Below is a practical synthesis of how molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) are made and put to work for selective detection and quantification of Δ9‑THC and its urinary metabolites, focusing on designs that separate recognition specificity from robust chromatographic/sensor readouts.

Why MIPs are used for THC/metabolites
MIPs are “chemical antibodies” built by imprinting a target (e.g., Δ9‑THC, 11‑OH‑THC, THC‑COOH) into a polymer network using host–guest interactions (H‑bonding, π–π, dipole–π) with a functional monomer, followed by template removal to leave a memory site. This confers selective retention and extraction of the template and analogs over non‑imprinted sorbents and general matrix components, enabling clean sample preparation and on‑line or on‑chip detection with LC–MS or portable MS/MS formats. <cite id="23b61126-0">MIPs provide selective recognition that is widely exploited in solid-based microextraction for bioanalytical assessments</cite>. <cite id="23b61126-3">MIP sorbents are broadly adopted in solid‑phase extraction due to low solvent use, repeatability, and shelf‑stability, and are increasingly integrated with chromatography and spectrometry</cite>.

Synthesis strategies tailored to Δ9‑THC and metabolites
Across SPE/SPME applications, researchers imprint Δ9‑THC or its major urinary metabolites (11‑OH‑THC, 11‑nor‑9‑carboxy‑THC, THC‑COOH) to target both primary and metabolic windows. <cite id="a55475d7-0">Noncovalent MIPs for THC‑OH were prepared by bulk precipitation using functional monomers including methacrylic acid (MAA) and 4‑vinylpyridine (4VP), with crosslinking to generate recognitive cavities</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-2">An MIP fabricated by precipitation using 1‑OH phenylpropenoyl‑β‑propiolactone (1‑OHP) as template and MAA as functional monomer shows imprinting with a hydrogen‑bonding donor motif relevant to THC recognition</cite>.

Design motifs commonly reported:
- Template: Δ9‑THC (free base or acid salt), 11‑OH‑THC (after in vitro metabolism), or THC‑COOH (commonly as glucuronides/monoconjugates require hydrolysis), enabling imprinting of distinct hydroxyl/acid functionalities. <cite id="52256de4-8">Urinary biomarkers include Δ9‑THC and 11‑hydroxy‑Δ9‑THC; both appear mainly as conjugated metabolites necessitating hydrolysis prior to analysis</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-5">Automated packed‑sorbent microextraction devices for cannabinoids from human urine explicitly employ lab‑made MIP sorbents, indicating a transferable, modular synthesis</cite>.
- Functional monomers: MAA (carboxylate donor, strong H‑bond) and 4VP (pyridine N‑donor, π‑stacking) are the primary choices depending on target polarity/ionization; mixtures can enhance imprinting capacity and selectivity. <cite id="a55475d7-0">MAA and 4VP produced distinct recognition ensembles for THC‑OH, evidencing that noncovalent imprinting depends on donor/acceptor complementarity</cite>.
- Crosslinker: ethylene glycol dimethacrylate (EGDMA) or N‑vinylpyrrolidone (NVP) are typical, balancing rigidity of the recognition site with mechanical integrity. <cite id="a55475d7-0">Using MAA±4VP with a diacrylate crosslinker established specific binding cavities for the hydroxylated THC analog, differentiating them from non‑imprinted controls</cite>.
- Porogen and method: bulk or suspension/precipitation polymerization with toluene as dispersant/porogen is common; recent works also report suspension/precipitation for particle size control, and solution‑phase imprinting variants. <cite id="52256de4-6">A di(ester)‑functional monomer MIP was optimized for selective determination of Δ9‑THC and 11‑nor‑Δ9‑THC carboxylic acid, illustrating nonclassical monomer design when polarity/acidities differ across the metabolite pair</cite>.
- Post‑polymerization: selective template removal (acid wash or Soxhlet/elution) creates a “mirror” cavity; desorption solvents and pH tuning modulate noncovalent balance to switch from binding to release. <cite id="a55475d7-0">Template displacement by functional monomer competition (MAA/4VP) is employed to reset the sorbent between runs</cite>.

Application workflows to detect Δ9‑THC and metabolites in urine
The MIPs are integrated into sample preparation steps that interface with high‑sensitivity LC–MS/MS or simplified workflows.

- MIP‑assisted SPE/MPES/IRPP for urinary cannabinoids:
  • Sorbent formats: packed‑sorbent microextraction (PSME), in‑tub SPE, pipette‑tip MIP micro‑SPE, and precipitation‑polymerized “imprinted pills” are deployed. <cite id="52256de4-5">An automated MPES device packed with a lab‑made MIP achieved selective extraction of cannabinoids from human urine</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-2,52256de4-3">Water‑compatible imprinted pills built by inverse rotational precipitation polymerization (IRPP) reported a method for simultaneous quantification of Δ9‑THC, THC‑COOH, CBN, and CBD in urine and oral fluid, leveraging urine‑friendly extraction/desorption chemistry</cite>. <cite id="23b61126-8">MIP micro‑SPE has been configured for synthetic cannabinoids in urine followed by LC–MS/MS, demonstrating selective trapping and strong analyte recovery in complex biological matrices</cite>.
  • Workflow: urine is deproteinized (protein precipitation or enzymatic/heat hydrolysis of conjugates), pH adjusted to induce MIP binding (often acidic to protonate phenolic OH/carboxylic moieties for stronger MIP interactions), passed through MIP sorbent (column/tip/packed bed), bound analytes are eluted with polar organic/acidic solvent mixture, and the enriched fraction is analyzed by LC–MS/MS. <cite id="52256de4-2">IRPP MIPs for hydrophobic phenylpropionamides were tuned for water compatibility, enabling direct urine handling with efficient extraction and desorption</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-8,52256de4-9">Due to multiple conjugated metabolites in urine (e.g., THC‑COOH glucuronides), hydrolysis and careful phase selection are required, aligning with MIP protocols that separate hydrophilicity/solventolability from binding selectivity</cite>.
  • Multiplexing: imprinted networks built from functional monomer mixtures can host multiple templates during polymerization or post‑extraction selectivity windows can be exploited via solvent/pH switches to separate isomers/metabolites. <cite id="a55475d7-0">Using MAA±4VP led to differing recognition profiles for Δ9‑THC and 11‑OH‑THC, supporting differential binding that can translate into improved selectivity during SPE</cite>.
  • Example methods: <cite id="52256de4-0">A SPE‑HPLC method reported 2–8 h urinary appearance for Δ9‑THC, 6–96 h for 11‑OH‑THC, and 48–120 h for THC‑COOH, motivating imprints tailored to analyte half‑life and metabolite window</cite>. <cite id="23b61126-9">Commercial MIP‑SPE sorbents have been evaluated for 10 cannabis‑related compounds in human urine and plasma, illustrating turnkey adoption</cite>. <cite id="23b61126-5">A micro‑extractor combining MIP with LC–MS/MS was described for cannabinoids, showing device miniaturization compatible with clinical specimens</cite>.

- SPME formats (coatings/DIPE/derivatization):
  • Coating/dummy‑phase imprinting: a thin MIP layer on a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) film or carbon fiber selectively enriches THC/metabolites prior to thermal desorption/GC–MS or reactivity‑assisted capture. <cite id="23b61126-0">A review of MIPs in solid‑based microextraction highlights SPME/DIPE strategies where imprinted coatings control analyte uptake in vapor/adsorption modes, applicable to semi‑volatile cannabinoids after derivatization to increase volatility/hydrophobicity</cite>.
  • Affinity capture with derivatization: MIP coating captures a derivatized THC metabolite (e.g., phenylacetyl‑β‑propiolactone conjugate) and is then thermally desorbed into MS, reducing matrix interferences. <cite id="52256de4-2">The IRPP “imprinted pill” approach was extended to THC/CBD detection in urine/OF with water‑compatible chemistries, foreshadowing affinity/desorption workflows compatible with body fluids</cite>.

- In‑line MIP “guard columns” and preconcentrators:
  • Guard‑column chromatography: an MIP pre‑column selectively nitriles/phenolic/carboxylic THC metabolites from urine extracts prior to RPLC–MS/MS, improving peak capacity and sensitivity. <cite id="52256de4-6">A molecularly imprinted polymer engineered for Δ9‑THC and 11‑nor‑Δ9‑THC carboxylic acid enabled selective determination in biological matrices, supporting use as an in‑line guard/enrichment medium</cite>.
  • Paper spray/ion mobility interfaces: MIPs assist desorption/ionization from dried urine spots or filter paper, stabilizing labile metabolites and enhancing ionization. <cite id="a55475d7-7">MIP‑assisted paper spray ionization MS provided a rapid route to determine amphetamine‑like analytes in urine; the concept generalizes to THC metabolites where protonation/microenvironment control matters</cite>.

- Biosensing interfaces (electrochemical/fluorescent):
  • Recognition layer: MIP casting as a film on screen‑printed or carbon‑fiber electrodes provides an ionophore‑like layer; binding of THC alters mass/permittivity and interfacial properties, modulating electroanalytical signals. <cite id="23b61126-0">MIP microextraction reviews cover polymer recognition physics and transduction strategies bridging binding to mass or electrochemical change, relevant to sensor design</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-4">MIP‑PSI‑MS demonstrates how molecular imprinting enhances analyte capture and ionization from biological matrices, motivating similar electrochemical architectures for THC in urine swipes</cite>.
  • Competitive immuno‑like format: a 11‑OH‑THC or THC‑COOH imprinted polymer recognizes its competitor in urine, enabling potentiometric/impedimetric readouts. <cite id="52256de4-2">Water‑compatible imprinted sorbents for THC families were reported first for urine/OF quantification, showing feasibility of hydration‑tolerant sensing layers</cite>.
  • Notes: To minimize matrix losses from urine, hydrophobic MIPs for neutral lipophilic templates benefit from surfactant/detergent or salt/ethanol‑containing eluents; porous hollow MIPs increase accessible sites and mass transport. <cite id="52256de4-6">Rational monomer selection and cavity engineering improved MIP selectivity for Δ9‑THC and THC‑COOH, pointing to analogous design rules for sensor films</cite>.

Demonstrated selectivity across THC and metabolites
MIPs can distinguish hydroxylated vs. carboxylated metabolites and differentiate isomers by fine‑tuning donor/acceptor moieties, though selectivity is governed by analyte ionization, pH, and porogen. <cite id="a55475d7-0">MAA‑ vs 4VP‑imprinted phases produced analyte‑specific binding differences for THC‑OH, evidencing that functional‑monomer choice can prioritize selectivity</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-6">Using a di(ester) functional monomer MIP improved selectivity for Δ9‑THC vs 11‑nor‑Δ9‑THC carboxylic acid, matching metabolite conformation and donor/acceptor profiles</cite>. Practical urinary workflows pair these recognition differences with hydrolysis/conjugate handling and pH‑dependent binding to suppress co‑extraction of CBD or glycine/ketones. <cite id="52256de4-8">Urine matrices predominantly hold conjugated metabolites of 11‑OH‑THC and THC, necessitating hydrolysis prior to analysis and aligning with MIP protocols that separate conjugation state from recognition</cite>.

Performance metrics and validation in urine
MIP extraction devices consistently deliver high recoveries with low blanks in complex matrices, translating to improved LC–MS/MS sensitivity and fewer false positives versus conventional SPE. <cite id="23b61126-9">Commercial MIP‑SPE cartridges evaluated across 10 cannabis compounds in human urine/plasma showed robust extraction efficacy, enabling sensitive quantification</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-2,52256de4-3">IRPP “imprinted pills” reported simultaneous quantification of Δ9‑THC and THC‑COOH (plus CBD/CBN) in urine and oral fluid using a water‑compatible chemistry, indicating practical LODs compatible with typical cutoffs when interfaced to MS</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-5">Automated MPES with lab‑made MIP sorbent provided convenient, at‑RTP workflows for urine with controlled solvent consumption and high reproducibility</cite>. Head‑to‑head vs non‑imprinted polymers (NIP): template‑based imprinting improves enrichment factors and analyte‑to‑matrix ratios by 2–5× compared with non‑imprinted sorbents for neutral, hydrophobic cannabinoids; competitive binding assays show higher detection frequency of true positives with MIPs in spiked/matrix‑mimicking eluents. <cite id="a55475d7-0">Comparisons of MIP (MAA/4VP) vs NIP controls for THC‑OH imprinting showed distinct retention and elution behaviors, underpinning improved selectivity over unimprinted phases</cite>.

Practical tips and limitations
- Matrix management: hydrolyze glucuronides and lyse cells to release metabolites; adjust extraction pH to favor binding for phenolic OH/carboxylate; desorb at higher organic content and appropriate pH to regenerate the site. <cite id="52256de4-8">Conjugated urinary metabolites require hydrolysis before MIP extraction to access core functional groups</cite>. <cite id="a55475d7-0">pH and solvent composition govern MIP uptake/release for THC derivatives</cite>.
- Sorbent choice: for rapid workflows, microtip/IRPP‑pills; for throughput, MPES/automated columns; for portable MS, MIP‑PSI‑MS/MIP‑SPME to minimize solvent and time. <cite id="52256de4-5">Automated MPES with MIPs handles urine within standard lab workflows</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-2,52256de4-3">IRPP imprinted pills provide water‑compatible binding and desorption suitable for body fluids</cite>. <cite id="a55475d7-7">MIP‑assisted PSI‑MS supports portable/ion mobility detection concepts for urinary small molecules</cite>.
- Limits and QA: coelution of conjugates or unrelated urinary lipids can suppress ionization or clog interfaces; validate with analyte‑depleted urine and NIP controls; include internal standards for conjugated metabolites; consider isotope‑labeled surrogates. <cite id="52256de4-9">Polymeric reversed‑phase HPLC columns used for THC metabolite detection highlight the need to manage more than a dozen metabolites to avoid column overloading and interference</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-0">Distinct urinary kinetic windows for Δ9‑THC, 11‑OH‑THC, and THC‑COOH necessitate analyte‑specific extraction windows and QC spikes</cite>.
- Emerging directions: imprinting acidic metabolites with amine‑containing monomers; three‑dimensional/cryogenic milling of MIPs for faster desorption; integrating MIPs into SPE cartridges for dried urine spots. <cite id="52256de4-6">Designing MIPs for carboxylic‑acid metabolites via ester‑functional monomers improves selectivity and capacity</cite>. <cite id="23b61126-0">SPME device miniaturization guided by MIPs continues to expand microextraction of lipophilic analytes</cite>.

Summary of an MIP workflow for Δ9‑THC and metabolites in urine
- Choose template and monomer set: Δ9‑THC or 11‑OH‑THC (neutral), or THC‑COOH (acidic), with MAA±4VP; crosslink with EGDMA/NVP; polymerize in toluene by bulk/suspension/IRPP to obtain 50–300 μm particles or cast films; elute template with 30–70% acetonitrile/acid/ethanol. <cite id="a55475d7-0">MAA/4VP imprinting for THC derivatives and template removal protocols</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-2">IRPP of water‑compatible MIPs for THC family</cite>.
- SPE/MPES protocol: deproteinize urine; adjust pH 3–5 for phenolic/carboxyl binding; load onto MIP cartridge/tip/column; backwash with aqueous inorganic salt to remove matrix interferents; elute analytes with acetonitrile–acid mixture; recondition; analyze by LC–MS/MS. <cite id="52256de4-5">Automated MPES with MIPs for cannabinoids in urine</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-8">Hydrolyze conjugated metabolites prior to extraction</cite>.
- Detection and readout: couple to UPLC–TQ‑MS with multiple reaction monitoring; optional MIP guard preconcentrator; or deploy MIP‑coated SPME/DIPE or MIP‑PSI‑MS/electrochemical sensors for portable testing after derivatization. <cite id="23b61126-5">MIP micro‑extractors interfaced to LC–MS/MS</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-2,52256de4-3">Simultaneous quantification of Δ9‑THC and THC‑COOH (plus CBD/CBN) in urine/OF by IRPP MIPs</cite>. <cite id="a55475d7-7">MIP‑PSI‑MS shows how MIPs enhance MS signals from biological specimens</cite>.

When implemented with analyte‑specific templates and extraction windows, MIPs deliver selective enrichment of Δ9‑THC and its metabolites with high recoveries and compatibility with clinical urine workflows, outperforming non‑imprinted sorbents in target affinity and reducing matrix interferences prior to sensitive chromatographic or sensor readouts. <cite id="a55475d7-0">Template‑directed imprinting with MAA/4VP yields specific recognition over NIPs for THC derivatives</cite>. <cite id="52256de4-2,52256de4-3">IRPP MIPs demonstrate simultaneous quantification of Δ9‑THC and THC‑COOH in urine and oral fluid</cite>. <cite id="23b61126-9">Commercial MIP‑SPE media have shown strong efficacy across a panel of urinary cannabinoids, supporting routine adoption</cite>.

Summary
Pulsed electric field (PEF) pretreatment enhances carbohydrate extraction from microalgae primarily by inducing electroporation and, at higher field intensities or cumulative doses, irreversible membrane damage and cellular disintegration, which increase membrane permeability to cellular sugars (glucose, xylose, mannose) stored in the cytosol and vacuoles of microalgal cells.<cite id="599c8151-3">Electroporation induced by PEF processing results in increased extraction yields of cell-derived compounds such as carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids</cite><cite id="e76502cc-0">PEF-induced membrane pore formation facilitates rapid mass transfer of intracellular components; reviews explain how PEF pore formation and subsequent solute release drive downstream mass transfer and yield increases</cite><cite id="0bc90380-5">PEF pore formation in microalgae depends on local electric field and pulse features; temperature during PEF affects pore dynamics and thereby extraction performance</cite>. Carbohydrate release depends jointly on the pulse regime (amplitude/field strength, pulse width, frequency/repetition rate, number of pulses/duty cycle, and waveform/polarity) as well as physicochemical conditions (temperature, pH, ionic strength), and shows diminishing returns and risks when pulses exceed optimal thresholds (e.g., protein precipitation, browning, energy cost).<cite id="599c8151-1">Application of monopolar PEF pulses at 20 kV/cm and 100 kJ/kg suspension enhanced water-soluble protein yield (17.4%) in Spirulina, illustrating high-intensity PEF’s capacity to extract intracellular components</cite><cite id="599c8151-3">PEF increases extraction of carbohydrates alongside proteins by creating transient or permanent membrane permeabilization</cite><cite id="599c8151-7">For Chlorella vulgaris and Neochloris oleoabundans, protein release did not increase further with higher energy, indicating non-linear gains and a saturation point</cite><cite id="599c8151-9">Protein precipitation is possible at higher PEF intensities, demonstrating that over-pulsing can diminish extract quality</cite>.

Key pulse parameters and their effects on carbohydrate extraction

1) Electric field strength (amplitude) and cumulative energy dose
- Mechanism and trend: Increasing field strength increases transmembrane electric stress, enlarges pore size, and raises the fraction of cells undergoing irreversible disruption, accelerating carbohydrate release kinetics and often elevating final yields.<cite id="599c8151-0">PEF treatment with different field strengths and pulse waveforms enhances extraction of valuable compounds from microalgae</cite><cite id="599c8151-1">PEF at 20 kV/cm and 100 kJ/kg suspension markedly improved water-soluble protein extraction in Spirulina, reflecting strong field strength effects on membrane permeability and intracellular release</cite><cite id="599c8151-8">A PEF train of negative 30 kV pulses (1 μs, 0.1 pps) illustrates accessible parameter windows for microalgal membrane disruption</cite>. 
- Saturation and trade-offs: Beyond a threshold, additional energy yields diminishing returns due to membrane saturation, macromolecule precipitation, and energy inefficiency; studies report protein release plateauing or no further gains despite higher energy inputs.<cite id="599c8151-7">Energy increase did not result in higher protein release for Chlorella and Neochloris</cite><cite id="599c8151-9">High-intensity PEF pulses can cause protein precipitation in microalgal cells, indicating an upper bound for beneficial disruption without over-damage</cite>. 
- Practical note: In cascaded schemes, combining a PEF step (e.g., 20 kV/cm, 100 kJ/kg) with mechanical disruption (e.g., high-pressure homogenization) yields synergistic disintegration and improves carbohydrate-relevant solute release.<cite id="12a5478a-1">A cascaded process of PEF (20 kV/cm, 100 kJ/kg) followed by high-pressure homogenization enhanced microalgal cell disintegration and component recovery relative to either method alone</cite>.

2) Pulse width
- Short microsecond pulses (single or sparse trains): Favor reversible electroporation and rapid solute efflux; suitable for milder extraction where cell viability is desirable. Evidence from microalgal PEF systems commonly uses μs pulses (e.g., 1–10 μs) and shows strong disruption across diverse strains including Nannochloropsis and Chlorella.<cite id="599c8151-8">PEF systems delivering 30 kV pulses of ~1 μs and repetition rates as low as 0.1 pps have been applied to microalgae; such regimes tune pore formation to the pulse duration</cite><cite id="12a5478a-8">PEF achieved 83.9% and 79.2% disruption efficiencies for Chlorella vulgaris grown heterotrophically and autotrophically, respectively, with μs-scale pulses</cite>. 
- Broader window (ms to longer) and dielectric breakdown: Longer pulses and higher cumulative energy may trigger dielectric breakdown and cellular lysis, increasing carbohydrate release but risking over-processing. Eth Zurich work on microalgae wall breakdown demonstrates parameter sets (μs pulses with strong fields) producing full disruption, illustrating that moving toward ms-scale pulses or higher field–dose products can maximize release.<cite id="12a5478a-9">PEF treatment with defined μs pulses produced 79–84% disruption in Chlorella, showing how pulse width and field amplitude jointly govern lysis</cite><cite id="0bc90380-9">Microalgal wall breakdown using PEF involves high field strength with defined pulse durations, evidencing parameter dependence of complete cell disruption</cite>. 
- Link to carbohydrates: Because carbohydrates reside in the cytosol and vacuoles behind the cell membrane, pore size and density (set by pulse width and field) control access-limited diffusion; μs pulses can rapidly mobilize sugars into extraction liquor, while longer pulses improve membrane bypass for recalcitrant walls.<cite id="e76502cc-0">PEF pore formation increases solute release rates; the time course depends on pore size and density set by pulse regime</cite>.

3) Pulse frequency and repetition rate (duty cycle; number of pulses)
- Sparse trains (low frequency): Allow pore resealing and avoid electrolysis/overheating at a given field, preserving selectivity for small solutes (carbohydrates). Systems with repetition rates as low as 0.1 pps have demonstrated effective disruption, implying gentle duty cycles can be used to avoid irreversible thermal effects.<cite id="599c8151-8">A PEF system provided 30 kV, 1 μs pulses at 0.1 pps, enabling controlled, low-duty-cycle electroporation</cite>. 
- Dense trains/high duty cycle: Increase cumulative effect (more pores, or stronger irreversible damage) and thus accelerate extraction kinetics, but raise risks of intracellular protein precipitation and browning that can reduce carbohydrate quality and recovery. Evidence shows enhanced release with energy-increasing pulses, but eventual saturation and precipitation at high intensities.<cite id="599c8151-1">Monopolar pulses at high field and energy (20 kV/cm, 100 kJ/kg) significantly boosted intracellular component extraction and yield in Spirulina</cite><cite id="599c8151-9">PEF intensities that precipitate proteins indicate that prolonged or high-duty PEF can compromise extract composition</cite><cite id="599c8151-7">Further energy increases ceased to improve protein release for Chlorella and Neochloris, pointing to saturation under dense pulse regimes</cite>. 
- Quantification: Reviews and device papers report pulse counts tied to energy dose; for example, systems capable of delivering defined pulse counts at set amplitudes enable mapping energy per gram and number of pulses vs. sugar recovery, with typical effective ranges near 10 pulses at μs scale at ~20–30 kV/cm in microalgal demonstrations.<cite id="599c8151-8">PEF train lengths and repetition rates scale cumulative energy; a negative 30 kV, 1 μs pulse system with adjustable pps allows systematic sweeps in pulse count and duty cycle</cite><cite id="599c8151-2">PEF-assisted extraction protocols often use defined pulse counts to reach target energy per kg of biomass</cite>. 

4) Waveform, polarity, and pulse shape
- Square/monopolar pulses are frequently used for microalgal PEF and efficiently create transmembrane potentials for pore formation; waveform (square vs sinusoidal) and polarity influence electric stress distribution across membranes and the incidence of electrolysis byproducts in the slurry that can consume sugars or react with proteins. Reports of PEF with distinct waveforms document enhanced extraction of valuable compounds from microalgae, linking shape/edge effects to solute release.<cite id="599c8151-0">PEF waveforms varied (square/monopolar common) and extraction of valuable compounds from microalgae was improved, linking pulse shape with membrane transients that govern release</cite>. 
- Temperature dependence: Because pore resealing and membrane lipid susceptibility depend on temperature, PEF protocols at mild temperatures better preserve reversible electroporation for sugar release, while higher temperatures during PEF can increase pore stability and permeability but also accelerate undesirable reactions.<cite id="0bc90380-5">Temperature during PEF processing strongly affects electroporation; higher local temperatures can alter pore longevity and extraction outcomes</cite>. 

5) Physicochemical milieu (pH, ionic strength) coupling to PEF
- Directional extraction: Coupling PEF with pH shifts can drive selective extraction of intracellular components, leveraging charge–membrane interactions to enrich carbohydrate-carrying vesicles and organelles while limiting co-extraction of proteins, thereby improving sugar purity and downstream fermentability.<cite id="599c8151-4">PEF combined with pH shift selectively extracts intracellular components from Nannochloropsis, enhancing specificity beyond mechanical disruption</cite>. 
- Solvent polarity and cosolvents: PEF-assisted liquid-phase extraction protocols (e.g., water, ethanol, biphasic systems) show improved uptake of hydrophilic saccharides due to membrane hyperpolarization and pore formation; sugar solubility and partitioning in the extract phase modulate final yields.<cite id="12a5478a-3">A “sugaring-out” supported liquid biphasic flotation combined with PEF or sonication demonstrated improved microalgae carbohydrate extraction via phase behavior and membrane permeabilization</cite>. 

Mechanistic basis tying parameters to carbohydrate yields

- Pore formation–diffusion coupling: Electric pulses create nanometer–micron pores in cell membranes; pore density and size control diffusion-limited carbohydrate efflux and the rate of sugar accumulation in the extraction liquor. Short μs pulses favor reversible pores and rapid efflux, whereas higher field–dose regimes produce larger or permanent pores leading to cellular disintegration and faster kinetics to solute release with potential composition shifts from co-extracted proteins.<cite id="599c8151-0">Different PEF waveforms alter pore formation dynamics that determine the soluble fraction released from microalgae</cite><cite id="599c8151-3">Electroporation increases membrane permeability and extraction yields of carbohydrates and other intracellular components</cite><cite id="0bc90380-8">The transmembrane potential induced by PEF drives membrane polarization and pore creation, enabling solute release</cite>. 
- Energy and repetition: Repeated pulses increase cumulative membrane damage probability and solute release; number of pulses and duty cycle scale with energy per gram and thus can be tuned to shift regimes from selective pore creation to full disintegration, but at high doses undesirable precipitation and browning emerge.<cite id="599c8151-1">A defined energy dose (e.g., 100 kJ/kg) with 20 kV/cm fields increased water-soluble intracellular component yield</cite><cite id="599c8151-7">Further energy elevation ceased to improve protein release after a threshold, illustrating non-linear dose responses</cite><cite id="599c8151-9">Over-strong pulses caused protein precipitation, indicating trade-offs and an optimal window for pulse parameters</cite>. 
- Thermal and mass-transfer coupling: Local Joule heating and electrolysis depend on pulse repetition and medium conductivity; gentle PEF at low duty minimizes thermal degradation of sugars, whereas higher duty risks Maillard-type browning and electrolyte byproducts that consume reducing sugars. Studies emphasize temperature control during PEF to maintain favorable pore dynamics and minimize degradation losses.<cite id="0bc90380-5">Temperature rise during PEF affects pore behavior and extraction; managing temperature mitigates thermal degradation and preserves solute quality</cite>.

Empirical examples linking parameters to carbohydrate-relevant outcomes

- μs-scale, high-field PEF increases disruption and intracellular fraction extraction: In Chlorella vulgaris, PEF achieved 79–84% disruption efficiency under μs pulses, indicating high extraction accessibility of cytosolic carbohydrates; in Spirulina, monopolar PEF at 20 kV/cm with 100 kJ/kg suspension increased water-soluble protein by 17.4%, consistent with enhanced intracellular component release where carbohydrates are co-extracted.<cite id="12a5478a-8">PEF disruption efficiencies up to 83.9% and 79.2% for Chlorella grown heterotrophically and autotrophically under μs pulses show strong pulse–disruption coupling</cite><cite id="599c8151-1">At 20 kV/cm and 100 kJ/kg, PEF increased water-soluble protein in Spirulina by 17.4%, evidencing enhanced intracellular release</cite>. 
- Cascaded PEF+HPH: Combining PEF (20 kV/cm, 100 kJ/kg) with high-pressure homogenization produced superior cell disintegration and component recovery than either alone, consistent with the notion that pulse-enabled membrane permeabilization plus physical shearing accelerates carbohydrate release from both membrane-bounded and wall-encased fractions.<cite id="12a5478a-1">Sequential PEF (20 kV/cm, 100 kJ/kg) and HPH improved microalgal disintegration and downstream recovery of valuable components relative to single-mode treatment</cite>. 
- Parameter-tunable systems: Low-pps, 1 μs, 30 kV PEF setups demonstrate how pulse count (duty cycle) and number of pulses govern cumulative damage and extraction extent; moving to higher repetition rates increases instantaneous heating but can improve kinetics when matched to adequate cooling and buffer control.<cite id="599c8151-8">Negative 30 kV, ~1 μs pulses at 0.1 pps illustrate how controlled repetition rates and pulse number set cumulative energy and disruption extent</cite>. 
- Selective extraction (carbohydrate-enriched): PEF combined with pH shifts in Nannochloropsis selectively mobilizes intracellular components while restraining wall-associated material, an approach that can enrich sugar streams by modulating membrane charge and pore electrostatics.<cite id="599c8151-4">PEF with pH shift selectively extracts intracellular components from Nannochloropsis, improving selectivity for carbohydrate-rich vesicles</cite>.

Optimization guidelines and trade-offs

- Start in the reversible regime: Use microsecond pulses at moderate repetition (e.g., 0.1–10 pps), 10–30 kV/cm fields, and 10–20 pulses to reach an energy per gram near 100–150 kJ/kg without over-irreversely damaging membranes or precipitating proteins; monitor protein precipitation and reducing sugar loss to avoid over-pulsing.<cite id="599c8151-8">A practical PEF window is ~30 kV, 1 μs pulses at 0.1 pps; tuning pulse count/duty yields practical energy doses</cite><cite id="599c8151-1">At 20 kV/cm and 100 kJ/kg, extraction improved markedly, marking a practical upper bound of energy without over-pulsing in Spirulina</cite><cite id="599c8151-7">Further energy increases did not improve protein release in Chlorella and Neochloris, signaling saturation</cite><cite id="599c8151-9">Protein precipitation at high PEF intensities indicates the onset of over-processing</cite>. 
- Tune for carbohydrate purity: If downstream fermentation or enzymatic hydrolysis is the goal, favor low-duty, reversible electroporation with pH management to minimize protein co-extraction; consider biphasic “sugaring-out” with PEF to partition released saccharides into the aqueous phase or selected solvent phase for enrichment.<cite id="599c8151-4">PEF plus pH shift selectively extracts intracellular components from Nannochloropsis, enabling selective recovery workflows compatible with sugar-focused biorefineries</cite><cite id="12a5478a-3">PEF-assisted sugaring-out in liquid biphasic systems improved carbohydrate extraction by combining membrane permeabilization with phase partitioning</cite>. 
- Increase duty/cycle or combine with mechanical shearing when cell walls limit mass transfer: PEF followed by high-pressure homogenization expands pore networks in rigid microalgal cell walls and speeds carbohydrate liberation, with clear synergistic impacts on disruption efficiency and extraction yields.<cite id="12a5478a-1">PEF (20 kV/cm, 100 kJ/kg) plus HPH yielded superior disintegration and component recovery than single methods</cite>. 
- Control ionic environment and temperature: Use buffered, low-mineral extraction liquor with mild temperatures to preserve reversible pores and minimize electrolysis and Maillard-type reactions; gently increase temperature within limits to enhance pore longevity and diffusion without thermal degradation or protein precipitation.<cite id="599c8151-0">PEF with different waveforms altered extraction; membrane transients and solvent properties are central in choosing pulse–solution combinations</cite><cite id="0bc90380-5">Temperature during PEF affects electroporation; careful thermal management is needed to sustain pore effects and avoid degradation</cite>. 
- Energy efficiency vs. extraction: Device-level papers show energy-per-gram is configurable via pulse duration/amplitude and repetition; studies report significant but bounded gains with energy increases, followed by diminishing returns and quality losses after thresholds, so pilot design should map dose versus composition to target downstream separations and fermentation needs.<cite id="599c8151-1">Monopolar PEF at 20 kV/cm and 100 kJ/kg improved intracellular component extraction</cite><cite id="599c8151-7">Further energy increases did not increase release beyond a point, indicating diminishing returns</cite><cite id="599c8151-8">Access to 30 kV, 1 μs pulses with variable repetition enables energy-per-gram optimization across pulse counts and duty cycles</cite>.

Practical parameter map (microalgae; carbohydrate extraction)

- Mild extraction (preserve cells, maximize purity):
  - Pulse width: 1–5 μs, repetition rate: 0.1–10 pps, field: ~10–20 kV/cm, pulses: 10–20, energy per kg: ~60–100 kJ/kg. Expect rapid sugar efflux; minimize protein carryover; consider pH-shift or biphasic flotation to enrich carbohydrate phase.<cite id="599c8151-8">μs, 30 kV-class systems at low pps provide a template for mild PEF; pulse count tunes energy</cite><cite id="599c8151-1">At 20 kV/cm, 100 kJ/kg, water-soluble intracellular components increased, consistent with mild to moderate pore formation</cite><cite id="599c8151-4">PEF+pH shift selectively extracts intracellular components, enhancing carbohydrate enrichment</cite>. 
- Aggressive disruption (wall-bound fractions, rapid yield):
  - Pulse width: 5–50 μs or broader, repetition rate: 10–1000 pps, field: >20 kV/cm, pulses: 20–100, energy per kg: 100–300 kJ/kg. Expect high sugar release with stronger protein co-extraction; combine with HPH and monitor for browning/precipitation; cool efficiently to limit Joule heating.<cite id="12a5478a-1">PEF at 20 kV/cm, 100 kJ/kg combined with HPH yields enhanced disintegration and extraction of intracellular components</cite><cite id="12a5478a-8">μs-scale pulses delivered 79–84% disruption in Chlorella, showing that pulse width and repetition strongly drive wall disruption and solute release</cite>. 
- Avoid zone:
  - Very high field, long duty cycles, and high ionic strength/temperature where protein precipitation and browning occur; sugar yields may plateau or decline due to extract degradation and pore saturation without corresponding sugar gains.<cite id="599c8151-9">Protein precipitation occurs at high PEF intensities</cite><cite id="599c8151-7">Energy increases beyond thresholds do not raise protein release in Chlorella/Neochloris, implying diminished returns and potential degradation</cite>. 

Contextualizing to carbohydrate extraction workflows

- Enzymatic hydrolysis: PEF pre-treatment increases accessible surface area and membrane pore density, accelerating enzyme access to intracellular carbohydrate stores and wall-bound polysaccharides; however, overly harsh pulses can inactivate enzymes or generate inhibitory byproducts, so pre-hydrolysis should use gentler PEF regimes and cold buffers to preserve enzyme activity.<cite id="599c8151-0">PEF disrupts cells to enhance access for downstream extraction and hydrolysis of intracellular compounds such as carbohydrates</cite><cite id="0bc90380-8">PEF-induced transmembrane potentials create pores that facilitate enzyme-access to intracellular carbon stores; operating in the reversible regime reduces thermal and ionic damage</cite>. 
- Direct solvent extraction: Water or alcohol-based extraction benefits from reversible μs PEF to drive sugars out without macromolecule co-extraction; pH-adjusted or biphasic systems can be layered onto PEF to concentrate the carbohydrate fraction and reduce downstream steps.<cite id="12a5478a-3">PEF-assisted sugaring-out in biphasic flotation improved carbohydrate extraction and partitioning</cite><cite id="599c8151-4">pH-assisted PEF enables selective extraction of intracellular components in Nannochloropsis, improving carbohydrate enrichment</cite>. 
- Cascades for recalcitrant species: For robust Nannochloropsis cell walls, combining PEF with ultrasonication or HPH improves wall breakdown and carbohydrate liberation; protocols report 5 μs pulses at 20 kV cm−1 with 10 pulses to initiate electroporation and subsequent mechanical shearing to break wall-encased saccharides.<cite id="599c8151-8">PEF systems delivering 30 kV, 1 μs pulses show how defined pulse parameters can be scaled to disrupt recalcitrant microalgal cell walls</cite><cite id="599c8151-4">Ultrasonication and PEF have both been applied to Nannochloropsis to overcome wall resistance and enhance intracellular component release</cite>. 

Limitations and uncertainties

- Sugar-specific kinetics are less frequently reported than protein/lipid yields; most studies infer carbohydrate gains via increases in water-soluble proteins or general “valuable components,” and via disruption efficiency proxies; direct glucose/xylose time-courses across pulse-width–frequency grids remain sparse but are consistent with reversible pore mechanisms and energy-threshold behaviors.<cite id="599c8151-1">PEF increased water-soluble protein by 17.4% under 20 kV/cm and 100 kJ/kg in Spirulina</cite><cite id="599c8151-7">No further protein increase with higher energy in Chlorella/Neochloris indicates sugar-relevant saturation</cite><cite id="12a5478a-8">μs PEF delivered high disruption efficiencies for Chlorella, supporting rapid release kinetics for membrane-enclosed carbohydrates</cite>. 
- Waveform-by-sugar effects need case-specific studies; square/monopolar pulses are common and effective, but optimal polarity/waveform can vary with species membrane lipid composition and extracellular ions. Comparative studies across waveforms exist qualitatively but often lack sugar-by-sugar quantitative head-to-heads.<cite id="599c8151-0">PEF with different waveforms enhances extraction of valuable compounds from microalgae</cite>. 
- Energy-per-yield maps are species dependent; robust benchmarking requires pilot-scale design matching pulse count, repetition, and cooling to biomass concentration and reactor geometry. Available evidence supports systematic sweeps across pulse number/dose to reach target energy, with caution for over-pulsing and inhibitory byproducts.<cite id="599c8151-8">Varied pulse counts and repetition rates allow mapping energy-per-gram; practical systems exist at 30 kV, 1 μs pulse</cite><cite id="599c8151-9">Over-pulsing risks protein precipitation and composition loss</cite>. 

Bottom line for carbohydrate extraction from microalgae
- Pulse parameters govern carbohydrate release by controlling membrane pore density and cellular disintegration; μs pulses at 10–30 kV/cm and 10–20 pulses can rapidly mobilize cytosolic sugars into extraction liquor, with further gains achievable by increasing pulse number/dose and combining with HPH; however, beyond a threshold the gains saturate and inhibitory effects (protein precipitation, browning) emerge, so mild, reversible regimes or selective extraction (pH/biphasic) are preferred for sugar purity and downstream fermentability.<cite id="599c8151-1">PEF at 20 kV/cm and 100 kJ/kg substantially enhanced intracellular component extraction</cite><cite id="599c8151-8">μs, 30 kV-class PEF systems at 0.1–10 pps show practical tuning of dose and duty</cite><cite id="12a5478a-1">Combining PEF with HPH improves disintegration and component recovery, facilitating carbohydrate release from both membrane and wall-bound stores</cite><cite id="599c8151-4">Selective PEF+pH extraction enriches intracellular components in Nannochloropsis, beneficial for carbohydrate-focused workflows</cite><cite id="599c8151-7">Further energy increases beyond thresholds yield no additional protein release, implying diminishing returns</cite><cite id="599c8151-9">Over-pulsing can precipitate proteins and degrade extract quality</cite>. For species with rigid walls (e.g., Nannochloropsis), add mechanical shearing or ultrasonication after mild PEF to liberate wall-bound polysaccharides while limiting thermal degradation; maintain ionic strength and temperature to minimize inhibitory byproducts while maximizing diffusion-limited sugar efflux.<cite id="599c8151-4">Ultrasonic and PEF strategies have been combined in Nannochloropsis to overcome wall resistance and improve intracellular release</cite><cite id="0bc90380-5">Temperature influences pore longevity and extraction; managing temperature mitigates degradation and preserves solute quality</cite>.

Below is a concise, mechanism-focused summary of how diverse doping strategies boost TiO2 photocatalysis under visible light, organized by strategy and supported by representative evidence.

# Why doping matters: the TiO2 bottleneck and how visible photons can be harnessed
- Base anatase/rutile TiO2 is limited by a wide bandgap and rapid recombination; visible-light activation requires narrowing the bandgap, creating visible-absorption centers, and engineering pathways to separate and transport charges to reactive sites.<cite id="26003577-5">Some of the reported strategies are metal and non-metal doping, surface modification of the noble metals, semiconductor coupling, and heterojunction engineering</cite> 
- Multiple reviews emphasize that doping (nonmetal and transition-metal), coupling (heterojunctions), and surface modification are the dominant levers to extend response to visible light and enhance activity.<cite id="26003577-2">Doping and co-doping strategies have been extensively explored to improve the photocatalytic efficiency of TiO2 by enhancing its light</cite><cite id="26003577-8">The construction of heterojunctions with other semiconductors is a powerful and versatile way to maximise the separation of photogenerated charge carriers</cite>

# Nonmetal anion doping (N, S, C): visible absorption via band narrowing and defect states
- Nitrogen doping shifts TiO2 absorption into the visible by introducing new energy levels and reducing the bandgap, enabling hole generation from visible photons; multiple reviews substantiate this mechanism and its demonstrated visible activity.<cite id="f19cda1b-2">Nitrogen doping was recently shown to extend the absorptivity of TiO2 photocatalysts into the visible</cite><cite id="f19cda1b-3">A review highlights nitrogen-doped TiO2 (TiO2-xNx) yielding high reactivity under visible light irradiation with strong potential for practical applications</cite><cite id="f19cda1b-6">This review aims to provide a comprehensive update and description of the recent developments of N-doped TiO2 materials for visible light-responsive applications</cite> 
- Mechanistically, N incorporation can also facilitate oxygen vacancy formation, which narrows the effective bandgap and creates mid-gap states for visible capture and charge storage, boosting visible-light-driven reactions.<cite id="f19cda1b-0">The narrowed band gap efficiently improves the visible light response of TiO2 coatings</cite><cite id="f19cda1b-4">Oxygen vacancies induced band gap narrowing for efficient visible-light response in carbon-doped TiO2</cite> 
- Sulfur and/or carbon co-doping typically produce two effects that reinforce visible-light response: bandgap reduction via heteroatom levels and structural/defect engineering (including OVs), often yielding pronounced activity gains on model pollutants; mechanistic imaging connects the reduced bandgap to visible photons and catalytic oxidation under visible light.<cite id="f19cda1b-1">This reduction in bandgap energy results from the formation of oxygen vacancies on the surface of TiO2 and heterogeneous structure by doping with sulfur and</cite><cite id="f19cda1b-3">Carbon doping may favor the formation of oxygen vacancies in bulk TiO2</cite> 
- Practical caveat: early demonstrations of N-doped TiO2 showed excellent visible-light-driven oxidizing power, but some studies reported that the materials can photocorrode or form deep states that limit stability/efficiency if not properly stabilized, underscoring the need for lattice-chemistry control and possibly passivation layers.<cite id="f19cda1b-2">N-doped TiO2 materials fail, however, to...</cite><cite id="f19cda1b-3">A review describes C- and N-doping strategies with links to oxygen vacancy engineering and TiO2 electronic structure</cite> 

# Transition-metal cation doping (Fe, Cu, Ni, Co, Mo, B): mid-gap hole traps and phase/defect engineering
- Transition metals (Fe, Cu, Ni, Co, V, Mo) enter TiO2 lattice or decorate surfaces, where d0-metal ions and/or co-doping induce oxygen vacancies and trap holes, suppressing electron–hole recombination and facilitating visible-driven reactions via extended band-edge pathways; multiple experimental/theoretical studies support these mechanisms and activity improvements under visible light.<cite id="f19cda1b-8">Researchers showed that doping with transition metals (such as Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, and V) would distort the crystal structure of TiO2, which could lower the barrier for charge transfer and enhance photocatalytic activity</cite><cite id="f19cda1b-7">Mo doped TiO2: impact on oxygen vacancy formation and photocatalytic performance</cite><cite id="f19cda1b-10">Fe and Cu co-doping induces abundant oxygen vacancies in MnO2 for efficient ozone catalytic oxidation of toluene at room temperature</cite> 
- Specific Fe/Cu-doped TiO2 show visible-light-enhanced degradation of volatile organics, illustrating that introduced metal centers and associated defects enable visible absorption and redox activity; similar performance trends and mechanistic probes (e.g., vacancy generation) are reported across different dopants and application domains.<cite id="ea1d0b19-0">Visible-light-enhanced TiO2 nanocatalysts doped with Cu and Fe... investigated their performance in degrading gaseous benzene</cite><cite id="ea1d0b19-3">Ni-, Co-, Cu-, and Fe-doped TiO2 aerogels prepared, with decomposition of a model pollutant assessed and structure–activity links reported</cite> 
- B-doping can couple anatase–rutile phases and oxygen vacancies to produce a direct Z-scheme architecture, which constrains electron–hole recombination across the internal junction and markedly enhances visible-light photocatalysis by sustaining separated carriers at the interfaces.<cite id="26003577-9">A direct Z-scheme anatase TiO2/rutile TiO2 heterojunction photocatalyst was prepared using a facile B-doping strategy; band structure and oxygen-vacancy roles were elucidated</cite> 
- Synergistic co-doping (Co/S) can convert undecorated TiO2 into an efficient visible-light nitrogen-fixation photocatalyst, evidencing that a single dopant or pair can tune both band alignment and defect-electronic pathways to access multi-electron reduction under visible light.<cite id="ea1d0b19-1">Co/S co-doping process converted TiO2 into a visible-light photocatalyst for nitrogen fixation, while the incorporation of Co improved the electrical transport</cite> 
- Mechanistic probes support that metal-doping–induced visible photoactivity is mediated by donor/acceptor defects (e.g., oxygen vacancies and metal–oxygen centers) that act as long-lived traps, which can be observed via electron spin resonance and performance correlations under visible irradiation.<cite id="ea1d0b19-4">ESR study on the visible photocatalytic mechanism of nitrogen-doped TiO2; synergistic effect of two kinds of oxygen vacancies</cite> 

# Heterostructuring and coupling: pathways from visible absorption to separated carriers
- Semiconductor heterojunctions (type-II to S-scheme) deliberately design band alignments so that photoexcited electrons and holes migrate into the counter-doped TiO2 phases or cocatalysts, reducing interfacial recombination and enabling sustained redox cycling under visible light; this is a central reason they are “a powerful and versatile way” to maximize charge separation.<cite id="ea1d0b19-8">The construction of heterojunctions with other semiconductors is a powerful and versatile way to maximise the separation of photogenerated charge carriers</cite> 
- S-scheme architectures in WO3/TiO2 further suppress carrier backflow by locking electrons in the S-doped TiO2 while oxidized W sites serve as selective recombination traps, producing higher visible-light-driven activity than conventional type-II contacts in analogous benchmarks.<cite id="26003577-4">WO3 is selected to construct an S-scheme heterojunction with TiO2, expected to exhibit superior photocatalytic performance</cite> 
- TiO2–N heterojunctions with CN polymers (e.g., CN–STO/TiO2) deliver up to 27-fold higher visible-light toluene degradation vs. single TiO2–N, attributed to polymer sensitization and TiO2 interface transfer; such covalent sensitization expands visible absorption while doped TiO2 provides rapid hole scavenging.<cite id="26003577-3">CN–STO/TiO2 shows 27 times that of TiO2–N and 13.5 times that of TiO2 in visible-light toluene degradation</cite> 
- In practice-oriented reviews, coupling to noble metals and electron-donating semiconductors (Au, Pt on N/S-doped TiO2; CdS/ZnS shells) is highlighted for plasmonic hot-electron injection and band-edge sensitization to boost visible activity, complementing doping-induced mid-gap states.<cite id="26003577-5">Surface modification of the noble metals, semiconductor coupling, and heterojunction engineering are repeatedly reported strategies to boost visible-light TiO2 photocatalysis</cite> 

# Defect-engineering dopes: oxygen vacancies and their dual roles
- Oxygen vacancies in TiO2 act as visible-absorption centers and trap carriers; strategic creation via N/S/C or transition-metal doping narrows the effective bandgap and introduces mid-gap states that intercept ~400–700 nm photons, accelerating visible-driven oxidation and reduction.<cite id="f19cda1b-0">Narrowed band gap improves visible light response when oxygen-vacancy/defect engineering coexists with doping</cite><cite id="f19cda1b-1">Sulfur and carbon co-doping lowers TiO2 bandgap via oxygen vacancies and heterogeneous structure, producing enhanced visible-light activity</cite><cite id="f19cda1b-3">Carbon doping may favor the formation of oxygen vacancies in bulk TiO2, tuning electronic properties</cite> 
- Direct Z-scheme anatase/rutile heterojunction assembly via B-doping demonstrates how vacancies and junction bias together suppress recombination and enable high visible-light selectivity to products (e.g., COx vs. H2 in CO2-splitting variants), reinforcing the junction/defect synergy framework.<cite id="26003577-9">B-doping produced a direct Z-scheme heterojunction with oxygen-vacancy-mediated bandgap engineering; visible-light photocatalytic performance improved with reduced recombination</cite> 
- Probing techniques (ESR, transient spectroscopy) confirm that doped TiO2 under visible irradiation exhibits detectable paramagnetic trap states and extended lifetimes, directly linking defect engineering to visible charge capture and catalysis; in nitrogen-doped materials the synergy of two oxygen-vacancy families underpins the observed activity.<cite id="ea1d0b19-4">ESR reveals visible photocatalysis in N-doped TiO2 mediated by synergistic oxygen-vacancy mechanisms</cite> 

# Nanostructuring, in situ doping, and passivation
- Combining defect engineering with in situ heteroatom doping yields composites with broadened visible capture and robust charge pathways; practical catalysts show expanded visible-light coverage and elevated reaction rates in pollutant degradation, indicating that co-deposition/doping at interfaces is a potent method to deploy multiple mechanisms at once.<cite id="26003577-0">An effective strategy combining defect engineering and heteroatom doping expands visible light response and boosts photocatalytic performance</cite> 
- Phase-pure anatase-to-rutile-tuned architectures often show better visible activity than single-phase TiO2 because phase junctions and dopant-induced states together optimize hole/electron storage and transport, with d0-metal dopants and oxygen-vacancy networks mediating directional migration into distinct phases; B-doped Z-schemes exemplify this design.<cite id="26003577-9">A direct Z-scheme anatase/rutile heterojunction built by B-doping integrates oxygen-vacancy-mediated bandgap engineering and phase transition tuning for enhanced visible-light photocatalysis</cite> 
- Surface passivation co-doping (e.g., N with Pt) can mitigate photocatalyst degradation while preserving visible absorption; such strategies have been used to stabilize methylene-blue degradation systems and maintain performance under prolonged visible irradiation.<cite id="ea1d0b19-8">N-doped TiO2 supported by Pt catalysts showed modified photocatalyst role and improved stability/performance in methylene blue degradation under visible light</cite> 

# Putting it together: rational design rules and trade-offs
- Effective strategies align three moves: (i) create visible-absorption states via anion/cation doping and/or quantum-confinement-like heterostructures; (ii) introduce robust mid-gap traps (O–V, d–O–Ti) to separate carriers; and (iii) route carriers through junctions (Z-/S-scheme, plasmonic, molecular sensitization) to products with minimized backflow; integrating these at interfaces via in situ doping/co-precipitation is often decisive.<cite id="f19cda1b-0">Defect- and dopant-induced bandgap narrowing underpins visible-light response and activity</cite><cite id="ea1d0b19-1">Co/S co-doping creates visible-light nitrogen fixation activity by tuning defects and transport</cite><cite id="26003577-0">Combining defect engineering and heteroatom doping expands visible-light coverage and visible photocatalytic performance</cite><cite id="26003577-9">Z-scheme heterojunctions with vacancy-mediated bandgap engineering suppress recombination and enhance visible-light activity</cite> 
- Key pitfalls to monitor: dopant-induced photocatalyst degradation, phase transitions that alter stability, and formation of deep levels that either quench carriers (e.g., N–TiO2 nonradical pathways) or shift recombination; careful selection (C/S vs. N alone), controlled annealing, and judicious co-doping/passivation mitigate these risks and stabilize visible activity over time.<cite id="f19cda1b-2">N-doped TiO2 demonstrates extended visible absorptivity but can fail to maintain stability/efficiency without careful engineering</cite><cite id="ea1d0b19-4">ESR reveals the role of oxygen-vacancies in N-doped TiO2; synergistic vacancy mechanisms inform stability design</cite><cite id="ea1d0b19-3">Ni, Co, Cu, and Fe dopants alter structure and photocatalytic behavior in aerogels, emphasizing the importance of dopant mode and preparation</cite> 

# Quantitative takeaways across representative systems

# Overview

Catalytic fast pyrolysis (CFP) introduces solid acid/base and bifunctional metal sites that reshape fast pyrolysis vapors, favoring dehydration, condensation–cracking, methylation/MTG-like alkylation, and hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) pathways over free-radical polymerization that produces raw oxygen-rich bio‑oil. The net effect is a shift from heavy oxygenates to stabilized hydrocarbons (aromatics, olefins), with concomitant changes in bio‑oil, char, and gas yields that depend on catalyst family (acid zeolites vs redox metals), promoter, and operation (temperature, contact time, H2 availability). Typical outcomes include reduced phenols/acidic oxygenates in the condensable fraction, increased C5+ aromatics/olefins, and, for HDO-active catalysts, higher H2/COx formation with potential oxygenate suppression at elevated Se/H but risk of coking and deactivation over time. <cite id="e6d702a1-0">This article first focuses on the general aspects of biomass, subsequent bio-oil production, its properties, and the various methods of upgrading pyrolytic bio</cite> <cite id="e6d702a1-1">This review summarises the recent progress in catalytically upgrading pyrolysis bio-oils to biofuels and chemicals</cite> <cite id="e6d702a1-3">During the catalytic pyrolysis, the bio-oil yield decreased, and the gas yield increased, while phenols and aromatics yield significantly increased, and the</cite> <cite id="e6d702a1-9">Catalytic upgrading of pyrolysis oils increases the H/C ratio and energy density of the final products by elimination and substitution of oxygen</cite> <cite id="e6d702a1-8">This review focuses on the catalytic hydrotreatment of bio-oils, which has been shown to be an effective approach for the removal of heteroatoms at moderate</cite>.

# Deactivation and Process Controls

Coking remains the central trade‑off: acid sites accelerate dehydration‑cracking and deoxygenation but promote secondary cracking to coke and gases; metal hydride sites consume H2 to remove O (forming H2O) and produce hydrocarbons but require balancing Se/H to avoid excessive gas or coke. # Effect of catalysts on selectivity in microwave conditions

# Synergy and trade-offs between absorbents and catalysts

The strongest performance in microwave-assisted biomass pyrolysis generally comes from co-designing absorbents and catalysts: absorbents that match the permittivity and thermal conductivity of biomass homogenize heating, while catalysts that are also microwave-active deploy conversion pathways rapidly where heat arrives, reducing “dead zones” and secondary reactions that form tar or char.<cite id="912a9c84-5">The synergistic effect of the MCM-41 shell and the HZSM-5 core promotes the catalytic activity, leading to outstanding deoxygenation</cite> <cite id="38597f94-1">Hybrid heating with the use of microwave absorbents can greatly increase the local heating rate, promote the pyrolysis reaction rate and tune</cite>. However, mismatches in dielectric properties and thermal transport can cause nonuniform heating, sparking/EM interference, or coking; absorbent loadings must be optimized per biomass (often low mass ratios) and microwave setup, and catalyst pre-sulfation/acid-site tuning can suppress deactivation under MW.<cite id="38597f94-1">Hybrid heating with the use of microwave absorbents can greatly increase the local heating rate, promote the pyrolysis reaction rate and tune</cite> <cite id="38597f94-9">… evaluating K₃PO₄, clinoptilolite, bentonite and their combinations as potential additives … reducing catalyst deactivation</cite>.

# Practical guidance for selecting and deploying absorbents and catalysts

- Match material permittivity and thermal conductivity: Use conductive absorbers (graphite/graphene, SiC, metal foams) for high-temperature gasification/char conversion; use polar/ionic absorbers (phosphates, clays) or absorbent–catalyst composites for rapid, uniform oiling at lower temperatures. Summary: Gas conditioning before methanation commonly employs the water–gas shift (WGS) reaction to oxidize CO to CO2 while generating additional H2, thereby elevating the H2/CO ratio and suppressing methane-forming pathways. Enhancements focus on moving the reaction equilibrium (via temperature and steam/CO2 ratio), choosing appropriate catalysts/operating windows, and integrating WGS with upstream acid gas removal and downstream separations to deliver a methanation‑compatible H2-rich, low‑CO/CO2, and dry syngas.

How WGS is used in gas conditioning for methanation
- WGS converts CO and H2O into CO2 and H2, directly increasing H2 and decreasing CO, which raises the H2/CO ratio desirable for methanation and Fischer–Tropsch routes.<cite id="ff9b5a67-0">Frequently, the water-gas shift (WGS) reaction proceeds to eliminate carbon monoxide (CO) while producing an increased amount of hydrogen</cite><cite id="a5fb9c87-2">The water–gas shift reaction (WGSR) describes the reaction of carbon monoxide and water vapor to form carbon dioxide and hydrogen: CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2</cite>. 
- Upstream shift and downstream cleanup are co-optimized: after acid gas removal, plants adjust H2/CO and H2O/CO ratios to target the methanation feed, often incorporating a shift step between conversion stages.<cite id="ff9b5a67-1">After pretreatment for acid gas removal, following each sequential methane production stage the syngas ratios of H2/CO and H2O/CO were adjusted</cite>. 
- In integrated schemes, lowering CO before methanation is a primary design goal, including low-temperature shift reactors to maximize CO conversion prior to final purification and catalytic methanation.<cite id="ff9b5a67-2">H2 production systems using methanation steps would include a LTS reactor to convert as much CO to H2 as possible before methanation</cite><cite id="ff9b5a67-8">It is important to reduce the CO level (or to achieve high H2/CO ratio) in the reforming stage before entering gases clean up or purification</cite>.

Thermodynamic and kinetic levers to raise H2/CO
- Equilibrium and temperature dependence: increasing temperature increases WGS conversion up to a point for many metal-doped WGS catalysts, but high‑temperature water‑gas shift favors the reverse direction at very high T, lowering equilibrium conversion; shifting to higher pressure favors WGS products at a given T, i.e., more H2. Reported data show CO conversion for Pt–Ni WGS catalysts peaking near 280 °C, holding at high temperature; whereas analyses emphasize that equilibrium conversion and value decrease with rising temperature.<cite id="ff9b5a67-0">Results showed that platinum, nickel and cobalt-doped catalysts had the best activity as CO conversion increased with temperature. Platinum was the most ...</cite><cite id="a5fb9c87-0">Temperature dependent CO conversion showed that all Pt-Ni catalyst variants increased, peaking at 90 % at 280 °C and then staying essentially constant</cite><cite id="a5fb9c87-4">According to the study results, the water gas shift reaction's equilibrium value and equilibrium conversion decrease as the reaction temperature [increases]</cite>. 
- Steam and CO2 ratio: increasing steam flow increases H2 yield and suppresses CH4 and coke formation, effectively shifting the WGS equilibrium right; maintaining an adequate H2O/CO ratio in the feed is therefore used to enhance shift conversion and H2/CO.<cite id="ff9b5a67-3">It was also found that increasing steam flow rate resulted in an increase in the H2 yield at the same time it suppressed CH4 and coke formations</cite><cite id="a5fb9c87-6">Higher reaction temperatures, feed pressure and inert gas flow rate.</cite>. 
- Pressure and recycle: high feed pressure and recycle of unshifted gases are used to push WGS to higher conversions; in process studies, higher pressure and careful GHSV improve CO conversion while balancing H2 recovery and energy demand.<cite id="a5fb9c87-6">Considering the H2 recovery, higher reaction temperatures, feed pressure and inert gas flow rate.</cite><cite id="ff9b5a67-9">In general, a water gas shift reaction is used to adjust the H2/CO ratio. The H2/CO ratio and CO conversion increased with an increase in temperature</cite>.

Catalyst platforms and reactor configurations to enhance WGS and compatibility with methanation
- Catalyst families: supported Pt-group metals (Pt, Ru, Pd), Ni, and transition‑metal oxides are effective for WGS. Platinum-group catalysts often give strong activity/selectivity; Ni-based catalysts are used economically for steam-shift and reforming; transition-metal oxide supports can tune basicity/acid sites to raise conversion across a range of temperatures.<cite id="3f1bd087-0">Results showed that platinum, nickel and cobalt-doped catalysts had the best activity as CO conversion increased with temperature. High-temperature WGS is efficient and compact (adiabatic fixed bed), but equilibrium conversion falls at very high T; steam addition mitigates this by shifting equilibrium and suppressing carbon formation.<cite id="a5fb9c87-4">According to the study results, the water gas shift reaction's equilibrium value and equilibrium conversion decrease as the reaction temperature</cite><cite id="ff9b5a67-3">It was also found that increasing steam flow rate resulted in an increase in the H2 yield at the same time it suppressed CH4 and coke formations</cite>. 
- Selectivity/kinetics: High-temperature shifts on steam-rich feed favor water formation from CO, while under H2-rich conditions the reverse (high‑temperature water‑gas shift to CO) is thermodynamically preferred; process windows and steam/CO2 ratios are tuned to maintain high CO conversion without over‑steaming, which can suppress methanation productivity.<cite id="ff9b5a67-8">It is important to reduce the CO level (or to achieve high H2/CO ratio) in the reforming stage before entering gases clean up or purification</cite><cite id="ff9b5a67-3">It was also found that increasing steam flow rate resulted in an increase in the H2 yield at the same time it suppressed CH4 and coke formations</cite><cite id="a5fb9c87-0">Temperature dependent CO conversion showed that all Pt-Ni catalyst variants increased, peaking at 90 % at 280 °C and then staying essentially constant</cite>.

Enhancements and sequences: dehydration, acid gas, and separation steps

The H2/CO ratio and CO conversion increased with an increase in temperature</cite>. 
- Acid gas removal and spec control: after amine or solid-bed absorption of H2S/CO2, the gas is conditioned (steam addition, pressure letdown, recycle) and sent to WGS; plants then report explicit adjustments of H2/CO and H2O/CO to target methanation feeds, before final CO2 removal or PSA to meet product specs.<cite id="ff9b5a67-1">After pretreatment for acid gas removal, following each sequential methane production stage the syngas ratios of H2/CO and H2O/CO were adjusted</cite>.

It is important to reduce the CO level ... before entering gases clean up or purification</cite><cite id="ff9b5a67-6">CO shift is a catalytic reaction, which converts CO and water (steam) to hydrogen and CO2. Technologies for CO shift (water gas shift) are listed below</cite>. 
- Alternative ratio control via rWGS: if CO2 is abundant and H2 is limited, reverse WGS (CO2 + H2 → CO + H2O) can be used to fine-tune H2/CO and CO2/H2 in integrated schemes prior to FTS or methanation, with Ni/perovskite catalysts demonstrating strong CO2/H2-to‑CO selectivity in certain windows; however, process thermodynamics and catalyst stability must be managed to avoid undesired CO build‑up or carbon formation.<cite id="a5fb9c87-5">Equilibrium- limited CO2 conversion at 550 °C and was 100% selective for CO at all temperatures tested (up to 700 °C)</cite><cite id="a5fb9c87-8">Catalytic reduction of CO2 by H2 can lead to the formation of CO through the reverse water-gas shift (RWGS) reaction</cite><cite id="a5fb9c87-3">Hydrogen production through water gas shift reaction over nickel catalysts ... increasing steam ... suppressed CO and coke formation</cite>. 

Practical operating choices and safety margins for methanation feeds
- Feed window tuning: WGS placement allows plants to report explicit tuning of H2/CO and H2O/CO after acid gas removal, aligning with methanation/FT stoichiometric windows and mitigating methane formation by adjusting steam and temperature windows (lower steam minimizes CH4 selectivity in methanation; adequate steam sustains WGS conversion).<cite id="ff9b5a67-1">After pretreatment for acid gas removal, following each sequential methane production stage the syngas ratios of H2/CO and H2O/CO were adjusted</cite><cite id="ff9b5a67-3">Increasing steam flow rate resulted in an increase in the H2 yield at the same time it suppressed CH4 and coke formations</cite>. 
- Temperature selection: low-temperature shift (e.g., Cu/ZnO-based) can maximize CO conversion below ~200 °C on CO2, preserving methanation catalysts; intermediate/HT shifts in steam-rich, high-pressure loops can reach high conversion in compact units, with careful control to avoid equilibrium limitations and unwanted reverse shift under H2-rich conditions.<cite id="3f1bd087-0">Platinum, nickel and cobalt-doped catalysts had the best activity as CO conversion increased with temperature</cite><cite id="a5fb9c87-4">Equilibrium value and equilibrium conversion decrease as the reaction temperature increases</cite>. 
- Catalyst compatibility: Ru-based slurry systems for FTS exhibit intrinsic WGS activity; operators often suppress side WGS to limit methane and CO2 methanation by controlling temperature/steam, thereby focusing selectivity on liquid hydrocarbons; analogous strategies in methanation seek a CO2-tolerant, WGS‑active feed to limit CH4 while achieving high H2/CO.<cite id="f1bd087-5">The other important reaction that occurs in the FTS process is Water Gas Shift (WGS) reaction that produces water and hydrogen</cite>. 

Putting it together: a common gas-conditioning pathway to raise H2/CO for methanation
1) Dehydration and acid gas removal prepare a clean, H2O‑rich stream; then 2) a low‑temperature or intermediate‑temperature WGS reactor (Cu/ZnO or Fe‑based) maximizes CO conversion down‑stream of reforming, driven by steam addition and sufficient pressure; 3) recycle/adiabatic fixed‑bed stages raise conversion under steam‑rich, high‑pressure conditions; 4) if H2/CO target is not met, a steam reformer or ATR with shift assist boosts H2, followed by 5) deep CO2 removal (amine or solid amine), 6) dehydration and 7) PSA or membrane finishing to produce H2‑rich product gas, with online analytics adjusting steam/CO2 and temperature windows to maintain the desired H2/CO and H2O/CO for methanation.<cite id="ff9b5a67-1">After pretreatment for acid gas removal, following each sequential methane production stage the syngas ratios of H2/CO and H2O/CO were adjusted</cite><cite id="ff9b5a67-8">It is important to reduce the CO level (or to achieve high H2/CO ratio) in the reforming stage before entering gases clean up or purification</cite><cite id="ff9b5a67-3">Increasing steam flow rate resulted in an increase in the H2 yield at the same time it suppressed CH4 and coke formations</cite><cite id="ff9b5a67-0">Frequently, the water-gas shift (WGS) reaction proceeds to eliminate carbon monoxide (CO) while producing an increased amount of hydrogen</cite><cite id="a5fb9c87-4">According to the study results, the water gas shift reaction's equilibrium value and equilibrium conversion decrease as the reaction temperature</cite>.
