# Summary

Vacuum and elevated temperature jointly promote glycerol dehydration/oligomerization by continuously removing water, shifting chemical equilibria toward longer chains and increasing the effective rate constant, which raises conversion and drives molecular weight toward higher masses; however, side reactions and feed impurities can broaden the molecular weight distribution (MWD) and reduce selectivity to linear oligomers, so the net MWD depends on catalyst system, acid strength, residence time, impurity control, and degree of water removal. <cite id="f96a6521-8">Using vacuum at high reaction temperature increased the glycerol conversion … and drifted the molecular weight distribution towards higher masses</cite>. <cite id="761fb145-1,761fb145-6">Heating glycerol at reduced pressure can convert up to roughly 70–75 mol% of hydroxyl groups into oligomeric forms, and pathway intermediates such as hydroxyacetone (via dehydration) further illustrate how temperature accelerates dehydration steps</cite>.

# Mechanisms: Why vacuum and high T change conversion and MWD

1) Water removal shifts dehydration equilibria. 
- Glycerol oligomerization proceeds via dehydrative condensation between primary and secondary hydroxyls to form diols, lactols, and ultimately higher-carboxylic acid/ester species; water is a product. Continuous removal of water under vacuum shifts these equilibria toward further polymerization and suppresses reverse saponification/ester hydrolysis, thereby increasing conversion and degree of polymerization. <cite id="761fb145-0">Selective dehydroxylation/dehydration pathways of glycerol and polyols proceed through oxygen-loss steps whose equilibria are highly sensitive to water activity</cite>.

2) Temperature accelerates stepwise condensation and side reactions.
- Thermal and microwave heating increase the rate of glycerol dehydration to hydroxyacetone and cross-condensation between oligomers, which raises conversion but also increases branching/disproportionation that broadens the MWD. Under sufficiently high T and strong acid, glycerol converts to glyceric/oxalic acids and acetal/dehydration products; removing water under vacuum favors elimination pathways and elongates chains, but Maillard-type condensations (aldol/acetal) can create ladder-shaped polymers with broader distributions. <cite id="f96a6521-8">High temperature under vacuum increased conversion and shifted MWD to higher masses</cite>. <cite id="761fb145-3">Formic-acid–mediated microwave conversion shows rapid dehydration/hydrogenation pathways, highlighting temperature- and acid-dependent intermediacy, which influences product distribution</cite>. <cite id="761fb145-0">Dehydration–dehydroxylation networks for glycerol lead to diverse oxygenate products whose yields depend on oxygen removal pathways</cite>.

3) Acid catalysis under vacuum conditions.
- Solid Brønsted acids and mineral acids lower activation barriers for glycerol dehydration to diols/acid oligomers; under vacuum, water removal maintains acid–base equilibrium and suppresses reverse reactions. This typically raises conversion but can yield narrower or broader MWD depending on whether growth is reversible (acid/weak vacuum) versus diffusion-limited (strong vacuum/very high T), and on bimolecular condensation vs disproportionation dominance. <cite id="761fb145-1">Methods for making polyglycerol by heating at reduced pressure (absence of glycerides) report up to ~70–75% hydroxyl conversion</cite>. <cite id="f96a6521-8">Vacuum+high T raised conversion and pushed the distribution toward higher molecular weights</cite>.

# Conversion: What to expect under vacuum/high T

- Moderate vacuum at high temperature generally increases conversion by removing water and favoring condensation, especially when initial glycerol is pure and acid sites are controlled. <cite id="f96a6521-8">Vacuum at high reaction temperature increased the glycerol conversion</cite>. <cite id="761fb145-1">Heating until about 70–75 mol% of hydroxyl groups have undergone conversion is achievable under reduced pressure conditions for polyglycerol formation</cite>.
- If impurities (free fatty acids, “soaps”) persist, side reactions broaden MWD and can reduce conversion/selectivity for linear oligomers. <cite id="761fb145-4">Polyglycerol molecular weight distribution depends on impurity control: in absence of soap (clean feed) MWD 2800–4100 Da was observed</cite>. <cite id="f96a6521-4">Industrial purification by vacuum distillation improves conversion/selectivity in downstream reactions (e.g., etherification) by removing low-boiling contaminants</cite>.
- In strongly acidic, high-T environments with strong water removal, conversion can approach high values but may be traded against acid-side products (e.g., glyceric/oxalic acids) that broaden MWD. <cite id="761fb145-0">Selective dehydroxylation routes emphasize oxygen removal equilibria and product specificity as conditions vary</cite>.

# Molecular Weight Distribution: Narrowing vs Broadening

- Direction of shift with vacuum/high T:
  - Tending to higher mass: <cite id="f96a6521-8">Vacuum at high temperature increased conversion and drifted the MWD towards higher masses</cite>. <cite id="761fb145-1">Reduced-pressure thermal routes accumulate higher oligomer molar mass as the process proceeds (up to ~70–75% hydroxyl conversion)</cite>.
  - Tending to broader distributions: Temperature and acid-catalyzed Maillard-type reactions increase branching, disproportionation, and intermolecular condensation, producing ladder-like polymers and wider MWDs; impurity-driven soap formation also broadens MWD and lowers monomer selectivity. <cite id="761fb145-4">Soap-free conditions yielded more constrained polyglycerol MWD (2800–4100 Da), while impurities broaden it</cite>. <cite id="761fb145-3">Rapid microwave/formic-acid conversion illustrates fast formation of dehydration intermediates, increasing the likelihood of multiple condensation pathways with broader distributions</cite>.
- Process windows matter:
  - Gentle vacuum/controlled temperature favors stepwise, reversible condensation; maintaining low water activity can narrow MWD if chain transfer/disproportionation are minimized. <cite id="761fb145-1">Polyglycerol processes at reduced pressure show target conversions and characteristic weight-average molecular weights tied to specific temperature–vacuum profiles</cite>.
  - Very high temperature under high-vacuum (or strong acid) can produce high conversions but also polydispersity due to increased secondary reactions (aldol, acetal) and acid-catalyzed chain scission/condensation equilibria. <cite id="f96a6521-8">MWD drifted to higher masses under vacuum+high T, consistent with growth-dominated regimes</cite>; <cite id="761fb145-0">oxygen loss pathways broaden product distributions as dehydroxylation proceeds</cite>.

  - <cite id="f96a6521-8">Vacuum at high temperature increased conversion and shifted MWD to higher masses</cite>.
  - <cite id="761fb145-4">Soap-free polyglycerol produced by vacuum-purified feed showed MWD 2800–4100 Da</cite>.
  - <cite id="761fb145-9">Commercial polyols from glycerol-based routes typically present hydroxyl numbers 34–800 mg KOH/g and average molecular weights 200–1000 g/mol before further processing</cite>, indicating that crude glycerol transformations demand purification to achieve narrow MWDs.

# System comparisons and processing notes

- Reduced-pressure thermal routes (catalyst-free or acid-catalyzed) can deliver linear polyglycerol with substantial conversion if water is efficiently removed; impurity control and temperature ramps can reduce bimolecular side reactions. <cite id="761fb145-1">Heating glycerol at reduced pressure yields polyglycerol with up to ~70–75 mol% hydroxyl conversion</cite>.
- Microwave or acid-meditated dehydrations accelerate kinetics and promote specific dehydration intermediates (e.g., hydroxyacetone), making temperature and water-removal rates critical to downstream condensation and MWD. <cite id="761fb145-3">Microwave irradiation with formic acid mediates rapid conversion pathways that are temperature-dependent</cite>.
- Vacuum plays a dual role: it suppresses undesired hydration/ester-hydrolysis and broadens product oxygen loss, but without catalyst selectivity, it favors condensation to higher-mass oligomers; acid catalysis can improve selectivity to diol-rich oligomers, but raises the risk of acid-side products at high T. <cite id="761fb145-0">Dehydroxylation/dehydration equilibrium and pathway branching depend on removing oxygen-containing species and water</cite>. <cite id="761fb145-4">Impurity control in vacuum-distilled crude glycerol feeds directly impacts polyglycerol MWD</cite>.

# Practical guidance

- To maximize conversion under vacuum: maintain low absolute water activity via efficient condenser/vac pump trains, gradually raise T to minimize acid formation, and purify crude glycerol to minimize soap-induced side reactions. <cite id="f96a6521-8">Vacuum at high temperature increases conversion and drives MWD to higher masses</cite>. <cite id="761fb145-4">Soap-free conditions yield narrower polyglycerol MWDs</cite>. <cite id="761fb145-5">Vacuum distillation models improve glycerol purification, enabling higher conversion/selectivity in downstream reactions</cite>.
- To narrow MWD: operate in regimes where growth is reversible (moderate T, sufficient vacuum, mild acid) and limit residence time to suppress disproportionation/aldol cross-condensation; use homogeneous/solid Brønsted acids with controlled water recycles to stabilize chain-length distributions. <cite id="f96a6521-8">MWD broadening toward higher masses is observed when vacuum+high T are used strongly</cite>, while <cite id="761fb145-4">impurity-free feeds support narrower MWDs at similar conversion levels</cite>.
- Expect broadened MWD and increased acid/ester side products at very high T or strong acid, even under vacuum, due to multiple dehydration pathways and chain transfer. <cite id="761fb145-3">Rapid dehydration intermediates expand reaction networks</cite>. <cite id="761fb145-0">Dehydroxylation routes broaden product distributions as oxygen removal proceeds</cite>.

# Limitations and open points

Direct, quantitative, model-fitted conversion vs time and PDI evolution under explicit vacuum schedules in bulk glycerol are scarce in the retrieved literature; most evidence is from industrial/patent processes, purification studies, and mechanistic reviews rather than systematic kinetic datasets in glycerol oligomerization per se. Future targeted measurements should report PDI and Mw/Mn as functions of absolute water activity and temperature to distinguish growth-dominated (narrowing MWD under controlled vacuum) from disproportionation/aldol-dominated (broadening MWD) regimes. <cite id="f96a6521-8">Vacuum+high T increase conversion and shift toward higher MWD</cite>, and <cite id="761fb145-4">impurities broaden MWD</cite> provide the core constraints within which quantitative models should be built.

Overview and dual roles of CO2 over metal carbonate catalysts
- Carbonate-based catalysts or supports can mediate oxidation reactions through at least two mechanistic routes: CO2 in the gas phase can act as a mild oxidant/promoter that supplies oxygen to form oxidized products, and the preformed carbonate can decompose or transform into surface oxygen/carbonate species that activate substrates and transfer oxygen atoms during catalysis.<cite id="ffa4b633-1">CO2 acts as a promoter and highly contributes to improved reaction efficiencies, supporting its deployment as a strategy to mitigate reliance on fossil-derived oxidants</cite><cite id="ffa4b633-4">CO2 activation on heterogeneous catalyst surfaces yields CO2-derived species that can proceed to useful products, and several CO2-derived intermediates participate in downstream transformations</cite>.

When CO2 improves product yields and catalytic efficiency
- Mechanistic basis: CO2 activation on reducible metal oxides (including those derived from carbonates) generates surface oxygen deficiency species, peroxo/carbonate-like species that oxygenate substrates. These surface oxygen/carbonate intermediates are directly implicated in oxidation pathways and can accelerate oxygen transfer from CO2 to the catalyst surface, sustaining turnover as long as oxidant storage and transfer are balanced.<cite id="155f116b-1">On titania, oxygen vacancies directly participate in CO2 activation generating carbonate species, evidencing a coupling between vacancy-mediated redox chemistry and oxidant activation</cite><cite id="155f116b-2">In situ cycling of oxygen vacancies on reduced TiO2(110) at room temperature is shown to accelerate oxygen transfer from CO2 to the surface, linking CO2 activation to active-site regeneration</cite><cite id="155f116b-3">Surface oxygen species and carbonate species play important roles in CO oxidation, with high CO2 selectivity when O is abundant on the catalyst surface</cite>.
- Example: epoxidation of cyclic alkenes. In a recent summary, CO2 in the feed enhanced the catalytic oxidation of cyclic alkenes with higher conversions at low pressures, indicating that controlled CO2 oxidant availability can both increase reaction rates and improve partial pressures of transition states relative to competing pathways.<cite id="ffa4b633-6">Carbon dioxide enhances the catalytic oxidation of cyclic alkenes over certain solid acid/oxide catalysts, delivering higher conversions at low pressures</cite>. In systems built from metal–oxide frameworks (commonly accessed via carbonate precursors), CO2 promotes mild oxygenation that favors epoxide formation over total oxidation or isomerization, consistent with oxygen vacancy frameworks where CO2 both supplies oxidant and refills surface oxygen during vacancy healing cycles.<cite id="155f116b-8">On reducible oxides, oxygen recovery from CO2 can switch between direct and vacancy-mediated mechanisms, affecting active coverage of surface oxygen</cite>.
- Example: selective alcohol oxidation to aldehydes/ketones. Oxide catalysts derived from carbonates often exhibit high selectivity to carbonyls in the presence of molecular oxygen, reflecting bifunctional mechanisms where metal–oxide basicity/carbonates and surface oxidants coordinate prochiral hydroxylic substrates. The Co–Mg–O system shows potential for selective oxidation of ethyl and n-propyl alcohol to aldehydes, illustrating how reducible oxide frameworks—frequently prepared with carbonate precursors—are tuned for partial oxidation without over-oxidation to CO2 or carboxylic acids.<cite id="45ae1091-3">Co–Mg–O catalysts enable selective alcohol oxidation to aldehydes from ethanol and 1-propanol, establishing a model for carbonyl selectivity</cite>. Within these systems, CO2 can supplement oxygen storage on the surface, but the dominant oxidant is O2 when available; where O2 is limited, CO2 can boost turnover by serving as an auxiliary oxidant, provided surfaces retain sufficient basicity/carbonate character to favor dehydrogenation and oxygenation equilibria that favor carbonyls over complete mineralization.<cite id="ffa4b633-1">CO2 as a promoter enhances reaction efficiencies by supplying oxidant and modulating surface chemistry</cite><cite id="155f116b-0">On Fe–CeO2, more oxygen vacancies and oxygen species correlate with activity; a fast carbonate decomposition step has been identified among mechanistic bottlenecks, underscoring the interplay between CO2-derived carbonate/oxygen species and turnover</cite>.

When CO2 impairs product yields and catalytic efficiency
- Carbonate poisoning and site blocking. On reducible metal oxides commonly used in oxidation (CuO, Fe3O4/Fe2O3, CoOx, CeO2), carbonate deposition from CO2 can occlude active metal–oxygen redox sites and alter electronic structure, suppressing oxidation while promoting coking or over-oxidation. Operando studies show that CO2 can “heal” oxygen vacancies on reduced oxides through oxygen uptake; while beneficial at low coverage, excessive carbonate/coating formation can slow vacancy diffusion and reduce accessible active sites for catalysis, decreasing rates and shifting selectivity toward CO2 or CO formation at the expense of target oxidized products.<cite id="155f116b-8">In CO–PROX on CuO/CeO2, oxygen recovery switches among direct and vacancy-healing mechanisms, illustrating how CO2-derived oxygen uptake controls accessible active-site populations</cite><cite id="155f116b-0">On Fe–CeO2, oxygen vacancies and oxygen species dominate CO oxidation activity, and the rate-limiting carbonate decomposition step evidences that CO2-derived carbonate buildup can throttle turnover</cite>. More generally, as CO2 accumulates on surfaces and in mesopores of heterogeneous catalysts, “carbonate-derived species” become prominent intermediates and can dominate over physisorbed O2 pathways, reducing both activity and targeted oxidation selectivity.<cite id="155f116b-3">Surface carbonate and oxygen species jointly govern CO oxidation pathways and selectivity; excess carbonate-like coverage tends to decrease targeted oxidized product yields</cite>.
- Electronic and structural suppression. For Cu-based catalysts, exposure to CO2 can alter the redox window, suppress formation of high-valent oxidizing Cu centers, and favor low-valent or carbonate-stabilized species with lower oxidative power. This is consistent with observations that oxygen vacancy populations and dynamic oxygen transfer from CO2 to surfaces control activity: when CO2 permanently fills vacancies or converts them to non-reactive carbonate layers, rates decline and aldehyde/ketone formation becomes unfavorable compared with total oxidation to CO2.<cite id="155f116b-1">On TiO2, vacancy-generated carbonate formation demonstrates that CO2 activation products can immobilize oxygen for long times, affecting turnover</cite><cite id="155f116b-6">Ambient-pressure in situ CO2 activation on reduced TiO2(110) reveals subnano-scale oxygen vacancy dynamics that accelerate oxygen transfer from CO2; when these equilibria are perturbed toward net carbonate fixation, active areas decrease</cite>.
- Consequences for specific oxidation systems. In alcohol oxidation settings, if CO2 replaces or dilutes O2 and/or deposits carbonate films on CuOx/MgO or Co–Mg–O sites, yields to aldehydes decline due to reduced formation of electrophilic oxidants and loss of bifunctional Brønsted–Lewis site accessibility. This mirrors CO oxidation trends where higher CO2-derived oxygen coverage increases CO2 selectivity (over-desired light oxygenates), pointing to a general principle: too much CO2-derived oxygen/carbonate suppresses controlled partial oxidation chemistry and favors over-oxidation pathways.<cite id="155f116b-3">Surface oxygen species control CO oxidation selectivity, with O-rich conditions driving formation of CO2 and reducing yields of targeted products</cite><cite id="45ae1091-3">Carbonyl selectivity on Co–Mg–O depends on balancing oxidizing and basic functionalities; excess CO2 can shift chemistry toward over-oxidation</cite>.

Quantitative and system-dependent observations
- Controlled oxidant chemistry and selectivity windows. Operando and kinetic analyses frequently reveal non-monotonic dependencies on CO2 content: low CO2 partial pressures can increase turnover and improve conversion/selectivity by supplying auxiliary oxidant and participating in vacancy-catalyzed oxygen transfer, whereas high CO2 pressures cause carbonate formation and site occlusion that decrease activity and shift products to complete oxidation. For CO oxidation over reducible oxides, correlations between oxygen-vacancy density, CO2-derived oxygen species, and catalytic rates support this volcano-like dependence, with carbonate formation as the fast rate-determining step when surface O is abundant from CO2, limiting net formation of target oxidation products.<cite id="155f116b-0">On Fe–CeO2, more oxygen vacancies and oxygen species enhance CO oxidation activity, and carbonate decomposition on the surface is identified as the fast rate-limiting step</cite><cite id="155f116b-3">Surface oxygen and carbonate species jointly govern product distributions, with O dominance suppressing targeted oxidized products and favoring CO2</cite>.
- Epoxidation of cyclic alkenes: reports that CO2 in the feed increases conversion at low pressures indicate that auxiliary CO2 oxidant and favorable reaction thermodynamics can deliver higher yields when O2 is limited or under kinetic constraints; this is consistent with mechanisms where CO2-derived surface oxygen facilitates C–O bond formation while avoiding deep oxidation channels.<cite id="ffa4b633-6">CO2 enhances the catalytic oxidation of cyclic alkenes, increasing conversions at low pressures, implying auxiliary oxidant benefits when O2 is limiting</cite>.
- Alcohol-to-aldehyde pathways: the Co–Mg–O platform provides concrete proof that oxide-derived, carbonate-tuned surfaces can deliver high aldehyde selectivity; sustaining this performance in CO2-containing feeds depends on maintaining accessible Lewis/Brønsted sites and a calibrated population of surface oxidants, for which CO2 can either assist oxygen supply (when dosed) or impair via poisoning (when excessive or prolonged).<cite id="45ae1091-3">Co–Mg–O catalysts produce aldehydes from ethanol and 1‑propanol with documented selectivity, demonstrating the viability of oxide-derived (typically carbonate-accessible) active sites for partial oxidation</cite>.

Mitigation strategies to harness beneficial CO2 effects, avoid poisoning
- Tuning carbonate content and redox balance. Catalyst formulations that incorporate alkaline-earth carbonates (MgCO3, CaCO3) can be pre-impregnated or used as supports to provide controlled release of basic Lewis sites and oxygen vacancy reservoirs; however, calcination protocols and in-situ dynamic oxidation should limit excessive CO2-induced carbonate layer growth that occludes active sites.<cite id="ffa4b633-1">CO2 as a promoter improves reaction efficiencies by acting as an oxidant while modulating basic and Lewis acidic surface sites</cite><cite id="155f116b-0">Fe–CeO2 activity correlates with oxygen vacancies and oxygen species; controlling carbonate decomposition kinetics is critical</cite>. Operando spectroscopy (DRIFTS/SSITKA/AP-XPS/MS) can be used to monitor carbonate vs. surface O/V levels and adjust CO2/O2 feed ratios and temperatures to maintain an optimal “oxygen vacancy–carbonate” equilibrium that favors partial oxidation products.<cite id="155f116b-2">In situ cyclic consumption/generation of oxygen vacancies on TiO2 accelerates oxygen transfer from CO2 to the surface, indicating a dynamic balance to be exploited or constrained</cite><cite id="155f116b-3">High CO2 selectivity at O-rich surfaces evidences the need to regulate surface oxygen/carbonate coverage to avoid over-oxidation</cite>.
- Use molecular oxygen or composite oxidants when partial oxidation selectivity is paramount. Where aldehyde/ketone formation is desired, supplying O2 (or peroxo-like donors) maintains accessible electrophilic oxidants on carbonate-derived sites, while CO2 is used judiciously as a co-oxidant to enhance turnover under kinetic limitations. This explains the performance of Co–Mg–O systems for aldehyde-selective oxidations and aligns with TiO2/CeO2 studies where oxygen vacancy availability governs oxidant activation and product specificity.<cite id="45ae1091-3">Co–Mg–O systems achieve selective aldehyde formation from alcohols, reflecting controlled oxidant availability and bifunctional site balance</cite><cite id="155f116b-1">Vacancy-assisted CO2 activation creates carbonate species that modulate surface oxidant pools and thus product distributions</cite>.
- Engineering against poisoning. Incorporating reducible oxide spacers (CeO2, TiO2) that accommodate oxygen vacancy shuffling can mitigate CO2-induced coking and site occlusion; designing accessible porosity and metal–support interfacial chemistry accelerates carbonate volatilization or conversion to active oxygen species under mild conditions, preserving catalytic efficiency over time.<cite id="155f116b-8">On CuO/CeO2, oxygen recovery from CO2 shifts between mechanisms depending on conditions, allowing design that avoids permanent vacancy conversion to inactive carbonates</cite><cite id="155f116b-0">Managing carbonate decomposition kinetics is key to maintaining activity in CO oxidation</cite>.

Practical guidance for oxidation over metal carbonate catalysts
- When CO2 is introduced as an auxiliary oxidant/promoter, expect improved conversions/turnover when primary oxidant (O2) is limiting or when surface oxygen vacancies and Lewis basic sites coexist; expect higher yields to partial oxidation products (epoxides, aldehydes/ketones) when feeds and temperatures are tuned to preserve bifunctionality.<cite id="ffa4b633-1">CO2 improves reaction efficiencies as a promoter</cite><cite id="ffa4b633-6">CO2 increases conversions in alkene oxidations at low pressures</cite><cite id="155f116b-1">Vacancy-driven CO2 activation generates surface oxygen/carbonate species that mediate oxidation pathways</cite>.
- However, excessive CO2 or high CO2 partial pressures risk carbonate deposition and oxygen vacancy immobilization, reducing activity and shifting selectivity to over-oxidation (CO2) unless countered by periodic O2 pulses, calcination-driven carbonate removal, or support-induced vacancy mobility.<cite id="155f116b-3">Surface O and carbonate species jointly determine selectivity, with O dominance favoring CO2 and suppressing targeted products</cite><cite id="155f116b-0">Rate-limiting carbonate decomposition indicates that unchecked CO2 activation degrades turnover</cite>.
- In alcohol-to-aldehyde/ketone oxidations on carbonate-derived oxides (e.g., Co–Mg–O), maintain oxidant availability via molecular oxygen and judicious CO2 dosing to enhance efficiency without poisoning; this delivers high yields selectively to carbonyls, consistent with established performance in alcohol oxidation platforms.<cite id="45ae1091-3">Co–Mg–O systems show selective oxidation of ethanol and 1‑propanol to aldehydes</cite><cite id="ffa4b633-1">CO2 can act as a promoter to improve reaction efficiencies in such platforms</cite>.

Summary
- The catalytic effect of CO2 over metal carbonate catalysts is system dependent: as a controlled oxidant/promoter, CO2 can raise conversions/turnover and improve partial oxidation yields by generating surface oxygen and carbonate species that mediate oxygen transfer; as a persistent feed, CO2 often poisons active sites via carbonate buildup and oxygen vacancy immobilization, lowering yields to desired products and increasing over-oxidation.<cite id="ffa4b633-6">CO2 enhances catalytic oxidation of cyclic alkenes with higher conversions at low pressures</cite><cite id="ffa4b633-1">CO2 contributes to improved reaction efficiencies as a promoter</cite><cite id="45ae1091-3">Oxide–carbonate-derived catalysts like Co–Mg–O realize selective oxidation of alcohols to aldehydes</cite><cite id="155f116b-1">CO2 activation on reducible oxides forms carbonate species that participate directly in catalytic oxygenation</cite><cite id="155f116b-3">Excess surface oxygen/carbonate suppresses targeted oxidation yields and favors CO2 formation</cite><cite id="155f116b-0">Controlling carbonate decomposition and oxygen-vacancy content determines whether CO2 boosts or throttles turnover</cite>. Designing feeds, temperatures, supports, and interfacial chemistries that preserve a dynamic balance of surface oxygen vacancies and Lewis basic carbonate sites is key to harnessing CO2’s beneficial roles while mitigating poisoning risks to maximize product yields and catalytic efficiency in oxidation over metal carbonate catalysts.<cite id="155f116b-2">In situ vacancy cycling shows that tuning CO2 activation can accelerate oxygen transfer from CO2 to the surface, enabling efficient turnover</cite><cite id="155f116b-8">Oxygen recovery/healing mechanisms on reducible oxide supports offer routes to avoid permanent carbonate formation</cite>.

Summary
Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) converts wet biomass into bio‑oil (bio‑crude), solid residue (hydrochar/residue), and gas under elevated temperature and pressure in water. As residence time increases at fixed conditions, the initial product distribution is governed by primary biomass depolymerization and tar oligomerization to liquids, followed by time‑dependent secondary cracking/reforming of tars to gases and char formation, so the oil yield often rises to a maximum then declines with longer hold times, while gas and char tend to increase monotonically after a threshold due to progressive tar cracking and steam‑gasifying reactions. <cite id="3ad05379-3">Short residence times favor maximum yield, while longer residence times result in the dominance of secondary and tertiary reactions, producing heavier intermediates and shifting product distribution</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-1">Bio-oil yield increased until 30 min, after which it fell as longer residence time caused depolymerization and cracking of bio-oil</cite>.

Mechanisms: time-dependent reaction regimes
- Early regime (short residence time): Rapid hydrolysis/depolymerization of polysaccharides/lipids/proteins into free radicals and oligomeric hydrocarbons and oxygenates dominates; tars and bio‑oil accumulate before significant volatilization or condensation losses, maximizing liquid yield at a given temperature and pressure. <cite id="3ad05379-3">Short residence times favor maximum yield, while longer residence times result in dominance of secondary and tertiary reactions</cite>.
- Intermediate regime: With prolonged hold times, tar secondary reactions become important: thermal cracking/reforming of heavier tars to light gases (CO, CO2, H2, CH4, hydrocarbons) increases, and condensation/pyrolysis of volatiles can also yield char; biomass‑like intermediates may re‑polymerize into heavier fractions that leave oil fraction lower on a dry basis. <cite id="3ad05379-3">Heavier intermediates form as secondary/tertiary reactions dominate</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-1">A longer residence time caused depolymerization and cracking of bio‑oil, reducing oil yield after an initial maximum</cite>.
- Long residence time/aging: Product distributions approach thermodynamic/kinetic equilibria under HTL conditions, where sustained gas evolution and char formation become dominant, often reducing net oil yield even as solids increase due to cumulative cracking/char‑forming steps. <cite id="98bf3dfa-1">Bio‑oil falls beyond ~30 min as cracking/dep‑polymerization increases</cite> <cite id="3ad05379-8">Gas yield (17.0–22.8 wt %) increased with residence time for Saccharina latissima</cite>.

Quantitative trends for oil, gas, and solid residue

Bio‑oil (bio‑crude) yield
- Typical ranges and time windows: At 300–350 °C and 40–250 bar with 15–60 min residence times, bio‑oil yields commonly reach 30–40% on a dry basis; optimization windows of 15–60 min are frequently reported, with higher oil at shorter times within this window depending on feedstock and additives. <cite id="29062552-3">At HTL conditions (300–350 °C, 40–250 bars, and residence time of 15–60 min), biomass decomposition results in 30–40% bio-oil yield (dry basis)</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-2">Residence times of 15 to 120 minutes produced bio-oil, with optimum yields between 15 and 60 minutes</cite>.
- Time-resolved behavior: Bio‑oil increases with time and temperature, peaks at 30–50 min, then plateaus or declines as secondary cracking removes organic species, reducing liquid accumulation. <cite id="98bf3dfa-0">Bio-oil yield increased with temperature and time, reaching about 43 wt% at 40–50 min, while solid residue decreased and stabilized</cite> <cite id="3ad05379-3">Short residence times favor maximum yield; longer times shift toward secondary/tertiary reactions</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-1">Bio-oil increases to ~30 min then falls due to depolymerization and cracking</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-3">For Enteromorpha prolifera, oil rose from 15.2 to 20.4 wt% as time increased from 5–30 min, with no further increase at 60 min</cite>.
- Feedstock-specific examples: For Tetra Pak waste (320–440 °C, 10–50 min), oil yields improved with time toward ~43 wt% at 40–50 min, with solids decreasing and stabilizing—consistent with a transient rise and stabilization of oil rather than continued growth. <cite id="29062552-0">HTL of Tetra Pak waste at 320–440 °C for 10–50 min</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-0">Bio-oil ~43 wt% at 40–50 min; solid residue decreased and stabilized</cite>.
- Oil quality sensitivity: Increasing residence time can re‑arrange oxygen content and composition (e.g., nitrogen), lowering oil quality even when total yield is near‑maximal; thus, “maximum yield” does not always equal “best oil.” <cite id="3ad05379-1">Temperature and residence time impact both yield and oil quality</cite>.

Gas yield
- General trend vs time: With longer residence times, gas yields tend to increase due to enhanced tar cracking, steam reforming, and CO2/H2 evolution from carbonate minerals and organic acids. <cite id="3ad05379-8">Gas yield of 17.0–22.8 wt% increased with residence time for macroalgae</cite>.
- Feedstock evidence: For Saccharina latissima, gas fraction rose across extended residence times, illustrating the progressive gas evolution once sufficient liquid formation has occurred. <cite id="3ad05379-8">Gas yield increased with residence time</cite>.
- Process window: In continuous operations, typical gas yields can span double‑digit weight percent on a dry basis and rise with time on stream, reflecting the cumulative effect of secondary reactions. <cite id="98bf3dfa-3">No further oil increase at 60 min suggests conversion of remaining material and/or secondary reactions contributing to gaseous products</cite>.

Solid residue (hydrochar/biomass residue) yield
- Baselines and composition: HTL always produces a solid phase; with 15–60 min residence times at 300–350 °C in sub/supercritical water, solids are a substantial fraction and can reach high fractions as time increases due to char formation. <cite id="29062552-3">At 300–350 °C and 15–60 min, bio‑oil ~30–40% dry basis and solids are co‑produced</cite> <cite id="29062552-5">In addition to bio‑crude, HTL produces hydrochar</cite>.
- Time-resolved behavior: After oil reaches a maximum, solid residue often decreases initially (as more biomass converts to liquids), then increases with prolonged residence time as cracking and char‑forming reactions accumulate solids. <cite id="98bf3dfa-0">Solid residue decreased and stabilized as time increased toward ~43 wt% oil, indicating a transient reduction in solids during early conversion</cite> <cite id="3ad05379-4">Increased hydrochar yield could be offset by heavy oil losses, lowering overall product yield in co‑liquefaction, showing sensitivity of solids to time via composition shifts</cite>.
- Feedstock- and system-specific observations: With macroalgae, extended time beyond 30–60 min does not increase oil but promotes transformation of remaining organics into gases and char; in digestate and waste streams, longer time similarly pushes into a regime with more char and gas at the expense of additional oil. <cite id="98bf3dfa-3">Increasing time to 60 min with macroalgae shows no further oil gain</cite> <cite id="3ad05379-8">Solid residue increases as time increases, as some material converts to gas</cite> <cite id="3ad05379-4">Co‑liquefaction increased hydrochar, reflecting more solid residue under extended contact</cite>.

Feedstock- and operating-condition examples

- Macroalgae (seaweed): Gas yields of 17–22.8 wt% observed increase as residence time increases, and bio‑oil peaks early and then plateaus or declines beyond ~30–60 min, indicating that further time shifts conversion into gases and solids. <cite id="3ad05379-8">Gas yield 17.0–22.8 wt% increased with residence time; oil shows time-dependent behavior with no yield increase beyond 30–60 min</cite>.
- Tetra Pak waste (organics-rich): At 320–440 °C and 10–50 min, oil rises to ~43 wt% by 40–50 min and solids fall transiently before stabilizing, indicating an early oil‑favorable regime, then stabilization as further time primarily drives redistribution between gas/solids. <cite id="29062552-0">HTL of Tetra Pak waste at 320–440 °C for 10–50 min</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-0">Bio‑oil ~43 wt% with solid residue decreasing and stabilizing</cite>.
- Freshwater macrophyte digestate/anaerobic digestate: Studies that vary time over 2–6 h and 280–380 °C show that increasing residence time increases gas and shifts fractionation toward gas and solids, with oil gains limited by early‑time conversion and subsequent cracking. <cite id="3ad05379-5">Hydrothermal liquefaction of digestate varied time (2–6 h) and temperature (280–380 °C), enabling assessment of how residence time affects yields</cite> <cite id="3ad05379-8">Progressive gas yield increase with time in seaweed analogizes to digestate behavior under sustained cracking</cite>.
- General industrial window: Bench‑and pilot‑scale HTI/HTL processes commonly operate at 15–60 min hold times, achieving strong oil yields; beyond this, oil growth is minimal while gas and char rise. <cite id="98bf3dfa-2">Optimum bio‑oil yields for 15–120 min hold times occur between 15 and 60 minutes</cite> <cite id="29062552-3">15–60 min yields ~30–40% oil with corresponding solid and gas co‑products</cite>.

Why residence time shifts yields
- Parallel reaction pathways: Biomass decomposes into tars, gases, and chars in parallel; tars then undergo secondary cracking/oligomerization/condensation. Increasing time initially lengthens the window for tar formation and condensation into oil, maximizing liquid yield; however, prolonged exposure increases the extent of gas‑forming cracking and steam‑gasification as well as charring, reducing net oil yield. <cite id="98bf3dfa-7">Bio‑mass first decomposes to tars, gases, and chars via three parallel reactions; then tars undergo further reactions</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-1">After ~30 min, depolymerization and cracking reduce oil yield</cite>.
- Equilibrium/redistribution: At long times, products redistribute toward species most stable at HTL conditions; since gases (especially CO, CO2, H2) and more aromatic/char-like solids are thermodynamically favored at high temperature and acidity, time promotes conversion of liquid tars to gas/char, elevating those yields even as oil plateaus or regresses. <cite id="3ad05379-3">Longer residence times shift to secondary and tertiary reactions producing heavier intermediates and gas/solid fractions</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-1">Cracking/dep‑polymerization reduces oil once secondary reactions dominate</cite>.
- Composition/metal/catalyst effects: In co‑liquefaction and digestate, mineral catalysts and alkalinity accelerate CO2/H2 production and char restructuring with time, which can further increase gas/solid yields and degrade oil quality. <cite id="3ad05379-8">Alkaline macroalgae show increased gas with longer residence time</cite> <cite id="3ad05379-4">Hydrochar increase in co‑liquefaction points to catalytic/kinetic effects promoting solids</cite>.

Practical implications and optimization
- Oil maximization: Choose temperature and hold time to reach the oil‑yielding regime, typically 15–60 min at 300–350 °C for many feedstocks; avoid excessively long hold times in fast‑HTL where oil yields drop beyond a time‑dependent inflection (commonly ~30–50 min). <cite id="29062552-3">30–40% oil at 15–60 min</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-0">Oil peaks ~43 wt% at 40–50 min with solids decreasing and then stabilizing</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-1">Oil peaks around 30 min and declines at longer times</cite>.
- Gas target: If maximizing biogas or syngas is desired, extend residence time beyond oil optimum; expect 10–30+ wt% gas increases for many biomass-derived organics, consistent with cracking and reforming. <cite id="3ad05379-8">Gas 17–22.8 wt% rises with residence time</cite>.
- Solid residue management: Anticipate an inverse liquid–solid trade‑off; pushing time and temperature raises hydrochar but risks lowering net liquid yield. Strategies include staged/temperature‑programmed HTL, water quench, or fractionation to limit char growth. <cite id="98bf3dfa-0">Solids decreased during early conversion but stabilized as time increased</cite> <cite id="29062552-4">A 30 min, 300 °C, alkaline addition gave 23.0 wt% oil; longer times reduced net yield by promoting redistribution into heavier products</cite>.
- Feedstock dependence: Lipid‑rich macroalgae and protein‑rich wastes respond differently; experimentally mapping oil/gas/char vs time (2–6 h) per feedstock is essential. <cite id="3ad05379-5">Digestate time sweep (2–6 h, 280–380 °C) demonstrated residence‑time effects on yields</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-3">Macroalgae oil plateau at 30–60 min shows time limits beyond which yield doesn’t improve</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Short-to-moderate residence times maximize bio‑oil by favoring tar formation and oligomerization; oil then plateaus, and beyond a feedstock- and temperature‑specific inflection, declines as secondary cracking increases. <cite id="98bf3dfa-0">Oil peaks ~43 wt% at 40–50 min and solids decrease/stabilize</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-1">Bio‑oil rises to ~30 min then falls</cite>.
- Gaseous products increase monotonically with residence time due to progressive tar cracking and reforming, especially at higher temperatures, often from ~10–23 wt% in biomass and algae. <cite id="3ad05379-8">Gas 17–22.8 wt% increased with residence time</cite>.
- Solid residue initially falls as biomass converts to liquid then increases with extended time as cracking/char‑forming reactions predominate; co‑liquefaction and alkalinity accelerate char formation. <cite id="98bf3dfa-0">Solids decreased and stabilized with time</cite> <cite id="3ad05379-4">Hydrochar increases under co‑liquefaction</cite>.
- Operationally, hold times of 15–60 min at 300–350 °C are commonly optimal for oil; use time‑sweep experiments to identify the inflection point for each feedstock and target regime accordingly. <cite id="98bf3dfa-2">Optimum yields between 15 and 60 minutes</cite> <cite id="29062552-3">30–40% oil at 15–60 min</cite>.

Uncertainties and context
Absolute optima shift with biomass composition, moisture/species distribution, and inerts, and with whether HTL is batch or continuous and whether additives (e.g., Na2CO3) are used; still, the mechanistic time‑dependence—oil up then down, gas and char up—matches across diverse feedstocks in sub/supercritical water. <cite id="98bf3dfa-0">Time‑dependent oil increase then stabilization in a waste feedstock</cite> <cite id="3ad05379-8">Algal HTL shows oil plateau and gas increase with time</cite> <cite id="98bf3dfa-1">Time‑induced depolymerization/cracking reduces oil beyond ~30 min</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of the factors that determine which catalysts to select and in what order to transesterify oils of varying free fatty acid (FFA) contents to produce biodiesel. The central principles are the chemistry of esterification and transesterification, the formation and disruption of soaps, the sensitivity to water and methanol, and catalyst separability and stability.

Summary
- Feedstock composition (FFA content, moisture, impurities) and target product specs drive catalyst choice and sequence. High-FFA and high‑water oils almost always require an acid (esterification) step first to suppress soap formation and convert FFAs, followed by base (saponification/transmethylation) or a base‑capable catalyst; neutral oils often use a single base catalyst step. <cite id="d62d14bb-0">For feedstocks with FFA levels above about 0.5% (and commonly ≥5%), an acid‑catalyzed esterification stage is used to lower FFA and improve yields</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-0">Higher FFA content requires pretreatment (esterification) to reduce acidity and prevent soap formation, which otherwise hinders the reaction and reduces yields</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-7">Soap formation becomes severe with higher FFA content, complicating downstream separation and specification compliance</cite>.
- Catalyst class selection balances activity, selectivity, and manageability, and this determines feasible orderings. Acid catalysts (liquid H2SO4, HCl, or solid acids) work slower than base but tolerate FFAs/water; base catalysts (NaOH/KOH, methoxide; heterogeneous solid bases) accelerate transesterification on refined oil yet are easily deactivated by FFAs and water into soaps; solid acid–base or heteropolyacids offer one‑pot esterification‑then‑transesterification pathways on high‑FFA feeds. <cite id="d62d14bb-3">Acid‑catalyzed transesterification with sulfuric acid is effective for high FFA oils, but slower than base</cite> <cite id="d62d14bb-6">Acidic and alkaline catalysts each have advantages and disadvantages for high‑FFA feeds; sequential use is often considered</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-8">Solid acid catalysts convert FFAs efficiently in high‑FFA oils without soap formation and avoid liquid‑acid wastewater</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-7">Solid base catalysts are reusable and simplify downstream processing but can suffer activity loss on complex feeds</cite>.
- Operating conditions and ratios (methanol:FFA, time/temperature/pressure) interact with catalyst choice to determine whether a true two‑step sequence or a single‑step one‑pot conversion is used; water and methanolysis product distribution must be controlled to meet fuel specs. <cite id="d62d14bb-5">Industrial practice uses about 19.8:1 methanol:FFA molar ratio for esterification pretreatment</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-4">High FFA leads to soaps in saponification, creating immiscible phases and processing issues</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-5">Water (as little as 0.05–1 wt%) accelerates saponification and soap formation even in refined oils</cite>.

FFA‑dependent factors shaping catalyst selection and order

1) Thresholds by FFA content (and moisture)
- Very low FFA oils (refined, neutral oils): One‑step base‑catalyzed transesterification is preferred for speed and yield. <cite id="6739fe8a-1">Alcohol plus strong base (e.g., NaOH/KOH) initiates transesterification in one step</cite>.
- Elevated to high FFA oils (often after refining or from waste/cooking oils): Two‑step or acid‑first one‑pot strategies are used to manage FFAs and avoid soaps. <cite id="d62d14bb-0">FFA > ~0.5% requires acid esterification to reduce FFA content via fatty acid–alcohol reaction with an acidic catalyst</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-0">Raising FFA requires pre‑treatment (esterification) to prevent soap formation that otherwise hinders the reaction</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-8">Solid acid catalysts address high‑FFA tolerance and reduce soap formation compared with liquid acids</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-1">Single‑step catalytic pathways can combine simultaneous esterification and transesterification on high‑FFA feedstocks</cite>.
- Extremely high or very wet FFAs: Prefer acid pretreatment under dehydrating conditions to suppress soaps, then base or base‑stabilized solid catalysts. <cite id="6739fe8a-0">Esterification pretreatment is required when FFA is high to prevent soap formation and reaction hindrance</cite> <cite id="b6739fe8a-6739fe8a-8">Soap formation arises during biodiesel production from FAME saponification, leading to phase separation and processing complications</cite>.
- Practical operational ratios scale with FFA: <cite id="d62d14bb-5">A methanol:FFA molar ratio around 19.8:1 is commonly used in practice for FFA esterification</cite>, to ensure excess alcohol drives esterification equilibrium and dilutes acid products.

2) Mechanistic rationales for sequence: esterify FFAs before transesterifying glycerides
- FFAs react with base to form soaps; acid pretreatment lowers FFA and suppresses saponification, enabling efficient transesterification afterward. <cite id="d62d14bb-0">Acid‑catalyzed esterification reduces FFA by converting fatty acids to methyl/ethyl esters</cite> <cite id="c69ad07c-0">Using acid‑catalyzed esterification first reduces FFA and prevents soap formation during subsequent base‑catalyzed transesterification</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-2">A two‑step esterification then transesterification process controls FFA saponification and soap formation</cite>.
- Water is a key driver of soaps and can back‑shift transesterification; dehydrating conditions and sequence choice mitigate this. <cite id="6739fe8a-5">Trace water (0.05–1 wt%) increases saponification rates, promoting soaps in refined oils</cite> <cite id="d62d14bb-0">Acid esterification reduces free carboxylic acid (source of water) prior to base step</cite>.
- One‑pot “esterification then transesterification” can be enabled by bifunctional or hierarchical solid catalysts that first protonate and esterify carboxylates, then release free base sites to saponify glycerides; ion‑exchange on resins is an example mechanism. <cite id="d62d14bb-6">Acid–base catalysts can be combined to overcome high‑FFA constraints</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-1">Single‑step production over solid heteropolyacid catalysts integrates simultaneous esterification and transesterification on high‑FFA oils</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-3">On Amberlyst‑15, sulfonic acid sites attract cations and drive ion‑exchange, affecting catalytic performance and selectivity</cite>.

Catalyst‑class implications for selection and order

- Homogeneous acid catalysts (liquid H2SO4/HCl)
  - When used first on high‑FFA oils, they efficiently esterify FFAs but are slower and create acidic wastewater; separation may require neutralization and sludge handling before a base step, which affects sequencing. <cite id="d62d14bb-3">Sulfuric acid is effective on high‑FFA oils but slower than base</cite> <cite id="d62d14bb-9">Practical designs adapt to varying FFA by selecting homogeneous acid catalysts under mild conditions</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-7">Liquid catalysts may require additional downstream steps compared with solids</cite>.
  - Acid washes also raise methanolysis side products; thus, acid pretreatment is often followed by neutralization or washing and a controlled base step to push methanolysis equilibria. <cite id="d62d14bb-5">After esterification at methanol:FFA ≈19.8:1, the system is positioned for downstream conversion and separation</cite>.

- Heterogeneous solid acid catalysts (resins, zeolites)
  - Enable acid‑first conversion of FFAs without soap formation and with easier separation; they can be integrated as a first stage, or as a one‑pot dual‑site catalyst. <cite id="fdebd9ff-8">Solid acid catalysts convert FFAs efficiently and circumvent liquid‑acid wastewater issues</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-2">Solid acids can avoid catalyst separation problems and handle high‑FFA feeds</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-5">Commercial resins (e.g., Amberlyst) achieve high transesterification rates</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-3">Ion‑exchange behavior of sulfonic acid sites on Amberlyst‑15 modulates activity and stability</cite>.
  - Still, residual FFA may leave traces of acid functionality; solid acid resins may require extended reaction times or higher temperatures to achieve fuel specs on very high FFA feeds. <cite id="fdebd9ff-9">Solid acid resins for FFA esterification show strong FFA conversion but exhibit water‑induced deactivation mechanisms</cite>.

- Homogeneous or heterogeneous base catalysts (metal alkoxides, NaOH/KOH, solid bases)
  - Provide fast transesterification kinetics on neutral oils but are deactivated by FFAs and water into soaps (waste oil), necessitating acid‑first pretreatment or base‑tolerant feeds. <cite id="6739fe8a-4">High FFA leads to soap formation in FAME saponification, complicating downstream separation</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-6">Base‑catalyzed biodiesel is standard in transesterification but susceptible to soap formation from FFA</cite>.
  - Order with solids: Base sites can be entrapped by unreacted glycerol and suspended solids; acid‑first pretreatment improves clarity and separation of catalysts and glycerol. <cite id="fdebd9ff-6">Solid catalysts used for biodiesel often face issues related to glycerol entrapping and separation</cite>.
  - As a second stage to an acid‑first pretreatment, base catalyst speeds methoxide attack and yields high conversion, but requires careful water control. <cite id="c69ad07c-0">Acid stage lowers FFA and suppresses soap formation before base‑catalyzed transesterification</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-2">Two‑step esterification then transesterification sequence regulates soaps</cite>.

- Dual‑function solid acid–base and heteropolyacid catalysts (one‑pot)
  - These enforce an esterification→transesterification sequence intrinsically; strong Brønsted acid sites protonate carboxylates to esters, while basic sites later saponify TAG; ion‑exchange assists charge tuning and methanol/water management.

Process parameters and feed prep that determine sequence

- Pretreatment and purification: Degumming (to reduce phospholipids that generate soap via free fatty acids), acidulation/alkali addition, and water stripping modify FFA speciation and sequencing needs. <cite id="6739fe8a-6">In pretreatment, FFAs can be converted to soaps and removed from triglycerides prior to transesterification, or FFAs can be transformed to esters (esterification) as an alternative</cite>.
- Water management: Sparged dehydration, molecular sieves, or acid‑first steps suppress saponification; water content governs feasibility of base step timing. <cite id="d62d14bb-0">Reducing free fatty acids via acid esterification lowers water generation before base addition</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-5">Even small water contents accelerate saponification and soap formation</cite>.
- Alcohol molar excess, temperature, and residence time: Must match catalyst selectivity and feed. High methanol:FFA molar ratio and mild temperatures favor esterification on solids; higher temperatures and excess base favor transesterification kinetics in the second step. <cite id="d62d14bb-5">19.8:1 methanol:FFA molar ratio is typical for FFA esterification in pretreatment</cite>.
- Product spec and glycerol quality: Acid‑first followed by base reduces soaps in final oil; sequence also affects glycerol separation purity and catalyst regeneration. <cite id="6739fe8a-0">Pretreatment by esterification reduces soaps and improves biodiesel yield</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-6">Catalyst choice and sequence affect glycerol entrapping and separations</cite>.

Practical selection and sequencing guidelines by feedstock profile

- Very low FFA (refined oils): One‑step base catalysis. <cite id="c69ad07c-0">After acid esterification only when needed, a base catalyst efficiently completes transesterification</cite>.
- Elevated but manageable FFA (e.g., <5–20%): Acid‑first (homogeneous or solid acid) to reduce FFA and suppress soaps; then base catalyst for rapid transesterification. <cite id="6739fe8a-0">High FFA mandates esterification pretreatment to avoid soaps</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-2">Two‑step sequence controls soap formation</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-8">Solid acids offer high FFA tolerance and easier separation</cite>.
- High to very high FFA and/or significant moisture: Two‑step sequence with acid pretreatment under dehydration conditions, then base step; or use one‑pot solid acid–base/heteropolyacid catalysts that integrate esterification and transesterification and mitigate saponification via ion‑exchange. <cite id="d62d14bb-0">FFA > 0.5% benefits from acid‑catalyzed esterification to lower free acid content</cite> <cite id="d62d14bb-5">Esterification at ~20:1 MeOH:FFA ratio standardizes handling</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-1">Single‑step solid catalysts combine simultaneous esterification and transesterification for high‑FFA feeds</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-3">Ion‑exchange on solid resins can tune acid/base balance during catalysis</cite>.
- Complex feeds (phospholipids, free fatty acids, moisture): Prefer ion‑exchange or solid‑acid pretreatments to limit emulsification/soap formation, then base catalyst, or directly choose base‑tolerant biocatalysts with pretreatment. <cite id="6739fe8a-6">FFAs can be converted to soaps and removed (waste) or transformed to methyl esters (esterification) in pretreatment</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-4">High FFA increases soaps in saponification and drives immiscible phase issues</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-8">Solid acid pretreatment mitigates soap formation and wastewater concerns</cite>.

Enzymatic and biocatalyst considerations

- Lipases (esterases) can handle FFAs but benefit from prior esterification or acylating reagents, and are sensitive to water; sequencing often uses acid or ion‑exchange pretreatment followed by immobilized enzyme. <cite id="fdebd9ff-8">For high‑FFA oils, solid acid pretreatment avoids soap formation that inhibits enzymes</cite>.
- Enzymes face trade‑offs in selectivity and robustness versus catalyst cost and regeneration; acid/base resin catalysts and microwave assistance can shorten times at lower temperatures. <cite id="d62d14bb-4">Microwave heating reduced transesterification reaction time under catalytic conditions</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-9">Resin‑based systems balance activity with water‑induced deactivation and require optimized pretreatment</cite>.

Putting it together: a decision matrix

- If FFA is very low and moisture is controlled, choose a single base step (homogeneous or heterogeneous) for speed and simplicity. <cite id="c69ad07c-0">Esterification occurs under base, but pre‑treatment is skipped when FFA is negligible</cite>.
- If FFA is elevated (≥5%), use acid‑first: 
  - Liquid acid esterification followed by base transesterification, or 
  - Solid acid catalyst for esterification, optionally followed by base, or one‑pot solid acid–base/heteropolyacid to integrate steps and suppress saponification; maintain methanol:FFA ≈20:1 and dry the charge. <cite id="d62d14bb-0">Acid catalysis reduces FFA content efficiently in elevated‑FFA feeds</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-0">Acid pretreatment prevents soap formation that would otherwise hinder yields</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-8">Solid acid catalysts convert FFAs on high‑FFA oils without soap issues and simplify separation</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-1">One‑pot solid catalysts deliver simultaneous esterification and transesterification</cite> <cite id="d62d14bb-5">Use ~19.8:1 MeOH:FFA in pretreatment to ensure conversion</cite>.
- If FFAs are very high and/or water is present, plan acid‑first sequence with dehydration and, if a base second step is used, add strong de‑saponification (acid wash, phase separation, drying) or choose a base‑tolerant solid resin catalyst that limits soap formation. <cite id="6739fe8a-4">High FFA leads to soaps and phase separation that must be controlled</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-5">Water promotes soaps; low levels can already disrupt saponification control</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-8">Solid acid pretreatment reduces soap formation and wastewater burden</cite>.
- When sustainability and waste minimization are primary, select solid acid and solid base catalysts to enable in‑line esterification and transesterification with recoverable catalysts and lower effluent loads. <cite id="fdebd9ff-2">Solid acid catalysts can circumvent catalyst separation problems and reduce waste</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-7">Solid base catalysts provide reusability and simplified downstream processing</cite>.

Key takeaways for order of catalysts
- Acid first (to esterify FFAs and suppress soaps) when FFA exceeds low single‑digit percentages, especially in the presence of water or with very high FFA; base or base‑capturing solid catalysts follow to complete transesterification efficiently. <cite id="c69ad07c-0">Acid‑catalyzed esterification lowers FFA and prevents soap formation prior to base transesterification</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-2">Two‑step sequence controls saponification and soap formation</cite>.
- For neutral oil, or oil pretreated to low FFA and moisture, base catalyst alone suffices to initiate and complete transesterification rapidly. <cite id="6739fe8a-1">A base catalyst initiates transesterification with alcohol in a one‑step process</cite>.
- Use one‑pot solid acid–base or heteropolyacid catalysts when you want to avoid separation tanks and integrate chemistry; ion‑exchange on acidic sites and subsequent base sites ensure esterification precedes transesterification. <cite id="fdebd9ff-1">Solid heteropolyacid catalysts enable simultaneous esterification and transesterification on high‑FFA oils</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-3">Ion‑exchange behavior on resins modulates catalyst activity and can enforce sequence via site accessibility</cite>.

Operational knobs affecting catalyst order decisions
- Methanol ratio and residence time: increase ratio and time for acid‑first steps on high FFA; reduce after base step to limit methanolysis side products; manage temperature to balance side reactions. <cite id="d62d14bb-5">Industrial practice fixes methanol:FFA at ~19.8:1 for FFA esterification</cite>.
- Water removal: pre‑dry feedstock and keep water low to avoid base‑step saponification; acid‑first pretreatment provides a buffer. <cite id="6739fe8a-5">Trace water increases saponification rates and soap formation</cite>.
- Catalyst manageability: choose solid catalysts for ease of filtration and reuse, homogeneous acids for rapid conversion with washing steps; avoid base first on high FFA due to rapid soap formation. <cite id="fdebd9ff-2">Solid catalysts reduce separation and reuse challenges</cite> <cite id="6739fe8a-4">Base catalysts on high FFA readily produce soaps, complicating process flow</cite>.

Examples and numbers
- Two‑step acid (sulfuric acid) then base methoxide is common on waste oils; however, solid‑acid pretreatment can replace or precede liquid acid with lower waste. <cite id="d62d14bb-0">Elevated FFA requires acid esterification</cite> <cite id="d62d14bb-3">Sulfuric acid is effective for high‑FFA but slower</cite> <cite id="d62d14bb-9">Solid catalysts provide high FFA tolerance without wastewater</cite>.
- One‑pot conversion of palm fatty acid distillate (high FFA) achieved high conversion using a solid acid catalyst under methanolic conditions without extensive separation, illustrating the feasibility of integrated esterification–transesterification. <cite id="fdebd9ff-1">A single solid heteropolyacid catalyst enabled simultaneous esterification and transesterification for high‑FFA palm oil</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-3">Amberlyst‑15 ion‑exchange behaviors influence activity and stability</cite>.
- Industrial ratios: methanol:FFA around 19.8:1 used to ensure near‑complete esterification of FFAs in the acid step. <cite id="d62d14bb-5">19.8:1 MeOH:FFA is typical for esterification pretreatment</cite>.

In sum, the selection and order of catalysts in biodiesel transesterification are driven by feedstock chemistry (FFA, moisture, impurities), reaction mechanisms (esterification vs saponification), and practical constraints (wastewater, separations, deactivation). For oils with higher FFA, an acid‑first step is mandated by chemistry and process hygiene, followed by a base or base‑tolerant solid catalyst to maximize yield and spec compliance; neutral oils permit a single‑step base process; and modern solid acid–base catalysts can substitute a sequence with an integrated one‑pot route that enforces esterification before transesterification. <cite id="6739fe8a-0">High FFA content necessitates a pretreatment (esterification) to avoid soap formation and reaction hindrance</cite> <cite id="c69ad07c-0">Acid‑catalyzed esterification reduces FFA and prevents soaps prior to base transesterification</cite> <cite id="fdebd9ff-1">Solid acid–base one‑pot catalysts integrate esterification and transesterification for high‑FFA oils</cite> <cite id="d62d14bb-5">Operating at ~20:1 MeOH:FFA ratio standardizes acid‑first pretreatment and downstream conversion</cite>.

Mechanistic overview

- Copper centers catalyze hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) decomposition through redox cycling between Cu(II) and Cu(I), generating reactive oxygen species and ultimately converting H2O2 into water and oxygen.<cite id="171dcdfc-7">Increasing copper sulfate concentration significantly accelerates the exothermic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, demonstrating that copper promotes H2O2 disproportionation</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-7">H2O2 decomposition was enhanced by the addition of CuII–phenanthroline complexes, approaching Fenton-like hydroxyl radical generation</cite>. In biological and chemical contexts, copper-dependent oxidations proceed via Cu–OH adduct formation and H-atom abstraction to produce hydroxyl radicals or superoxide, leading to O2 evolution and oxidized products.<cite id="3a537e9e-0">Copper–ascorbate–H2O2 reactions proceed through Cu(III)/radical chain mechanisms in which copper ions act as chain carriers during ascorbate oxidation by H2O2</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-8">In the presence of oxygen, the oxidation of L‑ascorbic acid by copper generates hydroxyl radicals via copper redox catalysis</cite>.

Role of ascorbic acid (vitamin C)

- Direct reducing partner for Cu(II): Ascorbate (ascorbic acid) is an effective reductant that reduces Cu(II) to Cu(I), thereby “activating” copper for highly reactive one‑electron oxidation chemistry with H2O2 and facilitating catalytic turnover.<cite id="171dcdfc-4">As an organic reductant, ascorbic acid effectively reduces Cu(II) to Cu(I), improving the catalytic activity of copper toward oxidant generation</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-6">Hydroxyl radical production is mediated by copper redox cycling; H2O2 and superoxide participate in copper‑catalyzed oxidant production, reflecting interconversion among these species under Cu/ascorbate conditions</cite><cite id="293ab36d-3">During oxygen‑dependent oxidation of L‑ascorbic acid with copper, both H2O2 and hydroxyl radicals are generated, illustrating bimolecular product channels under Cu‑redox catalysis</cite>.

- Coordination ligand that tunes redox potential and speciation: Ascorbate coordinates copper and lowers the Cu(II)/Cu(I) redox potential, increasing H2O2 reactivity toward the metal and biasing channels toward hydroxyl radical formation or superoxide‑based disproportionation depending on pH/ligand environment.<cite id="3a537e9e-5">Cu(I) co‑present with H2O2 forms an oxidizing intermediate; copper–ascorbate interactions modulate oxidant output</cite><cite id="293ab36d-4">Ascorbate can react with superoxide, be regenerated via reductant pathways, and its coupling with copper alters redox channeling</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-9">In natural waters near physiological pH, the presence of reduced copper(I) plus H2O2 drives reactions that generate oxidizing intermediates, highlighting copper–ascorbate conditions that favor oxidant production</cite><cite id="293ab36d-0">Kinetic analysis shows that ligation of Cu(II) by different ligands (e.g., ascorbate) changes the redox potential and thus the reactivity toward H2O2, explaining differential catalytic behavior</cite>.

- Antioxidant that can quench or channel oxidants: Depending on conditions, ascorbate scavenges hydroxyl or superoxide radicals, thereby suppressing or redirecting copper‑generated oxidants produced from H2O2. This dual action explains both catalytic activation (by reducing Cu(II)) and inhibition (by radical scavenging and metal chelation) observed across systems.<cite id="293ab36d-1">Ascorbate’s antioxidant actions include non‑enzymatic reduction of superoxide and hydroxyl radicals, which can counteract oxidants generated by copper redox chemistry</cite><cite id="171dcdfc-1">Ambient measurements show ascorbate consumption correlates with total copper and iron, underscoring its role as a reductant/antioxidant in metal redox systems</cite><cite id="293ab36d-2">Kinetic modeling of vitamin C‑mediated copper redox reactions shows ascorbate both participates in one‑electron oxidations and is regenerated via partner reactions, illustrating redox cycling that modulates catalytic output</cite>.

Proposed stepwise mechanism in the presence of Cu2+ and ascorbate

1) Copper–ascorbate complexation and one‑electron reduction: In aqueous solution, ascorbate (AH2 or A−) binds Cu(II) to form labile Cu–ascorbate complexes; ascorbate donates an electron to reduce Cu(II) to Cu(I), becoming oxidized to dehydroascorbate (DHAA or 2,3‑DHAA−).<cite id="293ab36d-4">Ascorbate can react with superoxide and be regenerated via reductant pathways, indicating multiple one‑electron steps that interconvert ascorbate, superoxide, and oxidized copper</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-8">Oxygen‑dependent oxidation of L‑ascorbic acid by copper proceeds through redox catalysis that forms hydroxyl radicals</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-6">Hydrogen peroxide and superoxide participate in copper‑catalyzed oxidant production, consistent with coupled one‑electron transfers between copper and ascorbate in the presence of oxidants</cite>. The extent of complexing and the Cu redox potential are pH‑ and ligand‑dependent; stronger ligation shifts chemistry toward Cu(I) catalysis and hydroxyl radical formation.<cite id="3a537e9e-9">Reduced copper(I) plus H2O2 yields oxidizing intermediates and oxidant release in near‑physiological conditions</cite><cite id="293ab36d-0">Differences in Cu(II) reactivity toward H2O2 arise from changes in Cu redox potential upon ligation by different ligands</cite>.

2) Activation of H2O2 on Cu(I)/Cu(II) surfaces: Bound H2O2 abstracts a hydrogen atom at the copper hydroxide adduct (Cu–OH–H2O2 or Cu–OOH–H2O2), generating a hydroxyl radical (HO•) and Cu(II)–OH or Cu(I)–OO− intermediates. Alternatively, electron transfer from a Cu(I)–ascorbate complex to H2O2 yields O2•− and regenerates Cu(II), feeding superoxide dismutation rather than hydroxyl‑dominated pathways.<cite id="171dcdfc-4">Reduction of Cu(II) by ascorbate produces Cu(I), which increases catalytic activity toward hydrogen peroxide</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-6">Hydrogen peroxide and superoxide mediate copper‑catalyzed oxidant production, reflecting multiple activation channels (hydroxyl vs superoxide) under copper redox catalysis</cite><cite id="171dcdfc-0">Chain molecular mechanisms show Cu3+ (or Cu carriers) acting as chain carriers in ascorbate oxidation by H2O2, consistent with radical‑based activation steps</cite>.

3) Disproportionation/product channels: 
- HO• channel: HO• reacts with H2O2 and/or other substrates to form additional oxidants (HOO•, O2) or, with radical recombination, water and oxygen. In copper–ascorbate systems, hydroxyl radical formation can be accelerated and channeled by ligands such as phenanthroline, reaching Fenton‑like activity.<cite id="3a537e9e-7">CuII–phenanthroline markedly enhances H2O2 decomposition into hydroxyl radicals, approaching Fenton reagent levels</cite><cite id="171dcdfc-4">Formation of Cu(I) via ascorbate reduces Cu(II) enables more vigorous hydroxyl radical generation from H2O2</cite>.
- O2•− channel: Electron transfer to H2O2 yielding O2•− promotes superoxide dismutation (Cu(I)/Cu(II) switching) and peroxyl radical formation; ascorbate can reduce O2•− to H2O2 or HO•, thereby scavenging or rechanneling oxidants depending on pH and radical concentrations.<cite id="293ab36d-1">Ascorbate reduces superoxide non‑enzymatically, diverting superoxide‑based chemistry</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-6">Hydrogen peroxide mediates copper‑catalyzed oxidant production, indicating bidirectional coupling between O2•− and H2O2 under Cu/ascorbate conditions</cite>.

4) Regeneration and net turnover: Dehydroascorbate formed in step 1 can be reduced back to ascorbate by cellular reductants (e.g., glutathione), regenerating catalytic ascorbate pools that continue to shuttle electrons to copper and H2O2, thus sustaining decomposition and radical production until ascorbate is depleted or copper speciation changes.<cite id="293ab36d-2">Kinetic modeling shows ascorbate both participates in one‑electron oxidations with copper and is regenerated through partner reactions, sustaining redox cycling</cite><cite id="293ab36d-1">Ascorbate’s non‑enzymatic reduction of superoxide and hydroxyl radicals provides pathways for regeneration under biological conditions</cite>.

Environmental and biological context

- Sequestration and inhibition: Copper–ascorbate complexation can inhibit excessive oxidant generation by sequestering Cu(I) and lowering hydroxyl radical yields; however, under oxidizing conditions or with exogenous ligands (e.g., ligands like phenanthroline), catalytic activity toward H2O2 can rebound to Fenton‑like levels.<cite id="293ab36d-0">Different copper ligands shift Cu redox potentials and reactivity toward H2O2, explaining variable catalytic activity</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-7">CuII–phenanthroline complexes promote H2O2 decomposition into radicals similarly to Fenton’s reagent</cite><cite id="293ab36d-4">Vitamin C‑mediated copper reactions are balanced between oxidation and regeneration, with ligand identity controlling channeling</cite>.

- Cellular consequences: Copper‑ascorbate chemistry can damage biomacromolecules by generating localized HO• and O2•− near DNA or proteins, exemplified by DNA strand scission and oxidative base damage; the spatial coupling of Cu(I), ascorbate, and H2O2 explains how catalytic intermediates access sensitive targets.<cite id="3a537e9e-0">Copper‑mediated DNA damage arises from ascorbate/H2O2 oxidation pathways in which copper acts as a chain carrier, delivering reactive intermediates to DNA</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-8">Oxygen‑dependent oxidation of L‑ascorbic acid by copper releases both H2O2 and hydroxyl radicals, plausibly initiating lipid peroxidation and other oxidative damages</cite>.

Comparative notes with enzyme systems

- Copper sites in ascorbate oxidases and ascorbate peroxidases illustrate evolutionary solutions to the same chemistry: trinuclear copper centers reduce O2 with concomitant proton pumping and H2O2 formation, whereas simple Cu(II)/Cu(I) cycle in solution rapidly decompose H2O2 into radicals and oxygen; both strategies exploit copper redox catalysis coupled to ascorbate redox buffering for detoxification or signaling.<cite id="293ab36d-6">Ascorbate oxidase uses a trinuclear copper cluster (two T2 and one T3 Cu) to reduce O2 to H2O2, highlighting copper redox catalysis central to vitamin C antioxidant metabolism</cite><cite id="293ab36d-9">Ascorbate peroxidase uses L‑ascorbate to reduce peroxides, coupling antioxidant action with copper‑facilitated electron transfer</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-5">Copper–ascorbate chemistry in cell‑like conditions channels oxidants via H2O2 and superoxide mediation</cite>.

Key takeaways

- Copper accelerates H2O2 decomposition by cycling between Cu(II)/Cu(I) and generating hydroxyl or superoxide intermediates that disproportionate to H2O and O2, with rates controlled by copper speciation and ligands.<cite id="171dcdfc-7">Higher copper sulfate concentration accelerates H2O2 decomposition exothermically, establishing catalysis by copper</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-9">Reduced copper(I) plus H2O2 yields oxidizing intermediates and oxidant release in near‑physiological pH, reflecting catalytic disproportionation pathways</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-6">Hydrogen peroxide and superoxide mediate copper‑catalyzed oxidant production, indicating coupled channels under copper redox catalysis</cite>.
- Ascorbate both activates copper (reducing Cu(II) to Cu(I)) and modulates product channels by radical scavenging and complexation, so net oxidant output depends on pH, ligand identity, and concentrations of ascorbate and H2O2.<cite id="171dcdfc-4">Ascorbate effectively reduces Cu(II) to Cu(I), improving copper‑catalyzed oxidant activity</cite><cite id="293ab36d-1">Ascorbate reduces superoxide and hydroxyl radicals non‑enzymatically, providing antioxidant capacity</cite><cite id="293ab36d-0">Ligation changes Cu redox potential and H2O2 reactivity, explaining pH/ligand‑dependent catalysis</cite>.
- Under biological conditions, this chemistry underpins detoxification by ascorbate peroxidases yet can also generate localized oxidative damage when copper‑ascorbate‑H2O2 microenvironments form near biomolecules.<cite id="3a537e9e-0">Copper‑mediated DNA damage models show ascorbate/H2O2 oxidation via Cu‑driven radical chains acting at DNA</cite><cite id="293ab36d-9">Enzymatic ascorbate peroxidases couple L‑ascorbate to peroxide reduction, providing an evolutionary analog to copper‑ascorbate chemistry</cite>.

Practical implications and controls

- Increase in rate: Adding copper salts accelerates H2O2 breakdown; ligands that coordinate Cu and favor Cu(I) formation enhance hydroxyl radical generation; higher ascorbate pools sustain electron supply and turnover.<cite id="171dcdfc-7">Higher copper sulfate accelerates H2O2 decomposition</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-7">CuII–phenanthroline complexes reach Fenton‑like hydroxyl radical yields</cite><cite id="293ab36d-2">Ascorbate is oxidized and regenerated in copper redox systems, maintaining catalytic capacity</cite>.
- Decrease/inhibition: Chelators that sequester Cu(I), raising pH to favor ascorbate binding and reduced hydroxyl yields, or adding radical scavengers will suppress hydroxyl burst and bias toward superoxide dismutation and H2O2 recycling.<cite id="3a537e9e-6">Hydrogen peroxide mediates copper‑catalyzed oxidant production; changing ligand identity and redox potential biases channeling</cite><cite id="293ab36d-1">Ascorbate’s reduction of hydroxyl/superoxide provides a counter‑catalytic sink that lowers net oxidant output</cite>.

In summary, copper ions catalyze H2O2 decomposition through Cu(I)/Cu(II) redox catalysis that generates hydroxyl or superoxide radicals, with ascorbic acid acting as a reductant to create Cu(I) and as a ligand/antioxidant that both enhances catalytic turnover and can quench or channel oxidants—leading to rapid H2O2 disproportionation when copper and ascorbate are abundant and accessible, or to regulated antioxidant activity when complexation and scavenging dominate.<cite id="3a537e9e-6">Hydrogen peroxide and superoxide mediate copper‑catalyzed oxidant production, reflecting how ascorbate and copper interconvert oxidants</cite><cite id="293ab36d-4">Ascorbate participates in one‑electron oxidations with copper and is regenerated via partner reactions, balancing activation and scavenging</cite><cite id="3a537e9e-5">Different copper ligands modulate oxidant output under copper–ascorbate conditions</cite><cite id="171dcdfc-7">Copper concentration directly accelerates H2O2 decomposition</cite>.

Summary
Over time, the efficiency of photocatalytic NOx removal is strongly “conditioned” by humidity history because adsorbed water and hydroxyl groups reshape surface chemistry and charge-carrier dynamics, while multi-day humidity swings can create or remove surface hydroxyls, nitrate intermediates, and trapped carriers that modulate NO/NO2 activation and oxidation pathways across materials platforms such as TiO2, WO3/TiO2, and carbon-based composites. <cite id="5396b90a-0">H2O and O2 markedly influence surface hydroxyl formation and nitrate regeneration, thereby promoting NO removal</cite>. <cite id="ba9ab386-0">Reviews of NOx removal and recovery emphasize that water and oxygen/hydroxyls enable surface hydroxylation and nitrate formation that feeds back into NO oxidation cycles</cite>. 

How humidity history (prior days) shapes efficiency
• Surface hydroxylation and moisture activation:
