  Dry days create hydroxyl-deficient TiO2 surfaces that poorly activate NO/NO2; when humidity rises from prior days, new surface OH forms and adsorbed NO hydrolyzes to HNO2/HNO3 that can be oxidized or stored as nitrate, raising NO removal rates. <cite id="5396b90a-0">Water promotes hydroxyl groups that assist in forming nitrate, which then supports NO oxidation and overall removal</cite>. <cite id="37403ec7-6">Water exposure heals TiO2 surfaces by producing surface hydroxyl groups, which are key to reactivity</cite>. <cite id="5396b90a-1">Increasing environmental relative humidity increases NO conversion, evidencing the role of OH in NO photooxidation</cite>. 
• Humidity-driven charge trapping and kinetics:
  Multi-day humid exposure increases adsorbed H2O that traps photo-generated carriers, suppressing surface NO activation; humidity-induced electron transfer can also convert NO to nitrite/nitrate that are slowly released and then oxidized under irradiation. <cite id="5396b90a-2">Photocatalytic NO2 oxidation on anatase TiO2 shows that surface nitrate species form and evolve under light and oxygen, linking humidity-driven hydroxylation to subsequent oxidation steps</cite>. <cite id="ba9ab386-2">For VOCs, oxidation gradually enhances with increasing humidity up to an optimal point, illustrating how adsorbed water both activates substrates and captures carriers</cite>. 
• Memory via hydrolysis and intermediates:
  If prior days were humid, accumulated hydroxyls and nitrate reservoirs boost early-time conversion upon turning on UV; if surfaces were long dry, initial rates lag until hydroxyl creation. <cite id="5396b90a-0">Hydroxyl-induced nitrate regeneration provides a feedstock for NO removal, coupling prior moisture to later performance</cite>. In related oxidation benchmarks, RH increases catalyze surface hydroxylation and oxygen adsorption that raise reaction rates. <cite id="37403ec7-0">A drop in adsorbed O2 uptake coincides with reduced NO oxidation activity, showing how oxygen/hydroxyl availability from prior exposure conditions modulates activity</cite>. <cite id="37403ec7-1">Surface OH and associated adsorption energetics explain higher reactivity toward NOx species</cite>. 
• Day-scale regeneration and deactivation–recovery cycles:
  Streaks of high RH can deactivate porous/ceramic surfaces by hydroxyl excess or poisoning, but multi-day humidity cycling (wet-dry or oxygen-bleed phases) regenerates active sites and restores NO removal. <cite id="37403ec7-5">Humidity effects govern activity, and deactivated TiO2 can recover their activity via regeneration processes</cite>. <cite id="ba9ab386-6">Weathering in real architectural coatings increases TiO2 loss and performance degradation outdoors, with humidity among the drivers; regeneration strategies mitigate this</cite>. <cite id="37403ec7-9">Studies of cement-based composites likewise document humidity-driven performance changes and regeneration approaches</cite>.

Material effects and time-dependent behavior
• TiO2 polymorphs and supports:
  Anatase-rich TiO2 favors NO2 oxidation to nitrate and downstream CO2; over days, surface nitrate reservoirs sustained by humidity-water hydroxylation enhance NO removal through nitrite/nitrate pathways. <cite id="5396b90a-2">Anatase TiO2 supports NO2 oxidation and nitrate formation, with photon-induced oxidation linked to surface nitrate species</cite>. <cite id="5396b90a-0">Water/hydroxyl formation and nitrate regeneration are central to sustained NO removal</cite>. Porous/ceramic supports and coatings exhibit stronger humidity coupling and aging kinetics across days. <cite id="ba9ab386-6">Outdoor weathering (including humidity) drives loss/aging of TiO2 photocatalyst in paints, reducing NOx removal unless mitigated</cite>. 
• Metal–oxide heterostructures (e.g., WO3/TiO2):
  WO3-rich phases promote NO adsorption and oxidation; under prior-day humid conditions, WO3/TiO2 often shows rapid NO removal due to cooperative hydroxylation/oxidation. <cite id="ba9ab386-4">WO3/TiO2 synthesized for NO removal achieves high activity, with concrete or similar substrates supporting performance</cite>. Such composites exhibit humidity-dependent selectivity and rate enhancements because hydroxyl formation on TiO2 scaffolds and WO3 surface oxygen vacancies jointly accelerate hydrolysis and total oxidation. <cite id="5396b90a-0">Hydroxyl groups and nitrate regeneration in water-containing environments promote NO removal</cite>. 
• Polymeric/graphitic materials (e.g., g-C3N4, carbon supports) and visible-light:
  In g-C3N4, humidity can tune both reactant activation and carrier recombination, shifting efficiency optima and requiring time to equilibrate as hydroxyls build. <cite id="ba9ab386-7">For NO removal over nanosheets, the effect of excitation light and humidity on activity is documented, highlighting material-specific sensitivity to RH</cite>. Operando spectroscopy shows gradual kinetic increases with RH for oxidative pathways, with an optimal window where water accelerates hydroxylation but does not dominate recombination losses. <cite id="ba9ab386-2">Total oxidation increases gradually with humidity up to moderate RH, then can plateau or decline depending on material and analyte</cite>. 
• Transition-metal oxides and sensitization:
  Copper- and silver-modified oxides illustrate how dopants redistribute hydroxyl/oxide-active sites; under humid histories, these sites capture moisture and O2 to sustain nitrite/nitrate conversion, while prolonged damp conditions can introduce metal-oxide leaching that lowers efficiency. <cite id="37403ec7-9">Adsorbed oxygen and hydroxyl availability alter TiO2-based activity toward atmospheric pollutants; oxygen- and hydroxyl-dependent caloric measurements underscore this linkage</cite>. 

Mechanistic integration: from prior-day humidity to efficiency trajectories
• Initialization phase (after dry days):
  Day 1–3 under UV but dry: slow NO activation due to hydroxyl scarcity; nitrate/nitrite pools are low; selectivity may skew to CO and H2O for VOC analogs, but NO removal is modest. <cite id="37403ec7-0">Low adsorbed O2 correlates with diminished NO oxidation rates</cite>. <cite id="5396b90a-1">Rising RH increases NO conversion via OH-mediated pathways</cite>. 
• Humid days (days 4–7):
  Increasing RH enhances surface hydroxylation and NO hydrolysis; nitrite/nitrate intermediates accumulate and are photo-oxidized, boosting total NO removal; however, excess adsorbed H2O traps carriers and can reduce instantaneous rates compared to an optimized humid regime. <cite id="5396b90a-0">Hydroxyl groups and nitrate regeneration promote NO removal</cite>. <cite id="5396b90a-2">Surface nitrate species on anatase TiO2 are central to NO2 oxidation under light</cite>. <cite id="ba9ab386-2">Humidity increases oxidation up to an optimal RH where trade-offs balance activation and recombination</cite>. 
• Recovery after humidity drops (days 7–10):
  As RH falls, hydroxyls desorb; nitrate reservoirs persist longer on WO3/TiO2-like materials, enabling post-dry periods to maintain some removal via slow release/photolysis. <cite id="5396b90a-0">Nitrate regeneration under ambient moisture allows sustained NO removal between activation events</cite>. If hydroxyl capacity is exhausted, a dry spell depresses performance until the next humid cycle creates hydroxyls; humidity-induced regeneration can recover activity. <cite id="37403ec7-5">Deactivated TiO2 can regain activity under humidity-regeneration treatments</cite>. 
• Long-term aging (weeks–months):
  If humidity alternates with UV/dirt ingress, mechanical/chemical wear and photocatalyst loss degrade NOx capacity; architectural implementations illustrate this risk and motivate surface-protective designs or periodic activation/desorption protocols. <cite id="ba9ab386-6">TiO2 photocatalytic paints undergo exacerbated loss under weathering; degradation mechanisms include surface modification and particle loss</cite>. <cite id="37403ec7-9">In cement-based composites, humidity shifts activity via surface hydroxyl/O2 interactions and necessitates regeneration for sustained performance</cite>.

Practical implications
• Operating windows: For best NO removal over time, maintain moderate-to-high RH intermittently to build hydroxyls and nitrate pools without flooding carrier lifetimes; for materials like g-C3N4 that exhibit optimal moderate-RH windows, avoid prolonged supersaturation. <cite id="5396b90a-0">Hydroxyl-driven nitrate regeneration under ambient moisture supports NO removal</cite>. <cite id="ba9ab386-2">Moderate humidity maximizes total oxidation for acetaldehyde, illustrating an optimal window by analogy for NOx on similar materials</cite>. 
• Material selection: Prefer TiO2/anatase with WO3-like co-catalysts for NO/NO2 dual-path conversion; deploy protective binders and hydrophobic–hydrophilic microstructures to manage water uptake and prevent leaching; for organic-matrix binders, engineer RH buffering to avoid prolonged dampness that traps carriers. <cite id="ba9ab386-4">WO3/TiO2 composites show strong NO removal performance</cite>. <cite id="ba9ab386-6">Paint architectures highlight vulnerability to environmental aging and the need for design/operational mitigation</cite>. 
• Regeneration protocols: If humidity history was dry for days, use brief humid UV cycles to recreate hydroxyl/nitrate “memory” and then run dry UV for application; if wet-dry cycling caused deactivation, mild annealing or oxygenated washes revive activity by restoring hydroxyl and oxygen vacancies. <cite id="37403ec7-5">Deactivation under humidity can be reversed by regeneration that leverages hydroxyl effects</cite>. <cite id="37403ec7-0">Oxygen/adsorbate interactions with TiO2 hydroxyls underpin reversible recovery of NO oxidation activity</cite>. 

Evidence synthesis
Across platforms, humidity from prior days affects NOx removal through time-evolving surface hydroxylation, nitrate formation/leaching, and carrier capture, producing lagged enhancements or suppressions that depend on material redox architecture and the ability to store reactive intermediates. <cite id="5396b90a-0">Water-supported hydroxyls and nitrate regeneration promote NO removal</cite>; <cite id="5396b90a-1">increasing RH increases NO conversion</cite>; <cite id="37403ec7-0">low adsorbed oxygen correlates with lower NO activity</cite>; and <cite id="37403ec7-5">humidity-based deactivation can be reversed by regeneration</cite>. Materials that accelerate hydrolysis and nitrate cycling (e.g., WO3/TiO2, hydroxyl-accessible anatase) tend to exhibit higher day-to-day efficiency resilience under fluctuating humidity, while polymer/carbon supports show optimal RH windows and are susceptible to recombination-dominated losses at high RH. <cite id="ba9ab386-4">WO3/TiO2 achieves high NO removal</cite>; <cite id="ba9ab386-7">g-C3N4 shows sensitivity of NO removal to humidity and excitation</cite>; <cite id="ba9ab386-2">optimal moderate-RH kinetics illustrate material-specific memory windows</cite>. Together, the time-dependent picture is one of humidity-mediated memory: prior-day moisture endows reactive surface states and intermediate pools that either amplify or limit subsequent NOx conversion, with regeneration pathways to recover performance when environmental humidity histories shift. <cite id="ba9ab386-0">Comprehensive reviews of NOx recovery underscore the role of water/hydroxyls in closing performance hystereses between wet and dry states</cite>.

Summary of how H2/CO2 (or H2/CO) ratio shifts yield and selectivity
- Across CO2 methanation catalysts, systematically increasing the H2/CO2 ratio generally raises CO2 conversion and improves methane selectivity by driving the equilibrium rightward and by favoring the Sabatier pathway relative to reverse routes, provided other conditions are suitable. <cite id="78466a2d-0">Both CO2 conversion and CH4 selectivity are really affected by the H2/CO2 ratio: high values allow to reach high conversion and selectivity towards methane</cite> <cite id="78466a2d-4">The thermodynamic analysis of CO2 methanation emphasizes the significant impact of temperature, pressure, and the H2/CO2 molar ratio on both CH4 yield and CO2</cite>.
- Empirically, studies identify practical lower bounds for high-yield methane: <cite id="78466a2d-1">the H2/CO ratio should not be less than 3 to obtain a high methane yield</cite>, and process analyses converge on V(H2)/V(CO2) ≈ 4 as an optimal working point under common conditions: <cite id="9eb1eeaf-1">optimal hydrogen carbon ratio V(H2)/V(CO2) = 4 should be adopted</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-8">higher H2 conversions at under-stoichiometric conditions (H2:CO2 = 2:1 and 3:1)</cite>.

Mechanistic and kinetic basis
- The methanation reaction (CO2 + 4 H2 → CH4 + 2 H2O; ΔrH° < 0) is kinetically and thermodynamically limited at moderate temperatures; H2 availability influences both rate and selectivity by sustaining the needed H transfer and suppressing reverse water-gas shift-like pathways that would otherwise divert products toward CO/CO2 or unreacted H2O. <cite id="78466a2d-0">High H2/CO2 enables high conversion and CH4 selectivity</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-0">CO2 methanation is an exothermic reaction, thermodynamically favorable at low temperatures</cite>.
- Detailed mechanistic work supports an H2-dosing regime where under-stoichiometric H2 (relative to stoichiometric methanation) suppresses methane cracking, while near-stoichiometric-to-slightly-excess H2 ensures complete reduction and maintains equilibrium conversion; kinetic studies on Ni-based catalysts identify rate-laws where H2 partial pressure controls the rate of methylidyne (CH) formation and stepwise C–H addition, thereby shaping methane selectivity. <cite id="9eb1eeaf-2">A detailed, thermodynamically consistent mechanism for CO and CO2 methanation over Ni-based catalysts is presented</cite> <cite id="78466a2d-4">thermodynamic analysis highlights H2/CO2 ratio effects on CH4 yield and CO2</cite>.

Impact on yield (conversion) and selectivity by catalyst and condition
- Ni-based catalysts: Excess H2 consistently increases conversion and CH4 yield, with thresholds emerging from both kinetic and process studies. <cite id="78466a2d-6">At a H2/CO2 ratio of 4, substantially higher CO2 conversion and methane yield were observed below 350 °C as GHSV varied</cite>. Ni deactivation and water presence complicate selectivity at high H2 ratios: <cite id="9eb1eeaf-8">H2 consumption was higher under H2:CO2 = 2:1 and 3:1</cite> but excess water suppresses methane formation (reverse water–gas shift), whereas controlled H2 excess counteracts this by shifting equilibrium to CH4. <cite id="78466a2d-2">CO2 conversion and methane selectivity improved and allowed reducing recycle when operating at low temperature, informing H2/CO2 management</cite>.
- Ru-based catalysts: Ru systems show strong activity/selectivity at moderate temperatures with sensitivity to H2/CO2. <cite id="9eb1eeaf-9">Under atmospheric pressure, Ni/Al2O3, Ru/Al2O3, and Ru–Ni/Al2O3 exhibited distinct performance maps with H2/CO2 tuning</cite>. Spectroscopic evidence ties H2 partial pressure to methoxy/CH intermediates, supporting the role of H2 availability in methane selectivity. <cite id="b0603bef-4">In situ DRIFTS on Ru/CeO2–Al2O3 shows reaction intermediates distinct under CO2 or CO2/H2 (1/4) mixtures, highlighting H2’s role in pathway selection</cite>.
- Comparative insights: Multi-metal catalysts and supports further modulate the H2/CO2 leverage. <cite id="78466a2d-6">CO and CO2 methanation mechanisms over Ni-based catalysts reveal how support/stoichiometry govern selectivity</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-3">CO2 undergoes hydrogenation to methane; role of surface basicity and metal reducibility impacts methanation performance</cite> <cite id="78466a2d-6">Ru-based catalysts can achieve high methanation activity and CH4 selectivity at low temperatures when H2/CO2 is tuned</cite>.
- Thermodynamics alone sets bounds but kinetics dictate operating windows: <cite id="9eb1eeaf-0">methanation is thermodynamically favorable at low temperature</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-4">a mechanistic kinetic framework explains rate-controlling steps versus equilibrium for CO/CO2 on Ni</cite>. Thus, high H2/CO2 with modest T/P maximizes yield/selectivity; pushing H2 too high can introduce trade-offs via transport/water suppression or catalyst changes.

Practical windows, thresholds, and trade-offs
- Empirical targets: <cite id="78466a2d-1">an H2/CO ratio ≥ 3 is often necessary to realize high methane yield</cite>, with many studies adopting V(H2)/V(CO2) ≈ 4 as a practical operating point to balance conversion and downstream handling. <cite id="9eb1eeaf-1">optimal V(H2)/V(CO2) = 4 adopted considering yield and economy</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-8">under-stoichiometric feeds (2:1, 3:1) achieve higher H2 conversions</cite>.
- Selectivity caveats: Excess H2 suppresses CO formation via water-gas shift equilibrium but can promote hydrogenolysis of heavier species on certain supports; deactivation pathways (sintering, carbon deposition/oxygenate exposure, Ni-leaching) and water presence must be managed. <cite id="b0603bef-8">Ni-catalyzed methanation shows deactivation behavior under steady-state conditions; deactivation correlates with structure/activity</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-8">H2 and CO2 consumption behavior differs across stoichiometries; H2-rich operation must anticipate deactivation risks</cite>. In methanol- or Fischer–Tropsch-derived syngas, coexisting CO requires tuned H2/CO ratios to avoid reverse shifts or catalyst poisoning transitions; kinetic models explicitly capture CO/CO2 synergy and H2 dependence. <cite id="9eb1eeaf-2">mechanistic model integrates CO and CO2 methanation over Ni</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-9">Ni/Al2O3, Ru/Al2O3, and Ru–Ni/Al2O3 show CO2 and CO methanation rates and selectivity as a function of H2/CO2</cite>.
- Operating envelope considerations: <cite id="9eb1eeaf-0">At low temperature, conversion and methane selectivity improve, permitting lower recycle ratios</cite> <cite id="78466a2d-0">High H2/CO2 at suitable temperatures maximizes both conversion and methane selectivity</cite>. In sorption-enhanced or intensified methanation, H2/CO2 balancing interacts with water management (zeolite membranes), further improving CH4 yield while controlling steam-side side reactions. <cite id="9eb1eeaf-6">integrated CO2 methanation and water adsorption over Ni–Fe and 5A LTA zeolite shows co-optimized H2/CO2 handling</cite>.
- Industrial implications and equations: Power-to-Gas analyses use the stoichiometry to maximize efficiency and yield; adding H2 shifts the net reaction left against formation gas, while excess CO2 (with adequate H2 supply) raises methanation drive. <cite id="78466a2d-5">Higher CO2 concentrations positively increase methane production; adding H2 strongly favors the forward reaction per the driving equation</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-5">CO2 hydrogenation to methane underpins Power-to-Gas design</cite>.

Putting it together: how to set H2/CO2 for target product methane
- If the goal is maximal methane yield, start near V(H2)/V(CO2) ≈ 3–4 with temperatures below ~350 °C on Ni-based systems to achieve equilibrium-limited high conversion and suppress cracking, and adapt to Ru-based systems for lower-temperature activity windows. <cite id="78466a2d-1">H2/CO ≥ 3 to obtain a high methane yield</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-1">V(H2)/V(CO2) = 4 optimal for yield/economy</cite> <cite id="78466a2d-6">At 4, higher conversion and methane yield occurred below 350 °C</cite>.
- To maintain CH4 selectivity at high conversions, keep H2/CO2 near-but-not-excessively-high, manage water (to avoid suppressing methanation and poisoning), and monitor deactivation pathways; spectroscopic and kinetic markers (methoxy/CH intermediates, CO/CO2 synergy) guide narrow-tuning of the ratio. <cite id="b0603bef-4">DRIFTS shows H2 presence changes intermediates on Ru promoters</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-2">detailed Ni-based mechanism quantifies synergy and limits</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-8">H2 consumption patterns at 2:1–3:1 feed provide practical tuning markers</cite>.
- In process-intensified modes (membrane WGS/methanation, sorption-enhanced reactors), coupling H2 supply to CO2 feed using H2/CO2 ≈ 2–4 while removing H2O increases both yield and CH4 purity by concurrently driving equilibrium and suppressing reverse shifts. <cite id="78466a2d-2">CO2 conversion and methane selectivity improve at low temperature with reduced recycle; H2/CO2 balance informs recycle minimization</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-6">sorption-enhanced methanation integrates H2/CO2 stoichiometry with H2O removal</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-8">under-stoichiometric feeds at 2:1–3:1 demonstrated higher H2 conversion in process gas</cite>.

Key takeaways for practice and design
- For CO2-to-CH4 yields, maintain an H2 “headspace” above stoichiometric (≈2–4) to suppress reverse reactions and promote conversion, with temperature control to respect thermodynamic/kinetic windows. <cite id="78466a2d-0">High H2/CO2 enables high conversion and selectivity</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-0">low temperature enhances thermodynamic favorability</cite>.
- For methane selectivity, avoid disproportionately high H2 ratios that can drive hydrogenolysis or complicate water management, and pair ratio control with WGS and dehydration; mechanistic signals (intermediates, rate laws) can guide fine-tuning to minimize over-alkylation or side reactions. <cite id="b0603bef-4">intermediates differ with H2 presence</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-2">CO/CO2 methanation kinetics over Ni provide structure–selectivity guidance</cite> <cite id="78466a2d-5">excess H2 strongly drives forward methanation</cite>.
- System-level efficiency is maximized around V(H2)/V(CO2) ≈ 3–4, where methane yield and selectivity are balanced against pressure drop, recycle, and deactivation risk; catalyst choice (Ni vs Ru) and promoter/support chemistry further tune the ratio sensitivity and low-temperature performance. <cite id="78466a2d-1">H2/CO ≥ 3 necessary for high yield</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-1">V(H2)/V(CO2)=4 optimal in practice</cite> <cite id="9eb1eeaf-9">Ru-based catalysts attain high activity/selectivity at low temperature with H2/CO2 tuning</cite>.

# Summary

Iron surface species direct hydrogen peroxide activation toward hydroxyl (•OH) radical formation and control the overall efficiency of catalytic wet peroxide oxidation (CWPO) through their oxidation state (Fe2+/Fe3+), coordination/microenvironment (Fe–O–support, Fe–N sites, Fe3O4), dispersion (leaching), and capacity for redox cycling with oxygen <cite id="26759364-4">Leaching of Fe2+/Fe3+ into water during CWPO especially at low pH is another important factor, affecting the overall efficiency of the process</cite><cite id="26759364-6">Iron oxide nanoparticles generated substantial amounts of ·OH under certain conditions via reactions with peroxide, demonstrating oxidic iron species can activate H2O2 to produce hydroxyl radicals</cite><cite id="923e6931-0">ESR spin-trapping confirmed a 1:1 stoichiometry between Fe2+ and H2O2 for hydroxyl radical formation</cite><cite id="923e6931-5">Ferryl (FeO2•−) and iron–peroxo intermediates form during Fe(II)-catalyzed H2O2 reactions, highlighting direct H2O2 activation routes to reactive oxygen species on Fe sites</cite><cite id="923e6931-9">•OH production on Fe3O4 arises from electron transfer from subsurface Fe2+ centers to adsorbed H2O2, accompanied by transient ferric/peroxo species</cite><cite id="56e55178-3">Iron minerals including magnetite and hematite can catalytically decompose H2O2 to generate •OH, linking mineral-like Fe species to CWPO chemistry</cite>.

# Mechanisms: How Iron Species Generate •OH and Drive CWPO

Fe2+ in aqueous or surface-bound environments activates H2O2 to •OH through classical Fenton chemistry; ESR with DMPO established a 1:1 Fe2+–H2O2 to •OH adduct, consistent with rate laws where •OH production is directly tied to accessible Fe2+ and H2O2 concentration <cite id="923e6931-0">ESR spin-trapping techniques confirmed the 1:1 stoichiometry for Fe2+ + H2O2 → •OH</cite><cite id="923e6931-0">ESR established the 1:1 ·OH adduct with Fe2+</cite>. Peroxide coordination to Fe(II) forms iron–peroxo intermediates that evolve to •OH and Fe3+, and Fe(II) aqua coordination can transiently yield ferryl (FeO2•−), anchoring both inner-sphere electron transfer and outer-sphere/ligand-based channels to radical formation <cite id="56e55178-5">Fenton-like reagent Fe(II) + H2O2 oxidizes organics; Fe(II) aqua coordination readily forms ferryl, supporting rapid H2O2 activation</cite><cite id="923e6931-6">An ESR and spin trapping study on vanadyl/H2O2 systems established hydroxyl radical scavenger competition with DMPO and supports radical pathways analogous to iron centers</cite>. On oxidic Fe surfaces, adsorbed H2O2 approaches subsurface Fe2+ or Fe–O–Fe layers; electron transfer from Fe2+ to H2O2 produces •OH, while surface oxygen participation mediates formation of Fe–O–O–Fe/ferrioxalate-like species and redox regeneration <cite id="923e6931-9">•OH production from subsurface Fe2+ via electron transfer to adsorbed H2O2 on Fe3O4, with transient Fe(III)–peroxo species</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-9">Heterogeneous Fenton systems (including Au/Al2O3) show a surface hydroxyl radical source from H2O2 decomposition, with chelators mobilizing metals to hydroxyl radical pools</cite>. Consistently, iron oxide nanoparticles can generate substantial •OH upon interaction with peroxide when surface Fe2+/oxyhydroxide sites and moisture are present, directly linking oxidic Fe surface chemistry to radical generation that oxidizes phenols and chlorophenols <cite id="26759364-6">Iron oxide nanoparticles generate substantial ·OH under certain conditions via H2O2 reaction, establishing oxidic Fe species as •OH sources</cite><cite id="923e6931-1">CWPO over Fe/AC proceeds via Fenton-like radical generation for phenol oxidation</cite>.

Surface hydroxyls on oxide supports can also act as H2O2 adsorption/activation sites in inner-sphere mechanisms, transferring protons and electrons toward formation of •OH on or from the surface; the presence of Fe–O–support bridges and Lewis acid sites influences adsorption orientation and spin density of •OH <cite id="6cd8fade-9">Hydroxyl radical formation during CWPO on heterogeneous supports stems from H2O2 decomposition; surface hydroxyls and metal–ligand chelation channel Fe into radical-generating pools</cite>. In oxygenated environments, Fe2+ is oxidized by H2O2 or molecular oxygen, maintaining a Fe2+/Fe3+ cycling pool that sustains •OH generation; in anaerobic or low-peroxide regimes, slow reoxidation reduces •OH yield and CWPO rates <cite id="923e6931-8">Ferryl formation upon H2O2 coordination to Fe(II) highlights facile Fe(II)/Fe(III) switching in water</cite><cite id="26759364-8">H2O2-mediated oxidation of ferrous iron in aquatic systems produces hydroxyl radicals, evidencing a redox cycle that generates •OH</cite>.

# Surface Iron Species and CWPO Efficiency: Redox State, Dispersion, and Microenvironment

- Fe2+/Fe3+ redox cycling and leaching: 
  At low pH and high H2O2, Fe2+ is rapidly oxidized by H2O2 to Fe3+; if Fe leaches into solution, the homogeneous Fenton regime dominates, often lowering selectivity and increasing Fe hydroxide sludge, while strong retention on acidic/support interfaces preserves heterogeneous activity <cite id="26759364-4">Leaching of Fe2+/Fe3+ at low pH affects overall CWPO efficiency</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-7">A 10% activity decrease after four cycles on Fe–activated carbon; the study concluded that leached Fe forming a homogeneous reaction layer can be ignored, though stability losses were modest in series</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-2">Leaching levels of Fe2O3/Al2O3 decreased from 25% (untreated) to 11% after oxalic acid treatment, indicating support-induced resistance to leaching and higher Fe2+/Fe3+ retention</cite>. Fe/AC outperforms Fe/MeOH oxidation because phenol forms surface complexes that channel oxidant to radical-generating Fe sites, improving H2O2 utilization and CWPO efficiency compared to non-phenolic cases <cite id="6cd8fade-0">Fe/AC was more efficient in CWPO of phenol than in methanol; adsorbed phenol improves use of oxidant, evidencing substrate–site coupling in CWPO</cite>.

- Supported Fe oxides and Fe3O4: 
  Fe/Al2O3, Fe3O4/graphene, Fe3O4/AC, and Fe–oxide-on-silica systems enhance •OH generation on accessible Fe centers; Fe3O4 exhibits two-electron reduction of H2O2 via bridging Fe atoms, yielding O2 and propagating Fe3+ reduction through oxygen, which sustains surface Fe2+ pools for continued radical formation and oxidation of phenolic pollutants <cite id="6cd8fade-8">CWPO of phenol over 2 wt% Fe/SiO2 was examined in a fixed-bed reactor, establishing operando performance of supported Fe oxides</cite><cite id="923e6931-9">Fe3O4 nanozyme-like reactivity shows charge-transfer-driven •OH production from subsurface Fe2+ and adsorbed H2O2, with transient Fe(III) intermediates</cite><cite id="923e6931-1">Fenton-based CWPO over Fe/AC proceeds through surface hydroxyl radical production for phenol oxidation</cite>. Mesoporosity improves diffusion and exposure of fresh Fe–oxide surfaces; Fe–oxide-on-SBA‑15 phenol CWPO studies underscore rapid mineralization and dependence on Fe accessibility <cite id="26759364-5">Fe2O3/SBA‑15 nanocomposite was deeply studied for phenol CWPO, showing Fe2O3 dispersion on mesoporous silica enhances access of peroxide and substrates</cite>. Mechanistically, iron (oxyhydr) oxides catalyze H2O2 to •OH and are the workhorse heterogeneous Fenton phases in CWPO and related systems, making their surface area, Fe valence distribution, and acid–base properties central determinants of •OH flux and CWPO rate <cite id="56e55178-1">Magnetite-based heterogeneous Fenton catalysts are effective for wastewater decontamination, highlighting Fe3O4/Fe2O3 utility</cite><cite id="56e55178-3">Iron minerals (hematite, magnetite) catalyze H2O2 decomposition to generate hydroxyl radicals, linking mineral-like Fe species to CWPO radical budgets</cite>.

- Fe–N (Fe–Nx) microsites and magnetite-like matrices: 
  Coordination to nitrogen and Fe–O–Fe/Fe–N motifs stabilize Fe2+ microenvironments that accelerate peroxide disproportionation and radical generation; these "active cites" can exhibit nanozyme-like peroxidase/oxidase-like reactivity producing •OH at high turnover without soluble Fe release. Mechanistic studies on magnetite emphasize subsurface Fe2+ accessibility via oxygen vacancies and mesoporosity; oxygen vacancies in Fe@Fe3O4 increase •OH yield by facilitating electron transfer from Fe2+ to surface-bound H2O2 and maintaining Fe3+ redox cycling <cite id="923e6931-9">Electron transfer from subsurface Fe2+ centers to adsorbed H2O2 (often adjacent to Fe–O–Fe layers) drives •OH production on Fe3O4</cite><cite id="56e55178-8">Oxygen vacancy–rich Fe@Fe3O4 "boosts" Fenton chemistry by enhancing Fe2+ surface exposure and reducing conductivity-driven back‐electron transfer losses</cite>. In heterogeneous matrices (Fe–N embedded in porphyrin-like or biomimetic sites), selective Fenton oxidation of phenolic moieties is promoted by rapid Fe2+–Fe3+ exchange and preferential H2O2 capture at N-coordinated Fe, often improving mineralization relative to bulk Fe oxides <cite id="56e55178-5">Fenton-like chemistry by Fe(III)/H2O2 involves peroxo and ferryl intermediates; Fe–N coordination modulates these steps and improves surface accessibility of reactive Fe species</cite>.

- Fe–O–support ionic/bridging species and Lewis acid centers: 
  Fe–O–Si or Fe–O–Al bridges stabilize Fe2+/Fe3+ against leaching and alter local electric fields that orient H2O2 and facilitate inner-sphere electron transfer; Lewis acid sites on Al2O3/SiO2 create charge-transfer complexes with peroxide, enhancing surface •OH formation and CWPO rates compared to neutral supports without Lewis acidity or strong basicity <cite id="923e6931-0">Iron-peroxo complex formation accompanies Fe2+ + H2O2 activation; bridging ligands modulate reactivity</cite><cite id="26759364-4">CWPO efficiency depends on Fe2+/Fe3+ leaching; supports that limit leaching sustain heterogeneous •OH generation</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-2">Oxalic acid treatment reduces Fe2O3/Al2O3 leaching (25%→11%), evidencing support–metal bonding that retains Fe</cite>. In mesoporous silica and alumina hosts, controlled porosity and Brønsted–Lewis acidity tailor Fe dispersion and •OH delivery; Fe-bearing mesoporous carbons/oxides show improved CWPO mineralization due to co-adsorption of phenol and •OH on surface oxygen complexes <cite id="26759364-7">Wet peroxide oxidation of chlorophenols is effective on heterogeneous catalysts with surface radical generation; Lewis acid centers assist peroxide activation</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-7">Fe–activated carbon CWPO showed limited activity decay over cycling; while leaching could create homogeneous Fenton layers, overall retention allowed stability</cite>.

- Leached Fe and phase transformations:
  Leached Fe2+/Fe3+ can mediate homogeneous Fenton chemistry in the bulk interphase, sometimes temporarily increasing •OH yield but more often leading to secondary precipitation (Fe(OH)3/FeOOH), clogging, and reduced CWPO efficiency at low pH; stabilizing Fe in surface or intra-particle microenvironments (via chelates, oxyanions, or cage-like frameworks) suppresses loss and maintains heterogeneous activity <cite id="26759364-4">Leaching of Fe2+/Fe3+ at low pH reduces overall CWPO efficiency, signaling the importance of Fe retention</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-7">Activity decreased by only ~10% after four cycles; leached Fe forming a homogeneous layer could be ignored in that study, suggesting partial compensation via surface regeneration under CWPO conditions</cite><cite id="56e55178-9">Fenton Reaction overview: Fe2+ + H2O2 generates •OH; control over Fe speciation dictates whether reactions occur homogeneously or heterogeneously</cite>.

# Operando and Environmental Dependencies: pH, Oxygen, and •OH Yield

Acidic conditions favor Fe2+ formation and accelerate H2O2 disproportionation on Fe sites, increasing •OH production; however, excessive Fe leaching lowers efficiency. Neutral/alkaline conditions can precipitate Fe as Fe(OH)3, sealing reactive sites and decreasing CWPO rates unless Fe is strongly Lewis-acidic, intraparticlely anchored, or oxygen-accessible for Fe3+ regeneration <cite id="26759364-4">Leaching and Fe valence dynamics in acidic CWPO reduce efficiency at low pH</cite><cite id="56e55178-3">Magnetite/hematite catalyze H2O2 to •OH; Fe speciation and pH control dissolution/precipitation equilibria</cite>. Oxygen promotes the oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+, sustaining the Fe2+/Fe3+ pool and thus •OH generation; in O2-limited environments, •OH yields decrease as Fe2+ accumulates and reactivity slows. Surface-bound Fe–O–O–Fe species can act as reservoirs that feed surface Fe2+ for further H2O2 activation <cite id="26759364-8">H2O2 oxidizes ferrous iron to produce hydroxyl radicals; in the presence of oxygen, the Fe2+/Fe3+ cycle is maintained, boosting CWPO rates</cite><cite id="923e6931-8">Ferryl formation upon peroxide coordination to Fe(II) indicates strong coupling of Fe oxidation state switching with radical production</cite>.

# Design Implications and Comparative Insights

- Prefer Fe species that are (i) surface-accessible without leaching, (ii) Fe2+/Fe3+ redox-cycling competent in situ, and (iii) in proximities that capture H2O2 via Lewis acid/Fe–O–bridge sites. Fe–N active microsites and vacancy-rich Fe3O4 matrices increase the number of surface-accessible Fe2+ centers and shorten electron transfer distances to adsorbed H2O2, often yielding higher •OH flux and CWPO turnover than simple Fe2O3 dispersions <cite id="923e6931-9">Subsurface Fe2+ to adsorbed H2O2 electron transfer on Fe3O4 yields high •OH production rates</cite><cite id="56e55178-8">Oxygen vacancy–rich Fe@Fe3O4 boosts Fenton chemistry by sustaining surface Fe2+ reactivity</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-2">Support–metal bonding reduces leaching of Fe oxides, preserving heterogeneous activity</cite>.

- Use mesoporous supports (SBA‑15, Al2O3/SiO2, activated carbon) to maximize fresh Fe–oxide interfacial area, enable substrate/oxidant co-adsorption near Fe sites, and confine Fe–O–support bridges against leaching; these features raise CWPO mineralization rates for phenols/chlorophenols by increasing radical delivery to bulk liquid and interfacial oxidation pockets <cite id="26759364-5">Fe2O3/SBA‑15 nanocomposites in phenol CWPO demonstrate dispersion-driven performance gains</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-8">Fe/SiO2 fixed-bed CWPO shows operando performance benefits of mesoporosity and surface Fe exchange</cite><cite id="26759364-6">Iron oxide nanoparticles generate substantial ·OH, underscoring the role of surface area and Fe valence distribution</cite>.

- Engineer against leaching: acid-washing, oxalic/EDTA passivation, and Fe–O–X covalent linkages or caging (e.g., zeolitic frameworks) reduce Fe2+/Fe3+ loss and maintain heterogeneous radical budgets; recognize that complete suppression is impractical; instead, aim for controlled slow release and rapid surface regeneration to maintain CWPO rates and reduce sludge <cite id="6cd8fade-2">Oxalic acid reduces Fe2O3/Al2O3 leaching from 25% to 11%, indicating passivation improves stability</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-7">Cyclability of Fe/AC CWPO showed modest activity decay; while some leaching occurred, activity was largely retained</cite><cite id="56e55178-9">Fenton chemistry is governed by Fe oxidation state; maintaining Fe2+/Fe3+ pools on supports is key</cite>.

- Leaching can be a double‑edged sword: transiently, dissolved Fe may increase •OH production in the near‑surface microlayer (heterogeneous Fenton), but long‑term it lowers global efficiency and introduces sludge; thus, catalysts should favor surface-immobilized Fe with strong Lewis acidity and short H2O2 diffusion lengths to maximize •OH generation per consumed H2O2 and minimize losses to leaching and precipitation <cite id="26759364-4">Leached Fe2+/Fe3+ at low pH reduces CWPO efficiency, emphasizing retention benefits</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-7">Some leached Fe can yield homogeneous reactions, but stability in CWPO systems can mask losses depending on cycling and loadings</cite>.

# Quantitative and Systems-Level Outcomes in CWPO

•OH yield from Fe2+–H2O2 is first order in Fe2+ and first/second order in H2O2 depending on surface saturation; ESR establishes a 1:1 Fe2+–H2O2 stoichiometry to •OH under spin‑trapping, a foundation for TOF calculations where accessible Fe2+ per unit area correlates with CWPO specific rate and mineralization per pass <cite id="923e6931-0">1:1 Fe2+–H2O2 to •OH; rate laws and accessibility of Fe2+ sites set CWPO performance</cite>. # Practical Guidance

- Favor Fe–oxide-supported systems with controlled Fe–O–support bonding and mesoporosity to maximize •OH generation per metal and minimize leaching; add Lewis acidity to enhance H2O2 capture and orientation near Fe2+ centers <cite id="26759364-5">Fe2O3/SBA‑15 improves dispersion and access in phenol CWPO</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-2">Oxalic passivation reduces Fe leaching, sustaining activity</cite><cite id="26759364-4">Leaching impairs overall efficiency at low pH</cite>.

- Prefer Fe3O4/Fe–N active-site architectures with oxygen vacancies and nitrogen coordination to increase surface Fe2+ availability for adsorbed H2O2 without bulk Fe loss; these architectures are increasingly shown to elevate •OH flux and CWPO rates while resisting leaching under mild conditions <cite id="923e6931-9">Electron transfer from subsurface Fe2+ to adsorbed H2O2 in Fe3O4 drives high •OH production</cite><cite id="56e55178-8">Oxygen-vacancy engineering in Fe@Fe3O4 raises Fenton reactivity</cite>.

- Operate near neutral pH with oxygen supply to maintain Fe3+ regeneration and avoid Fe(OH)3 precipitation that occludes active sites; employ chelating ligands or metal–organic frameworks judiciously to shuttle Fe2+/Fe3+ locally and sustain surface •OH generation without promoting indiscriminate leaching <cite id="56e55178-3">Iron minerals catalyze H2O2 to •OH; pH/complexation govern Fe speciation and radical generation</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-9">Chelates mobilize Fe to hydroxyl radical pools; controlled complexation can sustain heterogeneous activity</cite>.

- Monitor leaching and sludge: use filtration-resistant modules and recycle slurries where possible; for fixed-bed Fe–oxide catalysts, incorporate regeneration (oxygen bake, acid/oxalic passivation) to restore Fe2+/Fe3+ pools and reduce interfacial plugging from Fe hydroxides <cite id="26759364-4">Leaching affects CWPO efficiency; controlling Fe speciation reduces sludge formation</cite><cite id="6cd8fade-7">Fe/AC catalysts maintained only ~10% activity loss over four cycles; leached Fe can be tolerated but is not ideal</cite>.

In sum, Fe surface species determine CWPO efficiency by dictating how H2O2 is converted to •OH on or near the solid–liquid interface rather than in bulk solution. Accessible, redox-active Fe2+ centers anchored via Fe–O–support bridges and Fe–N microsites generate •OH rapidly and sustainably, whereas leached Fe shifts chemistry toward heterogeneous/batch Fenton regimes that are often less efficient over time. Catalyst design should prioritize intraparticle anchoring, Lewis-acidic activation sites, and oxygen-accessible Fe3O4/Fe–N architectures to maximize •OH productivity and CWPO performance while minimizing Fe loss and sludge formation <cite id="26759364-4">Leaching of Fe2+/Fe3+ influences overall CWPO efficiency and sludge formation</cite><cite id="26759364-6">Oxidic Fe species generate ·OH from H2O2, linking surface chemistry to radical budgets</cite><cite id="923e6931-0">Fe2+ + H2O2 produces •OH in a 1:1 stoichiometry per ESR, evidencing direct control of •OH yield by accessible Fe2+</cite><cite id="923e6931-9">Electron transfer from subsurface Fe2+ to adsorbed H2O2 on Fe3O4 produces •OH and maintains Fe redox cycling</cite><cite id="56e55178-3">Magnetite/hematite catalyze H2O2 decomposition to •OH; mineral-like Fe species are central heterogeneous Fenton/CWPO catalysts</cite><cite id="56e55178-5">Ferryl/peroxo intermediates and Fenton-like mechanisms highlight Fe–ligand coordination control over •OH formation</cite>

Summary: Potassium content shifts both the electronic structure and physical state of catalysts and supports, which in turn switches promotional roles between facilitation, protection, and poisoning across different metals and reactions. At sub-saturation loads K often strengthens charge-transfer pathways (e.g., heterolytic H2 activation, ERI oxygen/CO2 activation), tunes phase stability and creates active edges (e.g., Co2C, Co–C), and can add weak base sites to scavenge CO2, boosting activity, selectivity, and stability. Excess K can instead migrate to reduce/support sintering and create overly basic, oxygen-deficient surfaces that poison hydrogenation or otherwise degrade turnover, with outcomes strongly dependent on metal identity, dispersion, support, and environment. <cite id="28b13e80-2">Alkali metals have been widely used as promoters in heterogeneous metal catalysts to improve activity, product selectivity, and stability</cite> <cite id="28b13e80-0">Potassium can boost Ru/MgO hydrogenation activity via facilitated heterolytic H2 adsorption</cite> <cite id="28b1268-6">In Co–Mn catalysts, alkali promoters favor formation and stabilization of Co2C</cite> <cite id="28b13e80-3">On Ni/MnOx, K improves stability and carbon-resistance in selective removal of ethane</cite> <cite id="5970a7f0-2">Conversely, potassium is a promoter for Fe-catalyzed ammonia synthesis but a poison for Pt-catalyzed hydrogenations; electronic structure dictates this divergence</cite>.

1) How potassium “does” its job: mechanisms that evolve with loading

1.1 Electronic-structure tuning and facilitated charge-transfer
- Low-to-optimal K (sub-saturation) tunes work functions and d-band center, enhancing heterolytic H2 activation and polar reaction partners (O2, CO2, carboxylates). This role is central in hydrogenation and ERI pathways. <cite id="28b13e80-0">On Ru/MgO, K acts as a “facilitated heterolytic H2” promoter for LOHC hydrogenation, boosting turnover</cite> <cite id="28b13e80-7">On Pt(111), potassium promoters can enhance water-gas shift activity through ERI-like mechanisms on clean surfaces</cite>.
- As K loading increases, the likelihood of interfacial polarization and heterolytic intermediates grows; too much K can instead reduce H2-activation barriers on nonpolar planes or bias desorption channels, altering selectivity. <cite id="5970a4f0-5">On Pt–Co for PROX, K addition enhances activity by facilitating carboxyl dehydrogenation, switching the rate-determining step toward a more facile carboxyl pathway</cite>.
- The sign and magnitude of the effect depend on the metal’s frontier orbitals and adsorption geometry. <cite id="5970a4f0-2">In heterogeneous catalysis, alkali metals can be promoters or poisons depending on how the electronic structure of the metal and adsorbates respond</cite>.

1.2 Surface phase control and defect/edge generation
- Optimal K can stabilize active phases that otherwise reconform or sinter (e.g., Co2C, oxide-derived carbides and carbon interfaces), improving C–C cleavage and redox turnover on Co/oxide systems. <cite id="28b13e80-6">Alkali-metal promoters stabilize and create Co2C, crucial for C–C bond cleavage activity</cite> <cite id="28b13e80-0">Ru/oxide hydrogenation is promoted by potassium-mediated H activation</cite>.
- Adequate K promotes oxygen-vacancy or reducible-oxide “storage” that sustains redox cycles (CO oxidation, CO2 activation), but excessive K lowers oxide oxygen mobility and can suppress metal oxide activity. <cite id="5970a4f0-3">Oxygen vacancy concentration and mobility are key determinants of CO oxidation activity on metal oxides</cite> <cite id="5970a4f0-8">Base-promoted Au/oxide systems resist CO2 accumulation by base-site scavenging, improving high-T/H2O stability</cite>.

1.3 Base-site creation for CO2/CO2-derived poison management and coke mitigation
- K imparts weak Brønsted acidity when introduced to metal oxides and supports, scavenging CO2, carbonate, or formate intermediates that otherwise poison active sites, improving low-temperature oxidation and selective hydrogenation under humid feeds. <cite id="e5337e3e-8">Base-promoted Au/CO2-tolerant PROX activity emerges in presence of CO2 due to enhanced CO2 capture, with undercoordinated active sites remaining available</cite> <cite id="28b13e80-3">On Ni/MnOx SRE catalysts, K enhances resistance to carbon deposition, stabilizing performance</cite>.
- In CO oxidation, surface base sites convert adsorbed CO2 into bicarbonate/formate and desorb it, reducing site poisoning; K location and stability determine the strength of this effect. <cite id="e5329640-8">K-poisoned SCR catalysts recover activity via K removal or regeneration, demonstrating the reversible role of K species in adsorption/desorption cycles</cite> <cite id="e5329644-5">Species-resolved alkali desorption shows K stability and surface location depend on activation temperature and support, controlling their base-strength and CO2-removal efficacy</cite>.

2) System- and reaction-specific trends with potassium content

2.1 Hydrogenation and ERI-type conversions (Ru, Co–Ni/oxide, Pt/Co)
- Insufficient K: Weakens adsorbate polarization; hydrogenation or ERI rates are limited by poor charge-transfer to H2 or CO2. <cite id="28b13e80-0">Ru/oxide catalysts without sufficient K show lower LOHC hydrogenation rates due to limited heterolytic H2 activation at the interface</cite>.
- Optimal K: Enhances interfacial heterolytic H2, lowers activation barriers and improves enantioselectivity/stability in hydrogenation; in CO/PROX, routes via carboxyl intermediates dominate. <cite id="28b13e80-0">K-facilitated heterolytic H2 boosts Ru catalyst hydrogenation turnover</cite> <cite id="5970a4f0-4">K-PtCo/Al2O3 achieves higher PROX activity via carboxyl dehydrogenation, evidencing K-induced pathway engineering</cite>.
- Excess/immobile K: Can poison Pt hydrogenation by strong H binding and enantioselectivity reversal, or force phase reconstructions (e.g., Co2O3→Co2C) that favor undesired methanation or coke; the poison vs promoter boundary maps onto reaction chemoselectivity and metal d-character. <cite id="5970a4f0-2">Potassium is a poison for Pt hydrogenations, a promoter for Fe ammonia synthesis, highlighting metal-dependent electronic outcomes</cite> <cite id="28b13e80-6">High K favors Co2C stabilization, which increases C–C bond cleavage but may lower hydrocarbon selectivity</cite>.
- Designable regime: Confinement and activation temperature control K dispersion; smaller NPs and strong oxides increase base strength, improving CO2-tolerant hydrogenation. <cite id="e5329640-4">Undercoordinated Au sites and dynamic cluster structures regulate CO activation at low temperature; strong support and small size preserve dispersion</cite> <cite id="e5329640-5">EPR/DRIFTPD/TAD studies show K species states evolve with dopant level on Co3O4 and determine NO/soot oxidation activity</cite>.

2.2 CO oxidation and PROX on noble and bimetallic catalysts
- Insufficient K (or weakly held K): Limited CO2 capture; CO-poisoned sites persist, lowering low-temperature turnover. <cite id="28b13e80-0">Ru/oxide systems require K at near-optimal load to boost turnover; too little K yields lower activity</cite>.
- Optimal K: Adds surface base pockets and preserves undercoordinated metal sites, enabling simultaneous CO and O2 activation with minimal poisoning; Au/oxide systems and supported Au–Cu show high LT-TOF, with improved CO2-tolerant behavior if strong base sites are present. <cite id="e5329640-0">Supported Au nanoparticles exhibit low-temperature CO oxidation activity due to undercoordinated surface sites and support interactions</cite> <cite id="e5329642-3">Bimetallic Au–Cu/SiO2 shows promoter effects in CO oxidation, with activity tied to preserved Au dispersion</cite> <cite id="5970a4f0-8">Base sites in K-modified Au systems scavenge CO2, enabling stable PROX in SO2/H2O mixtures</cite>.
- Excess K or mobile K: Base-rich surfaces can dehydroxylate and sinter supports/active layers; in hydrogen environments, K accumulates as K2Ox and weakens O activation, reducing TOF. <cite id="e5329640-5">K-doped Co3O4 studies identify mobile/incorporated K species that correlate with oxidation activity changes; support interactions control migration</cite>.
- Environment dependence: In excess O2/H2O, K-driven CO2 capture and metal-oxide redox storage dominate; in CO-rich/humid feeds, base-induced deactivation requires balancing K mobility and strength. <cite id="72b636b6-0">Overlayer CO2 scavenge by alkali promoters stabilizes turnover for CO oxidation under CO2/H2O atmospheres</cite>.

2.3 Iron-based Fischer–Tropsch synthesis and methanation
- Low-to-optimal K (Duval-type storage): Creates reducible oxide storage for hydrogen and oxygen transfer, increases reducibility and stepwise C-chain growth; promotes chain termination control. <cite id="28b13e80-0">Ru/oxide example shows facilitated H2 activation mechanism analogous to optimal K-controlled Fe sites</cite> <cite id="5970a4f0-5">In CO2 activation/oxidation conversions, alkali metals act as ERI intermediates, suggesting a mechanistic analogy for FTS where oxygen transfer steps can be alkali-assisted</cite>.
- Excess K or strong basicity: Over-alkalization stabilizes highly oxidized phases (e.g., Fe3O4-like or Fe–O–C networks) and favors methanation, or poisons selective hydrogenation steps; sintering accelerates via K-assisted coarsening. <cite id="28b13e80-2">General trends show alkali promoters improve stability but can also cause deactivation pathways if base strength overwhelms acid–base balance</cite>.
- Practical evidence: On Ru-based LOHC hydrogenation (model for Fe systems), controlled K levels tune hydrogenation pathways and resistance to catalyst deactivation. <cite id="28b13e80-0">K-dose tuning on Ru/MgO adjusts hydrogenation rates and stability; similar levers apply to Fe-based FTS where K modifies reducibility and acid-base site balance</cite>.

2.4 Nickel-based selective oxidation and deoxygenation
- K improves carbon monoxide resistance and deposition control on Ni/oxide catalysts, but high K weakens Ni–support bonding and lowers dispersion. <cite id="28b13e80-3">Ni/MnOx with K shows improved stability and carbon-resistance under selective ethane removal</cite>.
- K can shift C–C bond cleavage pathways on Co/oxide catalysts; analogous Ni systems see oxygenate dehydration and partial oxidation routes modulated by base strength. <cite id="28b13e80-6">K promotes Co2C formation for stronger C–C cleavage; Ni-based systems respond via altered base–metal equilibrium</cite>.

2.5 Zeolite and mesoporous aluminosilicate systems
- Low-to-optimal K (exchangeable K+) converts lattice OH to strongly acidic Bronsted sites and increases cracking and shape-selectivity; content dictates acid-site density and coke deposition. At higher content, K impoverishes Brønsted sites (titration) and shifts to methanation/hydrocracking with higher coke. <cite id="28b13e80-2">Alkali promotion is widely used to improve activity/selectivity; acid–base balance and phase stability govern outcomes</cite>.
- In biomass conversion and methanol-to-olefins contexts, moderate K can improve oxygenate dehydration and suppress undesired condensation, while excess K promotes coke formation and reduces olefin selectivity; activation temperature and TAD determine long-term stability. <cite id="e5329640-4">Deactivation and regeneration studies emphasize that base strength and migration pathways control performance</cite> <cite id="28b13e80-5">Species-resolved alkali desorption maps K surface locations/loss, guiding dosing and activation</cite>.

3) Why K content matters more for some metals than others

- Promoter vs poison mapping by reaction chemistry: Hydrogenation (dihydrogen/CO2 coupling) benefits from strong interfacial heterolytic pathways and oxygen-vacancy storage, where K provides electrons and base character; hydrogenolysis and transfer hydrogenation can be inhibited by over-basic centers that bind H too strongly or bias to hydrosilylation/methanation routes. <cite id="5970a4f0-2">Alkali metals act as promoters in ammonia synthesis (Fe-based) and poisons in Pt hydrogenations, evidencing reaction-chemistry control</cite> <cite id="28b13e80-0">Ru/oxide hydrogenation exemplifies facilitated heterolytic activation by K</cite>.
- Support interactions and dispersion: Strong Lewis-acid supports (MgO, Al2O3, SiO2) stabilize K as near-surface bases; weak supports let K migrate to alumina or sinter the metal, eroding activity. <cite id="28b13e80-0">Ru/MgO shows facilitated H2 activation tied to oxide-supported, well-dispersed K</cite> <cite id="e5329640-5">K-doped Co3O4 shows mobile K species that change NO/soot oxidation activity</cite> <cite id="e5329640-5">EPR/TAD indicate K state and location control redox performance</cite>.
- Environment sensitivity: Water and CO2 feeds magnify K benefits (base capture) but can also trigger deactivation if K is not mobile enough to re-sequester intermediates; sintering in H2-rich environments requires limiting K content or controlling dispersion. <cite id="e5329640-8">PROX stability in CO2/H2O is improved by K-created base sites in Au systems</cite> <cite id="e5329640-9">K-poisoned SCR regains activity upon de-K or regeneration, underscoring reversible base-site interactions</cite>.

4) Practical guidance: choosing K content and environment

- Start with sub-saturation K to introduce interfacial heterolytic pathways without global base overload; optimize by TPR/DRIFTPD to locate K as near-surface oxides/hydroxides and by TAD to ensure mobility under operating conditions. <cite id="e5329640-5">Species-resolved alkali desorption shows K migration depends on temperature and support, guiding optimal dosing</cite>.
- For CO oxidation/PROX: moderate K that creates CO2-scavenging sites while preserving undercoordinated metal edges; avoid strongly basic supports that irreversibly deprotonate intermediates or sinter upon H2 exposure. <cite id="e5329640-0">Undercoordinated Au sites sustain low-T CO oxidation</cite> <cite id="5970a4f0-8">Base-site abundance dictates PROX robustness under CO2/H2O</cite>.
- For hydrogenation and ERI: K levels that weaken E–H or O–H bond scission without poisoning hydrosilylation or hydrogenolysis selectivity; bimetallics (Pt–Co, Ru–Cu) allow tuning via alloying to partially compensate for K effects. <cite id="5970a4f0-4">K-PtCo shifts the mechanism to facile carboxyl route, increasing PROX turnover</cite> <cite id="28b13e80-0">Ru/oxide hydrogenation improves with K at controlled content</cite>.
- For FTS/methanation: Duval-like “storage” K contents that maintain reducibility and acid–base balance; avoid high K that collapses TOF selectivity toward methanation and increases sintering. <cite id="5970a4f0-5">K acts as an ERI-like base/oxide intermediate in CO2 activation, analogous to storage oxygen-transfer steps in FTS</cite>.
- Use characterization–activity correlations: EELS/STEM for K migration and alumina phase formation; CO chemisorption and H2 pulse for acid–base strength; stepwise dehydration tests for biomass conversion to map optimal K windows. <cite id="28b13e80-6">XAS/XPS show alkali stabilization of carbide phases (e.g., Co2C) that are activity-linked</cite> <cite id="e5329644-5">EPR/TAD link K surface location to catalytic oxidation performance</cite>.

5) Remaining uncertainties and how to resolve them

Direct, monotonic K–activity curves rarely exist; instead, they bifurcate by mechanism (ERI vs Langmuir–Hinshelwood), support, and environment. Best practice is “iterative promotion”: add K in narrow increments, map surface composition/chemistry via operando DRIFTPD/DFR, and correlate to stepwise rate changes in model substrates (CO oxidation, methanol decomposition, PROX). <cite id="28b13e80-2">Structure–activity relationships for alkali promotion hinge on acid–base balance and phase evolution, which vary non-monotonically with dopant level</cite> <cite id="e5329640-5">Multi-species EPR/TAD analyses reveal alkali states responsible for observed activity swings</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Potassium content is a leverswitch that toggles catalysts between promotion, protection, and poisoning, depending on interfacial polarization, phase stability, acid–base balance, and environment. <cite id="28b13e80-2">Alkali promoters generally improve activity/selectivity/stability</cite> <cite id="5970a4f0-2">But their sign is metal- and reaction-specific</cite>.
- Optimal windows often arise where K creates near-surface, mobile base/oxide sites that scavenge CO2, stabilize active phases (e.g., Co2C, undercoordinated Au), and tune charge-transfer without overwhelming hydrogenation or oxygen-activation pathways. <cite id="28b13e80-6">K stabilizes Co2C for higher C–C cleavage activity</cite> <cite id="e5329640-0">Undercoordinated Au sites underlie LT CO oxidation, aided by K base sites</cite>.
- Excess or misplaced K (immobile K2Ox, overly basic centers) deactivates via poisoning or sintering; controlling dispersion, exchangeable fraction, and thermal mobility is central to performance. <cite id="e5329640-5">K species states on Co3O4 correlate with oxidation activity</cite> <cite id="5970a4f0-2">K can poison Pt hydrogenations and promote Fe ammonia synthesis, underscoring mechanism control</cite>.

2) Triangulation to 3D coordinates and time series
- For each matched pair, triangulation computes the 3D point by intersecting back-projected rays, leveraging parallax between cameras; repeated across the image set it reconstructs the 3D shape at a frame. Robustness is improved by epipolar-guided search and calibration-parameter constraints.<cite id="d65a3240-8">calibration and correlation are employed by Stereo-DIC based on epipolar geometry and how triangulation methods are used to perform</cite><cite id="a8d63220-2">The epipolar geometry of a stereo system allows us to search for corresponding points only along corresponding image lines</cite><cite id="d65a3240-1">acquires multi-view images ... detects and identifies target centers with</cite>. 
- Temporal tracking compares the registered 3D point fields between frames to obtain 3D displacement vectors and surface strain; this is the core of 3D DIC deformation analysis.<cite id="d65a3240-0">temporal tracking of pixel subsets, stereo-correlation of subsets, and stereo-triangulation</cite><cite id="3136e789-1">The DIC measurement helps to determine 3D displacements and surface strains, 3D velocities and 3D accelerations</cite><cite id="3136e789-3">Three-dimensional digital image correlation (DIC) is becoming widely used to characterize the behavior of structures undergoing 3D deformations</cite>.

3) Photogrammetric workflow and triangulation accuracy
- Practitioners employ photogrammetry-inspired calibration procedures (targets, bundle/block adjustment) to refine camera intrinsic and extrinsic parameters and tie points, thereby minimizing reprojection/ triangulation error for accurate 3D deformation retrieval.<cite id="d65a3240-1">a photogrammetry-based stereo calibration workflow acquires multi-view images of coded and non-coded targets, detects and identifies target centers with</cite><cite id="a9661721-9">Three-dimensional coordinates can be calculated from the overlap of two or more photographs</cite>.

Practical considerations for reliable deformation fields
- Speckle pattern design, image registration, and multi-view geometry guide robust triangulation; baseline and focal length set parallax and depth sensitivity, while strong epipolar constraints reduce erroneous matches and stabilize the 3D field for deformation extraction.<cite id="d65a3240-2">A Phantom DIC system includes synchronized high-speed cameras, precision stereo mounting hardware, matched lenses and LED lighting, calibration targets,</cite><cite id="3136e789-5">triangulation, and temporal matching to recover the 3D surface and track</cite><cite id="a8d63220-0">An epipolar line is defined as the set of points in one image that correspond to a specific point in another image, constrained by the fundamental matrix</cite>. 
- Open-source and commercial toolchains implement these steps (stereo calibration, epipolar search, triangulation, dense tracking) and report 3D displacement, velocity, and strain fields from time-resolved image series.<cite id="d65a3240-7">we present MultiDIC, a free open-source software library for analyzing multi-view stereo images and obtaining 3D shapes and full</cite><cite id="3136e789-1">The DIC measurement helps to determine 3D displacements and surface strains, 3D velocities and 3D accelerations</cite><cite id="d65a3240-9">Digital Image Correlation is a procedure to compute 2D or 3D coordinates from recorded single images or image series</cite>.

Putting it together: how 3D DIC leverages photogrammetry and triangulation
- Photogrammetric foundations: 3D coordinates from triangulation of projected image points, calibrated with pinhole models and poses; correspondence constrained by epipolar geometry reduces search and error.
- Triangulation role: back-projected rays from matched image points are intersected to yield 3D coordinates per pixel/subset; across frames, these yield 3D displacement vectors.
- Deformation/strain extraction: 3D coordinate time series are differenced to compute rigid-body motion, in-plane and out-of-plane displacements, and full-field strain (e.g., Green–Lagrange-type measures), with outputs including 3D velocity/acceleration in high-rate setups.
- Photogrammetric calibration and quality: target-based stereo calibration and bundle adjustment refine parameters and tie points; good practices emphasize matching criteria aligned to stereo-system calibration to ensure accurate triangulated shapes before temporal differencing for strain.

Key takeaways
- Without triangulation, 2D pixel shifts cannot be converted to true 3D deformation; photogrammetry supplies the mapping from 2D correspondences to 3D coordinates via calibrated camera geometry and ray intersections.<cite id="3136e789-5">3D DIC technique typically involves three key steps: stereo-matching, triangulation, and temporal matching to recover the 3D surface</cite><cite id="3136e789-7">Photogrammetry is a three-dimensional coordinate measurement technique based on triangulation principles</cite>.

Overview and scope
Organic solvent additives in CaCO3 precipitation systems shift thermodynamic and kinetic conditions in the super-saturated zone by introducing nonaqueous microenvironments, changing ionic association, and modifying crystal/solution interfaces, thereby altering nucleation rates, growth pathways, particle morphology, and colloidal stability of vaterite. Below, “additives” include polar solvents and cosolvents commonly used in aqueous carbonation systems: alcohols (ethanol, isopropanol), glycols/glycol ethers/acetates (ethylene glycol, diethylene glycol, glycol monoethyl ether/acetate), and aprotic solvents (acetone, cyclohexanone).

Mechanisms at a glance
- Microemulsion/dispersion control: Additives create mixed micelles/droplets or mixed-solvent microenvironments that increase nucleation sites and template curvatures/anisotropies, biasing vaterite over stable polymorph formation; dispersion state correlates strongly with product characteristics in microemulsion-like reactive precipitation routes <cite id="c77e9e3b-8">It was indeed suggested for microemulsion processes, which also occur in heterogeneous conditions, that the dispersion state impacts the characteristics of the solid products</cite> <cite id="ca1654ad-4">Influence of ethylene glycol on polymorphism and morphology of calcium carbonate has been studied; mixed-solvent systems can favor vaterite precipitation</cite> <cite id="ca1654ad-6">High concentration of ethylene glycol/water favored vaterite precipitation</cite>.
- Ion pairing and CO3^2− solvation shifts: Solvation shells and CO2–species interactions (e.g., bicarbonate/carbonate with organic groups) change ionic mobility and effective supersaturation, affecting nucleation and growth rates; lithium fission/cavity effects can promote vaterite nucleation and slow transformation <cite id="ca1654ad-3">Ca(OH)2 suspension in water containing acetone and a chelating agent undergoes carbonation to vaterite in the absence of CO2 and temperature increase; lithium carbonate in carbonated aqueous solution causes vaterite spontaneous precipitation</cite> <cite id="cb014429-2">Additives influence vaterite morphology and stabilize the mineral by preventing transformation to calcite</cite>.
- Surface adsorption and growth anisotropy: Organic molecules adsorb on vaterite faces, inhibit specific planes, and promote selective growth or aggregation to hierarchical shapes; microparticle growth can involve mixed vaterite–aragonite stages before phase assignment <cite id="c77e9e3b-2">Particles containing both vaterite and aragonite appear as intermediate growth stages</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-9">Surface-active organic molecules can stabilize vaterite, modulating Ostwald ripening via dissolution–reprecipitation on particle surfaces</cite>.
- Thermodynamic metastability management: Vaterite is intrinsically metastable; additives can suppress Ostwald ripening and slow transformation to calcite/aragonite through surface energy reduction and kinetic barriers, but insufficient suppression yields calcite content growth over time <cite id="c77e9e3b-4">The further ripening of vaterite is easily envisaged; Ostwald ripening occurs via dissolution–reprecipitation</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-3">All added organic solvents tested reduced the vaterite concentration both at reaction end and after aging, indicating partial transformation suppression rather than absolute prevention</cite>.

Nucleation: rates and pathway switching
- Increased apparent nucleation rates and metastable pathway selection: In aqueous systems with alcohol or glycol cosolvents, nucleation sites increase via micelles/droplets and mixed-solvent microphases, favoring vaterite formation over immediate calcite; kinetics of spontaneous vaterite precipitation have been tracked in ethanol/1‑propanol/isopropanol/diethylene glycol, with clear solvent-dependent profiles <cite id="ca1654ad-0">Kinetics of spontaneous precipitation of vaterite from aqueous solution in ethanol, isopropanol, and diethylene glycol was investigated</cite> <cite id="ca1654ad-3">Carbonation to vaterite proceeds even without CO2 or temperature increase in acetone-containing Ca(OH)2 suspensions, and lithium fission yields spontaneous vaterite precipitation</cite> <cite id="cb014429-0">Proportions of aragonite and calcite in vaterite can be modulated by isopropanol, demonstrating control over polymorph pathway</cite>.
- Trade-off at higher additive levels: Overloading with organics or inappropriate solvents lowers the final vaterite fraction due to enhanced secondary nucleation/secondary precipitation routes or faster transformation, emphasizing the need for optimized dosage/time windows <cite id="c77e9e3b-3">The presence of all added organic solvents reduced the vaterite concentration in the produced CaCO3 both during reaction and after aging, showing additive-specific suppression of vaterite content</cite>.
- Morphology-driven nucleation-assemblies: In mixed ethylene glycol/water, homogeneous nucleation can be superseded by nucleation at polymer-rich domains, producing porous/vaterite-dominant structures, again tying additive microchemistry to nucleation modes <cite id="ca1654ad-4">Ethylene glycol influences polymorphism and resulting morphology; activity-based control shows additive-rich domains can govern nucleation and growth</cite>.

Growth: linear growth, aggregation, and Ostwald ripening
- Slowed primary growth, selective inhibition, and curvilinear morphologies: Alcohol/glycol groups adsorb onto lattice faces and along edges, retarding certain growth directions while favoring others; this yields spheres, rods, prisms, or flower-like clusters; reactive precipitation studies show dispersion state controls crystal size distribution and anisotropy <cite id="c77e9e3b-8">In reactive precipitation analogs of microemulsions, dispersion state governs product characteristics</cite> <cite id="e79c1259-0">Interfacial control of crystallization pathways; solution surface tension governs vaterite morphology</cite> <cite id="e79c1259-4">Vaterite flowers synthesized using organic additives demonstrate additive-enabled hierarchical assembly</cite>.
- Ostwald ripening modulation: Additives stabilize small vaterite crystals by forming adsorbed layers that increase dissolution free energy of lattice and decrease transfer entropy to solution; reported pathways show reduced ripening compared to neat water, but vaterite remains susceptible to ripening and transformation without strong stabilization <cite id="c77e9e3b-4">Ostwald ripening of vaterite proceeds via dissolution–reprecipitation, and can be readily observed</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-9">Stabilization of vaterite via interfacial layers can impede Ostwald ripening</cite>.
- Polymorph switching during growth: Intermediate mixed vaterite–aragonite entities appear during microparticle growth, then assign to vaterite or aragonite depending on solvent/additive composition and supersaturation trajectories, indicating additive-modulated pathway branching <cite id="c77e9e3b-2">Particles with mixed vaterite and aragonite interpreted as intermediate stages in growth</cite>.

Morphology: solvent-specific shapes and porosity
- Spherical nanoparticles/microparticles and nanorods: Alcohols and polymeric additives often yield spherical vaterite composed of aggregated nanoparticles; acetone/cyclohexanone or glycol systems can drive rod-like or prism-like morphologies; acetone can promote near-in-situ vaterite-to-aragonite transitions as well <cite id="c77e9e3b-7">Vaterite microspheres form by reactive precipitation in organic-aqueous systems where dispersion and additive chemistry dominate</cite> <cite id="e79c1259-4">Acetone-based and other organic additives produced flower-like hierarchical structures; “any organic additives” yielded vaterite hierarchical forms</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-5">Oriented aggregation and novel vaterite-to-aragonite transformation observed in organic solvent/ionic media</cite>.
- Porous and hierarchical architectures: Mixed glycol/water and polymer-rich domains create templates for internal porosity and interparticle bonding, useful for biomedical and delivery applications; interfacial tension changes and adsorption layers explain reduced densification and increased specific surface area <cite id="ca1654ad-4">Ethylene glycol promotes mixed-solvent nucleation/growth that gives distinct morphology</cite> <cite id="ca1654ad-2">Vaterite microparticles show stable morphology consistent with hexagonal lattice with tapered corners</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-0">Vaterite’s higher solubility, hydrophobicity, and porosity under solvent-modified interfaces support its use in degradable systems</cite>.
- Solvent concentration dependence: Low levels can yield smooth spheres; increasing solvent fraction favors branching/flowers or rod growth via enhanced edge/face adsorption; too high additive fractions drive secondary precipitation pathways that reduce vaterite yield <cite id="ca1654ad-6">Higher ethylene glycol fraction favors vaterite; concentration tuning is key</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-3">At equal dosages, over time the organic additive decreased vaterite content, i.e., additive level must be optimized</cite>.

Stability: thermal/morphological stabilization and transformation suppression
- Chemical stabilization by additives: Additives slow calcite transformation by depressing surface energy and retarding diffusion-limited Ostwald processes; acetone and glycol systems specifically have been shown to prevent or delay conversion to calcite, stabilizing vaterite in the short to intermediate term <cite id="cb014429-2">Additives stabilize vaterite by preventing transformation to calcite; they also change crystal shapes</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-4">Ostwald ripening pathways of vaterite proceed via dissolution–reprecipitation on the particle–solution interface, modulated by interfacial layers</cite>.
- Kinetic stabilization and trade-offs: While many additives stabilize vaterite initially, insufficient or prolonged stabilization allows Ostwald ripening and polymorph transformation; data show that the same additives reduced the vaterite fraction during aging, implying dose–time windows are critical; acetone’s dual role (promoting nucleation yet potentially shifting pathways) illustrates this complexity <cite id="c77e9e3b-3">Organic solvents reduced the vaterite concentration both at reaction end and after aging</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-5">Acetone/ionic media observed vaterite-to-aragonite transformation, indicating additive-enabled pathway switching</cite>.
- Thermal/dispersion stabilization in synthesis: Microemulsion-like, solvent-bilayer-stabilized precursors yield uniform vaterite particles with small size and high stability; reactive precipitation in organic–aqueous media relies on droplet size and surfactant-like additives to maintain discrete reactive interfaces and narrow size distributions <cite id="c77e9e3b-8">Dispersion state in microemulsion-like heterogeneous conditions governs particle size and structure</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-7">Organic–aqueous reactive precipitation produces vaterite microspheres with controlled structure</cite>.

Solvent-by-solvent patterns within “organic additives”
- Alcohols (ethanol, isopropanol): Mediate rapid vaterite synthesis, accelerate nucleation, yield spherical or porous structures, and stabilize vaterite over calcite under appropriate dosing; however, too much alcohol or long aging reduces vaterite yield via Ostwald processes and transformation to calcite or aragonite <cite id="cb014429-0">Isopropanol mediates rapid, selective vaterite synthesis and controls aragonite/calcite proportions</cite> <cite id="ca1654ad-1">Ethanol/isopropanol addition strongly influences precipitation rate and final polymorph content</cite> <cite id="ca1654ad-0">Ethanol, 1‑propanol, and diethylene glycol modulate kinetic profiles of vaterite precipitation</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-3">At equal dosing, over time vaterite fraction declines, indicating transformation dominates without full stabilization</cite>.
- Glycols/acetates (ethylene glycol, diethylene glycol, glycol monoethyl ether/acetate): Create mixed-micellar reservoirs that favor vaterite at moderate supersaturation, produce prisms/rods or hierarchical “flower” morphologies, and improve interfacial energy balance leading to slower ripening and higher specific surface area; higher glycol fraction increases vaterite content up to a point, beyond which secondary precipitation reduces yield <cite id="ca1654ad-6">High ethylene glycol fraction favors vaterite precipitation</cite> <cite id="ca1654ad-4">Ethylene glycol/water systems control polymorph and morphology; additive microchemistry governs nucleation/growth</cite> <cite id="e79c1259-0">Interfacial tension regulation by solution surface tension shapes vaterite morphologies</cite>.
- Aprotic ketones/esters (acetone, cyclohexanone; glycol acetate): Provide nonpolar microphases that promote nucleation and alter ionic interaction, enabling rapid in-situ conversion pathways; acetone in particular has documented cases of carbonation-driven vaterite and even vaterite-to-aragonite transformation under ionic media, delivering rod/plate/hierarchical morphologies and good colloidal stability in short aging windows; longer aging shows reduction in vaterite fraction <cite id="ca1654ad-3">Carbonation to vaterite occurs in acetone-containing Ca(OH)2 without CO2/heat; lithium fission yields vaterite</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-5">Acetone/ionic systems show oriented aggregation and vaterite-to-aragonite transformation</cite> <cite id="e79c1259-4">Organic additive “any” (including acetone-derived systems) yields flower-like vaterite assemblies</cite>.

Colloidal behavior and interfacial physics
- Zeta potential and dispersion: While direct zeta potential datasets in carbonate systems are scarce, the literature consistently shows that organic additives increase hydrophobic character and reduce interfacial tension, which raises electrophoretic mobility magnitudes or improves repulsive stabilization at short range, leading to better redispersion of aggregated nanocrystals; mixed glycol/water and polymer-assisted routes achieve small, uniform, well-dispersed vaterite microspheres <cite id="e79c1259-0">Solution surface tension governs pathways and morphology; interfacial control regulates vaterite crystallization patterns</cite> <cite id="ca1654ad-2">Vaterite exhibits a stable hexagonal morphology consistent with anisotropic interfacial energy distributions</cite> <cite id="c77e9e3b-7">Organic–aqueous systems generate spherical, well-dispersed vaterite microspheres</cite>.
