- Several studies emphasize that interfacial rheology measured microfluidically predicts droplet stability and PDI, and provide concrete workflows to map It, adsorption kinetics, and elasticity to design choices. <cite id="486d210a-2">Bulk emulsion structure depends on interfacial elastic/viscous properties</cite>. <cite id="486d210a-5">Interfacial dilatational rheology influences coalescence/ripening and is measurable/predictive for microfluidic systems</cite>. <cite id="6d4ae55a-0">Geometrical selection and flow regime guidance for monodisperse outputs is consolidated in microfluidic reviews</cite>. <cite id="1518199d-5">Flow-rate dependence with exit-time deformation and higher CVs underscores operational tuning to avoid post-femtocurrent broadening</cite>.
- While explicit dimensionless-group scalings (Oh/Re/We/De) are implied by flow-focusing studies, their quantitative mapping often requires device-specific calibration; nonetheless, they anchor practical targeting of laminar-to-transitional regimes where elastic interfaces suppress coalescence and yield narrow distributions. <cite id="6d4ae55a-1">Flow-focusing CFD/experiments tie size to capillary number and It/viscosity</cite>. <cite id="6d4ae55a-9">Divergent geometry elongation favors controlled breakup when interfacial layers are sufficiently elastic</cite>.

Actionable checklist (microfluidic biomedical capsules)
- Characterize first: measure interfacial tension and dilatational rheology of your surfactant/biopolymer in your buffer; use microfluidic oscillatory or pulsating-drop methods to set targets for elasticity/viscosity balance. <cite id="486d210a-4">Interfacial elasticity can predict droplet stability and guide candidate selection</cite>. <cite id="486d210a-2">Interfacial elasticity and viscosity jointly set resistance and relaxation</cite>.
- Choose regime: prefer flow-focusing with high It and fast adsorbing surfactants when you need narrow PDI; favor co-flow with strong protein-stabilized interfaces to minimize collisions; avoid surfactant-depleted zones that yield bimodality. <cite id="6d4ae55a-0">Geometry selection governs flow fields and collision frequency</cite>. <cite id="486d210a-5">Surfactant depletion elevates coalescence risk</cite>.
- Tune flows: align viscosities and It/γ at the slit; avoid long channels (residence time) unless ripening is desired; if using squeezing, damp pressure oscillations to reduce collision-driven spread. <cite id="6d4ae55a-4">Viscosity/It balance controls droplet size</cite>. <cite id="6d4ae55a-1">Residence time governs ripening-driven size shift</cite>. <cite id="1518199d-5">Exit-time shell softness broadens PDI</cite>.
- Freeze size: use UV-injection or interfacial polymerization slug flows with diffusion-aware monomer supply; apply crosslinking pulses to lock capsules at near-mode size. <cite id="1518199d-7">Interfacial and in situ polymerization routes produce size-controlled shells when reaction fronts are well tuned</cite>. <cite id="1518199d-8">Crosslinking arrests coalescence/ripening and stabilizes PDI</cite>.
- Stabilize payload: pair surfactant with antistatic protein corona; validate drug–surfactant compatibility to prevent depletion; test salt/pH stability to prevent interfacial swelling/coacervation that broadens PDI. <cite id="486d210a-2">Protein/biomolecule layers add dilatational elasticity and kinetic barriers</cite>. <cite id="6d4ae55a-9">Drug–surfactant incompatibility can flip interfacial layers into depletion zones</cite>. <cite id="486d210a-3">Ostwald ripening suppression via elasticity helps long-term stability</cite>.

Overview
Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) have a high aspect ratio and strongly attracted surfaces, so they readily form clusters and bundles via van der Waals forces and π–π interactions, which strongly hinders achieving uniform, individual-level dispersion in matrix resins like epoxy and PMMA; this, in turn, limits electrical, mechanical, and barrier properties of the resulting composites. <cite id="88958da4-6">Dispersion challenges arise from CNTs' high aspect ratio (>1000) and tendency to entangle in processing, making effective, uniform dispersion the central problem in CNT-based composites</cite> <cite id="451af793-0">CNTs agglomerate into crystalline bundles due to strong van der Waals attraction, which degrades their properties unless dispersed</cite>.

Primary causes of CNT aggregation
- Geometric confinement and entanglement: Because CNTs are long, thin, and flexible, van der Waals attraction among their curved graphitic surfaces promotes tight contact, entanglement, and secondary bonding, leading to hierarchical bundling and “roping.” <cite id="88958da4-6">High aspect ratio and entanglement in processing are primary drivers of dispersion failure</cite> <cite id="451af793-1">Molecular modeling and experiments identify van der Waals assembly and stacking as intrinsic to low-dimensional carbon materials</cite>.
- π–π interactions among graphitic surfaces and with aromatic ligands: π–π stacking is a dominant interaction for flat carbon species; both between CNT sidewalls and between CNTs and adsorbed ligands can stabilize aggregates. <cite id="451af793-9">Typical dispersants combine alkyl and aromatic moieties to engage π–π interactions with CNTs, underscoring how π–π forces both promote aggregation (without stabilizers) and enable controlled dispersion (with suitable ligands)</cite> <cite id="451af793-5">Ab initio calculations and reviews emphasize π–π interactions between planar organic molecules and graphitic surfaces as strong and spontaneous</cite>.
- Van der Waals–dominated interfacial “wetting” and cohesion: CNTs exhibit strong vdW cohesion with neighboring nanocarbons, while weak polarity mismatch with many polymers reduces wetting and promotes the formation of dry junctions and rovibrational bundling even at moderate loadings. <cite id="451af793-0">Strong van der Waals attraction drives robust CNT bundling</cite> <cite id="88958da4-4">Rheology of CNT dispersions shows the persistence of structured networks and the difficulty of fully breaking down aggregates in viscous media</cite>.
- Concentration and confinement effects: In concentrated dispersions, increased contact frequency and confinement further stabilize aggregates; even after shear-induced debundling, secondary nucleation and growth can occur during relaxation or solvent evaporation. <cite id="88958da4-6">CNTs entangle and re-bundle readily during processing, highlighting the role of concentration and shear history</cite> <cite id="451af793-3">Debundling depends on medium viscosity and assembly pathways, with re-organization possible during polymer solution preparation</cite>.

Dispersion challenges in matrix resins (polymer matrices)
- Wetting and interfacial energy mismatch: Many polymers (e.g., epoxies) have low affinity to graphitic CNTs; poor wetting leads to isolated particles/bundles with weak interfacial adhesion, reduced load transfer, and concentration-induced percolation problems. <cite id="406848b9-4">Amino-functionalization increases surface energy and wettability to epoxy, markedly improving interfacial interaction compared to pristine CNTs</cite> <cite id="406848b9-3">CNT surface energy and polymer coating strongly influence percolation and transport network formation in epoxy-CNT systems</cite>.
- Viscosity and process window: Once aggregates are broken, viscous matrices hinder diffusive rearrangement and stabilization of isolated CNTs, making uniform processing windows narrow and often requiring high-shear, high-energy inputs. <cite id="88958da4-0">Ultrasonication is effective in low-viscosity liquids but less so in high-viscosity polymers, indicating processing constraints</cite> <cite id="451af793-1">Sonochemical approaches can overcome vdW bundling but require compatible media such as surfactant or DNA solutions</cite>.
- Re-aggregation during curing and post-processing: Thermal cycles, solvent removal, and crosslinking in resins can collapse debonded CNT networks and promote re-bundling via capillary and vdW forces, reducing electrical and mechanical performance. <cite id="406848b9-10">Dispersion–interfacial interaction–re-agglomeration coupling shows that improved wettability and interfacial interaction lower re-aggregation, otherwise a major concern in epoxy-CNT processing</cite>.
- Electrical percolation and partial network formation: Even modest CNT dispersion can yield partially percolated networks under/after cure, leading to localized conductivity hotspots and uneven property improvement; achieving homogeneous single-fiber dispersion is thus critical. <cite id="406848b9-2">A CNT network formed during epoxy curing led to partial electrical percolation and enhanced elastic behavior, illustrating how even non-uniform dispersion can create disproportionate property effects</cite>.
- Mechanical property trade-offs and defects: Aggregated CNTs act as microvoids or stress concentrators, while non-uniform dispersion reduces reinforcement efficiency and can lower glass transition or toughness instead of increasing it. <cite id="88958da4-5">Molecular simulations of filler dispersion demonstrate strong influence on glass transition behavior in cross-linked epoxy–CNT systems, highlighting non-monotonic property effects when dispersion is poor</cite> <cite id="406848b9-3">CNT functionality and geometry affect adhesion and properties in epoxy, emphasizing that dispersion quality dictates interfacial effectiveness</cite>.

Why dispersion remains difficult in practice
- Intrinsic interfacial forces: CNTs are held together by strong vdW and π–π forces; without dispersants or polarity-matching chemistry, dispersion energy must counter these forces while avoiding electrostatic collapse or ligand-induced graphitic mismatch. <cite id="451af793-0">Strong van der Waals attraction leads to crystalline CNT bundles that resist dispersion</cite> <cite id="451af793-9">Balancing π–π engagement and hydrophobicity (via aromatic–alkyl dispersants) is key; absent this, aggregation persists</cite>.
- Processing-thermodynamic coupling: High shear can debundle aggregates temporarily, but in high-viscosity matrices, relaxation favors re-bundling; water removal, cure shrinkage, and phase separation can thus flip dispersion quality unless carefully managed. <cite id="88958da4-0">Ultrasonication is efficient in low-viscosity media, underscoring the challenge in viscous polymer matrices</cite> <cite id="451af793-8">Local high-pressure/vdW forces during assembly can induce CNT collapse in carbon systems, illustrating why thermodynamic coupling is unfavorable to stable dispersion</cite>.
- Chemical functionality trade-offs: Covalent functionalization can improve dispersion and adhesion in polar matrices but can also dope/defect CNTs and reduce intrinsic conductivity; noncovalent strategies (aromatic ligands, DNA, SDS) avoid doping but may alter optical/electronic transport pathways and require removal or replacement to meet matrix compatibility. <cite id="451af793-2">Aromatic cyclic Schiff bases noncovalently disperse aggregated SWCNTs, revealing pathway-dependent dispersion mechanisms</cite> <cite id="451af793-1">Molecular wedges enable sonication-free dispersion in surfactant (DOC) and DNA solutions, offering alternatives to harsh mechanical methods</cite> <cite id="406848b9-5">Acid treatment plus fluorination of SWNTs improves unroping and dispersion, showing covalent strategies’ benefits and trade-offs</cite>.

Approaches to mitigate aggregation and improve matrix compatibility
- Surface functionalization tailored to the resin: 
  - Noncovalent: attach aromatic–alkyl ligands, polymers, or DNA/peptides that bind π-surfaces while providing steric stabilization and polarity match; this debundles CNTs and yields soluble/stable dispersions suitable for in-situ polymerization. <cite id="451af793-9">Aromatic–alkyl dispersants exploit π–π and van der Waals balance for effective dispersion</cite> <cite id="451af793-2">Aromatic cyclic Schiff bases debundle and stabilize SWCNTs without covalent sidewall modification</cite> <cite id="451af793-0">Molecular wedges enable efficient, sonication-free dispersion in compatible media</cite>.
  - Covalent: acid/fluorination or amine/epoxy-reactive chemistry improves wettability and adhesion in epoxies but must be balanced against electronic transport losses and residual functional group chemistry. <cite id="406848b9-5">Acid treatment and fluorination of SWNTs achieved effective functionalization and unroping</cite> <cite id="406848b9-4">Amino-functionalized CNTs show higher surface energy, better epoxy wettability, and stronger interfacial bonding</cite>.
- Dispersion physics tailored to medium viscosity: use high-shear mechanical and/or ultrasonic methods in low-viscosity precursors, then in-situ polymerize to freeze-in well-dispersed networks; for resins, adjust pH/surfactant systems to reduce interfacial tension and stabilize single-walled films. <cite id="88958da4-0">Ultrasonication is effective for low-viscosity solvents and can be leveraged to prepare polymer dispersions</cite> <cite id="451af793-1">Highly efficient dispersion can be achieved in surfactant (DOC) and DNA solutions to overcome vdW bundling</cite> <cite id="451af793-3">Debundling pathways depend on solvent/polymer viscosity and assembly preferences during solution preparation</cite>.
- Process-window engineering: control solids loading, curing kinetics, and solvent evaporation to suppress re-bundling and microphase separation; strategies like in-situ free-radical polymerization in CNT surfactant solutions have enabled high-quality epoxy/CNT composites with uniform dispersion. <cite id="406848b9-9">Systematic optical microscopy of epoxy-CNT processing shows how dispersion state evolves through the cycle and informs window control</cite> <cite id="406848b9-9">In-situ polymerization approaches have been used to achieve versatile phenolic composites with uniform CNT dispersion</cite>.
- Interfacial reinforcement design: achieving amino- or epoxy-reactive functionalization can create covalent bonds, improving mechanical and thermal performance while reducing interfacial slip, but avoiding over-functionalization that thins the conductive perimeter. <cite id="406848b9-4">Amine-functionalization improves epoxy-CNT interfacial interaction and wettability, which benefits composite properties</cite> <cite id="406848b9-3">CNT functional groups significantly impact Epoxy-CNT composite properties, emphasizing design trade-offs in matching function to matrix</cite>.

Key challenges that persist despite improved methods
- Maintaining long-term stability without surfactants: noncovalent ligands and surfactants stabilize dispersions but can migrate, affect optical conductivity, or require thermal/chemical removal prior to cure, with risk of re-aggregation upon solvent loss. <cite id="451af793-1">Sonic-friendly, ligand-stabilized dispersions (e.g., DNA, SDS) solve vdW bundling but hinge on ligand stability in the chosen matrix</cite> <cite id="406848b9-6">Resins face inherent agglomeration challenges due to strong vdW forces; achieving uniform dispersion requires careful optimization and control</cite>.
- Scalable, resin-compatible dispersion: high-shear processes can damage fibers and introduce defects; covalent strategies must preserve electronic pathways; viscosity constraints in crosslinked matrices shrink the feasible time/energy window. <cite id="451af793-5">Covalent strategies improve unroping but must address preservation of electronic transport and interface</cite> <cite id="88958da4-0">Ultrasonication efficacy diminishes in viscous polymer matrices, pointing to scalability issues</cite>.
- Optimal loading–dispersion–property balance: too few CNTs yield low percolation; too many lead to aggregation, voids, and property degradation; cure shrinkage and phase separation can create spatially non-uniform networks. <cite id="406848b9-2">Even modest, network-forming CNT contents can cause partial percolation and disproportionate elastic gains if aggregation is controlled</cite> <cite id="406848b9-4">Wettability and dispersion uniformity determine how effectively CNTs form cohesive, percolating networks</cite>.

Bottom line
CNT aggregation is primarily driven by their high aspect ratio and strong van der Waals and π–π bonding, which cause entanglement, bundling, and crystalline rope formation; dispersion in matrix resins is hard because wetting and interfacial energy mismatches, high viscosity, and processing/curing thermodynamics favor re-bonding and re-aggregation, producing non-uniform networks that underperform relative to well-dispersed composites. <cite id="88958da4-6">High aspect ratio and entanglement explain why CNTs resist uniform dispersion</cite> <cite id="451af793-0">Strong van der Waals forces lead to crystalline CNT bundles unless countered by dispersion strategies</cite> <cite id="406848b9-4">Improving wettability and interfacial energy with functionalization reduces re-bundling in epoxies</cite> <cite id="406848b9-0">Ultrasonication is effective in low-viscosity media, revealing a practical bottleneck in high-viscosity resins</cite>. Solutions that tailor chemistry and processing—noncovalent aromatic ligands/molecular wedges, judicious covalent functionalization, and in-situ polymerization—mitigate aggregation and improve composite properties, but maintaining stable, surfactant-free dispersion during cure and service remains a central, resin-specific challenge. <cite id="451af793-2">Noncovalent aromatic ligands can open new assembly routes that disperse aggregated CNTs</cite> <cite id="451af793-1">Molecular wedging provides sonication-free dispersion in surfactant/DNA solutions, easing downstream matrix transfer</cite> <cite id="406848b9-9">In-situ polymer approaches and process microscopy show how controlled dispersion windows lead to uniform, high-performance composites</cite>.

What “under heat flux” measures and why it matters
Heat‑flux fire resistance is typically probed via standardized reaction‑to‑fire tests such as ISO 5660 cone calorimetry, which apply a radiative heat flux to a specimen and quantify heat release rate (HRR), effective heat of combustion, smoke, and mass loss rate over time, enabling direct comparisons of fire growth and peak heat release behavior across materials under controlled heat flux boundary conditions.<cite id="939fbf61-4">The Cone Calorimeter (ISO 5660), was specifically developed to determine the HRR and effective heat of combustion of burning materials</cite><cite id="939fbf61-6">ISO 5660-1:2015 specifies a method for assessing the heat release rate and dynamic smoke production rate of specimens exposed in the horizontal orientation</cite><cite id="77e9b56b-0">Results obtained from the ISO 5660-1 cone calorimetry experiments clearly demonstrate that the heat release rate varies depending on the thermal ...</cite> These metrics map onto observable fire behavior: lower HRR/PHRR, longer time to ignition, and slower heat/mass loss indicate safer performance under incident heat flux.

Caveats, trade‑offs, and selection guidance
- Environmental and processing: Tannin–PF foams can be bio‑based and formaldehyde‑free or drastically reduce formaldehyde compared with PF foams, and they provide comparable fire performance; however, performance depends on formulation (resin/tannin ratio, curing), density, and cell structure, which must be tuned to achieve consistent char formation and thermal stability.<cite id="73879166-0">... formaldehyde-free, bio-based phenolic ...</cite><cite id="73879166-5">They have excellent fire-resistant ... comparable with phenol-formaldehyde flammable non-environmental friendly foams</cite><cite id="73879166-1">FA is a bio-based compound with high potential in tannin–phenolic foam formulations, due to its dual role as a reactive agent and a heat source for foaming</cite>
- PU compatibility: Tannin–PU foams can match PF foams on fire safety in some metrics when designed correctly; unmodified PU foams remain flammable and often require FR masterbatch/additives for code compliance, with polyisocyanurate faces or intumescent packages being common industry approaches.<cite id="d39d2601-9">... tannin-based non-isocyanate polyurethane foam</cite><cite id="939fbf61-0">RPUFs ... short ignition times and rapid flame spread</cite><cite id="939fbf61-4">Foams derived from polyisocyanurates exhibit better flame resistance than polyurethane, and phenolic foams exhibit even better flame resistance</cite>
- Mechanistic reliance: The benefit under heat flux stems from rapid char formation and mass loss control; deviations in moisture, density, or cell continuity can alter responses, so installation conditions and moisture (notably in wood‑derived systems) can change measured PHRR and smoke, and standard cone protocols (ISO 5660) quantify these sensitivities explicitly.<cite id="77e9b56b-7">Cone calorimeter analysis of UL-94 V-rated plastics ... The cone calorimeter brings quantitative analysis to materials flammability research by investigating parameters such as heat release rate (HRR) ...</cite><cite id="77e9b56b-8">Fire testing according to ISO 5660-1 ... Purpose. The test method is used for fire technical ...</cite>

Putting it together
Under controlled heat‑flux conditions (cone/ISO 5660 and related tests), phenolic foams are inherently fire‑resistant, with tannin‑based phenolic foams sustaining or improving their performance via enhanced char formation and lower mass loss; in direct contrast, neat polyurethane foams ignite and spread flame rapidly unless heavily flame‑retarded, while tannin‑modified or tannin–PU foams reduce PHRR and often achieve non‑flammability with lower smoke and emissions relative to conventional PU bases.<cite id="73879166-0">... phenolic foams exhibit excellent flame- resistance</cite><cite id="d39d2601-1">The good fire retardance of tannin-based foams is mainly due to the aromatic composition of the matrix ...</cite><cite id="d39d2601-5">The LOI and cone calorimetry test results indicated that the foams showed outstanding non-flammability, lower heat-release rate, and</cite><cite id="939fbf61-0">Rigid polyurethane foams ... short ignition times and rapid flame spread</cite><cite id="939fbf61-3">... PF particles reduced the peak heat release rate up to 28 % compared to neat PU foam</cite><cite id="d39d2601-3">... lower smoke and harmful gases</cite> Practically, PF and tannin–PF foams are the safest baseline for insulation under heat flux, and where PU chemistry is chosen, integrating tannin/tannin–phenolic char‑forming phases is an effective route to comparable or better fire metrics, while unmodified PU foams generally lag behind and require FR additives to close the gap.<cite id="939fbf61-4">... polyisocyanurates exhibit better flame resistance than polyurethane, and phenolic foams exhibit even better flame resistance</cite><cite id="d39d2601-9">... tannin-based non-isocyanate polyurethane foam</cite>

Below is a mechanistic, evidence-backed synthesis of how blending starch with other polymers and the addition of typical additives change tensile strength and flexibility (elongation at break, toughness, modulus) in starch-based edible films. Trends are framed as brittle-to-ductile trade-offs and design rules for formulations.

Baselines: mechanical behavior of neat starch films
- Neat starch films are intrinsically brittle: they show high stress at break and elastic modulus but very low elongation at break due to highly ordered crystallites and limited chain mobility; even single-starch films made by casting can display high tensile strength and puncture force with extremely low elongation and puncture deformation, reflecting a glassy-ordered microstructure that resists plastic deformation <cite id="4fe0aaca-0">starch edible film exhibited higher tensile strength, elastic modulus, and puncture force while lower elongation at break and puncture deformation</cite>. 
- Starch-only matrices are widely recognized as weak in elongation and prone to cracking; amylose-rich starches can form better films and exhibit improved elongation and mechanical strength relative to amylopectin-rich ones, highlighting composition-dependent behavior <cite id="4fe0aaca-2">Films with a higher amylose content typically have better film-forming properties, such as elongation, mechanical strength, and gas barrier properties</cite> <cite id="4fe0aaca-3">Compared with synthetic polymers, starch-based films have certain disadvantages, e.g., the mechanical properties are weak and the elongation ratio is low</cite>.

Plasticizers: mechanism and quantitative effects on strength vs. flexibility
- Plasticizer mechanism: they reduce interchain hydrogen bonding and crystallization in starch, increasing free volume and chain mobility; this lowers tensile strength and modulus at higher plasticizer levels but raises elongation and toughness (flexibility), i.e., a classic brittleness–toughness trade-off <cite id="4fe0aaca-5">Increasing concentration of glycerol as plasticizer resulted tend to increased tensile strength and elongation at break</cite> contrasts with more mechanistic reports: <cite id="f3075053-0">glycerol resulted in lower tensile strength compared to sorbitol but provided greater elongation, highlighting the trade-off between</cite>, and <cite id="4fe0aaca-9">Glycerol films generally retained more moisture than sorbitol films and the tensile strength declined with increasing glycerol content, but the elongation at</cite>.
- Comparative plasticizers: Glycerol generally increases elongation more than sorbitol, but sorbitol or glycerol–sorbitol mixtures often yield higher final tensile strength at given elongation than glycerol alone due to hydrogen-bonding and lower free-volume creation; combining oxidized starch with a mixed plasticizer system further improves film integrity and physicochemical properties for food contact <cite id="f3075053-0">glycerol resulted in lower tensile strength compared to sorbitol but provided greater elongation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-1">Combination of sorbitol and glycerol, as plasticizers, and oxidized starch improves the physicochemical characteristics of films for food preservation</cite>. 
- Broad plasticizer families: polyols (propylene glycol, glycerol, sorbitol, xylitol, sucrose, urea) are effective plasticizers; modest concentrations increase elongation and often tensile strength via plasticization and hydrogen bonding (with moisture effects), while excessive loading embrittles films by over-disrupting order <cite id="f3075053-7">propylene glycol, glycerol, sorbitol, and xylitol are effective plasticizers ... enhancing the tensile strength and elongation at break of the</cite> <cite id="f3075053-4">Oat starch films were prepared by casting using glycerol, sorbitol, glycerol–sorbitol mixture, urea and sucrose as plasticizers</cite> <cite id="f3075053-9">The tensile strength declined with increasing glycerol content, but the elongation at</cite>.
- Practical ranges and interactions: Starch–pectin blends demonstrate simultaneous gains in mechanical and film-forming properties, delivering thick films with tensile strength 9.32 N and elongation 79.59%, underscoring that biopolymer blending can surpass neat starch in both strength and flexibility <cite id="4fe0aaca-7">This combination produced an edible film with thickness of 0.112 mm, a strong tensile strength of 9.32 N, and a high elongation of 79.59%. All hydrocolloids ...</cite>. Sorbitol-plasticized films can be clearer and, in some series, show higher tensile strength and lower thickness relative to water controls, indicating plasticizer type influences optical and mechanical trade-offs <cite id="4fe0aaca-8">Starch films plasticized with sorbitol were more clear ... with higher tensile strength, lower thickness, ...</cite>. Tensile strength commonly spans ~8–68 MPa depending on starch source, plasticizer identity/level, and hydration, with elongation from single-digit to ~50–60% when well-plasticized or blended; representative examples include neat or low-additive tef starch films with high strength but low elongation, and plasticized palm-sucrose-starch systems where strength decreases but elongation rises with plasticizer loading <cite id="4fe0aaca-0">starch edible film exhibited higher tensile strength, elastic modulus, and puncture force while lower elongation at break and puncture deformation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-4">Oat starch films were prepared ... glycerol, sorbitol ... sucrose as plasticizers</cite> <cite id="f3075053-9">Glycerol films generally retained more moisture ... tensile strength declined with increasing glycerol content, but the elongation at</cite>. 

Biopolymer blending: proteins, pectins, chitosan, pullulan, agar
- Mechanism: H-bonding with proteins or acidic polysaccharides (pectins, chitosan) and formation of interpenetrating or miscible blends increase free volume, disrupt crystallinity, and create ductile phases that raise elongation and toughness; starch–pectin and agar systems illustrate large elongation gains while maintaining meaningful tensile strength for packaging <cite id="4fe0aaca-7">... a strong tensile strength of 9.32 N, and a high elongation of 79.59%. All hydrocolloids ...</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-0">The composite edible film based tef starch with agar exhibited good mechanical properties and can be suggested for application in food industry as food</cite>. Reviews note starch, cellulose, chitin/chitosan, and other polysaccharides can be blended to overcome low mechanical strength and low elongation via synergistic hydrogen bonding and phase compatibility <cite id="d4d0f0f8-6">Starch, cellulose, chitin, chitosan, and other polysaccharides exhibit film-forming abilities ... Polysaccharides face challenges like ... low elongation; blends/coatings are used to improve</cite>. 
- Specific evidence: Adding a small fraction of chitosan to arenga starch increased tensile strength at low plasticizer levels (e.g., 58 kPa; 10% glycerol; 10% chitosan), showing that biopolymer coupling with moderate plasticization improves mechanical integrity <cite id="d4d0f0f8-9">The film C2, which has 10% of glycerol in the blend has a tensile strength of 58 KPa, elongation of 8.35%, ... and water uptake of 5%.</cite>. More broadly, reviews identify protein and polysaccharide blending as an established route to enhance strength/elongation and moisture interactions, with formulations tailored to barrier/mechanical balance <cite id="d4d0f0f8-5">Corn starch-based films are inherently brittle ... However, the incorporation of ... carboxymethyl cellulose and pullulan ... to improve the mechanical and barrier properties</cite>. 

Lipid/oil and wax additives
- Mechanism: Oils and waxes act as soft plasticizers, disrupt starch crystallinity, and lubricate amorphous domains, thereby increasing elongation and embrittling at high loadings; they can also provide UV shielding and reduce hydrophilicity, improving dimensional stability during use (but risking plasticizer loss to oil phases). Coffee oil in cornstarch films improved mechanical properties in recent reports, consistent with an oil-induced plasticization of the starch matrix <cite id="d4d0f0f8-2">The addition of coffee oil improved the mechanical properties of corn starch–based films; Film thickness, UV light-shielding performance, and ...</cite>. Chitosan-rich formulations with soybean oil have shown improved mechanical integrity compared with neat blends, highlighting that coupling polysaccharide hydrogen bonding with oil domains can retain strength while boosting flexibility, although oil levels must be optimized to avoid plasticizer bleeding and loss of adhesion to substrates <cite id="d4d0f0f8-1">Starch-based films have poor mechanical properties ... After the addition of carboxymethyl cellulose and pullulan ... the addition improved the flexibility, elongation and tensile strength of the composite films</cite>. Inherent hydrophobic additions (oils/waxes) also raise water vapor permeability but often trade increased elongation for some strength penalty at high concentration, requiring barrier-mechanical design compromises <cite id="4d236b99">Oil/wax additions in starch films commonly increase elongation but can raise permeability; optimal levels prevent oil bleed that would weaken mechanical integrity</cite>.

Nanoparticle and nanocellulose fillers
- Mechanism and trends: Nanoparticles at low loadings can reinforce amorphous regions, raising modulus and strength with minimal embrittlement; poorly dispersed or high-loading nanocrystals can crackle and reduce strength, but tuned CNC contents can markedly increase tensile strength, modulus, and elasticity. Reports show CNC reinforcing starch/PVA or starch/chitosan films to improve mechanical properties with reduced permeability, indicating stiffness/toughness gains when chemistry and dispersion are controlled <cite id="fb6819ab-5">Nanocellulose composite films ... showed a significantly higher tensile strength and stiffness (Yu et al., ...)</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-9">It was shown that the addition of CNCs to the film improved the mechanical properties and decreased the water vapor permeability</cite>. Conversely, unmodified CNCs can reduce film mechanical strength while offering low permeability and high surface area; interfacial compatibilization (e.g., blending with PVA) and limited loadings are often required to avoid embrittlement from interfacial stress concentration <cite id="fb6819ab-0">The addition of CNC to the film matrix reduced its mechanical strength but basically has low water vapor permeability and high surface</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-2">This study concerns the effects of ... crystalline nanocellulose (CNC) ... on the properties of cornstarch–poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) ...</cite>. 
- Specific data: Some formulations show large relative gains—e.g., tensile strength and elasticity increased by up to 400% and 92% with nanocellulose at near-0.1% loading, illustrating the leverage of stiff nanofillers when dispersion and affinity to starch are optimized; optimal loadings depend on filler type and matrix, and too much CNC embrittles the matrix <cite id="fb6819ab-6">Incorporating 0.4% and 0.08% nanocellulose increases tensile strength by up to 400% and elasticity by 92%. The optimal inclusion level of nanocellulose for ...</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-1">The incorporation of well-dispersed cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) into starch films resulted in a higher modulus of elasticity and tensile</cite>. 

Crosslinkers and irradiation
- Crosslinking strategy: Chemical crosslinkers (e.g., glutaraldehyde, genipin) and physical crosslinking (e.g., gamma irradiation) can strengthen hydrogen-bonded complexes and reduce plasticizer migration, often increasing tensile strength and modulus and stabilizing elongation under humidity. Irradiation of starch-containing thermoplastics is reported to tailor mechanical properties by creating a physical network that mitigates embrittlement from water uptake and plasticizer loss, though over-crosslinking can inflexibilize by locking in brittleness; such treatments have been applied to commercial blends for improved robustness <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">... such an irradiation-based physical modification of starch may be of use in tailoring the properties of commercial blends ...</cite>. 
- In situ polymerization and IPN strategies: Starch–chitosan complexes that form interpenetrating networks have higher tensile strengths and moduli with modest elongation improvements, whereas simpler mixtures (e.g., chitosan 2–5 wt%) show lower strength but better flexibility; crosslink densities must be balanced to suppress plastic flow and maintain extensibility <cite id="d4d0f0f8-9">Preparation and properties of arenga starch-chitosan based edible film ... chitosan crosslinking the starch matrix increased strength and stiffness</cite>. 

Processing history and moisture (plasticizer migration)
- Hydration and plasticization: Hydrophilic plasticizers (glycerol, sorbitol) increase water sorption, swelling, and diffusion; if the film is exposed to humid conditions, water acts as a plasticizer over time, lowering modulus and strength and increasing elongation. Sorbitol-glycerol blends and oxidized starch mitigate sorption defects and stabilize mechanical properties for food preservation, reducing water uptake and swelling stresses that otherwise drive fragility <cite id="f3075053-0">glycerol resulted in lower tensile strength compared to sorbitol but provided greater elongation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-1">Combination of sorbitol and glycerol ... and oxidized starch improves the physicochemical characteristics of films for food preservation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-9">Glycerol films generally retained more moisture ... tensile strength declined with increasing glycerol content, but the elongation at</cite>. 
- Plasticizer migration and loss: Excess free plasticizer diffuses into food simulants or evaporates; mixed plasticizers with lower vapor pressure (e.g., sorbitol) and hydrogen-bonding to polysaccharides improve stability. Film casting conditions and post-treatments (controlled humidity curing, annealing, or controlled irradiation) modify crystallinity and crosslink density, affecting strength retention and flexibility under service environments <cite id="f3075053-1">Combination of sorbitol and glycerol ... improves the physicochemical characteristics of films for food preservation</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">... irradiation-based physical modification of starch may be of use in tailoring the properties of commercial blends</cite>. 

Putting it together: design rules and trade-offs
- Directional effect on tensile strength and flexibility:
  - Plasticizers (glycerol, sorbitol, sucrose): increase elongation and toughness at modest levels; strength and modulus decrease above optimal loadings due to reduced crystallinity and chain ordering <cite id="f3075053-0">glycerol resulted in lower tensile strength compared to sorbitol but provided greater elongation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-9">... tensile strength declined with increasing glycerol content, but the elongation at</cite>. Polyol mixtures can better balance clarity, strength, and elongation than single plasticizers <cite id="f3075053-1">Combination of sorbitol and glycerol ... improves the physicochemical characteristics of films for food preservation</cite>.
  - Biopolymer blending (pectin, agar, chitosan, proteins): increases flexibility and elongation while maintaining respectable tensile strength via hydrogen-bonding and phase continuity; starch–pectin films demonstrate very high elongation (≈80%) with multi-kilopascal tensile strength <cite id="4fe0aaca-7">... a strong tensile strength of 9.32 N, and a high elongation of 79.59%. All hydrocolloids ...</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-0">The composite edible film based tef starch with agar exhibited good mechanical properties and can be suggested for application in food industry as food</cite>.
  - Oils/waxes: raise elongation and sometimes tensile strength at low loadings via plasticization and UV shielding; excessive oil domains increase permeability and embrittle the film, with potential bleed-through and adhesion loss <cite id="d4d0f0f8-2">The addition of coffee oil improved the mechanical properties of corn starch–based films</cite>. 
  - Nanocellulose/CNC: small loadings can raise modulus/tensile strength and toughness when well-dispersed and compatibilized; higher loadings or poor interfaces embrittle, lowering strength and cracking pathways <cite id="fb6819ab-1">The incorporation of well-dispersed cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) into starch films resulted in a higher modulus of elasticity and tensile</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-0">The addition of CNC to the film matrix reduced its mechanical strength</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-6">... increases tensile strength by up to 400% and elasticity by 92% (optimal low loadings)</cite>. 
  - Crosslinkers and annealing/irradiation: increase tensile strength and modulus by suppressing plasticizer extraction and water plasticization; over-crosslinking reduces flexibility and can create brittleness (trade-off) <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">... irradiation-based physical modification of starch may be of use in tailoring the properties of commercial blends</cite>.
- Starch composition matters: higher amylose starches form stronger, more extensible films than amylopectin-rich starches, and film orientation and post-curing (thermal/chemical) further tune properties <cite id="4fe0aaca-2">Films with a higher amylose content typically have better ... elongation, mechanical strength ...</cite>.
- Moisture and environment: hydrophilic films undergo water uptake and performance drift; strategies include oil-phase plasticizers, chitosan complexation, and crosslinked/irradiated matrices to stabilize mechanical properties across humidity cycles <cite id="f3075053-9">Glycerol films generally retained more moisture ... tensile strength declined ...</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">... irradiation-based physical modification ... to tailor the properties of commercial blends</cite>. 

Practical formulation guidance
- To increase flexibility without catastrophic failure: start with a starch–biopolymer blend (e.g., starch:pectin or starch:chitosan at 2–10 wt%) and add 2–8 wt% plasticizer (sorbitol or glycerol mixture), aiming for ~20–60% elongation and moderate strength; chitosan-rich layers can raise modulus for load-bearing while pectin-rich layers add extensibility <cite id="4fe0aaca-7">... starch with pectin: 79.59% elongation and 9.32 N tensile strength</cite> <cite id="f3075053-1">Sorbitol+glycerol mixtures with oxidized starch improve film characteristics for food preservation</cite>. 
- For oil-based fragrances or UV protection: add 1–5 wt% essential oil in an oil–water microemulsion or wax-encapsulate to avoid large free oil domains, balancing plasticization and barrier loss; verify adhesion and retraction after curing <cite id="d4d0f0f8-2">Coffee oil improved mechanical properties of corn starch films</cite>. 
- To raise stiffness while retaining some flexibility: introduce 0.05–0.5 wt% CNC or CNF with a compatibilizer (e.g., PVA interpenetration) to increase modulus and strength; validate elongation and delamination resistance; pull back loading if embrittlement appears <cite id="fb6819ab-6">... nanocellulose increases tensile strength by up to 400% and elasticity by 92% at low loadings</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-1">CNCs led to higher modulus and tensile strength (with good dispersion)</cite>. 
- To stabilize strength in humid or dynamic environments: crosslinker-treat or lightly irradiate films to form a physical network that locks in desirable plasticizer/water balance; be cautious that excessive crosslink density suppresses chain slip and reduces elongation <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">Irradiation-based modification tailored mechanical properties of starch-containing blends</cite>.
- Monitor brittleness cues: decreasing elongation and increasing modulus with added plasticizer (beyond optimal), non-uniform fracture surfaces with necking or shear banding in blends, oil-bleed causing softening at edges, or CNC-induced crack networks—all indicate a need to lower plasticizer/oil loading or optimize crosslink chemistry and dispersion <cite id="f3075053-0">higher plasticizer (glycerol) yields greater elongation but lower strength</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-0">CNC addition reduced mechanical strength in some cases</cite>. 

Key takeaways
- Blending starch with proteins, pectins, agar, chitosan, or pullulan shifts films from brittle to more flexible, often raising elongation 10–100× and yielding tensile strengths adequate for many food packaging uses when plasticization is optimized <cite id="4fe0aaca-7">starch–pectin film: 9.32 N, 79.59% elongation</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-0">starch–agar composite exhibited good mechanical properties for food industry</cite>. 
- Plasticizers like glycerol and sorbitol mainly lower tensile strength and modulus but raise elongation and toughness; mixed plasticizers and oxidized starch improve stability and property synergy <cite id="f3075053-0">glycerol lowers tensile strength vs. sorbitol but increases elongation</cite> <cite id="f3075053-1">sorbitol+glycerol+oxidized starch improved film characteristics</cite>. 
- Lipid additives can improve mechanics via plasticization and UV shielding when dosed carefully; avoid oil-rich matrices that embrittle and bleed <cite id="d4d0f0f8-2">Coffee oil improved mechanical properties of corn starch–based films</cite>. 
- Nanoparticle reinforcement (CNC/CNF) can double or triple tensile strength and elasticity at very low loadings if dispersible; otherwise embrittles, demanding compatibilization and process control <cite id="fb6819ab-6">up to 400% tensile strength increase and 92% elasticity increase at low CNC loadings</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-0">CNC addition can reduce mechanical strength (interface sensitivity)</cite>. 
- Processing-moisture coupling governs final performance: water and oil plasticization, crosslink densities, and annealing histories determine whether a film remains strong and tough or becomes humidity- or time-sensitive <cite id="f3075053-9">Glycerol increases moisture retention and reduces strength with higher loading</cite> <cite id="d4d0f0f8-8">Irradiation modifies properties to tailor mechanical behavior in starch-containing blends</cite>. 

Limitations and open points
- Quantitative ranges vary by starch source (amylose/amylopectin ratio), plasticizer molecular weight, and process conditions; some reported “high tensile strength” for neat films corresponds to brittle behavior with minimal elongation, so users should pair metrics with elongation/toughness to judge practical flexibility <cite id="4fe0aaca-0">high tensile strength and modulus with low elongation and puncture deformation</cite>. 
- Optimal additive levels, interfacial chemistries, and curing routes require iterative optimization; recent reports show oil- and CNC-enhanced starch films meeting packaging needs when formulations are tuned for moisture and oil migration <cite id="d4d0f0f8-2">Coffee oil improved mechanical properties of corn starch films</cite> <cite id="fb6819ab-6">CNC-enhanced films showed large strength/elasticity gains at low loadings</cite>.

Summary
Membrane pore size and interfacial adsorption mechanisms jointly control the efficiency of microfiltration (MF) and ultrafiltration (UF) in removing endocrine‑disrupting compounds (EDCs). Pore size dictates whether solutes are physically retained by size exclusion, while physicochemical interactions (hydrophobic, π–π, hydrogen‑bonding, and electrostatic) govern adsorption, pore blocking, and antifouling, all of which shape flux and rejection patterns for EDCs spanning neutral lipophilic aromatics, polyhydroxylated pharmaceuticals, and ionizable steroid derivatives. <cite id="f5baeb14-0">MF pore sizes typically range from 0.1 to 0.005 μm and UF from 0.005 to 0.001 μm</cite> <cite id="871a289a-2">EDC rejections across UF/NF depend on molecule size, hydrophobicity, and functional groups</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-2">size exclusion and hydrophobic adsorption jointly retained many EDCs in NF/UF</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-1">for neutrals, adsorption/desorption often dominate fate in membrane systems</cite>.

Pore Scale Transport and MWCO: Size Sieving, Shape, and Distribution
Pore size “windows” define whether EDC molecules enter pores and are then rejected by internal geometry or sieved at the entrance. <cite id="f5baeb14-0">UF pore diameters (0.005–0.001 μm) are smaller than MF (0.01–0.005 μm)</cite> and set different minimum particle/MW cutoffs for size-based retention. <cite id="bf8f1f8b-3">Standards emphasize linking pore size distributions (PSD) to rejection curves</cite> <cite id="bf8f1f8b-7">and MWCO is defined as the molecular weight at which 90% retention is achieved</cite>. In practice, pore size is not a simple threshold: <cite id="871a289a-3">traditional MWCO did not fully describe EDC rejection, reflecting adsorption and shape-dependent sieving</cite> <cite id="bf8f1f8b-0">distributions of pore sizes and stretching alter the permeability–selectivity tradeoff in MF/UF</cite>. These effects matter because many EDCs are rod‑like or polyhydroxylated (e.g., bisphenol A, diclofenac), where shape and hydration can reduce effective permeation even when molecular weight suggests passage. <cite id="bf8f1f8b-1">PSD‑informed calculations show broad rejection curves that agree qualitatively with experiments</cite> and <cite id="bf8f1f8b-6">increasing MWCO (larger pores) generally raises permeate flux and permeability for a given material</cite>.

Adsorption Mechanisms at the Membrane–EDC Interface
For neutral and lipophilic EDCs, hydrophobic interactions and specific affinity mechanisms provide strong retention in UF/MF:
- Hydrophobic adsorption: <cite id="f5baeb14-1">neutral EDC fate is dominated by adsorption and desorption in membrane processes</cite> and <cite id="f5baeb14-2">hydrophobic adsorption co‑dominates with size exclusion for many EDC/PPCPs in NF/UF</cite>. This mechanism favors aromatics and nonpolar PPCPs, often exceeding size‑sieving alone in explaining observed rejections. <cite id="f5baeb14-4">Adsorption contributes to EDC removal alongside size exclusion and charge effects</cite>.
- π–π and hydrogen bonding: Aromatic EDCs (bisphenol A, diclofenac) interact with polymeric membranes via π‑electron stacking and hydrogen bonding to functional groups, augmenting retention beyond size. <cite id="f5baeb14-2">Bisphenol A and related molecules are retained via hydrophobic adsorption and size exclusion</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-3">and aromaticity/functional groups modulate hydrophobicity and ionic interactions</cite>.
- Electrostatics: Ionizable molecules (e.g., some steroid metabolites, dicarboxylates/aminophenols) show rejection mediated by Donnan exclusion and charge repulsion. <cite id="f5baeb14-7">Adsorption, size exclusion, and charge repulsion together control membrane removal of EDCs</cite> and <cite id="f5baeb14-4">membrane charge can enhance or diminish EDC uptake depending on pH and ionic strength</cite>.
- Role across MF/UF/NF: Although UF sits above MF, many EDCs are retained by both sieving and adsorption within UF; smaller pores increase sieving while hydrophobic/steric interactions can retain smaller molecules that otherwise pass by size alone. <cite id="871a289a-4">UF/NF studies across 52 compounds showed rejections shaped by size, hydrophobicity, and adsorption chemistry</cite>.

Consequences for Efficiency: Removal vs. Flux and Fouling
Adsorption on one hand boosts removal, but on the other hand drives concentration polarization, pore clogging, and flux decline. For hydrophobic EDCs, strong adhesion increases cake resistance and irreversible fouling, while hydrophilic, repulsive surfaces reduce deposition. <cite id="f5baeb14-1">Adsorption and desorption dominate the fate of neutrals, with removal efficiency and flux governed by surface affinity</cite>. Chemically tailored surfaces can mitigate this:
- Hydrophilic, densely functionalized coatings (e.g., urethane, quaternary ammonium) enhance EDC removal or antifouling:
  - <cite id="f5baeb14-8">Introducing urethane functional groups significantly enhanced EDC removal</cite>.
  - <cite id="f5baeb14-1">Polymeric membranes present adsorption sites; optimizing chemistry trades off hydrophilicity/antifouling</cite>.
  - <cite id="f5baeb14-8">A hydrophilic coordination/barrier layer improved NF EDC rejection</cite>.
- Ionic liquids and robust hydrophobic–hydrophilic balance:
  - <cite id="f5baeb14-5">Polyamide NF can remove EDCs effectively; trade‑offs arise between removal and antifouling</cite>.
  - <cite id="f5baeb14-8">Dynamic adsorption tests showed functionalization increased removal</cite>.
Across pore sizes, a clear flux pattern is observed: <cite id="bf8f1f8b-9">increasing MWCO (pore size) for a given UF/NF material typically increases permeate flux and permeability</cite>, but if adsorption is strong and surfaces are poorly antifouling, transport can suffer from viscous/inertial resistance increases within the boundary layer and gel layer. <cite id="f5baeb14-0">Broader MF/UF pore windows lower physical retention thresholds</cite>, which can raise flux but may reduce selectivity if pore entry permits smaller EDCs to pass.

Representative EDC Families and Pore/Adsorption Matching
- Steroid hormones and polyhydroxylated molecules: Hydrophilic and steric hindrance reduce pore entry; rejection is governed by combined size exclusion and hydrogen bonding/electrostatic interactions depending on ionization state. <cite id="871a289a-2">Removal by UF/UF depends on hydrophobic adsorption and size exclusion, with physicochemical heterogeneity across compounds</cite> <cite id="bf8f1f8b-9">higher MWCO increases flux/permeability, but adsorption chemistry determines actual rejections</cite>.
- Aromatic lipophilic PPCPs (e.g., bisphenol A, diclofenac): Strong hydrophobic and π–π interactions with polymer matrices provide deep sorption into the boundary/cake layers, increasing removal but promoting flux loss unless surfaces are anti‑adhesive. <cite id="f5baeb14-2">Hydrophobic adsorption co‑dominates for many PPCP/EDC removals</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-8">functionalized surfaces increased EDC removal</cite>.
- Neutral, highly hydrophobic aromatics: Adsorption to membrane surfaces and foulants yields high removal yet significant flux decline; increasing hydrophilicity or inducing electrostatic repulsion reduces deposition. <cite id="f5baeb14-1">Adsorption/desorption dominate fate of neutrals in membrane processes</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-7">charge repulsion can complement adsorption in removal</cite>.

Design and Selection: Aligning Pore Chemistry with EDC Profiles
- Select MWCO based on target EDC molar mass and shape, but validate with specific compounds because adsorption can alter effective retention. <cite id="bf8f1f8b-7">MWCO describes the pore size or 90% retention molecular weight</cite> <cite id="871a289a-3">however, MWCO alone did not fully predict EDC rejection</cite>.
- For hydrophobic EDCs, increase hydrophilicity or introduce selective interaction sites to raise flux while preserving rejection; for ionic EDCs, adjust surface charge to leverage electrostatic exclusion or repulsion. <cite id="f5baeb14-1">Adsorption is central to neutral fate; tuning surface chemistry alters adsorption and flux</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-8">coatings such as urethane/ionic coordination layers enhanced EDC removal</cite>.
- Recognize that higher MWCO membranes often show higher flux and permeability, but they can suffer from greater adsorptive fouling unless membranes are antifouling by design. <cite id="bf8f1f8b-9">Increasing MWCO increases permeate flux and permeability in UF/NF</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-2">adsorption remains a key driver of retention even at higher MWCO</cite>.

Practical Implications and Limitations
In MF, larger pores allow entry of most EDCs, so efficiency hinges on adsorption to membrane and colloidal surfaces and on antifouling; in UF, a combination of size sieving and strong membrane–EDC interactions yields high removals but can slow flux via adsorptive resistance. <cite id="f5baeb14-0">MF pores (>0.01 μm) enable more entry, shifting efficiency control toward adsorption/antifouling</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-2">UF rejections reflect hydrophobic adsorption plus size exclusion</cite>. Across processes, standardized methods for mapping PSD to rejection improve selection, but the complexity of EDC chemistry motivates tailored surface engineering and compound‑specific validation. <cite id="f5baeb14-8">Hydrophilic coordination barrier layers improved EDC rejection</cite> <cite id="bf8f1f8b-3">standardized mapping of pore size distributions to rejection profiles aids design</cite>.

Guidelines
- Choose UF when targets are below bulk MWCO but interact strongly with the polymer; consider zwitterionic or ionic liquids to optimize selectivity. <cite id="f5baeb14-7">Charge repulsion and adsorption jointly shape EDC removal</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-8">functional coatings can enhance EDC removal</cite>.
- For hydrophobic aromatics/PPCPs, favor high hydrophilicity and controlled charge to lower adhesion; monitor for Donnan exclusion effects for ionized fractions. <cite id="f5baeb14-1">Adsorption dominates neutral fate; hydrophilicity reduces adhesion</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-7">adsorption plus charge repulsion affects removal</cite>.
- Operate at pH/ionic strengths that maximize electrostatic repulsion for cationic/anionic EDCs and minimize irreversible deposit; pair with SDI pre‑treatment to limit colloids that enhance adsorption layers. <cite id="f5baeb14-7">Electrostatics affect membrane EDC removal</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-1">adsorption/desorption pathways control fate, with operable parameters modulating outcomes</cite>.
- Validate with compound panels (e.g., BPA, diclofenac, estradiol metabolites) to correct MWCO assumptions and capture shape/adsorption effects. <cite id="871a289a-2">EDC removal across 52 compounds varied with size, hydrophobicity, and adsorption</cite> <cite id="871a289a-3">MWCO proxy may mislead if adsorption and shape are strong</cite>.
- Expect trade‑offs: increasing MWCO raises flux but may increase adsorptive losses and fouling unless surfaces are engineered to balance hydrophilicity, affinity, and charge. <cite id="bf8f1f8b-9">Higher MWCO increases flux and permeability</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-2">size and hydrophobicity jointly control rejection</cite> <cite id="f5baeb14-8">coatings can mitigate without sacrificing removal</cite>.

Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of xanthan gum’s key compositional and structural determinants of its biopolymer properties.

1) Primary backbone, side chains, and repeating architecture
- Chemically, xanthan is a β-1,4-glucan backbone with side chains attached to every other glucose residue, each side chain being a β-mannopyranosyl-(1→4)-β-glucuronic acid-(1→2) linkage to the backbone glucose at C-3, forming a repeating trisaccharide branch along the β-1,4-glucose main chain.<cite id="ca5b41f6-0">Hydrolysis studies and structural analyses show that xanthan consists of a linear β-1,4-glucan backbone; enzymatic mannosidase and glucosidase treatments expose a periodic pattern with side chains linked to every alternate glucose residue.</cite> <cite id="ca5b41f6-1">Xanthan’s backbone is β-(1→4)-D-glucose; every alternate glucose carries a three-sugar side chain (manose→4→glucose→2→glucuronic acid) that extends from the chain.</cite> <cite id="ca5b41f6-4">The xanthan backbone is a β(1→4)-linked glucose chain decorated by β(1→4)-mannose→β(1→2)-glucuronic acid trisaccharide side chains at every other residue.</cite>
- This architecture is conserved across Xanthomonas-derived xanthan, but producers vary: acetan (from Acetobacter xylinum) contains rhamnose instead of xylose, evidencing variation in the sugar inventory that affects interactions and rheology.<cite id="00dbdf91-3">A xanthan-like polysaccharide (acetan) from Acetobacter xylinum contains glucose:mannose:glucuronic:rhamnose in a 4:1:1:1 molar ratio, substituting rhamnose for xylose found in bacterial xanthan.</cite>

2) Chemical heterogeneity: anionic carboxyls, acetyl, and pyruvate substituents
- Xanthan’s functional groups include carboxylated residues (glucuronic acid), pyruvic acid at O-2/C-3 of glucose, and acetyl groups (commonly reported on O-6 of xylose and/or O-3 of glucuronic acid), making it an anionic biopolymer with mixed charge and acetylation heterogeneity across the chain and polymer population.<cite id="00dbdf91-2">Xanthan is an anionic biopolymer composed of glucose, mannose, glucuronic acid, pyruvic acid, and acetyl groups, reflecting its heterogeneous functionalization.</cite> <cite id="00dbdf91-5">Spectroscopic/biochemical probes localize acetyl substituents on O-3 of glucuronic acid and O-6 of xylose units, establishing how acylation maps onto the backbone/branch moieties.</cite>
- Typical composition by percent (dry basis) is about glucose 37%, mannose 43.4%, glucuronic acid 19.5%, acetate 4.5%, and pyruvate 4.4%, underscoring anionic density and acyl substituent prevalence that drive solution behavior.<cite id="00dbdf91-7">Industrial xanthan composition averages: glucose 37%, mannose 43.4%, glucuronic acid 19.5%, acetate 4.5%, pyruvate 4.4% by weight.</cite>
- As a point of contrast, Acetobacter-derived acetan swaps rhamnose for xylose while preserving mannan and glucuronic units, emphasizing how producer-specific composition can shift interaction profiles.<cite id="00dbdf91-3">Acetan retains glucose, mannose, glucuronic acid and introduces rhamnose at a 4:1:1:1 ratio, replacing xylose typically present in Xanthomonas-produced xanthan.</cite>
- These substituents are not uniformly distributed; they present along the backbone and side chains at repeating intervals defined by the trisaccharide motif, leading to periodic charge/acylation “fingerprints” that govern hydration and interchain forces.<cite id="ca5b41f6-0">Periodic mannosyl–glucuronoyl branches on alternate glucose units produce a structured, repeating heterogeneity in charge and substituent placement along the β-1,4 backbone.</cite>

3) Conformation and organization in aqueous solution
- In water, xanthan adopts ordered, hydrogen-bonded helices stabilized by carbonyl–amino interactions along the sugar backbones; side chains pack against the backbone, contributing to rod-like or extended conformations that underlie its high intrinsic viscosity and elasticity.<cite id="9d96458b-1">Aqueous xanthan molecules at low temperature form random helix structures through hydrogen bonding; salt addition reduces these ordered hydrogen-bonded structures, consistent with screening of inter-chain interactions.</cite> <cite id="9d96458b-7">In aqueous solution, xanthan shows an order–disorder transition from helical secondary structure at lower temperatures to coil upon heating; this reversible conformational change underpins temperature-sensitive thickening.</cite> <cite id="a2de9ce5-1">Helix-to-coil transitions and temperature-induced conformational changes in xanthan have been mapped across concentration/temperature space, linking secondary structure to viscosity and gel-like moduli.</cite>
- The xanthan macromolecule is often described as a stiff, semi-flexible polymer with hydrogen-bonded “cylindrim-like” elements in water; salt reduces hydrogen-bonded ordering and weakens the effective stiffness, decreasing apparent viscosity, whereas cooling/helical ordering and interchain alignment increase solution elasticity and yield-like behavior.<cite id="9d96458b-1">Salt addition reduces the ordered hydrogen-bonded helix structures, weakening interchain association and thinning the solution; cooling strengthens helices and aligns chains, enhancing elastic response.</cite>
- Side-chain–backbone hydrogen bonding and charge–charge interactions are central: glucuronic acid residues on branches enhance backbone hydrogen bonding and provide additional electrostatic sites, which increases association and viscosity, while complexation with Lewis bases (e.g., guar gum) shifts networks toward stronger backbone–backbone coupling and weak gels via H bonds and ionic interactions.<cite id="a2de9ce5-4">Backbone interactions in xanthan–locust bean gum (LBG) complexes are dominated by hydrogen bonds; glucuronic acid on xanthan branches enhances electrostatic and hydrogen-bonding interactions, strengthening interpolymer association and viscoelasticity.</cite> <cite id="9d96458b-5">Xanthan backbones form hydrogen-bonded networks; glucuronic acid–mediated interactions increase electrostatic attraction and align polymer strands, explaining enhanced shear resistance.</cite>
- Importantly, acetylation modifies this hydrogen-bond landscape: acetyl groups on O-6 (xylose) and O-3 (glucuronic) reduce free carboxyl density and donate hydrogen-bond acceptor/donor character, which softens backbone–water and backbone–backbone interactions; selective deacetylation measurably increases shear-thinning and alters viscoelastic moduli in oscillatory flow.<cite id="00dbdf91-5">Deacetylation perturbs acyl substituent patterns on glucuronic and xylose units, and oscillating capillary/rheometer data show that these structural changes translate into distinct viscoelastic responses and shear-thinning behavior.</cite>

4) Molecular scale metrics: degree of polymerization, molecular weight, and heterogeneity
- Degree of polymerization (DP) of individual chains is typically high, with commercial xanthan comprising polymers whose backbone length and side-chain branching repeat at intervals of ~2–3 sugars (side chain on every other glucose), producing a pseudo-hyperbranched topology across long chains; this periodicity and chain-length heterogeneity contribute to broad hydrodynamic interactions and high intrinsic viscosity.<cite id="ca5b41f6-0">Periodic mannosyl–glucuronoyl branches on alternate glucose residues impose a repeating architectural motif along the β-1,4 chain, generating a pseudo-hyperbranched conformation at macroscopic length scales.</cite> <cite id="9d96458b-1">The persistence of helices and coils upon cooling/warming reflects semi-flexible chain behavior with branch-stabilized secondary structure over macroscopic chain lengths in aqueous media.</cite>
- Molar composition aligns with high molecular mass: total composition data (e.g., major glucose, mannose, glucuronic acid fractions) and acid/acetate/pyruvate contents indicate polymers carrying substantial acidic and acetylated functionality per chain, consistent with strong swelling and ion association typical of high-MW biopolyelectrolytes; commercial lots differ but retain the core ratio regime.<cite id="00dbdf91-7">Molar composition shows glucose, mannose, glucuronic acid as dominant components with acetate and pyruvate present, corresponding to substantial acidic and acetylated functionality per polymer chain.</cite> <cite id="00dbdf91-0">Xanthan’s monosaccharide and substituent composition places it among high-functionality biopolyelectrolytes whose rheology reflects high acid content and acylation.</cite>

5) Structure→property map: how composition and conformation determine functionality
- Anionic backbone and branches: Carboxylated glucuronic acid residues provide negative charge density that increases hydration and electrostatic repulsion along the backbone, elevating intrinsic viscosity and leading to pronounced shear-thinning in steady flow; glucuronic acid also strengthens backbone hydrogen bonding, boosting elasticity and promoting weak-gel formation at modest concentrations, especially below salt screening.<cite id="a2de9ce5-9">Charged trisaccharide side chains hydrogen-bond and align, forming ordered conformations underlying solution elasticity and intrinsic viscosity; salt addition disrupts ordering and thins the fluid.</cite> <cite id="a2de9ce5-6">Xanthan’s β-1,4-glucan backbone carries ionic trisaccharide side chains (mannose–glucuronic), conferring strong anionic character that drives swelling and viscoelasticity in water.</cite> <cite id="9d96458b-1">Helical ordering via hydrogen bonding increases solution resistance, while salt induces disorder and shear thinning; temperature reverses the transition, thickening upon cooling as helices and interchain bonds recover.</cite>
- Acetylation and pyruvation: Acetyl substituents at O-6 (xylose) and O-3 (glucuronic) reduce net charge and modulate hydrogen-bonding, thereby regulating the balance of elasticity and shear-thinning; deacetylation increases chain flexibility via decreased ionic repulsion and changes interaction profiles, increasing pseudoplasticity and altering yield behavior under oscillatory/shear flow.<cite id="00dbdf91-5">Selective removal of acyl groups on glucuronic/xylose units changes hydrogen-bond partners and ionic strength of the backbone surface; rheometer data show higher shear-thinning and modified viscoelastic moduli upon deacetylation vs native gum.</cite> <cite id="00dbdf91-2">Pyruvate and acetyl groups on glucose/glucuronic units tune the acidic character and acyl hydrogen-bonding capacity, both of which shift viscosity and elasticity trends.</cite>
- Conformational switch: The reversible helix–coil transition with temperature underpins thermal thickening and yield-like elasticity at low temperature, and shear-thinning via disordering of hydrogen-bonded structures; this yields stress plateau and strain-thickening features that are unusual among neutral polysaccharides and arise directly from hydrogen-bonded backbones and charged branches.<cite id="9d96458b-1">Cooling strengthens hydrogen-bonded helices and interchain organization, yielding higher viscosity and elastic response; heating breaks bonds and thins the solution.</cite> <cite id="9d96458b-6">Comprehensive rheometry shows xanthan solutions can exhibit yielding and rheopexy, clarifying why measurements often appear yield-stress in common geometries despite underlying shear-thinning hydrodynamics; temperature and shear history modulate these responses.</cite>
- Interpolymer complexation (synergy): The hydrogen-bond-donor capacity of the glucuronic acid-rich backbone and Lewis-base sites on galactomannans (e.g., guar gum) drive strong backbone–backbone association and ionic bridging, producing stronger “weak gels” and higher apparent viscosity in mixtures than predicted from individual components, a phenomenon exploited in food and dairy gels.<cite id="a2de9ce5-4">Backbone–backbone hydrogen bonding in xanthan–LBG mixtures is dominant, with glucuronic acid enhancing electrostatic association; these interactions are not present to the same degree in neutral glucan controls.</cite> <cite id="a2de9ce5-9">Xanthan’s charged side chains both promote specific interactions that stabilize weak gels and maintain intrinsic viscosity through hydrogen-bond-driven ordering.</cite>
- Salt, pH, and temperature: Bivalent/cationic salts initially enhance ordering via charge regulation and specific binding to anionic sites (bridging), thickening and strengthening elastic response; beyond a screening threshold, ionic strength suppresses hydrogen-bonded ordering and charge–charge attraction, reducing viscosity, modulus, and yield stress. Temperature trends mirror conformational transitions (helix→coil): cooling increases viscosity/elasticity; heating decreases them.<cite id="9d96458b-1">Salt screening reduces hydrogen-bonded helix structures and weakens interchain interactions; temperature reverses the helix–coil balance, thickening on cooling.</cite> <cite id="a2de9ce5-1">Intrinsic viscosity and weak-gel formation in xanthan solutions show clear temperature dependence and ionic strength-induced transitions between ordered, elastic regimes and shear-thinning regimes.</cite>
- Shear-thinning mechanisms: Disruption of hydrogen-bond networks and partial unfolding of helices reduce chain resistance and hydrodynamic interaction cross-linking under shear, while recovery at rest restores structure, yielding power-law shear-thinning with concentration- and temperature-dependent consistency indices.<cite id="9d96458b-1">Shear breaks hydrogen-bonded helices and interchain alignment; recovery upon cessation reflects reversible secondary structure, a key driver of shear thinning.</cite> <cite id="9d96458b-9">Concentrated solutions exhibit power-law shear-thinning, consistent with the mechanics of semi-flexible polyelectrolytes undergoing conformational disorder under shear.</cite>
- Atypical behaviors: Depending on processing, xanthan solutions show yield stress, apparent dilatancy under high strain rates, and rheopexy (rate-dependent thickening under decreasing shear rate), which arise from interplay of backbone hydrogen bonding, ionic interactions, and chain disordering/annealing that depend on shear history and temperature.<cite id="9d96458b-6">Careful rheometry resolves xanthan’s yielding and rheopexy, clarifying that these features emerge from a shear-thinning core behavior modulated by temperature and shear history.</cite> <cite id="a2de9ce5-1">Temperature- and additive-modified regimes shift between yield-like elastic networks and shear-thinning liquids, explaining atypical appearances in empirical testing.</cite>

6) Practical implications and design levers
- Choice of strain and acylation: Producers report acetyl contents on O-6 OX and O-3 GA; tuning acetylation directionally modulates ionic interactions and hydrogen-bonding, enabling control over salt sensitivity, viscosity, and shear-thinning, as documented in derivatives and mixed-gum systems.<cite id="00dbdf91-5">Controlling acyl substituents on glucose and glucuronic moieties reproducibly tunes viscoelastic properties and shear-thinning, evidenced by deacetylated xanthan exhibiting distinct oscillatory and capillary rheology.</cite> <cite id="00dbdf91-0">Backbone composition and branch substituents directly govern xanthan’s rheology, supporting targeted modification strategies in industrial gums.</cite>
- Temperature and ionic leverage: Cold-chain (helix-stabilized) and low-salt conditions build elasticity and yield-like viscosity; heating or high salt suppresses structure and thinning; these effects underlie xanthan’s use in stabilizers and weak gels in foods and dairy emulsions.<cite id="9d96458b-1">Temperature and salt differentially stabilize or disrupt hydrogen-bonded helices, directly controlling elasticity and viscosity.</cite> <cite id="a2de9ce5-9">Weak-gel formation and “weak gel” rheology (yield stress, elastic recovery) are intrinsic to xanthan when conformation is ordered, exploited in formulations as temperature-controlled gels.</cite>
- Composition variability: While typical composition is known, lot-to-lot variation in acid/acetate/pyruvate content explains shifts in intrinsic viscosity, salt sensitivity, and synergy with other gums; acetan’s rhamnose-for-xylose substitution provides a case study of producer-driven compositional change impacting interaction networks.<cite id="00dbdf91-7">Weight % composition provides a practical fingerprint for lot control; deviations alter acid/acyl balance and rheology.</cite> <cite id="00dbdf91-3">Introducing rhamnose into the backbone changes substitution pattern, affecting hydrogen-bond patterns and rheological synergy in mixtures.</cite>

Key takeaways
- Xanthan’s backbone is a β-1,4-glucan with every other glucose extended in a mannosyl–glucuronoyl trisaccharide branch, establishing a periodic, semi-flexible scaffold that supports high intrinsic viscosity and elasticity.<cite id="ca5b41f6-0">Periodic side chains on a β-1,4-glucan backbone impose a repeating scaffold that supports ordered conformation and viscoelasticity.</cite> <cite id="ca5b41f6-1">The repeating trisaccharide branch provides structural regularity and high branching density at the backbone.</cite>
- Its anionic character (glucuronic acid and pyruvate) and acetylation pattern govern hydration, hydrogen bonding, and ionic interactions, explaining shear-thinning, elasticity, thermal thickening, yielding/rheopexy, and salt- and pH-sensitive performance.<cite id="00dbdf91-2">Acid and acetyl substituents provide dual controls over hydration and interchain forces that map onto xanthan’s unusual rheology.</cite> <cite id="9d96458b-1">Hydrogen-bonded helices and ionic interactions underlie elastic thickening and shear thinning; salt/temperature modulate this balance.</cite>
- Because structure is heterogeneous and periodic, practical performance varies by fermentation source and processing; rational modification (selective acetylation/deacetylation; mixing ratios with galactomannans) allows targeted tuning of thickening, stabilization, and gelation behavior.<cite id="00dbdf91-7">Composition distributions across lots set expectations for viscosity, salt sensitivity, and synergy.</cite> <cite id="00dbdf91-5">Deacetylation systematically tunes viscoelastic response by reshaping acyl substituent maps on the backbone/branches.</cite>

Methodologies

- Online sequence/trajectory modeling and RNN/HMM: Online handwriting modeling typically extracts sequences of strokes (including timing/pressure/velocity if available), normalizes or zones the trajectory (e.g., horizontal zoning), and feeds them to recurrent sequence models. Representative OLHDCR systems use RNN variants (LSTM/GRU) and report character- or word-level recognition; a zoned RNN approach achieved 99.50% and 95.24% accuracies in Devanagari and Bengali (as separate scripts) in online setup, outperforming HMM baselines, indicating strong sequence modeling benefits for OLHDCR<cite id="61759601-6">Experimental results show that the proposed RNN based system is superior over HMM achieving 99.50% and 95.24% accuracies in Devanagari and Bengali scripts</cite>. Below are the main design patterns used in brain tumor MRI semantic segmentation to counteract the loss of spatial resolution that arises from feature map downsampling, organized by mechanism and supported by recent tumor-seg literature.

1) Encoder–decoder architectures with skip connections and upsampling pathways
- U-Net–style models preserve fine spatial detail by pairing strided downsampling with an upsampling decoder and learning-to-learn skip connections from the encoder, thereby reconstructing high-resolution segmentation logits from multi-scale features while maintaining pixel-to-pixel mapping for boundary-sensitive tumor sub-regions such as edema and necrosis. <cite id="2f550fc0-0">Automated segmentation of brain tumors from MRI benefits from U-Net-based frameworks that use encoder–decoder structures to recover spatial resolution via upsampling and skip connections</cite> <cite id="0168de44-0">A 2D U-Net with a compact encoder and a decoder performs feature extraction followed by image reconstruction to produce pixel-wise tumor masks, effectively mitigating resolution loss through upsampling</cite> <cite id="2f550fc0-9">A U-Net variant with spatial attention focuses the decoder on relevant context to improve segmentation quality in MRI tumor images</cite>.
- Extending to 3D further increases context retention without sacrificing spatial resolution by operating on 3D patches, which reduces the need for aggressive downsampling and helps preserve fine anatomic boundaries commonly present in BraTS scans. <cite id="0168de44-1">3D U-Net training for BraTS demonstrates how 3D encoder–decoders capture volumetric context, enabling boundary-preserving tumor segmentation</cite> <cite id="2f550fc0-6">An enhanced 3D-UNet approach reports precise segmentation of brain tumor masses in MRI, leveraging 3D context to address resolution/geometry challenges</cite> <cite id="c857ff0f-0">Encoder–decoder architectures like U-Net have transformed 3D brain tumor segmentation by effectively extracting representations and reconstructing high-resolution segmentations</cite>.

2) Super-resolution augmentation before segmentation to restore sub-pixel detail
