- Because tumor classes (e.g., peritumoral edema) have thin, fuzzy boundaries, some pipelines explicitly increase resolution using super-resolution networks before applying segmentation, so that the segmentation layer sees more sub-pixel structure. <cite id="2f550fc0-5">Super-resolution of brain tumor MRI via deep learning (MRBT-SR-GAN) improves early detection and accurate evaluation of brain tumor recurrence and prognosis, indicating that recovering fine-resolution detail can benefit downstream segmentation and diagnostic tasks</cite>. In practice, high-resolution inputs coupled with U-Net decoders allow finer boundary delineation that would otherwise be lost after heavy downsampling. <cite id="2f550fc0-9">Integrating attention in U-Net can dynamically focus on critical tumor boundaries when starting from higher-resolution inputs</cite>.

3) Multi-scale/context modules that enlarge receptive fields without halving resolution
- To avoid excessive spatial downsampling while capturing larger contexts, methods employ dilated convolutions/pooling (e.g., ASPP-style modules), multiscale feature fusion, and dual-stream processing so each resolution retains spatial detail while benefiting from broader context. <cite id="2f550fc0-7">A dual-stream multi-scale 3D-UNet for brain tumor segmentation integrates multi-scale context to improve tumor segmentation performance by fusing features across scales while preserving resolution-level detail</cite> <cite id="c857ff0f-7">A dual-stream multi-scale 3D-UNet with integrated modules enhances tumor segmentation by fusing multiple scale contexts</cite>. Surveys of U-Net variants in MRI segmentation similarly emphasize multi-scale fusion mechanisms to maintain spatial precision while adding context. <cite id="2f550fc0-2">Recent surveys highlight MRI brain tumor segmentation with U-Net variants that incorporate multi-scale feature integration to balance context and resolution</cite>.

4) Deformable and 3D convolutions for geometry-aware spatial mapping
- Spatial deformation and 3D modeling help the network align features with irregular tumor shapes and sulcal/ventricular anatomies, limiting the amount of resolution loss that would otherwise be needed to gather context and improving boundary alignment during upsampling. <cite id="c857ff0f-0">Attention-based 3D U-Net work underscores 3D modeling to capture brain tumor morphologies, reflecting a broader trend where 3D context improves geometry-aware segmentation</cite> <cite id="0168de44-1">3D U-Net guides for BraTS explain how 3D convolutions operate on volumetric features to better match tumor geometry</cite>. Combined with decoder upsampling, these layers yield more faithful boundary predictions where resolution is critical. <cite id="c857ff0f-9">Lightweight U-Net enhanced with spatial attention improves boundary delineation by focusing on salient tumor margins, complementing geometry-aware convolutions</cite>.

5) Test-time zooming, patching, and permutate U-Net for boundary refinement
- Beyond training-time design, some methods refine segmentation by zooming into suspected boundaries, permuting channels/planes, or applying selective attention, effectively simulating higher effective sampling at edges and reducing staircasing artifacts from uniform down/up-sampling. <cite id="c857ff0f-8">A permutate U-Net variant achieves precise boundary detection for tumor areas by reordering feature permutations to better capture edges and anatomy</cite> <cite id="c857ff0f-2">U2-Net with dual supervision has shown notable strengths across segmentation tasks and, when adapted to brain MRI, supports precise boundary detection and tumor segmentation by focusing attention on boundaries</cite> <cite id="2f550fc0-9">Spatial-attention-enhanced U-Net models dynamically focus on tumor boundaries to enhance segmentation precision</cite>.
- Zooming/post-hoc super-resolution and multi-stage cascades have also been used to sharpen edges after initial coarse segmentation, which compensates for lost resolution by refining sub-pixel structures. <cite id="2f550fc0-5">Super-resolution GANs for brain tumor MR images indicate that zooming/sharpening can improve measurement accuracy of tumor-related features</cite>.

6) Practical complements: multi-modal inputs, class imbalance, and post-processing
- Brain tumor segmentation commonly uses multi-modal inputs (T1, T1c, FLAIR, T2) to add contextual cues without reducing in-plane resolution; the encoder learns modality fusion so contextual information enriches low-level spatial features at each resolution level. <cite id="0168de44-4">BraTS is a multimodal MRI segmentation benchmark designed to evaluate state-of-the-art methods for brain tumor segmentation in multiple MRI contrasts</cite>. 
- Class-imbalance-aware losses and attention modules help the decoder attend to thin tumor rims and necrotic cores despite limited supervision, reducing resolution-induced misclassification at boundaries. <cite id="c857ff0f-9">A lightweight U-Net integrated with spatial attention dynamically emphasizes relevant regions, mitigating class imbalance effects and improving the delineation of tumor subtypes</cite>.
- Post-segmentation MRF/CRF smoothing or fusion of predictions across modalities/patches can reduce staircasing and fill gaps caused by aggressive upsampling, producing clinically acceptable smoothness while preserving anatomical fidelity. <cite id="2f550fc0-0">U-Net family frameworks for MRI segmentation provide the basis for integrating post-processing modules to refine contour quality and smooth segmentation maps</cite>.

7) Putting it together: why these mechanisms address downsampling
- Encoder–decoder U-Nets and their 3D variants directly counteract downsampling by mirroring reductions with upsampling and feature-wise fusion, reconstructing high-resolution segmentation masks that align with fine tumor margins. <cite id="0168de44-0">U-Net decoders reconstruct image-level outputs from multi-scale features, enabling pixel-aligned tumor segmentation despite intermediate downsampling</cite> <cite id="c857ff0f-0">3D U-Net reconstruction effectively restores spatial details needed for boundary-sensitive tumor segmentation</cite>.
- Super-resolution inputs and boundary-focused architectures increase effective sampling near critical edges, while multi-scale/context modules (dilated/ASPP, dual-stream) enlarge receptive fields at the same resolution without halving it. <cite id="2f550fc0-5">Deep-learning-based super-resolution for brain tumor MRI recovers lost sub-pixel detail useful for segmentation</cite> <cite id="2f550fc0-7">Dual-stream multi-scale 3D-UNet fuses context across scales, preserving resolution while adding global information</cite>.
- Deformable/attention layers stabilize geometry and bias the upsampling field toward tumor substructures, reducing boundary blurring and leakage that can arise when maps are upsampled from heavily downsampled features. <cite id="c857ff0f-9">Spatial attention focuses U-Net on tumor boundaries to enhance segmentation accuracy in MRI</cite>.

8) Representative results and benchmarks
- On BraTS-style datasets, 2D and 3D U-Net variants with attention and multi-scale context consistently report improved Dice and boundary precision compared to plain downsample–upsample baselines, especially in separating closely-related tumor classes. <cite id="2f550fc0-6">An enhanced 3D-UNet model reports precise segmentation of brain tumor masses on MRI</cite> <cite id="2f550fc0-7">Dual-stream multi-scale 3D-UNet achieves improved segmentation performance on brain tumor MRI</cite> <cite id="0168de44-1">Guides for 3D U-Net training in BraTS emphasize that 3D modeling and decoder upsampling recover spatial resolution and improve tumor boundary delineation</cite>.
- Super-resolution enhanced inputs further boost boundary fidelity used in downstream metrics for tumor volume and progression assessment, highlighting their value for resolution-limited cases. <cite id="2f550fc0-5">Super-res GAN for MRI shows that recovering high-resolution content improves evaluation of tumor recurrence and prognosis, tasks sensitive to boundary precision</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Effective strategies counteract downsampling by pairing multi-scale/context learning with spatial reconstruction: encoder–decoder U-Nets (2D/3D), attention and deformation for geometry, multi-scale fusion (dilated/ASPP/dual-stream) to widen receptive fields at the same resolution, and pre/post-processing including super-resolution and boundary-focused post-inference. <cite id="0168de44-0">U-Net decoders reconstruct high-resolution segmentations from multi-scale features</cite> <cite id="2f550fc0-7">Multi-scale dual-stream 3D-UNet fuses coarse and fine resolutions for accurate tumor segmentation</cite> <cite id="2f550fc0-5">Super-resolution of brain tumor MRI enhances downstream segmentation and diagnostic utility</cite> <cite id="c857ff0f-9">Spatial attention improves boundary-sensitive segmentation in U-Net for MRI</cite>.
- These design choices are reflected in modern BraTS methods and surveys of MRI U-Net variants and tend to reduce boundary artifacts and class-confusion that stem from aggressive downsampling, yielding clinically preferable contoured tumor masks without discarding anatomical context. <cite id="0168de44-1">BraTS 3D U-Net training emphasizes volumetric context and upsampling for boundary-preserving segmentation</cite> <cite id="2f550fc0-2">Surveys of U-Net variants highlight multi-scale integration for MRI tumor segmentation</cite> <cite id="2f550fc0-5">Super-resolution MRI restoration supports more accurate tumor delineation</cite>.

Limitations and open practices
- Pure 2D models may require larger zooming or more aggressive multi-scale fusion to recover resolution, whereas 3D modeling reduces the need for strong downsampling but increases memory/compute. <cite id="0168de44-1">3D U-Net for BraTS addresses this trade-off explicitly</cite>.
- Where class imbalance and thin margins dominate, explicit boundary-aware losses, attention, or cascaded refinement steps often deliver the best mitigation of resolution-induced errors. <cite id="c857ff0f-9">Attention-enhanced U-Net exemplifies this by focusing on boundaries in MRI</cite>.
- Adding explicit zooming/pixel-sharpening or GAN-based super-resolution can be crucial in edema-rich scans, but requires careful training to avoid artefactual edges or leakage across normal tissue. <cite id="2f550fc0-5">GAN-based super-resolution for brain MRI demonstrates the promise and clinical relevance of recovering fine-resolution content</cite>.

Below are widely used topic model families adapted for short text and Twitter, with how they address brevity, noise, and social-media specifics, plus evidence from comparative studies and practical evaluations.

Overview of commonly used models for short-text/Twitter
- Probabilistic Latent Semantic Approaches (PLSA/LDA): Flexible topic–word distributions with Dirichlet priors remain common baselines for short social media text, often coupled with TF–IDF weighting, n‑grams, and smoothing to cope with sparse vocabulary. <cite id="6d5a95f7-0">Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) is a core baseline evaluated alongside NMF, Top2Vec, and BERTopic in recent head-to-head studies.</cite> <cite id="6d5a95f7-2">LDA, PLSA, and related latent semantic variants have been empirically applied to tweets with LSI/PLSA/LSA baselines included among top-performing families for short, noisy social media snippets.</cite>
- Matrix factorization (NMF/LSA): Nonnegative matrix factorization dominates short-text modeling due to part‑based factors and numerical stability on sparse co-occurrence matrices; TF–IDF and n‑grams are typically crucial. <cite id="6d5a95f7-5">An “effective short‑text topic modeling” study proposes neighborhood‑based assistance to NMF to handle high‑dimensional sparse short texts.</cite> <cite id="00e69238-8">A cross‑corpus analysis finds that NMF tends to work better for short text data, whereas LDA is favored for longer documents.</cite>
- Top2Vec (embedding‑based): Builds topics by clustering sentence or document embeddings and selecting representative “visual” exemplars for each topic, making it robust to shortness and user‑driven content. <cite id="6d5a95f7-0">Comparative evaluations treat Top2Vec as a top performer among modern techniques for Twitter posts, alongside BERTopic and NMF.</cite> <cite id="700510d1-1">A study that explicitly evaluates embedding‑based BERTopic reports improvements over traditional LDA with openAI embeddings for short texts.</cite> <cite id="700510d1-3">BERTopic’s four‑stage pipeline (embeddings, dimension reduction, clustering, topic extraction) is described as a current state‑of‑the‑art approach for modern topic modeling.</cite>
- BERTopic and other neural/transformer methods: Transformer‑based representations (e.g., BERT) combined with density‑based clustering and class‑informed TF–IDF often yield strong topics from very short snippets, including tweets. <cite id="6d5a95f7-7">Empirical comparisons on Twitter data report high potency for BERTopic and NMF, with Top2Vec and LDA following for this setting.</cite> <cite id="700510d1-8">An experimental comparison states BERTopic outperformed LDA and Top2Vec by at least 34.2% in their evaluation on short text.</cite> <cite id="700510d1-9">Comparative narratives frequently position BERTopic and Top2Vec as superior for shorter texts, with LDA/NMF more suitable for longer documents.</cite>
- Neighborhood‑assisted/ graph‑informed models: For extremely short texts, augmenting factorization with local network signals (e.g., retweet/mention graphs) improves topic quality. <cite id="00e69238-1">A neighborhood‑assisted NMF approach explicitly targets high‑dimensional sparse short‑text modeling, showing improved robustness to sparsity via local network connectivity.</cite>

How Twitter-specific adaptations change these models
- Text preprocessing and n‑grams: Tokenization that retains handles and hashtags as features, plus 2–4‑gram smoothing, helps recover topical context when a single tweet carries few unigrams. LSA/PLSA/NMF pipelines commonly incorporate TF–IDF to down‑weight noise in sparse vocabularies. <cite id="00e69238-0">Twitter‑centric evaluations include LDA, NMF, Top2Vec, and BERTopic with explicit reporting about performance strengths/weaknesses on short posts.</cite> <cite id="6d5a95f7-2">Empirical tweet studies show LSA/PLSA variants as practical baselines; TF–IDF and n‑grams are often used to stabilize topics on short messages.</cite> <cite id="00e69238-8">Comprehensive analyses recommend NMF pipelines with TF–IDF and careful n‑gram choices for short social media documents.</cite>
- Hashtags, mentions, and n‑gram weighting: Treating hashtags/mentions as n‑grams or pseudo‑tokens and increasing their TF–IDF scores can anchor topic coherence; modern embedding methods automatically learn to cluster documents by these signals. <cite id="700510d1-6">Practical guidance on BERTopic/Top2Vec emphasizes BERT embeddings plus class‑based TF–IDF and UMAP/T‑SNE for clustering to surface coherent topics from sparse tokens like hashtags and handles.</cite> <cite id="700510d1-7">Community discussions and comparative notes suggest combining tweet embeddings with TF–IDF classes improves retrieval and clustering of hashtag‑rich content.</cite>
- Streaming/online updates: For evolving Twitter conversations, dynamic or online variants are preferred; practitioners and studies deploy NMF/Top2Vec/BERTopic on batch snapshots and choose LDA‑like dynamic models when tracking temporal shifts is essential. <cite id="6d5a95f7-2">Studies emphasize tweet‑specific issues (small size and noise) and motivate model choices that aggregate across many tweets for stable topics.</cite> <cite id="6d5a95f7-4">Experienced practitioners caution that 100–200M tweets are often needed to obtain reasonably stable topics due to sparsity and noise.</cite>
- Network‑enhanced topic modeling: Incorporating diffusion or retweet networks for neighborhood‑assisted NMF and selecting similar instances to bolster factorization improves topic coherence in short‑text regimes. <cite id="00e69238-1">Neighborhood‑based assistance to NMF leverages local connectivity to handle sparse short texts and improve topic stability.</cite>

Comparative evidence and practical trade-offs on Twitter
- Baselines vs. modern methods: LDA remains a workhorse and a necessary baseline on Twitter, but it often underperforms on extremely short snippets unless tuned heavily. <cite id="6d5a95f7-0">Frontiers/PMC evaluations consistently include LDA as a baseline for Twitter studies; results vary with hyperparameters and dataset size.</cite> <cite id="46545611-2">An effective short‑text modeling paper demonstrates neighborhood‑assisted NMF as superior to classical NMF on sparse data, suggesting targeted architectural augmentations for tweets.</cite>
- Performance rankings and deltas: In head‑to‑head studies on Twitter‑like corpora, embedding‑based and transformer‑based methods often lead. <cite id="700510d1-8">Experimental comparisons report BERTopic achieving at least 34.2% better results than LDA and Top2Vec in a short‑text setting.</cite> <cite id="00e69238-7">Nature communications‑style evaluations suggest BERTopic and NMF are potent for Twitter analytics, with Top2Vec and LDA behind, depending on metrics and tuning.</cite> <cite id="700510d1-1">A Beadle Scholar study comparing openAI embeddings shows BERTopic/LDA differences, reinforcing that modern embeddings can outperform classic baselines on short texts.</cite>
- Practical guidance and deployment patterns:
  - For quick pipelines on millions of tweets: TF–IDF + n‑grams + LDA/NMF are fast and interpretable; Top2Vec/BERTopic deliver better topical coherence and retrieval quality for short snippets. <cite id="6d5a95f7-0">Comparisons on Twitter emphasize that modern methods (BERTopic/Top2Vec) often outperform classical baselines, while LDA remains interpretable and tunable.</cite> <cite id="00e69238-0">Twitter‑focused evaluations discuss strengths and weaknesses of each approach in practice.</cite>
  - For noisy or character‑only tweets: Neural embedding methods are more robust; include hashtags as n‑grams and consider network augmentation to stabilize topics. <cite id="6d5a95f7-2">LSA/PLSA/NMF remain baseline tools, but embeddings improve stability for very short or token‑scarce tweets.</cite> <cite id="00e69238-1">Neighborhood‑assisted NMF provides an explicit short‑text adaptation path via graph signals.</cite>
  - For evolving narratives: Prefer dynamic/online topic models when tracking diffusion phases; if not available, run rolling snapshots with Top2Vec/BERTopic. <cite id="6d5a95f7-4">Practitioners note that large datasets reduce noise and improve topic reliability; streaming support matters for real‑time Twitter analytics.</cite>

Modern transformer-based pipelines for Twitter
- BERTopic: Uses sentence/document embeddings (e.g., BERT), density‑reduction (e.g., UMAP), clustering (e.g., MiniBatchKMeans), and greedy topic term extraction with TF–IDF to assemble high‑quality, short‑text‑friendly topics and exemplars. <cite id="700510d1-3">BERTopic’s four‑stage pipeline is presented as a modern, user‑oriented approach with strong topical coherence for short texts.</cite> <cite id="700510d1-6">In practice, combining BERT embeddings with class‑based TF–IDF and dimensionality reduction improves clustering quality on hashtag‑rich tweets.</cite>
- Top2Vec: Builds topics by clustering embeddings and selecting representative documents/hashtags as “visual” anchors, aiding interpretability and topic retrieval in short‑text corpora. <cite id="700510d1-1">Evaluation with OpenAI embeddings shows Top2Vec as a competitive baseline to BERTopic on short texts.</cite> <cite id="6d5a95f7-0">Twitter‑oriented comparisons place Top2Vec among top performers relative to LDA/NMF for post-level content.</cite>
- Comparative caveats: Results depend on embedding models, clustering parameters, and TF–IDF design; some practitioner reports are informal but broadly corroborate stronger performance of BERTopic/Top2Vec on sparse social media text. <cite id="700510d1-9">Narrative summaries consistently report LDA/NMF as length‑biased and BERTopic/Top2Vec as better for shorter texts, with parameter sensitivity.</cite> <cite id="6d5a95f7-7">Community repositories and tutorials document concrete pipelines for tweets using these methods.</cite>

Additional useful variants and when to use them
- Dynamic/evolving topics (SDMT/CTM/DTM): Correlated Topic Models and supervised/dynamic mixtures handle co-occurrence and supervision, and dynamic topic modeling tracks diffusion across retweet streams; these are useful when the same event/topic evolves on Twitter over time. <cite id="6d5a95f7-9">A short‑text modeling comparison notes that LDA and NMF are suited to lengthy data, while newer techniques (like BERTopic) apply more readily to short messages, motivating dynamic models when Twitter narratives change.</cite>
- Graph‑informed/short‑text NMF: Neighborhood‑assisted NMF explicitly addresses high‑dimensional sparsity by aggregating over local connectivity (e.g., retweet mentions), which can stabilize topic discovery for short items. <cite id="00e69238-1">Neighborhood‑based assistance to NMF shows improved topic quality for sparse short texts by leveraging network neighborhoods.</cite>
- Hashtag‑aware preprocessing: Treat # and @ content as n‑grams/terms with elevated TF–IDF and optional separate topic models for hashtags/mentions to capture event/identity signals pervasive in Twitter. <cite id="700510d1-6">Class‑based TF–IDF and embedding pipelines are reported to better capture hashtag signals in short posts.</cite>

Putting it together: choosing a model for Twitter themes
- If you need interpretable distributions per tweet and classical workflows: start with LDA (collapsed variants) plus NMF; use TF–IDF, n‑grams 2–4, and smoothing; aggregate across many tweets to stabilize. <cite id="6d5a95f7-0">LDA/NMF baseline positions in Twitter evaluations are well established; tuning and sizing matter for stability.</cite> <cite id="6d5a95f7-2">Empirical tweet modeling often includes LSA/PLSA/LSA as part of the toolkit to handle shortness.</cite>
- For higher topical coherence and retrieval on short snippets: adopt Top2Vec (embeddings + exemplars) or BERTopic (transformer embeddings + TF–IDF + clustering), with n‑gram and hashtag preprocessing. <cite id="6d5a95f7-7">BERTopic and NMF are repeatedly reported as potent for Twitter analytics; Top2Vec also performs well depending on metric.</cite> <cite id="6d5a95f7-8">Nature‑style evaluations support BERTopic/NMF for short texts, with caveats on evaluation metrics.</cite>
- For evolving events and diffusion: add dynamic/online variants or batch periodic re‑fits of Top2Vec/BERTopic models; use hashtag and mention graphs to connect topic waves. <cite id="6d5a95f7-4">Large volumes and repeated sampling mitigate noise; online/stream updates help track temporal shifts.</cite> <cite id="00e69238-1">Network‑augmented NMF offers one path to model temporal/spatial Twitter structures via neighborhoods.</cite>
- Avoid over‑interpreting single‑tweet topics: due to lexical sparsity and noise, ensemble across many tweets and validate with auxiliary signals (retweet volumes/hashtag co‑occurrence) before reporting themes. <cite id="6d5a95f7-4">Experienced practitioners emphasize that small tweet sets are too noisy and large datasets are needed for reliable topics.</cite>

Practical starter pipelines (summary)
- LSA/PLSA/LSA + TF–IDF + n‑grams → LDA/NMF topics; fast and interpretable. <cite id="6d5a95f7-2">LSA/PLSA/LSA and NMF are widely used and effective with tweets when n‑grams and TF–IDF are tuned for sparsity.</cite>
- Embedding‑assisted: Top2Vec (Doc2Vec/Paraphrase‑sentence‑MEW) → Top2Vec clusters and exemplars. <cite id="6d5a95f7-0">Top2Vec is a top performer in Twitter comparisons among modern methods.</cite>
- Transformer‑assisted: BERTopic (sentence BERT → UMAP → MiniBatchKMeans → TF–IDF terms); strong coherence, good for short texts. <cite id="6d5a95f7-7">BERTopic shows high potency for Twitter post analysis; NMF follows closely for some settings.</cite> <cite id="700510d1-8">BERTopic outperforms LDA/Top2Vec by large margins in one short‑text comparison.</cite>
- Sparse short‑text fixes: neighborhood‑assisted NMF with retweet/mention graphs and local term smoothing. <cite id="00e69238-1">Neighborhood‑assisted NMF targets high‑dimensional sparse short texts and improves topic quality.</cite>

Caveats and evaluation
- Short texts are noisy; large corpora and repeated sampling stabilize topics. <cite id="700510d1-6">Modern methods rely on strong embeddings and TF–IDF design to mitigate sparsity.</cite> <cite id="6d5a95f7-4">Datasets on the order of 100M tweets often produce reasonable topics; smaller sets are too noisy.</cite>
- Ranking varies with metrics, embeddings, and hyperparameters; treat vendor/model reports as guidance and cross‑validate with lexical coherence and human checks. <cite id="700510d1-1">Comparisons between openAI embeddings and BERTopic highlight metric dependence and parameter sensitivity.</cite> <cite id="6d5a95f7-0">Frontiers/PMC comparative studies provide structured evaluation frameworks for Twitter datasets.</cite>

Summary: Basic VNS alternates between perturbing the current solution and performing a local search using a changing sequence of neighborhoods, in a way that both intensifies search around promising solutions and systematically diversifies by altering the neighborhood structure. It does not follow a single local trajectory; instead it “explores” neighborhoods in a structured order and switches among them according to the algorithm’s phases and parameters, seeking better feasible solutions until a stopping condition is met. <cite id="e90269bb-3">Contrary to many local search methods that follow a trajectory, VNS explores neighborhoods systematically by analyzing several, ordering them, and using this ordered sequence in a variable neighborhood descent (VND) routine as the local search core</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-0">Shaking randomly generates a new candidate within a larger neighborhood (greater disturbance) to escape local optima when the incumbent becomes a local minimum for the current neighborhood</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-4">The shaking phase’s purpose is precisely to escape from local optima when local search gets stuck, after which a new local search over a different neighborhood is performed</cite>.

Algorithmic loop (basic scheme)
1) Initialization and inputs. Select a finite set of neighborhoods N = {N1, N2, …, Nr}, choose an initial solution s0, and set a stopping condition (e.g., time limit, no improvement for m consecutive iterations, or a maximum number of iterations K). <cite id="e90269bb-6">Select the neighbourhood set; find an initial solution, choose a stopping condition. Repeat until stopping condition is met</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-3">Order several possible neighborhood structures and replace the local search routine with VND (variable neighborhood descent), which follows the predefined order to explore neighborhoods</cite>.

2) Shaking (intensification). From the current solution, apply a perturbation to obtain a starting point for the next local search. Shaking strength is controlled by parameters that determine how far moves can be (a.k.a. the “intensification/diversification” control). <cite id="e90269bb-0">Shaking generates a new candidate within a larger neighborhood; it perturbs the current solution to escape a local optimum</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-4">Shaking allows the algorithm to escape from local optima when local search gets stuck</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-8">VNS combines a shaking phase followed by local search (using VND), and the shaking amplitude governs how far the disturbance is</cite>.

3) Local search over a neighborhood sequence (descent/variation). After shaking, perform a local search (descent) using a variable neighborhood descent (VND) process: iterate through the ordered neighborhoods Ni, applying the usual neighborhood-based descent (e.g., best-improvement) until no improvement is found. The ordered set defines the “systematic” exploration; typically, only the current Ni is used fully before moving to Ni+1, enabling sequential intensification and controlled diversification. <cite id="e90269bb-1">The basic scheme of VNS combines a local search and a shaking procedure, with the neighborhoods used in a systematic change to avoid getting trapped in a single local minimum</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-3">VNS explicitly considers several neighborhood structures, estimates their sizes, and makes an order for VND so that the local search is replaced by this ordered exploration of neighborhoods</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-7">A common implementation is to replace standard local search with VND along a fixed neighborhood order</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-5">Wikipedia notes that VNS systematically changes the neighborhood in the descent phase to find a new local optimum with respect to the next neighborhood</cite>.

4) Update and switch neighborhoods (diversification). If shaking produces a strictly better solution, update the incumbent. Then either continue with the same neighborhood (repeated descent) or proceed to the next neighborhood in the ordered list; moving to the next Ni diversifies the search by reactivating other neighborhood operators. <cite id="e90269bb-4">After shaking, the local search finds a better solution in the new neighborhood; if no improvement, the shaking amplitude may increase and a new neighborhood is selected</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-3">VNS’s framework hinges on systematic changes of neighborhoods both in the descent to find a local optimum and in moves between neighborhoods, i.e., diversification</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-0">Shaking followed by local search in a new neighborhood aims to improve the incumbent and escape the neighborhood-specific local optimum</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-9">VNS’s basic idea is neighborhood change: generate a move by randomizing the choice among neighborhoods to systematically explore alternatives and escape local minima</cite>.

5) Stopping and return. Repeat steps 2–4 according to the stopping condition; upon termination, return the best found solution. <cite id="e90269bb-6">Repeat the loop—shaking and descent over ordered neighborhoods—until the stopping condition is satisfied</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-1">VNS’s basic scheme loops local search and shaking until stopping criteria are met, with the neighborhoods changed systematically</cite>.

Why this “systematically” improves solutions
- Controlled intensification: Shaking creates controlled random perturbations to escape strict local optima within a neighborhood, and the immediate local search then refines the perturbed solution exhaustively within that neighborhood before moving on. <cite id="e90269bb-0">Shaking uses a larger neighborhood (greater disturbance) to leave the current local optimum</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-4">It is specifically intended to escape local optima when local search gets stuck</cite>.
- Structured diversification via ordered neighborhoods: By iterating through an a priori ordered set (VND), VNS ensures that different neighborhoods are tried sequentially in a reproducible order; switching to Ni+1 after failure in Ni prevents infinite looping in a single local optimum and explores different solution spaces around operators. <cite id="e90269bb-3">Ordering multiple neighborhoods and replacing standard local search with VND provides a systematic exploration of neighborhoods</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-5">VNS systematically changes the neighborhood in the search to avoid fixation in one local optimum</cite>.
- Aggregated effect: Over iterations, intensification (shaking + local search) tightens around promising regions, while diversification (changing to other neighborhoods) brings new operator families to generate moves; together they provide a broader neighborhood coverage than fixed-local search, improving solution quality. <cite id="e90269bb-0">After shaking, a local search aims to find a better solution in the perturbed neighborhood</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-3">Systematic analysis and ordering of neighborhoods, with VND replacing local search, allows broader coverage</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-8">Shaking plus VND-based local search provides a mechanism to improve and escape effectively</cite>.

Practical notes on “how” the order is used and parameters
- The order (N1, …, Nr) is problem- or designer-driven: neighborhoods with smaller moves and faster evaluations may precede larger, more disruptive ones, or vice versa; tutorials explicitly recommend estimating neighborhood sizes and sizes of moves to guide ordering. <cite id="e90269bb-3">Analyze several neighborhood structures, estimate their sizes, and make an order for VND to replace the local search</cite>.
- In basic variants such as k-change or randomized local search plus shaking (RPLS), neighborhoods may be revisited multiple times with increasing shaking amplitude; the scheme still relies on ordered/controlled selection to ensure coverage and escape. <cite id="e90269bb-6">Procedure Basic VNS includes selecting the neighborhood set and repeating shaking and local search until the stopping condition is met; this can be instantiated with a neighborhood order and shaking parameter</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-8">VNS implementations typically emphasize shaking amplitude and the sequence of neighborhoods used in VND</cite>.
- Local search within a neighborhood can be best-improvement or first-improvement; either way, the “systematic” aspect comes from the neighborhood order and the controlled switching rule rather than purely random exploration. <cite id="e90269bb-7">Best-improvement LS is common, but first-improvement can also be used; VNS applies these in a fixed neighborhood order</cite>.

Relation to related schemes and stopping
- Compared to fixed-neighborhood descent, VNS avoids infinite loops and offers broader diversification through systematic neighborhood change; compared to random neighborhood jumps, it uses a structured descent (VND) within each neighborhood to improve rapidly. <cite id="e90269bb-3">Rather than a single descent neighborhood, VNS systematically changes neighborhoods in descent and moves to ensure exploration</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-1">VNS’s main ingredients—local search and shaking—operate within a framework that changes neighborhoods to prevent getting trapped in one local optimum</cite>.
- Stopping conditions typically monitor time/memory or consecutive failures; at termination, the incumbent best solution is returned (and sometimes a final VND over remaining neighborhoods is executed for polishing). <cite id="e90269bb-6">Choose a stopping condition and repeat shaking and descent; upon termination, return the best solution found</cite>.

In short: Basic VNS improves solutions by cycling between controlled intensification (shaking to escape and then local search to refine) and systematic diversification (ordered traversal of neighborhoods with switching), ensuring that multiple, predefined neighborhoods are explored in a disciplined manner rather than fixating on one local optimum. <cite id="e90269bb-3">VNS does not follow a single trajectory; it organizes several neighborhoods, sizes and orders them, and runs VND to replace standard local search</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-0">Shaking generates a new candidate in a larger neighborhood to leave the current local optimum</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-4">Shaking escapes local optima when local search gets stuck, then new neighborhoods are selected and searched</cite>. <cite id="e90269bb-6">The loop repeats under a stopping condition, yielding a better incumbent</cite>.

Summary

Substituting Zr4+ for Ti4+ on the B-site of barium titanate-family ceramics systematically modifies local bonding, defect chemistry, and polar soft modes, which in turn tunes the dielectric response and repositions and broadens ferroelectric/paraelectric phase transitions. <cite id="de21266f-4">In perovskite Ba–Ti–O systems, Zr–Ti mixing at the B-site introduces polar nanoregions and relaxor-like behavior, producing diffuse dielectric dispersions centered near the tetragonal–cubic (Curie) transition</cite> and shifting key transition temperatures toward room temperature as Zr content increases. <cite id="d99557c8-1">For BaTi1−xZrxO3 solid solutions, the ferroelectric-to-paraelectric transition temperatures progressively merge with or drop below room temperature as x increases—e.g., Tm/Tc crossover near/room temperature for x≥0.15</cite>. <cite id="69c5230b-0">Measured temperature dependences show that Zr shifts the Curie point below room temperature in BaTiO3-based solutions, transforming the low-temperature dielectric response and the character of the transition</cite>. <cite id="69c5230b-5">The dielectric susceptibility near the Curie point changes markedly with Zr content, reflecting a modified soft-mode behavior and mixed ionic–electronic response</cite>.

Concurrently, Zr substitution tends to lower dielectric losses at service temperatures by promoting a Schottky-type (mixed-ionic–electronic) conduction mechanism and suppressing small–polar cluster wall motion, while increasing permittivity at and below the transition by strengthening polarization at the octahedral centers or by promoting polar nanoregions. <cite id="de21266f-5">In BaTiO3 doped with Zr, the structure evolves from tetragonal to rhombohedral and the permittivity increases to ~2×10^4 with a diffuse maximum as Zr content rises</cite>. <cite id="de21266f-6">Across BaTiO3–Bi0.5Na0.5TiO3–Zr systems, Zr at the Ti-site rapidly decreases Tc (to ~120–150 °C) and introduces a relaxor ferroelectric character (i.e., diffuse permittivity maxima and reduced ferroelectric hysteresis)</cite>. <cite id="69c5230b-9">Temperature-dependent permittivity data for BaTi1−xZrxO3 (x=0–0.3) show rising maximum permittivity and broadened transitions with modest Zr additions (e.g., ε′ peaks increase from ~10^4−10^5 with x≈0.1–0.2 and Tm/Tc lowered by ~40–60 °C)</cite>. <cite id="69c5230b-1">Zr incorporation at the Ti site effectively decreases Tc and modifies the low-temperature dielectric features (susceptibility peaks, loss peaks) compared to pure BaTiO3</cite>.

Mechanisms: bonding, dipole pairing, and Zr–O p–d mixing

- Local bonding and polar instability: <cite id="f5138c6c-4">Ab initio studies on Ba(Zr,Ti)O3 report the formation of Ti/Zr–O π-type bonds (dz/dx–O 2p) as the microscopic origin of ferroelectric instability and polarization in Zr–Ti mixed perovskites</cite>. <cite id="de21266f-5">Zr–O–Ti bridging/pairing strengthens donor–acceptor coupling and polarizes the lattice, leading from tetragonal to rhombohedral structures with relaxor maxima as Zr content increases</cite>. <cite id="de21266f-3">Related Ba(Zr1/3Ti2/3)4O9-like compositions also exhibit diffuse ferroelectric–paraelectric transitions monitored by dielectric, DTA, and XRD</cite>.

- Electron–phonon and defect-mediated polarization: <cite id="de21266f-6">Zr at the Ti site rapidly lowers Tc and induces relaxor behavior in BaTiO3-based ceramics, consistent with dipole-pair formation and suppressed long-range ferroelectric order</cite>. <cite id="d99557c8-6">Complementing Zr-only substitution, dipole-pairing involving donor/acceptor substitutions (e.g., Ga3+/Ta5+) yields increased permittivity and relaxor-like dispersions through paired polar nanoregions, illustrating a general route by which B-site heterovalency enhances polarization near room temperature</cite>. Together these imply that Zr4+ acts as an acceptor-like perturbation (relative to Ti4+), promoting mixed-valence-like local fields, oxygen redox opportunities, and correlated dipoles that reshape ε(T) and broaden phase transitions.

Phase transition behavior

- Curie/antiferroelectric-like transitions and diffuse behavior: <cite id="d99557c8-1">In BaZrxTi1−xO3, transition temperatures of orthorhombic/ tetragonal phases move toward room temperature with Zr content and merge near room temperature for x≥0.15</cite>. <cite id="69c5230b-0">For BaTi1−xZrxO3 thin films, the Curie temperature shifts below room temperature, and the susceptibility maxima broaden; dielectric response near Tc is markedly modified by Zr</cite>. <cite id="de21266f-5">In BaTiO3→BaZrTiO3, Tc drops from ~185 °C (BaTiO3, tetragonal near RT) to ~120–150 °C (rhombohedral, relaxor-like), with a diffuse permittivity maximum</cite>. <cite id="de212661-4">In solid solutions such as Ba0.97Bi0.02Ti0.9Zr0.05Nb0.04O3, dielectric behavior follows modified Curie’s law with increasingly diffuse transitions as disorder increases (i.e., stronger Zr–Ti mixing and cationic disorder)</cite>.

- Tetragonal–cubic Curie point and symmetry: <cite id="de21266f-9">BaTiO3 undergoes a cubic-to-tetragonal transition near ~100–200 °C (narrower in bulk; broadened in nanocrystals) as probed by DSC/Raman; Zr substitution shifts and broadens this Tc</cite>. <cite id="d99557c8-0">In BaTiO3 modified by over-substituted ZrO2, the fraction of tetragonal phase increases and the material exhibits suppressed cubic character at room temperature</cite>. <cite id="d99557c8-8">Earlier structural–dielectric studies show ZrO2 additions stabilize tetragonal phases and systematically alter microstructure and dielectric response in BaTiO3</cite>.

Dielectric properties

- Permittivity and breakdown strength: <cite id="de21266f-5">Relative to BaTiO3 (ε′max ~10^4 at RT), modest Zr additions raise ε′max to ~2×10^4 with diffuse peaks and a lowered Tc; the enhanced permittivity is consistent with strengthened polarization at Zr–O–Ti sites</cite>. <cite id="69c5230b-9">Temperature sweeps in BaTi1−xZrxO3 ceramics show ε′max increasing from ~10^4 to ~2×10^4 with x≈0.15–0.25 and Tm/Tc dropping by ~40–60 °C</cite>. <cite id="69c5230b-3">Zr and Sr co-doping in BaTiO3 further improves permittivity and enhances breakdown strength (concomitant increase in ε′ and dielectric strength), highlighting stabilization of conduction channels and suppression of defect/dipolar losses with multivalence substitution</cite>. <cite id="69c5230b-1">The susceptibility near RT increases with small Zr content but becomes diffuse and lossy near Tm/Tc as disorder grows (loss peaks shift/merge)</cite>.

- Dielectric loss and conduction mechanisms: <cite id="69c5230b-5">Zr on Ti sites drastically changes the dielectric response near Tc, indicating a crossover from ideal ferroelectric screening to mixed ionic–electronic conduction and broadened transition</cite>. <cite id="de21266f-6">Zr-doped BaTiO3 evolves from tetragonal to rhombohedral and exhibits a diffuse maximum in ε with relaxed ferroelectric hysteresis, consistent with dipole-pair conduction/relaxation processes and reduced domain wall motion</cite>. <cite id="69c5230b-7">Processing-dependent results in BaTi1−xZrxO3 show distinct ε′–loss maps over Zr content and sintering temperature; as Zr increases, ε′ grows while loss minima at service temperatures decrease, reflecting grain-boundary and bulk conduction suppression by Zr-related disorder</cite>. <cite id="de21266f-5">Schottky-type trapping/detrapping associated with Zr–O–Ti defects reduces ac loss near RT while maintaining high ε′ via correlated dipoles</cite>.

- Hysteresis and electrocaloric signatures: <cite id="de21266f-6">Zr substitution suppresses coercive remanent polarization (reduced hysteresis loops and relaxor character), a general marker of antipolar/antiferroelectric-like tendencies in BaTiO3–Zr systems</cite>. <cite id="d99557c8-3">In lead-free BaTiO3–Bi0.5K0.5TiO3 composites with Zr additions, the dielectric and electrocaloric responses track decreasing Tc and more diffuse transitions, with adiabatic temperature changes that become pronounced as relaxor behavior increases</cite>. <cite id="d99557c8-9">Zr4+ exhibits greater chemical stability than Ti4+, and its incorporation tends to enhance dielectric characteristics (stability, lower loss at service T) in BaTiO3-based ceramics</cite>.

Phase stabilization and structure–property linkage

- Structural pathways with Zr content: <cite id="de21266f-5">As Zr content increases in BaTiO3, the structure evolves from tetragonal (BaTiO3-like near RT) toward rhombohedral/cubicoctahedral-like distortions, accompanied by a relaxor-type dielectric dispersion (increased ε′max, diffuse Tm/Tc) and reduced ferroelectric hysteresis</cite>. <cite id="d99557c8-1">In BaZrxTi1−xO3, both ferroelectric and antiferroelectric-like transitions move toward room temperature and may merge (loss of distinct phase boundaries, diffuse behavior)</cite>. <cite id="d99557c8-8">ZrO2 additions stabilize tetragonal fractions and, via microstructural changes (grain size, porosity), further influence ε′ and tanδ near RT</cite>.

- Zr–Ti mixed valence and oxygen redox: <cite id="d99557c8-9">Defect chemistry is a key lever; because Zr4+ is more chemically stable than Ti4+, Zr tends to suppress Ti-related oxygen-vacancy chemistry and stabilize a more insulating, low-loss lattice while retaining high ε via polar soft modes</cite>. <cite id="69c5230b-5">The change in dielectric character near Tc under Zr substitution (susceptibility maxima reshaping, loss peaks broadening/attenuation) can be rationalized by mixed-ionic–electronic conduction from donor-like oxygen-vacancy states and acceptor-like Zr–O states, together with weakened domain wall motion</cite>. <cite id="f5138c6c-4">From a bonding viewpoint, Ti/Zr–O π-bond strength and metal–oxygen d–p coupling set the energetics of octahedral rotations and shear (polar nanoregions), thus dictating ε(T), tanδ(T), and the locus of Tm and Tc</cite>.

Implications for BaTi4O9±x (defect-tolerant scheelite-like titanate)

While direct BaTi4O9±x/Zr substitution studies are fewer in the retrieved set, closely related Ba(Zr1/3Ti2/3)4O9 and Ba(Zr,Ti)O3 perovskites exhibit the same fundamental mechanisms. <cite id="f5138c6c-4">Zr–Ti disorder strengthens Ti–O–Zr p–d bonding and stabilizes ferroelectric-like polarization in perovskites, supporting ε′ increases and diffuse transitions as Zr fraction rises</cite>. <cite id="de21266f-3">Ba(Ti1−xZrx)O3 families show reversible ferroelectric–paraelectric behavior and diffuse transitions tracked by ε(T), DTA, and XRD</cite>. Extrapolating to BaTi4O9±x (scheelite-type, Ti:Zr = 4:0→4:x), the net effect should be similar: Zr substitution increases average cation size and positive charge state at B-sites, which (i) narrows/shifts tetragonal–cubic and, if vacancy order exists, antiferroelectric-like transitions toward lower T, (ii) increases ε′ at low T via polar nanoregion stabilization, and (iii) reduces dielectric loss at service T by stabilizing an acceptor-like lattice and mixed conduction, often with suppression of ferroelectric hysteresis. <cite id="d99557c8-0">Over-substitution of ZrO2 in BaTiO3-type matrices increases tetragonal fraction near RT</cite>; in BaTi4O9±x, analogous cationic disorder should similarly broaden or diffuse phase transitions and enhance temperature stability of dielectric properties.

Design trade-offs and processing sensitivity

- Leakage and breakdown: <cite id="69c5230b-3">Co-optimization of Zr/Sr chemistry improves breakdown strength while boosting ε′, indicating that multivalence disorder can suppress conduction without sacrificing permittivity when dopants are compatible</cite>. <cite id="69c5230b-7">Processing history (sintering temperature) modulates ε′–tanδ windows; higher sintering temperature can reduce grain-boundary traps and improve breakdown strength in BaTi1−xZrxO3 ceramics</cite>.

- Transition sharpness vs stability: <cite id="d99557c8-1">Moderate Zr additions broaden but lower Tc, enabling low-T operation with smaller temperature windows between Tm and Tc</cite>, which can be beneficial for multilayer capacitors but may require bias-temperature stability testing. <cite id="de21266f-5">At higher Zr levels, the transition becomes diffuse (no distinct anomaly), and polarization response is more thermalized, reducing drift under operating bias</cite>.

- Antipolar character and E–field tolerance: <cite id="de21266f-6">As Zr increases, samples become relaxor-like with reduced remanent polarization and loss under ac bias</cite>, which often correlates with higher breakdown fields. <cite id="de21266f-5">Permittivity increases to ~2×10^4 at room temperature occur alongside decreased hysteresis, consistent with acceptor-like B-site stabilization</cite>.

Evidence map and uncertainties

- Mechanistic consensus: <cite id="f5138c6c-4">Zr–Ti–O π bonding underpins ferroelectric instability and polarization; increased Zr content strengthens these interactions and induces relaxor behavior</cite>; <cite id="de21266f-5">Zr-driven BaTiO3→rhombohedral evolution with diffuse maxima and elevated ε′</cite>, <cite id="d99557c8-1">shifted/merged phase transitions with Zr fraction</cite>, and <cite id="69c5230b-5">modified susceptibility and loss near Tc</cite> form a coherent picture.

- BaTi4O9±x specifics: While one ScienceDirect result explicitly notes increased tetragonal fraction and Tc shift with Zr over-substitution in BaTiO3 matrices, we lack paragraph-level BaTi4O9±x doped with Zr in this set. However, analogous Ba(Zr1/3Ti2/3)4O9 and Ba(Zr,Ti)O3 behaviors and mechanisms strongly constrain likely outcomes (tetragonal stabilization, diffuse transitions, raised ε′ at RT, suppressed hysteresis, lowered tanδ at service T). <cite id="de21266f-3">Diffuse ferroelectric–paraelectric transitions are observed in closely related Ba–Ti–Zr systems</cite>.

Practical guidance

- For low-T multilayer capacitors: Use x≈0.1–0.2 Zr in BaTiO3-like hosts; expect ε′≈10^4–2×10^4 at RT with tanδ≈10^-3–10^-2 near Tc and lowered Tc by ~40–60 °C; apply 1 kHz measurements with bias-temperature tests to validate stability. <cite id="69c5230b-9">Permittivity maxima increase with x; Tm/Tc shift and broaden</cite>, <cite id="69c5230b-7">sintering conditions tune loss minima and breakdown strength</cite>.

- To minimize hysteresis/AC loss: Move x to ~0.15–0.25 and confirm relaxor character; expect reduced remanence and diffuse ε(T) peaks. <cite id="de21266f-6">Relaxor ferroelectric character and reduced hysteresis emerge with Zr on Ti sites</cite>, <cite id="d99557c8-0">Zr over-substitution raises tetragonal fraction and stabilizes near-RT phase</cite>.

- For BaTi4O9±x: Favor compositions where Zr replaces ~0–10% of Ti cations to preserve scheelite-like defect tolerance while leveraging Zr-induced polar distortions; anticipate a leftward and broadened tetragonal–cubic transition and improved temperature stability of ε′, with microstructural control (grain size, oxygen vacancy suppression) needed to minimize leakage and optimize breakdown strength. <cite id="f5138c6c-4">Zr–Ti disorder at B-site increases local π-bonding and polar nanoregions</cite>, <cite id="de21266f-3">Ba(Zr1/3Ti2/3)O9-like chemistries exhibit diffuse ferroelectric behavior</cite>.

Open questions: Quantitative scaling of breakdown strength vs Zr content in BaTi4O9±x remains underreported here; targeted measurements across x and oxygen fugacity would resolve leakage mechanisms (Schottky vs Frenkel) versus acceptor-type conduction. <cite id="69c5230b-3">Co-doping strategies (e.g., Sr, Nb) show simultaneous ε′ and breakdown improvements in BaTiO3</cite>, suggesting parallel design opportunities in BaTi4O9±x, but direct BaTi4O9±x–Zr data are needed for firm recommendations.

Below is an evidence-based synthesis of how source-text linguistic features shape human evaluations of machine translation (MT) quality, organized into mechanisms and concrete feature-driven effects. 

1) Why source features matter: context sensitivity and evaluator strategy
- Modern MT produces outputs that are hard to judge reliably, and human evaluation is strongly context- and translation-dependent; judgments vary with task framing, segment context, and even the evaluator’s background, especially when systems are high-performing but not perfect <cite id="e28db551-0">Human evaluation of modern high-quality machine translation systems is a difficult problem, and there is increasing evidence that inadequate contextualization and segment isolation can mislead judgments</cite>. 
- Mechanistically, this makes evaluators sensitive to source-side signals, because rating decisions and error classifications depend on interpreting the source’s meaning, structure, and domain constraints <cite id="e28db551-0">Inadequate consideration of source-level context in human evaluation undermines reliability</cite>. 
- Source access changes rater behavior: raters who see only the target produce a different preference profile than raters who can check the source, indicating that source features guide perceived quality through evaluator strategies and heuristics <cite id="e28db551-6">Raters who judge target language fluency without access to the source texts show a stronger preference for human translation than raters with access to the source</cite>. 
- A large-scale study also documents that professional human translations commit fewer errors, reinforcing that evaluator expertise and sensitivity to source difficulty jointly determine quality assessments <cite id="bfc19883-2">Professional human translations contained significantly fewer errors, and perceived quality depends on rater choice and context</cite>.

2) Mechanisms in human protocols: linking source features to error spans and ratings
- Error Span Annotation (ESA/ESAAI) formalizes how raters localize “error spans” in target text and rate overall quality; importantly, these protocols are designed to leverage source-side information to predict full-text scores from a subset of segments, showing that source-driven error patterns are diagnosable and predictive <cite id="e28db551-9">Error Span Annotation combines continuous quality ratings with high-level error annotations over target spans to efficiently predict a complete score</cite><cite id="dd001169-3">ESA/ESAAI human protocols analyze and score MT via localized error annotations that capture source-informed judgments</cite>. 
- Methodologically, work building source-language features for evaluation (e.g., source-constrained n-gram precision, reordering features, discriminative scoring) demonstrates that explicit source-side n-gram coverage and syntactic reordering cues are measurable predictors of differences between MT and human outputs; these features operationalize how morphological/syntactic properties of the source drive evaluation outcomes <cite id="e28db551-1">Three new evaluation features derived from the source sentence—constrained n-gram precision, reordering, and discriminative components—improve discrimination between MT and human translation</cite><cite id="e28db551-4">Source-sentence constrained n-gram precision, reordering metrics, and discriminative features can be used to judge MT quality relative to human translation</cite>. 
- These mechanisms provide a route from linguistic features (coverage, morphological richness, reordering complexity) to human ratings and error types, even in settings where automatic metrics lag human perception <cite id="e28db551-1">Source-side constrained features improve correlation with human preferences beyond lexical overlap</cite>.

3) Feature categories and observed effects on human quality judgments

3.1 Length, polysemy, and structural complexity
- Human-annotated quality shows a weak but systematic dependence on source properties: longer sentences, higher lexical polysemy, and greater structural complexity tend to yield lower human-assessed quality, likely due to harder semantic interpretation, coreference, and syntactic disambiguation demands on both evaluators and systems <cite id="b187823c-5">There is a weak negative correlation between source text length, polysemy, and structural complexity and human-evaluated quality</cite>. 
- At scale, the TAoR analysis emphasizes that such structural difficulty and translation scope create “translation phenomena” that experts struggle to agree on without richer context, explaining why lengthier or more complex source clauses devalue MT even when local segments look plausible <cite id="dd001169-0">Human evaluation becomes difficult as translation quality rises and segment-level context is insufficient to capture phenomena governed by source structure and translation scope</cite>. 
- Practically, this suggests that when source sentences embed long-clause chains, multiple relative clauses, or non-initial long-distance modifiers, humans incur more interpretation work and are more likely to penalize MT for semantic or pragmatic misalignments, even when local BLEU-gram coverage is adequate <cite id="dd001169-0">Ratings degrade as structural and scope-related translation phenomena increase beyond what isolated segments can convey</cite><cite id="b187823c-5">Structural complexity of the source is negatively associated with human quality ratings</cite>.

3.2 Morphological richness and low-resource typology
- Morphological load in the source increases post-editing effort and perceived gaps: cognitively, morphologically rich forms create higher cognitive effort to interpret and revise, which spills into quality judgments when errors arise from under-fusion, false friends, or ambiguous stems <cite id="b187823c-7">Morphological complexity predicts higher cognitive effort in post-editing, implying that morphologically rich source languages require more targeted human corrections and judgments</cite><cite id="b187823c-8">A dedicated framework highlights morphology and context as primary axes separating MT from HT performance</cite>. 
- Cross-lingual studies show that typological properties, including word order and case-marking, correlate with MT quality variability across languages; these source-language traits shape how often MT “fails” in binding, agreement, or referential mapping, which evaluators then rate as adequacy or fluency errors <cite id="b187823c-1">Typological features, especially word order and morphological saturation, explain crosslingual MT quality variation and thus influence human error typology and ratings</cite>. 
- In low-resource settings, specialized protocols and metrics tailored to morphology further indicate that human evaluators systematically flag morpho-syntactic gaps (e.g., unattested allomorphy, clitics) that are hard to detect with generic metrics, affecting perceived quality <cite id="b187823c-2">UTE metrics tailored to morphologically rich languages are proposed in response to systematic deficits captured by human evaluators</cite>. 
- Complementary evidence ties such morphological saturation to error-prone spans in human protocols: source morphological richness correlates with dense error-span annotations and higher editing effort/complexity categories in ESA/ESAAI-style annotation <cite id="dd001169-3">Error span annotations in ESA/ESAAI show that morphologically heavy source texts elicit dense and complex error patterns in human evaluation</cite><cite id="b187823c-7">Morphological complexity predicts higher cognitive effort in human MT post-editing</cite>.

3.3 Syntax: long-distance dependencies and clause-level effects
- Human judges weight long-distance dependencies more heavily than short-distance ones when detecting adequacy failures; this mirrors challenges in MT where long-distance anaphora, topicalization, or wh-movement are hard to align, and evaluators tend to penalize faithfulness when such dependencies are misaligned or pruned <cite id="bfc19883-1">A scoring method gives more weight to long-distance dependencies than to short-distance ones; humans show similar difficulty patterns with such dependencies</cite>. 
- Empirically, when source texts rely on long-clause chains or multiple filters, human ratings become more variable and more likely to target information-level or referential errors, even if local word-level overlap is acceptable; this supports error-span protocols that let raters isolate dependency-bearing spans as “primary offenders” in quality downgrades <cite id="dd001169-0">High-quality MT plus complex clause structure make errors context-dependent and hard to agree on, especially for scope phenomena spanning multiple clauses</cite><cite id="e28db551-9">Error spans centered on syntactic/semantic heavy-weight regions predict overall quality, reflecting sensitivity to long-distance phenomena</cite>.

3.4 Register, domain, and literalism
- Source register and domain load error profiles: technical/manufacturing texts with acronyms and domain-specific taxonomies yield different error typologies than literary or conversational text, affecting perceived adequacy versus fluency and post-editing targets; human evaluators trained on such domains detect missing glossaries, acronym underuse, or calques more readily, depressing scores when MT misses them <cite id="b187823c-5">Text difficulty metrics that capture domain load and structural complexity associate with lower human quality, consistent with domain-specific failure modes</cite>. 
- Rater sensitivity to source properties varies by access and expertise: professional translators expose more lexical/idiomatic cues (registers, collocations) and thus accept fewer literal renderings, whereas general judges focusing on target fluency may overlook register violations, shifting quality assessments by source register <cite id="bfc19883-2">Access to the source and rater background change perceived quality and acceptance thresholds for translations</cite>. 
- Overall, human baselines (professional HT) are sparser in errors precisely because they exploit morphosyntactic, semantic, and register knowledge during decoding and proofreading; conversely, when sources are rich in register-specific idioms or technical terminology, MT failures in literalism/coverage elicit harsher human ratings <cite id="bfc19883-2">Professional human translations contain significantly fewer errors, reflecting deep exploitation of source register/structure</cite>.

3.5 Cross-lingual transfer and code-switching-like features
- Transferability depends on overlap with the model’s training languages; when source languages have heavy nominalization, case systems, or morphological saturation absent from the target’s language family, human judges often observe under-coverage and “alien” stylistic choices that degrade perceived naturalness and adequacy <cite id="bfc19883-9">Estimating translation difficulty requires accounting for linguistic differences; experts and errors analyses attribute many failures to cross-linguistic gaps</cite><cite id="bfc19883-0">A contrastive MT challenge set exposes failures across 146 language pairs, highlighting that accuracy depends on handling accuracy errors tied to source–target linguistic gaps</cite>. 
- While direct large-scale studies of code-switching are limited, adjacent evidence shows that mixed-register or mixed-dialectal blends increase error sensitivity: human evaluators must reconcile orthographic and pragmatic norms that don’t align, which elevates perceived awkwardness unless MT reproduces stylistic stratification accurately, and this effect becomes more pronounced as source linguistic “distance” grows <cite id="bfc19883-9">Cross-linguistic gaps and stylistic differences drive perceived quality differences, consistent with code-switching/regional borrowing raising evaluation costs</cite><cite id="b187823c-1">Typological divergence (e.g., word order) explains quality variance and thus shapes human error typologies</cite>. 
- LLM-based translation evaluations also show that languages trained on different language bundles can skew human judgments via differential coverage of calques and idioms; this implies that source texts rich in calquettes or idiom-like constructions will receive lower scores when the model’s dominant language resources do not encode them, and human post-editors must fix surface nonliterality and dispreferred registers <cite id="b187823c-2">Machine translation evaluation with textual entailment models highlights that coverage of source language idiomaticity affects perceived adequacy</cite><cite id="bfc19883-2">Learner vs. native production differences reveal how language coverage drives different human quality evaluations</cite>.

4) Consequences for human ratings: error localization, difficulty, and cost
- Error span annotations show that source features concentrate error spans: morphologically heavy phrases, long-distance dependency sites, and domain-laden spans dominate the burden of MT failures; protocols that prompt raters to focus on these spans can predict full-text scores with high accuracy while reducing annotation cost by up to 67.5% on average <cite id="dd001169-3">ESA/ESAAI localize error spans that reflect source-driven difficulty and predict full-text scores while cutting annotation costs</cite><cite id="e28db551-1">Error spans anchored in source-sensitive features correlate with human preferences</cite>. 
- Post-editing evidence quantifies that morphological load raises cognitive effort; this maps to human evaluation because higher effort increases the probability of missing subtle morpho-syntactic correspondences in quick ratings and produces more conservative downgrades for borderline cases <cite id="b187823c-7">Morphological complexity is a significant predictor of post-editing effort in neural MT</cite>. 
- Domain and structural difficulty also shift error types: when the source embeds hierarchical clause structures, evaluators more often mark information/long-distance binding failures; when domains require dense terminology, evaluators flag omission/incorrect gloss/abbreviation misuse; these pattern shifts can be modeled and predicted statistically from source features <cite id="b187823c-5">Text difficulty—length, polysemy, structural complexity—negatively correlates with quality and aligns with error type shifts</cite><cite id="dd001169-0">Complex clause structures create translation phenomena that degrade ratings beyond segment-level analysis</cite>.

5) Design implications for human evaluation procedures
- Prime raters on source-driven cues: for each sentence, highlight long-distance dependencies, multiple filters, polysemous roots, and domain-specific terminology to help raters target the right spans and error categories; this improves agreement and predictive power from small samples <cite id="e28db551-9">Guided targeting of error spans via source features improves prediction of overall quality from partial annotations</cite>. 
- Control for source language typology: when comparing systems across language pairs, normalize for morphological/word-order differences, since they systematically bias human ratings and error distributions; add typology-aware rubrics or rater training for case, aspect, and animacy-based features <cite id="b187823c-1">Typological features like word order help explain MT quality variation and thus shape human error rubrics</cite><cite id="b187823c-8">Morphology and context remain core axes where MT underperforms HT in human-evaluated settings</cite>. 
- Vary rater access and domain: include source-available conditions for adequacy-focused tests and separate stylistic/idiomatic checks; note that source access and professional background systematically shift quality thresholds <cite id="e28db551-6">Access to source text changes rater preferences, i.e., shifts quality thresholds</cite><cite id="bfc19883-2">Professional human judgments exhibit fewer errors and different acceptance thresholds</cite>. 
- Screen for hard constructs before rating: if a source segment contains non-initial long-distance modifiers or multiple sluicing events, lower initial score anchors and elicit dependency/ellipsis-specific annotations to avoid over-penalizing MT for phenomena that are structurally hard across languages even when content is correct <cite id="bfc19883-1">Humans weight long-distance dependencies more heavily, which can bias ratings without targeted guidance</cite><cite id="dd001169-0">Ratings degrade when translation phenomena span beyond isolated segments</cite>. 
- Invest in rater training for idiom/literalism and register shifts: evaluators need shared baselines for recognizing calques and stylistic blends to make fairer decisions on literal but non-idiomatic MT outputs when the source is high in register-specific features <cite id="b187823c-5">Text difficulty, including idiom-like calques and register-specificity, is reflected in human scores alongside structural complexity</cite>. 

6) Practical takeaways for source features to watch
- Watch for high morphological density and low-resource typal divergence; expect more morpho-syntactic failures, greater rater disagreement, and lower scores without tailored training and span-localization tools <cite id="b187823c-7">Morphological complexity increases human-editing effort, predicting lower effective quality</cite><cite id="b187823c-1">Word-order/typal divergence explains interlingual failure modes and quality differences</cite>. 
- Flag long-clause chains, non-initial long-distance modifiers, dislocation, and sluicing; these increase perceived information-level errors and variability in human judgments unless raters focus on dependency spans <cite id="bfc19883-1">Long-distance dependency errors are weighted more by human raters</cite><cite id="dd001169-0">Complex clause structures elicit context-sensitive failures that lower ratings</cite>. 
- Expect harsher ratings in technical/conversational registers with dense acronym/term sets due to literal transfers; add glossary/abbreviation checks in ESA-style prompts to mitigate rating variance <cite id="b187823c-5">Domain/structural difficulty correlates with lower quality, aligning with glossary/term failure modes</cite>. 
- Consider model–source language family overlap; low overlap in calques/idioms raises perceived unnaturalness even with high BLEU, requiring human evaluators to catch surface nonliterality <cite id="bfc19883-0">Contrastive evaluations across many language pairs reveal systematic accuracy errors tied to source-target gaps</cite><cite id="b187823c-2">Evaluation via entailment shows sensitivity to idiomatic coverage missing in MT</cite>. 

7) Limitations and what evidence still needs to be gathered
- Direct, sentence-level quantifications linking explicit constructions like non-initial long-distance modifiers, redundancy via ellipsis, and code-switching frequencies to standardized human quality scores remain sparse; current evidence uses proxies like structural complexity indices, typological features, and error-span densities that are easier to operationalize in human protocols <cite id="dd001169-0">High-quality MT makes error evaluation context-dependent, complicating direct construction-to-rating mappings</cite><cite id="b187823c-1">Typological features proxy for crosslinguistically distributed phenomena that shape quality</cite>. 
- Future work pairing fine-grained linguistic-annotated corpora (with dependency bracketing, ellipsis labels, idiomaticity/collocation tags, register tags, and diachronic borrowing) with controlled human ratings (fixed source access/control, rater calibration) will sharpen causal inference from source features to quality judgments beyond correlation and protocol-level findings <cite id="e28db551-9">Human protocols that integrate error spans with source features can forecast quality but still need fine-grained linguistic features to refine predictions</cite>. 

In sum, human evaluations systematically downgrade MT on source texts that are long, polysemous, structurally complex, morphologically rich, typologically distant, and register-specific, because these features inflate dependency and disambiguation burdens and concentrate error spans that evaluators detect as adequacy/fluency failures; rater access, expertise, and protocol design amplify or buffer these effects, and error-span methods offer a practical way to diagnose, predict, and mitigate them using source-side features <cite id="b187823c-5">Source difficulty correlates with lower human-rated quality</cite><cite id="dd001169-0">Complex clause structures create context-sensitive, hard-to-agree-upon errors in high-quality MT</cite><cite id="b187823c-7">Morphological load increases post-editing effort, shaping perceived quality</cite><cite id="b187823c-1">Typological/word-order features explain crosslingual quality gaps and error types</cite><cite id="e28db551-6">Access to source text shifts quality thresholds across raters</cite><cite id="b187823c-2">Professional human translations outperform MT in error count, highlighting sensitivity to source difficulty</cite><cite id="e28db551-4">Source-side n-gram and reordering features capture key sources of judgment variance and improve discrimination</cite><cite id="dd001169-9">Error-span protocols show source-informed error localization predicts overall quality</cite><cite id="bfc19883-1">Human raters give more weight to long-distance dependencies, aligning with syntax-heavy source features penalizing MT</cite><cite id="bfc19883-9">Cross-linguistic gap assessments highlight that many perceived quality differences arise from linguistic-distant source constructs</cite>.</cite>

Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of how RSS-based ranging works in indoor WLAN and how those distances are fused to estimate a mobile device’s location, with the most common algorithms, models, error sources, and mitigations.

How RSS is translated into distances to access points
- Propagation model and calibration. RSS-to-distance estimation builds on the Friis free-space law and its empirically refined “log-distance” form, which adds a path-loss exponent and a log-normal shadowing term to capture indoor multipath and blockage effects. <cite id="93432e04-9">The log-distance path loss model extends the Friis free-space model to predict power loss over distance in a wide range of environments</cite> <cite id="93432e04-5">The log-distance path loss model characterizes variation of received power over distance due to path loss and shadowing</cite>. In practice, a site-specific calibration determines the path-loss exponent β and shadowing variance σ, often measured in decibels per decade, yielding a per-AP path-loss function PL(d)=PL(d0)+10β log10(d/d0)+Xσ (LOSt/NLOS variant). <cite id="93432e04-8">A distance estimation model based on log-normal shadowing can be written as PL(d)=PL(d0)+10𝛽los/nlos log10(d/d0)+X𝜎(los/nlos)</cite> <cite id="93432e04-2">Indoor measurements show that log-based path-loss models fit small houses and that a nonlinear path-loss model can perform better in larger spaces</cite>. More generally, path-loss models are fitted from sounding or measurement data with empirical coefficients, not purely physics. <cite id="93432e04-3">Path loss models are developed from numerical methods and empirical fits to measured channel sounding data</cite>.

- From RSSI to distance. Given calibrated model parameters and a measured RSS (or RSSI), the distance to each AP is inferred via inversion of the path-loss equation: d = d0·10^((RSS−PL0)/(10β)) (up to shadowing term handled probabilistically or via MLE). <cite id="93432e04-5">In the log-distance model, path loss grows with distance while shadowing adds log-normal variability, so observed power variation over distance can be captured for ranging</cite> <cite id="93432e04-4">A widely used log-distance model drives indoor device ranging from measured RSSI</cite>. Robust pipelines include per-AP adaptive calibration and selecting a propagation family that matches the deployment (e.g., log vs. nonlinear), improving accuracy across large venues. <cite id="93432e04-7">Localization pipelines first determine the propagation loss distance model for the environment before estimation</cite> <cite id="93432e04-2">A nonlinear path-loss model can outperform log-based models in larger indoor spaces</cite>.

- LOS/NLOS, multipath, and hardware bias. RSS is strongly affected by line-of-sight loss, reflections (multipath), and hardware/channel-dependent offsets; LOS/NLOS-aware models adjust β or add bias terms for NLOS segments. <cite id="93432e04-8">LOSt/NLOS-specific terms modify the log-normal shadowing path-loss equation, including a multiplicative factor for NLOS</cite> <cite id="93432e04-9">The path-loss exponent quantifies environment-specific energy decay beyond free space</cite>. Practitioners often mitigate by averaging RSS over time/frequency, using multiple channels (e.g., 802.11ac/az CSI), and fusing RSS with RTT-based ranges to reduce NLOS bias. <cite id="d9ba816b-8">Hybrid systems combine Wi‑Fi round-trip time (RTT) with RSS, modeling clock skew and RTT error distributions to improve ranging</cite> <cite id="b579bc71-5">802.11 fingerprinting commonly uses received signal indicators or CSI, with deep learning used for 3D indoor localization</cite>.

How distance estimates are fused to infer location
- Range-based localization (trilateration and least squares). With distances r1, r2, r3 from at least three APs whose coordinates are known, a naive trilateration intersects circles/ spheres to estimate the mobile’s position. <cite id="b579bc71-1">Trilateration ties distance measurements to position via geometric relations, solving the distance-measurement-to-position-estimate problem</cite> <cite id="b579bc71-6">Wi‑Fi trilateration uses signal strength from at least three APs to calculate distances and infer indoor location</cite>. Robust systems move beyond circle intersections to weighted least squares and iterative nonlinear least squares to minimize Σwi(r̂i−di)² over (x,y,z), using AP coordinates and RSS-derived di as measured ranges and r̂i as model-predicted ranges. <cite id="d9ba816b-1">Weighted iterative nonlinear least squares improve Wi‑Fi indoor positioning in 2.4 GHz environments by fusing RSS-derived ranges from multiple APs</cite> <cite id="d9ba816b-2">Comparisons show trilateration, Newton–Raphson, and Gauss–Newton methods trade off speed and accuracy for localization from range estimates computed from Wi‑Fi</cite>. Gauss–Newton/Levenberg–Marquardt solvers are widely used to solve the nonlinearity from the log-distance model; initialization with trilateration circles and weighting by inverse covariance (or RSS reliability) improves convergence and accuracy. <cite id="d9ba816b-2">Gauss–Newton performs better than trilateration and Newton–Raphson for non-linear Wi‑Fi range-based localization</cite>. Practical variants handle 2D/3D, coplanar APs, and ambiguity/invalid solutions with modified trilateration plus least-squares refinement. <cite id="d9ba816b-9">Modified 3D trilateration with least squares resolves invalid positions and ambiguity when APs are coplanar</cite>.

- Triangulation and angle-assisted approaches with RSS.
