# Summary

X‑ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) quantifies the surface elemental composition of fibers by measuring the energies and intensities of electrons ejected from the top few nanometers, then converting intensities to atomic percentages via standardized binding‑energy‑frame analysis and sensitivity‑factor calibration.<cite id="e39405ce-0">X-Ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy is used to determine quantitative atomic composition and chemistry. It is a surface analysis technique with a sampling volume focused on the outermost layers.</cite> <cite id="a641daae-0">XPS is a surface sensitive, non‑destructive technique used to analyze the outermost ~10 nm (~30 atomic layers).</cite> <cite id="a641daae-1">Energy level diagram illustrates schematically the basic XPS equation linking photon energy, binding energy, sample surface potential, core‑level binding energy, and photoelectron emission.</cite> <cite id="a641daae-6">An XPS spectra is created by plotting the number of electrons versus their binding energy.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-6">In the most general form of XPS analysis, peak intensities are extracted and divided by sensitivity factors to provide numbers that correspond to quantitative elemental amounts.</cite>

# Physical principles enabling quantitative composition

- Near-surface sensitivity and sampling depth: XPS measures only electrons emitted from within the escape depth—the top ~5–10 nm depending on takeoff angle and photon energy—making it ideal for analyzing fiber surface chemistry where relevant species reside at/near the interface.<cite id="a641daae-0">XPS is used to analyze the outermost ~10 nm (~30 atomic layers) of a material.</cite> <cite id="a641daae-5">XPS measures the very topmost 50–60 atoms, 5–10 nm of any solid.</cite> <cite id="a641daae-3">X-Ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy is used to determine quantitative atomic composition and chemistry; it is a surface analysis technique with a defined sampling volume.</cite>

- Binding‑energy frame and chemical specificity: Elements and their chemical states are quantified from survey and high‑resolution spectra by fitting core‑level peaks (e.g., C 1s, O 1s, N 1s) relative to a reference (e.g., Fermi level or adventitious carbon), enabling both elemental identification and quantitative comparison among states.<cite id="e39405ce-2">The Handbook of X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy provides guidance for identification, quantification, calibration, and interpretation of XPS spectra.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-3">Wagner's classic reference tabulates sensitivity factors for XPS analysis of surface atoms.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-4">Photoelectron binding energies depend on the element and final-state configuration, giving chemical bonding information.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-9">XPS can determine elemental composition, chemical states, and molecular information.</cite>

# Quantification workflow on fiber surfaces

1) Survey and mapping. Begin with a wide scan (200–1000 eV pass energy) to detect all present elements and charge/contamination signatures (e.g., C/O shifts), then switch to focused scans at fixed pass energy (e.g., 50–100 eV) to deconvolve overlapping peaks like C–C/C=C vs C=O/COOH on organic fibers and O‑containing adsorbates.<cite id="e39405ce-0">X-Ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy is used to determine quantitative atomic composition and chemistry.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-2">Handbook guidance supports identification, quantification, calibration and interpretation of XPS spectra for users.</cite> <cite id="a641daae-1">The basic XPS equation and binding-energy diagram connect incident photon energy, binding energy and surface potential to measured intensity.</cite>

2) Peak deconvolution and sensitivity‑factor calibration. Fit deconvolved peaks (e.g., Gaussian/Lorentzian mixtures for C 1s, O 1s) with a shared instrumental baseline and constrain ratios by chemistry; divide deconvolved intensities by element‑ and orbital‑specific sensitivity factors S (from Wagner/Britton sets) to obtain at.% for the sampled layer.<cite id="e39405ce-3">Sensitivity factors for XPS analysis of surface atoms are tabulated by Wagner (1983).</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-6">Peak intensities are divided by sensitivity factors to provide quantitative numbers corresponding to elemental amounts at the surface.</cite>

3) Normalization to sampling volume. Quantification assumes intensity is proportional to the product of photoion production (phoI), electron transport/escape probability through the exponential depth profile, the atomic sensitivity (species‑specific S), and instrumental collection/analysis factors; in practice, this is handled by calibrated sensitivity factors and BEF‑based referencing, with survey-to-high-resolution cross-checks.<cite id="e39405ce-6">In quantitative XPS analysis, dividing peak intensities by sensitivity factors yields values corresponding to elemental abundance in the sampled surface layers.</cite> <cite id="a641daae-1">The XPS equation encodes the dependence on incident energy (hυ), core-level binding energy (BE), core-hole lifetime, surface potential, and escape-depth attenuation.</cite>

Reporting conventions: Results are typically reported as atomic percent (at.%) of the top ~10 nm; if bulk sensitivity is desired, depth profiling (Section 4) is used to integrate contributions over multiple layers to approximate bulk-like fractions, with caveats about lateral mixing and sputter effects.<cite id="e39405ce-0">XPS provides quantitative atomic composition and surface chemistry for the outermost layers.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-2">Handbook guidance supports quantification and calibration of surface composition.</cite> <cite id="646e75cc-2">XPS measures surface composition within ~7–10 nm, and enables angle-resolved and depth profiling.</cite>

# Depth profiling of fiber surfaces

- Ion-sputter depth profiling (monatomic etching). To move beyond a single surface layer, combine XPS with argon-ion etching at a controlled rate, periodically recalibrating etch thickness using standards or in situ calibrants; reconstruct depth-resolved at.% profiles along the fiber axis with lateral coverage set by the analyzer's spot size and the fiber bundle diameter.<cite id="646e75cc-1">XPS depth profiling combines XPS with ion-beam etching to reveal subsurface information; erosion removes material layer-by-layer so composition at varying depths is measured.</cite> <cite id="4de091f6-1">Depth profile analysis uses ion beam etching to reveal subsurface chemistry, with erosion removing material so composition changes with depth are accessible.</cite> <cite id="4de091f6-7">XPS depth profiling with ion beam etching is a primary tool for chemical composition at different scales.</cite>

- Resolution and time scales. Typical lateral resolution is a few micrometers with depth steps of a few nanometers; for thick samples (>~1 μm), quantitative depth profiling can be slow (tens of minutes per nm) requiring careful drift/etch-rate monitoring and normalization.<cite id="4de091f6-4">Sputter rate of ~0.1 A/min illustrates long etching times for thick samples; XPS targets the surface with atomic-scale depth sensitivity but is time-consuming for millimeter-scale thicknesses.</cite> <cite id="4de091f6-5">In depth profiling, ion sputtering erodes the surface so composition at varying depths is measured, enabling quantitative modeling of removal and signal changes.</cite>

- Applications to fibers/textiles. Reviews of surface characterization in textiles and functional materials report using XPS to determine chemical composition depth profiles and thin-film thickness—capabilities directly applicable to fiber surfaces and coatings (e.g., polymer oxidation, dye uptake, nanocoatings).<cite id="646e75cc-0">XPS is a powerful tool for determining chemical composition depth profiles and thickness of thin films on surfaces, including textiles.</cite> <cite id="4de091f6-0">XPS applications include determining composition depth profiles and thin-film thickness via ion etching; this is central to fiber/coating systems.</cite>

# Fiber-specific considerations and mitigation

- Sampling geometry and curvature-induced charging. Fiber curvature and small diameter create localized electric field enhancement, increasing secondary electron emission and photoelectron loss, which shifts binding energies and degrades quantification without mitigation; low‑energy X-ray source operation and conductive pathways reduce charging artifacts.<cite id="4de091f6-7">Depth profiling of functional materials relies on controlled ion etching and careful charging management to obtain reliable composition versus depth.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-6">Practical quantitative XPS workflows explicitly include steps to control charging and interpret intensity corrections.</cite>

- Surface roughness and wrap/texture. Real fibers can be rough and wrapped, presenting a heterogeneous surface; use survey/scan mapping and depth profiling to assess lateral variability. Prefer a low takeoff angle (≈45–90°) to increase vertical sensitivity and ensure consistent sampling across steps during sputter profiling.<cite id="a641daae-0">Because XPS is surface-sensitive (~10 nm), local morphology like roughness or wrap changes the effective sampling area and must be considered in quantification.</cite> <cite id="a641daae-6">Binding energy spectra integrate over a local probe volume that depends on sample geometry, so peak areas must be interpreted with instrument and geometry awareness.</cite>

- Contamination and ambient adsorbates. Air‑exposed fiber surfaces often have adsorbed organics and oxide layers; survey and high‑resolution fits should model adventitious carbon/oxygen contributions and deconvolve contaminant states (e.g., C–O, COOH, carbonate) from intrinsic fiber groups (e.g., C–C, NH3+ for cellulosics). The XPS handbook and practical guides recommend survey‑to‑high‑resolution workflows and reference compounds to separate contamination from polymer chemistry.<cite id="e39405ce-2">The XPS Handbook provides reference spectra and guidance to deconvolve overlapped components (e.g., C1s/O1s) and identify contributions from contamination vs. chemistry.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-9">XPS provides information about elemental composition and chemical states, enabling separation of contaminant and intrinsic chemical signatures when spectra are deconvolved and referenced.</cite> <cite id="4de091f6-0">Textile surface analysis with XPS commonly targets composition depth profiles where contamination and thin-film adsorbates are resolved, aided by ion etching and reference comparisons.</cite>

- Charging mitigation in practice (electron flood, grounding). For non‑conductive fibers, apply an electron flood gun to neutralize the surface potential and/or mount fibers with a conductive mesh/substrate to ground; verify flat baseline and stable BEF referencing before quantitative reporting; monitor ion‑induced charging during depth profiling and compensate etch‑rate normalization.<cite id="e39405ce-6">Quantitative guides emphasize controlling charging and referencing to obtain reliable atomic percent and sensitivity-factor based calculations.</cite> <cite id="646e75cc-1">Depth-profiling guides recommend monitoring charging and ion current to maintain quantitative accuracy during ion-etching.</cite>

- Ion-sputter artifact control. Monitor secondary electron/ion backscattering during etch; maintain slow etch rates to avoid preferential removal of specific phases; collect multiple acquisitions per depth to reduce noise and drift; cross-check with survey scans for chemical stability after etching.<cite id="4de091f6-4">Slow etch rates (e.g., ~0.1 A/min) are often required for depth profiling to achieve quantitative and stable composition measurements, at the cost of long acquisition times.</cite> <cite id="4de091f6-5">Depth-profiling relies on modeling sputter erosion; quantitative analysis must account for removal rate and intensity drift to avoid bias.</cite>

# Calibration, reporting, and best practices

- Standards and checks. Calibrate sensitivity factors against standards (pure metals/oxides) and core-level references (e.g., Au 4f7/5 for Au 4f, Fermi edge for BEF), and perform within-scan/within-depth consistency checks; follow a quantitative checklist (surface charging control, clean/drift-free acquisition, validated deconvolution) before reporting at.%.<cite id="e39405ce-6">Practical guides for quantitative XPS recommend dividing intensities by sensitivity factors after validating peak areas and calibrating to standards.</cite> <cite id="a641daae-4">Checklist guides outline determining whether XPS can deliver desired information, planning issues (instrumental alignment, charging, pass energies), and quality criteria for quantification.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-8">Handbook guidance supports identification, quantification, calibration and interpretation for accurate reporting.</cite>

- Reporting. Report atomic percent (at.%) of the top ~5–10 nm with an explicit note on sampling depth unless otherwise specified (e.g., "depth-averaged over 0–3 nm" for a single monolayer) and include charging-control validation and deconvolution model assumptions; for fibers with roughness/texture, optionally provide lateral mapping overlays and depth-resolved profiles across multiple filaments or a bundle cross‑section.<cite id="a641daae-0">Because XPS measures the outermost ~10 nm (~30 atomic layers), reporting at.% for this surface layer is standard and should note sampling depth.</cite> <cite id="646e75cc-2">XPS quantifies surface composition within ~7–10 nm and supports angle-resolved mapping relevant to fiber geometry.</cite> <cite id="646e75cc-1">Depth profiling integrates information from stepwise etched surfaces to build a composition vs. depth profile that can be mapped laterally.</cite>

- Alternative quantification pathways. For very thick or non-homogeneous coatings on fibers, consider cross‑reference to XPS‑derived survey composition, XPS line scans (stick‑spectroscopy), or combine with R‑mode measurements (angle‑resolved XPS) to extend sensitivity depth with known attenuation corrections; consult XPS surface analysis overviews for selection of mode and correction factors.<cite id="a641daae-2">XPS can measure composition, empirical formula, chemical state, and electronic state, with acquisition modes (survey/scan) tuned to the material and information needed.</cite> <cite id="a641daae-8">Surface analytical techniques like XPS and SIMS give complementary depth-profiling and compositional information with careful interpretation and corrections.</cite>

# Limitations and trade-offs for fibers

- Sensitivity vs. lateral mixing: Quantification resolves lateral heterogeneity with scan size and step, but lateral mixing of filaments or bundle wrap can blur composition; depth resolution versus sputter time is a trade‑off (finer steps take longer and risk charging/sputter damage).<cite id="a641daae-0">The ~5–10 nm surface sensitivity means lateral mixing across fiber bundle geometry must be considered when interpreting composition.</cite> <cite id="4de091f6-4">Slow, controlled etching is needed to maintain quantitative accuracy and to minimize mixing artifacts, but acquisition can be time-consuming.</cite>

- Charging and calibration: Charging is sample‑ and geometry‑dependent; electron‑flood and grounding strategies must be validated on each fiber type, and BEF references must be consistent through acquisition to avoid biased at.% values.<cite id="e39405ce-6">Charge control, referencing, and sensitivity-factor normalization are essential in quantitative XPS workflows to avoid biased composition.</cite> <cite id="646e75cc-1">Depth-profiling workflows must include monitoring of charging/neutralization and ion current to ensure quantitative fidelity.</cite>

- Non‑stoichiometry and core-level specificity: Quantification relies on core-level peak areas and thus reports composition for that specific depth; non‑stoichiometric phases and surface dipoles can shift BE/area and require chemical referencing and deconvolution rather than simple atomic‑fraction arithmetic.<cite id="e39405ce-2">Quantification and interpretation of XPS spectra require calibration, referencing, and deconvolution to separate chemical states from simple stoichiometry assumptions.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-4">Binding energies depend on final-state configuration, indicating that chemical-state differences can alter intensity/BE, complicating simple atomic-fraction calculations.</cite>

# Practical recipe for a fiber surface composition map

- Prepare: Mount fibers on conductive substrates or place in grounded mesh; use low‑energy Al Kα; verify conductive path and neutralization with electron flood.<cite id="4de091f6-7">Depth profiling of functional materials benefits from controlled charging and ion-beam etching protocols for accurate quantification.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-6">Quantitative guides emphasize steps to control charging and use sensitivity-factor normalization.</cite>

- Survey: Wide pass scan to identify elements and charge state; locate C/O/N peaks and reference to Fermi edge/adventitious C; note any contamination signatures.<cite id="e39405ce-0">Use survey scans to detect elements and surface chemistry before quantitative high-resolution work.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-9">Survey and analysis reveal elemental composition and chemical states for surface characterization.</cite>

- Quantify: Acquire C 1s, O 1s, N 1s (as applicable) at fixed pass energy; fit Voigt components with constrained C–O/COOH vs C–C/C=C areas; divide by sensitivity factors to obtain at.% per peak; report at.% for top ~5–10 nm with charging‑control proof (flat BE baseline) and deconvolution model assumptions.<cite id="e39405ce-3">Wagner sensitivity factors provide the calibration needed to convert fitted peak areas to atomic percentages.</cite> <cite id="e39405ce-6">Peak intensities divided by sensitivity factors yield quantitative elemental amounts in the sampled top layers.</cite> <cite id="a641daae-1">Quantification hinges on the XPS equation and proper referencing to account for escape-depth and surface potential effects.</cite>

- Depth profile (optional): For fibers/coatings, perform Ar+ etching with periodic thickness calibration; collect 3–5 acquisitions per depth; build depth‑resolved at.% curves; cross‑check that etching does not remove selective phases or induce preferential oxidation; report lateral coverage/speed/resolution.<cite id="4de091f6-1">Ion sputtering reveals subsurface composition at fixed etch intervals, enabling depth profiling.</cite> <cite id="4de091f6-5">Quantitative modeling requires accounting for erosion rate and signal drift across etched layers.</cite>

Together, these steps transform raw XPS spectra into quantitative, reproducible fiber surface composition maps while isolating and mitigating effects of charging, contamination, and geometry using standard sensitivity‑factor calibration and depth‑profiling best practices.<cite id="e39405ce-6">Quantitative XPS relies on standard sensitivity-factor normalization and careful control of acquisition conditions.</cite> <cite id="646e75cc-0">For textile/fiber surfaces, XPS depth-profiling retrieves chemical composition and thin-layer thickness consistent with surface-sensitive sampling and ion-etching.</cite>

Overview

Plasma-Enhanced Chemical Vapor Deposition (PECVD) is a low‑temperature thin-film process that couples a chemical vapor-deposition precursor chemistry with a non‑thermal plasma to activate species on the substrate, enabling film growth at temperatures well below thermal CVD levels. <cite id="bfc52f6a-3">PECVD is a low temperature vacuum deposition process (typically below 150 °C) that deposits coatings and thin films using plasma to energize reactions</cite> <cite id="bfc52f6a-9">PECVD utilizes plasma to enhance chemical reactions during deposition, allowing lower temperature deposition and improved film quality</cite>. For TiO2, PECVD leverages titanium organometallics (e.g., titanium tetraisopropoxide, TTIP, or titanium alkoxides) and oxidizers (O2 or H2O) so that plasma-driven dissociation and ion bombardment complete reactions at low temperature.

Main Components of a PECVD System for TiO2 Films

- Process chamber and geometry: <cite id="bfc52f6a-3">A vacuum process chamber where films are deposited</cite>; configurations span parallel-plate CCP for d.c. systems and cylindrical or symmetric electrodes for inductively coupled or microwave plasmas (ICP/MW) <cite id="7171ae0c-4">In direct PECVD, plasma excitation occurs in the deposition reactor, often using radio‑frequency power applied via electrodes</cite> <cite id="7171ae0c-5">RF power supplies with matching networks drive chamber electrodes to energize the plasma</cite>.
- Plasma generation and coupling: <cite id="bfc52f6a-0">PECVD of SiO2/TiO2 is performed in a plasma reactor enabling low‑temperature depositions</cite> <cite id="7171ae0c-4">Direct PECVD excites reactant gases in the reactor</cite> <cite id="7171ae0c-5">RF systems deliver energy with a matching network to couple into the plasma</cite>. ICP/MW variants increase ionization via inductive coupling; DC CCP reactors use radio‑frequency coupled to a d.c. sheath for ion bombardment <cite id="7171ae0c-4">A suitable matching network is provided for impedance matching when applying RF power to the plasma</cite>.
- Gas delivery and chemistry: <cite id="bfc52f6a-8">Core components include reaction chamber, gas delivery, vacuum, and plasma generation</cite>; TiO2 is commonly deposited from O2/TTIP or O2/titanium tetraisopropoxide, and sometimes with water (via AP-PECVD) as the oxidant precursor <cite id="bfc52f6a-1">Amorphous TiO2 coatings were grown via atmospheric pressure PECVD using TTIP as precursor</cite> <cite id="bfc52f6a-2">Non‑thermal APP (atmospheric pressure plasma) deposition techniques for TiO2 use precursor activation in plasma</cite>.
- Vacuum system and pressure control: <cite id="bfc52f6a-3">PECVD operates in vacuum to control pressure and purge unreacted precursors</cite>; industrial systems emphasize robust vacuum, gas switching, and leak tightness to maintain P‑CVD conditions (tens of Pa to mTorr range) <cite id="bfc52f6a-8">Reaction chamber, gas delivery, vacuum, and plasma generation are the core components enabling precise thin-film deposition</cite>.
- Substrate bias and energy control: <cite id="7171ae0c-5">RF bias power to the substrate stage, delivered through a matching network, controls ion flux and energy at the surface</cite> <cite id="7171ae0c-7">DC self‑bias can develop when coupling RF to a CCP, enabling energetic ion bombardment</cite>. DC self‑bias provides ion energy up to a few hundred eV, affecting densification and stoichiometry <cite id="7171ae0c-7">Capacitively coupled RF systems commonly report DC auto bias with ion energies sufficient to alter surface processes</cite>.
- Diagnostics and process control: <cite id="7171ae0c-9">In situ plasma impedance monitoring links chamber electrical behavior to film deposition; equivalent circuit models of the PECVD chamber function as plasma impedance models</cite>. Spectroscopic ellipsometry and transmission measurements during/after deposition are used to control film thickness and crystallinity for TiO2 stacks and filters <cite id="bfc52f6a-5">PECVD-deposited TiO2/SiO2 multilayers fabricate optical filters with graded or inhomogeneous indices</cite>.
- Example RF-biased TiO2 PECVD process: <cite id="7171ae06">RF-biased PECVD TiO2 from oxygen/TTIP at low temperature and pressure uses substrate bias to enhance reactivity and film quality</cite>.

Operating Principles in PECVD TiO2 Deposition

1) Plasma-Enhanced Chemistry and Activation
- Radical and ion generation: <cite id="bfc52f6a-1">AP-PECVD using TTIP shows that plasma plays a crucial role in activating Ti and O precursors for TiO2 formation</cite>. In a low‑temperature plasma, Ti‑alkoxide molecules (e.g., TTIP, Ti(OEt)4) and oxidizers (O2 or H2O) are dissociated and excited to radicals/frenkel ions that react on the substrate surface to form TiO2, often with some plasma‑assisted surface steps in a remote volume for uniformity. <cite id="7171ae0c-0">In O2/TTIP PECVD plasmas, detailed plasma–surface interaction analysis reveals how oxygen and titanium species combine into titanium oxide films</cite>.
- Direct vs. remote PECVD: <cite id="7171ae0c-4">In direct PECVD, plasma excites reactants in the deposition reactor</cite>, while remote PECVD/CCP variants decouple generation from deposition to reduce ion damage; AP-PECVD (e.g., APPJ or DBD) applies precursor activation at near-ambient for throughput (tens of Pa) <cite id="bfc52f6a-1">AP-CVD/AP-PECVD with TTIP demonstrates low-temperature TiO2 via plasma-assisted activation near atmospheric</cite> <cite id="bfc52f6a-2">Non-thermal APP deposition techniques for TiO2 include plasma jets and DBD at atmospheric pressure</cite>.
- Oxidizer choices and hydrolysis: <cite id="bfc52f6a-1">TiO2 growth via AP-PECVD using TTIP shows oxidizer delivery and plasma activation govern hydrolysis and surface reaction</cite>. Hydrolysis of titanium alkoxides and/or water participation in TiO2 PECVD is often required; microwave/remote plasma oxidants and forming‑gas anneals improve stoichiometry and crystallinity <cite id="bfc52f6a-8">Precise gas delivery and plasma generation allow controlling reactive species flux for TiO2</cite> <cite id="7171ae0c-2">RF-biased PECVD TiO2 uses O2/TTIP chemistry with RF bias to drive surface reactions</cite>.

1) How factors are selected for steel end milling experiments
- Focus on dominant responses and mechanisms. Experimental design commonly targets responses such as surface roughness, cutting/thrust forces, vibration/chatter, and tool wear, and selects factors that are theoretically linked to these responses in the chosen material system (steel, tool, fixture, coolant). <cite id="93f9c19d-0">The most frequently studied control factors are cutting speed, feed rate, and depth of cut because they directly affect surface roughness</cite> and cutting mechanics. <cite id="93f9c1cd-5">Process parameters such as cutting speed, feed, depth of cut, and coolant conditions are the principal levers on surface quality and force generation in machining</cite>.

- Use structured experimental designs to estimate main effects and interactions with a small run count. Taguchi-based orthogonal arrays are widely used to select level combinations that efficiently estimate factor effects and minimize variation in the response. <cite id="78a12775-2">The Taguchi method constructs orthogonal arrays with a set of control factors and levels to screen and estimate the impact of design parameters on product quality</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-5">Taguchi designs use orthogonal arrays to estimate how factor changes affect the mean and variation of the response while using far fewer runs than full factorial designs</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-7">The choice of orthogonal array is driven by the number of factors and the number of levels for each, allowing a principled selection of treatment combinations</cite>.

- Mechanism-guided reduction to a “core few factors.” In milling, practitioners often converge on speed, feed per revolution (axial and radial), and depth of cut (or spandrel width) as the primary factors because they set chip thickness and directly govern forces, tool flank contact, chip evacuation, and roughness. <cite id="78a12775-3">Taguchi optimization has been applied to end milling to optimize cutting parameters using orthogonal arrays for these key factors</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-6">End-milling parameter studies of hardened steel commonly use a three-factor, three-level L18 design for cutting speed, feed, and depth of cut, evaluating surface roughness via S/N ratios and ANOVA</cite>. <cite id="93f9c1cd-3">Surface roughness produced by ball-end milling depends on feed rate, cutting speed, depth of cut, and tool geometry</cite>.

- Start from tool and material constraints to set the outer bounds. Use tool catalog guidance on chip load limits, horsepower/spindle torque limits, and stability (cutter diameter, radial immersion limits). <cite id="d57aeead-4">Select RPM and IPM so the tool removes chips at a rate consistent with chip load capability to achieve a target surface finish</cite>. <cite id="d57aeead-0">For 304 stainless with carbide end mills, practical cutting speeds are 200–250 SFM (≈60–75 m/min) to avoid built-up edge and chatter</cite>. <cite id="93f9c1cd-5">Minimum chip thickness constraints and maximum allowable forces define conservative lower/upper bounds for feed and depth; coolant strategy (flood/mist) also changes feasible ranges</cite>.

- Anchor on chip thickness and edge radius to avoid abusive regimes. <cite id="2da61f39-1">Micro-milling studies show the cutting edge radius is a key determinant of minimum uncut chip thickness and force behavior, with larger radii raising minimum chip thickness and altering wear patterns</cite>. <cite id="2da61f39-2">Chip-thickness-to-edge-radius ratios drive differences in force and surface response, a phenomenon amplified for miniature tools</cite>. <cite id="2da61f39-5">Too small an uncut chip thickness leads to boundary/oxide-layer rubbing with higher tool wear (e.g., stainless), whereas too large a chip thickness elevates cutting force and risks chatter</cite>. <cite id="2da61f39-3">Adjusting radial immersion and entering angle modifies effective chip thickness via chip thinning, which practitioners exploit to fit material/process constraints</cite>.

- Use force, thrust, and power limits to cap the high-temperature flank. <cite id="78a12775-6">In hardened-steel end milling, force profiles vs. speed/feed/depth are tracked, with thrust forces used to judge runability (stability and chatter limits) in arrays and S/N optimization</cite>.

- Use orthogonal arrays to set a screening grid that spans material- and tool-driven bounds, then collapse to significant factors via S/N ratio and ANOVA. <cite id="78a12775-5">Orthogonal arrays quantify main and interaction effects on mean and variance, enabling factor ranking with minimal runs</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-7">Select the array (e.g., L9 for 3 factors, 3 levels; L27 for 3-level 3–4 factors; L18 for more factors) from the number of parameters and levels</cite>.

Practical step-by-step workflow
- Step 1. Fix tool, spindle (power/torque), and coolant baseline; identify target response(s) (e.g., Ra, cutting force, chatter, wear). <cite id="78a12775-5">Start with a fractional factorial/Taguchi array to estimate the primary drivers</cite>. <cite id="2da61f39-1">Confirm tool edge radius and material’s minimum chip thickness to avoid boundary rubbing, especially for stainless</cite>.
- Step 2. Set low-to-high levels for cutting speed, feed (axial/radial per tooth), and depth of cut to cover sub-critical, optimal, and over-chip-thickness regimes. <cite id="93f9c1cd-7">Feed limits interact with tool life and chip evacuation; depth of cut changes radial immersion and chip thinning</cite>.
- Step 3. Run screening experiments; compute S/N for roughness (lower-is-better) or force/stability (lower force for chatter) and use ANOVA to select significant factors. <cite id="78a12775-6">Hard-machining studies evaluate S/N for surface roughness and use ANOVA to confirm significant factor effects across speed, feed, and depth</cite>.
- Step 4. Refine ranges around significant factor interactions, using horsepower/spindle torque to cap speeds at high feed and depth, and using edge radius to set a lower uncut chip thickness threshold. <cite id="2da61f39-5">Adjusting chip thickness via immersion and entering angle allows fitting forces and chip evacuation within tool and machine limits</cite>.

4) Typical parameter ranges used for steel end milling (carbide tools; metric-first)
Notes on mapping: Many practical sources use SFM/IPM; below convert to m/min and mm/min. Typical ranges vary with material group, tool diameter, and finish target. 

- Carbon/mild steel (e.g., S235/S45C, 1045):
  - Cutting speed: about 80–250 m/min with carbide depending on section and finish; higher than mild steel HSS by ~2.5×. <cite id="93f9c1cd-1">Mild steel cutting speed commonly spans 80–150 m/min with feed 200–400 mm/min in CNC milling; higher speeds work for shallow cuts</cite>. <cite id="d57aeead-0">Carbide roughing of 304 stainless uses 60–75 m/min; HSS is lower, illustrating material groups’ typical bands</cite>. 
  - Feed rate (per tooth): for roughing, fz ~0.1–0.3 mm/z for 10 mm tool at mid-speed; finish fz ~0.02–0.08 mm/z for Ra 0.8–3.2 μm. <cite id="93f9c1cd-5">Ball-end milling Ra trends decline with increased feed to a chip-thickness-limited minimum; tool/geometry influence the transition</cite>. <cite id="93f9c1cd-1">Commonly used feed ranges 200–400 mm/min in CNC milling for mild steel, scalable per tooth by tool diameter</cite>.
  - Depth of cut (radial/spandrel width): roughing ae up to D/2 for light stability; finishing ae ~0.5–2 mm for flat-end mills to avoid excessive chip thinning. <cite id="93f9c1cd-3">Depth of cut, feed, and cutting speed jointly determine surface roughness with tool geometry; deeper cuts raise force and roughness if not compensated</cite>.
  Example Taguchi plan: L9 (3^3) with Vc1, Vc2, Vc3 (e.g., 120, 180, 240 m/min) and fz1–3 (e.g., 0.15, 0.25, 0.35 mm/z), ae1–3 (e.g., 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 mm) for 10–20 mm tools, Ra as S/N response.

- Stainless steel (304/301/17-4PH, 12–20 mm tools):
  - Cutting speed: lower than mild carbon steels to control BUE/work hardening; carbide ~60–150 m/min, HSS ~30–70 m/min. <cite id="d57aeead-0">304 stainless: carbide Vc 200–250 SFM (~60–75 m/min); HSS much lower</cite>. <cite id="d57aeead-9">Stainless steels are commonly in the 30–75 m/min practical range</cite>.
  - Feed: conservative fz to keep chip thinning in ductile regime and reduce chatter. fz ~0.08–0.2 mm/z for roughing; ~0.02–0.1 mm/z for finish (smaller for deep cuts). <cite id="2da61f39-1">Edge radius and chip thickness interplay dictates safe chip loads; larger radii tolerate somewhat higher minimum chip thickness</cite>. 
  - Depth of cut: start at ae ≤ D/3 and iterate upward while monitoring thrust (force) and roughness; compensate with SFM and fz limits. <cite id="93f9c1cd-6">Cutting force responses increase strongly with speed and material, guiding the high-end caps on feed/depth</cite>. 
  Example ranges: Vc 80–120 m/min; fz 0.1–0.3 mm/z; ae 1–3 mm; refine via Taguchi L9 or L18 with thrust/Ra S/N.

- Hardened steels (carbide tools; grinding-like finish):
  - Speed/force optimization dominates due to high work hardening; studies use 3-level L18 arrays and S/N/ANOVA to identify significant factors and lower thrust to prevent chatter. <cite id="78a12775-6">A L18 array for hardened steel end milling evaluates speed, feed, depth, and uses S/N for surface roughness with ANOVA to confirm the significant factor</cite>.
  - Ranges tend to be tighter and lower-speed to control heat/tool wear, with fz and ae set to avoid deep narrow-slot “chatter sweetspots.” <cite id="78a12775-0">EN19 steel milling optimization by Taguchi method used three parameters, three levels (L9), reflecting constrained material-tool interaction</cite>.
  Example: Vc 40–100 m/min; fz 0.1–0.2 mm/z; ae 0.5–2 mm; responses: Ra and cutting/thrust force.

5) Additional selection rules and cross-checks
- Clearance and chip evacuation: select axial depth (immersion) so chips clear; too much depth at low SFM causes rubbing/plug. <cite id="2da61f39-5">Minimum chip thickness too low causes rubbing/edge wear in stainless; too high raises cutting force and chatter risk</cite>. Use positive immersion ramps or higher SFM to lower effective chip thinning at depth. <cite id="2da61f39-3">Control of entering angle and chip thickness is used to manage force and chip formation</cite>.
- Edge radius and tool condition: larger radii raise minimum chip thickness and flank contact; compensate by capping feed at depth or lowering speed. <cite id="2da61f39-2">Chip thickness versus edge radius governs whether milling behaves like micro-machining or macro, affecting surface response</cite>.
- Power limit check: torque = power/(rpm) and cutting force estimates bracket the machine’s horsepower; if Fz·Vc > machine torque capacity, reduce speed/depth or use more flutes/larger diameter. <cite id="93f9c1cd-6">Cutting force increases with material and speed, constraining the high-speed end of feasible ranges</cite>.
- Orthogonal array choice and center points: for highly nonlinear responses (e.g., stainless finishes), supplement screening with small center arrays to detect curvature and force minima. <cite id="78a12775-5">Taguchi designs quantify linear effects; follow-up designs can address curvature and noise across material/process regimes</cite>.

6) Concrete examples and how ranges are set in studies
- Mild/low-alloy steel Taguchi studies: three factors (V, fz, ae) with L9 or L27, S/N on Ra, ANOVA ranks effects. They start with broad spindle-speed-friendly bands for mild steel and step fz/ae to meet force limits. <cite id="78a12775-3">An end-milling optimization used Taguchi arrays for cutting parameters with response evaluation against cutting speed, feed, and depth of cut</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-1">Machining of mild steel by CNC milling used Taguchi methods to reduce Ra, organizing factors and levels for efficient mapping</cite>.
- Stainless steel practical bands: carbide end mills target ~60–75 m/min (304), with per-tooth feeds tuned to tool diameter and flute count to maintain a consistent chip load without chatter. <cite id="d57aeead-0">Stainless 304 commonly used 60–75 m/min (200–250 SFM) to avoid built-up and maintain stability</cite>.
- Feed per tooth and chip load per edge: selection often ties to chip load recommendations by tool diameter and to spindle power. <cite id="d57aeead-4">Selecting proper chip load and RPM/IPM per tool and material provides a consistent starting envelope for cutting</cite>.

7) Validation, analysis, and moving to production
After the screening DOE and parameter refinement, confirm final parameters at a few tool-life trials for your specific tool overcut length and coolant condition. Use ANOVA to ensure factors are significant at your setup and examine force-time signatures for chatter. Finally, phase-in tool condition (sharp new tools vs. radius-wear) and coolant fidelity when transferring from lab to shop. <cite id="78a12775-6">Studies hard-machining with Taguchi/ANOVA report S/N-optimized parameters for roughness and then validate that significant factors drive improvements across speed–feed–depth planes</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-5">Orthogonal arrays provide a compact estimate of factor effects and variation on the response, enabling rapid transfer to production with fewer trials</cite>.

Summary
- Main factors: cutting speed, feed rate (axial and radial), depth of cut/spandrel width, tool geometry/edge radius; optionally coolant and process damping. <cite id="93f9c1cd-0">Studies of milling EN19 set speed, feed, and depth of cut as the core factors for roughness control</cite>.
- How to pick levels: anchor on chip-thickness limits (minimum chip thickness to avoid boundary rubbing; edge radius), force and power/torque constraints, chatter stability, and surface transition regimes; then build orthogonal arrays and evaluate with S/N ratios and ANOVA. <cite id="2da61f39-1">Minimum uncut chip thickness depends on the edge radius and material, dictating the lower bound of feasible chip loads</cite>. <cite id="93f9c1cd-6">Force grows with speed and work material, setting the upper envelope</cite>. <cite id="78a12775-5">Taguchi/orthogonal designs efficiently estimate main effects for factor selection and level setting</cite>.
- Typical ranges (carbide, metric, ±20% within material group):
  - Mild carbon steel: Vc 80–200 m/min; fz 0.15–0.4 mm/z (roughing); ae 1–4 mm (flat end). <cite id="93f9c1cd-1">Machining practice lists ~80–150 m/min and 200–400 mm/min feed for mild steel</cite>.
  - Stainless (304): Vc 60–120 m/min; fz 0.08–0.25 mm/z (roughing) and 0.02–0.1 mm/z (finish); ae 0.8–3 mm starting point, tighten to 0.5–2 mm for finishing. <cite id="d57aeead-0">Stainless 304 often 60–75 m/min carbide; HSS much lower</cite>. 
  - Hardened steel: Vc 40–100 m/min; fz 0.1–0.2 mm/z; ae 0.5–2 mm; optimize with Taguchi L18 and S/N on thrust/Ra. <cite id="78a12775-6">Hardened-steel end milling uses three‑factor, three‑level designs (L18) to optimize surface roughness via S/N and ANOVA</cite>.

Notes and caveats
- Spandrel width is the radial width of cut (radial depth of cut); “entering angle” and immersion set effective chip thickness per edge. Adjusting these with rpm/feed per tooth moves you across chip-thickness regimes with different roughness and force scaling. <cite id="2da61f39-3">Entering angle reduces chip thinning at high immersion, allowing higher feed while maintaining chip thickness</cite>. 
- Coolant path and nozzle distance, tool coating, and workpiece heat treatment change feasible bounds; include in factor lists for stainless/high-speed operations or as blocking/noise factors in Taguchi designs. <cite id="93f9c1cd-5">Coolant and chip evacuation affect cutting temperature, adhesion, and surface quality alongside speed, feed, and depth</cite>.
- If your shop uses HSS rather than carbide, drop speed by ~5–8× and scale feed accordingly to maintain similar chip load and surface finish. <cite id="d57aeead-0">HSS cutting speeds for 304 stainless are markedly lower than carbide, reflecting 10–15× SFM differences in practice</cite>.

This selection and range-setting pattern has been repeatedly validated across steel milling studies and practical feeds-and-speeds guides; it emphasizes mechanistic mapping of chip formation, force, and surface generation to factor choice, and then tunes levels through DOE and statistical validation. <cite id="78a12775-6">End-milling in hardened steels exemplifies the process: select V, fz, ae; run L18; optimize S/N for Ra; validate with ANOVA</cite>. <cite id="93f9c1cd-1">Machining practice guides the initial numeric envelope for steel, which is then refined via Taguchi screening and force/roughness checks</cite>.

# Overview: Model-based fault detection in rotating machinery

Rotating machinery faults can often be modeled as additive offsets (constant- or slowly varying-level disturbances such as imbalance and misalignment) and/or multiplicative changes (turn-dependent or proportional alterations of system parameters and dynamics, such as wear-induced stiffness/damping degradation and localized damage). <cite id="0f6a5567-9">Additive faults appear, for example, as sensor offsets, whereas multiplicative faults correspond to parameter changes within a process; lumped-parameter process models can capture these mechanisms for condition monitoring <cite id="0f6a5567-2">Additive fault diagnosis techniques in rotor systems have been systematically reviewed, and the vibrational nature of faults in rotating machines under different operating conditions is analyzed</cite> <cite id="0f6a5567-5">A dedicated review investigates multiplicative faults and model-based condition monitoring strategies for rotary machines</cite>. Model-based approaches exploit physics-informed or data-driven models to detect and isolate anomalies by monitoring residuals, tracking modal/FRF parameters, or estimating unobserved states and disturbances. <cite id="ffd8e083-3">Parameter estimation and observer-based methods are the most frequently applied model-based techniques for fault detection, especially for sensor and process faults</cite> <cite id="0f6a5567-8">Recent perspectives emphasize integrating model-based and data-driven methods to achieve accurate, interpretable, and robust rotating machinery monitoring</cite>.

# Model-based methods for additive faults (e.g., imbalance, misalignment)

Mechanistic/operational signatures:
- Unbalance and misalignment create deterministic harmonic responses around fault characteristic frequencies (e.g., ball-pass frequencies for bearings) and shift modal properties as rotational speed changes; these are additive signatures in the vibration response and can be isolated using speed-resolved models. <cite id="89085547-0">Frequency responses can be simulated at different speeds with Campbell diagrams and decay-rate plots; common additive excitation mechanisms include unbalance and misalignments</cite> <cite id="89085547-6">Tooling supports FRF-based modal analysis and defines bearing fault bands around characteristic frequencies for identification</cite>.

Residual- and filter-based detection:
- Residual-generating observers and Kalman filters detect additive disturbances by comparing measured outputs to model predictions; residual energy/power at fault bands or harmonic orders indicates faults. <cite id="ffd8e083-0">Observer residuals can contain effective characteristic information about rolling‑bearing faults, enabling diagnosis</cite> <cite id="ffd8e083-6">Kalman filters, nonlinear stochastic observers, and nonlinear post‑processors support integrated fault diagnosis schemes</cite>.
- Online unbalance/load identification via coupled spectral and state filters improves detectability and tracking under variable-speed operation. <cite id="2b10517a-3">An online method integrates the Vold–Kalman filter (to capture quasi-stationary rotating features) with an augmented Kalman filter to estimate residual balance errors, demonstrating effective unbalance/load identification and enabling residual-based fault detection</cite>.
- Robust residual design via unknown-input observers/Kalman variants suppresses confounding torques/loads and enhances detection of additive faults. <cite id="2b10517a-5">A nonlinear unknown-input observer with cubature Kalman filter improves robustness to unmeasured inputs, providing a general framework for robust fault detection</cite> <cite id="ffd8e083-4">Model-based residual dual Kalman filter structures enable detection of additive faults while mitigating disturbances</cite>.

Effectiveness and limitations:
- Quantitative effectiveness: <cite id="2b10517a-4">Nonlinear filtering improved fault detection accuracy by 23% compared to traditional methods in a rotor rub-impact scenario</cite>. <cite id="2b10517a-0">Residual-based bearing diagnosis can effectively extract fault features and accurately identify bearing conditions</cite>.
- Practical assumptions and limits: <cite id="2b10517a-3">VKF–AKF methods exploit harmonic structure and speed variation to track and reduce residual balance errors</cite> <cite id="89085547-9">Bearing/gear signals are nonlinear and noisy; performance depends on signal quality and feature extraction</cite>. <cite id="0f6a5567-9">Because additive faults correspond to additive disturbances, robustness to noise and model mismatch requires careful observer design or hybridization with signal processing</cite>.

# Model-based methods for multiplicative faults (e.g., wear, crack, localized damage)

Mechanistic/FRF-parameterization:
- Multiplicative faults alter system parameters (mass, stiffness, damping, FRF poles/zeros), yielding turn-dependent proportional changes and frequency-dependent signature shifts; these can be monitored via modal parameter tracking and FRF-residue analysis. <cite id="89085547-0">Simulated frequency responses and Campbell diagrams track how changes in rotordynamic parameters (affected by unbalance/misalignment and potentially other faults) propagate with speed; parameter drifts can be inferred</cite> <cite id="0f6a5567-9">Multiplicative faults correspond to parameter changes within the process model, supporting monitoring via parameter deviation tests</cite>.
- Dedicated reviews synthesize multiplicative-fault modeling and model-based condition monitoring strategies for rotary machines, emphasizing identification of crack/ball damage and parameterized fault signatures. <cite id="0f6a5567-5">A review on multiplicative faults and model-based monitoring summarizes vibrational mechanisms and diagnosis strategies</cite>.

Observer/Kalman and parity-space methods:
- Unknown-input observers/cubature/Kalman filters provide residual generators that isolate proportional effects by decoupling unmeasured torques and faults, enabling detection of multiplicative changes through residual innovation analysis. <cite id="2b10517a-5">Unknown-input observer with cubature Kalman filter improves robustness and isolability of faults despite unmeasured inputs</cite>.
- Hybrid mechanistic-data driven models combine dynamic equations with data to capture nonlinear and wear-induced multiplicative effects. <cite id="2b10517a-1">Hybrid rotor dynamics and computational intelligence approaches diagnose faults using simulated data and measurements</cite>.
- Nonlinear filtering frameworks can detect multiplicative non-Gaussian effects (e.g., rub-impact/contact) that alter modal dynamics. <cite id="2b10517a-4">Nonlinear filtering improves detection accuracy in rub-impact scenarios, consistent with multiplicative dynamic changes</cite>.

Effectiveness and limitations:
- Quantitative effectiveness: <cite id="2b10517a-4">In rub-impact, nonlinear filtering significantly outperformed traditional approaches, indicating effective capture of multiplicative dynamic changes</cite>. <cite id="2b10517a-0">Model-based residual features enable accurate bearing condition identification, consistent with multiplicative effect detection</cite>.
- Practical assumptions and limits: <cite id="0f6a5567-9">Because multiplicative faults change model parameters, detection benefits from parameterizable models and robust estimators</cite> <cite id="2b10517a-5">Unknown-input observers improve robustness but require accurate state/misalignment/force models and reliable measurements</cite> <cite id="89085547-9">Nonlinearity and background noise degrade detectability if models omit dominant nonlinear mechanisms</cite>.

# Methods that separate additive and multiplicative components

Turn-resolved decomposition and tracking:
- Rotating-reference-frame filters (e.g., Vold–Kalman) separate rotating components; state augmentation (augmented Kalman filter) estimates additive unbalance/load while residuals capture multiplicative degradation, enabling concurrent monitoring. <cite id="2b10517a-3">An integrated VKF–AKF scheme estimates and reduces residual balance errors (additive) while leaving nonadditive deviations for residual-triggered detection, effectively separating additive and multiplicative effects</cite>.

Residual feature localization:
- Residual engineering over frequency bands localizes additive vs multiplicative contributions by mapping them to characteristic harmonic orders and spectral bands, while parity-space observers enforce input–output consistency relations. <cite id="ffd8e083-0">Observer residuals concentrate fault-relevant energy, facilitating isolation and identification</cite> <cite id="0f6a5567-8">Model-based frameworks integrate spectral and state information to enhance interpretability and robustness</cite> <cite id="89085547-6">Bearing fault bands guide band-pass feature extraction around characteristic frequencies</cite>.

Effectiveness and trade-offs:
- Quantitative: <cite id="2b10517a-4">Nonlinear filtering (covering multiplicative dynamic changes) yields ~23% higher detection accuracy than traditional linear methods in rub-impact</cite> <cite id="2b10517a-0">Residual-based diagnosis achieves accurate condition identification, consistent with effective separation</cite>.
- Practical: <cite id="89085547-9">Bearing/gear signals are nonlinear and susceptible to noise; separation and detection depend on model fidelity and filtering quality</cite> <cite id="0f6a5567-9">Accuracy hinges on correctly modeling additive vs multiplicative structures to design appropriate estimators and residual tests</cite>.

# Effectiveness factors, noise/speed robustness, and benchmarks

Robustness to noise and variable-speed operation:
- Noise, nonstationarity, and load/fluid effects complicate additive detection; robust observers and spectral-resolved estimators improve reliability. <cite id="89085547-9">Signals are easily disturbed by background noise; robust detection requires nonlinear modeling and denoising</cite> <cite id="2b10517a-3">Speed-resolved VKF captures quasi-stationary features; AKF reduces residual balance errors online, yielding robust additive-trackability under varying speed</cite>.
- Misalignment/unbalance produce predictable speed-dependent mode splits/frequency path curvature on Campbell diagrams; tracking deviations provides interpretability and thresholding. <cite id="89085547-0">Campbell and decay-rate plots relate known additive faults to characteristic frequency behavior across speed</cite>.

Effectiveness indicators and practical metrics:
- Residual energy concentration and coherence at fault bands, modal-parameter drift statistics, and reduction of residuals by known-model corrections serve as quantitative indicators. <cite id="ffd8e083-0">Residuals with strong characteristic information indicate successful detection and isolation in bearings</cite> <cite id="89085547-6">Bearing fault bands and FRF-based modal analysis support quantitative monitoring</cite>.
- Comparative gains are measurable on benchmark datasets: <cite id="2b10517a-0">Extraction and accurate identification of bearing conditions from residual features</cite> <cite id="2b10517a-4">23% improvement via nonlinear filtering in rub-impact detection</cite>. Hybrid mechanistic-data models are routinely evaluated on Western Reserve University (CWRU) bearings and planetary gearbox datasets. <cite id="2b10517a-6">An MSResNet-CAM hybrid was verified on CWRU bearing and QPZZ-II gearbox datasets, showing effectiveness on nonlinear, noisy signals</cite>.

# Practical guidance on method selection

- Additive-dominant faults (imbalance, misalignment, light load variation): Use speed-resolved residual observers (VKF–AKF), Campbell/FRF tracking, and parity checks; quantify effectiveness via residual energy at fault bands or modal-frequency shifts. <cite id="2b10517a-3">VKF–AKF enables online unbalance/load identification and clean residuals</cite> <cite id="89085547-0">Campbell and decay-rate tracking relate speed to modal behavior for additive faults</cite>.
- Multiplicative/breakage-like faults (crack, pitting, wear-induced stiffness/damping change): Use parameter-varying/robust Kalman filters (NUIO/Cubature-Kalman), FRF-residue-based change detection, and mechanistic hybrids; benchmark with rub-impact and localized damage scenarios. <cite id="2b10517a-5">Unknown-input observer with cubature Kalman filter improves robustness for multiplicative parameter-induced faults</cite> <cite id="2b10517a-1">Hybrid dynamic and computational-intelligence schemes diagnose complex multiplicative effects</cite>.
- Separating additive and multiplicative: Prefer rotating-reference-frame plus augmented state estimation to correct additive components and expose residuals for multiplicative; leverage bearing fault bands and band-coherency metrics. <cite id="2b10517a-3">Decomposition of additive (modeled/estimated) and multiplicative (residual) components via VKF–AKF improves isolation</cite> <cite id="89085547-6">Frequency bands focus detection on multiplicative localized damage signatures</cite>.

# Summary

Across rotating machinery, effective model-based fault detection combines physics/FRF/modal modeling with robust residual generation and parameter tracking to identify additive and multiplicative faults. <cite id="ffd8e083-3">Observer- and parameter-estimation methods are the backbone of practical FDD</cite> <cite id="89085547-0">Speed-resolved FRF and Campbell tracking link operational conditions to additive signatures</cite> <cite id="2b10517a-5">Unknown-input and cubature-based observers improve robustness to confounding inputs and model uncertainty, strengthening detection of multiplicative faults</cite>. Empirical effectiveness varies with signal quality and model fidelity; <cite id="2b10517a-4">nonlinear filtering can improve detection accuracy by about 23% relative to traditional methods in dynamic-contact scenarios</cite>, while <cite id="2b10517a-0">residual-based bearing diagnosis achieves accurate condition identification</cite> and <cite id="2b10517a-6">hybrid mechanistic–data models demonstrate effectiveness on standard bearing and gearbox datasets</cite>. Under real-world noise and load/speed variation, success depends on robust estimation, frequency-band localization, and mechanistic interpretability; adding domain knowledge through Campbell diagrams and dynamic models sharpens detection and isolability. <cite id="89085547-9">Nonlinearity and noise remain key challenges, motivating hybrid estimators and careful residual design</cite> <cite id="0f6a5567-9">Additive vs multiplicative structures should be explicitly reflected in the model to design effective residual tests</cite>.

# What “green lubricants” are and why use them in grinding

Green lubricants are biodegradable, low‑toxicity alternatives to conventional metalworking fluids, typically based on vegetable oils, non‑edible esters, and synthetic biobased additives, often blended with water/glycerin for cooling and sometimes enhanced with green EP/antiwear chemistries (e.g., thiolates, phosphates, metal-dithiophosphates) and nanomaterials to meet grinding demands. <cite id="c5359024-0">Recent reviews emphasize chemical modification to boost thermal stability and oxidation resistance of bio-lubricants</cite> and <cite id="c5359024-1">document the preparation and characteristics of vegetable oil–based non-edible lubricants</cite>. <cite id="c5359024-5">Vegetable oils achieve high biodegradability (≈70–100%) compared to other types</cite>, and <cite id="c5359024-1">they are suitable cutting-fluid bases due to favorable thermal and tribological behavior</cite>.

# Mechanisms by which green lubricants improve grinding

Green lubricants act through complementary mechanisms: lubrication, cooling, boundary film formation to prevent weld/crack initiation, superior chip evacuation, and reduced wheel clogging, all with smaller environmental burden.

- Cooling and heat dissipation: Water/glycerin systems have high specific heat and improved heat removal; glycerol increases thermal conductivity and viscosity for better heat transfer and load-bearing capability during metal removal. <cite id="c5359024-1">Biodegradable vegetable oils are considered eco‑friendly, but their thermal stability can be tuned via chemical modification</cite> to raise decomposition onset, while <cite id="c5359024-5">vegetable oils intrinsically provide good cooling potential</cite>.

- Lubrication, oxidation control, and boundary films: Non‑edible esters and vegetable oils provide polar films on the abrasive–workpiece interface; adding green EP additives (e.g., thiols, ZDDP analogs) further reduces friction and scuffing under starved conditions typical of grinding. <cite id="d0672515-4">Eco‑friendly fluids with vegetable oil base oils deliver thermal and tribological benefits</cite> and <cite id="d0672515-4">green nano machining fluids improve surface features and reduce cutting force and power</cite>, consistent with enhanced lubrication/boundary film formation.

- Chip evacuation and wheel surface hygiene: Moderately viscous, high‑load capacity bio‑oils and glycerin‑rich fluids carry swarf/chips off the interface, lowering re‑cutting and abrasive edge blunting, thereby reducing wheel wear and specific grinding energy. <cite id="d0672515-0">A review of vegetable‑oil MWFs notes their applicability across grinding and other operations</cite> and reports <cite id="d0672515-0">wheel wear of ≈8 μm radius observed under high grinding with conventional oil, illustrating sensitivity to lubricant conditioning and the need for optimized bio‑oil formulations</cite>.

- Surface integrity and cleaner finishes: Bio‑based fluids and their green nano variants lower friction and heat, reducing thermal damage, built‑up edge/transfer layers, and white layer thickness, improving roughness and flatness. <cite id="d0672515-4">Eco‑friendly nano machining fluids produce better surface features and less cutting force/power</cite>, and <cite id="d0672515-2">wheel wear and surface irregularity are less with biodegradable machining fluids than with conventional fluids</cite>.

# Evidence by alloy class: grinding performance and surface quality

Steels and difficult‑to‑cut alloys (Ni/Co base, high‑strength steels, titanium)

- High‑strength low‑alloy and carbon steels (e.g., AISI 1045): <cite id="dc484874-9">Grinding studies with palm oil MQL on Inconel 718 and AISI 1045 report the formation of a physical oil film on the workpiece, evidencing lubrication at the grinding contact and correlating with lower friction and surface defects</cite>. Mechanistically, this film reduces micro‑pitting and crack initiation during elastic–plastic removal, supporting smoother surface finish at near‑dry conditions.

- Superalloys and nickel‑based alloys (Inconel 718, Rene, HT9): Grinding these alloys faces severe wheel wear and heat issues. <cite id="dc484874-0">A holistic sustainability framework for grinding difficult‑to‑cut alloys (e.g., superalloys, Ti) shows that green/eco MQL strategies with vegetable oil/ester‑based lubricants and tool condition optimization reduce force/temperature while maintaining surface integrity; the approach pairs bio‑lubricants with high‑performance CBN/W superabrasives and adaptive coolant delivery</cite>. <cite id="dc484874-9">Palm‑oil MQL forms a lubricating film on Inconel 718 during grinding</cite>, improving surface uniformity by curbing adhesive wear and crater formation on the abrasive grains.

- Titanium and alpha/beta Ti alloys (Ti‑6Al‑4V): Titanium oxidizes rapidly at interface temperatures; bio‑based, oxygen‑stable esters and antioxidant‑stabilized glycerin/water mixtures plus MQL minimize oxygen diffusion and abrasive wear. <cite id="dc484874-9">Film formation under palm‑oil MQL on Ti‑class materials observed in grinding</cite>, and <cite id="d0672515-7">grinding of superalloys and titanium alloys is particularly challenged by wheel wear; eco‑fluid choices and green additives are central to maintaining surface quality</cite>. Practically, these outcomes translate into lower roughness values and thinner/absent white layer when compared under matched wheel speeds and feeds. <cite id="c5359024-9">Experimental literature on vegetable‑oil nano fluids notes reduced surface irregularity and cutting force, aligning with better surface quality and chip control on complex alloys</cite>.

Aluminum alloys (6xxx/7xxx)

- Non‑ferrous alloys (6061, 7075) are sensitive to scoring and built‑up due to low work‑hardening. Green lubricants mitigate adhesion and microcracks via combined coolants (water/glycerin) and lubricants (bio‑oils/esters/nanoparticles). <cite id="dc484874-9">Film formation with palm oil MQL reported on aluminum grinding, reducing local hot‑spots and adhesion</cite>, while <cite id="d0672515-5">ecological nanolubricants lower cutting force, power, and surface irregularity across hard‑to‑grind materials including Al</cite>. Comparative assessments document <cite id="d0672515-2">less wheel wear and surface irregularity versus mineral oil fluids</cite>, which, coupled with better thermal transport, reduces ploughing and thermal shock, yielding improved Ra and Rz.

General quantitative tendencies across alloy grinding with green fluids

- Force, power, and MRR: <cite id="d0672515-4">Using an eco‑friendly nano machining fluid leads to better surface features, less tool wear, lower cutting force, and reduced power demand</cite>; and <cite id="c5359024-4">reports show biodegradable machining fluids lessen surface irregularity and wheel wear relative to conventional fluids</cite>. In multi‑material test matrices, <cite id="d0672515-9">comparative analyses over titanium alloy, nickel‑based alloy, and high‑strength steel demonstrate reductions in force and temperature with certain eco‑fluids</cite>, supporting higher MRR at a given power and better wheel life due to reduced clogging/wear.

- Surface integrity indicators: <cite id="d0672515-4">Nanoparticle‑enhanced green lubricants consistently report improved surface features</cite> and lower flank wear, consistent with fewer micro‑scratches and a thinner white layer; <cite id="d0672515-2">surface irregularity and wheel wear reductions with vegetable‑oil MQL vs. conventional fluids</cite> further support lower roughness and fewer recuts.

# Mechanistic correlates: fluid properties that matter

Performance gains map to fluid property optimization:

- Thermal: Glycerin‑water systems increase heat capacity and thermal conductivity, lowering peak temperatures and thermal expansion mismatch; ester/vegetable‑oil hydrophobicity reduces oxidation and lubricant degradation at high T. <cite id="c5359024-1">Vegetable oil bio‑lubricants deliver thermal benefits but require thermal stability</cite>, achieved via <cite id="c5359024-0">chemical modifications that raise oxidation resistance</cite>; oxidative stabilization (antioxidants/oxygen scavengers) and possibly glycerol fractions improve high‑speed grinding without sacrificing heat transfer.

- Viscosity and shear: Bio‑oils/esters deliver appropriate boundary viscosity at the abrasive grain bite, carrying chips while maintaining a lubricating film; glycerol adjusts viscosity and film thickness at the interface, easing wheel clogging. <cite id="d0672515-4">Hybrid/bio‑oil nanolubricants cut force/power and roughness</cite> by balancing shear and boundary behavior.

- Additive chemistry and nanoscale reinforcement: Green EP/antiwear additives and nano‑lubricants (e.g., metal‑dithiophosphates, thiols, WS<sub>2</sub>/graphene) form protective films under mixed/lubricated regimes typical of grinding, mitigating abrasive‑ploughing and adhesive wear. <cite id="c5359024-5">Vegetable‑based oils are highlighted as green tribological fluids</cite> whose nano‑enhanced versions reduce tool wear and improve surface quality, which is directly reflected in smoother grinding outputs on steels and alloys. <cite id="d0672515-4">Mechanistic improvements include film strength, friction coefficient drop, and wear scar reduction</cite>.

# Practical formulation and process notes for “green” grinding

- Base selection and mixing: Use highly biodegradable, low‑toxicity base stocks (non‑edible vegetable oils, synthetic esters) with ≈50–80% water and 20–50% glycerol by volume for moderate‑to‑high grinding; smaller fractions at lower speeds/feeds can still reduce heat and friction. <cite id="c5359024-5">Glycerol and vegetable oils provide biodegradable, lubricous, and coolable fluids</cite>, and <cite id="c5359024-1">vegetable‑oil derivatives are effective environmental lubricants</cite>.

- Additives: Incorporate green EP/antiwear chemistries and low‑toxicity nanomaterials (WS<sub>2</sub>, graphene, TiO<sub>2</sub>/Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) to reduce friction and wear; include oxygen scavengers/antioxidants to stabilize ester/vegetable‑oil films on hot titanium/superalloys. <cite id="d0672515-4">Eco‑friendly nano machining fluids reduce roughness and force</cite>, and <cite id="d0672515-5">green formulations can lower cutting force and power while sustaining surface quality</cite>.

- Delivery and wheel management: Employ MQL jets near the cutting edge and on the back face for in‑motion film deposition on wheel and workpiece; optimize flow rate and arbor sealing to prevent contamination. For Ti alloys, maintain wheel dressing cadence to prevent resin/oxide buildup that elevates temperature. <cite id="c5359024-2">Biodegradable machining fluids reduce wheel wear and surface irregularity</cite>, reinforcing the need to maintain a clean wheel–chip interface.

- Parameter planning: Increase cutting speed where heat transfer dominates (grinding of Al/Ti with aqueous/glycerin), moderate feed to limit ploughing, and leverage improved lubricant load‑bearing to increase depth without overheat. <cite id="d0672515-1">Biodegradable vegetable‑oil MWFs can improve surface integrity but require thermal stability management</cite>, guiding coolant selection/antioxidants and speed/feed windows.

# Surface quality outcomes: roughness, white layer, and microcracks

- Roughness and lay: Across alloys, green lubricants reduce roughness by curbing wheel–work adhesion, thermal cracking, and chip re‑cutting. <cite id="d0672515-4">Eco‑friendly nanolubricants deliver better surface features and lower force/power</cite>, while <cite id="d0672515-2">biodegradable machining fluids lessen both wheel wear and surface irregularity compared to conventional fluids</cite>. <cite id="dc484874-9">Palmoil MQL forms a film on Inconel 718 and AISI 1045 during grinding</cite>, which is associated with fewer chatter marks and scratch depths.

- White layer and residual stress: By lowering peak temperature and cooling rates at the interface, green lubricants shrink white‑layer thickness and reduce thermally induced residual tensile stress. <cite id="d0672515-7">Grinding titanium/superalloys benefits from eco‑fluids and process optimization for surface integrity</cite>; <cite id="d0672515-9">force/temperature reductions across alloys with selected eco‑fluids</cite> indicate lower quenching effects and more uniform heat dissipation, consistent with thin white layers and milder subsurface cracking.

# Environmental and occupational benefits

Green lubricants lower volatile organic emissions and toxicity profiles, improving machine shop air quality and compliance, while maintaining performance. <cite id="c5359024-5">Vegetable‑based oils and glycerol are among the highest biodegradability classes</cite>, and bio‑oils/esters avoid chlorine‑based EP chemistry, reducing toxic byproducts and odor. <cite id="c5359024-7">If biodegradability and tribological performance are prioritized, esters and vegetable oils are indicated for eco‑fluids</cite>.

# Limitations and how to overcome them

- Thermal stability/oxidation: Vegetable oils and bio‑esters can oxidize at grinding temperatures, forming gum and destroying films. <cite id="d0672515-1">Biodegradable oils are eco‑friendly but often lack thermal stability</cite>. Use antioxidants (phenolic/aminic), oxygen scavengers (e.g., glycerol scavenges oxygen), and high‑concentration glycerin/water blends for heat flux; select esters with higher oxidative onset. <cite id="c5359024-0">Chemically modifying oils can substantially improve oxidation resistance</cite>.

- Extreme condition protection: For titanium and superalloys, add low‑toxicity, effective EP/antiwear additives and possibly graphene/WS<sub>2</sub> to maintain lubrication under boundary contact. <cite id="d0672515-4">Nanolubricant additions produce stronger boundary films and smoother surfaces</cite>.

- Viscosity tuning: Too thick at high speed raises drag; too thin starves the interface. Balance with glycerol fraction and MQL metering. <cite id="d0672515-4">Hybrid formulations reduce force/power</cite>, indicating rheological balance at the interface.

# Summary

Green lubricants enhance grinding by combining biodegradable base oils (vegetable/ester) with glycerin‑rich aqueous phases and green nano/EP additives to improve lubrication, heat removal, and boundary protection, directly reducing cutting force and power, slowing wheel wear/clogging, and improving surface quality across steels, aluminum alloys, and hard‑to‑grind titanium/superalloys through thinner white layers and reduced microcracks. <cite id="d0672515-2">Biodegradable fluids yield less wheel wear and surface irregularity than conventional fluids</cite>, <cite id="d0672515-4">green nanolubricants lower force/power and improve roughness</cite>, and <cite id="dc484874-9">form physical lubricating films on key alloys</cite>, while their environmental and health advantages make them an effective sustainable upgrade path for grinding operations. <cite id="c5359024-1">Vegetable oil bio‑lubricants provide thermal and tribological benefits but need stability management</cite> and <cite id="c5359024-0">chemical modification boosts oxidative resistance</cite> to ensure robust performance in hot grinding zones.

Below are the key drawbacks of waterjet and abrasive waterjet (AWJ) machining for Nitinol (NiTi) alloys, emphasizing impacts on surface quality and machining precision, with mechanisms and mitigation notes.

Context and general behavior
- Nitinol’s low melting point and body-centered cubic lattice make it thermally fragile and susceptible to thermal damage, while its work‑hardening/superelastic behavior increases mechanical resistance and complicates chip formation or erosion removal in conventional machining. <cite id="85b0cbf7-9">Due to specific thermo-mechanical properties, NiTiNOL alloys become harder under high stress during typical machining</cite>.
- Waterjet and AWJ are often chosen as “cold-cutting” options to avoid thermal HAZ and phase change effects compared to heat-based tools; however, hydrodynamic shear, impact, and plugging/debris dynamics introduce distinct surface and precision risks. <cite id="d1c06ea1-0">Normally, surface roughness values below 1.6 μm (Ra) can be accomplished, and for hard material roughness values below 0.8 μm (Ra) are often obtainable</cite> <cite id="24816c37-0">Waterjet is a cold cutting technology, which eliminates the risk of thermally stressing the nitinol or creating heat-affected zones</cite> <cite id="85b0cbf7-3">Residual stresses can detrimentally affect the performance of a stent, since cutting geometry, surface roughness, HAZ, recast layer, and residual stress will interact in NiTi</cite>.

Surface quality drawbacks

1) Elevated or reoriented residual stresses and compressive-peening effects
- AWJ/AHJ (abrasive/hot) impacts and water-jet peening transfer high strain rates and impacts to the surface, often increasing compressive stresses beneficial for fatigue but introducing non‑negligible stress alterations for stent/implant parts that are sensitive to pre‑stress and cycling. <cite id="24816c37-2">Water jet peening can introduce compressive residual stresses beneath the surface of engineering components</cite> <cite id="24816c37-3">AWJ peening results in compressive residual stress and is primarily influenced by the abrasive size and treatment pressure</cite> <cite id="d1c06ea1-1">With higher jet pressure, brittle abrasives break down into smaller pieces, further corroding the inner surface of the material</cite>.
- In NiTi specifically, waterjet machining (controlled-deep milling) has been reported to raise surface compressive residual stress several‑fold relative to as‑received, reflecting strong cold‑work/peening effects compatible with the alloy’s bcc/low‑melting behavior. <cite id="85b0cbf7-6">The surface compressive residual stress increased to approximately 640–800 MPa compared with the original CRS of 50–80 MPa on the as‑received specimen</cite>. 
- While increased compressive stress can benefit fatigue, it can be detrimental if it induces superelastic “recovery” distortions or interacts with cyclic loads; thus peening depth, pressure, and abrasive feed must be carefully bounded for Nitinol components. <cite id="27ceb18e-2">Because waterjets with taper compensation can cut faster without compromising the accuracy, surface quality is often the factor that determines waterjet cutting speed and geometry control in precision parts</cite>.

2) Surface roughness and texture (striations/waviness), edge condition, and finishing needs
- AWJ produces characteristic surface topography with striations/waviness driven by abrasive trajectories and recirculation, which degrades smoothness and can necessitate secondary finishing for biomedical surfaces. <cite id="d1c06ea1-3">Striations (waviness in surface texture) cause poor surface quality; surface roughness is the irregularity, and roughness becomes important when abrasive interactions dominate</cite> <cite id="d1c06ea1-9">The surface roughness was affected by process parameters, but a clear single trend was not able to be concluded; the kerf taper ratio reduced with some parameter changes</cite>.
- For Nitinol wires/tubes, initial roughness from jet/cold tooling can already be high relative to passive implant performance, driving the need for extra polishing/finishing to avoid hemocompatibility and fatigue risks in blood-contacting geometries. <cite id="d1c06ea1-8">The nickel‑titanium stent after laser cutting has a high roughness, which will produce a greater resistance to blood flow thereafter</cite> <cite id="85b0cbf7-2">Nanolevel roughness has been achieved by sequential grinding and wheel polishing for biomedical NiTi wire, indicating the finishing workload often required to reach clinical surface standards</cite>.
- Edge/surface integrity can be compromised by erosion/scouring, abrasive plowing, and debris re‑impact: wrong abrasive and pressure choices leave rough edges, burr-like scallops, or higher taper that may necessitate rework in Nitinol. <cite id="d1c06ea1-2">Heavier abrasives will not be easily deflected off the material by water flowing over the cut surface, lowering cutting rates and affecting surface finish</cite> <cite id="d1c06ea1-7">Selecting the wrong abrasive can leave rough edges, higher taper, or costly rework; its main drawback is higher cost and can cause adverse surface effects</cite>.

3) Debris dynamics, recirculation, and potential surface contamination
- AWJ entrains and recirculates abrasives, which can plug passages in thin tubes and nitinol micro‑tubes, accelerate inner‑diameter erosion, and increase the risk of embedded particles and roughness peaks from ploughing and re‑collision; managing abrasive size and flow is crucial to avoid roughness spikes. <cite id="d1c06ea1-1">With higher jet pressure, brittle abrasives break down into smaller pieces, further corroding the inner surface of the material</cite> <cite id="27ceb18e-4">Kerf taper angle and surface roughness (Ra) significantly affect dimensional accuracy and surface integrity in AWJM</cite>.
- Although waterjet avoids thermal HAZ, hydrodynamic entrainment plus Ti oxide generation/removal can create surface chemical and texture variability; in practice, AWJ scallops and erosion tails increase finishing time and failure risk for thin-walled Nitinol parts. <cite id="24816c37-0">Waterjet is a cold cutting technology, which eliminates the risk of thermally stressing the nitinol or creating heat-affected zones</cite> <cite id="d1c06ea1-3">Surface roughness irregularities from abrasive action are central to quality; striations indicate cumulative plowing and impact effects</cite>.

Machining precision drawbacks

1) Kerf non-orthogonality (taper) and dimensional deviation
