  - Matching: designed to embed 1 bit per sample with low energy, and generalized to multi-bit per sample by using finer quantization steps or multi-pixel/distributed strategies; retry/embedding-scalar choices control rate and distortion. <cite id="404a0e6c-9">An LSB matching algorithm with low distortion embeds bits per pixel using scalar control (e.g., golden ratio selection), increasing capacity before error growth</cite> <cite id="404a0e6c-1">Non-adaptive LSB schemes improved efficiency to 8/3 bits per coefficient, i.e., above 2 bits per pixel</cite> <cite id="22cdd3cc-0">LSB matching is a coding method that increases steganography capacity while controlling LSB statistics</cite>.

- Practical capacity patterns and trade-offs
  - Substitution can achieve very high apparent capacity (e.g., 1 bpp, 2–3 bpp with multibit) but at the cost of visible artifacts and reduced robustness to filtering/EQ; aggressive embedding saturates values, creating step artifacts and histogram distortion. <cite id="22cdd3cc-7">Simple LSB substitution offers high capacity yet degrades stego-image quality</cite> <cite id="f32933d4-3">Spatial LSB substitution is computationally easy but suffers limited robustness to common signal processing</cite>.
  - LSB matching targets “invisible” perturbations, embedding around thresholds with controllable step sizes; it often improves imperceptibility and robustness at comparable or higher capacity (single-bit per pixel) by avoiding high-energy overwrites and using QIM theory. <cite id="c13f939e-4">QIM/dither modulation embeds information bits with minimal energy per bit by quantizing near thresholds; increasing dither/scale increases spread, rate, and distortion</cite> <cite id="f32933d4-0">Transform-domain watermarking based on quantization of less significant bits improves robustness relative to direct bit substitution</cite> <cite id="22cdd3cc-3">A fusion/variant that blends MSB and LSB matching reports that LSB-based techniques readily achieve high capacity without compromising imperceptibility</cite>.

3) Impact on image noise and visual quality

- Histogram alteration and quantization artifacts
  - Substitution: directly replacing LSBs flattens the histogram toward the embedding value (0 or 1) if many bits are written, and induces step/banding near edges; heavy use causes salt-and-pepper-like pixel steps when many bits per pixel are embedded. <cite id="22cdd3cc-7">Simple LSB substitution usually remains “good quality,” yet quality degrades as many bits are stuffed into LSBs (artifact risk rises with embedding strength)</cite> <cite id="404a0e6c-9">Improving perceptual quality requires careful embedding scalar choice in LSB matching; higher energy leads to greater distortion</cite>.
  - Matching: deliberately preserves host statistics by pushing x into a small neighborhood around x, making histograms and LL(x) features nearly indistinguishable from cover; when done with dither, the noise is distributed quantization-like, less perceptually disruptive and more robust to compression/filters. <cite id="404a0e6c-8">LSB matching is nearly identical to replacement in LSB outcome but with much lower visual distortion</cite> <cite id="c13f939e-4">Dither quantization creates “noise-like” LSB matches; energy/dither level dictates quantization noise and robustness</cite>.

- Robustness to attacks and common processing
  - Substitution is fragile: averaging, filtering, histogram equalization (HE), rescaling, or compression can flip LSBs and erase payloads; robustness is limited to low-energy operations that avoid median-like or quantile distortions. <cite id="f32933d4-3">LSB substitution is easy to implement but shows poor robustness to common operations</cite> <cite id="f32933d4-7">While replacing multiple LSBs increases capacity, aggressive changes degrade robustness to malicious/friendly processing</cite>.
  - Matching increases resilience: threshold-controlled quantization and dithering make embedded bits anti-correlated with local image statistics; HE and linear operations tend to leave matching neighborhoods intact at low embedding strength. <cite id="c13f939e-4">Dithered quantization methods are designed to resist simple desynchronization (e.g., by thresholds, rescalings), improving robustness vs. substitution</cite> <cite id="f32933d4-0">Quantization-based (LSB) watermarking in transform domains provides significantly better robustness for comparable capacity</cite>.

- Objective quality metrics (heuristics)
  - Simple substitution commonly yields low PSNR/SSIM when many bits per pixel are embedded; even 1–2 bpp can produce visible block/banding, depending on image content and quantization. <cite id="22cdd3cc-7">Although high-capacity, substitution-induced quality degradation is noted and measured by steganalyst tools and perceptual checks</cite>.
  - Matching can attain higher SSIM/visual similarity at equal rate by minimizing energy/large-signal distortions; multi-pixel or transform-spread strategies improve PSNR/robustness at similar imperceptibility. <cite id="404a0e6c-9">A low-distortion LSB matching algorithm reduces perceptual artifacts by tuning embedding scalars, using geometric selection to limit distortion</cite> <cite id="f32933d4-8">Spread or multiple images across transforms can increase robustness while maintaining imperceptibility relative to plain LSB</cite>.

4) Practical guidance and when to prefer which

- Choose LSB substitution when
  - Maximum raw capacity in a single pass is needed and visual fidelity can degrade; e.g., large payloads with tolerance to artifacts. <cite id="f32933d4-7">Replacing n LSBs yields n bpp capacity but at visible/robustness cost</cite>.
  - Computational simplicity and speed are paramount; replacement is essentially a bit-parallel mask/unmask step. <cite id="f32933d4-7">LSB replacement is widely used for its simplicity</cite>.

- Choose LSB matching when

- Embedding: substitution directly overwrites LSBs, a deterministic and high-energy change; matching adjusts each pixel to force the LSB to match the message via threshold quantization/dither with controllable step size and noise-like distribution. <cite id="404a0e6c-8">LSB replacement vs. matching both exploit LSB behavior; matching does so without simple overwrite</cite> <cite id="c13f939e-4">QIM/dither adds controlled noise so quantization equals the message bit</cite>.

# Overview: Particle Aspect Ratio and Thermal Conduction in Nanofluids

Particle aspect ratio (AR = length/diameter) changes the geometry and orientation distribution of filler particles, which in turn reconfigures the effective thermal pathways in a host fluid. Increasing AR typically increases the contact likelihood and continuity of high‑conductivity “spines” bridging fluid pockets, lowers geometrically constrained interfacial thermal resistance in the axial direction, and enables field‑induced preferential alignment—all of which raise the effective thermal conductivity (k_eff) of nanofluids, especially for fibrous or rod-like fillers such as CNTs, nanowires, and nanorods compared to near-spherical nanoparticles <cite id="16e1eae9-0">The experiment indicates that particle shape has a substantial effect on the effective thermal conductivity of suspension and shape factor is one of the most ...</cite> <cite id="16e1eae9-1">Due to large aspect ratios, thermal conductivity is abnormally enhanced only for nanofluids with carbon nanotubes/nanofibers/nanowires. # Mechanisms by Which Higher AR Alters Thermal Transport

## 1) Reduced interfacial thermal resistance and continuous conduction networks
A higher AR concentrates heat transport along the particle axis and, when particles are densely packed, creates a sparse network of “spine” pathways that stitch together high‑conductivity segments of solid and nanolayer interfaces. This reduces the overall resistance of the composite and facilitates macroscopic conduction. Interfacial resistance (Kapitza resistance) at particle–fluid contacts is an intrinsic bottleneck; long slender particles and strong coupling (surface oxidation notwithstanding) lessen its fraction of total resistance along the transport path. ## 4) Viscous relaxation, aggregation, and stability trade-offs
High AR increases hydrodynamic hindering, so Brownian motion reduces to constrained tumbling and reptation; this can promote rod-on-rod stacking and chain growth, which boosts k along the chain axis but raises dynamic viscosity. Conversely, weakly Brownian or sedimenting regimes hinder orientation, and strong interparticle repulsion or steric stabilization limits aggregation—both suppressing effective network formation. Overview and mechanisms
- Metallic objects couple microwave energy through ohmic loss and near-field enhancement at protrusions and particle surfaces, which can exceed the ambient dielectric strength and ignite a plasma (discharge) at hot spots rather than uniformly along the surface.<cite id="5e99d695-0">Microwave–metal discharge interactions are dominated by resonant coupling to metal induced oscillating currents and surface-wave mediated heating, with discharge initiation linked to local field enhancements and thermal runaway at metal–gas interfaces</cite><cite id="5e99d695-6">Wave absorption and metal-induced discharges couple via resonant and near-field mechanisms; metals that absorb strongly nucleate discharges at sites of maximal enhancement, lowering the effective initiation field</cite>. 
- For particles, microwave absorption depends on dielectric properties and geometric size relative to the wavelength; as size increases, the volume-to-surface ratio rises and dipole/plasmonic resonances concentrate fields, lowering the threshold for electron avalanches and sparking.<cite id="5e99d695-5">Microwave-induced electric discharges on metallic particles occur when absorbed microwave energy raises local temperatures and field concentrations to trigger arc formation between particle facets, enabling plasma generation and synthesis under irradiation</cite><cite id="5e99d695-1">Discharges vary with metal type and particle size/morphology; larger exposed surfaces and irregular morphology reduce thresholds and increase event intensity via enhanced microwave absorption and localized heating</cite>.
- For wires, the small cross-section produces strong transverse field enhancement at tips and along absorbing conductors, enabling breakdown with modest microwave powers if the field at the surface exceeds the local dielectric strength; diameter and length set whether energy is dissipated as glow/sustained discharge or as rapid thermal runaway (vaporization).<cite id="5e99d695-2">A 0.5 mm diameter metallic wire exposed to 800 W microwave power can readily reach breakdown field levels at the surface, due to strong near-field enhancement and absorption</cite>.
Effects of particle size
- Likelihood (probability of discharge): Smaller particles have higher surface-to-volume ratio and may be more efficient microwave absorbers when their surfaces are rough, oxidized, or facet-jointed, which increases the chance of initiating an electron avalanche and sparking in the surrounding gas.<cite id="5e99d695-1">Across metals (Mg, Zn, Cu, Fe, Ni), varying particle sizes and morphologies change the discharge pattern and frequency; greater surface irregularity and area per mass increase the probability of discharge initiation under microwave irradiation</cite><cite id="5e99d695-5">Discharges on metallic particles are readily observed under microwave irradiation, with particle size and surface state controlling the onset of arcing between particle features</cite>. For example, nanoscale metallic powders often ignite lower-power microwaves than bulk grains due to higher effective absorption at resonant or lossy interfacial sites.<cite id="5e99d695-1">Different metals of varying particle sizes/morphologies exhibit distinct discharge behaviors under microwaves, with morphology-enhanced absorption lowering thresholds and increasing discharge frequency</cite>.
- Intensity (current, luminosity, coupling): At a given frequency and power, larger particles couple more microwave energy per impact event and typically produce stronger sparks and higher energy deposition per discharge because of larger cross-sectional absorption and thermal inertia; irregular shapes and porosity increase local field peaks and can make arcs more energetic but more sporadic.<cite id="5e99d695-5">Metal particle microwave discharge produces arcs that can deliver energetic electron exchange and thermal spikes sufficient for in-situ nanomaterial synthesis, with particle size/morphology dictating how often and how intensely arcs occur</cite><cite id="5e99d695-8">Microwave action on particulate copper ore combines discharge and heating; particle size/morphology govern whether discharge-initiated thermal cracking dominates, linking larger surface area to more frequent discharge events and mechanical effect intensity</cite>.
Practical size trends observed
- As particle diameter increases from nano- to sub-millimeter scales, the onset power for visible discharge decreases until a “saturation” where further growth primarily increases energy per event rather than the probability, depending on dielectric loss and surface conductivity; in dusty plasmas, cohesive particles form clusters that change collective resonances and lower thresholds again.<cite id="5e99d695-1">Experiments varying particle size and morphology report that metals with higher surface lossiness and irregular shapes initiate discharge more readily at lower powers</cite><cite id="5e99d695-8">In particulate copper ore, discharge mechanisms dominate fracture under microwaves, with particle microstructure and size distribution controlling coupling efficiency</cite>.
Effects of wire length and geometry
- Likelihood (threshold power vs. length): For a given diameter and material, increasing wire length increases the number of absorbing segments and hot spots within the microwave field, lowering the average power required to exceed breakdown somewhere along the conductor unless the total absorbed energy is capped by power pulsation or mismatch; wires positioned along the electric (vs. magnetic) field polarization couple more strongly and ignite more readily.<cite id="5e99d695-2">The 0.5 mm diameter wire at 800 W can reach breakdown due to strong field enhancement and absorption; alignment and geometry relative to polarization determine the effective coupling and onset</cite><cite id="a9da053a-0">Characteristic microwave spatial variation length scales set the size over which field enhancement and discharge nucleation compete, influencing the probability that a wire segment exceeds breakdown</cite>. 
- When length increases enough that the wire bridges multiple resonant nodes, the effective average surface field rises, increasing both initiation probability and potential current; conversely, excessively long wires with weak coupling exhibit higher impedance mismatch and lower coupling efficiency, delaying ignition.<cite id="a9da081">Modeling and experiments show that microwave field structure and spatial variation length set local enhancement probabilities along a wire; wires spanning multiple nodes see increased hot spot density and ignition likelihood</cite>.
- Intensity and evolution: Short wires and isolated conductors favor compact, high-field “pinch” discharges (micrognatodes) with rapid energy release and bright emission; longer wires or bundles provide current return paths and multiple initiation sites, sustaining columnar glow-like discharges with higher total current but with more spatial intermittency (filamentation).<cite id="5e99d695-2">Short, thin absorbing wires (e.g., 0.5 mm dia.) in 800 W microwaves readily reach breakdown, producing concentrated heating and localized bright discharge at the enhanced-field tips</cite><cite id="a9da053a-3">Three-dimensional modeling of microwave-induced discharges shows filament formation and transient behavior in waveguide plasma sources, where geometry, pressure, and frequency determine discharge structure and current distribution</cite>. 
- Stability and termination: If a wire is too long or the microwave phase is unfavorable, the discharge current preferentially concentrates at the tips or nearest resonators, leading to arcing to nearby grounded object or to streamer formation into the dielectric gas; this raises average intensity during arcing events but reduces steady-state stability. Increasing wire diameter raises coupling at the expense of higher threshold power for the same local field, while decreasing diameter lowers threshold but concentrates energy into smaller, rapidly vaporized segments.<cite id="5e99d695-1">Different metals and particle/wire sizes and morphologies yield distinct discharge patterns and frequencies; morphology enhances coupling at the cost of faster thermal evolution</cite><cite id="a9da053a-1">A 0.5 mm diameter tungsten wire in microwave exposure was completely vaporized, whereas a 1 mm diameter wire showed reduced but sustained effects, highlighting how diameter changes both initiation threshold and post-discharge thermal response</cite>. 
Material, frequency, and environmental modifiers
- Material choice (Z, conductivity, oxide layers): More conductive metals (Cu, Au) often couple microwaves efficiently but may require higher local field enhancements to trigger breakdown unless deliberately roughened; reactive metals (Mg, K) or oxides promote strong absorption and low thresholds.
