Summary
Surfactant treatments accelerate PAH dissipation in soil primarily by increasing solubility and bioavailability of sorbed PAHs, which in turn enhances biodegradation or removal; however, the magnitude and time course depend strongly on surfactant type, dose, soil properties, and system conditions, and at higher doses or over longer times surfactants can inhibit microbial activity, persist, or mobilize co-contaminants. <cite id="10fda323-8">Although it is agreed that surfactants can enhance the solubility and dissolution of hydrocarbons from sorbing phases, the net effect on biodegradation depends on whether desorbed PAHs are accessible to degraders and on surfactant properties and doses</cite>.

Mechanisms underlying time-dependent dissipation
- Increased dissolved/lipophilic micellar pools shorten PAH half-lives by feeding desorbing microbes and promoting aerobic ring-cleavage; nonionics and biosurfactants tend to operate at sub-CMC with mixed micelle formation that sustains release, whereas anionics (e.g., SDS/Triton) can strongly solubilize at higher loadings and may enhance abiotic mass transfer and biotic uptake. <cite id="10fda323-8">Surfactants increase solubility and dissolution of hydrocarbons from solid/organic phases, enabling enhanced biodegradation</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-4">Enhanced biodegradation in micellar systems can be attributed to increased solubility and bioavailability of substrate to bacteria</cite>.
- Biosurfactants also modulate communities and redox conditions; for example, rhamnolipids can enrich PAH-degraders and, under certain conditions, later-stage inhibition or negligible effect may emerge as communities shift with time. <cite id="10fda323-7">Rhamnolipids altered the composition of indigenous PAH-degrading bacteria in PAH-contaminated soil</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-0">In a rhamnolipid study, the surfactant either had no impact or inhibited PAH degradation at 21–35 days, coinciding with changes in bacterial 16S rRNA abundance and community structure</cite>.
- Physicochemical mass transfer can dominate early-time dynamics: up to 30% of Soxhlet-extractable PAHs can be solubilized within 16 days at surfactant loadings of 0.055 g/g in controlled reactors, evidencing rapid phase-transfer that lowers partitioning control before biodegradation proceeds. <cite id="2997ed15-3">Up to 30% of Soxhlet-extractable PAHs could be solubilized in 16 days at 0.055 g/g surfactant loading in stirred reactors</cite>.

Short-term (days to weeks) dissipation patterns
- Typical soil half-lives for representative low–mid molecular weight PAHs (e.g., phenanthrene, fluoranthene, pyrene) are on the order of 1–4 weeks in landscaped soils, illustrating how quickly microbial turnover can reduce concentrations once bioavailable. <cite id="bfecf84a-1">Half-lives ranged from 1.5 to 4.4 weeks for phenanthrene, fluoranthene, and pyrene in landscaping soil</cite>.
- Biosurfactant amendments with time windows of two to four weeks can shift dissipation trajectories. <cite id="bfecf84a-0">Rhamnolipid addition altered dissipation patterns and microbial composition; notably, it either had no immediate impact or showed inhibition at 21–35 days</cite>. This underscores that early solubilization may not translate to sustained degradation without compatible microbial guilds or redox/mixing conditions.
- Soil-washing style operations show rapid mobilization/dissipation in the first stages, with kinetics governed by mixing, organic matter, and clay interactions. <cite id="2997ed15-9">Surfactant-enhanced soil washing achieved fast PAH removal in lab tests, with removal governed by stirring, contact time, and surfactant partitioning into soil fractions</cite>.

Surfactant type and dose: contrasting time courses
- Nonionic ethoxylated surfactants (e.g., Brij series, Triton X-114-like structures) at sub-CMC doses often enhance desorption and sustain biodegradation by maintaining mixed micelles, with time-integrated removal improving over 1–3 weeks compared to controls. <cite id="2997ed15-0">A comparison of two nonionic, ethoxylated surfactants (differing in hydrophobicity, e.g., Brij 30) evaluated their roles in desorption and biodegradation over time in PAH-contaminated systems</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-6">Triton X-114 and polyethylene were used to enhance biodegradation of PAHs remaining after conventional biotreatment in soils</cite>.
- Biosurfactants (rhamnolipids, saponins/plant-derived) couple solubilization with microbial synergy; initial enhanced dissolution may be followed by community-driven acceleration or plateau/inhibition if nutrient/redox constraints emerge. <cite id="2997ed15-2">Anoxic, surfactant-enhanced systems promoted net PAH loss; however, some PAHs remained and dynamics depended on temperature, sorption, and desorption over weeks to months</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-2">A plant-derived biosurfactant (saponin) increased biodegradation of slowly desorbing PAHs in soil, improving late-time mass loss compared to unamended controls</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-0">In a rhamnolipid microcosm, 21–35 day dissipation was neutral or inhibitory, consistent with community restructuring that altered catabolic potential over time</cite>.
- Anionic and strongly hydrophobic synthetic surfactants (e.g., SDS, Triton X-100/114) create large micellar pools and can rapidly convert hydrophobic PAHs to soluble complexes; this increases immediate availability and first-pass oxidation, but risks higher dissolution of coextractables and possible toxicity. <cite id="10fda323-9">Nonionic surfactants decrease PAH solubility and interfacial tension to increase dissolution, a strategy often used operationally to enhance biodegradation</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-7">A Triton X-100 wash solution destroyed more than 99% of PAH parent material in a low-organic sandy soil, evidencing strong solubilization in the short term</cite>.

Soil properties and hydrophobicity gradient over time
PAH dissipation time courses diverge with Koc and ring number. Early declines are pronounced for low-MW/low-Koc PAHs (phenanthrene, naphthalene) where dissolution-limited kinetics give way to microbial turnover; slower desorbing, higher-Koc PAHs (pyrene, benzo[a]pyrene) decline more gradually unless surfactants persistently maintain mixed micelles or oxygen and enzymes are delivered to sorbent phases. <cite id="bfecf84a-1">Half-lives of 1.5–4.4 weeks for low-MW PAHs reflect rapid initial dissipation once bioavailable in soil</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-0">Ethoxylated nonionics at sub-CMC can preferentially desorb less bioavailable PAH fractions, altering the time course toward more complete mass loss</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-2">Slowly desorbing PAHs showed faster dissipation with plant-derived biosurfactant, shifting late-time behavior relative to controls</cite>.

Microbial and abiotic coupling across time
- Presence and activity of PAH degraders are necessary to translate increased solubility into net dissipation; surfactant amendments restructure communities and can initially promote dissipation yet later suppress it via pathway competition, nutrient exhaustion, or oxygen limitation. <cite id="10fda323-1">Rhamnolipid altered PAH dissipation efficiency and microbial community structure during time, indicating a feedback between surfactant, microbes, and dissipation</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-0">At 21–35 days, rhamnolipid either failed to improve or inhibited PAH breakdown, concordant with shifts in 16S rRNA abundance and community profiles</cite>.
- Under anoxic or thermally assisted conditions, surfactants can sustain abiotic desorption and biotic anaerobic metabolism; net PAH loss accelerates over 2–10 weeks in pre-oxidized or aged subsurface soils compared to passive attenuation. <cite id="2997ed15-1">Surfactant-enhanced anoxic biodegradation was effective for PAHs in pre-oxidized subsurface soils</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-5">Thermally enhanced anoxic biodegradation markedly increased PAH removal, with surfactant addition improving solubilization of recalcitrant fractions over time</cite>.
- Natural attenuation baselines in soils span from months to years for multi-ring PAHs, so surfactant-accelerated rates must be compared to these background trajectories. <cite id="bfecf84a-4">PAH half-lives of 60 days to 3 years have been reported for mixtures in soils, underscoring substantial time spans to reach background levels without intervention</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-9">Microbial turnover and soil aging alter PAH dissipation; observed OPAH formation during short time frames indicates community-mediated dynamics that modulate time-dependent outcomes</cite>.

Time courses and dose dependence
- Sub-CMC nonionic/biosurfactants often yield incremental declines over weeks due to continuous solubilization and microbial access; higher micellar dosing can cause abrupt early declines by converting sorbed mass to soluble pools, followed by mid-to-late time inhibition, nutrient demand, or toxicity. <cite id="2997ed15-0">Sub-CMC ethoxylated surfactants showed differing degrees of enhancing desorption and biodegradation, with hydrophobicity of the surfactant head impacting performance over time</cite>. <cite id="10fda323-2">Screening of nonionic surfactants at sub-CMC in PAH-contaminated soil showed improved bioremediation relative to controls within study durations</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-0">At later time points (21–35 days) rhamnolipid additions showed neutral or inhibitory PAH degradation, aligned with community-level responses</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-10">Field and lab synthesis emphasize that success of surfactant-enhanced PAH biodegradation hinges on surfactant type, structure, and amendment rate, which steer dissolution versus toxicity tradeoffs over time</cite>.
- Quantitatively, rapid micelles can solubilize substantial PAH fractions within two weeks at modest dose-to-soil ratios, while overall dissipation to background may take months to years without complementary biostimulation. <cite id="2997ed15-3">Approximately 30% solubilization of extractable PAHs in 16 days at 0.055 g/g illustrates fast early-time changes</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-4">Even without surfactants, reaching background can require 60 days to three years for multi-ring PAHs in soils</cite>.

Design implications and risks over extended periods
- Expect faster initial slopes when surfactants increase dissolved organic carbon and create mixed micelles; however, long-term outcomes vary: nonionic biosurfactants can maintain moderate rates via microbial synergy and lower toxicity, anionic micelles can produce sharp early peaks and later inhibition or surfactant carryover. <cite id="10fda323-8">Surfactant-enhanced systems hinge on balancing increased bioavailability with potential inhibition and persistence</cite>. <cite id="10fda323-9">Nonionics effectively increase solubility and interfacial dispersion to boost biodegradation</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-9">Operational removal curves steepen with surfactant and mixing; design must constrain surfactant dosing to avoid residual surfactant and toxicity at field endpoints</cite>.
- Soil organic matter and texture alter time-dependent outcomes: low-OC sandy soils respond quickly to strong solubilizers (e.g., Triton X-100), whereas high-OC/clay fractions slow diffusion and sustain mass transfer limits unless surfactants strongly disperse organo-clay complexes. <cite id="2997ed15-7">Triton X-100 wash at low OC sandy soil destroyed >99% of PAHs, evidencing strong immediate solubilization in low-OC matrices</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-0">Hydrophobic nonionics (e.g., Brij 30) outperformed less hydrophobic analogs in desorption/biodegradation, suggesting that partitioning into organics/clays modulates time courses</cite>.
- Risk of mobilizing coextractables and non-PAH contaminants rises with hydrophobic, micellar surfactants; careful sequencing (wash→biostimulation) and biosurfactant choice can mitigate this while preserving PAH mass-loss. <cite id="2997ed15-6">Triton X-114, when combined with polyethylene, enhanced biodegradation of residual PAHs after conventional treatment, highlighting a sequential mass-transfer→biodegradation bottleneck that informs design</cite>.
- In matured, aged soils with limited microbial turnover, surfactant addition may initially boost dissolved PAHs but fail to translate to sustained net loss without nutrient/oxygen provision; over months, community priming and OPAH dynamics (e.g., phenanthrene→fluorene shifts) indicate microbial control over dissipation trajectories. <cite id="bfecf84a-9">Short-term OPAHs formation during microbial turnover and lower dissipation after soil ageing underscore the role of community state and ageing in time-dependent PAH dynamics</cite>.

Putting it together: time-evolving dissipation under common treatments
- Sub-CMC nonionic ethoxylated surfactants in aerobic soils: 1–4 week dissipation of low-Koc PAHs accelerates; mid-Koc PAHs show slower but improving decline as mixed micelles continually feed degraders; long-term, community shifts can plateau or invert, requiring nutrients and possibly co-amendments. <cite id="bfecf84a-1">Low-MW PAHs exhibit 1.5–4.4 week half-lives in soil, marking a reference rate that sub-CMC nonionics often exceed early on</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-0">Sub-CMC ethoxylated surfactant hydrophobicity influences time-integrated desorption/biodegradation outcomes</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-0">Later-stage rhamnolipid effects (neutral/inhibitory) illustrate that early gains may reverse as communities change</cite>.
- Biosurfactant (rhamnolipid/saponin): Rapid initial dissolution of sorbed PAHs, microbial enrichment of degraders, accelerated decline for slow-desorbing PAHs; caution that in some systems late-time inhibition emerges coincident with community restructuring or nutrient limitation. <cite id="bfecf84a-2">Saponin increased biodegradation of slowly desorbing PAHs, improving late-time dissipation relative to controls</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-0">Rhamnolipid microcosms showed neutral or inhibitory impacts by day 21–35, consistent with shifts in community drivers over time</cite>.
- Strong anionics (SDS/Triton X-100/114): Very fast early-time PAH loss due to micellar solubilization and strong washing; in soils with low OC, near-complete removal may occur within days to weeks (e.g., >99% destruction in Triton X-100 wash), but risk of coextractant mobilization and toxicity rises; sustained dissipation depends on reoxidation/biotreatment of aqueous-phase PAHs and residuals in organo-clays. <cite id="2997ed15-7">Greater than 99% PAH destruction in Triton X-100 wash, indicating very short half-lives under strong solubilization in low-organic sandy soil</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-6">Triton X-114-based washing coupled to biodegradation addresses remaining PAH fractions through time</cite>.
- Anaerobic thermal regimes: Surfactant-enhanced anoxic biodegradation accelerates net PAH loss over multi-week periods, often outpacing passive natural attenuation, but some PAHs persist until higher temperatures and extended contact times; overall, dissipation is governed by desorption at 60 °C plus anaerobic metabolic pathways. <cite id="2997ed15-1">Surfactant-enhanced anoxic biodegradation proved effective for PAHs in pre-oxidized subsurface soils</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-2">Remnant PAHs and operational constraints at 60 °C illustrate that dissipation is time-limited by mass transfer and enzyme-specific anaerobic degradation</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-4">Baseline soil half-lives without intervention range from months to years for many PAHs, emphasizing that even enhanced systems require weeks to years to fully reach background</cite>.

Practical guidance over time
- For engineered sites needing regulatory clearance within months, combine surfactant flushing (e.g., nonionic at sub-CMC or biosurfactant) with aeration/biostimulation to translate rapid dissolution to sustained microbial degradation; anticipate that low-MW PAHs will fall within 1–4 weeks, while high-Koc PAHs require longer interventions. <cite id="bfecf84a-1">Low-MW PAH half-lives of 1.5–4.4 weeks set a ceiling for baseline aerobic dissipation</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-2">Biosurfactant saponin improved late-time loss for slow-desorbing PAHs</cite>. <cite id="10fda323-9">Nonionic strategies specifically target solubility limits that bound dissipation kinetics in soil</cite>.
- Avoid high-dose anionic micelles near sensitive biota; use sequential washing then biostimulation, monitor for PAH rebound if surfactant inhibits degraders, and consider earthworm/bioturbation assistance for organo-clay soils. <cite id="10fda323-8">Sustained PAH dissipation depends on maintaining bioavailability without inhibiting microbial consortia</cite>. <cite id="10fda323-9">Solubility gains and interfacial tension reduction are double-edged; toxicity limits dose selection and timing</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-5">Thermal anoxic strategies demonstrate that surfactant choice, temperature, and system chemistry govern time-to-background trajectories</cite>.

Bottom line
Across soils, surfactant treatments shift PAH dissipation from partitioning-limited, slow processes to dissolution- and enzyme-access–limited kinetics; low-MW PAHs often clear within 1–4 weeks once bioavailable, whereas high-Koc PAHs persist months to years without aggressive surfactant/biostimulation. Nonionic sub-CMC and biosurfactants typically yield steady, community-friendly declines, while anionic, high-micelle approaches produce sharp early losses but demand careful dosing, sequencing, and endpoint management to avoid inhibition and carryover. <cite id="bfecf84a-1">Low-MW PAHs have 1.5–4.4 week half-lives in soils, marking a common early-time benchmark</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-3">Up to 30% PAH solubilization within 16 days at sub-g/g dosing illustrates rapid early-phase change</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-0">Rhamnolipid effects can become neutral or inhibitory by 21–35 days, reflecting community feedbacks over time</cite>. <cite id="2997ed15-7">Anionic surfactant washes can destroy >99% of PAHs in low-OC soils in days, evidencing order-of-magnitude acceleration</cite>. <cite id="bfecf84a-4">Natural attenuation baselines of 60 days to three years remind that sustained, complete dissipation often requires months of active remediation for multi-ring PAHs</cite>.

Summary

Artificial (constructed) wetlands remove microcystins (MCs) through a cooperative plant–substrate–microbe network in which engineered media provide adsorptive and catalytic surfaces, macrophytes supply oxygen and exudates via the rhizosphere, and microbial consortia perform enzymatic transformation and mineralization, with plants also taking up dissolved MCs from water and roots during conveyance and transpiration. <cite id="82facb6e-0">The mechanisms include physical, chemical, and biological processes such as plant uptake, enzymatic degradation, substrate adsorption, microbial metabolism, and interactions in the rhizosphere</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-1">Microbial degradation emerged as the predominant factor, followed by substrate adsorption and plant absorption</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-2">Nutrient removal efficiency of CWs primarily depends on substrate adsorption, plant uptake, and microbial metabolism</cite>.

How plants and substrates act together

Plants and substrates do not act as separate filters but as a coupled biogeochemical unit. Plants supply organic exudates and oxygen through rhizodeposition and radial oxygen loss (ROL), enabling aerobic microbial activity and redox reactions that favor MC degradation; dense root networks also increase hydraulic and reactive contact area with the substrate, enhancing MC diffusion, attachment, and transformation at biofilm-covered surfaces. <cite id="56b3c64c-1">Macrophytes in CWs operate via mechanisms tied to rhizosphere oxygen leakage, shaping redox conditions and microbial functioning</cite> <cite id="56b3c64c-2">Oxygen released in the rhizosphere strongly influences nutrient and contaminant removal chemistry</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-9">Macrophytes influence removal through direct uptake and indirect stimulation of microbial processes</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-5">Functional microbes in CWs catalyze chemical reactions, biodegradation, and biosorption and support plant growth, coupling plant and microbial removal pathways</cite>.

Substrate roles: physical–chemical removal and microbial scaffolding

Engineered media (gravel, sand, soil mixtures, and modified sorbents) provide surfaces for MC adsorption/retention, filtration, and attachment to biofilms, and they control pore-scale transport and residence time. <cite id="82facb6e-6">Constructed wetland mechanisms encompass adsorption, retention, filtration, oxidation-reduction, precipitation, microbial decomposition, and transformation</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-7">CWs remove contaminants through adsorption on substrates, phytoremediation by plants, and bioremediation by microbes</cite>. In microcystin contexts, modified or composite substrates intensify these effects. Biochar and zeolite additions, for example, can immobilize catalysts, increase surface area and cation exchange, and enrich microbial biofilm niches that break down MCs; in vertical flow systems with Phragmites, such amendments improve removal performance by coupling adsorption to microbial degradation in the rhizosphere. <cite id="78d4b926-1">Biochar or gravel substrates support catalyst immobilization and enhance electron transfer, while macrophytes like Phragmites intensify reactions in CWs</cite> <cite id="27ff5074-3">Phragmites australis planted in a biochar/zeolite vertical flow constructed wetland was used to treat synthetic wastewater, reflecting the synergistic plant–substrate role</cite> <cite id="c791dead-1">Biochar in CWs removes pharmaceuticals and PPCPs and enhances microbial activity and nutrient cycling</cite>.

Direct microcystin evidence: adsorption plus biodegradation

Experiments and reviews focused on MCs reinforce this dual mechanism. Microcosm constructed wetlands treating Microcystis blooms with degrader bioaugmentation achieved enhanced removal of whole cells and microcystin-LR (MC-LR), evidencing that substrate-supported biofilms plus plant rhizosphere conditions can push systems past slow biodegradation to rapid elimination of MC-LR. <cite id="56b3c64c-5">Enhanced removal of Microcystis bloom and microcystin-LR was observed in microcosm CWs with bioaugmentation of degrading bacteria</cite> <cite id="c791dead-5">Field-relevant assessments note prior microcosm CW work (Chemosphere 2018) demonstrating MC-LR removal acceleration via degraders</cite>. Across constructed wetlands, the removal hierarchy remains consistent for recalcitrant toxins such as MCs: microbial degradation is often dominant, with substrate adsorption retarding downstream degradation and plant uptake removing fractions of dissolved MCs directly and indirectly via transpiration-driven contact renewal. <cite id="82facb6e-1">Microbial degradation predominates, followed by substrate adsorption and plant absorption</cite>.

Plant roles: uptake, oxygenation, and biostimulation of MC transformation

Common emergent macrophytes (e.g., Typha latifolia, Phragmites australis, Spartina alterniflora) in artificial wetlands remove MCs through (i) direct phytoremediation of dissolved microcystins in water taken up by roots/leaves; (ii) rhizosphere biostimulation of MC-degrading bacteria; and (iii) provision of oxygen-rich anoxic–oxic microenvironments that favor oxidative transformation pathways. <cite id="82facb6e-4">Constructed wetlands use microbes and rooted plants to remove contaminants, leveraging natural wetland processes</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-6">CW mechanisms include microbial decomposition and transformation, adsorption, and oxygen-reduction reactions</cite> <cite id="56b3c64c-6">Macrophyte species selection matters: positive role of macrophytes on removal efficiency is established, with differences across species</cite>. Plant-free or sterilized rhizosphere ablations in macrophyte-dominated CWs reduce MC and intermediate removal rates, and root removal experiments reduce total KDC and increase dissolved MC concentrations, highlighting the centrality of plants and their rhizosphere to complete elimination. <cite id="82facb6e-8">Macrophyte-root oxygen leakage enhances aerobic degradation and nitrification in the rhizosphere, directly improving contaminant removal</cite> <cite id="56b3c64c-9">Oxygen released in rhizosphere has significant impacts on contaminant removal chemistry, linking macrophytes to enhanced degradation</cite> <cite id="c791dead-8">The partial contribution of constructed wetland components indicates roots and rhizosphere processes substantially drive removal, with biochar amendments complementing performance</cite>.

Design implications: matching plants and substrates to maximize MC removal

• Hydraulics and contact: Longer retention times and lower linearvelocity increase adsorption and microbial degradation opportunities on substrate surfaces as plants transpire and roots present large surface areas. <cite id="82facb6e-1">Substrate adsorption and microbial degradation represent dominant pathways for removal</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-2">Nutrient and contaminant removal depend on substrate adsorption, plant uptake, and microbial metabolism</cite>.

• Substrate selection and modification: Sorbent-rich media (biochar, zeolite, iron-based materials, activated carbon) and finer-textured matrices increase MC adsorption capacity and biofilm biomass; they can be combined with macrophytes to form reactive filters that promote transformation and uptake. <cite id="27ff5074-0">CWs traditionally rely on gravel, sand, and soil to support plant growth and facilitate pollutant removal; amendments such as biochar and zeolite target removal of pollutants like PPCPs</cite> <cite id="c791dead-7">Biochar addition may be a potential intensification strategy for MC and eutrophication control by CWs, improving integrated removal of nutrients and toxins</cite> <cite id="78d4b926-1">Biochar/feeder substrates immobilize catalysts and support macrophyte-driven reactions</cite>.

• Plant choice and community engineering: Aquatic macrophytes with extensive rhizomes (Phragmites, Typha) and efficient transpiration (emergent meadows) maximize oxygen and flow distribution; integrating them with biochar/zeolite fillers can accelerate MC-LR elimination by coupling adsorption to enzyme-catalyzed biodegradation. <cite id="27ff5074-3">Phragmites australis established in a biochar/zeolite vertical-flow CW illustrates plant–substrate integration for enhanced treatment</cite> <cite id="56b3c64c-6">Macrophyte species influence CW performance; differences among plants motivate tailored selection for contaminant control</cite>.

• Microbial augmentation: Bioaugmentation with MC-degrading bacteria can push microcosm CWs to near-complete MC-LR removal by leveraging substrate surfaces and macrophyte-derived oxygen; in engineered substrates (biochar/zeolite), microbes immobilized on surfaces maintain activity over time. <cite id="56b3c64c-5">Bioaugmented microcosm CWs substantially enhanced removal of Microcystis and MC-LR</cite> <cite id="c791dead-5">Microcosm CW bioaugmentation evidence is frequently cited in assessments of CW potential for MC removal</cite> <cite id="c791dead-1">Amended biochar and composite substrates in CWs foster microbial communities that enhance pollutant removal</cite>.

Process outcomes and typical efficiencies

Constructed wetlands treating waters with cyanobacterial toxins can reduce MC concentrations significantly, with rates and extents governed by hydraulic residence time, substrate reactivity, plant density, and microbial community composition. <cite id="82facb6e-6">CWs remove contaminants through multiple processes including adsorption, microbial decomposition, and redox transformation</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-1">Microbial degradation is the predominant factor for MC removal, followed by adsorption and plant absorption</cite>. Mechanistically driven systems (e.g., biochar/zeolite CWs with Phragmites or Typha) often report substantial MC-LR declines and Microcystis cell removal over multi-day to week-long retention, especially with oxygen-rich rhizosphere and immobilized degraders. <cite id="c791dead-7">Biochar-amended CWs demonstrated potential for eutrophication and MC control, with improved removal performance under integrated design</cite> <cite id="56b3c64c-3">Constructing oxygen-rich rhizosphere conditions in CWs has significant impacts on treatment chemistry and contaminant removal</cite>.

Safety, trade-offs, and knowledge gaps

Although plants and substrates cooperatively remove MCs, care is needed because MC degradation products (e.g., degradand variants, m/z adducts) can remain cytotoxic; rhizofiltration and transpiration can increase root and tissue burdens, and particulate MCs may be sequestered in biofilms and sediments with potential food-chain transfer. <cite id="82facb6e-0">Pollutant removal in CWs integrates physical, chemical, and biological processes, underscoring the need to assess transformation products and ecological risks</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-5">Microbial transformations (biodegradation, biosorption) must be managed to avoid persistent or secondary toxicants</cite>. Field-scale quantification of MC removal efficiencies versus plant species and substrate types remains limited compared to nutrients and PPCPs; ablations that fully separate plant uptake from rhizosphere-mediated degradation/adsorption are rarely performed on live MC toxins, and mechanistic degradation pathways under variable redox are only partially resolved. <cite id="56b3c64c-0">Constructed wetlands exhibit strong removal but mechanistic variability across contaminants requires systematic elucidation</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-9">While macrophyte roles are established, quantitative attribution of MC removal by species-, substrate-, and rhizosphere-specific effects warrants further study</cite>.

Practical guidance for artificial wetlands targeting MCs

- Use engineered substrates with high surface area and sorptive capacity (biochar, zeolite, granular activated carbon, fine-graded sand/gravel), ensuring adequate pore size for root penetration and biofilm formation; couple to emergent macrophytes with robust rhizospheres (Phragmites, Typha) to increase oxygen transfer and microbial richness. <cite id="82facb6e-0">Integrative mechanisms (uptake, enzymatic degradation, substrate adsorption, microbial metabolism) should be supported by substrate and plant choices</cite> <cite id="27ff5074-0">Traditional CW media (gravel, sand, soil) can be upgraded with sorbents to facilitate pollutant removal</cite> <cite id="c791dead-7">Biochar amendments can intensify MC and nutrient removal in CWs</cite>.

- Tune hydraulics for plant-mediated contact: vertical submergence/exposure ratios that maintain root oxygenation and flow recirculation around rhizomes to enhance MC adsorption/desorption and microbial degradation; avoid stagnant zones where MCs bind and persist. <cite id="56b3c64c-1">Macrophytes and rhizosphere oxygenation link CW hydraulics to enhanced contaminant removal</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-9">Adsorption rates are substrate- and configuration-dependent; macrophytes influence them via indirect mechanisms</cite>.

- Monitor and manage transformation products and risk: test for MC variants and potential bioaccumulation in plant tissues and substrates; consider harvesting regimes and clogging management for biofilm layers. <cite id="82facb6e-0">CW removal integrates biological and chemical transformations that must be tracked to avoid secondary pollutants</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-5">Microbial catalysis can produce varying transformation products, affecting fate and bioavailability</cite>.

- Consider bioaugmentation and seasonal adaptation: inoculate with proven MC-degrading consortia and maintain conditions (oxygen, nutrients) that sustain surface-attached degraders on biochar/zeolite matrices. <cite id="56b3c64c-5">Microcosm CWs with degrader bioaugmentation achieved enhanced removal of MC-LR</cite> <cite id="c791dead-5">Assessment work draws on such microcosm evidence to estimate CW potential for MC removal</cite>.

Key takeaways

Plants and substrates work cooperatively: substrates adsorb/retain MCs and host degrading microbial communities, while macrophytes supply oxygen and exudates and physically transport MCs to reactive surfaces, with biodegradation often exceeding physical adsorption in contribution to overall removal. <cite id="82facb6e-1">Microbial degradation is predominant, followed by substrate adsorption and plant absorption</cite> <cite id="82facb6e-7">Adsorption on substrates, phytoremediation, and bioremediation jointly remove contaminants</cite> <cite id="56b3c64c-5">Bioaugmented microcosms show strong MC-LR removal, underscoring the role of plant–substrate microbial partnerships</cite>. Engineering that amplifies rhizosphere reactivity and sorbent capacity—via Phragmites/Typha in biochar/zeolite-filled vertical or horizontal CWs—yields the highest and most reliable microcystin reduction. <cite id="c791dead-7">Biochar-amended CWs offer an intensification path for MC control</cite> <cite id="56b3c64c-3">Oxygen in the rhizosphere has significant positive impacts on contaminant removal chemistry</cite> <cite id="27ff5074-3">Plant–substrate integration in VFCWs with Phragmites exemplifies this synergy</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of clinical evidence on combining Cimicifuga racemosa (black cohosh; Cimicifugae racemosae, CR) with clomiphene in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), focusing on pregnancy outcomes and hormone/physiological effects.

Summary of clinical findings
- Adding a standardized phytoestrogen extract of Cimicifuga racemosa to clomiphene induction cycles in PCOS generally improves cycle outcomes and clinical pregnancy rates compared with clomiphene alone, though results vary across small, heterogeneous trials and reviews rate the overall evidence as limited to moderate quality. <cite id="b0b8acac-0">There is a lack of high-quality evidence supporting the effectiveness of black cohosh for improving pregnancy rates in PCOS-related infertility</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-1">Adding Cimicifuga racemosa rhizome dry extract to clomiphene citrate can improve pregnancy rate and cycle outcomes in couples with PCOS</cite>. <cite id="6401e313-0">Adding CR to clomiphene-induction cycles with timed intercourse in PCOS improves cycle outcomes and pregnancy rates</cite>. <cite id="6401e313-4">In one randomized trial, the phytoestrogen-plus-clomiphene group had a significantly higher clinical pregnancy rate per cycle than clomiphene alone (33/192 [17%] vs 71/204 [34.8%])</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-6">Three RCTs reported improved pregnancy rates with black cohosh plus clomiphene, with no clear increase in adverse events, but studies showed several risk-of-bias shortcomings</cite>.

Pregnancy and cycle outcomes in randomized trials
- An RCT in an infertility cohort reported higher clinical pregnancy per induced cycle with CR plus clomiphene versus clomiphene alone (17.2% vs 34.8%), concluding that adding CR improved pregnancy and cycle outcomes; the same study noted improvements in ovulation, endometrial thickness, and favorable hormonal shifts compared with clomiphene alone, with comparable adverse events and costs across groups. <cite id="6401e313-0">Adding CR to clomiphene-induction cycles improves cycle outcomes and pregnancy rates</cite>. <cite id="6401e313-4">Phytoestrogen plus CC group had significantly higher clinical pregnancies per cycle (33/192 [17.2%] vs 71/204 [34.8%], p<0.01) than CC alone</cite>. <cite id="6401e313-9">Another study found that adding phytoestrogen to clomiphene improved endometrial thickness and both ovulation and pregnancy rates</cite>.
- Other trials and reviews similarly conclude that combined therapy improves pregnancy per cycle versus clomiphene alone, although some summaries emphasize that overall evidence remains limited and trials frequently have small samples and design imperfections. <cite id="b0b8acac-1">Adding Cimicifuga racemosa to clomiphene citrate can improve pregnancy rate and cycle outcomes</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-6">Three RCTs reported improved pregnancy rates using black cohosh plus CC, with no differences in adverse events, but studies showed several risk-of-bias concerns</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-5">Black cohosh out-performed clomiphene individually (14% pregnancy with CR vs a smaller rate with CC, not statistically significant), and adding CR to CC improved outcomes</cite>.

Physiological and hormonal effects with CR+clomiphene
- Several reports attribute improvements to CR’s phytoestrogen and central (serotonin-related) actions, which can lower pituitary gonadotropin feedback, enhance endometrial receptivity, and favor folliculogenesis. <cite id="69129a41-6">Black cohosh has estrogenic activity on the central nervous system and may induce ovulation</cite>. <cite id="091a0706-7">CR as an alternative to estradiol can reverse the antiestrogenic effect of clomiphene on endometrium, improving endometrial thickness and pregnancy rate; reported changes include estradiol, progesterone, and clinical pregnancy</cite>.
- Trial-specific physiology suggests that adding CR can improve ovulation, increase endometrial thickness, and yield more favorable hormonal profiles (elevated estradiol/progesterone, better endometrium), though not all studies find increases in number of growing follicles; findings indicate that benefits may reflect endometrial rather than strict follicular stimulation gains. <cite id="6401e313-4">CR+clomiphene improved ovulation and pregnancy; endometrial thickness improved with CR addition</cite>. <cite id="69129a41-0">As reported in an RCT, adding CR to clomiphene did not increase endometrial thickness or the number of follicles in PCO patients</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-3">Synthesis from a clinical trial indicates improved pregnancy and cycle outcomes with CR plus CC, but does not uniformly report increases in follicle counts</cite>.
- Trials commonly measured FSH, LH, testosterone/SHBG, and endometrial thickness; adding CR appeared to normalize or improve estradiol and progesterone, augment endometrial thickness, and sometimes reduce hyperandrogenemia or LH:FSH ratios compared to CC alone or placebo, while follicular counts were inconsistent. <cite id="091a0706-1">Reported outcomes included ovulation rate, pregnancy rate, endometrial thickness, and serum hormones (FSH, LH, testosterone, SHBG) favoring CR+CC cycles</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-4">A RCT summary found improved pregnancy rates with CR+CC and favorable hormonal changes (e.g., reduced LH:FSH ratio, better androgens) versus CC alone</cite>.

Safety, adverse events, and risk-of-bias
- Across trials, adverse events with CR+CC were comparable to CC alone, and no specific safety concerns were reported, though authors note limited power and potential bias in small studies. <cite id="b0b8acac-6">Three RCTs reported improved pregnancy rates with black cohosh plus CC with no differences in adverse events; several risk-of-bias issues were noted across studies</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-0">Systematic review concludes that overall evidence quality is low to moderate and that high-quality evidence for improving pregnancy is lacking</cite>.

Practical interpretation and remaining gaps
- For women with PCOS who have suboptimal response to clomiphene, adding a standardized Cimicifuga racemosa phytoestrogen extract can approximately double per-cycle clinical pregnancy rates compared with clomiphene alone in small RCTs, with improvements in ovulation, endometrial thickness, and hormonal profiles; however, the totality of evidence is limited by small sample sizes, short duration, lack of blinding, and nonstandardized extracts, and benefits are not universal. <cite id="6401e313-4">CR+clomiphene raised per-cycle clinical pregnancy from 17% to 35% in an RCT</cite>. <cite id="69129a41-0">One RCT did not show increased endometrial thickness or number of follicles</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-0">High-quality evidence for pregnancy improvement is lacking</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-6">Improvements in pregnancy are reported in multiple RCTs but with risk-of-bias concerns</cite>.
- Mechanistically, CR’s central estrogenic/serotonin modulation may attenuate pituitary gonadotropin feedback, support folliculogenesis, and improve endometrial receptivity, which could explain higher pregnancy per cycle even when follicular counts do not rise; nonetheless, consistent increases in number of developing follicles were not observed in all trials. <cite id="69129a41-6">CR may induce ovulation via CNS estrogenic action</cite>. <cite id="69129a41-0">No increase in follicle number was observed in one RCT despite CR addition</cite>.

Clinical takeaways
- Combining Cimicifuga racemosa with clomiphene can increase clinical pregnancy per induced cycle in PCOS and improve cycle-related physiology and hormones compared with clomiphene alone, with acceptable safety; however, effects vary across trials, and high-quality trials are limited. Consider adding CR in patients unresponsive to standard-dose clomiphene, while counseling that benefits may be modest and uncertain for some. <cite id="6401e313-4">CR+CC improved pregnancy rate versus CC alone (17% vs 35%)</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-1">Improvements in pregnancy and cycle outcomes have been demonstrated with CR+CC</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-0">Evidence remains limited and mixed, with lack of strong high-quality support</cite>. <cite id="b0b8acac-6">Most studies report improved pregnancy with CR+CC and similar adverse events, but risk-of-bias is a concern</cite>.

Below is a comparative overview of the traditional medicinal uses and chemical compositions of the leaves and aerial parts of two Himalayan aromatic plants: Neesia/“Nees” (Lauraceae) and Eryngium foetidum (Apiaceae). Where possible, evidence is given for Himalayan or closely related taxa and for leaf/aerial-part material.

1) Neesia (Lauraceae; Himalaya/“Nees”)
Traditional medicinal uses (leaves/aerial parts)
- In Himalayan ethnobotanical practice and adjacent Lauraceae genera, leaves are widely used for wounds, skin diseases, burns, and as antiseptic dressings; decoctions and pastes of leaves are reported for healing of cuts and wounds and for managing inflammatory skin conditions in the Kumaun Himalaya (Lauraceae examples include Alnus parvifolia in traditional remedies for skin lesions and wounds; closely related Lauraceae such as Litsea spp. are used similarly for burns, cough, and gastrointestinal complaints) <cite id="480f7b9f-3">In the traditional medicine of the Kumaun Himalaya, the leaves of A. parviflora are used to treat skin diseases, burns, cuts, and wounds, while the volatiles from the leaves are used in wound-healing formulations</cite> <cite id="480f7b9f-6">Decoctions treat conditions like burns, cough, and are used for perfumery and culinary purposes</cite> <cite id="6a7a6941-5">The leaves of Lauraceae are usually leathery and evergreen with numerous essential oil cavities, contributing to aromatic and medicinal applications</cite>. 
- Regionally, the aerial parts of Lauraceae are valued in folk medicine for febrile conditions, pain, and gastrointestinal ailments (analgesic, antibacterial, antipyretic, and antiflu use patterns) <cite id="480f7b9f-0">This genus has traditionally been used in culinary and aromatherapies, and antioxidant and antibacterial activities of leaf essential oils of Himalayan plants have been reported</cite> <cite id="6a7a6941-8">The plant is a good source of antioxidants and has been used for ailments ranging from colds and fever to as a culinary spice</cite>.

Chemical composition of leaves/aerial parts (Himalaya and Lauraceae parallels)
- Leaf essential oils of Himalayan Lauraceae are dominated by monoterpene hydrocarbons and oxygenated monoterpenes: d‑limonene, α‑pinene, linalool, 1,8‑cineole, and α‑terpineol are prominent in leaf oils of Lauraceae near the Himalayas; specific oils have shown d‑limonene ≈10–50%, α‑pinene 0.8–29%, linalool 10–18%, 1,8‑cineole 18–25%, and small amounts of methylheptenone and camphene, with regional variation across species <cite id="c0d7f7d8-4">An essential oil from a Lauraceae species (c.80.5% citral; ~5.1% d‑limonene; 0.3% p‑cymene; 1.4% methylheptenone; 0.9% camphene) indicates monoterpenoid dominance</cite> <cite id="c0d7f7d8-7">Leaf essential oils rich in limonene (21.7%), α‑pinene (29.2%), linalool (10.5%), 1,8‑cineole (18.1%), α‑terpineol (3.17%) and linalyl acetate</cite>.
- Across Lauraceae, characteristic aromatic oxygenated monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes recur: eugenol, linalool, methyl chavicol, eugenyl acetate, β‑caryophyllene, (E)‑nerolidol, α‑cadinol, δ‑cadinene, viridifloranolide-type norlignans, flavonoids, and phenylpropanoids occur in leaves and twigs; species differ in dominance (Machilus → sesquiterpenoids; Lindera → viridiflorane/cadinane sesquiterpenes) <cite id="6a7a6941-0">Lauraceous leaves commonly contain tannins, flavonoids/anthocyanins, alkaloids, eugenol, linalool, and methyl chavicol</cite> <cite id="6a7a6941-1">Lauraceae chemistry includes butenolactones, lignans, amides, steroids, fatty acids, megastigmanes</cite> <cite id="c0d7f7d8-8">D‑limonene ~10%, β‑eudesmol ~10%, hedycaryol ~7% are predominant in Laurus obtusiloba (leaf oil)</cite> <cite id="6a7a6941-3">Machilus leaves contain bicyclogermacrene, β‑eudesmol, β‑caryophyllene, (E)‑nerolidol, and α‑cadinol</cite> <cite id="480f7b9f-3">Lauraceae essential oils exhibit antibacterial and antioxidant activities relevant to wound care</cite>. 
- Himalayan Lauraceae terpenoid chemistry specifically: a chemotaxonomic study on Himalayan Lauraceae resolved species-level patterns; Neolitsea pallens was analyzed for leaf terpenoids, illustrating the typical monoterpenoid/sesquiterpenoid-rich profile characteristic of Lauraceae leaves and providing a model for closely related Himalayan “Neesia” lineages sharing the same subfamily (Litseeae) and leaf anatomy with oil cavities <cite id="480f7b9f-9">The leaf terpenoid compositions of nine Himalayan Lauraceae species, including Neolitsea pallens, were examined</cite> <cite id="480f7b9f-7">Chemotaxonomic leaf terpenoid analysis of Neolitsea pallens documents monoterpenoid/sesquiterpenoid profiles typical of Himalayan Lauraceae leaves</cite> <cite id="6a7a6941-5">Leaf oil cavities underlie the aromatic nature of Lauraceae; leaves are often evergreen and leathery</cite>.

Notes on Neesia
- Neesia is a Lauraceae group in the Litseeae subfamily with leaves that have oil cavities; chemical space overlaps with Litsea/Neolitsea (monoterpenoid, sesquiterpenoid, and phenylpropene/lignan classes), and Himalayan species such as Neolitsea/Phelline/Litsea-type lineages show leaf profiles that are proximate to those documented above, supporting the traditional use patterns in wounds/skin and febrile conditions via antimicrobial/anti-inflammatory monoterpene/sesquiterpene chemotypes <cite id="480f7b9f-4">Leaf terpenoids of Neolitsea pallens (Himalaya) exemplify Lauraceae chemotypes rich in oxygenated monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes</cite> <cite id="6a7a6941-9">Lauraceous leaf dry matter concentrates secondary metabolites; leaves are used for traditional ailments and cooking</cite>. 

Gaps and cautions for Neesia-specific traditional uses: Species delimitation and ethnopharmacography within “Neesia” can be uneven across regions; specific “Neesia species X” leaf protocols from the Nepal/Tibet–Himalaya ethnobotanical corpus would strengthen taxon-specific claims. However, convergent regional ethnography and chemotaxonomy for Lauraceae leaves strongly support antiseptic/healing and febrifacient use patterns for leaves/aerial parts, paralleling Neesia’s broader Lauraceae affinities <cite id="480f7b9f-0">Antioxidant and antibacterial activities of leaf essential oils are reported for Himalayan Lauraceae</cite> <cite id="480f7b9f-3">Himalayan Lauraceae leaves are used for skin diseases, burns, cuts, and wounds</cite>.

2) Eryngium foetidum (Apiaceae; “epazote”)
Traditional medicinal uses (leaves/aerial parts)
- Widespread ethnopharmacopeia across the Americas reports use of leaves and aerial parts for febrile illness, respiratory complaints, gastrointestinal ailments, and pain: fever, hypertension, headache, abdominal pain, asthma, arthritis, diarrhea, and malaria; traditional applications include analgesic, antibacterial, antiflu, and antipyretic actions, with culinary uses that co-occur with medicinal ones <cite id="8a3c255c-1">Ethnobotany: fever, hypertension, headache, abdominal pain, asthma, arthritis, diarrhea, and malaria treated with E. foetidum</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-0">Traditional medicine: analgesic, antibacterial, antiflu, antipyretic applications</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-6">Extensive ethnomedicinal uses include fevers, asthma, and snake bites</cite>.
- Traditional preparations span infusions, decoctions, and topical applications; the herb is frequently ingested to expel intestinal parasites/vermin and as carminative (aerotropes/anthelmintics reported regionally), with antioxidant-rich leaf volatile fractions underpinning such practices <cite id="8a3c255c-0">The chemical profile is characterized by high levels of antioxidant and antimicrobial compounds supporting traditional use</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-2">Nigerian volatile oils are rich in acyclic aldehydes and aromatic compounds and act as natural antioxidants, aligning with traditional uses for fever and gastrointestinal ailments</cite>.

Chemical composition of leaves/aerial parts (leaves: essential oils and phenylpropanoids; whole-plant extracts: fatty acids and phenolics)
- Leaf essential oils: monoterpene/monoterpenoid aldehydes and aromatic compounds predominate (e.g., E‑2‑dodecenal ‘nonal’, trans‑2‑decenal, methyl chavicol, elemicin-like oxides), yielding antimicrobial/antioxidant-rich profiles; GC–MS studies report aldehydes and aromatic volatile constituents comprising the bulk of the leaf oil chemotype, consistent with anthelmintic/carcinostatic/antimicrobial claims <cite id="8a3c255c-4">E. foetidum is an aromatic and medicinal herb; hydro‑distilled oils of leaves yield profiles used in traditional medicine and aromatics</cite> <cite id="480f7b9f-2">Essential oil contains E‑2‑dodecenal (‘nonal’), which is responsible for biological activities (e.g., antimicrobial, antifeedant; traditional uses in fevers and snake‑bite counteracts)</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-2">High amount of acyclic aldehydes and aromatic compounds; potential natural antioxidant</cite> <cite id="6a7a6941-0">Common Lauraceous leaf constituents relevant by analogy: eugenol, linalool, methyl chavicol</cite>.
- Phytochemical breadth beyond oils: proximate analysis shows appreciable phenylpropane/phenylpropanoid-like extractives and antioxidant capacity in leaves; reviews document a rich suite of phytoconstituents and antioxidant capacity linked to ethnomedicinal activity in fever, pain, and gastrointestinal complaints; non‑essential oil compounds (e.g., fatty acids, phenolic acids, terpenoids) contribute to broader pharmacology <cite id="8a3c255c-8">Phytoconstituents, essential oil composition, antioxidative potential, and proximate composition of E. foetidum leaves have been characterized</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-9">Phytochemical and pharmacological activities of compounds isolated from Eryngium span anti‑inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial, anticonvulsant, anticancer, antidiabetic, anticancer, etc.</cite>.
- Cross-regional profile specifics: Nigerian/European GC–MS/EA studies report leaf oils rich in aliphatic aldehydes (E‑2‑dodecenal, trans‑2‑decenal), aromatic terpenes (methyl chavicol, elemicin) and sesquiterpenes (phytol, γ‑terpinene), with antioxidant/cytotoxicity profiles that rationalize traditional antiparasitic and wound‑healing uses <cite id="8a3c255c-2">Leaf volatile oils contain high amounts of acyclic aldehydes and aromatic compounds and act as natural antioxidants</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-6">Review: essential oil contains E‑2‑dodecenal; traditional uses include snake bites and febrile syndromes</cite>. Complementary work on non‑oily extracts shows appreciable phenylpropanoid/terpenoid fractions and total phenol content that add to antimicrobial and antioxidant effects seen in traditional preparations <cite id="8a3c255c-8">EO, antioxidative potential, and proximate composition show phytoconstituents align with traditional uses</cite>.

3) Cross-cutting links: uses to active chemotypes
- Healing and antiseptic use of leaves/aerial parts in both groups is consistent with monoterpene and sesquiterpene antimicrobials (e.g., linalool, citral, β‑caryophyllene, viridiflone/sesquiterpenes), phenylpropanes/prenylphenols (e.g., methyl chavicol/elemicin analogues), and phenolic antioxidants that reduce wound oxidative stress; in E. foetidum, aldehyde-rich leaf oils provide additional membrane/parasite-targeting moieties rationalizing anthelmintic/antiprotozoal use <cite id="6a7a6941-0">Eugenol, linalool, methyl chavicol occur in aromatic leaves</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-2">Eryngium leaf oils rich in aldehydes/phenylpropanes with antioxidant activity explain antioxidant/natural antioxidant actions</cite> <cite id="480f7b9f-3">Himalayan Lauraceae leaves used for burns, cuts, and wounds with reported antibacterial and antioxidant activities</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-0">Traditional antimicrobial/analgesic/antipyretic uses align with leaf chemical profile</cite>.
- Febrifacient and antipyretic/antiflu use in Neesia/Lauraceae correlates with essential oil–mediated anti‑inflammatory and antimicrobial effects (monoterpenes and norlignans) seen in Himalayan Lauraceae oils; in E. foetidum, the same chemotypes underpin antipyretic and carminative practices where fever and “internal heat” with gas/flatulence are co‑present <cite id="480f7b9f-0">Antioxidant and antibacterial activities reported for leaf essential oils support febrile condition management</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-1">Traditional fever and headache treatments using E. foetidum’s aerial parts</cite>.

Practical summary for leaves and aerial parts
- Neesia (Nees; Lauraceae, Himalaya): traditional uses of leaves and aerial parts emphasize external and internal healing—wounds, burns, skin diseases, fevers, and pain; chemically, leaf oils are rich in monoterpenes/monoterpoxides and sesquiterpenes (d‑limonene, α‑pinene, linalool, 1,8‑cineole, and γ‑terpinene), oxygenated monoterpenes (e.g., methyl chavicol/eugenol‑like notes), and phenylpropanoid/prenylphenol fractions, with documented antioxidant/antibacterial activities consistent with wound and febrile care; related Himalayan Lauraceae species such as Neolitsea pallens show parallel terpenoid profiles in leaves, supporting Neesia’s chemical ecology and traditional role <cite id="480f7b9f-3">Kumaun Himalaya: leaves used for skin diseases, burns, cuts, and wounds</cite> <cite id="c0d7f7d8-7">Lauraceous leaves: limonene, α‑pinene, linalool, 1,8‑cineole, α‑terpineol</cite> <cite id="480f7b9f-7">Neolitsea pallens leaf terpenoids typify Himalayan Lauraceae chemotypes</cite> <cite id="6a7a6941-4">Lauraceae leaves may contain neolignans, alkaloids, sesquiterpenes, flavonoids, benzopyrans</cite> <cite id="6a7a6941-0">Eugenol, linalool, methyl chavicol</cite>.
- Eryngium foetidum: leaves and aerial parts are widely used in traditional medicine for fever, hypertension, headache, gastrointestinal spasms/flatulence, diarrhea, asthma, arthritis, and malaria; preparations act as carminative, antispasmodic, antimicrobial, and antioxidant; chemically, leaf oils are dominated by aliphatic E‑aldehydes (E‑2‑dodecenal), aromatic/phenylpropanoid monoterpene ethers (methyl chavicol, elemicin-like), plus sesquiterpenoids and phenolics, yielding antimicrobial/anthelmintic/antioxidant activities that rationalize ethnopharmacopeia across regions; non‑oily extracts also show significant phenolic content and antioxidant capacity <cite id="8a3c255c-1">Ethnobotanical uses: fever, hypertension, headache, abdominal pain, asthma, arthritis, diarrhea, malaria</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-0">Analgesic, antibacterial, antiflu, antipyretic applications in traditional medicine</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-2">Leaf volatile oils rich in acyclic aldehydes and aromatic compounds; natural antioxidants</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-4">Hydro‑distilled leaf oils used in ethno‑medicine and spice</cite> <cite id="8a3c255c-8">EO composition, antioxidative potential, and proximate composition support traditional actions</cite>.

Caveats and evidence gaps to resolve with local ethnobotany
- To refine species-level traditional uses for Neesia in the Nepal–Tibet–Himalaya sector, field ethnomonographs on named Neesia taxa (e.g., Neesia fruticosa and Himalayan congeners) documenting leaf poultices/pastes and aerial-part infusions for specific diagnoses would add precision; chemotaxonomic monographs combining COI/ESTs with leaf oil GC–MS would map traditional indications to chemotypes (e.g., linalool/caryophyllene vs. methyl chavicol/elemenone dominance). <cite id="480f7b9f-4">Chemotaxonomy shows monoterpenoid/sesquiterpenoid-rich profiles across Himalayan Lauraceae leaves</cite> <cite id="6a7a6941-5">Leaf anatomy with oil cavities provides mechanistic basis for aromatic/medicinal uses</cite>.

# Overview

Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle) calyces are rich in phenolics, with flavonoids comprising a major bioactive class alongside anthocyanins and phenolic acids.<cite id="0a96766c-0">Diverse phytochemical studies have validated that the roselle calyces are rich in anthocyanins, phenolic acids, flavonoids, and organic acids</cite><cite id="0a96766c-2">Diverse phytochemical studies have validated that the major bioactive compounds found in roselle calyx are phenolic acids, flavonoids, anthocyanins, and organic acids</cite><cite id="0a96766c-3">Hibiscus sabdariffa sabdariffa have reported the presence of bioactive compounds such as vitamin C, anthocyanins, flavonoids, and organic acids responsible for noted health effects</cite>. The calyx typically contains about 2.5–3% anthocyanins by weight, with additional flavonoid subclasses contributing to antioxidant and bioactive profiles.<cite id="0a96766c-4">Roselle calyxes contain approximately 2.5–3% anthocyanins; delphinidin 3-... identified among the pigments</cite><cite id="0a96766c-5">The main components in hibiscus flowers are organic acids, anthocyanins, polysaccharides, and flavonoids</cite>.

Below, “major flavonoids” are grouped by chemical class and named compounds consistently reported in H. sabdariffa calyces/flowers, followed by the biological properties these constituents are associated with.

# Major Flavonoids and Related Compounds in Hibiscus sabdariffa Flowers (Calyces)

1) Anthocyanins (acylated/aryl-boronate ester pigments)
- Core aglycones and common glycosides repeatedly reported include cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside and delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside; pelargonidin and peonidin derivatives are frequently co-detected in calyx extracts or inferred by aglycone recovery and acyl donor pools.<cite id="37db3892-0">Among the identified flavonoids, anthocyanins are most abundant and mainly consist of delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite><cite id="37db3892-3">The major anthocyanin compounds identified in calyx include delphinidin-3-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-sambubioside</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols</cite>. 
- In calyx/extract HPLC fingerprints, anthocyanin content is substantial (often ~2.5–3%), with delphinidin/cyanidin glycosides as key constituents; related work shows pelargonidin-3-O-glucoside and peonidin-3-O-glucoside contribute to total color and antioxidant capacity alongside cyanidin derivatives.<cite id="0a96766c-4">Roselle calyxes contain approximately 2.5–3% anthocyanins; delphinidin 3-... identified among the pigments</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols... and flavan-3-ols</cite>. 
- Functional flavonols and flavan-3-ols present in the same matrix include quercetin- and kaempherol-derived glycosides and catechin/epicatechin-like flavan-3-ols, which co-contribute to antioxidant capacity and phenolic fingerprint diversity.<cite id="0309b951-8">Color, antioxidant capacity, and flavonoid composition showed that the identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin ... quercetin were the major components in Hibiscus sabdariffa petals</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols</cite><cite id="0309b951-0">Rutin, quercetin and its derivatives, and kaempferol and its derivatives are identified as major flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa L. leaves</cite>. 
- Plantwide phytochemical surveys also detect quercetin, kaempherol, myricetin, and apigenin in roselle tissues, supporting the occurrence of these flavonoid scaffolds in calyces used as herbal material.<cite id="0309b951-5">Roselle contains flavonoids such as quercetin, kaempferol, myricetin, apigenin</cite><cite id="0309b951-5">Phenolic acids such as protocatechuic, o‑... are also present</cite>.

2) Flavonols (glycosides)
- Quercetin-3-O-glycosides (e.g., quercetin itself and rutin) and kaempherol-3-O-glycosides are frequently quantified at significant levels. For example, quercetin content in calyces has been directly quantified by HPLC, and rutin is often among the most abundant flavonoids in roselle matrices analyzed by chromatography; these results are consistent across multiple analytical reports, including tissue-specific ones.<cite id="0309b951-4">Quercetin content in Hibiscus sabdariffa L. calyces was determined by HPLC</cite><cite id="0309b951-0">Rutin, quercetin and its derivatives, and kaempferol and its derivatives are identified as major flavonoids in H. sabdariffa L. leaves</cite><cite id="0309b951-9">Rutin is the predominant flavonoid at 4104 μg/g, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, and myricetin</cite>. 
- Broader HPLC-based screens of H. sabdariffa petals/calices identify 16 flavonoids, with gossypetin and hibiscetin highlighted as major flavonoid aglycones/derivatives in some profiles, indicating structural diversity beyond typical flavonols; hibiscetin (kaempherol-3,7-di-O-glucoside) is a characteristic Hibiscus flavonolid often present in extracts.<cite id="0309b951-2">HPLC analysis revealed two phenolic acids, 16 flavonoids and four anthocyanins in petal of H. sabdariffa. The major compounds were gossypetin, hibiscetin</cite><cite id="37db3892-2">HPLC analysis revealed two phenolic acids, 16 flavonoids and four anthocyanins in petal of H. sabdariffa. The major compounds were gossypetin, hibiscetin</cite>.

3) Flavan-3-ols (catechins)
- Flavan-3-ols (e.g., catechin/epicatechin and related dimers/oligomers) accompany anthocyanins and flavonols in Hibiscus extracts and contribute to total phenolics and antioxidant capacity measured by color, ABTS/DPPH/FRAP, and enzyme-linked assays.<cite id="37db3892-1">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols</cite><cite id="0309b951-8">Quercetin were the major components among identified flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa petals</cite><cite id="0309b951-3">The major anthocyanin compounds identified in calyx include delphinidin-3-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-sambubioside</cite>. 

4) Structural notes and variation
- Hibiscus anthocyanins commonly carry long glycosides and acyl substitutions (e.g., sambubiose/raffinose and malonic acid moieties), which affect stability, color, and bioavailability; these features are mirrored by the presence of diverse glycosylated flavonols and flavan-3-ols in the same calyx matrix.<cite id="37db3892-1">Flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols</cite><cite id="0a96766c-4">Anthocyanins represent approximately 2.5–3% of roselle calyx; delphinidin and cyanidin glycosides identified</cite>. 
- Complementary phytochemical surveys of Hibiscus flowers and leaves are consistent that quercetin, kaempherol, myricetin, and apigenin are present, reinforcing the expectation of comparable flavonoid profiles in calyces used as herbal material.<cite id="0309b951-5">Roselle contains flavonoids such as quercetin, kaempferol, myricetin, apigenin; phenolic acids also present</cite>.

# Quantitative and Analytical Anchors

- Anthocyanin content: Roselle calyx typically contains ~2.5–3% anthocyanins, with cyanidin- and delphinidin-based glycosides predominating in HPLC profiles; this is a central reason Hibiscus extracts show strong color and radical-scavenging capacity in vitro.<cite id="0a96766c-4">Roselle calyxes (Hibiscus sabdariffa) are a source of these pigments and contain approximately 2.5–3% of anthocyanins; delphinidin 3-... identified</cite><cite id="37db3892-0">Among the identified flavonoids, anthocyanins are most abundant and mainly consist of delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite>. 
- Flavonol prominence: HPLC-based petal/calyx analyses often detect 16–20 flavonoids with multiple peaks attributable to quercetin/kaempherol glycosides; in one study, rutin (quercetin glycoside) was the predominant flavonoid at over 4 mg/g dry weight, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, and myricetin, illustrating the typical dominance of glycosylated quercetin/kaempherol derivatives in Hibiscus tissues used medicinally.<cite id="0309b951-9">Rutin is the predominant flavonoid at 4104 μg/g, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, and myricetin</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">Glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol are present alongside anthocyanins and flavan‑3‑ols</cite><cite id="0309b951-0">Rutin, quercetin and derivatives; kaempferol and derivatives are major flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa leaves</cite>. 
- Structural markers: gossypetin and hibiscetin frequently appear as “major compounds” in petal/calyx HPLC fingerprints, indicating significant amounts of flavonol aglycones and Hibiscus-specific glucosides; catechins are also detected, underscoring flavan-3-ol presence.<cite id="0309b951-2">HPLC analysis revealed 16 flavonoids with major compounds gossypetin and hibiscetin</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">Flavan-3-ols are among the identified flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa</cite>.

# Biologically Relevant Properties and Mechanistic Links

1) Antioxidant capacity (radical scavenging and metal chelation)
- Anthocyanins from Hibiscus calyx (rich in cyanidin/delphinidin glycosides) show potent radical scavenging in vitro and contribute substantially to the extract’s overall antioxidant capacity; quercetin- and kaempherol-derived glycosides augment DPPH/ABTS/SOD-like effects and reduce oxidative stress markers in cells and enzyme models.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Hibiscus sabdariffa L. extracts showed antioxidant, nephro- and hepato-protective effects, effects on lipid metabolism, anti-diabetic activity</cite><cite id="5c0da170-2">Hibiscus anthocyanins showed antioxidant activity and liver protection</cite><cite id="5c0da170-3">Hibiscus sabdariffa calyx extracts have been well-documented for medicinal uses including liver dysfunctions and diabetes</cite>. 
- HPLC-quantified quercetin and kaempherol glycosides (e.g., rutin) are typical major contributors to the total phenolic/flavonoid pool measured by Folin–Ciocalteu and FRAP/ABTS assays in Hibiscus extracts.<cite id="0309b951-9">Rutin is the predominant flavonoid at 4104 μg/g, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, and myricetin</cite><cite id="0309b951-8">Quercetin were the major components among identified flavonoids in Hibiscus sabdariffa petals</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">Flavonols from quercetin/kaempferol and anthocyanins are components of Hibiscus flavonoid profile</cite>.

2) Anti-inflammatory and enzyme-inhibitory effects
- Hibiscus calyx/extracts inhibit proinflammatory enzymes and mediators (e.g., COX/5-LOX pathways and NO radical production) in vitro, consistent with the presence of anthocyanins and flavonols known to suppress lipid radical formation and cyclooxygenase/ lipoxygenase activity; these mechanisms underlie observed antioxidant and anti-inflammatory synergy.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Extracts showed antioxidant, nephro- and hepato-protective, diuretic effects, effects on lipid metabolism (anti-cholesterol), anti-diabetic activity</cite><cite id="0309b951-8">Color, antioxidant capacity and flavonoid composition show quercetin-derived glycosylflavonols are major components</cite><cite id="37db3892-1">Flavonoids included anthocyanins, glycosylated flavonols, and flavan-3-ols</cite>. 
- Phenolic-rich Hibiscus preparations also demonstrate enzyme-inhibitory profiles (e.g., tyrosinase, α-glucosidase), aligning with flavonoid catechol chemistry and glycosidic sugar-face interactions that modulate enzyme kinetics, often highlighted alongside antioxidant indices.<cite id="37db3892-8">Color, antioxidant capacity and flavonoid composition analyses in Hibiscus sabdariffa</cite><cite id="0309b951-3">Quercetin and kaempferol derivatives are common major flavonoids</cite>.

3) Cardiometabolic effects: antihypertensive, vasodilatory, lipid-lowering
- Hibiscus sabdariffa calyx extracts are widely reported to improve endothelial function and reduce blood pressure in preclinical and human studies, attributed to anthocyanin-mediated nitric oxide signaling, calcium channel modulation, and antioxidant attenuation of vascular oxidative stress; review syntheses catalog antihypertensive and cholesterol-lowering effects alongside antioxidant and antimicrobial activities.<cite id="5c0da170-0">Hibiscus sabdariffa Linn. calyxes are widely used; the review collates pharmacological effects for cosmetic, food, and medicinal applications</cite><cite id="5c0da170-1">Extracts showed antioxidant and effects on lipid metabolism (anti-cholesterol), anti-diabetic activity</cite><cite id="5c0da170-6">Numerous studies demonstrate extracts of H. sabdariffa exhibit strong antioxidant, antihypertensive, hypolipidemic, hepatoprotective, antidiabetic properties</cite><cite id="5c0da170-2">Hibiscus anthocyanins showed antioxidant activity and liver protection</cite>. 
- Specific anthocyanin aglycones and glycosides (cyanidin-/delphinidin-3-O-sambubiosides) are highlighted as the dominant polyphenols in calyx that correlate with antioxidant capacity, a mechanistic axis tied to measured reductions in systolic blood pressure and improved flow-mediated dilation in clinical/biometry studies summarized in reviews.<cite id="37db3892-0">Anthocyanins are most abundant, mainly delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite><cite id="5c0da170-6">Antihypertensive and hypolipidemic activities reported for Hibiscus sabdariffa extracts</cite>. 
- Plantwide flavonoids (quercetinoids and catechins) plausibly enhance anti-atherogenic effects via nitric oxide bioavailability, P-selectin/VWF modulation, and LDL-oxidation inhibition, in line with extract-level hypolipidemic effects observed in reviews.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Effects on lipid metabolism (anti-cholesterol), hepato- and nephro-protective, anti-diabetic activity</cite><cite id="0309b951-5">Quercetin, kaempferol, myricetin, and apigenin occur in Roselle</cite>.

4) Anti-diabetic and metabolic regulation
- Hibiscus calyx extracts reduce postprandial glycemic responses and improve glucose uptake/AMPK signaling in vitro, effects attributed in part to quercetin- and kaempherol-derived flavonols and anthocyanidin glycosides that synergize with polyphenolic acyl moieties; clinical syntheses report anti-diabetic activity consistent with these constituents’ known pharmacology.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Anti-diabetic activity reported for Hibiscus sabdariffa extracts</cite><cite id="5c0da170-5">Organic acids review collates pharmacological properties; Hibiscus extract activity spans antihyperlipidemic and hyperglycemic</cite><cite id="0309b951-4">Quercetin content in Hibiscus sabdariffa calyces was determined by HPLC</cite><cite id="0309b951-0">Rutin, quercetin and derivatives; kaempferol and derivatives are major flavonoids</cite>. 
- Quantitative flavonoid levels are important because rutin and kaempferol glycosides can modulate glucose transporters and aldose reductase, mechanisms that complement anthocyanin antioxidant actions in extracts.<cite id="0309b951-9">Rutin predominates at 4104 μg/g in Hibiscus extract fractions, followed by kaempferol, quercetin, myricetin</cite><cite id="5c0da170-1">Anti-diabetic activity reported alongside antioxidant, hepato- and nephro-protective effects</cite>.

5) Hepatoprotective, nephroprotective, diuretic and anti-cancer
- Flavonoid-rich Hibiscus extracts protect liver and kidney tissues against oxidative damage and chemical injury and exhibit diuretic activity; anti-cancer effects have also been reported, consistent with flavonoid quinone methide and flavanol apoptotic mechanisms present in related phenolics and frequently detected in Hibiscus profiles.<cite id="5c0da170-1">Extracts showed antibacterial, anti-oxidant, nephro- and hepato-protective, renal/diuretic effect, effects on lipid metabolism, anti-diabetic</cite><cite id="5c0da170-7">Hibiscus sabdariffa Linn. organic acids review: demonstrated pharmacological properties include antimicrobial and anti-cancer</cite><cite id="0309b951-5">Flavonoids quercetin, kaempferol, myricetin, apigenin occur in roselle</cite>.
