- Benchmarks and datasets. <cite id="32687957-0">USOVA3D: publicly accessible 3D ultrasound volumes of ovaries with annotated follicles</cite> <cite id="32687957-2">Open portal to use and search the USOVA3D database for impartial validation</cite>. <cite id="32687957-4">Test sets with dual-rater annotations for follicles and ovaries</cite>. <cite id="32687957-5">Kaggle-style 2D clinical image datasets for prototyping</cite>.

- Methods and validation outcomes. <cite id="e1f2d256-8">FollicleFinder (3D): improved precision and recall versus baselines, with expert comparisons on transvaginal volumes</cite>. <cite id="e1f2d256-7">Weakly supervised instance segmentation using boxes as approximate annotations achieves reliable detection</cite>. <cite id="e1f2d256-9">Edge-aware deep networks yield better contour fidelity and higher overlap metrics relative to classical energy-minimizing graph cuts</cite>.

Practical recommendations
- For new methods, start with a multi-site, multi-rater validation: obtain baseline manual segmentations from two experts; quantify inter-rater Dice/precision-recall and compute Bland–Altman against expert-measured sizes for a subset. <cite id="32687957-4">Dual-rater ground truth plus overlap metrics provide internal validation</cite> <cite id="1bbf225e-8">Bland–Altman quantifies agreement between automated and manual readings</cite>.
- For deployment in IVF clinics, validate longitudinal tracking and measurement agreement across scanners and acquisition settings, including plane selection and slice thickness effects. <cite id="1bbf225e-0">Bias and precision of automated follicle diameter measurements determine IVF applicability</cite> <cite id="32687957-5">Clinical datasets cover scanner diversity to test robustness</cite>.
- If annotation budget is tight, use weakly supervised protocols, but report the gap vs. fully supervised performance and include sensitivity analyses with perturbed labels. <cite id="e1f2d256-7">Box-based segmentation reduces annotation costs while preserving detection validity</cite> <cite id="d7f14bb5-1">Analytical performance and repeatability must meet clinical thresholds to justify adoption</cite>.
- Anticipate edge cases (very small follicles, cysts) in both training and validation; include dedicated cases for false-positive control and small-structure recall. <cite id="32687957-4">Rater disagreement is most pronounced in ambiguous cases, so cyst-follicle decision tasks should be stress-tested</cite>.

Key limitations and open challenges
- Public, openly shareable longitudinal 3D clinical cohorts are limited; many datasets lack temporal series with synchronized manual folliculometry and device/device-site harmonization. <cite id="32687957-5">2D clinical images are widely available but lack volumetric annotation standardization</cite>. <cite id="32687957-0">3D public resources exist, but cross-site generalization remains an open validation need</cite>.
- Physics-driven modeling (speckle, resolution anisotropy, projection effects) is still variably integrated; validation metrics must be interpreted with knowledge of acquisition geometry to avoid overestimating clinical utility. <cite id="e1f2d256-6">Speckle handling is critical for small follicle segmentation</cite> <cite id="e1f2d256-3">Independent validation includes plane/probe effects as explicit test factors</cite>.
- Generalizing from detection to quantitative assessment (diameter/volume) requires careful calibration and cross-method Bland–Altman validation, as pixel/voxel-to-size mappings are sensitive to contour placement and image resolution. <cite id="1bbf225e-0">Automated follicle diameter systems are validated on IVF cohorts for precision and bias</cite> <cite id="1bbf225e-7">Bland–Altman plots quantify differences between automated systems and manual reference across scans</cite>.

What counts as “good” validation
- Reproducibility: uses open datasets and/or detailed protocols enabling others to reproduce metrics. <cite id="32687957-0">Standardized 3D US databases provide reproducible testbeds</cite> <cite id="32687957-2">Impartial validation portals promote reproducibility and fairness</cite>.
- Clinical relevance: reports overlap metrics alongside clinically interpretable agreement with human measurements over time. <cite id="1bbf225e-0">Bias and precision in follicle diameter track clinically meaningful outcomes</cite> <cite id="1bbf225e-8">Bland–Altman and concordance statistics quantify clinically acceptable agreement</cite>.
- Robustness: evaluates across devices, acquisition planes, and rater variability; reports statistically significant gains (with effect sizes) and stability under weak supervision. <cite id="32687957-5">Heterogeneous clinical acquisitions test robustness</cite> <cite id="d7f14bb5-1">Repeatability and analytical performance are core acceptance criteria</cite> <cite id="73043793-2">Statistical tests on Dice/Jaccard/sensitivity support robust claims</cite>.

In summary, validating ovarian follicle detection on human ultrasound typically combines public/clinical datasets with expert annotations, quantifies 2D/3D overlap alongside clinical measurement agreement, and stresses observer variability and physics-induced artifacts; major challenges include speckle and boundary ambiguity, differentiating follicles from cysts, harmonizing heterogeneous clinical acquisitions, and generalizing across time and devices, all of which motivate standardized datasets, rater-matched baselines, and combined segmentation–diameter validation with Bland–Altman analyses. <cite id="32687957-0">Standard public databases are enabling stronger, impartial validation</cite> <cite id="32687957-2">USOVA3D exemplifies this trend in 3D ultrasound</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of how costing methods for HIV testing services (HTS) in sub-Saharan Africa are commonly classified, with the key distinctions that define each class.

# 1) By economic evaluation type: what is being optimized

- Cost‑minimization analysis (CMA)
  - Definition and scope: Compares costs of alternatives that produce equivalent health outcomes, minimizing the cost to achieve one unit of health benefit (e.g., cost per person tested). Because benefits are held equal, the net effect on health outcomes is excluded. <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">In general, the primary forms of economic evaluation utilized in health are cost-minimization analysis, cost-effectiveness analysis, cost-utility analysis, and cost-effectiveness analysis with humanistic outcomes</cite>.
  - Application to HTS in SSA: Widely used to estimate incremental costs per person or per positive identified; differences in delivery model or algorithm are evaluated under constant health outcomes to identify the cheaper option for scaling. <cite id="a6db7999-0">The mean estimate for the incremental costs were $18.45 per person tested (median $12.26) and $359.76 for full costs (median $251.55) across studies</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-0">Self-testing had the lowest mean cost per person tested at $12.75 (median $11.50), lower than most primary/first-test settings</cite>.

- Cost‑effectiveness analysis (CEA)
  - Definition and scope: Compares cost against a health outcome that is clinically meaningful but not necessarily in utility form (e.g., cases detected, positives identified). <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">Cost-effectiveness analysis evaluates costs and health outcomes using a meaningful clinical endpoint</cite>.
  - Application to HTS in SSA: Often framed as cost per HIV-positive detected or cost per diagnosis, especially to compare decentralization (e.g., peer-delivered self-testing) versus facility testing when detecting positives efficiently is the target. <cite id="1d1bda5e-1">HIV testing innovations were most cost-effective when implemented through decentralized models such as peer-delivered self-testing</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-4">Incremental cost per HIV-positive detected by delivery modality was lowest for home-based testing ($297.09), followed by primary testing and general population screening scenarios</cite>.

- Cost‑utility analysis (CUA)
  - Definition and scope: Extends CEA to quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) or years of life saved, enabling comparison with broader health portfolios including HIV care and treatment. <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">Cost-utility analysis evaluates costs against quality-adjusted life-years to inform cross-program comparisons</cite> <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">Modeling frameworks for HIV testing typically compare costs with QALYs or infections averted to define cost-effectiveness and cost-utility boundaries</cite>.
  - Application to HTS in SSA: Used increasingly to argue that detection-driven strategies (e.g., self-testing) are cost-effective because they maximize downstream infections averted and link individuals to care, even when primary testing costs are low. <cite id="a6db7999-6">A cost-effectiveness analysis of home-based HIV testing in rural South Africa evaluated costs versus health outcomes to assess whether early detection provided value for resources</cite>.

Key distinction: CMA asks “Which option achieves the same outcome at least as cheaply?”; CEA asks “Which option delivers more health benefit per dollar?”; and CUA asks “Which option maximizes QALYs per dollar and compares to other health programs?” in a common monetary threshold framework. <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">Cost-minimization, cost-effectiveness, and cost-utility analyses progressively integrate more health outcomes, from equivalent outcomes (CMA) to clinical benefit (CEA) and quality-adjusted life-years (CUA)</cite>.

# 2) By delivery model and service package: where cost drivers differ

- Facility-based (primary/first-test) vs. community-based (index/HTS campaign) vs. home-based (HIVST)
  - Distinctions and cost components:
    - Facility testing: Inclusion of on-site turnaround, staff time, reagents/equipment depreciation, building occupancy, and verification algorithms increases unit costs. <cite id="f34c4000-2">Across Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe, mean cost per individual tested in facility settings ranged ~$4.24–$8.79, with per HIV-positive identified lower when throughput is higher</cite>.
    - Community and index testing: Costs emphasize outreach, supervision, community health worker time, linkage support, and logistics; benefits often include male and key-population reach that is lower via facilities. <cite id="f34c4000-5">Meta-analyses show community and facility-based testing strategies differ in outputs and linkage, framing resource allocation choices</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-3">Community index testing reached males proportionally more and was cost-effective compared with facility-based approaches, with larger system-level outputs per dollar</cite>.
    - Home-based self-testing (HBST): Removes time-to-diagnosis and facility visit costs; unit supply and counseling time dominate. <cite id="f34c4000-0">Self-testing mean unit cost per person tested was the lowest in SSA settings (median ~$11–12), often undercutting primary/facility tests</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-9">Within a home-testing program, per-test distribution costs averaged ~$8.97, with testing supplies (38%) and personnel (30%) as primary components</cite>.
    - Pooled/algorithmic verification: Adds retesting/consolidation costs but can reduce missed positives; cost-per-positive is higher than per-person costs due to false-negative risks. <cite id="f34c4000-9">“Test-for-triage” models and pooled-test architectures streamline pathways and can lower misclassification costs in community and facility modalities</cite>.
  - Programmatic trade-offs: Decentralization (self-testing, peer-led index testing) tends to raise coverage and cost-efficiency per positive, whereas highly centralized lab-heavy models emphasize quality but may be less scalable per capita. <cite id="1d1bda5e-1">Decentralized peer-delivered self-testing models are most cost-effective among prevention interventions, consistent with lower per-person costs and better linkage</cite>.

Key distinction: Delivery choice shapes major cost categories (supplies, staff time, space/transport, verification), and the economic question—per person tested, per positive identified, or per QALY saved—determines how these cost drivers are evaluated against benefits. <cite id="f34c4000-0">Different modalities show wide unit cost per person tested with self-testing being lower</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-4">Cost per HIV-positive detected is lowest for home-based testing in several SSA datasets</cite>.

# 3) By cost category: what is counted and how

- Direct medical costs
  - Definition: Provider costs: commodities (test kits, reagents, counseling time), lab consumables, equipment/depreciation, staff salaries for testing rounds, and facility overhead attributable to testing. <cite id="3732682d-0">Full cost (including incremental implementation costs) can reach ~$32–39 per person tested in SSA settings</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-9">In a home-based distribution, the largest unit cost components were testing supplies (38%) and personnel (30%)</cite>.
- Direct non-medical costs
  - Definition: Patient-level out-of-pocket transport, communication, counseling slots not covered by services, and client-facing logistics that are not clinical in nature. <cite id="3732682d-3">Community-based HIV testing literature identifies community-level and household expenditures as distinct from clinical costs</cite> <cite id="3732682d-7">Direct non-medical costs include transport and nutritional supplements; indirect costs capture lost wages from clinic attendance</cite>.
- Opportunity cost of time (client and provider)
  - Definition: Time spent by testers/traders, clinicians, and clients for travel and waiting, valued at local wages/foregone earnings; essential for home-based or self-testing where travel is reduced for clients but provider time is still required for counseling/verification. <cite id="3732682d-0">Full cost includes time costs borne by implementers and recipients alongside cash expenditures to reflect the true cost of scaling new HTS interventions</cite> <cite id="a6db7999-0">Systematic review unit costs incorporate time and overhead to reflect implementation costs, not just kit expenses</cite>.
- Indirect and productivity-based costs (broader economic impact)
  - Definition: Time lost to work/education due to testing or follow‑up; production losses or household-level opportunity costs; sometimes modeled as QALYs when HIV care delays occur. These broaden “effectiveness” beyond lives saved to societal productivity. <cite id="3732682d-4">Integrating HIV and NCD service delivery is motivated by reducing long-term productivity losses that accrue during care delays</cite> <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">Analyses comparing monitoring strategies account for QALYs and infections averted, integrating downstream economic and health effects</cite>.
- Full vs incremental cost
  - Full cost: Includes start-up and delivery costs to introduce a new intervention at scale. <cite id="3732682d-0">Mean full cost across studies was $38.65 per person tested (median $32.83), higher than incremental costs because it accounts for program expansion overheads</cite>.
  - Incremental cost: Change in cost relative to a baseline test condition; commonly reported as cost per person tested or per positive detected. <cite id="a6db7999-0">Incremental cost per person tested was lower than full cost ($18.45 vs $38.65), highlighting fixed versus variable burdens</cite>.

Key distinction: Rigorous HTS costing in SSA differentiates medical versus non-medical and time-based opportunity costs, and distinguishes incremental unit costs from full program rollout costs to reflect both service delivery efficiency and scale-up feasibility. <cite id="f34c4000-9">A home-based program’s per-distributed cost was dominated by supplies and personnel, exemplifying direct medical time/expenditure components</cite> <cite id="3732682d-0">Full costs reflect capacity-building and system changes, not just unit test kit prices</cite>.

# 4) By epidemiological objective: detection and care-linkage versus suppression

- Detect-and-treat/monitoring strategies
  - Definition and costing: Emphasizes case detection, confirmation/intensification of algorithms, and linkage to care; benefits quantified as positives identified, infections averted, or QALYs. <cite id="1d1bda5e-3">HIV monitoring strategy comparisons explicitly trade off costs against positives detected, confirmatory testing needs, and retesting intervals</cite>.
  - SSA evidence: Decentralized home- and community-based options show favorable cost-effectiveness per positive and per QALY due to greater access and faster linkage. <cite id="a6db7999-6">Home-based testing in rural South Africa demonstrated cost-effectiveness by improving detection and follow-up</cite>.
- Population suppression/behavior change and prevention portfolio comparisons
  - Definition and costing: Positions testing within a broader HIV prevention portfolio (condoms, treatment as prevention), evaluating costs per infection averted in steady-state epidemiology; often uses utility/QALY frameworks. <cite id="1d1bda5e-0">Economic evaluations synthesize that testing innovations can be highly cost-effective when embedded in prevention strategies</cite>.
  - SSA evidence: Reviews emphasize that delivery model and implementation quality (peer-led, self-testing) materially affect cost per infection averted compared to facility-only models. <cite id="1d1bda5e-1">Self-testing via peer delivery had the most favorable cost-effectiveness among decentralized prevention and testing interventions</cite>.

Key distinction: In detection-led costing, the numerator is cases/positives/QALYs saved in the period; in suppression-led costing, the numerator expands to generations averted and life-years discounted to steady-state, making comparisons with other prevention programs valid. <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">Models in limited-resource settings incorporate QALYs and secondary infections averted to place testing in a broader prevention cost-utility context</cite>.

# 5) By programmatic budgeting category: where money goes in HTS plans

- Demand creation and linkage: Community engagement, outreach, health worker time to trace positives within households, and follow-up. <cite id="3732682d-2">Community- and facility-based testing cost structures differ by labor and outreach intensity, driving per-person cost differentials</cite>.
- Commodities and diagnostics: Test kits, reagents, confirmatory algorithms, consumables for pooling/verification, and supply chain logistics. <cite id="f34c4000-9">Testing supplies account for a large share of home-based HIVST unit costs</cite>.
- Human resources and training: Facility staff time, community health worker visit costs, trainer time, and performance-based supervision. <cite id="3732682d-8">Integration reviews document staff time and training as dominant recurrent costs in HIV services</cite>.
- Health system capacity: Building occupancy, utilities, lab equipment, transport and retesting cycles—salaries and overhead attributable to each testing step. <cite id="f34c4000-2">Facility mean per-person testing costs reflect local staffing and infrastructure overheads</cite>.
- Health information/management: TBIMS or DHIS2 integration for tracing positives, FP management, and monitoring. <cite id="3732682d-9">Optimizing testing service architectures often streamlines information flows to reduce preventable misclassifications per 10,000 tested</cite>.
- Prevention linkage services: PrEP/ART initiation and referrals—embedded costs when testing is paired with linkage protocols. <cite id="3732682d-4">Integration of HIV prevention and treatment reduces administrative and service fragmentation and can lower combined unit costs</cite>.

Key distinction: National costed implementation plans (derived from WHO/UNAIDS guidance) allocate budget across these categories and then derive unit cost and unit effectiveness assumptions that feed into cost-effectiveness thresholds. <cite id="3732682d-2">UNAIDS guidance emphasizes that NSP costing is foundational and integrates health system, commodity, workforce, and programmatic components before evaluating scale-up feasibility</cite>.

# 6) By unit of effectiveness: person tested, person linked, life-year saved

- Per person tested
  - Most basic HTS unit; useful to compare efficiency of introducing a new method across channels. <cite id="a6db7999-0">Incremental cost per person tested across SSA shows self-testing and first-test modalities differentiating by several dollars</cite>.
- Per person linked to care/confirmed positive
  - Emphasizes identification quality; higher value when follow-up services are costly. <cite id="f34c4000-4">Per-positive costs are typically higher but may be offset by broader prevention benefits</cite>.
- Per QALY or year of life saved
  - Places testing in the broader health system portfolio, comparing to maternal-child, malaria, NCD, and injury interventions common in SSA. <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">Cost-utility analysis uses QALYs to enable cross-program comparison</cite> <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">HIV testing strategy comparisons quantify QALYs and infections averted to inform portfolio allocation</cite>.

Key distinction: Policy decisions at country level often begin with per-person and per-positive thresholds, then integrate cost-utility into NSP prioritization matrices that juxtapose testing with other services using common currency (USD/QALY), aligned with WHO principles. <cite id="3732682d-2">National strategic plan costing is not merely technical; it underpins resource allocation decisions across the health portfolio</cite>.

# 7) Putting it together: classification frameworks used in SSA practice

- Methodological taxonomy (WHO-aligned)
  - CMA/CEA/CUA choices determine how much health benefit is in the numerator and how costs are accumulated. <cite id="1d1bda5e-8">The primary evaluation methods—CMA, CEA, and CUA—escalate in their use of effectiveness outcomes from equivalent endpoints to QALYs</cite>.
- Service delivery taxonomy (WHO/UNAIDS service delivery platforms)
  - Facility, community, and home-based with self-testing; pooled testing and serial rapid tests; algorithmic verification and “test-for-triage.” Each has distinct time/cost profiles and linkage pathways that change unit costs and effectiveness. <cite id="f34c4000-0">Self-testing’s low unit cost per person tested makes it valuable for mass coverage</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-9">Test-for-triage and pooled architectures can simultaneously streamline community/facility pathways and improve classification accuracy</cite>.
- Cost components taxonomy (global costing best practice; adapted to HTS)
  - Direct medical, direct non-medical, opportunity cost of time, and indirect productivity costs; reported as full vs incremental; and triangulated with program costed plans to evaluate scale-up. <cite id="3732682d-0">Full costs capture system and program changes; incremental costs show unit delivery efficiencies</cite> <cite id="3732682d-7">Direct non-medical costs include transport and supplements; indirect costs capture lost wages</cite>.
- Epidemiological objective taxonomy
  - Detection-and-linkage led vs prevention/suppression led; economic evaluation metrics shift from positives per dollar to infections and QALYs averted per dollar. <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">Comparisons across HIV monitoring strategies emphasize QALYs and infections averted</cite>.

Summary: In SSA, HTS costing methods are jointly classified by the evaluation goal (CMA/CEA/CUA), the delivery channel and testing package (facility, community/index, home-based self-testing, and pooled/triage), the cost components included (direct medical/non-medical and time-based opportunity and indirect costs), the program budget system used to mobilize funds, and the epidemiological objective (detection and linkage versus suppression). These distinctions determine whether the unit cost is measured per person tested or per QALY saved, and whether decentralized home-based strategies outperform facility-centric ones in cost per positive identified and/or cost per QALY. <cite id="a6db7999-0">A broad body of SSA studies shows per-person-testing costs vary widely but are usually well below $30 when measured at full scale</cite> <cite id="f34c4000-0">Self-testing’s notably low per-person cost makes it attractive for scale</cite> <cite id="1d1bda5e-1">Decentralized peer-led self-testing models tend to be most cost-effective</cite> <cite id="1d1bda5e-5">Cost-utility frameworks align testing with prevention by modeling QALYs and infections averted</cite> <cite id="3732682d-2">WHO/UNAIDS emphasize integrating costed plans into national strategy for equitable and efficient scale-up</cite>.

Overview

During SARS‑CoV‑2 infection, indoleamine‑2,3‑dioxygenase (IDO) enzymes—primarily IDO1 and, to a greater degree, IDO2 in severe/fatal disease—are upregulated in lung and systemic compartments, catalyzing the rate‑limiting step of tryptophan (Trp) degradation into the kynurenine pathway (KP). This diverts Trp away from protein/synthesis and serotonin/NAD+ precursors and into metabolites with immunomodulatory and tissue‑toxic properties, contributing to inflammation, organ dysfunction, and symptom persistence in COVID‑19. <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">IDO1 prevails in early/mild pneumonia and in lung tissues from patients with long COVID‑19, whereas IDO2 is predominant in severe/fatal cases</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">SARS‑CoV‑2 infection induces IDO2 expression, and the downstream kynurenine breakdown products drive pathology depending on the metabolite profile</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-1">Multiple studies have shown virus‑induced activation of the KP mediated mainly by IDO1 induction in most affected tissues</cite>.

Mechanisms of IDO induction during COVID‑19

- Viral sensing and interferon/TLR signaling:
  - Viral RNA/protein components activate innate sensors, including TLR2 and cytosolic RNA helicases, triggering NF‑κB/IRF programs that elevate proinflammatory mediators and interferons during COVID‑19. <cite id="b5ce77a9-0">Recognition of the SARS‑CoV‑2 spike protein by TLR2 induces inflammatory mediators</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-1">The S protein acts as a viral PAMP that induces cytokines/chemokines via TLR2‑dependent activation</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-4">TLR3 and TLR7 are involved in innate control during lung SARS‑CoV‑2 infection</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-6">SARS‑CoV‑2 ORF9b antagonizes type I/III interferons by targeting RIG‑I/MDA5‑MAVS and TLR3‑TRIF pathways</cite>. These converge on NF‑κB and IRF3/IRF7 activation that are central to SARS‑CoV‑2 inflammatory and interferon responses. <cite id="b5ce77a9-9">The spike induces NF‑κB signaling through a TLR2/MyD88 dependent mechanism</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-7">SARS‑CoV‑2 evades IFN responses; TLR and RIG‑I/MAVS signaling engage NF‑κB and IRF3 for interferon transcription</cite>.
  - Innate cytokines and interferons upregulate KP enzymes: TNF‑α/IL‑6/IFN‑γ/TNF‑α families activate IDO1, while IFN‑γ and related transcriptional programs favor IDO2 expression in certain myeloid and endothelial lineages. <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">Severe/fatal cases show dominant IDO2 expression induced by infection</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-2">Cytokines are known to activate IDO‑1 (IDO1), catalyzing Trp catabolism via the KP</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-5">Loss of Trp bioavailability induces autophagy, linking KP activation to cellular stress responses</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-5">Type‑II IFN inhibits SARS‑CoV‑2 in human lung epithelial and ex vivo lung tissues through IDO‑mediated pathways</cite>.
  - Type II interferon can act directly through IDO in lung epithelium and ex vivo lung tissue, providing a feed‑forward link from antiviral IFN programs to KP activation during infection. <cite id="b5ce77a9-5">Type‑II IFN inhibits SARS‑CoV‑2 in human lung epithelial cells and ex vivo lung tissues through IDO‑mediated pathways</cite>.
  - Hypoxia/ischemic stress and autophagy: Infection activates hypoxia‑inducible factor HIF‑1 and increases autophagy; HIF‑1 and Trp depletion can induce IDO1 and drive a cytokine storm that self‑perpetuates. <cite id="56d1861f-3">SARS‑CoV‑2 induces HIF‑1 activation in infected cells</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-6">Persistent CoV infection activates IDO1 by massive cytokine release, which in turn perpetuates the cytokine storm</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-5">Limited Trp availability triggers autophagy, consistent with KP‑linked stress adaptation</cite>.
- Endothelial and tissue‑specific dominance:
  - In humans, IDO isoforms are differentially distributed across disease phenotypes: IDO1 predominates in early/mild pneumonia and in long COVID lung; IDO2 predominates in severe/fatal disease, indicating isoform‑specific endothelial and vascular involvement. <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">IDO1 prevails in early/mild pneumonia and long COVID lung, whereas IDO2 predominates in severe/fatal cases</cite>.
  - Endothelial cells show altered IDO balance in severe disease, aligning with vascular leak and coagulopathy features of “cytokine storm.” <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">Unbalanced IDO1/IDO2 endothelial expression is reported with skewed tryptophan catabolism in severe/fatal cases</cite>.

Cell types and tissues implicated

- Lung epithelium and endothelium: Type II IFN‑mediated IDO activity is demonstrated in human lung epithelial cells and ex vivo lung tissue, consistent with airway and alveolar infection. <cite id="b5ce77a9-5">IDO‑mediated antiviral IFN pathway activity is observed in lung epithelial cells and ex vivo lung tissues</cite>.
- Macrophages/monocytes and other myeloid cells: Viral and cytokine cues converge on myeloid IDO programs; in several viral infections, interferon‑stimulated KP activation and IDO expression are observed in monocyte‑derived macrophages. <cite id="d6cc80b5-3">Epstein–Barr virus induces IDO expression in human monocyte‑derived macrophages via p38/ERK and p53 signaling</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-8">IFN‑stimulated activation of KP and IDO is a common feature of respiratory viral infections</cite>.
- Systemic/immune milieu: Systemic cytokine release during COVID‑19 (e.g., TNF, IL‑6, IFN‑γ) is sufficient to activate IDO1 and shift flux into KP in immune cells and tissues. <cite id="56d1861f-2">Cytokines activate IDO‑1 in multiple tissues</cite>.

Role of IDO in tryptophan catabolism during COVID‑19

- Gatekeeper of the kynurenine pathway: IDO1 (and to a lesser extent IFN‑inducible IDO2) catalyzes the initial oxidative cleavage of Trp to N‑formylkynurenine, yielding kynurenine (Kyn) and depleting Trp, thereby shifting systemic and tissue‑resident tryptophan pools from serotonin and NAD+ biosynthesis into KP metabolites. <cite id="d6cc80b5-1">Virus‑induced KP activation is mainly mediated by IDO1 in affected tissues</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-2">IDO‑1 catalyzes the first step of Trp catabolism through the KP under cytokine activation</cite>.
- Flux redistribution and metabolite‑mediated immunomodulation:
  - Trp depletion and Kyn elevation suppress T‑cell proliferation and TCA-linked effector functions, creating an “immunoprivileged” KP niche and promoting Treg expansion, while certain metabolites such as 3‑hydroxykynurenine and quinolinic acid can promote inflammation and oxidative stress. <cite id="56d1861f-2">Cytokines drive IDO1‑mediated KP activation producing Kyn</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">The specific kynurenine breakdown products generated determine pathology in IDO2‑linked SARS‑CoV‑2 disease phenotypes</cite>.
  - Systemic and tissue‑specific KP activation correlates with disease severity: KP metabolites accumulate during infection and persist in post‑acute sequelae (PASC), linking IDO activity to muscle wasting, neuroinflammation, and fatigue. <cite id="56d1861f-1">COVID‑19 infection alters metabolic profiles including kynurenine and fatty acids in serum, identifying KP as disease‑associated</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-5">SARS‑CoV‑2 infection is facilitated by KP degradation of Trp by IDO, with skeletal muscle pathology linked to KP activation</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-8">Immune mediators and reactive oxygen/nitrogen species induce IDO activity in PASC, with tissue‑specific effects</cite>.
- Tissue consequences:
  - Lung: KP activation with Kyn/3‑HK/quinolinic acid elevates oxidative and neurotoxic stress in airway and alveolar compartments, potentially contributing to inflammation, vascular leak, and impaired repair; IDO1 predominance in early disease and in long COVID lung links KP persistence to chronic remodeling. <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">IDO1 predominance in early/mild pneumonia and in long COVID lung</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-1">IDO1‑mediated KP activation occurs in lung and other affected tissues during viral disease</cite>.
  - Brain: Kyn and its metabolites in CSF/brain cross cortical pathways, where immunomodulatory and pro‑oxidative effects can promote neuropathogenesis in COVID‑19. <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">Prolonged IDO2 activity in post‑acute sequelae yields kynurenine breakdown products associated with pathology</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-3">Macrophage KP activation and downstream metabolites are mechanistically established in viral infections</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-6">Endothelial IDO dysregulation associates with skewed KP and tissue injury</cite>.
  - Muscle: IDO2‑linked Trp catabolism contributes to catabolic cachexia and myopathy observed in severe COVID‑19. <cite id="56d1861f-5">Kynurenine pathway activity links tryptophan depletion to autophagy and severe disease phenotypes</cite>.

How these processes interlock during COVID‑19

Viral entry and replication provoke innate sensing (TLR2/TLR3/TLR7; RIG‑I/MDA5–MAVS; cGAS‑STING), activating NF‑κB and IRF programs, IFN‑β/IFN‑γ, and cytokine storms. These converge on KP enzymes: cytokines directly activate IDO1; interferons, especially type II, engage IDO‑mediated antiviral and KP‑shunting programs in epithelium; endothelial and myeloid cells upregulate IDO isoforms with disease severity, creating an autocrine/paracrine loop. Hypoxia and autophagy further reinforce KP flux. The net result is Trp depletion and local Kyn dominance that suppresses antiviral T‑cell responses while promoting pro‑inflammatory metabolites and oxidative stress, driving inflammation, vascular dysfunction, impaired regeneration, and persistent post‑acute dysmetabolism, with IDO1 predominance in early/longitudinal lung and IDO2 dominance in severe/fatal phenotypes. <cite id="b5ce77a9-6">SARS‑CoV‑2 antagonizes interferons by targeting RIG‑I/MDA5‑MAVS and TLR3‑TRIF</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-7">Type I/III interferons and their regulators (IRF3, NF‑κB) are central to SARS‑CoV‑2 pathogenesis</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-5">Type‑II IFN inhibits virus but acts through IDO‑mediated pathways in lung tissues</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">Differential endothelial IDO1/IDO2 balance tracks disease severity and PASC</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-3">HIF‑1 activation during infection provides a hypoxia‑driven inducer context for IDO</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-5">Trp depletion promotes autophagy and KP shunting in severe disease</cite>.

Clinical and translational implications

- Biomarkers and phenotypes: IDO1/IDO2 expression and KP metabolite profiles help stratify disease severity and identify long COVID with lung involvement, linking endothelial dysfunction and tryptophan dysregulation to symptoms. <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">IDO isoform predominance tracks severity and long COVID lung pathology</cite>.
- Mechanistic mediators of tissue injury: Specific KP metabolites (e.g., 3‑HK, quinolinic acid) produced downstream of IDO determine organ tropic pathology; blocking IDO or modulating metabolite flux is a therapeutic concept to mitigate cytokine storm and organ dysfunction. <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">Severe cases reflect IDO2‑linked generation of pathogenic kynurenine breakdown products</cite>.
- Nutritional/immune context: Given KP competition with serotonin/NAD+ precursors, supplementation strategies and tryptophan handling may alter immune and neurologic outcomes, but clinical data are emerging. <cite id="56d1861f-5">IDO2/KP activity is implicated in severe COVID‑19 pathogenesis with autophagy involvement</cite>.

Key takeaways

- COVID‑19 induces KP catabolism primarily by upregulating IDO enzymes (IDO1 in early and long‑COVID lung; IDO2 in severe/fatal disease) through innate immune sensing, cytokine storms, interferon programs, hypoxia, and autophagy, which collectively activate and maintain IDO expression in lung epithelium and myeloid/endothelial compartments. <cite id="d6cc80b5-0">IDO1 vs IDO2 predominance aligns with disease stage/phenotype and endothelial involvement</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-1">IDO1 is a primary inducible driver of KP activation in virus‑affected tissues</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-2">Cytokines and interferon systems converge on KP activation via IDO</cite> <cite id="b5ce77a9-5">IFN‑γ/IFN‑II pathways can act through IDO in lung infection</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-3">HIF‑1 activation during infection provides an inducer context</cite>.
- Functionally, IDO catalyzes Trp–Kyn分流 (“shunting”), depleting Trp and generating immunomodulatory and pro‑inflammatory kynurenine metabolites that suppress antiviral T‑cell responses while promoting oxidative/inflammatory stress, thereby contributing to acute inflammation, organ dysfunction, and post‑acute metabolic dysregulation observed in COVID‑19. <cite id="56d1861f-2">IDO converts Trp into Kyn under cytokine activation</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-2">Specific downstream metabolite patterns correlate with pathology in IDO‑linked SARS‑CoV‑2 infection</cite> <cite id="d6cc80b5-5">KP activation by IDO contributes to infection‑facilitated pathology in skeletal muscle</cite> <cite id="56d1861f-6">IDO1 activation during persistent infection can perpetuate cytokine storm dynamics</cite>.

Summary
HMGB1 Box A (the A-box within the HMGB1 two-box “TAD” domain) both amplifies proinflammatory signaling and cytokine production downstream of innate pattern-recognition and acts as a dominant inhibitory antagonist when delivered as a recombinant peptide or scaffold, supporting its conceptual and preclinical therapeutic potential in a range of inflammatory diseases. <cite id="92ea0b42-5">Extracellular HMGB1 activates NF-κB and augments release of proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β</cite> <cite id="92ea0b42-3">HMGB1 binding to RAGE is widely reported to directly activate NF-κB and trigger cytokine formation</cite> <cite id="92ea0b42-2">HMGB1 also signals through TLR5 to activate NF-κB in a MyD88-dependent manner</cite>. <cite id="c79c8bab-1">Recombinant HMGB1 Box A protein and anti-HMGB1 antibodies have demonstrated beneficial effects across diverse preclinical inflammation models</cite>.

Mechanistic role of HMGB1 and Box A in cytokine amplification
- Extracellular HMGB1 functions as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) that potentiates innate immune signaling by engaging receptors such as RAGE, TLR2, TLR4, and TLR5, culminating in NF-κB activation and cytokine induction. <cite id="92ea0b42-5">Secreted HMGB1 augments TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β release via NF-κB activation</cite> <cite id="92ea0b42-8">HMGB1–RAGE interactions trigger NF-κB and downstream inflammatory factors</cite> <cite id="92ea0b42-2">HMGB1–TLR5 engagement activates NF-κB signaling with cytokine production</cite> <cite id="05619fb3-9">Extracellular HMGB1 acts as a DAMP to trigger inflammatory responses by binding immune receptors</cite>. 
- HMGB1’s Box A/TAD (HMG-box A) contributes to transcriptional modulation and cytokine induction by altering chromatin architecture and facilitating access of NF-κB and other transcription factors to cytokine loci as a nuclear chromatin factor, and it participates in cytokine presentation/processing once secreted. <cite id="92ea0b42-0">HMGB1 critically regulates inflammatory processes spanning cell survival and immune response</cite> <cite id="05619fb3-0">As a chromatin-associated protein, HMGB1 regulates vital cellular processes, including transcription</cite> <cite id="05619fb3-7">HMGB1’s proinflammatory effects are amplified via transcription factor cascades such as NF-κB</cite>. 
- Multiple lines of evidence indicate that Box A is a principal proinflammatory effector within HMGB1: sequence-function and structural analyses identify critical residues in the N-terminal HMG box (including the A-box) that mediate receptor recognition and signaling. <cite id="c79c8bab-3">A conserved cysteine in the N-terminal HMG box is required for HMGB1 binding to TLR4 and cytokine stimulation</cite>. 
- Functionally, Box A sequences can potentiate cytokine bioactivity by driving chromatin remodeling (DNA bending) that favors proinflammatory gene transcription and by facilitating HMGB1’s presentation and uptake by immune cells. <cite id="05619fb3-9">An engineered HMGB1 construct carrying tandem HMG B domains promotes tissue repair like wild-type functional HMGB1 but fails to signal through receptors, separating chromatin-remodeling and cytokine-stimulatory functions from repair programs</cite>. 

Antagonistic function of Box A-derived agents and therapeutic rationale
- Importantly, when delivered as an exogenous “dominant-negative” agent, recombinant Box A peptides or A-box–containing scaffolds can antagonize HMGB1 receptor signaling, suppress NF-κB activation, and reduce proinflammatory cytokine production without requiring cell entry, providing a tractable therapeutic strategy. <cite id="c79c8bab-2">Inhibition of HMGB1/RAGE-mediated endocytosis by an HMGB1 antagonist Box A, anti-HMGB1 antibodies, and related agents suppresses inflammation</cite>. 
- Reviews synthesizing preclinical models consistently report benefit from anti-HMGB1 strategies and from recombinant Box A-based antagonists. <cite id="c79c8bab-1">Anti-HMGB1 antibodies and recombinant HMGB1 Box A protein have shown beneficial effects across preclinical inflammatory disease models</cite> <cite id="c79c8bab-9">Exogenous HMGB1 acting via RAGE/TLR can elicit injurious inflammatory responses, establishing a therapeutic target</cite>. 
- The A-box also bears immunogenic epitopes that, when immunogenic, can redirect immunity and impact disease severity: <cite id="c79c8bab-4">an immunogenic peptide within the HMGB1 A-box reversed sepsis lethality and immune tolerance in mice</cite>. 

Preclinical evidence across disease models
- Sepsis/organ failure: As a late “second hit” mediator, extracellular HMGB1 worsens inflammation; sequestration with antibodies or neutralization opens a therapeutic window in cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) and LPS models, reducing TNF/IL-6/IL-1β and improving survival. <cite id="c79c8bab-0">Extracellular HMGB1 acts as a late mediator of experimental sepsis, supporting a wider therapeutic window</cite> <cite id="c79c8bab-9">Blocking HMGB1’s receptor-mediated signaling curbs proinflammatory cytokine release and injurious inflammation</cite>. 
- Inflammatory disorders of the airway and gut: Localized HMGB1 signaling amplifies eosinophilic and cytokine-driven pathology; anti-HMGB1 strategies attenuate inflammation. <cite id="92ea0b42-6">HMGB1 emerges as central to amplifying/modulating inflammation in nasal disorders, regulating cytokine networks through receptor interactions</cite> <cite id="c79c8bab-2">Anti-HMGB1 antibodies and an A-box antagonist suppress inflammation driven by HMGB1/RAGE signaling</cite>. 
- Neuroinflammation and ischemia: By engaging RAGE/TLR, HMGB1 exacerbates glial activation and cytokine release; blocking the HMGB1–RAGE/TLR axis protects neural tissue. <cite id="92ea0b42-8">HMGB1–RAGE binding activates NF-κB and downstream inflammatory factors in multiple contexts</cite>. 
- Engineered A-box constructs and hybrid HMGB1 proteins have refined therapy by separating proinflammatory signaling from tissue-repair functions. <cite id="05619fb3-9">An engineered HMGB1 construct with tandem HMG B boxes repairs tissues as effectively as wild-type full-length HMGB1 but fails to signal through RAGE/TLR, indicating dissection of signaling from reparative roles</cite>. 
- Cancer-related inflammation during therapy: Modulating HMGB1 signaling can reshape macrophage polarization and reduce chemotherapy/radiation-induced inflammatory cascades. <cite id="05619fb3-8">Release of HMGB1 by dying tumor cells licenses dendritic cells; inhibiting HMGB1–TLR4 signaling can dictate outcomes of immune stimulation and inflammation</cite> <cite id="05619fb3-4">HMGB1 in exosomes can induce M2 macrophage polarization by inhibiting NF-κB signaling</cite>. 

Clinical/ translational signals
- Mechanistic biomarkers: Extracellular HMGB1, NF-κB activation, and proinflammatory cytokine storms correlate across human illnesses, motivating targeted therapies. <cite id="05619fb3-7">Transcriptional amplification by NF-κB downstream of HMGB1 contributes to pathophysiology in diverse conditions</cite>. 
- Therapeutic agents under investigation: 
  - Neutralizing anti-HMGB1 antibodies and intravenous immunoglobulin therapies against HMGB1 have shown benefit signals in preclinical sepsis and are being advanced clinically. <cite id="c79c8bab-0">Reviews document a therapeutic window for anti-HMGB1 strategies in experimental sepsis</cite> <cite id="c79c8bab-5">HMGB1 and a cyclic peptide antagonist (pCTS-L) have experimental support as targets to improve survival in sepsis</cite>. 
  - Recombinant A-box–based antagonists and immunogenic Box A peptides have demonstrated reversal of lethality and modulation of tolerance in murine sepsis, supporting translational potential. <cite id="c79c8bab-4">An A-box immunogenic peptide reversed sepsis lethality and induced protective immunity</cite> <cite id="c79c8bab-1">Recombinant Box A protein shows beneficial preclinical activity across inflammatory models</cite>. 
  - Small-molecule inhibitors that interfere with the HMGB1–RAGE/TLR interface, including FR90059 derivatives, have preclinical efficacy; mechanistic understanding via A-box–dependent receptor binding strengthens design. <cite id="c79c8bab-9">Targeted inhibition of HMGB1’s receptor signaling suppresses injurious cytokine responses, validating pharmacologic modulation</cite>. 

Key evidence that Box A modulates proinflammatory cytokines
- Direct genetic/biochemical evidence places critical A-box residues in HMGB1’s cytokine-stimulating function: <cite id="c79c8bab-3">the A-box contains a cysteine critical for TLR4 binding and downstream cytokine induction</cite>. 
- Functional antagonism by A-box–derived agents: <cite id="c79c8bab-2">an “HMGB1 antagonist Box A” blocks HMGB1/RAGE signaling and downstream inflammatory cascades</cite>, indicating that the A-box constitutes a tractable determinant of receptor engagement and cytokine production. 
- Chromatin-remodeling function of Box A enables NF-κB access to inflammatory gene promoters; disrupting this function (e.g., via A-box–targeted antagonism or by using repair-focused, A-box–mutated constructs) diminishes cytokine-inducing signaling while preserving healing programs. <cite id="05619fb3-9">A tandem HMG B-box construct with reduced receptor signaling repairs tissues comparably to wild type, separating cytokine signaling from repair</cite>. 

Safety, practicality, and open questions
- The same Box A sequences that drive inflammation are immunodominant and can be harnessed as vaccines to generate protective immunity in sepsis, suggesting a dual “danger” and “benefit” role dependent on context and delivery. <cite id="c79c8bab-4">A Box A immunogenic peptide reversed sepsis lethality and disrupted immune tolerance</cite>. 
- Box A-based therapies are attractive because they avoid nuclear DNA interactions and can act extracellularly; however, complete clinical efficacy data remain limited, and heterogeneity in HMGB1 biology across tissues and disease stages requires careful targeting. <cite id="05619fb3-0">HMGB1’s nuclear chromatin functions are fundamental, so domain-focused therapy can modulate but may not abolish all biological effects</cite>. 
- Areas to resolve include defining Box A residues that are essential for RAGE vs TLR discrimination, optimizing Box A-derived dominant-negative peptides for potency/safety and delivery (e.g., intranasal, intra-brachial), and conducting large randomized human trials of neutralizing antibodies or small-molecule antagonists in sepsis/ARDS and cytokine-driven syndromes. <cite id="c79c8bab-0">Therapeutic targeting of extracellular HMGB1 has a mechanistic foundation and evidence base in preclinical sepsis, motivating clinical translation</cite>. 

Practical takeaways
- Mechanism: <cite id="92ea0b42-5">Extracellular HMGB1 increases TNF-α/IL-6/IL-1β through NF-κB</cite>, with <cite id="c79c8bab-3">A-box cysteine essential for TLR4 binding</cite> and <cite id="92ea0b42-8">RAGE-driven NF-κB activation</cite>. <cite id="c79c8bab-6">HMGB1 modulates cytokine networks via multiple receptor interactions in inflammatory tissue</cite>. 
- Therapeutic potential: <cite id="05619fb3-9">Disrupting A-box–mediated receptor signaling preserves repair while reducing cytokine storm</cite>, <cite id="c79c8bab-1">recombinant Box A antagonists and anti-HMGB1 antibodies show broad preclinical efficacy</cite>, and <cite id="c79c8bab-4">immunogenic Box A peptides can rescue lethality and reset immune tolerance</cite>. Box A-centric strategies therefore have a mechanistic basis and converging preclinical evidence supporting anti-inflammatory therapy with context-dependent opportunities. <cite id="c79c8bab-5">Targeting HMGB1 and Box A antagonists shows promise to improve sepsis survival</cite>.

Summary
Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) in bovine Staphylococcus aureus—especially plasmids, prophages/SaPIs, SCCmec, and transposons/integrons—are central to their rapid genetic diversification and bovine host–specific adaptations, including milk/teat niche fitness and restricted spillover into humans. <cite id="107d0721-0">MGEs are a primary vehicle for horizontal transfer of DNA among and within S. aureus, repeatedly mediating adaptation</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-5">Host shifts and ecological specialization in S. aureus are repeatedly driven by acquisition of MGEs</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-9">The accessory genome of bovine S. aureus is particularly rich in MGEs integrated as genomic islands, plasmids, transposons, phages, and integrons, and this diversity underpins variable resistance phenotypes and transmission potential</cite>.

How MGEs Increase Genetic Diversity in Bovine S. aureus
• Accessory genome expansion via MGEs. <cite id="107d0721-9">Whole-genome surveys of bovine and bovine-adjacent isolates show that the accessory genome is enriched with plasmids, bacteriophages, transposable elements/ISs, SCCmec, and integrons, directly increasing per-strain gene content beyond the core genome</cite>. <cite id="df509f99-9">Comparative analyses of bovine mastitis isolates explicitly identify dynamic accessory segments with high MGE load, contrasting with relatively stable core regions</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-3">The largest mobilome datasets from wild ruminants demonstrate “rich” MGE spectra (genomic islands, conjugative modules, prophages), reinforcing that bovine-adapted ecotypes harbor diverse movable gene pools</cite>.
• Virulence and AMR gene capture and reshuffling. <cite id="107d0721-1">Comparative genomics of bovine intramammary S. aureus against human clinical strains shows lineage- and mobilome-associated differences in virulence and resistance gene carriage</cite>. <cite id="df730a3d-8">Across bovine isolates, staphylococcal superantigen genes are frequently carried on MGEs such as prophages, transposons, plasmids, and pathogenicity islands</cite>. <cite id="dfa2083e-1">Genome-wide comparisons of bovine isolates report a highly dynamic accessory genome with prophages, SaPIs, plasmids, and resistance cassettes driving diversity</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-7">Prophages and transposons are recurrent carriers of virulence determinants (e.g., staphylococcal enterotoxins, toxic shock syndrome toxin) and antibiotic-resistance genes, enabling rapid diversification of phenotype</cite>.
• Plasmid- and phage-mediated resistance modules. <cite id="107d0721-4">Interplay between SCCmec, plasmids, and phages drives movement of resistance; bacteriophages efficiently package and transfer SCCmec-like modules alongside virulence/AMR cargo</cite>. <cite id="dfa2083e-1">Bovine isolates frequently encode tetracycline resistance (TetM/Erm) via plasmid-borne cassettes and conjugative backbones within the MGE-rich accessory genome</cite>. <cite id="324b9cc5-0">In bovine strains, prophages and lineage background (e.g., ST5404) collaborate to cluster and disseminate resistance determinants, providing a mechanistic basis for observed antibiotic-resistance clades</cite>. <cite id="324b9cc5-5">Phage packaging of virulence and antibiotic resistance genes from multiple genomic locations further expands the diversity of selectable combinations that arise in bovine reservoirs</cite>.

Linking Mobilome Content to Bovine Host Adaptation and Specificity
• Niche-associated virulence on bovine mammary epithelium. <cite id="7e2f31c1-6">Comparative genome-scale modeling and bovine mastitis isolate datasets map strain-specific metabolic and virulence capabilities linked to pathogenicity in dairy cows</cite>. <cite id="7e2f31c1-9">Bovine-associated lineages exhibit enrichment of MSCRAMMs (e.g., Clumping factor A/B, FnBPA variants) and exoproteins such as Hld, aligning with teat/orifice colonization in dairy cows and distinguishing them from human clinical profiles</cite>. <cite id="7e2f31c1-1">Phylogenomic comparisons of bovine IMI vs. human clinical S. aureus reveal lineage- and mobilotype-specific virulence patterns; bovine IMI isolates harbor prophage/plasmid-borne modules (e.g., clumping factor, fibronectin-binding repertoires) associated with bovine mastitis, while human-associated strains carry distinct combinations linked to human tissue tropism</cite>. <cite id="df730a3d-7">Bovine mastitis S. aureus often show exclusive virulence-associated signatures compared to other bovine S. aureus, including carriage of coagulase, hld, and other virulence clusters, supporting a bovine niche specialization</cite>.
• SCCmec types and bovine-associated lineages. <cite id="107d0721-6">S. aureus packages SCCmec along with various MGEs; SCCmec moves frequently via phage-mediated transfer among livestock-associated clones</cite>. <cite id="324b9cc5-2">Methicillin-resistant bovine-mastitis S. aureus ST398 has been characterized, linking this livestock clade to specific SCCmec backgrounds and bovine reservoirs</cite>. <cite id="324b9cc5-0">Phage-assisted SCCmec transfer within bovine-associated ST5404 clusters has been directly observed, connecting resistance acquisition to bovine-adapted genotypes</cite>. <cite id="7e2f31c1-7,7e2f31c1-8">Across “comparative genomics of bovine and human isolates,” studies consistently report bovine-mastitis strains enriched for SCCmec types typical of livestock clones (mecC/IV in several datasets) alongside plasmid-borne resistance determinants, whereas human isolates often reflect different SCCmec backgrounds</cite>.
• Limited multidrug resistance versus bovine-specific modules. <cite id="7e2f31c1-10">MDPI One Health analyses of bovine and human isolates find significantly greater genetic diversity and lineage distribution breadth in bovine S. aureus; yet bovine strains exhibit relatively fewer multidrug-resistant classes than human clinical MRSA, reflecting the presence of bovine-specific resistance modules (e.g., cTnT/tetM/Erm tetranetes) rather than the polyresistance typical of human community/international clones</cite>. <cite id="dfa2083e-4">Open veterinary genomics reports bovine S. aureus resistance phenotypes driven by acquired modules, aligning with plasmid/MGE-mediated traits rather than complex integronic stacks</cite>.

Mechanisms of Host Specificity: Mobilome-Mediated Constraints and Facilitators
• Facilitators: bovine-adapted mobilomes enhance bovine fitness. <cite id="107d0721-7">Phages and SaPIs deliver virulence determinants (Seg/Stl/Gas) and immune modulators that can be integrated in host-specific loci, increasing bovine niche fitness</cite>. <cite id="324b9cc5-0">Prophage integration sites in ST5404-like bovine clones facilitate clustering of resistance and virulence elements, forming bovine-associated “mobilome packages” selected in milk/teat environments</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-9">Bovine S. aureus accessory genomes carry abundant integrase genes, transposon ends, and integron backbones, enabling rapid assembly of niche-matched virulence suites</cite>.
• Constraints on human spillover: limited cross-host transfer of bovine packages. <cite id="107d0721-0">Despite S. aureus’ broad host range, adaptation is episodic and contingent on acquiring MGEs that confer new niche functions; failure to acquire human-specific determinants limits successful spillover</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-5">Host shifts occur via MGE acquisition, but each shift relies on appropriate gene modules; bovine-lineage isolates retain accessory genomes skewed to bovine colonization and resist factors, while human transmission typically requires additional virulence/AMR modules</cite>. <cite id="7e2f31c1-2">Comparative data show bovine IMI S. aureus have distinct SCCmec/plasmid/virulence profiles and reduced similarity to human pathogenic S. aureus, constraining efficient human adaptation</cite>.
• Ecological reinforcement by ruminant-adapted mobilomes. <cite id="107d0721-3">Wild ungulate S. aureus genomes harbor rich mobilomes indicating repeated horizontal transfers among ruminants; this supports a “host-associated” mobilome pool that seeds bovine reservoirs</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-9">Bovine lineages thus inherit ecological context (milk/teat biofilms) and MGE complements tuned to these niches, raising specificity for bovines through reinforced selection</cite>.

Representative SCCmec/Plasmid Modules and Their Distribution in Bovine Strains
• SCCmec carriage and transfer. <cite id="324b9cc5-5">Phages efficiently package SCCmec elements (types IV and variants) together with virulence and resistance cargo, allowing dissemination to bovine-adapted staphylococci</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-6">Environmental S. aureus efficiently package SCCmec with frequencies reflecting the strong role of bacteriophages in mobilizing resistance modules</cite>. <cite id="324b9cc5-2">Mastitis-associated ST398 bovine isolates have been resolved at geno-phenotypic levels with SCCmec characterizations, exemplifying livestock-typical mecC/IV associations</cite>.
• Tet- and erm-carrying conjugative plasmids and integron cassettes. <cite id="dfa2083e-1">Bovine S. aureus accessory genomes frequently encode tetracycline resistance (TetM/Erm) via plasmid-borne cassettes integrated within integron or transposon backbones</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-2">Bovine isolates recovered from farms carry genomic islands and integron-like modules with resistance determinants; mobilization hotspots are common</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-4">Bacteria-to-bacteria transfer of resistance is reinforced by phage–plasmid interactions, with SCCmec and genomic islands repeatedly exchanged in livestock settings</cite>.
• Bovine IMI-enriched virulence packages. <cite id="324b9cc5-0">Phage-mediated transfer synergizes with ST5404 background to consolidate virulence/resistance elements in bovine mastitis clusters</cite>. <cite id="7e2f31c1-7">Academic and eScholarship summaries of comparative bovine–human genomics converge on bovine-exclusive virulence patterns associated with mastitis, including hld, coagulase, and adhesin repertoires</cite>.

One-Health Perspective: Diversity Maintenance and Transmission
• Lineage diversity and AMR diversity in bovine systems. <cite id="7e2f31c1-5">Genomic evidence indicates bovine S. aureus displays broad genetic diversity and lineage distribution with antimicrobial resistance profiles shaped by MMEs; MRSA lineages like ST398/ST5404 dominate dairy cow reservoirs</cite>. <cite id="dfa2083e-1">Highly dynamic accessory genomes in bovine isolates reflect ongoing recombination and HGT, sustaining clonal diversity within bovine-adapted lineages</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-5">S. aureus diversifies via MGE acquisition across hosts; bovine lineages are an integral part of this continuum</cite>.
• Transmission potential mediated by MGEs. <cite id="107d0721-9">MGE-integrated virulence/AMR genes alter transmission potential; bovine isolates’ accessory-genome cargo packages traits that favor cow-to-cow spread (e.g., biofilm, mastitis virulence, plasmid-borne tetranetes)</cite>. <cite id="324b9cc5-0">Phage-mediated clustering of resistance genes promotes stable transmission within bovine clades like ST5404</cite>.
• Human risk depends on additional MGE acquisition. <cite id="107d0721-5">Successful host shifts to humans generally require additional MGEs conferring human-p niche functions; bovine-only packages alone do not ensure human adaptation</cite>. <cite id="7e2f31c1-2">Comparative genomics reveals bovine IMI strains are molecularly distinct from human clinical MRSA, with different SCCmec/plasmid/virulence complements and lower similarity, constraining immediate zoonotic virulence</cite>.

Open questions and evidence gaps
- Mutation–recombination balance. While multiple studies implicate MGEs in bovine accessory genome size and diversity, few provide quantitative partitioning of core vs. accessory evolution by site-frequency spectra across bovine-only clades; nonetheless, multiple bovine datasets explicitly attribute accessory diversity to plasmid/phage/SaPI/integron content. <cite id="dfa2083e-1">Highly dynamic accessory genome in bovine isolates</cite> and <cite id="107d0721-9">MGE enrichment in bovine accessory genomes</cite> indicate a strong recombination/HGT bias but do not compute mutation-to-recombination rate ratios.
- Prophage footprints and regulation in bovine niches. Some bovine prophage integrations (e.g., ST5404) are documented to cluster resistance/virulence; however, comprehensive bovine phage catalogs with integration-site preferences and regulatory takeover of virulence remain an area for expansion. <cite id="324b9cc5-0">Prophage synergy with ST5404 for clustered resistance transmission</cite>.
- Host specificity via teatpathogen modules. Direct demonstration that specific phage-borne adhesins (e.g., Hld-encoded ica/icaC/D regulatory determinants on SaPIs) are uniquely enriched in bovine isolates and control bovine host restriction would sharpen causality; comparative bovine–human virulence factor distributions support this hypothesis but more strain-level module mapping is needed. <cite id="7e2f31c1-1">Bovine IMI isolates exhibit distinctive virulence patterns</cite> and <cite id="7e2f31c1-7">bovine-exclusive virulence signatures</cite>.

Practical implications
- Diversity management. <cite id="107d0721-9">Targeting MGE hotspots (plasmid backbones, integrase/integron modules, prophage att sites) in bovine reservoirs can curb spread of virulence/AMR modules</cite>. <cite id="324b9cc5-0">Phage-aware interventions (e.g., temperate prophage interference) may disrupt SCCmec and resistance gene clustering characteristic of bovine STs</cite>.
- Host specificity mitigation. <cite id="107d0721-5">Reducing bovine-associated mobilome exchange (e.g., limiting phage-plasmid co-selection, prudent tetracycline use) can slow the formation of bovine-to-human transferable resistance/virulence packages</cite>. <cite id="7e2f31c1-2">Surveillance should prioritize bovine IMI SCCmec/plasmid profiles (mecC/IV, tetM/erm) and their virulence repertoires to predict spillover risk</cite>.

Key takeaways
- MGEs are engines of bovine S. aureus diversity: they expand the accessory genome with virulence and AMR determinants, often in prophage/plasmid/integron “packages,” and sustain lineage-specific trait suites in bovine clones. <cite id="dfa2083e-1">Dynamic accessory genomes enriched with prophages, SaPIs, plasmids, and resistance cassettes underpin bovine isolates’ diversity</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-7">Prophages and transposons frequently carry virulence/AMR genes, enabling rapid diversification</cite>.
- Bovine host specificity is shaped by mobilome-tuned virulence and resistance modules that confer advantage in milk/teat ecologies; however, human adaptation generally requires additional MGE acquisition beyond bovine packages. <cite id="7e2f31c1-1">Bovine IMI isolates carry bovine-specific virulence patterns distinct from human clinical S. aureus</cite>. <cite id="107d0721-5">Successful host shifts are MGE-mediated events, but selection on bovine niche fitness limits immediate human spillover</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of how plasmids and transposons promote horizontal transfer (HGT) of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) among Listeria species and other bacteria, organized by mechanisms, concrete examples, and ecological drivers.

# Overview: Plasmids and Transposons as Major Vectors of ARG Dissemination
Plasmids and transposons are primary mobile genetic elements that spread drug resistance across bacterial species and communities by packaging and moving resistance genes into new genomes through HGT, enabling rapid emergence and adaptation to antibiotics and heavy metals in the environment and clinical settings.<cite id="f33fbf8f-3">Plasmids and transposons are the leading mobile genetic elements responsible for spreading drug resistance among microbial pathogens implicated in persistent infections.</cite> In Listeria, both plasmids and transposons have been directly implicated in the acquisition of ARGs, including multi-gene composite transposons and plasmid-borne resistomes found across diverse sequence types.<cite id="f33fbf8f-7">Listeria monocytogenes can horizontally acquire ARGs via plasmids and transposons, including a composite transposon containing nine ARGs found in multiple strains; mgen 2023, PMID 37796356.</cite><cite id="f33fbf8f-8">Large-scale genome analysis across 1,924 Listeria strains revealed plasmids and mosaic sequences integrating transposon, phage, and plasmid modules, supporting repeated horizontal exchange among Listeria lineages.</cite>

# Mechanisms of Transfer: Conjugation Machinery on Plasmids and Transposons
Two complementary mechanisms dominate:
- Conjugation via plasmids: F-like and broad-host-range plasmids encode a Type IV secretion system (T4SS) in Gram-negatives (F pilus/T4SS) or conjugation complexes in Gram-positives that physically bridge donor and recipient cells to transfer single-stranded DNA; this route rapidly disseminates antibiotic resistance and virulence determinants in bacterial communities.<cite id="f33fbf8f-6">Conjugation of R plasmids is a major mechanism for spread of antibiotic resistance in bacterial communities; transposons also participate in HGT.</cite><cite id="f33fbf8f-3">Plasmids are key players in the rapid spread of antibiotic resistance by transferring resistance genes between bacteria via horizontal gene transfer.</cite><cite id="08d4134e-9">IncF plasmids encoding F-type T4SSs show high in vitro conjugation rates and are among the most frequent conjugative plasmids, facilitating rapid dissemination of resistance, including virulence and fertility genes.</cite><cite id="08d4134e-0">Direct single-particle and imaging evidence shows the F pilus functions as a conduit for DNA transfer during conjugation, resolving a 60-year debate and mechanistically underpinning plasmid-mediated ARG spread.</cite><cite id="08d4134e-3">F-like plasmid horizontal transfer by conjugation is responsible for disseminating antibiotic resistance and virulence factors in bacterial populations.</cite><cite id="08d4134e-1">Conjugative plasmids carry the genetic information enabling their own transfer into other cells, i.e., they encode the machinery for HGT.</cite><cite id="08d4134e-5">Reviews of conjugation in Gram-negative bacteria outline the life cycle of the F factor, including pairing, pore formation, and ssDNA transfer guided by conjugation machinery.</cite><cite id="08d4134e-2">Synthetic adhesins can be used to convert and target bacterial conjugation into programmable DNA delivery, illustrating how conjugation machinery physically mediates DNA transfer between cells.</cite>
- Conjugative transposons (integrative mobile elements): Composite, integrative transposons in gram-positive lineages encode both transposition enzymes and conjugation machinery (tra genes), enabling them to excise from a donor genome, traverse to a recipient via a pilus-like bridge, and integrate into host loci; canonical families include Tn916/Tn1545 that spread macrolide–lincosamide–streptogramin (MLS) resistance via gram-positive niches.<cite id="f33fbf8f-5">Conjugative transposons possess genetic machinery to facilitate their own transfer between bacterial cells; they mobilize themselves rather than relying solely on plasmid-borne conjugation machinery.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-0">The Tn916 and Tn1545 family predominates in clinically important gram-positive bacteria, disseminating antibiotic resistance via conjugative transposition.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-1">Tn916 contains erm(B), conferring resistance to macrolides, lincosamides, and streptogramins, and is mobile as a conjugative transposon in gram-positives.</cite>

Plasmids and transposons also synergize with integrons to assemble pan-resistance gene cassettes and adapt to antibiotic pollutants in the environment, facilitating diversification and persistence of resistance modules on mobile backbones.<cite id="03c432a4-6">Tn916-like elements are modular mobile genetic elements conferring antibiotic resistance through conjugation, supporting the spread of resistance determinants.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-4">Tn916-like elements form a diverse group of modular mobile elements that disseminate antibiotic resistance, reflecting extensive recombination and mobility among conjugative transposons in bacterial populations.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-9">Integrons, transposons, and IS elements promote diversification of multidrug resistance plasmids and their adaptation to antibiotic pollutants, enabling environmental persistence and transfer of ARGs.</cite>

# Listeria-Specific Pathways and Examples
Listeria monocytogenes and closely related species (e.g., L. innocua) have repeatedly acquired resistance via plasmids and transposons, and conjugation is a principal route for ARG dissemination within and beyond this genus. Reports document:
- Plasmid-borne resistance determinants in Listeria: Large surveys and strain analyses show frequent presence of extrachromosomal DNA, composite transposons, and mercury resistance modules in Listeria genomes from food isolates; novel Listeria-specific transposons and plasmids have been identified, including Tn7075 predicted to drive mercury resistance, and composite plasmid-ARG cargo including tetM and elements related to Tn916.<cite id="bc320fb0-1">A large-scale sequencing survey mapped the distribution of plasmids across 1,924 Listeria isolates, providing a comprehensive picture of Listeria plasmids and their roles in AMR.</cite><cite id="f33fbf8f-7">Composite transposons with multiple ARGs occur in Listeria, with nine-gene cassettes detected across multiple strains, evidencing significant horizontal acquisition via transposons; L. monocytogenes mgen 2023, PMID 37796356.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-7">A Listeria plasmid identified (p900703_1) contained genetic matches to a conjugative transposon Tn916 harboring tetM, consistent with tet resistance mediated by transposon-related mobility modules in Listeria.</cite><cite id="9212f1be-6">Novel environmental mercury resistance plasmids in Cronobacter (a Listeria-related genus) showed that Tn5042-type mercury transposons integrated via recombination into pQBR plasmids, demonstrating how Tn5042 spreads among plasmid backbones; this mechanism parallels transposon mobilization observed in Listeria.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-6">Tn916 was introduced into hemolysin determinants in Listeria, demonstrating site-specific transposon insertions and mutagenesis in L. monocytogenes, consistent with active transposon mobilization in this species.</cite>
- Transposon-mediated resistance determinants in Listeria: Direct characterization has shown Tn916-like elements in Listeria associated with resistance to trimethoprim (dfrG), and Tn916-family conjugative transposons predominate in gram-positive lineages including Listeria, facilitating spread of MLS resistance traits (erm) and tetracycline resistance (tetM).<cite id="03c432a4-2">Tn6198, a novel transposon in Listeria monocytogenes, embeds the trimethoprim resistance gene dfrG into a Tn916 element, representing a Tn916-based mobile module in Listeria.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-5">First fully characterized Tn916-like transposon in Listeria associated with dfrG confirms modular assembly where resistance gene cassettes are carried by Tn916-like backbones in Listeria, paralleling gram-positive dissemination of MLS/tet resistance.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-0">Tn916/Tn1545 family predominates in gram-positive bacteria and is a major vehicle of conjugative transposition and resistance dissemination in clinically relevant gram-positives.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-1">The erm(B) determinant within Tn916 confers resistance to macrolides, lincosamides, and streptogramins, providing an example of transposon-mediated MLS resistance that could move across gram-positives via conjugation.</cite>
- Cross-species transfer and experimental support: In Listeria, conjugation-mediated transfer from Gram-positive donors (e.g., Streptococcus) has delivered diverse antibiotic resistance elements into Listeria, demonstrating compatibility of mating pairs across species; this supports movement of plasmid-borne and transposon-borne ARGs into Listeria from commensals and food-associated bacteria and, by extension, out of Listeria into other recipients through similar conjugation pairings.<cite id="9212f1be-0">Elements encoding resistance to several antibiotics were transferred to Listeria species by conjugation with Streptococcus donor strains, demonstrating interspecies conjugation into Listeria.</cite><cite id="f33fbf8f-1">Conjugative transfer is one of the most important mechanisms for dissemination of antimicrobial resistance and stress adaptation determinants in Listeria monocytogenes, underscoring the central role of conjugation in its resistome evolution.</cite>
- Environmental and food niche selection: Large environmental surveys and genomic analyses support frequent HGT and selection of ARGs in natural and anthropized environments, providing selective contexts where plasmids and conjugative transposons thrive and exchange cargo, including ARG-rich composite transposons and heavy metal resistance modules shared among Listeria and non-Listeria lineages.<cite id="f33fbf8f-2">Recent HGT and environmental selection are implicated in acquisition and diversification of ARGs in natural environments, highlighting ARG mosaicism and mobilization under environmental pressure.</cite><cite id="f33fbf8f-8">Across 1,924 Listeria strains, integrated transposon–phage–plasmid mosaics were prevalent, indicating repeated horizontal exchanges involving mobile elements in environmental Listeria communities.</cite>

# Beyond Listeria: Plasmid-Mediated ARG Circulation Across Taxa
- Gram-negative systems illustrate plasmid-mediated spread of resistance determinants that Listeria can inherit via HGT or in commensal/food webs. F-like conjugative plasmids are efficient DNA transfer vectors encoding T4SS/pilus machinery, and their rapid spread underpins the dominance of IncF plasmids in resistance dissemination across Enterobacteriaceae, VIM-1 metallo-beta-lactamases on IncN plasmids in Enterobacteriaceae, and broader antibiotic resistance gene reservoirs on plasmids in food and humans.<cite id="f33fbf8f-3">Plasmids are key to rapid spread of antibiotic resistance via HGT.</cite><cite id="08d4134e-9">IncF plasmids with F-T4SSs exhibit high in vitro conjugation rates and are frequent types in bacterial communities, accelerating dissemination of resistance factors.</cite><cite id="bc320fb0-2">Nearly identical IncN-type VIM-1 plasmids circulated across different Enterobacteriaceae in one region, evidencing human, food, and environment movement of metallo-beta-lactamase resistance on conjugative plasmids.</cite><cite id="bc320fb0-5">In Enterobacteriaceae clinical specimens, six plasmids carried unit and composite transposons with AMR genes, with IS26 identified as a driver of composite transposon mobilization, underscoring plasmid-transposon synergy in resistance dissemination.</cite><cite id="bc320fb0-6">Plasmid-mediated colistin resistance (mcr-1) was first described in food animals, food, and humans in 2015, marking a paradigmatic case of rapid, global spread of a resistance determinant on conjugative plasmids.</cite>
- Conjugative transposons bridge gram-positive niches: Tn916/Tn1545 family has disseminated MLS resistance across gram-positive bacteria and serves as a reservoir for erm and lnu determinants that can enter or exit Listeria through conjugation with gram-positive donors/recipients such as Staphylococcus, Enterococcus, and Corynebacterium in the human microbiota and food chain.<cite id="03c432a4-0">The Tn916/Tn1545 family predominates among conjugative transposons in clinically relevant gram-positive bacteria, emphasizing their role in resistance dissemination across commensals and pathogens.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-1">Tn916’s erm(B) cargo provides a mechanistic example of mobile MLS resistance transfer via conjugative transposons in gram-positives, applicable to Listeria’s ecological partners.</cite><cite id="bc320fb0-3">LNU (lincomycin nucleotidyltransferase) family records in antibiotic resistance databases underpin the selective pressure and mobility of lincosamide resistance genes, often embedded in plasmid/transposon modules.</cite>

# Putting It Together: Routes, Determinants, and Outcomes in Listeria
- Donor–recipient encounters in food, gut, and environment enable conjugation-based transfer of plasmids and conjugative transposons into Listeria. Once integrated, resistance modules can include tetracycline (tetM), macrolide–lincosamide–streptogramin resistance (ermB), lincosamide inactivation (lnu/lin), and mercury resistance (mer operons/dfrG within Tn916-like cassettes) as mobile units or composite arrays, often assembled by integrative elements and IS transposons.<cite id="f33fbf8f-7">Listeria strains harbor composite transposons with multiple ARGs and have acquired ARGs via plasmids and transposons across diverse sequence types.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-1">Erm(B) within Tn916 exemplifies MLS resistance determinants movable by conjugative transposons among gram-positives.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-2">Tn6198 incorporates dfrG into a Tn916-like backbone in Listeria, demonstrating trimethoprim resistance gene capture by Listeria transposons and potential cross-species transfer as a conjugative unit.</cite><cite id="f33fbf8f-4">Mercury resistance Tn5042 and related transposons have been co-opted by environmental plasmids via recombination, illustrating a route by which mercury-resistance determinants reach bacteria across taxa and can be picked up by Listeria in environmental niches.</cite>
