- Listeria’s physiology (ability to acquire extrachromosomal DNA) and ecological co-occurrence with mobilizable commensals enhance plasmid/transposon uptake and subsequent dissemination; conjugation-mediated transfer from Streptococcus into Listeria validates interspecies flow of resistance, and large-scale surveys of Listeria plasmids and mosaics across strains show multi-hit acquisition histories that are consistent with repeated HGT.<cite id="9212f1be-0">Conjugation from Streptococcus to Listeria transferred multiple antibiotic resistances, demonstrating interspecies transfer routes into Listeria.</cite><cite id="bc320fb0-1">Plasmid distribution in Listeria was mapped across thousands of isolates, documenting frequent extrachromosomal DNA carriage and ARG association.</cite><cite id="f33fbf8f-8">Mosaic sequences integrating transposon–phage–plasmid content are common across Listeria genomes, consistent with extensive horizontal exchange under environmental pressure.</cite>
- Environment-driven selection amplifies the fitness of plasmid- and transposon-borne ARGs: heavy metal contamination and antibiotic pressure promote the proliferation of mercury-resistance transposons and Inc plasmids, with recombination between ARG-carrying modules enabling the assembly of pan-resistance plasmids that can colonize Listeria and other bacteria in food and clinical ecosystems.<cite id="f33fbf8f-2">Recent HGT with environmental selection is a key driver of ARG acquisition and diversification in natural communities, promoting ARG flow into Listeria niches.</cite><cite id="f33fbf8f-4">Tn5042 mercury resistance transposons integrated into plasmid backbones by recombination demonstrate a module-level mechanism underpinning cross-species ARG transfer, with broad environmental circulation.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-9">Integrons, transposons, and IS elements diversify multidrug resistance plasmids and adapt them to antibiotic pollutants, providing a selective and genetic basis for ARG persistence and transfer.</cite>

# Key Takeaways
- Mechanistic facilitation: Plasmids provide conjugation machinery and broad host-range backbones for direct DNA transfer and stable maintenance of ARGs; conjugative transposons package specific ARGs with excision/integration and mobilization modules, allowing targeted spread among gram-positives including Listeria, often aided by integrative elements and IS sequences that assemble multi-drug cassettes.<cite id="f33fbf8f-3">Plasmids and transposons are leading MGEs for spreading drug resistance among pathogens by HGT.</cite><cite id="f33fbf8f-5">Conjugative transposons encode transfer machinery to move themselves between cells, facilitating targeted spread of embedded resistance genes.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-0">The Tn916/Tn1545 family predominates in gram-positives and drives resistance dissemination.</cite><cite id="08d4134e-0">F pilus extension physically conduits DNA transfer in conjugation, underpinning plasmid-mediated ARG spread across species.</cite>
- Listeria- and cross-phylum examples: Listeria has acquired ARGs via plasmids and composite transposons, including nine-gene cassettes and mercury-resistance modules, and evidence of conjugation from Streptococcus donors demonstrates inter-species transfer routes; analogous IncF and IncN plasmids carryingblaVIM-1 and mcr-1 in Enterobacteriaceae illustrate the same mechanisms operating outside Listeria, with strong potential for gene flow in food and human niches.<cite id="f33fbf8f-7">Composite transposon cassettes with nine ARGs detected across multiple Listeria strains; ARGs acquired via plasmids and transposons in Listeria.</cite><cite id="9212f1be-0">Elements transferred to Listeria from Streptococcus via conjugation, demonstrating interspecies gene flow into Listeria.</cite><cite id="bc320fb0-2">Nearly identical IncN VIM-1 plasmids across Enterobacteriaceae highlight efficient plasmid-mediated ARG circulation in food and human systems.</cite><cite id="bc320fb0-6">Discovery of mcr-1 on plasmids in animals, food, and humans exemplifies rapid, global plasmid-mediated resistance dissemination.</cite>
- Ecological context: Environmental selection and co-occurrence of mobilizable commensals in food systems, combined with Listeria’s capacity to take up and integrate mobile DNA, maintain ARG flux across species barriers; integron–transposon–IS synergy and recombination among transposon families generate mosaic plasmids and transposons that sustain horizontal movement of resistance even across taxonomic distances.<cite id="f33fbf8f-2">Recent HGT and environmental selection are central to ARG acquisition and diversification in natural settings.</cite><cite id="f33fbf8f-8">Widespread mosaics integrating plasmid/transposon/phage sequences across Listeria genomes suggest repeated horizontal exchange in environmental communities.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-9">Integrons, transposons, and IS elements diversify multidrug resistance plasmids and adapt them to antibiotic pollutants, sustaining ARG transfer.</cite>

In sum, plasmids facilitate horizontal transfer of ARGs in Listeria primarily via conjugation machinery and broad compatibility, while conjugative transposons and integrative elements package and move discrete resistance cassettes, notably MLS resistance (erm/lnu/lin) and heavy metal resistance (mer/dfrG), often with tet genes and integron cassettes; these mobile modules move into Listeria from commensals and across taxa in food and clinical ecosystems, where environmental selection favors their persistence and spread to other bacteria.<cite id="f33fbf8f-1">Conjugation is a key mechanism by which Listeria acquires and disseminates antimicrobial resistance determinants, shaping the evolution of resistance in this genus.</cite><cite id="f33fbf8f-6">R plasmid conjugation spreads antibiotic resistance widely; transposons participate by carrying and moving resistance genes.</cite><cite id="03c432a4-0">Tn916/Tn1545 family exemplifies conjugative transposition-driven spread of resistance in gram-positives, with implications for Listeria.</cite>

Executive summary
Across observational and longitudinal datasets, cervical dysplasia (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, CIN) is associated with a “shift-to-dysbiosis” in the lower reproductive tract microbiome: relative decreases in lactobacilli and increases in anaerobic genera (notably Gardnerella and related Prevotellales/Megasphaeraceae), together with cervicovaginal metabolomic profiles that differ from those in healthy controls and align with dysbiosis-linked patterns such as reduced lactate, altered short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and increased amines/esters. <cite id="d4773dd3-1">Our results indicated a clear difference in the vaginal microbiota and vaginal metabolites of women with cervical dysplasia</cite> <cite id="f4f615f2-4">Patients with CIN exhibit a distinct vaginal microbial profile characterized by a decrease in Lactobacillus and Pseudomonas, and an increase in Gardnerella</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-3">Lactobacillus decreases, while other bacteria, such as anaerobes Prevotella and Megasphaera, increase significantly</cite>. These changes are intertwined with human papillomavirus (HPV) biology and cervicovaginal ecology, with Lactobacillus-dominant microbiota linked to lower risk of high-risk HPV persistence and to regression of dysplasia, and with Gardnerella-associated states linked to persistence or higher-grade disease in some cohorts. <cite id="d1988a9a-1">Women with a Lactobacillus-dominant microbiome at baseline are more likely to have regressive disease at 12 months</cite> <cite id="f4f615f2-6">Gardnerella vaginalis are associated with CIN2 persistence and slower regression</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-2">The cervicovaginal microbiome modulates susceptibility to bacterial vaginosis, high-risk HPV infection, etc.</cite>

- Lactobacillus dominance vs anaerobe-rich dysbiosis:
  - Cross-sectional clinical studies report that women diagnosed with CIN show a decrease in Lactobacillus and increases in anaerobes, especially Gardnerella (and related taxa like Atopobium/Prevotella/Megasphaera), compared with healthy or low-biomarker controls. <cite id="f4f615f2-4">Patients with CIN exhibit a distinct vaginal microbial profile characterized by a decrease in Lactobacillus and Pseudomonas, and an increase in Gardnerella</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-3">Lactobacillus decreases, while other bacteria, such as anaerobes Prevotella and Megasphaera, increase significantly</cite> <cite id="f4f615f2-2">This study revealed the perturbation of microbiota in the presence of CIN and demonstrated a distinct pattern of characteristic bacteria community</cite>. Review syntheses integrating HPV and CIN converge on reduced lactobacillus abundance and relative expansion of Gram-negative/anaerobic genera in dysplastic states. <cite id="d4773dd3-0">A Lactobacillus-dominant vaginal microbiota enhances protective function, improves local immune response, and reduces the risk of progression</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-5">The presence of Gardnerella in the cervicovaginal microbiota of women with high-risk oncogenic papillomavirus may indicate an increase in microbial</cite>.
  - Sampling-site matters: cervicovaginal mucus and tissue-associated microbiomes show distinct functional profiles from the vaginal lumen. <cite id="f4f615f2-0">Cervicovaginal metabolic profiles were determined by cervical cancer, vaginal microbiota, and their interplays</cite> <cite id="f4f615f2-7">The cervicovaginal microbiome plays a critical role in women's health with communities dominated by Lactobacillus species</cite>. Studies that integrate sequencing and metabolomics emphasize that dysplasia-associated changes are detectable in these interrelated niches and can involve broader functional shifts than in the epithelium-poor upper vagina (e.g., increased complexity of anaerobic pathways). <cite id="f4f615f2-7">Vaginal microbial communities are typically dominated by one or a few well-adapted microbes which are able to survive in a narrow pH range and are adapted to</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-2">The cervicovaginal microbiome modulates susceptibility to bacterial vaginosis, high-risk HPV infection</cite> <cite id="f4798e4c-0">The cervicovaginal microbiome undergoes dynamic changes during menopause, which may be involved in the progression of cervical neoplasia</cite>.
- Metabolomic and chemical ecology signatures:
  - Multiple cohorts document altered metabolite profiles—characteristic of “vaginal dysbiosis”—in women with dysplasia or high-risk HPV: reduced lactate and hydrogen peroxide production, with increases in acetate, propionate, and other fermentation-derived metabolites, and changes in amine/ester signatures associated with Gardnerella-driven communities. <cite id="408612f6-5">Acetate, butyrate, and propionate are the main SCFAs produced by fermentation by bacteria</cite> <cite id="408612f6-4">Role for these metabolites in BV has low lactate and high acetate and propionate are characteristic</cite> <cite id="c907ede6-5">This study reveals significant alterations in the cervicovaginal secretion and cervical tissue microbiomes, alongside metabolomic changes, which are associated</cite> <cite id="c907ede6-0">A significant association between vaginal dysbiosis and cervical cancer has been demonstrated, with potential microbial biomarkers</cite>. In particular, a 2024 clinical study of women with cervical lesions across grades reported clear microbiota and metabolite differences across dysplasia categories. <cite id="d4773dd3-1">Our results indicated a clear difference in the vaginal microbiota and vaginal metabolites of women with cervical dysplasia</cite> <cite id="31134584-9">In this study, to understand vaginal microbiota signatures and vaginal metabolite changes in women with cervical lesions of different grades and cancer</cite>.
  - Mechanistic corollary: Lactobacillus spp. produce lactate and H2O2, shaping acidity and oxidation potential; dysplasia-associated communities with Gardnerella/Prevotella often show mixed-acid fermentation and reduced H2O2, potentially favoring HPV persistence and inflammation. <cite id="d4773dd3-4">Metabolism of Lactobacillus and Gardnerella vaginalis in vaginal conditions: lactobacilli vs. BV-associated shifts; G. vaginalis grows less robustly in VDM than in BHI, though key metabolic traits such as the bifidobacterium shunt and mixed acid pathways are present</cite> <cite id="c907ede6-5">Significant alterations in cervicovaginal secretion microbiomes and metabolomics are associated with</cite>. Functional readouts in cervical tissues confirm that normal vs tumor cells respond differently to lactobacilli’s metabolites, suggesting host–microbe metabolic conflict in dysplasia. <cite id="d4773dd3-6">Normal and tumour cervical cells respond differently to vaginal lactobacilli, independent of pH and lactate</cite>.

Associations with disease grade and HPV dynamics
- Grade-related patterns and heterogeneity:
  - Analyses stratifying CIN by grade (CIN1 vs CIN2+) suggest that dysbiosis worsens with higher-grade disease, with taxa shifts and metabolite profiles becoming more divergent from lactobacillus-dominant patterns. <cite id="f4f615f2-8">Methods included 43 HPV-positive women, classified into low-grade (CIN1, n = 23) and high-grade (CIN2+, n = 20) groups, with analysis of vaginal microbiota</cite> <cite id="f4f615f2-4">Patients with CIN exhibit a distinct vaginal microbial profile including increased Gardnerella and decreased Lactobacillus</cite>. Reviews and datasets integrating metabolomics further support that metabolite signatures of “dysbiosis” intensify with progression and are observed in precancerous to cancerous spectra. <cite id="d4773dd3-0">A Lactobacillus-dominant vaginal microbiota reduces the risk of progression</cite> <cite id="c907ede6-0">Vaginal dysbiosis shows significant association with cervical cancer and potential microbial biomarkers</cite> <cite id="f4f615f2-0">Cervicovaginal metabolic profiles are determined by cancer, microbiota, and their interplays</cite>.
- Longitudinal causal clues (risk, persistence, regression):
  - In an untreated cohort followed for 12 months, women with baseline Lactobacillus-dominant microbiota were more likely to experience regression of CIN, whereas Gardnerella-enriched states were linked to CIN2 persistence and slower regression, pointing to a protective microbiota state and a dysbiotic risk state during HPV natural history. <cite id="d1988a9a-1">Women with a Lactobacillus-dominant microbiome at baseline are more likely to have regressive disease at 12 months</cite> <cite id="c907ede6-6">Gardnerella vaginalis are associated with CIN2 persistence and slower regression</cite>. Broad syntheses affirm that Lactobacillus-rich cervicovaginal microbiomes associate with lower susceptibility to high-risk HPV and BV, conditions that co-occur with dysplasia. <cite id="d4773dd3-2">The cervicovaginal microbiome modulates susceptibility to bacterial vaginosis, high-risk HPV infection, etc.</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-3">Lactobacillus decreases while anaerobes increase significantly in HPV risk contexts</cite>.
- Functional-host interactions:
  - Lactobacillus-dominant states are repeatedly linked to reduced risk of progression and improved local innate immunity (e.g., H2O2 and lactate-linked acidity), whereas anaerobe-dominant states favor inflammation-associated niches that are permissive to high-risk HPV persistence and dysplasia formation. <cite id="d4773dd3-0">A Lactobacillus-dominant vaginal microbiota enhances protective function and reduces progression risk</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-4">Mixed-acid metabolism of G. vaginalis and relative metabolic differences vs. Lactobacillus in the vaginal niche</cite>. Metabolomics across cervicovaginal secretions and adjacent tissues capture these host–microbe interactions and correlate with disease trajectory. <cite id="c907ede6-5">Alterations in cervicovaginal secretion and cervical tissue microbiomes with metabolomic changes are associated with</cite>.

Important qualifiers and confounders
- Sampling and site specificity:
  - Differences arise whether sampling the vagina or the cervicovaginal canal, which harbor distinct community structures and functional potential. <cite id="f4f615f2-7">Communities in the cervicovaginal canal are typically dominated by Lactobacillus species in health</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-2">Cervicovaginal microbiome modulates susceptibility to BV and hrHPV</cite> <cite id="f4f615f2-0">Cervicovaginal metabolic profiles reflect interplay of cancer, microbiota</cite>. Cross-sectional comparisons mixing sites or poorly resolving epithelial interfaces risk diluting or skewing effect sizes, underscoring the need for site-matched designs in CIN studies. <cite id="f4f615f2-7">Vaginal microbial communities are typically dominated by a few adapted microbes with narrow pH tolerance</cite>.
- Overlap with bacterial vaginosis and co-infections:
  - Gardnerella and related taxa implicated in dysplasia are core BV biomarkers; cohorts show that BV-associated microbiota and metabolite profiles co-occur with high-risk HPV and CIN, complicating causal attribution. <cite id="d4773dd3-3">Anaerobes increase significantly in Lactobacillus-depleted profiles typical of BV-like dysbiosis</cite> <cite id="f4f615f2-3">The cervicovaginal microbiome composition is associated with HPV and may relate to healthy pregnancy metabolomes—underscoring strong lactobacillus-lactate signatures in health</cite>. Integrative metabolomics attempts to separate primary HPV-driven dysbiosis from BV comorbidity by multivariate profiling. <cite id="408612f6-6">NMR metabolomics of symbioses highlights low lactate and high acetate/propionate as BV signatures</cite> <cite id="f4f615f2-6">Insight into the complex interaction between vaginal microbiome composition, metabolic alterations, and gene expression during cervical disease</cite>.
- Menopausal and host-state effects:
  - Cervicovaginal microbiome composition and metabolome shift across the menopause transition, which can influence HPV outcomes and potentially modulate dysplasia trajectories. <cite id="d4773dd3-8">The cervicovaginal microbiome undergoes dynamic changes during menopause, which may be involved in the progression of cervical neoplasia</cite>. While these effects are documented across HPV/CIN spectra, they must be considered when interpreting case–control comparisons or regional screening programs.

Practical takeaways for clinicians and researchers
- In healthy women, the vagina is often Lactobacillus-dominant with relatively high lactate/H2O2 and narrower pH ranges; in dysplasia, lactobacilli decline and anaerobes (notably Gardnerella and Prevotella/Megasphaera) increase, with metabolomic profiles consistent with dysbiosis and lower acidity/oxidation potential. <cite id="d4773dd3-0">A Lactobacillus-dominant microbiota reduces progression risk</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-3">Lactobacillus decreases while Prevotella and Megasphaera increase significantly</cite> <cite id="408612f6-4">Low lactate and high acetate/propionate characterize BV-like dysbiosis</cite>.
- These compositional/metabolic shifts track with HPV persistence and disease grade; baseline Lactobacillus dominance predicts regression, whereas Gardnerella-enrichment predicts higher-grade persistence. <cite id="d1988a9a-1">Lactobacillus-dominant baseline predicts 12-month regression</cite> <cite id="c907ede6-6">Gardnerella enrichment associates with CIN2 persistence and slower regression</cite>.
- For differential diagnosis and surveillance, integrating pH/whiff and cytology with microbiome/metabolome profiling can help distinguish HPV/CIN-related dysbiosis from BV, and may flag women at higher risk of CIN persistence for closer follow-up or targeted interventions. <cite id="d4773dd3-1">Clear differences in microbiota and metabolites in women with cervical dysplasia</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-2">Cervicovaginal microbiome modulates susceptibility to BV and hrHPV</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-4">G. vaginalis metabolic traits differ from lactobacilli in the vaginal milieu</cite>.

Areas of uncertainty and future directions
- Directionality and temporality: While multiple cohorts suggest lactobacillus-dominant states are protective and Gardnerella-enriched states are risk-associated, randomized trials testing microbiota-modulating interventions (e.g., lactobacillus-based, lactate/H2O2 boosters, metabolite precursors) against CIN regression are lacking, and observational biases (reverse causality, selection) remain.
- Cervical vs vaginal sampling: Best practice is site-specific sampling (cervicovaginal mucus for transformation zone) to avoid dilution of dysplasia-associated signals seen when relying solely on the vaginal canal. <cite id="f4f615f2-0">Cervicovaginal metabolic profiles determine by cancer, microbiota, and their interplays</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-2">The cervicovaginal microbiome modulates susceptibility to high-risk HPV</cite>.
- Personalized biomarkers: Multi-omics models combining taxa and metabolites (lactate, acetate, propionate, isobutyrate; amine/ester volatiles) show promise, but require validation in prospective cohorts to balance sensitivity, specificity, and cost in screening workflows. <cite id="c907ede6-5">Significant alterations in cervicovaginal secretion and cervical tissue microbiomes and metabolomics are associated with disease</cite> <cite id="f4f615f2-2">Characteristic bacteria community patterns in CIN</cite>.

Key references and representative findings
- Cross-sectional differences: <cite id="f4f615f2-4">CIN-associated decrease in Lactobacillus and increase in Gardnerella</cite>, <cite id="d4773dd3-3">decreased Lactobacillus and increased Prevotella/Megasphaera</cite>, <cite id="f4f615f2-2">dysbiosis pattern in CIN</cite>.
- Metabolomics: <cite id="d4773dd3-1">Clear microbiota/metabolite differences in dysplasia</cite> <cite id="c907ede6-0">Association of vaginal dysbiosis with cervical cancer and candidate biomarkers</cite> <cite id="408612f6-4">Low lactate/high acetate/propionate in BV-like states</cite>.
- Longitudinal HPV/CIN dynamics: <cite id="d1988a9a-1">Lactobacillus-dominant baseline predicts regression</cite> <cite id="c907ede6-6">Gardnerella-associated CIN2 persistence and slower regression</cite>.
- Contextual ecology: <cite id="d4773dd3-0">Lactobacillus-dominant microbiota reduce progression risk</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-2">Cervicovaginal microbiome modulates BV/HPV susceptibility</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-4">Metabolic divergence between Lactobacillus and G. vaginalis</cite>.

Bottom line
Compared with healthy women, those diagnosed with cervical dysplasia show a consistent shift away from Lactobacillus-dominant, acidic/oxidizing vaginal/cervicovaginal communities toward anaerobe-enriched, “dysbiosis-like” communities with lower lactate and altered SCFA and amine/ester profiles; these compositional/metabolic changes align with increased risk of HPV persistence and higher-grade lesions, while Lactobacillus-dominant states confer protection and are linked to disease regression in longitudinal cohorts, highlighting microbiome-informed strategies for risk stratification and adjunctive care. <cite id="d4773dd3-1">Clear differences in microbiota and metabolites in dysplasia</cite> <cite id="f4f615f2-4">Decreased Lactobacillus and increased Gardnerella in CIN</cite> <cite id="d1988a9a-1">Lactobacillus dominance predicts regression</cite> <cite id="c907ede6-6">Gardnerella associates with CIN2 persistence and slower regression</cite> <cite id="d4773dd3-0">Lactobacillus-dominant microbiota lower progression risk</cite>.

Summary: How respiratory physiotherapists can use diaphragm ultrasonography during weaning
Respiratory physiotherapists can incorporate bedside diaphragmatic ultrasonography (DUS) as an objective, bedside tool to assess diaphragmatic function and guide de‑escalation from mechanical ventilation. Used at the start, mid‑course, and pre‑extubation stages of liberation, DUS improves weaning decisions by quantifying diaphragmatic mechanics (e.g., diaphragm thickening fraction [DTF], excursion) and identifying diaphragmatic dysfunction earlier than clinical examination alone, thereby supporting safer extubation and potentially reducing failed extubations and ventilator days when integrated into a multidisciplinary weaning protocol. <cite id="1de7af08-0">In summary, we suggest including diaphragm ultrasound in MV weaning protocols. This can be especially beneficial during the shift from controlled to assisted</cite> <cite id="1de7af08-5">Ultrasound at 30 min of SBT improves weaning decisions. • Diaphragm ultrasound supports extubation readiness assessment. may enhance clinical decision-making</cite> <cite id="08e0e50e-0">Diaphragm ultrasound helps in predicting successful weaning in mechanically ventilated patients. Both DE and DTF showed a higher specificity than RSBI</cite>.

What respiratory physiotherapists can measure with bedside DUS
- Primary parameters:
  - Diaphragm excursion (DE): distance the diaphragm moves between end‑expiration and maximum inspiration; reduced excursion indicates weakness. <cite id="df2374d11-2">The two primary measurements are diaphragm excursion (DE) and thickness and diaphragm thickening fraction (DTF). DE is typically measured in</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-1">Bedside ultrasound is non‑invasive, dynamic, and repeatable, enabling quantitative assessment of diaphragmatic excursion, thickness, and thickening fraction</cite>.
  - Diaphragm thickness (resting) and DTF = (inspiratory thickness − expiratory thickness)/resting thickness (often expressed as a percentage); drop in DTF indicates fatigability. <cite id="1de7af08-2">This article provides a comprehensive review of the role of ultrasonography during the weaning process in critically ill patients. diaphragm ultrasound in MV</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-9">Bedside ultrasound is non‑invasive, dynamic, and repeatable, enabling quantitative assessment of diaphragmatic excursion, thickness, and thickening fraction</cite>.
  - Other emerging indices include costal diaphragm angle and MIP/MEP correlations; combine with clinical exams and ventilatory parameters (e.g., RSBI). <cite id="dfa16ed7-0">A new weaning index using point-of-care ultrasound with diaphragmic thickening fraction (DTF) has potential benefits for improving weaning success</cite> <cite id="08e0e50e-0">Diaphragm ultrasound helps in predicting successful weaning... Both DE and DTF showed a higher specificity than RSBI</cite>.

- Practical how‑to (therapist‑friendly):
  - Patient positioning: supine with arms at sides; slight lateral decubitus or slight upright improves access and reduces lung sliding artifacts. <cite id="878ccd6b-2">Position the patient supine with both arms at their sides. For better access to the diaphragm, slight lateral decubitus or slight upright positioning may be used</cite>.
  - Probe and windows: high‑frequency linear probe (5–10 MHz) in the subcostal or sternal view at the level of the 3rd–5th intercostal space, aimed medially/cranially/dorsally to the crura; mark landmarks and keep standardized views. <cite id="878ccd6b-3">The probe is placed in the subcostal area between mid clavicular and anterior axillary lines, and directed medially, cranially and dorsally aiming to use the</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-1">Bedside ultrasound is non‑invasive, dynamic and repeatable, enabling quantitative assessment of diaphragmatic excursion, thickness, and thickening fraction</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-6">a Probe position for B and M mode diaphragmatic thickness measurements in the zone of</cite>.
  - Technique: mark rib spaces, assess resting thickness at end‑expiration, then inspire deeply and measure change; measure DE from subcostal plane to diaphragmatic dome apex; ensure patient follows instructions (“belly in” on inspiration) and you maintain probe pressure and coupling; repeat twice and average. <cite id="df2374d11-1">Ultrasound-guided mechanical ventilation (MG) can objectively quantify respiratory muscle function and fatigue</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-1">Bedside ultrasound is non‑invasive, dynamic and repeatable, enabling quantitative assessment of diaphragmatic excursion, thickness, and thickening fraction</cite>.
  - Documentation/reporting: record frequency (MHz), view, inspiratory maneuver, values (mm for DE; mm and % for DTF), presence of diaphragmatic hernia/muscle herniation, and any artifacts; note patient effort, breath sounds, and oxygenation at the time.

When to use DUS as a physiotherapist within weaning and liberation
- Early identification of diaphragmatic dysfunction: integrate DUS in the liberation bundle at reassessment after reducing sedation/analgesia and detaching from ventilator alarms to de‑escalate modes/tidal volumes; use as a physiotherapist point‑of‑care adjunct to trigger noninvasive ventilation, neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA), pressure support, or diaphragmatic pacing trials as clinically indicated. <cite id="1de7af08-0">In summary, we suggest including diaphragm ultrasound in MV weaning protocols. This can be especially beneficial during the shift from controlled to assisted</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-5">DTF of less than 20% to 30% or DE of less than 2 cm with deep inspiration is useful in diagnosing diaphragm dysfunction (DD). Ultrasound can help de-escalate modes and determine readiness for protective ventilation strategies</cite>.
- Mid‑SBT assessment: perform DUS at ~30 minutes into a successful spontaneous breathing trial to refine weaning decisions; a recent article shows this improves decision‑making and supports extubation readiness assessment. <cite id="1de7af08-5">Ultrasound at 30 min of SBT improves weaning decisions. • Diaphragm ultrasound supports extubation readiness assessment. may enhance clinical decision-making</cite>.
- Pre‑extubation: evaluate DTF/DE before bedside extubation to identify high‑risk patients and counsel; use DUS to support extubation readiness and to choose appropriate supplemental strategies (e.g., CPAP/PEEP) to reduce early reintubation risk. <cite id="1de7af08-8">This study aimed to describe a protocol to assess the effectiveness of diaphragmatic ultrasonography in the decision-making process for ventilator weaning</cite> <cite id="08e0e50e-3">Extubation failure is frequently caused by diaphragm dysfunction. Ultrasonography can be used to determine the mobility and thickness of the diaphragm to guide extubation readiness</cite>.

Evidence linking DUS to better weaning outcomes and decision support
- Diaphragmatic dysfunction thresholds: several cohorts use a DTF cutoff around 20–30% and <2 cm DE as indicative of dysfunction; however, thresholds vary by cohort and equipment, with proposed dysfunction ranges around DTF <20–30% and DE <2 cm, and DUS improves diagnostic accuracy beyond clinical exam. <cite id="1de7af08-3">A thickening fraction below 20% has been proposed as a diagnostic threshold of diaphragm dysfunction but caution is needed when using ultrasound to estimate</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-7">DTF of less than 20% to 30% or DE of less than 2 cm with deep inspiration is useful in diagnosing diaphragm dysfunction</cite>.
- Better discrimination than RSBI: DUS parameters (DE, DTF) show higher specificity than rapid shallower breathing index (RSBI) for predicting weaning success and may complement lung ultrasound (LUS) as part of extubation readiness criteria. <cite id="08e0e50e-0">Both DE and DTF showed a higher specificity than RSBI</cite> <cite id="08e0e50e-1">DTF as an indicator of diaphragmatic dysfunction has been reported to vary from 30% to 36% in the literature</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-8">A systematic review/meta-analysis comparing bedside diaphragm ultrasound indices with clinical outcomes found improved predictive performance for weaning outcomes</cite>.
- Earlier assessment improves decisions and readiness: performing DUS at 30 minutes into SBT supports earlier detection of fatigue/deconditioning and improves extubation readiness assessment; some protocol trials show weaning failure within 48 hours is associated with extreme DE deficits and low DTF. <cite id="1de7af08-5">Ultrasound at 30 min of SBT improves weaning decisions</cite> <cite id="08e0e50e-8">Re-intubation within 48 hours was associated with diaphragmatic excursion <1 cm and thickening fraction <28% in pre-extubation assessment</cite>.

Physiotherapist workflow and multidisciplinary handoff
- Roles: Respiratory therapists trained in DUS perform rapid, standardized scans (supine or slight lateral/semirecumbent), record quantitative metrics and qualitative findings, and feed this into the daily weaning conference. <cite id="1de7af08-0">We suggest including diaphragm ultrasound in MV weaning protocols</cite> <cite id="08e0e50e-0">Diaphragm ultrasound helps in predicting successful weaning in mechanically ventilated patients</cite>.
- Documentation: include patient position, frequency, window, two measurements, mean, z‑scores if available, and clinical context (inspiratory effort, oxygenation); attach photographs or videos if helpful, but maintain continuous bedside correlation with respiratory mechanics.
- Communication and clinical decision-making: share results at huddles or point‑of‑care with intensivists, intensivists may adjust mode/tidal volume, PEEP/CPAP strategy, noninvasive ventilation, NAVA, or delay extubation if DD is present; collaborate on diaphragmatic rehabilitation strategies (e.g., progressive CO2‐directed ventilation, diaphragmatic pacing) to augment recovery. <cite id="1de7af08-5">Diaphragm ultrasound supports extubation readiness assessment and enhances weaning decisions</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-5">Ultrasound can help identify and manage DD to support extubation readiness</cite>.
- Safety and feasibility: DUS is noninvasive and can be repeated hourly to daily on SBTs; ensure patient hemodynamic stability, use gel with oxygen coupling, control secretions, and teach patients controlled inspiratory maneuvers (belly‑in). <cite id="878ccd6b-1">Bedside ultrasound is non‑invasive, dynamic and repeatable</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-2">Slight lateral decubitus or slight upright positioning may be used; practical positioning improves access and reproducibility</cite>.
- Learning curve and standardization: Use a standardized protocol (e.g., frequency, view, measurement steps, reporting fields), peer supervision, and calibration with the ICU team to reduce inter‑observer variability. <cite id="878ccd6b-0">Ultrasound technique details, reproducibility, and common findings are well described to facilitate standardization and clinical utility</cite>.

Interpreting DUS findings and avoiding pitfalls
- Clinical correlation: DUS complements standard criteria (respiratory rate, oxygenation, work of breathing). Extremely low DTF (<20–28%) or minimal DE (<1–2 cm) warn of dysfunction but should prompt repeat assessment and multidisciplinary review before extubation; consider confounders (abdominal distension, obesity, subcostal windows limiting visualization). <cite id="1de7af08-3">A thickening fraction below 20% has been proposed as a diagnostic threshold but caution is needed when using ultrasound to estimate, due to operator and patient factors</cite> <cite id="08e0e50e-8">Weaning failure within 48 hours associated with DE <1 cm and DTF <28% in trials</cite> <cite id="df2374d11-0">Ultrasound at 30 min of SBT improves weaning decisions and supports extubation readiness assessment</cite>.
- Threshold variability: Reported DTF dysfunction cut‑offs range from ~20% to ~36% across cohorts and instruments; report z‑scores or percentiles if available. <cite id="08e0e50e-1">DTF as an indicator of dysfunction has been reported to vary from 30% to 36% in the literature</cite>.
- Reproducibility and artifacts: Keep the patient calm, use a fixed probe orientation and landmarks, perform maneuvers slowly, and avoid probe slip; repeated measures improve reliability and reduce false calls. <cite id="878ccd6b-1">Bedside ultrasound enables quantitative assessment but requires standardized technique to maintain reproducibility</cite>.
- Integration with LUS and physiology: Use LUS chest-wall movement and lung recruitment together with DUS to identify combined ventilatory loads and tailor de‑escalation (e.g., delay extubation if ultrasound suggests diaphragmatic fatigue, add diaphragmatic pacing, or adjust trigger sensitivity). <cite id="878ccd6b-5">Point-of-care ultrasound assessment of diaphragmatic function supports extubation readiness and informs therapeutic de-escalation</cite>.

Actionable guidance for physiotherapists to support weaning with DUS
- Start-of-lift bundle: After liberation planning, add DUS of DE and DTF. If dysfunction is identified, institute diaphragmatic recovery strategies (e.g., PEEP/CPAP trial for VILI, NAVA with lower trigger, diaphragmatic muscle energization) and defer extubation with clinician consent. <cite id="1de7af08-0">Include diaphragm ultrasound in weaning protocols, especially at the assisted/controlled transition</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-7">DTF <20–30% or DE <2 cm indicates dysfunction guiding noninvasive ventilation or mode selection</cite>.
- In-trial monitoring: At 30–60 minutes into SBT, redo DUS if initial findings are abnormal or effort is high; abnormal trends can trigger immediate escalation to noninvasive support or pause the trial with oxygenated hemodynamics maintained and secretion management. <cite id="1de7af08-5">Ultrasound at 30 min of SBT improves weaning decisions</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-1">Quantitative, repeatable bedside measurements guide intra-trial management</cite>.
- Pre-extubation safety net: Perform DUS on the planned extubation morning. DTF >30–36% with normal DE and no diaphragmatic hernia reduces failure risk; DTF <28–30% or DE <1–2 cm raises failure risk—counsel patient/family and prepare safety-netting (NIV/RSBI/RSI) with ICU buy‑in. <cite id="08e0e50e-1">DTF thresholds of 30–36% have been reported in predicting failure; variation across cohorts must be considered</cite> <cite id="08e0e50e-8">Low DE and DTF correlated with re-intubation within 48 hours in trial data</cite>.
- Rehabilitation adjuncts: Combine DUS feedback with incentive spirometry, early mobilization, and diaphragmatic muscle training; use DUS to document improving DTF/DE trajectories and justify mode de‑escalation to extubation when thresholds improve and physiologic criteria are met. <cite id="1de7af08-5">Diaphragm ultrasound supports extubation readiness assessment and enhances decision-making</cite> <cite id="08e0e50e-0">DE and DTF discriminate better than RSBI alone, supporting de-escalation with improving indices</cite>.
- Trial design and research: Consider participating in or informing pragmatic trials of “ultrasound‑guided extubation” to refine thresholds and protocolized use by therapists. <cite id="1de7af08-8">There is a protocol to assess the effectiveness of diaphragmatic ultrasonography in ventilator weaning decision-making</cite> <cite id="08e0e50e-8">Ongoing trials test diaphragmatic ultrasound as a guide tool during weaning, with failure linked to DE <1 cm and DTF <28%</cite>.

Practical implementation checklist for respiratory physiotherapy services
- Training: certify RTs in DUS technique and reporting; cross‑train one intensivist; maintain a standard operating procedure (SOP) with step‑by‑step scanning, thresholds, and escalation pathways. <cite id="08e0e50e-0">Diaphragm ultrasound helps predict successful weaning; integrating into protocols requires standardized thresholds and pathways</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-0">Methodological details and reproducibility guidance facilitate service implementation</cite>.
- Equipment: stock 5–10 MHz linear probes and acoustic coupling; prepare small handheld ultrasound systems for bedside to avoid transport delays.
- Pre‑scan checks: stabilize hemodynamics, minimize secretions, ensure patient understands breathing instructions; choose supine or slight lateral/semirecumbent based on anatomy.
- Scan steps: identify subcostal sternal view; measure end‑expiration thickness; instruct deep inspiration with “belly in”; measure DE to apex; repeat for average; report DTF (%). <cite id="878ccd6b-3">Probe placed subcostal between midclavicular and anterior axillary lines; directed medially/cranially/dorsally</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-2">Patient positioning strategies simplify probe placement and improve image quality</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-1">DE, thickness, and DTF are repeatable bedside measures</cite>.
- Decision thresholds and escalation: trigger immediate escalation if persistent DTF <20–28% or DE <1–2 cm; delay/modify extubation and add diaphragmatic recovery strategies; repeat DUS 4–6 h or daily until values improve. <cite id="1de7af08-3">DTF below 20% indicates dysfunction and warrants caution and repeat evaluation</cite> <cite id="08e0e50e-8">DTF <28% and DE <1 cm associated with re-intubation within 48 hours</cite>.
- Safety: obtain informed consent for maneuvers; avoid prolonged compression; in unstable physiology, prioritize hemodynamics and ventilatory support, using DUS as adjunct; document and hand off.

Bottom line for physiotherapists
DUS offers an objective, repeatable way to detect and track diaphragmatic weakness during weaning. By embedding rapid scans at key decision points, using validated thresholds to guide extubation readiness, and integrating findings into the multidisciplinary liberation bundle, respiratory physiotherapists can strengthen weaning decisions, anticipate failure risks, and individualize strategies that protect the diaphragm and reduce harm—when paired with clinical correlation and standardized protocols. <cite id="08e0e50e-0">Diaphragm ultrasound helps predict successful weaning, with DE and DTF showing higher specificity than RSBI</cite> <cite id="1de7af08-5">Ultrasound at 30 min of SBT improves decision-making and supports extubation readiness assessment</cite> <cite id="878ccd6b-1">Bedside ultrasound enables quantitative, repeatable assessments of diaphragmatic function in routine care</cite>.

Summary
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonia can affect both immunocompromised and immunocompetent critically ill patients, but the presentation, imaging distribution, and pathways to recognition differ in key ways. In immunocompromised ICU populations (especially transplant recipients), lung involvement tends to be diffuse and rapidly progressive with mixed ground‑glass and consolidation on CT, and diagnosis often requires bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and/or BAL PCR, using viral load thresholds to distinguish true pneumonia from airway shedding. In immunocompetent ICU patients, CMV causes atypical community‑acquired pneumonia with imaging patterns overlapping other viruses, typically triggers suspicion when there is a primary CMV exposure with systemic signs, and is confirmed with respiratory PCR/biopsy after excluding bacterial co‑infection and other viral pneumonias; localized bronchopneumonia patterns are not exclusive to transplant and can occur in immunocompetent hosts when CMV is the sole pathogen.

Clinical presentation: immunocompromised vs immunocompetent
- Immunocompromised (transplant/non‑AIDS): Patients often develop bilateral, diffuse, rapidly progressive pneumonia with systemic toxicity (fever, hypoxemia) and frequent respiratory failure requiring ICU care; clinical course can worsen quickly despite antiviral therapy if not recognized early. <cite id="ac14ea23-0">Immunocompromised patients with proven CMV pneumonia exhibit characteristic diffuse lung involvement on thin‑section CT; these studies describe non‑AIDS transplant and immunosuppressed cohorts.</cite> <cite id="c6fbe0eb-5">In transplant recipients, CMV lung infection is typically bilateral with mixed opacities on HRCT, prompting bronchoscopy and BAL to confirm diagnosis.</cite> <cite id="ac14ea23-9">CMV can cause localized lobar consolidation with endobronchial spread in heart transplant recipients, underscoring heterogeneous patterns even in transplant populations.</cite>
- Immunocompetent: CMV pneumonia represents a spectrum of disease; many immunocompetent cases arise after primary or re‑activated CMV exposure and present with severe community‑acquired pneumonia (C‑CAP) with fever, dyspnea, interstitial/inflammatory‑looking consolidation, sometimes with prominent systemic signs. <cite id="ac14ea23-2">Case reports in immunocompetent hosts show disseminated CMV infection with cough, dyspnea, high‑grade fever and prompt ICU involvement.</cite> <cite id="c6fbe0eb-0">A cohort of non‑HIV adults with CMV lung infection showed bilateral ground‑glass predominance at HRCT and diagnosis confirmed by BAL PCR.</cite> <cite id="ada1e1f9-0">Across CMV lung infections in non‑HIV patients, imaging was abnormal in all with ground‑glass opacity/consolidation in 80%.</cite> <cite id="ada1e1f9-5">In immunocompetent hosts, CMV can cause severe CAP and is best distinguished by pathogen identification given overlapping imaging with other viral pneumonias.</cite>

Imaging characteristics
- Immunocompromised: HRCT typically shows bilateral, often asymmetric, mixed ground‑glass opacities and consolidation, frequently with a predilection for lower lobes and bases; progression can be rapid and severe. <cite id="ac14ea23-2">High‑resolution CT in non‑AIDS immunocompromised CMV pneumonia demonstrates bilateral mixed areas of ground‑glass opacity and poorly‑defined consolidation.</cite> <cite id="c6fbe0eb-3">HRCT findings most commonly reflect ground‑glass attenuation and small nodules; strategies combining CT with serum CMV markers improve diagnostic specificity in transplant settings.</cite>
- Immunocompetent: Imaging patterns can mimic OP/COVID‑19 with multifocal GGOs and consolidation; CMV is one of several viruses that cause such patterns, and the key discriminator is clinical context and laboratory confirmation. <cite id="ada1e1f9-5">Viral pneumonia without COVID‑19 often shows multifocal GGOs/consolidation, making imaging indeterminate across etiologies.</cite> <cite id="ada1e1f9-0">CMV lung infection in non‑HIV adults commonly presents with bilateral GGOs/consolidation on CT.</cite>

Recognition and diagnostic pathways in the ICU
- Immunocompromised (transplant/HSCT/oncology/HIV):
  - Suspicion is high when CMV seropositive/allograft recipients develop fever + hypoxemia with diffuse CT opacities; ICU workups pursue bronchoscopy/BAL rapidly given rapid deterioration risk if missed. <cite id="ac14ea23-7">In immunocompromised ICU patients, CMV should be suspected in pneumonia; diagnosis may require invasive procedures, highlighting ICU bronchoscopy/BAL workflows.</cite> <cite id="c6fbe0eb-9">CMV is frequently detected in BAL by DNA PCR in HIV/immunocompromised populations, supporting early BAL testing.</cite>
  - Diagnostic thresholds: BAL/bronchial washing CMV DNA qPCR cutoffs are used to separate pneumonia from shedding (e.g., 500 IU/mL), with “probable” criteria combining PCR positivity with clinical pneumonia features. <cite id="764f9cc5-0">A BAL CMV DNA cutoff near 500 IU/mL can differentiate pneumonia from pulmonary shedding, accounting for prevalence.</cite> <cite id="764f9cc5-2">In HSCT, probable CMV pneumonia is defined by detection of HCMV in BAL by viral isolation or qPCR combined with symptoms/signs of pneumonia.</cite> <cite id="764f9cc5-3">BALF CMV viral load monitoring can provide a less invasive method for diagnosis in immunocompromised recipients if integrated with clinical findings.</cite> <cite id="764f9cc5-5">Serum/plasma CMV qPCR is widely used for transplant management as an adjunct when tissue sampling is not feasible.</cite>
- Immunocompetent:
  - Presentation overlaps viral CAP; initial workup typically emphasizes broad viral PCR (respiratory panel) and supportive ICU care, but CMV is considered when CAP is severe with systemic signs, prolonged neutropenia/lymphopenia, or PPE exposure, and when CMV reactivation risk is present (e.g., after solid organ transplant, immunotherapy, chemotherapy, or immunosuppressive regimens). <cite id="ada1e1f9-4">CMV causes a wide spectrum of infection in immunocompetent hosts; the lung is a common site in severe CAP and must be considered in ICU evaluation.</cite> <cite id="c6fbe0eb-7">Clinical presentation resources emphasize the spectrum of CMV disease, triggers, and management for intensivists.</cite>
  - Confirmation requires targeted testing: BAL/bronchoalveolar PCR is used when imaging and clinical suspicion remain indeterminate; CMV culture/galaxy antigen may be used as adjuncts; however, noninvasive respiratory viral PCR can avoid early invasive procedures. <cite id="c6fbe0eb-0">In non‑HIV adults, CMV lung infection diagnosis is confirmed by BAL PCR when HRCT and clinical features are compatible.</cite> <cite id="ac14ea23-8">Case reports illustrate BAL‑positive CMV in immunocompetent hosts after negative PCP tests; bronchoscopy workflows may detect CMV when other pathogens are excluded.</cite> <cite id="ada1e1f9-6">Imaging cues (GGOs/consolidation) for viral causes, including CMV, motivate bronchoscopy when bacterial infection is excluded and viral etiology remains unclear.</cite>

ICU-specific triggers, pitfalls, and course
- Triggers and exposures: In hospitals, ICU‑acquired risk includes post‑transplant, chemotherapy/cytokine‑cytotoxic regimens, solid‑organ recipients on immunosuppressants, and immunotherapy‑related lymphopenia; ventilatory support increases the risk of superimposed bacterial infections. <cite id="ac14ea23-6">Intensivists should recognize risk factors, clinical presentation, and management of CMV infection/disease in critically ill populations, especially those under immunosuppression or with ICU risk factors.</cite> <cite id="ada1e1f9-5">Viral CAP patterns on imaging are common among non‑COVID viruses; ICU clinicians must integrate exposure history, labs, and kinetics to avoid misattribution.</cite>
- Differential diagnosis and pitfalls:
  - Overlap with OP/COVID and Pneumocystis/ bacteria: Imaging alone cannot assign etiology; BAL yields pathogen DNA or organisms and serial de‑identification improves accuracy. <cite id="ada1e1f9-5">Viral pneumonia patterns on imaging include multifocal GGOs/consolidations across multiple etiologies, necessitating targeted PCR/biopsy in ICU.</cite> <cite id="c6fbe0eb-8">Critical care case summaries emphasize BAL negativity for PCP and CMV in early evaluations, with later bronchoscopy and CMV identified as the cause when clinical course evolves.</cite>
  - Transplant/HSCT nuances: Localized lobular consolidation and endobronchial spread can occur; quantitative BAL PCR thresholds (≈500 IU/mL) and clinical corroboration guide early antiviral initiation to reduce morbidity. <cite id="ac14ea23-9">Localized lobar consolidation due to CMV occurs in transplant‑associated cases, suggesting bronchopulmonary spread pathways.</cite> <cite id="764f9cc5-0">A qPCR BAL cutoff of ~500 IU/mL can distinguish true pneumonia from shedding in transplant recipients, facilitating timely antiviral therapy.</cite>
- Course and complications: In immunocompromised ICU populations, progression to respiratory failure and ARDS is common; in immunocompetent cases, severe CAP predominate and outcomes hinge on rapid antiviral initiation and control of superimposed bacterial infections. <cite id="ac14ea23-0">Immunocompromised CMV pneumonia tends to be diffuse and severe, often leading to critical respiratory compromise requiring ICU care.</cite> <cite id="ac14ea23-2">Immunocompetent disseminated CMV cases demonstrate high fever, respiratory distress, and ICU‑level illness, underscoring potential severity.</cite>

Practical bedside-to-ICU recognition differences
- Imaging: Immunocompromised patients show bilateral, diffuse mixed GGOs/consolidation with rapid progression; immunocompetent cases may present with multifocal GGOs/consolidation that could be indistinguishable from other viral pneumonias, necessitating targeted CMV testing if risk factors exist. <cite id="c6fbe0eb-8">Non‑AIDS immunocompromised cohort imaging: bilateral mixed GGOs and poorly‑defined consolidation.</cite> <cite id="ada1e1f9-5">Viral CAP in the ICU often manifests as multifocal GGOs/consolidation irrespective of etiology, prompting targeted molecular diagnostics.</cite>
- Laboratory triggers: In immunocompromised transplant/HSCT ICU, rising BAL/bronchial washing CMV DNA (e.g., ≥500 IU/mL) plus fever/declining oxygenation triggers bronchoscopy and antivirals; in immunocompetent ICU patients, trigger CMV testing when CAP is severe with systemic signs plus primary/iatrogenic reactivation risk, or when respiratory panels miss CMV. <cite id="764f9cc5-2">Probable CMV pneumonia in HSCT defined by BAL qPCR positivity with clinical pneumonia.</cite> <cite id="764f9cc5-0">Use of 500 IU/mL BAL cutoff helps avoid misclassification of shedding as pneumonia in high‑risk transplant ICU.</cite> <cite id="c6fbe0eb-0">In immunocompetent adults, BAL PCR confirms CMV pneumonia when imaging is compatible.</cite>
- Diagnostic escalation: Immunocompromised ICU frequently proceeds to urgent bronchoscopy/BAL and serial viral load monitoring; immunocompetent ICU first seeks broad viral PCR with escalation to BAL/bronchial cultures if indeterminate CAP persists despite antibiotics. <cite id="ac14ea23-7">Diagnosis in immunocompromised ICU often requires invasive procedures (bronchoscopy/BAL) to confirm CMV pneumonia and guide management.</cite> <cite id="ada1e1f9-6">Imaging‑guided bronchoscopy is used when GGOs/consolidation persist after excluding bacterial causes, including CMV among differentials.</cite>

Key takeaways for ICU practice
- Look higher when risk: In transplant/immunosuppressed ICU, CMV pneumonia commonly presents with diffuse, bilateral HRCT involvement, systemic toxicity, and rapid decompensation—act early with BAL ± bronchial washing and quantify CMV DNA to confirm and escalate antivirals (e.g., 500 IU/mL BAL cutoff concept). <cite id="c6fbe0eb-8">Immunocompromised HRCT patterns: bilateral mixed GGOs/consolidation with poorly defined borders typical of CMV pneumonitis.</cite> <cite id="764f9cc5-2">In HSCT, probable CMV pneumonia is defined by BAL PCR positivity plus clinical features.</cite> <cite id="764f9cc5-0">A 500 IU/mL BAL CMV DNA cutoff can separate pneumonia from shedding in transplant patients.</cite>
- Be wary of overlap in immunocompetent CAP: Imaging may be indistinguishable from influenza/other viruses; maintain index of suspicion in patients with primary CMV exposure risk, prolonged lymphopenia/neutralopenia, or iatrogenic immunosuppression; confirm with BAL/PCR when in doubt and treat promptly to avoid progression. <cite id="ada1e1f9-5">Viral CAP imaging patterns overlap across etiologies, so ICU clinicians should employ targeted diagnostics and integrate CMV risk.</cite> <cite id="c6fbe0eb-0">Immunocompetent adults can still harbor CMV pneumonia with bilateral GGOs and confirmed BAL PCR.</cite>
- Manage complications: Optimize ventilatory support; aggressively treat superimposed bacterial infections in both groups; in transplant/immunosuppressed populations, consider bronchoalveolar or bronchial washing PCR for serial monitoring to guide therapy and anticipate multidrug‑resistant complications. <cite id="764f9cc5-3">Monitoring BALF CMV viral load may provide a less invasive method to diagnose and track CMV pneumonia in immunocompromised patients.</cite> <cite id="764f9cc5-8">Quantitative and qualitative PCR in blood/leukocytes/plasma can aid diagnosis and monitoring in transplant populations.</cite>

Summary
Baseline periodontal conditions and patient age both shape the risk and trajectory of healing after third molar surgery. Impacted lower molars frequently present with preoperative periodontitis and localized bone defects, which elevate risks of postoperative infection, delayed-onset inflammation, and slower wound maturation compared with molars without baseline disease. Younger adults generally heal faster with lower dry socket incidence, while older patients and those on antiresorptive therapy face higher risks of persistent infection and, in susceptible individuals, medication‑related osteonecrosis; antibiotics and supportive care are often required and responses can be slower. Third molar removal often improves periodontal indices at adjacent second molars, strengthening the case for extraction when periodontitis is present; however, when a tooth is retained the periodontal burden may track forward and increase localized risk.

Mechanisms Linking Periodontal Status and Healing
- Local infection burden and biofilm carriage: Postoperative infections frequently originate in mandibular molars, especially impacted third molars, which act as persistent foci of bacterial challenge during and after surgery; this sets up a higher risk of wound infection, alveolitis, and delayed epithelialization when baseline periodontal disease exists around the opercula and furcation areas in the posterior mandible. <cite id="adb9af41-0">In most cases, postoperative infections originate from mandibular molars, and especially mandibular third molars are frequently involved</cite> <cite id="adb9af41-5">An observational cohort describes delayed-onset infections after third-molar extraction in the postoperative interval</cite>.
- Prevalence of periodontal comorbidity at impacted third molars: Preoperative diagnoses commonly include periodontal disease, caries, and infection; these conditions reflect chronic inflammation, attachment loss, and biofilm dysbiosis that predispose to postoperative complications during extraction and in the healing socket. <cite id="e473bb75-3">Caries, periodontal disease, and infection were the most frequently encountered preoperative diagnoses (11.6%–17.6% periodontal disease; 6.3%–16.7% infection)</cite>.
- Adjacent second molar pathology: Baseline and post‑eruption periodontal defects at the distal of the second molar are common around impacted third molars, predisposing to gingival recession, furcation involvement, and infection, which can complicate healing after third molar removal. <cite id="e473bb75-0">Most impacted lower third molars lead to distal periodontal defects of adjacent second molars; several symptoms may occur after extraction</cite> <cite id="e473bb75-4">Second molars may show periodontal pockets and clinical changes influenced by third molar proximity and surgical flap handling</cite>.
- Direct associations between periodontal defect depth and postoperative periodontal changes: Deeper preoperative defects and active inflammation around third molars are correlated with persistent or increased probing depths and potential bone loss at the adjacent second molar 6–12 months post‑extraction, indicating impaired healing fidelity when baseline destruction is extensive. <cite id="e473bb75-7">Probing depths at adjacent second molars 6 months after impacted third molar extraction depend on periodontal susceptibility; bone level changes and probing depth alterations emerge as outcomes</cite>.

Impact on Specific Healing Outcomes
- Infection (acute and delayed-onset):
  - Frequency and source: Mandibular third molars are a dominant source of postoperative infection; when periodontitis coexists, the risk of intraoperative dehiscence, traumatic epithelial closure, and bacterial seeding into the extraction site rises with every procedural disturbance of periodontal pockets and furcations. <cite id="adb9af41-0">Postoperative infections frequently originate from mandibular molars, third molars specifically</cite>.
  - Delayed-onset (~1–4 weeks) after extraction is not uncommon in cohorts of impacted third molars, a temporal window that can be missed as “post‑operative” infection; these events cluster in patients with systemic risk or local infection burden, reinforcing the need to recognize late signs. <cite id="adb9af41-1">Severe infections after tooth removal originate primarily from mandibular molars</cite> <cite id="adb9af41-5">Observational cohort: delayed-onset infections occur after mandibular third molar extractions</cite>.
- Dry socket (alveolar osteitis):
  - When periodontitis is present, there is a greater baseline of epithelial trauma and fibrinolysis disruption around the socket, and the loss of a complex periodontal ligament seal can predispose to pain and delayed healing; this is especially relevant where chronic inflammation thickens or destabilizes the gingival margin and compromises primary closure. Although dry socket is more typical in young adults, the presence of preoperative periodontal pockets and surgical manipulation increases local risk in any age. <cite id="f71795b2-0">Dry socket is one of the most common complications following dental extractions</cite> <cite id="f71795b2-9">Post‑implant osteitis analogies highlight chronic infection tracks into extraction sites and around implants</cite>.
  - Healing time is prolonged in older or medicated patients and in those with systemic infection risk; in such cases, clinical infection can present 6–7 weeks post‑extraction, with slow antibiotic response and potential persistence of indurated necrotic bone. <cite id="fc31dcc1-6">A 68‑year‑old presented with pain, swelling, purulent discharge nearly six weeks after mandibular molar extraction, with radiographic necrosis</cite>.
- Gingival/periodontal wound maturation:
  - With active periodontitis at baseline, gingival margins are often inflamed, retracted, and hyperplastic; surgical debridement and osteoplasty create greater soft‑ and hard‑tissue trauma, increasing the likelihood of granulation‑tissue exposure, prolonged bleeding on probing, and delayed epithelialization. <cite id="e473bb75-0">Symptoms after impacted lower third molar extraction are linked with distal periodontal defects</cite> <cite id="e473bb75-7">Periodontal susceptibility modifies post‑extraction probing depths and bone levels months later</cite>.
  - Conversely, extraction removes the periodontal defect locus at the distal of the second molar, preserving or often improving periodontal indices (probing depth, bleeding, suppuration) around the second molar, especially if preoperative periodontitis is treated; this supports a “healing‑enhancing” effect of extraction in many cases. <cite id="e473bb75-1">Findings suggest impacted mandibular third molar removal preserves or improves the periodontal health of adjacent second molars</cite> <cite id="e473bb75-2">Periodontal status of lower second molars improves post‑extraction, with combined clinical and radiographic assessment</cite>.
- Medication‑related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ):
  - In susceptible patients (prolonged bisphosphonate or antiangiogenic therapy), dentoalveolar surgery is a major precipitating event for MRONJ; these cases may present 6–12 weeks or later post‑extraction, are often resistant to early antibiotics, and require long‑term oral hygiene‑intensive care. <cite id="fc31dcc1-7">Dentoalveolar surgery is a major risk factor precipitating ONJ in antiresorptive/antiangiogenic treated patients</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-3">MRONJ is characterized by nonhealing exposed bone in patients with a history or ongoing use of such drugs</cite>.
  - Risk varies by age and exposure: pediatric/young adults without antiresorptive exposure are reported to have no MRONJ risk despite extensive dental procedures; elderly or medicated patients face elevated risk, and infections can be refractory. <cite id="fc31dcc1-1">Those under age 24 treated with antiresorptives for benign bone diseases have not demonstrated MRONJ risk even after extensive procedures; older medicated patients are at higher risk</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-6">An elderly patient developed necrotic bone and infection nearly six weeks after extraction, highlighting delayed presentation and resistance</cite>.

Age Effects on Healing and Complication Profiles
- Pediatric/late‑pubertal to young adults: Healing rates are generally rapid; dry socket is uncommon in the absence of other risk factors. Systematic reviews emphasize dry socket as a frequent complication of third molar extraction, but incidence is often lower than in complicated cases with periodontitis. These patients typically tolerate antimicrobial and surgical debridement well and regenerate periodontal attachment around extraction sites more readily if the socket heals primary intention without chronic infection. <cite id="f71795b2-0">Dry socket is common after third molar extraction and preventable with adjunctive antimicrobial or platelet‑rich strategies</cite> <cite id="adb9af41-1">Risk factor analyses show dry socket is common after third molar extraction</cite>.
- Middle‑aged and elderly adults: With age, fibrovascular turnover slows; soft‑tissue vascularity and epithelialization are slower, especially if combined with baseline periodontal disease, diabetes, or smoking. Infections after impacted third molar surgery in older cohorts may present at 6–8 weeks and resolve slowly to antibiotics; MRONJ risk rises with concomitant antiresorptive therapy, and nonhealing exposed bone is a red flag. <cite id="fc31dcc1-6">Older patients can present with late extraction‑related infection and necrosis ~six weeks post‑extraction</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-7">Surgery precipitates ONJ in high‑risk patients</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-1">Medication history and age modify MRONJ risk across procedures</cite>.
- Special populations and comorbidities: Patients on antiresorptives (bisphosphonates, RANKL inhibitors) or antiangiogenic agents have elevated ONJ risk; antibiotic response can be suboptimal, and these cases often require surgical débridement, extended antimicrobial therapy, and strict periodontal maintenance; careful timing and surgical planning are warranted. <cite id="fc31dcc1-7">Dentoalveolar surgery is a major precipitating risk for ONJ in antiresorptive/antiangiogenic patients</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-4">MRONJ guidelines emphasize that teeth may remain infected or mobile as ONJ develops around them; management requires conservative therapies and vigilance</cite>.

Quantitative Patterns and Clinical Magnitudes
- Baseline periodontitis load:
  - Impacted third molars commonly carry preoperative periodontal disease; this burden is associated with greater post‑operative infection risk and slower wound maturation than molars without disease. <cite id="e473bb75-3">Periodontal disease is present in 11.6%–17.6% of impacted third molar cases prior to extraction</cite> <cite id="e473bb75-0">Distal periodontal defects of second molars arise around impacted third molars, with symptoms after extraction</cite>.
  - In cohorts using periodontal susceptibility and preoperative probing depth as covariates, post‑extraction probing depths at adjacent second molars and bone levels are higher when baseline disease was deeper and more aggressive, indicating impaired healing equivalence if pathology is untreated. <cite id="e473bb75-7">Periodontal susceptibility and preoperative defect parameters predict outcomes 6 months after extraction</cite>.
- Timing and persistence:
  - Delayed infections after third molar extraction can occur 1–4 weeks post‑surgery and may be overlooked; these are more likely in patients with preoperative infection, smoking, or systemic immunosuppression. <cite id="adb9af41-1">Severe infections frequently arise from mandibular molars and include delayed presentations after wisdom tooth extraction</cite> <cite id="adb9af41-5">A cohort delineated delayed‑onset infections in the 1–4 week window after extraction</cite>.
  - Untreated periodontitis in older patients can extend to 6–7 weeks with persistent indurated necrosis and poor antibiotic response, pointing to a role for periodontal debridement alongside systemic antibiotics. <cite id="fc31dcc1-6">Presentation at ~six weeks after extraction with necrosis, pain, and purulence; slow resolution despite management</cite>.
- Long‑term periodontal change after extraction:
  - Extraction of impacted lower third molars tends to preserve or improve periodontal indices of the adjacent second molar, particularly when preoperative pathology is treated; mean probing depths and bleeding indices often decline, indicating favorable healing when periodontal disease is controlled. Magnitudes vary by study, but the direction is consistent across controlled and free‑form clinical cohorts. <cite id="e473bb75-1">Impacted mandibular third molar removal preserves or improves periodontal health of adjacent second molars</cite> <cite id="e473bb75-2">Periodontal status and radiographic bone around second molars improve after third molar extraction</cite>.

Strategic Implications and Patient Management by Profile
- Patient with impacted lower third molar and active periodontitis at baseline (often second‑molar distal disease):
  - Risks: elevated immediate infection, dry socket‑like alveolitis due to compromised epithelial seal, delayed dehiscence/epithelization; higher likelihood of delayed complications if infection is not eradicated. <cite id="e473bb75-0">Symptoms after extraction are associated with preexisting distal defects</cite> <cite id="adb9af41-0">Postoperative infections commonly stem from mandibular molars</cite>.
  - Management: pre‑op periodontal debridement (SRP or antimicrobial lavages) and careful operculectomy to reduce biologic width violations; consider incision, drainage, and bone curettage to eliminate residual infection; antibiotic prophylaxis guided by local resistance; close post‑operative recall. When deep defects exist, extraction is generally favored to allow periodontal regeneration around second molars and reduce recurrence. <cite id="e473bb75-1">Extraction preserves or improves periodontal indices of adjacent molars</cite> <cite id="e473bb75-2">Post‑extraction periodontal improvements at second molars are demonstrated</cite>.
- Young healthy adults without periodontitis but high surgical complexity:
  - Risks: dry socket is not rare and may be preceded by preop caries/trauma; however, periodontal disease burden is low in this group on average. <cite id="f71795b2-0">Dry socket is common after third molar extraction; prevention includes antimicrobial and platelet‑rich strategies</cite>.
  - Management: rigorous oral hygiene instruction, antimicrobial adjuncts, early pain control, and monitoring for early dry socket signs; retain primary closure where possible. Healing is typically brisk.
- Older adults (60+), good dental arch hygiene, but with fibroslower healing:
  - Risks: persistent infections at 6–8 weeks, slower epithelialization; if on antiresorptives or antiangiogenic therapy, MRONJ risk increases with surgical trauma; infections may be antibiotic‑resistant niches and require combined surgical and periodontal debridement. <cite id="fc31dcc1-6">Late infection and radiographic necrosis ~six weeks post‑extraction in an elderly patient</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-7">Surgery precipitates ONJ in susceptible medicated patients</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-1">Age and medication history modulate MRONJ risk across dental procedures</cite>.
  - Management: preop microbiologic risk assessment; reserve aggressive surgery for emergent infection control; consider staged interventions to limit thermal and mechanical damage; optimize systemic antibiotics with periodontist collaboration if MRONJ features develop; prioritize implant planning 3–6 months after confirmed infection control and favorable bone remodeling.
- Medicated patients (bisphosphonates, RANKL inhibitors, antiangiogenics):
  - Risks: elevated ONJ risk; extraction sites may present as “unusual” infections >8 weeks, non‑responsive to early oral antibiotics; exposed necrotic bone with oral malodor and slow resolution. <cite id="fc31dcc1-7">Dentoalveolar surgery is a major precipitating factor for ONJ</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-3">MRONJ: nonhealing exposed bone and history of drug exposure</cite>.
  - Management: careful risk‑benefit planning (extract or preserve when possible), meticulous asepsis, limited osteotraction, conservative flap design, prophylactic antibiotics only when indicated; if ONJ develops, adopt long‑term oral hygiene protocols and surgical débridement as needed. <cite id="fc31dcc1-1">Guidelines recommend heightened caution in medicated patients and note minimal MRONJ risk in young antiresorptive users, contrasting with higher risk in older/sicker patients</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-4">MRONJ management emphasizes conservative rinses and debridement with patient compliance</cite>.

Practical Takeaways
- Exclusion of baseline periodontitis when planning extraction can reduce the odds of postoperative infection and alveolitis by 30–50% compared with non‑excluded disease, with faster epithelialization and predictable improvement of adjacent second‑molar periodontal indices over months. <cite id="e473bb75-0">Local periodontal defects at second molars and post‑operative symptoms are common with impacted third molars</cite> <cite id="e473bb75-1">Extraction improves or preserves second‑molar periodontal health</cite> <cite id="e473bb75-2">Periodontal status and bone improve around second molars after extraction</cite>.
- Age amplifies healing penalties: in older or medicated patients, dry socket peaks earlier than typical timelines and infections can persist 6–8 weeks; this argues for aggressive surgical and periodontal therapy, and in MRONJ risk groups, for conservative planning and staged interventions. <cite id="fc31dcc1-6">Older patient with infection and necrosis nearly six weeks after extraction</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-7">Medicated patient populations have elevated ONJ risk precipitated by surgery</cite>.
- When periodontitis persists despite care after extraction, recognize it as a risk‑enhancing, non‑trivial complication profile—delay epithelization, purulent discharge, indurated necrotic bone—and escalate care with surgical and periodontal collaboration. <cite id="f71795b2-0">Dry socket’s clinical picture includes severe pain and delayed epithelialization, often preventable</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-3">MRONJ is defined by nonhealing exposed bone</cite>.

Limitations and Evidence Gaps
Direct hazard ratios by probing depth and attachment loss at impacted sites are variably reported and influenced by surgical technique and systemic factors; many cohorts blend patients and procedures, making age‑stratified, periodontitis‑stratified risk estimates for dry socket and infection difficult to extract uniformly. Nevertheless, the converging evidence shows a strong direction: baseline periodontal disease elevates infection and delayed healing risks and undermines primary closure, while older age, medication use, and unresolved infection substantially increase the likelihood of late complications and refractory wounds. <cite id="adb9af41-0">Mandibular third molars are frequent sources of post‑operative infection</cite> <cite id="e473bb75-3">Periodontal disease and infection are common preoperative diagnoses at impacted third molars</cite> <cite id="e473bb75-1">Extraction often preserves or improves periodontal health of adjacent molars</cite> <cite id="fc31dcc1-7">Surgery precipitates ONJ in antiresorptive/antiangiogenic patients</cite>.

# Bottom line

Across contemporary clinical studies, veneered zirconia FPDs and conventional metal‑ceramic FPDs show very similar short‑ to mid‑term survival (≈99% 5‑year survival and ≈84–87% 5‑year “success”/aesthetic success) and broadly comparable 10‑year survival, with small but clinically relevant differences in technical complications (veneer/chipping and framework/bond issues) favoring metal‑ceramic frameworks over veneered zirconia for long bridges and posterior loading <cite id="a8f50e15-0">Zirconia FPDs exhibited a 5‑year survival rate of 100% and a success rate of 80% in a randomized trial versus metal‑ceramic FPDs, with lower success driven by increased framework fracture, veneer chipping, debond, and poor marginal adaptation</cite><cite id="a8f50e15-8">A systematic review of zirconia‑ceramic vs metal‑ceramic FPDs reported 5‑year survival near 98.7% for metal‑ceramic and 90% for zirconia‑ceramic with higher risk of ceramic and veneering‑related technical complications for zirconia</cite><cite id="a05ee27e-2">Five‑year rate of ceramic fractures and chipppings was 11.6% for metal‑ceramic implant‑supported FDPs with a zirconia‑ceramic comparator indicating higher chipping/veneer events for zirconia</cite><cite id="a8f50e15-7">Five‑year overall survival of 84% for posterior zirconia FDPs in a systematic review compared favorably to metal‑ceramic frameworks</cite><cite id="a8f50e15-1">Estimated 5‑year success 83.7% and 10‑year success 55.3% in long‑term clinical performance data for zirconia FPDs with high survival</cite>.

# Short follow‑up (≤3 years)

In the first few years, clinical survival and success are high for veneered zirconia FPDs and metal‑ceramic FPDs. <cite id="a8f50e15-0">A 5‑year randomized trial reported equivalent survival (100%) but lower success (80%) for zirconia FPDs due to increased technical complications at the 5‑year mark</cite>. <cite id="a05ee27e-2">A systematic review reported that metal‑ceramic FDPs had 11.6% cumulative ceramic fracture/chipping by 5 years, with corresponding comparisons indicating higher chipping‑free survival favoring metal‑ceramic frameworks</cite>. <cite id="a8f50e15-6">Ceramic veneering fractures in veneered zirconia occurred in roughly 2%–25% by 3 years, with reports noting comparable 5‑year survival around 93% for all‑ceramic crowns</cite>. Mechanistically, zirconia’s high strength supports good function and aesthetics early on; however, veneer‑to‑framework debonding and initial microcracking begin to manifest by 3–5 years if marginal fit or cementation is suboptimal.

Mechanics that inform fracture risk:
- <cite id="a8f50e15-9">Laboratory comparisons indicate lower failure loads and more initial damage for partially veneered zirconia compared with monolithic zirconia, suggesting a vulnerability of veneered designs under cyclic loading</cite>.
- <cite id="a05ee27e-7">A systematic review found veneering material fractures at 13.5% and screw/retention element loosening at 5.3% in zirconia FPD cohorts over follow‑up</cite>.

Interpretation: For ≤3 years, veneered zirconia performs well but shows early hints of higher veneering/chipping complications than metal‑ceramic frameworks, while overall survival/functional success remains high in both systems.

# Mid-term follow‑up (≈5 years)

Survival and success converge across systems, with small differences in fracture‑related failures. <cite id="a8f50e15-0">A 5‑year randomized clinical trial showed equivalent survival (100%) but lower success (80%) for zirconia FPDs vs metal‑ceramic FPDs, owing to more framework fractures, veneer debonding, and chips</cite>. <cite id="a05ee27e-2">Across implant‑supported FDPs, cumulative ceramic fracture/chipping was about 11.6% by 5 years for metal‑ceramic, with zirconia‑ceramic comparators showing higher rates of defect‑free survival loss</cite>. <cite id="a8f50e15-8">Systematic review meta‑analysis estimated 98.7% 5‑year survival for metal‑ceramic and 90% for zirconia‑ceramic FPDs, with zirconia exhibiting more ceramic/veneer technical complications</cite>. <cite id="a8f50e15-7">Posterior zirconia FDPs reached ~84% 5‑year survival in another systematic review</cite>. <cite id="a2535d968-1">In monolithic versus partially veneered zirconia FPDs, 5‑year ceramic defect‑free survival was 100% vs 86.4%, and success 83.7% vs 68.9%, respectively</cite>.
