Interpretation: By 5 years, survival gaps between veneered zirconia and metal‑ceramic are negligible overall, but zirconia shows a higher incidence of veneering defects (chips, cracks, debond) and framework fractures than metal‑ceramic frameworks, especially in multi‑unit posterior FPDs. This reflects the zirconia’s ceramic veneer’s susceptibility to microcrack coalescence and cement‑layer failure under long‑term occlusal and parafunctional loads.

# Long-term follow‑up (≥7–10 years)

Evidence remains scarcer but suggests a relative disadvantage of veneered zirconia in very long‑term durability due to veneer/chipping and framework fracture risks, whereas metal‑ceramic frameworks maintain high survival. <cite id="a8f50e15-1">Clinical performance to 10 years reported 55.3% “success” for zirconia FPDs with high survival at 5 years, underscoring a rightward shift of failures over time</cite>. <cite id="a05ee27e-5">A 10‑year randomized trial summary noted significantly higher rates in zirconia FPDs for framework fracture, debonding, major veneering ceramic fractures, and marginal inadequacy</cite>. <cite id="a33f19275-9">A systematic review across 13 studies (945 metal‑ceramic, 41 zirconia‑ceramic) reported a 10‑year survival of 86% for metal‑ceramic FDPs and 74% for zirconia‑ceramic, with higher risk of ceramic/veneer fractures and chippings</cite><cite id="a05ee27e-2">In the same dataset, 5‑year survival reached 98.7% for metal‑ceramic and 90% for zirconia‑ceramic, with zirconia showing higher chipping/defect‑free survival attrition</cite>. <cite id="a05ee27e-3">Reported 5‑year survival for posterior zirconia FDPs was ≈94%, but cumulative clinical and mechanical issues can lower long‑term survivorship</cite>.

Interpretation: Over ≥7–10 years, veneered zirconia FPDs show higher cumulative incidence of technical fractures/chips and debonding than metal‑ceramic frameworks, translating into lower long‑term survival/“success,” unless prostheses load on monolithic zirconia or are carefully cemented with optimized retention.

# Comparators and mechanisms across frameworks

- Veneered zirconia vs metal‑ceramic FPDs: <cite id="a8f50e15-0">Direct randomized evidence at 5 years showed equal survival but significantly higher “success” failures in veneered zirconia due to more framework fractures, veneer chippings/debonding, and marginal issues</cite>. <cite id="a8f50e15-8">Systematic review meta‑analysis corroborated better survival for metal‑ceramic and more frequent veneering/esthetic complications for zirconia‑ceramic FPDs</cite>.
- Monolithic vs partially veneered zirconia: <cite id="a2535d968-1">5‑year ceramic defect‑free survival of 100% (monolithic) vs 86.4% (partially veneered) highlights the vulnerability of veneered designs to fracture initiation at metal‑ceramic interfaces and ceramic microcrack propagation</cite>.
- Veneered zirconia vs all‑ceramic crowns: <cite id="a8f50e15-6">Reported veneer veneering fracture of 2%–25% by 3 years and ≈93% 5‑year survival for all‑ceramic crowns suggests that, for single‑tooth crowns, ceramic‑only frameworks achieve similar short‑term survival with potentially fewer veneer‑specific complications</cite>. <cite id="a8f50e15-7">However, posterior zirconia FDP survival around 84% by 5 years indicates that framework configuration and axial load distribution are key determinants</cite>.

Mechanisms:
- <cite id="a05ee27e-7">Fracture and chipping of veneering ceramic occur in ≈13.5% and screw/loosening in ≈5.3% in zirconia FDP cohorts</cite>.
- <cite id="a8f50e15-9">Failure load and initial microdamage data align with higher risk of veneer‑initiated fractures in partially veneered zirconia than in monolithic designs</cite>.
- Cement/bond interface and marginal fit are recurrent weak points for veneered zirconia under long loading cycles, explaining chipping/debond patterns over time <cite id="a8f50e15-0">increased debond and veneer loss</cite><cite id="a05ee27e-3">bond strength limitations noted for zirconia FDPs</cite>.

# Clinical takeaways by period

- ≤3 years: 
  - Similar survival; watch for first signs of veneer microcracks/chips and marginal issues; zirconia‑veneer complications may manifest as chip‑free survival loss but functional/esthetic success remains high <cite id="a8f50e15-6">veneer fractures 2%–25% by 3 years</cite><cite id="a8f50e15-0">initially equal survival, later success undermined by zirconia‑specific failures</cite>.
- 5 years:
  - Overall survival comparable; survival/esthetics slightly lower for veneered zirconia due to cumulative veneering and cement‑related failures; metal‑ceramic frameworks show edge in chipping‑ and debonding‑free survival <cite id="a8f50e15-0">100% survival vs 80% success for zirconia at 5 years</cite><cite id="a05ee27e-2">11.6% ceramic fracture/chipping for metal‑ceramic by 5 years in a comparative setting</cite><cite id="a8f50e15-8">90% survival for zirconia vs 98.7% for metal‑ceramic at 5 years</cite>.
- 7–10 years:
  - Veneered zirconia FPDs show higher cumulative fracture/chipping and debond rates; survival advantage shifts to metal‑ceramic frameworks in heavy function and multi‑unit posterior reconstructions; careful cementation, ferrule preparation, and load management remain critical for zirconia survival <cite id="a8f50e15-1">10‑year success 55.3% for zirconia, high 5‑year survival</cite><cite id="a05ee27e-5">10‑year RCT summary: higher framework fracture, debonding, and major veneering fractures for zirconia</cite><cite id="a33f19275-9">10‑year survival 86% metal‑ceramic vs 74% zirconia‑ceramic</cite>.

# Practical guidance

- For short‑term rehabilitation: either material achieves high survival if margins and cementation are optimized; zirconia offers excellent aesthetics but requires vigilant monitoring for veneer fractures and debonding <cite id="a05ee27e-2">chipping/defect rates and their implications</cite><cite id="a8f50e15-0">early success undermined by technical failures</cite>.
- For posterior multi‑unit bridges or heavy parafunctional loads: metal‑ceramic frameworks have evidence of better chipping/debond resistance over 5–10 years, translating to higher long‑term success and survival; choose monolithic zirconia or fully ceramic frameworks when possible for the abutment teeth to mitigate veneer stress concentrators <cite id="a8f50e15-0">more framework/debond failures in zirconia</cite><cite id="a8f50e15-9">lower failure loads in partially veneered zirconia</cite>.
- For single crowns: initial 5‑year survival is similar with all‑ceramic crowns; select ceramic‑only frameworks when esthetics and conservative preparation are paramount, but be mindful of patient parafunction and cement/bond longevity; posterior crowns benefit from metal frameworks for fracture resistance in long term <cite id="a8f50e15-6">93% 5‑year survival for all‑ceramic crowns; veneer fractures 2%–25% by 3 years</cite>.

# Uncertainties and bias

- Many head‑to‑head data are FPD vs FPD rather than explicitly crown vs crown; survival differences can reflect abutment tooth condition, treatment design, and loading, not solely the crown/ceramic framework <cite id="a05ee27e-2">study mix included implant‑supported FDPs with a zirconia comparator</cite>.
- Reporting varies in defining “success” vs “survival,” and loss to follow‑up may be asymmetric; survival curves show right‑censoring and higher dropout when complications occur <cite id="a8f50e15-0">success metric driven by technical failures in zirconia</cite><cite id="a05ee27e-7">veneer fracture and screw loosening rates summarize clinical follow‑up distributions</cite>.
- Long‑term data remain limited for cemented veneered zirconia in posterior regions beyond 10 years; reinforcement strategies (ferrule gain, 2‑slot designs, monolithic zirconia cores) may narrow gaps but require further prospective evidence <cite id="a05ee27e-3">bond strength limitations and design concerns noted</cite>.

In summary, over ≤3 years the fracture risks and survival between veneered zirconia FPDs and (metal‑ceramic or ceramic) crowns are similar, with zirconia showing early signs of more veneer/chipping complications; at 5 years survival is comparable but zirconia shows slightly higher venoer‑related failure rates; by 7–10 years, metal‑ceramic frameworks generally exhibit better survival and fewer technical fractures, especially under heavy posterior loading, while all‑ceramic crowns perform well for single units over 5 years. <cite id="a8f50e15-0">Zirconia and MC FPDs have equivalent 5‑year survival, but zirconia’s success is lower due to fracture/chip/debond</cite><cite id="a05ee27e-2">MC ceramic damage ~11.6% by 5 years with higher zirconia chippings</cite><cite id="a8f50e15-8">Systematic review: MC ~98.7% vs ZC ~90% 5‑year survival, with more zirconia veneer complications</cite><cite id="a8f50e15-1">By 10 years, zirconia success declines to ~55% while retaining high 5‑year survival</cite><cite id="a05ee27e-5">RCT meta‑summary: MC advantages in avoiding framework fracture, debonding, and major veneer fractures at 10 years</cite><cite id="a8f50e15-6">All‑ceramic crowns reach ~93% 5‑year survival with early veneer fracture rates 2%–25% by 3 years</cite>.

Summary
• Overall, adjunctive platelet-rich plasma (PRP) in maxillary sinus floor elevation produces variable effects: some histologic evidence of earlier bone maturation and reduced inflammation, but meta-analytic and trial data frequently show no clinically significant increase in hard-tissue volume or vertical height compared with bone graft alone, with uncertain benefits on long-term soft-tissue area that are inconsistent across studies.<cite id="664919ab-1">Meta-analyses found no additional beneficial effects of enriched platelet products in sinus augmentation for bone height and the percentage of soft tissue area</cite><cite id="664919ab-3,664919ab-7">Systematic meta-analyses reported no influence of PRP with bone graft on bone formation and implant survival in maxillary sinus augmentation</cite><cite id="664919ab-0">Comprehensive reviews of growth factor concentrates in sinus lift underscore that clinical gains often match bone graft plus time and periimplant maintenance, with limited additional benefit from PRP</cite>.

Effects on New Bone Formation
• Hard-tissue outcomes (height/apical fill and density at 3–6 months) show little to no advantage for PRP over bone graft alone when pooled across trials, despite biologic plausibility. A systematic review on autologous platelet concentrates reports that enriched-fibrin matrices can promote cellular proliferation and bone remodeling, but the net clinical bone-height gain in sinus augmentation remains modest and not consistently superior to graft-only approaches.<cite id="3878d692-3">Autologous growth factors released from platelet concentrates help promote bone remodeling and cell proliferation</cite><cite id="aa54eb11-1">Meta-analytic results found no additional beneficial effect of PRF compared with controls on bone height and percentage of soft tissue area</cite><cite id="664919ab-3,664919ab-7">Meta-analyses indicate no influence of PRP with bone graft on bone formation metrics in sinus augmentation</cite>.

• Mechanistic/early-bone data suggest PRP/PRF can accelerate maturation and vascularization, potentially shortening healing time, but these effects do not always translate into measurable increases in bone height by 3–6 months at harvest/implant placement. An experimental study in human maxillary sinus grafts observed increased early bone formation and a tendency to lower inflammation with PRP, yet the clinical sinuses (study design/grafting protocol) did not demonstrate a definitive increase in vertical bone height or density when compared over time.<cite id="aa54eb11-0">PRGF may lower surgical tissue inflammation, boost new bone production, and encourage bone vascularization</cite><cite id="aa54eb11-2">PRP enhanced early and late bone healing after autogenous maxillary sinus grafting in a histologic study</cite><cite id="664919ab-6">A clinical review highlights that leukocyte-rich matrices can lead to faster bone graft maturation and may shorten waiting time for implants in sinus augmentation</cite><cite id="a2d94ca0-1">Across RCTs/syntheses, healing time after sinus graft ranges 3–8 months; implant placement 3–6 months, but comparative bone-height gains of PRP over graft alone remain unproven</cite>.

• Comparative formulation appears important. Leukocyte-rich PRF (L-PRF) formulations often outperform leukocyte-poor PRP in growth factor yield and bioactivity; several clinical syntheses support faster graft maturation and earlier one-stage timing with L-PRF compared with standard PRP, although firm bone-height advantages are not uniformly demonstrated.<cite id="a2d94ca0-6">Adding leukocyte-rich PRF is associated with faster bone graft maturation and may allow shorter healing before implant placement in sinus augmentation</cite><cite id="aa54eb11-9">Recent reviews of concentrated growth factors in sinus lifts emphasize bioactive synergy with bone grafts where growth factor content and leukocyte composition modulate maturation speed</cite>.

Effects on Soft Tissue Area and Gingival Wound Healing
• Soft-tissue outcomes (gingival thickness, keratinized tissue width, recession, and “percentage of soft tissue area”) show no consistent improvement from PRP/PRF in sinus augmentation. Meta-analytic syntheses report no additional favorable effect on bone height or soft-tissue area percentage, and broader clinical summaries conclude that growth-factor–rich matrices do not reliably increase soft-tissue volume or coverage compared with grafting alone within 3–6 months.<cite id="664919ab-1">No additional beneficial effects of PRF on bone height and soft tissue area percentage in sinus augmentation</cite><cite id="664919ab-3,664919ab-7">Meta-analyses: no influence of PRP with bone graft on bone formation and implant survival; soft-tissue measures show no clear PRP benefit</cite>.

• That said, PRP/PRF can improve early wound healing and inflammation, which may transiently enhance gingival healing and reduce postoperative contour changes, but durable soft-tissue augmentation (e.g., keratinized width, marginal soft-tissue apical migration) has not been consistently observed. Contemporary clinical reviews note increased soft tissue dimension postoperatively with PRF in some cases, but these findings are heterogeneous and confounded by grafting technique and site-specific biomechanics.<cite id="aa54eb11-0">PRGF can reduce surgical tissue inflammation and promote vascularization</cite><cite id="aa54eb11-9">Platelet-rich concentrates can increase local growth factor load and may support faster tissue maturation, with reports of favorable early soft-tissue healing</cite>.

Timing, Formulation, and Survival Considerations
• Healing timelines remain the main driver of “bone formation” improvements: sinuses typically require 3–8 months to heal before graft placement and 3–6 months before implants. Where PRP/PRF show the greatest potential benefit is in shortening time-to-remodelation (particularly with leukocyte-rich matrices), enabling earlier one-stage procedures without necessarily increasing vertical bone height or density vs. graft alone.<cite id="a2d94ca0-1">Reported healing windows after bone graft (3–8 months) and implant placement (3–6 months) in sinus augmentation</cite><cite id="a2d94ca0-6">Leukocyte-rich PRF has been associated with faster maturation of grafts and shorter waiting time before implants</cite>.

• Implant survival: systematic reviews report uncertainty or at best minimal impact on implant survival with the addition of PRP. These findings caution that bone-level benefit (and thus survival) is not guaranteed by PRP adjuncts unless accompanied by demonstrable new bone formation at the sinus crest and apical fill by the edentulous interval.<cite id="664919ab-2">PRP use showed uncertain effect on survival of dental implants in sinus augmentation settings</cite><cite id="664919ab-3">Meta-analysis indicates no influence of PRP with bone graft on implant survival</cite>.

Clinical Synthesis and Practical Implications
• If the goal is new bone formation at the sinus floor, PRP/PRF is supportive but not transformative compared with autogenous bone graft plus time and meticulous surgical technique. Clinicians should expect gradual bone fill into the graft space over 3–6 months, with modest advantages when using leukocyte-rich, fibrin-based matrices, but without consistent, large increases in bone height or density over graft-only protocols. Persistent differences in outcomes likely require high-quality randomized trials with standardized timing, graft volumes, and imaging read methods.<cite id="664919ab-0">Contemporary reviews conclude that growth factor concentrates, including PRP, yield limited additional benefit beyond autogenous bone graft and predictable healing timelines</cite><cite id="a2d94ca0-6">Leukocyte-rich platelet concentrates may shorten healing while achieving similar graft-bone formation end points</cite><cite id="664919ab-1">Meta-analyses show no improvement in bone height and soft-tissue area percentage with PRF/PRP</cite>.

• For soft tissue area, PRP/PRF may aid early gingival wound healing and reduce postoperative recession or contour defects, but sustained increases in keratinized tissue width or overall soft-tissue area are inconsistent. Expect modest, case-dependent gains rather than predictable augmentation; practitioners targeting soft-tissue thickness should combine platelet therapy with flap management, primary closure, and guided tissue strategies, recognizing that PRP should not be viewed as a substitute for soft-tissue augmentation procedures.<cite id="aa54eb11-0">PRP-like platelet concentrates reduce inflammation and support vascularization, aiding gingival healing</cite><cite id="664919ab-1">No additional soft tissue area benefit detected in meta-analyses</cite><cite id="aa54eb11-9">Platelet-rich fibrin has been reported favorable for bone formation processes in grafted maxillae, consistent with improved tissue remodeling</cite>.

• Safety and feasibility: platelet concentrates are autologous, low-risk, and compatible with most bone grafts and membranes. Adverse events are rare when standard aseptic techniques are used, but exaggerated soft-tissue reactions are possible with leukocyte-rich products; patient expectations should be managed regarding magnitude and duration of soft-tissue gains.<cite id="aa54eb11-0">PRP/PRGF are autologous, reduce inflammation during surgery, and can accelerate vascularization</cite><cite id="aa54eb11-9">Clinical reviews document favorable biological effects and integration with bone grafts</cite>.

Bottom line for LeFort I sinus elevation/ridge augmentation:
1) New bone formation: PRP/PRF likely accelerates early bone maturation and remodeling within the graft space and may shorten healing, but the average increase in vertical bone height or sinus-floor density at 3–6 months is small or indistinguishable from bone graft alone; most meta-analyses detect no significant improvement in hard-tissue endpoints attributable to PRP.<cite id="aa54eb11-2">Histologic studies: PRP increases early bone formation</cite><cite id="664919ab-1,664919ab-3,664919ab-7">Meta-analyses: no PRP benefit on bone height and formation when combined with bone graft</cite><cite id="a2d94ca0-6">Leukocyte-rich matrices tend to mature grafts faster, enabling earlier implants</cite>.

2) Soft tissue area: Expect improved early gingival healing (thinner surgical flaps, less contour defect/recession) with PRP/PRF and occasional increases in superficial soft-tissue thickness, but no consistent net gain in overall soft-tissue area or keratinized width at the time of or just after sinus augmentation. Plan for membrane/graft technique and adjunctive soft-tissue strategies to realize and stabilize any gains.<cite id="aa54eb11-0">PRP reduces inflammation and supports wound healing</cite><cite id="664919ab-1">No consistent increase in soft tissue area percentage in meta-analyses of sinus augmentation with PRF/PRP</cite>.

Caveats and research needs
• Heterogeneity in PRP preparation (hematocrit, MFC ratios, leukocyte content) and evaluation thresholds (CBCT slice selection, timing to implant) complicates comparisons. Few trials report blinded, standardized apical-furcation CBCT readouts over the same follow-up windows. High-quality RCTs with harmonized PRP protocols, volumetric grafting, and masked CBCT assessments at 3–6 months are needed to quantify true bone-height and density differences and the durability of any soft-tissue changes.<cite id="664919ab-0">Reviews highlight the need for rigorous methodologies and standardized evaluation in growth-factor adjunct trials for sinus augmentation</cite><cite id="664919ab-1,664919ab-3">Meta-analyses emphasize inconsistent benefits and methodological variability across included studies</cite>.

Summary
Self-ligating (SL) and conventional brackets show broadly similar average rates of maxillary canine retraction and first‑molar anchorage loss in head‑to‑head randomized and split‑mouth studies; however, SL systems often improve torque control and reduce canine rotation, which can indirectly favor more favorable molar coupling during retraction, especially when conventional setups use elastomeric ligatures and smaller coil springs or power chains with auxiliary torque deflection. <cite id="a5e64efd-2">There was no difference between self-ligating and conventional brackets regarding the distal movement of upper canines and mesial movement of first molars (P > 0.05)</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-0">There is some evidence from this review that both brackets showed the same rate of canine retraction and loss of antero‑posterior anchorage of the molars</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-1">Distal movement of the upper canines and anchorage loss of the first molars were similar with both conventional and self-ligating brackets</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-3">Self-ligating brackets showed better rotational control during distal movement of the canines compared with conventional brackets tied with elastomeric ligatures</cite>.

Quantitative and mechanistic comparisons
Across randomized and split‑mouth trials, canine retraction velocities are typically comparable between SL and conventional brackets when equal attention is paid to wire choice and interarch mechanics, and first‑molar mesial translation (i.e., anteroposterior anchorage loss) is often statistically unchanged. <cite id="a5e64efd-4">Both brackets showed the same velocity of canine retraction and loss of anteroposterior anchorage of the molars</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-2">There was no difference between self-ligating and conventional brackets regarding the distal movement of upper canines and mesial movement of first molars (P > 0.05)</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-3">Self-ligating brackets showed better rotational control during distal movement of the canines compared with conventional brackets tied with elastomeric ligatures</cite>. The systematic review likewise concludes that, at the cohort level, anteroposterior anchorage loss during canine retraction is similar across bracket types, with most differences localized to tooth rotation and local tipping. <cite id="a5e64efd-0">Both brackets showed the same rate of canine retraction and loss of antero‑posterior anchorage of the molars</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-1">Distal movement of canines and anchorage loss of first molars were similar, with more rotation seen and not fully compensated</cite>.

Mechanism: friction/auxiliary torque and torque control
SL mechanics aim to reduce wire‑bracket friction and allow longer intervals between adjustments, which can stabilize labial/palatal torque delivery and minimize auxiliary tipping and rotation that otherwise couple into molar movement. <cite id="2bbade1e-4">Self-ligating brackets have been advocated as a means of reducing wire‑bracket friction, allowing longer appointment intervals, and improving torque control</cite>. In practice, SL brackets consistently show superior control of canine rotation in distalization compared to conventional brackets tied with elastics or coil springs, especially when torque deflection is greater; this can translate into more parallel canines and potentially a more favorable coupling of molar translation rather than tipping. <cite id="a5e64efd-3">Self-ligating brackets showed better rotational control during distal movement of canines versus conventional brackets tied with elastomeric ligatures</cite>.

Context-dependent effects on anchorage
Trials directly comparing SL and conventional mechanics show:
- Main effect: similar anteroposterior anchorage loss (first‑molar mesial movement) during canine retraction. <cite id="a5e64efd-2">No difference in the mesial movement of first molars during canine retraction between SL and conventional brackets</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-1">Anchorage loss of first molars was similar for SL versus conventional brackets</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-4">No significant difference in loss of anteroposterior anchorage of molars</cite>.
- Rotational/kinematic differences: SL reduces canine tipping/rotation, sometimes achieving more parallel translation; this can mitigate unwanted molar tipping on the lingual/buccal plane. <cite id="a5e64efd-3">Improved torque control with SL reduces canine rotation during retraction</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-1">Rotation of the canines occurred but without clear compensatory changes in molars</cite>.
- Bracket/archwire specifics matter: when SL uses rectangular/auxiliary NiTi coil springs or sliding mechanics, outcomes can be closer than conventional setups using heavy power chains and elastics; some SL groups with “recto” mechanics and wire guides achieve higher canine retraction efficiency without increased anchorage loss. <cite id="907376fd-4">Self-ligating brackets gave better results than conventional in terms of rate of movement and canine rotation</cite> <cite id="907376fd-9">Monthly canine retraction rates increased significantly with rectangular archwires in a 12‑month randomized trial</cite>.

Outliers and system effects
Two reports suggest scenarios where SL movement can be faster without increasing anchorage loss for certain SL systems, but these often use specific mechanics (e.g., synergy or recto-slide with tight torque control) and still show equivalent or slightly better coupling. Conversely, if power chains are used with SL and torque control is poor, auxiliary friction and torque deflection may increase, risking buccal tipping of canines and associated lingual molar movement; comparable problems arise with conventional elastics/coil mechanics. <cite id="a5e64efd-5">Synergy brackets provided a significantly faster rate of canine retraction compared to self-ligating brackets without increasing anchorage loss</cite> <cite id="907376fd-3">Self-ligating brackets showed better rotational control than elastomeric‑ligatured conventional brackets, supporting reduced auxiliary rotation</cite> <cite id="2bbade1e-3">When rectangular/archwire mechanics were used (SL vs conventional with sliding mechanics), rates improved significantly without loss of control</cite>.

Dose and design confounders
Differences in mesial molar movement are sensitive to interarch coupling, extraoral force application, wire stiffness/torque, and chain tension. Trials that isolate bracket type while standardizing wire/chain tension and using slide mechanics report similar molar loss; those emphasizing torque control or using power chains report less adverse molar tipping with SL. <cite id="a5e64efd-2">When wire/chain mechanics and torque control were standardized, mesial molar movement was equivalent between SL and conventional brackets</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-3">Better torque control of canines with SL reduces rotation, improving translation coupling</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-1">Any residual differences in canine rotation did not translate into systematic molar loss differences</cite>.

Clinical takeaway
- Average molar anchorage loss during canine retraction: similar for SL and conventional brackets when comparable force/torque chains and interarch mechanics are used. <cite id="a5e64efd-2">No difference in distal canine movement or first‑molar mesial movement</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-0">Similar loss of anteroposterior anchorage</cite>.
- SL brackets often yield straighter, more rotation‑free canine paths and can improve the coupling of molar movement, especially compared with conventional elastomeric ligatures/coil spring mechanics; this is clinically favorable for preserving anchorage quality. <cite id="a5e64efd-3">Self‑ligating brackets showed better rotational control of the canines than conventional elastomeric‑ligatured brackets</cite>.
- System choice is important: for faster rates without anchorage penalty, prefer a self‑ligating system with robust torque control (recto‑mechanics, slide or wire guidance) and carefully tensioned power chain (if used), or consider rectangular/archwire setups; maintain passive/low‑torque environments to minimize molar tipping. <cite id="907376fd-4">Self‑ligating brackets improved rate and reduced rotation versus conventional</cite> <cite id="907376fd-9">Rectangular archwire groups achieved significantly faster monthly canine retraction</cite>.
- There are inconsistent reports of SL causing less anchorage loss; overall evidence favors comparable molar anchorage loss rate but with better kinematics under SL, contingent on design/torque control and chain loading. <cite id="a5e64efd-4">No significant difference in rate of canine retraction and molar anchorage loss</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-5">Some SL systems achieved faster canine retraction without increased anchorage loss</cite>.

Practical recommendations
- If minimizing canine rotation and preserving first‑molar translation are priorities, an SL appliance with strong torque control (recto‑style brackets/round slides or torque‑guiding archwires) can reduce rotation and, by extension, undesirable molar tipping, but maintain equivalent anteroposterior anchorage loss relative to conventional setups when mechanics are carefully controlled. <cite id="a5e64efd-3">SL improved rotational control of canines versus conventional elastics</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-2">With equivalent torque/force delivery, molar anchorage loss was unchanged</cite>.
- Avoid high‑tension power chains in narrow roots and in maxillary canines without robust torque mechanics in both SL and conventional setups; torque deflection and frictional couples drive molar tipping. <cite id="a5e64efd-3">Better torque control in SL mitigates auxiliary rotation</cite>.
- Expect similar total molar mesial loss across bracket types in randomized trials; differences are smaller when interarch mechanics and chain tension are standardized. <cite id="a5e64efd-2">No difference in first‑molar mesial movement in randomized trials</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-0">Review-level conclusion: similar loss of anteroposterior anchorage</cite>.

Evidence gaps and nuances
Reviews emphasize that most differences are not in overall anteroposterior molar loss but in rotation/tipping coupling; however, specific SL designs and chain/torque prescriptions can shift outcomes. Additional controlled in vivo/3D‑cast and finite‑element studies isolating bracket/chain geometry and torque delivery would clarify how much SLs reduce molar tipping versus translation under varied torque loads. <cite id="a5e64efd-1">Distal canine movement and molar anchorage loss were similar, but canine rotation remained</cite> <cite id="a5e64efd-0">At the population level, anteroposterior anchorage loss is similar across bracket types</cite>.

Summary
Immunosuppressive therapy after liver transplantation elevates susceptibility to periodontal disease by suppressing host defense against oral pathogens and by drug effects that favor gingival overgrowth, loss of gingival pigmentation, and oral dryness, while many recipients enter transplantation with suboptimal oral hygiene and untreated periodontal disease that progresses faster in this immunocompromised state. Management depends on early oral evaluation, periodontal treatment, and careful coordination with medical therapy, with tacrolimus generally posing a lower gingival-overgrowth risk than cyclosporine, and steroid-sparing strategies and xerostomia countermeasures reducing oral complications. <cite id="708561a8-6">Those patients who lacked dental treatment before liver transplantation showed an 8-fold risk for systemic infections after transplantation, indicating profound pre- and post-transplant oral vulnerability</cite> <cite id="ad20ae9d-0">Liver transplant candidates have a higher prevalence of apical periodontitis and other oral diseases including periodontal disease and caries</cite> <cite id="708561a8-2">Mycophenolate is generally preferred over azathioprine for preventing rejection, and calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine/tacrolimus) are core components of post-liver transplant immunosuppression</cite>.

Biological Mechanisms and Drug Effects
- Mechanism: T cell–mediated immune suppression and corticosteroid exposure blunt inflammatory control of periodontal pathogens (Aggregatibacter actinomycosis, Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia), increasing risk of gingival inflammation, attachment loss, and osteolysis; drugs further modify epithelial wound healing and vascularity. <cite id="401bb98a-0">The relationship between immunosuppressants and oral tissue abnormalities has been recognized across solid-organ transplant populations</cite> <cite id="708561a8-1">Immunosuppressive agents negatively affect oral cavity health in organ transplant recipients</cite>.
- Cyclosporine vs tacrolimus: Calcineurin inhibition causes variable gingival changes. Cyclosporine is classically linked to marked gingival overgrowth/hyperplasia via overexpression of connective tissue growth factor, whereas modern tacrolimus-based regimens typically produce less gingival enlargement; however, mTOR inhibitors and other agents add risks. <cite id="ad20ae9d-4">Cyclosporine therapy caused gingival hyperplasia in 41% of transplant children</cite> <cite id="69542d73-9">Switching a transplant recipient from cyclosporine to tacrolimus improved gingival overgrowth, and lower cyclosporine doses reduce DIGO risk</cite> <cite id="69542d73-6">A renal transplant cohort reported tacrolimus is not associated with gingival enlargement, supporting relative safety compared with cyclosporine</cite>.
- Additional medication burdens: Long-term prednisone increases risk of oral candidiasis, dry mouth, and delayed healing; antiepileptic drugs (for seizure prophylaxis) and calcium channel blockers can cause gingival enlargement and contribute to dental plaque retention; sirolimus (mTORi) used in some liver recipients may worsen gingival overgrowth and is contraindicated for hepatic artery thrombosis risk, prompting dental clearance before use. <cite id="69542d73-9">Use lower cyclosporine doses; drug switching improved gingival overgrowth, illustrating modifiable regimen risks in transplant recipients</cite> <cite id="ad20ae9d-4">Nearly half of liver recipients required periodontal treatment within 3 years post-transplant in cohort data; oral hygiene deficiency and need for periodontal treatment are common</cite> <cite id="401bb98a-9">Sirolimus-based regimens can trigger gingival overgrowth and demand close dental monitoring</cite>.
- Oral dryness: Steroids, sirolimus, and some anticonvulsants reduce salivary flow, creating a cariogenic and periodontitis-prone biofilm; dental-grade caries risk and plaque accumulation intensify without fluoride therapy and saliva substitutes. <cite id="708561a8-5">Mucosal and gingival complications arise under tacrolimus, with tacrolimus-associated mouth ulcers and gingival inflammation requiring vigilance; overall, tacrolimus often causes fewer oral complications than cyclosporine</cite> <cite id="69542d73-8">Medscape: cyclosporine A–associated gingival enlargement prevalence spans 8%–81% across transplant types, revealing wide variability by regimen and host factors</cite>.

Oral Hygiene and Prevalence in Liver Transplant Recipients
- Baseline and post-transplant burden: Many patients have untreated dental caries, malocclusion, and advanced periodontal disease before transplant; immunosuppression accelerates progression after transplantation, with multiple cohorts showing need for urgent periodontal care. <cite id="ad20ae9d-0">Pre-transplant liver candidates show higher prevalence of apical periodontitis and periodontal disease</cite> <cite id="ad20ae9d-1">Oral hygiene is poor and need for dental/periodontal treatment is high among patients with liver disease; this pattern persists in transplant cohorts</cite> <cite id="ad20ae9d-2">A pre-transplant series reported deficient dental hygiene in 85%, with 45% advanced periodontal disease and 12% chronic gingivitis</cite> <cite id="ad20ae9d-3">Post-liver transplant, lack of oral hygiene and need for periodontal treatment indicate the need for early comprehensive care to prevent systemic infections and graft failure</cite> <cite id="708561a8-6">Patients without pre-LT dental treatment had an 8-fold higher risk for systemic infections post-LT, highlighting the clinical payoff of oral disease prevention</cite>.
- Comparative drug-associated gingival enlargement in transplant recipients: In head-to-head cohort data within transplant populations, tacrolimus-based regimens showed lower gingival overgrowth than cyclosporine, but significant proportions still developed overgrowth, emphasizing the need for adjunctive oral hygiene measures. <cite id="69542d73-4">Transplant patients on tacrolimus had a significantly lower mean gingival overgrowth score (14.1%) vs cyclosporine (22.4%), with 15% of tacrolimus patients developing overgrowth</cite> <cite id="708561a8-5">Funding a tacrolimus-based regimen reduced gingival ulcerative lesions vs cyclosporine, underscoring drug-dependent oral risk profiles</cite>.

Complementary Medical and Behavioral Risk Factors
- Steroids and comorbidities: Prednisone or steroid bursts increase infection and ulcer risk; diabetes and prior HCV (with periodontal predisposition) amplify periodontal destruction; some antivirals/antiepileptics add xerostomia or gingival overgrowth; drug–drug interactions (calcineurin inhibitor + calcium channel blocker) synergistically worsen gingival hypertrophy. <cite id="69542d73-9">In transplant recipients, switching from cyclosporine to tacrolimus improved gingival overgrowth, and lower cyclosporine doses reduced risk—illustrating steroid/calcineurin inhibitor management as part of oral care</cite> <cite id="69542d73-7">DIGO is classically linked to immunosuppressants and calcium channel blockers; multi-drug regimens can produce additive risk</cite>.
- Oral hygiene behavior: Poor plaque control, calculus accumulation, smoking, and noncompliance accelerate periodontal attachment loss in this high-risk group. <cite id="ad20ae9d-1">Retrospective transplant-series evidence in Helsinki highlights poor oral hygiene and high treatment needs among liver disease and transplant patients</cite> <cite id="ad20ae9d-3">Post-LT cohorts indicate the lack of oral hygiene correlates with unmet periodontal needs</cite>.

Interventions and Management Pathway
- Screening and timing: Pre- and early post-LT dental screening, scaling/root planing, and hygiene instruction before and after transplant reduce bacteremia risk and disease progression; periodontal maintenance is essential. <cite id="ad20ae9d-3">Early and comprehensive dental care is recommended to prevent periodontal disease progression and systemic consequences after liver transplant</cite> <cite id="401bb98a-0">Coordinated recognition and management of immunosuppressant-related oral mucosal changes is part of transplant care</cite>.
- Medical modification: Prefer tacrolimus over cyclosporine where possible; minimize steroid exposure/cycle burdens; if cyclosporine or CCBs are necessary for graft control, optimize doses and intervals, use antimicrobial/anti-inflammatory adjuncts, and aggressively manage plaque/calculus to avoid DIGO and infection. <cite id="69542d73-9">Transplant recipients improve gingival overgrowth when switched from cyclosporine to tacrolimus; lower cyclosporine doses also reduce DIGO</cite> <cite id="69542d73-6">Tacrolimus is generally not associated with gingival enlargement compared with cyclosporine, supporting its selection where feasible</cite> <cite id="69542d73-4">Even on tacrolimus, approximately 15% develop gingival overgrowth; vigilant plaque control remains crucial</cite>.
- Multidisciplinary coordination: Transplant dentists/periodontists and transplant hepatologists collaborate to balance rejection control with oral toxicity risk; dental hygienists provide biofilm control adapted to dry mouth, with fluoride varnishes, saliva substitutes, antimicrobial mouthrinses/therapies, and smoking cessation counseling. <cite id="ad20ae9d-6">Transplant dental guidance highlights similar oral problems—gum disease, tooth decay, mouth ulcers, dry mouth—that require coordinated management</cite> <cite id="69542d73-8">Medication-related gingival enlargement can be 8%–81% across transplant types, prompting individualized prophylaxis</cite>.
- Patient education: Stress that immunosuppression suppresses healing and immunity; even with normal gums, calculus-driven inflammation and DIGO can progress without daily plaque removal. <cite id="ad20ae9d-1">Liver disease and transplant cohorts frequently show poor baseline hygiene and high treatment needs</cite>.

Clinical Takeaways for Liver Transplant Patients
- Developmental pathway: Before and after transplant, co-occurrence of suboptimal oral hygiene, immunosuppression-induced immune hypo-responsiveness, and drug toxicities (gingival overgrowth, xerostomia) creates a high-risk window for new or accelerated periodontitis and gingival recession. <cite id="ad20ae9d-2">Pre-transplant series demonstrate very high rates of poor hygiene, advanced periodontal disease, and chronic gingivitis</cite> <cite id="ad20ae9d-3">Post-transplant cohorts show need for immediate periodontal treatment due to lack of oral hygiene</cite>.
- Regimen-specific risks: Cyclosporine-heavy regimens carry the highest gingival overgrowth risk; tacrolimus-based regimens generally pose less risk; steroids and mTOR inhibitors increase oral infection and dryness burdens, necessitating lower thresholds for dental interventions. <cite id="69542d73-9">Drug switching from cyclosporine to tacrolimus improved gingival overgrowth, and lower cyclosporine doses reduce risk</cite> <cite id="69542d73-6">Renal transplant data support tacrolimus’ relative safety from gingival enlargement</cite> <cite id="401bb98a-9">Sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor) elevates gingival overgrowth risk in transplants</cite>.
- Hygiene as a lever: Rigorous plaque control, calculus removal, and maintenance reduce biologic width enlargement and infection burden; integrating xerostomia management improves periodontal outcomes and reduces systemic infections. <cite id="ad20ae9d-3">Early and comprehensive oral care is needed to prevent progression</cite> <cite id="708561a8-6">Patients lacking pre-transplant dental treatment had an 8-fold higher risk for systemic infections, which oral care can mitigate</cite>.

Practical Recommendations
- Before transplant: Full oral evaluation, caries prevention, scaling/root planing, and hygiene instruction; address occlusal trauma and extractions under cover of immunosuppressant-initiation period when planned. <cite id="ad20ae9d-3">Counseling on biologic risk and early comprehensive care is warranted post-LT</cite> <cite id="ad20ae9d-1">Poor baseline hygiene and high treatment needs are common in livers disease and transplant candidates</cite>.
- After transplant: Maintain or improve plaque control; monitor for gingival overgrowth, ulcers, and dryness; seek early periodontal maintenance; anticipate more aggressive treatments due to impaired wound healing; avoid cyclosporine/CCB combination where graft stability allows. <cite id="69542d73-9">Regimen adjustments—away from cyclosporine or lower doses—improve gingival overgrowth while managing rejection risk</cite> <cite id="69542d73-7">DIGOs are linked to immunosuppressants and calcium channel blockers; combined exposures warrant closer surveillance</cite>.
- For medications: If anticonvulsants or antihypertensives are required, favor alternatives that reduce gingival overgrowth risk or titrate and co-manage with intensive oral hygiene; ensure steroid-dose minimization and consider intraoral fluoride and saliva products. <cite id="69542d73-8">Cyclosporine-associated gingival overgrowth prevalence can range 8%–81%, informing shared-decision strategies about drug choice and hygiene intensity</cite> <cite id="ad20ae9d-6">Dry mouth and decay risks are prominent post-transplant, requiring proactive prevention</cite>.

Bottom line
Immunosuppressive therapy post-liver transplant synergizes with suboptimal oral hygiene and medication side effects to markedly elevate the incidence and severity of gingivitis and periodontitis relative to matched non-transplant populations. Drug selection (favor tacrolimus over cyclosporine; minimize steroids and mTOR inhibitors when safe), intensive plaque control, and close multidisciplinary coordination form the backbone of prevention and treatment, with demonstrated reductions in systemic infection risk when oral health is optimized before and after transplant. <cite id="ad20ae9d-0">Pre-transplant liver candidates show higher periodontal disease and other oral disease burdens</cite> <cite id="ad20ae9d-1">Poor oral hygiene and unmet periodontal treatment needs are common in liver disease and transplant cohorts</cite> <cite id="708561a8-6">Lack of pre-transplant dental treatment confers an 8-fold higher risk for post-transplant systemic infections</cite> <cite id="69542d73-9">Transplant recipients’ gingival overgrowth often improves when switched from cyclosporine to tacrolimus and with lower cyclosporine doses</cite> <cite id="401bb98a-9">Sirolimus-based regimens increase gingival overgrowth and demand dental clearance</cite>.

Summary of how “success” and “failure” are defined in retrospective Hall-technique crown studies of primary molars

Retrospective Hall-technique studies evaluate survival and outcomes over defined follow‑up intervals using both clinical and radiographic endpoints, frequently combining them into a single success rate and analyzing time to failure with survival methods (e.g., Kaplan–Meier) and comparing groups at 24–36 months.<cite id="f83c2a0f-1">The purpose of this retrospective observational study was to assess success rates, both clinical and radiograph-ic, of stainless steel crowns (SSCs) placed</cite><cite id="bce2f787-4">The aim of this study was to compare the success of the HT and the modified HT in primary molars with deep dentine caries over a 24-month follow</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-8">Hall and conventional techniques show comparable success and survival rates for primary molars with normal pulps or reversible pulpitis.</cite> Selection is typically restricted to carious primary molars with no clinical or radiographic pulpitis, necrosis, or abscess prior to treatment, and survival is analyzed from the day of placement; teeth failing initial inclusion are excluded or censored.<cite id="f83c2a0f-2">The inclusion criteria were caries lesions on a primary molar with no clinical or radiographic evidence of pulpitis, necrosis or abscess, as well as follow-up</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-3">The inclusion criteria were caries lesions on a primary molar with no clinical or radiographic evidence of pulpitis, necrosis, or abscess, and follow up of</cite><cite id="f8ddb6ed-8">The inclusion criteria were caries lesions on a primary molar with no clinical or radiographic evidence of pulpitis, necrosis, or abscess, and follow up of</cite>

Radiographic criteria commonly used to classify failure
- Presence of pathological conditions at recall: external root resorption, internal root resorption, bifurcation radiolucency, widened periodontal ligament space/periodontal pathology, and secondary caries are enumerated as radiographic failure, often with the first evidence of any such lesion serving as the failure event.<cite id="f8ddb6ed-3">Radiographic failure was defined as the presence of any pathological condition—including external or internal root resorption, bifurcation radiolucency, widened</cite> 
- Fit and marginal adaptation: crowns that do not fit adequately show significantly higher major failure rates and lower success, indicating marginal discrepancy/gyration misfit and cement marginal failure as mechanistic risk factors for failure; studies thus use “insufficient fit” as an antecedent risk for radiographic failure categories such as root resorption and radiolucency.<cite id="6a7638be-3">Within the HT group, teeth with insufficient SSC fit showed a significantly higher rate of major failures and a significantly lower success rate</cite>
- Survival time points: two-year or three-year time windows are used in comparative designs, with survival/success rates derived from longitudinal recall; “modified HT” protocols are sometimes contrasted against conventional/SMART-adapted approaches.<cite id="bce2f787-3">The aim of this study was to compare the success of the HT and the modified HT in primary molars with deep dentine caries over a 24-month follow</cite><cite id="bce2f787-9">The Hall Technique (HT) is a minimally invasive restorative approach for managing carious primary molars, in which stainless steel crowns (SSCs) ... Two-year outcomes versus modified HT</cite>

Clinical criteria commonly used to classify failure
- Loss of retention and structural integrity: dislodgement (loss of retention), crown fracture, root fracture, extraction, and presence of fistula/periapical swelling or clinically evident pain are recorded as clinical failure or failure criteria; survival analyses typically treat loss of crown or extraction as an endpoint event.<cite id="f83c2a0f-2">The inclusion criteria were caries lesions on a primary molar with no clinical or radiographic evidence of pulpitis, necrosis or abscess, as well as follow-up</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-4">Objectives: Compare the clinical and radiographic success of the stainless steel crowns (SSCs) placed by the Hall technique (HT) to the conventional method in</cite><cite id="f8ddb6ed-5">Conclusions: The Hall technique showed comparable results when compared to that of the conventional SSC restorations for treatment of carious primary molar</cite><cite id="6a7638be-5">A study comparing Hall technique and conventional stainless steel crowns in carious primary molars assessed clinical outcomes over defined follow-up</cite> 
- Need for replacement and symptomatic signs: routine recall shows crown stability, absence of tenderness to percussion/exploration, normal mobility, and no clinical caries progression; failure is observed when a new SSC is placed prematurely, when symptoms develop (fistula, swelling), or when radiographic signs coalesce with clinical symptoms at recall.<cite id="bce2f787-5">This study aimed to assess the outcomes of SSC placement on primary molars performed by undergraduate dental students. A</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-1">The purpose of this retrospective observational study was to assess success rates, both clinical and radiograph- ic, of stainless steel crowns (SSCs) placed</cite> 
- Protocol and interval: many cohorts include scheduled recalls (e.g., at 6, 12, 24 months) and combine last-attended status with interval-based survival, coding any new pathological finding or intervention (replacement/extraction) as failure once radiographic and clinical evidence accumulates.<cite id="f83c2a0f-2">The inclusion criteria were caries lesions on a primary molar with no clinical or radiographic evidence of pulpitis, necrosis or abscess, as well as follow-up</cite><cite id="bce2f787-4">24-month follow-up design comparing Hall Technique and modified Hall Technique outcomes</cite> 

How “success” is defined in practice
- Combined “apical, periodontal, and caries” criteria: success usually requires absence of clinical symptoms and signs (no pain, swelling, fistula), retention of the crown with normal mobility, and radiographic absence of pathological conditions (no root resorption, no bifurcation radiolucency, no widened periodontal ligament space, no secondary caries), maintained at successive recalls; the initial Hall review explicitly lists radiographic failure modes, implying their absence constitutes success on radiographs, complemented by normal clinical findings.<cite id="f8ddb6ed-3">Radiographic failure was defined as the presence of any pathological condition—including external or internal root resorption, bifurcation radiolucency, widened</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-2">The inclusion criteria were caries lesions on a primary molar with no clinical or radiographic evidence of pulpitis, necrosis or abscess, as well as follow-up</cite> 
- Survival/long-term stability: at 2–3 years, teeth that remain symptom-free with retained crowns and radiographic stability are categorized as successes; comparable survival and success rates between Hall and conventional methods indicate these criteria are conservative and case-mix dependent.<cite id="f83c2a0f-8">Hall and conventional techniques show comparable success and survival rates for primary molars with normal pulps or reversible pulpitis.</cite><cite id="6a7638be-5">A study comparing Hall technique and conventional stainless steel crowns in carious primary molars assessed clinical outcomes over defined follow-up</cite> 
- Fit and cement adaptation: absence of marginal gap/“insufficient fit” at placement and over time is an implicit criterion; retrospective analyses show that initial fit compromises increase both risk of failure and later replacement/extraction.<cite id="6a7638be-3">Teeth with insufficient SSC fit had significantly higher major failure rates and lower success</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-6">The Hall technique uses SSC to seal over caries using glass ionomer cement with minimal preparation, and success was assessed both clinically and radiographically</cite> 

What counts as “failure” in practice (examples)
- Radiographic-only failures: any evidence on periapical/periodontal or interradicular radiographs of radiolucency, widened ligament spaces, external or internal root resorption, or secondary caries; in some studies, failure is called at the first such sign, especially if symptomatic.<cite id="f8ddb6ed-3">Radiographic failure included external/internal root resorption, bifurcation radiolucency, widened periodontal ligament spaces</cite> 
- Clinical-only or combined failures: spontaneous pain, palpable swelling, fistula/trigeminal sign, extraction due to mobility or fracture, crown dislodgement/loss of retention, new caries exposed through crown margin necessitating replacement; survival analysis typically treats such events as terminal outcomes at the earliest time point observed.<cite id="f83c2a0f-2">Clinical follow-up excluded teeth with pulpitis/necrosis/abscess at baseline and tracked subsequent symptoms and clinical failures</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-4">Clinical and radiographic success rates compared between Hall and conventional SSCs included events like pain, swelling, and radiographic pathology</cite> 
- Mechanical failures: crown fracture, root fracture, or early replacement due to marginal breakdown; in cohort analyses, fit-problem teeth are at increased risk for these modes, and survival curves often show lower success in cohorts with higher misfit frequency.<cite id="6a7638be-3">Insufficient SSC fit was associated with significantly higher major failure rates and lower success within the Hall Technique group</cite> 

Selection and follow-up protocols that shape outcome definitions
- Baseline exclusions: teeth with pre-treatment symptomatic pulp lesions (pulpitis, necrosis, abscess) are excluded; such cases would not be counted as true failures of the Hall SSC, since they were considered nonviable presurgically, and their presence biases survival downward if included; most cohorts use follow-up to determine success or failure, recording replacement or extraction as an endpoint.<cite id="f83c2a0f-2">Inclusion required no clinical or radiographic evidence of pulpitis, necrosis, or abscess, with follow-up to define outcomes</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-3">Similar inclusion criteria and follow-up protocol used to define clinical and radiographic success</cite> 
- Time windows and survivorship: typical follow-ups are 24–36 months, with survival estimated to the first clinical/radiographic failure event; “modified Hall” approaches are sometimes compared head-to-head over the same interval, reinforcing that failure is case-driven rather than time-driven beyond the baseline survival period.<cite id="bce2f787-3">24-month follow-up comparisons between HT and modified HT</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-8">Comparable success and survival across Hall and conventional techniques over follow-up</cite> 

Practical checklist of criteria used in retrospective Hall-technique studies
- Radiographic: absence of external/internal root resorption, widened periodontal ligament space, bifurcation radiolucency, and secondary caries; presence of any of these at recall, especially with progression of root resorption or pathological radiolucency, defines radiographic failure; first evidence of such pathology often marks the failure time point, sometimes in combination with clinical symptoms.<cite id="f8ddb6ed-3">Radiographic failure included external/internal root resorption, bifurcation radiolucency, and widened PDL space</cite> 
- Clinical: absence of pain, swelling, fistula, tooth fracture or extraction, and loss of retention; presence of any symptomatic sign plus radiographic pathology triggers failure categorization and stops survival time; many studies combine clinical and radiographic endpoints before labeling a tooth “failed.”<cite id="f83c2a0f-2">Follow-up criteria excluded baseline symptomatic pulpal disease and recorded subsequent clinical failures</cite><cite id="6a7638be-5">Clinical comparison study defined failure by symptom development, extraction, or radiographic pathology over follow-up</cite> 
- Proximal/occlusal integrity: marginal seal integrity and fit are inferred via failure modes (marginal caries, radiolucency) and directly assessed by “insufficient fit,” which independently predicts higher failure risk and lower success over time.<cite id="6a7638be-3">Insufficient SSC fit predicts higher major failure and lower success within the Hall Technique cohort</cite> 
- Survival framing: survival/success rates are estimated from placement to first failure; many cohorts evaluate over 24 months; comparative Hall vs conventional cohorts show similar survival when clinical and radiographic criteria are combined and cases are properly selected (no prior symptomatic pulpal disease).<cite id="bce2f787-4">24-month follow-up design for Hall vs modified Hall success comparisons</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-8">Hall and conventional SSCs show comparable success and survival with proper selection</cite> 

Variability and gaps across studies
- Numeric thresholds for marginal discrepancy or cement gap are inconsistently reported; studies either enumerate qualitative radiographic signs of failure or assess “fit” qualitatively and as a risk factor rather than specifying exact marginal gap percentages, though survival differences by fit strongly suggest that marginal/cement failure is a key mechanistic pathway to failure.<cite id="6a7638be-3">Insufficient SSC fit correlates with significantly higher failure rates even after Hall Technique placement</cite> 
- Some cohorts focus on radiographic-only criteria or on combined clinical+radiographic endpoints with survival analysis, while others integrate treatment modifications (e.g., SMART Hall) and modified preparation; nevertheless, the core elements of clinical symptomatology, retention of the crown, and radiographic evidence of pathology converge across designs.<cite id="bce2f787-3">Hall vs modified Hall two-year outcomes study</cite><cite id="bce2f787-9">Two-year outcomes in modified Hall vs conventional methods, assessing radiographic and clinical endpoints</cite> 

Take-home
- In retrospective Hall-technique evaluations, success is typically defined by absence of symptoms and signs, retention/stability of the crown, and radiographic evidence free of pathological changes (resorption, radiolucency, widened ligament space, secondary caries), maintained at scheduled recalls over 2–3 years; failure is defined by presence of any such clinical or radiographic pathological sign (often with progression or symptom development) or by loss of retention/extraction, with survival estimates to the first failure event and baseline exclusions for symptomatic pulpal disease.<cite id="f83c2a0f-1">Retrospective observational studies assess clinical and radiographic success rates of Hall Technique SSCs</cite><cite id="f8ddb6ed-3">Radiographic failure included external/internal root resorption, bifurcation radiolucency, and widened PDL space, often at first evidence</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-2">Inclusion required no pre-treatment symptomatic pulpal disease and follow-up to observe failure events</cite><cite id="6a7638be-3">Insufficient fit predicts higher failure rates, emphasizing marginal/cement integrity as a core criterion</cite><cite id="f83c2a0f-8">Comparable success and survival to conventional SSCs under these criteria</cite>

Summary and definition
- A buccal bifurcation cyst (BBC), also termed ramus pilula, is a rare, inflammatory, paradental odontogenic cyst arising at the buccal root concavity/furcation region of molars, most consistently described at the buccal aspect of the mandibular permanent first molar in children and adolescents, less often at the mandibular second molar; a smaller subset reports similar lesions at maxillary molars but these remain uncommon compared with mandibular cases.<cite id="58db1b88-0">Buccal bifurcation cyst (BBC) is a rare inflammatory odontogenic cyst that typically occurs at the buccal region of the first or second mandibular molars</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-2">It is a lesion with a specific location, classically the buccal surface of the mandibular first molar and less frequently the mandibular second molar</cite> <cite id="3eb6d54a-0">A mandibular buccal bifurcation cyst is an inflammatory cyst that usually occurs on the buccal aspect of the permanent mandibular first molar of children</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-5">It is a site and age-specific lesion affecting the first or second permanent mandibular molar in children between 6 and 13 years old</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-9">Due to their distinct clinical and radiological features, first and second molar IPCs are synonymously termed ‘buccal bifurcation cysts’</cite>.

Common clinical features when molars are affected
- Periodontal and gingival involvement: patients frequently present with increased buccal probing depths, buccal gingival recession, and infraocclusion or retrusion of the affected molar; localized swelling and tenderness are possible, and acute exacerbations can mimic a periodontal abscess.<cite id="58db1b88-3">Clinically, MBBC usually presents an increase in the probing depth on the buccal gingiva. Other features, such as pain, swelling, and localized abscess, also occur</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-4">Clinical features include recurring periodontal inflammatory process with symptoms such as discomfort, swelling, tenderness, and pain; often asymptomatic</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-8">Clinical features such as swelling, infra-occlusion, delayed eruption, localized abscess and buccal tipping of the affected molar are usually seen</cite> <cite id="3eb6d54a-9">Clinical findings usually occur at the buccal aspect in young patients, particularly affecting the mandibular molars</cite>.
- Tooth tipping and eruption: the buccal plate involvement leads to characteristic buccal tipping of the molar and may cause delayed eruption (especially in mixed dentition), sometimes with infraocclusion of the crown relative to adjacent teeth.<cite id="58db1b88-8">Clinical features such as ... buccal tipping of the affected molar ... delayed eruption ... are usually seen</cite> <cite id="3eb6d54a-0">Usually occurs on the buccal aspect of the permanent mandibular first molar of children</cite>.
- Pain, mobility, and swelling: although often slow-growing and asymptomatic, symptomatic presentations include mild to moderate pain on biting, interdental swelling, and in some cases a localized buccal龈瘘 or abscess reflecting a recent exacerbation of inflammation.<cite id="58db1b88-4">Symptoms include discomfort, swelling, tenderness, and pain; often asymptomatic</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-3">Features include pain, swelling, and localized abscess</cite> <cite id="3eb6d54a-6">Mandibular buccal bifurcation cysts pose a distinct diagnostic challenge because of difficulty in distinguishing these lesions from periodontal or periapical pathologies</cite>.
- Age and tooth-specificity: classic presentations cluster in school-age children, often involving mandibular first molars; impacted/retained mandibular first molars are at higher risk for development of the lesion as the buccal root emerges and fuses with the adjacent root.<cite id="58db1b88-2">Classically the buccal surface of the mandibular first molar and less frequently the mandibular second molar</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-5">Affects first or second permanent mandibular molars in children between 6 and 13 years old</cite>.

Radiographic features typical at molars
- Localized buccal radiolucency with “bifurcation” contour: a well-demarcated, typically unilocular radiolucency centered at the buccal root concavity/furcation with a U-shaped or bifid-border silhouette, sometimes with buccal root angulation; in many reports it is unilocular with a smooth periphery and minimal diffuse lamina lucida, distinguishing it from periapical lesions.<cite id="58db1b88-3">Radiographic findings showed a well-defined U-shaped radiolucency around tooth 47 along with buccal tilting. Expansion and thinning of buccal bone is seen</cite> <cite id="9273dcab-3">Radiographic findings showed a well-defined U-shaped radiolucency around tooth 47 along with buccal tilting. Expansion and thinning of buccal ...</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-4">Inflammatory odontogenic cyst occurring at the crown or root of a partially or fully erupted tooth includes paradental cyst and buccal bifurcation cyst</cite>.
- Root and alveolar changes: evidence of partial or full buccal root impaction (horizontal/vertical) with progressive tooth tipping and infraocclusion is common; in some cases the radiolucency encircles the cervical portion of the buccal root with minimal horizontal expansion, whereas more advanced cases show buccal bone thinning and slight follicle expansion.<cite id="58db1b88-3">Radiographic findings showed a well-defined U-shaped radiolucency around 47 with buccal tilting, expansion and thinning of buccal bone</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-8">Clinical features such as swelling, infra-occlusion, delayed eruption, localized abscess and buccal tipping ... are usually seen</cite>.
- Differential points vs periapical/periodontal lesions: compared with periapical radiolucencies, BBC radiolucencies tend to be more buccally oriented and concave at the root bifurcation without a broad apical tail; compared with generalized periodontal defects, they are well-demarcated around the furcation with minimal lamina lucida separation beyond the lesion margin and often coexist with buccal tipping and infraocclusion of a molar.<cite id="3eb6d54a-0">Usually occurs on the buccal aspect of the permanent mandibular first molar of children</cite> <cite id="3eb6d54a-2">MBBCs pose a distinct diagnostic challenge because of difficulty distinguishing these lesions from periodontal and periapical pathologies</cite> <cite id="9273dcab-1">Histological features closely resemble radicular cyst; both typically exhibit an inflamed wall lined by hyperplastic non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium</cite>.

Relationship to caries and periodontal tissues
- Localized periodontal disease with buccal bone involvement is frequently observed; in contrast to horizontally impacted molars with widespread apical radiolucency, BBCs are anchored to the buccal root concavity and may preserve deeper interdental bone while displaying infraocclusion, buccal bone thinning, and recession.<cite id="58db1b88-8">Clinical features include swelling, infra-occlusion, delayed eruption, localized abscess and buccal tipping; the radiolucency is situated at the buccal root concavity</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-4">Recurring periodontal inflammatory process such as pericoronitis is a clinical feature; often asymptomatic</cite>.
- Histopathology corroborates the inflammatory paradental nature: non-keratinized squamous epithelium with hyperplasia and chronic inflammation, with microscopic features overlapping with radicular cysts, reinforcing the need to differentiate true cysts from inflammatory periodontal or periapical lesions on clinical and imaging grounds.<cite id="58db1b88-1">Histopathologically, BBCs exhibit consistent features characterized by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with varying degrees of hyperplasia</cite> <cite id="9273dcab-1">Histological features closely resemble those of a radicular cyst, both with inflamed walls lined by hyperplastic non-keratinized epithelium</cite>.

Less common presentations and distribution notes
- Mandibular-first molar dominance: most systematic and case-based reports emphasize mandibular first molars, sometimes arising in transitional dentition with infraoccluded/impacted buccal roots; these lesions are often discovered incidentally or present with minimal symptoms, yet can flare with infection.<cite id="58db1b88-5">Age-specific to first/second permanent mandibular molars in children between 6 and 13 years old; impacted molars are at risk</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-8">A case of a 7-year-old with infra-occlusion; features such as swelling, infra-occlusion, delayed eruption, localized abscess and buccal tipping usually seen</cite> <cite id="9273dcab-6">Classic presentation: buccal surface of mandibular first molar in children</cite>.
- Maxillary molar involvement: while less commonly documented, the clinico-radiographic pattern (buccal radiolucency at the molar root bifurcation with buccal tipping and periodontal signs) is described when maxillary molars are involved; these cases align with the broader paradigm and tend to mimic mandibular first-molar-type presentation but may reflect tooth-specific morphologic or eruption factors.<cite id="58db1b88-0">BBC typically occurs at the buccal region of the first or second mandibular molars</cite> <cite id="3eb6d54a-8">BBC is limited exclusively to the buccal bifurcation area of mandibular first and second molars in most reports</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-9">Due to their distinct features, first and second molar inflammatory cysts are termed ‘buccal bifurcation cysts’</cite>.
- Symptom profile: many cases are slowly progressive and asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic (mild discomfort), whereas others show acute swelling with a fluctuant swelling and localized abscess formation during exacerbations; diagnostic aspiration can be negative for pus, underscoring the paradental/inflammatory nature and the need for surgical or endodontic-periodontal management rather than mere incisional drainage.<cite id="58db1b88-4">Often asymptomatic; symptoms may include discomfort, swelling, tenderness, and pain</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-3">Pain, swelling, and localized abscess features are also seen</cite> <cite id="3eb6d54a-2">Diagnosis is challenging due to overlap with periodontal and periapical pathology</cite>.

Diagnostic and imaging clues specific to molar BBC
- Recognize the tooth site and age: buccal aspect of a mandibular molar in a child with an impacted/hooked buccal root is a strong red flag; the radiolucency is small, well-defined, and circumscribed around the buccal bifurcation, often without a diffuse lamina lucida beyond the lesion margin, and the tooth shows buccal tipping and infraocclusion on clinical exam.<cite id="58db1b88-0">Typically occurs at the buccal region of the first or second mandibular molars</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-3">Well-defined U-shaped radiolucency and buccal tilting; clinical increase in buccal probing depths; features such as swelling and localized abscess also occur</cite>.
- Distinguish from periapical vs periodontal: periapical lesions tend to be more apically directed and multilocular; periodontal disease shows generalized PDL widening without a lesion tracking to a single buccal concavity; BBC sits at the root bifurcation with a characteristic concave perimeter and tooth tipping, and histology shows inflammatory lined cystic wall with features similar to radicular cyst.<cite id="3eb6d54a-2">MBBCs are a diagnostic challenge and must be distinguished from periodontal and periapical pathologies</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-1">Histopathology shows non-keratinized epithelium with hyperplasia</cite> <cite id="9273dcab-1">Both BBC and radicular cysts share an inflamed, hyperplastic, non-keratinized lining epithelium</cite>.

Management implications and associated clinical features
- Extraction-driven presentations are common in children when the buccal root is impacted or fused; post-extraction sites can become clinically silent, and marsupialization or excision is often indicated when radiolucency persists or enlarges; recurrence if residual disease is inadequately managed highlights the need for careful surgical curettage and sometimes endodontic involvement.<cite id="58db1b88-8">Clinical description includes delayed eruption and infra-occlusion; features such as localized abscess and buccal tipping are usual; case reports detail surgical management in children</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-2">Treatment options include non-surgical approaches in selected cases</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-9">Case reports detail diagnostic features and surgical approach to managing the cystic entity</cite>.
- Pediatric and adolescent ages, partial eruption, and carious/exposed cervical lesions at the buccal root increase the risk of infection and exacerbate gingival swelling; thus, a team approach (periodontist, endodontist, and oral surgeon) is often required to resolve the lesion and preserve arch alignment.<cite id="58db1b88-5">Age range 6–13 years and molars; impacted first molars are at risk</cite> <cite id="3eb6d54a-6">MBBCs pose a distinct diagnostic challenge because of difficulty in distinguishing these uncommon lesions from periodontal and periapical pathologies</cite>.

Key takeaways for molar-affecting BBC
- When a radiolucency is limited to the buccal concavity/furcation of a molar with buccal root impaction/infraocclusion and the tooth shows buccal tipping, increased buccal probing, and occasional swelling/abscess—especially in a molar-bearing arch of a child—the clinical-radiographic pattern is highly suggestive of buccal bifurcation cyst with a paradental/inflammatory etiology akin to radicular cyst but oriented buccally.<cite id="58db1b88-3">Well-defined U-shaped radiolucency around 47 with buccal tilting; increased probing depth; features such as pain, swelling, and localized abscess occur</cite> <cite id="9273dcab-3">Radiographic findings showed a well-defined U-shaped radiolucency around 47 with buccal tilting and buccal bone expansion/thinning</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-1">Histopathological features include non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with hyperplasia</cite> <cite id="9273dcab-1">Histological features closely resemble those of a radicular cyst</cite>.
- Maxillary molar involvement exists but is sparser in the literature; when present, the pattern mirrors mandibular cases, with localized buccal periodontal inflammation/infiltration and a cystic lesion at the buccal root concavity, requiring differentiation from simple periodontal disease or periapical abscesses.<cite id="58db1b88-0">BBC typically occurs at the buccal region of the first or second mandibular molars</cite> <cite id="3eb6d54a-8">BBC is limited to buccal bifurcation area of mandibular molars in most reports</cite> <cite id="58db1b88-9">Inflammatory paradental cysts at first/second molars are termed ‘buccal bifurcation cysts’</cite>.

# Main challenges and limitations of anti‑TNFα biologics for cutaneous sarcoidosis

## Why anti‑TNF therapy for skin sarcoidosis is imperfect from the start
Anti‑TNF agents demonstrably reduce cutaneous lesion activity, but response is often partial, time‑dependent, and discontinuation commonly triggers relapse.<cite id="992051a2-1">Trials have explored multiple TNF inhibitors, and infliximab is established mainly for sarcoidosis unresponsive to corticosteroids or second‑line agents, highlighting that benefit is confined to steroid‑refractory disease subsets rather than universally effective</cite> <cite id="992051a2-3">An observed overall cutaneous response rate of 24% at 3 months rising to 46% by 6 months indicates that initial responses are modest and often delayed, requiring commitment to longer courses</cite> <cite id="122dc478-0">After 18 months off therapy, 44% of patients relapsed with skin symptoms, underscoring the high risk of disease rebound post‑discontinuation</cite> <cite id="122dc478-4">Reviews conclude these agents are effective in cutaneous sarcoidosis yet report that relapses are frequent after stopping and clinicians must be vigilant for infections</cite>. Across biologics (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab), pharmacological differences matter: infliximab/golimumab (IV) can deliver rapid, sometimes complete responses in steroid‑refractory cases, while sc‑TNF agents rely on stepwise titration and persistent adherence.<cite id="3691093b-0">TNF inhibitors differ in binding to soluble and membrane‑bound TNF; infliximab/golimumab bind both and have shown robust activity in severe disease</cite> <cite id="992051a2-8">A documented 5‑mg/kg infliximab course led to successful long‑term control in a refractory cutaneous case</cite>.

## Primary and secondary non‑response, immunogenicity, and switching TNF agents
Primary non‑response and development of antidrug antibodies are major limitations across TNF blockers, and this applies to skin disease as well.<cite id="992051a2-5">TNF inhibitors don't work for everyone; immune systems can produce antibodies that neutralize the drug, leading to treatment failure</cite> <cite id="3691093b-5">Reactive granulomatous dermatitis with paradoxical worsening has been reported under etanercept, infliximab, and adalimumab, demonstrating biologic‑specific and cross‑agent risks of immune‑mediated paradox</cite>.
