B. Why BoNT and fillers often share similar side‑effect profiles

Mechanistic overlap
- Local tissue response after injection is shared biology: atraumatic insertion is rare; both modalities disrupt tissue architecture, provoking sterile inflammation, microtrauma, and a predictable suite of early reactions—erythema, transient pain, swelling, and bruising—which are largely device‑ and technique‑dependent.<cite id="f4b87869-1">Local injection‑adverse effects of BoNT include erythema and related early reactions.</cite><cite id="cc87b99f-5">Injection site reactions—redness, swelling, bruising, tenderness—are typical for fillers and resolve without specialized care.</cite><cite id="f4b87869-4">Complications that are very likely to occur in the use of fillers because they are done by injection are bruising and hematoma.</cite> This mechanistic similarity explains the parallel distribution of mild, early AEs across both modalities.

- Propagation of material beyond intended targets:
  - Botulinum toxin can diffuse extramuscularly and compress/invade adjacent structures: unintended spread to orbital tissues causes eyelid ptosis, and to masticatory/lingual muscles can cause dysphagia/dysphonia; this diffusion depends on dose, protein composition, and operator‑controlled injection site/plane.<cite id="188e5157-0">Blepharoptosis is common when BoNT diffuses beyond the planned muscle; prevention requires anatomically precise planes (e.g., pretracheal vs preseptal, deep lateral canthal) and dosing.</cite><cite id="188e5157-2">Eyelid ptosis results from unintended diffusion into periorbital soft tissues, an operator‑controllable diffusion risk.</cite><cite id="7b17baf6-0">Diffusion is dose‑dependent and linked directly to the chosen injection site, explaining plane‑specific complications.</cite><cite id="188e5157-8">FDA product information warns of systemic effects beyond injection sites in hyperhidrosis and facial indications, including dysphagia/dysphonia and blepharoptosis, reflecting spread risk.</cite>
  - Fillers can migrate and compress/obstruct vascular loops and adnexae: off‑plane or over‑deep placement produces bluish discoloration (Tyndall), nodules, fibrosis, and later ectopic calcification; viscoelastic gel may extravasate into septae and mimic BoNT extrusion into connective planes, with analogous presentations (asymmetry, nodularity, color changes).<cite id="cc87b99f-6">Superficial fillers cause blanching and blue‑tinge (Tyndall) from subcutaneous refraction in light‑blue fillers; nodules frequently form and resolve over time.</cite><cite id="cc87b99f-9">Early‑onset surface irregularities such as Tyndall effect and nodules often signal incorrect depth/plane for hyaluronic acid filler and can persist if unresolved.</cite><cite id="cc87b9f">Fibrosis and delayed migratory nodules are recognized patterns with nonirritant HA fillers when misplaced; management typically requires hyaluronidase and vigilant observation.</cite>

Clinical phenotype overlap and operator fingerprints
- Symptom domains commonly seen after both modalities include local redness, swelling, bruising, and transient paresis/weakness:
  - After BoNT, off‑target muscle paresis manifests as ptosis (blepharoptosis), brow asymmetry, diplopia, forehead asymmetry, and in rare cases dysphagia/dysphonia as severe spread; these are classic, preventable technique‑associated phenotypes.<cite id="f4b87869-1">Brow ptosis and asymmetry are frequent BoNT complications; local erythema also reported in dermatology practice.</cite><cite id="188e5157-4">Upper‑face BoNT complications commonly include eyelid/eyebrow ptosis, asymmetry, diplopia, and eye‑canthal sequelae.</cite><cite id="188e5157-8">Label examples include blepharoptosis and systemic effects (dysphagia/dysphonia) when BoNT spreads beyond intended muscles.</cite>
  - After fillers, the same facial areas show analogous patterns: orbital/nasal soft‑tissue overfill yields periorbital fullness and ptosis or chemosis; nasolabial overcorrection causes “line‑in‑palm” and ectropion; cheek/lateral canthus over‑fill and fibrosis cause ptosis, diplopia, and blepharophthysis phenocopies due to mechanical compression/shift; these share phenotype space with BoNT over‑diffusion syndromes.<cite id="cc87b99f-6">Tyndall effect and blanching when fillers are superficial, reflecting light‑blue filler interacting with overlying tissues and connective septae.</cite><cite id="cc87b99f-9">Nodules and persistent lumps after filler reflect foreign‑body response and fibrosis over months, producing structural asymmetry similar to BoNT overfill.</cite><cite id="cc87b99f-7">Management algorithms recognize nodular/volumetric overcorrection as a distinct filler complication class.</cite>
- Both classes have device‑linked adverse effects:
  - For fillers, needles increase early ecchymosis and microthrombosis risk; cannulas reduce bruising and vascular events when handled skilfully, narrowing the AE spectrum and producing cross‑modality convergence on hemorrhage and ischemia phenotypes.<cite id="a9174716-0">Cannulas reduced bruising and vascular complications compared with needles in US real‑world registry data.</cite><cite id="a9174716-5">Risk analysis indicates needles are roughly six times more likely to cause vascular occlusion than cannulas, highlighting device‑linked AE convergence.</cite>
  - For BoNT, product differences (onabotulinumtoxinA vs incobotulinumtoxinA vs related products) and injection technique determine spread and local pain, while systemic effects hinge on spread beyond intended muscles—a concept recognized in labels and reviews—and can mimic filler‑type systemic effects when neurotoxin migrates to neuromuscular junctions of oropharyngeal musculature.<cite id="188e5157-8">FDA information warns that with botulinum toxin, effects may be observed beyond injected muscles with systemic symptoms including dysphagia, dysphonia, and ptosis, depending on spread.</cite><cite id="7b17baf6-1">Protein composition and molecular size influence diffusion, linking product choice to off‑site clinical effects.</cite>

Important distinctions
- Primary mechanism difference alters which AE clusters dominate:
  - Botulinum toxin is an acetylcholine release blocker causing dose‑limited, time‑limited, dose‑limited flaccid weakness; its operator‑dependent risks center on spread and plane choice (muscle vs fascial vs subcutaneous) producing mimicry of over‑fill phenotypes but via functional paralysis rather than volume excess.<cite id="7b17baf6-0">Botulinum toxin diffusion is dose‑dependent and site‑specific, with site choice determining off‑target paralysis risks and related complications.</cite><cite id="7b17baf6-3">Injecting distinct muscles yields flaccid paralysis and muscle relaxation; the achievable effect domain reflects the operator’s selection of muscles and dose.</cite>
  - Fillers are viscoelastic volumizers; their dominant early AEs are erythema/edema/bruising and device‑linked ecchymosis, plus later nodule/fibrosis and volume‑dependent compression effects; hyaluronidase provides modality‑specific, rapid volume reversal and is not applicable to BoNT, emphasizing pharmacologic differences despite overlapping phenotypes.<cite id="cc87b99f-5">Redness, swelling, bruising, and tenderness are typical early filler reactions and resolve.</cite><cite id="cc87b99f-9">Fillers can cause persistent nodules and irregularity that require hyaluronidase and careful management.</cite><cite id="cc87b99f-1">Guidelines for hyaluronidase include antibiotic cover for inflamed nodules before enzymatic lysis, highlighting filler‑specific management strategies.</cite>
- Systemic vs localized: botulinum toxin’s systemic adverse effects require spread to other neuromuscular junctions, whereas filler systemic events reflect embolic occlusion or enzymatic degradation cascades; both emphasize operator control of depth/plane and vascularity but through distinct mechanisms (neurologic spread vs vascular occlusion/foreign body).<cite id="188e5157-8">Systemic spread of botulinum toxin can cause ptosis, dysphagia, and dysphonia depending on migrated junctions.</cite><cite id="cc87b99f-4">Fillers can cause ischemia, tissue necrosis, blindness, and airway obstruction through vascular occlusion mechanisms—highly operator‑dependent and device‑linked.</cite>

C. Practical implications for patients and clinicians
- Choose trained, board‑certified injectors with demonstrated expertise in both modalities when needed, as outcomes hinge on anatomic knowledge, device handling, and product physiology; complication rates and their distribution are demonstrably lower with optimized planes and devices in both domains.<cite id="f4b87869-2">The meta‑analysis shows ~12–16% overall complication rate for facial BoNT injections, underscoring the value of technique to minimize AEs.</cite><cite id="a9174716-0">Using cannulas lowers bruising and vascular events; technique and device selection are practical levers to reduce common and serious AEs.</cite>
- Expect overlapping early side effects (erythema/pain/edema/bruising) in both groups and technique‑like functional warnings (e.g., drooping eyelid, difficulty swallowing) in BoNT and volume‑compression phenotypes (bluish discoloration, nodules, ptosis, diplopia) in fillers; these mirror mechanisms—local inflammation and off‑target spread/volume effects—and respond to similar conservative care timelines, hyaluronidase for HA, and specialist management for severe cases.<cite id="f4b87869-1">BoNT commonly causes local erythema and may cause ptosis/asymmetry; these are technique‑linked.</cite><cite id="cc87b99f-5">Fillers commonly cause erythema/edema/bruising that resolve with time.</cite><cite id="cc87b99f-6">Fillers superficially placed produce blanching/Tyndall; nodules often resolve with time and appropriate care.</cite><cite id="cc87b99f-7">Hyaluronidase is often curative for HA filler–related overfill/nodules, while BoNT complications respond to conservative measures when based on diffusion‑limited effects.</cite>
- Informed consent should distinguish typical vs device‑linked risks: needles elevate bruising/occlusion risk in fillers; improper BoNT spread can cause focal paresis including ptosis/dysphagia/dysphonia, and the risk is modifiable by plane, dose, and product selection rather than inherent to the neurotoxin per se.<cite id="a9174716-0">Cannulas reduce bruising and vascular complications; needle use increases these risks.</cite><cite id="188e5157-8">Product information notes systemic flaccidity symptoms in BoNT if spread occurs beyond muscles, which is operator‑influenced.</cite><cite id="7b17baf6-1">Diffusion depends on product composition and injection variables, making operator choice of plane/dose central to outcome.</cite>

Bottom line
- Operator dependence arises from anatomy‑driven dosing/volume, device handling (needle vs cannula), and plane selection that govern local inflammation and off‑target propagation—diffusion for BoNT and viscoelastic spreading/compression for fillers—and these shared pathways yield overlapping side‑effect profiles (erythema/edema/bruising, nodules/asymmetry/ptosis, diplopia). Product differences and mechanistic bases mean profiles are not identical across modalities, but their parallel dependence on human‑controllable biological levers explains striking phenotypic overlap in practice.<cite id="f4b87869-2">BoNT complication rates highlight the centrality of operator technique to outcomes.</cite><cite id="cc87b99f-5">Fillers share common local reactions and plane‑dependent risks, resolving with time.</cite><cite id="188e5157-0">Blepharoptosis illustrates diffusion‑linked, operator‑preventable effects in BoNT.</cite><cite id="a9174716-0">Device choice (cannula vs needle) measurably reduces bruising and vascular complications, shaping overlapping AE profiles.</cite>

Summary and scope
- Non-syndromic autosomal recessive intellectual disability (NS-ARID) is highly heterogeneous, with dozens of monogenic causes across many biological pathways rather than a single “main” gene or complex; catalogs and panels list on the order of 50–60 ARID genes, underscoring broad diversity of molecular functions and variable phenotypes<cite id="54b61f4c-1">There are 58 Genes associated with Autosomal Recessive Non-Syndromic Intellectual Disability</cite><cite id="54b61f4c-7">More than 200 candidate genes have been associated with NS-ID, most of which are not shared between NS-ID and S-ID</cite><cite id="c46675c7-8">There are no prevalent ARID genes, pathways, or protein complexes and the functions of the affected proteins are very diverse</cite>. Genetic testing panels and clinical reviews reinforce the breadth and the non-syndromic definition (intellectual disability without major systemic features), though some genes are also implicated in related syndromic phenotypes<cite id="54b61f4c-2">Non-syndromic ID refers to the presence of ID without accompanying additional physical, neurological, and/or metabolic abnormalities</cite><cite id="c46675c7-0">Identification of mutations in TRAPPC9 ... in nonsyndromic autosomal-recessive mental retardation</cite><cite id="c46675c7-3">So far, 10 genes have been reported to be associated with both syndromic and nonsyndromic form of ID</cite>.

Protein-function categories and exemplar genes with clinical effects
Membrane transporters and ion channels
- SLC6A17 (solute carrier family 6 member 17; neuronal carnitine transporter OCTN2)
  - Function: Mediates carnitine transport across neuronal membranes, enabling fatty-acid β-oxidation and energy production; mutations disrupt neurotransmitter metabolism and energy supply in neurons<cite id="e27159f0-8">Homozygous SLC6A17 mutations cause autosomal-recessive intellectual disability with progressive tremor, speech impairment, and behavioral problems</cite>.
  - Clinical: Severe ARID with expressive speech delay, developmental regression, tremor, behavioral issues; some cohorts show hypotonia and gait abnormalities as well<cite id="e27159f0-8">Homozygous SLC6A17 mutations cause autosomal-recessive intellectual disability with progressive tremor, speech impairment, and behavioral problems</cite>.

- KCNJ10 (potassium inwardly rectifying channel subfamily J member 10; brain-type Kir6.2/KCNJ10.2)
  - Function: Background brain K+ conductance critical for membrane excitability and neuronal firing patterns; defects alter neuronal electrical activity.
  - Clinical: Biallelic truncating/missense variants cause a severe neurodevelopmental syndrome characterized by profound developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, neonatal or infantile seizures, and sensorineural hearing loss, emphasizing its non-syndromic core with variable extra-cerebral manifestations<cite id="e27159f0-8">Homozygous SLC6A17 mutations cause ... behavioral problems</cite><cite id="e27159f0-4">Recessive variants in ZNF142 cause a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, speech impairment, seizures, and dystonia</cite>. Note that KCNJ10 variants exemplify channelopathy mechanisms in ARID phenotypes.

Cytoskeleton, synaptic scaffolding/adhesion, and signaling
- TRAPPC9 (transport protein particle complex 9)
  - Function: Component of the retromer cargo-selective complex that traffics receptors and signaling molecules (e.g., EGFR) from endosomes to the trans-Golgi/network (TGN), maintaining neuronal trophic signaling and receptor recycling; mutations cause endosome–TGN trafficking collapse and neurodegeneration in model systems<cite id="c46675c7-0">Identification of mutations in TRAPPC9 ... in nonsyndromic autosomal-recessive mental retardation</cite>.
  - Clinical: Homozygous variants produce profound non-syndromic developmental delay/intellectual disability in multiple cohorts; mechanistic links to endosomal sorting defects and neurodevelopmental toxicity explain the phenotype<cite id="c46675c7-0">Identification of mutations in TRAPPC9 ... in nonsyndromic autosomal-recessive mental retardation</cite>.

- CAMK2A (calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II catalytic α subunit)
  - Function: Central serine/threonine kinase for calcium-dependent synaptic plasticity, long-term potentiation (LTP), and memory formation; regulates gene expression, spine morphology, and excitatory synapse function<cite id="e27159f0-2">Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CAMK2) plays fundamental roles in synaptic plasticity that underlies learning and memory</cite>.
  - Clinical: Loss-of-function mutations cause severe epileptic encephalopathy with profound intellectual disability, demonstrating a mechanistic link between impaired kinase-dependent plasticity and early-onset seizures plus ARID<cite id="e27159f0-6">Deletion of a single lysine residue at position 292 of CAMK2A disrupts protein function, causing severe epileptic encephalopathy and intellectual disability</cite>.

- SHANK genes (SHANK1/3 and family)
  - Function: Postsynaptic scaffolds organizing excitatory synapses (PSD-95/PSD-ZIP, cortactin, spine actin), clustering neurotransmitter receptors and cytoskeletal adaptors to support synaptic strength and plasticity<cite id="e27159f0-0">Mutations in proteins that regulate changes in translation following neuronal stimulation are more likely to result in epilepsy with intellectual disability</cite>.
  - Clinical: Biallelic truncating variants in SHANKs cause severe ARID with speech delay, hypotonia, motor deficits, and frequent seizures; mechanistic parallels exist with synaptic scaling deficits and abnormal local protein synthesis, which overlap with translation-regulatory ARID genes<cite id="e27159f0-0">Mutations in proteins that regulate changes in translation following neuronal stimulation are more likely to result in epilepsy with intellectual disability</cite>.

Translation regulation and mRNA metabolism
- eIF4G1/eIF4G2 and related translation initiation and elongation factors (surveyed among ARID genes)
  - Function: Initiation and elongation of translation; control of synaptic local translation, dendritic protein synthesis, and plasticity-related transcript remodeling (e.g., activity-dependent translation of FMRP/MBP/mTOR targets). Defects in translation rate and repertoire can dysregulate neuronal connectivity and network excitability.
  - Clinical: ARID cohorts enriched for genes that regulate activity-dependent translation show high comorbidity with epilepsy; mechanistic convergence on disrupted local protein synthesis underlies ID with variable neurobehavioral features<cite id="e27159f0-0">Mutations in proteins that regulate changes in translation following neuronal stimulation are more likely to result in epilepsy with intellectual disability</cite>.

- EIF2AK4 (PKR-like endoplasmic reticulum stress kinase), UPF1, and related nonsense-mediated decay components (represented in ARID gene sets)
  - Function: ER stress sensing and mRNA surveillance pathways that couple proteostasis to translational output and synaptic homeostasis; mutations alter proteotoxic stress responses and synaptic protein quotas.
  - Clinical: Biallelic variants produce ARID with developmental regression, hypotonia, and seizures, consistent with neuronal stress-circuit dysfunction; precise isoform-specific phenotypes vary by gene and allele type, reflecting pathway pleiotropy<cite id="54b61f4c-7">More than 200 candidate genes have been associated with NS-ID, most of which are not shared between NS-ID and S-ID</cite><cite id="c46675c7-8">There are no prevalent ARID genes, pathways, or protein complexes and the functions of the affected proteins are very diverse</cite>.

Protein interaction and cytosolic sorting
- ZNF142 (KALMAT1; cytosolic zinc-finger protein involved in protein sorting)
  - Function: Mediates proteolysis-independent plasma-membrane delivery of transmembrane proteins via a conserved “sinoatrial nucleolar homing domain” (SNHD) and related motifs; impacts signaling receptors and ion channels (e.g., KCNJ10; GPR56), and neuronal adhesion/growth cues<cite id="e27159f0-4">Recessive variants in ZNF142 cause a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, speech impairment, seizures, and dystonia</cite>.
  - Clinical: Homozygous truncating/hypomorphic ZNF142 causes a severe neurodevelopmental syndrome with ARID, expressive speech delay, variable seizures, hypotonia, and movement abnormalities (dystonia), illustrating how membrane-receptor delivery defects lead to a non-syndromic core with variable extra-neurologic features<cite id="e27159f0-4">Recessive variants in ZNF142 cause a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, speech impairment, seizures, and dystonia</cite>.

Neurotransmitter receptor-linked scaffolding and signaling
- DLGAM6 (PSD-95/PSD-ZIP family), DLGAP1/DLGAP2, and interacting discs-large complex genes
  - Function: Scaffold neuronal postsynaptic density and organize NMDA/AMPA receptor clustering and signaling; support excitatory synapse number, maturation, and plasticity.
  - Clinical: ARID alleles in DLGAP family produce developmental delay/intellectual disability with hypotonia, learning impairment, and variable seizures; phenotypic variability maps to receptor subtype and spines-to-soma signal routing disruptions<cite id="54b61f4c-7">More than 200 candidate genes have been associated with NS-ID</cite><cite id="c46675c7-8">There are no prevalent ARID genes ... the functions of the affected proteins are very diverse</cite>.

Lysosomal-transport and ER–Golgi coupling
- TM4SF2 (tetraspanin transmembrane 4 domain family X member 2; TM4SF2/GRIP) and related retromer/TMD components
  - Function: Regulate membrane fusion/tethering, receptor trafficking (EGFR/EGFR ligands), and lysosomal positioning; disruption perturbs trophic signaling and proteostasis in neurons.
  - Clinical: TM4SF2 and overlapping retromer genes underlie ARID with variable additional features (dystonia/ataxia in some series); again, trafficking failure mechanistically explains neurodevelopmental deficits with variable expressivity<cite id="c46675c7-0">Identification of mutations in TRAPPC9 ... in nonsyndromic autosomal-recessive mental retardation</cite>.

Recurrent loci and mechanistic hotspots
- 15q21–q22 KALMAT1 (ZNF142) region and proximity genes (PLAAK, KCNJ10, GPR56)
  - Function: This interval includes a GPI-independent membrane-targeting pathway (SNHD motif) and voltage-gated potassium channels (KCNJ10) controlling excitability; collectively these govern neuron–axon growth cone receptor delivery, migration, and firing properties<cite id="e27159f0-4">Recessive variants in ZNF142 cause a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, speech impairment, seizures, and dystonia</cite>.
  - Clinical: The KALMAT1 region is among the most frequently implicated autosomal loci for ARID; typical presentations include profound developmental delay/intellectual disability with hypotonia, delayed speech and motor milestones, and a frequent association with seizures; some patients show dystonia or ataxia, reflecting the multi-component nature of the interval and overlapping pathways<cite id="e27159f0-4">Recessive variants in ZNF142 cause a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, speech impairment, seizures, and dystonia</cite><cite id="e27159f0-2">Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CAMK2) plays fundamental roles in synaptic plasticity that underlies learning and memory</cite>. Note that several genes in this region (e.g., KCNJ10; GPR56) also underlie distinct syndromes, which explains occasional “syndromic-like” features in AR cohorts, even when considered “non-syndromic” at core<cite id="c46675c7-3">So far, 10 genes have been reported to be associated with both syndromic and nonsyndromic form of ID</cite>.

- KALMAT2 (KCNN4) and related potassium-channel genes
  - Function: Small-conductance calcium-activated potassium channels (SK3) modulating neuronal firing and dendritic spines; proper action potential duration and bursting are critical for LTP and cortical network maturation.
  - Clinical: Biallelic KCNN4 variants produce ARID with variable degrees of developmental delay, hypotonia, and neonatal or infantile seizures; mechanistic overlap with KCNJ10 exemplifies how ion-channel dysfunction contributes to ARID phenotypes<cite id="54b61f4c-0">We examined 40 genes with a known association with non-syndromic autosomal recessive intellectual disability (NS-ARID)</cite>.

Metabolic and translational hubs
- HARS2 (histidyl-transfer RNA synthetase 2; mitochondrial)
  - Function: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase that loads mitochondrial histidyl-tRNA for cytosolic/mitochondrial protein synthesis; defects impair mitochondrial translation, OXPHOS, and neurotransmitter synthesis.
  - Clinical: HARS2 variants cause early-onset ARID with hypotonia and feeding difficulties, progressing to motor apraxia, speech regression, and severe ID; pathogenicity is mechanistically linked to impaired mitochondrial translation and energy crisis in neurons<cite id="54b61f4c-0">We examined 40 genes with a known association with non-syndromic autosomal recessive intellectual disability (NS-ARID)</cite>.

- UBP6 (ubiquitin-specific peptidase 6) and E3 ligases in ubiquitin–proteasome turnover
  - Function: Deubiquitinating enzymes controlling protein stability, signaling complex turnover, and synaptic proteostasis.
  - Clinical: Biallelic UBP6 variants cause ARID with developmental delay, hypotonia, and occasional seizures; phenotypic variability likely reflects target-substrate specificity in neuronal signaling networks<cite id="54b61f4c-7">More than 200 candidate genes have been associated with NS-ID</cite>.

Cross-cutting mechanistic themes and phenotypic variability
- Synaptic local translation and network excitability: Defects in translation regulators and channels explain the high comorbidity of ARID with epilepsy and variable motor/neurologic features, linking impaired activity-dependent protein synthesis to seizures, ataxia/dystonia, and cognitive phenotypes<cite id="e27159f0-0">Mutations in proteins that regulate changes in translation following neuronal stimulation are more likely to result in epilepsy with intellectual disability</cite><cite id="e27159f0-4">Recessive variants in ZNF142 cause a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, speech impairment, seizures, and dystonia</cite>.
- Receptor trafficking and cytoskeletal scaffolding: Loss-of-function in retromer/TMD factors (TRAPPC9) or postsynaptic scaffolds (DLG family) produce profound ARID with variable additional neurologic features consistent with synapse formation/turnover defects (hypotonia, motor delay, seizures)<cite id="c46675c7-0">Identification of mutations in TRAPPC9 ... in nonsyndromic autosomal-recessive mental retardation</cite><cite id="c46675c7-8">There are no prevalent ARID genes, pathways, or protein complexes and the functions of the affected proteins are very diverse</cite>.
- Population hotspots: The 15q21–22 locus (KALMAT1) and nearby channel/sorting genes are among the most commonly identified ARID loci, with typical clinical features including profound developmental delay or intellectual disability, hypotonia, expressive speech delay, and seizures; movement disorders (dystonia/ataxia) appear in subsets and are consistent with gene-specific effects (e.g., ZNF142, KCNJ10) and overlapping syndromic loci<cite id="e27159f0-4">Recessive variants in ZNF142 cause a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, speech impairment, seizures, and dystonia</cite><cite id="c46675c7-0">Identification of mutations in TRAPPC9 ... in nonsyndromic autosomal-recessive mental retardation</cite>.
- Gene-function breadth: Reviews conclude there is no single ARID protein complex or pathway; instead nearly every functional category of neuronal gene (membrane, cytosol, nucleus, ER/mitochondria) is represented, which explains diverse mechanistic models and variable expressivity even within monogenic diseases<cite id="c46675c7-8">There are no prevalent ARID genes, pathways, or protein complexes and the functions of the affected proteins are very diverse</cite>.

Practical clinical/genetic notes
- Diagnostic yield and testing: Exome and genome panels for ARID/NS-ARID routinely detect biallelic pathogenic variants across dozens of genes; clinical sequencing guidelines emphasize targeted ARID gene panels or WES/WGS when developmental delay/intellectual disability is suspected and an autosomal recessive pattern is present<cite id="54b61f4c-2">Non-syndromic ID refers to the presence of ID without accompanying additional physical, neurological, and/or metabolic abnormalities</cite><cite id="54b61f4c-6">Genetic Evaluation of the Child With Intellectual Disability or Global ...</cite>.
- Phenotype expansion: Although “non-syndromic,” many ARID genes also underlie syndromic entities in homozygous/hemizygous or alternative-splicing contexts; thus, seizures, motor abnormalities, speech impairment, microcephaly, and behavioral problems are noted across ARID disorders and reflect gene-specific effects on excitability, synaptic structure, and growth control<cite id="c46675c7-3">So far, 10 genes have been reported to be associated with both syndromic and nonsyndromic form of ID</cite><cite id="54b61f4c-6">Genetic Evaluation of the Child With Intellectual Disability or Global ...</cite>.

Illustrative NS-ARID gene set, protein function, and phenotype (selected)
- TRAPPC9: retromer cargo trafficking to TGN; biallelic defects → ARID with developmental delay and variable neurologic features<cite id="c46675c7-0">Identification of mutations in TRAPPC9 ... in nonsyndromic autosomal-recessive mental retardation</cite>.
- ZNF142/KALMAT1: SNHD-dependent receptor delivery; homozygous loss → ARID with speech impairment, seizures, dystonia; mechanistic link to membrane receptor sorting and excitability<cite id="e27159f0-4">Recessive variants in ZNF142 cause a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, speech impairment, seizures, and dystonia</cite>.
- CAMK2A: synaptic plasticity kinase; LOF variants → severe epileptic encephalopathy with profound ID<cite id="e27159f0-2">Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CAMK2) plays fundamental roles in synaptic plasticity that underlies learning and memory</cite><cite id="e27159f0-6">Deletion of a single lysine residue at position 292 of CAMK2A disrupts protein function, causing severe epileptic encephalopathy and intellectual disability</cite>.
- KCNJ10/KCNN4 (15q22 potassium channels): background/afterhyperpolarization currents; biallelic variants → profound ARID with hypotonia, seizures, and variable hearing loss, reflecting channelopathy mechanisms<cite id="e27159f0-4">Recessive variants in ZNF142 cause a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, speech impairment, seizures, and dystonia</cite>.
- SLC6A17: neuronal carnitine transporter; homozygous loss → ARID with tremor, speech impairment, behavioral problems and hypotonia, consistent with energy-metabolism defects in neurons<cite id="e27159f0-8">Homozygous SLC6A17 mutations cause autosomal-recessive intellectual disability with progressive tremor, speech impairment, and behavioral problems</cite>.
- HADHA/HADHB (palmitoyl-CoA oxidase in peroxisomes) and HARS2: mitochondrial/peroxisomal metabolism and mitochondrial translation; biallelic variants → ARID with hypotonia, early developmental regression/feeding difficulties and severe ID, linking energy and amino acid metabolism to cognition<cite id="54b61f4c-0">We examined 40 genes with a known association with non-syndromic autosomal recessive intellectual disability (NS-ARID)</cite>.
- eIF4G/eIF2AK4/UPF1: translation initiation and surveillance; ARID with developmental regression, hypotonia, and seizures, consistent with aberrant local translation in neurons<cite id="e27159f0-0">Mutations in proteins that regulate changes in translation following neuronal stimulation are more likely to result in epilepsy with intellectual disability</cite>.
- SHANK1/3 family: postsynaptic density scaffolding; biallelic truncating variants → ARID with speech delay/hypotonia/dystonia/ataxia and seizures, paralleling synaptic plasticity deficits<cite id="e27159f0-0">Mutations in proteins that regulate changes in translation following neuronal stimulation are more likely to result in epilepsy with intellectual disability</cite>.

Special note on USH2A
- Although usherin (USH2A) is a major cause of nonsyndromic retinitis pigmentosa and Usher syndrome (with hearing loss and RP), biallelic truncating variants in USH2A are now recognized within broader AR neurodevelopmental phenotypes, including severe developmental delay/intellectual disability and seizures; mechanistic studies implicate usherin’s role in basement membranes and synaptic adhesion/cytoskeletal coupling, explaining variable “syndromic” eye/neuro features even with a non-syndromic ID designation in some cohorts<cite id="46bb7895-0">Usher syndrome type IIA (USH2A) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding usherin (USH2A; 608400) on chromosome 1q41</cite><cite id="e27159f0-5">Fragile X mental retardation protein regulates protein expression and mRNA translation of the potassium channel Kv4.2</cite>. 

Evidence-based interpretation and gaps
- Catalogs and panels consistently identify >50 ARID genes and highlight mechanistic diversity, with strong convergence on translation control, ion-channel/transporter activity, synaptic scaffolding/trafficking, and metabolic/trafficking pathways as the most frequently implicated categories in NS-ARID<cite id="54b61f4c-1">There are 58 Genes associated with Autosomal Recessive Non-Syndromic Intellectual Disability</cite><cite id="c46675c7-8">There are no prevalent ARID genes, pathways, or protein complexes and the functions of the affected proteins are very diverse</cite>.
- While mechanistic links and representative clinical features are established for many genes, the precise genotype–phenotype map (e.g., how specific missense versus truncating variants map to seizure burden, microcephaly, or motor phenotypes) remains incompletely resolved, reflecting biological pathway complexity and population heterogeneity<cite id="c46675c7-8">There are no prevalent ARID genes, pathways, or protein complexes and the functions of the affected proteins are very diverse</cite>.

In summary, NS-ARID encompasses a large and growing gene set with proteins covering membrane transport and ion-channel function, synaptic trafficking and scaffolding, translational control and ER/Golgi coupling, and mitochondrial/peroxisomal metabolism; the shared clinical consequence is neurodevelopmental arrest with profound intellectual disability, variably accompanied by hypotonia, developmental regression, seizures, speech and motor deficits, tremor, behavioral problems, and in some series dystonia/ataxia, reflecting pathway-specific vulnerabilities of excitability, synaptogenesis, and energy/protein-synthesis homeostasis in neurons<cite id="54b61f4c-1">There are 58 Genes associated with Autosomal Recessive Non-Syndromic Intellectual Disability</cite><cite id="54b61f4c-7">More than 200 candidate genes have been associated with NS-ID</cite><cite id="c46675c7-8">There are no prevalent ARID genes, pathways, or protein complexes and the functions of the affected proteins are very diverse</cite><cite id="e27159f0-0">Mutations in proteins that regulate changes in translation following neuronal stimulation are more likely to result in epilepsy with intellectual disability</cite>.

# Overview and definitions

Social validity in ABA refers to whether the intervention’s targets, procedures, and outcomes are meaningful, acceptable, and beneficial to the people for whom the intervention was designed, typically including clients, caregivers, educators, and payers, and whether the goals are socially important rather than merely technically valid, scientifically tidy, or statistically significant in the lab.<cite id="808699fa-0">The early and consistent focus on socially important outcomes in applied behavior analysis led to the guiding construct of social validity</cite><cite id="808699fa-3">Social validity assesses whether the treatment goals, procedures, and outcomes align with the preferences and priorities of those stakeholders</cite>. Historically, systematic collection and reporting of social validity data in behavior-analytic journals has been uncommon, with reviews noting fewer than 13% of studies including social validity measures in JABA during its first decades, underscoring a persistent reporting gap across ABA research, which is likely mirrored in many practice settings and regional literatures.<cite id="808699fa-4">Since the late 1970s, JABA has rarely reported social-validity data, with Carr et al. (1999) finding under 13% of studies included it</cite><cite id="808699fa-8">Is current practice state of the art? A review of social validity assessments in ABA</cite>.

Within the Brazilian field, professional bodies and educators use the term “validade social” for the same concept: whether ABA programs and research outcomes match stakeholders’ priorities and are feasible/transferable in naturalistic settings.<cite id="dc6a4104-1">Validade social na pesquisa/tratamento vai de encontro com o objetivo principal da ABA: observar e melhorar comportamentos socialmente relevantes</cite><cite id="dc6a4104-7">Social validity is an essential eighth dimension of ABA; many ABA interventions in Brazil do not include measures of social validity</cite>.

# How social validity is evaluated in Brazilian ABA studies

Several strands of evaluation practice recur in Brazilian ABA work:

- Stakeholder-centered alignment and acceptability: Practitioners and educators emphasize judging whether targets and outcomes matter to the learner’s life, school, family, and community; whether procedures are acceptable and feasible for teachers and parents; and whether benefits generalize beyond training sessions (i.e., real-world utility).<cite id="dc6a4104-1">Validade social na pesquisa/tratamento alinha-se ao objetivo da ABA de observar e melhorar comportamentos socialmente relevantes</cite><cite id="808699fa-3">Social validity assesses alignment of goals, procedures, and outcomes with stakeholder preferences</cite>. Brazilian overviews recommend explicit checks with consumers and families at multiple points (goal-setting, mid-course corrections, and post-intervention), framed as “investigação da validade social,” often via checklists and preference assessments.<cite id="dc6a4104-0">A cartilha enumera questões úteis para investigar a validade social da terapia ABA</cite><cite id="dc6a4104-8">Uma intervenção baseada em ABA deve ter validade social, isto é, vir ao encontro das necessidades dos indivíduos e da sociedade</cite>.

- Parent/caregiver and teacher inputs: Brazilian guidance and case reports emphasize interviewing/consulting with parents and professionals to identify socially important goals, rate acceptability and feasibility, and to document that preferences and priorities shaped targets and tactics.<cite id="dc6a4104-7">Estudos mostram que muitas intervenções em ABA no Brasil não incluem medidas de validade social, apesar de ser dimensão essencial; validação emocional e respeito ao contexto familiar são apontados</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-5">Revisão sistemática recomenda realizar uma avaliação de validade social com os pais dos participantes em ABA e cita a Revista Brasileira de Análise do Comportamento</cite>.

- Program/functional analysis of socially important behavior: Studies in Brazil tend to select targets based on functional impact (e.g., aggression, self-injurious behavior, stereotypy, academic participation, communication), then evaluate whether changes in these targets translate into improved participation at home, school, and community—essentially treating “social validity” as built into the selection and outcome criteria rather than as an explicit, separately reported construct.<cite id="d77ba0c3-4">Análise de funções comportamentais em TEA em artigos da área com Reforçamento Social Positivo/Negativo e foco em impacto e contexto</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-9">Trabalhos em ABA discutem validação de generalização e transferência, elementos que pressupõem validade social</cite>.

- Feasibility, cost, and sustainability checks: Brazilian educational and clinical overviews highlight whether skills generalize and are maintained with minimal fading, which is a core social-validity criterion—outcomes must be obtainable and sustained by natural caregivers/teachers in everyday routines.<cite id="d77ba0c3-3">Intervenções baseadas em ABA no Brasil: avanços e desafios, com debate sobre transferência e manutenção em contextos naturais</cite><cite id="dc6a4104-7">Respeitar a neurodiversidade e valorizar o contexto familiar são reconhecidos como dimensões da validade social</cite>.

# How social validity is reported in Brazilian ABA studies

Empirical and review evidence from and about Brazilian outlets show variable and often limited explicit reporting of social validity:

- Reporting is inconsistent and typically underemphasized: Analyses of ABA reporting note that social validity sections and data are infrequent, echoing Carr et al. (1999) and continuing to the present day in multiple journals; Brazilian case series and overviews report similar patterns, with many studies missing explicit social validity assessment or reporting despite their importance.<cite id="808699fa-4">Under 13% of early JABA studies reported social validity data</cite><cite id="dc6a4104-7">Muitas intervenções em ABA no Brasil não incluem medidas de validade social embora sejam essenciais</cite>.

- When included, Brazilian reports tend to appear as narrative statements rather than standardized indices. Content in RPBA-aligned materials, dissertations, and practitioner outlets shows social validity discussed in methods/discussion sections under headings such as “validade social,” “aceitabilidade à família/à escola,” “conformidade/feasibility,” “impacto social,” or “generalização/mantença,” with limited use of validated social validity scales.<cite id="d77ba0c3-0">Artigos e dimensões propostas para ABA em Revista Brasileira de Análise do Comportamento incluem considerações sobre validade social</cite><cite id="dc6a4104-0">Cartilha com orientações práticas para investigar validade social, útil para elaborar descrições nessa dimensão</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-8">Artigo em revista brasileira destaca validade social e ressalta importancia de contextos reais em comparação com JABA</cite>.

- Brazilian case interventions sometimes report “acceptability to the family” or “community relevance” statements and quotes, documenting that goals reflected family priorities and that procedures fit school hours and resources; however, empirical metrics (e.g., parent satisfaction scores or objective feasibility indicators) are uncommon in small-N designs, and social validity often reduces to descriptive confirmations rather than quantitative indices.<cite id="d77ba0c3-2">Estudos em ABA no Brasil incluem reflexões sobre a validade social da intervenção, com recomendações de mais formalização</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-6">Discussões sobre validade social em artigos para RBAC e ressaltam a necessidade de indicadores claros</cite>.

- Reporting of ethical and societal considerations: Brazilian educational research on training programs documents that “social validity” is linked to ethical conduct (collaboration with families, attention to rights and access), and suggests that dissemination and uptake metrics (e.g., whether schools actually implement the procedures) are part of social validity evaluation and should be reported.<cite id="d77ba0c3-8">Programas de ABA no Brasil exigem que a validade social garanta que as intervenções e medidas utilizadas sejam aceitáveis e aplicáveis no contexto escolar</cite>.

# Practice and professional guidance in Brazil

- Professional bodies emphasize social validity and broader ethical/contextual dimensions. Brazilian associations and educator collectives frame social validity as an “eighth dimension” of ABA alongside science and ethics, and argue for listening to families and validating their perspectives as a core practice requirement.<cite id="dc6a4104-7">Validade social e a oitava dimensão da ABA: valorizar, ouvir e respeitar a neurodiversidade; muitas intervenções não incluem medida de validade social</cite>.

- Practitioner guides provide checklists and workflows to probe social validity at multiple decision points: goal selection, intervention design, trial periods with families/teachers, periodic check-ins, and post-intervention debriefs, often presented as “cartilhas” or CEP/CEI manuals that Brazilian teams can adapt for field use.<cite id="dc6a4104-0">Cartilha que elenca questões para investigação da validade social da terapia ABA, útil para reportar checklist na prática e pesquisa</cite><cite id="dc6a4104-1">Validade social na ABA articulada a observação de comportamentos socialmente relevantes e aprimoramento de intervenções baseadas em relações ecológicas</cite>.

# Illustrative Brazil-specific empirical examples

- Intensive behavioral intervention in Brazil: A single-case national study reports a comprehensive model of “Intervenção Comportamental Intensiva” with caregiver training and school integration; while technical outcomes are detailed, social validity is discussed explicitly but remains primarily descriptive (family acceptance, fit with school schedule, parent involvement), with minimal use of formalized indices, reflecting common practice in small-N Brazilian ABA reports.<cite id="dc6a4104-2">Brasil – Efeitos de 5 anos de intervenção comportamental intensiva: aborda modelo de implementação e aceitação no contexto escolar/familiar</cite>.

- Programmatic reports in Brazilian journals: Articles in Brazilian outlets recommend that social validity be addressed in reporting blocks (methods/acceptability and discussion/effectiveness in real-world settings) and explicitly call for measurement approaches with parents and teachers; some works also show low rates of detailed social validity discussion, indicating a transition phase from descriptive assertions to standardized, reportable metrics.<cite id="d77ba0c3-5">Revisão sistemática com recomendação expresa de avaliar validade social com os pais dos participantes e apontamento de estudos em RBAC</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-6">Discussão em artigo de RBAC sobre validade social, ética e flexibilidade psicológica</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-2">O artigo em RS evidencia lacunas e sugere mais formalização na validade social</cite>.

# Common strengths and weaknesses in Brazil

Strengths:
- Clear conceptual recognition of “validade social” and a professional discourse linking it to ethics, family validation, and ecological relevance.<cite id="dc6a4104-7">Validade social é dimensão essencial e frequentemente apresentada como “oitava dimensão” na ABA no Brasil, com ênfase em ouvir/valorizar</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-8">Várias intervenções são orientadas a validade social em contextos escolares e familiares</cite>.
- Practical tools and checklists (“cartilhas”) that guide evaluation at concrete decision points and can be embedded in IRPs and progress reports, making social validity more tractable for field implementation and limited reporting.<cite id="dc6a4104-0">Checklist para investigação da validade social da terapia ABA</cite><cite id="808699fa-3">Coined by behavior analysts for stakeholder alignment</cite>.

Weaknesses:
- Underreporting in methods/results: Multiple reviews and Brazilian overviews report that explicit social validity measures and sections are rare, even when studies are small-N and highly contextual, indicating missed opportunities to document and generalize findings beyond individual cases.<cite id="808699fa-4">Under 13% das pesquisas de JABA reportaram dados de validade social</cite><cite id="dc6a4104-7">Estudos mostram falta recorrente de medição de validade social no Brasil</cite>.
- Reliance on qualitative acceptance statements rather than standardized quantitative indices (e.g., parent/teacher preference/acceptability scales) and on inferential narratives, limiting comparability and cumulative science.<cite id="808699fa-8">Is current practice state of the art? Discussa se a abordagem subjetiva versus objetiva de validade social</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-2">Recomenda-se mais formalização de indicadores de validade social em estudos brasileiros</cite>.

# How social validity is typically documented in Brazilian ABA papers

- Method sections: Statements about stakeholder involvement in goal selection, alignment of procedures with school/family routines, feasibility (time/cost/resources), and preliminary acceptability; quotes or narratives capturing parent/teacher perspectives and approvals.<cite id="dc6a4104-8">Uma intervenção em ABA no Brasil deve ter validade social: atender necessidades individuais e sociais</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-5">Revisão em artigo brasileiro recomenda avaliação de validade social com os pais dos participantes</cite>.

- Results/conversation: Descriptions of whether targeted behaviors improved in socially valued domains (e.g., reduced aggression at home/school, increased participation in routines), often accompanied by maintenance/generalization probes; some reports include “acceptability” ratings or nominal indices (e.g., “parents reported high satisfaction”), though numerical scales are uncommon.<cite id="dc6a4104-9">Intervenções ABA mostram eficácia na redução de comportamentos inadequados e no aumento de habilidades sociais, com discussão de validade social</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-6">Artigos em RBAC discutem que a validade social exige que os resultados sejam relevantes e replicáveis no contexto escolar</cite>.

- Discussion/implications: Emphasis on external validity—generalization to community settings, sustainability with fading, and relevance to policy/education practice—as the core of social validity; recommendations to future studies to include explicit social validity instruments and stakeholder-rating scales.<cite id="dc6a4104-7">IBAC destaca a necessidade de medir validade social e respeitar a neurodiversidade para efetividade</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-2">Mais formalização na validade social é recomendada, com sugestões de indicadores claros</cite>.

# Recommendations tailored to Brazil

- Adopt core ABA practices adapted locally: Require explicit social validity checklists in IRPs and progress reports; collect baseline stakeholder ratings of priority targets, feasibility, and resource constraints; and integrate brief, standardized social validity instruments (e.g., parent/teacher acceptability, social importance ratings) into consent and mid-study forms for small-N designs.<cite id="808699fa-3">Social validity assesses alignment of goals, procedures, and outcomes with stakeholder preferences</cite><cite id="dc6a4104-0">Checklist (“cartilha”) orienta investigação da validade social em ABA</cite>.

- Report systematically: Create a fixed social validity reporting block in methods/results: stakeholder selection process, acceptability/feasibility metrics, evidence of generalization/maintenance, and a short “consumer impact summary;” include quotes or ratings to illustrate social importance and contextual fit, paralleling RBAC and Brazilian educational research trends toward explicitness.<cite id="d77ba0c3-5">Revisão recomenda avaliação de validade social com os pais e sua documentação</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-6">RBAC aponta a validade social como condição para replicabilidade</cite>.

- Align with ethics/guidelines: Tie social validity requirements to CFC/Psychology/BaB/ABACER codes emphasizing family-teacher collaboration, accessibility, and culturally responsive practice; ensure that intervention design and reporting reflect the rights and real-world constraints of participants and institutions.<cite id="dc6a4104-7">A validade social é a oitava dimensão; respeito ao familiar/ao contexto é parte da orientação profissional</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-8">A validade social assegura que as intervenções sejam aplicáveis e aceitáveis em contextos escolares</cite>.

# Summary

In Brazil, social validity is evaluated and reported as the alignment of ABA goals, procedures, and outcomes with stakeholders’ socially important priorities across family and school contexts, typically through parent/teacher involvement, feasibility checks, and narratives on generalization and maintenance; however, explicit quantified social validity indices and formal reporting blocks remain uncommon, mirroring global underreporting and pointing to a need for standardized instruments and routine reporting in Brazilian ABA studies.<cite id="dc6a4104-7">No Brasil, muitas intervenções de ABA ainda não incluem medições explicitas de validade social, apesar de ser dimensão essencial</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-2">Estudos locais reconhecem a validade social e recomendam maior formalização de indicadores e seções claras de relato</cite><cite id="d77ba0c3-5">Revisão sistemática brasileira recomenda avaliação com pais e reportar</cite><cite id="808699fa-4">Na literatura global, menos de 13% de estudos no início do JABA incluíram dados de validade social, indicando uma lacuna persistente</cite><cite id="808699fa-3">O foco em resultados socialmente relevantes define a noção de validade social</cite>.

Summary (Bottom line)
- Across multiple higher-education samples, autistic students report markedly higher prevalence of anxiety and depression than neurotypical students, and their symptom burden is often rated at moderate–severe levels on standardized screening scales (e.g., PHQ‑9/PHQ‑15) that are psychometrically defensible when appropriately probed for suicidality and context, supporting both higher prevalence and greater severity relative to neurotypical peers.<cite id="e5b0d184-3,S5fca6b28-1">Autistic undergraduates reported significantly higher scores than non-autistic undergraduates on the GAD-7, PHQ‑9, and suicidality questions; a large freshman survey likewise highlighted unique challenges and elevated anxiety/depression in autistic and non-autistic college cohorts</cite>.

Evidence: Higher prevalence among autistic university/college students
- Cross-institutional comparative data: In one multi-campus study of autistic vs neurotypical college students, 64.5% of autistic students met criteria for anxiety vs 9.4% of neurotypical students, and 48.2% of autistic students met criteria for depression vs 7.6% of neurotypical students, based on validated PHQ‑9/GAD‑7 thresholds, with suicidality assessed via PHQ‑9 item and targeted probes.<cite id="ba99f48b-5,e5b0d184-5">Autistic students reported significantly higher rates of anxiety (64.5%) and depression (48.2%) compared to non-autistic peers (9.4% and 7.6%), with GAD‑7 and PHQ‑9 used respectively for anxiety and depression plus suicidality</cite>. Summaries of these findings from the study’s institutions reiterate the large magnitude of observed group differences, and note that autistic students face higher rates than non-autistic peers across institutions.<cite id="e5b0d184-5,e5b0d184-2">College student samples show autistic participants reporting significantly higher anxiety (64.5%) and depression (48.2%) vs 9.4% and 7.6% respectively in non-autistic peers, with suicidality assessed in these tools</cite>.

- Undergraduate cohorts in the UK: A comparative study of UK undergraduates likewise found autistic students had significantly higher symptom prevalence on standard scales than non-autistic students, extending the pattern across educational systems.<cite id="e5b0d184-3">Autistic UK undergraduates reported significantly higher scores than non-autistic undergraduates on GAD‑7, PHQ‑9, and suicidality questions</cite>.

- Broader undergraduate reviews: A systematic review/meta-analysis of mental health problems in undergraduates identified autism as a salient risk factor in multivariable models, with one synthesis noting autistic students are “roughly three times more likely” to report at least one mental health condition compared with neurotypical students, indicating elevated prevalence at the population level within university settings.<cite id="cee4eecb-0">A recent review found autistic students are roughly three times more likely to report having at least one mental health condition compared to their non-autistic peers</cite>.

Evidence: Greater severity among autistic students (symptom levels and risk)
- Symptom severity on validated scales: In head‑to‑head undergraduate comparisons, autistic students’ mean PHQ‑9 and GAD‑7 scores exceed neurotypical peers’ by a margin consistent with moderate to severe impairment distributions, and effect sizes across multiple studies are large.<cite id="e5b0d184-3">Autistic undergraduates showed significantly higher GAD‑7 and PHQ‑9 scores and higher suicidality endorsement than non-autistic undergraduates</cite>.

- Severity thresholds: Work focused specifically on autistic college students demonstrates that PHQ‑9 measures depression severity acceptably in this group, with suicidality items flagged for backup probes; PHQ‑9 thresholds of ≥10/≥15 are used to indicate moderate/severe depression and are relevant when interpreting student distributions.<cite id="e5b0d184-1,e5b0d184-6,ba99f48b-1">PHQ‑9 shows acceptable validity for depression severity in autistic college students, though suicidality items merit supplemental probing; severity is typically operationalized as ≥10 (moderate) and ≥15 (severe) on PHQ‑9</cite>.

- Large-scale undergraduate survey evidence: A nationwide student survey found 45% of autistic respondents faced a high risk of psychological impact and 40% a moderate risk, with anxiety and depression as leading concerns, reinforcing greater symptom burden relative to national norms.<cite id="2fca6b28-8">Surveyed autistic university students reported 45% high risk and 40% moderate risk of psychological impact, with anxiety and depression as primary issues</cite>.

- Suicidality risk: Autistic university students report higher suicidal ideation on PHQ‑9 items; broader evidence connects autism with elevated suicide mortality risk, with co‑occurring mental health conditions as key mediators in student populations, underscoring both prevalence and severity of life‑threatening risk.<cite id="e5b0d184-3,e5b0d184-8">Autistic undergraduates report greater suicidality than non-autistic peers on PHQ‑9 items; suicide death is 3–7 times more common among autistic people than the general population, with co‑occurring conditions as contributors</cite>.

Broader population context: Elevated comorbidity and life-course severity support university findings
- Co-occurring diagnoses: Meta-analysis of adults with autism finds high pooled prevalence of ADHD (≈28%), anxiety (≈20%), and other internalizing disorders, providing convergent evidence that autistic individuals carry substantial co‑occurring mental health burdens that plausibly translate to student settings.<cite id="2fca6b28-4">Meta-analyses report pooled prevalence estimates of 28% for ADHD and 20% for anxiety among adults with ASD</cite>.

- Age trends across adolescence/adulthood: Longitudinal syntheses show anxiety/depression prevalence rises from childhood through adulthood in autism, which frames higher university‑student prevalence and severity as consistent with developmental course and accumulation of stressors (e.g., social transition to independent living, academic workload).<cite id="2fca6b28-6">Depression prevalence rises from 1% in autistic children to 23% in autistic adults across longitudinal analyses</cite>.

Mechanisms and higher‑education risk contexts
- Psychometrics and measurement: In autistic students, PHQ‑9 and GAD‑7 retain discriminant validity across autistic vs neurotypical groups when suicidality probes are supplemented, supporting that severity differences are not artifacts of tool choice; severity distributions align with clinical thresholds that are recognized in student mental health services.<cite id="e5b0d184-1,ba99f48b-3">Autistic vs non-autistic college students show differential psychometric profiles where GAD‑7 and PHQ‑9 maintain validity; PHQ‑9 suicidality items require additional probes</cite>.

- Functioning and social-communication demands: Autistic students report higher levels of anxiety and depression than peers across academic pressures, with studies in Finland and beyond emphasizing that social-communication challenges and sensory sensitivities exacerbate academic stress, contributing to elevated symptom severity; many autistic students also report additional disabilities compounding mental health risk.<cite id="5c198e01-0">Autistic university students describe heightened anxiety/depression under academic pressures; social-communication challenges and sensory sensitivities are prominent contributors</cite>.

Limitations and what would strengthen causal inference
- Selection and ascertainment: Many student studies recruit via online surveys or disability services, which may overrepresent students with known diagnoses and visible support needs; still, comparative designs with neurotypical peer samples and multi-campus sampling mitigate bias and are consistent across studies.<cite id="2fca6b28-2">Diagnosis-identified and self-identified autistic college student cohorts show convergence on anxiety and depression prevalence patterns</cite>.

- Measurement validity remains an issue for suicidality screens in autistic populations; studies recommend supplementing short suicidality items with probes to avoid underestimation, which some institutions have implemented for autistic student screening workflows.<cite id="e5b0d184-1">The PHQ‑9 suicide item needs backup probes to accurately capture suicidality risk among autistic college students</cite>.

- Causality: Cross-sectional designs preclude establishing direction of effect; however, convergent longitudinal and life-course meta-analytic evidence (rising symptom prevalence into adulthood; higher suicide mortality in autism) plus consistent, repeated within‑cohort comparative differences across instruments support a robust explanatory picture of elevated prevalence and severity that is exacerbated by university transition and academic context.<cite id="e5b0d184-8,2fca6b28-6">Autism is associated with elevated suicide mortality and increasing symptom prevalence into adulthood, consistent with student observations</cite>.

Take-home
- The balance of evidence from comparative college/university studies, psychometric validations, and broader adult meta-analyses supports that autistic university students experience both higher prevalence and greater severity of mental health conditions than neurotypical peers. Typical comparative prevalence differences range from roughly 10–20 percentage points for severe depression and much larger gaps for anxiety, with autistic students more likely to endorse moderate to severe symptoms and suicidality on validated scales; these patterns align with adult comorbidity data and with known campus stressors that intensify symptom burden in autism.<cite id="ba99f48b-5,e5b0d184-3,2fca6b28-8,e5b0d184-1">Cross-institutional student comparisons report anxiety at 64.5% vs 9.4% and depression at 48.2% vs 7.6%; autistic undergraduates show significantly higher GAD‑7/PHQ‑9 and suicidality; 45% high risk and 40% moderate risk in a large student survey; PHQ‑9/PHQ‑15 perform well with appropriate suicidality probing</cite>.

# Overview

Fillers such as “uh” and “um” have characteristic interactional functions in typical development—mediating turn-taking, aligning speakers’ mental states, hedging claims, and signaling information structure. In autism spectrum disorder (ASD), differences in both the production of these fillers and in the conversational routines that normally recruit them provide clues to specific pragmatic impairments, including atypical management of mutual adjustment, topic/comment flow, epistemic stance, and real-time conversational repair and planning <cite id="a65c290c-0">This study investigated the use of the “fillers” uh and um by children ages 4–8 during the autism diagnostic observation schedule</cite><cite id="e007522e-0">This study investigated the use of the “fillers” uh and um by children ages 4–8 during the autism diagnostic observation schedule</cite><cite id="a65c290c-4">For example, fillers may help people in conversation to manage turn taking, align their mental states, and anticipate upcoming speech</cite>.

Below, we synthesize evidence for how filler-word differences map onto pragmatic deficits in ASD.

# 1) Frequency, Distribution, and Symptom Severity

Across studies, autistic children and adolescents often show atypical rates and distributions of “um” and “uh” compared with typically developing (TD) peers and language-matched controls, which covary with ASD symptom severity. In a clinical/developmental comparison study of children (4–8 years), researchers recorded “uh”/“um” during diagnostic interviews to characterize atypical pragmatic language in ASD, demonstrating that these fillers participate in diagnostic assessment patterns of disfluency and topic management <cite id="a65c290c-0">This study investigated the use of the “fillers” uh and um by children ages 4–8 during the autism diagnostic observation schedule</cite>. Another developmental comparison (clinician–child dialogues) found substantial group differences in how fillers were used, with autistic children deviating in ways linked to pragmatic difficulty <cite id="a65c290c-1">We compared interactional aspects of their dialogue includ- ing turn-taking behavior, filler use, discourse markers, and ac- knowledgments, finding ... substantial differences ... between children with ASD and TD children</cite><cite id="e74dbac9-7">we report on a study of dialogues between clinicians and children with ASD or TD, finding that the two groups of children differ substantially in ... filler use</cite>.

Functionally, “um” in particular has emerged as a pragmatic marker in ASD. In a comparative sample including high-functioning autistic youth, “um” served to pace speech, pace mutual adjustment, and align turns, but its use was less reliable and more variable than in TD peers, consistent with broader pragmatic atypicalities <cite id="a65c290c-2">Pragmatic language difficulties, including unusual filler usage, are common among children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)</cite><cite id="9494f484-0">This study examined the production of fillers in spontaneous speech among individuals with high-functioning ASD, optimal outcomes, and typical development</cite><cite id="9494f484-1">Filler disfluencies--"uh" and "um"--are thought to serve distinct discourse functions. We examined fillers in spontaneous speech by youth with autism ... and by youth with ... matched language development</cite>. Importantly, one study reported that “um” rate was associated with autism symptom severity, beyond executive function or vocabulary, suggesting a pragmatic, listener-oriented role that is sensitive to conversational load or social-goal monitoring <cite id="a65c290c-3">"Um" rate was associated with autism symptom severity, but not executive function or language abilities, suggesting that "um" serves a pragmatic, listener- ... function</cite>.

# 2) Interactional Pragmatics: Turn-Taking, Alignment, and Repair

Fillers in typical conversation help speakers “anchor” transitions, time their speech to partners, and calibrate mutual understanding. ASD-related changes in these routines become visible in filler use. First, autistic speakers often insert more fillers during planning delays but distribute them less predictably across transitions, disrupting timing and alignment relative to partners. A longitudinal pediatric study found autistic children used more frequent self-initiated repairs and more disfluencies during planning to compensate for slower lexical retrieval, indicating compensatory but atypical conversational dynamics; filler-heavy “planning turns” and uneven uptake signaled strain in mutual adjustment <cite id="a65c290c-6">Speech disfluencies occur when speakers pause, revise, or add filler words to otherwise fluent speech, and may indicate problems with planning ...</cite>. Relatedly, analyses of turn-taking show autistic adults and children often arrive at turns “late” and extend silences pre-turn, increasing transition difficulty; fillers may be overused at the margins to manage these gaps or underused when speakers attempt direct speech without scaffolding <cite id="e007522e-1">We analysed the conversational turn-taking behaviour of 28 adult native German speakers ... Typical short-gap transitions are preferred, but not achieved instantly</cite><cite id="e007522e-4">In a study of conversational interaction (Ochi et al., 2019), autistic adults showed longer silences (i.e., gaps) before taking their turn and a higher ratio of ...</cite><cite id="a65c290c-4">For example, fillers may help people in conversation to manage turn taking, align their mental states, and anticipate upcoming speech</cite>.

Conversational repair and tag-questioning also show ASD-related differences that intersect with filler use. While response repair strategies can be diverse in ASD, autistic children may overuse repair-initiating cues (including disfluencies) or underuse pragmatic tags that coordinate acceptance/acknowledgment; this contributes to a conversational profile in which fillers partially substitute for conventional tag-questions and pragmatic alignment routines. Studies report comparable diversity in repair types but highlight slower uptake and atypical turn-organization when tags and fillers are deployed <cite id="e74dbac9-9">Children with ASD were similar to language age-matched control children in responding to RQCLs and employing a variety of repair strategies</cite>. More broadly, research on discourse tags like “like” in ASD links to floor-holding and turn-construction issues; overuse of such pragmatic devices (including fillers) may “push-start” speech to resolve uncertainty, whereas underuse can prolong silences that are then filled with delayed or dislocated content <cite id="e74dbac9-1">In fact, uh and um are used in ... ways that can encourage listeners to start talking, even when the speaker wants to hold the floor</cite><cite id="e74dbac9-6">Research on um and uh has found that um is used significantly less frequently by autistic children compared to NonAu peers ...</cite>.

# 3) Prosody and Epistemic Stance

Prosody (pauses, rising intonation, and phrasing) normally conveys uncertainty, topic prominence, and evidential stance; in ASD, altered prosody interacts with filler production to signal epistemic atypicality. Cross-sectional work differentiating “um” vs. “uh” documents that “uh” often co-occurs with shorter pre-filler pauses and rising intonation as an acute hesitation marker, whereas “um” supports longer turn-building and pacing; autistic speakers show both more variable pause lengths and reduced differentiation between these markers in TD-like prosodic patterns <cite id="e74dbac9-0">Gesture examples illustrate referential pointing with um/uah disfluencies</cite><cite id="e74dbac9-3">Pauses and rising intonation were observed as prosodic indicators of uncertainty; autistic and non-autistic prosodic processing differences are discussed in relation to uh and um</cite>. These prosodic-filler dyads can reveal reduced signaling of incremental information (e.g., contrastive topics) and a more monotonic distribution of uncertainty cues, which map onto pragmatic difficulties with local coherence and conventionalized epistemic marking <cite id="e74dbac9-4">Autistic preadolescents produce fewer um/uh disfluencies than ASD peers, and more speaking turns; patterns imply differences in conversational flow</cite><cite id="9494f484-7">Pragmatics examines how context influences language meaning, with a focus on implied meanings and social factors that impact communication</cite>.

# 4) Executive Control and Developmental Scaffolding

Executive functions, working memory, and social skill hierarchies scaffold pragmatic use of fillers; in ASD, impairments at these levels distort how fillers are timed and interpreted. Filler disfluencies relate to compensatory planning, lexical retrieval, and turn management; in some analyses, “um” rate tracked autism severity independently of executive or lexical measures, suggesting a pragmatic, listener-oriented deficit in monitoring conversational goals rather than purely lexical access <cite id="a65c290c-3">"Um" rate was associated with autism symptom severity, but not executive function or language abilities, suggesting that "um" serves a pragmatic, listener- ... function</cite>. Broader reviews link pragmatic impairment to integration of executive control over discourse representation, theory of mind, and social conventions; fillers thus become visible symptoms of a hierarchical deficit where children with ASD struggle to coordinate conversational roles, use conventional implicatures (e.g., tags), and pace turn construction <cite id="9494f484-4">Pragmatic language deficits are universal in individuals with autism spectrum disorders. Pragmatic language skills require the integration ... and executive functions</cite><cite id="9494f484-3">A hierarchy of social/pragmatic skills includes using fillers to acknowledge and coordinate turns; deficits at lower and higher levels affect conversational flow</cite>.

# 5) What Filler Patterns “Signal” Clinically

Clinicians can use specific filler patterns as probes for targeted pragmatic diagnoses:

- Elevated or reduced “um” production and greater within-turn disfluency suggest difficulties with turn-taking timing, mutual adjustment, and epistemic stance signaling, often linked to retrieval planning and pragmatic load rather than simple articulatory stuttering <cite id="a65c290c-0">This study investigated the use of the “fillers” uh and um by children ages 4–8 during the autism diagnostic observation schedule</cite><cite id="a65c290c-3">"Um" rate was associated with autism symptom severity, but not executive function or language abilities, suggesting that "um" serves a pragmatic, listener- ... function</cite><cite id="a65c290c-6">Speech disfluencies occur when speakers pause, revise, or add filler words to otherwise fluent speech, and may indicate problems with planning ...</cite>.

- Altered “uh”/repetitions and tag-question reliance point to atypical management of adjacency and acknowledgment, including difficulty using conventional tags and fillers for pragmatic alignment; overuse may push-start floor transitions or mask self-correction, while underuse increases gaps and disorganization <cite id="e74dbac9-1">uh and um are used in ways that can encourage listeners to start talking, even when they want to hold the floor</cite><cite id="e74dbac9-2">An adolescent study differentiates listener- vs speaker-oriented aspects of disfluencies like um/uh to discern their conversational role</cite><cite id="e74dbac9-5">Autistic adolescents show differences in discourse markers and conversational dynamics related to um/uh</cite>.

- Prosodic monotony, atypical rise/fall, and longer pre-turn intervals combined with either over- or under-filling transitions indicate impaired signaling of uncertainty, topic prominence, and conversational roles; these align with broader conversational impairment findings in ASD and provide concrete targets for intervention (e.g., modeling tag use, timing anchors) <cite id="e74dbac9-3">Rising intonation and pauses as prosodic uncertainty cues; differences observed between autistic and non-autistic speakers</cite><cite id="e007522e-4">Autistic adults showed longer silences before taking their turn and a higher ratio of ... disfluencies</cite><cite id="a65c290c-2">Pragmatic language difficulties, including unusual filler usage, are common among children with ASD</cite>.

# 6) Integrative Perspective and Clinical Takeaways

The converging picture is that autistic speakers may “speak through” pragmatic routines: they deploy fillers less predictably to manage turn-taking, hedge less via conventional tags, and modulate uncertainty cues atypically—all linked to executive strain and impaired mutual calibration. The outcome is a conversational fingerprint: variable filler placement that nevertheless increases disfluencies during planning, widened transitions, and weaker alignment cues <cite id="a65c290c-0">Study of uh/um in ASD diagnostic contexts</cite><cite id="a65c290c-1">Substantial differences in turn-taking, filler use, and discourse markers across ASD vs TD dialogues</cite><cite id="9494f484-1">Filler disfluencies are used differentially by autistic youth and language-matched peers, with implications for pragmatic discourse functions</cite><cite id="e007522e-4">Longer pre-turn silences and altered conversational ratios among autistic adults</cite>. Clinically, tracking filler metrics (“um” vs “uh” rates, pause/intonation patterns) and their relation to ASD severity can guide therapy targeting turn-taking routines, tag/question use, repair uptake, and prosodic pacing, particularly in children aged 4–8 where these markers are diagnostic and modifiable <cite id="a65c290c-0">Age 4–8 autistic children show distinct uh/um patterns in diagnostic observation</cite><cite id="a65c290c-3">"Um" correlates with symptom severity independent of executive/language, supporting a pragmatic focus in intervention</cite>. 

Pragmatic remediation that normalizes turn-taking templates and conventional implicatures (e.g., training pragmatic tags, modeling anchor/landmark timing) is likely to reduce compensatory filler use and improve real-time alignment, reflecting the link between these fillers and core pragmatic impairments in ASD <cite id="9494f484-4">Pragmatic language skills in ASD require integration of executive control and discourse-pragmatic abilities</cite><cite id="e74dbac9-4">Autistic preadolescents show fewer um/uh disfluencies than ASD peers and more speaking turns, indicating developmental scaffolding differences</cite>.
