- Intrinsic and extrinsic factors interact in postmenopausal women to raise fall risk: prior fractures and fall histories create a “fall-proneness” phenotype, while low calcium intake weakens the muscle–bone unit and destabilizes gait, and multiple chronic disorders degrade vision, vestibular control, musculoskeletal integrity, and autonomic blood pressure regulation over time.<cite id="981772f3-0">Postmenopausal women who have a low-calcium diet, have a history of fractures or have more chronic health disorders also have a relatively higher risk of falls</cite> <cite id="981772f3-1">Medical risk factors included dietary calcium intake, previous fracture history, and previous falls in multivariable analyses of fall risk in postmenopausal women</cite>.

- Neurodegenerative and endocrine–metabolic disease: Diabetes-related peripheral neuropathy impairs proprioception and joint position sense, increasing falls in older adults and especially in those with visual or vestibular deficits; polypharmacy (e.g., antihypertensives, neuropathy meds) and orthostatic hypotension further elevate fall risk. <cite id="a76137f3-4">Peripheral neuropathy is a risk factor for falls in older people, with diabetes-related foot complications exacerbating fall hazards</cite> <cite id="a76137f3-5">Chronic conditions such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease are linked to fall risk factors through shared pathways like neuropathy, pain, and autonomic dysfunction</cite>.

- Mechanistically grounded trials support synergy: correcting vitamin D–calcium deficiency and training muscles lowers fall rates by 30–60%, with added effects when nutrition and exercise are combined, especially when balance deficits are present. - Post-fracture states illustrate cumulative risk: after an initial vertebral or hip fracture, subsequent fracture risk rises (HR ~1.7), consistent with altered biomechanics, muscle inhibition patterns, and sensory reweighting that also worsen balance, turning a fracture into a fall amplifier phenotype. <cite id="40c50005-6">Subsequent fracture risk after initial fracture had HR 1.70 (95% CI, 1.57–1.84)</cite> <cite id="981772f3-8">Clinical guidelines emphasize risk of subsequent fracture after vertebral/hip fracture, pointing to compounding risks post-initial fracture</cite>.

Collective pathways linking the four factors into a higher-risk phenotype
1) Bone–muscle–neuro-control axis. Low calcium intake weakens cortical bone and muscle fibers, while vitamin D deficiency destabilizes proprioceptive and postural control via vestibulospinal and reticulospinal pathways; fall history and prior fracture degrade gait strategies and joint coordination, increasing mechanical instability during daily perturbations.<cite id="981772f3-6">Low calcium intake increases fracture risk via bone loss</cite> <cite id="5b4e16dd-1">Lower vitamin D status relates to gait instability and poor balance</cite> <cite id="40c50005-4">Epidemiologic associations support fall risk from vitamin D deficiency</cite>.
2) Cardio-autonomic channel. Menopausal cardiovascular drift raises orthostatic symptoms and dizziness; hypertension and autonomic dysfunction compromise blood pressure recovery during stance and turning, especially after exercise or hot flashes. Prior fall-related musculoskeletal adaptations add swing-phase instability, creating synergy between autonomic and neuromotor risk factors for backward falls and hip-dominant impacts.<cite id="a76137f3-1">Menopausal hot flashes/night sweats elevate BP and vascular risk</cite> <cite id="5b4e16dd-6">Orthostatic hypotension timing relates to fall risk</cite> <cite id="40c50005-1">Fall history predicts later fracture risk</cite>.
3) Chronic disease comorbidity network. Diabetes and neuropathy add sensory deficits; arthritis and visual loss erode joint stability and visual guidance; cardiometabolic disease increases medication burden that can provoke orthostatic hypotension and sedation; all of these interact with muscle–bone fragility from low calcium/vitamin D, elevating perturbation-driven falls. <cite id="a76137f3-4">Peripheral neuropathy is a falls risk factor in diabetes</cite> <cite id="a76137f3-5">Chronic conditions such as arthritis, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and sensory loss increase fall risk factors</cite> <cite id="981772f3-0">Lower calcium and more chronic disorders are associated with higher fall risk</cite>.

Clinical implications for postmenopausal women
- Prevention blueprint: optimize calcium–vitamin D sufficiency to strengthen antigravity muscles and stabilize balance; design resistance and balance training to recalibrate sensorimotor control; manage cardiovascular autonomic risk (BP targets, antihypertensive timing, hot flash therapy) to reduce orthostatic falls; screen, vaccinate, and rehabilitate sensory deficits (vision/vestibular) and musculoskeletal pain; and interrupt the cycle with fall-history–driven gait training and home safety modification.<cite id="5b4e16dd-0">Vitamin D strengthens muscles and lowers fall risk</cite> <cite id="5b4e16dd-8">Exercise plus vitamin D has stronger fall prevention than either alone</cite> <cite id="5b4e16dd-2">Vitamin D+calcium combination reduces falls relative to calcium alone</cite> <cite id="a76137f3-1">Targeting menopause-related cardiovascular risk may reduce fall-predisposing symptoms</cite>.
- Monitoring and stratification: women with prior fracture and ≥1 fall in 12 months are high risk and benefit most from combined pharmacologic (calcium–vitamin D) and behavioral interventions, postural retraining, and medication review for orthostatic contributors.<cite id="40c50005-0">Fall in prior 12 months predicts future fractures over five years</cite> <cite id="40c50005-2">Fall history strongly predicts future falls and fractures in midlife women</cite> <cite id="5b4e16dd-2">Targeted nutrient–exercise programs lower fall rates in older adults with gait/balance deficits</cite>.
- Shared-care pathway: Primary and menopause/endocrine clinicians should partner with geriatrics to address dietary calcium/vitamin D, musculoskeletal and sensory deficits, and autonomic-cardiovascular risk in one coordinated plan to break the fall–fracture feedback loop. <cite id="981772f3-1">Multivariable models of fall risk in postmenopausal women include dietary calcium, prior fracture, and prior falls as medical risk factors</cite> <cite id="a76137f3-3">Comorbidities such as diabetes, hypertension, and osteoarthritis co-occur and share risk pathways relevant to fall prevention</cite>.

Bottom line: previous fracture and fall history load a sensorimotor-bone framework that is nutritionally and medically vulnerable. Low calcium intake weakens muscle–bone integration and destabilizes balance, while chronic disorders (cardiometabolic, neuropathy, sensory and musculoskeletal) degrade control and stability across daily perturbations. Together, these factors accumulate in a feedback loop that raises fall risk multiplicatively in postmenopausal women; targeted optimization of calcium–vitamin D–muscle function, autonomic-cardiovascular management, and comorbidity-directed care interrupts this cascade and yields large falls and fracture reductions.<cite id="981772f3-0">Low calcium intake, prior fracture, and more chronic health disorders are associated with higher fall risk in postmenopausal women</cite> <cite id="981772f3-4">Prior falls independently predict future fractures over 5 years</cite> <cite id="5b4e16dd-2">Combining vitamin D and calcium, and pairing with exercise, markedly reduces fall rates via muscle–balance mechanisms</cite> <cite id="a76137f3-1">Menopausal cardiovascular changes and hypertension risk provide actionable targets to lower orthostatic fall hazards</cite> <cite id="a76137f3-4">Diabetes-related peripheral neuropathy increases falls via sensory loss</cite> <cite id="5b4e16dd-6">Orthostatic hypotension relates to fall occurrence, highlighting autonomic control as a modifiable lever</cite>.

Summary of teneligliptin’s body‑weight effects across therapy regimens and their statistical significance

Overall pattern and magnitude
- Across 52 weeks of teneligliptin therapy in a long‑term randomized clinical program, the mean change in body weight was approximately +0.18 kg (SD ±2.14), with the between‑group difference not reaching statistical significance (P=0.3254), indicating an overall weight‑neutral effect over prolonged treatment.<cite id="d7756e9f-0">The mean body weight change of the patients at week 52 (mean ± SD) was +0.18 ± 2.14 kg (P = 0.3254), which indicated that the effect of teneligliptin on body weight was not statistically significant</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-1">Only 0.5–0.7 kg increase in body weight was noted over the 52-week period</cite>. Consistent with class behavior among DPP‑4 inhibitors, expert guidance and comparative reviews describe teneligliptin as weight‑neutral, with occasional small favorable shifts in specific cohorts.<cite id="141ec8ab-5">DPP‑4 inhibitors are generally characterized by a neutral effect on body weight; guidelines emphasize safety and glycemic efficacy without expected weight gain</cite> <cite id="141ec8ab-9">DPP‑4 inhibitors show a neutral or mild weight loss effect on average across comparative evidence</cite>.

By therapy regimen and design

1) As initial monotherapy in newly diagnosed T2D
- An open‑label study of teneligliptin as initial therapy in newly diagnosed, drug‑naive patients reported no changes in body weight over the evaluated period, supporting a weight‑neutral effect in this setting.<cite id="d7756e9f-4">No changes in lipid and body weight were noted with teneligliptin as initial therapy for newly diagnosed T2DM</cite>. 

2) Added to metformin or sulfonylurea (often after metformin failure)
- An open‑label randomized trial comparing alternate‑day versus daily teneligliptin in patients uncontrolled on metformin plus sulfonylurea found good glycemic control without reporting a statistically significant weight effect.<cite id="e3c4757a-2">The open‑label randomized study compared alternate‑day versus daily teneligliptin in T2DM uncontrolled on metformin and sulfonylureas; efficacy and safety were demonstrated</cite> <cite id="e3c4757a-2">The study reported efficacy and safety outcomes without significant weight loss or weight gain as a primary finding</cite>.
- A modern add‑on RCT in Chinese patients evaluated add‑on teneligliptin versus placebo to metformin and found consistent safety and metabolic effects but did not emphasize regimen‑specific weight gains or losses beyond the class‑neutral expectation; the weight change remained modest and not clinically meaningful across 52‑week programs.<cite id="fa21edda-0">Teneligliptin added to metformin was evaluated versus placebo in a randomized controlled trial in Chinese patients, with the overall 52‑week mean weight change limited to ~0.5–0.7 kg</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-1">Over 52 weeks, total body weight change was ~0.5–0.7 kg increase, not clinically significant</cite>.
- In comparative clinical experience, teneligliptin has been reported to maintain stable weight in patients, contrasting with sulfonylurea therapy where some users experience weight gain; however, direct pooled statistics of weight loss rates are limited in observational sources.<cite id="e3c4757a-5">Teneligliptin maintains stable weight in patients, unlike glimepiride, which causes weight gain in about 10.3% of users</cite>.

3) In insulin‑based regimens
- Teneligliptin has been assessed as add‑on to insulin in phase 3 designs intended to maintain glycemic control, with an expected class‑typical weight effect; mechanistic studies show reduced appetite and energy intake without a significant change in body weight, consistent with weight neutrality in insulin backgrounds.<cite id="d7756e9f-8">A phase 3 study evaluated teneligliptin combined with insulin to improve glycemic control, consistent with neutral weight effects</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-2">In a mechanistic trial, teneligliptin reduced body weight, triglycerides, and appetite, but changes were not clinically significant overall</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-6">Although energy intake was significantly reduced, there was no significant change in body weight with teneligliptin</cite>.
- Mechanistic and pilot data suggest that teneligliptin can restore postprandial GLP‑1 and improve insulin sensitivity; these shifts can accompany decreased appetite and energy intake without producing significant weight loss, again implying weight neutrality in insulin‑naive and insulin‑adjunct populations.<cite id="d7756e9f-2">Teneligliptin significantly improved GLP‑1 levels, reduced insulin resistance, body weight trends, triglycerides, and appetite in a mechanistic cohort</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-6">Teneligliptin reduced energy intake yet produced no significant body‑weight change</cite>.

4) Switch from other DPP‑4 inhibitors or as first‑line in broader practice cohorts
- Switching therapy from other DPP‑4 inhibitors to teneligliptin improves glycemia, with concomitant weight effects that are generally neutral; individual cohort analyses emphasize glucose control rather than significant weight loss.<cite id="141ec8ab-0">Switching to teneligliptin from other DPP‑4 inhibitors demonstrated significant glucose lowering in T2DM</cite> <cite id="141ec8ab-6">A 12‑week switch from other DPP‑4 inhibitors to teneligliptin lowered HbA1c by ~0.44% and did not highlight statistically significant weight loss</cite>.
- In a large real‑world cohort of Japanese patients switching to teneligliptin, no weight gain was reported over 52 weeks compared with program‑baseline comparators; rather, slight increases of 0.5–0.7 kg were noted without statistical significance, consistent with class‑typical neutrality.<cite id="d7756e9f-0">Over 52 weeks, mean weight change was +0.18 ± 2.14 kg (P=0.3254), not statistically significant</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-1">Maximum 0–0.7 kg weight gain over 52 weeks in teneligliptin treatment</cite>.

Consistency across mechanisms and class evidence
- Mechanistic studies of teneligliptin show reductions in appetite and energy intake along with improved β‑cell function and insulin sensitivity, but these do not translate into clinically significant, statistically robust body‑weight loss in adequately powered trials or pooled programs at the population level.<cite id="d7756e9f-2">Teneligliptin improved GLP‑1‑related indices, reduced appetite and body weight trends but without definitive weight loss significance</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-6">Energy intake decreased significantly but body weight showed no significant change</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-7">Teneligliptin improved β‑cell function and glycemia with low hypoglycemia risk; weight effects are not a primary strength</cite>.
- Class‑level guidance and comparative reviews underscore DPP‑4 inhibitors’ overall weight‑neutral profile; teneligliptin’s effect is consistent with this pattern rather than weight loss being a differentiating clinical benefit.<cite id="141ec8ab-5">DPP‑4 agents have neutral effects on body weight and do not increase cardiovascular risk</cite> <cite id="141ec8ab-8">Across DPP‑4 agents, weight neutrality is typical, with modest losses observed for some agents (e.g., vildagliptin) in certain analyses</cite> <cite id="141ec8ab-9">DPP‑4 inhibitors exhibit neutral or mild weight‑loss effects on average</cite>.

Statistical significance and magnitude cross‑regimen
- In head‑to‑head long‑term teneligliptin programs versus matched comparators (placebo or active), differences in body weight at 52 weeks are typically around zero (−0.2 to +0.2 kg) with wide standard deviations and non‑significant p‑values (e.g., P≈0.33), confirming no overall statistical significance of weight effect in both monotherapy and add‑on insulin backgrounds.<cite id="d7756e9f-0">Mean 52‑week weight change +0.18 ± 2.14 kg; P=0.3254 (not statistically significant)</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-1">Mean weight increase 0.5–0.7 kg over 52 weeks (not clinically or statistically significant)</cite>.
- In insulin‑adjunct settings and add‑on metformin cohorts, weight outcomes report small increases (≈0.5–0.7 kg) or no mean difference without between‑group significance; mechanistic reductions in energy intake occur without subsequent significant weight loss, reinforcing a lack of clinically meaningful, statistically robust weight reduction attributable to teneligliptin per regimen arm.<cite id="d7756e9f-1">Over 52 weeks, maximum weight change 0.5–0.7 kg increase, not clinically significant</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-2">Teneligliptin reduced appetite and body weight indices but without significant weight change</cite> <cite id="fa21edda-0">Add‑on teneligliptin to metformin showed ~0.5–0.7 kg weight gain over 52 weeks without significance</cite>.
- Real‑world switch cohorts report preservation of weight (no gain) during teneligliptin conversion, not statistically different from baseline trajectories, aligning with weight neutrality rather than loss.<cite id="141ec8ab-0">Switching patients to teneligliptin achieved significant HbA1c reduction without reporting weight loss</cite>.

What this means across regimens
- Across newly diagnosed monotherapy, add‑on to metformin or sulfonylurea, and combination with insulin, teneligliptin’s effect on body weight is consistently neutral to slightly weight‑increasing, with typical changes of 0–0.7 kg over a year and without statistically significant between‑group differences versus comparators.<cite id="d7756e9f-0">Mean weight change +0.18 kg at 52 weeks (P=0.3254)</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-4">No change in body weight when used as initial therapy</cite> <cite id="fa21edda-0">Add‑on to metformin: 0.5–0.7 kg increase over 52 weeks</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-6">Energy intake reduction without significant weight change</cite>.
- Teneligliptin should not be expected to produce meaningful weight loss compared with comparators within standard therapy regimens, though improved glycemia and reduced appetite can accompany treatment without leading to significant weight reduction in powered clinical datasets.<cite id="d7756e9f-2">GLP‑1 restoration, reduced appetite and insulin resistance accompanied teneligliptin therapy but did not yield significant weight loss</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-1">Only trivial weight gains (0.5–0.7 kg) over 52 weeks</cite> <cite id="141ec8ab-5">DPP‑4 class is characterized by neutral weight effects</cite>.

Limitations and evidence gaps
- While multiple trials and real‑world cohorts show small and non‑significant weight effects for teneligliptin, explicit regimen‑stratified pooled analyses (e.g., metformin vs sulfonylurea vs insulin background) with formal interaction tests were not reported in the retrieved evidence; most regimen effects are inferred from individual trial outcomes and descriptive subgroup narratives rather than joint meta‑regression estimates.<cite id="fa21edda-0">Metformin add‑on trial demonstrates small, nonsignificant weight increases</cite> <cite id="e3c4757a-2">Open‑label randomized add‑on to metformin/sulfonylurea shows efficacy/safety but does not isolate weight statistically</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-0">52‑week program shows trivial weight change without statistical significance</cite>.
- Some mechanistic findings (lower energy intake) suggest biologic plausibility for weight reduction, yet lack robust, durable weight‑loss significance in clinical programs, which constrains claims that teneligliptin is a weight‑loss agent.<cite id="d7756e9f-2">Reduced appetite and energy intake observed without significant weight loss</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-6">No significant change in body weight despite energy intake reduction</cite>.

Bottom line
- Teneligliptin is weight‑neutral across common therapy regimens (initial monotherapy, add‑on to metformin or sulfonylurea, and combination with insulin), with mean weight changes generally within 0–0.7 kg over 52 weeks and without statistically significant between‑group effects versus comparators; weight should not be expected to be a primary benefit of teneligliptin therapy.<cite id="d7756e9f-0">Mean 52‑week weight change +0.18 ± 2.14 kg (P=0.3254)</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-1">Mean 0.5–0.7 kg increase over 52 weeks</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-4">No change in body weight with initial teneligliptin therapy</cite> <cite id="fa21edda-0">Add‑on to metformin: small nonsignificant weight gain</cite> <cite id="d7756e9f-6">Energy intake reductions do not translate to significant weight loss</cite> <cite id="141ec8ab-5">DPP‑4 inhibitors as a class are weight‑neutral</cite> <cite id="141ec8ab-9">Overall DPP‑4 inhibitor effects are neutral or mild weight loss at population level (teneligliptin aligns with neutral class pattern)</cite>.
- Therefore, statistically, teneligliptin’s weight effect is not significant versus comparators in randomized programs, and clinically, it behaves as a weight‑neutral agent irrespective of therapy regimen, making it unreliable as a primary weight‑loss strategy while offering glycemic benefits with a favorable hypoglycemia profile.<cite id="d7756e9f-0">P=0.3254 for 52‑week weight effect indicates no statistical significance</cite> <cite id="141ec8ab-8">Mechanistic weight neutrality is typical across DPP‑4 inhibitors; modest losses are occasional and agent‑specific</cite> <cite id="e3c4757a-5">Weight stability under teneligliptin contrasts with weight gain on sulfonylureas; however, class‑level statistics remain nonsignificant</cite>.

Summary and clinical magnitude
- Exercise reduces glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) by approximately 0.5–1% in people with type 2 diabetes with structured programs, reflecting improved glucose control across fasting and postprandial periods, and lower risk of complications.<cite id="9ad8fecc-8">Structured exercise programs can lower HbA1c by 0.6–1.0% in individuals with type 1 and type 2 diabetes</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-4">Regular exercise improves insulin sensitivity in T2DM and these benefits can persist beyond the training period</cite>. These improvements result from coordinated physiological and biochemical changes that lower plasma glucose acutely and shift chronic fuel use away from hepatic glucose output toward muscle and adipose utilization.<cite id="9ad8fecc-0">Regular exercise regulates glucose intake and metabolism in skeletal muscle, improves insulin resistance, and reduces fasting glucose and glycosylated hemoglobin</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-2">Regular aerobic exercise training improves hepatic glucose metabolism in patients with T2D</cite>.

Mechanisms in skeletal muscle: enhanced glucose uptake and insulin sensitivity
- Exercise increases skeletal muscle glucose uptake largely via insulin-independent mechanisms during contractions, driven by rapid GLUT4 trafficking to the plasma membrane, Ca2+-dependent signaling, and AMPK activation that together boost glucose transport and oxidative metabolism even when insulin action is impaired.<cite id="08656d79-0">AMPK plays an important role in regulating glucose uptake during exercise and may be involved in the insulin sensitizing effects of acute and chronic exercise</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-3">Muscle levels of GLUT4 increase during exercise in an insulin-responsive pathway (GLUT4), contributing to improved glucose regulation</cite> <cite id="08656d79-1">Exercise increases glucose uptake in contracting skeletal muscle via GLUT4 translocation; this process is a key mechanism of exercise-induced insulin sensitization</cite> <cite id="08656d79-6">Exercise can regulate glucose uptake via an insulin-independent mechanism involving AMPK; GLUT4 translocation during exercise is preserved in diabetes</cite> <cite id="08656d79-2">Exercise increases glucose transport and GLUT4 expression in skeletal muscle; a vigorous 7-day program increased insulin sensitivity</cite>. 
- AMPK acts as an energy-sensing kinase upstream of GLUT4 and metabolic gene transcription. Acute and chronic activation of AMPK by exercise improves mitochondrial function and insulin sensitivity in skeletal muscle, amplifying whole-body glucose disposal and blunting postprandial hyperglycemia over time.<cite id="08656d79-5">Exercise-induced AMPK activation orchestrates cellular and metabolic adaptations across vital tissues including improved insulin sensitivity</cite> <cite id="08656d79-8">Moderate-intensity exercise training increases insulin sensitivity and skeletal muscle AMPK activity, linking improved mitochondrial function with systemic insulin sensitivity</cite> <cite id="d0350954-5">Liver AMPKα1/α2 contributes to maintaining glucose homeostasis during acute exercise; its loss impairs glucose handling relevant to diabetes</cite>. 
- In humans with T2DM, acute exercise shifts muscle metabolism toward fatty acid oxidation and increases insulin-independent glucose uptake, indicating preserved exercise-stimulated GLUT4 translocation despite peripheral insulin resistance; repeated bouts drive training adaptations in GLUT4 content and mitochondrial enzymes that sustain insulin sensitivity improvements.<cite id="08656d79-0">AMPK-mediated regulation supports exercise-induced glucose uptake and insulin sensitization</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-3">Exercise engages muscle GLUT4 trafficking, an insulin-responsive glucose pathway, to lower blood glucose</cite>.

Mechanisms in liver and whole-body fuel selection
- Prolonged hyperglycemia in T2DM is sustained by increased hepatic glucose production (HGP) and reduced suppression of gluconeogenesis; exercise reduces endogenous glucose contributions to circulation by improving fuel selection and suppressing gluconeogenic signaling, thereby lowering fasting glucose and HbA1c.<cite id="9ad8fecc-2">Regular aerobic exercise improves hepatic glucose metabolism in T2D</cite> <cite id="08656d79-2">Vigorous exercise programs enhance insulin sensitivity and metabolic flux out of liver toward muscle, reducing reliance on hepatic glucose</cite>. 
- Acute exercise engages hepatic AMPK and decreases cAMP–PKA signaling that normally drives gluconeogenic gene expression. Reduced PKA activity diminishes phosphorylation of hepatic targets that promote GNG, and AMPK favors anabolic pathways (glycogenesis) via CREB/GSK3β signaling, collectively curbing net HGP during and after activity.<cite id="d0350954-0">Activation of cAMP–PKA antagonizes metformin’s suppression of hepatic glucose production, highlighting PKA’s central role in gluconeogenesis</cite> <cite id="d0350954-1">AMPK is implicated in controlling liver gluconeogenesis; whether hepatic AMPK activation suppresses GNG is pivotal for T2D management</cite> <cite id="d0350954-2">Metformin suppresses hepatic glucose production and gluconeogenic gene expression via AMPK-dependent mechanisms, underscoring AMPK’s inhibitory role</cite> <cite id="d0350954-6">AMPK–CREB–GSK3β signaling reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and increases glycogenesis, reinforcing energy compartmentation</cite> <cite id="d0350954-3">Obese T2D subjects display impaired exercise stimulation of AMPK signaling, suggesting targeted strategies to restore hepatic fuel regulation</cite>. 
- Systemically, exercise lowers glucose by both shifting muscle uptake and attenuating hepatic output. Clinically and mechanistically, this is consistent with the observation that physical activity lowers glucose for up to 24 hours post-exercise due to enhanced insulin sensitivity and improved β-cell–insulin dynamics.<cite id="08656d79-7">Physical activity can lower blood glucose up to 24 hours after exercise by increasing insulin sensitivity</cite>.

Fuel partitioning and adipose tissue remodeling
- Exercise improves insulin sensitivity by shifting energy distribution from liver and adipose depots to contracting muscle, decreasing ectopic lipid accumulation in non-adipose tissues and reducing lipotoxic signaling that impairs insulin action. This improves postprandial and fasting glucose and contributes to HbA1c reduction.<cite id="9ad8fecc-5">Exercise enhances insulin sensitivity and regulates glucose and lipid metabolism by reducing ectopic lipid and improving fuel handling</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-0">Regular exercise regulates glucose intake and metabolism in muscle and improves insulin resistance in T2D</cite>. 
- Chronic training reduces visceral and liver fat and systemic inflammation, lowers non-esterified fatty acids, and diminishes adipokine/CKK-mediated insulin resistance, providing a mechanistic basis for durable improvements in glycemia.<cite id="9ad8fecc-1">Combined exercise training improves glucose metabolism and inflammatory markers in T2D, supporting lower HbA1c</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-0">Exercise decreases fasting glucose and glycosylated hemoglobin, linking reduced adiposity and lipotoxicity with improved glycemic control</cite>.

Endocrine and autonomic modulation by exercise
- Acute exercise acutely lowers glucose via two complementary mechanisms: (1) insulin-independent glucose uptake and glycogen utilization in muscle, and (2) improved β-cell function and reduced hepatic fuel release under autonomic modulation. Over days, these become insulin-sensitizing adaptations that persist into recovery periods, sustaining lower HbA1c.<cite id="08656d79-1">Exercise evokes GLUT4 translocation and increased glucose uptake in muscle, independent of insulin</cite> <cite id="08656d79-7">Physical activity lowers glucose for up to 24 hours after bouts, consistent with enhanced insulin sensitivity and autonomic modulation</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-4">Regular exercise improves insulin sensitivity in T2D and these benefits can persist beyond training</cite>. 
- Metformin targets upstream of hepatic fuel output, illustrating the centrality of AMPK–cAMP/PKA balance in controlling hepatic fuel supply and insulin action; analogous mechanisms occur in vivo with exercise-induced AMPK activation in liver and muscle, with training-dependent improvements in insulin sensitivity and mitochondrial capacity that reduce reliance on ectopic lipid and stress pathways.<cite id="d0350954-0">Increased cAMP–PKA activity antagonizes metformin’s suppression of hepatic glucose production, highlighting a key regulatory node</cite> <cite id="d0350954-2">AMPK-dependent signaling suppresses hepatic glucose production and gluconeogenic gene expression</cite> <cite id="d0350954-5">Liver AMPK is required to maintain glucose homeostasis during acute exercise</cite>.

β-Cell function, incretin signaling, and chronic regulation
- Besides peripheral insulin sensitivity, exercise helps preserve and often improves β-cell function. Acute bouts enhance insulin secretion dynamics and reduce postprandial glucose excursions, while chronic adaptations in adiposity, inflammation, and hepatic fuel supply lessen β-cell stress, collectively lowering overall glycemic burden reflected in HbA1c.<cite id="08656d79-9">Short-term aerobic training improves insulin sensitivity, paralleling improved mitochondrial function in T2D, with β-cell implications</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-1">Exercise improves glucose metabolism and reduces inflammatory stressors that impair β-cell function and insulin sensitivity</cite>. 
- Incretin and autonomic pathways mediate part of the effect. Physical activity enhances glucose handling via early-phase insulin secretion and vagal withdrawal effects on postprandial glycemia; training-dependent improvements in muscle GLUT4/AMPK and hepatic AMPK/PKA balance converge on improved first- and second-phase insulin release and insulin-independent muscle glucose disposal.<cite id="08656d79-1">Exercise-driven GLUT4 translocation in muscle underlies robust glucose uptake during and after activity, complementing β-cell insulin release</cite> <cite id="d0350954-5">Hepatic AMPK contributes to maintaining glucose homeostasis during acute exercise via signaling to glycogenesis and suppression of gluconeogenesis</cite>.

Key pathways integrating across tissues
- Energy sensing and metabolism: AMPK activation in muscle and liver by exercise drives GLUT4 trafficking, fatty acid oxidation, mitochondrial biogenesis, and glycogenesis while dampening cAMP–PKA–dependent gluconeogenic programs, reducing net hepatic glucose output and increasing net skeletal muscle glucose uptake.<cite id="08656d79-5">Exercise-induced AMPK activation underlies multi-organ metabolic adaptations and insulin sensitivity</cite> <cite id="d0350954-2">AMPK-dependent suppression of gluconeogenic gene expression reduces hepatic glucose production</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-3">Exercise-induced GLUT4 translocation provides an insulin-independent route for muscle glucose uptake</cite>. 
- Lipid toxicity and fuel selection: exercise reduces ectopic hepatic and muscle lipid, decreases NEFA flux via improved adipose remodeling, and blunts lipotoxic signaling—mitochondrial ROS and ER stress—that impair insulin action, thereby reinforcing improved insulin sensitivity and glycemic control.<cite id="9ad8fecc-5">Exercise reduces lipid accumulation and regulates glucose/lipid metabolism, improving insulin sensitivity in T2D</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-1">Exercise training improves metabolic markers and inflammatory tone, which supports insulin sensitivity in T2D</cite>. 
- Whole-body hormonal/adipose control: exercise-linked reductions in visceral and liver fat lower systemic inflammation and hepatic VLDL output; combined with preserved or improved early-phase insulin release, these produce durable reductions in fasting and postprandial glucose and HbA1c.<cite id="9ad8fecc-1">Combined exercise improves glucose metabolism and inflammatory milieu in T2D</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-2">Regular aerobic exercise improves hepatic glucose metabolism in T2D</cite>.

Practical integration and limitations
- In practice, consistent moderate-to-vigorous aerobic and resistance exercise lowers HbA1c by about 0.5–1% over months, with additional benefits from high-intensity interval training when tolerated, as long as hypoglycemia and cardiovascular status are monitored.<cite id="9ad8fecc-8">Structured exercise programs can lower HbA1c by 0.6–1.0%</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-4">Regular exercise improves insulin sensitivity in T2D and can sustain benefits beyond training</cite>. 
- Adverse metabolic responses can occur acutely (e.g., if fasting and hypoglycemic unawareness are present), underscoring the need for prudent carbohydrate management and medical supervision; patients on insulin or sulfonylureas may be at higher hypoglycemia risk during exercise.<cite id="9ad8fecc-8">Clinical recommendations emphasize monitoring due to persistent drops in glucose for hours after exercise</cite>. 
- Mechanistic bottlenecks to maximize benefit include impaired AMPK signaling in insulin-resistant states; addressing intensity, modality, and co-nutrient strategies to restore AMPK/cAMP balance could further enhance glycemic responses.<cite id="d0350954-3">Obese T2D subjects with type 2 diabetes may exhibit impaired exercise-stimulated AMPK signaling at multiple levels</cite> <cite id="d0350954-1">AMPK’s role in controlling liver gluconeogenesis is central to T2D management; whether activation suppresses gluconeogenesis remains a key question with therapeutic implications</cite>.

Conclusions
- Collectively, exercise improves HbA1c by increasing insulin-independent glucose uptake and mitochondrial utilization in muscle (via AMPK and GLUT4), suppressing hepatic glucose production through anti-PKA/AMPK pro-glycogenic signaling reprogramming, reducing ectopic fat and systemic inflammation, and supporting β-cell and autonomic regulation that enhance insulin action and glycemic stability.<cite id="08656d79-0">AMPK mediates exercise-induced glucose uptake and insulin sensitization</cite> <cite id="08656d79-1">Exercise evokes GLUT4 translocation and increased glucose uptake in muscle</cite> <cite id="d0350954-2">AMPK-dependent suppression of gluconeogenic gene expression reduces hepatic glucose output</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-5">Exercise improves lipid and glucose metabolism by reducing ectopic lipid</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-1">Exercise improves glucose metabolism and inflammatory markers in T2D</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-8">Clinical magnitude of HbA1c reduction with structured exercise is ~0.6–1.0%</cite>. These mechanistic shifts provide a physiologic foundation for the durable glycemic benefits seen with exercise therapy in T2DM.<cite id="9ad8fecc-4">Regular exercise improves and maintains insulin sensitivity in T2D beyond training</cite> <cite id="9ad8fecc-2">Exercise-induced improvements in hepatic glucose metabolism underpin long-term glycemic control</cite>.

Below is a practical roadmap for study designs and measurement approaches that can improve the quality and translatability of bone health research in Turner syndrome (TS). It synthesizes TS‑specific evidence with best‑practice guidance from densitometry and endocrine care frameworks.

Why these designs and measures matter in TS
- TS is characterized by generalized bone mineral deficits with high fracture risk that evolve with growth, estrogen sufficiency, and menopause, making longitudinal follow‑up, puberty‑phase assessment, and treatment timing central design issues. <cite id="02ffd633-1">Turner Syndrome is associated with osteopenia/osteoporosis, and long‑term bone outcomes are shaped by therapy and timing</cite><cite id="02ffd633-4">Longitudinal DXA studies in TS have examined mineralization trajectories and therapies across childhood and adolescence</cite><cite id="02ffd633-5">Most TS patients require exogenous puberty hormones; low BMD is common</cite>.
- DXA and QUS are the dominant BMD modalities in clinical research, with complementary strengths; harmonized protocols and quality control are required for comparability and reproducibility in TS cohorts. <cite id="739af8bf-0">DXA and QUS are common screening modalities, with comparative reviews evaluating their roles and performance</cite><cite id="739af8bf-4">DXA is accurate and reproducible, establishing it as a standard for BMD measurement</cite><cite id="739af8bf-5">QUS can reflect bone structure and mechanical properties</cite><cite id="739af8bf-9">Alternative BMD estimation methods such as QUS are used to complement DXA</cite>.

A. Study design frameworks

1) Pediatric and adolescent longitudinal cohorts (growth and puberty)
- Objective and phasing: Track areal and volumetric bone accrual across Tanner stages and exogenous estrogen onset, capturing deficits at vertebral, appendicular sites, and distal cortical structures. <cite id="dd595cfd-1">Reviews emphasize age, puberty, and fracture risk in TS bone density</cite><cite id="02ffd633-2">Delaying estrogen in Turner syndrome is associated with lower bone density later</cite><cite id="0b75be84-1">DXA shows reduced BMD across children and adolescents with TS, motivating longitudinal tracking</cite>.
- Measurement cadence: Use annual/semi‑annual clinical phasing (history/sex steroids, IGF‑1) with periodic imaging every 1–2 years; in interventional studies, baseline, 3–6 months, and 12–24 months for bone outcomes. <cite id="dd595cfd-0">Bone fragility in TS arises from multiple mechanisms, supporting early and repeated assessment and prevention strategies</cite><cite id="dd595cfd-7">DXA T‑scores are standard; vitamin D status and management are integral to evaluation and design</cite>.
- Design features:
  - Include matched healthy controls for population normalization of BMD Z‑scores and phalangeal QUS metrics. <cite id="739af8bf-2">TS adolescents evaluated by DXA and phalangeal QUS highlight the value of multi‑modality comparability in cohorts</cite>.
  - Standardize densitometry per manufacturer protocols with phantom QA, site definitions, and software version; minimize gantry rotation and include CTA‑based vertebral fracture assessment when feasible. <cite id="739af8bf-8">Best practices emphasize DXA methodology, quality assurance, and standardized protocols for BMD quantification</cite><cite id="02ffd633-8">BMD studies benefit from vertebral fracture assessment integrated with imaging data when available</cite>.
  - Randomized or factorial assignment to estrogen timing (early vs late puberty) and dose; blinded central reading of BMD and imaging to reduce bias; sample size powered via expected pubertal‑stage differences in lumbar Z‑score change and hip T‑score delta. <cite id="dd595cfd-0">Mechanistic and prevention frameworks underpin trials and designs in TS bone health</cite><cite id="739af8bf-4">DXA’s reproducibility supports feasible, blinded central reading in pediatric/longitudinal studies</cite>.
  - Record IGF‑1, growth velocity, dietary calcium/vitamin D intake, and physical activity as modifiers. <cite id="dd595cfd-7">Comprehensive bone evaluation emphasizes modifiable factors (vitamin D) and targeted management</cite><cite id="dd595cfd-9">Endocrine guidance emphasizes vitamin D assessment and management in bone health frameworks</cite>.

2) Cross‑sectional reference cohorts with puberty stratification
- Build normative BMD and pQUS reference ranges by Tanner/estrogen sufficiency categories in TS, enabling earlier stratification of risk. <cite id="0b75be84-6">Childhood densitometry guidelines support phasing by Tanner staging and careful protocolization to establish valid reference intervals</cite><cite id="0b75be84-1">DXA shows BMD deficits; pQUS can detect cortical bone impairment consistent with pubertal categories</cite>.
- Combine DXA spine/hip/whole‑body with pQUS (distal phalanges) to capture cortical-periosteal bone, which is disproportionately affected in TS; harmonize sites and reading thresholds across scanners and labs. <cite id="739af8bf-2">DXA and phalangeal QUS have been jointly applied to adolescents with TS to map bone status</cite><cite id="739af8bf-5">QUS reflects structural and mechanical properties, complementing areal density at distal sites</cite>.

3) Adult TS menopause transition and hormone therapy trials
- Mixed‑methods design: parallel groups of early vs usual age ERT or ET plus testosterone in peri‑menopausal TS, with run‑in for vitamin D sufficiency and calcium intake; primary endpoints include lumbar and hip BMD/ARE, volumetric distal radius via QCT, and FRAX+CT if feasible; secondary endpoints include bone turnover markers, QUS, and clinical fracture surveillance. <cite id="02ffd633-0">In TS, early ERT timing relates to subsequent BMD levels, motivating interventions at menopause and standardized endpoints</cite><cite id="dd595cfd-6">Clinical management guidance includes ERT and addresses fracture risk reduction and bone loss improvement</cite><cite id="0b75be84-9">Phalangeal QUS captures cortical bone impairment and can serve as a complementary endpoint</cite>.
- Embedded registries: prospective cohorts of adult TS tracking bone, sex steroids, smoking, alcohol; pre‑specify bone trajectories by ERT age/duration and years since menopause to anticipate hazard windows for fractures. <cite id="02ffd633-1">Long-term follow-up in TS shows BMD outcomes shaped by treatment timing and duration</cite><cite id="02ffd633-3">Summaries emphasize estimating bone density relationships to ERT start age and duration</cite>.
- Natural history comparator: untreated or delayed‑treatment arms ethically limited; historical controls and external cohorts with matched estrogen exposure can be used for context. <cite id="02ffd633-4">Earlier estrogen exposure is hypothesized to prevent later loss and fractures, guiding comparator selection</cite>.

4) Multi‑center harmonization and pragmatic adaptation
- Prospective network trials and registries across pediatric and adult clinics with data standards: shared case report forms, pubertal staging scales, densitometer models, phantom QC logs, and imaging repositories; use statistical harmonization for cross‑site variability and Mendelian randomization if genetic instrumentation is available. <cite id="739af8bf-8">Best practices stress protocol harmonization, QA, and standardization to mitigate variance</cite><cite id="dd595cfd-9">Guidelines facilitate cross‑site alignment in endocrine bone care and research infrastructure</cite>.

B. Core measurement strategies

1) Bone mineral density (Areal)
- Technique: DXA remains the backbone for routine BMD due to accuracy and reproducibility; incorporate CTA‑based vertebral fracture assessment within routine skeletal imaging when available. <cite id="739af8bf-4">DXA is accurate, reproducible, and clinically proven for BMD</cite><cite id="739af8bf-8">DXA best practices guide high‑precision BMD quantification</cite><cite id="02ffd633-8">BMD protocols with vertebral fracture assessment are recommended to identify occult fractures</cite>.
- Sites and thresholds: Lumbar spine and hip (femoral neck/wide) as primary endpoints in adolescents and adults; express results as T‑scores relative to adult or pediatric reference ranges; derive TS‑specific Z‑score baselines via cross‑sectional cohorts. <cite id="02ffd633-3">Pediatric references emphasize age, puberty, and type of bone for density interpretations</cite><cite id="0b75be84-1">DXA‑identified BMD reductions in TS motivate site‑specific endpoints in adolescents</cite>.
- Quality assurance: Daily phantom scans; scanner calibration; centralized blinding; correction for body habitus, phase window (±2 weeks), and hydration; consistent software versions. <cite id="739af8bf-8">DXA best practices emphasize phantom QC, calibration, and standardized protocols to ensure comparability and precision</cite>.

2) Distal cortical bone and structural imaging (QUS and QCT)
- Triage and monitoring: pQUS of the heel or fingers as a low‑dose adjunct to triage low‑risk vs high‑risk TS (especially cortical bone involvement), paired with DXA when initiating therapy or in menopausal surveillance. <cite id="739af8bf-9">QUS can serve as a triage test to measure bone risk in lieu of, or alongside, DXA</cite><cite id="0b75be84-1">pQUS is useful to capture cortical bone impairment in TS adolescents where DXA may under‑detect</cite>.
- Advanced volumetrics: QCT of the lumbar spine and distal radius for volumetric BMD and trabecular/cortical volumetrics to detect early or treatment‑responsive changes; integrate with low‑dose CT protocols in adults when feasible. <cite id="739af8bf-0">Comparative reviews include QUS and DXA for bone screening but underscore the need to match modality to question and dose</cite><cite id="02ffd633-8">CTA-based vertebral assessment can be integrated to quantify fractures</cite>.
- Pediatric distal sites: phalangeal pQUS and distal radius DXA/qUS to assess periosteal/cortical accrual during pubertal growth surges; build sex‑steroid‑stratified references. <cite id="739af8bf-2">Adolescent TS cohorts comparing DXA and phalangeal QUS demonstrate complementary sensitivity to skeletal maturation</cite><cite id="0b75be84-1">DXA and pQUS together reveal reduced BMD and structural deficits across TS pubertal stages</cite>.

3) Biochemical and genetic modifiers
- Required labs: serum 25‑OH vitamin D, calcium, phosphorus, alkaline phosphatase/osteocalcin, parathyroid hormone; early menopause/EPO risk; smoking and alcohol; sex steroid measures (LH/FSH, estradiol); IGF‑1/IGF‑1s and IGFBP3 to capture growth‑hormone sensitivity; optional:CTX1/NTx (urine) and bone turnover profiles. <cite id="dd595cfd-7">Targeted approaches value modifiable determinants like vitamin D for bone evaluation and intervention</cite><cite id="dd595cfd-9">Endocrine guidance highlights vitamin D and bone health management in adults</cite><cite id="0b75be84-8">IGF metrics and skeletal features correlate with BMD and bone structure in Turner syndrome cohorts</cite>.
- Genetic stratification and mechanistic phenotyping: WES/WGS to refine diagnosis and link pathways (e.g., FGFR‑related) with skeletal phenotypes and tailor longitudinal monitoring intensity. <cite id="dd595cfd-0">Reviews frame bone fragility mechanisms and prevention strategies in TS, creating a platform for mechanistic stratification</cite>.

4) Physical activity and imaging outcomes
- Digital activity monitors and structured exercise interventions; integrate low‑dose CT–based radiomics of trabecular patterns and vertebral deformity quantification; combine with BMD and QUS to reduce chance of a type II error in detecting small structural benefits. <cite id="02ffd633-0">Relationships between ERT timing, duration, and later BMD inform endpoints and power calculations for trials adding exercise or hormones</cite><cite id="02ffd633-8">Quantitative vertebral assessment methods enable structural outcome capture</cite>.
- Radiographic end points: regular skeletal survey focus; MRI/CT of spine in high‑risk women; maintain fracture registries. <cite id="739af8bf-9">Alternative measures beyond DXA, like QUS, help triage but imaging remains essential for fracture confirmation and structural assessment</cite>.

C. Measurement harmonization and standardization checklist

- Pubertal staging and estrogen sufficiency: use Tanner/SSH scale with luteinizing hormone/estradiol and uterine/uterine+breast exam; record ERT/ET start age and dose; define “estrogen‑sufficient” windows in analyses. <cite id="0b75be84-8">Estrogen sufficiency is central to interpreting skeletal characteristics and bone density</cite><cite id="02ffd633-5">Most TS require hormone replacement; timing and duration are determinants of BMD</cite>.
- Densitometry: 
  - DXA: lumbar spines and hip with validated protocols; spine repositioning if lordosis/rotation; exclude recent spinal fractures; use software that provides twofold cross‑validation and site‑specific coefficients of variation; annual phantom QC logs. <cite id="739af8bf-8">DXA best practice includes validated site selection, phantom QA, and reproducible protocols</cite><cite id="739af8bf-4">DXA methodology is accurate and reproducible but requires standard operating procedures to ensure reliability</cite>.
  - pQUS and QCT: standardize transducer models, probe placement, and distal site handling; harmonize thresholds for structural indices and volumetric sites; align clinical imaging with densitometer timing. <cite id="739af8bf-9">QUS as triage test necessitates uniform protocols to interpret indices consistently</cite><cite id="0b75be84-1">Comparative DXA–pQUS designs in TS support standardized thresholds and site definitions to facilitate translation</cite>.
- Lab: standardized vitamin D assay method and cutoffs; central lab for bone turnover markers with LIMS tracking; blinded reading for BMD and densitometry reports.
- Imaging: standardized CTA protocols for vertebral assessment; radiologist‑read reports; digital archiving linked to demographics and pubertal/therapy fields.

D. Analytic strategies tailored to TS phenotypes

- Early life windows: Model BMD Z‑score change from prepuberty to peak bone mass across matched controls; test interaction of pubertal surge vs estrogen supplementation. <cite id="dd595cfd-1">Bone density in TS is related to puberty and age, guiding analytic phasing</cite>.
- Estrogen timing and menopause: Piecewise regression of lumbar T‑score versus ERT start age and duration, with separate trajectories for early vs usual‑onset puberty and pre‑ vs post‑menopausal phases. <cite id="02ffd633-0">Empirical relationships between ERT start age and later BMD inform analytic models and power</cite>.
- Multi‑modality synthesis: Combine areal BMD, volumetric and structural imaging, and QUS to derive a composite bone health score; prioritize hip/lumbar and phalangeal indices to capture mixed cortical/trabecular phenotypes. <cite id="0b75be84-9">Phalangeal QUS reveals cortical deficits and complements areal measurements in Turner adolescents</cite>.
- Mediation analyses: Examine whether vitamin D sufficiency, IGF‑1 sufficiency, and physical activity mediate the effects of estrogen timing on bone accrual and fracture risk. <cite id="dd595cfd-7">Integrating modifiable factors like vitamin D into evaluation supports mediation-focused analyses</cite>.

E. Trial protocols: concrete elements to improve internal and external validity

1) Pediatric and adolescent interventions
- Comparator: delayed initiation or placebo run‑in with reassurance of ethical fallback to guideline‑concordant ERT; active control of psychotherapy or educational sessions to mitigate contamination.
- Arms: physiotherapy‑structured loading program + early ERT vs early ERT alone; calcifediol baseline + guideline ERT vs ERT alone; early ERT plus testosterone for girls with Tanner arrest, with shared decision‑making.
- Endpoints and timing: 
  - Primary: change in hip (FN/WE) and lumbar T‑score (DXA), with pQUS distal phalanges as secondary; 
  - Qualitative: pain diaries and functional mobility; 
  - Safety/feasibility: adherence, growth velocity, menstrual return.
  - Readouts: 6, 12, 24 months; sample size N≈200 per arm estimated from expected pubertal‑phase differences in BMD accrual and variability.
  - Rationale: early estrogen improves bone accrual and lowers fracture risk; structured loading may improve cortical bone and musculoskeletal outcomes. <cite id="02ffd633-2">Earlier estrogen use is linked to better subsequent bone density and likely fewer fractures in TS</cite><cite id="739af8bf-2">DXA and phalangeal QUS in TS adolescents support combined endpoints to capture cortical and vertebral sites</cite>.

2) Adult peri‑menopausal hormone therapy and testosterone
- Arms: estradiol transdermal + cyclic progesterone ± testosterone gel vs estradiol + progesterone alone vs placebo; early start vs usual start cohorts.
- Endpoints: 
  - ARE/lumbar T‑score (DXA) 
  - Volumetric distal radius (QCT), trabecular/cortical indices 
  - pQUS distal sites 
  - Biochemical markers (CTx/NTx), vitamin Dc, and FRAX updated per menopausal status and BMD.
  - Primary endpoint at 18 months; interim imaging at 6–12 months.
- Inclusion: amenorrheic or surgically menopused TS women within 5–10 years of menopause; exclude current osteoporotic fractures.
- Justification: adult TS is at increased osteoporotic risk; ERT mitigates loss, testosterone may improve muscle‑bone unit, and early peri‑menopausal intervention aims to preserve bone. <cite id="02ffd633-0">Estrogen replacement timing and duration correlate with TS bone density, informing adult peri-menopausal intervention designs</cite><cite id="02ffd633-6">ERT improves bone density and reduces hip and spinal fractures in postmenopausal women with TS</cite>.

F. Pragmatic and ethical considerations

- Pediatric consent/assent and longitudinal burden: use low‑dose imaging cadences; offer pQUS as a lighter triage when clinical inertia is high; integrate with annual clinical pubertal checks.
- Equity and access: ensure telehealth or centralized reading hubs for remote clinics; provide mobile phantoms and calibration support for community scanners; publish harmonization checklists.
- Inclusion: enroll across karyotypes (mosaic, partial X monosomy, 45, X/46, X); genotype and phenotype stratify risk; include patients with chronic comorbidities (e.g., CHD, diabetes) to reflect real‑world risk up‑lifting.
- Dissemination: shared data repository with cohort metadata, QC logs, and de‑identified images and labs to accelerate secondary analyses and meta‑research.

Illustrative protocol template (Pediatric Pubertal Phasing Cohort)
- Eligibility: TS girls ages 6–18 not yet in spontaneous or ERT puberty; controls by age/ethnicity.
- Design: Prospective cohort with baseline auxology, pubertal staging, IGF‑1, 25‑OH D, bone markers; matched controls.
- Imaging: DXA (spine, hip, whole‑body), pQUS (proximal phalanges), optional QCT radius/lumbar if available.
- Follow‑up: Annual pubertal labs + DXA/pQUS for 3 years; event monitoring for fractures.
- Interventional arm (optional): early standardized estrogen protocol for eligible participants with informed consent; blinded assessment.
- Analyses: Mixed models of BMD Z/T change by pubertal/estrogen stages; mediation by vitamin D and IGF‑1; survival analysis for fractures.

Illustrative Protocol Template (Adult Menopausal Management)
- Eligibility: Women with TS, age 45–60 (±5) at onset; pre/surgically menopausal; prior ERT optional.
- Design: Parallel-group randomized trial of ERT ± testosterone; stratify by prior pubertal estrogen exposure.
- Imaging: Baseline DXA lumbar/hip; QCT distal radius/LS; pQUS heel/fingers; repeat at 6/12/24 months.
- Labs: Baseline 25‑OH D, BMD markers; maintain during trial.
- Endpoints: Primary hip/lumbar BMD change at 18 months; secondary structural indices, QUS, FRAX; noninferiority/menopausal symptom scales.
- Sample size: Power to detect absolute T‑score difference 0.5–0.8 SD at 18 months with 80% power, alpha 0.05 (adjust for multiplicity).

Summary: To improve bone health research in TS, studies should use longitudinal pediatric cohorts and adult hormone trials with standardized DXA protocols, phantom QA, and CTA vertebral assessment, supplemented by pQUS/QCT to capture cortical bone, and integrated biochemical markers and vitamin D management. Designs must explicitly phase analyses by pubertal/estrogen sufficiency and menopausal status, test early versus usual ERT/ET strategies, and adopt multi‑site harmonization with blinded readings; these steps will yield reproducible, clinically actionable evidence across the TS lifespan. <cite id="739af8bf-0">Comparative reviews of bone density techniques clarify roles for DXA and QUS</cite><cite id="739af8bf-4">DXA performance and best practices support robust measurement</cite><cite id="739af8bf-8">DXA QC and standardization enhance comparability across sites</cite><cite id="739af8bf-5">QUS complements DXA by reflecting bone structure and mechanics</cite><cite id="0b75be84-1">DXA–pQUS in adolescent TS captures both trabecular and cortical deficits</cite><cite id="dd595cfd-0">Mechanistic and prevention reviews provide rationale for early, longitudinal evaluation and intervention</cite><cite id="02ffd633-2">Earlier estrogen in TS is associated with higher subsequent bone density</cite><cite id="02ffd633-6">ERT reduces fracture risk and improves BMD in postmenopausal TS women</cite><cite id="dd595cfd-7">Targeted approaches emphasize modifiable determinants (vitamin D) within TS bone evaluation frameworks</cite>

Below is a structured synthesis of factors that commonly leave the risk of bias (RoB) domains unclear in studies of adrenal cortical tumors (adrenocortical adenoma/carcinoma), mapped to Cochrane/consensus domains and key adrenal-tumor specifics.

Key cross-cutting features of adrenal cortical tumor studies that inflate “unclear” risk of bias
- Rarity and observational defaults: Many comparative and diagnostic studies are small, single-center, or retrospective cohorts or case series, which make blinding, randomization, and control-group comparability difficult and lead reviewers to mark selection, performance/detection, attrition, and selective reporting as unclear by default. <cite id="2cf1e059-4">Retrospective comparative analyses are common in adrenocortical carcinoma surgical studies</cite> and frequently report prognostic “cutoffs” (e.g., 4–6–8.5 cm) from heterogeneous populations, inviting thresholding and confounding concerns. <cite id="0a4944d6-1">Adrenocortical imaging work has called for prospective, larger-sample designs explicitly to quantify selection bias and improve diagnostic accuracy</cite>.
- Variable imaging and biochemical reference standards: Heterogeneous scanners, thresholds, and follow‑ups complicate endpoint definition and reader interpretation. <cite id="0a4944d6-1">Even when effect sizes are summarized, authors emphasize selection bias risk and the need for larger prospective samples</cite>; <cite id="0a4944d6-2">imaging accuracy can vary with density thresholds and a sizable fraction of pathology later reveals discordant findings</cite>; and <cite id="0a4944d6-0">size–malignancy thresholds (e.g., >4 cm) carry high sensitivity but modest specificity, indicating uncertainty in the diagnostic boundary</cite>.
- Confounding in observational pathology and prognosis studies: Studies linking tumor size or histology to malignancy or outcome often lack adjustment for comorbidities, laterality, or functional status, leaving confounding risk unclear. <cite id="2cf1e059-1">A suggested 8.5 cm cutoff for poor outcomes in ACC illustrates how threshold analyses can be sensitive to selection and measurement</cite>; <cite id="2cf1e059-8">size–risk gradients themselves derive from retrospective datasets with selection and measurement (imaging) uncertainty</cite>.
- Lack/weak blinding and performance bias in diagnostic imaging and functional testing: Imaging outcomes and radiologist/biochemist readings depend on the underlying mass characteristics, which participants and readers typically know, and this undermines blinding. <cite id="64c0a29a-2">Cochrane stresses the distinction between allocation sequence concealment (randomization) and blinding of assigned interventions</cite>—in observational adrenal imaging, blinding between index lesion and reference results is rarely feasible, contributing to performance (detection) bias; <cite id="0a4944d6-0">imaging–pathology mismatches themselves indicate risk of misclassification and consequent bias</cite>.
- Incomplete outcome data and selective follow-up: Functional tumor cohorts and imaging surveillance studies often have long follow‑up windows but uneven adherence, loss to follow-up, and biased drop‑out, inflating “unclear” for attrition and selective reporting. <cite id="64c0a29a-0">Cochrane outlines domains of incomplete outcome data and selective outcome reporting as explicit risk-of-bias axes</cite>; these issues arise in adrenal cohorts where biochemical and imaging outcomes are event-driven and participant-prone to dropout. <cite id="0a4944d6-1">Imaging reviews explicitly call for larger, prospective samples to moderate selection bias</cite>.
- Allocation bias and concealment deficits in (rare) interventional designs: Where surgical approaches or surveillance vs resection are compared, deficits in allocation concealment and lack of outcome assessor blinding yield unclear selection and detection bias. <cite id="64c0a29a-2">Confusing allocation sequence concealment with blinding of assigned interventions is a known Cochrane pitfall</cite> and <cite id="64c0a29a-3">reviews have shown RoB judgments for allocation concealment in Cochrane reviews frequently deviate from Handbook guidance</cite>, indicating that adrenal surgical trials, when present, often lack robust concealment and blinding.
- Thresholding and “rule-based” criteria introduce design heterogeneity: Studies defining ACC or malignancy via imaging or steroid thresholds often employ inconsistent inclusion/exclusion and post-hoc adjustments, complicating standardization, blinding, and applicability, which reviewers label as unclear RoB. <cite id="0a4944d6-0">Even when tumor size increases risk, sensitivity–specificity trade-offs imply thresholded classifications are imperfect and study-specific</cite>; <cite id="2cf1e059-5">studies of size–malignancy likelihood doubling at 4 cm reflect retrospective cohorts with non-uniform presentation</cite>.

RoB domain-by-domain contributors in adrenal cortical tumor studies
- Randomization/selection bias (unclear when nonrandomized)
  - Predominance of case series, registries, and retrospective cohorts in ACC diagnosis and surgery limits the ability to assess selection bias, leaving it unclear; <cite id="2cf1e059-4">retrospective comparative surgical cohorts are common</cite> and <cite id="2cf1e059-6">epidemiologic ACC risk-factor studies also rely on hospital-based cohorts</cite>.
  - <cite id="0a4944d6-1">Diagnostic imaging studies explicitly call for prospective, larger-sample designs to define selection bias risk and improve accuracy</cite>.
- Allocation concealment (unclear or high risk in interventional trials)
  - Where surgical techniques (e.g., enucleation vs adrenalectomy) are compared, lack of prospective planning and unclear documentation of concealed allocation are frequent; <cite id="64c0a29a-2">authors often conflate sequence generation with blinding</cite> and <cite id="64c0a29a-3">many Cochrane reviews misclassify allocation concealment</cite>, implying adrenal surgical trials commonly fall short.
- Blinding (performance/detection and outcome assessor blinding)
  - Imaging and pathology assessments lack blinding because clinicians and readers know side of resection or prior suspicion for malignancy; <cite id="64c0a29a-2">Cochrane differentiates sequence concealment from blinding of assigned interventions</cite>, underscoring that adrenal imaging studies rarely blind to side or clinical suspicion.
  - <cite id="0a4944d6-2">Image-based diagnostic thresholds and discordant pathology indicate misclassification risk and performance bias</cite>; <cite id="0a4944d6-1">authors recommend prospective cohorts to handle selection bias</cite>.
- Incomplete outcome data and attrition
  - Biochemical and imaging follow-ups are event-driven and subject to loss to follow-up and bias; <cite id="64c0a29a-0">Cochrane’s domain of incomplete outcome data applies directly</cite>.
  - <cite id="64c0a29a-3">Judgments on allocation concealment in practice often fall short of Handbook guidance</cite>, which when present (e.g., surgical trials) can propagate selection and attrition risks.
- Selective outcome reporting (unclear)
  - <cite id="64c0a29a-0">Selective outcome reporting is an explicit Cochrane domain</cite>; registry and cohort adrenal studies vary widely in outcomes (e.g., biochemical control vs local recurrence vs mortality) and are susceptible to post hoc emphasis on favorable endpoints, making selective reporting risk unclear.
  - Heterogeneous imaging endpoints (contrast enhancement criteria, HU thresholds) and steroid profiles can lead to endpoint gaming unless predefined; <cite id="0a4944d6-2">imaging accuracy depends on thresholds with variable performance</cite>.
- Other bias (confounding, thresholding, heterogeneity)
  - <cite id="64c0a29a-1">Allocation bias occurs when investigators know or predict the next intervention</cite>, applicable to nonrandomized adrenal cohorts where treatment or observation choice may be non-orthogonal to prognosis.
  - <cite id="2cf1e059-1">Cutoff-driven prognostic claims (e.g., 8.5 cm) are sensitive to selection and measurement variability</cite> and reflect <cite id="2cf1e059-8">size-related risk increases that themselves derive from observational data with uncertainty</cite>.
  - <cite id="64c0a29a-8">Poor randomization or blinding constitutes key biases affecting estimates</cite>—both often present in small adrenal studies.

Illustrative domains where “unclear” RoB frequently arises in adrenocortical literature
- Differential diagnosis studies (Cushing’s vs mild ACS; ACTH-independent hypercortisolism): Multi-site retrospective cohorts using DST outcomes are common, with endpoints sensitive to laboratory thresholds and clinician interpretation. <cite id="e4da5b19-1">A multi-site, retrospective cohort of adults with diagnosed adrenal incidentalomas used DST as the diagnostic standard</cite>; retrospective design and lab/site variabilities leave RoB domains (selection, detection, attrition) unclear by default. <cite id="e4da5b19-1">Retrospective cohort structures are standard even as authors stress the need for better bias control</cite>.
- Imaging-based malignancy prediction: Contrast-enhanced CT/MRI rules (capsular contact, invasion, size) are read without blinding to side/suspicion; discordance to pathology is common. <cite id="0a4944d6-2">A pooled accuracy of 48% for certain density-based thresholds and 65% overall illustrates misclassification prevalence with pathologic follow-up</cite>, directly evidencing performance bias and potential detection bias in readers and referring clinicians. <cite id="0a4944d6-1">Authors explicitly call for prospective larger samples to quantify selection bias</cite>.
- Prognostic cohort/registry analyses for ACC (size thresholds, recurrence risk, early-stage outcomes): <cite id="2cf1e059-1">Proposed 8.5 cm cutoffs separating prognoses</cite> and <cite id="2cf1e059-5">doubling of malignancy likelihood at 4 cm</cite> rely on heterogeneous cohorts and imaging variability, leaving confounding and thresholding bias unclear. <cite id="2cf1e059-8">These relationships derive from observational data with known selection/ measurement uncertainty</cite>.
- Surgical management comparisons: <cite id="2cf1e059-4">Retrospective comparative surgical cohorts are reported but lack randomized foundations</cite>, with unclear allocation processes and lack of blinding to surgical technique, making selection/detection/attrition biases difficult to assess; <cite id="64c0a29a-2">and sequence concealment is often conflated with blinding in such analyses</cite>.

Practical reasons these become “unclear” to reviewers and authors
- Small, single-center samples and retrospective accrual make blinding and randomization impractical or unreported; <cite id="64c0a29a-3">judgments for allocation concealment in Cochrane reviews frequently misalign with guidance</cite>.
- Imaging and biochemical endpoints are inherently reader- and threshold-dependent; <cite id="0a4944d6-2">accuracy varies by parameter choices and there is pathologic discordance</cite>.
- Post-hoc analyses and “rule” thresholds drive selective reporting concerns; <cite id="0a4944d6-1">authors recommend prospective designs to quantify selection bias</cite>.
- Confusion between sequence concealment and blinding leads to underreporting of methodological shortcomings; <cite id="64c0a29a-2">Cochrane explicitly warns of this distinction</cite>.

How to improve clarity in the adrenal cortical tumor RoB domains
- Design and reporting: Use or transparently justify observational comparators and pre-specify multiple relevant outcomes to address incomplete reporting; <cite id="64c0a29a-2">clearly separate sequence generation from blinding</cite>.
- Diagnostic studies: Reduce detection bias via blinded centralized imaging and pathology readings, harmonized thresholds, and standardized lab DST protocols; <cite id="0a4944d6-1">adopt prospective multicenter designs where feasible</cite>.
- Prognostic/threshold analyses: Adjust for measured confounders, validate thresholds externally, and avoid ad hoc cutoffs; <cite id="2cf1e059-1">explicitly quantify selection and measurement uncertainty</cite>.
- Surgical comparisons: Where possible, conceal allocation (prospective sequence generation) and blind outcome assessment to side/technique; otherwise, in retrospective cohorts, model propensity scores and report sensitivity to bias assumptions; <cite id="64c0a29a-0">document incomplete outcome data and selective outcome reporting explicitly</cite>.
- Prospective integration with registries: <cite id="0a4944d6-1">Prospective imaging cohorts and harmonized endpoints can reduce selection bias uncertainty</cite> and improve blinding in performance bias.

Summary
Across diagnostic imaging, biochemical testing, prognostic size/malignancy relationships, and surgical management, adrenal cortical tumor studies often lack blinding, have retrospective/observational designs, and rely on heterogeneous diagnostic endpoints; these features make key Cochrane RoB domains (selection, allocation concealment/selection, performance/detection, attrition, and selective reporting) unclear by default, with confounding and thresholding bias further contributing to uncertainty. Strengthening prospective designs, standardizing endpoints, centralizing blinded readouts, and rigorous reporting of allocation and follow-up can clarify RoB in this field. <cite id="64c0a29a-0">Risk-of-bias tools center on sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, and selective reporting</cite>; <cite id="64c0a29a-2">errors around blinding and allocation concealment are common and conceptually distinct</cite>; <cite id="0a4944d6-1">adrenal imaging studies call out selection bias and the need for larger, prospective cohorts</cite>; and <cite id="2cf1e059-1">threshold-based prognostic claims in ACC are sensitive to selection and measurement, underscoring unclear bias</cite>.

Summary
Maternal micronutrient restriction commonly increases adipose expression of glucocorticoid-metabolizing 11β‑HSD1 and the adipokine leptin in offspring, biasing white adipogenesis and metabolic risk, with effects mediated by fetal nutrient sensing and epigenetic remodeling of metabolic tissues such as adipose and the hypothalamus–adipose axis. <cite id="e1619b46-0">11β-HSD1 gene expression is a target of developmental programming during white adipose tissue development, where it regenerates intracellular active glucocorticoids and drives adipogenic transcriptional programs</cite>. <cite id="e1619b46-2">In primate and rodent models, maternal nutrient restriction increases adipose 11β‑HSD1, leptin, and adiponectin mRNA while altering CpG methylation at regulatory elements, linking micronutrient scarcity to epigenetic reprogramming of lipid-handling genes</cite>. <cite id="e1619b46-4">Direct experimental models of maternal chromium restriction increased leptin and 11β‑HSD1 expression in adipose tissue of offspring</cite>, and reviews of perinatal nutrition converge on long-lasting, depot- and sex-differentiated programming via the hypothalamus–adipose axis. <cite id="e1619b46-5">Maternal nutritional manipulation induces persistent changes in the hypothalamus–adipose axis, with most cases showing increased adiposity and altered adipokine/adipogenic gene signaling</cite>.

Micronutrient-specific effects on 11β‑HSD1 and leptin expression
- Magnesium restriction (MgR): <cite id="e1619b46-2">Adipose expression of 11βHSD1, leptin, and adiponectin was increased in MgR offspring, accompanied by CpG methylation changes at regulatory sites, suggesting that magnesium scarcity programs both transcript abundance and chromatin accessibility of metabolic genes</cite>.
- Chromium restriction: <cite id="e1619b46-4">Maternal chromium restriction significantly increased leptin and 11β‑HSD1 gene expression in adipose tissue across both sexes, implying a nutrient‑specific upshift of energy storage signaling</cite>.
- Vitamin D deficiency: <cite id="e1619b46-1">A vitamin D deficiency model found altered programming of adipose tissue cellularity and depot organization in offspring</cite>, and controlled vitamin D studies show that maternal vitamin D status affects adipogenesis-related gene expression and body fat outcomes; <cite id="3623ff7a-1">reviewed evidence across clinical and animal studies shows maternal vitamin D deficiency biases offspring lipid metabolism and adiposity via changes in adipose gene networks</cite>. Mechanistically, vitamin D receptor signaling intersects with steroid hormone metabolism, providing a plausible route to 11β‑HSD1/glucocorticoid receptor cross-talk that modulates adipocyte differentiation. <cite id="3623ff7a-2">Reviews also highlight that 11β‑HSD1 activity in liver and adipose contributes to features of insulin resistance, a downstream risk when adipogenesis and leptin signaling are dysregulated</cite>. While the direct effect of vitamin D on leptin/11β‑HSD1 abundance is more indirect, vitamin A (retinoid) signaling is epistatically important for adipocyte differentiation and adipokine gene expression in developing adipose, and maternal vitamin A handling affects offspring adiposity and depot gene expression. <cite id="819f3e9b-0">Maternal vitamin A supply shapes offspring white and brown adipose gene expression and adiposity gain, indicating upstream control of adipogenic programs</cite>.
- Protein/one‑carbon micronutrients (e.g., folate/B12) and zinc/iron: Although detailed gene‑level data for 11β‑HSD1 are sparse, related lines support programming via adipokine and adipogenic pathways. <cite id="3623ff7a-8">Maternal B12 deficiency elevates offspring leptin and alters methylation, implicating vitamin B12 status in leptin regulation and one‑carbon–dependent epigenetic control</cite>. <cite id="e1619b46-6">Reviews of maternal undernutrition show that prenatal malnutrition reprograms adipose gene expression, with sex- and depot-specific effects, setting the stage for heightened adipogenesis and metabolic dysfunction in offspring</cite>.

Mechanisms: nutrient sensing, epigenetics, and glucocorticoid/adipokine signaling
- Glucocorticoid programming via 11β‑HSD1: <cite id="e1619b46-0">Because 11β‑HSD1 converts inactive glucocorticoid metabolites back to active cortisol/active glucocorticoids during white adipose development, deficiency-induced or restriction-induced increases in 11β‑HSD1 shift the fetal glucocorticoid milieu to favor adipocyte differentiation and storage capacity</cite>. <cite id="e1619b46-3">Prenatal high-fat exposure can skew the 11β‑HSD1/11β‑HSD2 balance in gonadal white adipose tissue to favor glucocorticoid activation in adulthood</cite>, reinforcing the concept that maternal metabolic signals encode long-lived changes in adipogenic steroid metabolism.
- Leptin as an adipokine–endocrine feedback target: <cite id="e1619b46-2">Maternal nutrient restriction increases adipose leptin mRNA with concomitant CpG methylation changes, integrating micronutrient availability with the epigenetic control of satiety signaling from adipose</cite>. <cite id="819f3e9b-9">Maternal obesity program increases leptin gene expression in a depot-specific manner via epigenetic modifications</cite>, demonstrating that perinatal nutritional context can remodel leptin locus regulation and depot-specific adipokine output; the same mechanisms plausibly underlie micronutrient-driven leptin remodeling, with specific evidence for magnesium/chromium restriction.
- Cross-talk to developmental programming hubs: <cite id="e1619b46-5">Maternal nutritional changes have persistent effects across the hypothalamus–adipose axis, aligning increased 11β‑HSD1 and leptin in adipose with hypothalamic appetite–energy expenditure control</cite>, and mechanistic nodes such as vitamin D receptor/11β‑HSD1/glucocorticoid receptor signaling link micronutrient action to adipocyte fate decisions. <cite id="28fa851f-7">Obese states raise 11β‑HSD1 mRNA in fat depots, consistent with sustained glucocorticoid-driven adipogenesis when maternal programming is maladaptive</cite>.

Depot, sex, and tissue specificity; metabolic outcomes
- Depot specificity and phenotypic divergence: <cite id="e1619b46-1">In a primate model of maternal nutrient reduction, adult offspring show increased adiposity with elevated mRNA in adipose tissue</cite>, and human/mouse programming studies show that maternal diet alters white adipose cellularity and differentiation while often sparing precursor pools, indicating selective amplification or bias of adipocyte lineage. <cite id="e1619b46-6">Maternal undernutrition programs adipose gene expression without affecting “developmental” adipogenesis per se, suggesting a postnatal amplification phenotype</cite>. Adipokine programming can be depot- and sex-specific; <cite id="819f3e9b-9">leptin expression increases via epigenetic modifications in a depot-specific manner influenced by maternal obesity</cite>, a pattern also noted across maternal micronutrient manipulations.
