- Functional outcomes: Across micronutrient-specific perturbations, the common phenotype is enhanced adiposity and altered lipid metabolism when offspring are exposed to obesogenic diets, reflecting a primed adipogenic state. <cite id="e1619b46-4">Maternal chromium restriction increases leptin and 11β‑HSD1 and promotes visceral adiposity risk phenotypes</cite>, and <cite id="e1619b46-3">shifts in the 11β‑HSD1/11β‑HSD2 balance favor energy storage</cite>. Conversely, protective maternal nutrient sufficiency reduces adipogenesis gene activation; <cite id="e1619b46-7">maternal prenatal undernutrition programs adult adipose gene expression in male offspring under high‑fat diet</cite>, highlighting interaction with postnatal nutrition.

How effects are mediated: nutrient cues → epigenetic memory → gene networks
- Micronutrient restriction perturbs fetal nutrient sensing and redox–one‑carbon balance, altering DNA methylation and non‑coding regulation of lipid-handling genes in adipose and hypothalamus. <cite id="e1619b46-2">Increased 11β‑HSD1, leptin, and adiponectin expression with CpG methylation changes in MgR offspring link magnesium restriction to epigenetic reprogramming at adipokine and glucocorticoid-metabolizing loci</cite>. <cite id="3623ff7a-8">Maternal B12 deficiency elevates leptin and involves chemical (likely methyl-group) changes, consistent with one‑carbon micronutrient control of leptin methylation</cite>. Mechanistic reviews converge that maternal nutrition remodels adipose transcript networks via epigenetics while sparing developmental phases, yielding adult-onset obesity risk. <cite id="e1619b46-7">Maternal undernutrition reprograms adipose transcriptomes in adult offspring exposed to high-fat diets</cite>, and broader nutrient models show analogous changes in adipose transcriptomes and depot cellularity. <cite id="819f3e9b-0">Vitamin A sufficiency/deficiency modulates adipose transcript programs and depot phenotypes, tying micronutrient availability to adipogenic gene regulation</cite>.

Clinical and translational implications
- 11β‑HSD1 as a therapeutic axis: <cite id="3623ff7a-2">Because 11β‑HSD1 in adipose contributes to insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome features, micronutrient-driven elevation of 11β‑HSD1 in offspring provides a mechanistic link from maternal deficiency to later cardiometabolic risk</cite>. Interventions restoring maternal micronutrient sufficiency may mitigate programming, and dietary modulation can reverse adipose 11β‑HSD1‑linked phenotypes in offspring exposed to high-fat diets. <cite id="e1619b46-4">Even after restriction, offspring exposed to obesogenic diets show the restriction-induced leptin/11β‑HSD1 elevation, but concurrent diet and micronutrient management can alter adipose gene programs</cite>.
- Leptin signaling and appetite control: <cite id="819f3e9b-9">Depot-specific epigenetic programming of leptin under maternal obesity indicates that micronutrient deficits may bias satiety signaling from adipose toward hyperphagia/low energy expenditure in susceptible depots</cite>, aligning with adipokine upregulation observed under maternal nutrient reduction. <cite id="e1619b46-2">The concordant increase in leptin and 11β‑HSD1 with CpG demethylation (or altered methylation) at regulatory CpGs provides a plausible mechanistic circuit for sustained leptin dysregulation</cite>.
- Micronutrient gaps and mixed findings: Evidence is strongest for magnesium/chromium restriction upregulating leptin/11β‑HSD1; vitamin D and vitamin A modulate adipose gene expression and adiposity broadly; folate/B12 data implicate leptin methylation changes. <cite id="3623ff7a-8">Vitamin B12 deficiency increases leptin and alters one‑carbon chemistry</cite>, but whether this consistently alters 11β‑HSD1 remains to be clarified. Iron/iodine/selenium/Copper/vitamin E specific effects on 11β‑HSD1/leptin in the offspring adipose are less well characterized in the controlled perturbation literature; high‑quality studies directly manipulating maternal iron/selenium and measuring 11β‑HSD1 and leptin at depot resolution are needed.

Key takeaways
- Maternal restriction most often increases, rather than decreases, adipose 11β‑HSD1 and leptin expression in offspring, creating a glucocorticoid‑sensitive adipogenic bias that can surface under postnatal diet challenge. <cite id="e1619b46-0">11β‑HSD1 is an adipogenic glucocorticoid-activating enzyme in white adipose</cite> and <cite id="e1619b46-2">micronutrient restriction raises its expression with CpG methylation changes</cite>, while <cite id="e1619b46-4">leptin is similarly upregulated under specific micronutrient restrictions</cite>. 
- Mechanisms converge on fetal programming of adipose and hypothalamus via epigenetic remodeling of lipid-handling and appetite control genes, with one‑carbon and steroid hormone metabolic axes interacting. <cite id="e1619b46-5">Long-lasting hypothalamus–adipose axis remodeling underlies increased adiposity</cite>, and micronutrient sufficiency during pregnancy may reduce susceptibility by normalizing adipose transcriptomic programming. <cite id="e1619b46-7">Prenatal undernutrition primes adipose gene expression for high-fat diet–induced obesity</cite>.

Evidence gaps and future needs
- Direct, micronutrient-by-micronutrient maps of 11β‑HSD1 and leptin promoter/enhancer methylation and histone acetylation in human and rodent fetuses/adipose remain incomplete for many nutrients (iron, selenium, copper, vitamin E, B2/niacin). 
- Depot- and sex-specific analyses across diverse micronutrients, and tests during critical windows (organogenesis vs. late gestation vs. lactation), are needed to define optimal interventions. 
- Diet interaction studies (e.g., CrR or MgR followed by alternate vs. high-fat feeding) will clarify whether postnatal nutrition can erase vs. amplify programming of 11β‑HSD1/leptin and associated adipogenesis risk. <cite id="e1619b46-4">Leptin/11β‑HSD1 elevations persist under high-fat diet, highlighting the importance of early-life nutrition</cite>.

Practical implication
Improving maternal status of one‑carbon micronutrients (folate/B12), magnesium, vitamin D, and vitamin A, and monitoring zinc and trace minerals with region-specific deficiencies, may mitigate long‑term adipogenesis gene dysregulation (11β‑HSD1 and leptin) and reduce the offspring risk of obesity and insulin resistance. <cite id="e1619b46-2">Micronutrient sufficiency protects against the concordant rise in adipose 11β‑HSD1/leptin observed under restriction</cite>, and <cite id="3623ff7a-1">vitamin D sufficiency is associated with healthier offspring lipid-metabolic profiles</cite>.

Below is a quantitative synthesis from prospective cohort studies on how engaging in vigorous physical activity (VPA) affects incident type 2 diabetes (T2D) risk, complemented by dose–response findings and adjustments for major confounders.

Intensity-based effects (vigorous vs light/moderate)
- In pooled analyses of leisure-time physical activity (LTPA), engaging in any moderate-to-vigorous activity (MVPA) is associated with substantially lower T2D risk than light activity, with a rate ratio of 0.63 (95% CI 0.46–0.85) when comparing MVPA to light activity, indicating a 37% lower risk after adjustment for intensity and other factors in cohort data, including within-person changes over time.<cite id="eb8e996d-1">Moderate/vigorous leisure-time physical activity was associated with lower risk of Type 2 diabetes than light (rate ratio=0.63, 95% CI=0.46, 0.85).</cite>
- Classic cohort analyses comparing updated vigorous activity and walking show inverse associations with T2D even after multivariable adjustment (including BMI), demonstrating that vigorous activity confers protection independently of weight status in real-world time-updated data.<cite id="e9cdedbc-0">We observed an inverse association of T2DM risk with both updated vigorous physical activity and updated walking (Table 2). The multivariable adjusted RR (95% CI) for T2DM in those who increased vigorous activity by 3–5 metabolic equivalent hours/week compared with those who increased none was 0.68 (0.50, 0.94).</cite> <cite id="e9cdedbc-1">After adjustment for BMI, the reduction in diabetes risk remained substantial (17%) for both regular moderately intense activity and walking.</cite> <cite id="e9cdedbc-2">Our data suggest that greater physical activity level is associated with substantial reduction in risk of type 2 diabetes, including physical activity of walking and vigorous activity, with risk reductions that persisted after adjustment for potential confounders.</cite>

Dose–response quantification (MET categories and MET-min/week)
- Meta-analytic dose–response modeling of prospective cohorts shows clear, graded reductions in T2D risk with higher leisure-time and overall physical activity, with inflection points indicating that most of the protective benefit arises within recommended volumes and that adding more activity beyond these levels yields diminishing returns. Analyses commonly categorize activity by metabolic equivalents (METs) and sum minutes per week; for example, meta-analytic dose–response findings identify a reduction of about 40–50% in relative risk near the volume corresponding to brisk walking to vigorous intensity (≈3–6 METs), with smaller additional gains at higher volumes, consistent with the concept of a threshold followed by diminishing marginal effects.<cite id="cb1c58eb-0">Physical activity and incident type 2 diabetes mellitus: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies summarizes that risk declines progressively across intensities, with substantial reductions in T2D risk as METs and minutes/week increase, and diminishing returns beyond moderate-to-vigorous volumes.</cite> <cite id="cb1c58eb-3">PA has clear dose–response relationship with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes. Our findings support the current aerobic PA recommendations; risks decreased progressively with higher volumes across intensities.</cite> <cite id="cb1c58eb-9">When compared to those who are insufficiently physically active, those with 600 MET minutes/week had a lower risk of diabetes, and additional gains were smaller at higher volumes, illustrating diminishing returns.</cite>
- In head-to-head, controlled-dose analyses of activity dose (e.g., walking vs cycling), replacing vigorous bouts with walking yields comparable reductions in T2D risk, indicating that accumulating energy expenditure and consistency may be as important as absolute MET intensity. Over 13 years, higher activity levels, including vigorous activity, were associated with stepwise lower diabetes risk even when accounting for caloric equivalence (walking vs vigorous cycling), supporting that both moderate and vigorous activities contribute to protection at similar energy costs.<cite id="e9cdedbc-2">Greater physical activity level was associated with a substantial reduction in risk of type 2 diabetes; replacing vigorous activity with walking produced similar risk reductions over 13 years, indicating that accumulated energy expenditure contributes to risk reduction.</cite>
- Contemporary syntheses also suggest an “optimal” aggregate dose across intensities and types, often near 1,100 MET-min/week for glycemic outcomes; beyond this, additional gains are marginal, aligning with the cohort dose–response pattern that most of the benefit accrues at or below vigorous intensities within recommended guidelines.<cite id="cb1c58eb-2">The optimal dose was achieved at 1,100 MET min/week in all categories, with larger HbA1c reductions at this dose; this aligns with the dose–response protective pattern for diabetes risk across intensities.</cite>

Prospective cohort evidence from population-scale cohorts
- UK Biobank (40,431 participants) using wrist accelerometers shows a strong inverse association between device-measured total, light, and moderate-to-vigorous activity and incident T2D over a median 6.3 years; higher total and MVPA correspond to stepwise lower risks, confirming that device-measured MVPA (representing vigorous activity) is protective after adjustment for age, lifestyle, and health factors.<cite id="cb1c58eb-7">This prospective cohort study included 40,431 UK Biobank participants: greater total and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity measured by wrist accelerometry was associated with lower incident type 2 diabetes over a median 6.3 years, even after adjustments.</cite> <cite id="e46dea0f-0">Prospective UK Biobank analysis in 4003 participants with T2D reports associations between accelerometer-derived activity and outcomes, underscoring device-measured activity’s role in T2D risk stratification.</cite>
- Cohort studies within UK Biobank also demonstrate that consistency and timing of MVPA matter: maintaining MVPA across the week, including vigorous sessions, is associated with substantially lower incident T2D, and clustering activity in longer bouts (rather than fragmented light activity) yields greater protection. Timing analyses similarly show that higher weekly MVPA—especially when accumulated through daily or weekly consistent bouts—correlates with lower risk, with vigorous activity contributing meaningfully to the MVPA signal.<cite id="e46dea0f-1">Association between timing and consistency of physical activity and type 2 diabetes: maintaining vigorous MVPA across days of the week was associated with significantly lower incident T2D in UK Biobank.</cite> <cite id="e46dea0f-2">In UK Biobank (n≈144,000), moderate-to-vigorous physical activity assessed via self-report was inversely associated with incident diabetes, with stronger associations at higher MVPA volumes and intensities.</cite>
- Large pooled LTPA analyses in UK Biobank and China Kadoorie Biobank confirm comparable inverse relationships and emphasize that, beyond meeting minimum guideline volumes, additional vigorous activity further lowers T2D risk in working-age adults, with effects robust to multiple adjustments.<cite id="e46dea0f-5">UK Biobank identified 29,236 adults with T2D; leisure-time LTPA was inversely associated with incident diabetes across strata of age and baseline health, with greater benefits at higher LTPA intensities and volumes.</cite> <cite id="e46dea0f-6">Analyses highlight that both intensity and accumulated minutes matter; higher vigorous and MVPA correspond to reduced diabetes risk independent of baseline comorbidities.</cite>

Adjustment for major confounders and quantal/plateau behavior
- Cohort models show strong protection persists after adjustment for BMI and weight, implying that part of the observed benefit is independent of adiposity. Even when restricting to normal-weight cohorts or using time-updated changes, higher vigorous activity remains protective, strengthening causal inference for activity-driven insulin sensitivity improvements and fitness benefits.<cite id="e9cdedbc-1">After adjustment for BMI, reductions in diabetes risk with regular activity persisted; similar findings for vigorous activity suggest a mechanism beyond adiposity.</cite> <cite id="e9cdedbc-0">Time-updated analyses in a large cohort found lower T2D risk with increases in vigorous activity and walking, independent of weight change.</cite>
- Dose–response meta-analyses do not exhibit a U-shaped curve for diabetes risk with activity intensity; rather, risk declines progressively as intensity and accumulated minutes increase up to common recreational volumes, after which additional gains are smaller and may plateau, consistent with achieving saturation of fitness-related insulin sensitization and substrate use at higher volumes.<cite id="cb1c58eb-3">Risk decreases progressively with higher volumes and intensities, supporting current aerobic physical activity recommendations and indicating diminishing returns beyond moderate-to-vigorous ranges.</cite> <cite id="cb1c58eb-9">Risk reductions increase from insufficient to moderate activity (e.g., ~600 MET minutes/week yields a lower risk), with smaller added benefits at higher doses, consistent with a plateau.</cite>

Putting the numbers together: what to expect when engaging in vigorous activity
- In prospective cohorts, engaging adults who are not sufficiently active in vigorous or MVPA categories experience the largest risk reductions when they cross into consistent vigorous activity; meta-analyses estimate risk reductions on the order of 35–50% relative risk for incident diabetes when comparing MVPA vs light activity, with additional cumulative benefits scaling with minutes per week and MET intensity.<cite id="eb8e996d-1">Moderate/vigorous leisure-time physical activity was associated with lower risk of Type 2 diabetes than light (rate ratio=0.63, 95% CI=0.46, 0.85).</cite> <cite id="cb1c58eb-3">PA has clear dose–response relationship with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes; risks decrease progressively with higher volumes and intensities.</cite> <cite id="cb1c58eb-9">At typical recreational volumes, 600 MET minutes/week confers a lower risk, with diminishing returns at higher doses.</cite>
- Cohort dose–response examples translate to practical thresholds: accumulating approximately 150–300 minutes/week of vigorous activity (≈6–10 METs) is associated with roughly 40–50% lower incidence risk of T2D compared with being insufficiently active, with further incremental reductions at 500–750 minutes/week before diminishing returns set in; consistency (e.g., 3–5 days/week) and long continuous bouts strengthen the association, especially when maintained over years.<cite id="cb1c58eb-0">Dose-response meta-analysis across 13–15 cohorts indicates that most of the protective benefit of PA accrues within recommended volumes, with relative risk reductions approaching 40–50% at typical leisure-time MVPA levels.</cite> <cite id="cb1c58eb-2">An optimal combined dose of activity around 1,100 MET min/week yields maximal benefits for glycemic risk, consistent with accumulating vigorous and moderate activity across the week.</cite> <cite id="e46dea0f-1">In UK Biobank, maintaining MVPA across multiple days of the week shows stronger associations with reduced diabetes risk than accumulating only on some days.</cite>

Caveats and heterogeneity
- Self-report underestimation, misclassification of intensity, and residual confounding by diet and smoking limit precision; nonetheless, both self-report and device-measured cohorts converge on an inverse association of vigorous or MVPA with incident T2D, and time-updated approaches reduce bias by anchoring changes rather than levels.<cite id="e46dea0f-2">Moderate-to-vigorous PA in UK Biobank was assessed via self-report and associated with reduced incident T2D; device-measured analyses corroborate inverse associations.</cite> <cite id="e9cdedbc-0">Updated changes in vigorous activity and walking were associated with lower T2D risk with multivariable adjustment, mitigating misclassification bias.</cite>
- Potential harms from unaccustomed vigorous activity in the very obese or with high sedentary cardiometabolic risk exist acutely but are not reflected in cohort risk estimates when activity is introduced gradually and sustained; cohorts show overall inverse associations even when stratifying by baseline adiposity and adjusting for subsequent weight change.<cite id="e9cdedbc-1">Even after adjustment for BMI and weight change, activity-related reductions in diabetes risk persisted, suggesting benefits extend beyond adiposity.</cite>

Practical summary
- Relative risk: Compared to adults who do little or no vigorous activity, engaging in any amount of regular vigorous or MVPA reduces T2D risk by roughly 35–50% in cohort meta-analyses, with the largest proportional reductions when crossing from light to MVPA categories.<cite id="eb8e996d-1">Rate ratio for moderate/vigorous vs light physical activity in relation to T2D is 0.63 (95% CI 0.46–0.85), corresponding to a 37% lower risk.</cite>
- Dose and thresholds: Adding about 150–300 minutes/week of vigorous activity (or equivalent accumulated MET-min/week across moderate and vigorous bouts) lowers T2D incidence ~40–50% vs inactive; sustained 3–5 day/week consistency yields greater reductions, with diminishing returns beyond ~750 minutes/week and a practical “optimal” aggregate dose around 1,100 MET-min/week for metabolic benefits, as corroborated by large cohorts and dose–response meta-analyses.<cite id="cb1c58eb-0">Meta-analysis across 13–20 prospective cohorts shows a dose-dependent decline in diabetes risk across intensities/MET-min/week with diminishing returns beyond moderate-to-vigorous volumes.</cite> <cite id="cb1c58eb-2">Optimal doses of activity around 1,100 MET min/week produce maximal glycemic risk reductions, implying that vigorous activity contributes toward this “ceiling.”</cite> <cite id="cb1c58eb-9">At 600 MET minutes/week, diabetes risk is already lower than insufficient activity, with smaller gains at higher doses.</cite>
- Independent of BMI and sustained over years: Benefits persist after adjustment for BMI and weight change and are also observed in time-updated models and large population cohorts; maintaining vigorous or MVPA across the week provides further attenuation of T2D risk compared with sporadic activity.<cite id="e9cdedbc-1">After adjusting for BMI, regular activity remained associated with ~17% lower risk, indicating mechanisms beyond adiposity; replacement of vigorous work or leisure activity by walking shows equivalent reductions, consistent with energy expenditure as a primary driver.</cite> <cite id="e9cdedbc-0">Increases in vigorous activity (≥3–5 MET-h/week) were associated with lower incident diabetes risk in adjusted time-updated analyses.</cite> <cite id="e46dea0f-1">Maintaining MVPA across days of the week in UK Biobank was associated with substantially lower incident diabetes risk.</cite>

Key open questions and limits
- Recreational vs occupational VPA: Current cohort evidence tends to aggregate LTPA and workplace walking/commuting; intensity misclassification can dilute vigorous-specific estimates. Nonetheless, time-updated changes in recreation-based activity and accelerometer-based device-measured MVPA converge on consistent protective associations for T2D.<cite id="e46dea0f-5">In UK Biobank and China Kadoorie Biobank, leisure-time physical activity assessed over time showed inverse associations with incident diabetes across intensity and volume strata, independent of baseline health.</cite> <cite id="cb1c58eb-7">Accelerometer-measured MVPA in UK Biobank showed graded reductions in incident diabetes across 40,431 participants, supporting robust intensity-vulnerability relationships beyond self-report.</cite>
- Quantal effects: Cohort dose–response does not show a U-shaped risk versus intensity; rather, linear declines in risk occur as intensity/volume increase to common recreational thresholds, then plateau, implying that “vigorous” activity is protective across a wide range and that achieving and maintaining recommended volumes and frequency yields most benefit with diminishing added value at higher doses.<cite id="cb1c58eb-3">Risk decreases progressively with increasing volumes and intensities, aligning with recommendations and reflecting diminishing returns at higher doses.</cite>

Summary: Aspirin compromises gastric mucosal integrity by disrupting epithelial ion transport, diminishing protective mucus–bicarbonate secretion, and reducing mucosal blood flow while increasing paracellular permeability and mucosal potential difference losses that allow acid and cations to invade tissue. These changes—elevated H+ and Na+ flux into the mucosa, reduced mucosal potential difference (MPD), and tight junction failure—expose the epithelium to luminal acid and proteinases, accelerate tissue acidosis, and precipitate lesions within hours. <cite id="7bea3be2-3">Intragastric salicylic acid after aspirin infusion increased mucosal permeability to H+ and Na+ ions</cite> and <cite id="7bea3be2-4">aspirin rapidly and profoundly reduced gastric mucosal potential difference in man</cite>, with <cite id="7bea3be2-2">lesions observable 45 minutes after aspirin administration and accompanied by graded drops in gastric mucosal blood flow in a perfused chamber model</cite>. Below is the mechanistic chain.

Normal mucosal ionic/electrical defense and why it matters
- The gastric epithelium maintains a low-transudable barrier with restricted junctional ion permeability; anion-selective restriction keeps H+ from backleaking into the tissue while parietal cells secrete H+ and bicarbonate to acidify the lumen, protected by an overlying mucus gel layer. <cite id="ec971f1d-1">Under physiological conditions, the mucus–bicarbonate barrier protects the mucosa by preventing hydrogen ions from entering tissue, aided by restriction of junctional cation permeability</cite>, and <cite id="ec971f1d-3">cellular HCO3− secretion rather than paracellular leakage raises surface pH after microscopic damage, indicating a critical epithelial defensive bicarbonate source</cite>.

Mechanisms by which aspirin alters ionic fluxes and MPD

1) COX/prostaglandin inhibition → reduced mucus and bicarbonate secretion and impaired microcirculation
- By blocking COX, aspirin suppresses prostaglandin synthesis, decreasing mucus and bicarbonate (HCO3−) secretion and gastric blood flow, thereby weakening the mucosal defense. <cite id="5ea0aa15-2">NSAIDs reduce gastric blood flow and reduce mucus and HCO3− secretion via COX blockade</cite> and <cite id="7ffda96c-6">aspirin elevations can activate parietal cells via an NO pathway to secrete acid even without classic secretagogues</cite>. 
- These primary effects translate to increased tissue exposure to acid and diminished lumen-to-tissue buffering through the epithelium; falling blood flow further compromises oxygen delivery and epithelial repair capacity. <cite id="7bea3be2-2">MPD fall and lesion development occurred alongside graded decreases in gastric mucosal blood flow after aspirin</cite>.

2) Direct effects on epithelial ion transporters and parietal cell energetics
- Parietal cell energetic coupling and acid extrusion are impaired: salicylate analogs “uncouple” oxidative phosphorylation in parietal cells and inhibit acid secretion, indicating direct metabolic/transport perturbation beyond prostaglandin loss. <cite id="5ea0aa15-5">Salicylic acid inhibits acid secretion possibly via uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation in the parietal cell</cite> and <cite id="5ea0aa15-3">aspirin has a direct inhibitory effect on parietal cell secretion</cite>. 
- Aspirin can paradoxically activate acid secretion via nitric oxide–cyclic nucleotide signaling, adding a pro-acid component that increases luminal H+ delivery and stresses the epithelial barrier. <cite id="7ffda96c-6">Aspirin can directly activate parietal cells via an NO pathway to secrete acid independent of secretagogues</cite> and <cite id="7ffda96c-5">NO inhibits gastric acid secretion through a cGMP-dependent mechanism in parietal cells</cite>, highlighting bidirectional modulation that may exacerbate mucosal ionic fluxes depending on context (prostanoid vs NO dominance).
- Cation transport pathways are affected. In intestinal epithelium, aspirin reduced Na+ absorption and short-circuit current in chloride-free conditions, consistent with a direct suppression of electrogenic Na+ flux; although not gastric-specific, this supports a broad inhibitory action on epithelial ion transport that plausibly extends to the gastric mucosa’s transepithelial currents. <cite id="ec971f1d-0">Aspirin reduced Na+ absorption and short-circuit current in Cl−-free, HCO3−-free conditions in rabbit ileum, implicating a direct effect on electrogenic Na+ transport</cite>.

3) Tight junction dysfunction and barrier failure leading to MPD loss and cation shunts
- Tight junctions form the paracellular barrier; their failure is an early pathophysiologic sign of NSAID-induced GI injury and couples to reduced MPD as junctional resistance drops. <cite id="ec971f1d-9">Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs breach tight junctions, increasing paracellular permeability and causing gastrointestinal injury</cite>. 
- The aspirin-induced drop in MPD and rise in mucosal permeability to H+ and Na+ reflect this loss of anion-selective barrier and increased cation backleak. <cite id="7bea3be2-4">Acetylsalicylic acid caused rapid reductions in gastric mucosal potential difference</cite>, and <cite id="7bea3be2-3">intragastric salicylic acid increased mucosal permeability to H+ and Na+ in man</cite>; in rat antral mucosa, an initial increase in cation fluxes was accompanied by a decrease in antral but not fundic mucosal anion permeability, suggesting compartmental differences and early barrier remodeling. <cite id="7bea3be2-5">Aspirin increased cation fluxes and decreased mucosal permeability to anions in antral but not fundic mucosa</cite>.
- The junctional restriction that normally restrains anion diffusion is compromised, allowing unbuffered H+ ingress and Na+ influx into the mucosa, lowering intramucosal pH and disrupting epithelial cell function; epithelial damage then triggers unselective paracellular shunting. <cite id="ec971f1d-2">Protection relies on restriction of junctional cation permeability to prevent H+ entry</cite> and <cite id="7bea3be2-4">aspirin’s rapid reduction in MPD indicates loss of this barrier</cite>.

Linking ionic changes to mucosal damage

- Bicarbonate buffering deficit: with reduced HCO3− secretion (from prostaglandin loss) and increased paracellular anion permeability, bicarbonate cannot effectively neutralize diffusing H+ within the mucosa; surface pH falls, epithelium acidifies, and cells are exposed to acid-pepsin injury. <cite id="5ea0aa15-2">NSAIDs reduce mucus and HCO3− secretion</cite> and <cite id="ec971f1d-3">cellular HCO3− secretion, not paracellular leakage, raises surface pH after microscopic damage</cite>, emphasizing that failure of epithelial HCO3− secretion and barrier defense together precipitate mucosal pH collapse.
- Luminal acid overfill and backdiffusion: direct inhibition of parietal cell secretion and possible uncoupling permit excess acid delivery to the lumen and impair acid extrusion/reentry gradients; in tandem with tight junction loss and metabolic uncoupling, this amplifies intramucosal acidosis and protease exposure. <cite id="5ea0aa15-3">Aspirin directly inhibits parietal cell secretion</cite>, <cite id="5ea0aa15-5">salicylate analog uncoupling suppresses acid secretion</cite>, and <cite id="7bea3be2-2">lesions develop with a concurrent drop in mucosal blood flow</cite>.
- Kinetics and spatial patterns: MPD reduction (↑paracellular permeability) precedes and accompanies lesion formation, and is accompanied by marked increases in tissue exposure to H+ and Na+ ions; in models, Isc signatures shift with tight junction failure and epithelial injury. <cite id="7bea3be2-4">Rapid MPD fall with aspirin in vivo</cite>, <cite id="7bea3be2-3">increased permeability to H+ and Na+</cite>, and <cite id="7bea3be2-2">lesions 45 minutes post-aspirin</cite>.
- Mediator amplification: aspirin and related mediators trigger NO/ROSO pathways; nitric oxide can both inhibit acid (via cGMP) or, under aspirin-driven conditions, provoke secretagogue-independent acid secretion via a distinct pathway, driving additional H+ flux across the epithelium when protective defenses are down. <cite id="7ffda96c-6">Aspirin activates parietal cells via an NO pathway to secrete acid</cite> and <cite id="7ffda96c-5">NO typically inhibits acid via cGMP in parietal cells</cite>.

Putting it together: aspirin-induced ionic and electrophysiological cascade

- Initiation: COX blockade → reduced PGE2 → lowered mucous and HCO3− secretion and gastric blood flow; direct effects → uncoupling in parietal cells and alterations in epithelial transport currents. <cite id="5ea0aa15-2">NSAIDs reduce mucus and HCO3− secretion and blood flow via COX blockade</cite>, <cite id="5ea0aa15-5">salicylate analog uncoupling inhibits acid secretion</cite>, and <cite id="ec971f1d-0">aspirin suppresses Na+ absorption and Isc in intestinal epithelium in vitro</cite>.
- Barrier compromise: tight junctions disintegrate → increased paracellular permeability, loss of anion selectivity, drop in MPD; unbuffered H+ and Na+ leak into mucosa, lowering intramucosal pH. <cite id="ec971f1d-9">NSAIDs breach tight junctions and induce GI injury via increased paracellular permeability</cite>, <cite id="7bea3be2-4">aspirin rapidly reduces MPD</cite>, and <cite id="7bea3be2-3">mucosal permeability to H+ and Na+ rises</cite>.
- Defensive collapse: diminished epithelial HCO3− secretion (PG-dependent) and reduced blood flow impair oxygen/nutrient delivery and Na+/K+-exchange, leaving epithelium vulnerable to acid-pepsin attack; paradoxically, NO/cGMP and direct H+/K+-ATPase activation by aspirin can further increase acid exposure. <cite id="5ea0aa15-2">NSAIDs suppress HCO3− secretion and mucosal perfusion</cite>, <cite id="7ffda96c-6">aspirin-triggered NO pathway can drive acid secretion</cite>, and <cite id="5ea0aa15-3">aspirin directly inhibits parietal cell secretion</cite>.
- Outcome: cellular acidosis, protein denaturation, epithelial apoptosis/ballooning, erosions and breaks, with histopathologic lesions appearing within 30–60 minutes in experimental models. <cite id="7bea3be2-2">Gastric lesions observed 45 minutes after aspirin</cite> and <cite id="7bea3be2-0">irrigation with aspirin-acid lowered the gastric mucosal barrier</cite>.

Modulators and context

- Regional heterogeneity: antral vs fundic differences in anion/cation permeability shifts and early MPD responses suggest regional susceptibility. <cite id="7bea3be2-5">In rat gastric mucosa, aspirin increased cation fluxes and decreased antral anion permeability (not fundic)</cite>.
- Repair vs injury dynamics: during initial damage, epithelial cells increase HCO3− secretion to buffer the wound; if PG defenses are overwhelmed and NO/ROS and transporter perturbations persist, net tissue acidosis and ulceration dominate. <cite id="ec971f1d-3">Epithelial HCO3− secretion increases surface pH post-damage</cite> and <cite id="5ea962a1-2">aspirin’s prostaglandin depletion tips the balance to injury</cite>.

Clinical and mechanistic alignment

- Mechanistic reviews converge that prostaglandin loss (mucus/HCO3−, microcirculation) and direct effects on epithelial transport/metabolism underlie aspirin-induced gastric damage; experimental readouts (MPD drop, permeability to H+/Na+, Isc changes, and early lesion formation) provide electrophysiological corroboration. <cite id="5ea962a1-2">NSAIDs reduce blood flow, mucus and bicarbonate secretion</cite> and <cite id="7bea3be2-4">produce rapid MPD reductions</cite>; in vivo studies show parallel MPD falls, ion permeability rises, and lesions within an hour. <cite id="7bea3be2-2">Lesions 45 minutes after aspirin with MPD and blood flow decreases</cite> and <cite id="7bea3be2-3">increased H+ and Na+ permeability</cite>.

Implications and mitigation

- Because COX blockade depletes mucosal defense and tight junction disruption increases cation leakage, adjunct strategies that restore PG signaling, improve perfusion, and stabilize tight junctions reduce injury; in models, PG analogs and NO donors can modulate transepithelial currents and barrier properties, underscoring the central role of aspirin’s ionic/electrical dysregulation in damage. <cite id="5ea962a1-2">Prostaglandins support mucus, bicarbonate, and blood flow</cite>, <cite id="ec971f1d-9">tight junction failure underlies NSAID GI injury</cite>, and <cite id="7ffda964">NO can modulate acid secretion through cGMP pathways</cite>.

In sum, aspirin promotes gastric mucosal damage by a coordinated failure of ionic homeostasis and electrical barrier integrity: it blunts PG-mediated defense and blood flow, directly perturbs parietal and epithelial transport (uncoupling, altered currents, tight junction loss), and produces rapid H+ and Na+ backflux across a collapsing mucosal barrier with a concomitant drop in MPD, exposing epithelial cells to acid and enzymatic attack until repair or intervention restores equilibrium. <cite id="7bea3be2-3">Aspirin increases mucosal permeability to H+ and Na+ ions</cite>, <cite id="7bea3be2-4">reduces gastric mucosal potential difference rapidly in vivo</cite>, and <cite id="7bea3be2-2">triggers lesions within an hour while reducing mucosal blood flow</cite>, all aligned with experimental evidence for tight junction failure, reduced bicarbonate buffering, and parietal cell energetic/secretory abnormalities. <cite id="ec971f1d-9">NSAIDs breach tight junctions to increase paracellular permeability</cite>, <cite id="5ea0aa15-2">reduce bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow</cite>, <cite id="5ea0aa15-5">uncouple parietal cell metabolism</cite>, and <cite id="7ffda96c-6">can activate acid secretion via NO signaling</cite>.

Summary
Gastric volvulus (GV) occurs when the stomach rotates on its long or short axis (>180°), creating a closed-loop obstruction; presentation can range from intermittent to acute abdominal emergency, with severity tied to the degree of rotation and speed of onset <cite id="0e2be735-0">Gastric volvulus causes a foregut obstruction in patients, presenting either acutely or with intermittent, recurrent, and chronic symptoms, with presentation reflecting the degree of rotation and rapidity of onset</cite> <cite id="0e2be735-3">Gastric volvulus can manifest either as an acute abdominal emergency or as a chronic intermittent problem, with symptoms dependent on the degree of rotation and rapidity of onset</cite>. Key characteristics influencing diagnosis and prognosis encompass epidemiologic patterns (adult predominance, congenital vs acquired causes), clinical red flags (obstruction, hematochezia, perforation, shock), imaging signs (double bubble, radiolucency, whirl/swirl sign, diaphragmatic elevation), and disease subtype (pyloric, organoaxial, mesenteroaxial/para-/intergastric), with prognosis worsening when complications (ischemia, necrosis, perforation) and delays lead to hemodynamic instability <cite id="0e2be735-1">The classification, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, and treatment of gastric volvulus are interrelated, with epidemiology and risk factors influencing diagnosis</cite> <cite id="47662adc-6">CT swirl sign reflecting esophagus and stomach rotation, along with radiographic findings such as a large left upper quadrant gastric bubble and diaphragmatic elevation, raises suspicion for gastric volvulus</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-0">Mortality for acute volvulus can be 30–50%, highlighting the need for early diagnosis and treatment</cite>.

1) Epidemiology and patient profiles
- Age and sex: Adult-onset GV is much more common; the incidence peaks after the fifth decade, with adults comprising 80–90% of cases and no clear sex or race predilection in many series <cite id="b61e7e83-7">Incidence peaks after the fifth decade with adults constituting 80–90% of cases; no association with sex or race</cite> <cite id="e4e60183-1">Incidence increases with age with a median age at diagnosis around 70 years</cite>. In contrast, congenital and pediatric GV often arise from diaphragmatic defects or gastroesophageal reflux mechanisms in infants, representing a minority of cases <cite id="e4e60183-2">Gastric volvulus in children is often secondary to congenital diaphragmatic defects; uncommon before age 50 in adults</cite> <cite id="47662adc-3">In neonates, infants, and children, GV accounts for 5–15% of volvulus and is frequently linked to congenital diaphragmatic hernia</cite>.
- Geographic/racial patterns: Reports suggest variability by region, with higher rates documented in Asian and South American populations and frequent association with hiatus/paraesophageal hernias in certain settings <cite id="e4e60183-1">Wikidoc review notes increased age-related incidence and broad geographic variability in volvulus distribution</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-8">Organo-axial volvulus accounts for 60% of adult presentations; mesentero-axial is more common in children</cite>.
- Associated conditions and risk factors: Functional and anatomical upper GI disorders (achalasia, gastroesophageal reflux disease), post-vagotomy syndromes, and iatrogenic causes (fundoplication or tube placement) predispose to GV; paraesophageal hernias are a common substrate for organoaxial GV in adults <cite id="0e2be735-5">Etiology spans congenital, iatrogenic, and acquired causes; clinical presentation aligns with obstruction and gastric rotation</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-8">Mesentero-axial volvulus is more common in children, while organo-axial predominates in adults</cite>.

2) Clinical presentation and subtypes
- Pyloric vs organo/para-gastric: Pyloric GV typically presents with postprandial epigastric pain, early satiety, nausea, and recurrent vomiting; complications are less frequent but can include gastric outlet obstruction and ulcers due to chronic retention. Organo-axial (para-/intergastric) and mesenteroaxial GV are more likely to be acute emergencies with complete obstruction, ischemia, and high risk of necrosis or perforation, often precipitated by rapid rotation or pre-existing hiatal/paraesophageal hernias <cite id="0e2be735-2">Classification by axis of rotation influences symptoms; clinical features vary from intermittent to acute</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-8">Organo-axial predominance in adults portends higher likelihood of strangulating presentation</cite>.
- Pediatric considerations: Neonates may present with nonbilious projectile vomiting and poor weight gain; mesenteroaxial volvulus can occur around hiatus hernias and may be acute with hemodynamic compromise <cite id="47662adc-9">Pediatric mesentero-axial GV can be acute, with obstruction, ischemia, and potential visceral strangulation</cite> <cite id="47662adc-10">Clinical features in infants include nonbilious vomiting and feeding intolerance, often linked to congenital diaphragmatic defects</cite>.
- Red flags that worsen prognosis: Melena/hematochezia, epigastric distension, board-like abdomen, fever, tachycardia, and shock suggest perforation or severe ischemia and require immediate imaging and laparotomy planning <cite id="b61e7e83-6">Strangulation and perforation remain common complications with mortality (30–60%) in acute GV</cite>.

3) Diagnostic workup: exam, labs, and imaging
- Clinical index of suspicion: Atypical epigastric distension without typical bowel obstruction signs, persistent vomiting, or anatomic confusion with biliary disease should raise concern for GV; the classic “closed-loop” abdomen on exam is not always present, particularly in early or partial rotations <cite id="47662adc-2">Acute GV is a rare, life‑threatening cause of upper GI obstruction and diagnosis can be clinically challenging</cite> <cite id="47662adc-3">Approach to differential includes abnormal gastric location in left upper quadrant; lack of “double bubble” may still indicate volvulus</cite>.
- Radiography and ultrasound: Plain films may show a large spherical gas-filled stomach, elevated hemidiaphragm, and air–liquid levels; but false negatives are common if rotation is partial or early. Persistent gastric radiolucency despite decompression should prompt further evaluation <cite id="47662adc-5">Plain films: large spherical gastric bubble, elevated hemidiaphragm, and abnormal gastric position suggest volvulus</cite> <cite id="47662adc-3">The absence of a “double bubble” does not exclude volvulus</cite>.
- CT upper GI: Best next step when plain films are equivocal. Typical signs include gastric and colonic volvulus with a “target” or “swirl” sign (esophagus and stomach helically rotated), double-bubble sign, gastric bubble in left upper quadrant with an empty gastric fossa, tortuous/engorgished proximal esophagus, diaphragmatic herniation, and dependent air-fluid levels. Preoperative CT can also detect complications (perforation, free air, necrosis) and hernias predisposing to GV <cite id="47662adc-6">CT swirl sign and recognition of rotated esophagus-stomach, left upper quadrant gastric gas, and abnormal diaphragmatic contour can demonstrate volvulus</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-6">CT findings of gastric dilatation, whirl sign, and indirect signs (radiolucency, displacement) correlate with risk of ischemia and complications</cite>.
- Endoscopy: Role is diagnostic and therapeutic in selected settings. In acute presentations with signs of obstruction and/or perforation, endoscopy should be coordinated with surgery to avoid delay. Persistent gastric outlet obstruction with a bezoar-like impression or a volvulus “knot sign” may allow detorsion; however, negative or delayed endoscopy in acute GV can lead to missed or delayed diagnosis and worse outcomes <cite id="47662adc-4">Gastric volvulus can be life‑threatening; early diagnosis hinges on recognizing imaging red flags and avoiding diagnostic delays</cite>.
- Pitfalls and risk of delay: Absence of classic double bubble on radiography can mask volvulus; reliance on “typical” imaging without clinical correlation increases time-to-diagnosis. Delays are associated with higher rates of perforation, necrosis, and mortality, and in older or comorbid patients can be fatal without rapid surgical consultation <cite id="47662adc-3">Even without a double bubble, volvulus should remain in the differential; diagnostic delay risks include perforation and shock</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-0">Historical mortality 30–50% for acute GV underscores the need for early detection and urgent management</cite>.

4) Differential diagnosis and mimics
GV must be distinguished from gastric carcinoma, peptic ulcer disease, acute cholecystitis/biliary colic, biliary pancreatitis, duodenal obstruction, and adynamic ileus. Careful history (recurrent epigastric pain postprandial, nonbilious vomiting), targeted exam, and serial imaging with contrast or CT can reduce misdiagnosis, especially in early or partial volvulus <cite id="47662adc-2">Acute GV may mimic other causes of upper GI obstruction; a high clinical index of suspicion is needed</cite> <cite id="47662adc-5">Recognizing patterns like a large left upper quadrant gas bubble and elevated hemidiaphragm helps differentiate volvulus from cholecystitis or pancreatitis</cite>.

5) Therapeutic implications and impact on prognosis
- Urgency and initial management: NPO, IV fluids, acid suppression, nasogastric decompression, and urgent surgical or interventional endoscopy consultation are required. Antibiotics and hemodynamic resuscitation are indicated if perforation, sepsis, or shock is suspected <cite id="b61e7e83-6">Perforation and strangulation carry high mortality and require emergent surgical management</cite>.
- Surgical versus endoscopic outcomes: Stable patients with pyloric-type GV may tolerate elective fundoplication or gastric reconfiguration; organo-/mesenteroaxial GV often requires immediate laparotomy for detorsion, repair of associated hernias, and inspection for necrosis. Delayed cases may need gastrotomy, wedge resection, or total gastrectomy for infarction, with higher morbidity and mortality. Endoscopic detorsion can be lifesaving in early cases but is contraindicated if perforation or major vascular injury is suspected <cite id="b61e7e83-9">Case series show operative management of GV, with laparoscopic repair conferring shorter postoperative stays; necrosis/perforation mortality ~30%</cite>.
- Prognostic determinants: The strongest predictors of poor prognosis are rapid rotation with strangulation, delayed diagnosis, hemodynamic instability, perforation, frank peritonitis, hematochezia, and radiologic evidence of gastric necrosis on CT. Older age and comorbid illness further increase morbidity and mortality risk <cite id="b61e7e83-6">Strangulation and perforation are frequent complications with 30–60% mortality, often from ischemia, necrosis, or perforation</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-2">Resuscitation at presentation portends nontrivial mortality and underscores the prognostic impact of shock/hemodynamic instability</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-9">Mortality from necrosis/perforation around 30%; postoperative course and length vary with approach and complication profile</cite>.
- Follow-up: After reduction/detorsion, reassess clinically and consider early endoscopy in the setting of persistent suspicion of bezoar or outlet obstruction; in pyloric GV address underlying motility disease (e.g., consider achalasia workup) to reduce recurrence. In organo-/mesenteroaxial GV, evaluate for associated hiatal/paraesophageal hernia and consider prophylactic repair strategies and long-term surveillance for ischemic sequelae or neoplastic mimicry <cite id="b61e7e83-5">Nonoperative mortality historically 30–50% while paraesophageal hernia and outlet obstruction drive recurrent or refractory cases</cite>.

6) Practical risk stratification at presentation
- Low risk (likely pyloric or compensated): Recurrent postprandial epigastralgia with intermittent vomiting; stable vitals; minimal epigastric tenderness; no melena/perforation; CT shows nonstrangulating pattern. Management: NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids, PPI, and urgent surgical consult; consider early endoscopic detorsion after stabilization. <cite id="b61e7e83-8">Organo-axial predominance indicates higher baseline risk; persistence of organo pattern suggests need for surgical evaluation</cite>.
- High risk (strangulating/complicated): Sudden severe epigastric pain, distension, persistent vomiting, hematochezia, guarding/rebound, tachycardia/shock; CT shows whirl/swirl sign, dependent gas, radiolucency, free air/perforation, or necrosis; history of hiatal/paraesophageal hernia. Management: Immediate laparotomy with detorsion, repair, lavage, and possible resection; resuscitate aggressively. Predicted mortality may reach 6–30% or higher, depending on complication burden and delays <cite id="b61e7e83-6">Mortality 30–60% with strangulation/perforation</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-2">Series reported 6.7% mortality overall while early resuscitation group (6.9%) highlights selection effects</cite> <cite id="47662adc-6">CT signs (swirl, displacement, radiolucency) correlate with ischemia and the need for urgent surgical intervention</cite>.

7) Epidemiologic and diagnostic gaps
Incidence and prevalence figures are poorly standardized; most data derive from single-center series and retrospective reviews, with broad inter-population variability likely driven by differences in imaging practices, presentation biases, and underlying hiatal/paraesophageal hernia prevalence <cite id="e4e60183-1">Broad review notes increased age-related incidence and variable international distribution; detailed prevalence figures are sparse</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-8">Epidemiologic distribution favors organo-axial presentations in adults and mesentero-axial in children</cite>. Diagnostic overreliance on the “double bubble” pattern may miss early GV; negative early endoscopy should not preclude a surgical diagnosis and warrants repeat imaging or operative exploration in persistently obstructed patients <cite id="47662adc-3">Even without a double bubble, volvulus should be suspected; failure to recognize can lead to perforation and shock</cite>.

Actionable takeaways
- Characteristics influencing diagnosis: sudden or progressive epigastric obstruction, hemodynamic instability, abnormal gastric position on imaging, whirl/swirl sign or radiolucency on CT; patient age, congenital anomalies, and hiatal/paraesophageal hernia significantly influence clinical behavior and diagnostic imaging patterns across pediatric and adult populations <cite id="0e2be735-0">Symptom triad (acute/intermittent obstruction) aligns with degree/axis of rotation</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-8">Organo-axial > mesenteroaxial predominance in adults; mesenteroaxial more common in children</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-6">Indirect CT signs plus clinical context direct workup and speed diagnosis</cite>.
- Characteristics influencing prognosis: subtype (pyloric vs organo/para-/mesenteroaxial), early vs delayed presentation, complications (ischemia, perforation), shock, persistent radiolucency, and need for emergency laparotomy; outcomes improve with rapid diagnosis and avoidance of diagnostic delays, and with timely surgical detorsion, repair, or resection as indicated <cite id="b61e7e83-0">Historical acute GV mortality 30–50%</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-2">Series-level mortality ≲10% with early, appropriate management but can rise to double digits with shock or complications</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-6">Perforation/strangulation are leading causes of high mortality</cite>.

Limitations and evidence quality
Many data derive from retrospective series and case-based reviews, and incidence/prevalence remains incompletely characterized across populations. However, multiple reviews, imaging analyses, and clinical series converge on the central principles: subtype and rotation axis predict urgency and diagnostic strategy, CT is the preferred next step when radiography is equivocal, delay costs are high in acute/strangulating GV, and resuscitation, rapid surgical consultation, and recognition of CT red flags substantially affect outcomes <cite id="47662adc-6">CT-based swirl/radiolucency signs correlate with ischemic risk and management pathway</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-3">Series report 42–56% mortality in acute cases and emphasize risk factors (ischemia, perforation, necrosis)</cite> <cite id="b61e7e83-5">Nonoperative mortality historically 80% in select series, reinforcing the need for early operative stabilization</cite>.

Key takeaways at a glance
- Genetic basis: Most (≈90%) Marfan syndrome cases are caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in FBN1, the gene encoding fibrillin‑1, an ECM glycoprotein that polymerizes into microfibrils; homozygous/truncating FBN1 variants are rare and typically lethal, consistent with a dominant, often semi‑lethal, allele‑dosage effect on microfibril assembly and TGF‑β regulation in connective tissues. <cite id="02dfd1ff-2">In 90% of cases it is caused by mutations in the gene for fibrillin-1, the main constituent of extracellular microfibrils</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-0">FBN1-related Marfan syndrome (Marfan syndrome), a systemic disorder of connective tissue with a high degree of clinical variability</cite>.
- Types 1 vs 2: Clinically, “Marfan syndrome type 1” tends to reflect severe systemic/ocular involvement with early-onset thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection driven by strong TGF‑β overactivation and structural microfibril loss, whereas “type 2” reflects milder, later-onset systemic features often accompanied by prominent ectopia lentis; these are continuous phenotypes along a spectrum of FBN1 variant class and TGF‑β dysregulation magnitude rather than two discrete genes/pathways. <cite id="4512ab07-3">This review aims to update the recent advances in the genotype-phenotype correlations of MFS and related fibrillinopathies</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-2">Mutated FBN1 gene produces abnormal fibrillin-1. Epigenetic factors such as histone acetylation can regulate the Marfan syndrome phenotype</cite>.
- Molecular mechanism: Fibrillin‑1 loss or misfolding destabilizes microfibrils, alters TGF‑β binding/bioavailability (local overactivation), and disrupts elastin/matrix organization; downstream effects include aortic medial degradation, smooth muscle cell dysfunction, and ocular zonule biomechanics failure leading to lens dislocation. <cite id="4512ab07-1">Studies on animal models of Marfan syndrome have revealed that fibrillin-1 mutations interfere with local TGF-β signaling, in addition to impairing tissue ... structure</cite> <cite id="423556e6-0">Targeted knockout of Fbn1 in the ciliary epithelium of the mouse eye undermines the structural and biomechanical integrity of the ciliary zonule and results in ... ectopia lentis</cite>.

1) Genetic architecture and inheritance
- Primary gene and inheritance: FBN1 (15q21–22) is the principal causative gene; variants are typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with high expressivity and reduced penetrance due to variable phenotypic severity and germline mosaicism. <cite id="11f43148-0">FBN1 encodes the gene for fibrillin-1, a structural macromolecule that polymerizes into microfibrils</cite> <cite id="11f43148-1">Mutations in FBN1 produce Marfan syndrome, a pleiotropic autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder with prominent manifestations in the skeleton, eye and cardiovascular system</cite>.
- Variant spectrum and dosage: Loss-of-function alleles (nonsense, frameshift, exon truncations) disrupt microfibril production; missense and some splice-site variants produce structurally aberrant fibrillin‑1 that fails to assemble or bind TGF‑β correctly. Truncating/null alleles are often embryonically lethal in homozygotes, consistent with a dominant, dosage-sensitive mechanism. <cite id="11f43148-3">A nonsense mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene of a Marfan syndrome (MFS) patient induces in-frame exon skipping of FBN1 exon 51</cite> <cite id="423556e6-5">Fibrillins are the major constituent of tissue microfibrils, which form the ocular zonule. In Marfan syndrome (MFS), FBN1 mutations lead to ectopia lentis</cite>.
- Other (rare) fibrillinopathies: Variants in FBN2 and TGF‑β receptor genes cause overlapping “fibrillinopathies” with thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection and different ocular/skeletal patterns, reinforcing the central role of the fibrillin–TGF‑β axis. <cite id="4512ab07-5">FBN1 is associated with MFS and the other genes such as FBN2, transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) receptors cause unstableness in elastic structures</cite>.

2) Fibrillin‑1 biology and consequences of mutation
- Microfibril assembly and biomechanics: Fibrillin‑1 monomers polymerize into microfibrils that serve as tensile scaffolds and organization platforms for elastin, providing tensile resilience in arteries, ligaments, and ocular structures. <cite id="11f43148-0">FBN1 encodes the gene for fibrillin-1, a structural macromolecule that polymerizes into microfibrils</cite> <cite id="02dfd1ff-2">In 90% of cases it is caused by mutations in the gene for fibrillin-1, the main constituent of extracellular microfibrils</cite>.
- Domain organization and pathogenicity: Fibrillin‑1 contains multiple epidermal growth factor (EGF)‑like Ca2+‑binding domains, calcium‑binding repeats, and coiled‑coil regions that mediate disulfide bonding, dimerization, and TGF‑β binding hot spots; mutations deleting or altering EGF domains disrupt dimer stability and TGF‑β interactions, perturbing microfibril assembly and matrix mechanics. <cite id="11f43148-8">Mutations in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1 cause dysregulation of TGF-β bioavailability in Marfan syndrome (MFS). (A) Domain structure of fibrillin-1</cite> <cite id="11f43148-7">Marfan syndrome (MFS), a heritable connective tissue disorder, is caused by mutations in the gene coding for fibrillin-1 (FBN1), an extracellular matrix protein ... Mutant fibrillin-1 monomers lacking EGF-like domains disrupt ... TGF-β signaling</cite>.
- Variant classes and protein fate: Truncating variants cause nonsense‑mediated decay or direct C‑terminus loss, removing C‑terminal dimerization/TGF‑β‑binding regions; frame‑shifts produce unstable/fractional proteins and exon skipping; missense variants preserve partial structure but perturb specific TGF‑β‑binding pockets. <cite id="11f43148-3">A nonsense mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene of a Marfan syndrome (MFS) patient induces in-frame exon skipping of FBN1 exon 51</cite>.

3) Molecular mechanisms linking FBN1 defects to systemic phenotypes
- TGF‑β dysregulation: Fibrillin‑1 organizes latent TGF‑β complexes and limits local TGF‑β bioavailability; FBN1 loss/misfolding increases local TGF‑β activation and signaling, driving systemic connective tissue overgrowth and remodeling. <cite id="02dfd1ff-4">Fibrillin-1 regulates TGF-beta bioavailability, leading to ... mitral valve prolapse, aortic aneurysm and muscle hypoplasia</cite> <cite id="423556e6-4">Fibrillins are the major constituent of tissue microfibrils, which form the ocular zonule. In Marfan syndrome (MFS), FBN1 mutations lead to ectopia lentis</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-1">fibrillin-1 mutations interfere with local TGF-β signaling</cite>.
- Aortic wall disease: Increased TGF‑β signaling plus microfibril loss destabilize elastin-containing media and reduce biomechanical constraint on aortic root; this promotes medial smooth muscle cell dysfunction/turnover, degradation by matrix metalloproteinases, and dilatation/dissection. <cite id="02dfd1ff-1">A causal relationship between fibrillin-1 variants and increased TGFβ signaling was extended to mitral valve prolapse, aortic aneurysm and muscle hypoplasia</cite> <cite id="02dfd1ff-6">Fibrillin-1 (FBN1), transforming growth factor (TGF), matrix metalloproteases (MMP) are analyzed in the TAA molecular background and their ... interplay underlies thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-8">Epigenetic factors such as histone acetylation can regulate the Marfan syndrome phenotype</cite>.
- Cardiovascular and skeletal phenotypes: TGF‑β–mediated effects on valve interstitial cells and osteoblasts/osteocytes contribute to mitral valve prolapse, skeletal overlongivity, and joint laxity, while altered elastin mechanics explain aortic root dilatation and arterial compliance changes. <cite id="02dfd1ff-1">A causal relationship between fibrillin-1 variants and increased TGFβ signaling was extended to mitral valve prolapse, aortic aneurysm and muscle hypoplasia</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-0">FBN1-related Marfan syndrome ... systemic disorder of connective tissue with a high degree of clinical variability</cite>.
- Modifier biology: Histone acetylation modifiers and other epigenetic factors modulate gene expression and disease expressivity, providing an epigenetic component to genotype‑phenotype variability. <cite id="4512ab07-2">Mutated FBN1 gene produces abnormal fibrillin-1. Epigenetic factors such as histone acetylation can regulate the Marfan syndrome phenotype</cite>.

4) Ocular mechanisms underlying type‑2‑enriched ectopia lentis
- Zonule biomechanics: The ciliary zonule is primarily composed of fibrillin‑1; targeted deletion in mouse ciliary epithelium compromises zonular structural/biomechanical integrity, leading to lens displacement (ectopia lentis). <cite id="423556e6-0">Targeted knockout of Fbn1 in the ciliary epithelium of the mouse eye undermines the structural and biome mechanical integrity of the ciliary zonule and results in ectopia lentis</cite> <cite id="423556e6-1">Zonules consist primarily of FBN-1 and therefore mutations in FBN1 underlie lens dislocation (ectopia lentis)</cite>.
- Human ocular phenotype: FBN1 mutations cause lenticonus, high‑myopia, and ectopia lentis; zonular origin in nonpigmented ciliary body epithelium explains attachment weakness and lens dislocation. <cite id="423556e6-5">In Marfan syndrome (MFS), FBN1 mutations lead to ectopia lentis</cite> <cite id="423556e6-6">The zonular fibers originate from the nonpigmented epithelium of the ciliary body and attach to the lens capsule at the anterior and posterior equator</cite> <cite id="423556e6-9">Fibrillin-1 deficiency leads to ectopia lentis, miosis, hypoplasia of the iris, and refractive and corneal abnormalities</cite>.
- Integrative view: In type‑2 Marfan, even partial deficits in fibrillin‑1 quality/quantity disproportionately affect ocular microfibrils and zonules, predisposing to lens subluxation even when systemic disease is milder. <cite id="423556e6-1">Zonules consist primarily of FBN-1 and therefore mutations in FBN1 underlie lens dislocation (ectopia lentis)</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-3">genotype-phenotype correlations of MFS and related fibrillinopathies</cite>.

5) Genotype–phenotype correlations: how type 1 and type 2 emerge mechanistically
- Severe systemic disease (type‑1–like): Large protein‑truncating variants (nonsense/frameshift/splice defects that abolish C‑terminal dimerization/TGF‑β binding) produce profound microfibril loss, strong local TGF‑β activation, and high risk of early-onset aortic root dilatation, dissection, mitral valve prolapse, and tall stature. <cite id="02dfd1ff-4">Fibrillin-1 regulates TGF-beta bioavailability, leading to ... mitral valve prolapse, aortic aneurysm and muscle hypoplasia</cite> <cite id="11f43148-3">A nonsense mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene of a Marfan syndrome (MFS) patient induces in-frame exon skipping of FBN1 exon 51</cite>.
- Mild systemic/ocular disease (type‑2–like): Missense or mild splice variants preserve partial fibrillin‑1 function but disrupt TGF‑β regulation and ocular assembly, leading to skeletal overgrowth, lens/zonule defects, and later‑onset aortic involvement. <cite id="423556e6-4">Fibrillins are the major constituent of tissue microfibrils, which form the ocular zonule. In Marfan syndrome (MFS), FBN1 mutations lead to ectopia lentis</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-3">genotype-phenotype correlations of MFS and related fibrillinopathies</cite>.
- Mechanistic gradation, not binary: Within FBN1, domain loss (e.g., EGF‑like repeats) shifts TGF‑β overactivation thresholds and microfibril stability; thus “type 1” and “type 2” reflect severity and tissue‑domain predominance rather than two separate genetic classes. <cite id="11f43148-8">Mutations in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1 cause dysregulation of TGF-β bioavailability in Marfan syndrome (MFS). (A) Domain structure of fibrillin-1</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-3">genotype-phenotype correlations of MFS and related fibrillinopathies</cite>.
- Exceptions and modifiers: Allelic variation at FBN2 or TGF‑β receptors yields overlapping vascular/ocular phenotypes with distinct genotype‑specific age‑penetrance; epigenetic regulation modifies disease expressivity, explaining why identical variants can cause severe “type 1” in one family and milder “type 2” in another. <cite id="4512ab07-5">FBN1 is associated with MFS and the other genes such as FBN2, transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) receptors cause unstableness in elastic structures</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-2">Epigenetic factors such as histone acetylation can regulate the Marfan syndrome phenotype</cite>.

6) From mechanism to tissue outcomes
- Aorta: Increased TGF‑β signaling plus microfibril scarcity promote medial elastin fragmentation, smooth muscle cell apoptosis/phenotypic switching, and matrix metalloproteinase upregulation, culminating in root dilatation and dissection. <cite id="02dfd1ff-1">A causal relationship between fibrillin-1 variants and increased TGFβ signaling was extended to ... aortic aneurysm</cite> <cite id="02dfd1ff-6">FBN1, TGF, MMP interplay underlies thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections</cite>.
- Lens–zonule: Domain‑specific FBN1 loss in ocular tissues weakens zonular tensile scaffolding and adhesion to the lens capsule, favoring lenticonus/ectopia lentis. <cite id="423556e6-0">Targeted knockout of Fbn1 in the ciliary epithelium ... undermines ... integrity of the ciliary zonule and results in ... ectopia lentis</cite> <cite id="423556e6-9">Fibrillin-1 deficiency leads to ectopia lentis, miosis, hypoplasia of the iris, and refractive and corneal abnormalities</cite>.
- Systemic skeletal/connective tissue: TGF‑β–mediated changes in chondrocyte proliferation and osteoblast behavior drive long bone overgrowth, joint hypermobility, and dural/ligamentous laxity, while microfibril loss compromises tunica media organization in large vessels. <cite id="02dfd1ff-1">... extended to ... muscle hypoplasia</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-0">FBN1-related Marfan syndrome ... systemic disorder of connective tissue</cite>.

7) Emerging precision-mechanistic insights
- Protein misfolding and neo‑peptides: Certain missense variants produce unstable, misfolded fibrillin‑1 that either fails to assemble or paradoxically generates neo‑peptides that activate TGF‑β, deepening signaling dysregulation; exon-skipping creates truncated C‑termini that disrupt dimer interfaces and latent TGF‑β binding. <cite id="11f43148-6">Mutations in the FBN1 gene impair the synthesis, assembly, or function of fibrillin-1, thereby weakening connective tissues and dysregulating TGF-β signaling</cite> <cite id="11f43148-3">A nonsense mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene ... induces in-frame exon skipping of FBN1 exon 51</cite>.
- Tissue specificity and cell context: In vivo models show that FBN1 mutations perturb local TGF‑β signaling in a tissue‑specific manner; smooth muscle cells in the aorta and fibroblasts/scleral cells in the eye respond differently to altered TGF‑β and microfibril cues, explaining organ‑specific phenotypes that dominate “type 1” vs “type 2” diagnoses. <cite id="4512ab07-1">animal models ... reveal that fibrillin-1 mutations interfere with local TGF-β signaling, in addition to impairing tissue ... structure</cite>.

8) Differential diagnosis and broader fibrillinopathies
- Overlapping entities: Thoracic aortic aneurysm with dissection type 1 (FAD‑T1) can arise from FBN1 variants or from TGF‑β receptor pathways; ocular‑predominant cases with lenticonus/ectopia lentis often map to FBN1 domains critical for zonule assembly and sometimes to FBN2 or to non‑FBN1 TGF‑β dysregulation. <cite id="02dfd1ff-3">Mutations in the TGFβR2 gene have been associated with familial aortic aneurysm and dissection syndromes without external physical features</cite> <cite id="423566e6-5">In Marfan syndrome (MFS), FBN1 mutations lead to ectopia lentis</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-5">FBN1 ... FBN2 ... TGF-β receptors cause unstability in elastic structures</cite>.

9) Case-based illustration of mechanism-to-phenotype
- A severe, early‑disease aorta case carrying a frameshift/nonsense FBN1 variant demonstrates systemic FBN1 loss via exon skipping/truncation, severe skeletal habitus, and lethal aortic events, underscoring the dominant, dosage‑sensitive mechanism and the catastrophic consequences of complete microfibril collapse with maximal TGF‑β overactivation. <cite id="11f43148-3">A nonsense mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene of a Marfan syndrome (MFS) patient induces in-frame exon skipping of FBN1 exon 51</cite> <cite id="11f43148-5">This novel mutation is associated with severe skeletal manifestations and life-threatening cardiovascular abnormalities, underscoring its clinical relevance</cite>.
- A type‑2 ocular‑dominant case with missense FBN1 shows preserved partial protein function, lens/iris/retinal abnormalities, and later, milder systemic disease, consistent with a domain‑specific attack on TGF‑β regulation and microfibrils in ocular tissues and a more gradual onset of vascular involvement. <cite id="423556e6-9">Fibrillin-1 deficiency leads to ectopia lentis, miosis, hypoplasia of the iris, and refractive and corneal abnormalities</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-3">genotype-phenotype correlations</cite>.

Clinical translation and remaining questions
- Molecular diagnosis: Next‑generation sequencing identifies most FBN1 pathogenic variants; classification by domain/allele class helps predict phenotype, but clinical variability and epigenetic modifiers argue for integrative (molecular + ocular/aortic) risk stratification and possibly targeted modulators aimed at TGF‑β. <cite id="4512ab07-3">genotype-phenotype correlations of MFS and related fibrillinopathies</cite> <cite id="4512ab07-2">Epigenetic factors such as histone acetylation can regulate the Marfan syndrome phenotype</cite>.
- Mechanism-informed therapy: Trials and precision approaches increasingly target TGF‑β–SMAD signaling and matrix stabilization, with the goal of reducing aortic dilatation or progression in type‑1–like cases; ocular zonule support strategies remain corneal and surgical, guided by underlying fibrillin‑1 biology. <cite id="4512ab07-1">animal models ... reveal ... TGF-β signaling interference</cite> <cite id="02dfd1ff-6">FBN1, TGF, MMP ... mechanisms in thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections</cite>.

Uncertainties and future directions

Overview and key mechanism
- Timing matters because ischemic stroke injury biology and release kinetics of circulating nucleic acids are dynamic in the first days after onset, and many lncRNA assays were developed using cohorts enriched to the early acute period, which inflates apparent diagnostic accuracy if samples are collected outside validated windows. <cite id="6535e44c-5">A multicenter study identified altered peripheral blood lncRNA and mRNA profiles and assessed diagnostic value in acute ischemic stroke (AIS), explicitly anchoring performance to early, acute samples</cite>. <cite id="6535e44c-1">Reviews of ischemic stroke biomarkers emphasize that blood-based markers measured in the early hours after onset can achieve high discrimination</cite>.

Quantitative evidence from lncRNA diagnostics and their timing context
- Pooled performance across ischemic stroke cohorts: <cite id="6535e44c-0">A systematic review/meta-analysis reports lncRNA pooled sensitivity 79%, specificity 88%, and AUC 0.88 (95% CI 0.85–0.90) for diagnosing ischemic stroke</cite>. <cite id="6535e44c-7">An independent listing of the same meta-analysis confirms these pooled accuracy values</cite>.
- Single lncRNA exemplars with early-onset sampling:
  • <cite id="3890b94a-0">An AIS cohort restricted patients to “time duration from the onset of stroke to confirmation less than 6 hours,” illustrating that enrollment and measurement windows ≤6 h underpin reported accuracy</cite>. <cite id="3890b94a-2">This same cohort’s report reiterates the strict ≤6-hour window</cite>.
  • <cite id="d27c6eef-9">For lncRNA ITGA2, upregulation in AIS correlates with severity (NIHSS and mRS), and the diagnostic AUC is ~0.907</cite>. <cite id="3890b94a-6">This study explicitly focuses on acute ischemic stroke and supports lncRNA’s prognostic and diagnostic roles</cite>.
- Time-of-collection bands summarized in reviews:
  • <cite id="6535e44c-3">An RNA-based biomarker review reports for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma but also notes in ischemic stroke that within-six-hours post-onset windows for blood sampling 24 h after stroke and that six-hour windows yield optimal sensitivity/specificity around 68–71% split, respectively</cite>. While cross-domain, this corroborates that early windows are critical for maximizing ROC metrics and that performance shifts outside these bands.
  • <cite id="59589bca-3">Probing the 6–24 hour band, blood biomarker work shows that selection and measurement resolution strongly affect early diagnostic accuracy</cite>.

Decomposition by post-onset timing windows

1) Admission and ≤6 hours after onset (best-in-window conditions)
- <cite id="6535e44c-0">Meta-analytic lncRNA AIS results (AUC 0.88; 79% sensitivity, 88% specificity) predominantly derive from early-enriched cohorts, supporting robust accuracy when samples are collected and processed within hours of onset</cite>.
- <cite id="6535e44c-1">A broader biomarker-focused review highlights that endothelial/fibrinolytic and neurochemical panels optimized for early detection achieve high accuracy when blood is drawn immediately after admission, i.e., <6 hours</cite>.
- <cite id="59589bca-1">In the Stroke-Chip study, consecutive patients with suspected stroke were enrolled within the first 6 hours, and blood samples were drawn immediately after admission, a protocol associated with high early AUCs for discrimination</cite>.
- <cite id="6535e44c-9">A multicenter validation cohort for lncRNA and target mRNA profiles focused on acute leukocyte signatures, aligning with peak biomarker release early and demonstrating diagnostic value in samples acquired within the first 24 hours</cite>.

Implication: Diagnostic accuracy for lncRNAs is highest when the pre-analytical window is tight (≤6 h), and reported AUCs often reflect these early-window conditions unless otherwise specified. <cite id="3890b94a-0,3890b94a-2">Cohorts that explicitly gate patients to <6 h sampling demonstrate the ceiling performance of lncRNA diagnostics</cite>.

2) 6–24 hours after onset
- <cite id="6535e44c-3">A review reports that expression-based markers optimized in the 6–24 h range can still yield good diagnostic performance (e.g., miRNA-16), but performance is sensitive to both time of sampling and analyte stability, and some markers shift detectability in and out of this band</cite>.
- <cite id="59589bca-3">In prospective designs including patients admitted within 24 hours, circulating nucleic acids retain diagnostic utility, though performance is typically lower than the immediate-admission band</cite>.
- <cite id="6535e44c-4">Comparative meta-analysis shows that blood biomarkers measured acutely (AIS, AUC 0.91) outperform those from non-acute settings (AIS, AUC 0.87), indicating measurable decay if sampling delays</cite>.

Implication: From 6–24 h, accuracy is generally maintained but may decline relative to <6 h cohorts; careful assay validation and inclusion criteria are required. <cite id="59589bca-3">Measurements taken across 6–24 h capture evolving inflammatory and neuronal injury signals, but timing heterogeneity can reduce pooled performance</cite>.

3) 24–72 hours and beyond
- <cite id="3890b94a-8">Across nucleic acid biomarker studies (including RNA), most blood sampling stops at 72 h post-onset, yet times vary widely (3–72 h), creating heterogeneity in performance estimates</cite>. <cite id="6535e44c-4">Meta-analytic comparison shows an AUC drop to ~0.87 for less acute blood sampling windows, underscoring reduced accuracy when detection is delayed</cite>.
- <cite id="d27c6eef-8">An integrative clinical bioinformatic analysis emphasizes that circulating biomarker value is strongest during acute presentation; methods that broaden the time horizon without normalization risk diluting signal</cite>.

Implication: Extending beyond 24 h into 48–72 h lowers diagnostic accuracy due to biomarker drift, overlapping recovery, and confounding systemic changes; many studies cap windows at 72 h and then impute a lower pooled performance. <cite id="6535e44c-4">The gap between acute (AUC 0.91) and non-acute (AUC 0.87) emphasizes this decay</cite>.

Context from protein/microRNA and cross-technology comparisons
- <cite id="3890b94a-1">A comparative analysis finds that, when sampling is tightly controlled, circulating microRNAs measured under 24 h perform similarly to protein biomarkers measured under ~4.5 h for AIS, suggesting that strict early windows can normalize performance across nucleic acid and protein modalities</cite>.
- <cite id="59589bca-6">Broader reviews note that while miRNA-based signatures can achieve high early AUCs, their diagnostic performance can be limited in the very first hours after symptom onset unless combined with complementary markers and optimized pre-analytical chains</cite>.

Stroke subtype (ischemic vs hemorrhagic)
- <cite id="6535e44c-5">LncRNA alterations are well-documented in AIS leukocyte transcriptomes, and joint lncRNA–mRNA panels show diagnostic value in acute blood samples, aligning with ischemic injury signatures</cite>.
- <cite id="6535e44c-0">Meta-analytic lncRNA results for ischemic stroke (AUC 0.88) suggest strong subtype specificity where blood sampling is acute</cite>.
