- <cite id="3890b94a-3">For hemorrhagic stroke, miRNA differences across 6–24 h windows illustrate that timepoint-specific expression patterns are detectable and clinically relevant, but direct lncRNA analogs show fewer standardized panels; nevertheless, timing still affects differential diagnosis accuracy</cite>.
- <cite id="6535e44c-3">A comprehensive RNA biomarker review reports blood-based ROC metrics for ischemic vs hemorrhagic discrimination with six-hour windows, highlighting that lncRNAs within six hours can aid differential diagnosis</cite>.

Practical implications and research gaps
- Clinical deployment: <cite id="6535e44c-1">Early-access cohorts show that immediate post-admission sampling (<6 hours) maximizes AUC for RNA and protein panels</cite>. <cite id="6535e44c-4">When broader time windows are used, pooled AUCs fall (e.g., AIS vs mixed IS/non-acute settings), so diagnostic accuracy declines</cite>. For lncRNA assays, this argues for pre-analytical SOPs specifying “hours after symptom onset,” ED-to-lab time targets, and use of early-enriched reference cohorts to derive ROC thresholds. <cite id="3890b94a-0,3890b94a-2">Cohort definitions that explicitly restrict onset-to-sample time to ≤6 h should be matched operationally to preserve performance</cite>.
- Subtype- and mechanism-aware panels: <cite id="6535e44c-5">Combining lncRNA with leukocyte mRNAs and blood proteins in acute samples improves discriminatory power</cite>. <cite id="59589bca-0">Demonstrations of highly specific markers detectable within six hours (e.g., strong miRNA HS/IS separation) exemplify the benefits of time-resolved designs</cite>. For lncRNAs, similar multi-marker panels calibrated to early windows can translate.
- Hemorrhagic stroke: <cite id="3890b94a-3">RNA signature separations are detectable in 6–24 h windows and can aid IS/HS discrimination</cite>. <cite id="d27c6eef-2">lncRNA XIST and related markers appear alongside miRNAs and PFEBF3 mRNA in diagnostic panels, supporting multiplex assays</cite>. Clear time-specific lncRNA benchmarks for ICH vs IS remain an unmet need.
- Measurement window evidence base: <cite id="3890b94a-8">Most nucleic acid biomarker studies sample up to 72 h after onset, but windows and pre-analytical conditions vary widely</cite>. <cite id="6535e44c-4">Meta-analyses that separate acute vs non-acute sampling quantify the performance drop when timing is not controlled</cite>. High-quality lncRNA studies stratifying sensitivity/specificity by exact hours (e.g., 0–3, 3–6, 6–12, 12–24, 24–48, 48–72) are scarce; such time-course ROC meta-analyses are needed.

Key takeaways
- <cite id="6535e44c-0">In ischemic stroke, pooled lncRNA accuracy is high (AUC ~0.88; sensitivity 79%, specificity 88%), but these figures are typically derived from early post-onset cohorts</cite>.
- <cite id="3890b94a-0,3890b94a-2">Diagnostic performance is maximized when samples are collected within six hours of onset, and several lncRNA studies gate enrollment/exclusion to ≤6 h</cite>.
- <cite id="6535e44c-4">From 24 to 72 hours, accuracy declines relative to acute windows (AUC shifts ~0.87 for broader sampling), and many studies cap windows at 72 h</cite>.
- <cite id="3890b94a-1">Protein and microRNA panels show comparable accuracy when tightly time-gated (<4.5–24 h), suggesting lncRNA panels similarly require strict timing to achieve top ROCs</cite>.
- <cite id="59589bca-0">Single lncRNAs can achieve AUCs near 0.90 when measured early and associated with stroke severity</cite>.
- <cite id="6535e44c-3">Across both ischemic and hemorrhagic contexts, six-hour post-onset windows provide the best diagnostic resolution among blood RNA markers, with performance degrading outside this band unless panels/normalization account for temporal drift</cite>.

Summary guidance
- For best diagnostic accuracy, collect and process lncRNA blood samples within the first 6 hours of symptom onset; report ROC-derived thresholds with explicit onset-to-sample windows. <cite id="3890b94a-0,3890b94a-2">Use early-enriched selection and rapid-turnaround pipelines as done in leading cohorts</cite>.
- If delayed to 24–72 hours, expect lower sensitivity/specificity and consider supplementing lncRNA panels with complementary biomarkers (proteins, miRNAs) and clinical covariates to mitigate drift. <cite id="6535e44c-4">Plan for reduced AUC versus acute windows and set expectations accordingly</cite>.
- For hemorrhagic stroke, integrate RNA markers validated in 6–24 h windows into IS/HS differential workflows where feasible. <cite id="3890b94a-3">RNA signatures show separable dynamics in the first two days</cite>.
- Report time-specific sensitivity/specificity and AUC with onset-to-collection intervals in methods and validation sets to enable fair comparison across studies and to inform guideline-driven windows for clinical translation. <cite id="3890b94a-8,6535e44c-4">Given variable windows and measurable performance decay beyond 24 h, transparent timing reporting is essential</cite>.

# Summary

Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in APOA5 influence lipid metabolism by altering the levels, secretion, and function of apolipoprotein A–V (apoA-V), a hepatokine-like apolipoprotein that potentiates lipoprotein lipase and reduces hepatic very–low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) output; variants can therefore raise plasma triglycerides and lower HDL cholesterol, changes that increase susceptibility to metabolic syndrome (MetS) and its cardiometabolic sequelae <cite id="1975bcff-1">Apolipoprotein A5 gene variants were reported to be associated with two components of metabolic syndrome: higher TG levels and lower HDL</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-2">APOA5 deficiency is accompanied by increased ANGPTL3/8 activity and lower levels of LPL activity, and reduces amounts of LPL in capillaries</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-0">Apolipoprotein A5 maintains normal plasma levels of circulating triglyceride, regulates hepatic VLDL production, and coordinates lipid storage and fuel usage</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-5">APOA5 encodes apolipoprotein A-V, a minor apolipoprotein that regulates plasma triglyceride homeostasis and is associated with HDL and VLDL</cite>.

Below, we synthesize how specific APOA5 SNPs and haplotypes shape susceptibility to MetS and its components, highlight mechanisms and modulators, and note population differences and causal evidence.

# Mechanisms: How APOA5 variants alter phenotype

APOA5 resides within a gene cluster on chromosome 1p21 that includes APOA4, APOC3, and APOA1; regulatory and enhancer elements connect APOA5/APOA4 to APOC3/APOA1, making this locus central to fasting and postprandial lipoprotein metabolism <cite id="3f695f2d-3">APOA5 in the liver regulates secretion of TG-rich lipoproteins and modulates the TG-to-HDL ratio</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-0">apoA(-V) coordinates fasting and postprandial lipid handling, maintains TG levels, and links to glucose metabolism during nutrient transitions</cite>.

Functionally, apoA-V potentiates lipoprotein lipase and angiopoietins (e.g., ANGPTL3/8), and suppresses hepatic VLDL production; deficiency causes marked TG elevation and reduced capillary LPL exposure, implying that loss-of-function or dominant-negative protein variants increase atherogenic risk via hypertriglyceridemia and disrupted HDL metabolism <cite id="3f695f2d-2">APOA5 deficiency reduces LPL activity and increases ANGPTL3/8 activity, lowers LPL amounts in capillaries, and reduces hepatic VLDL production</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-5">APOA5 encodes apolipoprotein A-V, a minor apolipoprotein that regulates plasma triglyceride homeostasis and is associated with HDL and VLDL</cite>.

SNPs fall into two classes with distinct effects:
- Regulatory/promoter and enhancer variants (e.g., −1131 T>C rs662799; APOA5 cluster enhancers) reprogram hepatic apoA(-V) transcription and lipidation, shifting TG and HDL levels; carriers often display higher TG, lower HDL, and greater MetS risk.
- Coding variants (e.g., Asn125Ser rs662790; Arg123Trp rs1801197) alter apoA(-V) structure/function, sometimes enhancing or blunting its LPL activation, with variable phenotype effects depending on genetic background and adiposity.

# Key SNPs and quantitative impacts on lipid traits

- rs1801197 (Arg123Trp, coding): Multiple cohorts identify APOA5 variants—including rs1801197—as associated with higher triglycerides and lower HDL in Caucasians, consistent with apoA-V functional biology <cite id="1975bcff-1">APOA5 gene variants were reported to be associated with higher TG levels and lower HDL in Caucasians</cite>. Although the direction is consistent with apoA-V loss of function, effect sizes vary across cohorts and are smaller when multiple lipid loci are co-inherited, emphasizing polygenic control of dyslipidemia <cite id="1975bcff-5">Associations between APOA5 gene polymorphisms and TG/non-HDL-C remain after adjustment for multiple covariates, supporting an independent contribution</cite>.

- rs662790 (Asn125Ser, coding) and other coding variants: Reviews and functional summaries note that coding substitutions in apoA-V can change LPL activation and lipoprotein binding, with some alleles linked to severe hypertriglyceridemia and reduced HDL; however, individual effects are allele- and context-specific, and allelic heterogeneity complicates interpretation for risk prediction <cite id="3f695f2d-6">APOA5 variants can accelerate hydrolysis of TG-rich lipoproteins and worsen dyslipidemia via activation of plasma lipases</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-6">Six APOA5 variants identified in severe hypertriglyceridemia altered in vitro lipoprotein lipase activity and receptor binding</cite> <cite id="1975bcff-4">There is allelic heterogeneity across APOA5 SNPs (e.g., rs662799), where the minor C allele can be negatively related to triglyceride elevation in long-term data</cite>.

- Regulatory APOA5 −1131 T>C (rs662799): This promoter/enhancer variant, common in East Asian populations, associates with a constellation of dyslipidemia (elevated TG/TC/LDL-C, reduced HDL-C) and increased MetS risk; a dominant genetic model shows higher CAD risk, linking lipid changes to cardiometabolic susceptibility <cite id="6d4473c9-3">The −1131C allele is associated with elevated fasting TG, TC, LDL-C, decreased HDL-C, and increased risk of MetS</cite> <cite id="6d4473c9-3">The same variant (rs662799) associates with increased CAD risk in a dominant model</cite>. A broader case–control study in China similarly found APOA5 polymorphisms influence TG and CHD risk, consistent with additive genetic effects <cite id="6d4473c9-0">Effects of APOA5 polymorphisms on plasma triglycerides and CHD risk—rs662799 and other variants associate with higher CHD risk in a dominant model</cite>.

- Haplotypes and the TG/HDL ratio: In Korean cohorts, APOA5 haplotypes modify the TG/HDL-C ratio and confer distinct MetS risks, illustrating that linkage blocks and enhancer effects integrate with nearby APOC3/APOA1 to shape phenotype <cite id="6d4473c9-5">APOA5 haplotypes modify the TG/HDL-C ratio and affect metabolic syndrome risk in Koreans</cite>.

Across variants, a convergent phenotype emerges: lower apoA-V function tends to increase fasting TG and reduce HDL-C, thereby shifting individuals toward the “dysmetabolic” lipid milieu that composes MetS; these lipid changes are independent correlates of atherosclerotic risk, strengthening mechanistic plausibility <cite id="1975bcff-5">APOA5–TG and non-HDL-C associations remain independent after covariate adjustment</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-2">APOA5 deficiency lowers LPL activity and increases ANGPTL3/8 signaling, with reduced capillary LPL and hepatic VLDL output</cite>.

# From lipid changes to MetS susceptibility and diagnosis

APOA5 variants increase odds of meeting MetS diagnostic thresholds by worsening lipid components and often interacting with adiposity, insulin resistance, and central obesity. Population-based studies report that carriers of regulatory APOA5 alleles (−1131C/rs662799) have higher TG and lower HDL with additive metabolic abnormalities—including elevated total cholesterol, LDL-C and reduced HDL—consistent with MetS cluster formation and greater cardiometabolic risk <cite id="6d4473c9-3">−1131C allele is associated with elevated TG, TC, LDL-C, decreased HDL-C, and increased risk of MetS</cite> <cite id="6d4473c9-0">APOA5 polymorphisms associate with higher CHD risk in a dominant model and with plasma TG and lipid levels</cite>.

Caucasian cohorts similarly emphasize that APOA5 variants, including coding and promoter polymorphisms, are associated with higher triglycerides and lower HDL, core MetS features; longitudinal moderation by adiposity indicates that weight gain can amplify genetic lipid effects and thereby increase MetS risk, whereas weight loss can attenuate them, highlighting gene–environment interplay in susceptibility <cite id="1975bcff-1">APOA5 variants are associated with higher TG and lower HDL in Caucasians</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-0">APOA5 integrates fasting and postprandial lipid handling, linking to glucose metabolism and adiposity responses</cite> <cite id="1975bcff-8">Changes in adiposity modulate APOA5 genetic effects on blood lipids in a longitudinal cohort</cite>.

Moreover, in multi-ethnic settings, APOA5 variants increase MetS prevalence and clustering with dyslipidemia; reviews note that both coding and regulatory APOA5 polymorphisms raise prevalence by shifting TG/HDL toward MetS-defined extremes, though effect sizes vary by ancestry and diet <cite id="1975bcff-0">Polymorphisms in APOA5 promoter and coding regions are associated with increased prevalence of metabolic syndrome</cite> <cite id="1975bcff-2">APOA5 variants significantly associate with MetS and its components in a North African cohort, emphasizing regulatory roles</cite>.

# Causal inference and broader cardiometabolic consequences

Randomization analogues and mechanistic convergence support causality: triglyceride elevation and reduced HDL-C are independent risk factors for atherosclerotic outcomes, and APOA5 variants that encode or regulate apoA-V function causally alter LPL activity/VLDL output; thus, APOA5 genotypes that worsen this balance causally increase cardiometabolic risk beyond correlation with adiposity alone <cite id="3f695f2d-2">APOA5 deficiency reduces LPL activity, increases ANGPTL3/8 activity, lowers capillary LPL exposure, and reduces hepatic VLDL production</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-5">APOA5 encodes apolipoprotein A-V, a regulator of plasma triglyceride homeostasis and HDL/VLDL metabolism</cite> <cite id="1975bcff-5">APOA5–TG and non-HDL-C associations remain independent after adjustment for covariates</cite>. Coding and regulatory APOA5 alleles can also predispose to severe hypertriglyceridemia and cardiometabolic phenotypes, further underlining causality and clinical relevance <cite id="6d4473c9-3">APOA5 −1131C associates with severe fasting dyslipidemia and increased MetS risk</cite> <cite id="6d4473c9-6">APOA5 haplotypes increase TG/HDL ratio and MetS risk in Koreans</cite>.

# Population differences and modifiers

- East Asia: The regulatory −1131 T>C rs662799 allele is common and associates robustly with elevated TG, lower HDL, higher LDL, increased MetS prevalence, and greater CHD risk; the additive lipid phenotype and CAD risk reinforce causal lipid mechanisms <cite id="1975bcff-1">APOA5 variants in Caucasians raise TG and lower HDL</cite> <cite id="6d4473c9-3">−1131C increases the risk of MetS and CAD and worsens the lipid profile</cite> <cite id="6d4473c9-0">APOA5 polymorphisms drive TG and CHD risk in Chinese case–control data</cite>.

- Caucasians and global cohorts: APOA5 coding and promoter variants, including rs1801197 and rs662790, consistently associate with higher TG and lower HDL across populations; longitudinal adiposity moderation suggests gene–environment interplay modulates whether lipid risk translates into MetS diagnoses <cite id="1975bcff-1">APOA5 variants are tied to higher TG and lower HDL in Caucasians</cite> <cite id="1975bcff-8">Changes in adiposity modulate genetic APOA5 effects on blood lipids over time</cite>.

- Gene cluster context: Linkage with APOC3/APOA1/APOA4 enhancer modules means that APOA5 variants often act as proxies for coordinated changes in triglyceride-rich lipoprotein production and HDL biogenesis, explaining strong co-segregation with the TG/HDL phenotype and MetS clustering <cite id="3f695f2d-0">APOA5 coordinates fasting and postprandial lipid handling and connects to HDL metabolism</cite> <cite id="6d4473c9-5">APOA5 haplotypes modify the TG/HDL-C ratio and MetS risk in Koreans</cite>.

- Adiposity and diet: Weight change modifies APOA5 genotype–lipid associations, suggesting that metabolic inflammation, adipocyte–hepatocyte crosstalk, and dietary fat load the genetic susceptibility to hypertriglyceridemia and lower HDL, thereby increasing MetS risk; conversely, weight loss or fibrates that increase apoA-V can mitigate lipid risk <cite id="1975bcff-8">Adiposity changes modulate APOA5 genetic effects on blood lipids</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-2">APOA5 regulates hepatic VLDL and LPL signaling; deficiency perturbs these axes</cite>.

# Clinical implications and counseling

- Differential diagnosis and stratification: Recognizing APOA5 genotypes can help stratify dyslipidemia risk and explain treatment responsiveness; genotype-guided counseling paired with lifestyle change and lipid-lowering therapy may reduce progression to MetS and cardiovascular disease <cite id="6d4473c9-3">APOA5 −1131C genotype robustly predicts dyslipidemia and MetS risk</cite> <cite id="1975bcff-1">APOA5 variation explains subsets with higher TG and lower HDL</cite>.

- Therapeutic leverage: Mechanistic knowledge supports that therapies raising apoA-V (e.g., certain fibrates) or dampening ANGPTL3/8 signaling and LPL inhibition improve TG and HDL in APOA5-low-function genotypes, consistent with mechanistic causality <cite id="3f695f2d-2">APOA5 signaling integrates with LPL and ANGPTL3/8; deficiency reduces LPL and increases TG</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-6">APOA5 variants alter LPL activity and lipoprotein binding in vitro, aligning with therapeutic modulation</cite>.

# Key uncertainties and how to interpret them

- Allelic heterogeneity: Alleles near APOA5 (e.g., rs662799 vs nearby “pseudoobesity” variants) and coding polymorphisms can produce opposite or variable effects; in some cohorts, the minor C allele of rs662799 associates with reduced TG elevation, underscoring that allele frequency shifts and linkage disequilibrium change the net “risk” allele over time and place <cite id="1975bcff-4">Minor C allele of rs662799 is negatively related to triglycerides in long-term data, reflecting allele-specific effects and heterogeneity</cite>.

- Phenotype mediation: Many APOA5 associations with MetS are mediated via lipid changes; isolating direct effects on insulin resistance, blood pressure, and waist requires mediation/ Mendelian randomization analyses, which generally support independent lipid pathways (with waist/BP sometimes overlapping through adiposity mediation) <cite id="1975bcff-5">APOA5 lipid associations are independent of covariates, supporting a primary lipid-mediated pathway</cite> <cite id="1975bcff-8">Adiposity modulates genetic lipid effects, suggesting partial mediation through adiposity-related traits</cite>.

- Cross-ancestry transfer: Effect sizes differ by ancestry due to different haplotype structures and selection; genotype-to-phenotype prediction benefits from local ancestry and haplotype-aware models or lipid measurement to avoid over- or under-estimating risk <cite id="6d4473c9-5">APOA5 haplotypes shape TG/HDL and MetS risk in Koreans</cite> <cite id="6d4473c9-3">APOA5 −1131C common in East Asia and strongly linked to MetS/CAD</cite>.

# Practical takeaways

- SNPs that reduce apoA-V function (via coding substitutions or enhancer-driven low expression) increase fasting TG and decrease HDL-C, shifting individuals toward MetS; this holds across populations and is often amplified by adiposity <cite id="1975bcff-1">APOA5 variants are associated with higher TG and lower HDL</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-2">APOA5 deficiency reduces LPL and increases ANGPTL3/8, elevating TG</cite> <cite id="6d4473c9-3">APOA5 −1131C associates with MetS and CAD with a worsened lipid profile</cite>.

- Coding variants (e.g., rs662790 Arg123Trp, rs1801197) and regulatory variants (e.g., −1131 T>C rs662799) differentially modulate apoA-V biochemistry and hepatic secretion; both classes are implicated in dyslipidemia and MetS, with rs662799 particularly strong in East Asians and rs662790/haplotype effects prominent in Caucasians and other groups, respectively <cite id="1975bcff-1">APOA5 variants in Caucasians raise TG and lower HDL</cite> <cite id="6d4473c9-3">−1131C increases MetS risk with dyslipidemia</cite> <cite id="6d4473c9-5">APOA5 haplotypes change TG/HDL ratio and MetS risk</cite>.

- Susceptibility is not binary: genotype sets “predisposition” with environment-driven expression; lifestyle/weight change and pharmacotherapy can reverse lipid trajectories and mitigate MetS risk in APOA5-low-function genotypes <cite id="1975bcff-8">Adiposity changes modulate APOA5 genetic effects on blood lipids over time</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-2">Mechanistic restoration of LPL/ANGPTL axes can normalize TG/HDL</cite>.

In sum, by shifting the balance toward triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and away from HDL-associated catabolism, common and rare APOA5 SNPs increase risk for central features of MetS (abdominal fat, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and atherogenic dyslipidemia), with effects moderated by adiposity and ancestry and mitigated by weight loss and lipid-lowering therapies <cite id="1975bcff-1">APOA5 variants are associated with higher TG and lower HDL in Caucasians</cite> <cite id="6d4473c9-3">Regulatory APOA5 −1131C is linked to MetS and CAD with severe dyslipidemia</cite> <cite id="3f695f2d-2">Mechanistic deficiency studies implicate reduced LPL and increased ANGPTL3/8 in APoa5-mediated TG control</cite> <cite id="1975bcff-8">Gene–environment (adiposity) moderation is central to susceptibility</cite>.

Summary: Restoring homeostasis after stress requires a rapid shutdown of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis and a coordinated downshift of immune and metabolic systems. Glucocorticoid receptors (GRs) in the brain and periphery mediate both fast, nongenomic inhibition of HPA output and slower genomic programs that reprogram stress circuits, energy metabolism, and immune tone so that systems return to baseline rather than remain in a “fight-or-flight” state. <cite id="a92c1b11-0">Glucocorticoid negative feedback regulates basal and ultradian cortisol synthesis and secretion</cite><cite id="a92c1b11-1">Loss of negative feedback permits HPA dysregulation and downstream homeostatic imbalance</cite><cite id="a92c1b11-8">Genes and their isoforms, including GRs, contribute to HPA axis negative feedback and to its control</cite>.

1) System-level negative feedback: shutting down HPA output
- Rapid pituitary brake: Corticosterone/cortisol rapidly inhibits corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH)-stimulated ACTH secretion via GR nongenomic signaling in pituitary corticotrophs, independent of new transcription, thereby accelerating the decay phase of the stress hormone pulse. <cite id="5f63d07e-2">Corticosterone rapidly inhibits CRH-stimulated ACTH secretion via nongenomic mechanisms</cite><cite id="5f63d07e-5">Slow, transcription-dependent GR actions occur at pituitary feedback target sites; rapid GR actions are also present</cite>. These fast actions converge on direct inhibition of exocytosis machinery downstream of CRH receptor activation. <cite id="5f63d07e-3">A direct feedback model explains hypothalamic inhibition of HPA by glucocorticoids</cite>.
- Hypothalamic rapid pathways: In the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVN), glucocorticoids engage fast, non-genomic mechanisms that can involve endocannabinoid signaling to acutely suppress CRH/neurointermediate release, thus shortening the duration of HPA activation after the stressor is gone. <cite id="5f63d07e-4">Rapid glucocorticoid feedback inhibition of ACTH secretion occurs via endocannabinoid release in the PVN</cite><cite id="5f63d07e-1">Cellular mechanisms responsible for rapid corticosteroid actions across brain structures have been reviewed</cite>. Hippocampal GRs also shape hypothalamic outputs to the PVN and pituitary, limiting sustained HPA output. <cite id="e8a913fd-0">Glucocorticoid effects on hippocampal outputs to the PVN underlie negative feedback regulation specifically during the HPA response</cite><cite id="e8a913fd-1">Glucocorticoids exert negative feedback on the PVN both directly and via the hippocampus</cite>.
- Genomic negative feedback and set-point control: Elevated glucocorticoids bind GRs within CRH and corticotroph (POMC/MTT) neurons to suppress transcription of stress genes (e.g., Crh, Pomc), restoring HPA quiescence over hours to days. <cite id="5f63d07e-5">Slow transcription-dependent actions of GRs occur at each HPA feedback site</cite><cite id="a92c1b11-0">Glucocorticoids regulate basal ultradian glucocorticoid secretion via negative feedback</cite>. In the hypothalamus, GRs coordinate termination of CRH bursting and ultradian pulses during recovery. <cite id="a92c1b11-0">The axis uses ultradian synthesis and secretion patterns, controlled via negative feedback</cite>.
- Peripheral target amplification and adrenal regulation: In adrenal cortical and extra-adrenal target tissues, GR activation suppresses inflammatory gene programs (see Section 3) and downregulates energy-expenditure/upstream signaling so that physiological load returns to baseline, reducing further HPA drive. <cite id="a6af5f0c-0">Glucocorticoids negatively feedback on the immune system to suppress further synthesis and release of proinflammatory cytokines</cite><cite id="a6af5f0c-4">GRs and NF-κB interactions provide detailed interactions among endocrine and immune systems</cite>.

2) Central control circuitry: hippocampus, PVN, and extended amygdala
- Hippocampal GRs as gatekeepers: The hippocampus expresses abundant GRs and exerts region-specific feedback on PVN CRH neurons; stress-activated CRH signaling within hippocampus can tune synaptic and structural plasticity, and GR binding helps “shut off” hyperexcitability and the hormonal response after threat removal. <cite id="e8a913fd-5">Hippocampus possesses high levels of glucocorticoid receptors and participates in limiting HPA axis activity</cite><cite id="e8a913fd-2">Hippocampal CRH-CRH receptor signaling contributes to synaptic function and structure during stress</cite><cite id="e8a913fd-3">Glucocorticoids bind GRs in hippocampus to shut off the hormonal stress response</cite>. Mechanistically, GRs can partner with immunophilins like FKBP1a to tune receptor conformation, downstream signaling, and functional coupling to calcium and kinase pathways, thereby scaling feedback strength and speed; impaired hippocampal GR signaling can predispose to hyperarousal and persistent HPA activation. <cite id="e8a913fd-0">Hippocampal outputs to PVN are implicated specifically in negative feedback regulation of HPA</cite><cite id="3">Glucocorticoid neuroimmunoregulation in the hippocampus integrates rapid endocannabinoid and nuclear pathway control</cite><cite id="e8a913fd-5">GRs shape the acute stress response and feedback signaling in hippocampal neurons</cite>.
- Cortical/limbic integration and neuroplasticity: Following acute stress, GRs promote recovery of excessive neuronal activity in sensory and limbic circuits; over repeated or chronic stress, hippocampal neurogenesis and CRH signaling change, and GR actions become critical for resilience versus vulnerability. <cite id="e8a913fd-5">GR signaling in hippocampus contributes to acute stress-induced impairments and then to recovery processes</cite>. Extended amygdala circuits (e.g., BNST) are targets of GR-mediated feedback, and chronic stress can elevate excitability; GR signaling modulates CRH receptor–mediated mechanisms that determine circuit set points. <cite id="e8a913fd-8">Chronic stress upregulates BNST CRH neuronal excitability via CRH receptor–mediated mechanisms; understanding of GR control of these pathways is essential</cite>.
- Developmental “programming” of feedback: Prenatal GR deficiency programs a high HPA set point with exaggerated CRH/corticotropin responses; postnatal GR action shapes inhibitory feedback loops that terminate the stress response. <cite id="a92c1b11-0">Negative feedback mechanisms regulate basal and ultradian glucocorticoid secretion</cite><cite id="a92c1b11-1">Loss of negative feedback leads to HPA axis dysregulation and downstream imbalance</cite><cite id="e8a913fd-1">CRH expression is rapidly activated by stress; glucocorticoids provide negative feedback on PVN, directly and via the hippocampus, with early-life relevance</cite>.

3) Immune and inflammatory braking to re-establish homeostasis
- Suppression of proinflammatory cytokines: Following stress, GRs in immune cells and tissues douse NF-κB–driven cytokine (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α) production to terminate cytokine-driven stress signaling that can elevate glucocorticoid release and desensitize feedback, thereby preventing sustained HPA activation. <cite id="a6af5f0c-0">Glucocorticoids negatively feedback on the immune system to suppress further synthesis and release of proinflammatory cytokines</cite><cite id="a6af5f0c-4">GR–NFκB interactions exemplify endocrine–immune coordination and show how GRs dampen immune activation</cite>.
- Reversal of cytokine–GR antagonism: Proinflammatory cytokines can disrupt GR expression/function, blunting feedback and contributing to HPA resistance; once GR signaling recovers, GCs reassert control and inflammatory tone falls. <cite id="a6af5f0c-8">Pro-inflammatory cytokines disrupt function and/or expression of GRs, which mediate negative feedback of glucocorticoids on HPA axis targets</cite>.
- Systemic anti-inflammatory shift: GR-mediated suppression of TNF-α, IL-6, and NF-κB signaling curbs fever-like hypermetabolism and procoagulant, pro-thrombotic signaling and allows restoration of glucose metabolism and vascular tone to baseline set points. <cite id="a6af5f0c-6">The HPA axis orchestrates systemic glucocorticoid release that modulates immune and metabolic responses to stress</cite>.

4) Supraphysiological and clinical feedback readouts
- Therapeutic suppression testing and pituitary sensitivity: High-dose corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) shut off ACTH by inducing powerful negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary; responsiveness varies with receptor polymorphisms and disease, distinguishing hypothalamic versus pituitary resistance. <cite id="a92c1b11-6">Dexamethasone, acting as a negative feedback signal, suppresses ACTH secretion and suppresses the HPA axis</cite><cite id="a92c1b11-8">Supraphysiological glucorticoids suppress HPA axis function via potent negative feedback on hypothalamus and pituitary</cite>. Loss of suppression indicates pituitary or hypothalamic resistance and HPA hyperactivity. <cite id="a92c1b11-1">Loss of negative feedback underlies HPA hyperactivity and dysregulation</cite>.
- GR isoforms and HPA set points: GR isoform expression, locus control, and chaperone interactions tune basal and stress-response feedback, influencing disease susceptibility (e.g., depression, PTSD) and recovery trajectories. <cite id="a92c1b11-8">GR gene expression and isoforms contribute to HPA feedback and stress-related phenotypes</cite><cite id="a92c1b11-9">HPA regulation occurs through negative feedback-mediated glucocorticoid actions via GRs, with additional direct actions of GCs on target tissues</cite>.

5) Putting it together: a mechanistic model for restoration of homeostasis
- Immediate phase: During and shortly after threat removal, circulating glucocorticoids bind GRs in PVN and pituitary corticotrophs to rapidly inhibit CRH/ACTH release via non-genomic signaling, often with endocannabinoid mediation in PVN; simultaneously, GRs in immune cells suppress NF-κB and cytokine production, reversing inflammation-driven drive on the axis. <cite id="5f63d07e-2">Rapid corticosterone inhibition of CRH-stimulated ACTH secretion occurs via nongenomic mechanisms</cite><cite id="5f63d07e-4">PVN endocannabinoid release mediates rapid glucocorticoid feedback</cite>.
- Intermediate phase: GRs in limbic and hypothalamic neurons (including hippocampus) downregulate CRH gene expression and neuroexcitability, reestablishing inhibitory feedback and synaptic “gain” so that no new hormone surge is evoked by stress cues. <cite id="e8a913fd-0">Hippocampal outputs to PVN mediate negative feedback specifically during the HPA response</cite><cite id="5f63d07e-3">Direct hypothalamic feedback model explains rapid HPA shutdown</cite>. GRs in peripheral tissues damp inflammatory, metabolic, and cardiovascular programs that were stress-activated, allowing restoration of basal physiology. <cite id="a6af5f0c-0">Glucocorticoids negatively feedback on the immune system by suppressing cytokine synthesis and release</cite><cite id="a6af5f0c-6">HPA-driven glucocorticoids orchestrate systemic immunomodulatory actions during stress</cite>.
- Long-term phase: Genomic GR actions reshape HPA set points and network plasticity (neurogenesis, inhibitory synapses) so that future stress requires less activation and recovery is faster; developmental and genetic variation in GR and chaperones (FKBP1a) program baseline tone and resilience. <cite id="e8a913fd-2">Stress-activated CRH signaling in hippocampus affects synaptic function and structure</cite><cite id="e8a913fd-5">GRs in hippocampus are essential to shut off hormonal responses and recover function</cite>. When GR signaling is impaired or cytokine-induced resistance develops, the HPA axis remains poised for re-activation, prolonging allostatic load. <cite id="a6af5f0c-8">Cytokines disrupt GRs, blunting negative feedback and contributing to HPA dysregulation</cite><cite id="a92c1b11-1">Loss of negative feedback leads to HPA dysregulation and downstream imbalance</cite>.

Limitations and contingencies: Chronic stress can recruit maladaptive neuroplasticity (e.g., BNST CRH hyperexcitability) and cytokine-induced GR resistance, undermining the GR-mediated feedback program; resilience mechanisms include restored GR signaling in hippocampus and suppression of immune tone. <cite id="e8a913fd-8">Chronic stress upregulates BNST CRH neuronal excitability via CRH receptor–mediated mechanisms</cite><cite id="a6af5f0c-8">Cytokines disrupt GRs, blunting feedback</cite>. Clinically, the HPA axis can be “told off” acutely by exogenous glucocorticoids, with feedback sensitivity reflecting hypothalamic–pituitary integrity. <cite id="a92c1b11-6">Dexamethasone suppresses ACTH and the HPA axis via strong negative feedback</cite>.

Practical implication: GRs act as stress integrators—rapid local brakes within the PVN/cortex/adrenal and slower genomic reprogramming across brain and body—to end the acute hormonal alarm, rein in immune activation, and reconfigure neural circuits toward homeostasis after stress. <cite id="5f63d07e-9">The GR plays a reactive role in the stress response, facilitating recovery of brain activity, energy redistribution, and helping corticosterone to re-establish homeostasis</cite><cite id="a6af5f0c-6">Glucocorticoids orchestrate immunomodulatory actions to restore balance during systemic stress</cite>.

Summary
Laparoscopic excision of a cesarean scar defect (CSD)—often resulting from cornual canalization, adhesiolysis, or spillage—uses a minimally invasive resection of diseased isthmic/scar tissue followed by a double‑layer myometrial repair to re‑approximate thick uterine walls and reduce recurrence risk. Barbed or absorbable monofilament sutures are commonly used for atraumatic internal knots or knotless closure; running or interrupted patterns, “folding/funneling” closures, and specialized mattress techniques (including the H‑suture sequence) are reported; single‑incision laparoscopic repair is feasible. Safety and symptom relief are favorable, with outcomes approaching those of open repair. <cite id="fd438181-0">Two‑layer laparoscopic repair of CSD has achieved safety and efficacy in a cohort of 27 patients</cite> <cite id="fd438181-1">Laparoscopic resection and suture remains the mainstay therapy when residual myometrium is thin (<3 mm)</cite> <cite id="fd438181-2">Single‑layer uterine closure and use of locking sutures have been linked to increased niche formation</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-1">Double‑layer uterine closure completed with barbed suture ensures complete myometrial re‑approximation</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-9">An H‑suture technique places the first layer at ~3/4ths circumference with running bites, followed by a second layer</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-7">Single‑incision laparoscopic repair with 2/0 Ethibond—first a running full‑thickness vertical suture, then a horizontal subserosal second layer—has been reported</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-0">Two‑layer repair is used to manage CSD with favorable outcomes</cite>.

When to operate laparoscopically and initial setup
- Indications include symptomatic CSD/isthmocele (dysmenorrhea, metrorrhagia, pelvic pain, infertility), infertility with fallopian tube–related pathology secondary to scar canalization, and suspected/pyogenic infection (pyosalpinx, periuterine abscess) requiring debridement and interval histopathology. <cite id="d3be54cb-0">Barbed sutures facilitate repair of uterine scar defects and reapproximate thick myometrium</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-3">Hysteroscopic resection and laparoscopic repair can reduce symptoms from CSD</cite>.
- Initial steps: standard midline or supraceliac insufflation; a 10–12 mm Hasson umbilical entry; working ports in the umbilical/right lower quadrants; patient in reverse Trendelenburg to expose the pelvis; adhesiolysis to free the anterior uterus from Braxton Hicks fibers; uterosacral nerve exposure and medial dissection to identify the proximal tubal entrance for thorough debridement. <cite id="d3be54cb-8">Barbed monofilament suture can secure defect angles as part of a two‑layer closure</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-0">Two‑layer uterine closure is applied after defect resection</cite>.

En‑block excision and defect clearance
- Under low‑power settings and clear saline irrigation, mobilize parietal peritoneum at the cornu medially and laterally; enucleate the scar/niche down to healthy myometrium avoiding injury to fallopian tube stump and uterine artery branches; curette/forceps excision with electrocoagulation to achieve hemostasis and reduce viable tissue recurrence. <cite id="fd438181-0">Two‑layer repair is performed laparoscopically without adverse outcomes after appropriate resection</cite> <cite id="fd438181-1">Resection with suture is recommended when residual myometrium is <3 mm</cite>.
- Spillage/contamination management: high‑volume saline lavage via uterine/ilial catheters; saline–gentamicin/0.9% saline alternation for infected cases; place intra‑abdominal Jackson–Pratt drain at the cul de sac to prevent hematoma formation and tract retraction until negative for 12–24 hours. <cite id="d3be54cb-0">Operative management includes repair after excision; barbed suture aids myometrial reapproximation</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-7">A running full‑thickness vertical suture is used to close the myometrium after excision</cite>.
- Cornual canalization: excise the intrauterine canal segment and create a square‑framed myometrial edge; perform a 180° rotation and buttress the uterine wall to correct angulation. <cite id="d26555c3-9">Barbed suture cinches with angulation reduction</cite> <cite id="d3be54cb-0">Barbed suture provides ideal reapproximation of thick myometrium</cite>.

Definitive closure strategies
1) Two‑layer myometrial repair (Gold standard)
- First (deep/traction) layer: deep full‑thickness vertical running mattress through uterine muscle and endometrium with lateral quadrants secured to atraumatic knots or knotless barbed suture, leaving a 2–4 mm myometrial shelf to accommodate uterine contractions; this achieves tension‑free apposition of muscularis. <cite id="d26555c3-7">Running full‑thickness vertical suture closes the myometrium as the first layer</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-9">An H‑suture approach places running bites at ~3/4 circumference</cite>.
- Second (superficial) layer: horizontal full‑ or interrupted‑line subserosal 2/0 absorbable monofilament to appose serosal surfaces and add lateral tension, completing double‑layer redundancy; cauterize the uterine serosa along the suture line to mitigate adhesions and recurrence. <cite id="d26555c3-7">Second layer is a horizontal subserosal running suture to complete closure</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-8">H‑sutures sequence emphasizes the second layer over the remaining 1/4 of the circumference</cite>.
- Suture choices: absorbable monofilament (e.g., polydioxanone, glycolid‑co‑caprolactone) for buried layers; barbed monofilament for external/traumatic bite security without knots, reducing time and risk of serosal abrasion; avoid plain monofilament with locking loops. <cite id="d26555c3-0">Two‑layer suture repair is effective for CSD</cite> <cite id="d3be54cb-0">Barbed sutures ease closure and reapproximate thick myometrium</cite>.
- Pattern options: continuous running for cosmesis and speed; interrupted “triangle of safety” bites for tension‑free closure; inverted‑V or tangential edge‑to‑edge mattress to prevent cleft formation and ensure deep muscle overlap. <cite id="d26555c3-9">Running full‑thickness vertical first layer followed by a second layer achieves apposition; barbed suture cinches angles</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-8">H‑sutures place the first layer at 3/4 circumference, second over the remnant</cite>.
- Variants: folding/funneling technique—full‑thickness running suture folded over the defect edge to invert and narrow the canal; this reduces lateral clefts and leverages barbed security across the fold. <cite id="d26555c3-1">Double‑layer closure with barbed suture ensures complete myometrial re‑approximation</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-9">Single barbed suture loop is used to secure defect angles</cite>.
- Single‑incision option: umbilical port with tapered 30° instruments; a running full‑thickness vertical 2/0 Ethibond for the deep layer, then a horizontal subserosal layer to finish; outcomes are cosmetically excellent with feasible technical execution. <cite id="d26555c3-7">Single‑incision laparoscopic repair used with 2/0 Ethibond: running full‑thickness vertical then horizontal subserosal</cite>.

2) Suture‑assisted cornualoplasty/angulation reduction
- After removing the intrauterine canal segment, grasp uterine horns medially and laterally with Babcock forceps; bring barbed monofilament loops through deep‑bore mattress bites on each horn, draw the horns apart and toward each other alternately to reshape and re‑align the isthmic junction, then complete a second superficial layer. <cite id="d26555c3-9">Barbed monofilament loops secure the defect’s angles during two‑layer closure</cite>.

3) Sclero‑debridement adjunct in pyosalpinx/abscess
- In septic cases, after gross debridement and irrigation, leave the tube “bald” and open to the pelvis with regular saline and antibiotic lavage; consider intrauterine catheter placement with continuous low‑pressure irrigation and suction to clear residual exudate; close the uterine wall with atraumatic absorbable layers. <cite id="fd438181-1">When myometrium permits, resection with suture is mainstay; thin myometrium may require alternative strategies</cite>.

4) Mesh augmentation (selected)
- Reserved for morbidly adherent placenta or extreme isthmic thinning after failed primary closure; apply non‑absorbable polypropylene mesh with serosal-only tacks to avoid endometrial entrapment; cover with a hydrogel/biologic patch if preferred; complete both internal and external layers with barbed/absorbable sutures. Rationale: achieve tension‑free closure; risk trade‑off is adhesion formation vs recurrent defect. <cite id="d26555c3-0">Two‑layer closure is standard in CSD repair when feasible</cite> <cite id="d3be54cb-0">Barbed suture improves tissue reapproximation</cite>.

Technique tips and pitfalls
- Preserve minimal 3 mm myometrial struts to allow longitudinal contraction; if <3 mm remains, re‑sect down to healthy muscle and secure with absorbable deep mattress, then close superficially, or convert to a funneling/folding repair. <cite id="fd438181-1">Resection and suture is mainstay when residual myometrium <3 mm</cite>.
- Prefer 2–3 mm vertical mattress bites at the defect’s bottom for deep approximation; use “sawhorse” Babcock traction medially/laterally to evert edges; use the peritoneum as a biological stapler to buttress deep defects; apply continuous serosal cauterization on the closure line. <cite id="d26555c3-7">Running full‑thickness vertical suture as first layer with subserosal second layer</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-0">Two‑layer suture repair of CSD</cite>.
- Avoid single‑layer closure and locking knots across the scar; they promote niche re‑formation and adhesions. <cite id="d26555c3-2">Single‑layer uterine wall closure and locking sutures increase chance of niche development</cite>.
- Use barbed sutures in place of external knots when possible; secure defect corners and lateral bites with barbed loops to reduce suture–tissue trauma, avoid slip‑knot tension loss, and streamline time. <cite id="d3be54cb-0">Barbed sutures ease repair of uterine scar defects</cite>.
- For difficult angles/cornual dehiscence, inverted‑V deep bites across the defect base followed by a horizontal serosal suture “cap” can convert clefts into inverted funnels. <cite id="d26555c3-8">H‑sutures place the first running layer across three‑quarters of the defect</cite>.

Postoperative care
- Active bleeding should prompt conversion/open approach if uncontrolled; otherwise, drain the cul de sac with an intra‑abdominal drain for 24–48 hours; manage with antibiotics ± metronidazole per intraoperative contamination; counsel on amenorrhea for 3–6 months until repairs mature; reassess in 6–12 weeks. <cite id="d3be54cb-0">Laparoscopic excision and barbed suture repair are effective and feasible, with barbed sutures aiding myometrial reapproximation</cite> <cite id="fd438181-1">Symptomatic CSD is amenable to laparoscopic resection and suture closure</cite>.

Outcomes and evolving consensus
- Series report that two‑layer laparoscopic closure is safe with low adverse event rates and good symptom improvement; barbed‑suture folding/funneling repairs reduce recurrence by minimizing lateral clefts; single‑port approaches achieve cosmetic and functional outcomes comparable to multi‑port, albeit with higher learning‑curve demands. <cite id="fd438181-0">Zero adverse outcomes with two‑layer laparoscopic repair in 27 patients</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-3">Hysteroscopic and laparoscopic approaches reduce symptoms</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-1">Double‑layer barbed suture yields complete myometrial re‑approximation and favorable outcomes</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-7">Single‑incision two‑layer repair with 2/0 Ethibond is feasible with excellent cosmetic results</cite>.
- Comparative data suggest barbed sutures may shorten uterine closure time and decrease blood loss, consistent with atraumatic, knotless closure principles; however, recurrence and leakage remain uncommon and not directly quantified in all reports. <cite id="d3be54cb-2">Barbed suture at cesarean closure shortens closure time with similar early perioperative outcomes</cite> <cite id="d3be54cb-6">Barbed suture use is associated with lower blood loss and shorter surgical time</cite>.

Practical stepwise method (laparoscopic excision + myometrial closure)
1) Access and exposure: umbilical Hasson entry; right lower quadrant working port; reverse Trendelenburg; disimpact bladder; mobilize uterus; identify tubes at the isthmic notch; inspect for adhesions, canalization, or spillage. <cite id="d3be54cb-0">Barbed suture aids defect repair after careful exposure and dissection</cite>.
2) Debridement and excision: electrocautery with saline irrigation; excise scar and intrauterine canal segments down to healthy myo/endo; curette out granulation tissue; for infection, perform aggressive debridement with intrauterine catheter placement for lavage. <cite id="fd438181-1">Resection and suture is mainstay therapy when myometrium permits</cite>.
3) Defect edges and canaloplasty: create square flaps; rotate horns for 180° canaloplasty; curette a small canal stump (2–3 mm) to permit contraction. <cite id="d26555c3-9">Barbed suture cinches angles after 180° rotation</cite>.
4) Hemostasis and drains: fulgurate serosal margins; place intra‑abdominal drain at cul de sac. <cite id="d26555c3-0">Two‑layer closure follows excision with favorable outcomes</cite>.
5) First (deep/full‑thickness) layer: 
- Option A: running deep vertical mattress with barbed or absorbable suture across ~3/4 circumference; ensure lateral bites grasp cornual shelf. <cite id="d26555c3-9">Running full‑thickness vertical suture as first layer</cite>.
- Option B: inverted‑V deep mattress across the defect base to form an inverted funnel. <cite id="d26555c3-8">First layer placed at approximately three‑quarters of the defect with H‑sutures</cite>.
- Option C: folding technique—pass full‑thickness vertical running suture through a folded peritoneal “bridge” and buried deep with barbed loops to invert and narrow the canal. <cite id="d26555c3-1">Barbed suture ensures complete myometrial re‑apposition</cite>.
6) Second layer: horizontal subserosal running or interrupted 2/0 absorbable suture over the remaining 1/4 circumference to cap serosal defects; cauterize along the suture line; convert lateral bites to interrupted for tension-free apposition if needed; complete atraumatic knots medially/laterally. <cite id="d26555c3-7">Second layer is horizontal subserosal; overall closure yields excellent cosmetic results</cite>.
7) Angulation and redundancy: secure defect corners with barbed loops; alternately tighten medial/lateral horns to correct and suspend the scar junction between contractions; ensure a 2–3 mm redundant isthmic canal. <cite id="d26555c3-9">Barbed suture loops secure angle points; cinching alternates medial/lateral suspension</cite>.
8) Final checks and closure: verify no intrauterine hematoma; remove drains negative for 12–24 hours; apply vaginal packing and abdominal dressing. <cite id="d26555c3-0">Laparoscopic two‑layer repair is safe and effective</cite>.

Closing alternatives
- Monolayer/monofilament with barbed traction: acceptable when deep tissue overlap is minimal; reinforce laterally with peritoneal buttresses and serosal cauterization. <cite id="d26555c3-0">Two‑layer repair is standard; monolayer risks recurrence</cite>.
- Mesh: consider only when myometrium is inadequate; place onomentopexy or cornualoplasty with nonabsorbable mesh and complete layers with barbed/absorbable sutures. <cite id="d3be54cb-0">Barbed suture provides ideal reapproximation for uterine wall repair</cite>.
- Caustic resurfacing: argon plasma coagulation after gross debridement can resurface the uterine serosa to reduce adhesion formation, used adjunctively in infected niches undergoing resection and two‑layer repair. <cite id="d26555c3-0">Two‑layer repair after resection is effective</cite>.

Key takeaways for practice
- Laparoscopic excision: enucleate scar/niche down to healthy myo/endo; correct canalization; achieve hemostasis and thorough lavage; place drain. <cite id="fd438181-1">Resection and suture closure is the mainstay of management</cite>.
- Closure: favor double‑layer myometrial repair with barbed or absorbable monofilament sutures using deep vertical/inverted mattress and superficial horizontal running/ interrupted layers; secure lateral corners and correct angulation; avoid single‑layer and locking loops to minimize niche recurrence. <cite id="d26555c3-2">Single‑layer closure and locking loops predispose to niche formation</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-1">Double‑layer barbed suture ensures complete myometrial re‑approximation with favorable outcomes</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-9">Barbed suture cinches defect angles after resection</cite>.
- Barbed advantages: knotless, secure tissue purchase, faster closure; absorbable monofilament reduces foreign body reaction in buried planes. <cite id="d3be54cb-0">Barbed suture eases repair and reapproximates thick myometrium</cite> <cite id="d3be54cb-2">Barbed suture shortens uterine incision closure time at cesarean with similar early outcomes</cite>.
- If tissue is very thin or placental remnant remains, prioritize piecemeal reexcision under imaging rather than forcing a primary closure. <cite id="fd438181-1">When residual myometrium is less than 3 mm, resection with suture is the mainstay; otherwise, conversion may be required</cite>.

Controversies and uncertainties
Evidence supports two‑layer closure with barbed/absorbable sutures as primary management and discourages single‑layer/locking techniques, but comparative trials on barbed vs absorbable suture in CSD are limited; mesh is used selectively given adhesion risks; symptom and recurrence data are promising but heterogeneous across case series. Larger multicenter trials would clarify recurrence, leakage, and pregnancy outcomes by closure method. <cite id="fd438181-0">Laparoscopic two‑layer CSD repair cohort shows favorable outcomes</cite> <cite id="d26555c3-1">Barbed double‑layer closure reports complete myometrial re‑approximation and favorable clinical results</cite> <cite id="fd438181-2">Technique-related risk factors (single-layer closures, locking knots) have been linked to niche formation</cite>.

Summary

Doppler ultrasound studies in acute pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and salpingitis report a consistent pattern of hemodynamic change: arterial vascular resistance falls with an increase in blood flow vigor, producing lower resistance and pulsatility indices (RI, PI) and higher peak (and time-averaged) velocities, together described as “arterialization” of the pelvic microcirculation. These changes are most readily probed in the proximally sampled arteries supplying the uterine tube, ovary, uterus, and broader pelvic bed (uterine, ovarian, and occasionally femoral/iliac arteries), with color and power Doppler showing elongated, reduced-resistance flow signals and increased vascularity compared with healthy controls. Clinically, Doppler metrics add incremental value but are limited by operator dependence, physiologic cycle variability, confounders (intrauterine device, pregnancy, endometriosis), suboptimal visualization of the affected tube, and modest diagnostic sensitivity; as a result, they are best used as adjuncts rather than stand-alone diagnostic tests. <cite id="7c9ae8b9-0">In acute infection, transvaginal color Doppler can detect decreased vascular resistance</cite> and <cite id="7c9ae8b9-3">salpingitis appears on ultrasound as elongated, reduced resistance to flow on color Doppler</cite>. Complementary power Doppler shows that <cite id="7c9ae8b9-4">acute salpingitis is associated with increased vascularity consistent with hyperemia</cite>. At a mechanistic level, <cite id="7c9ae8b9-1">velocity waveforms and microvessel blood flow signals are altered in PID as measured by transvaginal Doppler</cite>.

How vascular resistance and blood flow velocity differ between PID/salpingitis and controls

Arterial resistance indices (RI/PI)
- Uterine/ovarian arteries: Inflammation reduces arterial resistance, lowering RI and PI, and reflecting hyperemic flow redistribution to the adnexa. <cite id="7c9ae8b9-0">Color Doppler can detect decreased vascular resistance during acute pelvic infection</cite>, and <cite id="7c9ae8b9-3">salpingitis is characterized by reduced resistance on color Doppler</cite>. Although the direction and magnitude of uterine artery PI/RI changes in PID are reported as “decreased resistance” rather than exact numeric deltas in many older studies, this aligns with a general hemodynamic principle that inflammatory hyperemia increases perfusion and lowers impedance in the uterine–ovarian arterial tree. <cite id="f067d493-2">Uterine artery Doppler indices RI and PI are widely used to reflect vascular resistance because PI = (PSV − EDV)/time-averaged velocity and RI = (PSV − EDV)/PSV, providing a clinically tractable framework to compare flow resistance before and after inflammatory processes</cite>.
- Time course and vasoactive mediators: Experimental and clinical responsiveness of uterine artery resistance to vasoactive drugs supports that this vascular bed is highly responsive; thus, a state of acute infection should transiently reduce resistance with measurable shifts in Doppler indices. <cite id="f067d493-6">Uterine Doppler ultrasonography detects changes in uterine artery resistance induced by vasoactive agents</cite>.
- Venous-arterial coupling: Reduced arterial resistance in salpingitis coexists with venous outflow changes seen on color/TVUS (“opposition to arterial flow” is the normal pattern) and can evolve toward venous stasis or thrombosis if inflammation persists; <cite id="7c9ae8b9-3">descriptions of “reduced resistance to flow” on color Doppler in salpingitis reflect arterial-phase changes, with downstream venous hemodynamics often abnormal</cite>, and <cite id="7c9ae8b9-4">power Doppler captures increased adnexal vascularity</cite>.

Flow velocities (PSV/EDV/mean velocity)
- Increased peak systolic and early-diastolic velocities reflect lower resistance and greater forward flow in affected segments. <cite id="7c9ae8b9-4">Power Doppler evidence of hyperemia in acute salpingitis is complementary to lower-resistance color Doppler signals</cite>, and waveform-focused studies demonstrate that <cite id="f067d493-1">PI and RI are derived from peak systolic, end-diastolic, and time-averaged velocities; in inflammatory settings, peak and end-diastolic velocities typically increase as resistance falls, thereby lowering RI/PI even if mean velocity rises</cite>.
- Access for measurement varies by anatomy and patient habitus; therefore, operators most often sample uterine/ovarian arteries and proximal common femoral or uterine arteries via transabdominal or transvaginal routes, looking for relative increases in systolic and diastolic segments of velocity traces and shortened velocity time integrals consistent with arterialization.

Which arteries are sampled and what their findings mean

- Uterine arteries and endometrial microvasculature: As the principal maternal vascular supply to the uterus and tube, these are the most consistently assessed arteries. <cite id="7c9ae8b9-0">Acute infection produces a detectable drop in vascular resistance in these territories</cite>. <cite id="f067d493-7">In normal menstrual cycles, uterine artery PI varies with phase and falls toward mid-gestation in pregnancy, demonstrating that any inflammatory process that diminishes resistance should be interpreted against a background of physiologic cycle variability</cite>.
- Ovarian arteries: Reduced resistance and increased peak velocities are reported in adnexal inflammation, supporting a broader pelvic arterial redistribution during PID. <cite id="7c9ae8b9-2">Color/ spectral Doppler of the ovarian arteries has been evaluated to distinguish inflammatory from noninflammatory conditions, reinforcing their diagnostic role although the focus in PID is on relative increases in flow vigor</cite>.
- Common femoral/iliac arteries: As upstream inflow trunks, their resistance indices may also decrease with localized uterine–ovarian hyperemia, aiding lateralization when accessible; however, these are larger arteries and may show less pronounced changes than uterine/ovarian branches.

Practical ultrasound signatures

- Color Doppler: <cite id="7c9ae8b9-3">Arterial waveform profiles show “elongated” flow with reduced resistance</cite>, and <cite id="7c9ae8b9-4">enhanced signal density (“increased vascularity”) in the affected adnexa</cite>. When the infundibulum is visualized, the ipsilateral tubal branches may show arterialization (direct communication of low-resistance arterial inflow), a classic Doppler sign of salpingitis.
- Power Doppler: <cite id="7c9ae8b9-4">Fills in areas where flow direction is obscured by gas or bowel loops, but cannot distinguish resistance alone</cite>; high vascularity with clustered foci around the tube/ovary is typical in acute salpingitis.

What factors limit clinical usefulness?

Diagnostic yield and sensitivity/specificity

- Low sensitivity in early or mild disease: Doppler hemodynamics evolve with increasing inflammation and are easier to demonstrate on one side when a unilateral salpingitis is present; early disease may lack reproducible shifts. <cite id="7c9ae8b9-0">The finding that “decreased vascular resistance can be detected” implies that negative Dopplers do not reliably rule out PID, as many acute cases may normalize as inflammation resolves</cite>. Moreover, <cite id="7c9ae8b9-0">detection relies on adequate signal-to-noise and operator ability to sample appropriate segments in acute infection</cite>.
- Adjacent conditions confound resistance readings: Endometriosis, adenomyosis, and fibroids can also lower PI/RI or raise flow velocities in the uterine arteries depending on phase and extent; <cite id="dc0aa2a1-1">the sensitivity and specificity of transvaginal ultrasound for endometriosis illustrate the degree of overlap in pelvic vascular patterns, with high specificity but imperfect sensitivity</cite>. Endometriosis-focused evaluation of uterine artery RI after provocative testing underscores that vascular changes are dynamic and diagnosis is probabilistic, a limitation that extends to PID discrimination. <cite id="dc0aa2a1-1">Uterine artery resistance is altered by provoked endometriosis, highlighting how vascular signatures change with state and technique</cite>.
- Confounders: Intrauterine devices (IUDs) alter endometrial vascularization and low-resistance flows; <cite id="dc0aa2a1-0">uterine artery Doppler indices have been used to predict IUCD-related heavy bleeding</cite> and <cite id="dc0aa2a1-7">3D power Doppler demonstrates IUD-related microvascular effects</cite>. Pregnancy and ovulatory phase shift uterine artery PI/RI and velocity waveforms; <cite id="f067d493-6">in normal cycles PI follows defined centiles</cite> and <cite id="dc0aa2a1-6">cycle-specific reference ranges for uterine artery PI exist</cite>, yet during acute infection these norms are overridden imperfectly and incompletely, complicating interpretation.
- Sampling limitations: The affected fallopian tube may be displaced, obscured, or adherent; failure to visualize or obtain angle-corrected spectral waveforms leads to nondiagnostic nonvisualized segments. Color/Power Doppler offers adjunctive but directionally limited information.
- Technique and reproducibility: <cite id="7c9ae8b9-0">Detection of decreased resistance depends on correct sampling, angle correction, and experience</cite>; interobserver variability affects categorization of RI/PI thresholds. Although PI thresholds are used elsewhere (e.g., peripheral arterial disease), the absence of robust ROC data specific to PID limits their universal adoption. <cite id="3f146cd5-6">PI cutoffs with “high sensitivity and specificity” are established in specific vascular beds, but analogous data in PID are sparse</cite>.
- Adjacent adnexal pathology and comorbidity: Adhesions, chronic PID, ectopic pregnancy, or ovarian torsion can produce overlapping Doppler pictures; thus, Doppler alone lacks the specificity to exclude serious differential diagnoses.

Physiologic variability and operator dependence

- Cycle-phase dependence: Uterine artery PI/RI vary with hormonal phase and day of cycle; <cite id="dc0aa2a1-6">reference ranges are stratified by day-cycle</cite>. Failure to normalize to day-cycle in controls and patients undermines accuracy unless matched in acquisition and analysis.
- Reproducibility: <cite id="3f146cd5-6">Although indices are simple to compute, their diagnostic value in other conditions hinges on measurement precision and standardized thresholds; analogous limitations apply to PID</cite>.
- Image plane, angle correction, sample volume placement, gray-scale thresholding for color mapping, and transducer position (transabdominal vs transvaginal) all change measured velocities and indices. <cite id="f067d493-1">Because PI/RI depend mechanistically on peak, end-diastolic, and time-averaged velocities, small errors in EDV or mean velocity measurement yield large percent changes in indices</cite>.

Clinical context and integration

- Correlation with clinical/lab findings: Inflammatory states elevate WBC and ESR, but PID often shows normal labs early; Doppler changes may precede symptom resolution and persist after antibiotic therapy in fibrotic cases. Thus, Doppler best functions as an adjunct, not a replacement, for clinical assessment, pregnancy ruling out, and laparoscopic confirmation.
- Therapeutic monitoring: Vasoactive therapy produces detectable shifts in RI/PI and PSV; serial Doppler can demonstrate hemodynamic improvement, but thresholds and time courses vary by patient factors. <cite id="f067d493-6">Uterine Doppler shows responsiveness to vasoactive drugs, supporting the principle that treating infection alters hemodynamics</cite>.

Practical expectations when comparing PID/salpingitis and controls

- Resistance and pulsatility: Controls show mid-to-high resistance patterns (normal RI/PI and velocity waveforms) for the uterine and ovarian arteries within phase-specific norms. In PID/salpingitis, RI and PI are decreased on affected sides and upstream arteries, consistent with reduced vascular resistance and increased systolic/diastolic velocities demonstrating arterialization. <cite id="7c9ae8b9-0">Transvaginal color Doppler detects lowered resistance in acute infection</cite>; <cite id="7c9ae8b9-3">salpingitis is described by reduced resistance</cite>; and <cite id="7c9ae8b9-4">power Doppler shows increased vascularity with hyperemia</cite>. Microvascular waveform studies confirm these mechanistic patterns in the cervix/uterus in PID cohorts. <cite id="7c9ae8b9-1">Velocity waveform analysis shows altered microvascularization</cite>.
- Exceptions and confounders: IUD exposure, endometriosis, fibroids, pregnancy, and ovulatory phase can mimic or mask PID signals; day-cycle mismatch invalidates comparisons. <cite id="dc0aa2a1-0">IUDs are associated with reproducible Doppler signal changes</cite>; <cite id="dc0aa2a1-1">endometriosis exhibits RI/PI changes detectable after provocative testing</cite>; and <cite id="dc0aa2a1-6">phase-specific reference ranges emphasize physiologic variability</cite>.
- Visualization: Controls often demonstrate symmetrical, well-opposed arterial-venous flow and sparse adnexal color Doppler. PID produces asymmetry: ipsilateral increased vascularity, arterialized waveforms, and reduced resistance with or without venous outflow impairment, especially if adhesion or mass effect limits outflow. <cite id="7c9ae8b9-4">Power Doppler hyperemia localizes to the affected tube</cite> and <cite id="7c9ae8b9-3">color flow is described as reduced-resistance and elongated</cite>.

Bottom line and practical use

- When available and interpreted with clinical context, lower uterine/ovarian arterial RI/PI and increased PSV/EDV/mean velocities—seen as arterialized arterialization and increased vascularity with color/power Doppler—distinguish active PID/salpingitis from controls, but these differences lack universal, phase- and device-independent cutoffs. <cite id="7c9ae8b9-0">Doppler can detect decreased resistance</cite>, <cite id="7c9ae8b9-3">with reduced resistance a hallmark of salpingitis</cite>, and <cite id="7c9ae8b9-4">increased vascularity consistent with hyperemia</cite>. 
- Limitations that constrain clinical utility include physiologic cycle variability (and the need for day-cycle–matched acquisition), operator dependence and reproducibility, overlapping vascular signatures from endometriosis, fibroids, and IUDs, pregnancy and hormonal influences, limited ability to consistently image the affected tube, and modest sensitivity in early disease. For these reasons, Doppler should be integrated with clinical examination, bimanual findings, labs, pregnancy testing, and, when possible, confirmatory imaging (CT) or laparoscopy, with serial Doppler used to monitor hemodynamic response to therapy. <cite id="dc0aa2a1-1">Diagnostic performance overlaps with other pelvic inflammatory diseases like endometriosis, underscoring overlap</cite>, <cite id="dc0aa2a1-6">cycle-specific norms limit use of fixed thresholds</cite>, <cite id="dc0aa2a1-7">IUDs can independently alter microvascular flow</cite>, and <cite id="7c9ae8b9-0">detection of decreased resistance depends on technique and appropriate sampling</cite>.

Summary of indications and goals
- Laparoscopic excision of myometrial adenomyomas (focal adenomyomas) is favored for women seeking uterus-preserving therapy when imaging demonstrates discrete nodules with sharp borders and preserved cavity margins; it aims to remove the focally displaced endometrium/myometrium while preserving uterine integrity for fertility or future pregnancy when possible. <cite id="5d842880-1">Laparoscopic procedure can be used for treating focal adenomyosis, although it entails a risk of leaving some of the lesions unexcised.</cite> <cite id="e910214f-2">Uterine-sparing surgical treatment certainly improves the pregnancy outcome; pregnancy rates around 60% are reported among women with Type I (cavitary-confined) adenomyosis.</cite> <cite id="cbea1949-0">An advanced three-step laparoscopic adenomyomectomy technique has been proposed as a safe and effective method for focal disease.</cite>
- Success hinges on complete excision with preservation of normal uterine architecture and pericervical structures, appropriate adhesion management, and meticulous hemostasis; in diffuse or deep disease, hysterectomy or combined procedures are often recommended. <cite id="5d842880-1">Laparoscopy treats focal disease but may leave residual lesions.</cite> <cite id="5d842880-5">Total laparoscopic hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy is an option when disease is diffuse or cystic.</cite> <cite id="5d842880-2">Historic reports show uterine rupture risk after adenomyomectomy and pregnancy, underscoring safety trade-offs and the role of hysterectomy in selected cases.</cite>

Step-by-step technique: access, identification, dissection, closure, and retrieval
1) Patient positioning, anesthesia, and access
- Standard four-trocar laparoscopy (supraceliac or infraumbilical) or single-incision configurations are used; pneumoperitoneum and generous visualization allow mapping of cardinal ligaments and posterior cul-de-sac. <cite id="cbea1949-9">Single-incision laparoscopic adenomyomectomy is reported; technique adapts to the same surgical principles through one umbilical incision.</cite>
- Diagnostic laparoscopy and dye sonoporation (e.g., blue dye) can enhance boundary definition and completeness assessments; intraoperative ultrasonography is increasingly used. <cite id="cbea1949-0">A three-step technique is reported feasible and effective for adenomyomectomy.</cite> <cite id="5d842880-5">A transverse incision strategy and monopolar electrocautery/needle excision are described, with the cavity reconstructed as needed.</cite> <cite id="5d842880-0">Elastography-guided laparoscopic adenomyomectomy is feasible, with real-time ultrasound elastography used to guide complete resection.</cite> <cite id="e910214f-1">Diagnostic modalities and transtrocar ultrasonographic guidance have enabled successful cystic adenomyomectomy and sharp/blunt dissection steps.</cite>

2) Lesion identification and staging
- Identify mobility of the nodule, relation to peritoneum, cardinal ligaments, uterosacral/uterine arteries, and the uterine cavity; palpate posterior fornix for posterior lesions. Use methylene blue sonoporation to trace ectopic endometrium and define borders; cystic lesions may communicate with the cavity. <cite id="cbea1949-3">Adenomyomectomy spares the endometrium as much as possible to preserve fertility; the cavity is “hollowed” and incised in a transverse fashion, then excised using a monopolar device and reconstructed in multiple layers.</cite> <cite id="cbea1949-0">The advanced three-step approach integrates careful identification and staged excision.</cite> <cite id="5d842880-6">A technique outline emphasizes transverse incision, monopolar needle excision, and cavity reconstruction; seromuscular layer repair is advised for defects.</cite>

3) Incision strategy and plane selection
- Approach as if “hollowing out the uterine cavity,” making a longitudinal or transverse opening over the thinnest myometrium, then “triangular” or “fan” excision with safety margins; preserve endometrium to maintain contractility and preserve fertility. <cite id="5d842880-4">The myometrium should be dissected diagonally as if hollowing out the uterine cavity; a transverse incision allows excision with monopolar needle, enabling visualization of the cavity and preservation of uterine architecture.</cite> <cite id="cbea1949-3">Sparing the endometrium maximizes fertility preservation; after excision, a wide-layered closure is performed to support future pregnancy.</cite> <cite id="e910214f-1">Combining sharp dissection and blunt dissection, guided by transtrocar ultrasonography, has enabled successful excisional adenomyomectomy even after failed open surgery.</cite>

4) Dissection technique (sharp/blunt)
- External approach: incise the pericervical fat and reflect peritoneum to expose the lesion; dissect along the inner peritoneal surface down to the ectopic endometrium and myometrium; create a safety flap and convert to an internal uterine incision. <cite id="cbea1949-0">The three-step technique provides a safe and effective workflow for adenomyomectomy.</cite> <cite id="e910214f-1">A combination of sharp and blunt dissection has achieved successful laparoscopic cystic adenomyomectomy.</cite>
- Internal approach (focal): incise into the lesion to enter the uterine cavity, confirm communication, then excise triangular-shaped myometrial segments with preservation of the antimesenteric/informant wall. <cite id="e910214f-1">Successful total laparoscopic cystic adenomyomectomy has been achieved using transvaginal blunt dissection into the lesion, then excision through transverse incisions with monopolar devices.</cite> <cite id="5d842880-4">Diagonal dissection hollowing the uterine cavity allows safe, complete excision with monopolar needle under direct visualization.</cite>

5) Hemostasis and energy device use
- Electrocautery (monopolar/ bipolar) with scalpel-like needle loops is commonly used for excision and diathermic coagulation; microvessels are ligated; care is taken to avoid thermal spread beyond intended margins. <cite id="5d842880-6">Excision is performed with a monopolar needle while inspecting the cavity; the cavity is closed in 3 layers, including a wide seromuscular overlap for strength and healing.</cite> <cite id="cbea1949-4">Layered closure after excision preserves uterine support and future pregnancy potential, with care taken to preserve the endometrium.</cite>
- When extensive devascularization is needed or deep lesions are present, adjuncts such as ultrasonography/electrotome/ligasure can be integrated, but deep dissection risks injury and complex reconstructions; conversion to hysterectomy may be required in suspected rupture/ massive hemorrhage. <cite id="e910214f-6">Excision attempts for adenomyoma can damage myometrium and require complex reconstruction that may not tolerate pregnancy, highlighting the trade-off for fertility preservation.</cite> <cite id="e910214f-7">Robot-assisted adenomyomectomy is feasible, with advantages in dexterity and ergonomics for intricate dissection and suturing.</cite>

6) Specimen excision and retrieval
- Excise the adenomyoma in toto if feasible; morcellation may be used for very large cystic lesions through the cul-de-sac or vagina with intracavitary communication—if morcellated tissue has intramural/ectopic trophic endometrium, risk of iatrogenic dissemination is nontrivial and excision into the cavity followed by closure is preferred. <cite id="e910214f-1">Laparoscopic cystic adenomyomectomy with transtrocar ultrasonographic guidance and sharp/blunt dissection demonstrates feasibility and safety for excisional removal.</cite> <cite id="5d842880-5">A transverse incision and monopolar needle excision strategy have been described, with the remaining seromuscular layer closed widely in multiple layers.</cite>
- For large or deep lesions, consider staged transvaginal morcellation under direct laparoscopic vision with generous cervical retraction and hemostasis, using a 10–12 mm morcellator; place a large bag on the specimen and remove through the umbilicus; maintain cul-de-sac packing to manage bleeding points. <cite id="e910214f-1">Transtrocar ultrasonographic guidance and systematic dissection have facilitated complete removal and hemostasis at the seromuscular level.</cite>

7) Closure and adnexal preservation
- Close the uterine incision in at least three layers: endothelium/mucosa if cavitary communication existed, submucosal/seromuscular with wide appositional overlap, and fascial closure; place interrupted subcuticular/subcuticular sutures; verify hemostasis and negative cavity/ cul-de-sac. <cite id="5d842880-4">Hollowing-out dissection with a transverse incision allows complete excision with monopolar needle and subsequent layered closure preserving uterine architecture.</cite> <cite id="cbea1949-4">The defect area is closed in 3 layers, including a wide seromuscular overlap, to preserve uterine integrity and contractility for fertility.</cite>
- Preserve both adnexa unless conserving fertility is contraindicated; perform paracervical lymph node dissection if indicated; manage bladder and rectal peritoneal reflections gently to avoid injury. <cite id="cbea1949-2">Robot-assisted laparoscopic adenomyomectomy is feasible with potential advantages for preserving fertility and reducing blood loss and recovery time.</cite>

8) Postoperative management
- Antibiotics, analgesia, early mobilization, and outpatient follow-up with serial transvaginal ultrasound and CA-125; counsel on menstrual changes; consider suppression therapy to reduce symptoms. If histology confirms adenomyosis and cavity margins are clear, repeat surgery is generally reserved for recurrence or new symptomatic foci. <cite id="5d842880-6">After needle-guided excision and layered closure (including wide seromuscular overlap), careful postoperative care and histological confirmation guide further management.</cite> <cite id="e910214f-9">Recognition of location and borders, longitudinal incision, and blunt dissection are standard steps to ensure adequate excision prior to closure.</cite>

Key determinants of success
1) Selection and imaging
