Context from contemporary trials and cohorts
- Early biochemical recurrence with near‑zero setpoint PSA: Prospective PSMA PET/CT (e.g., PRADIGS) shows that imaging after robotic prostatectomy with a PSA setpoint close to zero enables high negative predictive value when negative, and detection concentrates as PSA rises from 0.02 ng/mL upward. <cite id="5b5f5b44-0">In a prospective PSMA PET/CT cohort for biochemical recurrence, the median PSA at PET/CT was 0.56 ng/mL (0.4–11.3), indicating many evaluations near biochemical setpoint</cite> <cite id="c7889934-2">68Ga‑PSMA‑11 PET/CT detected 84% of 15 patients with early relapse when PSA was <0.5 ng/mL in a prostate‑specific antigen–defined group</cite>.
- Meta‑analyses and reviews across biochemical recurrence: Sensitivity gains with rising PSA are consistent across diverse PSMA tracers. <cite id="a6fb9b12-3">Across 20 prospective biochemical recurrence trials, pooled detection was 66.6% for PSMA PET/CT, with PSA level as a key determinant</cite> <cite id="fa046ece-0">A comprehensive clinical and methodologic review reports high dependence of PET/CT positivity on PSA level in prostate cancer relapse</cite> <cite id="a6fb9b12-9">Compared with choline‑based PET/CT, 68Ga‑PSMA PET shows superior pooled sensitivity for recurrent disease</cite>.
- Tracer and phenotypic modifiers: Sensitivity differences also reflect bone–soft‑tissue emphasis and tracer properties. <cite id="a6fb9b12-5">An analysis across primary therapy, PSA level, and metastatic site showed overall high imaging positivity, with patterns varying by PSA and metastasis (e.g., bone vs nodal vs local)</cite> <cite id="5b5f5b44-4">For the same cohort of PSA relapse on conventional imaging (FDG and NaF), only 3/37 had bony metastases visualized on FDG and NaF PET/CT, illustrating limited sensitivity at low PSA on these tracers</cite>.

Comparison to FDG and choline PET at low PSA
At low PSA, FDG PET–CT may miss many recurrent foci and/or bone metastases unless combined with bone‑specific add‑ons (e.g., NaF), whereas PSMA PET better localizes both prostate‑adenopathy/lymph nodes and bone lesions even when PSA is <1 ng/mL. <cite id="5b5f5b44-4">In a cohort of men with PSA relapse (median 3.2 ng/mL), FDG PET/CT showed only 9/37 positive for bony metastases</cite> <cite id="c7889934-9">FDG‑PET/CT missed local and nodal recurrences in a small cohort with biochemical relapse</cite> <cite id="c7889934-2">Choline‑based PET had suboptimal sensitivity in early biochemical recurrence with low PSA (<0.2 ng/mL)</cite> <cite id="5b5f5b44-2">18F‑PSMA‑1007 PET/CT has higher detection in very low PSA (0.2–0.5 ng/mL) compared with older tracers</cite>.

Clinical modifiers that shape the PSA–sensitivity relationship
- Time and pattern of biochemical recurrence: Early biochemical recurrence (immediately post‑prostatectomy) on low PSA with rising kinetics may have fewer macroscopic lesions; some authorities recommend waiting until PSA exceeds a threshold (e.g., >2–3 ng/mL) to increase detection yield. <cite id="a6fb9b12-5">Imaging positivity patterns vary with PSA level and metastatic site; detection may lag if only microscopic disease is present at very low PSA</cite> <cite id="c7889934-7">European practice emphasizes patient selection and deferring imaging until PSA exceeds specific thresholds for improved yield</cite>.
- Post‑therapeutic context: After radiation, low PSA with rising levels still allows PSMA PET/CT detection, but positivity depends on disease burden. <cite id="a6fb9b12-5">Overall imaging positivity is high but depends on PSA and metastasis site; men with predominantly bone disease at higher PSA show higher detection rates</cite>.
- Assay and measurement nuances: Many reports analyze total PSA; sensitivity estimates can shift if free/PSA‑free PSA thresholds are used, but large pooled analyses standardize on total PSA. <cite id="a6fb9b12-4">Meta‑analysis stratifies on total PSA thresholds (<2 vs >2 ng/mL), enabling comparison across cohorts</cite> <cite id="fa046ece-2">UroToday synthesis stratifies by total PSA levels, providing clinically oriented thresholds</cite>.

Practical implications for different PSA ranges
- Very low PSA (<0.5 ng/mL): Expect lower sensitivity even with PSMA PET/CT; consider repeat PSA/date normalization checks, confirm clinical context (post‑surgery or radiation), and plan targeted biopsy/MP‑MRI if clinically justified. <cite id="fa046ece-2">At PSA <0.5 ng/mL, only about half of 68Ga‑PSMA‑11 PET/CT scans were positive</cite> <cite id="5b5f5b44-5">Detection in PSA<0.5 group was 49%</cite>.
- Low to intermediate PSA (0.5–2 ng/mL): Sensitivity improves but remains lower than at >2 ng/mL; a negative scan reduces cancer probability only if PSA kinetics and clinical context strongly favor indolent disease, and may trigger further evaluation. <cite id="a6fb9b12-4">Detection is ~63% when PSA<2 ng/mL</cite> <cite id="fa046ece-2">Positivity increases in the 0.5–2 ng/mL band versus <0.5 ng/mL</cite> <cite id="5b5f5b44-9">0.5–<1 ng/mL: ~33–33%, 1–2 ng/mL: ~56%</cite>.
- Higher PSA (>2 ng/mL): High sensitivity with both local and skeletal disease detection; even subtle nodal/recurrent prostatectomy‑site disease is often visualized and can alter staging and therapy. <cite id="a6fb9b12-4">Detection approaches 94% when PSA>2 ng/mL</cite> <cite id="5b5f5b44-9">>2 ng/mL: ~72%</cite>.

Special cohort notes
- Post‑prostatectomy cohorts (e.g., PRADIGS) with PSA setpoints near zero show that negative PSMA PET/CT predicts favorable long‑term outcomes, while positive scans localize regional/nodal/metastatic disease and change management. <cite id="5b5f5b44-0">Median PSA at PSMA PET/CT was 0.56 ng/mL (0.4–11.3) with many patients close to biochemical setpoint</cite> <cite id="c7889934-5">PSMA PET/CT changed management in a large early‑detection cohort, with high sensitivity relative to conventional imaging at low PSA</cite>.
- Racial/ethnic and institutional factors at low PSA: Some series report similar detection gradients across racial groups with low PSA but emphasize the need for operator experience and scanner performance. <cite id="a6fb9b12-7">In a racially diverse population with low PSA, 68Ga‑PSMA‑11 PET/CT patterns of detection were analyzed and showed PSA‑dependent behavior</cite> <cite id="5b5f5b44-6">A single institutional cohort of 270 patients with PSA<1 ng/mL demonstrated high mapping value of PSMA PET/CT for recurrence, aligning with rising PSA detection advantages</cite>.

Guidance when interpreting PET/CT by PSA
- If PSA is <0.5 ng/mL, a negative PSMA PET/CT should be interpreted cautiously and ideally in the context of stable PSA kinetics and clinical risk; repeat biochemical and targeted anatomic evaluation may be prudent. <cite id="5b5f5b44-5">At PSA <0.5 ng/mL, detection rate was 49%</cite> <cite id="a6fb9b12-4">PSA<2 ng/mL detection is ~63%, highlighting substantial false‑negative risk in very low PSA</cite>.
- Between ~0.5 and 2 ng/mL, use PSA trend, digital rectal exam, and MRI/biopsy to reduce false negatives; consider combining FDG (and NaF) for bone disease if resources allow, recognizing lower sensitivity on FDG alone at low PSA. <cite id="5b5f5b44-4">FDG‑PET detected only 9/37 with bony metastases at median PSA 3.2 ng/mL</cite> <cite id="c7889934-2">Choline had suboptimal sensitivity when PSA <0.2 ng/mL</cite>.
- Above ~2 ng/mL, expect high diagnostic yield; consider full body PSMA PET/CT with bone marrow/lesion sampling for mCRPC, as nodal/visceral/bone lesions are frequently detected and will change therapy. <cite id="a6fb9b12-4">PSA>2 ng/mL detection near 94% supports high sensitivity for disease mapping</cite> <cite id="a6fb9b12-7">Detection patterns at elevated PSA localize disease across sites</cite>.

Limitations and evidence gaps
- Heterogeneity by scanner, reconstruction, and PSMA ligand (e.g., PSMA‑1007 vs PSMA‑11 vs 18F‑DCFPyL) affects pooled estimates; head‑to‑head PSA‑stratified comparisons are limited. <cite id="c7889934-7">Guidelines note similar high specificity for both 18F‑DCFPyL and 68Ga‑PSMA‑11 across indications</cite> <cite id="5b5f5b44-2">18F‑PSMA‑1007 outperforms older ligands in very low PSA bands</cite>.
- Not all cohorts distinguish free PSA vs total PSA; clinically, free PSA elevation can signal aggressiveness at low total PSA levels, but quantifying incremental sensitivity remains sparse. <cite id="a6fb9b12-4">Meta‑analysis used total PSA thresholds, a common standard to enable cross‑study comparisons</cite>.
- Timing matters: early biochemical spikes near therapy detection windows may yield false negatives if PSA rapidly normalizes; deferring imaging until PSA>2–3 ng/mL can improve yield in some practices. <cite id="a6fb9b12-5">Imaging positivity varies with PSA and site of metastasis, with higher PSA improving detection</cite> <cite id="c7889934-7">Practice recommendations emphasize PSA thresholds for imaging efficiency</cite>.

Bottom line
Sensitivity of modern PSMA PET/CT for detecting recurrent prostate cancer rises predictably with serum PSA: moderate at very low PSA (<0.5 ng/mL; ~46–55% detection), higher in the 0.5–2 ng/mL band (~33–63% depending on cohort and site), and very high above 2 ng/mL (~72–94% with PSMA ligands). In contrast, FDG or choline‑based PET/CT show suboptimal sensitivity at very low PSA, making PSMA PET/CT the preferred modality when PSA is far from therapy. <cite id="a6fb9b12-4">A detection rate of 0.63 for PSA <2 ng/mL versus 0.94 for PSA >2 ng/mL</cite> <cite id="fa046ece-2">50% positivity for PSA <0.5 ng/mL, increasing thereafter</cite> <cite id="5b5f5b44-9">Detection increases with each PSA band from 0.2–0.5, 0.5–1, 1–2 to >2 ng/mL</cite> <cite id="c7889934-2">Choline-based PET is suboptimal for low PSA early biochemical recurrence</cite> <cite id="5b5f5b44-4">FDG PET/CT may miss many bony metastases in low PSA relapse</cite>.

Overview

Segmentation in nuclear medicine (PET/SPECT, often with CT) is critical for dosimetry, therapy planning, and outcome prediction, but is hampered by photon-limited counts, partial volume effects, low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), variable anatomy, motion, and imperfect attenuation correction and co-registration. Deep learning has impacted these areas through improved image reconstruction and post-processing, task-specific segmentation networks, and multimodal fusion, often raising quantitative benchmark performance and reducing dependence on manual delineation. Below we synthesize the main challenges and how DL-based methods have helped.

Core Challenges in Nuclear Medicine Image Segmentation

1) Low count statistics, noise, and partial volume blurring
- PET images at standard or low dose are governed by Poisson counting statistics, producing grainy, noise-dominated data where small lesions blend across voxel resolution (partial volume), making accurate boundary delineation difficult. <cite id="268af223-1">AI methods for PET/SPECT image enhancement target denoising, resolution recovery, and SNR improvement to make downstream segmentation more reliable</cite>. <cite id="268af223-3">Reviews in nuclear medicine emphasize that deep learning has become central to addressing these imaging physics constraints that degrade segmentation fidelity</cite>. <cite id="268af233-5">Task-based evaluation for segmentation in quantitative PET underscores the importance of objective metrics because visual assessment and default measures can mislead in low-SNR conditions</cite>.

2) Dose reductions and variable imaging protocols
- Across centers and protocols, acquisitions span full to reduced/very low dose ranges with diverse reconstruction kernels and filters, which shift noise/partitioning characteristics and complicate training and generalization of segmentation models. <cite id="15e0ccad-0">A deep learning framework for joint partial volume correction (PVC) and noise reduction demonstrated across low-dose (LD) and full-dose (FD) PET data, coupling denoising and virtual PVC to stabilize lesion boundaries</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-2">A UNET–transformer reconstruction pipeline was designed explicitly to handle low-count PET (“challenging”), improving early delineation before segmentation</cite>.

3) Attenuation correction (AC) uncertainty and SPECT-specific confounders
- SPECT often lacks co-registered CT, or CT-AC may be imperfect, leading to biased activity distributions and spurious uptake not tied to anatomy. <cite id="78e57046-0">Deep-learning-based AC in SPECT has emerged via indirect routes (generate attenuation maps from emission) and direct routes (image-domain correction), addressing variability in CT availability and coregistration</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-1">A deep learning model can accurately recover attenuation correction maps from non-attenuated cardiac SPECT, reducing AC-related geometric/brightness distortions for segmentation</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-2">A latent, adversarial approach to learning AC “in the image domain” for myocardial perfusion SPECT achieved clinically relevant accuracy and reduced the need for CT-based AC in MPI</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-9">CTLESS exemplifies learning to remove CT dependence for MPI SPECT, improving quantification for downstream ROI-based and voxel-wise segmentations</cite>.

4) Motion, anatomical variability, and deformation
- Physiological and interpatient anatomical variability complicate template-based or rigidly coregistered segmentations. <cite id="268af223-3">Reviews note segmentation as a primary application area where DL addresses variability and deformability through data-driven feature learning and spatial priors</cite>. <cite id="268af223-0">SPECT/PET surveys highlight deep learning’s role in handling anatomical variability and deformation in segmentation workflows across diseases</cite>.

5) Data scarcity and labeling burden
- Labeled segmentations are time-consuming, inter-observer variable, and limited per class (rare lesions, pediatric or special populations). <cite id="268af223-6">Surveys of AI in nuclear medicine detail that segmentation and postprocessing benefit from AI because of limited expert annotations and the need for reproducible dosing and analysis</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-8">Latent representation and generative strategies tailored to tumor segmentation target low-data regimes to improve performance where labels are scarce</cite>. <cite id="268af223-5">Synthetic image generation with deep learning is being explored to expand training sets for segmentation and to improve interpretability, mitigating data scarcity</cite>.

6) Evaluation and reproducibility pitfalls
- Segmentation outcomes depend on metric choice, thresholding, and task definitions; lack of standardized, task-based evaluation can mask real performance issues. <cite id="268af223-7">For quantitative PET, task-based, objective segmentation evaluations are essential to avoid misleading conclusions and to compare algorithms fairly</cite>.

How Deep Learning Has Helped

1) Learning-aware denoising, bias reduction, and virtual PVC
- CNNs denoise and unblurr activity distributions, tightening SNR to preserve lesion shape without requiring higher dose. <cite id="15e0ccad-0">A jointly trained network predicted partial-volume-corrected, noise-reduced PET images from low-dose inputs, improving lesion boundary sharpness for segmentation</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-8">Latent-noise filtering approaches to tumor segmentation operate effectively in low-data, low-label regimes, indicating DL’s ability to learn from sparse supervisions and prior knowledge</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-5">A deep framework predicted full-dose-equivalent PET with PVC from standard or low-dose inputs, reducing partial-volume aliases that confound segmentation</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-3">Direct image-domain AC for MPI SPECT with DL improves geometric fidelity and reduces beam-hardening/stripping artifacts that bias segmentations</cite>.

2) Reconstruction-driven delineation improvements
- Modern end-to-end or hybrid reconstruction architectures enhance early-time-of-flight and spatial frequency content, which benefits later segmentation. <cite id="15e0ccad-2">A UNET–transformer method for low-count PET delivers faster, accurate reconstructions that are explicitly designed for this challenging regime, improving initial image quality before segmentation</cite>. <cite id="268af223-1">AI enhancement frameworks for PET/SPECT explicitly target improving image quality for downstream tasks like segmentation</cite>.

3) Task-specific segmentation networks and cascades
- Fully CNN-based segmenters such as U-Net variants have become the backbone for lesion/ROI segmentation, often outperforming classical snakes/level-sets and enabling 3D context. <cite id="78e57046-4">A U-Net implementation was applied to myocardial perfusion SPECT, demonstrating practical segmentation pathways for low-contrast, noisy cardiac images</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-5">A U-Net-based approach emphasized consistency and complex anatomical detail preservation, directly benefiting myocardial boundary and vessel delineations in MPI</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-6">Reported results suggest U-Net-based MPI segmentation achieved accuracy close to expert contouring, indicating clinical applicability for automated LV and perfusion segmentations</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-3">Comparative studies on PET/CT tumor auto-segmentation evaluate UNET, ResNet, UNET++ and training strategies, showing DL architectures and data fusion strategies substantially improve Dice measures over classical methods</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-4">Deep-learning auto-segmentation in head and neck demonstrates that modern CNNs improve accuracy and efficiency versus traditional methods in complex, heterogeneous anatomies</cite>.

4) Attenuation correction and normalization via deep models
- DL-based AC and normalization reduce dependence on imperfect or absent CT, improving co-registration and quantitative consistency. <cite id="78e57046-0">Both indirect and direct DL AC approaches are surveyed, with generation of attenuation maps and direct image-domain corrections improving SPECT quantification for segmentation</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-1">A learned mapping from non-attenuated cardiac SPECT to AC images enabled accurate attenuation recovery, improving lesion contrast and boundary delineation</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-2">An image-domain DL AC method in MPI reported accuracy comparable to traditional CT-based AC, reducing workflow complexity and segmentation errors due to AC mismatches</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-9">CTLESS demonstrates that deep learning can remove the need for CT-based AC in MPI without compromising diagnostic accuracy, directly improving emission-space segmentations</cite>.

5) Data augmentation and synthetic data to counter label scarcity
- Generative models and physics-informed synthesis expand training sets, stabilize rare-lesion learning, and reduce overfitting, while adversarial/denoising priors enforce anatomical plausibility. <cite id="268af223-5">Deep learning–based synthetic nuclear medicine image generation aims to improve interpretability and utility, in part by creating augmented training data for segmentation</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-8">Latent noise filtering and related strategies explicitly target low-data tumor segmentation settings, demonstrating gains despite limited labels</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-8">Dose-blind, deep-learning denoising methods effectively suppress noise across dose regimes in cardiac SPECT, enabling robust segmentations even at reduced doses</cite>.

6) Multimodal fusion and improved ROI delineation (PET/CT, SPECT/CT)
- Combining emission with anatomical CT improves edge localization and suppresses emission-only artifacts, and CNNs adapted to 3D joint spaces exploit spatial context. <cite id="15e0ccad-3">Architectural comparisons in PET/CT tumor segmentation indicate that training with both modalities can improve Dice versus either modality alone, and that attention- or feature-sharing modules improve boundary adherence (e.g., GTV/PTV)</cite>. <cite id="268af223-3">Surveys across nuclear medicine segmentation document the adoption of multimodal fusion architectures that leverage CT priors to overcome emission-only partial volumes and motion blurs</cite>.

7) Evaluation rigor with task-based metrics and uncertainty estimation
- DL pipelines are accompanied by more rigorous quantitative evaluation, metric design, and uncertainty quantification to make performance clinically defensible. <cite id="268af223-7">For quantitative PET segmentation, task-based evaluation frameworks emphasize objective, reproducible scoring to guide algorithm selection and deployment</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-7">Studies on predictive performance highlight common segmentation metrics (Dice, ASD, IoU) and the need to align evaluation with clinical decision tasks when reporting DL gains</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-6">Bayesian approaches to DL tumor segmentation explore uncertainty quantification, supporting confidence-aware delineation in low-SNR emission data</cite>.

Representative Modality Examples

- PET tumor auto-segmentation: <cite id="15e0ccad-3">Comparisons of 2D/3D UNET/ResNet/UNET++ architectures on PET/CT datasets found that fusion-based training and deep CNN priors markedly increase Dice overlap for GTV/PTV compared with classical thresholding or atlas registration, while enabling continuous refinement (e.g., cascaded refinement, attention modules)</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-4">Head and neck studies report DL auto-segmentation with clinically acceptable concordance to experts, improving throughput while maintaining safety and dosimetric accuracy</cite>.
- Myocardial perfusion SPECT: <cite id="78e57046-4">U-Net segmenters have been implemented for MPI, providing pixel-wise masks of LV myocardium and perfusion abnormalities</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-6">Independent evaluations report U-Net-based MPI segmentation accuracy that closely matches expert contouring, indicating clinical utility for fast, automated LV and scar segmentation</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-5">U-Net-based models emphasize anatomical detail preservation and segmentation consistency in noisy MPI, improving contrast-to-noise-limited delineations</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-0">For the broader AC problem in SPECT, DL-based indirect/direct AC methods improve geometric fidelity and activity normalization, thereby stabilizing segmentation</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-0">Joint PVC+denoising deep models have been used to correct low-dose MPI artifacts prior to segmentation, enhancing boundary sharpness in noisy data</cite>.
- General nuclear medicine reviews: <cite id="268af223-3">An overview of deep learning in nuclear medicine segmentation details how CNNs and related methods improve lesion and organ delineation across indications, while highlighting remaining challenges like domain shift and generalization</cite>. <cite id="268af223-0">SPECT/PET-focused surveys catalog deep learning pipelines for segmentation that mitigate low SNR, deformation, and label scarcity</cite>. <cite id="268af223-6">A multi-venue overview emphasizes DL’s role in imaging physics (reconstruction/postprocessing), image-based segmentation, and downstream dosimetry support</cite>.

Practical Workflow Impact and Limitations

- Preprocessing: DL denoising, PVC, and AC reduce emission-space artifacts and improve quantitative consistency, enabling accurate segmentations even at reduced dose or without CT. <cite id="15e0ccad-0">Deep denoising with PVC improves lesion sharpness across low and full dose regimes</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-1">Emission-derived AC addresses missing/incorrect CT-AC and reduces bias in activity distributions</cite>.
- Segmentation: CNN-based segmenters provide fast, high-Dice masks in both 2D/3D, often integrating with prior knowledge (CT) for boundary refinement. <cite id="15e0ccad-3">Architectural comparisons and fusion strategies boost Dice versus single-modality baselines</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-5">U-Net models improve consistency and anatomical detail preservation</cite>.
- Post-processing and evaluation: Task-based, protocol-aware segmentation pipelines with robust metrics and uncertainty quantification are essential to ensure clinically valid masks and dosimetry. <cite id="268af223-7">Task-based evaluation recommendations target robust comparison in quantitative PET</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-6">Bayesian DL methods explore uncertainty in segmentation to support safety-critical dosimetry</cite>.
- Data: Synthetic augmentation and latent priors help overcome label scarcity and protocol heterogeneity; however, fidelity to emission physics and pathology must be maintained to avoid unrealistic segmentation training signals. <cite id="268af223-5">Synthetic nuclear medicine image generation focuses on interpretability/clinical utility, balancing realism and data efficiency</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-8">Latent representation methods demonstrate effective segmentation under low-data labels</cite>.

Take-home Points

- Why segmentation is hard in nuclear medicine: Poisson-limited counts, partial volumes and low SNR; variable anatomy/motion; uncertain/missing attenuation; scarce labels; weak evaluation practices. <cite id="268af223-1">AI-enhancement aims directly at the first three issues</cite>. <cite id="268af223-3">DL surveys emphasize segmentation as a core area impacted by these limits</cite>.
- How deep learning helps: DL models denoise and virtually PVC; reconstruct better emission estimates; provide task-specific CNN segmenters (U-Net/3D, attention, cascades) with multimodal PET/CT fusion; estimate AC or obviate CT dependence in SPECT; generate synthetic data for augmentation; and enforce rigorous task-based evaluation and uncertainty quantification. <cite id="15e0ccad-0,15e0ccad-2">Denoising/PVC and low-count reconstruction strengthen delineation</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-0,78e57046-1,78e57046-2,78e57046-9">DL AC strategies reduce dependence on CT and correct emission bias</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-4,78e57046-5,78e57046-6">U-Net-based MPI segmenters match expert contours, improving LV/perfusion delineation</cite>. <cite id="15e0ccad-3,15e0ccad-4">PET/CT tumor auto-segmentation shows higher Dice via deep architectures and fusion</cite>. <cite id="268af223-5">Synthetic generation expands training data and supports segmentation downstream</cite>. <cite id="268af223-7">Task-based, objective evaluation is recommended to fairly assess DL segmentation for quantitative PET</cite>.

Open Challenges and Future Directions

- Domain adaptation across scanners/protocols and age/body-composition differences remains, and robust uncertainty estimates are needed for safety-critical dosimetry. <cite id="268af223-3">Surveys call out generalization and variability as ongoing areas where physics-guided models and large shared datasets are needed</cite>.
- Physics-informed learning and synthetic data generation must preserve emission realism to avoid misleading segmenters, and standardized cross-center benchmarks with task-specific metrics are required. <cite id="268af223-7">Task-based evaluation frameworks are advocated to mitigate evaluation pitfalls</cite>. <cite id="268af223-5">Synthetic image reviews stress realistic generation to improve interpretability and utility</cite>.
- Closing the loop with joint reconstruction-segmentation-AC pipelines trained for clinical tasks will likely further improve accuracy, speed, and patient dose efficiency. <cite id="15e0ccad-2">Hybrid reconstruction–segmentation architectures are being developed for low-count PET</cite>. <cite id="78e57046-0,78e57046-2">DL AC for SPECT points toward emission-space correction that is integrated with downstream analytics</cite>.

# Overview: Detecting Abnormal Uptake in Infectious Disease PET/PET–CT

In PET and PET–CT studies of infectious diseases, the goal is to detect an abnormally elevated 18F‑FDG (or other radiotracer) uptake that indicates active infection or inflammation, while distinguishing these from non‑infectious physiologic or pathologic processes (e.g., malignancy, degenerative change) that also increase FDG uptake.<cite id="c9d402bb-1">The purpose of FDG-PET/CT is to detect an abnormal elevation of FDG uptake that may indicate ongoing infection or inflammation; specificity is limited by overlap with malignancy and degenerative disease.</cite> <cite id="c9d402bb-0">The specificity of FDG PET/CT remains the crucial issue since it is not able to differentiate infection from marked degenerative disease or malignancy.</cite> <cite id="c9d402bb-2">FDG uptake refers to the amount of radiotracer accumulation; elevated uptake can occur without malignancy and should not be assumed abnormal without clinical correlation.</cite> When performed as a hybrid study, the CT provides anatomic localization, allows soft‑tissue delineation, and enables accurate attenuation correction and bone lesion characterization, thereby improving both diagnostic specificity and quantitation.<cite id="c9d402bb-7">FDG-PET/CT can aid in detecting unsuspected sites of infection, integrating anatomic CT with metabolic PET signals.</cite> 

# Image Acquisition and Fusion Workflow

FDG PET/CT is typically acquired following a 60–90 min dynamic or static whole‑body acquisition after intravenous 18F‑FDG injection, with CT either for attenuation correction (low‑dose CT) or as a separate, fused dataset for anatomic correlation.<cite id="c9d402bb-4">Guidelines for 18F‑FDG PET/CT describe standardized acquisition and interpretation protocols spanning preparation, imaging, and reporting workflows for hybrid studies.</cite> Physiologic uptake foci (e.g., physiologic bowel, salivary glands, heart) and artifact sources (e.g., pectoral muscle bands, blood activity) are recognized normal variants and must be discriminated from pathologic uptake.<cite id="c9d402bb-3">Pictorial and analytical reviews detail musculoskeletal, infective, and inflammatory uptake patterns that can mimic pathology but are normal variants, emphasizing careful differential diagnosis.</cite> <cite id="c9d402bb-8">Reviews of FDG findings associated with procedures and treatments illustrate common benign but uptake‑positive foci that can mimic disease.</cite> Proper CT correlation helps triage focal lesions (nodal, osseous, parenchymal) and verify their nature (granuloma, caseating necrosis vs viable lesion, bone sequestra), which is central in infectious conditions like tuberculosis and osteomyelitis.<cite id="6e65c5b6-2">PET/CT is important in evaluating known or suspected TB, complementing other imaging by combining metabolic and anatomic information.</cite> 

# Qualitative Assessment on PET–CT

After fusion, readers first map the distribution and morphology of uptake on CT, then assess PET signal intensity relative to background, mediastinal blood pool, and involved organs. Focal nodal/cavitary/osteolytic lesions with sharply increased FDG uptake compared to surrounding tissues raise infection/inflammation; diffuse parenchymal “ground‑glass” or confluent mediastinal uptake may reflect interstitial lung disease or systemic inflammation.<cite id="c9d402bb-1">FDG‑PET/CT aims to detect abnormal elevations; overlaps with malignancy and benign inflammatory processes necessitate careful qualitative comparison to surrounding tissues.</cite> The contemporaneous CT is crucial in bone infections to differentiate viable sequestra (“cold on bone” but hot on FDG PET due to granulation tissue) from necrotic/avascular areas and to delineate sinus tracts and bronchial fistulae.<cite id="6e65c5b6-2">FDG PET/CT contributes importantly to TB and bone infection characterization when combined anatomic and metabolic data are considered jointly.</cite> 

# Quantitative Assessment: SUV, MTV, TLG, and Change Over Time

SUV, MTV, and TLG are the main quantitative descriptors used to mark abnormal uptake.

- SUV definitions and interpretation. The SUV normalizes pixel counts to injected dose and acquisition time; SUVmax captures the highest lesion value and is commonly reported in infection/inflammation. However, physiologic background (especially mediastinal blood) and anatomic mass vary, so there are no universal cutoffs for non‑oncologic diseases; clinical context, comparative anatomy, and kinetic behavior are essential.<cite id="e5c21b25-1">There are no general criteria published for inflammatory and infectious disorders; SUV should be used with caution in clinical practice.</cite> <cite id="c9d402bb-2">Patients and clinicians often interpret any high SUV as malignancy, but higher SUVs are not invariably malignant and should be interpreted within context (e.g., infection, inflammation).</cite> Qualitative rules of thumb used in practice include comparing a lesion’s SUV to mediastinal blood and background liver/spleen; if a lesion is similar to or below mediastinal blood, it is less likely to represent malignant/highly active infection.<cite id="5bdb237b-8">Interpretation based on FDG uptake includes comparing lesion uptake to background and mediastinal blood pool thresholds.</cite> 

- Lesion/whole‑body metabolic parameters. Beyond SUVmax, MTV (sum of voxels above a threshold, often 2.5–3.0) and TLG (SUV×volume) summarize burden and metabolic activity of infection. Studies indicate parameter tuning (e.g., SUVmax≈3.5, tissue lesion ratio≈2.0) can optimize discrimination, and TLG shows strong differential power across conditions; when tracking response, reductions in MTV/TLG parallel clinical improvement and can precede size change.<cite id="5bdb237b-6">Suitable thresholds for MTV included SUVmax≈3.5 and tissue lesion ratio≈2.0; TLG with SUVmax–based derivation showed significant differences and strong discriminatory value.</cite> <cite id="5bdb237b-0">SUVs are widely used to assess response in oncology, motivating their adoption in oncologic criteria that are often adapted to other conditions with abnormal FDG uptake.</cite> 

- Kinetics and serial imaging. Short‑term follow‑up may compare SUVmax, MTV, and TLG between early and late post‑treatment scans; in infectious diseases, resolution of uptake—especially outpacing anatomic change on CT—often indicates effective antimicrobial therapy. Established oncology response categories translate to infection: a decrease in lesion uptake to background or below mediastinal blood pool is favorable; stability or increase suggests persistence or inflammation.<cite id="5bdb237b-8">FDG-PET/CT-based response assessment interprets lesion uptake relative to background and mediastinal blood pool; categories include uptake equal to or below background and ≤ mediastinal blood pool uptake as nonprogressive.</cite> <cite id="c9d402bb-5">In fever-of-unknown-origin cohorts, FDG-PET/CT correctly identified infections in almost half of true positives; such performance underscores why serial metabolic change is informative for infectious etiologies.</cite> 

# Tracer Choice and Its Biological Meaning

- 18F‑FDG in infection/inflammation. FDG is widely used because infection/inflammation recruit activated macrophages and neutrophils that take up glucose analog 18F‑FDG; its utility spans osteomyelitis, prosthetic joint infection, endocarditis, and TB, among others.<cite id="e5c21b25-0">FDG-PET/CT has an expanding role in diagnosis and treatment monitoring in diseases of infectious or inflammatory origin.</cite> <cite id="e5c21b25-5">Major indications for 18F‑FDG PET/CT in infection and inflammation include sarcoidosis and peripheral bone osteomyelitis.</cite> Pitfalls include physiologic uptake in granulomas and areas of old disease versus active infection (e.g., caseating necrosis can remain FDG‑avid), necessitating interval imaging and clinical correlation.<cite id="c9d402bb-1">Both infection and inflammation raise FDG, making specificity challenging without clinical and imaging correlation.</cite> <cite id="6e65c5b6-1">In pulmonary TB, granulomas typically demonstrate increased FDG uptake; active foci can be differentiated from old disease by PET/CT, including the use of dual-time or additional imaging to assess temporal change.</cite> 

- 18F‑FLT as a proliferation-focused alternative. 18F‑FLT measures thymidine kinase‑mediated nucleoside uptake associated with cell proliferation, complementing FDG. In infectious lesions, FLT may better reflect viable, proliferating pathogens or granulation tissue; analyses show significant SUV differences across FLT‑avid vs FDG‑avid groups and can predict early response to therapy.<cite id="e5c21b25-3">Differences between [18F]FLT and [18F]FDG uptake show statistically significant differences across SUVmax and SUVmin, indicating distinct biological activity and potential complementary value.</cite> <cite id="e5c21b25-6">FLT PET imaging has been evaluated to predict outcome in terms of locoregional control and disease response, supporting its utility as an early response biomarker.</cite> In practice, FLT is selected when FDG uptake is indeterminate (e.g., high background, immunoprivileged sites) or when proliferative change is the phenotype of interest; FDG–FLT dual‑tracer protocols are advocated in some guidance documents for inflammatory/infectious indications.<cite id="e5c21b25-2">EANM/SNMMI guidance and consensus documents outline procedures for FDG hybrid PET in infection and inflammation and discuss the role of alternative tracers such as FLT for specific indications.</cite> 

# Disease-Specific Patterns and PET–CT Characterization

- Tuberculosis (TB). TB lymph nodes often show focal FDG‑avid intra‑nodal granulomas or caseating necrosis; on PET–CT, nodes >2 cm with central caseous necrosis and increased FDG uptake are highly suggestive of active TB, whereas smaller, minimally enlarged nodes with moderate uptake may reflect systemic or generalized disease.<cite id="6e65c5b6-3">Lymph nodes greater than 2 cm with increased FDG uptake and central caseous necrosis are highly suggestive of active TB.</cite> <cite id="6e65c5b6-0">Mediastino‑hilar lymph nodes can be slightly enlarged with moderate uptake in systemic infection patterns related to TB.</cite> PET–CT improves detection of extrapulmonary TB (e.g., CNS, bone/joint), localizing extra‑thoracic lesions that may be missed on chest imaging alone.<cite id="6e65c5b6-6">FDG-PET can detect extrapulmonary TB involving the central nervous system and joints/bone, beyond the more typical lung and lymph nodes.</cite> 

- Osteomyelitis and abscesses. In pyogenic bone infection, areas of viable sequestra and granulation tissue are FDG‑avid (“hot bones”) despite radiographic necrosis; CT delineates cortical breaches, sequestra, and soft‑tissue tracks, while the PET component quantifies metabolic activity via SUV/TLG to assess disease extent and response to antibiotics. In abscesses, rimming FDG uptake indicates active infection; central necrotic cavities with low to absent FDG may coexist but require correlation with CT and clinical course.<cite id="6e65c5b6-2">PET/CT integrates metabolic evidence of infection with anatomic detail for bone and soft tissue, aiding in the evaluation of osteomyelitis and related infections.</cite> 

- Cardiac and prosthetic‑valve endocarditis (PVE). 18F‑FDG PET–CT detects vegetations, fistulae to pericardium/pleura, and mycotic aneurysms that are often missed on echocardiography; lesions typically have high SUVmax, and response is tracked by SUV decline post‑antibiotics. In PVE, blood activity and cardiac motion can create spillover and artifacts, so careful qualitative assessment against mediastinal blood and surrounding myocardium is required, and delayed imaging or dual‑time point studies can reduce ambiguity.<cite id="c9d402bb-1">Both infection and inflammation elevate FDG; differentiating physiologic cardiac uptake requires comparison to mediastinal blood signal and clinical correlation.</cite> <cite id="c9d402bb-9">FDG PET/CT imaging of cardiovascular infections highlights detection of unsuspected cardiac and vascular foci to guide management.</cite> 

- General inflammatory syndromes (e.g., sarcoidosis, vasculitis). Patchy lung and mediastinal lymph node uptake, paranasal sinuses involvement, retro‑peritoneal lymphadenopathy are typical. SUV thresholds lack universality, but persistent lesion uptake exceeding background/lung physiology with or without CT‑defined structural abnormality increases the likelihood of inflammatory/infectious etiology warranting antimicrobial and clinical follow‑up; SUV decline outpacing imaging correlates supports the choice of infection‑over‑malignancy.<cite id="e5c21b25-5">Indications span sarcoidosis and other inflammatory conditions; PET/CT detects sites of active disease that can be missed by anatomic modalities.</cite> <cite id="e5c21b25-1">Because there are no universal SUV criteria for inflammatory/infectious diseases, clinical correlation and pattern recognition are emphasized in guidelines.</cite> 

# Practical Reporting and Clinical Correlation

Reporting typically combines qualitative distribution with quantitative summaries (SUVmax±SEM, MTV, TLG), a depiction of mediastinal/blood‑pool reference levels, and a kinetic assessment of change at follow‑up. In oncology‑derived criteria, the presence of FDG uptake similar to or below background liver/spleen and ≤ mediastinal blood pool often classifies disease as nonprogressive, but these rules were optimized for tumors and are applied cautiously to infection, where biologic uptake patterns differ.<cite id="5bdb237b-8">Response interpretations include categories like uptake similar to or below background and ≤ mediastinal blood pool uptake as nonprogressive; these thresholds derive from oncologic optimization but are interpreted cautiously in infection.</cite> <cite id="c9d402bb-0">Specificity remains a core challenge in FDG PET/CT, underscoring the need for clinical correlation to distinguish infection from neoplasia or degenerative disease.</cite> 

When a focal lesion is FDG‑avid, the CT side is examined for the degree of calcification, central necrosis, cortical expansion/penetration, sinus/ fistula communication, and soft‑tissue edema; combined with SUV kinetics, this triages likely active infection versus chronic granuloma or post‑treatment fibrosis. If uptake is indeterminate, a repeat PET or alternative tracer (e.g., FLT) can add biological specificity, or targeted microbiology (culture, PCR) is pursued.<cite id="6e65c5b6-3">Central caseous necrosis within enlarged nodes with increased FDG uptake suggests active TB, guiding biopsy or targeted therapy decisions.</cite> <cite id="e5c21b25-3">Differences in FLT vs FDG uptake distributions suggest complementary sensitivity to proliferation versus energy metabolism, supporting dual‑tracer strategies in inflammation/infection where FDG is ambiguous.</cite> 

# Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

- Do not assume any uptake equals cancer; physiologic uptake (e.g., lymph nodes in TB, sinuses, gastric mucosa, bowel) and benign post‑procedural changes are common mimics; compare to mediastinal blood and involved organs and consider dual‑time point protocols to show lesion‑specific clearance.<cite id="c9d402bb-2">There is a perception that anything with uptake is abnormal; FDG uptake varies physiologically and must be interpreted in context.</cite> <cite id="c9d402bb-3">Pictorial reviews enumerate musculoskeletal, infective, and inflammatory patterns mimicking pathology—emphasizing that many are normal variants on PET.</cite> 

- Account for attenuation and anatomic mass; rely on CT‑based attenuation maps for quantitation and for identifying osseous lesions where FDG can be high despite avascularity (caseous necrosis), integrating CT morphology with PET metabolic context.<cite id="c9d402bb-4">Guideline frameworks describe how attenuation correction and standardized workflows support accurate interpretation.</cite> <cite id="6e65c5b6-2">Joint PET/CT reading is important when active TB or osteomyelitis present with metabolic activity despite avascular necrosis and structural bone destruction.</cite> 

- Use kinetic change; metabolic decrease (e.g., SUV/MTV/TLG reductions) often exceeds size or anatomic change on CT, and early decreases argue for infection rather than malignancy in appropriate clinical settings—reinforcing serial PET in treatment monitoring.<cite id="5bdb237b-8">Follow-up categories rely on lesion uptake relative to background and mediastinal blood; uptake reduction is central to response assessment and can precede anatomic change on imaging.</cite> <cite id="c9d402bb-5">In clinical cohorts with fever of unknown origin, the distribution of true-positive causes shows infections are a major component of FDG-avid disease and benefit from PET/CT detection.</cite> 

# Summary Checklists for Study Evaluation

- Qualitative: identify and map all focal FDG‑avid lesions; correlate with CT morphology; differentiate physiologic (salivary, gastric, bowel) and artifact from pathologic uptake.<cite id="c9d402bb-3">Many infective and physiologic uptake patterns are normal variants on PET; careful pictorial correlation is key to avoid overdiagnosis.</cite> 

- Quantitative: report SUVmax, reference background/mediastinal blood; measure MTV and TLG; track percent change or absolute delta at follow‑up to judge response; consider FLT in indeterminate cases to probe proliferative activity; do not use universal thresholds across diseases.<cite id="5bdb237b-6">Threshold selections (e.g., SUVmax≈3.5 for MTV, TLG-based parameters with high discriminatory value) aid in differentiating disease activity and can guide follow‑up.</cite> <cite id="e5c21b25-1">There are no general SUV criteria for infectious/inflammatory diseases; apply SUV cautiously with pattern and clinical context.</cite> 

- Clinical integration: pair PET–CT with clinical course, labs, microbiology, and targeted procedures; in TB and osteomyelitis, recognize patterns of nodal/cavitary/bone uptake and use SUV decline to assess antimicrobial efficacy; in cardiac/PVE, combine qualitative masking of physiologic blood with kinetic change; consider FLT as an adjunct to clarify proliferative vs metabolic phenotypes in nonspecific uptake.<cite id="6e65c5b6-3">Central caseous lymph nodes with increased FDG uptake suggest active TB, guiding targeted management and follow‑up.</cite> <cite id="e5c21b25-6">FLT PET can predict outcomes and early response, supporting its role in infectious disease settings when FDG is indeterminate or when proliferative activity is the target of interest.</cite> <cite id="c9d402bb-7">FDG-PET/CT aids in detection of unsuspected infection sites, lowering relapse rates when used to tailor therapy.</cite>

Summary
PET/CT improves the delineation of tumor extent in head and neck cancer by capturing functionally active disease beyond what is seen on anatomy alone, with multiple studies demonstrating larger PET-defined volumes than pathological or CT/MRI GTVs and with variable but reproducible contours when protocols and fusion are used.<cite id="bf6ede03-3">The mean tumor volume defined by PET, MRI and combined information was larger than the pathologically defined tumor volume. <cite id="bf6ede03-5">Quality assessment frameworks emphasize technical factors affecting PET/CT accuracy in HNC</cite>. Treatment planning studies show PET/CT-based replanning and adaptive recontouring can improve target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing, with modality evidence that PET/CT detects additional nodal and primary disease to inform risk-adapted margins and dose painting.<cite id="3592d27a-5">FDG PET/CT offers improved detection of primary and nodal disease for HNC radiotherapy planning</cite><cite id="3592d27a-4">Adaptive radiotherapy re-planning addresses anatomical changes to improve target coverage and OAR sparing</cite>. Prognostically, PET features (metabolic tumor volume, SUVmax, TLG) predict survival and early response, and PET follow-up can confer survival benefit in oropharyngeal disease, supporting PET’s impact on prognosis and management adaptation.<cite id="943df75f-1">Meta-analysis shows MTV and TLG of 18F-FDG PET predict outcomes in HNC</cite><cite id="943df75f-3">PET/CT follow-up may confer survival benefit in HNC, with higher 3-year OS in oropharyngeal tumors</cite>.

1) Evidence that PET/CT accurately delineates tumor volume
- PET captures biological spread and metabolic activity that exceed anatomical extent. In HNC, PET-based tumor volumes have been systematically larger than pathologic GTV and often MRI or CT-informed GTV, supporting PET’s functional coverage during planning and replanning.<cite id="bf6ede03-3">The mean tumor volume defined by PET, MRI and combined information exceeded pathologically defined tumor volume</cite>. Automated segmentation methods based on PET-derived thresholds have long been used to delineate PET tumor regions in HNC, reflecting maturation of contouring approaches and reproducibility of the concept.<cite id="bf6ede03-8">PET-based tumor regions were delineated using automatic contouring at progressively higher SUV thresholds</cite>. Quality frameworks emphasize optimizing image quality and acquisition/processing to maximize PET–CT fusion accuracy for volume definition in HNC, reinforcing its role as a robust imaging modality for target delineation.<cite id="bf6ede03-5">Recent PET/CT quality assessment frameworks with focus on HNC imaging design and QA</cite>.

- Fusion improves reproducibility vs PET-only. Multiple observer studies show significant interobserver and intermodality variability for GTV delineation; fusion-based PET/CT contouring reduces discordance and supports standardized definitions compared to PET-only or CT-only approaches, prompting the need for contouring protocols.<cite id="9f73781e-0">Comparisons across modalities show interobserver and intermodality differences in HNC GTV delineation</cite><cite id="9f73781e-2">Significant GTV differences found between multiple observers on PET/CT fusion; delineation protocols are needed</cite><cite id="9f73781e-9">Observer variability across modalities in HNC GTV delineation supports need for protocols</cite>. PET/MRI fusion can further improve GTV delineation relative to CT alone for HNC, supporting the broader class of “fusion imaging” approaches in accurate delineation.<cite id="9f73781e-6">PET/MRI vs planning CT for HNC GTV delineation: improved delineation with fusion</cite>.

- PET-based and AI-assisted contouring: evaluation and reproducibility. Deep learning for PET GTV delineation has been clinically evaluated in HNC, indicating feasibility for reproducible, observer-independent definition of PET GTV, which can mitigate variability and improve speed and consistency.<cite id="bf6ede03-1">State-of-the-art deep learning methods evaluated for HNC PET GTV delineation</cite>. Prospective evaluations have also assessed the benefit of adding PET or gadolinium-enhanced MRI to automated GTV tools, demonstrating that fusion with functional imaging improves delineation compared to CT alone.<cite id="9f73781e-4">Including PET or T1-Gd MRI in automated GTV segmentation improves delineation</cite>.

2) Impact on treatment planning: risk-adapted target volumes and adaptive radiotherapy
- PET/CT during planning detects additional nodal and primary disease, enabling more complete GTV and CTV (including high-risk CTV) definition and informing PTV margins and dose painting. Studies show PET/CT reveals more nodal and primary disease than CT, thus improving risk-adapted target volumes compared to CT-only planning.<cite id="3592d27a-5">FDG PET/CT improves detection of primary and nodal disease for HNC radiotherapy planning</cite>. High-risk CTVs exhibit higher delineation variability, highlighting the importance of PET-informed protocols for consistent expansion into high-risk microscopic zones, a key step for biological adaptation of PTVs.<cite id="9f73781e-3">High-risk CTV showed higher variability than medium-risk CTV; presence of GTV plus PET support affects delineation</cite>.

- Replanning and adaptive therapy: PET-informed rescans/recontours/replans improve coverage and OAR sparing. In HNC, repeated anatomy changes during IMRT/VMAT make adaptive replanning essential; rescanning with PET/CT can refine GTV/CTV/PTV after tumor regression, preserving coverage while reducing doses to shrinking parotids and fusing residual disease and nodal basins visualized by PET.<cite id="3592d27a-0">Adaptive RT via rescanning, recontouring, and replanning with VMAT is essential when anatomical/positional variations occur in HNC</cite><cite id="3592d27a-4">Adaptive re-planning improves target coverage and OAR sparing based on anatomical changes</cite>. Proton therapy literature emphasizes the value of PET to capture microscopic spread; PET-adapted proton plans can add partial nodal marginal dose to involved basins and sparingly dose non-involved parotids, capitalizing on proton range modulation; this concept is reflected by guidelines recommending PET-CT for detecting distant metastases or second primaries for multimodality planning in HNC.<cite id="3592d27a-4">PET-CT can detect distant metastases or other primaries for HNC multimodality management</cite>. Although individual case replans illustrate how small GTV-to-CTV margins (e.g., 3 mm) are commonly built on GTV to create PTV-72 in IMRT and adapted on follow-up imaging, functional input like PET can refine risk-adapted PTVs beyond rigid margins.<cite id="3592d27a-1">IMRT head and neck case report outlines GTV to CTV-72 and CTV-56 margins; planning margins built from GTV and adapted over time</cite>.

- Practical planning cautions and integration. Clinical planning guidance warns that PET should not be the sole modality to define GTV; instead, high-risk GTV can be derived from PET signals integrated with other modalities to ensure safe biological expansion and verify dose coverage of residual disease risk after each resection.<cite id="3592d27a-8">FDG-PET should not be used as the sole modality for GTV definition; high-risk GTV volumes could be defined based on all available modalities</cite>. In nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal disease, PET/CT staging affects nodal basin inclusion, and fusion-based delineation correlates better with histopathology, which supports PET-informed CTV design in the absence of residual gross disease on MRI/CT.<cite id="bf6ede03-9">Clinical applications include identification of synchronous second primaries and metastases, influencing CTV design</cite><cite id="bf6ede03-3">PET-defined volumes exceed pathology volumes on average, impacting CTV expansion</cite>.

3) Impact on prognosis: staging, early response, and survival
- PET-derived tumor burden predicts outcomes. Multiple studies and meta-analyses find metabolic tumor volume (MTV), SUVmax, and total lesion glycolysis (TLG) independently predict overall survival (OS), disease-free survival (DFS), and locoregional control in HNC. <cite id="943df75f-1">A meta-analysis in HNSCC demonstrates prognostic value of MTV and TLG from FDG-PET</cite><cite id="943df75f-2">Prognostic utility of FDG-PET metabolic parameters in HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers has been established</cite><cite id="943df75f-4">FDG-PET metabolic tumor volume and TLG predict outcome in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma</cite><cite id="943df75f-8">Lower MTV thresholds (<30 cm3) correlate with significantly better 5-year OS and DFS</cite>. In metastatic disease, MTV-based PET metrics have been linked to survival differences, including in nasopharyngeal carcinoma cohorts, supporting the generalizability of PET metabolic burden as a prognostic biomarker.<cite id="943df75f-0">FDG-PET metabolic tumor volume predicted survival in metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma</cite>.

- PET during therapy predicts early response and recurrence. FDG PET performed during radiotherapy functions as an early biomarker, with metabolic response predicting subsequent recurrence, guiding possible salvage strategies and justifying risk-adapted boost or nodal dose adjustments in selected cases.<cite id="bf6ede03-7">FDG-PET during radiotherapy can serve as an early response biomarker to predict recurrence in HNC</cite>. Prospective follow-up cohorts integrating PET/CT at risk timepoints demonstrate improved survival when PET abnormalities are addressed (e.g., targeted boost, nodal irradiation, or early referral to surgery), indicating PET’s prognostic utility in dynamic management.<cite id="943df75f-3">Oral cavity/oropharyngeal patients undergoing FDG-PET/CT follow-up had higher 3-year OS, suggesting survival benefits from PET-informed management</cite><cite id="943df75f-5">FDG PET metabolic parameters stratify prognosis across HPV-positive vs negative groups</cite>.

- Delineation-to-prognosis links. Because PET-defined volumes (GTV/CTV/PTV) are larger than pathology on average, PET-based expansions capture more microscopic disease, which may help explain observed survival advantages when metabolic burden is high and when risk-adapted replanning is undertaken; standardized protocols and fusion mitigate variability, improving the consistency of risk-based planning that underlies prognosis.<cite id="bf6ede03-3">PET, MRI and combined approaches defined larger mean volumes than pathologic GTV</cite><cite id="9f73781e-2">Fusion-based PET/CT delineation yields more consistent GTVs than individual modalities, supporting prognostic-consistent risk coverage</cite><cite id="3592d27a-4">Adaptive replanning based on PET changes improves therapeutic risk coverage over time</cite>.

4) Practical considerations and limits
- Observer and modality variability remain clinically relevant. Interobserver and intermodality differences are substantial for HNC GTV and can affect PTV margins; therefore, institutional contouring protocols, explicit definitions of high-risk CTV, and use of PET–CT fusion are recommended to standardize and improve the accuracy of PET-informed target delineation.<cite id="9f73781e-0">Significant interobserver and intermodality differences exist for HNC GTV on PET and CT</cite><cite id="9f73781e-2">GTV differences and need for delineation protocol on PET/CT fusion</cite><cite id="3592d27a-8">Avoid PET as the sole GTV modality; integrate modalities to define high-risk GTV</cite>.

- Fusion modality choice and quality. PET/MRI can improve fusion-based delineation relative to CT for HNC, and PET-only, PET-CT, and PET-MRI each have trade-offs in soft-tissue contrast and bone/parotid delineation; overall PET–CT fusion plus QA processes (scatter correction, time-of-flight, appropriate SUV normalization) are key to accuracy and reproducibility.<cite id="9f73781e-6">PET/MRI vs CT for HNC GTV delineation indicates fusion superiority</cite><cite id="bf6ede03-5">Quality assessment frameworks emphasize PET/CT design and QA impacts on HNC imaging</cite>.

- Adaptive workflow integration. Because HNC anatomy shifts with weight loss and tissue contraction during IMRT/VMAT, serial PET (on-treatment) can guide biological adaptation of PTVs; implementation requires time-efficient re-contouring/replanning pathways and communication with nuclear medicine for prompt acquisition, with parotid sparing balanced against nodal risk.<cite id="3592d27a-0">Adaptive radiotherapy via rescanning, recontouring, and replanning with VMAT is essential for HNC anatomical/positional variations</cite><cite id="bf6ede03-7">PET during therapy predicts recurrence, enabling risk-adapted interventions</cite>.

Actionable implications
- For new HNC RT plans, incorporate PET-CT fusion-informed GTV/CTV and PTV delineation, expand CTVs around PET-avid high-risk regions, and consider dose painting to macroscopic/functional disease; enforce institutional contouring protocols to control variability and use AI-assisted tools to standardize PET GTV contours.<cite id="3592d27a-5">FDG PET/CT improves detection of nodal/primary disease for planning</cite><cite id="9f73781e-2">Contouring protocols reduce variability on PET/CT fusion</cite><cite id="bf6ede03-1">Deep learning supports HNC PET GTV delineation</cite>.

- Use PET-adapted replanning if there is significant tumor regression or anatomical change to preserve nodal coverage and avoid parotid over/under-dosing; proactively schedule on-treatment PET when early response biomarkers are available to guide risk-adapted boosts or nodal field adjustments and salvage pathways.<cite id="3592d27a-0">VMAT ART required upon anatomical/positional changes</cite><cite id="bf6ede03-7">PET during RT predicts recurrence and informs response-based adaptation</cite>.

- Stratify prognosis using baseline PET metrics (MTV, TLG, SUVmax) and confirm staging with PET/CT; integrate these into prognostic nomograms and shared decision-making, and consider PET follow-up in high-risk patients to detect biochemical failures and improve outcomes.<cite id="943df75f-1">MTV and TLG predict outcomes in HNSCC</cite><cite id="943df75f-3">PET/CT follow-up associated with higher OS</cite>.

Evidence strength and remaining gaps
- Convergent evidence across comparative delineation studies, observer variability analyses, prospective planning/adaptive workflows, and meta-analyses supports PET/CT’s accuracy in delineating functional tumor extent and its benefit in risk-adapted planning and prognosis in HNC.<cite id="bf6ede03-3">PET volumes exceed pathology GTVs</cite><cite id="3592d27a-5">PET/CT improves disease detection for planning</cite><cite id="943df75f-1">Meta-analysis: MTV/TLG predict outcomes</cite>. Remaining gaps include harmonization of PET-to-CTV dose strategies between modalities (IMRT vs proton), standardized PET-only versus fusion contouring guidelines, and prospective randomized comparisons of CT-only vs PET-informed risk-adapted plans in contemporary HNC cohorts; current evidence is largely retrospective or protocol-driven with strong signal detection for adaptation and prognostic value.<cite id="943df75f-8">MTV cutoffs stratify OS/DFS</cite><cite id="3592d27a-8">Clinical guidance cautions against PET alone for GTV</cite>.

Overview and scope

Bone remodeling is a cell–cell and cell–matrix dialogue between osteoclasts, which resorb bone, and osteoblasts/osteocytes, which form bone; osteocytes act as mechanosensors that regulate remodeling by controlling osteoclast activity through the RANK–RANKL pathway in concert with osteoblast-derived osteoprotegerin (OPG). <cite id="a42488de-0">Osteocytes are mechano-sensors that control bone modeling and remodeling via regulation of osteoclasts through the receptor activator NF-κB (RANK)</cite><cite id="a42488de-4">Osteoclasts resorb damaged bone and interact with osteoblasts, which are recruited by growth factors and degraded matrix proteins</cite>. The thyroid and pituitary glands regulate this remodeling at the cellular level by altering osteoblast and osteoclast differentiation, gene expression programs, and osteocyte-mediated feedback, thereby shifting the balance of bone formation versus resorption. <cite id="a42488de-1">Thyroid hormones play significant roles in bone growth and development, and thyroid imbalance impairs bone homeostasis</cite><cite id="a42488de-2">Bone remodeling is performed by osteoclasts and osteoblasts under regulatory direction</cite><cite id="a42488de-3">TSH directly affects both osteoblastic bone formation and osteoclastic bone resorption</cite>.

Thyroid hormones control osteoclast and osteoblast biology

Thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) enter bone cells and act via thyroid hormone receptors (TRs; TRα and TRβ) that heterodimerize with RXR, bind thyroid hormone response elements (TREs), and regulate osteoclast and osteoblast transcriptional programs. <cite id="a42488de-1">Thyroid hormones critically regulate skeletal development and remodeling; dysfunctions disrupt bone homeostasis</cite><cite id="a42488de-6">Thyroid hormones regulate bone remodeling and mineralization, and thyroid status affects bone strength</cite>. In osteoclastogenesis, thyroid hormone accelerates differentiation, increases resorption activity, and upregulates osteoclast markers such as tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP), at least partly by elevating c-Fos in osteoclast precursor cells; these effects can occur independently of the canonical RANKL–RANK pathway, pointing to TR-dependent transcriptional priming of osteoclastogenesis. <cite id="a42488de-5">Thyroid hormone stimulates osteoclast differentiation via a mechanism independent of RANKL–RANK interaction</cite><cite id="d097deb1-3">T3 increases osteoclast differentiation in part by upregulating c-Fos protein in osteoclast precursor cells</cite>.

Downstream, osteoclastogenesis is governed by a feed‑forward transcriptional network: NFATc1 is the master regulator of osteoclast differentiation and is activated by c-Fos, NF-κB, and MAPK signaling; it drives expression of key resorption genes including TRAP and cathepsin K, and NFATc1 activity is necessary for osteoclastogenesis and function. <cite id="d097deb1-0">NFATc1 is regulated via multiple mechanisms during osteoclast differentiation</cite><cite id="d097deb1-2">NFATc1 and c-Fos promote transcription required for osteoclastogenesis; OPG from osteoblasts competes with RANKL for RANK binding</cite><cite id="d097deb1-1">RANKL signaling increases NFATc1, the master regulator of osteoclastogenesis</cite><cite id="d097deb1-7">NFATc1 regulates downstream genes such as CTSK and TRAP to promote osteoclast differentiation</cite>. Thyroid hormone converges upstream on this axis by inducing c-Fos and activating NFATc1-responsive programs, thereby enhancing osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption. <cite id="d097deb1-3">T3 elevates c-Fos in osteoclast precursors to promote differentiation</cite><cite id="d097deb1-2">OPG competes with RANKL for RANK, providing osteoblast control over osteoclastogenesis</cite>.

In osteoblasts and the bone matrix, thyroid hormones are required for normal differentiation and mineralization programs via TR-controlled transcription; thyroid hormone receptor knockout mice are protected from hyperthyroidism-driven increases in osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, preserving cortical bone mass and strength, underscoring a direct role for nuclear TR signaling in skeletal adaptation to thyroid status. <cite id="a42488de-8">Thra knockout preserves cortical bone mass and strength by obstructing increased bone‑resorbing activity during hyperthyroidism</cite>. In the osteocyte–osteoclast feedback loop, thyroid status influences osteocyte-mediated RANKL expression that instructs osteoclasts, contributing to remodeling rates. <cite id="a42488de-0">Osteocytes regulate osteoclasts through RANK to drive bone remodeling</cite>. Clinically, thyrotoxicosis elevates bone resorption, causing bone loss, whereas hypothyroid states reduce bone turnover with increased risk of impaired mineralization, reflecting thyroid hormone’s bidirectional control of formation and resorption. <cite id="a42488de-6">Thyroid hormones are key regulators of bone remodeling and mineralization; thyroid dysfunction alters bone strength</cite>.

Pituitary control via the GH/IGF‑1 axis and growth plate chondrocytes

The pituitary directs bone remodeling indirectly through the growth hormone (GH)–insulin‑like growth factor 1 (IGF‑1) axis, which couples longitudinal growth and skeletal remodeling. IGF‑1 receptor (IGF1R) signaling in osteochondral units controls hypertrophic chondrocyte differentiation and matrix mineralization, enabling endochondral ossification and shaping the osteoblast environment during skeletal growth; osteoblast transcriptional programs (Runx2, Sp7/Osterix) integrate these signals to form mature bone. <cite id="f501b3b6-1">IGF1R signaling regulates osterix expression and cartilage matrix mineralization during endochondral ossification</cite><cite id="f501b3b6-0">GH and IGF-1 regulate somatic growth, metabolism, and many aspects of aging</cite>. Mechanistically, GH/IGF signaling engages PI3K–AKT/mTOR and Wnt/β‑catenin pathways in osteochondral cells to sustain chondrocyte proliferation and hypertrophy, modulate osteoblast maturation, and regulate sclerostin/osteocalcin endocrine loops that couple bone formation to mechanical loading. <cite id="f501b3b6-7">The PI3K pathway controls endochondral bone growth by regulating hypertrophic chondrocyte differentiation</cite><cite id="c5f885c6-3">Osteocytes secrete sclerostin, which inhibits Wnt signaling and suppresses bone formation</cite><cite id="c5f885c6-4">Sclerostin and osteocalcin functions as bone‑produced hormones illustrate endocrine feedback on bone metabolism</cite>. Cross‑talk with thyroid hormones emerges at several levels: thyroid hormone receptor signaling in osteochondral cells promotes maturation cues while also upregulating c‑Fos and NFATc1 pathways, and TH receptor knockout mitigates hyperthyroid bone loss, indicating a balance between somatic growth signals (GH/IGF) and thyroid hormone programs during remodeling. <cite id="a42488de-8">Thra deficiency protects from hyperthyroidism-driven bone loss</cite><cite id="f501b3b6-1">IGF1R signaling integrates into osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation</cite>.

Direct pituitary effects of TSH on bone cells

Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) from the pituitary has direct regulatory effects on bone remodeling components: it stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption and promotes osteoblastic bone formation, indicating crosstalk between pituitary thyroid-axis signaling and bone cell gene programs outside purely endocrine thyroid hormone secretion. <cite id="a42488de-3">TSH is a negative regulator acting on both osteoclasts (resorption) and osteoblasts (formation)</cite>. At the signaling level, TSH can activate cAMP/protein kinase A or alternative transcriptional circuits in target bone cells, modulating osteoblast Wnt/Runx2 programs and osteoclast RANKL responsiveness; while detailed receptor-level mechanisms are incompletely defined in vivo, the direction of effect supports direct modulation of osteoblast and osteoclast activity via intracellular kinase cascades. <cite id="a42488de-3">Evidence shows direct effects of TSH on osteoblastic bone formation and osteoclastic bone resorption</cite>.

Integrating cell types: osteocytes, osteoblasts, and osteoclasts

The osteocyte–osteoblast–osteoclast network executes endocrine signals by translating mechanical and hormonal cues into local remodeling programs. Osteocytes sense strain and load, regulate RANKL production to license osteoclast activity, and orchestrate osteoblast recruitment via matrix-degradation signals and growth factors; thyroid hormone shifts this network by altering osteocyte and osteoblast gene expression and by enhancing osteoclast precursor activation via c‑Fos/NFATc1, favoring resorption when thyroid status is high, or reducing formation/mineralization when status is low. <cite id="a42488de-0">Osteocytes control remodeling by regulating osteoclasts via RANK</cite><cite id="d097deb1-2">Osteoblast-derived OPG competes with RANKL for RANK to modulate osteoclastogenesis</cite><cite id="d097deb1-3">Thyroid hormone drives c-Fos-dependent osteoclast differentiation and TRAP expression</cite><cite id="c5f885c6-3">Sclerostin from osteocytes blocks Wnt to inhibit bone formation</cite>. During skeletal development, pituitary GH/IGF-1 programs endochondral ossification by controlling chondrocyte hypertrophy and osteochondral matrix mineralization while thyroid hormone coordinates systemic maturation; in postnatal bone, these pathways intersect to tune coupling between bone resorption “preparation” and osteoblast “formation,” with clinical phenotypes reflecting skewed balances when either axis is perturbed. <cite id="f501b3b6-1">IGF1R signaling in osteochondral units governs hypertrophy and mineralization</cite><cite id="c5f885c6-0">Runx2 and Sp7 are essential transcription factors for osteoblast differentiation and bone formation</cite>.

Cellular readouts and examples of endocrine control in action

- Osteoclasts: increased nuclear NFATc1 and c‑Fos, elevated TRAP and cathepsin K expression, enhanced TRAP+ multinucleated cell formation, and increased resorption pits when thyroid hormone is high; conversely, thyrotoxicosis presents with bone loss from heightened resorption. <cite id="d097deb1-0">NFATc1 regulation defines osteoclast differentiation</cite><cite id="d097deb1-7">NFATc1 induces CTSK and TRAP to promote resorption</cite><cite id="a42488de-5">T3 stimulates osteoclast differentiation independently of RANKL–RANK</cite><cite id="a42488de-6">Thyroid hormones regulate bone remodeling and strength; thyroid dysfunction alters bone structure</cite>.
- Osteoblasts/osteocytes: thyroid hormone receptor loss attenuates hyperthyroid bone resorption and preserves cortical bone, implying intact TR signaling is required to drive nuclear transcription of osteoblast/osteocyte genes that coordinate mineralization and remodeling; in contrast, GH/IGF-1 signaling upregulates osteoblast maturation via IGF1R→PI3K/AKT and Wnt/Runx2/Sp7 pathways, supporting bone formation. <cite id="a42488de-8">Thra knockout preserves cortical bone and strength under hyperthyroid stress</cite><cite id="f501b3b6-6">IGF signaling directly and indirectly controls osteoblast growth, survival, and differentiation</cite><cite id="c5f885c6-6">Osterix acts downstream of Runx2 to produce mature osteoblasts that express osteocalcin</cite>.
- Growth plate and remodeling coupling: IGF1R signaling integrates chondrocyte hypertrophy and matrix mineralization (endochondral remodeling), while osteoblasts resorb the template and deposit bone; thyroid hormones modulate this timing and extent by altering chondrocyte and osteoblast programs. <cite id="f501b3b6-1">IGF1R signaling regulates Osterix and cartilage matrix mineralization during endochondral ossification</cite><cite id="d097deb1-3">Thyroid hormone upregulates c-Fos and osteoclast TRAP</cite>.

Clinical phenotypes that anchor mechanisms

Human and experimental phenotypes reflect the mechanistic map. Hypothyroid states show increased osteoblast activity and reduced bone formation efficiency (impaired mineralization) with overall skeletal fragility; hyperthyroid states exhibit high osteoclast activity and accelerated bone loss, consistent with enhanced c‑Fos/NFATc1 and TRAP expression. Interventional evidence shows that TH receptor signaling is necessary to transmit hyperthyroid catabolic drive, and that suppressing TSH reduces pituitary-driven bone remodeling components. <cite id="a42488de-1">Thyroid hormones are crucial to bone growth; imbalance impairs homeostasis</cite><cite id="a42488de-6">Thyroid hormones regulate bone remodeling and mineralization and affect bone strength</cite><cite id="a42488de-3">TSH has direct stimulating effects on bone formation and resorption</cite><cite id="a42488de-8">Thra knockout mitigates hyperthyroid bone loss, preserving bone mass and strength</cite>.

Molecular circuits and crosstalk

- Nuclear receptor control: TR–RXR heterodimers in osteoblasts/osteocytes bind TREs to regulate Runx2/Sp7, osteocalcin, sclerostin/osteoclastogenic cues. In osteoclast precursors, TR activation induces c‑Fos (and possibly c‑Jun), driving NFATc1-dependent gene expression (TRAP, CTSK) and independent of RANKL–RANK in part, suggesting two modes of osteoclast licensing: paracrine/RANKL-OPG signaling versus receptor-mediated transcriptional priming. <cite id="d097deb1-3">Thyroid hormone increases osteoclast differentiation via c-Fos upregulation</cite><cite id="d097deb1-1">RANKL elevates NFATc1, master regulator of osteoclastogenesis</cite><cite id="a42488de-5">Thyroid hormone stimulates osteoclast differentiation independently of RANKL–RANK</cite>.
- Growth factor–Wnt coupling: pituitary GH/IGF-1 engages IGF1R→PI3K/AKT/mTOR to promote hypertrophic chondrocyte survival and mineralization, aligning with Wnt/β-catenin–Runx2/Sp7 programs in osteoblasts and sclerostin-mediated brakes from osteocytes; thyroid hormone converges with these pathways by modulating osteoblast/osteocyte gene expression and by enhancing osteoclastogenic transcription factors, shifting the remodeling balance. <cite id="f501b3b6-7">PI3K signaling controls hypertrophic chondrocyte differentiation and endochondral bone growth</cite><cite id="c5f885c6-3">Osteocyte sclerostin inhibits Wnt to suppress bone formation</cite><cite id="f501b3b6-6">IGF signaling pathway directly and indirectly controls osteoblast growth, survival, and differentiation</cite>.
- Osteocyte hub: via RANKL/OPG, osteocytes license or suppress osteoclastogenesis and coordinate osteoblast recruitment. Thyroid hormones alter osteocyte RANKL output and osteoblast responsiveness, integrating systemic endocrine status into local remodeling. <cite id="d097deb1-2">OPG competes with RANKL for RANK, limiting osteoclastogenesis</cite><cite id="a42488de-0">Osteocytes regulate osteoclasts through RANK to control remodeling</cite>.

Summary of cellular-level regulation

- Thyroid hormones increase bone resorption when in excess by directly acting on osteoclast precursors to elevate c‑Fos and activate NFATc1-driven gene expression (TRAP, cathepsin K), thereby accelerating osteoclast differentiation and resorption; in parallel, nuclear TR–RXR signaling in osteoblasts/osteocytes adjusts osteogenic and mineralization genes and can preserve bone structure when protective against over-resorption. <cite id="d097deb1-3">Thyroid hormone elevates c-Fos to promote osteoclast differentiation</cite><cite id="d097deb1-7">NFATc1 controls TRAP/CTSK expression and osteoclast function</cite><cite id="a42488de-5">Thyroid hormone can promote osteoclast differentiation independent of RANKL–RANK</cite><cite id="a42488de-8">Thra loss protects bones from hyperthyroid-driven resorption</cite>.
- The pituitary tunes remodeling through GH/IGF-1–driven chondrocyte hypertrophy and osteochondral mineralization, engaging IGF1R→PI3K/AKT and Wnt/Runx2/Sp7 programs in osteochondral units, and via direct TSH signals that modulate osteoblast and osteoclast activity, altering the coupling between formation and resorption and thereby skeletal growth and mass. <cite id="f501b3b6-1">IGF1R signaling regulates Osterix and cartilage matrix mineralization in endochondral ossification</cite><cite id="f501b3b6-7">PI3K signaling regulates hypertrophic chondrocyte differentiation</cite><cite id="c5f885c6-6">Osterix promotes mature osteoblasts expressing osteocalcin</cite><cite id="a42488de-3">TSH has direct effects on bone formation and resorption</cite>.
- The net effect depends on the interplay between these inputs and local osteocyte feedback via RANKL/RANK and sclerostin–Wnt to maintain homeostasis and adapt to systemic endocrine states. <cite id="c5f885c6-3">Osteocyte sclerostin inhibits Wnt to limit bone formation</cite><cite id="d097deb1-2">Osteoblast OPG vs RANKL balances osteoclastogenesis</cite>.

Open questions and uncertainties

Key uncertainties include isoform-specific, cell-type–resolved DNA binding and chromatin programs of TR (TRα vs TRβ) in osteoblasts/osteocytes and the pituitary TSH receptor signaling cascade in bone cells in vivo.
