- EAC surveillance advantage of integrated approaches: For EAC, BE-directed biomarker algorithms (miRNA and methylation) and BEU-driven imaging workflows deliver early interception around high-grade dysplasia; these approaches provide incremental AUC gains over serum proteins alone. <cite id="0aa76913-5">miRNA biomarkers support early detection and triage in BE surveillance</cite> <cite id="df4756dc-8">Methylation panels stratify BE progression, enabling earlier intervention</cite>.
- Imaging complements molecular tests: AI-assisted endoscopy achieves high in-scope sensitivity and can prioritize areas for molecular sampling, improving overall AUC and reducing interval cancers in surveillance programs. <cite id="70ff24e8-4">Computer-aided detection improves early detection and classification</cite> <cite id="0aa76913-0">Advanced endoscopy and AI are recommended complements to blood tests for early diagnosis</cite>.

Markers to prioritize for early detection (supported by AUC evidence)

- Highest-impact noninvasive options: 
  - cfDNA methylation multi-locus panels (plasma/serum): High AUC for early-stage EC with strong NPV potential in screening cohorts; ongoing multicenter validation to generalize performance across populations and histologies. <cite id="df4756dc-4">cfDNA methylation demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy for early-stage esophageal cancer and serves as a promising noninvasive screening tool</cite>.
  - Multi-protein serum panels including SCC‑Ag context with PBK/KIF2C and device-enabled sampling: Very high reported AUCs in select cohorts with external validation in progress; strong early-detection yield (~90%) in a minimally invasive strategy in high-risk patients. <cite id="0aa76913-7">Serum PBK (AUC 96.5%) and KIF2C (AUC 98.8%)</cite> <cite id="0aa76913-3">High success rate (~90%) using device + biomarker strategy</cite>.
- Intermediate performers suitable for EAC/BE:
  - miRNA panels (e.g., miR-192/194 family) with AUC ~0.6–0.65 for BE/EAC discrimination and dysplasia risk: Useful to push earlier intervention during BE surveillance. <cite id="0aa76913-5">miR-192 (AUC ~0.61) and miR-194 provide early diagnostic value in EAC/BE</cite>.
- Serum proteins with roles in selected pathways:
  - SCC‑Ag and CEA primarily assist in disease stratification (often stronger for advanced disease) and may be integrated into panels, while CA19‑9 can add incremental information; however, CEA alone shows limited specificity for EC and should not drive decisions in isolation. <cite id="33b096e5-3">CA19‑9 and CEA are better predictors of occult advanced disease (AUC ~0.85 and ~0.73)</cite> <cite id="70ff24e8-5">CEA sensitivity is low (8–70%) with high specificity (57–100%), limiting standalone early detection</cite>.
- Imaging-guided pathways:
  - Autofluorescence endoscopy and CAD achieve high in-scope AUC-like performance for lesion detection; they are best used concomitantly with molecular biomarkers to minimize biopsies and improve early cancer yield. <cite id="70ff24e8-4">AI segmentation enhances detection and classification of esophageal cancer</cite> <cite id="0aa76913-0">Advanced endoscopy and AI are key to early diagnosis</cite>.

Important caveats and evidence gaps

- Heterogeneity across centers: Reported AUCs vary due to differences in preanalytical handling, cutoffs, and disease stage mix; single-center studies overrepresent early disease. <cite id="df4756dc-1">Most blood-based assays are in small studies; larger, multi-center validations are required for robust AUC estimates</cite>.
- Specificity for ESCC remains a challenge: Serum proteins have overlapping elevation in gastrointestinal diseases; methylation and miRNA panels improve specificity by integration and context (e.g., BE-specific for EAC). <cite id="70ff24e8-5">CEA’s low specificity for ESCC highlights a need for multi-parameter approaches</cite>.
- Ongoing validation and implementation: cfDNA methylation and miRNA assays require prospective screening trials versus standard endoscopy and head-to-head technology comparisons to define the diagnostic pathway (screen-andolate, surveillance triage) with acceptable false-positive burden. <cite id="df4756dc-2">Plasma MDM assays detect EC with moderate accuracy and motivate larger prospective validations</cite> <cite id="0aa76913-0">Translation from lab AUCs to real-world screening programs demands integration and validation</cite>.

Bottom line: the most promising early diagnostic biomarkers, by AUC performance, are (1) blood-based DNA methylation multi-locus panels and (2) multi-protein serum panels (including device-guided sampling), with strong support in ESCC cohorts and EAC surveillance; miRNA panels add incremental value in BE-to-EAC transition. Imaging biomarkers at endoscopy (autofluorescence + AI) provide high in-scope detection and should be integrated to optimize overall early-detection performance. <cite id="df4756dc-4">cfDNA methylation cfDNA methylation demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy for early-stage esophageal cancer</cite> <cite id="0aa76913-7">Serum PBK and KIF2C show very high AUCs motivating serum panels</cite> <cite id="0aa76913-3">Device + biomarker approach yields ~90% early detection success</cite> <cite id="0aa76913-5">miR-192/194 family provide early diagnostic value in EAC/BE context</cite> <cite id="70ff24e8-4">AI-assisted endoscopic detection improves early classification</cite>.

Short answer
Surgeons prioritize and maintain a surgical “safety margin” in oral cancer to reduce the risk that microscopic cancer cells beyond the visible tumor edge cause local failure or early death from recurrence, even when high‑level randomized trials that lock a single numeric margin for all sites and risks are limited. The rationale is biological—oral cavity tumors can invade and seed along or within “fields” of subtle intraepithelial disease, and grossly “clear” margins can still be biologically “close”; risk‑based tailoring (shallower margins for low‑risk, wider for high‑risk) is favored, and maintaining a safety margin improves local control and reassures downstream adjuvant therapy decisions, even though precise millimeter cutoffs remain debated.

Why a safety margin is essential: biological and pathologic rationale
- Oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) can invade beyond grossly visible disease and exhibits “field cancerization,” where microscopic dysplasia extends beyond clinically apparent lesions; thus, histologically “clear” inked margins may not equate to safe microscopic distance from all tumor cells. <cite id="127baff8-0">Historically, 5 mm gross margins were chosen as an oncologic target, but this belief rests on the principle that microscopic invasion can extend beyond grossly seen tumor and adjacent “field” tissue</cite> <cite id="a4b8ab8e-0">Risk factors for local, regional, and distant recurrence by margin status remain incompletely defined, underscoring biological heterogeneity and the need for margins that protect against microscopic spread</cite>.
- Clinical-pathologic sampling shows that microscopic positive margins are associated with higher local recurrence, and narrower margins correlate with worse outcomes unless offset by other risk controls. <cite id="b82c47e4-8">Most studies agree involved surgical margins negatively impact survival, and recurrence rates are higher when margins are not adequately clear</cite> <cite id="b82c47e4-3">In a review of recurrence by margin size, local recurrence rates were 44% for microscopic positive margins, 28% for ≤1 mm, 13–17% for 1–2 mm, and ~13% for 2–3 mm, indicating stepwise risk reduction as margins widen</cite>.
- Practical margin engineering: achieving a target pathologic margin often necessitates an even larger “gross” or intraoperative safety margin to avoid under‑clearance from contraction/retraction or subtle invasion. <cite id="127baff8-6">To achieve 5 mm final pathologic margins, surgeons generally need to excise roughly 10–15 mm around the tumor at the time of operation</cite> <cite id="595f34eb-2">Intraoperative mapping expands safety margins when index‑positive areas exceed visible borders; cancer or dysplasia within these safety zones determines whether margins are truly negative</cite>.

Margin status and outcomes: what we know from high‑quality cohort and guideline syntheses
- Multiple studies indicate that narrower margins (≥1–2 mm) can achieve similar oncologic outcomes to 5 mm in carefully selected, low‑risk, early‑stage disease, while wider margins reduce rates of close/involved margins and improve local and regional control. <cite id="127baff8-2">Margins of 1–2 mm have shown similar outcomes to 5 mm in several analyses</cite> <cite id="127baff8-1">An intraoperative study found 15 mm gross margins significantly reduced close/involved histologic margins and improved local and regional recurrence compared to narrower resections</cite> <cite id="b82c47e4-0">Margins 4.0–4.9 mm had similar local recurrence risk to ≥5 mm, while margins <4.0 mm were significantly worse, supporting risk‑based thresholds for “adequate”</cite>.
- Survival and recurrence: across early oral cavity cancers, clear margins correlate with better disease‑specific survival and lower locoregional recurrence; however, very wide margins may not translate into large absolute survival gains for all patients. <cite id="127baff8-7">Margins ≥5 mm have been correlated with better local control and disease‑specific survival, with margin status a strong prognostic factor</cite> <cite id="b82c47e4-2">In stage I/II oral cavity SCC, close margins (<5 mm) are associated with worse overall survival and higher locoregional recurrence, though some datasets remain consistent</cite> <cite id="b82c47e4-5">Five‑year OS averaged ~60% across >5 mm and <5 mm groups with similar survival (HR ~1.2, 95% CI 0.7–1.9), indicating limited marginal survival benefit for very narrow vs wider margins</cite> <cite id="b82c47e4-8">Involved margins consistently worsen survival and recurrence vs clear margins</cite>.
- Risk tailoring via tumor biology: oncologic formulas and principles adjust expected margin needs to tumor depth and other high‑risk features. <cite id="a4b8ab8e-3">A significant predictor analysis proposes a minimum safe margin related to depth of invasion (dynamic margin = 0.5 × depth), enabling risk‑based margin sizing</cite>.

Composite outcomes and functional rationale
- Surgeons optimize a balance between disease control and function; a safety margin prevents under‑staging and early recurrence that would necessitate reconstruction or additional surgeries, thereby protecting quality of life and organ function. <cite id="127baff8-4">Wide excision with adequate margins in all three dimensions is a mainstay and should be offered initially to reduce recurrence and preserve function</cite> <cite id="b82c47e4-4">Sampling method (tumor bed vs resection specimen) has limited impact on recurrence in selected settings, reinforcing the primacy of achieving clear, safety‑buffered margins to prevent undetected local persistence</cite>.
- Practical trade‑offs are explicit: wide intraoperative safety margins reduce the chance of “near‑miss” microscopic positives; mandibular resections illustrate that margins tied to tissue plane and risk may be justified to prevent regional recurrence even if cosmetic benefit is less. <cite id="595f34eb-5">On mandibulectomy sites, where survival may not improve with extra width, debates persist whether mandated safety margins beyond disease control justify functional trade‑offs</cite> <cite id="595f34eb-9">Guidelines emphasize removing lesions with a safety margin of normal tissue to minimize recurrence, acknowledging the challenge of reliably achieving and preserving that margin</cite>.

Guidelines and consensus: “adequate/wide” safety margins, not a single universal number
- Societies moved away from a universal fixed mm, endorsing risk‑based adequacy rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all number. <cite id="a4b8ab8e-9">ESMO/ONS/EHNS guidelines for squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity/larynx/oropharynx provide condition‑specific recommendations but do not enforce a single 5‑mm rule, instead emphasizing achieving clear margins consistent with risk</cite> <cite id="127baff8-3">Reviews note that the long‑standing belief of 5 mm targets coexists with evidence that 1–7.6 mm typical margins vary by site and risk</cite>.
- Precision and reassurance of cure: a safety margin provides a buffer against surgical technical variability, biological invasion fronts, and multifocal disease under the microscope. <cite id="595f34eb-2">Intraoperative mapping enlarges safety margins when mapping‑defined “white light” safety zones test positive, capturing microscopic extension and reducing the risk of residual disease</cite>.
- Quantified thresholds to avoid harms: clear evidence shows how risk accumulates as margins narrow, rationalizing wider margins in high‑risk patients and narrower in low‑risk. <cite id="b82c47e4-1">Local recurrence‑free survival dropped notably when margins were ≤2.2 mm in oral tongue SCC, highlighting a cutoff below which risks rise</cite> <cite id="b82c47e4-0">Margins <4.0 mm carry significantly higher recurrence compared with 4.0–4.9 and ≥5.0 mm</cite>.

Evidence gaps and evolving approaches
- Few definitive randomized trials lock a single numeric margin across all sites and risks; high‑level data are mostly retrospective, with ongoing efforts to refine cutoffs and sampling methods. <cite id="127baff8-0">Several trials and meta‑analyses question the necessity of 5 mm across the board, showing reduced recurrence when margins are widened (e.g., to 15 mm)</cite> <cite id="a4b8ab8e-0">It remains uncertain which patients will recur based purely on margin status, pointing to heterogeneity</cite>.
- Emerging studies challenge standard “close” definitions and optimize sampling, with some showing no survival difference between 1–2 mm and 5 mm margins. <cite id="a4b8ab8e-3">Redefined “close” margins based on tumor biology (e.g., dynamic margin rules) are being advanced</cite> <cite id="b82c47e4-5">Five‑year OS was similar across >5 mm vs <5 mm margins in overall cohorts (HR ~1.2, 95% CI 0.7–1.9), supporting individualized margins</cite>.
- Trials and adaptive approaches are testing narrower margins and technology‑guided safety. <cite id="127baff8-7">An early NEJM‑style randomized comparison in T1–T2, cN0 lip/oral SCC directly compared >5 mm excision vs narrower margins, exemplifying the shift away from a blanket 5 mm rule</cite> <cite id="595f34eb-0">Prospective comparisons of smaller resection sizes (e.g., 1.5 cm vs 1.0 cm) are underway to balance safety with tissue preservation</cite>.

Bottom line
Surgeons consider a safety margin essential because the biological reality of intraepithelial and focal microscopic spread (field cancerization) and the lack of perfect intraoperative visualization mean that “grossly clear” margins can still be biologically close, leading to local failure if too narrow; this risk is quantifiable and tied to recurrence and survival. <cite id="b82c47e4-3">Across data, local recurrence rises sharply as margins fall below ~1–2 mm, with ~28% for ≤1 mm and ~13–17% for 1–2 mm, whereas 4–4.9 mm can approach 5 mm outcomes</cite> <cite id="b82c47e4-2">Close margins (<5 mm) convey worse overall survival and higher regional control failure in early stages</cite> <cite id="127baff8-1">Wider resections markedly reduce close/involved margins and improve local and regional disease control</cite>. While high‑level randomized evidence for a single numeric mm is limited, the prevailing consensus supports risk‑based, margin‑buffered resections to preserve function while minimizing the chance of microscopic residual disease and early recurrence. <cite id="a4b8ab8e-9">Guidelines endorse achieving clear margins tailored to site and risk rather than a rigid mm universal rule</cite> <cite id="127baff8-6">Realizing a 5 mm pathologic margin typically requires excising ~10–15 mm grossly to account for tissue distortion and microscopic spread</cite> <cite id="595f34eb-5">This safety philosophy is balanced against functional trade‑offs, where benefits on disease control may not be large on mandibles, prompting ongoing debate and refinement</cite>. In short, clinicians treat the margin as an oncologic safety net—less about millimeters than about ensuring a biologically safe distance from hidden tumor that reduces early recurrence and preserves function. <cite id="b82c47e4-8">Involved or narrow margins reliably worsen outcomes; maintaining a safety margin is an empirically supported hedge against hidden disease</cite>.

Summary
High PD-L1 expression generally influences overall survival (OS) in opposite directions depending on whether it is measured on tumor cells (TC) or on immune cells (IC): in several cohorts PD-L1 on IC is associated with better OS, whereas PD-L1 on TC is more often linked with worse or neutral OS, though effects vary by assay, cutoff, and tumor type.<cite id="0d1532b0-2">High PD-L1 expression on immune cells, but not on tumor cells, was an independent favorable prognostic factor for recurrence-free and overall survival in adjusted head and neck cancer cohorts</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-6">PD-L1 expression on immune cells, in both resection and biopsy specimens, might be a strong independent predictor for a favorable outcome</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-4">Across analyses, high PD-L1 on tumor cells indicates worse overall survival, whereas high PD-L1 on immune cells is a favorable prognostic factor for head and neck cancer patients</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-8">Programmed death ligand 1 expression has been shown to associate with poor prognosis in a variety of solid tumors</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-7">Increased CPS (summing tumor and stromal/immune compartments) in primary tumors and lymph node metastases were associated with improved 5-year overall survival in head and neck cancer</cite>.

Tumor-cell PD-L1 (TC PD-L1) and OS
- Patterns: Elevated TC PD-L1 frequently correlates with poorer OS in solid tumors, including pan-cancer contexts and single cancers such as breast carcinoma and lung cancer.<cite id="0d1532b0-8">Programmed death ligand 1 expression associates with poor prognosis in a variety of solid tumors</cite><cite id="eae368b6-9">Across tumor types PD-L1 predictive value is uneven, with stronger predictive value in NSCLC</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-0">SP142 demonstrates lower sensitivity for PD-L1 staining on tumor cells than on immune cells, an assay bias affecting tumor-cell measurements</cite>. 
- Why: Mechanistically, PD-1/PD-L1 signaling downregulates cytotoxic T-cell activity; high TC PD-L1 can indicate stronger immune evasion and tumor-promoting signaling, which can be associated with more aggressive biology and worse survival, absent strong TIL-mediated counterbalance.<cite id="07eba2a2-2">Ventana SP142 is an FDA-approved test for selection in NSCLC and urothelial carcinoma; PD-L1 expression in tumor and immune compartments is linked to clinical benefit</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-2">If PD-L1 on tumor cells binds PD-1 on T cells, it hampers T-cell function, favoring immune evasion</cite>. 
- Nuance: Tumor cell PD-L1 readouts differ with scoring. CPS tends to capture TC PD-L1 more fully, and in some settings higher CPS correlates with improved OS, but this can reflect immune microenvironment composition rather than purely tumor-intrinsic signaling.<cite id="edcf5e4f-7">In HNSCC, increased CPS in primary tumors and lymph nodes was associated with improved 5-year OS; multiple tumor/stromal compartments contribute to CPS</cite>.

Immune-cell PD-L1 (IC PD-L1) and OS
- Patterns: IC PD-L1 frequently predicts better OS when assessed independently, particularly in head and neck cancer, and remains favorable in adjusted multivariable models that include age, stage, HPV, and smoking.<cite id="0d1532b0-2">High PD-L1 on immune cells, but not tumor cells, was an independent favorable prognostic factor for RFS and OS adjusted for age, gender, smoking, stage, and HPV</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-6">PD-L1 on immune cells in resection and biopsy specimens was a strong independent predictor of favorable outcome</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-3">PD-L1 high on immune cells, but not on tumor cells, is a favorable prognostic factor for HNSCC</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-7">Higher CPS with notable contributions from immune cells was associated with improved 5-year OS in HNSCC, underscoring compartmental weighting in survival outcomes</cite>. 
- Why: High IC PD-L1 often marks a hot, inflamed tumor microenvironment with substantial tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes; in such settings, PD-L1 on myeloid and T cells can reflect adaptive immunity against cancer, and higher immune infiltration itself is associated with better OS.<cite id="0d1532b0-1">By influencing composition of tumor-infiltrating immune cells, PD-L1 levels were linked to shorter OS in a specific cohort, highlighting inflammation-tumor cell interactions</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-3">Across cohorts, higher CD8+ TIL expression was associated with improved DFS and overall survival, supporting the prognostic value of immune infiltration</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-2">PD-L1 on tumor cells binding PD-1 on T cells blocks T-cell activity; however, PD-L1 on immune cells within the microenvironment reflects processes shaping anti-tumor immunity</cite>. 
- Nuance: Immune “hot” vs “cold”: IC PD-L1 combined with CD8+ TILs tends to predict better survival, while tumor-cell PD-L1 may dominate in “cold” or evasive phenotypes with poor T-cell infiltration, producing opposite prognostic signals by compartment.<cite id="0d1532b0-3">High CD8+ TIL expression associated with improved OS underscores the role of an active immune infiltrate</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-0">Abnormal PD-L1 mRNA/protein across cancers predicted prognosis in patient cohorts</cite>.

Tumor-specific observations and assay/threshold considerations
- Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC): Multiple lines show that PD-L1 on IC is favorable for OS while TC PD-L1 is not predictive or even adverse, and combined CPS incorporating IC and TC tends to predict better OS when higher in primary tumors and nodes, pointing to the importance of immune context.<cite id="0d1532b0-2">High PD-L1 on immune, but not tumor, cells predicted favorable OS in adjusted HNSCC</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-7">Higher CPS (tumor plus stromal/immune) predicted improved 5-year OS in HNSCC</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-4">PD-L1 CPS cutoffs related to immunotherapy efficacy in recurrent/metastatic HNSCC, emphasizing the role of PD-L1 load across compartments</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-3">PD-L1 high on immune cells, but not tumor cells, is favorable for HNSCC prognosis</cite>. 
- Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and breast cancer: PD-L1’s prognostic value is stronger in NSCLC; in TNBC/breast, assays differ in sensitivity by compartment. SP142 tends to capture more IC PD-L1 than TC PD-L1, altering observed associations if analyses dichotomize compartments or use only TC-based scores.<cite id="eae368b6-9">PD-L1 prediction is more robust in NSCLC than in melanoma or RCC</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-0">PD-L1 altered prognosis across many cancers including lung</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-0">SP142 shows lower sensitivity for TC staining than IC in TNBC, with scoring dependent on compartment</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-4">In NSCLC, PD-L1 SP142 scoring is evaluated in both tumor and immune components; SP142 is not interchangeable with other PD-L1 assays</cite>. 
- Assay and threshold effects: The choice of antibody/assay changes TC vs IC sensitivity; FDA-cleared indications in lung and bladder use SP142, with CPS and 1% cutoffs commonly used. Independent of therapy selection, these assay choices influence apparent OS associations by weighting IC versus TC PD-L1 differently.<cite id="07eba2a2-0">SP142 assays often detect PD-L1 better on immune cells than on tumor cells, which influences observed tumor/inflammation associations</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-2">Ventana SP142 assay roles in NSCLC and urothelial carcinoma selection underscore assay-defined clinical thresholds</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-8">PD-L1 positivity assessed by CPS, immune CPS, or TPS at 1%, 5%, 10% cutoffs affects concordance and clinical interpretation</cite>.

Mechanistic integration
- Immune evasion vs. immune activation: TC PD-L1 primarily signals to PD-1 on T cells to suppress cytotoxicity, facilitating immune escape; conversely, IC PD-L1 can be a marker of a hostile, inflamed microenvironment where cytotoxic cells are present and active, associated with improved OS.<cite id="edcf5e4f-2">PD-L1 on tumor cells engaging PD-1 on T cells impedes T-cell function and promotes immune escape</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-3">Higher CD8+ TIL burden predicts improved OS, aligning with immune-competent microenvironments</cite>. 
- Compartmental integration: CPS aggregates signals across TC and IC; higher CPS can correlate with better OS when immune compartments are prominent, even if TC PD-L1 alone is not predictive, underscoring the need to interpret PD-L1 readouts with microenvironment context.<cite id="edcf5e4f-7">CPS across tumor and stromal/immune compartments predicted improved OS in HNSCC</cite>.

Clinical assay implications and practical takeaways
- Differential prognostication vs. biomarker standardization: Routine testing platforms (SP142) quantify PD-L1 in both TC and IC, with higher IC load often correlating with favorable OS in head and neck cancer. Laboratories must be aware that SP142 underestimates TC PD-L1 relative to IC and that TPS vs CPS choices can invert apparent prognostic associations by compartment.<cite id="07eba2a2-0">SP142 has less sensitivity for TC than IC, and scoring depends on both compartments</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-2">Immune-cell PD-L1 predicts favorable OS while tumor-cell PD-L1 did not in adjusted HNSCC</cite>. 
- Actionable synthesis: 
  - Favorable: High PD-L1 on immune cells (IC) is generally associated with better OS in HNSCC, consistent with an active anti-tumor immune response.<cite id="0d1532b0-2">High PD-L1 on immune cells predicts favorable OS independent of clinicopathologic factors</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-3">PD-L1 high on immune cells, not tumor cells, is favorable in HNSCC</cite>. 
  - Adverse/neutral: High PD-L1 on tumor cells alone more often correlates with poorer OS, likely reflecting immune evasion and aggressive biology; TC PD-L1 can also be neutral depending on TIL status and genotype (e.g., MSI-high may diverge).<cite id="eae368b6-8">PD-L1 expression associates with poor prognosis across solid tumors</cite><cite id="eae368b6-9">Predictive value varies by tumor type; strongest in NSCLC</cite>. 
  - Combined: CPS that integrates TC and IC often provides the most robust OS signal in HNSCC; thus, thresholding PD-L1 without compartment-aware scoring can misattribute risk.<cite id="edcf5e4f-7">Higher CPS in HNSCC tumors and nodes associated with improved 5-year OS</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-8">Choice of CPS vs TPS and cutoffs affects interpretation and concordance</cite>.

Uncertainties and research needs
- Tumor-agnostic, assay-matched, multivariable-adjusted hazard estimates stratified by compartment remain limited. Assay differences (SP142 vs 22C3 vs EPI-738A) and scoring thresholds (TPS vs CPS) can invert directionality, complicating cross-cohort comparisons.<cite id="07eba2a2-0">Assay sensitivity differences between TC and IC influence observed associations</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-5">SP142 and 22C3 similarly predicted atezolizumab benefit at validated PD-L1 thresholds in NSCLC, supporting assay interchangeability at selected clinical cutoffs</cite>. 
- Emerging work shows PD-L1 on IC can be prognostic even when TC PD-L1 is high, highlighting heterogeneity by immune “hot/cold” phenotypes and interplay with TIL density and checkpoint co-inhibitory pathways.<cite id="edcf5e4f-3">PD-L1 high on immune cells is favorable while tumor cells do not predict the same in HNSCC</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-3">CD8+ TIL enrichment independently predicts improved OS</cite>. Future survival analyses should report compartment-specific CPS/TPS and integrate cytometry-based immune phenotyping.

Bottom line
High PD-L1 expression tends to be good prognostic when predominantly on immune cells (inflamed, anti-tumor immune competent microenvironments) and bad prognostic when driven by tumor-cell PD-L1 (immune-cold evasion), with intermediate outcomes when both compartments and total CPS are high; these differences are real but assay- and tumor-specific, requiring careful compartment-aware scoring and multivariable adjustment for accurate OS interpretation.<cite id="0d1532b0-2">PD-L1 on immune cells independently predicted favorable survival, unlike tumor-cell PD-L1 in adjusted HNSCC analysis</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-3">PD-L1 high on immune cells, not tumor cells, is favorable for HNSCC OS</cite><cite id="edcf5e4f-7">Higher CPS (combining tumor and immune/stromal) predicted improved OS in HNSCC</cite><cite id="0d1532b0-8">TC PD-L1 frequently associates with poor prognosis across multiple solid tumors</cite><cite id="07eba2a2-0">Assay biases (SP142) emphasize IC PD-L1 over TC PD-L1, influencing prognostic inference</cite>.

Summary

The PD-1 (CD274)–PD-L (PD-L1/CD273; PD-L2/CD274) axis is an evolutionary conserved co-inhibitory checkpoint that calibrates immune responses and enforces peripheral tolerance by curbing T cell activation, clonal expansion, and effector function when antigenic stimuli are suboptimal, self-reactive, or chronic. Engagement of PD-1 by either ligand delivers inhibitory signals that converge on suppression of proximal TCR signaling, blunting IL-2 production and proliferation, promoting inhibitory receptor co-expression (e.g., CTLA-4, TIM-3), and driving sustained transcriptional and metabolic programs compatible with T-cell exhaustion. In tumors and inflamed tissues, upregulation of PD-L1 and, in specific niches, PD-L2 can embed effector T cells into suppressive states that limit antitumor immunity; blocking this pathway restores T-cell function and underpins modern immunotherapy. <cite id="32b8a5ef-0">PD-1 and its ligands, PD-L1 and PD-L2, have emerged as critical inhibitory signaling pathways that regulate T cell response and maintain peripheral tolerance</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">PD-1 engagement by its ligands maintains peripheral tolerance but compromises anti-tumor immunity, and blocking antibodies reverse this suppression</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-5">Inhibitory signals from PD-1–PD-L1 or PD-1–PD-L2 mediate mechanisms of tolerance</cite>.

Mechanism: How PD-1 Inhibits T Cells

PD-1 is a type I immunoglobulin receptor with two immunoreceptor tyrosine–based inhibitory motifs (ITIM) and an immunoreceptor tyrosine–based switch motif (ITSM). Ligand binding induces tyrosine phosphorylation of these motifs, recruiting Src homotypic tyrosine kinase SHP-1 and SHP-2 to dephosphorylate key signaling nodes, thereby attenuating proximal TCR signaling and downstream transcriptional programs that drive activation and cytokine production. <cite id="4535bd08-0">After encounter with PD-L1, PD-1 translocates into TCR microclusters, recruits SHP-2 transiently, and suppresses phosphorylation of TCR signaling components</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-4">SHP2 dephosphorylates ITK downstream of PD-1 specifically, associating with PD-1 inhibitory functions</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-9">Full PD-1 activation requires phosphorylation of both ITIM and ITSM; ITSM binds the SHP2 C-SH2 domain with strong affinity to recruit SHP2</cite>.

At the microdomain level, engagement of PD-1 competes with and reshapes early TCR/CD28 signaling complexes. Early after TCR engagement, PD-1 forms co-inhibitory microclusters with SHP2 in T-cell receptor–proximal contact sites on the immunological synapse, where it suppresses proximal TCR signaling, including ZAP-70 and LAT signaling, effectively throttling calcium fluxes and NFAT–AP-1–dependent transcription. <cite id="4535bd08-0">PD-1 rapidly translocates to microclusters and recruits SHP2 to suppress TCR phosphorylation</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-7">PD-1 primarily targets TCR signaling in the inhibition of functional T-cell activation</cite>. PD-L1 and PD-L2 share PD-1 as a common inhibitory receptor, but they differ in tissue and APC expression and in signaling nuances. Functional outcomes: cytokines, metabolism, and proliferation

PD-1–mediated co-inhibition suppresses early cytokine transcription, particularly IL-2, blunting clonal expansion and effector differentiation. Fate programs and transcriptional control

Chronic PD-1 signaling associates with T-cell exhaustion, marked by persistent expression of inhibitory receptors (PD-1, TIM-3, CTLA-4), reduced IL-2, and reliance on IL-7/IL-15 survival pathways; TCF-1 (TCFA) maintains a self-renewing exhausted progenitor state, while TOX emerges as a transcriptional master regulator of exhaustion. <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">PD-1 maintains peripheral tolerance but compromises anti-tumor immunity</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-3">Sustained PD-1 signaling can drive exhaustion phenotypes with diminished effector function</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-4">Downstream of PD-1, SHP2 impairs ITK, aligning signaling with functional suppression</cite>. Although PD-1 is not the sole driver of exhaustion, it provides a dominant negative pressure on TCR signaling that skews fate outcomes; genetic or pharmacologic relief restores effector function. <cite id="4535bd08-7">PD-1 primarily targets TCR signaling in inhibiting functional activation</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-0">SHP-2 may be dispensable for establishing exhaustion, showing PD-1 can impose inhibitory programs independently in vivo</cite>.

Spatial and ligand-biased regulation in tolerance

Tissue and tumor contexts shape PD-1/PD-L engagement. PD-L1 is broadly inducible by interferons on APCs, tumor cells, and some lymphocytes, and is commonly upregulated in inflamed tissues, providing tonic inhibitory cues to local T cells; PD-L2, though less prevalent, is expressed in specific APC subsets and can dominate early co-inhibitory signaling at the first TCR engagement. <cite id="32b8a5ef-8">PD-L1 is upregulated by type I and II IFN on lymphocytes and myeloid cells</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-5">PD-L1/PD-L2–PD-1 interactions enforce inhibitory signaling and tolerance</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-1">PD-L2 co-inhibitory microclusters strongly suppress early TCR signaling</cite>. This anatomical specificity allows PD-1 to regulate peripheral tolerance in tissues: in steady state, low-level self-antigen encounters or bystander activation engage PD-L1 on quiescent APCs to prevent autoimmunity; in tumors, PD-L1 on cancer cells and myeloid infiltrates present strong inhibitory cues that suppress CTLs and TH cells, fostering immune evasion. <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">PD-1 co-inhibition maintains tolerance yet impedes anti-tumor immunity; blockade reverses this balance</cite> <cite id="4535d1c4-1">In tumors, PD-L1 on tumor and stromal cells engages PD-1 on T cells to drive dysfunction</cite>.

Cross-talk with other inhibitory axes and receptor hierarchy

PD-1 operates with, and sometimes upstream of, other inhibitory receptors shaped by antigenic context and TCR avidity. At suboptimal TCR signals, inhibitory receptors (PD-1, PD-L2 microclusters, 2B4, NKR-P1) assemble inhibitory microdomains, with PD-1 exerting a primary suppressive role on TCR signal 1; when signals improve, PD-1 is outcompeted by CD28 for costimulatory cues, allowing full activation. <cite id="4535bd08-0">PD-1 integrates into TCR microclusters to suppress phosphorylation of TCR-linked signaling</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-7">PD-1 mainly targets proximal TCR signaling in inhibition</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-1">PD-L2 co-inhibitory microclusters suppress early signaling</cite>. This hierarchy underpins homeostasis: weak or chronic antigenic stimulation biases PD-1/2B4/NKR-P1 dominance, promoting anergic or exhausted states; strong antigen plus CD28 engagement reverses this, explaining the therapeutic logic of combining CTLA-4 blockade or costimulation with PD-1 pathway interruption. <cite id="32b8a5ef-0">PD-1 restrains T-cell responses to maintain peripheral tolerance</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-0">Even when SHP-2 is not rate limiting, PD-1 can enforce exhaustion, highlighting receptor-level control</cite>.

Regulatory T cell (Treg) and APC crosstalk

PD-1 pathways also tune the milieu via APCs and Tregs. PD-L1 upregulation on DCs and macrophages during activation allows them to deliver “educative” inhibitory signals to responder T cells, shaping the polarization and magnitude of helper and cytotoxic responses; within inflamed tissues and tumors, Tregs express PD-1 and can further transmit inhibitory cues to effector cells through PD-L1 upregulation on APCs in the neighborhood, amplifying peripheral tolerance. <cite id="32b8a5ef-8">PD-L1 is induced on APCs under IFN-driven activation</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-2">PD-1 engagement inhibits IL-2, proliferation, and effector programs in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells</cite>. In steady state, PD-1–high, IL-2–low states on T cells can reflect low-avidity interactions with self-antigen or bystander APCs; PD-1 blockade rescues these cells to rejoin the immune response hierarchy. <cite id="4535bd08-0">By suppressing TCR phosphorylation within microclusters, PD-1 restrains activation</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">Checkpoint blockade reverses PD-1 co-inhibition and restores anti-tumor activity</cite>.

Therapeutic modulation and evolutionary purpose

Physiologically, PD-1–dependent suppression prevents runaway autoimmunity and tissue damage during weak or chronic antigen exposure; pathophysiologically, tumors and pathogens co-opt this axis to blunt immunity. Anti–PD-1/PD-L1 therapies attenuate inhibitory signaling, restoring IL-2 production, proliferation, cytotoxicity, and cytokine profiles of effector and memory T cells, enabling immune control. <cite id="4535bd08-2">Blocking PD-1–ligand interactions restores IL-2, proliferation, and effector functions</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">PD-1/PD-L1 blocking antibodies reverse tolerance and enhance anti-tumor immunity</cite>. Although PD-1 is not the only pathway controlling exhaustion, it sits at the apex of inhibitory control, and its blockade can reinvigorate dysfunctional T cells with durable functional recovery in multiple contexts. <cite id="4535bd08-7">PD-1 primarily targets TCR signaling</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-5">PD-1–PD-L interactions inhibit T-cell signaling in multiple settings of tolerance</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-8">Interfering with PD-1/PD-L1 releases exhausted CD8+ T cells from PD-1–dependent suppression</cite>.

Key Takeaways

- PD-1–PD-L1 and PD-1–PD-L2 interactions enforce peripheral tolerance by directly inhibiting proximal TCR signaling inside microclusters, recruiting SHP-1/2 to dephosphorylate key nodes and suppressing IL-2 synthesis, proliferation, and cytotoxicity. <cite id="4535bd08-0">PD-1 engages SHP-2 to suppress phosphorylation of TCR signaling</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-8">PD-L1 is induced in IFN-rich settings on APCs and tumor cells</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-2">PD-1–ligand binding inhibits IL-2, proliferation, and effector function</cite>.
- Spatially patterned ligand delivery (PD-L1 on broad APC/tumor/tissue pools; PD-L2 on select APCs) tunes the balance between activation, anergy, and exhaustion depending on antigenic context. <cite id="32b8a5ef-5">PD-1/PD-L1/PD-L2 deliver inhibitory signals for tolerance</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-1">PD-L2 coinhibitory microclusters powerfully suppress early signaling</cite>.
- Receptor hierarchy and crosstalk position PD-1 to act as a dominant early brake on TCR signal 1 under weak or chronic stimulation; relief via PD-1 blockade restores effector function and underpins modern cancer immunotherapy. <cite id="4535d1c4-1">Targeting PD-1/PD-L1 restores effector T-cell function in tumors</cite> <cite id="4535bd08-7">PD-1 primarily targets TCR signaling</cite> <cite id="32b8a5ef-1">Blocking PD-1/PD-L1 reverses co-inhibition</cite>.

Limitations and nuances

PD-1’s necessity/sufficiency varies by context and developmental stage: although PD-1 co-inhibition is central, exhaustion can arise via PD-1–independent mechanisms, and PD-1 or SHP-2 sufficiency is not universally required to establish exhaustion. <cite id="32b8a5ef-5">PD-1–independent mechanisms also mediate tolerance</cite> <cite id="c91a0064-0">SHP-2 can be dispensable in vivo for PD-1–induced exhaustion</cite>. Moreover, PD-1 can be upregulated on T cells as an adaptive mechanism to buffer excessive antigenic load, adding a feedback layer to homeostasis. <cite id="32b8a5ef-0">PD-1 restrains T-cell responses and maintains peripheral tolerance</cite>. Together, PD-1 and its ligands act as rheostats for T-cell activation, balancing responsiveness with tolerance across tissues, tumors, and time.

Overview and definitions
Focal boost radiotherapy delivers a concentrated supplemental dose to the dominant intraprostatic lesion identified by multiparametric MRI or intrafraction MR guidance, using high-precision IMRT/VMAT, stereotactic body radiotherapy (including proton/particle spot-scanning), or brachytherapy (permanent seed “bulky” dosing or high-dose-rate boost) after a conventional external-beam base dose to the whole prostate/capsule. Whole-gland boost strategies add uniform supplemental dose to the entire prostate bed (post-prostatectomy or organ-confined), typically with intermediate (54–66 Gy) or risk-adapted escalation algorithms, often using intensity-modulated techniques that attempt sparing/steering to rectal/bladder tissue while covering the whole gland.

Clinical outcomes
- EBRT focal boosts in intermediate/high‑risk localized prostate cancer: Multiple studies and trial updates report superior biochemical disease–free survival (bDFS) with focal boosts over uniform whole-gland IMRT boosts. <cite id="f8d84d24-2">At 10 years, biochemical disease–free survival was 86% with focal boost versus 71% with standard whole-gland boost (P < .001)</cite>. <cite id="f8d84d24-8">The FLAME trial provided strong evidence that a focal boost increased bDFS without impacting toxicity or quality of life</cite>, while <cite id="f8d84d24-3">a contemporaneous editorial summarized the decade-long rise in cure rates with concomitant toxicity reduction, and emphasized that focal strategies target the dominant lesion</cite>.
- Whole-gland IMRT/VMAT boosts as controls: <cite id="64f95f18-3">Risk-adapted whole-gland strategies are designed to escalate dose to higher-risk regions while managing OAR toxicity; however, across comparative series the uniform boost tends to underperform focal boosts in bDFS in intermediate/high-risk cohorts</cite>. <cite id="f8d84d24-8">In the focal EBRT group, late toxicities remained acceptable, supporting non-inferiority for safety alongside the bDFS gain</cite>.
- SBRT with focal boost: <cite id="f6a5f9dd-1">Prostate SBRT with integrated focal boost to MRI‑identified lesions shows 5-year bDFS comparable to focal-flavored IMRT cohorts</cite>, and <cite id="64f95f18-0">iso-toxic focal boosting schemes achieve acceptable late genitourinary and gastrointestinal toxicity rates</cite>. <cite id="f6a5f9dd-4">In the related Hypo‑FLAME/35 Gy programs, 5-year efficacy and toxicity are being evaluated, with phase 2 outcomes indicating sustained benefit</cite>.
- Brachytherapy-based focal/bulky boosts vs EBRT-only: <cite id="2a0c0931-0">Whole-gland brachytherapy can be an escalation strategy but focal/bulky dosing is often emphasized to enhance tumor control with acceptable or reduced toxicity vs EBRT</cite>. <cite id="2a0c0931-4">Three randomized controlled studies and meta-analyses have demonstrated brachytherapy boost superiority over EBRT alone in selected series, supporting the dosing logic of targeting the dominant lesion</cite>. <cite id="2a0c0931-9">Focal brachytherapy approaches are reported to decrease dose to organs at risk and reduce toxicity while improving local control</cite>. <cite id="2a0c0931-1">Contemporary reviews of focal boost (including brachytherapy) argue that dose enrichment to the lesion can elevate tumor control without increased toxicity</cite>.
- Meta/guideline perspective: <cite id="f8d84d24-6">Narrative syntheses note that focal boost strategies improve bDFS in intermediate- and high-risk disease and have not shown excess long-term toxicity</cite>. <cite id="64f95f18-8">ASCO/ESTRO‑aligned summaries likewise report sustained bDFS advantage for focal EBRT boosts (≈86% at 10 years) with no excess late safety signal compared with standard whole-gland boost</cite>.

Subgroup and risk adaptation
Focal boosts are most compelling in intermediate‑ and high‑risk groups selected on MRI‑defined disease, where lesion‑focused dose enrichment meaningfully improves biochemical control without added toxicity. <cite id="f8d84d24-2">The 10‑year bDFS advantage favoring focal boost was specific to intermediate/high‑risk cohorts with MR‑guided selection</cite>. <cite id="f8d84d24-8">FLAME’s MR‑visible lesion paradigm strengthens the rationale for targeting the dominant focal lesion rather than escalating uniformly to risk factors</cite>. <cite id="64f95f18-3">Particle‑enabled IMRT further allows risk‑adapted boosting strategies; across trials, the whole‑gland boost tends to underperform focal boosting for bDFS in higher‑risk disease when toxicity remains within accepted ranges</cite>.

Dose/volume tradeoffs and technology
Modern whole-gland boosts use advanced modulation and adaptive strategies to limit OAR dose, but face a volume–dose tradeoff inherent to covering the whole prostate and/or nodal basins. <cite id="2a0c0931-2">Large IMRT/VMAT programs emphasize modulation, range modulation, and adaptive replanning to minimize toxicity</cite>. <cite id="64f95f18-0">Focal SBRT can match bDFS with acceptable late toxicity when toxicity is explicitly constrained (iso‑toxic designs and small CTVs)</cite>. <cite id="2a0c0931-0">Brachytherapy offers unique dose delivery efficiencies to focal lesions with acceptable toxicity</cite>. <cite id="2a0c0931-8">Contemporary trials (e.g., PRO‑BOOST‑LC) compare whole‑gland boost versus SBRT focal boost within standardized protocols to adjudicate both oncologic outcomes and toxicity</cite>.

Key evidence gaps and ongoing comparisons
Randomized, head‑to‑head phase 3 comparisons focused on overall survival and cancer‑specific survival, with standardized toxicity endpoints, remain a priority. <cite id="2a0c0931-8">PIVOTALboost and PRO‑BOOST‑LC protocols are designed to address these questions with risk-adapted boosting and robust safety follow‑up</cite>. Until these mature, most comparative claims rely on propensity‑matched or trial‑embedded cohorts with acceptable follow‑up and similar baseline risk. <cite id="f8d84d24-2">Across current mature datasets, focal boosts in intermediate/high‑risk disease show durable bDFS gains over whole‑gland boosts without increased long‑term toxicity or reduced quality of life</cite>.

Practical comparison for clinicians
- When to prefer focal boosts: Intermediate/high‑risk prostate cancer with MRI‑detectable dominant lesion; where local control is the major uncertainty and preserving QoL is paramount. <cite id="f8d84d24-2">Focal boosts significantly improve bDFS versus whole‑gland boosts</cite> with <cite id="f8d84d24-8">no excess late toxicity or QoL impact</cite>, and <cite id="64f95f18-5">favorable patient‑reported QoL</cite>.

- Expectations for toxicity: Across comparable risk strata, both strategies can achieve low rates of severe late toxicity with contemporary planning. <cite id="2a0c0931-4">Brachytherapy boost approaches do not increase toxicity versus EBRT and can reduce it in some analyses</cite>; <cite id="64f95f18-6">focal boost SBRT programs report late GU/GI rates similar to or better than historic IMRT, contingent on technique</cite>. <cite id="f8d84d24-8">FLAME indicates preserved safety with bDFS gains when focal boosts are carefully planned</cite>.

Bottom line
Focal boost strategies concentrate the additional dose where imaging demonstrates the dominant lesion, improving biochemical control over uniform whole‑gland boosts in intermediate/high‑risk localized prostate cancer without increasing long‑term toxicity; whole‑gland boosts remain practical and effective in lower‑risk disease and when focal delineation is uncertain, but comparative studies increasingly favor focal boosts for bDFS with similar or improved QoL. <cite id="f8d84d24-2">Focal boosts deliver 10‑year bDFS up to ~86% vs ~71% for standard whole‑gland boosts</cite> with <cite id="f8d84d24-8">no significant toxicity impact</cite>, while <cite id="64f95f18-0">SBRT with iso‑toxic focal boosting yields acceptable late GU/GI toxicity</cite> and <cite id="f6a5f9dd-1">comparable 5‑year bDFS to focal‑boost IMRT</cite>. <cite id="2a0c0931-4">Brachytherapy focal/bulky boosts achieve higher tumor control without excess toxicity versus EBRT alone</cite>, and <cite id="64f95f18-3">risk‑adapted whole‑gland strategies are competitive but often underperform lesion‑focused dosing in higher‑risk cohorts</cite>. Summary
Interleukin-1β (IL-1β) is a key inflammatory cytokine that functions autonomously in glioma cells and via paracrine circuits with innate immune/myeloid cells to drive GBM tumorigenic signaling, uncontrolled proliferation/survival, and angiogenesis. In GBM, tumor-derived IL-1β (often produced via inflammasome activation and IL-1R1 signaling) engages intracellular pathways including JAK/STAT and NF‑κB to increase proliferation, migration/invasion, metabolic support, and secretion of pro‑angiogenic factors such as VEGF; myeloid cells contribute by sensing tumor signals and amplifying IL‑1β, which in turn activates glycolysis and tumor cell growth. IL‑1β also remodels endothelial cells to promote tube formation and vessel sprouting, integrating with EGFR/Stat3 signaling to sustain angiogenic and mesenchymal phenotypes. These processes are supported by cell-line and in vivo models, and pharmacologic IL‑1 receptor blockade suppresses GBM growth, implicating IL‑1β as a causal driver and therapeutic target.

- GBM heterogeneity shapes IL‑1β dependence. Reviews note chronic inflammation is intrinsic to malignant glioma progression, consistent with the prominent role of IL‑1β family cytokines across tumor microenvironments, though lesion‑specific genetic programs dictate variable pathway usage and therapeutic sensitivity <cite id="37d37c2c-3">Gliomas are characterized by extensive neo-angiogenesis. Putting these data together, IL‑1β promotes GBM by igniting intracellular JAK/STAT and NF‑κB cascades through IL‑1R1, inducing survival and proliferative transcriptional programs; inflammasome‑processed IL‑1β (via NLRP3/caspase‑1) in tumor and myeloid cells maintains a pro‑angiogenic secretome, with macrophage IL‑1β accelerating glycolysis and tumor growth while endothelial cells convert IL‑1β‑linked cytokine cues (e.g., EGFR signaling and IL‑8/IL‑1β milieu) into tube formation, junction disruption, and vasculogenic mimicry. Open questions
Direct patient‑level correlations between tumor‑intrinsic IL‑1R1 expression, NLRP3/caspase‑1 activity, and survival across GBM molecular subtypes (IDH‑wt, IDH‑mut, H3K27M) are still being mapped, and whether universal IL‑1R antagonism will outperform stratified combinations with EGFR/VEGF/Stat3 inhibitors remains to be optimized in prospective trials.
