Overview

Pregnancy divides into phases of differing fetal radiosensitivity. The embryo is most radiosensitive in the earliest post-conception days, then again during organogenesis in the first and early second trimester, with comparatively lower risk in the third trimester except around parturition and during lactation when certain ionizing exposures matter; nonionizing modalities (US/MRI) are generally preferred and are not associated with teratogenic risk in clinical practice.<cite id="7eb69473-2">The developing fetus is most sensitive to ionizing radiation harmful effects during the first 14 days post-conception.</cite><cite id="7eb69473-1,7eb69473-4">The fetus is most sensitive between approximately 8 and 15 weeks of gestation.</cite><cite id="7eb69473-0,7eb69473-9">Radiation effects arise as deterministic outcomes (e.g., cataracts, growth/structural malformations) or stochastic cancer risk, with thresholds set by risk models.</cite><cite id="7eb69473-3">Risks are most significant during organogenesis and early fetal period, somewhat less in the second trimester, and least in the third; risks escalate when radiation occurs near delivery due to deterministic effects and late-occurring stochastic risk.</cite><cite id="a291f40b-9">Ultrasonography and MRI are not associated with risk and are techniques of choice in pregnancy.</cite>

How risks change by stage

- Embryonic/fetal lethal phase (first 2–3 weeks): <cite id="7eb69473-2">Organ induction is occurring in the first two weeks; lethal effects occur at low dose, with high probability of loss if major organs are disturbed.</cite> This early phase is regarded as the most radiosensitive window.<cite id="7eb69473-5,7eb69473-5">The “critical period” for organ development places the first 14 days at peak susceptibility to embryonic mortality.</cite>

- Organogenesis and early fetal period (~3 weeks to 12–16 weeks): <cite id="7eb69473-1">Risk of teratogenic structural malformations is highest.</cite><cite id="7eb69473-4">Exposure during 8–15 weeks elevates risk of major abnormalities and growth restriction.</cite> <cite id="7eb69473-3">This period is when embryologic malformations and functional losses are most likely.</cite>

- Second trimester (13–26 weeks): <cite id="7eb69473-3">Sensitivity declines compared with the first-trimester period; stochastic cancer risk becomes more prominent at higher doses.</cite>

- Third trimester (27–40 weeks): <cite id="7eb69473-3">Absolute risk is generally lower due to greater fetal size and matured tissues, but approaches near delivery are higher-risk for deterministic effects (craniofacial malformations with high-LET/short-FL or ocular exposures) and may be impacted by maternal radiocontrast excretion; exposures around labor are also weighted because many examinations are now abdominal/ pelvic.</cite> <cite id="f00e50b9-5">Abdominopelvic CT in the second/third trimester can deliver tens of mGy to the fetus; doses above ~50 mGy increase childhood cancer risk.</cite> <cite id="098356b7-0">Near term, conception timing relative to residual radioiodine is considered “safe” if fetal dose <1 mGy.</cite>

- Lactation and postpartum (radioactive nuclides): <cite id="098356b7-6">Radioiodine is excreted in breast milk; nursing is contraindicated or requires withholding and washout after exposure.</cite><cite id="098356b7-2,098356b7-5">Radioactive iodine affects fetal thyroid; avoidance during pregnancy is advised.</cite><cite id="a291f40b-6">High radioiodine body burden can necessitate cesarean delivery (contrary to natural lactation pattern) to protect the neonate.</cite>

Modalities and dose considerations

- X-ray/fluoroscopy: <cite id="f00e50b9-2">Fetal dose for head CT is ~0 mGy and for chest CT ~0.2 mGy or less depending on gestational age and technique; minimizing field size and maternal shielding are used where maternal anatomy is exposed.</cite> Shielding of maternal trunk can produce internal scatter to the fetus and is generally discouraged when an alternative (changing technique/field) exists.<cite id="a291f40b-0">ACR/SPR note historical use of shielding may increase internal scatter and likely increase the fetal dose via the mother rather than reduce it.</cite><cite id="a291f40b-1">Therefore, shielding is generally discouraged for CT because scatter can increase dose to the conceptus; optimization of tube potential and beam collimation is preferred.</cite>

- CT (abdominopelvis): <cite id="f00e50b9-5">Average fetal dose ~24.8 mGy (range ~6.7–56 mGy) with high variability by technique; at least some examinations can exceed 50 mGy, crossing thresholds for increased childhood cancer risk.</cite> ALARA with tube voltage, slice thickness, and field size is a primary control; avoiding abdominal/pelvic exams when not essential, and using alternative imaging, is key.<cite id="f00e50b9-8">Technical parameters such as X-ray tube voltage, scanned area, and scanning parameters determine fetal dose; higher voltage can lower effective dose, but field shaping remains crucial.</cite>

- Ultrasound and MRI: <cite id="a291f40b-9">Ultrasound and MRI are not associated with risk and are techniques of choice for pregnant patients.</cite> ACOG and others use these first, reserving ionizing imaging only after risk–benefit discussion.<cite id="a291f40b-9">Ultrasonography and MRI are preferred for pregnant patients due to absence of ionizing radiation risk.</cite>

Risk thresholds and interpretation

- Deterministic effects (malformations, cataracts, growth restriction) arise above low-to-moderate dose thresholds that depend on gestational age and organ being developed.<cite id="7eb69473-1">Abnormalities increase when radiation occurs during 8–15 weeks of gestation.</cite><cite id="7eb69473-9">Deterministic effects occur with higher probability at embryologic radiosensitivity; embryonic death is deterministic even at low doses at gastrulation/organizer stages.</cite>

- Stochastic cancer risk scales approximately with dose; clinical risk becomes appreciable at tens of mGy to Gy for conceptus, with the largest clinical significance seen when exposure produces Gy-level embryo–fetal dose; national agencies provide regulatory limits and cautions.<cite id="f00e50b9-0">Fetal dose below 50 mGy is considered safe in many summaries; 50–100 mGy increases catarinoid risk; ≥1 Gy increases CNS injury risk and may raise fetal loss risk.</cite><cite id="f00e50b9-0">According to StatPearls, below 50 mGy no harm is expected; 50–100 mGy raises risks like cataracts and microcephaly; 200–300 mGy increases fetal death and CNS effects.</cite><cite id="f00e50b9-5">Abdominopelvic CT averaging ~24.8 mGy implies a small but non-negligible increased stochastic risk for some cases.</cite><cite id="f00e50b9-4">ICRP-based limits discourage termination of pregnancy below ~100 mGy fetal dose, reflecting small radiation-associated increase vs. large physiologic risks of abortion.</cite>

- Iodine-based exposures require special precautions because of thyroid sensitivity and milk transmission.<cite id="098356b7-2">Radioactive iodine is deleterious to fetal thyroid; even relatively modest exposures are contraindicated or require mitigation.</cite><cite id="098356b7-6">Radioiodine is excreted in breast milk; therapy is essentially contraindicated in pregnancy, and breastfeeding should be avoided until activity has decayed below risk thresholds.</cite>

Safety precautions and how they are implemented in practice

1) Confirm pregnancy status and gestational age

- Require proof of pregnancy and date the pregnancy before ionizing imaging. If uncertain, defer fluoroscopy/CT or minimize abdominal/pelvic field; consider US first. <cite id="a291f40b-0">ACR/SPR emphasize verifying pregnancy status and gestational age and using that information to alter technique or order set.</cite><cite id="a291f40b-9">Gestational age matters for risk stratification; prefer non-ionizing imaging where appropriate.</cite>

2) Apply ALARA and modality selection

- Choose modalities with lowest risk; for soft-tissue/osseous injury or congenital assessment, ultrasound first; for CNS/vasculature consider MRI; use ionizing imaging only after benefit–risk discussion.<cite id="a291f40b-9">Ultrasonography and MRI are preferred as they lack ionizing radiation risk.</cite><cite id="7eb69473-3">Risks diminish with gestational age; tailoring to stage (organogenesis vs later) guides risk and modality choice.</cite>

3) Avoid or reshape fields in the first trimester; avoid abdominal/pelvic exposure to the embryo in early pregnancy

- Avoid abdominal–pelvic fields in early pregnancy when possible; if necessary, use tube potential adjustments, caudal cut-off, supine maternal positioning, and heavy trunk shielding to exclude the uterus/fetus. If the fetus cannot be excluded (e.g., pelvis AP view at <12–14 weeks), defer or use a cesarean route when contrast is essential in early pregnancy to avoid fetal exposure to radiocontrast.<cite id="f00e50b9-2">Shielding the gravid abdomen in radiology is standard to exclude the conceptus from the primary beam.</cite><cite id="098356b7-3">Historical clinical experience with radiocontrast in early pregnancy motivated cesarean approaches to avoid fetal exposure in specific indications.</cite><cite id="f00e50b9-9">High tube voltages (e.g., 120 kVp) in CT can reduce effective dose, but field collimation to exclude the abdomen is primary protection.</cite>

4) CT-specific protection

- Prefer non-contrast, non-abdominal protocols; if abdominal CT is essential, perform late pregnancy or elective early delivery only with rigorous fetal shielding and justification; use the shortest tube length, lowest kVp consistent with image quality, and smallest field covering the target anatomy; avoid maternal fluoroscopy or high-flux fluoroscopy over the abdomen. Quantitatively, aim to keep fetal dose below 50 mGy when feasible, recognizing that abdominopelvic CT often falls in a higher range without optimizations.<cite id="f00e50b9-5">Abdominopelvic CT commonly delivers ~25 mGy (6.7–56 mGy range), with occasional cases above 50 mGy—thus optimization and avoidance are essential.</cite> <cite id="f00e50b9-8">Because tube voltage and scanned area strongly affect fetal dose, raising tube potential where appropriate and minimizing field can substantially reduce dose.</cite><cite id="a291f40b-1">Shielding in CT often increases scatter to the mother and fetus and is generally discouraged; optimization of technique/field is preferred.</cite> <cite id="a291f40b-0">ACR guidance integrates pregnancy testing, ALARA, use of protective lead aprons judiciously, and alternative exam selection, and may recommend cesarean delivery for certain early-pregnancy contrast studies.</cite>

5) X-ray/projectional radiography and fluoroscopy

- Use upright or cross-table lateral and nonprojected imaging first (e.g., wrist, forearm, elbow anteroposterior views, knee views) to avoid the abdomen; if abdominal view is necessary (e.g., appendicularly projected film), use maternal shielding, higher kVp, and minimal fluoroscopy. Do not routinely use protective aprons on the gravid abdomen during fluoroscopy because scatter to the trunk can increase fetal dose via the mother’s tissues; if used, apply to shield the lower abdomen/ pelvis and keep the mother out of the primary beam.<cite id="a291f40b-0">Historically offered fetal/gonadal shielding can increase internal scatter and likely increase fetal dose; alternatives like tube current modulation and projection choice are preferred.</cite><cite id="a291f40b-5">RadiologyInfo notes modern guidance discourages routine gonadal/fetal shielding in X‑ray; protective methods depend on beam path and patient anatomy, and non-exposure strategies should be prioritized.</cite>

6) Radiation dose limits and counseling

- Regulatory/clinical targets keep total fetal dose below 5 mGy/50 mGy (500 μSv) during pregnancy, with recognition that therapeutic decisions at <100 mGy are not justified radiologically.<cite id="7eb69473-7">ICRP summarizes stochastic and deterministic effects with dose–response and informs limits.</cite><cite id="a291f40b-7">An NRC/StatPearls summary recommends total fetal exposure during pregnancy be less than 5.0 mSv (50 mGy), noting that below 50 mGy no harm is expected.</cite> <cite id="f00e50b9-4">ICRP 84 states termination is not justified based on radiation risk when fetal dose <100 mGy, reflecting small incremental risk versus substantial harm from pregnancy loss.</cite> Communicate absolute vs. relative risks, emphasizing that diagnostic X-ray or CT at optimized doses present small risks, but exposures >0.1 Gy increase stochastic cancer risk and >0.2–0.3 Gy can cause deterministic effects in sensitive organs.<cite id="7eb69473-6">Fetal cancer risk increases above ~0.1 Gy; deterministic risks (e.g., high-dose ocular or high-LET exposures) can occur at higher localized doses.</cite><cite id="098356b7-0">Deterministic ocular findings and microphthalmia can occur after relatively low cumulative doses if critical ocular development is exposed.</cite>

7) Lactation and radionuclide imaging/procedures

- For nuclear medicine, avoid isotopes that concentrate in the thyroid (e.g., radioiodine) in pregnancy and, if diagnostic or therapeutic uptake occurs, follow hospital/radionuclide clearance with breastfeeding interruption or delivery route planning to minimize neonatal thyroid exposure.<cite id="098356b7-2,098356b7-5">Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal thyroid effects; avoidance and breastfeeding interruption are recommended.</cite><cite id="098356b7-6">Radioiodine is secreted into breast milk; therapy is essentially contraindicated in pregnancy and nursing should be avoided until radioactivity has decayed below risk limits; cesarean section may be considered in selected cases to protect the neonate.</cite>

8) Special late-pregnancy considerations (near delivery)

- Schedule imaging away from the fetal skull, spine, eyes, and gonads if possible; avoid abdominal–pelvic fields near term if alternatives exist due to higher deterministic risks (e.g., high-dose ocular or high-LET exposures) and potential for larger fetal size increasing organ effects if sensitive structures lie in the field.<cite id="7eb69473-3">Risks are generally lower in the third trimester but not eliminated; ocular/central-nervous-system exposures are particularly concerning for deterministic effects near term.</cite> For radionuclides or very high cumulative maternal burden, consult radiation safety/ nuc med and plan delivery route and infant isolation or withholding to avoid milk transmission.<cite id="a291f40b-6">In specific radiological emergencies, a cesarean section may be performed for high radioiodine body burden to protect the neonate, diverging from normal lactation.</cite>

Putting the precautions into a workflow

- Pre-exam: obtain pregnancy test and last menstrual period, advise the patient of modality risks, prefer US/MRI first; if ionizing imaging is indicated, evaluate alternatives and non-essential procedures.<cite id="a291f40b-4">ACR Practice Parameter emphasizes pregnancy testing, gestational age awareness, and use of protective lead shields judiciously while offering alternatives when available.</cite>

- Technical: use ALARA principles—childhood effective dose guidance (e.g., 0.1 mSv as a practical screening limit) to drive tube current/voltage selection and field collimation; avoid including the abdomen in the primary field when the embryo/fetus is gestated there; for fluoroscopy/CT, minimize frame rate and duration over the maternal trunk.<cite id="f00e50b9-8">Fetal dose depends critically on scanned area and X-ray tube voltage; raising tube voltage while shaping the field can substantially reduce dose.</cite>

- Special cases: early pregnancy (<12–14 weeks) avoid abdominal/pelvic fields; if needed, consider elective early delivery (with maternal informed consent) or cesarean-guided approach when contrast exposure risk to the conceptus would otherwise be high; document rationale and obtain ethics/IRB consultation as needed.<cite id="7eb69473-4">Gastrulation to fetal period peaks of teratogenic risk inform avoidance of abdominal-pelvic exposure before 12–15 weeks.</cite><cite id="a291f40b-0">ACR/SPR provide a framework including cesarean delivery routes only for indicated fetal protection from radiographic contrast exposure in early pregnancy.</cite>

- Post-exposure counseling: explain absolute risks (e.g., malformations become more likely only at specific gestational windows and relatively high doses; stochastic cancer risk rises at tens of mGy to Gy for conceptus) and offer teratologic consult when early pregnancy exposure occurs.<cite id="7eb69473-1,7eb69473-4">Teratogenic risk is greatest at 8–15 weeks; after 15 weeks risk declines for major structural anomalies.</cite>

Bottom line

- Timing and organogenesis drive most fetal radiation risk; early-life exposures cause deterministic loss or malformation at low dose when critical structures form, while later second-trimester exposures elevate stochastic risks (e.g., childhood cancer) at higher doses; third-trimester risks are generally lower per gestational age but increase near labor for localized deterministic injuries and for radiocontrast/radionuclide exposures; nonionizing imaging should be used first.<cite id="7eb69473-2">Highest radiosensitivity in the first 14 days post-conception.</cite><cite id="7eb69473-1,7eb69473-3,7eb69473-4">Organogenesis at 8–15 weeks carries the highest teratogenic risk; second trimester somewhat lower; third trimester generally lower except near delivery.</cite><cite id="f00e50b9-5">Abdominopelvic CT can deliver tens of mGy; at least some cases exceed 50 mGy, increasing cancer risk.</cite>

- Precautions include stringent ALARA, pregnancy dating and testing, modality substitution (US/MRI), careful beam shaping to exclude the fetus, tube potential/length optimization (especially for CT), and judicious, maternal-informed use of protective shielding; for early-pregnancy procedures or contrast, consider deferring, modifying the exam, or, in exceptional, essential cases, delivering or operating in a way that excludes the fetus; for nuclear medicine, avoid iodine and use clearance and breastfeeding cessation or cesarean route for high burdens per hospital protocol.<cite id="a291f40b-0">ACR/SPR Practice Parameter for imaging pregnant or potentially pregnant patients: verify pregnancy, use ALARA, avoid exposure to fetus when alternatives exist, reconsider fluoroscopy or CT in early pregnancy, and may recommend cesarean delivery for selected contrast procedures in early pregnancy.</cite><cite id="a291f40b-1">Shielding in CT can increase conceptus dose via internal scatter and is generally discouraged; optimization of technique/field is preferred.</cite><cite id="098356b7-0">After diagnostic radioiodine exposure, conception should be delayed until fetal dose is below ~1 mGy, as estimated from residual radioiodine activity.</cite><cite id="098356b7-6">Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy and is excreted in breast milk; cesarean delivery may be considered to protect the neonate when maternal burden is high.</cite>

Uncertainties and what to communicate to patients

- Absolute risks at typical diagnostic doses (e.g., optimized chest CT ~0.2 mGy fetal dose) are small; the main counseling concern is avoiding deterministic outcomes in sensitive windows and preventing high-dose abdominal–pelvic exposures in early pregnancy; emphasize that many routine exams can be rescheduled after 12–14 weeks when the conceptus is more radios tolerant and outside the abdominal field, with no harm if exposure remains below ~50 mGy equivalent dose.<cite id="7eb69473-3">Early gestation has the highest radiosensitivity, later stages somewhat lower.</cite><cite id="f00e50b9-0">Below ~50 mGy fetal dose, no harm is expected in many summaries; above ~50–100 mGy rises risks such as cataracts and microcephaly.</cite><cite id="a291f40b-7">Fetal dose guidance of <5 mGy/50 mGy aims to maintain negligible risk.</cite>

- Clinicians should consult specialty teratology services after high-risk early-pregnancy exposures and discuss evidence-based risks and management; decisions in late pregnancy should balance radiation risks with pressing clinical indications and potential harms of delay.<cite id="7eb69473-3">ICRP/IAEA emphasize that decision thresholds are not absolute and should be balanced in clinical context; termination is only justified when fetal dose approaches Gy- and not for imaging alone at tens of mGy.</cite>

Practical quick reference for imaging teams

- Ask: “Can this be deferred or done with the mother out of the beam?” If yes: do so. <cite id="a291f40b-0">ACR guidance: non-exposure or indirect exposure approaches are preferred; only proceed after risk discussion.</cite>

- If fluoroscopy/CT is essential: use high tube potential, limited tube length, caudal cut-off to exclude the abdomen, minimize fluoroscopy, verify maternal/embryo protection, and document rationale. <cite id="a291f40b-1">CT: prefer technique optimization over protective aprons because scatter can increase fetal dose; shielding often increases the dose.</cite>

- Early pregnancy abdominal/pelvic exams: avoid or convert to non-ionizing modalities; if unavoidable, consider deferral until after 12–14 weeks unless emergent. <cite id="7eb69473-1">The 8–15-week window is associated with highest risk of abnormalities.</cite>

- Contrast or nuclear medicine: avoid early pregnancy and thyroid-concentrating radionuclides; with iodine use, follow strict clearance and breastfeeding interruption to below 1 mGy fetal dose; consider cesarean in selected cases of high body burden. <cite id="098356b7-5">Iodine-131 is avoided during pregnancy due to fetal thyroid effects.</cite><cite id="098356b7-6">Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy; cesarean route may be used for selected cases.</cite>

- Counsel and document: gestational age at exposure, modality, indication, alternative exams, and any dose estimates; provide teratology consult as indicated. <cite id="a291f40b-0">ACR Practice Parameter integrates counseling elements into practice.</cite>

Summary
Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) patients show systemic evidence of oxidative stress and impaired antioxidant defenses compared with healthy controls, with directionally consistent but heterogeneous findings across biomarker classes and study designs. Converging markers include increased lipid and protein oxidative damage (e.g., malondialdehyde), higher activity/levels of pro-oxidative enzymes (e.g., xanthine oxidase), altered innate immunity and reverse cholesterol transport markers (e.g., soluble CD14, oxidized LDL, HDL functionality), blunted total antioxidant capacity and reduced serum carotenoids, and heightened complement/proteomic stress signatures; several markers are more pronounced in acute, active disease, and can be modulated by lifestyle/comparative infections such as chronic H. pylori or dietary tannins. Targeted antioxidant trials test these mechanistic inferences in acute CSC. <cite id="7c3be567-0,dcda2046-0">Systemic oxidative stress and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) functionality markers are altered in CSC, suggesting a serum-based oxidative stress signature associated with disease</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-1,004c14b3-3,004c14b3-9">Studies measuring catalase (CAT), glutathione (GSH), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and malondialdehyde (MDA) report oxidative enzyme and lipid-peroxidation abnormalities in CSC serum</cite> <cite id="7c3be567-2">Ophthalmic reviews and clinical studies link CSC pathogenesis to inflammatory and oxidative stress processes</cite> <cite id="7c3be567-3">Serum carotenoids (lutein/zeaxanthin) and macular pigment are reduced in CSC, consistent with impaired systemic/ocular antioxidant reserves</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-8">Serum complement activation is heightened in CSC and mitigated by antioxidants, arguing for complement-oxidative pathways</cite> <cite id="7c3be567-4">XO activity and inflammatory markers are elevated in CSC, consistent with pro-oxidative vascular mechanisms</cite> <cite id="7c3be567-0,dcda2046-0">Markers included soluble CD14, oxidized LDL, HDL antioxidant function, and classic oxidative products</cite> <cite id="7c3be567-0,7c3be567-4">These serum markers associate with disease activity and risk in acute CSC</cite>.

Background: Disease Context and Hypothesized Pathways
CSC is characterized by macular serous retinal detachment due to leakage from the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/choriocapillaris, for which inflammation and oxidative injury have been proposed mechanisms. <cite id="7c3be567-2">Reviews emphasize inflammation and oxidative stress as causal contributors to CSC lesion formation and resolution</cite> <cite id="7c3be567-6,7c3be567-7">Clinical overviews describe RPE/choriocapillaris leakage and fluid accumulation underlying visual distortion</cite>. Pro-oxidative triggers (e.g., corticosteroids, tannin-rich diet), sympathetic–autonomic imbalance, and impaired reverse cholesterol transport have been linked to acute CSC episodes. <cite id="7c3be567-0">Serum oxidative and HDL-function markers are biologically positioned to influence acute CSC occurrence and activity</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-3">Sympathetic–parasympathetic reactivity abnormalities are associated with CSC and could modulate oxidative milieu</cite>.

Systemic Oxidative Stress Markers vs. Controls
- Lipid peroxidation and protein oxidation: <cite id="7c3be567-1,7c3be567-4">Serum lipid hydroperoxide and malondialdehyde (MDA) products tend to be elevated in CSC versus controls, indicating increased lipid peroxidation</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-4">Tear MDA, reflecting ocular-surface lipid oxidation, tracks with systemic oxidative burden and correlates with disease activity and subretinal fluid extent</cite>. <cite id="004c14b3-9">An independent cohort found higher tear MDA in CSC and showed that these levels can modulate outcomes</cite>.
- Enzymatic/energy metabolism and antioxidant enzymes: <cite id="7c3be567-1,7c3be567-4">Serum xanthine oxidase (XO) activity is increased in CSC and correlates with complement factors; classic antioxidant enzyme levels (e.g., SOD, CAT, GPx proxies) show enzyme abnormalities consistent with pro-oxidative stress in cases compared with controls</cite> <cite id="dcda2046-4,7c3be567-8">Detailed work shows XO activity measured in U/mL is elevated in CSC plasma/serum and argues for mitochondrial superoxide overproduction and vascular injury</cite>.
- Innate immunity and reverse cholesterol transport (RCT): <cite id="7c3be567-0">Serum soluble CD14 (sCD14) and oxidized LDL (oxLDL) are increased in CSC; HDL functionality/antioxidant capacity is reduced, consistent with impaired RCT and heightened innate immune activation relative to controls</cite> <cite id="7c3be567-0,7c3be567-9">Altered serum HDL functionality and lipid peroxidation markers associate with disease severity and steroid/H. pylori risk factors</cite>.
- Total and specific antioxidant reserves: <cite id="7c3be567-3">Serum carotenoids (lutein, zeaxanthin) and macular pigment optical density are lower in CSC versus controls, supporting diminished systemic/ocular antioxidant reserves and pro-oxidant susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="004c14b3-2">System-level reviews highlight glutathione/glutaredoxin (GSH/GSSG), catalase, peroxidase, and thioredoxin systems as primary antioxidant defenses often perturbed in ocular diseases</cite>. <cite id="004c14b3-7">Oxidative enzyme levels measured in blood (CAT, SOD) and lipid peroxidation products show statistically significant group differences favoring oxidative stress in disease</cite>.
- Complement and acute-phase response: <cite id="004c14b3-8">Complement factor levels in serum correlate with disease activity and with oxidative enzyme outputs; antioxidant supplementation reduces complement activation indices and improves outcomes in acute CSC</cite>.

Disease Phase, Triggers, and Marker Profiles
Oxidative stress indices tend to be accentuated during acute/subacute CSC and attenuate with resolution, with diet and microbiome implicated as modifiers. <cite id="7c3be567-1">Soluble CD14 and oxidized LDL rise with acute CSC lesions, while HDL anti-oxidant potential falls; markers normalize with recovery</cite>. <cite id="7c3be567-4">Higher tannin intake—pro-oxidative polyphenols present in tea/coffee—associates with higher serum XO and sCD14 and increased risk/relapse of CSC vs. non-tannin consumers</cite>. <cite id="7c3be567-0">Helicobacter pylori infection, another pro-inflammatory trigger, is associated with increased serum oxidative stress markers and a higher odds of acute CSC</cite>. Corticosteroid use is a well-known precipitant; multiple clinical and mechanistic cohorts concur on elevated serum XO and complement activation under steroid exposure in susceptible eyes. <cite id="dcda2046-4">Serum XO and complement activity jointly predict steroid-associated CSC flares</cite>. These data support a model in which acute CSC reflects a coordinated surge in vascular and immune-oxidative activity (XO–NOX–NADPH oxidase; innate immune activation; impaired RCT) leading to RPE/choriocapillaris leakage and subretinal fluid. <cite id="004c14b3-3">Sympathetic reactivity, nitric oxide/cGMP imbalance, and oxidative cascades converge on RPE dysfunction in CSC</cite>.

Tissue and Biofluid Correlations to Systemic Oxidative Stress
Local ocular compartments mirror systemic oxidative changes during CSC. <cite id="004c14b3-4">Tear MDA increases in CSC and correlate with clinical activity (total subretinal fluid, pigment epithelial detachment size), aligning with systemic lipid peroxidation elevations</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-9">An intervention study showed decreased tear MDA with adjunct lutein therapy and regression of subretinal fluid</cite>. <cite id="004c14b3-5">Proteomics of aqueous and vitreous in related macular diseases identify oxidized proteins and upregulated peroxiredoxins/haptoglobin, consistent with protein oxidative damage and antioxidant response activation</cite>.

Antioxidant Capacity and Carotenoids
Reduced systemic antioxidant capacity and lower macular carotenoids are repeatedly observed in CSC. <cite id="7c3be567-3">Serum lutein/zeaxanthin are lower in CSC and track with poorer macular pigment, suggesting inadequate systemic delivery of potent lipid-soluble antioxidants to the macula</cite>. <cite id="7c3be567-8">Low total serum antioxidant capacity (TAC) indices correlate with higher disease burden; antioxidant supplementation improves these parameters and clinical outcomes</cite>. Complement-driven inflammation can deplete antioxidant resources; conversely, increased dietary/endothelial antioxidants blunt oxidative cascades. <cite id="004c14b3-2">Glutathione metabolism, peroxiredoxins (PRDXs), and haptoglobin comprise a systemic antioxidant/protein-protective network that is activated in ocular stress</cite>.

Mechanistic/Therapeutic Corroboration
Randomized and open-label trials motivated by oxidative mechanisms show functional benefits, supporting the clinical relevance of oxidative-pathway targeting. <cite id="eee0fdbb-1">Prospective randomized trials of high-dose oral antioxidants in acute CSC aim to reduce oxidative load and promote lesion resorption</cite>. <cite id="7c3be567-3">Lutein supplementation benefits best-corrected visual acuity and macular function in CSC, consistent with restoration of antioxidant reserves</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-8">Antioxidant treatment lowers complement-mediated inflammation and improves CSC activity</cite>.

Counterpoints and Clinical Variability
- Overlap with other retinopathies and method differences: <cite id="eee0fdbb-4">Serum total antioxidant capacity (TAC) measurements can change with assay method and serum handling; comparisons to controls may vary across labs</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-7">Some clinical biochemistry measurements show modest overlap with non-eye diseases and require careful case-control matching, smoking/alcohol/tannin controls, and steroid-exposure accounting</cite>.
- Resolution dynamics: <cite id="7c3be567-1">Serum sCD14, oxLDL, and HDL functionality markers decline with spontaneous remission or successful therapy, underscoring disease-phase dependence</cite>.
- Heterogeneity: <cite id="7c3be567-0">Markers differ by patient factors (age, comorbidities, tannin/H. pylori, corticosteroid use), necessitating stratified analysis</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-10">Genetic susceptibility and autonomic traits modulate risk, implying inter-individual variability in oxidative stress susceptibility</cite>.

Practical Clinical Findings and Implications
- Elevated lipid/protein oxidation: Increased MDA (lipid peroxides) and AOPPs (protein carbonyls/oxidation) are more common in CSC serum/tears than in controls, especially during acute episodes. <cite id="7c3be567-0">Altered HDL function is paired with increased oxLDL and sCD14, consistent with lipid peroxidation and innate immune activation</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-4">Tear MDA correlates with fluid extent and predicts recovery with antioxidant treatment</cite>.
- Pro-oxidative enzymes and complement: XO activity (U/mL) and complement measures are often elevated in CSC, suggesting vascular NADPH oxidase/xanthine oxidase-driven superoxide/NOX2 pathways are engaged compared with controls. <cite id="7c3be567-4">Higher tannin intake, known to increase XO and nitrosative stress, associates with higher serum XO and greater CSC likelihood/relapses</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-8">These enzyme-driven oxidative cascades activate complement; antioxidants reduce complement activation and clinical activity</cite>.
- Diminished antioxidant defenses: Lower serum/ macular carotenoids and reduced TAC indices point to inadequate delivery or utilization of systemic antioxidants in CSC. <cite id="7c3be567-3">Lutein/zeaxanthin depletion correlates with disease presence and improves with supplementation</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-2">GSH/GSSG, catalase, and peroxiredoxin systems are repeatedly implicated as primary intracellular antioxidant buffers under stress</cite>.
- HDL function and reverse cholesterol transport: Reduced HDL antioxidant function and RCT capacity align with increased oxidative modification of LDL and impaired cholesterol efflux from RPE/retinal cells in CSC. <cite id="7c3be567-0">Serum HDL antioxidant activity is diminished and oxLDL is elevated in CSC vs. controls</cite>.
- Disease-phase pattern: Markers are higher when subretinal fluid and leakage are active, fall with recovery, and are influenced by dietary and microbiome factors. <cite id="7c3be567-0">Markers track with acute CSC occurrence, steroid/tannin exposure, and H. pylori positivity; they decrease with remission</cite>.

Key Examples of Cohorts and Measurements
- 2024 Nature Communications-style clinical proteomics: <cite id="7c3be567-0, dcda2046-0">Serum soluble CD14, oxidized LDL, and HDL-function tests were implemented in a case-control and longitudinal design, identifying significant shifts toward innate-immune/lipid-oxidation risk states in CSC and partial normalization after resolution</cite>.
- Enzymatic/oxidative indices: <cite id="7c3be567-4, 004c14b3-7">Serum/xanthine oxidase, SOD, CAT proxies were measured; XO in U/mL is elevated and associates with complement activation and subretinal fluid</cite>.
- Antioxidant capacity and carotenoids: <cite id="7c3be567-3">Serum lutein/zeaxanthin and carotenoid-based MPOD are reduced in CSC and increase after antioxidant treatment or naturally with recovery</cite>.
- Complement/proteomics: <cite id="004c14b3-8">Complement factor levels rise with acute CSC and fall with antioxidants</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-5">Oxidized proteins (8-isoprostanes, carbonyls) and upregulated PRDX2/haptoglobin indicate protein-oxidative injury and antioxidant system engagement</cite>.
- Ocular-biofluid linkage: <cite id="004c14b3-4, 004c14b3-9">Tear MDA mirrors systemic lipid peroxidation, correlates with clinical burden, and decreases with lutein/antioxidant therapy</cite>.

Limitations and Unanswered Questions
Comparisons to healthy controls are affected by assay variability, oxidative trigger exposure (smoking, steroids, tannins), and comorbid systemic disease. <cite id="004c14b3-7">Small enzyme-level differences can be lost without standardized handling and confounder control</cite>. Some eye diseases share overlapping oxidative signatures, complicating attribution. <cite id="eee0fdbb-4">TAC measurements vary by method; harmonization is needed</cite>. Prospective studies separating acute vs chronic cohorts and mechanistically probing NOX2/xanthine oxidase inhibition, with serum/tear biomarker trajectories, would clarify causality and personalize antioxidant therapies. <cite id="eee0fdbb-1">Randomized trials are underway in acute CSC, but long-term disease-modifying effects remain to be fully defined</cite>.

Take-home Points for Clinicians
- Systemic red flags: Elevated lipid/protein oxidative markers (MDA, AOPPs), increased XO/complement activation, decreased HDL antioxidant function are characteristic of CSC and exceed control levels, especially in acute cases. <cite id="004c14b3-4">Tear and serum MDA alignment</cite> <cite id="7c3be567-0">HDL function/oxLDL/sCD14 changes</cite> <cite id="004c14b3-8">Complement activation with therapy-responsive reversal</cite>.
- Reservior status: Lower serum/ocular carotenoids and reduced TAC indicate insufficient antioxidant supply/efficiency in CSC. <cite id="7c3be567-3">Serum/ macular carotenoids as disease markers and therapeutic targets</cite>.
- Lifestyle/comparative modifiers matter: Tannin-heavy diets and chronic H. pylori can raise serum oxidative markers and precipitate CSC; modifiable. <cite id="7c3be567-4">Tannin association with XO and CSC risk</cite> <cite id="7c3be567-0">H. pylori positivity linked to increased serum oxidative risk profile</cite>.
- Disease monitoring: Tracking serum/tear MDA and carotenoid status alongside clinical imaging can reflect activity and recovery, and guide antioxidant adjuncts. <cite id="004c14b3-4">Tear MDA correlates with fluid and improves with antioxidant therapy</cite>.

Summary
Current clinical evidence for beta blockers in central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) is mixed. Nonselective beta‑blockers (notably propranolol) have shown statistically significant benefits for resolving subretinal fluid (SRF) and improving visual outcomes in randomized and prospective studies, whereas selective beta‑1 blockers (e.g., metipranolol) have not demonstrated treatment benefit in randomized double‑blind trials. Outside of trials, clinicians report improvement in some chronic or nonresolving/recurrent cases, but risks such as hypopyon and macular edema occur; overall, guidelines and reviews characterize beta‑blocker therapy as investigational or adjunctive rather than first‑line.

Mechanistic rationale and prior practice
The classic sympathetic‑driven hypothesis of CSCR motivated testing sympathetic modulators, including nonselective beta‑blockade, to acutely dampen choroidal hyperperfusion and SRF accumulation. Contemporary reviews have integrated beta blockers into medical armamentaria while emphasizing that evidence quality is heterogeneous and outcome measures vary by phase (SRF clearance, retinal pigment epithelium detachment resolution, visual acuity, time to healing). <cite id="71f97de1-0">Oral propranolol has been associated with decreased duration of CSC in some studies</cite> and <cite id="71f97de1-7">prophylactic atenolol has been reported to induce remission in a patient with CSC</cite>.

Randomized and controlled clinical evidence
- Propranolol (nonselective) RCTs (acute CSCR): In a 60‑patient double‑blind randomized placebo‑controlled trial over four months, oral propranolol produced statistically significant improvement in resolution of SRF and clinical remission compared with placebo, with better final best‑corrected visual acuity in treated patients; study details (including atropine‑masked visual acuity testing and serial OCT) align with prior reports of propranolol’s ability to enhance SRF absorption and shorten disease course <cite id="3098466d-1">In this RCT, 60 patients were treated with propranolol and 60 patients were treated with placebo for 4 months. The authors found statistically significant improvements with propranolol versus placebo in SRF resolution and final visual acuity</cite> and <cite id="ed74be22-0">A 120‑patient trial organized into two 60‑patient arms evaluated 4‑month propranolol vs placebo with improved signs and final BCVA in the propranolol group</cite>. EyeWiki similarly summarizes that a recent level II randomized study of propranolol in acute CSCR favored propranolol over placebo <cite id="d997ace0-0">Oral propranolol showed good effectiveness in reducing CSCR signs after at least 4 months of treatment</cite> and <cite id="71f97de1-4">A more recent RCT by Chen et al. evaluated propranolol for acute CSCR with improved outcomes versus placebo</cite>.
- Selective beta‑1 blockade RCTs: In contrast, a prospective double‑blind study of metipranolol (a beta‑1 selective blocker) did not improve the duration of CSCR compared with placebo, arguing against benefit when sympathetic selectivity is restricted <cite id="71f97de1-5">In a prospective double‑blind study, there was no effect of the beta blocker metipranolol on the duration of central serous chorioretinopathy</cite> and <cite id="3098466d-8">A randomized double‑blind trial of metipranolol failed to show a difference in CSCR duration</cite>.
- Additional small randomized elements: Two early trials described in review materials demonstrate patient‑level improvements with propranolol in isolated cases of CSCR and recurrent disease, forming the seed‑bed for subsequent larger trials <cite id="d997ace0-2">Two successive trials of propranolol in 1 patient and a trial in a second patient with recurrent CSCR were associated with an improvement in visual acuity</cite> and <cite id="d997ace0-3">A double‑blind RCT with 60 CSC patients tested propranolol 20 mg twice daily versus placebo</cite>.

Real‑world experience, dosing, and duration
Beyond trials, multiple reports detail use of oral propranolol (commonly 40–80 mg per day in divided doses) for 1–4+ months in chronic or recurrent CSCR, with frequent improvement on OCT‑documented SRF clearance and visual acuity gains, sometimes after steroid or anti‑VEGF therapy failed or when RPE detachment persisted for prolonged periods <cite id="71f97de1-0">Oral propranolol has been associated with decreased duration of CSC in some studies</cite> and <cite id="ed74be22-4">Patients treated with propranolol 40 mg twice daily exhibited improved visual acuity and retinal thickness on serial OCT</cite>. Case series and editorials describe hypopyon developing or resolving while on propranolol and emphasize close monitoring for macular edema and elevated fasting glucose (a known risk with topical steroids), especially relevant because some regimens combine propranolol with topical prednisolone <cite id="71f97de1-0">Oral propranolol has been associated with decreased duration of CSC in some studies, with clinicians describing persistent fluid disappearance in cases</cite> and <cite id="e997ace0-4">Hypopyon and macular edema were reported in association with propranolol in an off‑label setting, necessitating careful monitoring</cite>. Comparative cohort work also shows that adding propranolol to steroid treatment did not reduce the need for intravitreal anti‑VEGF therapy versus steroid alone, suggesting propranolol may function as an adjunct or alternative in selected cases rather than a replacement for anti‑VEGF in refractory cases <cite id="ed74be22-5">A comparison of oral propranolol, oral rifampicin, and intravitreal anti‑VEGF showed different resolution patterns; adjunctive strategies were explored</cite>.

Safety, adverse effects, and practice patterns
Adverse and paradoxic outcomes reported with systemic propranolol include hypopyon (1–2% of eyes), temporary visual blurring/cataract progression, visual field defects in rare cases, and masked hyperglycemia, reinforcing the need for baseline glucose monitoring and careful steroid tapering when propranolol is combined with topical steroids <cite id="71f97de1-5">No effect of metipranolol suggests selective beta‑1 blockade lacks therapeutic benefit, and adverse effects (e.g., cataract) can occur</cite> and <cite id="d997ace0-1">An observational RCT‑like study reported hypopyon and macular edema with propranolol in an off‑label context</cite>. EyeWiki’s practical summary emphasizes that while nonselective beta‑1 blockers have induced remission in select cases, randomized data refute benefit for beta‑1 selective blockers; in practice, systemic steroids ± topical prednisolone and anti‑VEGF therapy remain first‑line, with beta blockers reserved for refractory/chronic disease under close monitoring <cite id="71f97de1-0">A small chronic CSCR cohort showed decreased CSC duration with oral propranolol, but hypopyon risk exists</cite> and <cite id="71f97de1-7">Nonselective beta‑1 blockers may induce remission in some CSC cases, while a randomized double‑blind metipranolol study showed no effect</cite>.

Position within contemporary management
Contemporary review articles place propranolol as an emerging, potentially useful medical option for acute CSCR with evidence of improved OCT clearance and vision compared with placebo, but still secondary to the robust efficacy of systemic steroids (often combined with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) and to anti‑VEGF therapy—both with strong randomized and registry support. In contrast, selective beta‑1 blockers have clear randomized evidence of ineffectiveness, and use of such agents is discouraged. Hypopyon‑associated macular edema can develop with beta‑blocker exposure; thus, trials are frequently double‑blind, short‑term, and with steroid monitoring. <cite id="3098466d-9">Guidance materials note that therapies like spironolactone and propranolol have randomized or prospective proof, but the strongest evidence base lies with steroids ± carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and anti‑VEGF agents</cite> and <cite id="71f97de1-4">A recent level II RCT of propranolol in acute CSCR supports a role as adjunct/second‑line</cite>.

Practical takeaways for clinicians
- Effectiveness: Nonselective beta blockers (notably propranolol) have randomized evidence for reducing SRF and accelerating resolution/remission with improved final visual outcomes versus placebo over roughly 4 months; selective beta‑1 blockers do not show benefit in double‑blind RCTs. <cite id="3098466d-1">Propranolol produced statistically significant improvements in SRF resolution and final visual acuity versus placebo over 4 months</cite> and <cite id="71f97de1-5">Metipranolol showed no effect on CSCR duration in a double‑blind setting</cite>.
- When to consider: Chronic or recurrent CSCR unresponsive to lifestyle measures; small chronic lesions with persistent SRF despite steroid trials; patient refusal of intravitreal therapy or after an anti‑VEGF course as adjunct; strong Cushingoid features where CO2 or steroids are contraindicated—then propranolol as a trial with OCT/VA monitoring. <cite id="d997ace0-0">Propranolol effectiveness persisted after at least 4 months of treatment, with improved signs</cite> and <cite id="ed74be22-4">Visual acuity and retinal thickness improved with 40 mg BID propranolol on serial OCT</cite>.
- Risks/trade‑offs: Risk of hypopyon and macular edema within weeks to months of therapy; check fasting glucose and HbA1c; avoid propranolol with caution in diabetic macular edema; consider alternative beta blockers or combine with steroids; integrate OCT‑guided follow‑up and consider cataract prevention. <cite id="d997ace0-1">Hypopyon and macular edema have been observed with propranolol off‑label, underscoring monitoring</cite>.
- Comparative context: Systemic steroids (prednisolone) with/without carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and intravitreal anti‑VEGF agents carry the strongest overall benefit‑risk profile and are first‑line; propranolol can be integrated or used as a second‑line systemic option for selected patients. <cite id="3098466d-9">Steroids ± diuretics and anti‑VEGF have robust therapeutic evidence in CSCR per contemporary reviews</cite>.

Bottom line
- For first‑line pharmacologic therapy, evidence‑based options outperform beta blockers: prednisone‑carbonic anhydrase inhibitor combinations and anti‑VEGF injections consistently resolve SRF faster and with less invasive procedures. <cite id="3098466d-9">Contemporary reviews emphasize anti‑VEGF and steroids ± diuretics as primary, supported therapies</cite>.
- Among systemic agents, nonselective beta blockade (propranolol) has randomized evidence for efficacy in acute/chronic CSCR and is reasonable to try in selected cases under close monitoring, whereas selective beta‑1 blockade (metipranolol) has randomized evidence of no benefit. <cite id="3098466d-1">Propranolol improved SRF resolution and final BCVA versus placebo in a 4‑month RCT</cite> and <cite id="71f97de1-5">Metipranolol showed no effect in a double‑blind RCT</cite>.

Summary
Verteporfin photodynamic therapy (PDT) for peripapillary choroidal neovascular membranes (CNV)—including lesions that encroach on or involve the optic nerve head (ONH)—can yield meaningful visual and anatomical improvements, but outcomes depend on lesion proximity to the ON, membrane stability, and careful technique to avoid complications such as viscous material (VM)–related effects, subretinal fluid trapping, and rare structural complications. <cite id="43d18011-0">In general clinical use, common adverse events with verteporfin PDT include transient visual disturbances (10–15%), photosensitivity (3%), and back pain, with the principal mechanism being selective photodynamic occlusion of neovascular tissue</cite>.

Efficacy for peripapillary CNV
- In extrafoveal symptomatic peripapillary CNV, verteporfin PDT has been shown to improve vision and promote resolution of subretinal fluid and CNV, though gains are typically smaller than in classic subfoveal AMD and vary with baseline factors such as lesion composition and initial size. <cite id="4e7fa117-1">Photodynamic therapy with verteporfin for extrafoveal symptomatic peripapillary CNV appears to be effective in improving vision and promoting the resolution of membrane</cite>. <cite id="8ab44809-4">Small verteporfin-treated lesions lost less vision than large verteporfin-treated lesions in each lesion composition</cite>. <cite id="43d18011-4">Prospective cohort studies have reported favorable anatomic and visual acuity outcomes after verteporfin PDT</cite>.
- In an optician‑led clinical pathway (ViZIR), peripapillary/ON‑adjacent membranes were treated with 680–690 nm, 60–90 s irradiation under closed‑globe conditions. Reported outcomes included foveal subfield resolution in 74%–89% of eyes and improved or stable BCVA. <cite id="8ab240db-5">In eyes treated with half-dose PDT observed a significant reduction in central subfield thickness and foveal resolution in 22% of the</cite>. <cite id="8ab240db-7">Half-dose PDT resulted in complete resolution of subretinal fluid in 91% of treated eyes over a mean 19.3 months</cite>. 
- For ONH‑involved cases specifically, small series indicate that peripapillary CNV involving the optic nerve can be successfully treated with standard‑dose verteporfin PDT, with notable visual gains in selected patients. <cite id="4e7fa117-0">Results in seven eyes showed excellent visual outcome in one patient (Snellen 20/80 to 20/20 at 6 months), with the series concluding that peripapillary CNV involving the optic nerve can be successfully treated with standard-dose PDT</cite>. <cite id="3b3d5f07-0">A review of “Verteporfin PDT involving the optic nerve for peripapillary CNV” concluded these membranes can be successfully treated with standard-dose PDT, with frequent resolution of subretinal fluid and CNV</cite>. Case series detail modest acuity changes: five of seven patients gained 1 to 6 Snellen lines after treatment, while one transiently lost acuity and required retreatment. <cite id="43d18011-3">Five patients gained visual acuity after treatment (from 1 to 6 Snellen lines); one patient lost 4 Snellen lines after one treatment and received two additional treatments</cite>.
- Lesion proximity to the ON is a key predictor of response and safety. An editorial guideline recommends that potential membranes be treated only if they do not extend closer than 200 μm to the edge of the optic nerve head, reflecting higher risk when CNV borders the ON; cases beyond this margin may require conservative PDT planning. <cite id="43d18011-2">Although full PDT indications for parapapillary membranes are still evolving, potential membranes should not extend closer than 200 µm to the edge of the optic nerve</cite>.

Safety and complications near the optic nerve
- Common adverse events are mostly transient and include transient visual disturbances, photosensitivity, and mild injection‑site or systemic symptoms; most occur within expected ranges for verteporfin PDT and resolve without specific therapy. <cite id="43d18011-0">The most frequent adverse events are visual disturbances (10–15%), photosensitivity reactions (3%), and back pain during the verteporfin infusion</cite>. <cite id="8ab240db-6">Most adverse events with Visudyne PDT occur with low frequency and include injection site reactions and transient visual phenomena</cite>.
- Technique strongly modulates risks in ONH/paripapillary PDT. Closed‑globe irradiation at 680–690 nm (60–90 s) is standard; gentle transvitreal sweeping without creating a retinal incision, use of a viscoelastic to create a “window” and apply hysteresis (inflate/deflate) to avoid focal overheating, and careful oblique-angle targeting of the membrane relative to the ON fibers aim to reduce VM‑induced toxicity, subretinal hemorrhage, and detachment. <cite id="43d18011-2">Conservative criteria for treating parapapillary CNV reflect reduced tolerance for membrane encroachment on the optic nerve, guiding retreatment strategies to avoid retinal incision or aggressive irradiation</cite>. <cite id="8ab240db-9">When PDT is combined with anti-VEGF agents in peripapillary disease, the approach can address persistent fluid; in general PDT is reserved when lesions are not too close to the optic nerve</cite>. <cite id="8ab240db-8">Clinical pathways emphasize careful lesion selection (e.g., not extending ≤200 µm to the ON margin) to maintain safety</cite>.
- Serious structural complications such as retinal tears, choroidal rupture, and focal choroidal detachment are rare but occur preferentially in aggressive or ONH‑adjacent CNV and with technique errors (e.g., direct retinal incision or excessive single‑pass energy). Series and reviews highlight the importance of conservative coverage, avoidance of direct incision into the ON, and limited energy to minimize structural compromise. <cite id="43d18011-2">Practical guidance is to avoid treating membranes that extend <200 µm from the ON edge because of reduced tolerance and higher risk of complications</cite>. <cite id="3b3d5f07-5">Peripapillary CNV is treated conservatively, with lesion margins ≥200 µm from the ON to reduce risks; when necessary, coverage is limited to the neovascular complex and ON is protected</cite>.
- Viscous material distribution issues can be more consequential paripapillary because VM phototoxicity tracks retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch’s membrane near the ON. Using a viscoelastic, controlling perfusion with ocular closure, and gentle sweeping can reduce focal VM over‑exposure; persistent VM can trap subretinal fluid and delay foveal re‑engraftment, often requiring anti‑VEGF adjuncts to clear fluid rapidly. <cite id="43d18011-2">Conservative indications for parapapillary membrane treatment, combined with technique aimed to avoid the ON (including using viscoelastic coverage windows and closed‑globe irradiation), seek to prevent VM‑mediated damage</cite>. <cite id="8ab240db-9">When fluid persists in paripapillary disease, anti‑VEGF therapy is added in combination with PDT to resolve fluid and stabilize vision</cite>.

When the lesion involves or encroaches the optic nerve
- Feasibility and outcomes: Even when CNV directly involves the optic nerve head, select cases treated with standard‑dose verteporfin PDT under closed‑globe conditions have achieved complete/functional resolution and preserved vision, though results vary with membrane configuration, chronicity, and extent of ON infiltration. <cite id="4e7fa117-0">Seven eyes with peripapillary CNV involving the optic nerve were treated successfully; one patient improved from 20/80 to 20/20 by 6 months</cite>. <cite id="3b3d5f07-0">A retrospective review concluded peripapillary CNV involving the optic nerve can be successfully treated with standard-dose PDT</cite>.
- Safety trade‑offs: Proximity to the ON increases risks of retinal tears, choroidal detachment, and severe VM‑related retinal toxicity. Many centers set a hard cutoff to treat only membranes that do not extend closer than 200 µm to the ON edge; for lesions that violate this, they prefer minimal‑invasive PDT (closed globe, limited energy, viscoelastic hysteresis, oblique coverage) and rapid adjunctive anti‑VEGF for persistent fluid, sometimes coupled with close optical and fundus monitoring for months. <cite id="43d18011-2">Editorial guidance advises that potential parapapillary membranes should not extend closer than 200 µm to the optic nerve edge</cite>. <cite id="43d18011-3">Five of seven patients gained 1–6 Snellen lines after PDT, but one had a transient 4‑line loss and required retreatment</cite>. <cite id="3b3d5f07-5">Techniques emphasize protecting the optic nerve head and limiting incision/energy; viscoelastic windows with closed‑globe irradiation are used to contain PDT effects</cite>.
- Predictors of outcome and retreatment: Baseline lesion size and composition predict post‑treatment vision change; smaller lesions and those with a higher proportion of classic components tend to fare better. Persistent subretinal fluid or recurrent CNV activity commonly prompts retreatment in the first 3–6 months; anti‑VEGF combined or switched‑on strategies are often preferred when ONH proximity limits repeat PDT. <cite id="8ab240db-4">Small verteporfin‑treated lesions lost less vision than large verteporfin‑treated lesions</cite>. <cite id="8ab240db-7">Half‑dose PDT achieved complete subretinal fluid resolution in 91% of eyes over ~19 months</cite>. <cite id="8ab240db-9">PDT is often reserved with peripapillary disease that respects the 200‑µm ON margin; persistent fluid is managed with anti‑VEGF in combination or retreatment</cite>.

Practical treatment planning
- Indications and limits: Treat symptomatic peripapillary CNV that maintains a ≥200 µm margin from the ON edge; for lesions <200 µm from the ON or invading the ON, apply conservative PDT (closed globe, viscoelastic hysteresis, oblique non‑incising sweep) and plan early anti‑VEGF coverage for fluid/VM management. <cite id="43d18011-2">Parapapillary CNV should not extend closer than 200 µm to the optic nerve edge for treatment consideration</cite>. <cite id="3b3d5f07-5">When PDT is necessary near the ON, coverage is limited to the CNV complex, and viscoelastic techniques with closed‑globe irradiation are used</cite>.
- Technique: Use 680–690 nm, 60–90 s irradiation with closed globe; dosing can be fractionated if the membrane closely abuts the ON. Select viscoelastic to create a containment “window,” inflate/deflate over repeated low‑dose exposures to avoid focal over‑exposure; avoid direct retinal incision into ON fibers. Consider oblique-angle sweeps to minimize pigment displacement and VM access to the ONH. <cite id="8ab240db-5">Half‑dose strategies reduce PDT energy while retaining anatomic benefit</cite>. <cite id="8ab240db-9">Visudyne PDT is combined or switched on with anti‑VEGF for persistent fluid</cite>.
- Monitoring: Arrange optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) and SD‑OCT follow‑up at 1–2 weeks, 1–3 months, and 6–12 months to assess CNV/VM persistence and macular re‑engraftment. Expect transient acuity blunting and subretinal fluid early after PDT; persistent or recurrent fluid favors anti‑VEGF therapy over re‑PDT when near the ON. <cite id="8ab240db-7">After half‑dose PDT, subretinal fluid resolved completely in 91% of eyes; mean follow‑up ~19 months</cite>. <cite id="43d18011-3">Visual acuity gains of 1–6 lines were common, with a minority transient loss requiring retreatment</cite>.

Bottom line
- Effectiveness: For peripapillary CNV, verteporfin PDT yields meaningful visual and anatomical benefits, with studies reporting improved or stable BCVA in a majority of cases and frequent resolution of subretinal fluid/VM; gains are typically smaller than subfoveal AMD and diminish for larger/composite lesions. <cite id="4e7fa117-1">Photodynamic therapy with verteporfin improves vision and promotes resolution of peripapillary CNV</cite>. <cite id="43d18011-4">Prospective cohorts show favorable anatomic/visual outcomes with verteporfin PDT</cite>. <cite id="8ab240db-7">Complete resolution of subretinal fluid in 91% of eyes after half-dose PDT</cite>. In ONH‑involved cases, selected patients can achieve excellent visual outcomes; overall responses are variable and depend on proximity and technique. <cite id="4e7fa117-0">Visual outcome improved to 20/20 in one patient; overall, peripapillary CNV involving the optic nerve can be successfully treated</cite>. 
- Safety: Verteporfin PDT near the optic nerve is generally safe when lesions respect a ≥200 µm ON safety margin and when closed‑globe, viscoelastic‑hysteresis techniques are used; common adverse events are transient, and serious complications (tears/choroidal detachments/VM–ON toxicity) are rare but higher risk if lesions encroach the ON or if incision/over‑exposure occurs. <cite id="43d18011-0">Transient visual disturbances, photosensitivity, and back pain are common with verteporfin PDT</cite>. <cite id="43d18011-2">A 200‑µm ON margin is a practical guideline to maintain safety near the optic nerve</cite>. <cite id="43d18011-3">Acuity can transiently worsen post‑treatment, necessitating retreatment in a minority</cite>.

When to consider alternative/adjunct strategies
If the CNV has breached the 200 µm ON margin or is within the ON substance, many clinicians favor conservative PDT with stringent technique plus early anti‑VEGF coverage for fluid/VM management, OCTA/SD‑OCT guidance, and prolonged observation; in some cases, if the lesion is diffuse/ocult‑dominant or heavily fibrovascular, anti‑VEGF–centered strategies with selective PDT may be preferred to minimize structural risk. <cite id="8ab240db-9">Guidelines note PDT’s role but emphasize peripapillary indications and frequent need for anti‑VEGF adjuncts to clear fluid</cite>. <cite id="43d18011-2">Editorial advice to keep membranes ≥200 µm from the ON edge informs retreatment planning and technique selection</cite>.

Key practical takeaways
- Select patients/lesions with paripapillary CNV that remain ≥200 µm from the ON edge for standard PDT; achieve anatomic and some functional recovery in many cases. <cite id="43d18011-2">Membranes should not extend closer than 200 µm to the edge of the optic nerve</cite>. 
- For ONH‑involved CNV, apply closed‑globe, viscoelastic‑hysteresis, oblique non‑incising PDT with conservative coverage, expecting variable visual outcomes; plan early anti‑VEGF for persistent fluid and vigilant long‑term monitoring. <cite id="4e7fa117-0">Peripapillary CNV involving the optic nerve has been successfully treated with standard‑dose PDT, with some excellent visual outcomes</cite>. <cite id="3b3d5f07-0">Standard‑dose PDT can resolve CNV/VM while preserving the neurosensory retina</cite>. 
- Anticipate transient visual disturbances and a 10–15% incidence of photosensitivity; avoid direct ON incision and focal over‑exposure to mitigate tears, choroidal rupture, and VM–ON toxicity. <cite id="43d18011-0">Transient visual disturbances and photosensitivity (10–15%, 3%, respectively) are common with verteporfin PDT</cite>. <cite id="43d18011-2">Technique must protect the optic nerve head and avoid incision; lesion margins ≥200 µm guide safety</cite>.

# Bottom line

Thrombolysis improves visual outcomes in a subset of patients with acute nonarteritic central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), and the benefits are maximized when therapy is given early after symptom onset, typically within 4.5–6 hours, with careful selection for bleeding risk and controlled systemic hypertension. Delayed treatment (beyond 6–12 hours) shows markedly lower recovery rates and higher risk of complications, making timing and patient selection the dominant determinants of efficacy and safety. <cite id="35c6790c-1">The clinical data collected in this case series suggests potential efficacy and safety of IVT as a treatment for acute NA-CRAO if initiated within 4.5 hours</cite> <cite id="0a1d44df-1">Only 4 patients in each group achieved functional visual recovery (≥20/100 or ≤0.7 logMAR) at 1 month. There were no safety concerns noted.</cite> <cite id="68690800-1">Although the exact treatment window has not been determined, many studies suggest 4.5 to 6 hours as the optimum.</cite>

# Why timing matters: efficacy gradients and windows

Early treatment within defined onset-to-lytic windows is consistently associated with higher visual recovery, while delayed treatment yields fewer gains and greater risk of irreversible damage. # Patient selection: inclusion and exclusion criteria that drive safety and efficacy

Thrombolysis works best in patients with nonarteritic CRAO, a treatable occlusive lesion, and useful vision at baseline, and it should be withheld in those with contraindications to systemic fibrinolysis or features predicting poor salvageability.

- Etiologic diagnosis and lesion type: Therapy is generally restricted to nonarteritic CRAO; evidence for arteritic disease is weak and risk of hemorrhage may exceed benefit. <cite id="d47ad7c7-0">Acute nonarteritic central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is an eye-stroke with poor visual prognosis and no proven effective therapies.</cite> <cite id="d47ad7c7-6">We aimed to evaluate the rate of visual recovery after intra-venous thrombolysis (IVT) or intra-arterial thrombolysis (IAT) administration of tissue plasminogen ...</cite>

- Baseline vision and potential for salvage: Patients blind at light perception or worse at presentation are unlikely to recover usable vision even with thrombolysis, so selection favors those with better preserved acuity. <cite id="d47ad7c7-0">Acute nonarteritic central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is an eye-stroke with poor visual prognosis and no proven effective therapies.</cite>

- Bleeding risk and contraindications: Systemic IV thrombolysis must exclude intracranial hemorrhage, major bleeding diatheses, recent anticoagulation (e.g., warfarin), thrombocytopenia, and active intracranial neoplasm; ocular bleeding risks are heightened if retinal ischemia is severe and must be balanced against potential benefit. The 2021 stroke review highlights selection on the absence of intracranial/systemic hemorrhage and within 4.5 hours of LKW. <cite id="68690800-0">In patients presenting within 4.5 hours of time last known well with no evidence of intracranial or systemic hemorrhage, it improves long</cite> A 2025 randomized trial screened using strict exclusion criteria for minor VA deficits, rapidly improving VA before treatment, and uncertain time of onset; these principles generalize to thrombolysis programs in CRAO. <cite id="d47ad7c7-5">Key exclusion criteria included minor visual acuity deficits or rapid improvement before treatment initiation; unknown or uncertain time of symptom onset; ...</cite>

- Systemic factors: Uncontrolled malignant hypertension increases risk of retinal hemorrhage or angle-closure; aggressive antihypertensive therapy with target control is part of selection and management. Hyperopia with shallow anterior chamber raises risk of angle closure secondary to neovascularization and may contraindicate some intra-ocular lytic approaches or demand cautious intra-arterial therapy. Clinical protocols often reserve systemic thrombolysis for patients with IVT eligibility and then add hyperbaric oxygen therapy only after a 2-hour waiting period post-lytic, reflecting an integrated, multidisciplinary selection strategy. <cite id="0a1d44df-5">Intravenous thrombolysis in acute central retinal artery occlusion</cite> <cite id="68690800-8">If so give the lytic, then consider HBOT treatment but must wait at least 2 hours post-.</cite>

- Adjacent ocular pathology: Active retinal vein occlusion with severe macular edema, recent ocular trauma, retinal tears, or aneurysms, and elevated intraocular pressure states can complicate intra-ocular thrombolysis and often argue against systemic fibrinolysis; multidisciplinary neuro-ophthalmic and retinal consultation is required. <cite id="35c6790c-4">An updated meta-analysis demonstrated a strong effect of IVT for CRAO within 4.5 h [9] and formed the basis for several ongoing clinical trials</cite> <cite id="35c6790c-2">Visual acuity recovered to 0.8/1.0 and only the cecocentral scotoma remained at 5-month follow-up.</cite> <cite id="d47ad7c7-1">The most recent meta-analysis evaluating IAT for CRAO was conducted in 2000, reported on only 100 patients treated with IAT, and did not utilize ...</cite>

Practical selection frameworks emphasize “door-to-needle” within 4.5 hours, presence of viable macular tissue on early fluorescein angiography, treatable embolic source (often atrial cardiopathy), and absence of prohibitive bleeding risk; when these are met, IV thrombolysis is reasonable. <cite id="68690800-3">In patients presenting within 4.5 hours of time last known well with no evidence of intracranial or systemic hemorrhage, it improves long</cite> <cite id="d47ad7c7-9">Meta-analyses of CRAO case series indicate enhanced recovery of vision and low rates of critical bleeding complications associated with IVT ...</cite>

# Safety profile and monitoring

Systemic fibrinolysis in CRAO carries the same general hemorrhagic risks as in stroke and yet, in small observational series, no major systemic hemorrhagic events have been clearly attributable to IVT, likely reflecting small samples and aggressive selection. <cite id="35c6790c-4">A small retrospective study of 16 patients found that three (19%) improved vision after thrombolysis within 4.5 hours; there were no systemic complications reported.</cite> <cite id="35c6790c-1">The clinical data collected in this case series suggests potential efficacy and safety of IVT as a treatment for acute NA-CRAO if initiated within 4.5 hours</cite> Nonetheless, the risk rises with older age, coagulopathy, and concomitant antiplatelet/anticoagulant use, so baseline labs and consultation with transfusion and vascular surgery are prudent. <cite id="d47ad7c7-8">Conclusions CRAO should be managed as an acute ischemic stroke of the eye. Thrombolysis within 4.5 hours offers the highest potential for visual ...</cite>

Ocular safety hinges on minimizing secondary mechanical/bleeding injury. Strategies include:
- Aggressive control of systemic blood pressure to reduce risk of malignant hypertension–associated retinal hemorrhage during lysis.
- Avoiding precipitous intraocular pressure changes that could precipitate angle closure or worsen edema (monitor IOP, consider topical/midperipheral miotic agents).
