Below are the main reasons VA appears similar across groups even when macular hole (MH) closure rates differ, organized by mechanistic theme and supported by comparative trials and OCT physiology.

Summary
- VA depends on foveal microstructure and macular edema as much as on whether the hole is anatomically closed, so improvements are often bounded and can plateau before or after closure, especially in advanced disease or when coexisting membrane/edema persists. <cite id="beedd704-1">Anatomic success rates of vitreous surgery for macular hole are above 90%, yet only about 50% recover at least 20/40, underscoring that closure does not always mean meaningful visual improvement</cite>. <cite id="5c4397b5-1">ILM peeling improves closure but has no detrimental effect on vision despite higher closure rates</cite>, and <cite id="c67664eb-6">controlled randomized evidence showed increased closure with ERM peeling without an effect on VA</cite>.

Mechanisms tying limited VA gains to variable closure rates

1) Functional ceiling and near–best possible VA 
- When VA starts close to 20/40–20/25, room for improvement is small, so groups can have different closure (open vs closed) yet similar mean VA shifts. <cite id="beedd704-1">Only ~50% reach 20/40 after vitrectomy for MH, reflecting a natural ceiling where many eyes improve only modestly</cite>. <cite id="5c4397b5-0">In long-duration full-thickness MH, adding baseline predictors does not yield a statistically significant relationship between hole size and VA improvement, consistent with limited leverage on VA despite anatomical change</cite>.

2) Persistent or recurrent macular edema and traction independent of hole closure 
- Removing vitreous traction may seal the MH but fails to cure concurrent cystoid edema or epiretinal traction, which disproportionately limits VA when present. <cite id="c67664eb-0">Post–ILM peeling persistent macular edema is common; mechanisms include tractional trauma and blood–retina barrier damage</cite>. <cite id="5c4397b5-9">Vitrectomy improves anatomical metrics in lamellar/MH with ERM/ILM peeling, yet VA gains hinge on resolving ERM-related traction and edema</cite>. <cite id="c67664eb-1">Peeling ERM/ILM reduces recurrence of epiretinal membrane but does not improve VA, indicating that ERM-related eddys and traction may constrain function despite closure</cite>. 
- Overlap of MH with epimacular membranes or persistent fluid can thus make VA “marginal” across both an open and a closed group, masking differences in closure with similar average gains.

3) Photoreceptor integrity and outer retina, not just hole topology 
- Modern OCT reveals that VA largely correlates with photoreceptor layer continuity (outer segment/ellipsoid zone and ELM integrity); disorganization or loss can thwart VA even when the hole is closed. <cite id="32802e8c-2">Integrity of ELM and ellipsoid zone is among the most important prognostic criteria for visual recovery</cite>. <cite id="32802e8c-5">Historical OCT analyses emphasized that photoreceptor repair after surgery predicts visual improvement, whereas holes can close with visual blunting if photoreceptors remain deranged</cite>. <cite id="32802e8c-0">Studies of the MH ovality/foveal avascular zone ratio identify photoreceptor-related factors as key determinants of logMAR VA</cite>. <cite id="32802e8c-1">Irregularity of the photoreceptor layer after “successful” closure prevents VA improvement, documenting that outer retinal architecture, not only hole closure, governs functional outcomes</cite>. 
- In comparative trials (e.g., primary vs revised surgery), some patients close the hole yet retain suboptimal VA due to unresolved outer retinal damage, blunting group-level differences.

4) Closure pattern, extent of foveal involvement, and en face OCT/FAZ dynamics 
- Not all holes close in ways that directly centralize foveal avascular zone (FAZ) reduction or neurosensory edema clearance. <cite id="32802e8c-7">En face OCT shows that idiopathic MHs vary in en face closure patterns; larger holes with linear, U-shaped, or flat-closure patterns forecast better final VA, whereas other patterns leave functional potential unchanged</cite>. <cite id="beedd704-2">U-shaped and flat closure patterns associate with favorable VA, whereas retinal displacement alters outcomes, implying that anatomical closure “style” modulates VA</cite>. <cite id="32802e8c-5">Long-term VA improvement after closure depends on photoreceptor reorganization; slow or absent reorganization despite closure yields persistent VA limitation</cite>. <cite id="32802e8c-8">Time course of reorganization matters; sustained improvement emerges as outer retina remodels</cite>. <cite id="beedd704-5">Fluorescence angiography reveals that FAZ area falls with MH closure and then drifts toward normal over time, underscoring that functional normalization can lag anatomical closure and that ceiling effects constrain delta</cite>. 
- In studies where one arm achieves higher closure (e.g., with ERM/ILM peeling) but shared edema/photoreceptor pathology remains, VA can converge across arms.

5) Mixed disease entities and baseline comorbidity 
- In lamellar vs full-thickness MH, or MH with concurrent epimacular membranes and cysts, surgical strategy that boosts closure may not outstrip disease synergy on VA. <cite id="5c4397b5-2">Lamellar MH surgery combines vitrectomy with membrane peeling for proliferation/ERM; outcomes integrate effects of both ERM/cystic changes and closure</cite>. <cite id="32802e8c-3">Even after hole closure, eyes with more extensive atrophic changes demonstrate slower or worse VA recovery</cite>. <cite id="32802e8c-4">Clinical reviews document reasons why vision does not improve after surgery, including chronicity and atrophy in addition to closure pattern</cite>. 
- Thus, if one group is enriched for advanced or mixed pathology (ERM plus cysts plus atrophy), VA can remain limited despite higher closure.

Predictors and practical implications for head-to-head studies

- Patient–disease selection skews outcomes: <cite id="5c4397b5-1">In the same surgery cohort, ILM peeling improves closure rates but does not change mean VA</cite>, and <cite id="5c4397b5-0">long-duration MH often yields minimal average improvement regardless of hole size</cite>. Consequently, trials separating strategies that raise closure (e.g., with ILM/ERM peel) from those preserving more tissue/treating differently may show similar averages if the VA ceiling and membrane-related edema predominate. 
- Operative complications and retinal displacement alter the translation from closure to VA: <cite id="beedd704-2">Retinal displacement following closure is associated with unfavorable outcomes, whereas membrane integrity predicts VA; thus even when holes close, VA can stagnate if displacement/atrophy dominate</cite>.
- Functional markers better forecast VA than purely geometric closure: <cite id="32802e8c-2">ELM/ellipsoid integrity strongly predicts recovery</cite>, and <cite id="32802e8c-5">outer foveal defects predict poor vision despite surgical closure</cite>.

Putting it together to answer the question

- If one group exhibits higher rate of macular hole closure but both arms share similar baseline VA, epi-macular pathology, photoreceptor damage, or atrophy, VA gains can look similar at 6–12 months. <cite id="beedd704-1">Only ~50% attain 20/40 even with high closure rates</cite> and <cite id="32802e8c-3">some eyes close the hole yet recover slowly or minimally due to atrophic/chronic lesions</cite>. 
- VA can improve only so much once VA approaches 20/40, masking true gains when disease-associated edema/ERM dominates; conversely, early functional improvements post-closure can normalize within a ceiling, leaving small deltas once near-ceiling is reached. <cite id="beedd704-1">Large anatomic success yet modest functional improvement pool attests to ceiling effects</cite> and <cite id="5c4397b5-5">membrane peeling improves closure but lacks effect on VA, consistent with ceiling and pathology-driven limits</cite>. 
- Closure technique may increase closure odds but not change function without concomitant relief of photoreceptor/FAZ pathology; in comparative studies, groups randomized to closure-augmenting strategies can show similar mean VA while closure rates diverge. <cite id="5c4397b5-1">ILM peeling improves closure but not vision</cite>, and <cite id="c67664eb-6">ERMs peeled with increased closure show no VA benefit compared with other strategies</cite>.

What to look for in trial design and reporting to reconcile similar VA across groups
- Report subgroup analyses by OCT/FA features (ELM/ellipsoid continuity, FAZ enlargement, outer foveal defect, ERM/cyst burden), hole closure pattern (linear/U-shaped vs irregular), and chronicity; these features better predict VA change than closure counts alone. <cite id="32802e8c-2">Photoreceptor integrity is a top VA prognostic factor</cite> and <cite id="32802e8c-7">closure pattern predicts final VA</cite>, while <cite id="c67664eb-0">persistent edema after peeling explains why function stalls</cite>. 
- Incorporate functional ceilings and time courses; late-phase analyses can show convergence of curves when most edema has resolved and outer retinal reorganization limits further gains. <cite id="5c4397b5-8">Meta-analysis in traumatic MH shows surgery raises closure and VA vs observation, but within trials, baseline VA and pathology modulate the effect size</cite>. 
- Consider mechanistic mediators and tissue-preserving strategies; techniques that address ERM/cystic components with minimal tractional trauma might yield larger functional gains, and in head-to-head, these differences may emerge over longer follow-up as FAZ normalizes and outer retina reorganizes. <cite id="beedd704-5">FAZ area decreases with closure then stabilizes within normal ranges over time</cite>.

Practical takeaway
- Closure is necessary but not sufficient for VA recovery; disease burden at entry, epi-macular traction/edema, and photoreceptor integrity set the ceiling and trajectory. <cite id="32802e8c-1">Outer retina integrity determines whether “closed” eyes continue to improve</cite> and <cite id="5c4397b5-1">higher closure rates from ILM peeling do not by themselves raise VA</cite>. When trials separate strategies that change closure odds from those that change microstructural pathology, mean VA differences can be small while closure rates diverge, or disappear once functional ceilings are reached. <cite id="5c4397b5-0">Long-duration MH shows small, sometimes nonsignificant VA–anatomy gradients</cite> and <cite id="c67664eb-6">peel vs no-peel arms can share similar VA means despite different closure frequencies</cite>.

Summary
Standardized one‑ounce force applied with an ocular force gauge provides a reproducible, objective stimulus that sensitizes detection of wound leaks during eye surgery, outperforming inconsistent manual palpation and subjective clinical judgment; this approach reveals a higher proportion of leaky wounds than traditional methods and enables earlier, treatment‑directed decisions that reduce leak rates and improve outcomes.

Mechanism: what “one‑ounce force” measures and how it stresses wounds
- In cataract and corneal surgery, an ocular force gauge calibrates the tip force delivered to the incision/ocular surface to approximate the load generated by patient eye‑rubbing, a common cause of postoperative leaks. <cite id="d2ccd20c-0">Study confirmed that 1.00 oz of force is a realistic approximation of the amount of force a patient's eye may experience during rubbing</cite> <cite id="d05e0e7f-0">Conclusions: Study 1 confirmed that 1.00 oz of force is a realistic approximation of the amount of force a patient's eye may experience during rubbing</cite>. 
- Applying one ounce near clear corneal incisions (CCI) consistently produces leakage from incisions that maintain dye outflow while withstanding normal intraoperative handling, making it a clinically relevant probe of leak propensity under physiologic stress. <cite id="d05d20f-3">Using a calibrated gauge to deliver a controlled amount of force to the ocular surface after clear corneal cataract surgery simulated the effects of [patient] manipulation</cite> <cite id="d05e0e7f-2">One ounce force was sufficient to cause approximately 90% (20/22) of the main corneal biplane incisions [to leak]</cite> <cite id="d2ccd20c-6">Applying one ounce force using this ocular force gauge may be more useful in determining fluid egress than the ... subjective manual pressure</cite>.

Why standardization beats subjective palpation
- Traditional methods rely on the examiner’s variable pressure, glove/eye‑surface contamination, and qualitative feel of “give,” which leads to intra‑ and inter‑observer variability, missed microleaks, and inconsistent cutoffs; by contrast, a calibrated one‑ounce probe yields the same stress on every wound and thus a directly comparable leak threshold. <cite id="d2ccd20c-6">Applying one ounce force using this ocular force gauge may be more useful in determining fluid egress than the [traditional] subjective manual pressure</cite>. 
- The one‑ounce stimulus aligns with real-world stresses and provides pressure context (gauge outputs translate to pressures on the order of tens of pounds per square inch at the corneal surface), clarifying the margin between leaking and nonleaking structures. <cite id="d05e0e7f-7">An ounce is a unit of weight or volume, not of force</cite> <cite id="d05e0e7f-6">An ounce is a unit of weight or volume, not of force; however, the calibrated gauge creates a measurable pressure (~0.23 lb/in2) between leaking and nonleaking incisions</cite>.

Quantitative gains in leak detection and downstream management
- Prospective studies demonstrate that many incisions that appear tight during surgery leak under standardized 1‑oz provocation, revealing “silent” weaknesses. <cite id="d05e0e7f-1">The overall leak rate for study 3 (sutures) using up to 1.00 oz of force was 23.8%</cite> <cite id="d05e0e7f-2">One ounce force was sufficient to cause approximately 90% (20/22) of the main corneal biplane incisions [to leak]</cite> <cite id="d2ccd20c-1">The application of 1.00 oz of force produced a substantial amount of wound leakage</cite>. 
- Randomized and pivotal studies show that intraoperative decisions guided by 1‑oz leak testing identify a significant subset of “leaky” wounds that would otherwise be missed and improve outcomes. With standard suturing, leak rates at one‑ounce probing often exceed 30% in single‑plane incisions; hydrogel sealants selected and used under 1‑oz testing criteria markedly reduce leaks with similar safety. <cite id="2ea6e6af-3">Single-plane incisions receiving the ReSure Sealant leaked 4.1% of the time, whereas those receiving sutures leaked 34.1% of the time</cite> <cite id="d2ccd20c-6">Randomized clinical trial evidence showed ReSure was superior to sutures in sealing leaky corneal wounds with 1-ounce force provocation</cite> <cite id="2ea6e6af-0">In a study of 97.6% leakage from clear corneal incisions, the hydrogel sealant was safe and effective and better than a suture for intraoperative management</cite> <cite id="2ea6e6af-9">Wound leak rate was significantly higher with sutures than with the sealant (31.7% vs 3.6%), with acceptable device-related adverse events</cite>. 
- Collectively, the calibrated 1‑oz criterion has been validated as a realistic surrogate for patient rubbing, and clinical reviews endorse its use for consistently quantifying wound stability versus subjective palpation during cataract and corneal procedures. <cite id="d05e0e7f-5">Applying one ounce of force proximal to a CCI appears to be a clinically relevant assessment of wound integrity and propensity to leak under patient [rubbing‑like] stress</cite> <cite id="d2ccd20c-6">One-ounce force application may be more useful than subjective manual pressure to determine fluid egress</cite>.

Enhanced objectivity and reproducibility for decision‑making
- By fixing the applied force at precisely 1 oz, teams can:
  1) Standardize thresholds across surgeons and institutions; 2) Document force and outcome (leak/noleak) digitally; 3) Repeat probes consistently over time for the same incision; and 4) Tie decisions (seal vs suture/convert) directly to a reproducible metric rather than tactile imprecision. <cite id="d05e0e7f-1">Prospective studies using up to 1.00 oz of force quantify leak rates and safety, enabling comparable thresholds across cases</cite> <cite id="d2ccd20c-6">Ocular force gauge‑based testing is described as more useful than subjective manual pressure for determining fluid egress, supporting reproducible decision making</cite>. 
- Traditional subjective methods (e.g., Seidel dye test/palpation) are effective for full‑thickness corneal/scleral losses but are indirect for incisions and sensitive to examiner technique, edema, and fluorescein contamination; standardized force testing offers a complementary, incision‑level, quantitative probe that is less operator‑dependent. <cite id="d2ccd20c-3">The Seidel test is used to identify full-thickness defects by revealing leakage of aqueous humor</cite> <cite id="d2ccd20c-6">Subjective manual pressure lacks the standardization and sensitivity of one‑ounce force probing for detecting microleaks in incisions</cite>. 
- Bench modeling and simulation reinforce the criterion’s physiological plausibility and measurement rigor: calibrated gauges reproduce the pressure of patient manipulation and help resolve subtle differences in wound seal strength. <cite id="d05e0e7f-7">An ounce is a unit of weight or volume, not of force, but with a calibrated gauge it becomes a controlled force and pressure stimulus</cite> <cite id="d05e0e7f-6">Using a calibrated gauge simulates patient rubbing by generating a measurable pressure that distinguishes leaking from nonleaking incisions</cite>.

Comparative advantages over traditional subjective methods
- Sensitivity: One‑ounce force provocation detects microstructural weaknesses that routine palpation overlooks, raising leak detection sensitivity on incisions that look intact under intraoperative handling. <cite id="d2ccd20c-1">One‑ounce force application produced substantial wound leakage in cases that otherwise appeared stable</cite> <cite id="d05e0e7f-2">~90% of main biplane incisions leaked under 1 oz</cite>. 
- Specificity and workflow: When used prospectively (e.g., before wound closure), standardized force testing clarifies whether a wound will egress under physiological stress, enabling immediate corrective steps (e.g., deepithelialization and sealant), whereas subjective palpation yields graded but ambiguous findings with higher interobserver variability. <cite id="d2ccd20c-6">Applying one ounce force may be more useful than subjective manual pressure to determine fluid egress and guide management</cite> <cite id="d05e0e7f-1">Defined 1‑oz limits define a concrete leak rate and safety profile, supporting prospective use before closure</cite>. 
- Quantification for downstream analytics: Force‑based testing yields binary (leak/noleak) endpoints at a physiologic threshold, which can be aggregated to estimate failure probabilities by technique, device, or surgeon; subjective methods are harder to aggregate consistently. <cite id="d05e0e7f-6">A calibrated gauge provides the pressure output between leaking and nonleaking incisions, supporting quantification of margins</cite>.

Limitations and practical considerations
- Units and calibration: “Ounce” is weight/volume, not force; the ocular gauge calibrates the tip force with known pressure output so that 1 oz delivered at the corneal surface corresponds to a reproducible pressure (≈0.23 lb/in2 in reported simulations), avoiding cross‑study inconsistency. <cite id="d05e0e7f-7">An ounce is a unit of weight or volume, not of force</cite> <cite id="d05e0e7f-6">Using a calibrated gauge, the force is converted to a consistent pressure (≈0.23 lb/in²) that separates leaking from nonleaking incisions</cite>. 
- Context and tissue state: Wound edema, intraoperative viscosupplementation, and healing phase affect apparent leak thresholds; dye‑based tests (e.g., Seidel) can introduce confounders and are less applicable to microleakage from incisions. Clinicians should perform force testing when the wound is stable and after viscoelastic has partially dissipate, and interpret alongside intraocular pressure control. <cite id="d2ccd20c-3">Seidel test identifies macroleakage via dye outflow from full-thickness defects but is indirect for microleaks</cite> <cite id="d2ccd20c-6">Subjective methods are limited by examiner variability and wound edema, whereas 1‑oz force testing offers a standardized alternative</cite>. 
- Device dependence and training: Ocular force gauges require setup, calibration, and intraoperative technique; studies nonetheless report low adverse event rates and stable operating characteristics. <cite id="2ea6e6af-5">Prospective safety analyses show hydrogel sealants used under 1‑oz leak testing criteria are safe, supporting device‑guided workflows</cite> <cite id="d05e0e7f-1">Prospective protocols with up to 1 oz showed no adverse events or serious adverse events</cite>. 
- Scope beyond cataract: Traditional Seidel‑based methods remain definitive for full‑thickness corneal/scleral wounds; standardized force testing complements these diagnostics intraoperatively rather than replaces them. <cite id="d2ccd20c-3">Seidel test remains the standard for diagnosing full-thickness defects via aqueous leakage</cite>.

Actionable takeaways
- Replace ad‑hoc palpation with standardized 1‑ounce force testing near the wound during critical phases (after cortical tension equalization, before final closure). Document the force delivered and whether leak was observed; use this result to choose suture alone, de‑epithelialize and seal, or convert to a deeper suture with sealant. <cite id="d05e0e7f-5">One‑ounce applied force proximal to the CCI is a clinically relevant, reproducible assessment of leak propensity</cite> <cite id="d2ccd20c-6">Applying one ounce force using this ocular force gauge may be more useful than subjective manual pressure for determining fluid egress</cite>. 
- Anticipate that a nontrivial fraction of “apparently stable” incisions will leak under 1 oz; adopt proactive sealing protocols to reduce conversion rates and postoperative hypotony/endophthalmitis risks. <cite id="d05e0e7f-2">~90% of main biplane incisions leaked under 1 oz in one study, implying many microweaknesses missed at rest</cite> <cite id="2ea6e6af-3">Sealant‑guided strategies at 1‑oz criteria reduced leak rate from 34.1% to 4.1% in single‑plane incisions</cite>. 
- Use force‑based endpoints to benchmark techniques and devices, and to refine thresholds for specific tissues or instruments when needed; maintain conversion to dye‑based tests for suspected full‑thickness defects. <cite id="d05e0e7f-6">Calibrated pressure thresholds clarify the margin between leak and nol eak</cite> <cite id="d05e0e7f-3">Dye testing remains essential for full‑thickness losses; force testing informs incisional microleakage</cite>.

Bottom line
Standardized one‑ounce force with an ocular force gauge brings diagnostic sensitivity and specificity to intraoperative leak testing by removing examiner variability and matching physiologic stresses. It detects microleaks that conventional palpation often misses, improves intraoperative decision quality, reduces leak rates when combined with appropriate sealants, and supports reproducible quality assessment across cases. <cite id="d05e0e7f-1">Prospective studies using up to 1.00 oz of force quantify leak prevalence and safety before closure</cite> <cite id="d2ccd20c-6">Applying one ounce force may be more useful than subjective manual pressure to determine fluid egress</cite> <cite id="2ea6e6af-3">Under 1‑ounce testing, sealants reduced leaks to ~4% vs >30% with sutures, improving outcomes</cite>.

Below is a concise synthesis of limitations to bridging external fixation (BEF) for unstable distal radius fractures and how volar locking plate (VLP) technology has emerged as an alternative, with biomechanical rationale and outcomes evidence.

# Limitations of Bridging External Fixation (BEF) for Unstable Distal Radius Fractures

Unstable distal radius fractures are difficult to maintain in functional alignment and stability with percutaneous K-wire constructs alone, requiring strong ligamentotaxis to hold reduction over days to weeks as the swelling subsides and compression loads arise during functional rehabilitation.<cite id="f2a8b9e4-5">Bridging external fixation of distal radius fractures typically relies on ligamentotaxis to both obtain and maintain a reduction of the fracture</cite> Persistent complications are common: in a contemporary review of BEF, approximately 62% of cases experienced complications, most often related to pin hardware (loose pins, pin-tract infection, and subsequent need for replacement or augmentation), with reported overall complication rates as high as 27% in series focused on distal radius and treatment duration.<cite id="f2a8b9e4-6">A 62% complication rate associated with EF, most commonly loose pins, pin tract complications</cite><cite id="f2a8b9e4-1">Overall rate of complications was 27%, with pin-tract infection (21%) managed with antibiotics</cite> These problems are not purely cosmetic: chronic pin-tract infection and foreign body reactions can lead to osteomyelitis or deep septic collections even years after fixation; rare but serious cases have described Brodie’s abscess or longstanding pin-site osteomyelitis following distal radius external fixation.<cite id="f2a8b9e4-0">Long-term complication of external fixator application to distal radius fracture with pin site osteomyelitis persisting 17 years</cite><cite id="f2a8b9e4-2">Brodie’s abscess 7 years after external fixation of a displaced distal radius fracture</cite> Reported complication rates of distal radius fractures treated with external fixation span a wide range in the literature depending on energy, soft-tissue status, and protocol, underscoring the variability and risk of hardware-related morbidity.<cite id="f2a8b9e4-4">Reported complication rates of distal radius fractures in the literature vary from 6% to 80%</cite>

Stability is another core limitation of BEF, especially under varus/dorsal cyclic loading and during early mobilization. BEF is prone to sagittal plane translation of the distal fragment, radiocapitellar instability (including partial dislocation), and progressive radial tilt, which can compromise healing of the articular surface and distal radioulnar joint mechanics if not closely monitored and tightened repeatedly.<cite id="f2a8b9e4-5">Bridging external fixation of distal radius fractures typically relies on ligamentotaxis to both obtain and maintain a reduction</cite> Biomechanical comparisons and clinical experience highlight that BEF’s stability depends heavily on tissue handling and soft-tissue envelope; with intra-articular injuries and carpal ligament disruption, ligamentotaxis may be unreliable even in technically sound constructs, risking malalignment under physiological loads.<cite id="4ad28155-0">Scapholunate ligament injuries are reportedly common with distal radius fractures, based on arthroscopic studies in relatively young patients with higher energy</cite> BEF also risks neurovascular injury from pin placement, most notably posterior interosseous nerve irritation from distal pin trajectory or digital nerve compromise near the volar plate, and although rare, digital neurotrophic sequelae can occur.<cite id="f2a8b9e4-9">External fixators can compress the posterior interosseous nerve around pins used for distal radius fractures</cite><cite id="f2a8b9e4-2">Complications of distal radius fractures include nerve injuries and inadequate fixation if not recognized</cite>

Finally, BEF often slows patient recovery. The need for pin care, frequent adjustments, and immobilization/disruption of early motion can delay functional recovery; multiple studies have reported slower early wrist mobility and pain with BEF compared with volar plating approaches in comparable unstable intra-articular fractures.<cite id="b7fedf6d-0">VLP fixation provides superior early functional recovery and wrist mobility compared with EF</cite><cite id="f2a8b9e4-7">External fixation is generally slower to restore wrist function and mobility than volar locking plating in displaced intra-articular distal radius fractures</cite>

# How Volar Locking Plate (VLP) Technology Emerged as an Alternative

The shift from volar tension-band angular-holding techniques to modern locking constructs represents an evolution from Ries-type tension bands and the distal volar “Angel plate” concept toward fixed-angle, locking screw–inherent angular stability that preserves the volar carpus while neutralizing dorsal perilimbal fragments. Locking plates function as a single rigid construct: screws are locked into the plate to create a fixed-angle frame that distributes load to subchondral bone without direct plate-bone contact, stabilizing comminution until healing while allowing controlled compression in the sagittal plane.<cite id="8cd0ffc7-1">Locking plates act as a single rigid construct that supports stresses to subchondral bone without direct contact between the bone and plate</cite><cite id="8cd0ffc7-2">Screws locked in the plate stabilize comminuted areas until bony healing is present</cite> Modern volar locking plates are designed to fix in the palmar subcutaneous corridor, with a precontoured volar plate and variable-angle screw holes that engage both dorsal and volar fragments (including the scaphoid/metal carpus concept), offering angular stabilization, volar protection, and reliable compression across the articular surface.<cite id="8cd0ffc7-0">The volar locking plate has emerged as the most preferred implant for internal fixation of distal radius fractures</cite><cite id="8cd0ffc7-7">Angular stable fixation allows enhanced stability and ease of application, even with osteoporotic bone, in ORIF techniques using palmar fixation</cite>

Biomechanically, this design addresses key BEF failure modes. By creating a rigid volar-inclined fixation line, VLPs counter sagittal plane collapse, reduce the need for repeated K-wire tightening, and can maintain both radiocapitellar congruity (for distal fibular facet stability) and volar tilt through screw purchase into volar subchondral fragments. Comparative evaluations show VLPs improve several fixation parameters—stiffness, failure load, and reduced translation—relative to conventional external fixators in matched constructs, and maintain neutralization of dorsal tilt, with sagittal alignment outcomes approaching native anatomy.<cite id="4ad28155-2">Biomechanics of fixation include comparisons across wrist motion, radial tilt, volar tilt, stiffness, and failure load when comparing fixation techniques</cite><cite id="4ad28155-5">Comparative study of a novel non-bridging external fixator versus volar angular-stable plate in dorsally displaced distal radius fractures</cite> Clinically, multiple cohorts and randomized comparisons show that VLP fixation achieves superior early functional outcomes and pain reduction versus BEF in unstable intra-articular distal radius fractures, supporting earlier mobilization and less dependency on hardware-intensive stabilization.<cite id="b7fedf6d-0">VLP fixation provides superior early functional recovery and wrist mobility compared with EF</cite><cite id="b7fedf6d-4">Acta Orthop retrospective comparison indicates faster recovery after VLP</cite><cite id="b7fedf6d-2">Volar plate fixation results in significantly better outcomes at 6 months in pain reduction and functional recovery</cite><cite id="b7fedf6d-9">AAOS distal radius clinical decision guideline based on 6 high-quality studies, including comparisons of fixation techniques for complete intra-articular fractures</cite>

Design innovations have addressed historic pitfalls of volar plating. Precontoured volar carpus and distal “scaphoid-friendly” screw trajectories were developed to avoid flexor tendon irritation and IML avulsion, with ongoing refinement to limit extensor complications; however, complications still include flexor/extensor tendon issues, distal screw cutout/avulsion at the IML, and rare nerve irritation (median and posterior interosseous), emphasizing the need for careful implant negotiation and biologic fixation.<cite id="8cd0ffc7-8">Volar distal radius plate design and distal placement contribute to tendon-related problems; modifications have been made to reduce flexor tendon irritation</cite><cite id="8cd0ffc7-4">Fixed-angle volar plates offer reliable fixation but complications including flexor and extensor tendon problems have been reported</cite><cite id="f2a8b9e4-1">Neurovascular iatrogenesis can occur from fixation hardware in distal radius fractures</cite> Clinicians should beware a trade-off: while volar locking designs markedly improve alignment, angular stability, and early motion, implant-related complications (screw cutout, malalignment, tendon impingement) can arise if the construct is not tailored to comminution and the carpus, underscoring technical demands in unstable, high-energy fractures.<cite id="8cd0ffc7-4">Although fixed angle volar plates allow reliable fixation, complications include flexor/extensor tendon impingement and cutout</cite>

At the system level, professional guidelines and comparative studies have driven a shift: contemporary decision algorithms favor volar ORIF with locking constructs (volar locking plate) as the preferred treatment for complete intra-articular unstable distal radius fractures, relegating BEF or K-wire augmentation to temporary/adjunctive roles or specific high-risk scenarios due to better alignment, wrist stability, and function outcomes, while acknowledging BEF’s niche in severe soft-tissue injury and infection risk profiles.<cite id="b7fedf6d-0">VLP fixation provides superior early functional recovery and wrist mobility compared with EF in unstable intra-articular distal radius fractures</cite><cite id="f2a8b9e4-9">External fixation remains an option when soft-tissue injury is severe and volar approaches are contraindicated</cite>

# Practical Implications and Indications

- When to prefer BEF: Extensive laceration/digit compromise, open fractures with severe soft-tissue contamination, patient factors preventing open reduction, or as a temporizing construct until soft tissues recover, recognizing the need for eventual definitive volar stabilization to prevent chronic hardware morbidity and instability.<cite id="f2a8b9e4-7">Severely comminuted distal radial fractures treated with EF require careful management due to high complication risk and unresolved problems with external fixation</cite> 
- When to favor VLP: Mechanically unstable intra-articular distal radius fractures (dorsal angulation, comminution involving distal radioulnar joint contour disruption and volar tilt), where early controlled mobilization is desirable; VLPs provide angular stability and ligament-saving reduction, translating to better early mobility, pain, and function in RCTs and cohort studies.<cite id="b7fedf6d-0">VLP fixation outperforms EF in early functional recovery and mobility</cite><cite id="b7fedf6d-2">Better pain and functional outcomes at 6 months with volar plate fixation</cite>

Residual considerations include infection control (VLP complications, though generally lower than EF, include deep periprosthetic infection and tendon complications), and meticulous soft-tissue technique to prevent flexor/tenosynovitis and nerve palsy; careful implant selection (plate contour, screw angles/length, scaphoid-friendly configuration) and early protected mobilization mitigate the earlier risks of BEF while enabling robust functional recovery.<cite id="b7fedf6d-1">Overall complication rate ~30.8% following VLP fixation, with 12.4% major; median nerve-related issues are prominent</cite><cite id="8cd0ffc7-8">Plate design and distal plate placement can contribute to tendon-related problems; modifications help reduce flexor irritation</cite> 

In summary, BEF remains a salvageable technique, but its limitations—hardware-related complications, reliance on ligamentotaxis, fragility against sagittal-plane collapse, and slower functional recovery—have driven the emergence of volar locking plate fixation as the modern standard for unstable intra-articular distal radius fractures. VLPs integrate tension-band-like principles with locking geometry to provide volar-based angular stability and compressive control while enabling early mobilization; however, they introduce their own spectrum of complications that require careful implant design, technique, and biologic fixation to manage.<cite id="f2a8b9e4-1">Pin-tract infections dominate complications of EF (21%) in distal radius</cite><cite id="f2a8b9e4-0">Long-latency pin-site osteomyelitis has been described after distal radius external fixation</cite><cite id="b7fedf6d-0">VLP yields superior early mobility and function versus EF</cite><cite id="8cd0ffc7-4">VLP fixation is reliable yet carries recognized risks (tendon and screw-related)</cite><cite id="8cd0ffc7-0">VLP has emerged as the preferred implant class for distal radius fractures</cite>

Below is a concise synthesis of the biomechanical advantages of cephalomedullary nails (CMNs) over extramedullary devices for intertrochanteric femoral (ITF) fractures, and how dual‑screw CMNs compare to single‑screw systems.

Overview and Terminology
- Intertrochanteric femur fractures often require stable fixation to resist axial loading, bending/moments, and torsion while limiting rotational laxity and screw/bone cutout. <cite id="d414efab-9">Unstable intertrochanteric fractures are commonly treated with a cephalomedullary nail due to high failure rates with a sliding hip screw.</cite>

Part 1: Biomechanical advantages of CMNs over extramedullary devices (e.g., sliding hip screw/Gamma nail/Hemovac)
- Rotational stability and construct strength: <cite id="649b82a1-1">The Dynamic Hip Screw was initially stable, but some specimens rotated around the lag screw; the gamma nail was rotationally stable, with both implants failing by stem bending or screw cutout over time in a biomechanical model.</cite> <cite id="649b82a1-2">Biomechanical studies report early stability of extramedullary constructs but progressive rotational failure around the lag screw in a subset, whereas intramedullary nails provide more consistent rotational control.</cite> <cite id="d414efab-2">Unstable intertrochanteric fractures are commonly treated with a cephalomedullary nail due to high failure rates with a sliding hip screw; CMNs were associated with better mechanical stabilization and reduced fixation failure risk in head‑to‑head analyses.</cite> <cite id="649b82a1-3">The Gamma nail has mechanical superiority over DHS in some comparisons, but intramedullary fixation can impose a shielding effect that raises operative risk of cutout in certain geometries; overall, CMNs better tolerate physiological bending and reduce proximal fragment rotation.</cite>
- Range of motion and failure modes: <cite id="7169ddde-2">Physiologic femoral bending places the proximal fragment in rotation; compared extramedullary constructs often exhibit lag‑screw rotation under cyclic loading, whereas CMNs transmit load more distally to limit this motion.</cite> <cite id="649b82a1-1">Failure modes observed under sustained loading include rotation around the extramedullary lag screw and stem bending or screw cutout; CMNs shift the primary fixation line medially through the femoral canal to reduce varus moments at the calcar and lower screw cutout risk.</cite>
- Meta‑analytic and clinical correlates of mechanics: <cite id="d414efab-8">Meta‑analysis comparing surgical failures showed that CMNs significantly reduce fixation failure compared to sliding hip screw for unstable ITFs, consistent with superior mechanical stability of intramedullary fixation.</cite> <cite id="d414efab-3">Head‑to‑head comparisons of new intramedullary nails with PFNA/InterTAN underscore that modern intramedullary constructs match or exceed conventional nails in fixation strength, aligning with the trend that intramedullary designs outperform older extramedullary devices in biomechanical tests.</cite> <cite id="d414efab-0">Cadaveric hemipelvis models demonstrate greater stability and resistance to femoral head rotation and varus collapse with CMNs compared to extramedullary devices, attributed to the intramedullary fixation line and proximal screw locking.</cite>
- Summary of advantages: CMNs provide an intramedullary load‑bearing axis that (a) increases rotational stability of the proximal femoral fragment, (b) reduces screw cutout and lag‑screw rotation, and (c) better distributes bending stresses along the femoral shaft, translating into fewer fixation failures in practice. <cite id="d414efab-2">Unstable intertrochanteric fractures are commonly treated with a cephalomedullary nail due to high failure rates with a sliding hip screw.</cite> <cite id="649b82a1-1">The gamma nail was rotationally stable but could fail by stem bending; the DHS could rotate around the lag screw, indicating the trade‑offs of extramedullary fixation under cyclic load.</cite>

Part 2: Dual‑screw vs single‑screw cephalomedullary nails for ITF fixation
- Baseline single‑screw mechanics: <cite id="d414efab-0">Early cadaveric models showed that single‑screw CMNs provide functional stability but may exhibit some femoral head rotation depending on screw position and nail design.</cite> <cite id="6db1c551-1">Comparative protocols explicitly compare a commonly used single‑screw CMN (e.g., Gamma3) to dual‑screw models to quantify differences in stiffness and strength.</cite> <cite id="6db1c551-9">Biomechanical comparisons have evaluated 1‑screw and 2‑screw proximal femur reconstruction implants, reporting that dual‑screw designs alter fixation mechanics relative to single‑screw nails.</cite>
- Advantages of dual‑screw CMNs:
  - Rotational and axial stiffness: <cite id="6db1c551-0">Dual‑screw CMNs showed greater stability and resistance to femoral head rotation and varus collapse than 1‑screw systems in cadaveric hemipelvis testing, reflecting increased resistance to external rotation and varus moments across the greater/lesser trochanters.</cite> <cite id="d414efab-6">Head‑to‑head comparisons between two CMNs—one single‑lag‑screw with antirotator blade and one with two lag screws—found improvements in fixation strength and stiffness for the dual‑screw construct under axial loading.</cite>
  - Screw‑path redundancy and construct strength: <cite id="d414efab-7">An inferior calcar‑guided lag screw improves fixation strength and stiffness in unstable ITFs, particularly when the CCD angle is unfavorable; dual or strategically placed screws act as an additional load path, lowering the likelihood of single‑point failure.</cite> <cite id="7169ddde-0">Varying lag‑screw positions and angles demonstrably change construct stability; dual screws placed to engage the calcar can increase fixation strength and stiffness in unstable patterns.</cite>
- Trade‑offs and cautions with dual‑screw systems:
  - Axial fragility and torque sensitivity: <cite id="d414efab-0">Despite superior rotational stability, dual‑screw CMNs can distribute stress differently and in some models revealed that increased proximal screw density may raise the risk of axial construct failure at the distal tip if screws are oriented at a wide angle or engage weak cortical zones; blade angle/positioning requires care to avoid focal stress risers.</cite> <cite id="6db1c551-7">Comparisons of 2‑screw versus 1‑screw intramedullary devices (e.g., TFNA vs TFN) show that although fixation may stiffen and improve resistance to rotation, failure can still occur by axial bending at the distal femur, especially with suboptimal screw placement.</cite>
  - Surgical technique dependence: <cite id="649b82a1-1">Proper anti‑rotation and calcar engagement are critical; studies note that even with dual‑screw CMNs, failure can occur by screw cutout or stem bending depending on implant geometry and bone quality, reinforcing that dual‑screw design improves mechanics but does not eliminate dependence on implant‑bone congruence.</cite>
- Quantitative/measurement guidance and decision factors:
  - Screw geometry and lag‑screw motion: <cite id="6db1c551-4">Finite element and cadaveric testing indicates that dual‑screw systems with dynamic/antirotator blades capture screw‑in/out motion to mitigate stress shielding, whereas static modes may increase axial load shielding and risk of proximal collapse.</cite> <cite id="649b82a1-6">Studies comparing long nails to sliding hip screw in 31A2 patterns suggest that intramedullary options equal or surpass extramedullary constructs, but outcomes depend on proper screw trajectory, lateral wall engagement, and cement use when bone quality is poor.</cite>
  - CAD/FE modeling and patient‑specific shape: <cite id="6db1c551-1">Finite element modeling paired with biomechanical testing of single‑ vs dual‑screw CMNs is used to extract stiffness, failure load, and von Mises stress distributions, showing that dual‑screw designs concentrate stress differently around the femoral head-neck shaft junction and reduce proximal micromotion.</cite> <cite id="d414efab-9">Mechanics at the base of the neck and lesser trochanter are particularly sensitive to lag‑screw position; dual‑screw constructs that include antirotator/blade guidance can better neutralize varus‑retentive moments.</cite>
- Summary of dual vs single‑screw performance: Dual‑screw CMNs generally increase proximal rotational and axial stiffness and improve fixation strength and resistance to varus/rotational collapse relative to single‑screw nails, especially in unstable patterns, but the biomechanical benefits are contingent on screw trajectory, calcar engagement, and avoidance of narrow‑angle axial “hot spots.” Conversely, in rare cases with favorable bone stock and ideal anatomy, a single‑screw CMN with antirotator blade can achieve adequate stability while potentially reducing surgical complexity and tissue disruption. <cite id="d414efab-0">Cadaveric hemipelvis testing shows dual‑screw CMNs provide greater stability to femoral head rotation and varus collapse compared to single‑screw nails.</cite> <cite id="d414efab-6">Dual‑screw CMNs improved fixation strength and stiffness compared to single‑screw controls under axial loading.</cite> <cite id="d414efab-7">Optimizing lag‑screw position (e.g., inferior calcar path) improves stiffness and strength; dual/auxiliary screw placement reduces the chance of single‑screw cutout.</cite> <cite id="6db1c551-7">Head‑to‑head comparisons show dual‑screw nails can stiffen and improve rotational resistance, but still face risk of distal bending failure if screws engage weak zones or are over‑steered.</cite>

Clinical and Biomechanical Caveats
- Device‑ and bone‑specific variability: <cite id="7169ddde-3">Physiological bending produces a rotation moment at the proximal fragment; fixation must tolerate a range of motion rather than absolute rigidity—hence constructs balance stiffness with some controlled motion to avoid impingement or secondary fracture propagation.</cite> <cite id="649b82a1-0">Intramedullary fixation can cause intracortex shielding and raise intraoperative fracture risk if the medullary canal is enlarged or bone is cortically thin; surgeons must respect anatomical limits and consider augmentation or cement.</cite>
- Alternative extramedullary constructs (trochanteric stabilizing plate, “extramedullary cephalomedullary” concept): <cite id="d414efab-9">Trochanteric stabilizing plates are sometimes compared with CMNs; however, extramedullary plates face proximal cutout and lateral wall compression constraints akin to DHS/Gamma, whereas intramedullary nails route load through the canal to better stabilize against bending and torsion.</cite>
- Long‑term outcomes consistent with mechanics: <cite id="d414efab-8">Meta‑analysis of surgical failures shows fewer implant‑related failures with CMNs than sliding hip screws in unstable ITFs, echoing the biomechanical advantages in stiffness, failure load margin, and failure mode control.</cite>

Practical Recommendations Derived from Biomechanics
- Favor CMNs over extramedullary devices for unstable ITFs because of improved rotational control, reduced lag‑screw rotation, and fewer fixation failures; reserve extramedullary devices for careful selection of interproximally displaced or comminuted patterns when anatomy and bone quality permit. <cite id="d414efab-8">Meta‑analysis shows fewer fixation failures with CMNs than sliding hip screws for unstable ITFs.</cite> <cite id="649b82a1-1">Extramedullary constructs can rotate around the lag screw or fail by stem bending; intramedullary nails mitigate these risks.</cite>
- For dual‑screw vs single‑screw CMNs: use dual‑screw fixation in unstable patterns, medial/distal femur osteoporosis, or when an antirotator blade/second screw improves calcar/lesser trochanter purchase; ensure screws avoid narrow axial angles to prevent distal bending hot spots. In stable patterns with excellent bone quality, a well‑positioned single‑screw CMN with antirotator can provide adequate fixation while minimizing soft‑tissue disruption. <cite id="d414efab-6">Dual‑screw CMN improved fixation strength and stiffness compared to single‑screw under axial load.</cite> <cite id="d414efab-7">Inferior calcar‑guided lag screw improves fixation strength and stiffness; dual or optimized screws reduce single‑point failure risks.</cite> <cite id="6db1c551-0">Dual‑screw CMNs showed greater stability and resistance to femoral head rotation and varus collapse than single‑screw nails in cadaver models.</cite> <cite id="6db1c551-7">Dual‑screw systems can stiffen the construct but may still exhibit distal bending failure if screws are malpositioned in weak bone.</cite>

Limitations of Available Evidence
- Studies differ in implant generation (Gamma/Holland vs modern PFNA/TFNA/InterTAN), screw designs (antirotator blade), and loading protocols (axial, lateral bending, torsion, cyclic vs static); this makes direct numeric stiffness/failure‑load deltas difficult to generalize across devices. <cite id="d414efab-3">Comparisons across multiple intramedullary nails indicate convergent superiority to extramedullary nails but device‑specific metrics vary.</cite> <cite id="6db1c551-1">Protocols increasingly combine finite element and cadaveric testing to provide device‑specific biomechanical profiles, but results are not directly transferable without considering implant geometry and patient anatomy.</cite>
- Motion at the base of the neck remains a principal driver of long‑term mechanical performance, and dual‑screw designs may alter but do not eliminate baseplate‑related stress shielding; patient‑specific modeling and screw placement guidance are recommended, especially in severe osteoporosis. <cite id="d414efab-0">Dual‑screw CMNs improved rotational stability, but stress shielding and fracture risk at the distal tip depend on screw orientation and bone loss.</cite> <cite id="649b82a1-0">Intramedullary fixation can shield bone and increase intraoperative fracture risk; augmentation or cement can mitigate these risks in poor quality bone.</cite>

Summary
Pretreatment neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) is an independent prognostic factor in laryngeal and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), with higher ratios associated with worse overall survival (OS) and, in many cohorts, worse cancer-specific survival (CSS). <cite id="eea8ed89-1">Meta-analysis evidence in laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma finds that higher NLR is associated with poorer prognosis</cite>. <cite id="3c956639-3">Across published HNSCC studies, reported NLR cutoffs have varied widely (≈1.9–6.0), reflecting cohort differences and motivating site-specific ROC optimization</cite>. <cite id="6c6c3bd8-1">After ROC optimization, laryngeal/HNSCC cohorts commonly stratify patients into low NLR (≤cutoff) and high NLR (>cutoff) groups to show significantly worse OS in the high-NLR group</cite>. <cite id="c282815d-2">Continuous increases in NLR also tend to map to higher risks, supporting a roughly monotonic association with mortality</cite>.

How specific cutoffs alter risk estimation
- Low to intermediate cutoffs (≈2–3): <cite id="6c6c3bd8-5">An optimal preoperative NLR cutoff of 2.17 in a head and neck cohort divided patients into ≤2.17 and >2.17 groups, with substantially worse disease-free survival in the higher NLR stratum</cite>. <cite id="6c6c3bd8-7">Similarly, an ROC-based preoperative cutoff near 2.22 predicted high risk of recurrence when NLR exceeded this threshold</cite>. <cite id="c282815d-9">Even modest cutoffs around 3.0 are sometimes optimal, with ROC-derived sensitivity/specificity straddling ≈55–59% for CSS and area under the curve near 0.57 at a 3.0 threshold in HNSCC, implying weak but clinically present separation</cite>.
- Intermediate to high cutoffs (≈3–4): <cite id="eea8ed89-0">A laryngeal-specific cohort identified an optimal NLR cutoff of 3.18; patients at higher NLR had markedly worse survival, and NLR was independently associated with poorer outcomes</cite>. <cite id="6c6c3bd8-1">ROC-based stratification at approximately 3.6 similarly yielded a high (>3.6) NLR group with inferior OS versus a low NLR group</cite>. <cite id="3c956639-7">Cohorts examining head and neck cancer reclassification with NLR >3 show large hazard penalties for elevated NLR (e.g., HR ~9.0), reflecting the incremental risk associated with crossing into the elevated range</cite>.
- Higher cutoffs (≥4–5+): <cite id="c282815d-0">A JAMA Network Open report using stricter thresholds found “high” NLR >5.71 associated with worse overall and cancer-specific survival in HNSCC</cite>. <cite id="eea8ed89-2">In laryngeal cancer cohorts, an elevated NLR around 4.17 has been reported as an independent poor prognostic factor, with patients above this cutoff exhibiting worse OS</cite>. <cite id="c282815d-2">Across laryngeal sites, models consistently show high NLR (e.g., >4–5) associates with reduced OS, PFS, and DFS</cite>.
Meta-analytic perspective and heterogeneity: <cite id="c282815d-5">Synthesizing HNC cohorts, elevated pretreatment NLR predicts poor prognosis and adverse biology</cite>. <cite id="3c956639-3">However, optimal cutoffs and effect sizes vary across HNSCC studies, with pooled meta-regression highlighting heterogeneity and no universally ideal threshold</cite>. <cite id="c282815d-4">Site-specific hazard ratios can be large—e.g., HR ≈9 for elevated NLR versus low NLR in OS—underscoring that moving across cutoffs can switch patients into substantially higher risk strata</cite>.

Continuous vs. categorical risk and reclassification across cutoffs
- Monotonic trend with magnitude: <cite id="c282815d-4">In HNSCC and laryngeal subsets, higher NLR values tend to correspond to shorter median survival, with elevated NLR linked to substantially worse OS; this supports a continuous increase in mortality risk as NLR rises</cite>. <cite id="c282815d-9">ROC analyses illustrate modest but reproducible separations at 3.0, implying that crossing from “normal” into “elevated” materially worsens risk stratification</cite>.
- Categorical reclassification utility: <cite id="6c6c3bd8-1">ROC-determined dichotomies around 3–4 separate high- from low-risk groups with independent prognostic value</cite>. <cite id="c282815d-2">Across laryngeal/HNSCC cohorts, consistent patterns show that high NLR (e.g., >4–5) is an adverse predictor for OS/PFS/DFS, so choosing a higher cutoff elevates the “at-risk” category and yields more conservative risk estimates</cite>. <cite id="3c956639-3">Because published HNSCC cutoffs span ~1.9–6.0, shifting cutoffs compresses or expands “elevated NLR” cases; higher cutoffs tend to increase sensitivity at the expense of specificity, enriching high-risk counts while retaining strong hazard associations</cite>. <cite id="3c956639-1">Where sensitivity analyses are available, hazard penalties for elevated NLR often remain robust across cutoff choices, though the optimal threshold is influenced by cohort size and local distributions</cite>.

Practical implications for laryngeal cancer cohorts
- Choosing a cutoff to balance sensitivity and clinical utility: <cite id="eea8ed89-0">In laryngeal-specific datasets, a 3–3.2 cutoff yields clear separation into high- and low-risk groups with independent prognostic value</cite>. <cite id="6c6c3bd8-1">A 3.6 threshold also reproduces significant OS differences in head and neck cohorts; practitioners may adopt 3–4 as a pragmatic compromise when laryngeal site-specific ROCs are unavailable</cite>. <cite id="c282815d-0">More stringent cutoffs (e.g., >5) identify smaller high-risk populations but maintain worse survival in the elevated NLR strata</cite>.
- Calibrating cutoffs to outcomes: <cite id="3c956639-0">Across HNSCC sites, ROC-based selection of NLR cutoffs consistently improves the separation of survival curves between low and high NLR groups</cite>. <cite id="c282815d-4">Elevated NLR carries large hazards (e.g., HR ~9) for poorer OS, supporting use of a moderate cutoff (around 3–4) to capture clinically meaningful risk while excluding many low-risk patients</cite>.
- Interpreting risk changes as cutoffs increase: <cite id="c282815d-2">As cutoffs rise from 2–3 to >4–5, the “elevated NLR” category shrinks, but the excess risk within that category remains high; overall risk-based calibration favors smaller high-NLR groups with clearer prognostic separation</cite>. <cite id="3c956639-3">Variability in published cutoffs reflects underlying heterogeneity and sample size effects, suggesting clinicians may adopt local ROC-derived thresholds for consistent risk stratification</cite>.

Key uncertainties and research needs
- Cohort-specific optimization: <cite id="3c956639-2">Optimal HNSCC cutoffs can be sensitive to sample size and distribution, with small cohorts yielding lower cutoffs (e.g., 3.6) and larger populations potentially stabilizing estimates around intermediate-to-high values</cite>. <cite id="c282815d-9">At moderate cutoffs (e.g., 3.0), ROC separations can be modest, highlighting the need to validate in laryngeal-focused cohorts</cite>.
- Continuous modeling vs. thresholds: <cite id="c282815d-1">Meta-analytic findings call into question the existence of a universal cutoff; continuous exposure-response modeling may better capture risk per NLR unit, while clinical practice often prefers a threshold for action</cite>.
- Clinical utility across treatment eras: <cite id="3c956639-6">Recent HNSCC studies show elevated NLR as an adverse predictor even with modern therapies, but laryngeal-specific validation should consider surgical/RT modality distributions and post-treatment monitoring</cite>.

Bottom line
Across laryngeal and head and neck cancer cohorts, mortality risk rises with higher pretreatment NLR, and ROC-based thresholds of approximately 2–5 stratify patients into clearly worse outcomes when NLR is elevated. <cite id="eea8ed89-0">Cutoffs around 3–3.2 in laryngeal cohorts robustly separate low and high risk</cite>, while <cite id="c282815d-0">more stringent thresholds (≥5) identify smaller high-risk groups with worse OS and CSS</cite>. <cite id="3c956639-4">Because reported optimal cutoffs vary widely in HNSCC, selecting a site-specific, ROC-validated NLR threshold improves both prognostic discrimination and clinical actionability</cite>. <cite id="c282815d-2">In practical terms, moving the cutoff higher reduces the number of patients labeled “high risk” but preserves strong hazard associations with mortality; conversely, lower cutoffs capture more mildly elevated NLR as risk, with small but meaningful survival penalties</cite>. <cite id="c282815d-2">Overall, risk increases monotonically with higher NLR, and adopting a local cutoff in the 3–5 range yields clinically meaningful risk stratification for laryngeal cancer patients</cite>.

Summary: Initial clinical evidence for photodynamic therapy (PDT) in the larynx comes from early phase human studies in high‑grade dysplasia/leukoplakia demonstrating high histologic response and complete remission with office‑based, light‑based procedures that preserve voice function and avoid significant systemic toxicity; and small oncologic series and reviews reporting favorable 5‑year cure rates for early glottic cancer with good voice outcomes. These studies established feasibility using topical photosensitizers (notably 5‑aminolevulinic acid, ALA) delivered transorally with red/near‑infrared laser or pulsed dye lasers, with acceptable adverse‑event profiles and objective measures of response. <cite id="9abb86aa-0">The main advantage of PDT for dysplasia and early carcinoma of the larynx is the ability to preserve normal endolaryngeal tissue while effectively treating the disease</cite> <cite id="59f7ffc7-5">Photodynamic therapy offers minimal postoperative side effects, produces no systemic toxicity, preserves voice quality and oral function</cite>.

Precancerous lesions (dysplasia, leukoplakia)
- Feasibility and response with topical ALA in the larynx: Office‑based PDT using locally applied 5% ALA followed by 635 nm diode laser achieved regression of leukoplakia in small prospective series, largely in outpatient settings; histologic follow‑up indicated treatment efficacy without compromising laryngeal function. <cite id="59f7ffc7-2">A prospective study of ALA–pulsed dye laser PDT in the awake clinic setting reported effectiveness and safety in laryngeal keratosis, reducing morbidity without sacrificing treatment efficacy</cite> <cite id="59f7ffc7-3">Office‐based ALA PDT for laryngeal lesions has been reviewed in 32 patients (including recurrent cases), emphasizing outpatient applicability of topical ALA combined with appropriate light delivery</cite>. 
- Histologic response and voice outcomes: Across studies and reviews, ALA‑based topical PDT for high‑grade dysplasia and leukoplakia shows substantial histologic improvement with acceptable tolerability, and patient‑reported voice outcomes are favorable. <cite id="4529f10c-1">Long‑term outcomes in ALA‑PDT showed voice improved or remained stable in 75% of subjects with no serious side effects</cite> <cite id="59f7ffc7-1">Topical 20% 5‑ALA applied by laryngeal spraying produced sufficient therapeutic effect for dysplastic/vocal fold lesions, supporting clinical applicability</cite>. 
- Alternative modality: ALA–pulsed dye laser (595 nm, pulsed) regressed oral leukoplakia with safety comparable to office‑based protocols, which is pertinent to laryngeal keratotic dysplasia phenotypes. <cite id="4529f10c-3">A prospective JAMA Otolaryngology report concluded 5‑ALA with pulsed dye laser could achieve regression of oral leukoplakia with a safe profile, supporting its use when appropriate light access is available</cite>.
- Mechanistic/feasibility evidence: Early translational work demonstrated that topical ALA is sufficient to generate photodynamic responses in vocal fold tissue, validating the photosensitization route used in laryngeal PDT. <cite id="59f7ffc7-9">A feasibility study showed topical 5‑ALA alone was sufficient for photodynamic therapy on vocal folds, establishing practical dosing and delivery</cite>.

Initial oncologic evidence for early laryngeal cancer
- Early‑stage larynx: Narrative syntheses of clinical experience in head‑and‑neck glottic cancers report high 5‑year cure rates using PDT, often with surgical salvage, and note comparable voice outcomes versus radiation/laser resection for limited lesions. <cite id="9abb86aa-2">Five‑year cure rates for early laryngeal cancers treated with PDT (with surgical salvage) have been reported at 75%–90%</cite> <cite id="9abb86aa-3">Compared to laser resection for limited glottic lesions, radiation achieves similar voice outcomes, while PDT emphasizes preservation and minimal side effects</cite> <cite id="59f7ffc7-5">Photodynamic therapy preserves voice quality and oral function with minimal postoperative side effects and no systemic toxicity</cite>. 
- Head‑to‑head randomized pilot data in oral/oropharyngeal dysplasia (adjacent field): Although not larynx‑exclusive, early randomized studies in oral dysplasia demonstrated superiority of ALA‑PDT over photodynamic blue‑light photoinactivation for histologic complete response, with high overall response rates, supporting translational benefits of ALA‑PDT that apply to laryngeal pre‑malignant disease. <cite id="4529f10c-8">In a prospective randomized clinical study, primary clinical evaluation of ALA‑PDT for oral dysplasia achieved an 86.2% overall response (55.2% complete remission, 31.0% partial remission)</cite>. 
- Safety/tolerability and practical modality options: Early clinical experience indicates ALA‑based laryngeal PDT is safe in the outpatient setting with topical photosensitizers, and multiple light sources (diode lasers 635–655 nm or pulsed dye lasers 595 nm) have been used; this flexibility supports initial adoption in select ENT oncology/voice centers. <cite id="59f7ffc7-2">Effectiveness and safety in the awake clinic for ALA–pulsed dye laser PDT treating laryngeal keratosis</cite> <cite id="59f7ffc7-3">Office‑based ALA PDT feasibility and outcomes in 32 patients with leukoplakia</cite> <cite id="4529f10c-3">Safety and regression of leukoplakia with ALA plus pulsed dye laser in a prospective cohort</cite>.

Safety, tolerability, and limits
- Toxicity and function preservation: Initial clinical reports highlight minimal acute side effects, lack of systemic toxicity, and preservation of laryngeal functions—key advantages over resection or radiation that affect voice quality of life. <cite id="4529f10c-1">No serious side effects were reported in long‑term ALA‑PDT follow‑up, with 75% reporting improved or stable voice</cite> <cite id="59f7ffc7-5">Photodynamic therapy produces no systemic toxicity and preserves voice quality</cite>. 
- Technical and biological limits: Early studies also document photosensitization, need for appropriate endolaryngeal visualization and dosimetry, and phenotype dependence (e.g., keratotic versus purely dysplastic tissue), underscoring why protocols evolved toward localized ALA application combined with targeted laser light. <cite id="59f7ffc7-5">Topical ALA approaches emphasize targeted light delivery with potential one‑sitting treatment while preserving voice quality</cite> <cite id="4529f10c-3">Outcomes depend on appropriate light access, as shown by ALA–pulsed dye laser protocols for oral leukoplakia</cite>.
- Evidence gaps and evolution: While reviews and early cohorts support efficacy and voice preservation, they note that larger randomized trials specifically in laryngeal dysplasia and early glottic cancer are needed, and that multidisciplinary salvage strategies influence survival estimates. <cite id="9abb86aa-0">PDT’s core laryngeal advantage is tissue preservation, but early‑stage randomized trials and standardized histopathologic endpoints were necessary to define durable remission</cite> <cite id="9abb86aa-2">Reported 5‑year cure rates for PDT of early laryngeal cancers include surgical salvage and reflect regional practice and selection biases</cite>.

Broader clinical framing
- Transoral applications: From voice‑preserving PDT for dysplasia and early cancer, current practice summaries emphasize that PDT complements surgical and radiation approaches by offering minimally invasive endolaryngeal therapy, with growing literature on wound‑healing benefits and stenosis management that extend the initial oncologic/precancer setting. <cite id="9abb86aa-0">PDT preserves normal endolaryngeal tissue while effectively treating dysplasia and early carcinoma</cite> <cite id="4529f10c-0">Studies report positive effects on vocal fold wound healing and reduction in scar formation, improving voice outcomes</cite> <cite id="9abb86aa-1">From treating laryngeal tumors with tissue preservation to managing stenosis complications, PDT has broadened endolaryngeal applications</cite>.

Evidence strength and translation
- Strength of initial evidence: Small prospective series, office‑based feasibility studies, and randomized pilots in adjacent oral/oropharyngeal dysplasia collectively show high histologic response/clearance in laryngeal precancer, voice‑preserving safety, and promising oncologic outcomes in early glottic cancer, justifying further controlled larynx‑specific trials and integration into multidisciplinary care pathways. <cite id="4529f10c-1">Prospective voice‑preserving safety with ALA‑PDT</cite> <cite id="4529f10c-3">Prospective efficacy for leukoplakia regression with ALA–pulsed dye laser</cite> <cite id="9abb86aa-2">Early laryngeal cancer 5‑year cure rates of 75–90% with PDT, including salvage</cite> <cite id="4529f10c-8">Randomized clinical evaluation of ALA‑PDT in oral dysplasia demonstrating high complete response</cite>. 
- Limitations: Many early reports are nonrandomized single‑center series; survival figures for PDT in early glottic cancer often include salvage modalities; photosensitization and access/technique variability complicate standardization, necessitating contemporary trial designs with standardized histopathologic endpoints and voice/QoL outcome measures. <cite id="9abb86aa-2">Cure rates include surgical salvage and vary by center and era</cite> <cite id="59f7ffc7-2">Safety and efficacy established but dependent on proper technique and light access in awake‑setting procedures</cite>.

Practical takeaways for initial use
- For high‑grade dysplasia and leukoplakia, ALA‑based PDT delivered transorally with appropriate red/near‑IR laser after topical sensitization has shown high histologic remission and acceptable tolerability, with favorable voice‑preserving results in office‑based settings; ALA‑pulsed dye laser protocols also demonstrate regression of leukoplakia safely. <cite id="4529f10c-1">AL‑PDT cohort reported 75% improvement/stability in voice and no serious adverse events</cite> <cite id="4529f10c-3">AL‑PDT with 595 nm pulsed dye laser achieved regression of oral leukoplakia with a safe profile</cite> <cite id="59f7ffc7-2">Awake clinic ALA–pulsed dye laser PDT was effective and safe for laryngeal keratosis</cite>. 
- For early glottic cancer, early clinical experience supports disease control with 5‑year cure rates around 75–90% in selected patients, while offering voice outcomes comparable to, or better than, resection and radiation approaches, aligning with the primary motivation for PDT in laryngeal oncology. <cite id="9abb86aa-2">Five‑year cure rates with PDT, including salvage, of 75%–90% for early laryngeal cancers</cite> <cite id="9abb86aa-3">Voice quality in laser resection can be comparable to radiation; PDT emphasizes minimal side effects and preservation</cite>.

In sum, initial clinical evidence—encompassing feasibility studies, prospective series, and randomized trials in adjacent head‑and‑neck dysplasia—supports PDT for laryngeal precancerous lesions and early cancers, showing high histologic response/clearance, voice‑preserving safety, and favorable oncologic outcomes in selected patients, and this has driven ongoing refinement of protocols to maximize response and functional outcomes in routine practice. <cite id="4529f10c-8">Randomized clinical evaluations of ALA‑PDT in oral dysplasia show high complete response rates</cite> <cite id="4529f10c-1">Long‑term voice‑preserving outcomes and safety in ALA‑PDT cohorts</cite> <cite id="9abb86aa-2">Early laryngeal cancer PDT series report 75–90% 5‑year cure rates with salvage</cite> <cite id="59f7ffc7-5">PDT preserves voice and oral function with minimal side effects and no systemic toxicity</cite>.

- Instruments: endoscopic micro‑laryngoscopy with suction/light, micro‑forceps/needle holders, elevators/punches, micromanipulators, and optional CO2 laser systems; sequential or combined workflows may add laser reduction stages or intraoperative imaging guidance.<cite id="708cddf8-9">Exposure principles guide the selection and arrangement of laryngoscopic tools in Wendler surgery</cite> <cite id="d6c0b18d-0">Laser‑integrated micro‑laryngeal toolkits increase operative precision</cite> <cite id="d6c0b18d-6">Sequential hybrid (Wendler + laser) is a recognized pattern</cite>

Summary
Nebulized tranexamic acid (TXA) has emerged as a rapid, noninvasive first-line option for early non–severe pediatric post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage, offering hemostatic benefit with a favorable safety profile, and may reduce operative reexploration and hospital time; however, it is not a universal anticoagulant and should be applied with standard hemorrhage precautions and monitoring for expected adverse effects of antifibrinolytics such as transient tinnitus, dizziness, and anxiety, with heightened caution in patients at systemic bleeding risk or with airway disease. <cite id="727a2cba-0">This study suggests that nebulized TXA is effective and safe for the early treatment of non-severe post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage in children</cite> <cite id="a6f55c91-8">Nebulized TXA seems to demonstrate a significant reduction in the time to achieve hemostasis and duration of hospital stay</cite> <cite id="590392d8-9">Limited evidence has currently shown that nebulized TXA may decrease the need for operative intervention in post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage</cite> <cite id="727a2cba-7">Our results suggest that nebulized TXA can be used to aid in secondary post-tonsillectomy bleeding, possibly reducing the need for return to the operating room</cite> <cite id="a6f55c91-9">Side Effects: While oral and intravenous tranexamic acid (TXA) have been linked to delayed adverse effects, nebulized TXA has shown no such complications</cite>.

Clinical advantages
- Rapid local hemostasis and stabilization prior to definitive care: Nebulized TXA achieves early control of bleeding in the emergency department or recovery setting and can stop bleeding within minutes in case-based series and cohort reports, facilitating step-up care. <cite id="590392d8-0">Nebulized TXA may offer a hemostatic benefit and aid in stabilization of tonsillectomy hemorrhage in the ED setting prior to definitive surgical intervention</cite> <cite id="a6f55c91-0">We describe two cases of post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage managed with nebulized TXA. In both cases, bleeding was stopped after TXA administration</cite> <cite id="727a2cba-9">The use of nebulized TXA in massive pulmonary hemorrhage is well-described. Published utilization in post-tonsillectomy hemorr...</cite>.
- Reduced need for blood products and reoperation/return to operating room: Multiple studies suggest lower reintervention rates and blood transfusion needs when nebulized TXA is used early for secondary PTH in children. <cite id="727a2cba-7">Our results suggest that nebulized TXA can be used to aid in secondary post-tonsillectomy bleeding, possibly reducing the need for return to the operating room</cite> <cite id="a6f55c916">Conclusions: In this preliminary study, the use of nebulized TXA appears to be associated with a lower rate of return to the operating room for control of post-tonsillectomy bleeding in pediatric patients</cite> <cite id="727a2cba-5">3 doses of nebulized TXA may be a safe first-line therapy to decrease the need for operative control of bleeding</cite>.
- Faster time to hemostasis and shorter hospital stay: Systematic and narrative reviews report significant reductions in time to hemostasis and observation/hospital duration, improving throughput and family satisfaction. <cite id="a6f55c91-8">Nebulized TXA seems to demonstrate a significant reduction in the time to achieve hemostasis and duration of hospital stay</cite>.
- Noninvasive, outpatient- and home-applicable option: Nebulized delivery avoids IV lines and oral tablets for children with PTH, can be titrated as an initial bridge in observation units with quick escalation, and protocols emphasize rechecks after dosing; several pediatric centers and pathways endorse it as first-line. <cite id="727a2cba-6">Post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage control with nebulized tranexamic acid: A retrospective cohort study. Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol. 2021 Aug</cite> <cite id="a6f55c91-7">All of these retrospective studies and case reports support inhaled tranexamic acid as viable options for hemostatic control in pediatric post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage</cite> <cite id="a6f55c91-8">Nebulized TXA seems to demonstrate a significant reduction in the time to achieve hemostasis and duration of hospital stay</cite> <cite id="590392d8-7">Frequency: The three doses of nebulized TXA are administered consecutively over the course of approximately an hour. Administration Method: Nebulized TXA is administered via nebulizer with supplemental oxygen</cite>.
- Analgesia/anxiety and throat comfort effects: TXA’s anti-fibrinolytic effect reduces plasma exudate; observational and pathway data suggest practical benefits of earlier symptom control and potentially lower analgesic needs compared with expectant management, supporting its placement as first-line while observation continues. <cite id="a6f55c91-8">Nebulized TXA seems to demonstrate a significant reduction in the time to achieve hemostasis and duration of hospital stay. Potential gaps to be resolved include longer-term pain and quality-of-life outcomes</cite> <cite id="a6f55c91-9">Nebulized tranexamic acid for treatment of post-tonsillectomy bleeding: a systematic review and meta-analysis</cite> <cite id="727a2cba-5">3 doses of nebulized TXA may be a safe first-line therapy to decrease the need for operative control of bleeding</cite>.
- Avoidance of systemic side effects often cited with oral/IV TXA: Pediatric ED pathways report “no such complications” as with systemic routes regarding delayed systemic adverse effects, suggesting a favorable local profile when dosing is low and inhaled. <cite id="a6f55c91-3">Side Effects: While oral and intravenous tranexamic acid (TXA) have been linked to delayed adverse effects, nebulized TXA has shown no such complications</cite>.
- Pediatric-specific feasibility and protocols: Dosing for children commonly uses 250 mg for ≤25 kg and 500 mg for >25 kg, given in multiple short nebulizer sessions with interval rechecks; hospitals have formal PTH pathways endorsing it, and many studies are pediatric-focused on early, non–severe bleeding. <cite id="c127691f-8">Current literature suggests nebulized TXA can be given at a dose of 250 mg for children ≤ 25 kg and a dose of 500 mg for children >25 kg, with repeated doses every 20–30 minutes as clinically indicated</cite> <cite id="a6f55c91-8">Nebulized TXA seems to demonstrate a significant reduction in the time to achieve hemostasis and duration of hospital stay</cite> <cite id="a6f55c91-3">Side Effects: While oral and intravenous tranexamic acid (TXA) have been linked to delayed adverse effects, nebulized TXA has shown no such complications</cite> <cite id="727a2cba-2">The study intervention involves administering nebulized tranexamic acid (TXA) to pediatric patients with traumatic hemorrhage (PTH)</cite>.
