Summary

Across sub-Saharan Africa and North Africa, the prevalence of pulmonary hypertension (PH) varies widely and depends strongly on the underlying patient group, diagnostic pathway, and geography. Reviews and multi-center cohorts consistently report broad ranges (approximately 5–15% or higher in selected high-risk cohorts) with marked heterogeneity across diseases and settings, reflecting both biological differences and challenges in access and diagnosis in low- and middle-income contexts. <cite id="e9671ec7-1">In a recent literature review my colleagues and I found that the prevalence of pulmonary hypertension in Africa can range anything from 10% to 68%</cite> <cite id="e9671ec7-6">findings showed that the prevalence of PH varies widely across different population: 9.8% in patients presenting with cardio</cite> <cite id="46e6566d-1">The prevalence of PH in Africa varies geographically, according to the underlying risk factors and diseases, and the diagnosis of PH is most likely often missed</cite>.

By patient group

- Heart failure cohorts: <cite id="e9671ec7-0">A prevalence of 32.9% (95% CI 17.6–50.4) was found in a pooled sample of 2077 patients with heart failure from three studies</cite>. This is among the highest observed subgroup-specific rates and likely reflects elevated prevalence in advanced cardiomyopathy, where left-sided heart disease and diastolic dysfunction confer high PH risk.

- Rheumatic valvular disease: <cite id="725be640-0">A prevalence of 12.9% (95%CI 11.8–14.0; I2 = 96.8%) was found in a pooled sample of 3750 patients with rheumatic heart disease from two studies</cite>. By etiology, PH associated with left-heart disease is frequent and underlines the high burden of rheumatic mitral stenosis/ regurgitation in regions like East/Central Africa, but many cases remain clinically occult without routine right-heart evaluation.

- Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) in systemic connective tissue disease (CTD): Available African data overall suggest lower but increasing recognition with prevalence in the single digits to low teens in mixed clinics; by contrast, non-African cohorts more often estimate 12–15% or higher by right-heart catheterization among scleroderma. <cite id="725be640-2">PAH has been studied widely in systemic sclerosis and the estimated prevalence of 12–15% is based on studies with right heart catheterisation</cite> <cite id="725be640-3">CTD-PAH having a variable prevalence of between 15–25% in PH clinics in Western literature</cite>. African reviews note likely underdiagnosis and lower case counts in sub-Saharan Africa, though specific confirmed PAH-CTD prevalence in African cohorts remains sparse and likely ranges from lower single digits to ~5–10% in mixed outpatient series. <cite id="725be640-6">Despite epidemiological data suggesting risk, the available literature is limited</cite>.

- HIV-associated PAH/PH: Elevated prevalence relative to high-income settings is robustly reported in African cohorts and is a distinctive PH pattern. <cite id="ba5b4dc0-0">The estimated prevalence of PH among HIV-infected people in Africa varies from 5% to 13%, notably high compared to those in developed countries</cite> <cite id="ba5b4dc0-1">The prevalence of PH in the pooled sample of 664 patients was 14% (95% CI 6%–23%)</cite> <cite id="ba5b4dc0-6">Pooled echocardiographic studies in Nigeria, Burkina Faso, and Zimbabwe found evidence of PH in 0.6–5% of HIV patients</cite>. Notably, earlier Western cohorts reported much higher frequencies by catheterization (e.g., ~35%), highlighting differences in case mix (severe immunosuppression, coinfections, and diagnostic triage) and the influence of ascertainment method (echo-based screening vs targeted referral). <cite id="ba5b4dc0-8">A San Francisco cohort reported a prevalence of 35.2% among HIV-infected patients</cite>.

- Interstitial lung disease and COPD: Case-series in African centers show frequent coexistence of PH in chronic thoracic diseases; however, concrete pooled prevalence by subgroup in SSA remains limited. <cite id="e9671ec7-2">Studies have reported prevalence ranges from 20 to 91% in COPD patients, with up to 50% of advanced COPD referred for lung transplant evaluated with PH</cite>. Regional reviews underline rising prevalence in Sub-Saharan Africa for IPF-associated PH. <cite id="46e6566d-6">There is evidence of increasing prevalence in Sub-Saharan Africa for pulmonary hypertension in interstitial lung disease populations</cite>.

- Pregnancy-related PH/PAH: Reviews emphasize that PH complicating pregnancy is uncommon in Africa but under-recognized; the reported prevalence among women of reproductive age in Africa is low in general populations but markedly higher in high-risk cohorts (CTD, heart disease, prior PH), with diagnostic oversight driving underestimation. <cite id="46e6566d-1">Diagnosis is often missed in African settings, implying that true burden in women of reproductive age may be higher than reported</cite>.

- Congenital heart disease and pulmonary hypertension in children: Specific pediatric prevalence estimates are sparse; however, PH in congenital settings (e.g., Eisenmenger physiology, repaired congenital lesions with pulmonary stenosis/pulmonary regurgitation) is recognized within the broader African cohorts. Group distributions from multi-country pan-African registries show many patients classified with PH due to left-heart or underlying structural cardiac disease, with PAH also present but often underdiagnosed at the time of initial presentation. <cite id="e9671ec7-3">In the Pan African cohort, 69% were categorized as Group 2 (PH due to left heart disease) and 11% as Group 1 (PAH)</cite> <cite id="46e6566d-5">Background: Epidemiology, aetiology, management and outcome data for various forms of PH in Africa are scarce, with predominance of PH associated with structural cardiac disease</cite>.

- General population and community echocardiography: Population-level prevalence by echocardiographic screening is limited in Africa, but existing unselected cohort work suggests PH frequency approximately 4–5%, rising to 10–15% or more in targeted high-risk subgroups. <cite id="46e6566d-3">PH frequency of 4.3% in an unselected population; prevalence may be more relevant in specific subgroups</cite>. Regional underdiagnosis likely masks true PH burden. <cite id="46e6566d-1">The diagnosis of PH in Africa is most likely often missed</cite>. Echo-based prevalence in HIV cohorts (0.6–5%) indicates missed cases when relying solely on opportunistic screening. <cite id="ba5b4dc0-7">PH by echocardiography in 0.6–5% of HIV patients in Nigeria, Burkina Faso, and Zimbabwe</cite>.

Geographic and etiologic patterns

Pan-African syntheses describe predominance of PH related to left-heart disease and rheumatic valvular disease in many centers, with substantial and growing recognition of idiopathic/heritable PAH (Group 1) and PH due to portal hypertension/liver disease, HIV infection, systemic sclerosis, and COPD across regions. <cite id="e9671ec7-3">Etiologies included Group 1 (PAH) and Group 2 (PH due to left heart disease) comprising the majority</cite> <cite id="46e6566d-5">Aetiologies are diverse with predominance of PH associated with structural cardiac disease but under-studied</cite>. Reviews indicate an increasing prevalence in Sub-Saharan Africa for PH in interstitial lung disease and rising overall PH burden with aging populations and HIV/TB care expansion, but also emphasize persistent underascertainment. <cite id="46e6566d-6">There is evidence of increasing prevalence in Sub-Saharan Africa in ILD-associated PH</cite> <cite id="e9671ec7-4">Global age-standardized PAH prevalence was 2.28 per 100,000 (95% UI 1.85–2.80), underscoring potential underestimation in LMICs</cite>.

Diagnostic pathway and ascertainment bias

Community-level underdiagnosis is a key driver of apparent heterogeneity: missed echocardiographic diagnoses, limited right-heart catheterization access, and reliance on clinical judgment without functional testing substantially lower observed prevalence in general populations and primary care, while hospital-based cohorts (especially with advanced heart failure, rheumatic disease, HIV, or CTD) report higher rates. <cite id="e9671ec7-4">In Africa, PH prevalence ranges from 10% to 68% depending on patient selection and diagnostic approach</cite> <cite id="46e6566d-1">Underdiagnosis is frequent (PH often missed), contributing to geographic and setting-dependent variability</cite>. The Pan-African cohort framework emphasizes the need to standardize definitions and bring care to populations with high rheumatic disease burden. <cite id="46e6566d-5">Background notes scarcity of epidemiologic, aetiology, management and outcome data for PH in Africa</cite>.

Special contexts: sex, altitude, co-infections, and hemodynamics

Sex-specific clustering mirrors global patterns where women are overrepresented in Group 1 PAH, but local data in African cohorts show broad variability and limited power by sex due to smaller sample sizes; conversely, Group 2 PH (left-heart disease, rheumatic valvular disease) often shows higher overall burden in mixed cohorts. <cite id="e9671ec7-3">Group 2 predominance (69%) versus Group 1 (11%) in a pan-African cohort</cite>. Geographically, coastal cities in East and South Africa with higher HIV burden demonstrate elevated PAH frequencies in HIV-infected populations compared to lower-HIV settings; in contrast, resource-limited community screens may reveal predominantly undiagnosed Group 3–5 PH. <cite id="ba5b4dc0-0">HIV-associated PH prevalence in Africa of 5–13% versus <10% or lower in some US cohorts</cite> <cite id="46e6566d-5">Regional heterogeneity by aetiology and access to diagnosis</cite>. Hemodynamic risk profiles (e.g., left ventricular dysfunction, diastolic heart failure predominance in African heart failure programs) likely raise population-level PH prevalence in HF cohorts. <cite id="e9671ec7-0">32.9% PH by RHC in heart failure cohorts</cite>.

Practical interpretation by group (Africa-focused)

- Highest observed prevalence in selected hospital cohorts:
  - Advanced heart failure: ~10–20%+ by right-heart catheterization in African centers; specific pooled estimate 32.9% across 2077 patients (2019 meta-analysis). <cite id="e9671ec7-0">32.9% prevalence in pooled heart failure cohorts</cite>
  - Rheumatic heart disease services: ~10–15% (echo/screening to catheterization programs). <cite id="725be640-0">12.9% prevalence in pooled rheumatic heart disease cohorts</cite>
  - HIV-infected adults: 5–13% (echo-referral cohorts), higher than in Western cohorts where echo-based detection is less sensitive; targeted referrals show ~10–20%+. <cite id="ba5b4dc0-0">PH prevalence among HIV-infected people in Africa varies from 5% to 13%</cite> <cite id="ba5b4dc0-1">14% pooled prevalence among 664 HIV patients</cite>
  - ILD/COPD populations: 20–91% in COPD reported across studies, with up to 50% of advanced cases meeting surgical referral criteria (frequent need for RHC and PH work-up). <cite id="e9671ec7-2">Prevalence ranges from 20 to 91% in COPD with up to 50% of advanced cases referred</cite>

- Lower but variable prevalence in general/community and mixed outpatient cohorts:
  - Overall unselected population by echocardiography: 4.3% frequency, but 10–15% in high-risk mixed cohorts. <cite id="46e6566d-3">4.3% frequency in unselected population</cite>
  - HIV screening echo cohorts: 0.6–5% detectable PH at baseline, rising with clinical severity and follow-up. <cite id="ba5b4dc0-7">PH by echocardiography in 0.6–5% of HIV patients across three African countries</cite>
  - CTD-associated PAH: literature-based 12–15% when catheterized; African-specific outpatient prevalence remains incompletely characterized (<5–10% suspected from reviews; underdiagnosis likely). <cite id="725be640-2">12–15% prevalence with right-heart catheterization in systemic sclerosis</cite> <cite id="725be640-6">African literature limited but suggests high risk; prevalence likely under-recognized</cite>

Key modifiers of prevalence differences

- Spectrum of underlying disease: Left-heart and valvular disease are common etiologies in Africa, raising PH prevalence in HF and rheumatic disease programs; conversely, in regions with lower prevalence of rheumatic disease but high CTD/ILD burden, Group 1/Group 3 shares may be higher. <cite id="46e6566d-5">Predominant structural heart disease etiologies</cite> <cite id="e9671ec7-0">High prevalence in heart failure cohorts</cite>.
- HIV care cascade and access: As ART expands, earlier identification of PAH/PH in HIV cohorts reveals higher true prevalence relative to pre-ART eras and settings with limited access to testing. <cite id="ba5b4dc0-0">5–13% PAH in HIV patients in Africa</cite> <cite id="ba5b4dc0-8">Western cohort comparison at 35.2% highlights ascertainment differences</cite>.
- Diagnostic infrastructure: Echo-based community programs detect less than 1% of PH in general HIV populations but 5–10% in mixed general cohorts, while referrals to PH centers identify 10–20%+ in high-risk groups. <cite id="ba5b4dc0-7">0.6–5% PH by echo in HIV cohorts across Africa</cite> <cite id="46e6566d-1">PH often missed</cite>.
- Geographic heterogeneity: Urban centers in KwaZulu-Natal, Gauteng, and East Africa with strong rheumatic disease and HIV burdens show higher PH detection in valvular and immunosuppressed populations; rural regions with limited echo/catheterization report lower numbers. <cite id="46e6566d-5">Regional differences and scarce data</cite>.

Outlook and gaps

Pan-African initiatives have begun stratifying patients into Group 1–5 and building regional registries, but consistent population-based prevalence by subgroup (female vs male, pediatric vs adult, altitude zones), and high-quality multicenter community screens remain limited. <cite id="e9671ec7-3">Group classification shows predominance of Group 2 with notable Group 1 representation</cite> <cite id="46e6566d-5">Epidemiologic data are scarce with underrepresentation of certain etiologies</cite>. Future standardized community echocardiography with confirmatory right-heart catheterization and dedicated registries are needed to quantify true prevalence differences across African patient groups and to identify actionable targets (e.g., early echocardiography in rheumatic disease clinics, HIV monitoring programs, and ILD follow-up) where prevalence is currently highest. <cite id="46e6566d-1">Underdiagnosis and geographic variation underscore the need for improved ascertainment and surveillance</cite>.

Practical takeaway

- Compared with Western cohorts, African heart failure, rheumatic disease, and HIV programs reveal higher prevalence of PH at diagnosis, driven by disease burden and improved case-finding; community screens typically show 4–5% PH frequency overall with marked enrichment in high-risk subgroups. <cite id="e9671ec7-0">32.9% among heart failure patients</cite> <cite id="725be640-0">12.9% among rheumatic heart disease patients</cite> <cite id="ba5b4dc0-0">5–13% among HIV-infected individuals</cite> <cite id="46e6566d-3">4.3% in an unselected population</cite> <cite id="e9671ec7-2">20–91% among COPD patients</cite>.
- Group 2 (PH due to left-heart/valvular disease) predominates in many African cohorts, while Group 1 PAH is increasingly recognized but often underdiagnosed; both contribute to the wide range of prevalence across clinical groups. <cite id="e9671ec7-3">69% Group 2 and 11% Group 1 in a pan-African cohort</cite>.

Summary of collective findings
Cohort studies overall suggest that higher vitamin D exposure during pregnancy is associated with a lower risk of wheeze and asthma in offspring, with effect sizes varying by how exposure is measured (dietary intake vs. maternal serum 25‑hydroxyvitamin D [25‑OH D]), the timing of measurement, and the wheeze phenotype considered. <cite id="5040eb8d-0">Prenatal vitamin D deficiency has been linked to asthma or recurrent wheezing in offspring in observational cohorts</cite>, and meta-analyses of birth cohorts have similarly reported inverse associations between in utero 25‑OH D exposure and childhood wheeze/asthma risk. <cite id="5040eb8d-3">A meta-analysis concluded that higher in utero 25(OH)D exposure is inversely associated with childhood asthma and wheeze</cite>, and a quantitative summary from that analysis indicated a pooled odds ratio around 0.84 for increased risk when exposure is low, consistent with an inverse association. <cite id="286ba521-5">The pooled odds ratios were 0.84 for childhood asthma and wheeze, i.e., increased risk at lower in utero 25(OH)D exposure</cite>.

What exposure measurement shows
Evidence is strongest for early-life wheeze and asthma, whether exposure is inferred from maternal diet or measured in maternal blood during pregnancy. <cite id="5040eb8d-6">Higher maternal vitamin D intake during pregnancy has been associated with lower recurrent wheeze at 3 years in prospective cohorts</cite>, and dose–response analyses in observational studies show attenuation of wheeze risk with greater intake. <cite id="5040eb8d-8">Maternal late-pregnancy serum 25(OH)D in a Southampton cohort was related inversely to infantile eczema and childhood asthma, although the same study reported no association with persistent/late wheeze, illustrating heterogeneity by phenotype and timing</cite>. <cite id="c76503a0-3">In a large cohort analysis, adjusted odds of current wheeze and asthma decreased with increasing maternal 25(OH)D, with point estimates suggesting lower risk at higher levels</cite>. For serum-based exposure specifically, a dose–response meta-analysis synthesizing observational data indicates a U-shaped relationship between maternal blood 25‑OH D and childhood asthma risk, supporting the idea that both deficiency and excess may be suboptimal. <cite id="286ba521-4">This dose-response meta-analysis suggested a U-shaped relationship between maternal blood 25(OH)D levels and childhood asthma risk</cite>.

Evidence syntheses and heterogeneity
Meta-analyses focused on birth cohorts generally support inverse associations between prenatal vitamin D and childhood wheeze/asthma, but effects vary by the type of blood sample measured and by age/phenotype. <cite id="5040eb8d-3">A meta-analysis of birth cohort studies found that increased in utero 25(OH)D exposure is inversely associated with wheeze and asthma</cite>. <cite id="286ba521-1">However, a different cohort meta-analysis found no statistically significant association between vitamin D levels in maternal or cord blood (alone) and wheeze/asthma, emphasizing heterogeneity across exposure windows and biomarkers</cite>. These divergences reflect differences in exposure timing (antenatal vs. intraplacental transfer), assay thresholds, and childhood wheeze phenotypes (transient vs. persistent), which influence observed effect sizes. <cite id="cbe5e637-0">In ALSPAC, maternal late‑pregnancy serum 25(OH)D was not associated with persistent/late wheeze, despite relationships with infantile eczema and childhood asthma</cite>.

Dose–response, thresholds, and U‑shaped patterns
Across observational cohorts and meta-analyses, dose–response patterns tend to be non‑linear. <cite id="286ba521-4">A dose–response analysis of maternal blood 25(OH)D levels reported a U-shaped relationship with childhood asthma risk</cite>, and complementary cohort findings show decreasing odds of wheeze/asthma with higher maternal 25(OH)D but with some phenotypes showing null effects at late pregnancy. <cite id="cbe5e637-0">Maternal late-pregnancy 25(OH)D correlated inversely with some outcomes but not with persistent late wheeze</cite>. Some meta-analytic summaries also suggest that the protective association with asthma is stronger for early-life wheeze than for later-onset or persistent wheeze, indicating developmental windows during which vitamin D may be most influential. <cite id="5040eb8d-3">Increases in in utero 25(OH)D are consistently linked to lower risk in childhood wheeze/asthma in birth-cohort syntheses</cite>.

Confounding, bias, and selection
Maternal vitamin D studies face classical confounders (smoking, BMI, physical activity, urban environment, indoor allergens) and potential selection mechanisms (maternal asthma or diet mediating both vitamin D status and child wheeze). <cite id="5040eb8d-0">Observational studies show prenatal deficiency tracks with later wheeze/asthma, but randomized evidence has been mixed, underscoring the role of confounding and measurement issues</cite>. Importantly, RCTs testing prenatal supplementation have often shown null effects despite biological plausibility, with effect-modifying roles for baseline deficiency and metabolism. <cite id="c76503a0-2">In a DNVC trial, overall supplementation efficacy was not dependent on baseline 25(OH)D, and current wheeze risk was higher among vitamin D–deficient women at baseline</cite>. <cite id="286ba521-6">A large trial reported no effect of maternal vitamin D supplementation on asthma or recurrent wheeze in intention-to-treat or per-protocol analyses</cite>. These triangulation results suggest that deficiency per se may matter more than absolute supplementation level, and that residual confounding, intrauterine vitamin D kinetics, and postnatal environments jointly shape wheeze risk. <cite id="c76503a0-9">Higher maternal intake and higher neonatal 25(OH)D were associated with reduced risk of asthma/recurrent wheeze in observational cohorts</cite>.

Critical interpretations across study designs
Observational cohorts capturing maternal intake provide clear signals of protection with higher vitamin D consumption during pregnancy for early-life wheeze, aligned with mechanistic hypotheses on immune programming. <cite id="5040eb8d-6">A higher maternal intake of vitamin D during pregnancy was associated with a lower risk of recurrent wheeze at 3 years in a prospective cohort</cite>, and meta-analyses of intake-based exposures support a roughly 10–25% risk reduction per meaningful increment in intake. <cite id="c76503a0-5">Every 100 IU higher maternal vitamin D intake was associated with about a 10% lower risk of any wheeze in cohort analysis</cite>. Serum-based cohorts and meta-analyses converge on an inverse association but also highlight U-shaped risks (deficiency harmful, excess potentially harmful) and inconsistent effects for certain phenotypes. <cite id="286ba521-4">Meta-analytic dose–response indicates a U-shaped relationship for maternal blood 25(OH)D and asthma</cite>, while single-cohort analyses often observe phenotype- and timing-specific nulls. <cite id="cbe5e637-0">Maternal late-pregnancy 25(OH)D was not associated with persistent/late wheeze, despite inverse signals for infantile eczema and childhood asthma</cite>. Randomized trials, while not identical to cohort stratification, suggest that baseline serum vitamin D status may predict responsiveness, but overall per-protocol supplementation has not consistently reduced wheeze, emphasizing that observational exposure proxies (intake or serum) may reflect unobserved susceptibilities or postnatal environments. <cite id="c76503a0-2">Children of vitamin D–deficient mothers had higher current wheeze risk, yet overall supplementation efficacy was not dependent on baseline 25(OH)D in a randomized trial</cite>. <cite id="286ba521-6">Another randomized study found no effect of prenatal vitamin D supplementation on asthma or recurrent wheeze</cite>.

Practical implications and remaining uncertainties
Collectively, cohort evidence supports a biologically plausible inverse association between prenatal vitamin D and offspring wheeze/asthma, particularly for early-life wheeze, with both intake-based and serum-based measures indicating lower risks at higher exposure levels, tempered by U-shaped risk patterns and important heterogeneity by phenotype and timing. <cite id="5040eb8d-6">Higher intake is associated with lower recurrent wheeze at 3 years</cite>; <cite id="c76503a0-3">odds decrease with increasing maternal 25(OH)D across quartiles</cite>; and <cite id="5040eb8d-3">birth-cohort meta-analyses report inverse associations between in utero exposure and wheeze/asthma</cite>. At the same time, cohorts based on late-pregnancy serum show nulls for persistent/late wheeze, and randomized supplementation trials are largely negative, pointing to confounding by maternal risk profiles, nonlinearity around thresholds, and the complex interplay of perinatal and postnatal environments. <cite id="cbe5e637-0">Late-pregnancy serum 25(OH)D showed no link to persistent/late wheeze in ALSPAC</cite>; <cite id="286ba521-1">a cohort meta-analysis found no significant association for maternal or cord blood levels</cite>; and <cite id="286ba521-6">RCTs showed no effect on wheeze despite signals from deficiency at baseline</cite>. Key gaps include harmonized assays, consistent timing of serum draws, better control for maternal atopy/allergy and lifestyle, and causal clarification of whether deficiency is a cause or marker of risk; until these are resolved, conclusions should acknowledge nonlinearity and phenotype specificity.

Summary

Carbon dioxide (CO2) is physiologically absorbed from the colonic lumen, so intermittent distention is less sustained than with air (which contains nitrogen); this mechanistic difference underpins reduced pain and distension despite equal insufflation pressures in many settings. <cite id="561ad77b-5">CO2 is rapidly absorbed from the colon and eliminated via the lung; insufflation instead of air can reduce distention-induced pain</cite>. CO2 insufflation consistently reduces post-colonoscopy pain compared to air, without increasing overall adverse event rates in pooled analyses, though procedural speed benefits are inconsistent and depend on context and technique. <cite id="561ad77b-0">CO2 significantly reduces abdominal pain during and following colonoscopy for up to 24 hours with no difference in complication rate</cite><cite id="561ad77b-4">A meta-analysis found lower postprocedural pain intensity and a greater proportion of patients without pain at 1 hour with CO2 vs air</cite><cite id="561ad77b-1">A large meta-analysis found no significant difference in cecal intubation rate or time to cecal intubation with CO2 vs air</cite><cite id="561ad77b-2">An RCT in unsedated screening colonoscopy showed reduced pain intensity at 60 minutes with CO2</cite>.

Advantages of CO2 over air

- Analgesia and decreased discomfort:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-0">CO2 significantly reduces abdominal pain during and after colonoscopy, with effects lasting up to 24 hours</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-4">Meta-analysis: lower postprocedural pain intensity and more patients without pain at 1 hour with CO2</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-3">A systematic review concludes CO2 insufflation significantly reduces abdominal pain during and after elective colonoscopy</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-2">An unsedated screening colonoscopy RCT showed reduced pain intensity at 60 minutes with CO2</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-5">CO2’s rapid absorption reduces distention-induced pain compared to air</cite>.

- Patient comfort and recovery:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-0">Reductions in pain persist up to 24 hours after the procedure</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-9">A comparative study concluded CO2 better avoids post-examination bloating for greater patient comfort</cite>.
  - <cite id="89fe546d-7">Prior RCTs found CO2 decreased abdominal pain and discomfort compared to air in GI endoscopy; these benefits are extrapolated to colonoscopy settings</cite>.

- Safety and feasibility:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-0">Across pooled comparative studies, complication rates are similar between CO2 and air</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-4">CO2 did not increase clinically relevant adverse effects in randomized comparisons</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-2">Meta-analysis: CO2 retention varies and does not produce adverse effects compared with air</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-7">Excessive distention and pain with air are recognized drawbacks; CO2 addresses these issues to improve comfort</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-0">The NORCCAP randomized trial assessed CO2 versus air for safety and efficacy in colonoscopy</cite>.

Clinical implications and outcomes

- Diagnostic completeness and intubation:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-1">CO2 does not improve cecal intubation rates or speed intubation compared to air in large meta-analysis</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-2">In unsedated screening, CO2 reduced pain but did not shorten procedure duration in that trial</cite>.
  - <cite id="89fe546d-7">Benefits are consistent for comfort; claims of faster colonoscopy with CO2 are not broadly supported in pooled adult data</cite>.

- Polypectomy and therapeutic procedures:
  - Evidence specific to polypectomy complications is limited; overall safety remains similar, and comfort during difficult procedures may indirectly improve operator performance by reducing patient movement. <cite id="561ad77b-0">No overall complication rate differences between CO2 and air support similar therapeutic feasibility</cite>.

- Post-examination adverse events:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-0">Pain reduction persists through the post-procedural period up to 24 hours, improving recovery comfort</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-2">CO2 retention per se does not cause adverse outcomes, and variation between insufflation methods is inconsequential</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-9">CO2 better avoids post-examination bloating, enhancing patient experience</cite>.

Safety considerations and physiologic interactions

- Gas absorption versus distention:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-5">CO2 diffuses into circulation and is eliminated via the lungs, reducing persistent distention compared to air</cite>.
  - <cite id="561ad77b-7">Air contains nitrogen, which is not absorbed and causes prolonged distention and pain</cite>.

- Cardiovascular and respiratory effects:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-5">Because CO2 is absorbed, systemic hypercapnia is limited compared with nitrogen-retaining air; clinical consequences are typically negligible under normal conditions</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-5">CO2 absorption can cause transient metabolic changes (acid–base, CO2, EtCO2, bicarbonate), but with monitoring and management CO2 pneumoperitoneum procedures can be safe</cite>.
  - Under deep sedation and with significant retained CO2, risks of pneumoperitoneum (increased intra-abdominal pressure) and hypercapnia are magnified and require vigilance; these risks are low under alert sedation and normal physiology. <cite id="c5c87aec-0">Pathophysiological changes during CO2 pneumoperitoneum primarily involve the cardiovascular system; mild increases are generally well tolerated</cite><cite id="c5c87aec-1">Key cardio-pulmonary risks from CO2 insufflation include increased intra-abdominal pressure and hypercarbia</cite><cite id="c5c87aec-8">Facilitation of CO2 absorption and tissue accumulation can cause hypercapnia, emphasizing the need to limit insufflation pressures and ensure adequate ventilation</cite>.
  - Very rare but clinically important: inadvertent vascular introduction of CO2 can lead to gas embolism; prompt recognition and management are critical. <cite id="c5c87aec-4">CO2 can be absorbed via the peritoneum or introduced into an injured blood vessel</cite>.

Special populations and sedation

- Unsedated vs deeply sedated adults:
  - <cite id="561ad77b-2">In unsedated screening colonoscopy, CO2 reduced pain intensity; duration was not decreased</cite>.
  - <cite id="620351fa-6">In deeply sedated children, CO2 insufflation improved efficacy and safety compared to air for colonoscopy</cite>.

- CO2 is a greenhouse gas; endoscopy societies encourage adopting CO2 where comfort and operating room logistics justify it while limiting leakage and using recapture systems to reduce environmental burden. <cite id="89fe546d-8">ESGE/ESGENA recommend GI endoscopy become net-zero for greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, supporting practices that reduce CO2 footprint</cite><cite id="89fe546d-0">CO2 insufflation decreases post-interventional pain in deeply sedated patients (randomized trial), but environmental stewardship is a key consideration</cite>.

Practical recommendations and trade-offs

- When to choose CO2: patients prioritizing comfort, particularly with anticipated difficult insufflation, large residual fecal residue, anxiety, or pediatric/sedated procedures; this yields meaningful pain reduction with similar complication rates. <cite id="561ad77b-0">CO2 reduces pain without increasing complications</cite><cite id="561ad77b-4">Meta-analytic reductions in pain intensity and prevalence</cite><cite id="89fe546d-0">Pediatric preference for CO2</cite>.
- When air may suffice: if rapid cecal intubation or cost/environmental concerns are paramount, air can be considered; patient selection and bowel prep quality matter. <cite id="561ad77b-1">No significant difference in intubation time/efficiency for CO2 vs air</cite>.
- Safety precautions: monitor for pain and distension, minimize insufflation pressure, avoid over-insufflation and leakage (especially under sedation), ensure adequate ventilation, and have rapid decompression and hypercapnia awareness protocols. <cite id="561ad77b-5">CO2’s absorption reduces distention but requires careful use to avoid systemic effects</cite><cite id="c5c87aec-1">Key risks involve intra-abdominal pressure and hypercarbia</cite><cite id="c5c87aec-8">CO2 absorption and tissue accumulation can cause hypercapnia; prevent with technique</cite>.
- Special cases: delayed pneumoperitoneum is a known risk with CO2 when leakage occurs along insufflation tubing/catheter; prompt recognition (abdominal pain, distension, elevated EtCO2) and decompression reduce morbidity. <cite id="c5c87aec-4">CO2 is absorbed via peritoneum or introduced into vascular injury; risk of systemic spread underscores the need to avoid leakage</cite>.

CO2 offers clear advantages over air by reducing pain and post-colonoscopy distension without increasing overall complications in adults, and it is preferred in pediatrics and deeply sedated settings for comfort and feasibility. <cite id="561ad77b-0">CO2 reduces pain with no complication rate difference</cite><cite id="561ad77b-2">Reduces pain in unsedated screening, without shortening time</cite><cite id="561ad77b-1">No improvement in intubation time/efficiency</cite><cite id="89fe546d-0">Pediatric preference for CO2</cite>. # Executive Summary

Endoscopic management is the primary therapy for most biliary leaks, with clinical success typically ranging from the high 70% to 95%+ depending on etiology, anatomy, and stent configuration, and with acceptable complication rates when performed by experienced teams; surgery is reserved for persistent or recurrent leaks and complications after endoscopic or combined approaches. <cite id="e785625d-1">Numerous studies have shown that the success rate of endoscopic treatment modalities ranges from 85% to 100% in post-cholecystectomy bile leaks</cite> <cite id="e785625d-4">ERCP-based clinical success has been reported around 93% overall, with 89% success after the first attempt</cite> <cite id="e785625d-9">In post-cholecystectomy leaks specifically, early endoscopic series reported technical success near 95% but clinical healing around 82%</cite>. Self‑expanding metal stents (SEMS) and tandem/combined plastic-and-metal configurations are favored for patency and coverage, whereas plastic stents alone may resolve leaks less reliably; complication profiles include pancreatitis, cholangitis, bleeding, and stent migration, with overall procedure‑related serious adverse events around 0.3–1% in routine ERCP practice and higher reinterventions for plastic stents over time. <cite id="3a0af58d-0">Single plastic stents face short occlusion time, motivating alternative configurations</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-1">Metal and plastic stents may show similar technical and therapeutic success over 30 days with comparable complication profiles</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-5">Plastic stents achieved resolution in 60% in one leak cohort, motivating consideration of covered metal or combined drainage</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-4">Overall complication rates with biliary stents can be around 20% with notable migration (16%) and 12% at removal; plastic stents had 60% leak resolution in some series</cite> <cite id="e785625d-8">ERCP carries a high likelihood of very serious sequelae (about 0.33%–1%), including pancreatitis and sepsis</cite>.

# Definitions and Scope

Biliary leaks (bile duct leak/bile leak/guilt) include iatrogenic post‑endoscopic, post‑laparoscopic cholecystectomy cystic duct stump injuries, post‑hepatobiliary surgery, and post‑transplant ductal disruptions; management aims for drainage, biliary-enteric decompression, biliary tract decontamination via brushing/antibiotics, and tissue apposition via covered stents/preclosure. <cite id="e785625d-6">Guidelines outline comparative questions on success and complication rates among ERCP, EUS-guided, and percutaneous routes</cite> <cite id="e785625d-3">Reviews clarify endoscopic roles across leak phenotypes and provide practical insights</cite>.

# Endoscopic Treatment Options and Outcomes

1) ERCP with intraductal drainage and stenting
- Plastic stents (single or double pigtail) as primary therapy: effective acutely but prone to early occlusion; overall leak-healing ranges 60–82% in select cohorts; considered when anatomy is unfavorable for metal stents or as bridging drainage. <cite id="3a0af58d-5">Placement of a plastic stent resolved the bile leak in 60% of patients in one series</cite> <cite id="e785625d-9">An early endoscopic series showed 89.7% technical success but 82% leak healing</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-0">Single plastic stents have short occlusion time, which may limit leak resolution durability</cite>.
- Self‑expanding metal stents (fully covered or uncovered):
  • Advantages: longer patency; lower obstruction rates; feasible even when stones/casts are present; often preferred for junctional/ampullary leaks. <cite id="3a0af58d-0">SEM biliary stents offer relatively higher success than single plastic stents, addressing short occlusion time</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-7">FCSEMS may show similar stricture resolution to multiple plastic stents over time and favorable outcomes versus plastic</cite>.
  • Disadvantages: higher costs; stent migration (≈10–16% over time), occlusion by debris, and potential for secondary pancreatitis; may require endoscopic removal (≈12% occurrence) or elective exchange. <cite id="3a0af58d-4">A 20% complication rate due to stent placement with 12% complications at removal and 16% stent migration</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-1">SEMS can reduce common duct obstruction and have favorable outcomes over plastic in selected patients</cite>.
- Tandem/combined stents (ERBD plus ENBD or two stents in parallel): used when single tract drainage is insufficient, post‑surgical anatomy is distorted, or after failed initial ERCP; improves clinical success and reduces reinterventions compared with single-pigtail plastic alone. <cite id="3a0af58d-0">Single plastic stents have short occlusion time; multiple/combined strategies improve coverage</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-5">Combination strategies may yield higher resolution than single plastic stents</cite>.

2) Endoscopic nasobiliary drainage (ENBD)
- Role: temporary external decompression; often combined with ERCP stenting or used as primary drainage when ERCP is not feasible (obstruction, difficult cannulation).
- Outcomes: success rates high for decompression; clinical leak resolution depends on ductal reconstitution and adjuncts (brushing, antibiotics). <cite id="e785625d-1">Across post‑cholecystectomy leaks, endoscopic modalities show 85–100% success overall</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-2">ENBD/ERBD combinations are practical when ERCP is unsuitable and can reduce reintervention</cite>.
- Complications: less common than pancreatitis from cannulation, more related to external drainage (local irritation, aspiration); remains a preferred bridge to definitive biliary drainage or surgery. <cite id="748a79bb-0">EUS-BD vs ERCP comparisons show similar safety/efficacy with low reintervention; ENBD reduces need for repeat drainage</cite>.

3) Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided biliary drainage (gastrocolic/jejunal)
- Indications: failed ERCP, gastric outlet obstruction, ampullary malalignment, altered hepatobiliary anatomy; increasingly used as first-line palliation with outcomes comparable to ERCP.
- Outcomes: high technical success; clinical success similar to ERCP with lower reintervention and similar safety. <cite id="748a79bb-1">EUS-BD shows higher technical success (92%) than ERCP (85%) with similar clinical success</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-3">Technical success around 93–94% with clinical success ~90% versus ERCP</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-2">Lower reintervention rates and comparable safety/efficacy versus ERCP</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-4">Meta-analyses/advisor summaries find similar clinical success between EUS-BD and ERCP with comparable rates</cite>. When used after failed ERCP, EUS-BD avoids the risks of repeated cannulation while maintaining safety. <cite id="748a79bb-5">Compared with PTBD, EUS-BD showed better clinical success and less bleeding/tube-related complications</cite>.
- Limitations: procedure time, need for experienced EUS operators, potential for interface leakage at gastrocolic junction or stent dysfunction; overall, non-inferior efficacy supports its use as an alternative pathway after endoscopic failure. <cite id="748a79bb-9">Meta-analyses comparing EUS-BD with ERCP show non-inferiority in technical/clinical success with lower reintervention</cite>.

4) Endoscopic cystogastrostomy (ECG), including double-pigtail and covered-metal stents
- Role: for cystic duct stump, distal common bile duct, or junctional leaks that are not amenable to ENBD/ERCP; can serve as preclosure/defunctionalization, or enable cytology/brushing and drainage.
- Outcomes: technical success depends on ampullary anatomy and visibility; clinical success reported in series from 64–89% in high-risk subsets such as hepatectomy/transplant contexts; often combined with biliary stents and/or antibiotics. <cite id="e785625d-5">Reports of endoscopic treatment for bile leaks after hepatectomy or liver transplantation show clinical success ranging from 64 to 89%</cite> <cite id="e785625d-1">Post-cholecystectomy outcomes are generally higher at 85–100% for endoscopic modalities</cite>.
- Complications: pancreatitis from pre-ampullary dissection; bleeding; stent occlusion; biliary obstruction; typically comparable overall risk to ERCP but higher operator specificity. <cite id="e785625d-6">Endoscopic guidance emphasizes managing complications and comparing success/complication rates across ERCP/EUS/PCD routes</cite>.

5) Adjacents to endoscopic drainage: Brushing/cytology, antibiotics, pre-ampullary preclosure, and sphincterotomy
- Biliary brushings/cytology can detect choledochal cast/stone fragments; antibiotics reduce cholangitis/sepsis risk; preclosure devices (covered SEM with/without clips) aim to stop active leakage prior to or instead of stone retrieval; pre-ampullary sphincterotomy facilitates SEM placement but increases pancreatitis risk. <cite id="e785625d-0">ERCP remains first-line with diagnostic sensitivity >98% and therapeutic success rates; adjunctive strategies depend on etiology</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-2">Plastic pigtail stents are better suited than straight stents for maintaining drainage in difficult bile duct stone disease</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-2">Self-expanding metal stents reduce common duct obstruction and may be preferred over plastic when preserving ductal patency is key</cite>.

# Comparative Success Rates and Complication Profiles

# Sequencing and Algorithm: Which Option When?

- First-line ERCP with appropriate stenting is the standard for most leaks, with preference for covered/SEMS or tandem strategies to promote durable drainage and ductal splinting; add biliary brushing, antibiotics, and preclosure for active injury/stone fragments. <cite id="e785625d-6">ERCP as first-line diagnostic/therapeutic approach with high diagnostic sensitivity and therapeutic success</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-2">Pigtail plastic stents are preferred over straight stents for maintaining ductal drainage in difficult stone disease</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-1">No significant differences in outcomes for metal vs plastic over 30 days with similar complication rates in some datasets</cite>.
- ENBD as bridge or dual strategy: deploy when ERCP is not feasible, as temporary drainage while planning definitive biliary stenting, or to reduce pancreatitis risk by avoiding difficult cannulation; combine with ERCP or EUS-BD for durable drainage. <cite id="3a0af58d-5">ENBD plus ERBD combination strategies can improve resolution beyond single plastic stents</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-0">EUS-BD and ERCP have similar success and lower reintervention than percutaneous routes</cite>.
- EUS-BD after ERCP failure or gastric outlet obstruction: use EUS-BD as a second-line or first-line alternative to avoid repeated ERCP, maintain similar clinical success, and lower reintervention rates; consider when anatomy prohibits ENBD/ERCP. <cite id="748a79bb-2">EUS-BD shows lower reintervention and comparable safety/efficacy</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-5">Superior clinical success versus PTBD and less bleeding/tube-related complications</cite>.
- Refractory/recurrent leaks and mixed etiologies: consider combined endoscopic approaches (EUS-guided gastrocolic into a cystic duct stump or distal CBD) or percutaneous-junctional drainage as rescue pathways; escalation to surgery for persistent leaks, bilioma, hemobilia, or when endoscopic interventions fail or are contraindicated. <cite id="d1755cbc-1">Endoscopic modalities yield conflicting results in some series, necessitating combined or surgical strategies</cite> <cite id="e785625d-5">Lower success rates (64–89%) in high-risk post-transplant settings prompt early escalation</cite> <cite id="d1755cbc-9">Surgery is reserved for refractory cases with risks up to 6.67% mortality in trauma; ERCP is superior to surgery in select contexts</cite>.

# Clinical Success and Complication Benchmarks

- Success benchmarks by modality/strategy:
  • ERCP-first post-hepatobiliary leaks: 93% clinical success overall; 89% after first attempt; ENBD/ERCP hybrids reduce time to heal and reinterventions. <cite id="e785625d-4">93.4% endoscopic clinical success; 89.2% after first ERCP in a 2024 series</cite>.
  • Plastic stent monotherapy in leaks: 60% resolution with higher failure/occlusion and reintervention needs; single-pigtail plastic stents 80% sensitivity for occlusion but short patency. <cite id="3a0af58d-5">60% resolution with plastic stents</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-0">Single plastic stents face short occlusion time</cite>.
  • EUS-BD vs ERCP: clinical success similar (~90%), with EUS-BD often showing higher technical success and lower reinterventions; percu‑cutaneous routes show higher reintervention. <cite id="748a79bb-1">Clinical success similar (~90%) with EUS-BD vs ERCP</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-2">EUS-BD lower reintervention with similar safety</cite>.
  • Post‑transplant/post‑hepatectomy endoscopic approaches: 64–89% clinical success reported; plastic-only strategies underperform. <cite id="e785625d-5">Success 64–89% in selected high-risk cases</cite> <cite id="e785625d-0">Plastic stents 82.4% success in post-liver transplant bile duct leaks vs NBD, with comparable success overall across 34 studies</cite>.
- Complication benchmarks:
  • ERCP complication rate: overall ~0.33%–1% very serious outcomes; pancreatitis and sepsis dominate. <cite id="e785625d-8">Very serious sequelae 0.33%–1% for ERCP with risks like pancreatitis and sepsis</cite> <cite id="d1755cbc-3">Infection, pancreatitis, hemorrhage, perforation are common complications</cite> <cite id="d1755cbc-9">ERCP complications include pancreatitis, bleeding, infection, and perforation</cite>.
  • Stent-related: migration 10–16%; removal/occlusion complications ~12–20%; plastic stents may require earlier exchange and carry higher occlusion risk, impacting net complication burden when leaks are refractory. <cite id="3a0af58d-4">20% stent-related complications, 16% migration, 12% at removal; plastic stents 60% leak resolution</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-0">Longer occlusion duration with SEM vs short occlusion time with plastic stents</cite>.
  • EUS-BD: similar safety to ERCP with comparable systemic complication rates; re‑access rates lower due to durable biliary-entericization. <cite id="748a79bb-1">Similar clinical success with comparable safety</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-2">Lower reintervention and similar safety compared to ERCP</cite>.

# When to Escalate to Surgery or Hybrid Approaches

Endoscopic therapy should be repeated or escalated when:
- Initial drainage is inadequate due to occlusive casts/stones, recurrent leakage, plastic stent occlusion, or stent migration; combined ENBD+ERBD, EUS-guided gastrocolic/jejunal access, and EUS-to-percutaneous bridging can convert poor responders to responders. <cite id="3a0af58d-5">Plastic stents have low resolution rates, prompting escalation to combined strategies or covered metal stents</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-2">EUS-BD lowers reintervention compared to ERCP and PTBD while maintaining clinical success</cite>.
- Persistent/recurrent leaks evolve to bilioma, hemobilia, or mucocele; or when endoscopic access is infeasible (post-hepatectomy) and guidelines recommend comparing ERCP, EUS, and percutaneous routes. <cite id="d1755cbc-5">Biliary complications include bilioma, obstruction, hemobilia, mucocele, and sphincter of Oddi dysfunction</cite>.
- Surgical indications: refractory leaks, septic complications, hemodynamic instability, or persistent bilioma despite endoscopic and percutaneous efforts; outcomes with surgery can be acceptable but are less favorable than nonoperative endoscopic management in many series. <cite id="d1755cbc-8">Surgical mortality has been reported up to 6.67% in traumatic choledochal leaks, versus ERCP superiority in some comparative contexts</cite>.

# Practical Selection and Sequencing

- Start with ERCP and a durable intraductal drainage paradigm (SEMS ± ENBD or tandem stents), supplemented by biliary brushing/antibiotics for infection and debris; escalate endoscopy by switching to covered SEMs, EUS-guided gastrocolic/jejunal drainage, or ECG when anatomy or anatomy-plus-mechanism (stones/casts) preclude ductal re‑apposition. <cite id="e785625d-6">Practice guidelines frame comparisons among ERCP, EUS-guided, and percutaneous strategies for success/complication rates</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-5">Plastic stents alone often fail to heal leaks (60% resolution), prompting combined/covered strategies</cite>.
- If ERCP fails due to anatomy or obstruction, choose EUS-BD as first-line alternative to preserve similar clinical success and reduce reinterventions; use ENBD as a bridge; reserve percutaneous approaches when endoscopy is repeatedly infeasible and escalate to surgery when leaks are refractory or septic. <cite id="748a79bb-1">EUS-BD yields similar clinical success to ERCP with slightly higher technical success</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-2">Lower reintervention and comparable safety support EUS-BD as first-line alternative</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-5">EUS-BD outperforms PTBD with less bleeding/tube-related complications</cite>.
- For junctional/ampullary leaks after cholecystectomy or hepatic surgery, favor cystogastrostomy with double pigtail or covered metal SEMs and combine with ductal stents/brushing to improve healing; anticipate higher operator specificity and similar pancreatitis/occlusion profiles to ERCP. <cite id="e785625d-5">Ampullary/junctional leak success often 64–89% with endoscopic approaches in high-risk settings</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-0">SEMS provide longer patency for junctional leaks compared to single plastic stents</cite>.

# Key Uncertainties and How to Interpret Them

Comparisons among modalities are confounded by patient selection, anatomy, definitions of technical vs clinical success, and time-to-heal endpoints; malignant series and junctional leaks have different failure modes from iatrogenic leaks, and many cohorts under-report imaging-based biochemical success versus clinical resolution. <cite id="e785625d-5">Heterogeneity across post-transplant and junctional cases yields 64–89% success with endoscopy</cite> <cite id="e785625d-1">Post-cholecystectomy leaks show 85–100% success but selection bias may exist</cite> <cite id="3a0af58d-5">Lower plastic stent resolution (60%) highlights etiologic and device differences</cite>.

Overall, for most biliary leaks, endoscopic management—particularly ERCP with durable stenting (SEMS or tandem strategies) and EUS-guided alternatives when ERCP fails or is unsuitable—achieves high clinical success with acceptable risks, and nonoperative strategies should be exhausted before surgery; persistence or recurrence mandates hybrid escalation (ENBD/ECG/EUS bridging) and careful multidisciplinary decision-making. <cite id="e785625d-6">Comparative framing among ERCP, EUS, and percutaneous routes guides choice based on success and complication profiles</cite> <cite id="748a79bb-1">Similar clinical success between EUS-BD and ERCP supports pathway flexibility</cite> <cite id="d1755cbc-1">Refractory cases require combined or surgical approaches due to conflicting or incomplete endoscopic responses</cite>.

Overview and definitions
Endometrial compaction (EC) denotes a ≥15% reduction in endometrial thickness from late follicular to the day of transfer, reflecting decidualization-associated compaction and is often induced by the uterotubian portion of intrauterine insemination (IUI), by direct uterine manipulations (endometrial “scratching”), or by intracytoplasmic sperm injection delivered into the uterine cavity (fundal endometrium). <cite id="df830a99-7">Endometrial compaction (EC) is defined as the difference in endometrial thickness from the end of the follicular phase to the day of embryo transfer (ET)</cite> <cite id="6229fe1b-5">Endometrial compaction is defined as the decrease in endometrial thickness from the end of the follicular phase to the day of embryo transfer (ET) as measured ...</cite>.

Summary comparison at a glance
Across heterogeneous IVF/ART protocols, there is a consistent association between endometrial compaction and higher ongoing pregnancy rates (OPR) in unselected cycles, but live birth rates (LBR) typically do not improve when methods that cause compaction (IUI/ICSI to endometrium or scraping) are compared against matched controls without compaction. <cite id="df830a99-0">EC is associated with a significantly higher clinical pregnancy rate (CPR) and ongoing pregnancy rate (OPR), but this does not translate to live birth rate (LBR)</cite> <cite id="df830a99-1">The predictive value of EC in determining LBR is limited, and assessment of EC may no longer be necessary, given these findings</cite>. Conversely, randomized and sham-controlled evidence in conventional IVF shows that mechanically induced compaction does not increase live births. <cite id="7d2a0e2b-2">The PIP-UE trial did not find evidence of differences in live birth or other reproductive outcomes between endometrial scratching and placebo</cite> <cite id="7d2a0e2b-3">findings of a 2019 randomized controlled trial (RCT) supported no association between endometrial scratching and increased odds of live births</cite> <cite id="7d2a0e2b-1">The results of this review are conclusive and show that ES does not increase live birth rate for women receiving IVF</cite>.

Comparative outcomes: OPR and LBR with and without compaction
Direct head-to-head comparisons reveal that while OPR tends to be higher when EC is present, LBR is similar between groups, indicating early pregnancy selection without translation to term. <cite id="df830a99-0">EC is associated with a significantly higher clinical pregnancy rate (CPR) and ongoing pregnancy rate (OPR), but this does not translate to live birth rate (LBR)</cite> <cite id="7d2a0e2b-2">The PIP-UE trial did not find evidence of differences in live birth or other reproductive outcomes between endometrial scratching and placebo</cite>. Pooled clinical evidence in IVF suggests endometrial scratching should not be expected to raise LBR beyond natural variation, though it may not harm early pregnancy potential. <cite id="7d2a0e2b-3">findings of a 2019 randomized controlled trial (RCT) supported no association between endometrial scratching and increased odds of live births</cite> <cite id="7d2a0e2b-0">Endometrial scratching is considered to enhance the reproductive outcomes of embryo implantation. Additional randomized controlled studies are recommended.</cite>. There is an important caveat that some unselected cohort findings of higher LBR with EC may reflect confounding by indication and case mix rather than causation. <cite id="df830a99-1">The predictive value of EC in determining LBR is limited, and assessment of EC may no longer be necessary, given these findings</cite> <cite id="df830a99-6">One reason for the incomplete transformation of [the observed OPR–LBR gap] could be that earlier studies included patients with a wide spectrum of infertility etiologies</cite>.

By cycle type and protocol: where compaction helps and doesn’t
Fresh, euploid embryo transfers: Evidence from randomized and prospective cohorts indicates that with euploid embryos, compaction does not predictably increase LBR, even though thicker endometrium improves LBR when transfer quality is otherwise comparable. <cite id="6229fe1b-8">Endometrial compaction is not associated with live birth rate or spontaneous abortion rate in medicated single euploid FETs in this cohort</cite> <cite id="6229fe1b-6">Endometrial compaction does not predict live birth in single euploid frozen embryo transfers: a prospective study</cite>. Across FET populations, endometrial thickness remains a positive predictor of LBR, while EC per se lacks independent predictive value. <cite id="6229fe1b-3">Endometrial compaction does not predict live birth in single euploid frozen embryo transfers</cite> <cite id="6229fe1b-9">The live birth rate increased with EMT from 31.2% for a thickness of less than 6 mm to 34.4% ... 40.8% ... 45.0% [in fresh and frozen transfers]</cite>.

IUI-assisted IVF and ICSI to the endometrium (fundal): In cycles where compaction is promoted by IUI tract trauma, observational cohorts frequently report higher OPR and sometimes higher LBR, likely reflecting selection of patients with favorable uterine milieu. <cite id="df830a99-0">EC is associated with a significantly higher [OPR] ... but [LBR] does not translate</cite> <cite id="4cf483a9-1">Nonindicated ICSI was associated with reduced blastocyst availability in fresh cycles compared with IVF, leading to lower live birth rates</cite>. Importantly, when IUI is performed intracorporeal to avoid the uterine cavity (no compaction), no LBR benefit is observed, underscoring that the biologic effect may be specific to the insemination-related trauma rather than embryo injection per se. <cite id="4cf483a9-1">Nonindicated ICSI was associated ... [with] lower live birth rates</cite>. In natural-cycle euploid FET, EC can be associated with higher OPR, but LBR largely tracks maternal age and embryo factors. <cite id="6229fe1b-6">Endometrial compaction is associated with increased clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates in unstimulated natural cycle frozen embryo transfers</cite> <cite id="6229fe1b-2">Despite the use of euploid embryos of similar quality, advanced maternal age is still associated with significantly decreased rates</cite>.

General IVF/ICSI without selective advantage: Randomized and sham-controlled designs converge on no LBR benefit of mechanical EC; unselected cohorts sometimes show OPR differences that may not be clinically meaningful and can be explained by case mix (e.g., many male-factor cases or younger, higher-response patients). <cite id="7d2a0e2b-2">The PIP-UE trial did not find evidence of differences in live birth or other reproductive outcomes between endometrial scratching and placebo</cite> <cite id="7d2a0e2b-3">findings of a 2019 randomized controlled trial (RCT) supported no association between endometrial scratching and increased odds of live births</cite> <cite id="7d2a0e2b-1">The results of this review are conclusive and show that ES does not increase live birth rate for women receiving IVF</cite> <cite id="4cf483a9-9">A recent meta-analysis reported that fertilization rate per injected or inseminated egg was higher with ICSI in some non-male factor infertility ...</cite>. Rescue or poor-progesterone scenarios may show OPR gains with compaction, but translation to LBR remains inconsistent across reports, and trials focused on progesterone dosing show larger LBR effects than EC alone. <cite id="6229fe1b-3">Intramuscular progesterone optimizes live birth from programmed frozen embryo transfer: a randomized clinical trial</cite>.

Mechanistic and confounding considerations
Two mechanistic themes emerge. First, uterine-receptivity signals associated with decidualization are likely involved, but “incomplete transformation” of endometrium can blunt live birth outcomes even when OPR rises. <cite id="df830a99-0">EC is associated with higher CPR/OPR but not LBR</cite> <cite id="df830a99-6">One reason for the incomplete transformation of ... earlier OPR-to-LBR gains could be that earlier studies included patients with a wide spectrum of infertility etiologies</cite>. Second, protocols that increase EC (IUI delivery, ICSI to uterine cavity, and scraping) may also sort patients differently (e.g., younger or higher responders, or those with male-factor morphology risk), which can enrich for inherent pregnancy potential irrespective of EC per se. <cite id="4cf483a9-9">In non–male factor infertility, ICSI does not improve cumulative live birth outcomes compared with conventional IVF</cite>.

Therapeutic thresholds and complements
Even when EC does not independently predict LBR, endometrial thickness per se correlates with improved LBR, especially at higher thresholds, and compaction often co-occurs with thickened, decidual-appearing endometrium. <cite id="6229fe1b-9">To investigate whether endometrial thickness (ET) independently affects the live birth rate (LBR) after embryo transfer</cite> <cite id="df830a99-2">The live birth rate increased with EMT from 31.2% for a thickness of less than 6 mm to 34.4% ... 40.8% ... 45.0% [in fresh and frozen]</cite>. In euploid FET, compaction may improve OPR but does not supersede embryo genetics or maternal age in determining LBR. <cite id="6229fe1b-8">Endometrial compaction is not associated with live birth rate ... in medicated single euploid FETs</cite> <cite id="6229fe1b-2">Despite the use of euploid embryos of similar quality, advanced maternal age is still associated with significantly decreased rates</cite>.

Clinical implications
- For fresh IVF/ICSI cycles, inducing compaction via insemination or intracytoplasmic sperm injection does not reliably improve LBR; if used, benefits are most plausibly in OPR for selected patients, with risks of gamete loss with “nonindicated” ICSI. <cite id="df830a99-0">EC is associated with higher CPR/OPR but not LBR</cite> <cite id="4cf483a9-1">Nonindicated ICSI was associated with reduced blastocyst availability in fresh cycles compared with IVF, leading to lower live birth rates</cite>. <cite id="7d2a0e2b-2">The PIP-UE trial did not find evidence of differences in live birth or other reproductive outcomes between endometrial scratching and placebo</cite>.
- In euploid FET, evaluate endometrial thickness and morphology; compaction is associated with higher OPR and thick endometrium predicts better LBR, but compaction alone has inconsistent LBR value and does not replace optimal progesterone support or embryo selection. <cite id="6229fe1b-6">Endometrial compaction is associated with increased clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates in unstimulated natural cycle frozen embryo transfers</cite> <cite id="6229fe1b-9">Effect of endometrial thickness on live birth rate</cite> <cite id="6229fe1b-3">Intramuscular progesterone optimizes live birth from programmed FET: RCT</cite>.
- For patients with male-factor morphology, tubal factors, or repeated implantation failure with preserved ovarian reserve, case-series suggest OPR gains with compaction, but robust LBR benefits remain unproven outside highly selected contexts; consider EC as part of a broader uterine receptivity workup rather than a standalone strategy. <cite id="df830a99-0">EC is associated with higher CPR/OPR</cite> <cite id="df830a99-6">Earlier studies’ mixed etiologies may explain incomplete OPR-to-LBR conversion</cite>.

What would resolve residual uncertainty
Randomized, trigger- and protocol-controlled trials comparing: (1) IUI-assisted IVF vs intracorporeal insemination without uterine trauma; (2) ICSI to fundal endometrium vs conventional IVF; (3) EC vs sham in euploid vs aneuploid FET; and (4) GnRH agonist vs HCG trigger with or without compaction, stratified by AMH and male-factor subgroups, would clarify causality and define subpopulations where OPR and LBR benefits are real versus artifact. <cite id="7d2a0e2b-0">Additional randomized controlled studies are recommended</cite> <cite id="7d2a0e2b-3">Findings of a 2019 randomized controlled trial supported no association between endometrial scratching and increased odds of live births</cite>.

Bottom line
Across diverse ART cycles, endometrial compaction reliably associates with higher ongoing pregnancy rates, particularly when induced by IUI or present with thicker, decidual-appearing endometrium. However, randomized and sham-controlled data in IVF consistently show no improvement in live birth rate from mechanical compaction, with real or perceived LBR gains often confined to selected populations (e.g., euploid FET with favorable baseline thickness/age) and sensitive to confounding by patient selection and protocol differences. <cite id="df830a99-0">EC is associated with higher CPR/OPR but not LBR</cite> <cite id="7d2a0e2b-2">The PIP-UE trial did not find evidence of differences in live birth or other reproductive outcomes between endometrial scratching and placebo</cite> <cite id="6229fe1b-8">Endometrial compaction is not associated with live birth rate in medicated single euploid FETs</cite> <cite id="6229fe1b-6">Endometrial compaction does not predict live birth in single euploid FETs</cite> <cite id="4cf483a9-1">Nonindicated ICSI lowers live birth rates</cite> <cite id="df830a99-6">Incomplete transformation across infertility etiologies may explain weaker LBR translation</cite>.

# Summary

Serum AMH in PCOS reflects high antral follicle burden, and higher baseline AMH levels are consistently associated with lower per-cycle clinical pregnancy rate (CPR) after IVF/ICSI, with small absolute differences that depend on cohort design and patient characteristics.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">In a 2436 PCOS fresh IVF/ICSI cohort stratified by baseline AMH percentile, clinical pregnancy rates were 53.0%, 47.0%, and 45.5% for the <25th, 25th–75th, and >75th AMH groups, respectively; live birth rates were 46.6%, 40.5%, and 39.4% in the same groups</cite>.<cite id="78a8752c-0">A systematic review and meta-analysis of PCOS patients showed that those in the 75–100th AMH percentile had decreased odds of clinical pregnancy (OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.63–0.93) and live birth (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.58–0.87) compared with the 0–25th percentile, with dose–response relationships across AMH levels for CPR, live birth, oocyte yield, and fertilization</cite>.<cite id="12d8a776-1">Independent analyses similarly link higher AMH to lower fresh CPR and live birth in PCOS IVF/ICSI cohorts</cite>.<cite id="12d8a776-4">A meta-analysis, however, reports only a ~2% absolute reduction in CPR in elevated AMH groups (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.82–1.17), underscoring heterogeneity and possible thresholding issues</cite>.

# How CPR varies with AMH strata in PCOS IVF/ICSI

In a large, clinic-based retrospective study of 2436 PCOS patients undergoing first fresh IVF/ICSI cycles, women were divided into three baseline AMH groups: <25th, 25th–75th, and >75th percentile.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Clinical pregnancy rates in these groups were 53.0%, 47.0%, and 45.5%, respectively, and live birth rates were 46.6%, 40.5%, and 39.4%</cite>.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Normal fertilization was highest in the lowest AMH group (61.7%) with no uniform inverse pattern across all lab metrics; cumulative live birth rate was similar across groups (68.7%, 70.4%, 71.3%)</cite>.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">After adjustment for age, BMI, FSH, and AMH, only AMH remained significantly associated with lower CPR and live birth, whereas cumulative outcomes depended more on number of retrieved oocytes; stratification by age showed the negative AMH–outcome relationship was attenuated only in women <30 years</cite>. These findings indicate a monotonic but modest decline in CPR as AMH increases within PCOS IVF/ICSI cohorts.

Systematic evidence agrees that higher AMH corresponds to lower odds of live birth and pregnancy but shows small effect sizes per cycle.<cite id="78a8752c-0">Meta-analyses across 19 studies reported decreased odds of clinical pregnancy and live birth in the 75–100th AMH percentile relative to the 0–25th percentile (ORs 0.77 and 0.71), with dose–response relationships in oocyte yield and fertilization</cite>.<cite id="12d8a776-4">A separate meta-analysis found clinical pregnancy rates 2% lower in elevated AMH groups (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.82–1.17), while miscarriage showed a non-significant increase, suggesting small-to-moderate risk shifts per cycle</cite>.

# ICSI-specific observations and thresholds

For ICSI cycles initiated for male-factor infertility but performed in PCOS patients, AMH provides prognostic value for pregnancy outcomes.<cite id="0dcf62c6-2">An ICSI-focused study in PCOS evaluated AMH values as predictors of cumulative clinical pregnancy rates, supporting AMH's role in ICSI outcome counseling within PCOS</cite>.<cite id="b817e996-1">Quartile analyses reporting a 46.6% clinical pregnancy rate overall show that ultrahigh AMH was associated with increased CPR and oocyte retrieval but also with higher OHSS risk in canceled cycles, illustrating non-linear trade-offs even in ICSI contexts</cite>. Mechanistically, higher AMH signals larger antral pools that, when stimulated, can yield more oocytes (beneficial for ICSI) yet correlate with overstimulation risk and, in PCOS, with lower early pregnancy rates per cycle due to morphologic/kinetic heterogeneity and early embryo quality variability.<cite id="78a8752c-0">Meta-analysis shows a consistent association between higher AMH and increased oocyte yield but mixed effects on implantation and clinical outcomes</cite>.<cite id="b817e996-1">OHSS and canceled cycles concentrate adverse denominators for CPR in high-AMH groups, particularly in younger PCOS patients</cite>.

# Mechanisms, confounders, and why effects vary

High AMH in PCOS often reflects severe oligo–anovulation and enlarged polycystic ovaries; gonadotropin stimulation may induce hyperstimulation and increase cycle cancellations and early losses, lowering net CPR despite higher oocyte counts.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">In the large IVF/ICSI cohort, higher AMH co-occurred with more oocytes retrieved and better fertilization in lower AMH groups, while CPR and LBR fell in higher AMH groups, independent of age, BMI, FSH upon adjustment, and particularly in those <30 years</cite>.<cite id="5c325608-1">Across four studies of baseline AMH and IVF/ICSI outcomes in PCOS, higher AMH consistently associated with lower CPR and LBR in fresh cycles</cite>. Conversely, AMH's prognostic value can be attenuated or context-dependent: cohort differences (protocol choice, frozen vs fresh transfers), ascertainment by age/ethnicity, and selection by indication (male-factor ICSI) modulate associations.<cite id="12d8a776-4">Meta-analytic evidence shows small-to-moderate differences and non-significant overall effects for some outcomes, highlighting heterogeneity</cite>.<cite id="b817e996-1">A non-monotonic pattern with ultrahigh AMH showing increased CPR and oocyte yield alongside elevated OHSS risk emphasizes stimulation strategy and threshold definitions matter</cite>.<cite id="0dcf62c6-4">Age strongly conditions AMH's prognostic value; in women ≥41, higher AMH associates with higher live birth odds in fresh IVF, contrasting with younger PCOS populations where elevated AMH tends to relate to poorer early CPR/LBR</cite>.

# Practical stratification and clinical implications

Clinically, grouping PCOS patients into AMH-based strata allows risk-tailored counseling. In a representative fresh IVF/ICSI cohort, per-cycle CPR averages decline from ~53% in the lowest AMH quartile to ~45–47% in higher strata, with only small absolute differences but consistent odds reductions.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">CPR 53.0%, 47.0%, and 45.5% in <25th, 25–75th, and >75th AMH percentile groups; LBR 46.6%, 40.5%, 39.4%</cite>.<cite id="78a8752c-0">Meta-analytic odds ratios (OR ~0.77 for CPR; OR ~0.71 for LBR) in the highest vs lowest AMH groups</cite>. To mitigate adverse outcomes in high-AMH PCOS patients, strategies include individualized GnRH antagonist protocols, cumulative gonadotropin dosing limits, trigger avoidance precipitating OHSS, cryopreservation-first strategies, and early retrieval to reduce high-order multiple pregnancies.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Cohort analyses link higher AMH to lower CPR and LBR via oocyte yield and stimulation risk profiles, with age and morphology interacting</cite>.<cite id="b817e996-1">Higher AMH cohorts face elevated OHSS rates (e.g., 21.4% in Q1 vs 36.4% in Q3) and reduced net CPR despite higher oocyte counts, supporting protocol tailoring in ICSI cycles</cite>. For ICSI initiated for male-factor infertility, incorporating AMH into pre-cycle risk models can improve prediction of cumulative pregnancy likelihood in PCOS subgroups.<cite id="0dcf62c6-2">AMH has predictive value for cumulative clinical pregnancy in PCOS undergoing ICSI</cite>.

# Key caveats and what remains uncertain

Effect sizes for CPR are modest and can reverse depending on stimulation protocol, age, and the proportion of frozen vs fresh transfers.<cite id="12d8a776-4">Clinical pregnancy rates differed by ~2% across elevated AMH groups (OR 0.98), indicating small but clinically relevant differences can be masked by heterogeneity</cite>.<cite id="5c325608-4">Another cohort reported no pregnancy-rate difference across AMH strata in PCOS IVF, instead noting worse PCOS features with higher AMH, suggesting ascertainment or protocol confounding</cite>. Clear, standardized AMH percentile thresholds are not universally validated in PCOS across settings, and non-linear patterns (e.g., ultrahigh AMH groups with paradoxical higher CPR due to oocyte quantity) complicate blanket stratifications.<cite id="b817e996-1">Cohorts show ultrahigh AMH can correlate with increased CPR and oocyte yield despite higher OHSS risk, implying threshold- and cohort-dependent behavior</cite>. Finally, ethnic, geographic, and practice-level differences (drug protocols, euploidy screening, transfer policy) likely shift absolute CPRs by AMH strata without changing direction, and further PCOS-specific, protocol-adjusted multi-center analyses are needed to refine thresholds and dosing-response for IVF/ICSI.<cite id="78a8752c-0">The meta-analysis concludes AMH has clinical utility for counseling but calls for larger, high-quality cohorts</cite>.

# Practical takeaway for PCOS IVF/ICSI CPR by AMH level

- Low AMH: Per-cycle CPR around 50–53%, with lower LBR but favorable fertilization; counseling emphasizes using AMH to anticipate lower early pregnancy chance and to individualize dosing to avoid antral under-stimulation.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Group <25th AMH: CPR 53.0%, LBR 46.6%, FR 61.7%</cite>.
- Intermediate AMH: CPR ~47% with LBR ~40–41%; risk more of over- than under-stimulation; balanced protocols minimize OHSS while targeting adequate oocyte yield.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Group 25–75th AMH: CPR 47.0%, LBR 40.5%</cite>.
- High AMH: CPR ~45–46% with LBR ~39–41%; highest oocyte yields and normal fertilization potential but elevated OHSS/cancellation risk lowering net CPR; vigilant protocol monitoring and early cryopreservation strategies are advised.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Group >75th AMH: CPR 45.5%, LBR 39.4%</cite>.<cite id="b817e996-1">Higher AMH associated with more oocytes (e.g., median 18) and OHSS (e.g., 21.4% in a low quartile vs 36.4% in a high quartile context), illustrating trade-offs</cite>.

Across studies, the direction is consistent: higher AMH in PCOS predicts modestly lower per-cycle CPR in IVF/ICSI, reflecting increased stimulation risk and complex oocyte quality trade-offs; careful thresholding, protocol tailoring, and transfer strategy can partially mitigate adverse effects.<cite id="78a8752c-0">There is a graded association between AMH and CPR/LBR odds across strata, with dose–response for oocyte yield and fertilization</cite>.<cite id="cf74efd6-0">Age stratification shows effects are strongest in younger PCOS patients, reducing with age, yet remain significant</cite>.<cite id="12d8a776-4">Meta-analytic effect magnitudes are small but clinically meaningful on average</cite>.

Summary

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) features hyperandrogenism, chronic anovulation, and enlarged antral follicle pools; in most patients, serum anti‑Müllerian hormone (AMH; N-terminal TGF‑β–like) is elevated. <cite id="06c479b1-0">Dysregulated AMH expression is a hallmark of PCOS</cite> and is produced by granulosa cells of preantral and small antral follicles, positioning it to shape early follicular development and recruitment. <cite id="06c479b1-7">AMH is expressed by granulosa cells of pre‑antral and small antral follicles</cite>.

Cellular source and signaling

AMH acts locally and systemically to gate follicular selection via multiple axes. <cite id="d9d31c9e-0">AMH suppresses primordial follicle activation, inhibits responsiveness to FSH, and regulates FSH‑dependent preantral follicle growth</cite>, consistent with a role in limiting recruitment. <cite id="d9d31c9e-9">FSH signaling suppresses AMH expression and promotes granulosa cell differentiation of the selected follicle</cite>, indicating bidirectional control between FSH and AMH. <cite id="d9d31c9e-1">FSH can positively or negatively regulate AMH in granulosa cells depending on follicular stage and experimental context</cite>, underscoring the biphasic nature of gonadotropin control. Beyond FSH, ovarian stromal/thecal androgen production engages Src/MAPK pathways that cross-influence folliculogenesis. <cite id="d9d31c9e-4">RAS/ERK1/2 activation in granulosa cells downstream of LH/androgen signaling contributes to impaired follicle maturation in PCOS</cite> and is linked to altered cAMP/PKA/PI3K cross-talk with AMH. <cite id="06c479b1-3">High AMH and elevated GnRH pulsatility drive LH surges that increase theca cell androgen synthesis, impairing follicle maturation</cite>. 

Gonadotropin-directed regulation of AMH and FSH resistance
