In summary: Before initiating a JAK inhibitor in refractory RA, clinicians should screen for and quantify cardiovascular, thrombotic, oncologic, infection, hepatic, hematologic, reproductive, and drug–drug interaction risks; individualize agent choice (often favor upadacitinib when risks are balanced) and tailor dose, vaccinations, and monitoring; counsel extensively on contraception and fertility; and adopt a formal risk‑management plan with early lab and symptom surveillance, team involvement, and clear escalation pathways when adverse events arise<cite id="b5c034bb-0">Risk profiles differ across JAK inhibitors, with baricitinib associated with higher CV and cancer risk and careful selection based on patient-specific factors</cite><cite id="b5c034bb-2">Guidelines emphasize patient-specific risk assessment, infections (including TB), malignancy, cardiovascular risk factors, and drug interactions when prescribing JAK inhibitors in RA</cite><cite id="b5c034bb-4">Regulatory and pharmacovigilance updates list major CV risk, malignancy, VTE, serious infections, teratogenicity, and P‑gp/ABCB1 and CYP interactions as key risk factors/management elements</cite><cite id="e8c44156-2">JAK inhibitors increase MACE risk, especially stroke, with shorter time to onset compared to anti‑TNF therapies</cite><cite id="e8c44156-3">Baseline cardio‑metabolic comorbidities, age, and disease activity all raise baseline MACE risk and should guide JAK use and monitoring</cite><cite id="0570ec05-1">Risk‑management plans should include pregnancy testing, contraception, and fertility counseling to mitigate teratogenic risks</cite><cite id="0570ec05-6">Discontinuation planning in women of childbearing potential requires counseling on flare risk to inform shared decisions</cite><cite id="0570ec05-4">Pregnancy outcomes with upadacitinib, baricitinib, and tofacitinib demonstrate increased adverse outcomes, reinforcing avoidance and planning</cite>.

Summary
MRI is an adjunctive imaging modality in carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS), with good-to-excellent reported sensitivity and specificity for median nerve pathologic cross‑sectional area (CSA) measurements, but it should not be used routinely as first-line diagnostic testing for typical CTS without strong clinical or electrodiagnostic indications <cite id="d3717a2b-1">MRI has good-to-excellent sensitivity (84–100%) and specificity (85–94%) for diagnosing CTS when using median nerve CSA thresholds</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-6">Do not routinely use MRI for the diagnosis of CTS; prioritize diagnostic questionnaires and/or electrodiagnostic studies</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-3">This guideline addresses diagnosis and treatment of adult CTS and emphasizes non‑routine use of imaging</cite>.

Clinical situations where MRI is particularly useful
- Conflicting clinical or electrodiagnostic findings: MRI delineates soft‑tissue and neural morphology and can resolve discordant diagnoses when symptoms, signs, and nerve conduction studies are inconsistent <cite id="d3717a2b-0">MRI provides information on morphological changes in CTS</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-6">Guidelines caution that MRI should not be used as a standalone routine test</cite>.
- Persistent/recurrent symptoms after release: MRI detects signs of incomplete decompression, persistent median nerve edema or fibrosis, failed carpal ligament release, or proximal tunnel compromise following open or endoscopic release <cite id="d3717a2b-5">MRI is useful for detecting signs of nerve dysfunction—gadolinium‑enhanced areas, fibrosis, abnormal nerve width/ratio, and insufficient carpal release—in recurrent CTS after open release</cite>.
- Suspected coexisting structural wrist pathology: MRI characterizes synovial/mucous cysts, ganglion cysts, ganglion‑like dorsal wrist/TFCC lesions, ligament or joint pathology, fractures, or dislocations that can narrow the carpal canal or compress the median nerve (e.g., volar retinacular thickening, ulnar impingement), which can mimic or exacerbate CTS <cite id="d3717a2b-1">MRI depicts the carpal tunnel and potential pathology with high soft‑tissue contrast</cite> <cite id="cf32d56b-1">Pictorial review of MRI findings in multiple pathologies implicated in CTS causation</cite>.
- Ulnar‑deviated/varus wrist phenotypes and “deklinning”: MRI shows groove formation and neural impingement under the transverse carpal ligament and at the ulnohamate hook, as well as volar ulnar retinaculum thickening; during MRI, positioning variability can change the apparent looped ulnar artery’s course, correlating with symptoms reproduced in ulnar deviation, supporting an ulnocarpal impingement contribution in ulnar‑deviated hands <cite id="d3717a2b-1">MRI sensitivity/specificity rely on CSA and morphology, enabling detection of tunnel narrowing/grooving</cite> <cite id="cf32d56b-1">Review catalogs MRI signatures in median nerve entrapment variants</cite> <cite id="bcede944-1">With radial deviation, the ulnar artery shifts ulnarly within Guyon’s canal by a few millimeters; similar alignment‑dependent neural/groove dynamics underpin tunnel compression</cite>.
- Radial‑sided symptoms or borderline median/radial nerve issues: MRI clarifies multineural involvement and variant tunnel anatomy in radial-sided symptoms, helping distinguish median vs radial nerve dominance and identify proximal carpal tunnel variants or midcarpal narrowing that may explain symptoms labeled as “radial tunnel syndrome” but demonstrate median nerve involvement on MRI <cite id="cf32d56b-3">The carpal tunnel is the most common compression site; 7–10% of cases show entrapment at sites along the median nerve’s course</cite> <cite id="cf32d56b-3">MRI depicts the carpal tunnel and potential pathology with high spatial resolution and soft tissue contrast</cite>.
- Early disease or disproportionate clinical severity: Where median nerve CSA enlargement and tunnel stenosis are asymmetric between wrists, MRI helps identify focal ligamentous pathology (e.g., trauma, prior microtrauma, or synovitis) out of proportion to physical signs, and can detect early pathological changes before severe degenerative alterations <cite id="d3717a2b-0">MRI provides information on morphological changes relevant to CTS</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-2">MRI is limited by expense/time, supporting selective use when morphological clues justify cost</cite>.
- Complex or unusual acquisition or occupational mechanisms: MRI’s multiplanar reformation and soft‑tissue contrast aid in evaluating repetitive loading injuries, scar tissue at the wrist from prior lacerations or surgeries, and subtle distal extrinsic neurodynamic constraints, scenarios where US or plain radiography may be inconclusive <cite id="d3717a2b-1">MRI has good-to-excellent diagnostic accuracy using CSA thresholds</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-6">MRI should be used judiciously based on clinical need</cite>.
- Multimodal diagnostic puzzles: When electrodiagnostic studies are nondiagnostic or unavailable, MRI combined with careful clinical examination can provide the anatomical substrate (median nerve enlargement/positional grooving within the carpal canal) to support a targeted operative plan <cite id="d3717a2b-1">MRI’s soft‑tissue depiction enables identification of morphological changes correlating with symptoms</cite> <cite id="cf32d56b-1">Pictorial review demonstrates MRI features of entrapment</cite>.

How MRI complements ultrasound and electrodiagnostics
MRI and ultrasonography (US) are comparable for measuring median nerve CSA in the carpal canal, with both tracking severity trends; CSA is a robust parameter, but modalities differ in portability, cost, and acquisition time, so they are often used together to improve diagnostic confidence <cite id="8df93e6f-2">USG and MRI are comparable for median nerve CSA measurement</cite> <cite id="8df93e6f-1">US can be complementary but not conclusive for CTS severity classification; CSA-WFR increase with CTS severity</cite> <cite id="8df93e6f-5">US and MRI CSA measurements show close agreement under current technology</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-1">MRI shows good-to-excellent sensitivity/specificity using CSA thresholds</cite>. Together with electrodiagnostic studies, MRI improves localization and surgical planning by identifying ligament thickening, synovial hypertrophy, ganglia or cysts affecting the canal, thus clarifying whether symptoms are due to median nerve compression or other coexisting pathology <cite id="d3717a2b-0">MRI provides morphological change information used in CTS evaluation</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-5">Postoperative MRI detects incomplete release, fibrosis, and abnormal nerve morphology</cite>.

Special clinical scenarios and indications
- Suspected ulnar/cubital tunnel overlap or cervical radiculopathy mimic: MRI of the wrist and forearm reveals radial nerve dominance in cubital tunnel syndrome and can delineate cervical radiculopathy patterns versus tunnel pathology; alignment maneuvers on MRI that reproduce symptoms support tunnel dynamics and ligament groove involvement, favoring focal wrist decompression <cite id="cf32d56b-3">The carpal tunnel is the most common site of median nerve compression but entrapment can occur at other sites along the nerve</cite> <cite id="bcede944-3">Radial tunnel syndrome involves radial nerve compression on the thumb side; clinical differentiation benefits from MRI localization</cite>.
- Ganglion‑like wrist lesions and TFCC pathology: MRI differentiates dorsal wrist ganglia, synovial cysts, and TFCC lesions associated with ulnar impingement that can mimic CTS; sagittal STIR and axial T2 planes show fluid collections, synovitis, and ligament morphology guiding decompression vs cyst excision choices <cite id="cf32d56b-1">Pictorial review details MRI features across median nerve pathologies</cite>.
- Post‑traumatic and post‑operative: MRI after fractures, dislocations, ligament avulsions, and prior wrist surgeries (including failed carpal ligament release) identifies scar tissue, incomplete ligament release, and recurrent synovitis, justifying revision strategies <cite id="d3717a2b-5">MRI detects gadolinium‑enhanced areas, fibrosis, abnormal nerve width/ratio, and inadequate release</cite>.
- Proximal carpal canal stenosis and extra‑tunnel entrapment: MRI extends visualization caudal to the distal radioulnar joint and proximal into the wrist/forearm to detect congenital or acquired proximal tunnel stenosis and interosseous membrane variants, as well as non‑wrist entrapment sites contributing to symptoms <cite id="cf32d56b-3">Entrapment can occur at various sites along the median nerve’s course, not only at the wrist</cite>.
- Volar wrist pain and midcarpal instability: When ulnar‑sided, midcarpal instability causes volar carpal ligament impingement or midpalmar synovitis, MRI and MRI‑AR can confirm instability and synovial proliferation compressing the distal median nerve branches or dorsal/lateral cutaneous branches, directing surgical stabilization and débridement <cite id="bcede944-8">Ulnar‑sided wrist pain may arise from midcarpal instability with loss of coupled motion</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-0">MRI depicts soft‑tissue changes and their relation to symptoms</cite>.

Practical approach and limitations
- Selective use: Use MRI when CTS is suspected but unproven, when electrodiagnostics are nondiagnostic yet surgery is being considered, or when anatomical coexisting lesions are suspected on clinical exam <cite id="d3717a2b-6">Do not routinely use MRI; consider when cost and time are justified</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-3">Guideline emphasizes judicious use within an overall diagnosis and treatment pathway</cite>.
- Acquisition: Include both sagittal and axial T2‑weighted/STIR planes of the wrist focused on the carpal canal with nerve tracking; add coronal planes if ulnar side or TFCC pathology is suspected. In ulnar deviation/deklinning phenotypes, perform images with patient in mild radial deviation and, if feasible, correlate with provocative maneuvers <cite id="cf32d56b-1">MRI pictorial review highlights plane selection to demonstrate carpal canal and entrapped structures</cite> <cite id="bcede944-1">Alignment affects ulnar artery position in Guyon’s canal and can guide imaging positioning</cite>.
- Correlation: Combine MRI with clinical correlation and, when possible, US for rapid CSA measurement, and ensure electrodiagnostic evaluation if omitted; avoid unnecessary imaging in mild, straightforward cases <cite id="8df93e6f-1">US and MRI are comparable and complementary for CSA grading</cite> <cite id="8df93e6f-3">US achieves excellent accuracy for CTS evaluation with high AUC</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-0">MRI augments noninvasive evaluation but is not a replacement for clinical reasoning</cite>.

Bottom line
MRI is particularly useful in CTS when anatomy must be resolved (grooving/impingement, ulnar deviation/deklinning, volar retinaculum thickening), when symptoms persist or recur after release (to identify incomplete decompression, fibrosis, synovitis), when coexisting wrist lesions (synovial/mucous cysts, ganglia, TFCC lesions, fractures/dislocations) are suspected, for radial‑sided or borderline median/radial syndromes (to clarify neural involvement), and in complex cases where surgery is contemplated or revision may be necessary. It should be ordered when its cost and time are justified and in conjunction with clinical and electrodiagnostic findings to refine diagnosis and tailor management <cite id="d3717a2b-0">MRI provides morphological change information supporting CTS evaluation</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-1">Sensitivity 84–100% and specificity 85–94% using CSA criteria</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-5">MRI identifies incomplete release and neuropathic changes after recurrent CTS</cite> <cite id="cf32d56b-1">Review of MRI findings across median nerve pathologies</cite> <cite id="8df93e6f-2">USG and MRI are comparable for CSA measurement, enabling combined use</cite> <cite id="d3717a2b-6">Guidelines counsel against routine MRI, reserving it for selected cases</cite>.

Summary
Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) preserves more native knee anatomy than total knee arthroplasty (TKA) because it replaces only one compartment while sparing ligaments, menisci, and the patellofemoral joint; this typically translates into faster recovery, shorter hospital stay, and better short‑term function, though mid/long‑term revision risk can be higher outside optimal candidates. <cite id="5b3f753b-4">UKA holds several potential advantages over TKA, including less invasive surgical exposure, reduced morbidity and mortality, preservation of ... [anatomical structures] in selected patients</cite> <cite id="34dfc9d0-0">Uka resulted in higher function scores compared to TKA without increased revision rate during short-term follow-up</cite> <cite id="5b3f753b-9">UKA had better knee recovery and a shorter length of stay compared to TKA, per a large meta-analysis</cite>.

Anatomical preservation (biologic knee preservation, ligaments, bone, kinematics)
- Ligaments and cruciate integrity: <cite id="f9c65854-8">The femoral condyles roll-back and the screw-home mechanics of the tibia are preserved only if the ACL is maintained, as in UKA or bi-UKA implants</cite>. <cite id="f9c65854-4">Compared to TKA, patellofemoral arthroplasty (PFA) preserves the tibiofemoral joint, the medial and lateral meniscus, and the cruciate ligaments</cite>. <cite id="f9c65854-4">Contemporary UKA/bi-UKA strategies are presented as preserving the tibiofemoral joint, menisci, and cruciate ligaments compared to TKA</cite>.
- Bone and condyles: <cite id="f9c65854-9">Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty is a safe and effective surgical treatment option for isolated end-stage unicompartmental knee osteoarthritis</cite>. <cite id="f9c65854-8">By retaining the ACL, UKA/bi-UKA preserves femoral condyle rollback and the tibial screw‑home mechanics</cite>. <cite id="5b3f753b-4">Modern UKA is less invasive and aims to preserve native bone and ligament structures compared with TKA</cite>.
- Patellofemoral and medial/lateral structures: <cite id="f9c65854-4">Compared to TKA, UKA (and associated PFA) preserves the tibiofemoral joint, menisci, and cruciate ligaments, emphasizing biologic preservation of non-replaced compartments</cite>. <cite id="5b3f753b-5">At 10 years, survivorship was similar between PFA+UKA and TKA (97.3% vs 95.1%), with functional improvements favoring TKA overall in one cohort, underscoring that preserved anatomy does not preclude good outcomes, and vice versa</cite>.
- Indication-based anatomy matching: <cite id="34dfc9d0-3">Clinical guidance indicates UKA is indicated when only one compartment is affected, whereas TKA is used for more extensive disease</cite>. <cite id="5b3f753b-9">Screening emphasizes predominantly unicompartmental degeneration and acceptable patellofemoral joint skyline without lateral facet involvement</cite>.
- Biomechanical rationale for preservation: <cite id="f9c65854-1">Studies model tibial slope changes in fixed-bearing medial UKA in ACL-deficient knees, demonstrating stability considerations that inform implant design when native ligaments are compromised</cite> <cite id="f9c65854-8">Preservation of screw-home mechanics hinges on maintaining the ACL, which UKA/bi-UKA accommodates</cite>.
- Safety and suitability caveats: <cite id="34dfc9d0-0">Better short-term function after UKA versus TKA was observed without increased short-term revision rate</cite> <cite id="5b3f753b-9">UKA is advantageous for patients with isolated compartment pathology, and benefits may be context- and patient-dependent</cite>.

Postoperative recovery and early outcomes
- Functional recovery and PROs: <cite id="34dfc9d0-0">Uka resulted in higher function scores than TKA in 12‑month short-term follow-up, without increased early revision, supporting earlier goal attainment</cite>. <cite id="34dfc9d0-9">Randomized evidence shows that UKA and TKA yield comparable functional outcomes overall, highlighting that patient-reported outcomes can converge over time</cite> <cite id="34dfc9d0-4">One RCT reported larger ROM and increased return to activity after UKA, but noted higher revision rates, illustrating a classic early-benefit/long-term-risk trade-off</cite>.

- Isolated unicompartmental disease: <cite id="34dfc9d0-3">Guidelines consider UKA appropriate when only one compartment is affected</cite>. <cite id="5b3f753b-9">Selection criteria stress predominantly unicompartmental degeneration and a clinically acceptable patellofemoral joint skyline</cite>. <cite id="f9c65854-9">Medial UKA is effective for isolated end-stage unicompartmental osteoarthritis, supporting limb- and joint-sparing goals</cite>.

- Anatomy-sparing benefits of UKA:

For patients with isolated compartment osteoarthritis and acceptable ligament and patellofemoral anatomy, UKA offers superior anatomical preservation—retaining cruciate ligaments, menisci, and native femoral/tibial kinematics—while yielding faster recovery, earlier better function, and shorter hospitalization compared to TKA; however, careful patient selection and long-term surveillance are essential because early advantages like increased ROM and return to activity may coexist with higher revision risk in some subgroups. <cite id="5b3f753b-4">UKA’s less invasive approach and preservation of native structures are key benefits versus TKA</cite> <cite id="34dfc9d0-0">UKA delivers higher function scores without increased short-term revision</cite> <cite id="5b3f753b-9">UKA often shortens hospital stay and reduces complications relative to TKA</cite> <cite id="34dfc9d0-8">Greater ROM and return to activity come with revision risk trade-offs for some patients</cite> <cite id="34dfc9d0-3">UKA is most appropriate for isolated compartment disease</cite>.

# Summary Answer

Aerobic exercise interventions in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) consistently lower circulating inflammatory markers, particularly CRP and TNF‑α, with smaller or inconsistent effects on IL‑6 and ESR, and concurrently improve disease activity and physical function, including reductions in DAS28 and pain/fatigue and gains in functional ability and aerobic capacity.<cite id="953ae1df-5">Exercise interventions in RA show variable effects on inflammatory biomarkers.
