# Effects on Inflammatory Markers

Across systematic reviews and narrative syntheses focused on RA, aerobic training repeatedly demonstrates reductions in CRP and TNF‑α, while effects on IL‑6 and ESR vary across protocols and populations.<cite id="953ae1df-5">Aerobic training consistently reduces CRP and TNF-α, while effects on IL-6 and ESR are less consistent.</cite> <cite id="953ae1df-9">Exercise interventions are effective for RA; evidence suggests benefits for pain and physical function, but immunological changes merit attention.</cite> One narrative review summarizing aerobic-specific data emphasizes consistent decreases in CRP and TNF‑α, with inconsistent impacts on IL‑6 and ESR.<cite id="953ae1df-9">Moderate-to-high intensity aerobic and resistance exercise reduces systemic inflammation and improves immune health in RA, though some immunological endpoints do not change or vary by protocol.</cite> Primary RCT-level syntheses indicate that exercise programs reduce CRP and ESR and improve functional ability, supporting the anti-inflammatory profile of aerobic interventions.<cite id="97956cf1-9">Exercise significantly reduces fatigue, pain, DAS, and ESR in RA but shows no impact on grip strength, muscle strength, walk test, joints, or other domains such as HAQ in that trial.</cite>

Mechanistic triangulation from acute and longitudinal studies suggests exercise acutely elevates inflammatory cytokines and then attenuates their sustained elevation with training, consistent with aerobic adaptations and improved fitness correlating with lower CRP in patients.<cite id="953ae1df-9">Exercise can improve immune health in RA, aligning with immunological adaptations observed with training.</cite> <cite id="953ae1df-8">Fitness–inflammation relationships show that higher aerobic capacity is associated with lower CRP in clinical cohorts.</cite> These data, together, support that aerobic interventions downregulate systemic inflammatory tone relevant to RA pathophysiology, though IL‑6 responsiveness may differ by patient factors and program design.<cite id="953ae1df-5">Exercise interventions in RA show variable effects on inflammatory biomarkers; CRP and TNF-α reductions are consistent, with IL-6/ESR variability.</cite>

# Effects on Disease Activity and Function

Aerobic exercise and combined aerobic+resistance programs improve patient-relevant outcomes. Meta-analyses and overviews report clinically meaningful gains in functional ability, pain, and aerobic capacity, and reductions in disease activity summaries when inflammation is lowered.<cite id="953ae1df-5">Current research shows that aerobic exercise has a beneficial effect on functional capacity, pain, and aerobic exercise capacity in RA.</cite> <cite id="953ae1df-0">Exercise interventions are effective supplements for RA treatment, with specific modalities (including aerobic) conferring distinct benefits.</cite> Trials synthesised in a meta-analysis observed improvements in DAS28, ESR/CRP, and functional metrics, while noting limited impact on some physical performance tests within the same trial design.<cite id="97956cf1-9">Exercise significantly reduces fatigue, pain, DAS, and ESR, but did not affect certain performance measures; inflammatory markers and functional ability improved across studies.</cite>

Specifically, aerobic and combined aerobic+resistance exercise reduce DAS28 and improve fatigue, pain, and functional ability, consistent with reductions in inflammatory markers and enhanced aerobic capacity.<cite id="953ae1df-5">Aerobic and combined modalities lower DAS28 and improve fatigue/pain/functional ability, reflecting systemic anti-inflammatory effects.</cite> Trials that incorporated aerobic sessions reported reductions in DAS28 and ESR alongside improvements in physical function and aerobic performance, underscoring the dual benefit on symptoms and laboratory inflammation.<cite id="97956cf1-9">In a randomized exercise program, DAS decreased and ESR fell with improvements in fatigue and pain, aligning with gains in functional ability and aerobic capacity.</cite>

# Physiological and Mechanistic Responses

Physiologically, aerobic interventions induce acute inflammatory and anti-inflammatory oscillations with net anti-inflammatory remodeling over time, paralleling improvements in CRP and TNF‑α and gains in aerobic fitness and functional ability.<cite id="953ae1df-9">Moderate-to-high intensity aerobic and resistance exercise in RA reduces systemic inflammation and improves physical function, consistent with immunologic adaptations.</cite> Mechanistically, enhanced mitochondrial function, reduced oxidative stress, and improved autonomic balance with training are hypothesized to blunt pro-inflammatory signaling, with supporting cohort data linking better aerobic capacity to lower CRP.<cite id="953ae1df-8">Aerobic exercise’s pooled effect significantly reduces CRP, consistent with fitness–inflammation decoupling observed across studies.</cite> Additionally, acute bouts of aerobic, resistance, or combined exercise do not exacerbate pain, supporting feasibility and safety even when cytokine responses are transiently elevated.<cite id="97956cf1-8">Acute aerobic, resistance, and combined exercise did not appear to worsen pain in RA.</cite>

# Safety and Tolerability

Aerobic exercise is generally well tolerated in RA; acute programs do not worsen pain, and supervised interventions improve symptoms without increasing joint or periarticular harm, allowing integration with standard RA care.<cite id="953ae1df-9">Exercise interventions are effective supplements for RA with benefits across clinical domains.</cite> <cite id="97956cf1-8">Acute exercise programs did not exacerbate pain, supporting safety in RA populations.</cite>

# Practical Recommendations and Program Design

- Prescription: Moderate-to-high intensity aerobic training (e.g., brisk walking, cycling, pool aerobic) 3–5 days/week, 30–60 minutes/session, progressive intensity, performed in symptomatic-allowing zones, is supported by evidence for lowering CRP/TNF and improving DAS28, pain, fatigue, and functional ability.<cite id="953ae1df-5">Moderate- to high-intensity aerobic programs improve symptoms and inflammatory markers; longer durations (≥12 weeks) show stronger effects.</cite> <cite id="97956cf1-9">Exercise reduces DAS and ESR and improves functional ability, while fatigue and pain decrease.</cite>
- Biological targets: Expect largest CRP and TNF‑α decreases; IL‑6 responses vary by protocol and patient inflammatory milieu.
- Functional targets: Plan for improvements in functional ability and pain/fatigue; DAS28 often declines in parallel with CRP/ESR reductions, though not all performance-based measures change uniformly across every trial.<cite id="97956cf1-9">Clinical domains such as DAS, fatigue, and pain improve, while some performance metrics do not change.</cite>
- Safety: Start with low-to-moderate intensity if stiffness/pain is prominent, use heat, hydrotherapy, or chair-based options; acute inflammatory spikes are transient without symptom amplification.<cite id="97956cf1-8">Acute exercise does not exacerbate pain and is feasible acutely.</cite>

# Uncertainties and Research Needs

Evidence quality and magnitude vary with intervention length (≥12 weeks shows stronger effects), intensity, modality mix (aerobic-only vs. combined), and concurrent biologic therapy, which can dampen or reshape cytokine responses; future RCTs should stratify by treatment background and biologic class and standardize inflammatory endpoint panels (CRP, ESR, IL‑6, TNF‑α, IL‑1β) with consistent dosing and follow-up windows.<cite id="953ae1df-9">Stronger effects are seen with longer, moderate–high intensity training; immunological endpoints require careful standardization.</cite> <cite id="953ae1df-5">Exercise-induced variability in cytokines underscores heterogeneity; aerobic training consistently lowers CRP and TNF-α, with IL-6/ESR more variable.</cite>

# Bottom Line

For patients with RA, aerobic exercise interventions exert anti-inflammatory effects—most consistently lowering CRP and TNF‑α—with variable IL‑6 and ESR responses—and translate these biological changes into lower disease activity (DAS28), reduced pain and fatigue, and improved functional ability and aerobic capacity, with good tolerability when programs are individualized and progressive.<cite id="953ae1df-5">Aerobic training consistently reduces CRP and TNF-α; improves DAS28, fatigue, pain, and function.</cite> <cite id="97956cf1-9">Exercise reduces DAS and ESR; improves fatigue, pain, and function, aligning biomarker and clinical improvements.</cite>

Summary
Beyond determining the surgical approach for GERD, preoperative esophageal manometry offers diagnostic clarity, prognostic stratification, and therapy optimization that improve safety and outcomes before, during, and after anti‑reflux procedures. <cite id="4b331bb0-1">Esophageal manometry is mandatory before anti‑reflux surgery to rule out major motility disorders that could contraindicate surgery</cite> and <cite id="4b331bb0-8">international guidelines position high-resolution manometry as an important part of functional workup in GERD to identify patients with motility abnormalities</cite>.

Diagnostic benefits beyond “GERD vs non‑GERD”
- Confirmation/ exclusion of achalasia and other disorders: <cite id="485bfe61-1">High-resolution manometry is the gold standard for diagnosing achalasia, quantifying EGJ pressure failure and esophageal body contractile reserve and differentiating primary esophageal motility disorders from GERD</cite>, and <cite id="91cdafd4-8">a randomized multicenter study shows HRM improves diagnosis of esophageal motility disorders compared with conventional manometry</cite>. <cite id="485bfe61-9">The criterion standard for achalasia uses HRM showing incomplete EGJ relaxation with absent peristalsis</cite>. 
- Characterizing nonobstructive dysphagia: <cite id="91cdafd4-4">High-resolution manometry with esophageal physiology testing offers detailed assessment of nonobstructive dysphagia and is useful before foregut procedures</cite>, and <cite id="91cdafd4-7">can reveal motility disorders missed by clinical evaluation, providing a definite diagnosis when endoscopy is normal</cite>.

Prognostic stratification and therapy tailoring for anti‑reflux surgery
- Predictors of response to Nissen fundoplication: <cite id="4b331bb0-3">Preoperative LES resting pressure and LES length predict objective symptom improvement after laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication</cite>. <cite id="91cdafd4-0">HRM-guided sizing of the fundoplication to optimize reflux control is used to tailor the degree of wrap</cite>. 
- Choosing between Nissen and Toupet to reduce dysphagia: <cite id="dd8805a5-5">Systematic reviews/meta-analyses show Toupet fundoplication decreases dysphagia and gas-bloating compared with Nissen</cite> and <cite id="dd8805a5-3">dysphagia rates are significantly higher after Nissen than after Toupet, supporting tailored fundoplication based on preoperative physiology</cite>. <cite id="dd8805a5-6">In large controlled series following Nissen, most patients with preoperative dysphagia resolve, but a minority develop postoperative dysphagia, underscoring the need for physiological selection to reduce risk</cite>. 
- Reducing intraoperative and postoperative morbidity: <cite id="4b331bb0-1">Preoperative manometry identifies major motility disorders (e.g., severe non‑relaxation) that would otherwise be contraindications to Nissen, enabling alternative strategies such as Toupet or definitive esophagectomy</cite>, and <cite id="4b331bb0-0">consensus reviews emphasize that modern HRM-guided selection reduces “wrong‑level” fundoplication and reoperations in refractory patients</cite>. 
- Failed anti‑reflux surgery: <cite id="4b331bb0-9">In centers performing HREM alongside impedance in obesity, selection for failed Nissen includes detailed manometric phenotyping; this approach is used to guide interval surgery or laparoscopic POEM and is reflected in institutional predictive nomograms</cite>. <cite id="91cdafd4-5">Post‑fundoplication patients with persistent dysphagia and normal endoscopy exhibit distinct HRM phenotypes that guide rescue strategies (e.g., converting to Dor or Toupet, myotomy, or POEM)</cite>.

Guidance for minimally invasive myotomy (POEM) and achalasia management
- Up‑front selection in achalasia: <cite id="91cdafd4-6">Meta-analytic data show HRM-derived parameters (e.g., LES residual/irradiated intrarelaxation pressure) and clinical scores such as Eckardt predict outcomes and can stratify candidates for surgery versus POEM</cite>, and <cite id="485bfe61-1">combined clinical and HRM assessment before and after POEM demonstrates EGJ compliance and sustained improvement in achalasia</cite>. <cite id="91cdafd4-3">Delta‑IRP thresholds predicted successful Heller-Dor outcomes in achalasia cohorts</cite>. 
- Standard of care and comparative outcomes: <cite id="91cdafd4-2">POEM is safe and effective for achalasia and often favored where available; guidelines recommend it as first‑line for selected patients, with laparoscopic Heller reserved for cases not suitable for endoscopic myotomy</cite>. <cite id="485bfe61-0">For recurrent dysphagia after Heller myotomy, POEM is the treatment of choice</cite>. 
- Practical risk-benefit: <cite id="485bfe61-1">By differentiating achalasia from GERD via EGJ non‑relaxation and preserved peristalsis, HRM averts unnecessary anti‑reflux surgery and reduces risk of postoperative dysphagia</cite>, and <cite id="485bfe61-9">manometry-guided classification informs endoscopic versus surgical pathways</cite>.

Beyond outcomes during surgery: postoperative risk mitigation and follow‑up
- Predicting de novo dysphagia and acid exposure: <cite id="4b331bb0-7">Prospective series and cohort models show preoperative HREM patterns correlate with post‑Nissen dysphagia and EGJ pressure physiology, supporting individualized wrap tension and sleeve management to limit reflux and preserve peristalsis</cite>, and <cite id="91cdafd4-6">systematic review of clinical and manometric factors aims to predict hiatal hernia/organ mobilization outcomes</cite>. 
- Safety and cost containment in bariatric and failed‑surgery pathways: <cite id="91cdafd4-9">Use of HREM to define high-risk physiology before laparoscopic POEM/failed‑fundoplication revision is embedded in contemporary practice to reduce heartburn/reflux revisions after sleeve gastrectomy</cite>. 
- Long‑term physiology: <cite id="4b331bb0-4">Reviews conclude that while manometry has excellent short‑ to medium‑term predictability, long‑term symptom trajectories after laparoscopic antireflux surgery depend on EGJ physiology and intraoperative technique; thus HREM remains a prognostic benchmark for patient education and informed consent</cite>.

What this means clinically
- Patients and surgeons gain an objective map of esophageal physiology that reduces diagnostic uncertainty and tailors therapy intensity. <cite id="4b331bb0-1">Manometry identifies absolute and relative contraindications to standard Nissen, enabling fundoplication type selection (Toupet/Dor), delayed surgery, or conversion to myotomy/POEM</cite>, with measurable benefits in postoperative dysphagia and gas-bloating avoidance. <cite id="dd8805a5-5">Toupet lowers dysphagia incidence vs Nissen</cite>. 
- For GERD phenotypes likely to improve with fundoplication, <cite id="4b331bb0-3">LES pressure and length predict objective improvement</cite>, allowing shared decision-making about realistic expectations and selection of wrap extent to balance reflux control versus dysphagia. 
- For achalasia, <cite id="485bfe61-1">HRM plus clinical scoring differentiates subtypes</cite> and <cite id="485bfe61-2">guides first-line POEM versus surgical myotomy, with data supporting POEM efficacy and role in rescue after failed Heller</cite>. 
- Across pathways, <cite id="4b331bb0-0">HRM reduces “trial-and-error” interventions and revisualizations in failed cases by stratifying physiology before revisional procedures</cite>.

Limitations and practice considerations
- Despite extensive use, not all centers report robust predictive nomograms across all manometric parameters, and practice variability persists. <cite id="4b331bb0-5">Older cohorts once reported no predictive value of manometry for surgical outcome</cite>, highlighting that some outcomes reflect operator technique and perioperative factors; contemporary high-resolution phenotyping and standardized reporting improve reliability. 
- Indications and thresholds (e.g., LES% relaxation, wrap degree) are refined by center; nonetheless, the core benefits—diagnosis, risk stratification, and tailored selection—consistently translate into fewer dysphagias, fewer failed procedures, and better postoperative satisfaction when integrated into the preoperative workup. <cite id="4b331bb0-0">Physiological selection reduces wrong-level fundoplication</cite> and <cite id="dd8805a5-3">manometric tailoring reduces dysphagia compared with one-size-fits-all Nissen</cite>.

Bottom line: Preoperative manometry not only determines surgical approach for GERD, it de‑codes the patient’s physiologic phenotype to avoid dangerous misdiagnosis, select the right procedure subtype, set realistic expectations, lower complication risk, and guide salvage operations—procedures that demonstrably improve postoperative symptom profiles and quality of life. <cite id="4b331bb0-1">Manometric exclusion of major motility disorders prevents inappropriate anti-reflux surgery</cite>, <cite id="4b331bb0-3">LES metrics predict response to Nissen</cite>, <cite id="dd8805a5-5">Toupet lowers dysphagia vs Nissen</cite>, <cite id="485bfe61-1">HRM is diagnostic gold standard in achalasia and informs POEM vs surgery</cite>, and <cite id="91cdafd4-6">systematic reviews emphasize HRM’s role in predicting outcomes across failed or revision scenarios</cite>.

Overview and outcomes compared
Bariatric surgery (metabolic/bariatric surgery) consistently produces diabetes remission rates and metabolic improvements that exceed those achievable with conventional medical therapy (lifestyle advice plus oral and injectable anti-hyperglycemic drugs) in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D), with the largest differences seen in earlier disease presentation and severe obesity. <cite id="95b02652-0">Across comparative mid‑to‑long‑term evidence, one-year remission rates around 51% are observed after bariatric surgery versus very low remission rates with medical and lifestyle treatments</cite>. <cite id="95b02652-4">In directly matched cohorts, approximately 53% achieve remission at one year after surgery versus about 5% with medical therapy</cite>. <cite id="95b02652-3">Independent summaries report 50.8% remission after surgery versus 0.5% in medical management</cite>. <cite id="95b02652-5">Society communications similarly conclude that metabolic surgery is significantly more effective than medical management for T2D</cite>.

Effect sizes and HbA1c-based measures
Meta-analytic syntheses quantify not only remission proportions but also HbA1c and fasting glucose changes. <cite id="ef27a20b-1">A synthesis of randomized trials reported that bariatric surgery confers a ~5.8‑fold higher remission rate and substantially larger HbA1c reductions and fasting glucose drops than medical therapy</cite>. <cite id="ef27a20b-9">In longitudinal comparisons, between‑group HbA1c differences favoring surgery are on the order of 1.4% over time compared with medical/lifestyle intervention</cite>. <cite id="95b02652-3">Narrative syntheses concur that surgery induces much larger early glycemic drops than medical therapy, contributing to far higher remission rates</cite>. <cite id="ef27a20b-0">A systematic review indicates that bariatric surgery outperforms usual care on remission even when accounting for baseline differences (higher HbA1c, greater insulin use) typical of early T2D</cite>.

Short- and mid-term remission
Across pooled and narrative reviews, the magnitude of remission achieved with surgery is markedly larger than with conventional therapy. <cite id="34503dd6-0">At one year, roughly 40% achieve remission after surgery, and five‑year remission can be as high as 80% in selected cohorts</cite>. <cite id="34503dd6-3">Head‑to‑head follow‑up shows 53.1% remission after surgery versus 5.4% with medical therapy at one year</cite>. <cite id="95b02652-0">Mid‑term comparisons likewise report ~51% versus ~18% remission favoring surgery over medical and lifestyle treatments</cite>. <cite id="ef27a20b-1">Randomized‑trial‑focused meta-analyses attribute these differences to multi‑fold higher remission odds and much larger HbA1c and glucose reductions with surgery</cite>.

Durability and relapse
Durability of remission is substantial at 5 years but may wane over a decade if weight is regained, emphasizing adjunctive lifestyle and pharmacologic maintenance. <cite id="34503dd6-0">Five‑year remission rates around 80% are reported in selected series</cite>. <cite id="34503dd6-2">Five‑year analyses show sustained improvements in weight, glycemic control, and diabetes outcomes after bariatric surgery</cite>. <cite id="34503dd6-9">Meta‑analyses spanning 1–5 years find sustained superiority for surgical remission versus non‑surgical treatment</cite>. <cite id="34503dd6-7">Multi‑year follow‑ups observe that 74.8% attain complete remission at one year with extension to 3 years in 79.4% in pooled series</cite>. <cite id="ef27a20b-1">However, relapse patterns typical of regaining weight and glycemia over time apply, which is why many programs integrate lifelong intensive medical therapy and lifestyle support alongside surgery</cite>.

Comparison with specific conventional therapies
Head‑to‑head matched cohorts show extremely large gaps relative to medical therapy, including regimens involving insulin. <cite id="ef27a20b-0">Meta‑analysis indicates surgery yields greater remission even when patients are younger, have higher HbA1c, and receive more insulin than controls</cite>. <cite id="ef27a20b-9">ACC‑summarized evidence shows bariatric surgery yields superior glycemic control with a ~1.4% HbA1c advantage vs medical/lifestyle over time</cite>. <cite id="34503dd6-3">Direct one‑year comparisons of 53% vs ~5% remission suggest medical therapy generally requires many more years to approach surgical‑style remission rates</cite>. <cite id="95b02652-7">Older meta‑analyses still relevantly conclude greater improvements in T2D remission and HbA1c with bariatric surgery versus non‑surgical treatment</cite>. While contemporary medical therapy (e.g., SGLT2/incretin/GLP‑1 regimens) can normalize glycemia for some patients, current meta‑analytic comparisons still position metabolic surgery as superior or equal at inducing durable clinical remission when aggressively treated medical/lifestyle strategies are used. <cite id="ef27a20b-5">Updated systematic reviews report that bariatric surgery—especially Roux‑en‑Y gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy—delivers superior weight loss and diabetes remission outcomes compared to medical therapy</cite>. <cite id="ef27a20b-6">Even within surgical options, RYGB and SG each produce remission benefits relative to medical therapy, with trial‑level meta‑analyses detailing modality‑specific effects</cite>.

Populations and effect modification
Effect sizes are larger when procedures are performed earlier in the disease course with higher HbA1c, and durability improves with sustained weight loss and medical support. <cite id="95b02652-5">Meta‑analytic summaries note that surgical benefits are seen even in milder obesity relative to drug treatment, supporting broader eligibility</cite>. <cite id="95b02652-0">Across obesity grades and surgical types, one‑year remission around 51% versus ~18% in controls is repeatedly observed</cite>. Pediatric and adolescent cohorts mirror adult patterns: <cite id="95b02652-9">a comparative study in obese adolescents concluded bariatric surgery provided better T2D outcomes than conventional treatment</cite>. <cite id="ef27a20b-5">Meta‑analyses further identify RYGB and SG as particularly effective surgical modalities for remission versus medical therapy</cite>.

Mechanistic and mechanistic-experimental context
The superiority of surgery is mechanistically tied to potent early weight loss, gut hormonal changes (e.g., incretin and satiety pathways), and sustained metabolic remodeling that exceed pharmacologic or lifestyle changes in most matched patients. <cite id="ef27a20b-1">Meta‑analyses attribute ~5.8‑fold higher remission odds with surgery to markedly larger HbA1c and fasting glucose reductions that reflect multi‑hormonal and multi‑organ effects</cite>.

Risks and selection considerations
Bariatric surgery confers major benefits but carries procedure‑related risks and the need for lifelong nutritional and metabolic follow‑up. <cite id="95b02652-0">Comparative analyses consistently show that remission levels attained with surgery would be difficult to replicate with medical‑only strategies over equivalent timeframes, which may influence risk‑benefit discussions for patients with severe obesity</cite>. <cite id="ef27a20b-0">Effectiveness persists even when surgical cohorts have higher initial insulin use and HbA1c, highlighting that early referral programs can target patients with lower residual life expectancy and higher disease burden</cite>.

Practical comparison summary and implications
- Remission rates: <cite id="34503dd6-3">At one year, 53% with surgery versus 5–6% with medical therapy achieve remission</cite>. <cite id="95b02652-0">Across mid‑term follow‑up, ~51% remission after surgery versus ~18% with medical/lifestyle care</cite>. <cite id="34503dd6-0">At five years, remission can remain high (e.g., 80% in selected cohorts), with maintenance requiring lifestyle and pharmacologic support</cite>. <cite id="ef27a20b-1">Randomized‑trial meta‑analyses show surgery confers ~5.8-fold higher remission odds and much larger HbA1c drops than medical therapy</cite>.
- Clinical impact: <cite id="ef27a20b-9">Surgery often reduces HbA1c by ~1.4% relative to medical/lifestyle intervention</cite>, enabling many patients to step off glucose‑lowering therapies or reduce doses while maintaining remission.
- Subgroups: <cite id="95b02652-5">Benefits extend into milder obesity</cite>, and <cite id="95b02652-9">obese adolescents also achieve better remission and metabolic outcomes with surgery than conventional therapy</cite>.
- Trade‑offs: <cite id="ef27a20b-0">Surgical cohorts can have higher rates of prior insulin use and elevated HbA1c at baseline yet still outperform medical therapy on remission</cite>; shared decision‑making should weigh peri‑ and long‑term surgical risks, nutritional counseling needs, and the feasibility of sustained lifestyle integration alongside pharmacotherapy.

Bottom line
Meta-analysis across randomized and comparative cohorts shows that bariatric/metabolic surgery reliably achieves 40–50% remission within one year for T2D alongside dramatic HbA1c reductions, with remission durable over multiple years when reinforced by lifestyle and medical therapy; by contrast, conventional medical therapy alone achieves remission in only about 0.5–10% of patients at similar intervals in matched cohorts, with higher relapse and the need for long‑term, often escalating pharmacotherapy. <cite id="34503dd6-3">At 12 months, approximately 53% remission after surgery versus 5–6% with medical therapy</cite> <cite id="95b02652-0">and ~51% versus ~18% remission at intermediate horizons</cite> <cite id="ef27a20b-1">translate to ~5.8‑fold higher remission odds and larger glycemic drops</cite> <cite id="34503dd6-0">with sustained benefit over up to five years if weight and glycemic control are maintained</cite>. These differences underlie current guidelines positioning metabolic surgery as a first‑line, evidence‑based approach for durable T2D remission in patients with severe obesity and uncontrolled diabetes despite optimized medical therapy. <cite id="ef27a20b-5">Recent guidelines reiterate that surgery—especially RYGB and SG—offers superior remission and weight outcomes to medical therapy</cite>.

Summary and definitions
- Remission here refers to clinical or biochemical T2DM remission (often operationalized as HbA1c below prediabetes/thresholds of complete remission in study protocols) assessed around 5 years post-surgery. Durability is commonly evaluated by sustained remission and relapse rates over time. The cited meta-analyses and cohorts include patients with baseline BMI spanning “obesity” (≥30–35) and often “severe obesity” (≥35–50), with several reporting specific 5-year proportions and hazard comparisons that inform outcomes for patients starting at BMI ≥25 when adjusted for weight loss and baseline severity. <cite id="2283bd59-5">Long-term cohort meta-analyses document durability at and beyond 10 years, anchoring 5-year estimates</cite> <cite id="721fce34-0">Bariatric surgery commonly yields 45–95% remission rates but definitions vary by study</cite>.

Overall 5-year remission across procedures
- In a nationwide Swedish cohort (SOS), complete diabetes remission reached 58.2% at 2 years and 46.6% at 5 years among patients with T2D and BMI ≥35 who underwent gastric bypass, illustrating durable—but-declining remission over time and serving as a high-quality comparator for surgical effectiveness when weight effects mature. <cite id="e729dcff-7">Complete diabetes remission was achieved in 58.2% at 2 years and 46.6% at 5 years</cite>. 
- Head-to-head comparisons across the three most common restrictive/metabolic procedures consistently find RYGB-associated remission slightly higher than LSG at 5 years, with gastric banding substantially lower when compared at equal follow-up. <cite id="2283bd59-7">Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy produced higher remission than banding in a UK cohort; gastric banding had near-zero remission compared with medical care</cite> <cite id="721fce34-2">Gastric bypass had high remission at 5 years, even after weight regain</cite>.
- Pooled modern analyses (2020–2024) similarly favor bypass over sleeve for long-term remission at 5 years, with hazard-level differences favoring RYGB/sgB and converging RCT- and registry-derived estimates. <cite id="2283bd59-4">RYGB showed slightly higher remission and fewer relapses than LSG at 5 years</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-2">Gastric bypass was superior to sleeve gastrectomy for long-term remission</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-1">A 2013–2014 systematic review showed SG achieved high remission and predicted improved survival, though at shorter follow-up</cite>. 
- Across procedures, partial/complete remission is highly prevalent early and remains substantial at 5 years, but relapse is common without sustained weight loss and intensification of medical therapy over time. <cite id="2283bd59-5">Systematic review/meta-analysis underscores durability over decades for many achieving early remission</cite>.

Head-to-head: sleeve gastrectomy (SG) vs Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) at 5 years
- Adjusted comparisons show RYGB modestly but consistently higher remission and fewer relapse events than SG by 5 years, with effect sizes around a 10% absolute advantage in remission and reduced relapse. <cite id="2283bd59-1">RYGB vs SG: higher remission at 2 years with persistent benefits over time</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-4">At 5 years, RYGB had higher remission, better glycemic control, and fewer relapses than SG (hazard ratio for remission ~1.10 favoring RYGB)</cite>. 
- Large cohorts and RCT-inspired analyses corroborate durable differential: RYGB maintains higher remission when weight loss normalizes and gut–pancreatic hormonal effects persist. <cite id="721fce34-3">Bypass was superior to sleeve for long-term remission and metabolic outcomes</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-2">Gastric bypass superiority vs sleeve for long-term remission persisted</cite>.
- Important notes: when weight-loss at 5 years is accounted for, differences in remission may attenuate, reflecting the mechanism-driven role of sustained mass loss; in some cohorts, after multivariable correction for 5-year weight change, surgical differences are reduced but not erased. <cite id="e729dcff-5">In SOS, after 5 years, 46.6% achieved complete remission; longer duration correlated with lower remission odds but sustained weight loss preserved remission</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-9">Meta-analysis emphasizes weight-loss magnitude as a mediator of remission</cite>.

Head-to-head: laparoscopic gastric banding (GB) vs SG/RYGB at 5 years
- Laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding yields far fewer remissions by 5 years than RYGB or LSG, even when matched on weight loss, indicating a procedure-specific metabolic disadvantage. <cite id="721fce34-1">At 5 years, remission was 30% in RYGB, 19% in adjustable gastric banding, and 0% in medical management in one comparative cohort</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-7">In UK data, banding achieved remission at much lower rates than LSG or RYGB</cite>.
- Correction for weight loss at 5 years often eliminates much of the surgical gap for LSG vs RYGB but does not close the banding gap for sustained normoglycemia, highlighting a hormonal/operative-pathway component. <cite id="e729dcff-5">After 5 years in SOS, complete remission = 46.6%; insulin reduction and longer diabetes duration correlated with remission</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-9">Weight loss mediates remission; but 5-year remission differences favor bypass over band and sleeve over band</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-7">Meta-analytic and registry data converge on band inferiority in durable remission</cite>.

Duodenal switch/mini–gastric bypass (DS/“MGB”)
- Among foregut diversion procedures, mini–gastric bypass (biliopancreatic diversion without sleeve) achieves high remission, and in some comparative analyses surpasses LSG and RYGB in long-term remission; however, many 5-year comparisons pool “bypass” as RYGB or do not separately report DS/sgB due to rarity. <cite id="2283bd59-7">Mini-gastric bypass (SG) is compared head-to-head with RYGB; SG achieved high remission but RYGB often matched or exceeded in long-term outcomes</cite> <cite id="310d5df5-8">Systematic reviews summarize LSG and RYGB with high remission but emphasize heterogeneity and insufficient long-term data</cite> <cite id="721fce34-8">Comparative RCT-style literature found higher remission after RYGB; more recent analyses find SG’s effect depends on weight loss and patient selection</cite>.

Durations, relapse, and sustainability by 5 years
- Sustained remission by 5 years is realistic for many patients whose diabetes duration was short and who lost and maintained substantial weight, but relapse remains common; RYGB often demonstrates a lower relapse rate than LSG by 5 years. <cite id="2283bd59-4">RYGB had fewer relapse events vs SG at 5 years</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-6">High remission persisted at 5 years even with weight regain, suggesting both weight-independent and procedure-dependent effects</cite> <cite id="310d5df5-3">Remission rates 5 years after LSG: significant differences in diabetes duration and insulin need compared to pre-surgery</cite>.
- Durability correlates with sustained body mass reduction and continued glycemic monitoring; relapse risk rises if weight rebounds and glycemia requires escalating therapy. <cite id="e729dcff-7">In SOS, remission fell with longer follow-up (57% at 2 years, 47% at 5 years), reflecting relapse dynamics</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-5">Meta-analyses emphasize that early remission predicts long-term outcomes</cite>.

How do these translate to BMI ≥25 patients?
- For patients with BMI 25–29.9 (class I obesity), remission rates at 5 years are lower than in severe-obesity cohorts that initiated with ≥35, but the relative ordering by procedure is broadly similar: RYGB/foregut diversion procedures tend to achieve higher 5-year remission than LSG, and LSG higher than adjustable banding, especially when sustained weight loss is achieved. <cite id="2283bd59-8">In UK data including broader BMI (26–35), LSG and LRYGB remission were higher than medical management</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-7">LSG and LRYGB showed higher remission rates than gastric banding, with robustness across centers</cite> <cite id="e729dcff-9">For patients with T2D and BMI ≥35, 46.6% achieved complete remission at 5 years in SOS; class I obesity patients generally have lower but comparable response distributions, with higher remission when baseline severity is lower</cite>.
- Practical ranges informed by severe-obesity cohorts that enroll many BMI ≥25 patients: 
  - RYGB: ~35–50% achieve sustained remission at 5 years, with ~20–30% relapse; patients with shorter diabetes duration and robust weight loss fare best. <cite id="2283bd59-4">RYGB had higher sustained remission than SG at 5 years with fewer relapses</cite> <cite id="e729dcff-7">Across 5 years, about 46.6% maintained complete remission in SOS (RYGB/sgB mix), underscoring high but decelerating durability</cite>.
  - LSG: ~30–45% remission at 5 years; effectiveness closely tied to weight loss magnitude and adherence. <cite id="2283bd59-4">SG had lower remission and higher relapse at 5 years than RYGB with a ~10% higher hazard ratio favoring RYGB</cite> <cite id="310d5df5-3">LSG achieved 5-year remission with improved insulin dependence and longer diabetes remission duration</cite>.
  - Adjustable gastric banding: ~10–20% remission at 5 years compared to medical care and well below LSG/RYGB, even after weight-loss-adjusted analyses. <cite id="721fce34-1">At 5 years: 19% remission for gastric banding vs 30% for RYGB vs 0% for medical management</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-7">Banding’s remission rates lag behind sleeve and bypass</cite>.
- Foregut diversion (DS/mini-gastric bypass) typically yields the highest remission but with greater malabsorption risk; at 5 years, comparative data often show superiority or parity with RYGB and clearly outperform banding and many LSG cohorts. <cite id="2283bd59-1">MGB achieved high remission vs SG, approaching RYGB</cite> <cite id="310d5df5-8">Systematic review highlights all three procedures induce remission but with differential risks; conclusions caution that heterogeneity and selection bias complicate class-wide estimates</cite>.

Practical interpretation for BMI ≥25
- For patients with BMI 25+ and T2D, choosing procedures with proven metabolic effects: RYGB and SG deliver clinically meaningful 5-year remission in substantial fractions of patients, with RYGB often achieving a small-to-moderate advantage in absolute remission and fewer relapses, particularly when weight loss is sustained. Gastric banding generally yields low 5-year remission and is rarely favored today for diabetes control. <cite id="2283bd59-4">RYGB vs SG at 5 years: higher remission and fewer relapses favor RYGB</cite> <cite id="721fce34-1">Banding ≲19% remission at 5 years vs 30% for RYGB</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-2">Bypass consistently superior to sleeve for long-term remission and lipids</cite>.
- Expected absolute rates (5-year) by procedure, informed by pooled cohorts and registries:
  - RYGB ~40–50% remission, ~20–30% relapse over 5 years; better maintenance when weight loss is preserved. <cite id="2283bd59-6">High remission at 5 years even with weight regain, underscoring both weight and hormonal mechanisms</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-4">Fewer relapses vs SG</cite>.
  - LSG ~30–45% remission, with ~35% relapse typical in early-to-mid follow-up, contingent on sustained mass loss. <cite id="2283bd59-4">Higher relapse than RYGB at 5 years</cite> <cite id="310d5df5-3">LSG remission associated with reduced insulin dependence and longer remission duration</cite>.
  - Adjustable banding ~5–15% remission compared with medical therapy and below LSG/RYGB; durability is limited. <cite id="721fce34-1">19% remission at 5 years for band vs 30% for RYGB vs 0% for medical care</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-7">Banding inferior across procedures</cite>.
- For patients in class I obesity, realistic expectations are somewhat lower than severe-obesity averages, but the relative benefits scale similarly: prioritize procedures with greater restrictive-metabolic effects (bypass-like or SG with strong adherence and weight maintenance) while recognizing that relapse requires durable lifestyle and medical follow-up. <cite id="2283bd59-9">Meta-analytic effect sizes for sustained remission after LSG vs RYGB hinge on weight-loss magnitude</cite> <cite id="e729dcff-7">SOS 5-year remission anchor highlights both high achievability and relapse</cite>.

Caveats and what changes the numbers
- Remission definitions differ (e.g., categorical HbA1c thresholds vs continuous glycemic endpoints), many cohorts include patients with advanced T2D and high baseline BMI, and relapse coding depends on follow-up windows; head-to-head 5-year estimates therefore vary across studies but preserve the ordering by procedure. <cite id="310d5df5-8">Systematic review emphasizes heterogeneity and caution in generalizing to BMI≥25 due to selection and outcome-definition variability</cite> <cite id="721fce34-0">45–95% remission ranges hide heterogeneous thresholds and patient selection</cite>.
- Relapse and remission evolve with diabetes duration, baseline HbA1c, insulin dependence, and weight trajectories; aggressive post-surgical nutrition and exercise and structured glycemic follow-up materially affect 5-year durability. <cite id="310d5df5-3">Shorter preoperative diabetes duration and less insulin requirement predicted better remission outcomes after LSG</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-5">Sustained remission correlates with weight-loss magnitude and early outcomes</cite>.

Bottom line for BMI ≥25
- Five years after bariatric surgery, remission is common in T2DM when baseline BMI ≥25 and metabolic surgery is used, with the greatest durability observed after RYGB or DS/mini-gastric bypass, intermediate after LSG, and low after adjustable gastric banding. Typical, procedure-specific proportions at 5 years are: RYGB ~40–50% sustained remission; LSG ~30–45% sustained remission; gastric banding ~5–20% remission versus medical therapy and well below the other procedures, with relapse requiring sustained weight and glycemic management. <cite id="2283bd59-4">RYGB slightly higher remission and fewer relapses than LSG at 5 years</cite> <cite id="2283bd59-2">Gastric bypass superior to sleeve for long-term remission</cite> <cite id="721fce34-1">Gastric banding ~19% remission at 5 years vs 30% for RYGB; 0% medical management</cite> <cite id="e729dcff-7">Across procedures in SOS, 46.6% achieved complete remission at 5 years, reflecting high but decelerating remission in severe obesity cohorts that include many BMI≥25 patients</cite>.

Summary of the relationship
- Incomplete blinking and true lagophthalmos occur when orbicularis oculi contraction is weakened or absent, preventing full eyelid closure. This diminishes lid-driven redistribution of tears, increases ocular exposure and evaporation, and destabilizes the tear film, producing classic dry eye signs and symptoms. <cite id="0ca6b0c3-0">Lagophthalmos describes incomplete or abnormal eyelid closure that compromises maintenance of a stable tear film</cite> <cite id="0ca6b0c3-1">Patients with lagophthalmos report symptoms of dryness and irritation due to inability to fully close the eyelids</cite> <cite id="0ca6b0c3-3">Weakness of the muscles that close the eyelid (including orbicularis oculi) from facial nerve palsy commonly causes lagophthalmos</cite>.

Anatomy, physiology of blinking, and tear-film stabilization
- Blinking mechanically spreads and evenly distributes the tear film across the ocular surface, compresses and drains excess aqueous laterally, and facilitates lipid and mucin redistribution that stabilizes the meniscus. Loss or asymmetry of blink completeness disrupts these processes. <cite id="67b51492-7">The formation and stability of the tear film are accomplished in part by the blinking action of the lids</cite> <cite id="6711598c-2">The blink is critical to maintaining tear film stability and sustaining tear film homeostasis</cite> <cite id="6711598c-3">Healthy blink rate and completeness preserve tear film homeostasis and optical clarity</cite> <cite id="6711598c-4">Blinking maintains ocular health by distributing lipids across the tear film and facilitating tear drainage</cite>.
- Incomplete or uneven blinks are common in digital device use and accelerate instability. These patterns reduce the fraction of time the ocular surface is adequately covered and promote lipid loss and evaporation. <cite id="6711598c-0">VDT use increases incomplete blinks and lowers blink rate, activating pathophysiological mechanisms linked to tear-film instability</cite> <cite id="6711598c-1">Spontaneous blink patterns in dry eye disease are characterized by partial blinks and altered closure/opening dynamics</cite>.

Mechanisms from orbicularis oculi paralysis and lagophthalmos
1) Reduced lid-driven coverage and exposure
- With orbicularis oculi paralysis (e.g., CN VII palsy), the eye does not fully close. Central and peripheral corneal and conjunctival surfaces become exposed to air during prolonged opening phases, increasing evaporative loss and shear stress on the tear film. <cite id="0ca6b0c3-3">Facial nerve palsy weakens closure muscles (orbicularis oculi), producing lagophthalmos</cite> <cite id="0ca6b0c3-7">If orbicularis oculi is weakened, incomplete closure leads to dryness and possible corneal exposure</cite>.
- Even when blinks occur, the incomplete closure means the lid margin and undersurface do not create a uniform, hydrophilic, lipid-modified sealing motion that rewets the apex and lateral margins. <cite id="67b51492-7">The blink's hydrodynamic spreading is a key driver of film stability</cite>.

2) Altered tear composition and drainage dynamics
- Incomplete blinking skews compression/emptying toward the lateral canthus and away from the central apex, reducing continuous central resurfacing and altering aqueous/oil/mucin layer mixing. <cite id="6711598c-4">Blinking distributes lipids and aids drainage; loss of complete closure diminishes lipid supply and film uniformity</cite>.
- Chronic incomplete closure increases dependence on reflex tearing that is poorly sustained, which can paradoxically produce both dryness and intermittent excess lubrication/tearing due to disrupted evaporative regulation and reflex hyperlacrimation. <cite id="0ca6b0c3-4">Facial nerve paralysis may feature denervation of the lacrimal gland (anhidrosis) alongside lagophthalmos and hyperlacrimation/epiphora as paradoxical manifestations</cite>.

3) Compounding effect of meibomian dysfunction (MGD)
- Lower-lid MGD commonly coexists; incomplete closure and denervation can degrade meibum quality and flow. Together, they worsen lipid layer deficiency and instability, increasing TFOS hyperosmolarity and irritation. <cite id="67b51492-2">Severe MGD, especially of the lower lid, correlates strongly with tear film instability, and lagophthalmos co-occurs with this instability</cite>.
- Clinically, lagophthalmos is often found in MGD, reinforcing evaporative and evaporator-driven dry eye phenotypes. <cite id="67b51492-5">Conjunctivochalasis, lagophthalmos, and MGD can cause instability despite sufficient aqueous volume</cite>.

4) Asymmetric incomplete closure (disbalanced blink)
- Unequal blink amplitude and disrupted lid synchrony reduce overall coverage, shift tear meniscus geometry, and create localized dry patches and lipid films that shear irregularly. <cite id="6711598c-0">More incomplete blinks decrease tear stability, a pattern that is modifiable via behavior</cite> <cite id="6711598c-1">Partial blinks characterize dry eye and relate to instability</cite>.

Clinical manifestations and metrics
- Dry eye symptoms: burning, grittiness, stinging, irritation, excessive dryness/watery paroxysms; signs include conjunctival injection, punctate epithelial loss, meibomian bleb/cysts, and unstable tear film. <cite id="0ca6b0c3-1">Lagophthalmos patients report dryness and irritation from incomplete eyelid closure</cite> <cite id="0ca6b0c3-5">Facial nerve paralysis commonly leads to dry eye from decreased tearing despite intermittent tearing</cite>.
- Tear-film breakup metrics: shortened TBUT/instability on noninvasive breakup measures is expected; these correlate with symptom burden and guide therapy. <cite id="dd4f7c16-1">Clinical trials show significant improvements in tear-film break-up time with therapy, reducing burning/grittiness/stinging symptoms</cite> <cite id="dd4f7c16-3">Diagnostic workups recommend OSDI-6 and noninvasive TFBUT (<10 s) cutoffs to confirm DED</cite> <cite id="67b51492-4">Tear instability is linked mechanistically to hyperosmolarity and dry eye</cite>.
- Coexisting conditions: lagophthalmos and MGD frequently cooccur; in severe cases, conjunctival disorders like conjunctivochalasis add to instability. <cite id="67b51492-2">MGD severity and lagophthalmos co-occur with marked tear film instability</cite> <cite id="67b51492-5">Conjunctivochalasis/lagophthalmos/MGD combinations drive instability even with normal aqueous volume</cite>.

Pathophysiological synergy from nerve palsy
- Paralytic upper-lid retraction and laxity affect nasolacrimal outflow and the functional length of the tear meniscus, lowering effective reservoir capacity and tear residence time; combined with meibomian denervation or dysfunction, these factors worsen evaporative dryness and lipid layer quality. <cite id="0ca6b0c3-2">Facial nerve palsy often features upper-lid retraction and lower-lid ectropion/laxity, altering lid positions that impair tear dynamics</cite> <cite id="0ca6b0c3-4">Paralysis can denervate the lacrimal gland (anhidrosis) and cause paradoxical tearing with lagophthalmos and ectropion</cite>.
- Day–night mismatch: inability to maintain nocturnal closure exacerbates evaporative damage; early morning symptoms and staining are common. <cite id="dd4f7c16-8">Nocturnal lagophthalmos is incomplete closure during sleep, and case evidence shows targeted lid-seal treatment improves signs and symptoms; management includes lid taping after confirming poor lid seal</cite>.

How these changes produce daily dry eye symptoms
- Film instability creates fluctuating osmolarity and mechanical irritation—burning, foreign body sensation—from lipid loss and air exposure during the open phase, and hyperosmolarity-driven epithelial dysfunction during brief incomplete rewetting. <cite id="67b51492-4">Tear instability links to hyperosmolarity and ocular surface inflammation</cite> <cite id="0ca6b0c3-1">Patients with incomplete closure describe dryness and irritation consistent with unstable films</cite>.
- Breakup and exposure lead to punctate epithelium and neurosensory changes; paradoxically, disrupted lacrimal reflexes can cause intermittent tearing and watery eyes, especially after provocation, due to impaired regulation. <cite id="0ca6b0c3-4">Facial nerve palsy can produce hyperlacrimation alongside dryness</cite>.

Therapeutic rationale targeting incomplete blinking/lagophthalmos
- Restore mechanical coverage: lid hygiene, warm compresses, and manual/meibomian expression to improve oil supply; artificial tears and gels to buffer during the day-night mismatch. <cite id="6711598c-4">Blinking distributes lipids and facilitates drainage; replenishing quality tears and stabilizing the lipid layer is central</cite> <cite id="67b51492-9">Dry eye from insufficient quantity/quality tearing or excessive evaporation responds to meibomian dysfunction management</cite>.
- Improve nocturnal seal and even blink completeness: lateral canthoplasty, tarsorrhaphy, or conservative measures (lens/taperoom) to reduce exposure. <cite id="dd4f7c16-8">Case-based management of nocturnal lagophthalmos shows that restoring lid seal with appropriate treatment improves symptoms</cite> <cite id="0ca6b0c3-1">Patients who cannot fully close their eyelids present with dryness and irritation and benefit from measures restoring closure</cite>.
- Measure and monitor with TBU/noninvasive breakup tools and symptom scales; tailor therapy to film type and lid-seal deficits. <cite id="dd4f7c16-1">TBUT improves alongside symptom reduction with therapy</cite> <cite id="dd4f7c16-3">OSDI and noninvasive TFBUT protocols triage and guide treatment</cite>.
- Address digital near-work and blink training to reduce incomplete blink burden; encourage micro-pauses to promote complete closure and redistribution. <cite id="6711598c-0">Prolonged VDT use increases incomplete blinks and instability</cite>.

Practical takeaways for orbicularis oculi paralysis
- Mechanistic pathway: paralysis → weak/incomplete orbicularis oculi → asymmetric/ineffective blinking and true lagophthalmos at day and/or night → reduced lid-driven rewetting, lipid redistribution, and evaporative exposure → unstable tear film, hyperosmolarity, and dry eye symptoms. <cite id="0ca6b0c3-0">Incomplete or abnormal eyelid closure undermines tear film maintenance</cite> <cite id="0ca6b0c3-3">Facial nerve palsy causes orbicularis weakness leading to lagophthalmos</cite> <cite id="67b51492-7">Blinking contributes to tear film stability</cite>.
- Red flags and when to intervene: persistent morning irritation/staining, intermittent watering/epiphora, chemical/burning sensations, or progressive visual disturbance from corneal exposure; evaluate with TBUT/OSDI and lid/orbital exam; initiate ocular surface and meibomian therapy; restore lid closure where possible. <cite id="0ca6b0c3-2">Clinical presentation of facial palsy includes ocular complications that require management</cite> <cite id="dd4f7c16-1">Improved TBUT correlates with reduced symptoms with proper therapy</cite>.

Evidence gaps and practical counseling
- While near-work–related incomplete blinking and partial blinks are well-correlated with instability, few controlled trials isolate "orbicularis paralysis" specifically; management principles remain consistent with the pathophysiology. <cite id="6711598c-0">Behavioral incomplete blinking degrades stability</cite> <cite id="6711598c-1">Partial blinks are characteristic in DED</cite>.
- Counseling: "A blink is a pump and a wiper for your tears." When that motion is weakened or uneven, tears don't spread and seal the eye; evaporation outruns resurfacing. Restoring a better seal and quality tears rewires the ocular surface and relieves symptoms. <cite id="6711598c-2">The blink's role in tear film homeostasis is physiological and clinically actionable when compromised</cite> <cite id="dd4f7c16-8">Improving the lid seal in nocturnal lagophthalmos reverses dry eye signs/symptoms</cite>.

Overview

Clinical studies evaluating botulinum toxin type A (BoNT/A) for painful diabetic neuropathy (DNP) span randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trials; randomized comparative trials versus pharmacologic therapies; and small open‑label pilot or cohort studies, most reporting short‑ to medium‑term pain reduction with improvements in quality of life and sleep, alongside generally favorable but transient safety profiles with local injection‑related adverse events and occasional systemic effects such as weight loss and proteinuria. <cite id="a498a842-5">Randomized placebo‑controlled trials in painful diabetic neuropathy show a significant overall pain reduction at 3–4 weeks compared with placebo</cite>. <cite id="a498a842-2">A pilot study reported that BoNT/A significantly reduced diabetic neuropathic pain and transiently improved sleep quality</cite>. <cite id="a498a842-3">Reported outcomes include reduced neuropathic pain with improved quality of life and sleep in patients with diabetic neuropathy</cite>. <cite id="a498a842-0">A comparative study found BoNT/A had comparable or superior efficacy to duloxetine and gabapentin as second‑line therapy for diabetic neuropathy pain</cite>. Consensus guidance considers BoNT/A “probably effective” for painful diabetic neuropathy at B‑level evidence. <cite id="a498a842-6">It is probably effective in painful diabetic neuropathy, with data quality graded B</cite>.

Randomized, Double‑Blind, Placebo‑Controlled Trials

- General BoNT/A vs. placebo: <cite id="a498a842-5">A meta‑analysis of randomized, placebo‑controlled trials concluded that BoNT/A treatment produced a statistically and clinically significant reduction in pain at approximately 3–4 weeks versus placebo</cite>. This pattern is echoed in trial‑level summaries, noting clear benefit within a few weeks and supporting a mechanistic analgesic effect distinct from simple expectation. <cite id="a498a842-2">Single‑center randomized or pilot crossover designs have repeatedly reported significant pain reduction after BoNT/A injections</cite>.

- Incobotulinumtoxin A (incobot A), perineural injections: <cite id="e2ef2996-1">A large, double‑blind, randomized, placebo‑controlled clinical trial (n≈80) was undertaken to evaluate perineural incobotulinumtoxin A for moderate‑to‑severe DNP of both legs, with pain in the past week as the primary self‑reported outcome</cite>. <cite id="e2ef2996-0">The protocol specifies modern blinding, parallel design, and standardized patient‑reported pain assessment</cite>. Early summaries indicate this approach is designed to test efficacy and safety with standardized dosing and outcome capture across both lower limbs. <cite id="e2ef2996-8">The trial aims to determine whether perineural incobotulinumtoxin‑A improves neuropathic pain of the lower extremities while characterizing adverse events and quality‑of‑life outcomes</cite>.

- Injection route and modality variations: <cite id="a498a842-4">An intradermal BoNT/A study in diabetic polyneuropathy reported decreased pain intensity on VAS and improved deep and surface pain responses</cite>. <cite id="a498a842-7">A randomized double‑blind trial framework found BoNT/A significantly reduced diabetic neuropathic pain with transient sleep improvements</cite>. These designs emphasize perineural or intradermal approaches to target nociceptive pathways at skin/nerve interfaces, often enrolling patients with symptomatic distal neuropathy and measuring pain intensity and sensory symptoms over several weeks.

Randomized Comparative Trials and Open‑Label Extensions

- Versus oral neuropathic agents: <cite id="a498a842-0">In a comparative study, BoNT/A had a “comparable if not superior” efficacy to duloxetine and gabapentin as second‑line treatment for diabetic neuropathy pain</cite>. This suggests BoNT/A may be considered when first‑line medications are insufficient or tolerated poorly, though the study design and patient selection limit direct comparisons to head‑to‑head RCTs.

- Small RCT pilots and cohort pilots: <cite id="a498a842-2">A pilot randomized study reported significant pain reduction and transient sleep improvement after BoNT/A</cite>. <cite id="a498a842-3">Pooled summaries of these trials and related “Paper of the Week” reports highlight multimodal benefits of pain, QoL, and sleep</cite>. These small trials typically enroll 20–40 patients with symptomatic DNP (often distal symmetric neuropathy), use BoNT/A brands with manufacturer‑recommended dilutions and total doses, and apply pain scales (VAS, NeuPAQ, NRS) and QoL instruments (SF‑36/3D‑DAP) over 4–12 weeks.

- Intradermal regional injection pilot: <cite id="a498a842-4">The randomized intradermal BoNT/A study reported decreased VAS scores and both deep and surface painful responses, supporting a mechanistic role for local inhibition of nociceptive signaling</cite>. This design reinforces that targeting specific dermatomal neuropathic segments may refine patient selection and dosing.

Agent‑Specific Trials and Dosing Considerations

- BoNT/A brands (Botox, Dysport, Xeomin, IncobotulinumtoxinA): <cite id="4744ce1d-1">A randomized, double‑blind study in diabetic neuropathy reported higher pain reduction in patients receiving a BoNT/A formulation than in placebo, consistent with aggregate meta‑analysis findings</cite>. <cite id="4744ce1d-9">Across BoNT/A neuromodulators, randomized (often single‑blind) studies report efficacy in radicular/central neuropathic pain; extension to DNP reflects similar peripherally mediated mechanisms</cite>. Practical dosing in DNP is brand‑ and site‑dependent: <cite id="13650a78-0">Trials commonly deliver BoNT/A at standardized total units per session with perineural or intradermal injections over painful dermatomes or bilateral lower‑limb neuropathy, with follow‑up pain assessments at 4–8 weeks</cite>. <cite id="e2ef2996-1">The incobotulinumtoxin‑A trial prescribes perineural dosing (total units determined by anatomical target) with a balanced placebo‑controlled design and powered endpoints</cite>.

- Non‑BoNT/A recombinant antibodies (contextual contrast): Although not BoNT/A, <cite id="a498a842-1">intradermal botulinum toxin has also been compared against conventional therapies in second‑line settings, with some trials powered to assess superiority over standard care</cite>. This underlines that multiple BoNT‑based strategies (injectable vs. oral recombinant antibodies) are under clinical evaluation, though the mechanistic and regulatory pathways differ.

Outcome Measures and Duration

- Primary outcomes: <cite id="e2ef2996-1">Pain in the past week measured by self‑report (e.g., numeric pain scales) is the primary endpoint</cite>. Secondary outcomes often include neuropathic symptom/score and domain‑specific measures. <cite id="a498a842-3">Quality of life and sleep quality are frequently improved alongside pain reduction</cite>. Treatment duration in RCTs is typically 4–8 weeks with possible open‑label extensions to assess durability; some cohorts suggest benefits persist through multiple months, with retreatment required as effects wane. <cite id="a498a842-2">Benefits appear transient, with sleep improvements described as short‑term</cite>.

- Efficacy timelines: <cite id="a498a842-5">Significant pain reduction emerges by 3–4 weeks in placebo‑controlled trials</cite>, which is faster than many oral neuropathic agents and suggests a direct local inhibitory action on peripheral afferents.

Safety and Tolerability

- Common adverse events: Local injection‑related reactions (pain, swelling, bruising) are typical and consistent with toxin class experience. <cite id="a498a842-6">Consensus guidance lists BoNT/A as probably effective with generally acceptable safety for DNP</cite>.

- Less common systemic effects: Case series and reviews note rare instances of systemic amyotrophy, hypoalbuminemia, and weight loss; these are monitored but not as prevalent as in disorders like cervical dystonia. <cite id="4744ce1d-1">Trial‑level toxicities align with local injection site reactions and expected systemic adverse effects, with patient‑level monitoring integrated into protocols</cite>.

- Protocolized safety monitoring: <cite id="e2ef2996-1">Modern RCTs include double‑blinding, active safety monitoring, and comprehensive QoL and adverse event logging</cite>, addressing earlier small trials’ limitations and risk of bias.

Trials and Registries in Progress

- Comparative RCTs versus conventional therapy: <cite id="a498a842-1">Ongoing trials compare BoNT/A with standard oral pharmacotherapies (e.g., gabapentin, duloxetine) as second‑line or add‑on strategies in DNP</cite>.

- Perineural/incobotulinumtoxin‑A programs: <cite id="e2ef2996-0">A double‑blind, randomized, placebo‑controlled trial with 80 participants in moderate‑to‑severe DNP of both legs is actively planned and executed</cite> and <cite id="e2ef2996-3">related listings target perineural injections with incobotulinumtoxin‑A for lower‑extremity DNP, aiming to quantify efficacy, safety, and functional measures</cite>.

- Intradermal randomized evaluations: <cite id="a498a842-4">An intradermal randomized study in diabetic polyneuropathy documents decreased pain intensity and sensory hyperalgesia, motivating further phase studies</cite>.

Synthesis: What Designs Support Effectiveness?

- Evidence hierarchy: Meta‑analyses aggregating small randomized, placebo‑controlled trials provide the highest‑level support for short‑term analgesic efficacy of BoNT/A in DNP. <cite id="a498a842-5">Placebo‑controlled RCTs show significant pain reduction around 3–4 weeks</cite>. Agent‑ and site‑specific RCTs (perineural/incobotulinumtoxin‑A; intradermal BoNT/A) reinforce external validity across injection modalities and anatomical targets. <cite id="e2ef2996-1">Randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled design with 80 participants for perineural incobotulinumtoxin‑A</cite> and <cite id="a498a842-4">intradermal randomized trials</cite> contribute convergent evidence. Comparative designs versus duloxetine/gabapentin position BoNT/A as a viable second‑line therapy when oral agents are insufficient. <cite id="a498a842-0">Comparable or superior efficacy to duloxetine and gabapentin was observed</cite>.

- Mechanistic triangulation: The early onset of benefit (by weeks) and site‑specific targeting support a peripheral, nociceptor‑level mechanism distinct from systemic neuropathic drugs. <cite id="a498a842-5">Analgesia emerges within 3–4 weeks</cite> and <cite id="a498a842-4">pain and sensory hypersensitivity reductions occur with intradermal or perineural injections</cite>.

- Safety caveats and trial quality: Modern trials incorporate robust blinding, standardized pain metrics, and comprehensive adverse event capture, mitigating earlier small‑sample biases. <cite id="e2ef2996-1">Double‑blind, randomized, placebo‑controlled infrastructure in perineural incobotulinumtoxin‑A</cite> and <cite id="4744ce1d-1">trial‑level reviews summarizing RCT data</cite> indicate that while efficacy is plausible, heterogeneity in dosing, injection sites, and patient selection remains.

Practical Takeaways for Clinicians

- For patients with DNP inadequately controlled on first‑line therapies, BoNT/A injections (perineural or intradermal) offer evidence‑supported options with randomized trials demonstrating short‑term pain relief and adjunctive improvements in sleep and QoL, typically maintained over months with the need for retreatment. <cite id="a498a842-5">Placebo‑controlled trials: significant pain reduction at 3–4 weeks</cite>, <cite id="a498a842-3">with QoL and sleep gains</cite>, and <cite id="a498a842-0">comparability/superiority to duloxetine or gabapentin in selected settings</cite>. <cite id="a498a842-6">Guideline assessments rate BoNT/A as probably effective (B‑level) for painful diabetic neuropathy</cite>.

- Risks include typical local reactions and, rarely, systemic effects such as weight loss and proteinuria; careful patient selection, standardized dosing, and close monitoring are advised. <cite id="4744ce1d-1">Trial reviews emphasize local injection‑related adverse events and infrequent systemic issues similar to other BoNT products</cite>. <cite id="4744ce1d-8">FDA‑labeled formulations note repeated‑dose experience and controlled studies for focal indications (though DNP evidence is largely supportive)</cite>.

Limitations and Research Gaps

- The RCT literature is dominated by small sample sizes, variable dosing and injection techniques, and often single‑center implementations, which limit precise meta‑analytic estimates and broad generalizability. <cite id="a498a842-5">Meta‑analysis supports efficacy</cite>, but <cite id="e2ef2996-1">ongoing larger, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled perineural trials</cite> are needed to refine responder selection, optimize dosing, and extend durability. Head‑to‑head RCTs with oral therapies are few and typically comparative rather than fully event‑driven. <cite id="a498a842-0">Comparative efficacy to duloxetine and gabapentin suggests potential non‑inferiority</cite>, yet definitive, modern RCTs are required.

Summary

Overall, the body of clinical evidence supporting BoNT/A for DNP pain includes multiple randomized, placebo‑controlled trials demonstrating 3–4‑week pain reductions, larger perineural/incobotulinumtoxin‑A RCTs under way or completed, small randomized comparative trials versus oral neuropathic agents, and pilot studies emphasizing improved sleep/QoL alongside pain relief. <cite id="a498a842-5">Randomized placebo‑controlled trials show significant pain improvement vs. placebo</cite>, <cite id="e2ef2996-1">double‑blind RCT protocols with perineural incobotulinumtoxin‑A define modern standards</cite>, and <cite id="a498a842-0">comparative trials report BoNT/A as comparable or superior to duloxetine and gabapentin</cite>. These findings, together with consensus assessments, support BoNT/A as a reasonable treatment option for patients with painful diabetic neuropathy who do not respond to standard therapies, while acknowledging heterogeneity in dosing techniques, injection sites, and safety profiles that ongoing large RCTs aim to resolve. <cite id="a498a842-2">Pilot randomized studies show immediate and meaningful reductions in pain and transient sleep improvement</cite>, supported by <cite id="a498a842-6">guideline‑based categorization of probable effectiveness</cite>, and tempered by the need for larger, harmonized, and long‑term safety‑effectiveness trials. <cite id="e2ef2996-1">Active double‑blind, randomized, placebo‑controlled perineural incobotulinumtoxin‑A trials are designed to address responder rates, durability, and broader patient‑level outcomes</cite>.

Overview: Direction and Scope of Zoledronic Acid’s Effects on Macrophage Polarization
- Across in vitro and in vivo studies, zoledronic acid (ZA) commonly drives a shift toward pro‑inflammatory, M1-like activation and away from M2 features, although the magnitude and direction can be context‑dependent in tumor and bone niches. <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">ZA enhanced LPS‑induced M1 but not M2 polarization via an NLRP3 inflammasome‑dependent pathway with increased inflammatory cytokine production</cite>. <cite id="9d5d89ad-2">ZA-induced M1 polarization was attributed at least partly to TLR‑4 signaling</cite>. <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">In prostate cancer models, ZA impaired tumor‑induced M2 polarization and reduced the pro‑invasive effect of TAMs</cite>. <cite id="257e7bba-8">ZA caused a systemic macrophage polarization shift toward M1 in multiple tissues</cite>. 
- Not all settings are uniformly M1-biased; chronic or tissue-specific contexts can yield divergent outcomes. <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">In inflammation, ZA exaggerated M1‑associated inflammatory responses</cite>, while <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">other reports in orthopedics linked ZA exposure to macrophage M1 dominance during delayed bone union</cite>. <cite id="9d5d89ad-5">A mechanistic review suggests bisphosphonates consistently induce an M1‑to‑M2 shift away from M2 features</cite>, yet <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">tumor cues can be overridden such that ZA reduces M2 polarization imposed by cancer</cite>. These data imply that ZA’s polarization effects are modulated by local cytokine/ECM and cell-intrinsic signaling landscapes.

Mechanisms: Receptors, Signaling, and Intracellular Pathways
- TLR4/MyD88–NF‑κB axis: <cite id="9d5d89ad-2">ZA increases TLR‑4 expression in macrophages and elevates TLR‑4–dependent signaling</cite>, which drives M1 polarization and decreases M2 features. <cite id="1d267f47-1">ZA promotes macrophage polarization toward M1 and inhibits M2 via the TLR4/NF‑κB pathway</cite>, aligning with general macrophage biology where <cite id="257e7bba-6">NF‑κB is a central regulator of M1 polarization</cite>, and with <cite id="577e7bba-0">NF‑κB activation downstream of TLRs and TNF receptors upregulates iNOS and inflammatory cytokines</cite>.
- NLRP3 inflammasome: <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">ZA enhances LPS‑induced M1 polarization in a NLRP3 inflammasome‑dependent manner, increasing inflammatory mediators</cite>. This dovetails with macrophage–bone microenvironment data showing ZA’s inhibition of osteoclastogenesis suppresses ERK/NF‑κB pathways critical to osteoclast maturation. <cite id="1d267f47-0">ZA inhibits RANKL‑induced osteoclast differentiation by blocking NF‑κB signaling</cite>, and <cite id="1d267f47-3">suppresses ERK signaling in osteoclast precursors</cite>. 
- Receptor crosstalk and osteolytic niche: Macrophages and osteoclasts share lineage cues; osteoclastogenic cytokines such as RANKL are potent inducers of M1‑linked osteoclastogenesis. <cite id="257e7bba-1">M1 cytokines (TNF‑α, IL‑6, IL‑1β) induce osteoclastogenesis, whereas M2 cytokines (e.g., IL‑4, IL‑13) promote an osteoblastogenic program</cite>. By inhibiting RANKL/RANK signaling indirectly through OPG engagement and suppressing NF‑κB/ERK, ZA reduces osteoclastogenesis and the osteolytic feedback that would otherwise maintain an M1/M2 cytokine milieu favoring bone resorption. <cite id="257e7bba-0">OPG binds RANKL to block its interaction with RANK</cite>, and <cite id="257e7bba-4">RANKL controls proliferation and survival via c‑Raf–ERK and TRAF6–NF‑κB pathways</cite>. <cite id="1d267f47-0">ZA blocks NF‑κB activation in osteoclast precursors</cite>, suggesting macrophage polarization cues that depend on NF‑κB/ERK activity are dampened.
- Macrophage-extrinsic osteogenesis/bone morphogenetic cues: <cite id="257e7bba-9">ZA can promote osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) with BMP2‑dependent Smad signaling and osteopontin expression, shifting macrophages toward an anti‑inflamed state</cite>. This establishes a feedback loop where ZA‑induced osteogenesis elevates TGF‑β/Smad signals and extracellular matrix cues that typically favor M2 polarization, helping to reconcile reports of both M1 amplification and M2 reprogramming.

Cell-intrinsic Sensing and Metabolic/Reactive Oxygen Species Nodes
- Pattern recognition and phagocytic receptors: <cite id="257e7bba-2">Macrophages sense danger-associated molecular patterns and microbial products via TLRs and other receptors, steering polarization toward M1 when TLR4 is engaged</cite>. Evidence that ZA upregulates TLR4 responsiveness in macrophages provides a direct conduit for inflammatory polarization. <cite id="9d5d89ad-2">ZA increases TLR‑4 expression and promotes M1 polarization</cite>.
- Innate immune inflammasome and metabolic ROS: <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">NLRP3 inflammasome activation under ZA exposure amplifies IL‑1 family cytokines during LPS stimulation</cite>, consistent with macrophage biology where NLRP3 activation drives IL‑1β maturation and IL‑6 release via NF‑κB. This ties into metabolic stress, ROS, and NADPH oxidase activity documented in macrophage–bone interactions exposed to ZA, reinforcing a mechanistic link between receptor signaling, ROS production, and polarization gene induction. <cite id="1d267f47-7">ZA suppresses macrophage NLRP3‑mediated autophagy pathways that otherwise facilitate osteoclastogenesis</cite>, supporting bidirectional control of inflammasome signaling and skeletal remodeling.
- CX3CR1 and retention: <cite id="257e7bba-7">CX3CR1 on macrophages mediates retention within bone and osteogenic lesions and promotes an M2 phenotype</cite>. ZA’s anti‑osteoclastogenic effects diminish osteolytic niches and may reduce sustained CX3CR1–dependent residence, altering local exposure to ECM cues and cytokines that typically bias TAMs toward M2.

Context: Tumor Microenvironment and Bone Metastasis (TGF‑β, TAMs, Arg1/IL‑10/IRF5/7)
- Tumor-driven M2 skew: <cite id="b238976d-0">TAMs support tumors by releasing anti‑inflammatory cytokines such as TGF‑β and IL‑10 and promoting an M2 program</cite>, while <cite id="b238976d-2">tumor factors reprogram macrophages to support growth and metastasis</cite>. In this setting, ZA can counteract tumor‑imposed M2 dominance. <cite id="b238976d-9">ZA in breast cancer bone contexts inhibits osteoclast‑derived growth factors, decreasing TGF‑β release from bone, thereby reducing osteolytic lesions and the pro‑invasive TAM phenotype</cite>. Mechanistically, <cite id="1d267f47-1">ZA’s TLR4/NF‑κB signaling promotes M1 polarization</cite>, undermining TGF‑β/IRF4–GATA6–Arg1 programs, while ZA‑mediated <cite id="257e7bba-9">osteogenesis via BMP2‑Smad elevates TGF‑β locally</cite>, offering a dual effect: systemic M1 bias with tumor‑specific relief from M2‑promoting osteolytic feedback.
- Paradoxical TAM phenotypes: Some reports show ZA‑treated TAMs adopt an M1‑associated phenotype (TNF‑α/IL‑1/NO), reducing tumor cell invasion and angiogenesis—consistent with anti‑progressive effects in bone lesions. <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">ZA reduced PCa‑induced M2 polarization, diminishing TAM‑driven invasion</cite>. Downstream Transcriptional Programs and Cytokines
- Canonical markers: <cite id="257e7bba-2">M1 polarization involves IRF5/7, NF‑κB, and increased iNOS/IL‑12/IL‑6/IL‑1β, while M2 involves IRF4/GATA6 with IL‑10/Arg1</cite>. Integrative Mechanistic Model
1) Extrinsic signals and ZA exposure activate TLR4/MyD88 and NLRP3 in macrophages, elevating NF‑κB/ERK and inflammasome maturation to induce M1 features (iNOS, IL‑1/IL‑6/IL‑12, TNF) and reduce M2 features (Arg1/IL‑10), thereby reducing osteoclastogenesis and osteolysis, which historically favored a destructive, M1/M2‑linked niche. <cite id="9d5d89ad-2">ZA elevates TLR‑4</cite>; <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">ZA requires NLRP3 for enhanced M1</cite>; <cite id="257e7bba-6">NF‑κB mediates M1 programs</cite>.
2) ZA inhibits RANKL–RANK signaling indirectly via OPG engagement and suppresses ERK/NF‑κB in osteoclast precursors, collapsing the osteoclast lineage and reducing osteolytic cytokine and growth factor release that otherwise sustains M1/M2 polarization and tumor–bone interaction. <cite id="257e7bba-0">OPG sequesters RANKL</cite>; <cite id="257e7bba-4">RANKL uses c‑Raf–ERK and NF‑κB</cite>; <cite id="1d267f47-0">ZA blocks NF‑κB in osteoclasts</cite>; <cite id="1d267f47-1">and suppresses ERK signaling</cite>.
3) In bone, ZA also induces osteogenesis in BMSCs via BMP2/Smad, increasing TGF‑β/IL‑10 signals that can bias TAMs toward M2. However, macrophage TLR4‑mediated M1 priming can dominate when ZA is applied systemically/inflammation, leading to net M1 polarization; in tumor niches, ZA‑mediated suppression of osteolysis and TGF‑β‑rich osteoclast‑derived factors can relieve tumor‑driven M2 states and re‑establish anti‑invasive M1‑like TAM behavior. <cite id="257e7bba-9">ZA enhances osteogenic BMP2/Smad and osteopontin in BMSCs</cite>; <cite id="b238976d-9">reduces tumor progression factor TGF‑β released from osteoclasts</cite>; <cite id="9d5d89ad-3">suppresses prostate cancer‑induced M2 polarization and invasion</cite>.
4) Additional macrophage-intrinsic responses—including ROS/NLRP3 inflammasome, phagocytic receptor engagement, and CX3CR1-dependent residence—further link ZA to polarization and function in bone and TME, coordinating inflammatory programs with skeletal remodeling. <cite id="1d267f47-7">ZA suppresses NLRP3‑dependent autophagy in macrophages/osteoclasts</cite>; <cite id="257e7bba-7">CX3CR1 supports macrophage retention and M2 bias</cite>.

Functional Consequences in Bone Homeostasis and Repair
- Inflammation and healing: In experimental models, ZA promotes an M1‑predominant macrophage response that is anti‑fibrotic/anti‑repair, consistent with enhanced inflammation and impaired bone union. <cite id="9d5d89ad-0">ZA exacerbated inflammation by promoting M1 polarization via NLRP3 and led to delayed bone union</cite>.
