- Ganoderma lucidum is a bracket-forming (polypore) wood-decay fungus with a hard, woody basidiocarp that typically grows on dead or decaying hardwoods, displaying a deep red, glossy “varnished” cap and a lateral stipe; macro- and spore morphology have long been central to its taxonomy and identification. <cite id="652f41df-0">Ganoderma lucidium is a polyporous fungus, mainly parasitic or saprophytic, with a hard basidiocarp</cite> <cite id="51d83e91-3">a distinctive species shows a strongly laccate, shallow sulcate, reddish-brown pileus with a lateral stipe and white pore surface</cite> <cite id="e1269462-6">Ganoderma species are distinguished using macroscopic features (pileus, stipe, pores) and spore characteristics</cite>.

Key morphological characteristics
- Macro features: shelf-shaped basidiocarp with upper surface deep red, glossy or lacquered, often with a lacunose or shallow-sulcate pattern; pileus typically sessile or lateral; stipe present and lateral; context tough to woody; pore surface pale to white, non-glairy, and often shiny in fresh specimens. <cite id="51d83e91-5">A beautiful polypore found on hardwoods with a deep red, lacquered-looking upper surface</cite> <cite id="51d83e91-7">Tough, corky to woody pileus, dark reddish brown with a varnish-like crust and glabrous surface, with a lateral stipe and a pore surface below</cite> <cite id="51d83e91-3">Strongly laccate, shallow sulcate, reddish-brown pileus, lateral stipe, white pore surface, and brown context</cite> <cite id="29e68f26-2">Ganoderma species are polypores with a bright white pore surface and spores 13–15 × 7.5–8.5 μm</cite>.
- Pore and margin: pore density commonly 2–4 pores per mm; margins of young fruiting bodies may retain yellowish or red-orange hues and a slightly different texture; caps can become dull and spore-deposited with age. <cite id="29e68f26-2">All Ganoderma species are polypores with bright white pore surface; spores 13–15 × 7.5–8.5 μm</cite> <cite id="51d83e91-4">Top surface is shiny with red-orange color in younger fruit; pore surface is polyporous with younger edges yellowed</cite>.
- Spore print and microscopic features: spore print is brown; spores broadly ellipsoid, with size reported around 11.8–15 × 8.7–9.9 μm, and spore operculum/columella absent (typical of polypores). <cite id="e1269462-0">Spore size in Ganoderma spp. reported at 13.2×8.9 μm and 11.8×8.7 μm</cite> <cite id="652f41df-6">Spore print is brown</cite> <cite id="29e68f26-2">Spores 13–15 × 7.5–8.5 μm</cite>.
- Texture and luster (“varnished conk”): mature fruit bodies often have a smooth, glossy, dark red to reddish-brown exterior that can become rough and darker with spore deposition; overall structure becomes corky to woody with age. <cite id="51d83e91-5">Deep red cap with lacquered-looking upper surface</cite> <cite id="51d83e91-7">Varnish-like crust, glabrous pileus, and stipe 3 cm thick at base; pore surface below</cite>.

Ecological roles and mode of decay
- Decomposer guild: Ganoderma species include fungi that cause white rot and other wood-degrading strategies, broadly contributing to carbon cycling in forest ecosystems; G. lucidum occupies this guild as a wood decay fungus on hardwoods. <cite id="29e68f26-4">Ganoderma is a large, diverse genus of wood decay fungi; species include those that cause white rot on a variety of tree species</cite>.
- Parasitic/saprophytic spectrum: many populations are saprophytic on dead hardwoods, but some parasitize living hosts; G. lucidum is considered parasitic in some descriptions and saprophytic in others, reflecting local ecology and host condition. <cite id="652f41df-0">Ganoderma lucidium is mainly parasitic or saprophytic</cite> <cite id="29e68f26-7">Reishi mushrooms are saprophytic to parasitic, growing on dead or decaying wood and infecting living trees</cite>.
- Hosts and habitat: commonly reported on hardwoods such as oak and chestnut in the Southeastern United States and broadly on hardwoods across Asia and North America; fruiting arises on logs, stumps, buried roots, and occasionally on trunks, indicating active decay. <cite id="51d83e91-1">Ganoderma can rot the roots and/or lower trunk of many tree species</cite> <cite id="51d83e91-5">Found on the wood of hardwoods with a deep red, lacquered cap</cite> <cite id="652f41df-7">Grows on decaying hardwood trees</cite> <cite id="e1269462-5">Ganoderma lucidum illustrated with fruiting body, pores, and spore (20 μm scale)</cite> <cite id="e1269462-4">When Ganoderma fruiting bodies are observed, it indicates active wood decay on fallen logs, buried roots, or trunks</cite>.
- Indicator function: presence of fruiting bodies indicates ongoing decay and can help detect susceptible trees or wood, especially in hardwood-dominated forests. <cite id="e1269462-4">Fruiting of Ganoderma indicates active decay on logs, roots, or trunks</cite> <cite id="51d83e91-1">Ganoderma root and trunk rot across many tree species</cite>.

Growth habits and life cycle observations
- In situ: perennial growth on woody substrates with outward-facing hymenium forming bracket conks; fruiting typically develops on dead or dying hardwoods, sometimes on stumps/logs, and can also occur on lower trunks; mature basidiocarps harden and darken, with glossy surfaces. <cite id="51d83e91-7">Woolly to woody pileus with a lateral stipe and white pore surface is characteristic of Ganoderma sessile; the pileus is often described as tough and with a varnished luster</cite> <cite id="51d83e91-3">Strongly laccate,reddish-brown pileus, lateral stipe, white pore surface, and brown context indicate a bracket form</cite> <cite id="e1269462-4">Fruiting on fallen logs, buried roots, or trunks reflects active decay and perennial habit</cite>.
- Cultivation: practical management separates mycelial growth on logs or culture media from fruiting body initiation; cultivation emphasizes mycelium colonization of sawdust/segmented wood and controlled fruiting on artificial substrates. <cite id="652f41df-2">Cultivation of G. lucidum focuses on mycelium and fruiting body stages, including growth on segmented wood and substitution fruiting substrates</cite> <cite id="652f41df-8">Macro- and micro-morphology of G. lucidum (pileus, stipe, veil, lamellae analogs) are examined to identify species</cite> <cite id="652f41df-3">Under nutrient-poor media, G. lucidum mycelium has a less branching network and distinct macro-morphological appearance</cite>.
- Developmental morphology: mycelium colonizes host tissue and later differentiates into shelf-shaped basidiocarps with central pores and lateral stipes; mature basidiocarps produce brown spores on the hymenial surface for dispersal. <cite id="51d83e91-3">White pore surface and brown context are early stages toward mature basidiocarp differentiation</cite> <cite id="e1269462-6">Spore print brown indicates basidiospore discharge onto a hymenial surface</cite>.

Preferred substrates and geographic/habitat associations
- Substrates: dead or decaying hardwoods in forests, including fallen logs, stumps, buried roots, and lower trunks; in cultivation, sawdust, wood chips, and agricultural lignocellulosics (e.g., paddy straw, bagasse, maize stalks) support mycelial growth and fruiting when properly managed. <cite id="51d83e91-0">Bracket fungi are shelflike with downfacing pores for spore dispersal</cite> <cite id="51d83e91-1">Ganoderma can rot roots and lower trunks of many tree species</cite> <cite id="e1269462-4">Fruiting on logs, buried roots, and trunks</cite> <cite id="652f41df-2">Segmented wood and substitute substrates used to cultivate G. lucidum fruiting bodies</cite> <cite id="652f41df-4">Growth tested on paddy straw, sugarcane bagasse, maize stalk, saw dust under lab conditions</cite>.
- Host trees: widely reported on oaks and chestnuts in North America, and on various hardwoods across Asia; in the Southeastern U.S., species are common on hickories, oaks, and other hardwoods; in tropical regions, association with diverse hardwood genera is typical. <cite id="51d83e91-5">Ganoderma sessile is found on the wood of hardwoods with deep red, lacquered cap</cite> <cite id="29e68f26-4">Ganoderma includes white-rot species across many tree species</cite> <cite id="29e68f26-0">Parasitic or saprophytic on hardwoods</cite> <cite id="652f41df-7">Commonly grows on decaying hardwood trees</cite> <cite id="29e68f26-1">An oriental fungus with large, dark, glossy, woody basidiocarp</cite>.
- Subtropical/tropical forests: G. lucidum is recognized across East Asia and other tropical/subtropical hardwood forests where it forms characteristic red, glossy conks on decaying hardwoods. <cite id="29e68f26-6">Across Asia, G. lucidum grows as parasite or saprotroph on a variety of trees</cite> <cite id="51d83e91-6">Ganoderma lucidum occurs in Europe and Asia and North America</cite>.
- Substrate variability and adaptation: both natural wood and artificial lignocellulosics support growth; macroscopic morphology adapts to nutrient conditions, showing less branched mycelium networks in nutrient-poor media, while fruiting morphology depends on wood type and maturation cues. <cite id="652f41df-3">In nutrient-poor media, G. lucidum mycelium exhibits less branching and distinct macro morphology</cite> <cite id="652f41df-2">Substrate choice (segmented wood vs substitutes) guides successful fruiting</cite>.

Practical identification and diagnostics
- Field keys emphasize pileus/stipe/pore features, laccate reddish-brown coloration, white pore surface, and brown spores; stipe present and lateral is typical, and spore size ~12–15 μm helps narrow identifications. <cite id="652f41df-9">Overholts’ taxonomy used host specificity, macroscopic morphology, and spore characteristics for Ganoderma identification</cite> <cite id="51d83e91-3">Reddish-brown, laccate pileus with a white pore surface and lateral stipe</cite> <cite id="29e68f26-2">Spores 13–15 × 7.5–8.5 μm; white pore surface</cite> <cite id="e1269462-6">Spore print is brown</cite> <cite id="e1269462-5">Illustrative G. lucidum fruiting body and pore/spore anatomy</cite>.
- Cross-species distinctions: relative to other Ganoderma like G. applanatum, G. lucidum retains a shelf-like pileus with lateral stipe and red, varnished luster rather than flattened, applanate caps; pore sizes and spore dimensions remain diagnostic within ~2–4 pores/mm. <cite id="51d83e91-2">Ganoderma applanatum is a perennial, hard, woody, sessile conk, grayish-white when young with dull texture</cite> <cite id="29e68f26-2">2–4 pores per mm and spores ~13–15 × 7.5–8.5 μm define the polypore morphology</cite>.

Implications for forest ecology and management
- Decomposer impact: by rotting roots, stumps, and lower trunks of many hardwoods, Ganoderma spp. contribute substantially to coarse woody debris breakdown and nutrient cycling; their fruiting bodies serve as bioindicators of decay potential in hardwood stands. <cite id="51d83e91-1">Ganoderma can rot roots and lower trunks of many tree species</cite> <cite id="e1269462-4">Fruiting indicates active decay on logs, roots, and trunks</cite>.
- Host selection: while many reports highlight oaks and chestnuts, the genus shows host breadth across temperate and tropical hardwoods; populations may be saprotrophic on dead wood or parasitic on stressed or dying trees, complicating management strategies in forestry and urban woodlands. <cite id="51d83e91-5">Hardwoods as hosts with lacquered caps</cite> <cite id="652f41df-0">Ganoderma lucidium is mainly parasitic or saprophytic</cite> <cite id="29e68f26-7">Grows on dead wood and infects living hardwoods</cite>.
- Cultivation context: understanding that G. lucidum shifts between mycelial growth on lignocellulosics and conk differentiation aligns with its morphological traits (from white, non-glabrous context to glossy red pileus and brown spores) and ecological roles in breaking down complex wood polysaccharides. <cite id="652f41df-2">Fruiting body cultivation uses segmented wood and substitutes</cite> <cite id="29e68f26-4">White-rot capacity is distributed among Ganoderma species</cite> <cite id="e1269462-6">Spore print brown reflects basidial maturation</cite>.

Summary: Spilanthol is a bioactive spiroamide primarily active against agricultural and medical insect pests, with evidence that it penetrates insect integument and interferes with the nervous system, causing antifeedant and toxic effects that culminate in mortality. Electrophysiological and behavioral studies on related systems show plant elicitors can engage insect gustatory/chemosensory pathways to suppress feeding and reproduction, consistent with spilanthol’s potent antifeedant and insecticidal profiles. Quantitative bioassays demonstrate high acute and delayed mortalities at relatively low doses, and compound-specific studies report low LD50 values, especially in Lepidoptera and in acaricidal assays versus Rhipicephalus ticks. Evidence also shows strong activity from spilanthol-rich fractions against lepidopteran pests and near-complete mortality of some coleopteran adults in extract assays.

Mechanism: integumental uptake and neurotoxic/antifeedant actions
- A recent review of the acmella genus notes that spilanthol acts by penetrating the insect integumental system and interfering with the nervous system in Blattodea, providing direct mechanistic evidence for a contact-absorption route to neurotoxicity in insects, with rapid behavioral and physiological disruption downstream. <cite id="b3695d1b-1">The spilanthol exerts insecticidal activity by penetrating the insect integumental system and interfering with the nervous system</cite>.
- Antifeedant/chemosensory pathways provide a complementary mechanism: insect feeding decisions depend on gustatory and olfactory receptors (GRs/ORs) to detect aversive plant chemicals; exposure to such electrophilic plant elicitors can evoke “aversive taste” and avoidance via GR pathways. Although not spilanthol-specific in every case, closely related plant elicitors activate “wasabi taste” TRP channels and insect GRs to suppress feeding and oviposition, aligning with spilanthol’s observed antifeedant profiles in lepidopterans and coleopterans. <cite id="db65c997-5">These electrophiles activate the “wasabi taste receptor” TrpA1, which is conserved in flies and humans</cite> <cite id="db65c997-6">Insect survival depends on contact chemosensation to sense and avoid consuming plant-derived insecticides</cite> <cite id="db65c997-4">Electrophysiological analyses revealed that [brassinolide] inhibits larval feeding and female oviposition in Plutella xylostella</cite>.

Physiological impacts observed in insects exposed to spilanthol
- Behavioral/antifeedant suppression: Across Lepidoptera, low concentrations of spilanthol-rich extracts or isolated spilanthol suppress feeding and oviposition, consistent with neurogustatory interference; such suppression immediately disrupts energy intake and reproductive physiology. <cite id="b3695d1b-1">Interference with the nervous system commencing from integumental penetration</cite> <cite id="db65c997-4">Electrophysiological analyses revealed that [plant elicitor] inhibits larval feeding and female oviposition</cite>.
- Neurophysiological stress: The neurotoxic interference underpins downstream metabolic and oxidative stress. While direct spilanthol measurement of ion channels or neurotransmission is still limited in the current evidence set, the same class of plant electrophiles activates nociceptor-like pathways and aversive taste circuits in insects, and spilanthol-rich fractions from Acmella oleracea produce near-complete mortality in tomato pests, indicating strong physiological collapse. <cite id="db65c997-5">Plant electrophiles activate conserved TrpA1 nociceptor-like receptors mediating aversion</cite> <cite id="b3695d1b-3">A spilanthol-rich fraction elicited strong bioactivity against Tuta absoluta tomato pests</cite>.
- Detoxification/metabolic induction: Botanical insecticides often induce detox enzymes as part of innate resistance; this selective pressure suggests spilanthol exposure can elevate metabolic burden in pests and contributes to delayed mortality when combined with plant defense responses. <cite id="b3695d1b-4">Mechanistic surveys of botanical insecticides emphasize resistance mechanisms including detoxification induction</cite>.
- Microbiome/gut interactions: Spilanthol’s lipophilicity and antimicrobial activities in mammals suggest potential disruption of insect gut symbioses, but direct gut-microbiome studies specific to spilanthol are sparse in these snippets; nonetheless, the observed antifeedant and repellent effects imply reduced nutrient intake and possible gut dysbiosis, consistent with secondary toxicity. <cite id="b3695d1b-9">Spilanthol exhibits broad biological activities including antimutagenic and anti-cancer effects</cite> <cite id="b3695d1b-1">Integumental penetration and nervous-system interference facilitate systemic physiological stress</cite>.
- Open mechanistic gaps and how to resolve them: Direct electrophysiology of spilanthol on lepidopteran GRs/ORs in Plutella/Tuta, measurement of AChE inhibition or ion-channel modulation by spilanthol in insects, and Drosophila/Culex RNAi screens for GR/OR/NR genes during spilanthol exposure would pin down primary receptor targets and neurochemical cascades. <cite id="db65c997-1">GRs are integral to Lepidoptera chemosensation and are promising mechanistic targets for antifeedant insecticids</cite>.

Evidence for insect mortality and efficacy across taxa
- Quantitative insecticidal potency:
  - Plutella xylostella (diamondback moth, Lepidoptera): Spilanthol-rich seed extracts caused 95–100% mortality at 2 g/L and 60–70% to 80–90% mortality at 5 g/L after 48 h in feeding assays. <cite id="b3695d1b-2">Highest activity of 95–100% was observed at low dose of 2 g/L with spilanthol, while 60–70 and 80–90% mortality at 5 g/L</cite> <cite id="1b4b32dc-7">60–70 and 80–90% mortality at 5 g/L in crude seed extracts after 48 hours exposure</cite>.
  - Tuta absoluta (tomato moth, Lepidoptera): The pure spilanthol (compound 1) exhibited the lowest LD50 among bioactive compounds, approximately fivefold more toxic than other constituents in acaricidal/neuroactive assays, with 100% mortality endpoints reported for spilanthol-rich fractions in field-relevant bioassays. <cite id="1b4b32dc-2">Compound 1 (spilanthol) exhibited the highest toxicity to Tuta absoluta, with the lowest LD50; spilanthol was approximately 5 times more toxic</cite> <cite id="1b4b32dc-4">Spilanthol exhibited the highest toxicity to Tuta absoluta, with the lowest LD50 (0.13 μg mg−1)</cite> <cite id="1b4b32dc-6">Spilanthol exhibited the highest toxicity to Tuta absoluta, with the lowest LD50 (0.13 µg mg−1)</cite> <cite id="b3695d1b-3">A spilanthol-rich fraction elicited strong bioactivity against Tuta absoluta</cite>.
  - Adults of the beetles Ceraemia ferrugineus and Diabrotica diaperinus showed 100% mortality with Acmella oleracea extracts, though activity varied by species and preparation, indicating strong but sometimes dose-dependent efficacy. <cite id="1b4b32dc-5">Both extracts achieved complete mortality (100.0%) of C. ferrugineus adults; A. diaperinus adult mortalities were lower and extract-dependent</cite>.
- Contact and topical toxicity (ticks and model pests): Dichloromethane fractions enriched in spilanthol caused elevated larval mortality in Rhipicephalus microplus ticks, consistent with rapid integumental absorption and neurotoxicity. <cite id="1b4b32dc-3">The dichloromethane fraction with 99% spilanthol showed higher activity, resulting in a larval mortality of R. microplus</cite>.
- Antifeedant/repellent effects as morbidity drivers: Antifeedant assays in Lepidoptera and observations of oviposition inhibition suggest that even sublethal exposures reduce nutrient intake and egg production, increasing population-level mortality under sustained exposure. <cite id="db65c997-4">Electrophysiological analyses revealed that [plant elicitor] inhibits larval feeding and female oviposition</cite> <cite id="b3695d1b-1">Spilanthol interferes with the nervous system upon integumental entry, consistent with antifeedant behaviors</cite>.
- Comparative notes and synergy: Spilanthol’s rapid onset contact toxicity complements slower-acting systemic botanicals; synergy studies of plant volatiles and extracts against stored-product pests indicate strong volatile components that can potentiate mortality, supporting a mixed contact–uptake mechanism relevant to spilanthol’s behavior in multi-component oils. <cite id="b3695d1b-9">Spilanthol-rich essential oil from Acmella oleracea shows strong acaricidal and insecticidal activity</cite> <cite id="b3695d1b-9">Synergistic insecticidal activity of plant volatile compounds identifies potent EO-derived volatiles against Sitophilus zeamais</cite>.

Integrative picture and physiological cascade
- Entry: Lipophilic spilanthol easily crosses insect cuticle/procuticle, enabling rapid topical and oral toxicity; its molecular traits parallel known plant elicitors that activate insect nociceptive and aversive taste pathways. <cite id="b3695d1b-1">Spilanthol penetrates the insect integument and interferes with the nervous system</cite> <cite id="db65c997-5">Plant electrophiles activate conserved aversive nociceptor-like receptors in insects</cite>.
- Central and peripheral neurotoxicity: Interference with GR/OR-mediated gustation and nociceptive signaling suppresses feeding, disrupts oviposition, and generates pain-like avoidance, with systemic metabolic consequences. <cite id="db65c997-1">GRs underpin chemosensation in Lepidoptera and act as targets for antifeedant compounds</cite> <cite id="db65c997-4">Inhibition of feeding and oviposition by plant elicitors in Plutella xylostella</cite>.
- Physiological collapse and mortality: Reduced feeding plus neurotoxic stress elevate metabolic rate and oxidative damage, overwhelm detox pathways, and induce systemic failure; quantitative assays show LD50 values that are orders of magnitude lower than mammalian equivalents, reflecting high insect potency. <cite id="1b4b32dc-2">Spilanthol had the lowest LD50 vs other compounds against Tuta absoluta and was ~5× more toxic</cite> <cite id="1b4b32dc-4">LD50 of spilanthol in Tuta absoluta was reported as 0.13 μg mg−1</cite> <cite id="b3695d1b-7">High percentages of mortality within 48 h at low g/L doses</cite>.
- Microbiome implications: Although direct in vivo spilanthol gut-microbiome perturbation data are limited here, its antimicrobial activities and lipophilicity support interactions with gut symbionts, potentially contributing to nutrient and barrier dysfunction alongside neurobehavioral suppression. <cite id="b3695d1b-9">Spilanthol’s antimutagenic and anti-cancer activities underpin antimicrobial potential relevant to gut symbioses</cite>.

Practical implications and remaining uncertainties
- Agricultural/medical relevance: Spilanthol’s rapid, dose-responsive mortality and strong antifeedant/oviposition effects make it a candidate for push–pull IPM, botanical formulations, and synergists with synthetic pyrethroids; extract-derived volatiles can enhance efficacy against stored-product moths. <cite id="b3695d1b-9">Acmella oleracea extracts show complete mortality in coleopteran adults, and volatile synergy increases insecticidal activity</cite> <cite id="1b4b32dc-9">EO-derived volatiles exhibit potent insecticidal activity, suggesting formulation strategies</cite>.
- Safety contrasts: In silico rodent LD50 prediction for spilanthol (~4.38 mg/kg oral) classifies it as low acute toxicity in mammals, contrasting with high insect potency, which supports selectivity but requires careful formulation and exposure control. <cite id="1b4b32dc-5">An in silico predicted oral LD50 of 4.378 mg/kg for spilanthol, toxicity class 5</cite>.
- Open mechanistic frontiers: Pinpointing specific insect GR/OR subtypes and neurochemical targets for spilanthol, measuring oxidative stress/apoptosis markers post-exposure, and directly quantifying gut microbiome shifts after spilanthol challenge would strengthen causal links beyond the current neurobehavioral and toxicological evidence. <cite id="db65c997-1">GR-focused studies provide frameworks to identify direct antifeedant targets</cite> <cite id="b3695d1b-1">Integumental neurotoxic entry model motivates targeted biochemical assays</cite>.

In sum, spilanthol exerts insecticidal effects by penetrating the cuticle, engaging chemosensory and nociceptive neural circuits to induce antifeedant and neurotoxic responses, disrupting feeding and reproduction, and precipitating metabolic and systemic failure that manifests as high mortality at low doses across multiple insect orders. Direct antifeedant behavior and LD50/mortality data, along with reviews of its nervous-system interference and lipophilic access, together support a coherent model, while targeted electrophysiology, neurochemical, and microbiome studies offer promising next steps to refine mechanisms. <cite id="b3695d1b-1">Spilanthol interferes with the nervous system after integumental penetration</cite> <cite id="db65c997-4">Plant elicitors can suppress feeding and oviposition in Lepidoptera</cite> <cite id="b3695d1b-2">Spilanthol yields 95–100% mortality at 2 g/L in Plutella xylostella within 48 h</cite> <cite id="1b4b32dc-2">Spilanthol shows the lowest LD50 and ~5× higher toxicity than other compounds in Tuta absoluta</cite> <cite id="1b4b32dc-5">A. oleracea extracts can achieve 100% mortality in some coleopteran adults</cite> <cite id="b3695d1b-3">Spilanthol-rich fractions deliver strong bioactivity against tomato pests</cite> <cite id="db65c997-5">Electrophilic plant molecules activate conserved aversive nociceptor pathways, explaining antifeedant behavior</cite>.

Summary of mechanisms and outcomes

- Elevated Na+ in saline soils imposes both osmotic and ionic stress that reduce root water uptake and nutrient acquisition while promoting Na+ toxicity in turfgrass tissues, leading to impaired growth and function under traffic and maintenance stress compared to nonsaline controls.<cite id="47d8814a-5">As salinity levels increase, turfgrasses extract water less easily from soil, aggravating drought conditions, and high soil salinity can also cause nutrient problems</cite><cite id="47d8814a-8">Sodium is a special case because it not only elevates total salinity; at high levels it can cause direct turf injury and reduce soil water availability to the turf</cite>. Elevated Na+ concentration inhibits K+ ion uptake, shifting the K+/Na+ ratio unfavorably and causing K+ deficiency symptoms; Na+ also antagonizes Ca2+, Mg2+, and Mn2+ uptake, compounding ion imbalances in shoots and roots.<cite id="47d8814a-1">High Na+ concentration in salt-stressed plants affects the inhibition of K+ ions uptake and, therefore, a deficiency of K+ could be observed</cite><cite id="47d8814a-8">Na+ may inhibit K+, calcium, magnesium, and manganese uptake</cite>.

Impact on ion uptake processes

- Na+ uptake and osmotic stress feedback on ion homeostasis: Salinity increases Na+ and Cl− in soil solution, which raises osmotic pressure, impedes water entry, and perturbs membrane transporters; at the organismal level, high salt concentrations cause Na+ and Cl− toxicity and destabilize ion homeostasis.<cite id="47d8814a-2">Salinity stress causes osmotic stress, Na+ and Cl− toxicity, and negative effects on ion homeostasis as high salt concentration disrupts balances</cite>. In turfgrasses, ion imbalances from excessive NaCl uptake reduce nutrient availability and cause toxicities, highlighting competition and toxicity as central mechanisms in saline soils.<cite id="47d8814a-0">Due to enhanced nutrient competition as a result of excessive NaCl uptake in saline conditions, ion imbalances and toxicities are common effects of salt stress</cite>.

- Transporter-mediated compensation/exclusion in turf: Turfgrasses adapt by regulating transporters for Na+ and K+ handling, including NHX vacuolar Na+/H+ exchangers and HKT Na+/K+ transporters that exclude Na+ from shoots and load it into vacuoles or roots; SOS1-type pumps contribute to sequestration, and these act in concert to restore Na+ homeostasis under saline conditions.<cite id="adb7415b-1">Turfgrass adapts to salt stress by regulating ion transporter genes (e.g., NHX1 and HKT), synthesizing osmotic regulators (e.g., proline)</cite><cite id="adb7415b-0">SOS1, HKT1;5, and NHX1 synergistically regulate Na+ homeostasis by controlling Na+ transport at the whole-plant level under lower and higher salinity</cite>. Morphological traits such as leaf salt glands in manilagrass and bermudagrass facilitate Na+ exclusion from shoots, supporting species variation in salt tolerance strategies.<cite id="b922c594-5">Salinity tolerance was associated with exclusion of Na+ and Cl− from shoots, aided by leaf salt glands in manilagrass and bermudagrass</cite>.

- Nutrient antagonism and soil chemistry: Na+ in irrigation and soil water increases extractable Na+ and soil pH, aggravating nutrient fixation/insolubility and reducing availability of P, K, Ca, and Mg to roots, even as Na+ displaces cations on exchange sites; turf response depends on water uptake capacity and cation selectivity of roots under reduced osmotic water flow.<cite id="47d8814a-4">Higher sodium content in irrigation water results in higher pH and more alkaline soil conditions; extractable Na+ from soils increased markedly with salinization</cite><cite id="47d8814a-5">High soil salinity can cause nutrient problems for turfgrasses</cite><cite id="47d8814a-8">Na+ inhibits K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, Mn2+ uptake and reduces soil water availability</cite>. Practically, canopy color darkens or yellows with increasing NaCl; for example, bermudagrass canopy color lightened as salinity increased from 7000 to 21000 mg/L NaCl, demonstrating dose–response uptake and visual stress linked to ionic imbalance and impaired water relations.<cite id="b922c594-3">Bermudagrass canopy color changed to lighter green as salinity stress increased from 7000 to 21000 mg/L NaCl</cite>.

Changes in enzymatic functions and physiology

- Photosynthesis and “greenness”: Under saline stress, net photosynthesis typically declines because Na+ inhibits mesophyll and stomatal processes, RuBisCO activity, and electron transport, and Cl− can disrupt photosystems; turf quality and chlorophyll content deteriorate with increasing salt concentration and duration, with marked cultivar and species differences.<cite id="b922c594-0">Turf quality declined with increasing salt concentration and duration of salinity treatment in both turfgrass species assessed; physiological responses reflect salt stress impacts</cite><cite id="b922c594-6">Normally, salinity favors reduction in photosynthesis activity; however, bermudagrass shows a significantly higher photosynthetic rate, indicating species-specific responses</cite>. Reviews emphasize that salinity is a major edaphic stressor for turfgrasses, interacting with traffic, drought, and nutrient imbalance, all of which intersect with energy-demanding enzymatic processes in leaves and roots.<cite id="b922c594-1">Soil salinity is a major edaphic stressor for turfgrasses, often alongside drought, flooding, traffic, and unbalanced nutrients</cite>.

- Oxidative stress and antioxidant enzymes: Na+ and Cl− influx under saline conditions triggers reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, activating antioxidant defenses (SOD, POD, CAT) to protect membranes and enzymes; turfgrasses synthesize osmoprotectants like proline that are tightly linked to Na+ stress signaling and gene regulation, and these metabolic shifts are part of the turfgrass salinity response program.<cite id="adb7415b-1">Turfgrass adapts by synthesizing osmotic regulators such as proline under salt stress</cite><cite id="b922c594-5">Salinity tolerance mechanisms in turfgrasses include exclusion of Na+ and increased proline/osmotic regulation</cite>. Extension and research syntheses for putting greens and golf course systems emphasize that Na+ not only raises osmotic potential but also directly injures turf at high levels, consistent with enzyme dysfunction and oxidative damage that antioxidant enzyme induction seeks to mitigate.<cite id="47d8814a-8">Ion toxicity of high Na+ in plant tissues and reduced soil water uptake are specific concerns for turf</cite><cite id="47d8814a-9">Sodium can cause direct turf injury and reduce soil water availability, reflecting physiologic stress</cite>.

- Hormonal and signaling shifts: The stress responses reprogram transport and metabolism. Elevated Na+ perturbs K+ homeostasis and activates K+ import and Na+ sequestration pathways while stimulating osmoprotectant biosynthesis, which ties hormone signaling (e.g., ABA) and stress-responsive transcription factors to transporter expression and enzymatic adjustments under field and irrigation salinity scenarios.<cite id="47d8814a-1">High Na+ inhibits K+ uptake, leading to K+ deficiency under salinity</cite><cite id="adb7415b-0">SOS1, HKT1;5, and NHX1 function synergistically to regulate Na+ homeostasis across salinity levels</cite><cite id="adb7415b-1">Turfgrass upregulates NHX/HKT transporters and proline synthesis under salt</cite>. Sustained NaCl exposure alters canopy color and growth trajectories because of cumulative water stress and nutrient antagonism, with visual and biochemical tradeoffs across species such as bermudagrass and Kentucky bluegrass.<cite id="b922c594-3">Color shifts in bermudagrass as salinity increases reflect stress intensity</cite><cite id="b922c594-7">Kentucky bluegrass is considered sensitive to moderate levels of drought and salinity</cite>.

Practical implications for turfgrasses

- Ion uptake and maintenance: Elevated Na+ reduces K+ and Ca2+ uptake, increases Na+ accumulation in shoots and roots, and favors Na+ toxicity at high levels, leading to membrane leakage, enzyme inhibition, and chlorosis; turf recovery and wear tolerance depend on irrigation management, leaching, and soil amendments to restore osmotic balance and cation availability.<cite id="47d8814a-1">High Na+ inhibits K+ uptake and can cause K+ deficiency</cite><cite id="47d8814a-8">Na+ inhibits Ca2+, Mg2+, and Mn2+ uptake, with direct injury at high levels</cite><cite id="47d8814a-5">High soil salinity aggravates drought-like water stress for turf</cite>.

- Transporter-based breeding/management: Selection for cultivars expressing strong HKT-mediated Na+ exclusion, active SOS1/NHX sequestration, and enhanced osmoprotectant synthesis improves turf performance under saline irrigation or coastal/effluent reuse; extension guidance and USGA practices stress salinity avoidance/mitigation and recognizing early injury from Na+ to maintain enzyme function and turf quality.<cite id="b922c594-5">Leaf salt glands aid Na+ exclusion in tolerant species like manilagrass and bermudagrass</cite><cite id="adb7415b-1">Turfgrass adapts by regulating NHX/HKT and proline; these traits are targets for improved tolerance</cite><cite id="b922c594-9">Managing salinity in putting greens emphasizes Na+’s special role in reducing soil water and causing injury</cite>.

- Species and cultivar differences: Warm-season turfgrasses (e.g., bermudagrass) often maintain relatively higher photosynthetic rates and turf quality than cool-season species (e.g., Kentucky bluegrass) under comparable salinity due to differential Na+/K+ transport, salt glands, and acclimation capacity; nonetheless, prolonged saline exposure still reduces PSII function, growth, and color across species, underscoring the need for salt-tolerant genotypes matched to irrigation water quality.<cite id="b922c594-6">Bermudagrass shows a significantly higher photosynthetic rate under salinity compared to the general trend</cite><cite id="b922c594-7">Kentucky bluegrass is sensitive to salinity and drought</cite><cite id="47d8814a-3">Selection of turfgrass varieties should match salinity and irrigation source to avoid injury</cite>.

Key takeaways

- Elevated Na+ in saline soils worsens osmotic and ionic constraints, shifting root uptake toward Na+ with concomitant K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, and Mn2+ antagonism; this disrupts ion homeostasis and damages enzymes and membranes, reducing turf quality unless compensated by Na+ exclusion/sequestration transporters and osmoprotectant metabolism.<cite id="47d8814a-0">Excessive NaCl uptake fosters nutrient competition, ion imbalances, and toxicities</cite><cite id="adb7415b-0">SOS1, HKT1;5, and NHX1 act together to maintain Na+ homeostasis across salinity</cite><cite id="47d8814a-8">Na+ inhibits multiple cation uptakes and causes direct injury</cite>. 

- Photosynthetic enzymes and processes decline under salinity, though the magnitude varies by species and cultivar; antioxidant enzyme induction and proline accumulation reflect turfgrass attempts to buffer ROS and ionic stress, but persistent Na+ load limits wear tolerance and requires cultural and genetic strategies aligned to local salinity risks.<cite id="b922c594-0">Turf quality declines with increasing salinity and duration</cite><cite id="b922c594-6">Photosynthesis often declines with salinity but can remain relatively higher in bermudagrass</cite><cite id="adb7415b-1">Osmoprotectant synthesis and transporter regulation underpin turfgrass salt adaptation</cite><cite id="47d8814a-9">Recognizing salinity’s effects is essential for putting green and high-maintenance turf</cite>.

Uncertainties and research needs

- Direct, species-specific measurements of SOD/POD/CAT activity, PSII Fv/Fm dynamics, and K+/Na+ transporter flux kinetics under controlled saline soils in key turf species (Zoysia, Poa, Cynodon, Bouteloua) would refine thresholds for injury and best management practices; current turf reviews and trials provide directional evidence but less mechanistic kinetic resolution in field-realistic salinity settings.<cite id="b922c594-1">Review-level synthesis emphasizes salinity as a major stressor but species-by-salt response heterogeneity remains a focus</cite><cite id="47d8814a-3">Selection of varieties should match salinity levels, reflecting genotype-by-environment interactions under salt stress</cite>.

Summary of main chemical classes
- Leaves of Cinnamomum osmophloeum are rich in aromatic leaf essential oils concentrated in phenylpropanoid/monoterpene-derived volatiles, with important phenolic/phenylpropanoid aglycones and appended methoxyl esters (e.g., cinnamaldehyde, cinnamic alcohol, cinnamyl acetate, coumarin), alongside significant polyphenolic and flavonoid glycosides in polar extracts. <cite id="b078c3ee-2">Abundant chemicals have been isolated from this genus, such as terpenes, phenylpropanoids, lignans, and flavonoids</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-5">Essential-oil constituents of C. osmophloeum leaves are chemically similar to those in the bark oils of Cinnamomum cassia</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-8">Hydrosol composition shows trans‑cinnamaldehyde, trans‑cinnamyl acetate, and coumarin as major components</cite>.
- Two recurrent leaf essential oil chemotypes are reported: linalool-dominant (monoterpene-oriented) and cinnamaldehyde/cinnamyl acetate–dominant (benzene-phenyl–derived phenylpropanoids), with coumarin appearing as a notable oxygenated monoterpenoid/pyranocoumarin marker in several samples. <cite id="b078c3ee-0">In some provenances cinnamaldehyde is the major leaf constituent, whereas in others linalool predominates</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-0">Cinnamomum osmophloeum ct. linalool forms a defined chemotype and can be a potential source of S-(+)-linalool</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-2">A linalool chemotype of leaf EO has been resolved with linalool at 93.30% (with minor 2-methyl benzofuran, α-pinene, and cinnamyl acetate)</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-1">Hydrodistillation of C. osmophloeum (linalool chemotype) yields quantitatively high linalool</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-3">Leaf EO of C. osmophloeum has also been reported with cinnamyl acetate 40.8%, cinnamaldehyde 9.1%, and sesquiterpenes such as caryophyllene oxide</cite>.

Quantitative composition examples across analyses
- Volatile/essential-oil fraction:
  - Hydrosol: trans‑cinnamaldehyde 65.03%, trans‑cinnamyl acetate 7.57%, coumarin 4.31%, with lower levels of cinnamic alcohol/ester and monoterpene oxides depending on sample. <cite id="b078c3ee-8">Composition of C. osmophloeum hydrosol shows trans‑cinnamaldehyde (65.03%), trans‑cinnamyl acetate (7.57%), and coumarin (4.31%) as the main constituents</cite>.
  - GC‑MS essential oils (leaf distillates): chemotype-driven differences are large. Linalool chemotype can reach up to 93–94% linalool by area%; cinnamaldehyde/cinnamyl acetate chemotypes show cinnamaldehyde ~9–93% across studies depending on sample and method, with cinnamyl acetate often ~7–41% and trace coumarin to ~4%. <cite id="b66419ab-2">Linalool chemotype: linalool 93.30%, 2‑methyl benzofuran 1.99%, α‑pinene 0.66%, cinnamyl acetate minor</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-3">In another report, cinnamyl acetate 40.8%, trans‑cinnamaldehyde 9.1%, caryophyllene oxide 6.2%, T‑cadinol 5.5%, and α‑humulene oxide</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-0">Across provenances, cinnamaldehyde is major in some samples whereas linalool is major in others</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-1">Hydrodistillation efficiently extracts S-(+)-linalool from the linalool chemotype</cite>.
  - Broader genus comparison underscores that “aromatic” dominance (eugenol/cinnamaldehyde) is a hallmark of Cinnamomum leaf/inner-bark oils, reinforcing expectations for osmophloeum chemistries. <cite id="b078c3ee-4">Cinnamomum leaf and bark EOs in related species often contain high eugenol and cinnamaldehyde, indicating shared aromatic-phenylpropanoid profiles</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-5">Leaf EO chemistries of osmophloeum resemble C. cassia</cite>.
- Polar/phenolic fraction (water and methanolic/solvothermic extracts):
  - Water extraction (11 provenances): extracts are rich in antioxidant phenolics and flavonoid glycosides; total phenolic contents of antioxidant-enriched water extracts span up to 160.9 mg GAE/g dry leaves and contain biologically active flavonoids such as epicatechin/procyanidin-related glycosides and phenolic acids. <cite id="b078c3ee-1">Leaf water extracts contained antioxidant phytochemicals and showed antioxidant efficacy</cite> <cite id="c2599a94-0">Highest total phenolic content reported 160.9 mg/g in antioxidant-enriched leaf water extracts, with bioactive flavonoid glycosides identified across 11 provenances</cite>.
  - LC‑MS metabolomics resolves dozens of phenolics (phenolic acids, flavonoids, other polyphenols), consistent with “osmophloeum rich in aromatic oils” statements that include cinnamic acid, cinnamaldehyde, coumarin, and tannins/mucilage in extracts. <cite id="b078c3ee-7">Extracts contain essential oils (cinnamaldehyde, cinnamic acid, coumarin), tannin, mucus, and other phenolics</cite> <cite id="c2599a94-2">LC‑ESI‑QTOF‑MS/MS identified 47 phenolic compounds in C. osmophloeum leaves, including 13 phenolic acids, 28 flavonoids, and 4 other polyphenols</cite>.

What shifts the “proportions” across studies
- Chemotype and provenance: Leaves can be grouped into chemotypes (linalool vs cinnamaldehyde/cinnamyl acetate) depending on genotype and environment; in turn, these determine which class dominates the EO profile. <cite id="b66419ab-0">A distinct linalool chemotype exists in C. osmophloeum</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-2">In linalool chemotype EOs, linalool can reach 93%+</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-0">Cinnamaldehyde may be the major constituent in some provenances while linalool is major in others</cite>.
- Extraction method and time/temperature: Hydrodistillation, headspace/hydrosis, and solvent workups differentially partition volatiles vs polars. Short hydrodistillation can fully extract S-(+)-linalool within 1 h, affecting apparent “percent composition” recovered; hydrosols often retain higher benzoic-derivative volatiles (cinnamaldehyde, cinnamyl acetate) relative to full EO fractions. <cite id="b66419ab-1">Hydrodistillation extracts S-(+)-linalool from leaves completely within 1 h</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-8">Hydrosol analysis shows very high cinnamaldehyde content</cite>.
- Extraction solvent and polarity: Water extracts concentrate polar phenolics and glycosides (anthocyanidin/epicatechin-type glycosides, chlorogenic/cinnamic acids) and can achieve total phenolic contents up to ~161 mg/g (GAE/g), whereas nonpolar/methanolic extracts will enrich terpenes/phenylpropanoids; comparing methods across the same material thus alters apparent “percent composition” among classes. <cite id="b078c3ee-1">Leaf water extracts show high antioxidant phenolics</cite> <cite id="c2599a94-0">Water extracts from 11 provenances: 160.9 mg/g total phenolics and multiple bioactive glycosides</cite>.
- Location/genotype, seasonality, and processing: Provenance-specific chemotypes and regional genotypes alter monoterpenoid vs phenylpropanoid ratios; processing (age at harvest, curing/wounding, extraction batch) can bias yields toward volatilization or polymerization, changing measured percentages. <cite id="b66419ab-9">Across Cinnamomum species collected in Sarawak, cinnamaldehyde dominance is common in leaf oils</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-5">Osmophloeum leaf EOs resemble C. cassia, supporting regional consistency within benzene-phenyl chemistries</cite>.
- Analytical technique sensitivity: GC‑MS emphasizes volatilizable/thermally stable constituents, whereas LC‑MS resolves polar phenolics/oligomers; differences in detection range explain why some studies emphasize “essential oil monoterpenes (e.g., linalool)” while others highlight “phenylpropanoid/coumarin-rich essential oils” and “high phenolic glycosides in water extracts.” <cite id="b66419ab-3">GC‑MS profiles list cinnamyl acetate, cinnamaldehyde, and sesquiterpenoids in osmophloeum EO</cite> <cite id="c2599a94-2">LC‑MS detects numerous phenolic acids and flavonoids in the leaf matrix</cite>.

Practical synthesis and comparability across analyses
- “Main constituents” commonly reported for osmophloeum leaves include: (1) volatile phenylpropanoids/monoterpene derivatives—trans‑cinnamaldehyde, trans‑cinnamyl acetate, coumarin, linalool, terpinen‑4‑ol—with chemotype-driven dominance; and (2) polar phenolics/flavonoids—procyanidin/epicatechin glycosides and cinnamic/phenolic acids—enriched in water/methanol extracts. <cite id="b078c3ee-0">Cinnamaldehyde may be major in some provenances and linalool major in others</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-8">Hydrosol: cinnamaldehyde > cinnamyl acetate > coumarin as main constituents</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-2">Linalool EO with >90% linalool is documented</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-3">Alternative EO profile: high cinnamyl acetate with ~10% cinnamaldehyde</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-1">Water extracts are rich in antioxidant phenolics and flavonoid glycosides</cite> <cite id="c2599a94-0">Water extracts can reach 160.9 mg/g total phenolics</cite>.
- Proportions differ among analyses due to: chemotype/provenance (linalool vs cinnamaldehyde-based), extraction route (hydrodistillation vs partial volatilization vs hydrosis), solvent/polarity (water vs methanol vs ethyl acetate), detection mode (GC‑MS vs LC‑MS), and processing/seasoning, which shift apparent “percentages” of each class and compound. <cite id="b66419ab-0">Defined linalool chemotypes indicate monoterpenoid-dominant potential</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-0">Across provenances, major constituents vary between cinnamaldehyde and linalool</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-1">Hydrodistillation time/efficiency can fully extract linalool within 1 h, altering EO-reported composition</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-8">Hydrosols report very high cinnamaldehyde percentages</cite> <cite id="c2599a94-0">Water extraction enriches phenolics up to ~161 mg/g</cite>.

Illustrative quantitative ranges for comparability
- Essential oils (leaf):
  - Linalool chemotype: linalool ~90–93% by GC area% in hydrodistillates; minor monoterpene oxides and some cinnamyl acetate, with trace coumarin. <cite id="b66419ab-2">Linalool 93.30%; minor 2‑methyl benzofuran and α‑pinene; small cinnamyl acetate</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-1">S-(+)-linalool is recoverable in full within 1 h of hydrodistillation from linalool chemotype</cite>.
  - Cinnamaldehyde/cinnamyl acetate chemotype: cinnamaldehyde typically ~9–93% (sample- and method-dependent), with cinnamyl acetate ~7–41%, plus terpenoids and coumarin often below single digits. <cite id="b66419ab-3">Cinnamyl acetate 40.8%, trans‑cinnamaldehyde 9.1% in one EO; caryophyllene oxide and T‑cadinol present</cite>.
  - Hydrosol (related sample set): trans‑cinnamaldehyde ~65%, trans‑cinnamyl acetate ~7–9%, coumarin ~4%, demonstrating hydrosis and polarity partitioning that enriches phenylpropanoid volatiles. <cite id="b078c3ee-8">Hydrosol: trans‑cinnamaldehyde 65.03%, trans‑cinnamyl acetate 7.57%, coumarin 4.31%</cite>.
- Polar extracts (leaf):
  - Water extracts (11 provenances): total phenolics as high as 160.9 mg/g (GAE/g), with multiple bioactive flavonoid glycosides indicating substantial antioxidant capacity in the polar fraction. <cite id="c2599a94-0">Highest reported total phenolic content 160.9 mg/g; antioxidant-enriched water extracts across 11 provenances</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-1">Water extracts contained antioxidant phytochemicals and showed efficacy as antioxidants</cite>.
  - LC‑MS profiling confirms extensive phenolic classes (47 compounds) representing phenolic acids, flavonoids, and other polyphenols as the principal polar phytochemicals in leaves. <cite id="c2599a94-2">47 phenolics identified, including 13 phenolic acids, 28 flavonoids, and 4 other polyphenols</cite>.

Takeaway
- Expect two major chemical clusters in Cinnamomum osmophloeum leaves: (A) volatile phenylpropanoid/monoterpene-rich essential oils with either linalool- or cinnamaldehyde/cinnamyl acetate–dominant chemotypes and coumarin present; and (B) polar phenolic/flavonoid-rich fractions with high total phenolic and flavonoid glycoside content in water and methanolic extracts. <cite id="b078c3ee-0">Across provenances, cinnamaldehyde or linalool can be the leaf EO major constituent</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-8">In hydrosols, cinnamaldehyde commonly dominates at >60%</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-2">Linalool chemotype distillates can be >90% linalool</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-3">Alternative composition with high cinnamyl acetate and cinnamaldehyde</cite> <cite id="c2599a94-2">LC‑MS reveals abundant phenolic acids and flavonoids in leaf matrix</cite> <cite id="c2599a94-0">Water extraction can yield very high total phenolics (160.9 mg/g)</cite>.
- Reported proportions vary because different studies select different chemotypes, use distinct extraction techniques and solvents, and apply different analytical platforms (GC‑MS vs LC‑MS), which differentially partition and quantify volatile vs polar classes and their subcomponents. <cite id="b66419ab-0">Defined linalool chemotype explains monoterpene-dominant profiles</cite> <cite id="b66419ab-1">Hydrodistillation recoveries affect measured linalool percentage</cite> <cite id="b078c3ee-8">Hydrosol quantification favors phenylpropanoid volatiles</cite> <cite id="c2599a94-0">Water-based methods emphasize phenolic glycosides/phenolics</cite>.

Below are commonly used RGB-based indices for estimating plant traits such as SPAD (chlorophyll) and grain yield, together with their mathematical formulations and evidence from the literature. I group indices by how they are computed from red (R), green (G), and blue (B) channels and by the trait they target.

Key principles and RGB-only proxies
- RGB “greenness/redness” and simple ratios: Many field-deployable methods compute greenness or redness from R and G (or R and B) to approximate the red-edge/NIR behavior of classical NDVI-type indices, because NIR is not available in pure RGB sensors. <cite id="49b49858-0">Mobile-phone RGB cameras have been widely used to assess greenness/“redness” of leaves while correlating with chlorophyll status</cite>. <cite id="49b49858-7">Empirical analyses of RGB-derived VIs from UAS imagery have compared linear relationships between indices and reference traits</cite>. 
- Approximating chlorophyll indices without NIR: Green-based chlorophyll indices substitute G for R in NDVI-like formulas (GRVI, GNDVI) and are often preferred under visible-only constraints. <cite id="49b49858-3">NDVI-type sensors are sensitive to red and NIR and can estimate leaf chlorophyll content; the green-based approach adapts this principle to visible green and red channels</cite>. <cite id="bb342472-7">Broge and Leblanc’s approach motivates green/red-based chlorophyll indices due to strong chlorophyll absorption in red and high reflectance in green</cite>.

Commonly used RGB-based indices (formulations)
- Red–Green–Blue “vigor” ratios and VIs
  - R/G or G/R “redness/greenness” ratio: Widely used as a fast proxy for vegetation vigor and chlorophyll content, especially in cereals. <cite id="49b49858-7">In barley, SPAD correlated best with estimated chlorophyll using R/G with low RMSE (0.072), suggesting the simple R/G ratio as an effective proxy</cite>. <cite id="49b49858-9">A low-cost smartphone-based pipeline retrieves rice leaf chlorophyll from images, enabling SPAD estimation without specialized sensors</cite>. 
  - Green Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (GNDVI) in RGB: Uses visible green as a proxy for NIR. Formula: GNDVI = (G − R)/(G + R). <cite id="bb342472-6">GNDVI substitutes visible green for red in NDVI to better measure photosynthesis and chlorophyll status</cite>. <cite id="49b49858-7">In barley, G-based redness/greensness indices outperform red-only ratios for chlorophyll/SPAD estimation</cite>. <cite id="49b49858-4">Machine-learning-driven models on RGB images have been proposed to rapidly estimate SPAD with non-destructive imaging</cite>. 
  - Green–Red Ratio Index (GRVI) and Simple Green/Red “chlorophyll” indices: GRVI = G/R; sometimes scaled to avoid negative values. <cite id="bb342472-7">The strong reflectance peak near green and deep chlorophyll absorption near red underpin GRVI/GNDVI as chlorophyll-sensitive</cite>. <cite id="bb342472-5">Index databases list RI = (R − G)/(R + G) (redness index) and related formulations; GNDVI = (G − R)/(G + R) as a chlorophyll index</cite>. 
  - Variable Importance Index (VARI) and variations: Uses R, G, B to emphasize green reflectance while accounting for attenuation. Examples and practical formulations appear in UAV/ag software guides. <cite id="bb342472-1">Interpretations of common vegetation indices emphasize NDVI/GNDVI-like behavior and green/red reflectance-absorption contrasts</cite>. <cite id="bb342472-4">Practical guides define VARI as a ratio of R, G, B to assess plant health from RGB imagery</cite>. 
  - Triangular Vegetation Index (TVI) and related polygons: TVI approximates NIR-like behavior with red-edge/green sensitivity but can be adapted to RGB by substituting visible “greenness.” <cite id="bb342472-7">TVI is based on an area spanning green, red, and near-infrared sensitivity, providing a chlorophyll-sensitive metric</cite>. 
  - Redness Index (RI) / Redness-based “vigor” proxies: RI = (R − G)/(R + G), where higher values indicate more redness (less chlorophyll/greenness); sometimes reported as RED or RVI. <cite id="bb342472-5">Index databases explicitly list R/G redness indices (e.g., RI) and RGB-only variants as “redness” metrics</cite>. 
  - CIE L*a*b* “greenness” and smartphone proxies: Mobile-phone RGB pipelines convert sRGB to CIE L*a*b* and use a* or b* “greenness” to correlate with SPAD. <cite id="49b49858-0">Low-cost phone RGB greenness measurements have been paired with SPAD reference readings</cite>. <cite id="49b49858-6">Smartphone imaging methods model approaches to retrieve rice leaf SPAD values under field conditions</cite>. 
  - Composite or multispectral-influenced RGB indices: Green–Red–Blue “broadband greenness” and related combinations aim to place green and red at contrasting ends of chlorophyll response. <cite id="bb342472-0">Broadband greenness indices take the ratio of the band with highest vegetation reflectance to the band of deepest chlorophyll absorption, often implemented as a green/red ratio in RGB-only sensing</cite>. <cite id="49b49858-1">Linear relationships between VI and references (e.g., SPAD or yield) have been analyzed from RGB imagery under different scales</cite>. 

- Chlorophyll-sensitive RGB indices (explicit formulas)
  - NDVI-like, green-based:
    - GNDVI = (G − R)/(G + R) [chlorophyll index; substitutes visible green for NIR] <cite id="bb342472-6">GNDVI uses visible green and red to assess chlorophyll; it is often more sensitive than red-only NDVI</cite>. 
    - GRVI = G/R (or scaled GRVI = (G + K)/(G − R + K); K avoids division-by-zero) [chlorophyll/redness proxy] <cite id="bb342472-1">Green-based indices interpret higher green reflectance and lower red absorption as higher chlorophyll</cite>. <cite id="bb342472-6">GNDVI and related green-based indices are emphasized for photosynthesis and chlorophyll monitoring</cite>. 
  - Redness-based vigor proxies (for trait screening/canopy cover):
    - RI = (R − G)/(R + G) [redness index; lower values imply more green/chlorophyll] <cite id="bb342472-5">Red/green ratio indices and similar formulations appear in index databases and RGB toolchains</cite>. 
    - VARI-style enhancements: VARI = 3G − R − B divided by 3G + R + B, emphasizing green while accounting for blue/red attenuation; many RGB software libraries use variants of this family. <cite id="bb342472-4">VARI is presented as an RGB-based vegetation index for assessing plant health</cite>. 

Using RGB indices to estimate SPAD (chlorophyll)
- Empirical evidence and formulations
  - Simple ratios and green-based VIs correlate well with SPAD. <cite id="49b49858-7">In barley, the best correlation between SPAD and estimated chlorophyll came from R/G with RMSE 0.072, indicating that a simple red/green ratio can serve as an effective SPAD proxy</cite>. <cite id="49b49858-4">Machine learning on RGB-derived features and hand-crafted indices has been proposed to improve SPAD estimation accuracy and robustness</cite>. 
  - Mobile phone-based pipelines. <cite id="49b49858-0">RGB phone cameras capture leaf greenness paired with SPAD meters to estimate chlorophyll status in the field</cite>. <cite id="49b49858-2">A practical, low-cost solution monitors SPAD and chlorophyll via mobile-image analysis in field crops</cite>. 
  - Green-based indices vs red-only NDVI. <cite id="49b49858-3">Because NDVI sensors rely on red and NIR, a GNDVI-like substitution with green (instead of NIR) is a common visible-only adaptation for chlorophyll estimation</cite>. <cite id="bb342472-9">In practice, GNDVI measures chlorophyll content more accurately than NDVI and detects wilt or aging, aiding nutrient management</cite>. 

Using RGB indices to estimate grain (maize/cereal) yield
- Time-series and greenness-based strategies
  - Greenness and chlorophyll dynamics during mid-to-late growth stages improve yield estimation. <cite id="75f72745-1">Time-series NDVI-derived greenness indices (GSIs) improved maize yield estimation with machine-learning models</cite>. <cite id="bb342472-8">Key: GNDVI more accurately measures chlorophyll than NDVI; practical yield modeling benefits from robust chlorophyll estimates</cite>. 
  - Green-based chlorophyll indices as predictors. <cite id="75f72745-4">Across time, GNDVI had the highest correlation with maize yield and was suggested for inclusion alongside yield predictors</cite>. <cite id="75f72745-2">Identifying the best phenological stage and VI type improved rainfed corn yield estimation</cite>. <cite id="75f72745-0">Analyses of vegetation indices, canopy cover, and plant height from multispectral and RGB imagery have informed grain yield estimation in corn</cite>. 
- UAV and smartphone-based yield mapping
  - RGB-only VIs and canopy cover from UAV imagery feed into yield models. <cite id="75f72745-0">Different RGB vegetation indices, canopy cover, and plant metrics were evaluated for predicting corn grain yield; RGB pipelines are competitive</cite>. <cite id="75f72745-1">Greenness-based time series from NDVI-like metrics improved maize yield estimation</cite>. 
  - Practical index sets from UAV RGB. <cite id="75f72745-8">RGB-based vegetation indices derived from UAV imagery were optimized; small saturation effects relative to red-edge NDVI persisted at higher biomass</cite>. <cite id="75f72745-9">Time-series indices (e.g., based on NDVI/GSI) enhanced accuracy for estimating growth and yield</cite>. 

How to choose and deploy indices (practical guidance)
- For SPAD/chlorophyll, prefer green-based formulas that approximate NIR using visible green:
  - GNDVI = (G − R)/(G + R) 
  - GRVI = G/R (or scaled GRVI) 
  - Use a* from CIE L*a*b* derived from sRGB as a fast “greenness” proxy with regression to SPAD. <cite id="49b49858-7">R/G performed best among simple ratios in barley for SPAD estimation</cite>. <cite id="49b49858-0">Mobile-phone greenness measurements can align with SPAD references</cite>. <cite id="49b49858-6">Smartphone-based modeling retrieves SPAD with field-deployable accuracy</cite>. 
- For grain yield, combine RGB-chlorophyll indices (GNDVI, GRVI) with canopy metrics and time:
  - Build time-series greenness/smelting curves (GSI) from repeated RGB flights; use GNDVI as a key feature; feed into RF/XGBoost/LightGBM; tune by phenological stage. <cite id="75f72745-1">Time-series GSIs improved maize yield predictions</cite>. <cite id="75f72745-4">GNDVI showed the highest correlation with maize yield and was recommended for yield modeling</cite>. <cite id="75f72745-2">Stage–index matching boosted corn yield estimation under field conditions</cite>. <cite id="75f72745-0">RGB-based VIs plus canopy/height features were effective predictors of corn yield</cite>. 
- Be aware of limitations:
  - Without red-edge sensitivity, indices can saturate at high biomass; incorporating red-edge-aware features (unavailable in pure RGB) reduces saturation. <cite id="75f72745-8">Optimized RGB indices showed small saturation at higher biomass compared with red-edge NDVI</cite>. 
  - Simple ratios may degrade under non-uniform lighting/shading; calibrate per scene or use GNDVI-style formulations that normalize by sum denominators. <cite id="49b49858-1">Scaling effects on chlorophyll estimation were investigated by analyzing linear relationships between RGB-based VI and references</cite>. <cite id="49b49858-9">Adaptable shade-aware ML models plus VI improve low-cost SPAD estimation</cite>. 

Examples across crops and scenarios
- Barley SPAD: <cite id="49b49858-7">R/G achieved the best SPAD–chlorophyll correlation with low RMSE (0.072), indicating a simple, robust proxy from RGB</cite>. 
- Rice SPAD (smartphone): <cite id="49b49858-6">A smartphone-based imaging method retrieves rice SPAD via modeling, demonstrating RGB-based chlorophyll retrieval in the field</cite>. 
- Maize/corn yield: <cite id="75f72745-1">GSIs from NDVI-like greenness improved yield estimation</cite>; <cite id="75f72745-4">GNDVI had the highest correlation with yield</cite>; <cite id="75f72745-0">RGB VIs with canopy cover and plant metrics predicted grain yield</cite>. 
- General RGB toolbox: <cite id="bb342472-5">Index databases enumerate common RGB-only ratios (RI, NDVI-like GNDVI) and their purposes</cite>; <cite id="bb342472-4">VARI shows how to weight RGB bands for chlorophyll–vigor assessment</cite>.

Summary: Commonly used RGB-based indices and their use
- SPAD/chlorophyll: 
  - GNDVI = (G − R)/(G + R) (green-based NDVI) 
  - GRVI = G/R (or scaled GRVI) 
  - Redness index RI = (R − G)/(R + G) 
  - VARI = (3G − R − B)/(3G + R + B) 
  - CIE L*a*b* greenness (a*) from sRGB, trained to SPAD 
  - TVI-style indices adapted to RGB green/red channels 
  Empirical performance: <cite id="49b49858-7">R/G correlates best with SPAD/chlorophyll in barley and has low RMSE</cite>; <cite id="49b49858-6">smartphone RGB enables rice SPAD retrieval</cite>; <cite id="bb342472-6">GNDVI improves chlorophyll monitoring relative to red-only NDVI</cite>. 
- Grain yield:
  - Greenness-based time series GSIs (from NDVI/GVI) and GNDVI are key features in ML yield models.
  - Use canopy cover and plant height from RGB/UAV imagery alongside chlorophyll indices.
  Evidence: <cite id="75f72745-1">GSIs improved maize yield predictions</cite>; <cite id="75f72745-4">GNDVI correlated most strongly with yield</cite>; <cite id="75f72745-0">RGB-based VIs predicted corn grain yield with canopy/height features</cite>. 
- Practical notes:
  - When selecting indices, prefer green-based chlorophyll proxies (GNDVI/GRVI) for SPAD; for yield, integrate time-series greenness and GNDVI with structural canopy metrics.
  - Anticipate saturation at high biomass and adjust by stage, lighting normalization, or adding red-edge channels when available. <cite id="75f72745-8">RGB-only indices show modest saturation at higher biomass relative to red-edge NDVI</cite>; <cite id="49b49858-1">scale effects on RGB-derived VI-to-SPAD relationships require calibration</cite>; <cite id="75f72745-2">matching stage and VI type improves yield estimation</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of chemotypes and specific compounds reported across organs of Rhizophora stylosa, drawing on phytochemical reviews, GC–MS profiling, and ethnopharmacology-guided extraction studies. Where possible, compound names and classes are backed by analytical identification; where data are limited, related Rhizophoraceae evidence and screening results are noted with caveats.

Summary of major classes found in R. stylosa tissues
- Across roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits, evidence repeatedly shows polyphenols (phenolic acids, flavonoids), tannins (condensed/proanthocyanidins), triterpenes/steroids, monoterpenoids/phenylpropenes, saponins, alkaloids, and gums/resins as recurring classes. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">R. stylosa is rich in alkaloids, flavonoids, phenolic acids, tannins, terpenoids, saponins, and steroids</cite> <cite id="aea5f1c4-0">R. stylosa is rich in alkaloids, flavonoids, phenolic acids, tannins, terpenoids, saponins, and steroids</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-0">R. stylosa is rich in alkaloids, flavonoids, phenolic acids, tannins, terpenoids, saponins, and steroids</cite>. 
- Class-level screening in leaves (ethym acetate extracts) also reports cardiac glycosides in addition to alkaloids, saponins, phenols, flavonoids and tannins. <cite id="188b1452-3">Preliminary screening of ethyl acetate leaf extract of R. stylosa showed alkaloids, cardiac glycosides, saponins, phenols, flavonoids, and tannins</cite>.

Roots: Tannins, triterpenes, phenolics; specific monoterpene evidence suggested in rhizophoreae
- Chemical profile and activity: GC–MS–based antioxidant profiling of R. stylosa extracts attributes activity in part to lupeol, demonstrating the presence of triterpene backbones in root and other extracts. <cite id="aea5f1c4-4">GC–MS analyses identified lupeol as a contributor to antioxidant activity in R. stylosa root/stem/leaf extracts</cite> <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol was detected by GC–MS and linked to antioxidant activity in R. stylosa extracts</cite>. 
- Constituents: Root extract programs (e.g., antioxidant/phytochemical screening) consistently detect phenolics, condensed tannins, triterpenoids, and sterols across R. stylosa tissues; these classes are considered typical of mangrove roots. <cite id="14cfa313-2">A study on R. stylosa extracts from flower, leaf and stem bark reported antioxidant potential via GC–MS profiling, implicating bioactives such as triterpenes/phenolics</cite>. 
- Note on monoterpenes: While specific root-side identification of linalool/eugenol is not explicitly shown in the roots snippets, flowers within the same species contain these monoterpenes, and cross-generic Rhizophoraceae chemistry supports their occurrence in aerial roots/secretions; more targeted root LC–MS or isolation studies are needed for definitive assignment in R. stylosa roots. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Flowers of R. stylosa contain linalool and eugenol</cite>.
- Example compounds representative of roots (identified or plausibly present): lupeol (triterpene); β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol (steroids/phytosterols); phenolic acids and condensed tannins (tannin-class markers). <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol detected by GC–MS</cite> <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">GC–MS profiles of leaves show campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, lupeol</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-5">Phytochemicals in leaves, stems, flowers, roots, and fruits include flavonoids, saponins, reducing sugars, tannins, gums, anthocyanins</cite> <cite id="aea5f1c4-4">GC–MS antioxidant study notes lupeol as contributor</cite>.

Stem and heartwood (bark/inner stem): Phenolics, triterpenes/sterols, lignan-like polymeric tannins; extract-guided profiling
- Chemical profile: Studies that tested “stem bark” fractions of R. stylosa using GC–MS report sterol/triterpenoid profiles (e.g., β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol) and identify lupeol as a bioactive component, indicating that heartwood/bark contributes the same triterpenoid classes detected in leaves. <cite id="14cfa313-2">R. stylosa flower, leaf, and stem bark extracts were evaluated by GC–MS; antioxidant results implicate triterpenes/phenolics</cite> <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">Leaf GC–MS shows campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, lupeol</cite>.
- Example compounds representative of stem/bark: β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol (phytosterols); lupeol (triterpene); phenolic acids and condensed tannins; lignans/oligomeric procyanidins may be present as polymer markers by Folin–Ciocalteu/DCP assay screens. <cite id="14cfa313-2">Stem bark extract profiling and antioxidant activity</cite> <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol detection in GC–MS</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-5">Tannins and phenolics are common across stems and roots</cite>.
- Note on alkaloids: Review-level statements support alkaloid occurrence, but explicit stem-bark alkaloid identification in R. stylosa needs targeted isolation confirmation. <cite id="aea5f1c4-0">Alkaloids are among the major classes in R. stylosa</cite>.

Leaves: Diverse polyphenols, triterpenes/steroids, and other secondary metabolites; named molecules by GC–MS
- Leaf-specific chemistry: GC–MS of R. stylosa leaves detects the triterpenes/sterols lupeol, campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, cycloartenol, and β-amyrin. <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">GC–MS analysis showed campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, and lupeol in leaves</cite> <cite id="aec8d568-3">Metabolites composition includes campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, lupeol</cite>.
- Qualitative screening: Ethyl acetate leaf extracts show alkaloids, cardiac glycosides, saponins, phenols, flavonoids and tannins by preliminary tests. <cite id="188b1452-3">Preliminary screening of ethyl acetate leaf extract of R. stylosa shows alkaloids, cardiac glycosides, saponins, phenols, flavonoids, tannins</cite>.
- Example compounds representative of leaves: lupeol (triterpene); β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol (sterols); phenolic acids and flavonoids/tannins (polyphenols); potential cardiac glycosides. <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">Triterpenes/sterols and lupeol in leaves</cite> <cite id="188b1452-3">Alkaloids, cardiac glycosides, saponins, phenols, flavonoids, tannins present in leaf extracts</cite>.

Flowers: Monoterpenes/phenylpropenes; additional polyphenols
- Flower-specific compounds: Linalool and eugenol are reported in R. stylosa flowers, representing terpenoid phenylpropene/monoterpenoid chemotypes common in essential oils. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Flowers of R. stylosa contain linalool and eugenol</cite>.
- Broader metabolite scope: Flower, leaf, and stem-bark extracts collectively show sterols/triterpenes and phenolics by GC–MS, underpinning the polyphenolic-rich profile. <cite id="14cfa313-2">Extracts from flower, leaves, and stem bark of R. stylosa show GC–MS–detectable sterols/triterpenes and phenolics</cite>.
- Example compounds representative of flowers: linalool; eugenol; flavonoids/phenolic acids present as floral co-extractives. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Linalool and eugenol identified in flowers</cite>.

Fruits and seeds: Polysaccharides/gums, tannins, sugars, anthocyanins; general Rhizophoraceae patterns when R. stylosa data are sparse
- Fruits/seeds across Rhizophoreae commonly contain sugars, gums/polysaccharides, tannins, and anthocyanins, aligning with pericarp mucilage and seed coat phenolics typical of red mangroves; while R. stylosa fruit-specific compound lists are limited in open-access GC–MS reports, ethnopharmacology and cross-generic chemistry point to these matrices. <cite id="14cfa313-1">Seeds, roots, stems, and leaves are used ethnomedicinally in R. stylosa</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-5">Phytochemicals in leaves, stems, flowers, roots, and fruits include flavonoids, saponins, reducing sugars, tannins, gums, anthocyanins</cite>.
- Example compounds representative of fruits/seeds: reducing sugars; pectin-like gums/polysaccharides; condensed tannins; anthocyanidin glycosides; phenolic acids. <cite id="14cfa313-5">Fruits contain gums, tannins, anthocyanins, sugars</cite>.

Representative compounds by class with organ-association where available
- Tannins/condensed tannins/proanthocyanidins: Reported by chromatographic and antioxidant assays across leaves, stems/bark, and roots; serve as major astringent/antioxidant pool in R. stylosa. <cite id="14cfa313-5">Tannins are present in leaves, stems, flowers, roots, and fruits</cite> <cite id="188b1452-1">Preliminary screening indicated phenolic acid, phenolic, flavonoid, flavanol, condensed tannin, and triterpenoid in all R. stylosa fractions tested</cite>.
- Phenolic acids and anthocyanins: Leaf and fruit fractions show phenolic acids and anthocyanins, supporting pigment/phenylpropane contributions; these contribute to color and antioxidant capacity. <cite id="14cfa313-5">Phenolic acids and anthocyanins occur in leaves, stems, and fruits of Rhizophoraceae</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-2">Phenolic/sterol/triterpenoid profiles in leaves and stem bark</cite>.
- Flavonoids/glycosides: Screening and profiling indicate flavonoids in leaves and cross-tissue fractions; these are common in mangrove leaves’ UV/antioxidant profiles. <cite id="14cfa313-5">Flavonoids present across leaves, stems, flowers, roots, fruits</cite> <cite id="188b1452-3">Flavonoids detected in ethyl acetate leaf extract</cite>.
- Triterpenes/steroids: 
  - Leaves: campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol; lupeol is a key leaf/whole-plant bioactive. <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">Campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, lupeol in leaves</cite>.
  - Stem/bark: same sterol/triterpenoid classes are implicated in antioxidant activity; GC–MS–linked lupeol contributes to activity. <cite id="14cfa313-2">Stem bark extract antioxidant results and GC–MS profiles</cite> <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol detected in R. stylosa extracts</cite>.
  - Roots: sterols/triterpenoids and phenolics are the dominant classes by GC–MS–based profiling and activity. <cite id="14cfa313-2">Root extract participation in antioxidant effects</cite> <cite id="188b1452-2">Lupeol identified and active in GC–MS</cite>.
- Monoterpenoids/phenylpropenes: Flowers contain linalool and eugenol; these compounds may also occur in aerial root exudates/heartwood but require organ-specific confirmation. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Flowers contain linalool and eugenol</cite>.
- Alkaloids: Reviews and ethnopharmacology of R. stylosa list alkaloids among major classes; specific isoquinoline/indole alkaloids analogous to other mangroves may occur but need isolate-level confirmation per organ. <cite id="aea5f1c4-0">Alkaloids are among major phytochemicals in R. stylosa</cite>.
- Saponins and cardiac glycosides: Leaf ethyl acetate extracts show saponins and cardiac glycosides in preliminary tests; these are consistent with triterpene-derived biosurfactants present in R. stylosa tissues. <cite id="188b1452-3">Saponins and cardiac glycosides present in leaf extracts</cite>.
- Polysaccharides/gums and reducing sugars: Fruits/seeds commonly contribute pectic gums and sugars in Rhizophoraceae; R. stylosa fruits/seeds are implicated in traditional remedies for respiratory and inflammatory ailments, consistent with these bulk-phase chemistries. <cite id="14cfa313-5">Fruits contain gums and reducing sugars</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-1">Ethnomedicinal uses of seeds, roots, stems, leaves of R. stylosa for cough, boils, skin diseases, hepatitis, asthma, joint inflammation</cite>.

Notes on methodology and quality of evidence
- Analytical GC–MS is the strongest evidence for specific compound identities (e.g., lupeol, campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol) in leaves and across extracts; such studies directly link structures to antioxidant/bioactivity readouts. <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">GC–MS–identified leaf triterpenes/sterols and lupeol</cite> <cite id="188b1452-2">GC–MS identification of lupeol in R. stylosa extracts</cite>.
- Qualitative phytochemical screening (e.g., ethyl acetate extracts) shows broad classes (alkaloids, cardiac glycosides, saponins, flavonoids, tannins) and supports diversity within leaves; however, these screens do not specify single structures or resolve polymeraceous tannins into oligomer sequences. <cite id="188b1452-3">Ethyl acetate leaf extract screens positive for multiple classes</cite>.
- For roots and stem-bark, the best-documented metabolites are phenolics/tannins, sterols/triterpenoids; explicit compound-level isolation from these tissues in R. stylosa remains relatively underreported in open-access snippets, though extraction/bioactivity data imply their presence. <cite id="14cfa313-2">Stem bark extract and GC–MS profiles indicate triterpenes/phenolics</cite> <cite id="aea5f1c4-4">Root/stem/leaf GC–MS profiles implicate lupeol and other triterpenes</cite>.

Conclusions
- Across all parts of Rhizophora stylosa, the chemistry is dominated by polyphenolic pathways: phenolic acids, flavonoids/tannins (condensed and hydrolysable), and extensive triterpenoid/steroid backbones (β-sitosterol, campesterol, stigmasterol, lupeol) with significant contributions from monoterpenoid phenylpropenes (linalool, eugenol) in flowers. <cite id="dcf8d64b-0">Flowers contain linalool and eugenol</cite> <cite id="188b1452-3">Tannins, phenols, flavonoids, saponins, alkaloids, cardiac glycosides detected in leaf extracts</cite> <cite id="dcf8d64b-3">Leaves contain campesterol, stigmasterol, β-sitosterol, lanosterol, β-amyrin, cycloartenol, and lupeol</cite> <cite id="14cfa313-2">Stem bark shows similar GC–MS–detectable sterols/triterpenes and phenolics</cite>.
