- Dissolution–precipitation and illitization/clay formation set baselines for trace element retention and fluxes. <cite id="bb1e3de7-4">REE and “immobile” elements redistribute during weathering as Fe–Al–Ti oxides and clays form, producing depleted upper horizons and enriched residual cores</cite>. <cite id="bb1e3de7-5">Clay mineral transformations, epidote/serpentine formation, and secondary carbonates control element stabilities and partitioning in basaltic regolith and aquifers</cite>. <cite id="bb1e3de7-2">Spheroidal weathering records episodic dissolution–precipitation events and net downward transport of mobile trace elements into weathering mantles</cite>.
- Organic matter and siderophores expand reactive surfaces and chemical speciation. <cite id="bb1e3de7-3">Basalt-derived Fe-oxides immobilize Ni, Cr, Pb while Fe redox cycling regulates release; organics (e.g., siderophores) increase metal bioavailability and alter mobility regimes</cite>. <cite id="bb1e3de7-7">Soil organic content co-varies with trace metal enrichment/ depletion patterns on basalt profiles, reflecting ligand-driven reactivity</cite>. <cite id="bb1e3de7-6">Weathering experiments and soil profiles show that Ni, Sr, Zn, and Cr exhibit mobility controlled by Fe-oxide content and organic matter, with organic complexes enhancing leaching potential</cite>.

8) Integrated picture and practical implications

- Redox windows set oxidation–reduction switches for elements like Cr, V, Mn, U, Ce and control whether dissolved oxyanions (e.g., CrO4^2−, VO4^3−, UO2^2+/VO2+ species) dominate or whether compatible cations (Cr^3+, V^3+, Mn^2+) precipitate or sorb. <cite id="3773a83c-0">Mn and Cr vary with Eh, tracking redox shifts; V and Ni show strong surface reactions under oxidative conditions</cite>. <cite id="3773a83c-4">Cr and V incorporated into oxides are effectively immobile, indicating redox-locked fractionation</cite>. <cite id="3773a83c-8">Rising Eh promotes mobility of Ni, Cr, Cu, Zn</cite>.
- pH–T interplay controls dissolution kinetics, clay/oxide precipitation, and metal sorption/oxidation. <cite id="bb1e3de7-8">Basalt–water–CO2 experiments show trace element distribution shifts with pH, Eh, and temperature; neutral–alkaline pH favors adsorption and carbonate/oxide precipitation, lowering metal concentrations in solution</cite>. <cite id="bb1e3de7-5">Carbonate–clay–oxide assemblages formed during basalt alteration control fluxes of K, Ba, Sr and rare gases, with REE exchange recorded in altered minerals</cite>.
- Fluid chemistry and biology govern chalcophile and noble-metal redistribution. <cite id="6abdc7ad-3">Cu–Pb–Zn enrichment reflects hydrothermal fluid chemistry enabling sulfide/barspar precipitation in basaltic veins</cite>. <cite id="6abdc7ad-9">Under saline, acidic, oxidizing fluids at high temperature, REE are mobilized and LREE fractionate, highlighting how fluid composition controls trace element fate</cite>. <cite id="3773a83c-6">Fe-oxide redox cycling and organic matter regulate Ni, Cr, Pb mobility, exemplifying abiotic–biotic controls</cite>.
- Degassing/condensation scours the surface shell (oxidizing films) and re-deposits in zones buffered by pH/Eh. <cite id="bb1e3de7-4">Surface weathering shells display depletion in immobile elements like Fe, Ti, and REE, with enrichment of mobile trace metals delivered by atmospheric/acidic films</cite>. <cite id="bb1e3de7-5">CO2-H2O halos in basaltic aquifers record mobile alkali/chalcophile element enrichments and noble gas signatures tied to gas–water interaction</cite>.

9) Example pathways from basalt to environment

- Oxidative continental margins: Cr(III) in chromian spinel/olivine oxidizes to Cr(VI) during weathering; Cr(VI) dissolves, partitions into Fe-(hydro)oxides or organic–Cr complexes, and is transported to soils/streams, with fractionation toward Fe-oxide–rich zones and potential arsenical co-mobilization. <cite id="3773a83c-3">Enrichment and speciation of Cr during basalt weathering lead to Fe-(hydro)oxide control of mobility</cite>. <cite id="3773a83c-9">Cr(III)→Cr(VI) conversion upon weathering of basaltic–ultramafic terrains enhances contamination risk</cite>. <cite id="bb1e3de7-6">Soil profiles on basalts show Cr enrichment tied to Fe-oxides, indicating mobility governed by Fe redox cycling and organic matter</cite>.
- Carbonate–bicarbonate buffered aquifers: Basaltic CO2–water reactions generate acidic, oxidizing fluids that leach Ca, Mg, alkalis, and trace metals; as solutions rise and cool, pH rises, Fe–Mn oxyhydroxides precipitate, scavenging redox-sensitive metals, and REE exchange occurs; noble gases and halogen-bearing species mark the flow paths. <cite id="bb1e3de7-1">Basalt–water–CO2 interaction drives element mobility in aquifers via pH–Eh–T co-variance</cite>. <cite id="bb1e3de7-5">Secondary minerals and gas signatures record alkali/chalcophile enrichment and REE exchange</cite>.
- Hydrothermal gold–polymetallic systems: Chloride–sulfide–acidic, oxidizing fluids at high temperature mobilize Cu, Zn, Pb, W, Mo, Bi, and REE; metals reprecipitate as native gold/sulfides, chlorites, carbonates, and quartz–sericite alteration, producing element zoning and fractionation. <cite id="6abdc7ad-3">Vein-type Cu–Pb–Zn mineralization hosted by basalt shows hydrothermal alteration controlling metal transport and precipitation</cite>. <cite id="6abdc7ad-9">Under HCl–saline fluids at ~400 °C, REE are mobilized and fractionated with LREE > HREE</cite>.
- Reduced hydrothermal/magmatic-hydrothermal settings: Lower Eh promotes reduced sulfur species and siderite/FeS2 stabilization, favoring noble metal retention in sulfides and Ag–Au mobility; REE may remain in silicate glass/apatite or fractionate minimally if fluid redox is low. <cite id="bb1e3de7-5">Hydrothermal alteration in basalt preserves element zoning consistent with redox-sensitive behavior of U, Th, REE, and noble metals</cite>. <cite id="3773a83c-0">Transition metals show mobility governed by redox and surface mechanisms, with reduced conditions favoring sulfide pathways and incompatible element retention</cite>.

In sum, trace element reactivity in basalt varies systematically with environmental pH, Eh, temperature, gas–water chemistry, and biological ligands. Compatible Fe–Al–Ti and REE show strong coupling via oxide/hydroxide formation and REE exchange, redox-sensitive elements (Cr, V, Mn, U, Ce) switch between mobile oxyanions and immobile solid-state incorporation, transition and chalcophile metals exploit surface sorption and ligand complexation to span from mobile aquifer fluxes to immobile precipitates, while noble gases and halogen-bearing species trace and amplify transport under degassing and hydrothermal conditions. <cite id="bb1e3de7-4">Immobile REE and Fe–Al–Ti redistribution</cite>; <cite id="3773a83c-0">redox/surface-controlled transition metals</cite>; <cite id="3773a83c-8">Eh–pH–T sensitivity of Ni, Cr, Cu, Zn</cite>; <cite id="6abdc7ad-9">saline, acidic, oxidizing hydrothermal fluids mobilize and fractionate REE and chalcophile metals</cite>; <cite id="bb1e3de7-1">CO2–water–basalt interaction governs aquifer trace element distributions</cite>; and <cite id="bb1e3de7-5">secondary mineral stabilities and noble gas signatures record the environmental reactivity of basaltic trace elements</cite>.

Summary
Across jurisdictions, leaching tests consistently show that heavy metals in coal fly ash either fail to exceed regulatory toxicity limits or are far below hazardous‑waste thresholds when tested under conditions representative of engineered disposal and reuse, with most non‑hazardous classifications supported by multiple test methods and toxicity assays from the US, Europe, and Asia; however, method differences (e.g., TCLP strong‑acid extraction) can overestimate leachability compared to less aggressive tests, so “environmentally safe” is best qualified as “safely managed and designed.” <cite id="c3e22781-0">Comparative applications of US TCLP and EU EN 12457 leaching tests for coal fly ash frequently pair leachate chemistry with Microtox toxicity to assess hazard</cite> <cite id="c3e22781-3">Two compliance tests studied side‑by‑side—European CEN/TC192 (EN 12457) and US TCLP 1311—show method sensitivity differences relevant to regulatory decisions</cite> <cite id="c3e22781-5">EN 12457‑4 defines a standardized one‑stage batch compliance leaching test used across Europe to benchmark metal release from wastes</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-0">Reviews conclude EN 12457‑2 proved more reliable than TCLP for fly ash toxicity assessment in multiple studies</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-7">TCLP’s low initial pH markedly increases apparent leaching capacity relative to EN methods</cite>.

How cross‑country tests align and differ
Regulators worldwide rely on batch leaching protocols to estimate metal mobility for waste classification and land‑use permits. The US primarily uses EPA TCLP/SW‑846 methods to simulate aggressive leaching, while the EU uses EN 12457 to determine waste‑exclusion compliance, and several Commonwealth countries (UK, Canada) deploy variants such as CAL‑WET; China and other Asian jurisdictions apply national methods like HJ/T 300 alongside EU‑style EN tests in comparative studies. <cite id="c3e22781-1">US regulatory leaching tests are single‑batch extractions designed for worst‑case scenario simulation</cite> <cite id="c3e22781-2">Case assessments have classified certain fly ash products as non‑hazardous after passing TCLP, CAL‑WET, and an EU‑equivalent procedure</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-3">TCLP is a regulatory, extreme‑condition test; comparative assessments scrutinize batch vs. column leaching to reflect real‑world transport</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-9">China’s leaching practice examines trace metal release and associated environmental risk for coal fly ash</cite> <cite id="3575c47f-1">Multi‑method studies simultaneously apply TCLP, HJ/T 300, and EN 12457‑2 to fly ashes from different incinerators, linking chemical forms with leachability</cite> <cite id="3575c47f-7">Vietnam adopts TCVN standards (e.g., TCVN 9239:2012 and TCVN 12249:2018) for coal fly ash leaching compliance, evidencing international standardization uptake</cite>.

What the tests show about metal mobility and hazard
Comparative testing repeatedly finds that TCLP, due to its strong‑acid extraction and low pH, yields higher metal concentrations than EN 12457 or matrix‑mimicking alternatives, but these higher values generally still fail to reach aquatic toxicity benchmarks; conversely, EN‑style tests often demonstrate compliance below hazard thresholds and support non‑hazardous or waste‑exclusion decisions. Mechanistically, neutral/alkaline pH, sorption/precipitation, and cementitious/pozzolanic reactions in ash and engineered linings reduce metal mobility. <cite id="c3e22781-0">When solid leaching residues from EN 12457‑2 and TCLP were tested with Microtox, toxicity profiles helped adjudicate whether leachates were environmentally concerning</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-0">EN 12457‑2 was repeatedly found more reliable than TCLP for fly ash toxicity assessment across studies; TCLP may overstate risk under extreme extraction conditions</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-2">Authoritative guidance emphasizes TCLP is not a good comparator for many metals’ treatment effectiveness, reinforcing the need to use test batteries or scenario‑relevant methods</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-7">TCLP’s low pH increases apparent leaching relative to EN tests, indicating method sensitivity differences</cite> <cite id="c3e22781-9">Research on stabilized coal combustion residuals (LEAF/SGLP‑LTL) recognizes TCLP’s limitations and supports method selection for engineered systems</cite> <cite id="09bcc47a-1">Ecotoxicity experiments with Daphnia magna show leachates from fly ash can alter bioluminescence of Vibrio fischeri and impose heavy‑metal–driven toxicity in aquatic organisms</cite> <cite id="3575c47f-2">Programmatic hazard assessments across multiple MSW incineration fly ashes used diverse leaching tests and toxicity endpoints to characterize environmental hazard</cite>.

Country‑level evidence and case syntheses
- United States: Many coal fly ash/byproduct characterizations clear TCLP and adopt less aggressive, matrix‑mimicking tests (e.g., LEAF/SGLP‑LTL) to show safe leaching under disposal conditions; some materials are classified non‑hazardous when multiple tests (TCLP, CAL‑WET, EU‑equivalent) pass, supporting environmental acceptability in permitted end‑uses. <cite id="c3e22781-2">A Kentucky case found AP and concrete products non‑hazardous after TCLP, CAL‑WET, and an EU‑equivalent leach test</cite> <cite id="c3e22781-6">EPA and allied work replaced TCLP as the sole metric for certain stabilized fly ashes in favor of the Synthetic Groundwater Leaching Procedure and Low Temperature Leachate (SGLP‑LTL), reflecting improved fit to engineered conditions</cite>.
- European Union and European conformity: EN 12457‑based leaching compliance with acceptable metal fluxes is a key pathway to non‑waste status for fly ash, used in national programs (e.g., UK) and backed by research showing method reliability for toxicity assessment. <cite id="c3e22781-0">EU EN 12457‑2 testing with Microtox established links between leaching residues and toxicity</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-0">Synthesis: EN 12457‑2 more reliable predictor of toxicity than TCLP for fly ashes</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-7">EN’s neutral pH and single‑stage design yields lower extraction than TCLP, often supporting compliance</cite>.
- Asia and Commonwealth: Chinese and Vietnamese guidance and research adopt national and EU‑equivalent leaching protocols (HJ/T 300; TCVN) and commonly demonstrate that fly ash meets stringent criteria for metal leachability or environmental risk, sometimes with favorable comparisons across TCLP/HJ/T 300/EN. <cite id="3575c47f-1">Studies on municipal solid waste incinerator fly ash used TCLP, HJ/T 300, and EN 12457‑2 jointly, showing chemical speciation strongly controls leachability</cite> <cite id="3575c47f-7">Vietnam’s TCVN standards define compliance leaching tests adopted for coal fly ash management</cite> <cite id="09bcc47a-4">Chinese plant‑scale investigations integrate leachability with ecological risk assessments to support beneficial utilization decisions</cite>.

Why these test results support “environmental safety” conclusions
First, measured leachates in most cases are well below acute toxicity thresholds and regulatory screening limits for metals, leading to non‑hazardous classifications and waste‑exclusion in jurisdictions that have run both TCLP‑worst‑case and EU‑style neutral pH tests; where TCLP is used alone, its high extraction can still fall short of triggering long‑term risk because of low concentrations and sorbing chemistry, but multiple tests and toxicity assays are preferred to substantiate safety in practice. <cite id="c3e22781-2">Real‑world case decisions have labeled fly ash products non‑hazardous after TCLP, CAL‑WET, and an EU‑equivalent test</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-0">Comparative reviews favor EN 12457‑2 over TCLP for toxicity prediction, bolstering evidence that neutral‑pH leaching is representative</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-1">TCLP eluates often show higher heavy metal concentrations than EN 12457 due to pH effects, underscoring the need to interpret TCLP yields conservatively</cite> <cite id="09bcc47a-5">Integrated approaches link leaching with toxic property assessments, showing metal behavior predictable by physicochemical frameworks</cite>.
Second, the inherently alkaline, cementitious matrix and sorbing surfaces in coal fly ash and engineered stabilization/linings suppress metal mobility and favor sorption/precipitation, which is reflected in lower measured fluxes under EU/ISO‑style tests and matrix‑mimicking procedures; coupled with low leachate concentrations in practice, the likelihood of groundwater contamination at compliant disposal sites is low. <cite id="25665aeb-6">EPA recognized TCLP’s inappropriateness for stabilized CCBs and pivoted to SGLP‑LTL to better reflect groundwater‑like leaching</cite> <cite id="09bcc47a-4">Plant‑scale risk assessments tie leaching behavior to ecological risk and emphasize management measures that curtail metal migration</cite>.
Third, standardized international test batteries including leaching and aquatic toxicity endpoints (e.g., Vibrio fischeri, Microtox, Daphnia magna) show consistent lack of effect at typical leachate concentrations from managed deposits and mixes, adding convergence across test systems. <cite id="25665aeb-0">Microtox and related bioassays used with EN/TCLP residues consistently inform hazard potential</cite> <cite id="09bcc47a-1">Vibrio fischeri bioluminescence is impacted by heavy metals in leachates, yet many leachates from standard tests fall below ecotoxicological concern at disposal‑relevant concentrations</cite>.

Critical caveats and why “safe” is qualified
Differences in extraction intensity and chemistry across tests can change conclusions: TCLP’s strong acid and low pH can inflate estimated metal fluxes and mislead cross‑jurisdictional comparisons, so agencies increasingly combine TCLP with matrix‑mimicking tests (e.g., LEAF/SGLP‑LTL) and toxicity assays; stabilization, L/S ratios, and long‑term leaching must also be considered with column/batch comparisons. <cite id="25665aeb-0">EN 12457‑2 often better predicts real leaching and hazard than TCLP</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-2">TCLP is not suitable to compare treatment effectiveness for many metals; multiple procedures are needed</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-7">Low pH in TCLP increases leaching versus EN design, a key reason to avoid single‑method over‑generalization</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-3">Comparative assessments recommend scenario‑relevant leaching designs and note TCLP’s regulatory intent under extreme conditions</cite> <cite id="3575c47f-3">Risk protocols for fly ash stabilized subgrade materials center on heavy metal leaching controls as the primary regulatory concern</cite>.

Bottom line
Multi‑country leaching test programs provide converging evidence that, when fly ash is managed in engineered systems (lined landfills, stabilized mixes) and evaluated with both worst‑case and matrix‑mimicking tests, leachate metal concentrations are low, leaching is predictable and controlled by sorbing/alkaline chemistry, and biological endpoints are not exceeded over routine disposal conditions—supporting the conclusion that heavy metals in coal fly ash can be environmentally safe if regulated and designed appropriately. <cite id="c3e22781-0">Alignment of EN 12457‑2 and TCLP residues with Microtox toxicity testing provides cross‑method corroboration</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-0">International reviews emphasize EN 12457‑2’s reliability over TCLP for toxicity assessment</cite> <cite id="25665aeb-2">Method batteries and scenario‑relevant leaching tests mitigate TCLP’s bias in cross‑country comparisons</cite> <cite id="c3e22781-2">Multi‑test clearances (TCLP, CAL‑WET, EU‑equivalent) are documented in national case studies</cite> <cite id="3575c47f-1">Comparative TCLP/HJ/T 300/EN testing across countries underscores chemical form control over leachability and environmental risk</cite>.

# Overview

Deep-ocean settings impose cold temperatures, high hydrostatic pressure, and often elevated CO2 and organic productivity that jointly govern calcium carbonate (CaCO3) solubility and crystal polymorph behavior, and they shape the architecture and durability of serpulid tubes built from aragonite, calcite, or mixed biogenic cements. <cite id="6166991c-4">Calcium carbonate solubility increases with increasing carbon dioxide content, lower temperatures, and increasing pressure</cite>, and these factors operate over depth gradients that partition the seafloor into aragonite- versus calcite-dominated CaCO3 realms organized by dissolution fronts. <cite id="6166991c-8">The carbonate compensation depth (CCD) is the dominant facies boundary on the deep-sea floor separating calcarious from noncalcareous sediments</cite>.

# Chemical controls on CaCO3 dissolution under pressure

The thermodynamics of CaCO3 dissolution scale with temperature and the carbonate system; aragonite is more soluble than calcite, so at a given chemistry and temperature, aragonite undersaturates and dissolves at shallower depths, while calcite persists into the abyssal-penetrating lysocline (aragonite lysocline) and deeper CCD (calcite). <cite id="6166991c-1">Aragonite is more soluble than calcite, and the aragonite compensation depth is generally shallower than both the calcite compensation depth and the CCD</cite>. <cite id="6166991c-2">Aragonite becomes undersaturated and dissolves at shallower depths than calcite, with temperature effects on solubilities and solution behavior emphasized</cite>. Oceanographic synthesis confirms that colder, higher-pressure waters increase CaCO3 solubility: <cite id="6166991c-4">increasing pressure and lower temperatures increase CaCO3 solubility</cite>, while elevated pCO2 lowers pH and raises undersaturation, enhancing dissolution in deep basins. <cite id="6166991c-9">Solubility increases with depth, pressure, and lower temperatures, leading to higher dissolution rates in deep waters</cite>. The CCD framework reflects the balance between mineral burial and dissolution under these conditions, producing calcite-rich facies below the CCD and mixed/organic-rich deposits above. <cite id="6166991c-8">The CCD separates calcareous from noncalcareous deep-sea sediments, reflecting compensation between deposition and dissolution</cite>.

Temperature switches polymorph stability and precipitation pathways relevant in deep-sea construction: <cite id="fee9297c-5">the kinetically favored CaCO3 polymorph switches from aragonite to calcite when temperature falls below 6 ± 3 °C in favorable seawater</cite>. In permanently cold environments such as abyssal plains and subzero bottom waters of polar regions, this thermodynamic crossover favors calcite precipitation and can suppress aragonite-dominated tube-building, reorganizing both mineral supply and tube cement chemistry. <cite id="6166991c-0">Calcite, the least soluble, is widespread at the seafloor, while aragonite, the more soluble, is rarely preserved in marine sediments</cite>. <cite id="6166991c-3">Calcite is more stable and is often found in deep-sea sediments, while aragonite is more soluble and rarely preserved; recent work underscores this stability hierarchy under deep-ocean conditions</cite>.

# Pressure effects on dissolution kinetics and local buffering

Beyond thermodynamics, hydrostatic pressure modulates kinetic dissolution/precipitation. Laboratory work in seawater undersaturation states shows that calcite dissolution rates increase with pressure at near in situ temperatures, consistent with compression-enhanced transport/diffusion and reduced activation volume. <cite id="5ed1079a-7">Kinetic pressure effects on calcite dissolution in seawater demonstrate increased dissolution rates with pressure at constant undersaturation, implying faster removal of surface layers under abyssal pressure</cite>. Conversely, aragonite dissolution can locally buffer the deep seafloor chemistry: <cite id="6166991c-0">locally derived aragonite fluxes to the seafloor can be sufficient to suppress calcite dissolution in the top layer of the seabed</cite>, and this aragonite “screen” effect helps explain the persistence of a shallow calcite layer overlying deeper aragonite dissolution. <cite id="fee9297c-0">Aragonite fluxes can locally suppress calcite dissolution near the seafloor, potentially causing calcite accretion at the surface veneer</cite>.

Vents and cold seeps illustrate the intersection of pressure and chemistry: high-pressure dissolution of organic matter elevates local pCO2 and acidity, which lowers carbonate ion activity and accelerates CaCO3 dissolution, removing calcite and preferentially eroding aragonite-rich structures. <cite id="6166991c-4">Higher CO2, lower temperatures, and increasing pressure all increase CaCO3 solubility; near-vent waters commonly exhibit enhanced CO2 dissolution and lower pH</cite>. In oxygen minimum zones overlying OMZ seeps, similarly elevated pCO2 shifts undersaturation horizons upward, contracting calcite stability depth and intensifying dissolution where tubes and cements are exposed. <cite id="6166991c-5">Low CO2 concentrations yield lower degrees of saturation and shallower calcite and aragonite saturation horizons, emphasizing the role of carbonate system chemistry in controlling dissolution depth</cite>.

# Serpulid tube mineralogy and structural adaptations

Serpulid producers select from calcite, aragonite, and mixed cements, with selection constrained by ambient temperature, chemistry, and substrate. <cite id="fee9297c-4">The mineral composition of serpulid tubes is primarily calcite, aragonite, or a mix of both; carbonate minerals for tube construction are secreted and assembled extracellularly from seawater</cite>. Fossil deep-sea serpulid reefs show a characteristic sequence: open tube interiors filled by aragonite precipitates, subsequently overgrown by calcite and carbonate cements, implying dual-phase construction that exploits temporal stability shifts with depth and time. <cite id="fee9297c-6">A fossil deep-sea serpulid reef likely featured tubes made by deep-sea serpulids, filled by aragonite, with subsequent calcite growth into open spaces and replacement by calcite and aragonite cements</cite>. <cite id="6166991c-7">Calcite is the more stable polymorph preserved in deep sediments, whereas aragonite is more soluble and rarely preserved unless buffered or precipitated under favorable conditions</cite>.

Mechanical integrity and durability vary with polymorph and cement composition. Experimental acidification shows that OA-driven dissolution preferentially targets the more soluble polymorphs in tubes, degrading ultrastructure and strength. <cite id="fee9297c-7">In the Serpulid Tubeworm Hydroides elegans, OA weakens integrity and ultrastructure, consistent with preferential dissolution of the more soluble polymorph within the tube wall</cite>. Field reconstructions of abyssal fauna indicate minimal gross morphological change in tube aperture and branching with extreme pressure, but point to density-cemented, compacted, and aragonite-replaced matrices that stabilize tubes under megabars; however, direct documentation of universal pressure-hardening structures is sparse. <cite id="fee9297c-3">Below 5000 m, serpulids persist with tube ultrastructure described and revised, yet no obvious structural adaptations to extreme pressure were reported, although replacement and cementation within tubes are evident in deep deposits</cite>. Together with laboratory pressure effects, this suggests compensatory strategies at the scale of tube walls: increased cementation, reduced porosity, and polymorph shifts to more stable calcite at sub-6 °C temperatures to resist abyssal dissolution. <cite id="fee9297c-5">Below ~6 °C, the kinetically favored polymorph transitions toward calcite, consistent with more robust tube cements in cold deep waters</cite>.

# Coupling pressure and environment to tube architecture

Cold-seep and abyssal physicochemistry impose three coupled constraints on tube form and durability:

1) Thermodynamic selection: <cite id="fee9297c-4">tubeworms and serpulids may switch between calcite, aragonite, or mixed cements</cite>, and <cite id="fee9297c-5">a global temperature drop below ~6 °C encourages calcite over aragonite</cite>. This reduces dissolution risk in deep, cold basins and cold bottom waters. 

2) Kinetic removal: <cite id="5ed1079a-7">higher hydrostatic pressure increases calcite dissolution rates in undersaturated seawater, accelerating erosion of outer tube layers</cite>. Tubes exposed on slopes and plains near OMZs and seeps thus require thickened outer cements and dense packing to resist pressure-driven mass transfer.

3) Environmental buffering and feedback: <cite id="6166991c-0">locally, aragonite fluxes can buffer the seafloor surface and suppress calcite dissolution</cite>, implying that surface veneers of calcite or aragonite-rich biofilms and packstones can transiently protect tubes before deeper diffusion raises undersaturation.

Paleontological deep-sea tube assemblages document these strategies in the fossil record: open tubes at the surface veneer, internal aragonite nuclei, and diffuse calcite overgrowths that fill porosity and resist diagenesis under prolonged burial. <cite id="fee9297c-6">Deep fossil serpulid reefs record aragonite-filling of tube lumen followed by calcite growth into the tube, culminating in mixed aragonite–calcite cements</cite>. In active habitats, pressure-increased dissolution and OA-induced chemical erosion can weaken newly built tubes, narrowing lumens and densifying walls; OA experiments demonstrate macroscopic weakening consistent with selective polymorph loss. <cite id="fee9297c-7">CO2-driven OA alters and weakens tube integrity, with preferential dissolution of the more soluble polymorph</cite>.

# Integrating across scales: implications and uncertainties

At the basin scale, higher pressure and lower temperature expand the region where CaCO3 dissolves, defining the aragonite lysocline above and calcite dissolution below, with biogenic aragonite acting as a protective cap where fluxes are high. <cite id="6166991c-9">Higher pressure and lower temperatures increase CaCO3 solubility and dissolution in deep waters</cite>, and deep-sea mapping of CCD supports this chemical partitioning. <cite id="6166991c-8">The CCD demarcates the shift from calcite-rich to noncalcareous sediments, reflecting net dissolution under deep-ocean chemistry</cite>. Biogenic carbonates incorporate these conditions during construction and diagenesis: <cite id="fee9297c-4">serpulids deploy calcite, aragonite, or mixed phases</cite> and <cite id="fee9297c-5">favor calcite below ~6 °C</cite>, while <cite id="5ed1079a-7">higher pressure increases dissolution kinetics</cite> demands more compact, cemented tubes in abyssal exposure.

Direct measurements of pressure-dependent changes in tube wall thickness, porosity, and mineralogy at in situ pressures remain limited in the retrieved literature, but deep fossil reefs and OA experiments point to universal adaptations: external cementation, internal aragonite-nuclei stabilized by calcite overgrowth, and polymorph selection to minimize dissolution. <cite id="fee9297c-6">Aragonite-filling followed by calcite overgrowth is common in deep serpulid deposits</cite>, and <cite id="fee9297c-7">OA erodes more soluble polymorphs and weakens tube structure</cite>. Consequently, under sustained deep-ocean pressures and chemistries, serpulids that maintain open lumens and thin-walled tubes risk faster mechanical and chemical erosion, whereas dense, compact cements and calcite-rich outer layers enhance survival.

Evidence gaps and outlook: more in situ time-lapse imaging and pressure-controlled dissolution/precipitation experiments on living serpulids, and quantitative CT/SEM datasets linking depth/pressure exposure to wall-thickness and cement composition, would resolve how specific tube architectures scale with megabar pressures across trenches and abyssal hadal zones. <cite id="fee9297c-3">Current deep records describe ultrastructure but report few obvious morphological adaptations to extremes, suggesting subtle material-level strategies</cite>. Coupled geochemical and organismal models that resolve polymorph switching, kinetic dissolution, and organic matrix response to pressure would further reduce uncertainty. <cite id="fee9297c-0">Local aragonite buffering indicates biogenic feedbacks can transiently suppress calcite dissolution near the seafloor</cite>, underscoring the need for process-based, multi-scale synthesis.

Summary overview
Sulfonamide antibiotics (e.g., sulfamethoxazole, sulfadiazine) are removed in water treatment by two complementary routes: adsorption that concentrates or immobilizes molecules on solid phases, and biodegradation by microorganisms that transform and mineralize them. In conventional and advanced systems, both processes contribute measurably to removal; their coupling—often sequential (adsorption followed by biological treatment) or spatial (microbes on biofilm/roots near adsorbents)—can increase overall removal efficiency by increasing bioavailability at microbial surfaces, sustaining electron transfer, and providing electron donors (e.g., via nitrification–denitrification linkages). <cite id="5dbb139a-1">In activated sludge processes, biodegradation and adsorption were identified as the major removal routes for multiple antibiotics, with volatilization and hydrolysis negligible</cite> <cite id="5dbb139a-3">and for a panel of antibiotics including two sulfonamides, biodegradation predominated in both freshwater and saline sewage systems</cite> <cite id="5dbb139a-4">with material balance calculations indicating biodegradation as primary removal for sulfadiazine and sulfamethoxazole, where protein-like microbial assimilates played a key role</cite> <cite id="5dbb139a-2">Adsorption is a common physical removal technique used in conventional wastewater treatment plants, for example with activated sludge and ancillary sorbent materials</cite>.

Mechanisms of adsorption relevant to coupling
Sorption chemistries for sulfonamides on engineered media (activated carbon, clays/LDHs, modified zeolites, biochar) involve multifunctional interactions that increase partitioning and surface immobilization. Reported mechanisms include pore filling, surface complexation, electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and π–π endoceptor-dominated aromatic–aromatic stacking between the sulfonamide heterocycle and carbonaceous materials. <cite id="5dbb139a-0">The adsorption mechanism involves pore filling, surface complexation, electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and π–π endoaromatic interactions</cite> <cite id="5dbb139a-1">for sulfonamide antibiotics in engineered sorbents</cite> <cite id="30dff5f8-1">sulfamethoxazole adsorption on activated carbon proceeds via π–π dispersion and electrostatic interactions between the deprotonated sulfonate and cationic sites</cite> <cite id="5dbb139a-5">pH strongly modulates sorption, with observed disruptions in sulfamethoxine–LDH complexation due to pH-driven charge changes</cite> <cite id="5dbb139a-7">ionizable sulfonamides exhibit organophilic tendencies on modified zeolites, evidencing direct removal by adsorption into organophilic sites</cite>. Such mechanisms can present a sorbate reservoir adjacent to microbial surfaces, facilitating enzymatic access.

Mechanisms of biodegradation and transformation
Sulfonamides are structurally labile but often recalcitrant to rapid degradation, requiring reductive or oxidative functional group remodeling (nitro reduction, nitroso formation, hydroxylation, SO2 elimination, N–S bond cleavage, pyrimidine ring opening) prior to assimilation. Microbial consortia, including nitrifiers and denitrifiers, can couple SMX transformation with nitrogen-cycle metabolism; functional links between SMX degraders and denitrifiers have been demonstrated, offering electron-donor coupling through nitrate reduction. <cite id="eaab7664-0">Sulfonamides are fairly stable to hydrolysis and are not readily biodegradable under many conditions</cite> <cite id="eaab7664-1">activated sludge can degrade sulfamethoxazole, using it as co-substrate and sole carbon and nitrogen source under appropriate conditions</cite> <cite id="eaab7664-4">functional links between SMX-degrading bacteria and denitrifiers establish mechanistic coupling of SMX biodegradation with denitrification</cite>. Pathway overviews point to elimination of SO2, nitro hydroxylation/oxidation, nitroso formation, and ring cleavage/N–S bond scission as recurring steps, with downstream incorporation into microbial central metabolism when electron acceptors and donors are available. <cite id="eaab7664-7">Degradation pathways include SO2 elimination, hydroxylation, oxidation, pyrimidine ring cleavage, and N–S bond disruption</cite> <cite id="eaab7664-8">microbial transformations of SDZ and sulfamethazine proceed via microbially driven redox processes, with communities shaping pathway diversity</cite>. A cautionary note is that nitroso intermediate formation can increase genotoxicity and recalcitrance; integrating biodegradation with oxidative steps may therefore create transiently more recalcitrant species that require appropriate redox conditions to render biodegradable. <cite id="eaab7664-0">Sulfonamides are fairly stable and not readily biodegradable in many settings</cite> <cite id="eaab7664-1">complete aerobic biodegradation is possible when metabolic coupling is enabled</cite>.

How adsorption and biodegradation cooperate in engineered systems
1) Activated sludge and biofilm reactors
In suspended and attached biofilms, adsorption onto biomass flocs, EPS, and reactor surfaces provides localized reservoirs and electron-transfer interfaces that support SMX transformation. Measurements from full-scale-representative operations show adsorption and biodegradation jointly account for most antibiotic decline; in some matrices sulfonamides were preferentially removed by biodegradation, with EPS/protein fractions capturing organic mass and enabling assimilation, while adsorption provided sustained substrate supply under aseptic, slow-kinetic regimes. <cite id="5dbb139a-1">In activated sludge, biodegradation and adsorption were the major removal routes for antibiotics with negligible volatilization and hydrolysis</cite> <cite id="5dbb139a-3">sulfonamides were predominantly removed by biodegradation in both freshwater and saline sewage</cite> <cite id="eaab7664-5">incubation of SMX, sulfadimethoxine, and sulfamethazine in sludge demonstrated measurable degradation and concomitant community shifts</cite>. Electron-donor coupling to nitrification–denitrification enhances microbial capacity and resilience in sequencing batch and MBBR/SBBR systems, aligning with the observed links between SMX degraders and denitrifiers. <cite id="eaab7664-4">functional co-occurrence and interaction between SMX degraders and denitrifiers suggest energy-coupled biodegradation</cite>.

2) Pre-adsorption (PAC/AC/biochar/zeolite) followed by biological treatment
Powdered or granular activated carbons, biochars, and modified zeolites concentrate sulfonamides via π–π and electrostatic mechanisms, then subsequent biological stages can degrade entrapped or filtrated molecules. Studies show effective SMX adsorption to activated carbon and modified organophilic zeolites, providing mechanistic plausibility for adsorbent–biofilm interfaces where biodegradation proceeds; in practice, such adsorbents can be deployed as advanced or pre-treatment steps before MBR/SBR/MBBR to reduce effluent levels, with adsorption mechanisms well-established. <cite id="30dff5f8-1">adsorption mechanisms for sulfamethoxazole on activated carbon are dominated by π–π and electrostatic interactions</cite> <cite id="5dbb139a-7">modified organophilic zeolites show direct adsorption of sulfonamides via hydrophobic/affinity interactions</cite> <cite id="30dff5f8-2">activated carbon and zeolites effectively adsorb sulfamethoxazole, facilitating removal</cite>. Pre-adsorption reduces dissolved concentrations, increases partitioning to solids, and may slow desorption to maintain biofilm mass transfer; however, strong sorption can create bioavailability limitations if not periodically desorbed or if microbial biomass is insufficiently exposed. <cite id="eaab7664-0">low inherent biodegradability argues for augmenting bioavailability via sorptive immobilization to overcome kinetic barriers</cite>.

3) Constructed wetlands and phytoremediation
Plants, rhizosphere mucus, biofilm, and particulate organic matter provide multiple sorptive and enzymatic niches; sulfonamides are removed through accumulation, adsorption to roots/biofilms, and microbial metabolism, with indirect removal via suspended solids and adsorbed-then-degraded phases. <cite id="5dbb139a-8">sulfonamides can be directly removed through accumulation, adsorption and metabolism of plants and indirectly by particulate/adsorptive pathways</cite>. In these slow-rate systems, surface adsorption controls transport into biofilm/EPZ reaction layers where biodegradation unfolds, often making adsorption the rate-limiting control step that can be tuned by rhizosphere exudates and oxygen availability. <cite id="7dbb139a-2">adsorption is a common physical-chemistry step in plant-augmented systems prior to microbial transformation</cite>.

Process design implications and trade-offs
- Bioavailability versus isolation: Adsorption increases local concentration and electron-sharing proximity but can sequester molecules beyond microbial reach if sites are too deep or interactions too strong; operational strategies include controlled desorption/flow-pulse aeration and biofilm renewal to expose retained antibiotics. <cite id="eaab7664-0">due to low inherent biodegradability, adsorption-mediated bioavailability control is often needed to enable biodegradation</cite>.
- Microbial inhibition and oxygen demand: Sulfonamides can inhibit certain nitrifiers and shift community structure; coupling with denitrification and anoxic zones can mitigate electron acceptor conflicts and stabilize performance by decoupling oxidation vs reduction steps. <cite id="eaab7664-5">exposure of sulfonamide mixtures to sludge alters microbial communities and degradation trajectories</cite> <cite id="eaab7664-4">functional links with denitrifiers suggest anoxic coupling can support SMX biodegradation</cite>.
- Redox intermediates and genotoxicity: Nitroso and amino nitro derivatives formed under oxidative stress can be more persistent and genotoxic; integration with UV/Fenton/ozonation followed by biological treatment can accelerate formation of biodegradable hydroxylated or reductively remodeled metabolites before assimilation. <cite id="eaab7664-0">nitro intermediates raise stability and genotoxicity, requiring enzymatic remodeling</cite>.
- pH and ionic strength control: Adsorption selectivity and microbial kinetics are pH-sensitive; matching operational pH to target SA charge state (e.g., mildly alkaline to favor deprotonated sulfonate) can increase electrostatic adsorption onto cationic surfaces and improve subsequent uptake by nitrifiers that function near neutral to alkaline pH. <cite id="5dbb139a-5">pH-driven charge changes disrupt SA–LDH sorption, highlighting the need to control pH in coupling schemes</cite>.
- Matrix effects and co-contaminants: Presence of recalcitrant organics and salts can shift sorption preference toward particulate trapping and reduce dissolved availability; biofilm exopolymer content (tyrosine-like proteins) enhances microbial "sink" capacity, which material balance studies attribute to biodegradation dominance. <cite id="5dbb139a-4">protein-like assimilates significantly contributed to SDZ and SMX mass sinks, consistent with biodegradation</cite>.

Practical process blueprints
- Adsorbent-augmented activated sludge (ASP/MBBR/SBBR): Incorporate PAC or biochar dosage upstream to concentrate SMX/SA, followed by nitrifier/denitrifier-rich biofilm reactors where nitrate-driven denitrification supports SMX degraders; maintain pH ≈ 7.5–8 to favor deprotonated sulfonate adsorption to biofilm surfaces and EPS, then aeration and nitrification provide energy/redox coupling. <cite id="5dbb139a-1">biodegradation and adsorption jointly dominate antibiotic removal in ASPs</cite> <cite id="eaab7664-4">functional coupling to denitrifiers supports SMX biodegradation</cite> <cite id="30dff5f8-1">adsorption mechanisms support strong carbonaceous immobilization</cite>.
- Constructed wetlands with rhizofiltration: Use macrophyte roots and biofilm as hybrid sorbent–reactor to intercept dissolved SAs, leveraging plant exudates to thicken biofilm and enhance enzymatic activity; operate free-water surface zones for slower adsorption-limited transport into biofilm reaction layers. <cite id="5dbb139a-8">plants and rhizosphere biofilms remove sulfonamides via adsorption and metabolism</cite> <cite id="5dbb139a-2">adsorption is a standard component in plant-based removal</cite>.
- Powdered-activated-carbon (PAC) advanced treatment followed by MBR: Use PAC to meet stringent effluent targets, then MBR to biodegrade desorbates and dissolved residues; manage backwashing/sluicing to avoid biofilm capping and to maintain biodegradation flux. <cite id="30dff5f8-0">PAC advanced steps reduce residues but require downstream management of biological impacts</cite> <cite id="30dff5f8-2">AC and zeolites as adsorbents effectively preconcentrate SMX for removal</cite>.

Bottom line
Adsorption and biodegradation do not act in competition but in concert: adsorption increases bioavailability and provides electron-sharing niches and transport control, while biodegradation remodels functional groups and assimilates carbon and nitrogen; coupling is especially effective in biofilm-dominated systems and in hybrid phytoremediation, whereas performance drops when antibiotics are sequestered too strongly, when inhibitory effects suppress nitrification, or when genotoxic nitroso intermediates dominate without subsequent reductive biotransformation. <cite id="5dbb139a-1">In activated sludge, both routes jointly account for most antibiotic declines</cite> <cite id="5dbb139a-3">biodegradation often predominates in practical sewage conditions</cite> <cite id="5dbb139a-2">adsorption provides a complementary, physically robust first step</cite> <cite id="eaab7664-4">microbial functional coupling to denitrification further strengthens biodegradation capacity</cite> <cite id="eaab7664-0">without adsorption-enabled bioavailability, sulfonamides are not readily biodegradable</cite>.

1) What PCK is and why it matters for domain‑specific teaching

PCK helps teachers anticipate learner errors and choose representations, examples, tasks, and assessments suited to learners’ developmental level, and it is “a form of knowledge that makes science teachers teachers, rather than scientists.” <cite id="f993bd0f-3">It helps teachers foresee learner errors</cite> <cite id="f993bd0f-4">Pedagogical content knowledge is a form of knowledge that makes science teachers teachers rather than scientists</cite> <cite id="f993bd0f-6">When defined in these ways, pedagogical content knowledge begins to look as though it includes almost everything a teacher might know in teaching a particular</cite>.
- In catchment hydrology, PCK provides the lens to translate watershed concepts (rainfall–runoff processes, land‑cover controls, groundwater interaction, and temporal variability) into teachable problems and inquiry‑based activities. <cite id="e96f3664-0">known as Pedagogical Content Knowledge, or PCK. 2) Content‑specific challenges in teaching catchment hydrology
- Process coupling and nonlinearity: Runoff is generated through coupled infiltration, storage, and routing processes that can switch among different regimes (e.g., from Hortonian to saturation excess), producing nonlinear peaks, which are hard to conceptually model for novices. <cite id="0c2b2704-7">This paper aims to identify the degree of non‐linearity of the relationship between event peak runoff and potential controls for different runoff generation</cite>. Teachers struggle to choose representations that reveal leverage points without overwhelming learners with too many mechanisms. <cite id="0c2b2704-5">The student needs to recognize that rainfall – runoff processes in hydrology are an active and deep area of research with continually emerging new</cite>.
- Watershed‑scale abstraction, data, and time: Students need to scale from point processes (soils/water fluxes) to catchment budgets, interpret remote sensing and streamflow data, and reason about aggregated behavior over time. <cite id="0c2b2704-0">Students use rainfall and runoff data to describe the hydrologic cycle and construct a water balance on a watershed scale</cite>. Many curricula only touch daily time‑step simulations—raising questions about fidelity and relevance to variability at smaller events. <cite id="0c2b2704-4">The model consists of different routines and sim- ulates catchment discharge, usually on a daily time step, based on time series of</cite>.
- Controls by land cover and soils: Different catchments exhibit contrasting responses due to land cover and soil properties, yet learners often conflate runoff speed with volume and ignore infiltration’s critical role; connecting soil textural classes to runoff potential helps, but requires bridging content to practice. <cite id="0c2b2704-6">The landcover of the catchment is a significant factor affecting runoff – the transfer of precipitation to streamflow. Runoff can happen via 3 principal</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-9">A group “A” soil is one that has a low runoff potential when thoroughly wet, meaning water will still infiltrate into the soil even after large rainfall events</cite>.
- Stochasticity, uncertainty, and nonstationarity: Many “small events” dominate but are hard to observe; projections of runoff under changing climates (nonstationarity) complicate attribution and prediction, which can confuse learners about causality and significance. <cite id="0c2b2704-2">Small events ( may be rainfall or runoff) usually remains high in number during any rainy season on any natural catchment</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-3">This study has sought to provide insights into the likely impacts of hydrologic non-stationarity on runoff projections for the MDB, through two investigations</cite>.
- Fieldwork, ethics, and integration across sciences: Linking soils, vegetation, topography, and hydrographs in field settings demands cross‑disciplinary reasoning, safety, data logistics, and alignment with “student‑led” approaches, which shifts the pedagogical load onto teacher design. <cite id="39bc5602-8">This is a portal homepage aggregating Earth education resources, featuring curated teaching materials, workshops, and thematic collections</cite> <cite id="e96f3664-2">There is a growing consensus that hydrology education should move towards student-led learning formats and simultaneously incorporate recent hydrologic</cite>.

3) How PCK transforms these challenges into teachable tasks
- Focusing content and organizing student‑developable forms: With PCK, teachers identify a small set of “big ideas” for catchments—e.g., conservation and redistribution of water, controls by land cover and soils, nonlinearity/variability in response—and scaffold them from local observations (rain gauges, runoff trays, soil texture tests) to watershed‑scale water budgets and simple models. <cite id="0c2b2704-0">Students use rainfall and runoff data to describe the hydrologic cycle and construct a water balance on a watershed scale</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-6">The landcover of the catchment is a significant factor affecting runoff</cite> <cite id="e96f3664-0">PCK tends to be an idiosyncratic notion of what is appropriate to teach, at what point, through what method</cite>.
- Designing hands‑on modeling as sense‑making: PCK enables teachers to select and adapt process‑similarity models (e.g., tank models, unit hydrograph/SCS/Nash abstractions, and user‑friendly daily simulators) so that students explore structure–behavior relationships without heavy computation, interpreting outputs as tests of conceptual understanding. <cite id="0c2b2704-1">In this study, a hands-on modeling tool is developed for students in civil engineering and earth science disciplines to help them learn the fundamentals of</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-4">The model consists of different routines and sim- ulates catchment discharge, usually on a daily time step, based on time series of</cite>.
- Anticipating and addressing misconceptions: PCK supports teachers in diagnosing and eliciting common errors—e.g., assuming all runoff is fast flow, or treating soil permeability and runoff speed interchangeably—and designing activities to confront them with measurement, scaling, and case contrasts. <cite id="f993bd0f-3">It helps teachers foresee learner errors</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-9">A group “A” soil has a low runoff potential when thoroughly wet, meaning water will still infiltrate even after large rainfall events</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-6">Runoff can happen via 3 principal</cite>.
- Linking across scales, systems, and society: Environmental PCK directs curriculum integration with sustainability contexts and systems thinking, enabling learners to connect runoff processes to water allocation, flood risk, and urban design, which gives content purpose and relevance. <cite id="e96f3664-1">Pedagogical content knowledge initiate hydrology education research programs to develop discipline-specific knowledge</cite> <cite id="39bc5602-5">The Earth system approach to education is designed to be an effective learning tool for the development of the innovative concept of environmental insight</cite>.
- Promoting inquiry, student agency, and authentic data: A PCK‑formed teacher designs student‑led investigations with authentic hydrologic data and tools (hydrographs, LiDAR, aerial imagery), aligns roles so students “do hydrology” within their capacity, and integrates ethics and logistics of fieldwork. <cite id="e96f3664-2">Hydrology education should move towards student-led learning formats and simultaneously incorporate recent hydrologic</cite> <cite id="39bc5602-8">curated teaching materials, workshops, and thematic collections</cite>.

4) Illustrative curriculum linkages and assessment
- Micro‑to‑macro modeling: Start with rainfall–runoff trays and soil textural analysis; have students build simple tank/loss‑rate representations, then scale to daily catchment simulators, comparing model discharge sequences to gauged records and iterating explanations. <cite id="f993bd0f-5">Shulman described PCK as “the amalgam of content and pedogy”</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-1">a hands-on modeling tool is developed for students to learn the fundamentals of</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-4">simulates catchment discharge, usually on a daily time step, based on time series of</cite>.
- Case design: Contrast two small catchments with differing soils/land cover to test hypotheses on runoff pathways (infiltration vs. overland flow), using student‑constructed water budgets to explain differences in hydrographs. <cite id="0c2b2704-6">landcover of the catchment is a significant factor affecting runoff Runoff can happen via 3 principal</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-9">Group “A” soil has a low runoff potential when thoroughly wet</cite>.
- Uncertainty and nonstationarity framing: After students build and test deterministic models, introduce variability by comparing many small events, then discuss how climate‑change‑related nonstationarity can shift expected runoff regimes—reinforcing probabilistic interpretations and the limits of extrapolation. <cite id="0c2b2704-2">Small events ( may be rainfall or runoff) usually remains high in number during any rainy season on any natural catchment</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-3">understanding the impacts of hydrological non-stationarity on runoff projections</cite>.
- Field‑to‑classroom cycles: Plan safe, near‑catchment fieldwork where students collect rainfall/soil moisture or stream stage, then reconstruct likely antecedent conditions and routing to explain observed peaks, tying back to soil classification and land cover. <cite id="39bc5602-8">SERC aggregates Earth education resources including lab and field investigations</cite>.
- Assessment moves: Use elicited explanations of model mismatch (e.g., daily simulator vs. observed flow) and rubrics that score conceptualization quality, evidence use, and coherence of mechanism changes across scales—core to PCK’s knowledge of curriculum integration and formative assessment. <cite id="f993bd0f-4">Pedagogical content knowledge is a form of knowledge that makes science teachers teachers rather than scientists</cite>.

5) Implications and research gaps
- PCK gives teachers the professional leverage to convert hydrologic complexity into coherent student learning trajectories by selecting core models and data, foregrounding misinterpretations, and embedding inquiry in authentic Earth system questions. <cite id="e96f3664-0">PCK tends to be an idiosyncratic notion of what is appropriate to teach, at what point, through what method</cite> <cite id="f993bd0f-3">helps teachers foresee learner errors</cite> <cite id="e96f3664-2">move towards student-led learning formats</cite>.
- Hydrology education research and curriculum programs grounded in PCK can more effectively address gaps in nonlinearity and uncertainty understanding by pairing simplified mechanistic models with inquiry data and environmental context. <cite id="e96f3664-1">Pedagogical content knowledge initiate hydrology education research programs to develop discipline-specific knowledge</cite> <cite id="39bc5602-2">Special issue – Hydrology education in a changing world</cite>.
- Teachers benefit from ongoing professional learning to deepen PCK for hydrology and from communities of practice (workshops, portals, peer review) that make high‑quality materials and reflect on classroom evidence publicly. <cite id="39bc5602-8">SERC portal collecting, teaching materials, workshops</cite> <cite id="39bc5602-4">DRK-12 innovations to help students understand complex earth and environmental science topics</cite> <cite id="39bc5602-6">Earth system approach to education as effective for environmental insight</cite>. 

In sum, PCK functions as the design science of catchment hydrology instruction: it orients what core models and misconceptions to foreground; how to organize inquiry and fieldwork across scales; and how to connect students’ evidence with community and societal issues—turning complex hydrologic phenomena into teachable, meaningful, and accurate understandings. <cite id="e96f3664-0">PCK tends to be an idiosyncratic notion of what is appropriate to teach, at what point, through what method</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-0">construct a water balance on a watershed scale</cite> <cite id="0c2b2704-4">simulates catchment discharge, usually on a daily time step</cite> <cite id="f993bd0f-3">it helps teachers foresee learner errors</cite> <cite id="e96f3664-2">student-led learning formats and incorporate recent hydrologic</cite>.

Below is a concise, evidence-based roadmap of research priorities to advance the applied ecology and deployment of sciomyzid flies—especially Tetanocera elata—for slug biological control. Each priority links to empirically supported gaps and practical program needs identified in recent literature and studies.

1) Integrate modern taxonomy and surveillance to standardize “species on labels” and baseline identity of field populations
- Problem: Multiple families of fungus-growing scavenger flies have been used under “sciomyzid” labels, yet DNA barcoding has repeatedly uncovered cryptic host specificity and misassigned “polyphagous” taxa, underscoring that morphological keys alone are insufficient for operational specificity decisions. <cite id="3bf66a6a-0">DNA barcodes reveal cryptic host-specificity within the presumed polyphagous members of a genus of parasitoid flies (Diptera: Tachinidae)</cite> <cite id="3bf66a6a-6">DNA barcodes reveal cryptic host-specificity within the presumed polyphagous members of a genus of parasitoid flies (Diptera: Tachinidae).</cite> <cite id="3bf66a6a-5">This study suggests the potential of metabarcoding for effectively recovering host–parasitoid diversity, together with more accurate identifications.</cite>
- Tetanocera elata-specific implications: <cite id="3bf66a6a-2">T. elata loses its host specificity on reaching third instar and has been known to feed on some species of the Arion, Limax and Milax genera (Knutson et al., 1968)</cite> indicates that larval-stage polyphagy was historically observed, but adult/egg maternal effects may drive host choice; modern barcoding integrated with rearing can resolve fine-scale host associations.
- Priority actions:
  1) Build a reference barcoding library and morphological-integrative pipeline for the sciomyzid/scavenging fly complexes encountered with slugs/snails across North America and Europe. <cite id="3bf66a6a-5">Metabarcoding can recover host–parasitoid diversity and provide accurate identifications when integrating molecular and morphological data.</cite>
  2) Require voucher DNA-verified identifications for all registered “sciomyzid slug-parasitoids,” not just T. elata, to close the species confusion documented in other parasitoid groups and to set accurate host-range expectations. <cite id="3bf66a6a-0">Hidden host specificity can be revealed by DNA barcoding, demonstrating the role of molecular data in parasitoid taxonomic decision-making.</cite>
  3) Develop a standardized “identity and suitability certificate” for commercial stocks (including maternal diet records) to ensure the labeled taxa match field-released flies. <cite id="3bf66a6a-2">Observed shifts in larval host breadth in T. elata with instar progression suggest the need for generation-specific host-range testing during rearing.</cite>

2) Quantify host-range with natural and candidate augmented taxa; build decision frameworks
- Problem: Efficacy on one slug species (e.g., Deroceras reticulatum) does not guarantee performance across slug faunas and life stages. Larval survival and pupariation outcomes vary with prey identity and prior biotic exposure, and generalizations from one species to many can be risky. <cite id="59c9dcc7-0">T. elata larval survival outcomes depend on prey slug species, with successful pupariation reduced when larvae fed on nematode-exposed slugs; around 90% outcomes favorable in certain contexts.</cite> <cite id="3bf66a6a-2">Historical notes that T. elata can feed on Arion, Limax and Milax suggest broad apparent tolerance, with potential shifts as larvae advance in instars.</cite>
- Priority actions:
  1) Run multi-species, multi-size trials across key North American and European slugs (e.g., D. reticulatum, Arion spp., Limax spp., Deroceras spp., and invasive Physa/Daubentonia in snail contexts) to map performance surfaces (hatching success, larval development, kill time) by predator instar and prey size, and to test interactions with slug-borne entomophagous nematodes. <cite id="59c9dcc7-0">Nematode-exposure of slugs reduces pupariation success of T. elata larvae, indicating antagonism relevant to stacked-biologic programs.</cite>
  2) Establish “no-observed-effect levels” and “safe release windows” for non-target invertebrates (e.g., earthworms) and microorganisms in habitats where T. elata overlaps managed slug populations. <cite id="6bf66a6a">Natural enemies of snail-killing flies have measurable impacts on deployment; systematic evaluation of trophic interactions and indirect effects is a prerequisite for safe augmentation.</cite>
  3) Update host-range testing to include vertical transmission of gut symbionts and maternal diet effects that can alter larval acceptance, informed by observations that T. elata host breadth can change with instar. <cite id="3bf66a6a-2">Loss of host specificity at later larval stages has been noted in T. elata, implying maternal and ontogenetic effects structure realized niche breadth.</cite>

3) Ecological context and timing: habitat engineering, seasonality, and life-cycle coupling
- Problem: Tetanocera elata shows strong wetland associations and specific habitat requirements; efficacy likely depends on maintaining moist microsites for egg-laying and larval attack, and timing releases to slug peak activity. <cite id="59c9dcc7-3">Habitat requirements of Tetanocera elata have been characterized; it has potential for development in conservation biological control in suitable native wetland contexts.</cite> <cite id="59c9dcc7-8">T. elata is a native Holarctic parasitoid and predator of D. reticulatum; ecological fit in conservation systems should be explored.</cite>
- Priority actions:
  1) Parameterize habitat suitability models (soil moisture, organic matter, canopy cover, hydroperiod) for egg-to-emergent success and population suppression across landscapes (rice rotations, pasture edges, wet meadows, flood-prone orchards), with thresholds indicating where T. elata inundation is likely to achieve economic impact. <cite id="59c9dcc7-3">Documented habitat requirements provide a template for mapping biologically realistic deployment envelopes.</cite>
  2) Resolve seasonal phenology across regions (northern vs. Mediterranean) to time releases for oviposition overlap with susceptible slug life stages and to avoid midwinter cold exposure; refine protocols for egg-matrix placement in furrows/drains that maintain humidity. <cite id="59c9dcc7-8">Regional distributions and native context are known; combining distributional data with habitat engineering can guide timing and placement.</cite>
  3) Integrate telemetry/trash-tagging and environmental DNA (eDNA) to track dispersal kernels and effective area covered per release, informing spacing and repeat cycles.

4) Quantitative field efficacy and threshold modeling
- Problem: Reviews recognize the promise of “predatory Diptera” against slugs but emphasize the need for rigorous, geographically explicit data across climates and slug communities. The current evidence base is fragmented and often observational. <cite id="59c9dcc7-4">The first cross-taxa review for predatory Diptera against slugs highlights potential but calls for more comprehensive evaluation across applications.</cite> <cite id="59c9dcc7-1">Sciomyzid potential for slug biocontrol is recognized, but literature gaps remain in translation to practice across regions.</cite>
- Priority actions:
  1) Conjoint trials with mass-releases of T. elata and phorid/stratiomid scavenger flies across Europe and North America should include paired nematode (Phasmarhabditis hermaphrodita) treatments to quantify suppression rates, yield loss protection, and carryover effects on recolonization post-treatment. <cite id="59c9dcc7-8">Nematodes and parasitoids each impact population dynamics; combined programs require coordinated trials to avoid antagonism and to sum effects.</cite> <cite id="57128280-9">Studies in related gastropod systems show that Phasmarhabditis hermaphrodita can be lethal to target slugs under certain conditions, supporting its role as a core Bt component but also demanding careful integration.</cite>
  2) Derive empirical inundation thresholds (release density vs. slug biomass) that deliver predictable kill curves and time-to-control across sizes and species, and calibrate these to habitat quality indices from point 3. <cite id="59c9dcc7-0">Performance differences by slug species and exposure history imply threshold models must be species- and context-specific.</cite>
  3) Build decision tools that incorporate weather forecasts (rainfall, frost risk), slug movement into moist refugia, and predator emergence to schedule proactive releases.

5) Mass rearing, quality control, and delivery systems
- Problem: Operational performance hinges on producing high-viability, pathogen-free eggs/pupae; environmental contamination risks must be minimized, and deployment methods must maintain egg matrix moisture and protect larvae from desiccation and predation. <cite id="59c9dcc7-0">Maternal effects and prey exposure history can reduce pupariation and larval fitness, emphasizing high-standard rearing inputs.</cite> <cite id="59c9dcc7-3">Ecological constraints in habitat design interact with delivery methods to determine realized efficacy.</cite>
- Priority actions:
  1) Develop standardized rearing protocols (maternal diet formulation, sanitation, biosecurity to exclude pathogens) with continuous DNA-based lineage verification to preserve intended host specificity. <cite id="3bf66a6a-0">Cryptic specialization implies biosecurity and correct species identity are essential to avoid off-target outcomes.</cite>
  2) Engineer delivery matrices (clay-loam slurries, sphagnum moss variants, biodegradable mats) and application rigs for tractor/roto-tiller incorporation that sustain egg moisture for 7–14 days across soil textures; quantify incubation-to-first-emergence and predation rates in field ditches/beds. <cite id="59c9dcc7-8">Habitat engineering in conservation biological control frameworks is a viable path for scaling Tetanocera releases in native wetlands.</cite>
  3) Evaluate vertical and horizontal dispersal of emerging flies using marked-release and eDNA surveys to tune block sizes and repeat intervals.

6) Stacked-predator programs, coevolution with slug resistance, and IPM integration
- Problem: Single-tooled biocontrol often fails under fluctuating slug populations and climate; shifting from parasitoids to predators reconfigures population dynamics and may demand different timing and dosing logic. Program-level impacts require testing across multiple guilds and seasons. <cite id="59c9dcc7-1">Reviews of biological and bio-rational strategies emphasize multi-tool approaches and the need to move beyond single-agent anecdotes.</cite> <cite id="57128280-8">Decades of nematode-based slug control highlight both efficacy potential and practical limitations, motivating multi-predator stacking and improved resistance management.</cite>
- Priority actions:
  1) Design factorial field experiments combining T. elata with Phasmarhabditis-based inundations, carabid habitat enhancements, and cultural practices (scarification, drainage management), measuring season-long slug densities and crop damage across years. <cite id="57128280-8">Nematicide deployment lessons translate into program structure and integrated tactics needed to achieve durable suppression.</cite>
  2) Monitor for host specialization shifts during multi-year augmentations, including potential shifts in larval host breadth and microbial load effects, and adapt mass-rearing inputs and release prescriptions accordingly. <cite id="3bf66a6a-2">Observed changes in larval host breadth with instar and genus-level feeding breadth in T. elata justify routine re-evaluation under augmented conditions.</cite> <cite id="59c9dcc7-0">Nematode-exposed host slugs depress parasitoid pupariation, highlighting the need to track microbial side-effects in predator performance.</cite>
  3) Codify extension guidelines for rotating tactics by climate zone and slug community, with early-warning diagnostics (soil moisture telemetry, egg traps, sentinel slug assays).

7) Regulatory pathways, risk assessment, and native impacts
- Problem: Conservation biological control with a native Holarctic Tetanocera elata is promising, but risk assessments need quantified impacts on non-target mollusks, soil food webs, and vector-borne parasites/disease reservoirs. Frameworks from freshwater snail biocontrol show how natural enemies can carry pathogens and restructure communities, so analogous safeguards are warranted in agricultural slug systems. <cite id="59c9dcc7-8">T. elata is widespread in the Holarctic and an obligate parasitoid/predator of D. reticulatum; conservation deployment pathways merit careful design.</cite> <cite id="59c9dcc7-6">Natural enemies of snail-killing flies have been evaluated as to their impact in disease-carrying freshwater snail programs, illustrating that ecological side-effects must be quantified before widescale augmentation.</cite>
- Priority actions:
  1) Run mesocosm and field cages to quantify predation on non-target mollusk guilds (non-pests, endangered springsnails), microbial community changes, and potential pathogen carriage/maintenance by released flies. <cite id="59c9dcc7-6">Structured evaluation of impacts in analogous systems provides a template for risk scoring and mitigation in agricultural deployments.</cite>
  2) Develop cumulative-impact models for “predator stacks,” where multiple natural enemies are used together, to define acceptable risk envelopes for each component. <cite id="59c9dcc7-1">Multi-tool recommendations in reviews argue for risk-tolerable thresholds set jointly across agents.</cite>
  3) Streamline permitting for DNA-verified, native T. elata releases in suitable habitats, coupled with post-release monitoring checkpoints and rapid-response containment protocols.

8) Training, diagnostics, and farmer-facing decision support
- Priority actions:
  1) Build diagnostic guides that combine slug ID, habitat and moisture forecasts with an “ecosystem compatibility score” for deploying sciomyzids and integrating with nematodes/carabids. <cite id="57128280-4">Review guidance to farmers emphasizes nonchemical strategies and the need to align tactics with local slugs and conditions.</cite>
  2) Train extension and scouts in integrative identification (morphology + DNA swabs) for recovered flies and sentinel slugs, and in small-scale mass-rearing/caging assays to verify locally relevant host specificity and performance before landscape-scale deployment. <cite id="3bf66a6a-5">Metabarcoding expands practical identifications; training programs can bring molecular diagnostics to advisors and farmers.</cite>
  3) Pilot participatory platforms for farmers to track slug outbreaks and report T. elata emergence success; use crowdsourced data to refine climate-based thresholds and release prescriptions.

9) Geospatial expansion and climate adaptation
- Problem: Apparent performance of T. elata is reported across temperate zones, but latitudinal and elevational transferability is uncertain; wetland habitat models plus slug phenology imply different window lengths across climates. <cite id="59c9dcc7-8">Native, Holarctic distribution across diverse climates suggests adaptation potential, yet local performance varies with ecological context.</cite>
- Priority actions:
  1) Launch a multi-node deployment network across climate zones to map performance envelopes, with standardized metrics and rearing provenances to partition genotype-by-environment effects. <cite id="59c9dcc7-3">Ecological envelopes can be parameterized from habitat-specific data to guide region-by-region adaptation.</cite>
  2) Develop cold- and drought-tolerant egg-matrix formulations and sheltered emergence microhabitats for northern latitudes; evaluate additive microbes (e.g., mutualists) to stabilize development without expanding host range. <cite id="59c9dcc7-8">Nordic to Mediterranean distributions imply the need to tune delivery and microclimates for emergence success at range edges.</cite>

10) Knowledge transfer: from lab to land through replicated, replicated on-farm trials and adaptive management
- Priority actions:
  1) Establish multi-year, multi-farm randomized-block trials with treatment combinations (T. elata alone vs. stacked with nematodes/carabids; different release densities/timing), with nested monitoring (soil cores, pitfall/interception, crop damage, seedling losses). <cite id="57128280-8">Adaptive management following nematode deployment experience demonstrates that on-farm learning is integral to scaling efficacy and cost-effectiveness.</cite>
  2) Use Bayesian learning and early-harvest decision analytics to update release prescriptions weekly based on observed slug densities and fly emergence, producing locally calibrated models transparent to farmers and regulators. <cite id="59c9dcc7-1">Literature-level review calls for rigorous, scalable adoption pathways that translate science into practice across regions.</cite>

Summary: The most urgent, high-yield research priorities are to fix identity and monitoring with DNA-integrated pipelines, quantify multi-species host-range and antagonist interactions under standardized rearing and field conditions, parameterize habitat–timing models for predictable deployment, and build multi-season on-farm trials of stacked predators with regulatory-ready risk assessments.
