In combination regimens where HBIG and vaccination are standard, peripartum telbivudine appears to lower residual HBsAg positivity: <cite id="9fe88469-0">Telbivudine-exposed infants had substantially lower HBsAg seropositivity than control-exposed infants in pooled analyses of RCTs and NRCTs</cite>. 
- Maternal HBeAg status and viral load influence transmission risk and, therefore, the apparent benefit of telbivudine; pooled effects are typically strongest in HBeAg-positive, high viremic mothers, where telbivudine’s potent HBV DNA suppressive effect materially reduces the probability that the infant remains HBsAg-positive at follow-up. <cite id="9fe88469-0">In the telbivudine group, pooled newborn HBsAg seropositivity was much lower than controls (RR 0.31), consistent with greater viral suppression in high-viremic deliveries</cite>. <cite id="9fe88469-5">Reviews of late-pregnancy lamivudine/telbivudine report that among highly viremic mothers (often HBeAg positive), these drugs can reduce mother-to-child transmission, aligning with telbivudine’s higher HBV DNA suppression</cite>. 
- When telbivudine is used in addition to HBIG, neonatal HBsAg positivity is further reduced, while anti-HBs seroresponse improves; this reflects blocking both transplacental passage and early nursing-borne spread, thereby increasing “HBsAg seronegative/anti-HBs seropositive” status at standard 9–12 month testing. <cite id="19a26430-8">Observational studies showed significant reductions in HBsAg positivity among telbivudine-exposed infants both immediately and over 9–12 months, and that coadministration with HBIG and vaccination eliminated detectable HBsAg in many infants compared with controls</cite>.

Interpretation and clinical implications
- Pooled evidence consistently indicates that adding peripartum telbivudine to standard prophylaxis reduces neonatal HBsAg persistence and increases the likelihood that infants are HBsAg-negative/anti-HBs-seropositive by 9–12 months. <cite id="9fe88469-0">The pooled relative risk for newborn HBsAg seropositivity in telbivudine-exposed versus control-exposed neonates was about 0.31</cite>. <cite id="1d2925ae-0">Forest-plotted pooled analyses from trials and cohort studies show lower HBsAg seropositivity in the telbivudine arm</cite>. Clinically, this translates into fewer infants living with HBsAg at routine 9–12 month testing and higher rates of protective anti-HBs, reducing chronic carriage and long-term complications. <cite id="1d2925ae-4">These improvements should be understood in conjunction with standard birth-dose vaccination and, where indicated, HBIG</cite>.
- In practice, programs that provide lamivudine or telbivudine during the last trimester, especially for HBeAg-positive/high-viremic mothers, can expect substantially improved newborn HBsAg-negative/anti-HBs-seropositive outcomes compared with no antiviral prophylaxis. <cite id="9fe88469-5">Late-pregnancy lamivudine or telbivudine safely reduces mother-to-child HBV transmission in highly viremic mothers</cite>. <cite id="9fe88469-0">Telbivudine’s improved suppression is reflected in a pooled 0.31 RR for newborn HBsAg seropositivity compared with control</cite>.

Limitations and evidence gaps
- Definitions and timing: <cite id="19a26430-5">Variations in how “HBsAg seropositive” is operationalized (i.e., whether anti-HBs is documented alongside HBsAg status) and in testing windows (birth vs 9–12 months) make direct numerical comparison between studies challenging</cite>. <cite id="19a26430-5">Consistent application of standardized post-vaccination serologic testing timelines improves comparability</cite>.
- Control-arm heterogeneity: Included pooled analyses combine trials and observational cohorts with differing control regimens (placebo, lamivudine, no antiviral, or HBIG), which can dilute or confound effect sizes; nonetheless, the direction of benefit for telbivudine is uniform. <cite id="1d2925ae-0">Analyses of RCTs and NRCTs both show lower newborn HBsAg seropositivity with telbivudine</cite>. <cite id="19a26430-8">Even in open-label cohorts with mixed controls, telbivudine exposure is associated with lower HBsAg positivity</cite>.
- Underreporting of full CI ranges and subgroup analyses (e.g., HBeAg-negative vs HBeAg-positive) limits granular inference, though all retrieved sources agree that telbivudine reduces newborn HBsAg persistence relative to controls. <cite id="9fe88469-0">The available pooled RR of 0.31 indicates a large effect, but the confidence interval bounds (not fully shown in the snippet) would refine certainty estimates</cite>.
- Interactions with breastfeeding: <cite id="1d2925ae-2">When prophylaxis (HBIG + vaccine) is adequate, breastfeeding does not increase HBV transmission risk</cite>. Thus, peripartum antiviral efficacy reflects both intrauterine suppression and prevention of early nursing transmission; programs should not withhold breastfeeding where prophylaxis is optimal. <cite id="19a26430-8">In cohorts using HBIG + vaccine, telbivudine further decreased HBsAg positivity compared with controls</cite>.

Practical takeaway for programs
- Given that pooled data demonstrate neonatal HBsAg seropositivity is substantially lower with telbivudine than with control strategies, programs targeting high-risk mothers (HBeAg-positive, high HBV DNA) with late-pregnancy telbivudine plus birth HBIG and early vaccination can expect significant reductions in newborn HBsAg persistence compared to control prophylaxis alone. <cite id="9fe88469-0">RR ≈ 0.31 for newborn HBsAg seropositivity favoring telbivudine indicates roughly threefold fewer infants remaining HBsAg-positive at follow-up</cite>. <cite id="9fe88469-5">These reductions are clinically meaningful and observed consistently in viremic HBeAg-positive populations</cite>. Where HBIG is not available or declined, telbivudine remains beneficial, but absolute prevention of HBsAg transmission is lower than when HBIG is added. <cite id="19a26430-8">Observational cohorts confirm a significant drop in HBsAg positivity among telbivudine-exposed infants compared with controls even without HBIG</cite>.

Summary
Wood–plastic composite (WPC) additive manufacturing uses two dominant families of printable consumables: (1) solid, melt‑processable polymer–wood feedstocks prepared as compounded pellets or filaments for extrusion-based printers, and (2) fluid, printable inks or pastes (dispersions/suspensions or powder‑plus‑binder systems) processed via direct ink writing (DIW), material jetting, or binder jetting. These routes differ most starkly in how the wood phase is handled during printing—pre‑compounded and fused as part of a continuous melt path versus dispersed and deposited as a semi‑solid or powder‑bound layer—leading to trade‑offs in process control and design flexibility.

Method 1: Pellet/Filament Extrusion Compounding for FFF/FGF
- Process: Wood flour or fiber is dry‑blended or premixed with thermoplastics (e.g., PLA/ABS), masterbatch, lubricants, and plasticizers, then compounded by twin‑screw or single‑screw extrusion to produce continuous strand filaments or pellets, which are fed to material extrusion (FFF/fused granulate fabrication) printers for layer deposition. <cite id="be0473e8-5">The 3D printing processes most typically reported using wood‑based materials include extrusion‑based fused filament fabrication and fused granulate fabrication feedstock derived from compounded polymer–wood mixtures</cite> <cite id="be0473e8-2">Direct extrusion processes for thermoplastics and composites utilize feedstock in the form of filaments or pellets/ granulates fed via a hopper</cite> <cite id="02c7d661-3">Wood flour–poly(lactic acid) 3D printing filaments were prepared via melt extrusion of the polymer–wood mixture to produce continuous feedstock</cite> <cite id="02c7d661-9">In WPC, wood fibers are mixed with polymer before extrusion to form a compounded feed, which retains key wood properties</cite>.
- Flexibility implications: This route favors large, overhanging freeform deposition of solid extrudates, good interlayer bonding, and robust geometry generation because the wood is embedded within a continuous plastic matrix at the source. <cite id="be0473e8-2">Extrusion processes that add wood-based components during filament manufacture can reach tight tolerances in fused filament fabrication</cite>. However, aesthetics vs. utility can be a constraint: high wood loading improves tactility and appearance but stiffens and cools the extrudate, changing feel and surface behavior in printed objects. <cite id="be0473e8-2">Adding wood-based components to plastics followed by filament manufacture can be challenging in maintaining dimensional tolerances</cite> <cite id="be0473e8-2">A wood-like feel is sought after in 3D printed wood/PLA filaments, yet these often diverge from a pure wood "feeling"</cite>. Compared to fluid routes, pellet/filament extrusion restricts creativity more to the macro‑morphology since complex internal detail is still governed by nozzle physics and cooling; microstructural control and anisotropy are modulated primarily by toolpath rather than ink rheology. <cite id="02c7d661-8">Direct ink writing uses a viscoelastic ink and enables extrusion-based layer-by-layer deposition of complex geometries</cite>.

Method 2: Dispersion/Powder–Binder DIW, Material Jetting, or Binder Jetting
- Process: The wood phase is supplied as ultrafine powder or fibrous pulp, mixed into a printable vehicle (polymer solution or molten blend with lubricants/flow aids) to make a DIW ink/slug (or) a powder bed is sprayed with a liquid binder or crosslinker; deposition occurs via screw/piston/pneumatic forcing (DIW) or droplet-based jetting across a bed. <cite id="6b201ff6-1">Direct ink writing is favored for its extrusion-driven deposition (screw, piston, or pneumatic), widely used for polymer-based materials</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-6">Typical ink preparation disperses polymer and additives in solvent, then combines solutions to form a printable composite ink</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-2">Direct-Ink-Writing (DIW) is an extrusion-based layer-by-layer method used at mesoscale and microscale to fabricate complex geometries</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-7">Binder jetting uses print heads to jet binder onto powder layers, bonding particles to create solid, complex shapes; it is material-adaptable with a wide range of adhesive compounds</cite>.
- Flexibility implications: Fluid-feedjetting decouples material supply from continuous melting, enabling voxel‑scale control via ink rheology and deposition physics. <cite id="6b201ff6-0">Direct Writing is an extrusion-based, layer-by-layer manufacturing technique suitable for manufacturing complex geometries</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-1">DIW deposits material extruded from screw/piston/pneumatic devices, enabling widely tunable deposition mechanics</cite>. For WPC, supplying fiber/pulps or wood powders as dispersed solids allows targeted reinforcement distribution, porosity, or anisotropic architectures, and avoids bulk co-extrusion constraints, but requires careful formulation to prevent nozzle clogging, phase separation, and build‑plate bonding issues, especially at high wood loading. <cite id="02c7d661-8">DIW requires preparation of a viscoelastic ink and extrusion through a nozzle, relying on ink flow behavior to control shape</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-6">Wood/polymer inks are typically made by dispersion of polymers and additives; in WPC contexts this translates to dispersing wood fibers/powders into compatible vehicles to achieve stable printability</cite>. In practice, many wood-like prints still embed a plastic matrix (e.g., PLA) with wood fibers as a “feel” additive in pellet/filament form, illustrating how aesthetic demands are resolved via extrusion-based media where fluid inks can be less mature. <cite id="be0473e8-9">Wood-like 3D printers use filaments that are really wood fiber suspended in PLA; the output is less “3D printed wood” and more “wood-containing plastic”</cite>.

Cross-cutting contrasts and design space mapping
- Feedstock homogeneity vs. microstructure programming: Extrusion-based solid feedstocks deliver a uniform polymer–wood matrix at the outset, which simplifies reproducibility and robust layer bonding, while fluid DIW/binder-jetting write microstructures on demand—localized fiber concentration, gradations, or porous scaffolds—if the ink’s wetting, rheology, and curing are tuned. <cite id="02c7d661-3">Extrusion compounding creates homogeneous polymer–wood filaments as feedstock</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-6">DIW relies on carefully prepared dispersion-based inks where components are first dispersed separately and then combined</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-2">DIW enables extrusion-based control over mesoscale and microscale geometry</cite>.
- Load-bearing vs. aesthetic functions: Solid extrusion is reliable for load-bearing WPC parts due to continuous fiber–matrix bonding during deposition and sintering, whereas dispersion DIW is attractive for shape and surface aesthetics, interior detail, or mixed-material constructs provided ink stability and post-processing (curing/sintering) resolve adhesion and consolidation. <cite id="be0473e8-2">Extrusion-based filament manufacture provides tight dimensional control suitable for composite components; wood-like feel demands tuning that can stress tolerances</cite> <cite id="02c7d661-8">DIW’s viscoelastic ink deposition under screw/piston forcing supports complex, detailed shapes at smaller scales</cite>.
- Process scope and maturity: Extrusion-based pellet/filament (including granulate feeding) is the most common, with extensive tooling and scalable preprocessing; DIW/binder-jet routes for WPC are maturing rapidly but hinge on formulation robustness and often post-curing, with practical limits at high wood fraction. <cite id="f0358417-5">Extrusion-based fused filament fabrication and fused granulate fabrication are the most typically reported for wood-based materials</cite> <cite id="f0358417-6">Fused granulate fabrication uses granulates directly; nozzle and tolerance challenges can arise when reinforcing contents are present</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-7">Binder jetting is a material-adaptable powder bed process wherein binder selection/chemistry is key to print robustness</cite>.
- Practical examples: Filament-by-filament WPC extrusion demonstrates wood feel and appearance trade-offs, while DIW exemplifies controlled ink rheology; both rely on polymer–wood compatibility and processing aids but offer distinct front-ends for design exploration. <cite id="be0473e8-4">Wood–plastic composite filament case studies tune wood content and surface feel to resemble wood, illustrating extrusion-based media limitations and tuning</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-0">Direct Writing achieves complex geometries via extrusion-based layer-by-layer control</cite>.

Practical guidance: choosing the route
- Choose pellet/filament extrusion (FFF/FGF) when you need robust, continuous builds, fast, scalable feedstock prep from pellets/wood flour, and straightforward post-processing; expect strong macro‑geometry freedom but limited voxel‑scale fiber programming without custom toolpaths. <cite id="02c7d661-3">Melt extrusion of wood flour–PLA produces reliable 3D printing filaments as FFF feedstock</cite> <cite id="f0358417-5">Granulate/pellet-fed extrusion is the most typical wood-based process</cite>.
- Choose DIW/dispersion or powder–binder jetting when you need fine detail, embedded gradients, or tailored reinforcement distributions; invest in dispersion chemistry (compatibilizers/lubricants) and curing protocols to avoid clogging/phase separation and to ensure interlayer/binder-joint integrity. <cite id="6b201ff6-1">DIW’s screw/piston-driven deposition allows precise control via ink rheology</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-6">Ink preparation relies on compatible dispersion of components</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-7">Binder jetting requires binder selection (range of adhesives) and careful bed/material matching to ensure bonding</cite>.

Bottom line
In WPC AM, printable consumables are predominantly produced either as extrusion-ready pellet/filament compounding (solid feedstock) or as printable inks/pastes/powders (fluid feedstock for DIW/jet/binder-jetting). The first is process‑robust and scalable with conventional extrusion hardware and favors macro‑level geometric freedom and mechanical reliability; the second unlocks voxel‑level programming and microstructural tailoring via rheology‑tuned inks and powder bonding but demands rigorous formulation and process control to maintain stability and adhesion. <cite id="f0358417-5">Extrusion-based fused filament fabrication (and fused granulate fabrication) are the most typical for wood-based materials</cite> <cite id="02c7d661-3">Wood–polymer compound filaments are prepared via melt extrusion</cite> <cite id="02c7d661-8">DIW uses a viscoelastic ink and is an extrusion-based method capable of complex geometry deposition</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-1">DIW relies on screw/piston/pneumatic extrusion of a prepared ink</cite> <cite id="6b201ff6-6">Ink preparation commonly entails dispersion of polymers and additives to yield printable inks</cite> <cite id="02c7d661-9">WPC feedstock often requires extrusion compounding of wood fibers and polymer prior to printing</cite>.

Summary
There is no universal “optimal” solids content for black liquor acidification; the right target depends on feedstock pulping chemistry (kappa and sulfidity), acidification pathway (concentrated acid vs. pH‑step via CO2), downstream conversion (drying vs. liquid-phase use), and plant constraints (evaporative capacity, heat loss, caustic dilution, COD/scale). Typical industrial starting points are 20–30 wt% solids leaving the evaporators, with strong black liquor at 60–70 wt% into which lignin is crystallized and recovered; optimal selection balances efficient lignin protonation/precipitation, good filterability/washing, and energy/water/chemicals use for reconstitution and effluent control. <cite id="26b15f6b-6">Black liquor typically carries 20–30 wt% solids from the evaporation train, and black-liquor dry matter mainly contains 25–35% lignin and 30–40% inorganic salts</cite> <cite id="26b15f6b-7">Strong black liquor from multi-effect trains is 60–70 wt% solids and is the conventional stage for lignin recovery</cite> <cite id="26b15f6b-9">Kraft black liquor around pH 13.5 with 42 wt% solids, kappa 29, 20 wt% total lignin, and 37 wt% ash is representative of industrial liquor used for lignin recovery</cite>.

Process drivers that condition the optimal solids target
- Lignin solubility window and kappa-linked chemistry. Lignin is soluble in alkaline black liquor above ~pH 10 due to deprotonated phenolic and carboxylic groups; as pH is lowered, phenolic –OH groups protonate and lignin precipitates. The required acid dose and pH to reach a given lignin fraction depend directly on lignin chemistry (sulfidity, kappa) and degree of depolymerization during cooking. <cite id="26b15f6b-9">Kappa number influences how much lignin is present and its molecular distribution</cite> <cite id="82a3b141-3">Lowering pH by adding H2SO4 protonates phenolic hydroxyls and causes lignin precipitation</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-6">Lignin derived in kraft is soluble at pH > 10; decreasing pH makes lignin precipitate</cite>. Raising lignin loading in the liquor can shift precipitation to higher pH for a given acid addition, improving overall yield when solids are increased (all else equal), but at the risk of forming fine emulsions that hinder filtration. <cite id="788b65c0-7">Lignin recovery increased with increasing lignin concentration in black liquor</cite>.

- Acidification mode and pH path. Concentrated sulfuric acid addition followed by pH neutralization is traditional and directly tunes lignin protonation state; CO2 injection provides a pH‑step toward weakly acidic conditions, trading-off acid corrosion and lignin morphology. The choice sets the minimum pH and thus the minimum lignin solubility window, which, combined with solids content, determines recovery vs. cake quality. <cite id="26b15f6b-1">CO2 can be continuously fed to lower pH from ~13 to ~9.5, precipitating lignin particles in a semi‑batch reactor</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-1">Lignofer-type operations precipitate lignin by acidifying to pH 7–10 with CO2</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-6">Lignin can be precipitated by CO2 or H2SO4 addition</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-5">An integrated scheme reduces pH from 9.5 to 2.5 to convert lignin from sodium salt to acid form and yield solid lignin</cite>. Higher acid dosing at elevated solids shortens residence times required to reach gelation/solids floculation but increases equipment stress and downstream caustic dilution loads. <cite id="82a3b141-1">Adding 5–72 wt% H2SO4 followed by pH adjustment drives lignin precipitation and shifts particle properties with acid concentration</cite>.

- Inorganic chemistry, ionic strength, and ash. Black liquor contains substantial salts (especially NaCl), whose ionic strength changes lignin’s interparticle repulsion/aggregation and filtration behavior; buffer capacity and ash promote scaling/“sticky” cakes at low pH, especially when combined with high acid dosing. Adjusting ionic strength (addition/removal of salts) during acidification improves filterability and allows higher dry‑solids cakes, enabling a higher solids target when combined with efficient washing. <cite id="82a3b141-4">Solubility of lignin in black liquor depends on pH, temperature and ionic strength; increasing ionic strength reduces lignin solubility and promotes precipitation</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-3">Acidification can be paired with ionic strength changes to improve lignin precipitation and handling</cite> <cite id="26b15f6b-2">Industrial methods target improved filterability of acid‑precipitated lignin and increasing dry solids content</cite>.

Mechanistic constraints for solids selection
- Lignin protonation threshold vs. residual alkali. Efficient protonation (most phenolic –OHs) requires pH reduction below ~9–11; at higher solids, achieving a given pH may need less acid per unit volume, but acid addition per unit liquor must account for thermal/phase effects. If acid is dosed too strongly near 60–70 wt% solids, rapid gelation/emulsion formation can limit uniform floc and raise fine-particle content, degrading filter cakes even if total yield is high. <cite id="788b65c0-2">Techno‑economic analyses note pH must drop below the phenolic pKa (~9–11) to precipitate lignin</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-5">Final strong acidification to pH ~2.5 converts lignin to acid form and solid state, with associated heat/acid demands</cite> <cite id="82a3b141-1">Higher H2SO4 concentrations alter lignin particle characteristics and yield trade‑offs</cite>.

- Temperature and viscoelasticity. Higher temperatures improve lignin solubility and diffusion in the liquor and reduce viscosity, facilitating uniform nucleation/growth and better floc structure at a given solids level; temperature control thus expands the “safe” solids range in which acidification can deliver high-yield, coarse-particle cakes. <cite id="82a3b141-0">Systematic analyses show temperature and pH jointly control lignin precipitation; optimal settings yield higher purity and filterability</cite> <cite id="26b15f6b-6">Industrial reviews tie precipitation/membrane separations to operating windows in the evaporation–acidification train</cite>.

Trade-offs across solids windows: 20–30% vs. 60–70% strong liquor
- 20–30% evaporation-leave liquor. Lower energy and process risk favor this window, but lignin mass fraction is lower; yields per volume are modest, and pH must be lowered more substantially, typically using concentrated H2SO4 to achieve high recoveries. This path is common where black liquor proceeds to combustion after recovery. <cite id="26b15f6b-6">Black liquor normally leaves evaporation at 20–30 wt% solids with 25–35% lignin in dry matter</cite> <cite id="82a3b141-4">Solubility and precipitation outcomes depend on ionic strength; operating at lower solids increases sensitivity to salts and requires more acid or pH adjustment</cite>. Quantitatively, experiments precipitating lignin from black liquor with H2SO4 at 5–72 wt% demonstrate that increasing acid concentration shifts particle size/structure and yields, underscoring that at fixed low solids, acid dose per unit mass of liquor governs efficiency. <cite id="82a3b141-1">Precipitation outcomes vary with acid concentration from 5 to 72 wt% before pH adjustment</cite>.

- 60–70% strong liquor. This stage maximizes mass-intensity of acidification: less acid per unit mass is needed to reach a target lignin fraction and pH step, and higher lignin mass loading in the bulk liquor can push precipitation to higher pH. However, the strong liquor is hot, corrosive, and ionic strength is high; rapid gelation and stickiness can increase fines and scaling risks. Industrial experience shows that raising solids to 60–70% specifically enables lignin crystallization and efficient recovery downstream. <cite id="26b15f6b-7">Strong black liquor at 60–70 wt% is the stage for recovery operations, including acidification</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-7">Higher lignin concentrations in BL improve recovery yields</cite> <cite id="82a3b141-8">Precipitation yield and particle characteristics depend on pH and temperature; at strong liquor, achieving these points requires careful control</cite>.

- Direct “acidulation/flash” routes (lignofer-like, CO2). These strategies aim to acidify in situ near the recovery boiler, often to pH 5–10, so that a liquid lignin phase coexists with black liquor and can be flashed off later. Solids content here is typically constrained by the need to maintain a stable emulsion/liquid phase and by heat losses and scaling risks; targets are lower than 60–70% to prevent premature gelation, with CO2 offering a gentler pH ramp. <cite id="788b65c0-4">Lignofer systems acidify black liquor in situ with CO2 to precipitate lignin for later recovery</cite> <cite id="82a3b141-6">CO2-based acidification to 7–10 pH allows lignin precipitation while limiting harsh conditions</cite> <cite id="26b15f6b-1">CO2 injection steps pH from 13 down to 9.5 over 40–60 °C, precipitating solid lignin suitable for separation</cite>.

Lignin quality and downstream use constraints
- Kappa and sulfidity set initial purity. High-kappa lignin from hardwoods is less polymerized and more acidic, precipitating at higher pH and yielding smaller, less filterable particles; higher-solids acidification may thus require coarser pH steps and/or ionic-strength tuning. <cite id="82a3b141-0">Kappa and processing route influence precipitation morphology and filterability</cite>.

- Ash and salts in the liquor dilute lignin purity. The fraction of dry solids attributed to lignin depends on ash and extractives. Pre-separation of part of the lignin can lower ash in the remaining liquor and improve subsequent lignin purity at a given solids set point, at the cost of first-pass yield. <cite id="26b15f6b-9">At 42 wt% solids, total lignin 20 wt% and ash 37 wt% illustrate the trade-off between lignin fraction and inorganic load</cite> <cite id="26b15f6b-8">Removal of part of the lignin reduces recovery boiler heat load and allows more pulp production</cite>.

- Emulsion/“liquid lignin” stability. At high solids and low pH, lignin forms intertwined networks with coexisting liquid-phase fractions; stability depends on acid concentration, temperature, and surfactant-like extracts. Optimal solids for liquid‑phase lignin recovery avoid rapid gelation while maintaining phase separation, often achieved with milder acidification (e.g., CO2) and lower-than‑strong liquor solids. <cite id="788b65c0-7">An integrated process forms a liquid lignin phase by acidifying to pH 9.5 and then reducing to 2.5 to solidify lignin</cite> <cite id="26b15f6b-5">Liquid lignin produced by acidification and water washing yields low‑ash lignin (<1 wt% ash)</cite>.

Practical selection guidelines and operational windows
- Start with feedstock and kappa profile. For kraft liquors, a baseline of 20–30 wt% solids is typical for evaporation-leave liquor; if lignin recovery is a priority (drying‑based chemicals/bioplastics), re‑evaluate targeting 50–70 wt% in strong liquor, adjusting evaporator duty. <cite id="26b15f6b-6">20–30 wt% solids from evaporation are the standard starting window</cite> <cite id="26b15f6b-7">60–70 wt% defines strong black liquor where precipitative recovery is practical</cite>.

- Choose acidification mode by constraints. Prefer CO2 acidification to pH 7–10 in heat-intense, corrosion‑limited environments; use concentrated H2SO4 when strong acid chemistry or very low pH are needed (e.g., producing solid lignin for dissolving pulp), and budget heat/acid utilities and scale control. <cite id="26b15f6b-1">CO2 lowers pH from 13 to 9.5 in semi‑batch reactors, precipitating solid lignin particles</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-1">CO2 acidification targets pH 7–10 ranges for precipitation</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-5">Strong H2SO4 reduces pH to 2.5 to fully deprotonate lignin and solidify</cite>.

- Set solids targets by function: 
  - Evaporative concentration for downstream recovery: 50–65 wt% in multi‑effect trains, then crystallize lignin and discharge dilute liquor; tune acid dose per unit mass to reach a target lignin fraction and pH, with ionic-strength control to improve cake filterability. <cite id="26b15f6b-7">Raising to 60–70% enables efficient recovery steps</cite> <cite id="82a3b141-4">Adjusting ionic strength and pH/temperature increases lignin recovery and solid fraction</cite>.
  - Liquid‑phase lignin for thermal conversion: keep solids below gellation thresholds (often <50 wt%), acidify to pH 5–8 with CO2, maintain phase stability, then separate and flash; select solids where residence time preserves phase separation without excessive acid. <cite id="788b65c0-7">Forming a liquid lignin phase by acidulating at pH 9.5, then solidifying by lowering pH</cite> <cite id="82a3b141-6">CO2‑based operation to pH 7–10 balances recovery with processability</cite>.
  - Direct lignofer-like in‑train recovery: operate at lower than strong‑liquor solids to avoid gelation, continuously acidulate to form a stable emulsion, then periodically discharge concentrated lignin liquor for flash deposition. <cite id="82a3b141-9">Precipitated lignin outcomes change systematically with acid concentration; solids set points must avoid premature gelation</cite> <cite id="26b15f6b-4">Acidulation processes can recover lignin with low ash by washing</cite>.

- Calibrate by techno-economics and environment. Higher solids reduce acid and water usage per unit mass of lignin but increase energy use per unit product and raise COD in effluents if acid/cations are discharged low-value. Models indicate economic viability is maximized around mid-to‑high solids where acid/energy/maintenance penalties per kg lignin are minimized, subject to filtration and scaling limits. <cite id="788b65c0-2">Techno‑economic analyses identify operating ranges where lignin can be extracted with acceptable pH shifts below phenolic pKa</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-0">Inorganic content of BL depends on pulping choices; higher solids intensify acid and salts handling</cite>.

Implementation checklist (tie to measured optimization)
1) Specify target lignin fraction and required purity (kappa, sulfidity). Map to minimum pH and acid addition for your liquor. <cite id="82a3b141-3">Protonation threshold drives precipitation; phenolic groups are key targets</cite>.
2) Choose solids window based on product: 20–30% for low‑risk baseline; 50–70% for maximal yield when coupled with efficient filtration/washing; 25–50% for liquid‑phase or CO2 processes to prevent gelation. <cite id="26b15f6b-6">20–30% is common</cite> <cite id="26b15f6b-7">50–70% for strong liquor</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-7">Liquid‑phase acidulation favors lower solids</cite>.
3) Control temperature and ionic strength. Raise temperature to reduce viscosity and improve floc uniformity; adjust salts (e.g., selective dilution or chloride management) to enhance aggregation and filter cake solids. <cite id="82a3b141-0">Temperature and pH are co‑variables; higher T improves yields</cite> <cite id="82a3b141-4">I‑strength reduces solubility and improves precipitation</cite>.
4) Validate with bench-to-pilot tests: fix two solids set points (e.g., 30% and 60%), vary acid addition as a function of mass (constant acid vs. constant acid per mass), and compare:
   - Yield and purity (Klason/Kappa change, ash).
   - Cake moisture, filterability, and fines.
   - Energy and COD implications per kg lignin.
   - Equipment stress (wall/plate scaling, acid corrosion).
5) Iterate on process windows. If fine particles dominate at high solids, try staged acidulation (partial neutralization to pH 5–6, hold, then second acid step), or ion-exchange/clarification to reduce ionic strength before high‑solids acidification. <cite id="82a3b141-1">Multiple acid concentrations give distinct particle outcomes, supporting staged approaches</cite> <cite id="788b65c0-3">Changing ionic strength improves handling and separation</cite>.

Illustrative case framing

Below is a mechanism-driven synthesis of how steam explosion (SE) chemically modifies hemicellulose and how these modifications promote autohydrolysis during biomass processing.

Overview: conditions and initial reactions
- SE exposes lignocellulosic fibers to high-pressure hot steam followed by rapid decompression. Under these conditions, water autohydrolyzes at elevated temperature and pressure, generating acids and reactive hydronium species that hydrolyze hemicellulose and some cellulose while disrupting the lignin–hemicellulose–cellulose matrix. <cite id="d353069c-7">Steam explosion involves exposing lignocellulosic biomass to high-pressure saturated steam and then swiftly reducing pressure, causing rapid physical and chemical changes</cite> <cite id="db338cb5-0">Liquid hot water/steam explosion induce high-temperature autohydrolysis and structural alteration by explosive decompression</cite> <cite id="db338cb5-8">Steam explosion is a highly efficient and environmentally friendly pretreatment of lignocellulosic biomass</cite>.

Chemical modifications to hemicellulose
- Deacetylation and removal of labile functional groups: Hemicellulose is often O-acetylated and carries uronic/phenolic groups that affect sugar solubility and accessibility. SE conditions increase acidity and heat, leading to loss of acetyl groups and release of organic acids, which together promote solubilization of hemicellulose and reduce re-binding of sugars. <cite id="4ebdf112-1">A permeate from steam-exploded wood showed a globally lower acetylation content (5.4% w/w), consistent with acetyl loss into the hydrolysate</cite> <cite id="4542b7a6-1">Condensed steam promotes debranching reactions that release acetic and uronic acids during autohydrolysis</cite>. Phenolic acids and other phenolics associated with the carbohydrate fraction can migrate into the liquor during pretreatment. <cite id="4ebdf112-2">SE alters chemical composition, with increased total phenolic content, particularly phenolic acids and flavonoids</cite>.
- Sugar release and redistribution: High-temperature water and transient acids cleave short hemicellulose segments and remove acetylated and uronic sugars, shifting them into the aqueous phase where they act as solubilized intermediates or catalysts. <cite id="d353069c-1">Steam explosion operations separate acetylated polymeric hemicelluloses; the permeate contains small pectic sugars and lignin-sugar complexes are redistributed, with lignin retentate and permeate streams reflecting extraction of hemicellulosic sugars</cite> <cite id="db338cb5-4">In the first process stage, optimal autocatalytic hydrolysis of hemicellulose yields a hydrolysate enriched in solubilized sugars</cite>.
- Degree of polymerization (DP) decrease and backbone fragmentation: Thermal–acid conditions degrade hemicellulose and reduce DP, especially at higher temperatures, which increases susceptibility to hydrolysis and enzymatic access. <cite id="4ebdf112-6">Steam explosion at 160–205 °C degraded hemicelluloses and reduced cellulose DP</cite>. Quantitatively, milder SE conditions can decrease the DP of pretreated cellulose fractions to values around 300, evidencing structural remodeling by hydrolytic cleavage and swelling under steam. <cite id="4ebdf112-4">Adjusting SE decreased polymerization degree to 302 while modulating crystallinity and accessibility</cite>.

Disruption of lignin–hemicellulose–cellulose networks and structure
- Linkage cleavage and network loosening: SE cleaves ether and glycosidic linkages between hemicellulose and cellulose, and partially decomposes lignin–hemicellulose crosslinks, thereby improving access of water and acids to cellulose microfibrils and disrupting fiber fusions. <cite id="4542b7a6-0">Breaking linkages between hemicellulose and cellulose improves subsequent steam explosion efficiency, and dilute acid presoaking further weakens these bonds</cite>. <cite id="4542b7a6-5">Hybrid organosolv–steam pretreatment fractionates birch biomass via ether bond cleavage in lignin and hemicellulose, enabling efficient separation</cite>.
- Defibrillation, porosity, and surface exposure: The explosive decompression and swelling–collapse cycle fragment bundles, split lignin domains, and expose amorphous regions, enhancing diffusivity of water and acid to reactive sites. <cite id="db338cb5-2">SE gently and rapidly alters structure via high-temperature autohydrolysis and explosive decompression-driven structural changes</cite> <cite id="d353069c-3">SE effectively destroys lignin structure to enhance release of hemicellulose and cellulose, evidencing network opening and fiber exposure</cite>.
- Pore formation, swelling, and recrystallization suppression: After SE, residual solids are hydrophilic, swollen, and less prone to tight recrystallization; sugars and organic acids remain in the aqueous phase rather than re-adsorbing onto cellulose, which suppresses re-binding and increases the apparent rate of hydrolysis. <cite id="db338cb5-1">Acids released during SE autocatalyze hemicellulose saccharification, accelerating initial hydrolysis</cite> <cite id="4542b7a6-1">Released acetic and uronic acids catalytically hydrolyze hemicelluloses during autohydrolysis</cite>. <cite id="d353069c-1">SE separates acetylated hemicelluloses and small pectic sugars into the permeate, indicating reduced wall reconstitution and lower recrystallization propensity</cite>.

How these changes promote autohydrolysis
- Autocatalytic acid generation from biomass itself: The debranching of hemicellulose and lignin during SE yields acetic, formic, and levulinic acids that acidify the liquor and accelerate hydrolysis of both hemicellulose and cellulose. <cite id="db338cb5-1">During SE, acids released from the lignocellulosic matrix autocatalyze hemicellulose saccharification</cite> <cite id="4542b7a6-1">Autohydrolysis debranching yields acetic and uronic acids that catalyze hemicellulose hydrolysis</cite>. Phenolic species migrate to the liquid and can further protonate or chelate metal centers, amplifying catalytic activity. <cite id="4ebdf112-2">SE increases phenolic acids and flavonoids in the liquor</cite>.
- Reduced sugar re-binding and recrystallization to cellulose surfaces: By deacetylating hemicellulose, removing small sugars, and disrupting the interfibrillar network, SE lowers the thermodynamic driving force for sugar adsorption onto cellulose surfaces and hemicellulose–lignin aggregates, keeping the aqueous phase enriched in acids and hexoses. <cite id="4542b7a6-0">Breaking hemicellulose–cellulose linkages improves subsequent steam explosion hydrolysis efficiency, consistent with reduced wall reattachment and sugar recapture</cite> <cite id="d353069c-1">Solubilized pectic sugars and lignin–sugar complexes move into permeate, evidencing reduced wall reconstitution</cite>.
- Faster hydrolysis kinetics and lower activation energies: The combined effects—higher temperature/pressure, acid catalysis, disrupted crystallinity/entanglements, and acid-sugar–mediated suppression of recrystallization—lower activation barriers and increase rate constants for hydrolysis of hemicellulose and cellulose. <cite id="4ebdf112-6">SE at 160–205 °C degraded hemicelluloses and reduced DP, consistent with accelerated hydrolytic cleavage</cite> <cite id="db338cb5-4">SE operates in a stage with optimal autocatalytic hydrolysis of hemicellulose, producing a sugar-rich hydrolysate</cite>. Enzymatic saccharification then benefits from higher exposed surface area and labile sites on depolymerized cellulose/hemicellulose. <cite id="db338cb5-2">SE improved enzymatic hydrolysis by exposing fibers and modifying structure</cite>.
- Acid catalyst recovery to sustain autohydrolysis: Closing the acid loop captures volatiles and reintroduces acid catalysts into subsequent SE/autohydrolysis, maintaining low activation energies and avoiding external acid addition. <cite id="d353069c-5">A closed-loop SE process recovers volatiles produced during pretreatment and reintroduces them as acid catalysts</cite>. Hybrid fractionation routes likewise combine mild SE with selective cleavage to create an autocatalytic milieu in the liquor while yielding structurally accessible solids. <cite id="4542b7a6-5">Hybrid organosolv–steam pretreatment depolymerizes lignin via ether bond cleavage and produces pretreated solids suitable for hydrolysis</cite>.
- Process windows and feedstock dependence: SE and autohydrolysis promote hemicellulose removal and network disruption; however, hardwoods can form problematic acid-soluble lignin under severe conditions, and milder SE may be more suitable for acid hydrolysis. <cite id="4542b7a6-7">SE is not a suitable pretreatment for acid hydrolysis of hardwood lignocellulosic biomass in some conditions</cite> <cite id="4ebdf112-9">Operating at high temperature under autogenous steam and acid strength governs whether hemicellulose, cellulose, and lignin are preferentially solubilized or degraded</cite>.

Integrating the evidence
- Chemically, SE acts as a thermo‑acidic “softening” process: it deacetylates/defats hemicellulose, releases soluble sugars/phenolics, and partially hydrolyzes glycosidic/ether linkages, thereby lowering the DP of polysaccharides and weakening lignin–hemicellulose–cellulose crosstalk that otherwise restricts water and acid ingress. <cite id="4ebdf112-1">SE lowers acetylation content in permeates</cite> <cite id="4542b7a6-0">Disrupting hemicellulose–cellulose linkages improves subsequent hydrolysis</cite>. <cite id="4ebdf112-6">SE degrades hemicelluloses and reduces cellulose DP at 160–205 °C</cite>.
- Mechanistically, those modifications create a self-amplifying autocatalytic cycle: acids and sugars produced during SE increase hydrolysis rates of remaining hemicellulose and cellulose, while acid-catalyzed suppression of sugar re-binding on cellulose prevents product inhibition, enabling rapid autohydrolysis at comparatively milder conditions than acid-only hydrolysis. <cite id="db338cb5-1">Autocatalytic hemicellulose saccharification driven by in-situ acid generation</cite> <cite id="4542b7a6-1">Acetic/uronic acids catalytically hydrolyze hemicelluloses</cite>.
- Practically, the degree of modification is tunable with temperature/time/pressure and acid strength: higher severity increases hemicellulose removal and cellulose damage; lower severity increases deacetylation and network loosening with less polymer loss, enabling closed-loop autohydrolysis and enzymatic hydrolysis depending on downstream goals. <cite id="4ebdf112-6">Severity-controlled degradation of hemicellulose and cellulose</cite> <cite id="4ebdf112-9">Tailored steam/acid conditions govern selective release of hemicellulose from exploded stalks</cite> <cite id="d353069c-5">Acid recovery loops reintroduce catalysts to sustain autohydrolysis</cite>.

Caveats and open points
- Quantitative activation-energy reductions after SE are feedstock- and condition-dependent; several mechanistic sources report faster hydrolysis and lower recrystallization but fewer head‑to‑head Eyring/kinetic comparisons. <cite id="db338cb5-1">Autocatalytic hemicellulose saccharification is established</cite> <cite id="4542b7a6-1">Acid-catalyzed debranching is well-described</cite>. More controlled TGA/FTIR–kinetic studies across DP ranges would further resolve activation barriers.
- Acid catalyst recycling must balance corrosivity and silicon/copper toxicity from boiler and feed returns; hybrid SE routes and membrane separations (e.g., diafiltration) improve selectivity and longevity of equipment. <cite id="d353069c-1">Diafiltration separates acetylated hemicellulosics and small sugars while differentiating retentate/lignin from permeate</cite> <cite id="d353069c-5">Closed-loop recovery of volatiles as acid catalysts</cite>.

Summary
SE chemically modifies hemicellulose by deacetylating and solubilizing it, cleaving glycosidic branches, and reducing polymer chain lengths, while concurrently disrupting the lignin–hemicellulose–cellulose network via ether/glycosidic bond cleavage and defibrillation. These structural and chemical transformations acidify and solubilize the liquor with sugars and phenolics that autocatalyze hemicellulose and cellulose hydrolysis, suppress sugar re-binding and recrystallization, and expose reactive sites, thereby promoting rapid autohydrolysis at elevated but often milder process windows than standalone acid hydrolysis. <cite id="db338cb5-1">Autocatalysis by in situ acids accelerates hemicellulose saccharification</cite> <cite id="4542b7a6-1">Autohydrolysis debranching yields acids that catalyze hemicellulose hydrolysis</cite> <cite id="4ebdf112-1">Acetylation content decreases with SE, reflecting hemicellulose modification and acid-soluble byproduct formation</cite> <cite id="4ebdf112-6">SE degrades hemicellulose and lowers cellulose DP, evidencing chemical and structural remodeling that enhances hydrolysis rates</cite> <cite id="d353069c-0">Linkage cleavage improves subsequent steam explosion hydrolysis efficiency</cite> <cite id="d353069c-1">Diafiltration separates acetylated hemicelluloses and small sugars, reducing wall reconstitution and promoting autohydrolysis</cite> <cite id="d353069c-5">Closed-loop acid recovery sustains autocatalysis for efficient autohydrolysis</cite>.

Overview

During the evaporation stage of drying cellulosic materials (paper, fiber mats, wood), liquid–vapor interfaces (menisci) form around shrinking wetting films, in capillaries of cell walls, and at fiber crossings. These interfaces have curved surfaces that give rise to Laplace pressures, generating capillary forces that pull or push nearby surfaces. As water leaves, menisci shrink and reorganize; attractive capillary actions draw hydrophilic cellulose surfaces together, enabling the formation of fiber contacts and bridges, whereas other configurations can produce transient repulsion. These evolving capillary interactions drive fiber rearrangement, densification, and bonding, while moisture gradients also produce shrinkage stresses and defects if not accommodated. <cite id="266ec689-2">A meniscus with negative radius of curvature produces an attractive capillary force, and upon water removal the radius becomes smaller, enhancing capillary attraction</cite> <cite id="7f4285d8-6">Capillary forces are due to a meniscus mainly around fiber crossings, with the dominant capillary force the wetting force acting along fiber intersections</cite>.

1) Mechanisms: How capillary forces arise during evaporation

- Meniscus curvature and Laplace pressure in narrow channels:
  <cite id="266ec689-2">As free water evaporates from wetting films at fiber surfaces, a capillary meniscus forms with negative mean curvature that yields an attractive Laplace pressure toward the curved region—this pull intensifies as the meniscus area (negative radius) diminishes with evaporation</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-1">At the fiber–cell-wall–lumen scale, capillary pressure in micropores and the elastic response of cellulosic elements compete: elastocapillary models show capillary suction in lumens and capillary micropores controls collapse depending on pore size and wall stiffness</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-5">In wood, theory posits that negative pressure (tension) develops when air–water menisci reach capillary pores in cell walls, drawing water through walls and promoting capillary action</cite>.

- Air entrapment, diffusion, and capillary condensation at drying fronts:
  <cite id="266ec689-0">In drying wood, the interplay of capillary pressure, permeability, and diffusion determines where evaporation occurs; air entrapment at drying fronts reduces effective permeability and focuses capillary suction into weak pathways</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-4">Within cell lumens and walls, water can be held by capillary condensation and capillary action; capillary condensation describes liquid formation at adsorbed monolayers in hydrophilic pores even below bulk saturation</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-8">As free water content declines, menisci at the drying front with the largest openings may rupture under suction, re-retreating into narrower neighboring capillaries and forcing liquid redistribution</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-7">Free water transport in wood is enabled by capillary forces created by evaporation from fibers near or at surfaces, with permeability governing withdrawal as bound water moves through walls</cite>.

- Bridge-mediated capillarity at fiber contacts:
  <cite id="7f4285d8-6">In wet paper, menisci concentrate at fiber crossings where capillary forces (dominant “wetting forces”) promote inter-fiber draw-in along crossing lines</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-2">In the early drying stage, the main capillary force is surface-tension-driven bridge formation; liquid bridges between fibers are the primary capillary agents</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-0">As highly adhered (HR) water is removed, high capillary (attractive) forces draw fibers closer together, enabling fiber–fiber bonding</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-3">Conversely, when a meniscus in a wide pore cannot sustain suction, it retracts into narrower channels, redistributing liquid and altering the capillary net</cite>.

2) Role of capillary forces in fiber bonding during evaporation

- Fiber–fiber drawing, contact formation, and capillary bridging:
  <cite id="dccef780-6">Water capillary bridges during drying pull hydrophilic cellulose surfaces into very close contact (nanometer gaps), facilitating hydrogen bonding between hydroxyl groups on adjacent fibers to form a primary, capillary-bridged bond</cite>. <cite id="7f4285d8-1">When capillary bonding is strong, fiber shrinkage during drying can impose lengthwise crimping, indicating formation of robust, mechanically effective bonds that constrain relative motion</cite>. <cite id="7f4285d8-2">Capillary attraction can overcome lumen elastic restoring forces, producing partial collapse of fibers and closer packing</cite>.

- From attractive to repulsive interactions depending on geometry and phase changes:
  <cite id="7f4285d8-3">Near a receding water drop on a cellulosic surface, fibers may initially be pulled together by capillary action; however, as the contact line withdraws, capillary geometry can yield a net repulsive interaction that resists wetting and can oppose further draw-in</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-4">Paradoxically, microscopic experiments report that capillary forces within fiber crossings can decrease as solids content increases yet wet paper strength continues to rise; this implies evolving macroscopic adhesive networks and structural densification despite diminishing bridge surface tension, where early capillary “surface-tension bridges” transition toward solid/bridged contacts and hydrogen-bonded junctions</cite>.

- Microstructural densification and adhesion strengthening:
  <cite id="7f4285d8-6">By concentrating menisci at crossings, capillary forces align and compress fiber junctions, increasing local contact area and real contact load; the wetting junction is the dominant capillary action locus and underpins paper’s tensile and bonding behavior</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-1">An elastocapillary framework shows that in lumen-micropore systems, capillary pulling and elastic recoil jointly set collapse thresholds, linking capillary pressure at drying to pronounced fiber bending and interlocking geometry</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-9">Classification of incomplete (teardrop/pendant) bridge shapes and stability using the Delaunay capillary surface solution shows how contact angle and bridge topology determine whether a capillary bridge holds or ruptures, directly conditioning adhesive contact formation</cite>.

- Stage-wise contributions to the overall drying process:
  • Constant-rate/initial fast-drying regime: <cite id="dccef780-2">Surface-tension-dominated capillary bridges rapidly draw fibers together at crossings, maximizing liquid uptake by bridges and driving wet strength rise through junction densification</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-0">Capillary pressure and local permeability/diffusion control evaporation sites; this stage exhibits rapid free-surface loss and mobile wetting films in cell walls/fiber lumens</cite>.
  • Transition/falling-rate stage: <cite id="7f4285d8-0">Removal of highly adhered (HR) water generates strong capillary attraction that collapses inter-fiber spacings and stabilizes fiber contacts</cite>; <cite id="7f4285d8-1">bonding becomes sufficiently strong that fiber shrinkage triggers crimping, producing strain-compatible, interlocked joints</cite>.
  • Late-stage redistribution/entrapment: <cite id="266ec689-8">As free water reduces, main-pore menisci may rupture under suction, causing liquid re-entry into narrower channels; capillary condensation maintains films in small pores until vapor transport dominates</cite>, producing a residual network of capillary water and bridges that lock the mat.

3) Key parameters and surface phenomena controlling capillary bonding

- Contact angle and hysteresis:
  <cite id="dccef780-9">Analytical capillary-bridge analyses (Delaunay) delineate incomplete bridge morphologies versus complete wetting for given contact angles; bridge detachment at receding contact lines correlates with contact angle hysteresis and determines adhesion duration and rupture</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-6">Highly hydrophilic cell wall channels generate large negative pressures (capillary water tension) that pull water into and along conduits, emphasizing that low contact angles favor suction and bonding while higher hysteresis increases pinning and bridge instability</cite>.

- Capillary number and time scales:
  <cite id="266ec689-5">Capillary pressure scales with liquid surface tension and curvature and must overcome viscous and elastic resistance as water leaves; the capillary timescale sets how quickly bridges nucleate and lock, structuring the sheet’s junction network</cite>.

- Air–liquid interfaces and vapor diffusion:
  <cite id="266ec689-4">Capillary condensation can supply water to narrow pores even below ambient RH, sustaining bridges; during evaporation, non-condensable vapor buildup adjacent to drying menisci modifies local vapor pressure and curvature, affecting bridge stability and capillary pressure</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-0">Air entrapment at the front reduces permeability and focuses suction into weak pathways, promoting localized capillary bonding and later cracking if moisture loss is uneven</cite>.

4) Outcomes and trade-offs in drying-related bonding

- Strength, toughness, and shrinkage adaptation:
  <cite id="dccef780-6">Capillary-bridge–driven nanometric gap closure enables covalent hydrogen bonding between cellulose hydroxyls, forming a primary, high-shear, moisture-sensitive bond within junctions</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-1">Bond development mechanisms also include 3D fiber mixing and mechanical entanglement; capillary forces are central in bringing fibers together for these processes</cite>. <cite id="dccef780-4">Strength can keep rising even as individual capillary force magnitudes decrease with solids increase because junctions evolve from transient liquid bridges to dry, hydrogen-bonded contacts and interlocked morphologies</cite>.

- Morphology changes and defects:
  <cite id="7f4285d8-2">Capillary attractions can partially collapse fibers and reduce luminal cross-sectional area</cite>, <cite id="7f4285d8-1">which may translate into crimping and strain hardening</cite>. <cite id="266ec689-8">Alternatively, suction-driven meniscus retraction and heterogenous drying can cause bridging loss, path reshaping, and microcracking that interrupt bonding continuity</cite>.

Practical implications

- To maximize fiber bonding during evaporation: control surface wettabilities and drainage to favor stable, concave menisci and low hysteresis over contacts; maintain uniform evaporation fronts to avoid localized suction damage; use topologies (fiber load, cross-section, additives) that promote rapid bridge formation and junction densification without over-collapse. <cite id="7f4285d8-0">Highly adhered water removal triggers strong capillary pulling</cite>, <cite id="dccef780-6">but close contact must be followed by hydrogen-bond formation and moisture redistribution for durable bonds</cite>.
- To mitigate defects: manage permeability and humidity gradients to limit air entrapment and rupture of main-pore menisci; allow late-stage capillary condensation to maintain junction moisture until bonds lock; recognize that <cite id="7f4285d8-3">receding contact lines can produce repulsive capillary stresses that resist wetting and delay or reduce bonding in narrow channels</cite>.

Summary

Capillary forces during drying arise from curved air–water interfaces at shrinking wetting films, fiber crossings, and microcapillaries of cell walls and lumens. Their magnitudes and signs depend on meniscus curvature, contact angle and hysteresis, and evolving pore occupancy (free water, capillary condensate, vapor). These forces attract and compress hydrophilic cellulose surfaces, closing gaps to form liquid bridges and then hydrogen-bonded fiber–fiber contacts that become the structural and adhesive backbone of the sheet; they also generate shrinkage and collapse modes that induce crimping and interlocking. In wood, analogous capillary turgor drives suction in cell walls as free water leaves lumens, reshaping cells and reinforcing mat bonding through cell wall–lumen coupling. Control of these processes across the evaporation stages determines whether drying yields strong, dense, crack-resistant structures or weaker, fractured networks. <cite id="266ec689-2">Meniscus curvature produces attractive capillary pressure that increases as bridges shrink</cite> <cite id="dccef780-6">to form hydrogen-bonded junctions</cite> <cite id="7f4285d8-1">that translate shrinkage into crimp and enhanced strength</cite> <cite id="266ec689-5">while capillary condensation and vapor diffusion sustain liquid films in narrow pathways to lock bonds upon completion of drying</cite>.

Notes on unresolved physics: Evaporation-induced non-condensable vapor layers and Kelvin/Poisson curvature corrections in very narrow channels can modulate local capillary pressures; quantitative modeling suggests they significantly affect bridge lifetimes and junction wetting in late-stage drying, but their magnitude depends on material roughness, humidity boundary layers, and temperature gradients that require site-specific modeling and measurement. <cite id="266ec689-4">Capillary condensation and evaporation at adsorbed layers</cite> <cite id="266ec689-0">and air entrapment effects</cite> underscore the need to integrate interfacial thermodynamics with transport to predict capillary bonding evolution. <cite id="dccef780-1">Adhesion of fiber junctions is multifactorial—capillary action plus mixing and mechanical interlock—so bond strength integrates both capillary-driven contact creation and post-drying structural evolution</cite>.

Overview and mechanisms: Why mixing fuels matters in SCS
- In solution combustion synthesis (SCS), exothermically mixed oxidizer and fuel solutions self‑ignite and propagate, and mixing two or more fuels systematically changes the ignition delay, peak temperature/time profile, heat release rate, viscosity, and gas‑phase chemistry, which in turn governs nucleation and growth during the synthesis burst and the ensuing consolidation behavior in nanocomposites. <cite id="93e33ae2-3">Solution Combustion Synthesis is a liquid-mediated process where dissolved precursors and fuels ignite to form nanoparticles</cite> <cite id="60ac4dd5-1">In SCS, the exothermic reaction of oxidizer and fuel must be sufficient to sustain propagation and rapid heating</cite>. 
- By pairing fuels with different heats of combustion and transport/viscosity profiles, mixed-fuel SCS decouples ignition and peak temperature from total energy release, homogenizes local redox, and can suppress soot while tuning post‑combustion gas evolution. <cite id="60ac4dd5-2">Citric acid provides relatively low heat of combustion and yields lower-temperature processing, whereas glycine has a higher heat of combustion and raises peak temperatures</cite>. 
- Empirically, such combinations often yield more complete reactions and smoother particle size distributions at lower shrinkage contrasts during the initial combustion burst, enabling finer crystallites and better green-to-bulk densification in nanocomposites. <cite id="93e33ae2-0">Mixed-fuel SCS can produce smaller crystallites that in turn improve sintering relative to single-fuel routes</cite>.

Phase formation: Selectivity, reaction completeness, and secondary phases
- Mixed fuels can stabilize or favor targeted solid solutions by shifting the thermal budget and gas composition during ignition and propagation. In ceramics and nanocomposites, this can promote phases that are thermodynamically accessible only within a narrow temperature/气氛 window produced by a single-fuel profile. <cite id="93e33ae2-1">Mixing fuels favored formation of the perovskite CeAlO3 over compositions attainable with single-fuel routes, with smaller crystallites and enhanced sintering capability</cite>. 
- Alumina case studies illustrate the role of mixed-fuel thermal control in phase selection: alpha‑alumina predominance versus transient or residual gamma‑phase depends on peak temperature and cooling rate shaped by fuel choice and ratio. <cite id="35fae3c9-2">XRD of alumina powders synthesized by mixed-fuel SCS showed a phase transition from alpha alumina to a mixture of alpha and gamma alumina, indicating that combustion conditions critically determine phase fraction</cite>. 
- Mixed organic fuels also improve reaction completeness and reduce carbonaceous residue, which otherwise can act as impurity phases or sintering inhibitors in nanocomposites. <cite id="c2609312-2">Using urea–glycine mixed fuels for gamma‑alumina synthesis produced ~5 nm crystallites and the glycine component moderated exothermicity, reducing excessive carbon buildup relative to single-fuel cases</cite>.

Crystallite size and microstructure: Nucleation density and growth suppression
- Mixed-fuel processing typically raises nucleation rates and constrains growth, producing smaller crystallites than single-fuel conditions that reach higher peak temperatures or have longer high‑temperature holds. <cite id="93e33ae2-1">Mixed-fuel synthesis of CeAlO3 yielded smaller crystallites than a solely urea fuel, an effect linked to enhanced sintering capability</cite>. 
- The thermodynamic and transport rationale follows from mixed-fuel thermochemistry and viscosity: pairing slow‑burning, viscous polyfunctional acids (e.g., citric) with fast‑burning amino fuels (e.g., glycine or urea) shortens ignition delay and sharpens the temperature-time profile, increasing nucleation density while moderating peak temperatures that otherwise drive Ostwald ripening. <cite id="60ac4dd5-2">Because citric acid provides low heat of combustion and tends to lower peak temperatures, pairing it with high‑heat glycine or urea can moderate thermal runaway and constrain crystallite growth</cite> <cite id="93e33ae2-0">Reported mixed-fuel alumina powders exist in amorphous or crystalline forms depending on the mixed-fuel thermal history, and mixed-fuel samples exhibited smaller crystallites than urea-only</cite>. 
- Systematic comparisons across fuels document microstructural differences consistent with mixed-fuel tuning. <cite id="c2609312-4">Glycine, urea, and citric-acid-fueled SCS of oxide nanopowders produced distinct phase formation and microstructural evolution pathways, with mixed-fuel conditions mapping near intermediate XRD profiles indicative of suppressed grain growth</cite>. 
- In nanocomposites, mixed fuels can also reduce agglomeration risk by modifying combustion gas composition and viscosity—particularly when a polyol or polyfunctional acid is blended with an amino fuel—helping to preserve narrow size distributions after consolidation. <cite id="60ac4dd5-0">Glycerine combined with urea or other amino fuels is recommended for bimetallic/bimetal oxide systems, consistent with mixed-fuel strategies that suppress lumped growth and encourage uniform nucleation</cite>.

Sintering behavior: Green density, densification kinetics, and grain-boundary diffusion
- Mixed-fuel SCS often delivers powders with higher apparent reactivity, narrower size distribution, and lower oxygen vacancy content, which raise green density and accelerate densification on heating. Reports attribute improved “sintering capability” to mixed-fuel–induced finer crystallites and gentler cooling through the critical densification regime. <cite id="93e33ae2-1">Mixed fuels favored CeAlO3 formation with smaller crystallites, leading to enhanced sintering capability compared with single-fuel synthesis</cite> <cite id="93e33ae2-0">A mixed-fuel synthesized alumina sample showed smaller crystallites and improved sintering versus urea-only, illustrating the link from combustion-derived crystallite size to densification</cite>. 
- In nanocomposites containing fillers (e.g., SiO2, Al2O3 glass networks, CNTs/graphene), mixed-fuel processing can mitigate deleterious reactions and maintain phase purity during sintering. When single fuels push peak temperatures too high, they can cause unwanted secondary reactions (e.g., graphitization, volatilization), whereas mixed fuels lower the thermal load and homogenize the heat flow, improving densification without catastrophic property loss. <cite id="35fae3c9-2">Phase fraction maps across mixed-fuel alumina show that adjusting the fuel blend modifies the alpha/gamma balance, evidencing control over phase stability windows relevant to sintering behavior</cite> <cite id="c2609312-2">Urea–glycine mixed-fuel synthesis of gamma‑alumina produced nanocrystalline products with moderated exothermicity, a condition conducive to avoiding graphitization and maintaining phase purity during sintering</cite>. 
- Case studies in ferrites show mixed-fuel choices can tune lattice strain and defect chemistry, which in turn influence shrinkage kinetics and final density; across fuels, crystallite sizes typically range from ~120–180 nm and phase purity (e.g., cubic YIG) remains high when synthesis is carefully controlled. <cite id="35fae3c9-4">For YIG ferrites, XRD indicates main cubic phase with crystallite sizes of 121–181 nm, varying with fuel type; mixed-fuel strategies are used to stabilize the cubic structure and reduce secondary phases under sintering</cite>.

Practical implications for nanocomposite design
- Redox and oxygen vacancy control. Mixing fuel pairs that release different gaseous products and oxygen affinities (e.g., amino fuels for rapid N2/NOx release plus polyfunctional acids for CO2/H2O buffering) can stabilize desired oxidation states and oxygen vacancy concentrations, improving phase formation and densification without grain growth at the expense of strength. <cite id="60ac4dd5-2">Because glycine supplies higher heat and citric acid lowers peak temperature, pairing them adjusts the combustion redox/thermal window to stabilize targeted phases</cite>. 
- Viscosity/ignition synergy. Slow-burning, viscous fuels (citric acid, glycerol) delay ignition and improve mixing; fast-burning amino fuels accelerate reaction and raise effective heat flux. Mixtures reduce burst-shrinkage contrast, improving particle-level uniformity and green density. <cite id="93e33ae2-0">Mixed-fuel alumina powders exhibit smaller crystallites leading to improved sintering compared with urea-only, indicating that combustion-derived microstructure controls densification</cite> <cite id="60ac4dd5-0">Glycerol–urea mixtures are recommended for complex nanocomposites, consistent with viscosity-heat synergy</cite>. 
- Residue management. Mixed fuels mitigate soot and carbon residue, reducing pore collapse problems and carbon-related phase impurities during sintering, in contrast to single-fuel conditions that can carbonize and trap gaseous products. <cite id="c2609312-2">Urea–glycine mixed-fuel synthesis reduces carbonaceous residues and yields nanocrystalline alumina with minimal side reactions during consolidation</cite>. 
- Design workflow. Use mixed-fuels when: (i) targeting narrow size distributions with small crystallites, (ii) stabilizing perovskites or solid solutions that phase‑separate under high single‑fuel peaks, or (iii) sintering nanocomposites with sensitive fillers. Validate via coupled TGA–DTA/SEM mapping, XRD (Scherrer), and shrinkage/density curves across composition, then fine‑tune fuel ratio to hold the lattice‑parameter‑temperature window constant. <cite id="c2609312-4">Systematic SCS with glycine, urea, and citric acid shows distinct phase evolution across fuels, motivating composition-tuning of mixed-fuels to control microstructure</cite> <cite id="93e33ae2-1">Mixed-fuel SCS favorably altered phase formation and crystallite size in CeAlO3, enabling enhanced sintering</cite>. 

Limits and how to assess trade-offs experimentally
- While many reports show improved sintering with mixed fuels via reduced crystallite size and moderated peaks, quantitative deltas depend on system-specific kinetics and oxidizer/fuel stoichiometry. Direct head‑to‑head XRD peak narrowing and densification shrinkage comparisons across explicit mixed‑fuel ratios are necessary for robust design. <cite id="93e33ae2-0">Mixed-fuel samples produced smaller crystallites than urea-only and improved sintering, but the exact magnitude depends on the specific fuel blend</cite>. 
- Mixed fuels can also create new challenges: excessive dilution lowers reaction completeness and increases amorphous phases; certain fuel pairs form intermediate salts or residues that alter sintering atmospheres. Use proximal diagnostics—DTA/TGA to lock ignition/peak temperatures, XRD line‑profile analysis for crystallite size/strain, STEM–EDS for carbon/oxygen mapping, and isothermal density/sHRK curves during sintering—to verify that mixed-fuel adjustments actually improve densification and phase purity. <cite id="c2609312-2">Urea–glycine mixing lowers exothermicity and carbon content, which must be balanced to retain sufficient reaction completeness</cite> <cite id="35fae3c9-2">Alumina phase fraction shifts (alpha/gamma) reflect the need to calibrate fuel mix to the desired thermal path</cite>. 

Examples and representative outcomes
- Ferrites: Mixed-fuel SCS across glycine/urea/citric acid keeps the cubic YIG phase dominant with crystallite sizes on the order of 120–180 nm, demonstrating that mixed-fuel tuning preserves phase while varying microstructure. <cite id="35fae3c9-4">Cubic YIG remains the main phase with 121–181 nm crystallites across fuel types, with mixed-fuel strategies used to suppress secondary phases</cite>. 
- Perovskites: In CeAlO3, mixed-fuel processing favored perovskite formation with smaller crystallites and improved densification versus single-fuel glycine/urea routes. <cite id="93e33ae2-1">Mixed fuels enhanced CeAlO3 phase formation and produced smaller crystallites that improved sintering</cite>. 
- Alumina nanocomposites: Mixed glycine–urea or urea–citric-acid blends produce nanocrystalline alumina with suppressed gamma content and improved green density/densification, including evidence for ~5 nm gamma‑alumina nuclei under optimized mixed-fuel conditions; glycine moderates exothermicity compared with citric‑acid‑only synthesis, reducing agglomeration and carbon residues. <cite id="c2609312-2">Urea–glycine mixed-fuel synthesis of gamma‑alumina yielded ~5 nm crystallites with moderated exothermicity</cite> <cite id="35fae3c9-2">Mixed-fuel SCS shifts alumina phase fractions (alpha/gamma), evidencing thermal-path control</cite> <cite id="c2609312-0">Alumina powders made with glycine/urea mixed fuels appear as amorphous/crystalline depending on mixed-fuel thermal history and mix ratio</cite>. 

Summary
- In nanocomposites made by SCS, mixing fuels is a practical lever to tailor the combustion pulse and thermal history. By coupling a high‑energy amino fuel with a slower, more viscous polyfunctional/polyol fuel, you can obtain shorter ignition delays, moderated peak temperatures, improved reaction completeness, and finer crystallites—leading to better phase formation and more reproducible sintering behavior. <cite id="93e33ae2-1">Mixed-fuel SCS can favor target phase formation (e.g., CeAlO3) and yield smaller crystallites</cite> <cite id="93e33ae2-0">These smaller crystallites enhance sintering relative to single-fuel synthesis</cite> <cite id="60ac4dd5-2">Citric/glycerol act as thermal buffers relative to glycine’s stronger exotherm</cite>. 
- For nanocomposites with sensitive fillers or reactive phases, mixed fuels reduce carbon residues and phase decomposition risk, preserving green density and densification kinetics at lower peak-dwell times; design by XRD/TGA/SEM coupling and by incremental fuel-mix swaps around the optimal temperature–time profile yields predictable crystallite sizes and sintering shrinkage on heating. <cite id="c2609312-2">Urea–glycine mixtures reduce carbonaceous problems and deliver nanocrystalline alumina</cite> <cite id="35fae3c9-2">Phase maps across mixed-fuel alumina highlight the controllability of alpha/gamma fractions</cite> <cite id="93e33ae2-0">Smaller crystallites in mixed-fuel powders translate into improved sintering behavior</cite>.

Summary and motivation
- Engineers historically design propellers by first achieving acceptable aerodynamic performance, then iteratively “retune” geometry (skew, twist, chord, count) to cut aeroacoustic tones, using fast, mid‑fidelity tools and experiments to validate far‑field noise versus regulatory targets. <cite id="d1f82bdb-1">Generally, the aim of the propeller design process is to find the best aerodynamic performance without considering aeroacoustic behaviour</cite>. <cite id="d1f82bdb-6">Quiet‑propeller design uses multidisciplinary optimization processes that explicitly impose constraints on noise</cite>.

How the classical iterative process works
- Step 1: Propose a baseline planform. Teams start from an initial geometry in terms of chord distribution, mean camberline (or NACA-type approximations), and prescribed spanwise/axial twist distribution, often inspired by prior data and desired performance targets. <cite id="8d43019b-7">RANS‑based propeller noise prediction approaches compute blade loads from aerodynamic solvers, then apply Ffowcs‑Williams–Hawkings (FW–H) analogy to obtain far‑field noise in take‑off or hover/forward‑flight regimes</cite>. <cite id="ce300269-6">Design goals are jointly reduced acoustic noise and improved performance (efficiency or thrust per torque)</cite>.
- Step 2: Trim/resolve loading. A boundary element or potential/BEM-based solver predicts loaded/unloaded blade pressure distributions and inflow conditions. This may be potential (inviscid) for fast first-pass loads or BEM/RANS for higher fidelity off‑design performance. <cite id="8d43019b-9">A BIE-based low‑noise design procedure computes the aerodynamic field via a potential boundary element discretization and couples it to an acoustic integral equation</cite>. <cite id="ce300269-1">Adjoint-based workflows couple time‑dependent aerodynamic models with aeroacoustic responses to enable optimization of flexible rotors</cite>.
- Step 3: Predict near‑ and far‑field noise using linearized acoustics. Tonal propeller noise is commonly modeled through Lighthill’s stress‑tensor formulation (or its quadrupole strength evaluated from surface pressure) and the FW–H acoustic analogy for blade‑passing and vortex‑shedding tones in mean/rotating frames. The surface pressures and loading from Step 2 feed a far‑field directivity/intensity model. <cite id="8d43019b-0">Propeller aeroacoustic studies adopt RANS for loads with an FW–H acoustic analogy to compute far‑field noise</cite>. <cite id="8d43019b-8">Coupling BEM/FW–H to assess tonal noise has been used routinely, discussing strategies to link aerodynamics to the FW–H integral formulation for propellers</cite>. <cite id="ce300269-8">The FW–H method extends Lighthill’s approach to compute noise from turbulence in the presence of mean flow, widely used for propellers</cite>.
- Step 4: Evaluate far‑field patterns and metrics. The acoustic model computes directivity, spectra, and SEL/LT‑SPeL at representative off‑body points, and compares against constraints (e.g., rotorcraft AGARD or aviation noise envelopes) for the target flight regime. <cite id="ce300269-3">A boundary‑integral‑equation (BIE) aeroacoustic design procedure computes pressure and noise and uses the results in a feedback loop to adjust geometry</cite>.
- Step 5: Geometry edit and feedback. Based on the noise map and dominant tones (e.g., blade‑passing frequency ± hub passage and higher harmonics), designers adjust skew (spanwise incidence), local twist, chord distributions, or add micro‑features (gurneys/slots) and re‑run loads+acoustics. <cite id="ce300269-0">Trade‑off optimization between aerodynamics and aeroacoustics can be cast by varying weighting factors to reach quiet–efficient designs</cite>. <cite id="d1f82bdb-0">Optimized propellers can reduce maximum total sound pressure level by several decibels</cite>. <cite id="ce300269-5">Efficient optimization approaches have been presented to reduce tonal noise of isolated propellers</cite>.
- Step 6: Experimental validation and scaling. Changes are propagated to detailed geometry and fabricated as full‑span or representative blades; wind‑tunnel/flight trials confirm far‑field changes and do not match model assumptions, so iteration continues (or surrogate models are constructed). <cite id="d1f82bdb-6">The quiet‑propeller workflow is a multidisciplinary design optimization under constraints, reflecting practical trade‑offs</cite>.

Design levers and objectives
- Performance efficiency vs noise reduction.
