Teams optimize the efficiency frontier under acoustic constraints, often balancing reduced torque at fixed thrust with acceptable efficiency or increased thrust at fixed torque while lowering noise. <cite id="ce300269-6">Operational improvements include increasing efficiency by reducing torque at fixed thrust, or increasing thrust at fixed torque, while concurrently reducing acoustic noise</cite>.
- Geometric controls. Spanwise skew and twist distributions shift discrete tones (BPF and harmonics) and their amplitude through changes in local angle of attack and surface pressure spectra. Chord and camber set energy content feeding the acoustic analogy. <cite id="8d43019b-9">Potential BIE aeroacoustic procedures couple geometry variables to load and noise, enabling low‑noise design</cite>. <cite id="ce300269-6">High‑fidelity CFD and FW–H have been applied to tailor performance–noise trade‑offs for specific propellers</cite>.
- Isolated vs coupled rotor. Many loops begin with “isolated propeller” calculations to isolate tonal mechanisms, later reintroducing inflow/interactions when predicting far‑field at vehicle scale. <cite id="ce300269-5">Propeller aeroacoustic optimization frameworks target isolated propeller tonal noise in controlled settings before integrating vehicle effects</cite>.

Key challenges posed by the classical loop
- Load prediction fidelity and turbulence/complexity. Linear or potential aerodynamic models used for speed are crude in complex, viscous, rotating wakes, where separation and unsteady vorticity concentrate noise sources. High‑fidelity RANS/URANS improve physics but slow the loop and may still miss highly non‑linear effects. <cite id="8d43019b-1">RANS is used to provide blade loads before the FW–H analogy, but the fidelity trades with computational cost</cite>. <cite id="8d43019b-3">Challenges ahead include reducing CPU and memory requirements when coupling high‑fidelity CFD with FW–H for propellers</cite>. <cite id="d1f82bdb-1">The conventional aero‑then‑acoustics sequence decouples mechanisms, creating blind spots when aeroacoustic features arise from complex flow physics</cite>.
- Linear acoustics limitations for rotating blades in mean flow. Lighthill/FW–H treat noise as a linear response to unsteady loading, which can miss strong non‑linear mixing-layer/wake/shock interactions, vortex mergers, and turbulence–turbulence coupling. The analogy works well for tonal blade‑passing and shedding but is limited if mechanisms are highly non‑linear or when convective/acoustic Mach effects dominate. <cite id="ce300269-8">The FW–H analogy extends Lighthill’s model to include mean flow, but remains fundamentally based on a linearized source–field split</cite>. <cite id="8d43019b-5">Surveys of FF–H show its widespread use in marine/air propeller applications, but emphasize model formulation choices and applicability boundaries</cite>.
- Frequency/discretization and mapping. The accuracy of tonal predictions hinges on resolving discrete blade events (BPF, skew‑passing, tip/retreating interactions) and their harmonics; if the numerical discretization (spanwise/axial nodes, time steps, microphone sampling) misses critical spectral peaks or their phase, the design feedback can be misleading. <cite id="8d43019b-1">RANS‑based FW–H implementations for propellers must discretize in space/time and couple carefully to avoid loss of tonal fidelity</cite>. <cite id="ce300269-9">FW–H applications to UAV propellers demonstrate practical forward flight far‑field simulation, but also highlight modeling choices (source terms, near‑field integration) affecting spectra</cite>.
- Inflow and vehicle environment. Helicopter/turboprop design hinges on inflow state, ground effect, clearance, and fuselage ducting; classical “isolated propeller” loops require re‑integration with vehicle CFD/FEA and measured environments to achieve robust designs. <cite id="ce300269-4">An iterative feedback process between mid‑fidelity vehicle trim and aeroacoustic models improves reliability of outcome in rotorcraft contexts</cite>.
- Cavitation and ventilation (marine) / compressibility and shock‑related tones (air). The classical FW–H/Lighthill chain treats compressibility via equations but misses cavitation/cloud cavitation dynamics and ventilation; these mechanisms alter source strength patterns and broadband content, requiring specialized models and experiments. <cite id="d1f82bdb-2">A hydro‑acoustic review emphasizes integrating noise attenuation strategies and methods for evaluating hydroacoustic performance, underscoring mechanism‑specific modeling needs</cite>. <cite id="d1f82bdb-8">Hydro‑acoustic optimization reviews the strategies and evaluation methods for propellers, highlighting domain‑specific phenomena beyond linearized acoustics</cite>.
- Computational cost and design space. Running a load+FW–H pass can cost hours per cycle; exploring realistic design spaces (continuous skew/twist maps, chord families, manufacturing constraints) demands surrogates or adjoint gradients; otherwise, convergence to globally quiet, efficient designs is slow or brittle. <cite id="ce300269-3">A propeller low‑noise design procedure is presented, with coupling and feedback between aerodynamic and acoustic solvers</cite>. <cite id="ce300269-1">Time‑dependent adjoint methods provide design sensitivities for flexible rotors to accelerate aeroacoustic optimizations</cite>. <cite id="ce300269-7">RANS‑based aeroacoustic global sensitivity studies define far‑field tonal models via FW–H, enabling uncertainty and sensitivity quantification but at nontrivial computational cost</cite>. <cite id="8d43019b-3">Open challenges emphasize CPU/memory reductions in FW–H integrals for fast evaluations</cite>.
- Uncertainty, correlation, and validation. Because mechanisms are complex and models are approximate, wind‑tunnel or flight data are indispensable to confirm trends; design changes that “look good” in the loop can fail in real inflow or produce unexpected tonal comb filtering due to misaligned assumptions. <cite id="ce300269-0">Weighted trade‑off methods can deliver acceptable quiet–efficient designs, yet hinge on accurate predictions and robust constraints</cite>. <cite id="ce300269-4">Iterative coupling of vehicle trim with aeroacoustics enhances reliability when translating blade‑level changes into far‑field behavior</cite>. <cite id="d1f82bdb-0">Measured improvements (e.g., −5 dB max SEL) validate optimization value but depend on correct model‑to‑experiment alignment</cite>.
- Mechanism ignorance at early stages. Many programs start from aerodynamic “best” geometries that were never quiet; the loop must rediscover and engineer against dominant mechanisms. Reviews emphasize that the design process often inverts this order region‑by‑region (e.g., tip–hub, midspan “quiet zones”). <cite id="d1f82bdb-1">The conventional practice emphasizes aerodynamic performance first, leading to the need to revisit designs for aeroacoustic behavior</cite>. <cite id="d1f82bdb-9">UAV propeller studies analyze noise‑reduction techniques and select design changes (reduced tip speed, more blades) that improve quietness while understanding performance trade‑offs</cite>.

Practical implications and trends
- Coupled “trim‑loads‑acoustics” loops are now typical at agency and OEM centers, with adjoint/surrogate accelerators and high‑fidelity CFD hybrids (e.g., potential/BEM for fast loading to RANS/LES at critical points) to keep iteration feasible. <cite id="ce300269-4">Iterative feedback between mid‑fidelity vehicle trim and aeroacoustic models improves reliability</cite>. <cite id="ce300269-1">Adjoint-based aeroacoustic design optimization for flexible rotors has been developed and applied</cite>. <cite id="ce300269-7">Far‑field tonal noise models based on FW–H over RANS enable sensitivity studies and uncertainty quantification in the design loop</cite>. <cite id="8d43019b-9">BIE-based coupled procedures provide a design pattern for low‑noise propeller optimization</cite>.
- Expectation management: Even well‑tuned loops produce modest dB‑level gains in the best cases and hinge on correct identification of dominant tones and geometry levers; blind scaling of “quiet” blade shapes can degrade hub/thrust efficiency without a structured trade‑off framework. <cite id="ce300269-6">Reducing noise and improving performance are traded off; “best” designs balance efficiency and acoustic goals</cite>. <cite id="d1f82bdb-0">Optimized propellers can achieve around −5 dB reductions in maximum total sound pressure level, demonstrating feasible gains under constraints</cite>.

Takeaway
- The classical quiet‑propeller process iterates aerodynamic trimming, fast source‑strength prediction from blade loading, linearized acoustic propagation to far fields, and geometry edits guided by spectral targets and constraints; it has produced meaningful noise reductions and is increasingly coupled with higher‑fidelity aerodynamics and gradient‑based optimization. Yet it remains challenged by non‑linear source physics, inflow/vehicle interactions, cavitational/ventilated effects, computational cost, and the need for experimental cross‑validation, driving current research into adjoint/surrogate frameworks, hybrid CFD–analogy chains, and mechanism‑aware extensions. <cite id="ce300269-8">FW–H extends Lighthill’s analogy for propeller noise in mean flows, forming the backbone of engineering prediction</cite> <cite id="d1f82bdb-9">Design trade-offs often emphasize reduced tip speeds and increased blade count</cite> <cite id="ce300269-1">Adjoint-based design–optimization links aerodynamics to acoustic objectives</cite> <cite id="ce300269-6">The twin goals are reduced noise and improved performance</cite> <cite id="d1f82bdb-0">Documented optimizations have delivered decibel‑level noise reductions</cite>.

Below is how “fundamental physical units” are organized and used in volcanic modeling and how they drive scaling equations via dimensional analysis and similitude.

1) Core physical quantities and units that structure volcanic models
Volcanic models are built from conservation of mass, momentum, and energy, with material properties and source terms representing magma, gas, and fragmented particles at eruption. In practice, analyses rely on SI base units (seconds, meters, kilograms) and the corresponding derived units for mechanical, thermal, and fluid-dynamical quantities: density (kg m−3), pressure (Pa), force (N), momentum flux (kg m s−2), viscosity or yield strength (Pa·s), surface tension (N m−1), heat capacity and latent heat (J kg−1), and mass eruption rate (kg s−1). <cite id="1200bc54-2">Dimensional analysis reduces a physical problem by combining variables to honor dimensional homogeneity, i.e., quantities must have consistent units for balancing and scaling</cite>. <cite id="1200bc54-6">For multiphase gravity-driven flows, governing balances imply invariance under changes of units only when non-dimensionalization by key field groups (e.g., Reynolds and Mach) is performed</cite>.

In volcanic models, eruption source terms introduce:
- Eruption mass eruption rate (MER) Q (kg s−1) and bulk densities; plume physics then convert MER into plume momentum and buoyancy fluxes with characteristic densities and vent geometry. <cite id="79fae2f0-0">The mass flux Q appears explicitly in plume models (e.g., the Bristol plume) with the total mass flux at neutral buoyancy and bulk pumice density terms in the momentum/ buoyancy balances</cite>. <cite id="79fae2f0-4">Column height and collapse depend sensitively on a given mass flux or MER, providing a scaling lever from observations of MER</cite>.
- Gas–particle interaction and drag organize momentum exchange in columns and PDCs; drag depends on relative velocity, particle density/size (invoking Reynolds/Ohnesorge numbers) and ambient density (kg m−3).
- PDCs are modeled as particle- and gas-laden gravity currents where gravitational driving stems from density contrasts (kg m−3) and particle concentration; runout and thickness decay are tied to rheology, inertia, and ambient shear/viscous effects. <cite id="076abd62-8">Particle-laden gravity currents are driven by mass differences between the heavy mixture and lighter ambient</cite>. <cite id="076abd62-2">Empirical scaling between runout and mass yields a power-law dependency where runout scales with total mass flow and deposit thickness decays with flow extent</cite>. <cite id="076abd62-4">Depth-averaged multiphase PDC models capture dilute-turbulent ash suspension regimes in which particle-gas drag and gravity set the dynamics</cite>.

2) From quantities to dimensionless groups: how units contribute to non-dimensionalization
Volcanic modeling uses canonical dimensionless groups whose definitions derive directly from the above quantities. These groups are unit ratios that isolate dominant physical balances for scaling:
- Froude number Fr = U√(A/gA), or equivalently the ratio of inertial to gravitational (buoyancy) terms; for ash-gas mixtures and PDCs Fr compares flow inertia to gravitational driving from density contrasts and cross-sectional area. <cite id="1200bc54-3">Dimensional homogeneity guarantees that only combinations of variables producing dimensionless ratios can change form-invariant governing equations across scales</cite>. <cite id="da1ebf4f-3">The Froude number is the ratio of flow inertia to external field (often gravity) and targets gravity–inertia balance in open flows</cite>. <cite id="da1ebf4f-1">General scaling laws derive dimensionless numbers and matching criteria to align model and prototype flow physics</cite>.
- Reynolds number Re = UL/ν (or UL2/Q for pipe-like flows), comparing inertial to viscous or turbulent transport terms; in volcanic gases/ash mixtures Re guides the transition between viscous and turbulent regimes for both gas and particle-laden flows. <cite id="1200bc54-9">Buckingham Pi analysis constructs dimensionless parameters from independent dimensions and quantities such as length L and kinematic viscosity ν, yielding the Reynolds group</cite>.
- Mach number Ma = U/c (gas sound speed), used where compressibility of gas-rich plumes matters; matching Ma in high-temperature, gas-dominant plumes preserves compressibility effects across scales. <cite id="1200bc54-6">Mach number arises as a key parameter alongside Reynolds in ensuring similarity and scaling of compressible effects</cite>.
- Weber number (or Ohnesorge/Keulegan-Carpenter) We = ρU2L/σ (or variants) compares inertial to surface-tension or drag forces; this matters in bubbly or atomized magma/gas mixtures and in particle-particle/gas-particle interactions that control suspension and fragmentation. <cite id="1200bc54-5">The Pi theorem formalizes that such force ratios are the building blocks for valid similarity and scaling</cite>.
- Archimedes/Grashof number Ga or Gr = gβΔT L3/ν2 (buoyancy term) in thermal plumes; for dense PDCs “thermal” is often replaced by density contrast Γ = (ρm−ρa)/ρa, which plays the same dimensional role in mechanical buoyancy. <cite id="1200bc54-4">Froude and Reynolds matches are often jointly required in geometrically scaled experiments to reproduce simultaneous gravity and inertia–viscosity balances</cite>.

These groups ensure that equations are unit-consistent and dynamically similar. For example, volcanic plume rise and stability scaling ties plume top height to entrainment and momentum/buoyancy fluxes built from mass density and MER; collapsing the height versus MER data across events uses a Fr/Re/So–U number framework to collapse curves. <cite id="79fae2f0-0">The mass flux Q with bulk density enters directly into plume force balances, providing the dimensional basis for scaling top height as a function of Q</cite>. <cite id="79fae2f0-8">Three-dimensional plume intercomparisons use shared volcanological inputs (mass flux, ambient wind) to test whether scaling via momentum/ buoyancy balances reproduces heights and collapse</cite>.

3) How these units and groups contribute to scaling equations in volcanic modeling
Dimensional analysis produces explicit, unit-homogeneous scaling laws used in three contexts: predictive scaling from MER, geometric/transect scaling, and lab-to-field scaling.

- Predictive scaling using eruption metrics. Plume and deposition models express top-of-column height H as a function of MER Q, gas pressure/temperature (through sound speed and density), and ambient wind/stability; dimensional groups (Ma, Fr, Re) organize the dependence so that H scales with U, A, and Q/A balances. <cite id="79fae2f0-0">PlumeRise encodes H as a function of Q and material densities in momentum/ buoyancy balances via mass flux at neutral buoyancy</cite>. <cite id="79fae2f0-4">Column top height and collapse mode depend for a given MER but also on gas content/mass loss pathways, highlighting why non-dimensionalization around inertia–buoyancy (Fr/Re/Ma) is key to collapsing curves across eruptions</cite>. In PDCs, unit-consistent rheology–topography balances yield runout–thickness laws where runout X scales with total mass flow rate and deposit thickness thins with distance, with decay exponents tied to rheological and gravitational balances. <cite id="076abd62-2">Runout–mass flow scaling provides a first-order closure used to estimate event energies and source discharge from observed deposits</cite>. <cite id="076abd62-3">Sensitivity analysis shows runout depends primarily on mass flow rate, and thickness decay encodes initial rheology and emplacement energy</cite>.

- Lab-to-field scaling and similitude. Laboratory analog experiments for PDCs and columns “recover” field dynamics only if multiple unit-based groups are matched: e.g., Froude number to match gravity–inertia balance, and Reynolds (or Weber/Weis) to preserve viscous/drag effects; compressible Ma is matched where gas-rich dynamics dominate. <cite id="da1ebf4f-4">Froude matching ensures equality of gravity effects (inertial to buoyancy force ratios), and in many practical models Reynolds equality is also needed to preserve viscous/drag similarity</cite>. <cite id="da1ebf4f-1">General rules for scaling laws stress deriving dimensionless numbers from variables like length, velocity, and density to set matching criteria for model–prototype similarity</cite>. If experiments only scale one group (e.g., Fr) and not Re or We, mismatches appear in entrainment, viscosity-dominated boundary layers, or fragmentation thresholds. <cite id="79fae2f0-1">Experimental constraints can provide a scaling law to estimate total mass and mass discharge rate of natural eruptions, but only when model physics and unit-based criteria are well matched</cite>.

- Eruption source-region scaling (fracture/melt mass flux, energy, pressure). Process models from dike/foam/fracture evolution to fragmentation scale mass flux and energy release via conservation laws expressed in SI units of mass/time, pressure (force/area), and internal energy/time; when upscaled, these terms form dimensionless criteria like yield/fragmentation energy ratios to predict column base pressure and MER, with Fr/Re–based criteria controlling ascent transition to column dominance. <cite id="79fae2f0-3">Outgassing through magmatic fractures sustains effusive or hybrid eruptions by supplying mass and energy fluxes quantified in mass/time and heat/time to maintain eruption vigor</cite>.

4) Practical unit-guided workflows for scaling equations
A practical route for building scaling equations is:
- Identify variables with their SI dimensions that span mass, momentum, and energy balances (e.g., Q [kg s−1], ρp, ρa [kg m−3], U [m s−1], L [m], μ [Pa·s], σ [N m−1], Cp [J kg−1 K−1]); form dimensionless groups (Fr, Re/We, Ma, Ga/Γ) that isolate dominant balances. <cite id="1200bc54-2">Dimensional analysis reduces variables by forming dimensionless groups that ensure unit-consistent balances</cite>. <cite id="1200bc54-5">Buckingham Pi shows how n−k dimensionless groups control similarity</cite>.
- Build unit-homogeneous, group-based scaling laws: e.g., column height vs. Q and Mach/Froude criteria; PDC runout vs. Q and Fr/Re–dependent rheology; crater/sill geometry and exhumation tied to dynamic pressure and energy units. <cite id="79fae2f0-0">Plume top metrics are expressed via mass flux and material densities in unit-consistent force balances</cite>. <cite id="076abd62-3">Runout and deposit thickness patterns scale with discharge and initial parameters, enabling source inference from deposits</cite>.
- Match groups for laboratory to field transfer: set Fr equal to reproduce gravity–inertia balance; set Re (or We) equal to preserve viscous/drag balance; set Ma equal in gas-rich regimes; only then do scaling curves collapse and parameters translate consistently across unit systems. <cite id="da1ebf4f-4">Froude-number scaling preserves gravity effects; Reynolds-number equality is also needed in many cases to capture viscous/drag effects simultaneously</cite>. <cite id="1200bc54-4">Simultaneous Fr and Re matching is often required to avoid mismatch between inertial and viscous similarity</cite>.

Caveats
- Missing-group mismatch. Scaling based on a single group (e.g., only Fr) can mis-predict drag-dominated entrainment, boundary-layer viscosity, or fragmentation, producing divergent heights or runout when compared to field data. <cite id="da1ebf4f-4">Equality of Fr is necessary but may be insufficient; additional group matches (e.g., Re) are required for dynamic similarity</cite>. <cite id="79fae2f0-4">Column response for a given MER depends on mass loss pathways and gas–particle coupling, i.e., beyond simple gravity balance</cite>.
- Units and data homogenization. Because volcanic datasets span lab, field, satellite, and model outputs, scaling requires consistent SI handling of density contrasts and MER; non-SI analogs (e.g., “venticle” counts in lab) must be translated through unit-based relations before comparison. <cite id="79fae2f0-1">Laboratory laws can back-calculate MER and total mass, enabling cross-domain scaling if unit-consistent relations are enforced</cite>.

Summary
Fundamental physical units—length (m), time (s), mass (kg), and their derived counterparts for density, pressure, momentum flux, viscosity, and mass flux—anchor volcanic models and make scaling possible. These units enter conservation laws and constitutive relations, which are then non-dimensionalized into volcanic scaling equations using groups like Froude (gravity–inertia), Reynolds (inertia–viscosity), Mach (inertia–acoustic), and Weber/Archimedes-like (surface tension/buoyancy), ensuring dynamic similarity across lab and field. Explicit scaling examples include plume top-of-column rise as a function of mass flux with Mach/Froude criteria, and PDC runout/thickness as power laws of total mass flow with Fr/Re/Γ–dependent exponents. Successful scaling requires matching multiple groups simultaneously; otherwise, unit-based balances and their implied physics will not transfer consistently. <cite id="1200bc54-2">Dimensional analysis ensures unit homogeneity and parameter reduction</cite> <cite id="1200bc54-3">and formalizes non-dimensionalization to make equations invariant under scale changes</cite> <cite id="1200bc54-4">so that Fr and Re (and others) dictate when scaling is physically consistent</cite> <cite id="79fae2f0-0">in plumes, mass flux and density terms set the rise</cite> <cite id="076abd62-3">and in PDCs, runout scales with mass flow while thickness decay encodes rheology and initial energy</cite> <cite id="da1ebf4f-4">and only simultaneous Fr–Re (and Ma/We when relevant) matching yields predictive, unit-consistent scaling</cite>.

Limitations of the evidence base. While the unit and group structure is well-supported and used in volcanic modeling, we did not retrieve a snippet specifically defining a standardized “Sill unit” or named volcanic SI-derivative unit set. In current practice, experiments are scaled to SI discharge and density contrasts and compared via dimensionless groups rather than a fixed named derived unit; if you do encounter proprietary “S_l”/“Sill unit” notation in a specific lab protocol, treat it as a shorthand for a predefined set of SI base-unit-derived scaling parameters and translate back to SI for cross-domain comparison.

Below is a practical, evidence-based procedure to determine how the mass fraction of nanoparticles evolves with time using a sedimentation balance (gravitational or centrifugal sedimentation analysis), including the physical principles, measurements, and conversions to mass fraction.

Summary overview and principles
- Sedimentation balance methods infer particle size and concentration from the time-dependent movement of particles under gravity or centrifugation, via their settling velocity; size and density determine whether sedimentation is slow enough to be measured before hindered effects dominate or separation into a concentration gradient (or pellet) occurs.<cite id="63f5767c-5">Sedimentation methods are classically divided into “equilibrium” (monitoring until a concentration profile forms) and “velocity” (measuring terminal settling rate before full separation), and both rely on size- and density-dependent drift under buoyancy-drag balance.</cite> <cite id="63f5767c-8">For colloids and nanoparticles, settling velocities are commonly analyzed via Stokes’ regime where terminal velocity scales with (density contrast)×diameter²/viscosity, enabling sizing from measured fall times before density gradients build up.</cite>

Instrumentation and detection
- In a sedimentation balance, a sample is allowed to sediment (or centrifuge) while a probe records the mass or optical response versus position and time. Two common approaches are: (a) direct mass sensing, where a time-varying mass at a given height or in a moving window is reported; and (b) optical readout (e.g., UV–Vis), where transmitted or scattered intensity across the cell yields a sedimentation profile that is time-resolved and converted to mass/volume fraction using Stokes’ relations and density inputs.<cite id="d8904757-4">Particle mass is determined from particle size and density; in sedimentation analysis the settling rate is measured by non-optical probes (e.g., X-ray/optical density sensors) to derive size and hence mass contribution.</cite> <cite id="d8904757-7">Commercial sedimentation analyzers compute particle size from the measured settling velocity under centrifugal force (centrifugal sedimentation), which directly constrains concentration-derived mass fractions when combined with particle density.</cite>

Data acquisition: height vs time and signal-to-time mapping
- Velocity-based sedimentation balances acquire a time series of sediment heights or velocity profiles; plotting sediment height vs time gives the characteristic settling rate and equilibrium approach time, while optical methods record transmission/intensity as a function of height and time.<cite id="63f5767c-7">Plotting sediment height versus time yields the sedimentation rate; with Stokes’ law, one estimates size and associated time constants for settling to equilibrium.</cite> <cite id="63f5767c-3">A practical approximation is that full sedimentation equilibrium is reached after about 1.4 times the single-particle time-to-sediment, which sets the acquisition window for mapping mass fraction evolution.</cite> <cite id="d8904757-4">In optical sedimentation setups, transmission or density-like signals across the cell height provide the time-resolved mass distribution; equivalent spherical diameters are then inferred from sedimentation times with Stokes’ equation and combined with density to get mass contributions per size class.</cite>

From sedimentation signal to mass/volume fraction
- Step 1: derive settling velocity distributions. Differential centrifugal sedimentation (and high-resolution gravitational sedimentation) obtain differential mobility (settling coefficient) from time-resolved motion under increasing centrifugation; equivalent spherical diameters are derived from sedimentation times and particle densities using Stokes-type relations, then deconvoluted into size distributions.<cite id="c030585f-0">Differential centrifugal sedimentation separates nanoparticles by centrifugal field and then analyzes their sedimentation coefficients to recover size distributions before mapping to physical sizes; software models the time-dependent separation.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-1">Equivalent spherical (Stokes) diameter is calculated from sedimentation time if particle density is known, using the Stokes equation, which links velocity to size and density; integrating this over the cell yields the size-resolved mass contribution.</cite>
- Step 2: compute volumetric fraction and convert to mass fraction. Under Stokes flow, the local volumetric concentration profile c(z,t) rises with time at a rate set by the hindered settling velocity; multiplying by density contrast and the fraction of nanoparticle volume gives the buoyant mass fraction ϕ_m(z,t) = c(z,t) (ρ_p−ρ_m)/(ρ_m) approximately, then integrating over the sampled height (or using balance mass readout) gives the total mass fraction at time t. When hindered settling is negligible (dilute), use c(z,t) = c0 [1 − erf(z/(2√Dt))], with D inferred from Stokes mobility; in concentrated suspensions, use hindered laws (e.g., Richardson–Zaki) to scale terminal velocity with local volume fraction, which updates D or the drift law.<cite id="c030585f-6">Empirical hindered settling: v_hindered = v_Stokes (1 − φ)^n (Richardson–Zaki), where φ is volumetric particle concentration and n adjusts for interaction; this is used to correct terminal velocity at finite concentrations before converting to diffusion/drift and mass fraction profiles.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-8">Quantitative experiments show how nanoparticle sedimentation establishes a solute-like concentration gradient across the cell with time; velocity-based monitoring captures both diffusion and hindered-settling contributions, enabling c(z,t) extraction and downstream conversion to mass-based fractions using density.</cite>
- Step 3: optical-to-mass mapping. In UV–Vis sedimentation balance, transmission decreases at lower heights as mass accumulates; intensity I(z,t) is proportional to the total scattering/absorbance of nanoparticles in that slice, which equals the mass times an optical factor; dividing by density yields volume fraction, and using density contrast yields mass fraction via ϕ_m(z,t) = [I(z,t) − I0(z)]/I_sat ≈ c(z,t) (ρ_p−ρ_m)/ρ_m under dilute conditions, with deconvolution for polydispersity using Stokes sizes from the same sedimentation data.<cite id="d8904757-4">Particle mass relates to size and density, and sedimentation analyzers use measured settling rates and optical-density-type inputs to deduce size distributions and mass contributions at a given time.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-9">Diffusion-deconvoluted sedimentation/flotation analysis recovers s and D distributions and jointly fits mass and intensity signals to produce high-resolution nanoparticle mass distributions versus size and time.</cite>

Time-evolving mass fraction over time
- Time course from equilibrium vs velocity modes:
  1) Velocity sedimentation (gravitational or moderate centrifugation): integrate the local mass (direct balance) or intensity (UV) from a moving window to compute the time-resolved mass fraction in that window; extrapolate to full-cell integration as equilibrium is approached. The characteristic rise time to equilibrium is set by the smallest settling velocities, often approximated as 1.4 times the time for a representative particle to traverse the cell, defining when ϕ_m(t) stabilizes for averaging.<cite id="63f5767c-3">Time-to-equilibrium for nanoparticle suspensions is approximately 1.4× the single-particle sedimentation time, guiding when time-resolved mass fractions converge.</cite> <cite id="63f5767c-7">Height-versus-time trajectories and Stokes-law conversions to size allow tracking equilibrium approach and extraction of size-resolved mass contributions at each moment.</cite>
  2) Centrifugal sedimentation (analytical ultracentrifuge/disk/tubular centrifuge): differential times resolve distinct size classes; mass fractions per class evolve as s_i(t) curves rise and separate under centrifugal acceleration a(r), with ϕ_i(t) = A_i ∫ a(r) s_i(t) dr, where A_i includes density and optical/scattering factors; software deconvolves overlapping signals to return per-class mass fractions versus time without reweighing.<cite id="c030585f-0">Analytical centrifugal sedimentation yields s and D distributions, enabling class-specific mass fraction recovery from the time-dependent sedimentation profile under a known centrifugal field.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-5">Dynamic models for tubular centrifuges simulate nanoparticle fractionation over sedimentation time, mapping process variables to time-resolved particle mass distributions.</cite>
- Accounting for aggregation/coagulation and density gradients: monitor apparent settling velocities and mass changes; slowing rise times or irregular profiles indicate aggregation/hindered motion; density stratification can be exploited to quantify density-resolved mass fractions via buoyant density fractionation under increasing centrifugation steps.<cite id="c030585f-2">Settling behavior depends on size distributions and interactions; bidisperse silica studies show how different size classes settle at distinct rates, enabling time-resolved separation into partial fractions.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-9">High-resolution sedimentation/flotation distribution analysis fits intensity and mass transport to extract size-resolved mass distributions, resolving density-driven partial flotation and sedimentation simultaneously.</cite>

Calibration and corrections (critical for mass fraction accuracy)
- Density and size calibration: measure or input solvent density and nanoparticle density; compute equivalent spherical diameter (d) from Stokes sedimentation times via v = [(ρ_p−ρ_m)/3ζ] d²; report mass fraction per size bin using ϕ_m = ϕ_v (ρ_p−ρ_m)/ρ_m approximately (dilute), or exact ϕ_m = ϕ_v (1 − ρ_m/ρ_p) if buoyancy term is preferred; polydispersity is handled by deconvolution or by modeling the convolution of size-resolved d² contributions.<cite id="c030585f-1">Equivalent spherical diameters are explicitly calculated from the sedimentation time using the Stokes equation using the known particle density.</cite> <cite id="d8904757-4">Because particle mass follows from size and density, density inputs and equivalent-sphere assumptions must be specified when translating sedimentation time into mass contribution.</cite>
- Hinderance correction: apply Richardson–Zaki-type scaling v = v0 (1 − φ)^n or related hindered laws to the terminal velocity before converting to time constants, particularly at higher initial concentrations; iterative fitting of c(z,t) with hindered diffusion/drift yields improved mass fractions at early and late times.<cite id="c030585f-6">Hindered settling models v_hindered = v_Stokes (1 − φ)^n correct terminal velocities in concentrated suspensions, improving agreement between predicted and observed sedimentation profiles.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-8">Quantitative monitoring captures hindered settling effects, enabling c(z,t) extraction and conversion to mass fractions when hinderance is modeled.</cite>
- Optical pathline calibration: for UV-based sedimentation analyzers, calibrate I(z,t) against known nanoparticle concentrations at fixed size to obtain a linear-to-quasilinear mapping to mass in each slice (Beer–Lambert limited) or account for multiple scattering; cross-validate with mass flow fractionation under the same centrifugation to align mass fractions across methods.<cite id="d8904757-7">Centrifugal sedimentation analyzers compute size from settling velocity and combine with concentration-derived signals to output mass distributions without destructive sampling; calibration against known dispersions ensures mass-to-signal mapping.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-9">Coupling diffusion-deconvoluted sedimentation with scattering/absorbance resolves overlapping mass transport processes, supporting robust conversion from optical signals to mass fractions.</cite>
- Concentration windows and sample prep: keep initial mass fraction below ~5–10% to delay aggregation and maintain Stokes regime; otherwise, add degassing/agitation steps and apply density-gradient or staged-centrifugation to mitigate hinderance; for very high solids, report “partial fractions” recovered at specific rotor angles/tempos and convert each partial mass fraction by mass balance.<cite id="63f5767c-0">Magnetic nanoparticle dispersions of modest mass fraction (a few to ~15%) sediment within tens of minutes, illustrating the timescale sensitivity to concentration and magnetic forces in sedimentation-type analysis.</cite> <cite id="63f5767c-6">Differential centrifugation and density gradients fractionate nanoparticles by sedimentation rate and density, producing time-resolved partial mass fractions that sum to the input mass fraction when properly normalized.</cite>

Practical workflow to report ϕ_m(t)
1) Specify system: particle density ρ_p, dispersant density ρ_m, viscosity η(T), temperature, geometry, detection window or beam height(s) z_i, and whether free sedimentation or centrifugation a(r) is used.<cite id="c030585f-1">Sedimentation time-to-size conversion requires density and viscosity inputs; equivalent-sphere diameter and thus mass contribution follow from these.</cite>
2) Initial baseline: measure I0(z) or m0(z) to correct for instrument offset and density background; record background slope to correct drift (temperature/pressure, gas solubility).<cite id="d8904757-4">Sedimentation analyzers separate particle-induced signals from background by reference measurements and density-aware calibration.</cite>
3) Run sedimentation: allow particles to settle under constant a(r) or g; record I(z,t) or m(z,t) at fixed heights or via a moving balance window at Δt intervals until I changes minimally across heights (or reach the 1.4×tsed criterion).<cite id="63f5767c-3">Use equilibrium time approx 1.4×tsed to decide when to stop acquisition for time-resolved mass fractions.</cite> <cite id="63f5767c-7">Height-time plots visualize the approach to equilibrium; early-time slopes give settling velocities and characteristic times.</cite>
4) Convert to concentration/mass per height:
   - If direct mass balance: m(z,t) = m0(z) + Δm(z,t); ϕ_m(z,t) = m(z,t)/M_total(t), where M_total(t) is the total nanoparticle mass inferred by integrating m(z,t) over the window or by mass conservation from initial mass M0 (for closed system). 
   - If optical intensity: c(z,t) = [I(z,t)−I0(z)]/I_sat(z) via Beer–Lambert or instrument transfer function; apply hindered-velocity correction to c(z,t) using Richardson–Zaki; convert to mass using ϕ_m(z,t) = c(z,t) (ρ_p−ρ_m)/ρ_m (dilute), or exact buoyancy term, then integrate window or normalize by M_total(t) = ∫ ϕ_m(z,t) dz.<cite id="d8904757-4">Analytical mapping from sedimentation rate (and density) to mass relies on knowing density and size to compute mass fractions per slice.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-6">Hindered settling corrections are applied to local volume fractions before converting to mass to recover realistic time profiles at higher concentrations.</cite>
5) Derive time-evolving global mass fraction:
   - Window integral: ϕ_m(t) = ∫ m(z,t) dz / M0 or ∫ ϕ_m(z,t) dz = ∫ c(z,t) (ρ_p−ρ_m)/ρ_m dz; for UV, normalize by initial mass fraction so ϕ_m(t) is tracked without reweighing.
   - Size-resolved ϕ_i(t): if multiple sizes, deconvolute I(z,t) or m(z,t) into size distributions via Stokes sedimentation curves and compute mass fractions per size bin; in centrifugation, use s/D distributions to report ϕ_i(t) per class.<cite id="c030585f-0">S and D distributions from sedimentation yield per-class contributions to the observed signal, enabling ϕ_i(t) extraction.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-9">Diffusion-deconvoluted s/D analysis fits mass transport data to produce size- and time-resolved nanoparticle mass distributions.</cite>
6) Validate and refine:
   - Cross-check by independent method (e.g., centrifugation at a higher g to recover lower size classes and compare partial mass fractions by mass balance); compare early-time slopes (t→0+) with Stokes expectations (Δϕ_m ∝ a d² Δt) and late-time plateau with total mass M0/M_cell·(ρ_p−ρ_m)/ρ_m (buoyancy-corrected for dilute suspensions).<cite id="63f5767c-7">Early-time height-versus-time slopes yield settling velocities and thus can be tested against Stokes predictions for size estimates.</cite> <cite id="d8904757-4">Density-aware calibration allows validation of mass-vs-height profiles by direct comparison to known dispersions.</cite>

What to report and how errors propagate
- Typical outputs: ϕ_m(t) globally and per size/density class; timescales t90/t95 for 90–95% equilibration; characteristic settling velocities v90 for the slowest class; and residuals vs. Stokes prediction with hindered corrections.<cite id="63f5767c-3">Equilibrium times scale with 1.4×tsed; use this to report t90/t95 and associated uncertainty in ϕ_m(t).</cite> <cite id="c030585f-6">Hindered-settling residuals quantify interactions and aggregation; significant deviations motivate density-gradient or staged centrifugation protocols.</cite>
- Error budget: include particle density uncertainty (ρ_p), dispersant density (ρ_m), viscosity (η), temperature, and instrument sensitivity; for optical methods, include baseline drift and multiple-scattering nonlinearity, and calibrate with known nanoparticle standards at controlled solids.<cite id="d8904757-4">Instrument datasheets quantify how density inputs and signal transfer functions translate measurement uncertainty into mass fraction.</cite> <cite id="d8904757-7">Analytical centrifugation methods propagate size and concentration uncertainties through the settling-velocity model to mass distributions, documented in instrument manuals.</cite>

Limitations, troubleshooting, and when to switch methods
- Slow sedimentation (μm/min): use centrifugation to increase a; however, high accelerations can compress size distributions due to compression and hydrodynamic coupling; model with DCS/tubular centrifuge simulations to correct for residence-time effects.<cite id="c030585f-0">DCS models the response of nanoparticles under centrifugal fields to recover true s/D distributions from measured separation curves.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-5">Process models for tubular centrifuges predict how residence time and acceleration shape the recovered mass distributions, guiding instrument settings and interpretation.</cite>
- Aggregation/heterotypic interaction: non-Stokesian velocities and changing I(z,t) profiles indicate flocculation; use dispersant controls and anticoagulants, and measure zeta potential; if aggregation persists, report time-resolved partial fractions under defined centrifugation steps and combine by mass balance with density-gradient elution.<cite id="63f5767c-5">Classical sedimentation theory distinguishes velocity and equilibrium modes; transitions between them inform how to interpret changing mass distributions with time.</cite> <cite id="63f5767c-6">Density-gradient and staged centrifugation mitigate hinderance and improve fraction purity and reproducibility of mass fractions over time.</cite>
- Polydispersity: broad size distributions produce overlapping v(z,t) features; deconvolution via s/D analysis or multi-Gaussian fitting to intensity profiles improves fidelity of ϕ_m(t) and reveals slow vs fast components.<cite id="d8904757-7">Modern sedimentation analyzers resolve overlapping components by fitting size distributions to the time-resolved sedimentation signal, yielding mass-based fractions without physical separation.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-2">Bidisperse systems show separated settling velocities enabling component-resolved mass fraction extraction over time.</cite>

Example summary for clarity
- In a UV-based sedimentation balance cell: inject a known mass M0 of 50 nm PSL in toluene (ρ_p≈2.0 g/cm³, ρ_m≈0.867 g/cm³, η≈0.58 mPa·s at 25 °C); set z-intervals Δz. Monitor I(z,t) every 10 s under 1 g. From I(z,t) compute c(z,t) via Beer–Lambert cross-validation with a 1 wt% standard; apply Richardson–Zaki hindered correction locally; convert to mass using ϕ_m(z,t) = c(z,t)*(ρ_p−ρ_m)/ρ_m and integrate to ϕ_m(t)=∫ ϕ_m(z,t) dz/Δz. Track t90 using the 1.4×tsed rule; report ϕ_m(t) per 10-min bins and per size bin after s/D deconvolution validated against an analytical centrifuge; compute error from density/viscosity and instrument noise. <cite id="d8904757-4">Equating particle mass to size and density and measuring sedimenting rate via optical density underpins this conversion.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-6">The hindered-velocity correction adjusts terminal velocities at finite concentrations to match observed drift, improving ϕ_m(t) accuracy.</cite> <cite id="c030585f-0">Deconvolution of s/D distributions from the same data stream yields the size-resolved ϕ_m(t) consistent with centrifuge reference.</cite>

Caveats
- Near-packing and gelation invalidate Stokes/hindered models; measure equilibrium by density gradient and read off density-resolved fractions directly rather than extrapolating time series.<cite id="c030585f-8">When hindered settling is strong and evolving, equilibrium concentration profiles are best captured by time-resolved density mapping and then converted to mass fractions using density differences.</cite>
- Magnetic or electric sedimentation can introduce anomalous accelerations; report net effective a(z,t) in instrument settings and calibrate using magnetic bead standards to avoid biased ϕ_m(t).<cite id="63f5767c-1">Magnetic sedimentation analysis directly monitors how magnetic nanoparticles are pulled by external fields; calibration with bead standards is essential to map force fields to particle mass fraction over time.</cite>

Summary
X‑ray diffraction (XRD) detects cellulose loss in waterlogged archaeological wood by tracking declines in crystallinity index (CrI), shifts in crystalline reflection intensities (e.g., 2θ≈18° amorphous shoulder and 200/110), and growth/shifting of broad amorphous halos from lignin and substituted amorphous cellulose; crystallite size also shrinks as crystalline content declines, and these features correlate with chemical depolymerization of cellulose chains. The main challenges are high and variable moisture, matrix changes from decay and burial products (e.g., lignin-rich walls or silica), and polymorph transitions; careful dehydration, reference standards, and cross-validation (e.g., FT‑IR, size-dependent fitting, wide-angle scans) mitigate biases. <cite id="3adc54ce-4">An X‑ray diffractometer was employed to investigate the cellulose crystalline structure of waterlogged archaeological wood, with changes in crystallinity indices quantified by XRD</cite><cite id="3adc54ce-5">Moisture content has a significant bearing on XRD‑estimated CrI and I200 metrics, especially for Segal CrI<90%</cite><cite id="3adc54ce-8">Archaeological waterlogged and artificially degraded wood showed concurrent XRD and FT‑IR signatures of reduced cellulose crystallinity</cite><cite id="3adc54ce-7">Cellulose preferentially decays in waterlogged wood, leaving lignin‑rich matrices that dominate amorphous scattering in XRD</cite>.

What XRD measures in wood cell walls
Wood’s diffraction pattern includes: (i) sharp cellulose reflections near 2θ≈15–25° (h00 series; e.g., cellulose I/Iβ 100/200), whose intensity and width report crystallinity and crystallite size, and (ii) a broad amorphous halo from the noncrystalline lignin–hemicellulose matrix and substituted amorphous cellulose that grows in as crystalline cellulose declines. XRD therefore captures both absolute crystallinity (CrI) and relative changes in the crystalline/amorphous balance. <cite id="9f793099-0">The Segal method estimates the amorphous fraction of cellulose Iβ from the intensity at 18° 2θ to approximate CrI</cite><cite id="9f793099-2">Crystallinity changes in cellulose can be evidenced by XRD peak evolution and baseline changes measured after modifying the material</cite><cite id="3adc54ce-2">A common practice is to grind wood to ~60‑mesh granules for XRD analysis of cellulose crystallinity</cite>. The rise of the broad amorphous halo with decay reflects increasing lignin/cellulose substitution content. <cite id="0b8a7155-4">On never‑dried wood and treated wood, XRD profiles show broadening (full‑width at half‑maximum) consistent with loss of sharp crystalline order and growth of amorphous scattering</cite>.

Practical workflow for waterlogged archaeological wood
1) Sample preparation and state control: measure moisture by oven‑drying small aliquots, then rehydrate or gently dehydrate to a target moisture (e.g., 5–15%) to minimize artifacts; otherwise, correct CrI/I200 values for moisture using reference data or in‑lab calibrations. Report moisture before/after XRD to meet Segal method assumptions. <cite id="3adc54ce-5">Moisture significantly affects XRD‑estimated cellulose CrI and the 200 peak intensity; controlled moisture or correction is essential</cite>. 
2) Scanning strategy: use Cu Kα, step 0.02–0.1°, 2θ range ~10–40° for cellulose I reflections and amorphous halo; optionally add wide‑angle (WAXS) to ~60–100° for finer lignin/amorphous characterization and cellulose I/II identification if needed. <cite id="0b8a7155-5">WAXS/XRD profiles and derived equations enable more accurate lignocellulose crystallinity determination than conventional models</cite>. 
3) Sample presentation: polish or plane surfaces to reduce preferred orientation; for powders, screen‑mesh sizing improves randomness; however, be alert that cellulose polymorph (Iα/Iβ/II) and added silica/amorphous organics can alter apparent intensities. <cite id="3adc54ce-7">Waterlogged wood often lacks cellulose and is lignin‑dominant, making preferred orientation and amorphous growth major factors in diffraction</cite>.
4) Reference standards: run cellulose I (powdered cotton/wood pulp), cellulose II (regenerated cellulose), and lignin standards in the same conditions to benchmark lattice spacing d(hkl), halo position/intensity, and enable mixed‑phase quantification. <cite id="9f793099-7">Segal CrI depends on crystallite size and cellulose polymorph; simulations across crystallite sizes and I/II distinguish effects on the 100/200 spacings and shoulder height</cite>. 
5) Cross‑validation: collect FT‑IR alongside XRD to corroborate hemicellulose/cellulose loss and to interpret amorphous halo trends; chemometric multi‑metric diagnostics strengthen attribution. <cite id="3adc54ce-8">In waterlogged/chemically degraded wood, coupled FT‑IR/XRD analyses revealed hemicellulose degradation and cellulose crystallinity reduction; chemometric classification mapped these changes across depth</cite>.

Quantifying cellulose loss and crystallinity changes
Crystallinity index (CrI) and crystallite size (L):
- CrI by Segal/Saxton: approximate CrI from the ratio of total crystalline intensity to the sum of crystalline plus amorphous contributions at ~18° 2θ (I_total − I_amorphous)/I_total; report alongside the peak identity and moisture content. <cite id="9f793099-0">The Segal method estimates the amorphous fraction of cellulose Iβ materials from the 18° 2θ intensity shoulder</cite><cite id="3adc54ce-3">For cellulose materials, CrI = (I_total − I_amorphous)/I_total is a standard XRD‑based estimator</cite><cite id="9f793099-4">Implementations differ (valley vs. baseline subtraction) but follow (I_valley/I_total) or (1 − I_amorphous/I_total) formulations</cite>. 
- Peak intensity ratios and Scherrer equation: monitor intensities of cellulose reflections (e.g., 200 vs 110) as relative indicators of crystallinity and chain order; compute crystallite size L via Scherrer by the width of the (100)/(200) peaks at FWHM after baseline/clearing background attributable to moisture halo. <cite id="9f793099-1">Cellulose polymerization degree and crystallinity influence peak width and height; Scherrer analysis (with known wavelength and camera constant) gives crystallite size from diffraction peak widths</cite>. 
- Wide‑angle/Guinier limits: for very low crystallinity or very small L, prefer Guinier analysis of lattice fringe spacings (d100, d200) to estimate intrinsic crystallinity independent of crystallite size; WAXS and least‑squares fits with amorphous standards improve accuracy in complex lignocellulosics. <cite id="0b8a7155-5">WAXS‑based equations for cellulose crystallinity improve accuracy over conventional models</cite><cite id="0b8a7155-6">Fitting with an amorphous standard yields the smallest crystallite‑size dependence and robust CrI estimates even as crystallites shrink</cite><cite id="9f793099-8">A method combining WAXS/least‑squares fitting and perpendicularly incident scans improves crystallinity determinations for challenging cellulose I specimens</cite>. 
- Cellulose depolymerization signatures: loss of degree of polymerization (DP) accompanies lower L and narrowed peaks if chain fragmentation is homogeneous; conversely, partial removal of amorphous matrix (lignin extraction) can transiently sharpen peaks. Track CrI, L, and relative intens (I200/I110) across treatments that chemically depolymerize cellulose to establish calibration curves in your material system. <cite id="3adc54ce-1">XRD and FT‑IR measured surface crystallinity changes in cellulose during degradation, showing concurrent intensity/width changes that reflect chain shortening and disorder</cite>. 
- Mixed phase and polymorph watch: rising lignin fraction shifts the amorphous shoulder upward in 2θ and can obscure cellulose peaks; if cellulose II appears (common after partial depolymerization/regeneration), the I200/I110 pattern and d‑spacing shift from cellulose I to II, requiring polymorph‑specific calibration. <cite id="9f793099-7">Simulated cellulose Iβ vs II show distinct CrI/spacing trends versus crystallite size, showing how polymorph and size jointly affect 100/200 spacings and the 18° shoulder</cite>.

Interpreting signals in waterlogged wood
- Chemical/physical decay mapping: in waterlogged contexts, cellulose is preferentially lost, often leaving lignin‑rich walls; this raises the amorphous halo and lowers the relative intensities of cellulose reflections, producing a lower CrI, smaller apparent L (Scherrer), and a more disorderly I200/I110 ratio compared to sound wood. <cite id="3adc54ce-7">Cellulose preferentially decays in waterlogged wood, leaving high lignin content matrices</cite><cite id="3adc54ce-3">In waterlogged wood, hemicellulose degradation and cellulose crystallinity reduction were shown by FTIR and XRD</cite>. 
- Depth/texture heterogeneity: decay can be non‑uniform; planed faces or polished cross‑sections with stepwise ablation paired with IR/XRD show that crystallinity decreases from intact to degraded surfaces, consistent with selective cellulose loss and matrix densification. <cite id="3adc54ce-8">XRD/FT‑IR mapping in waterlogged/chemically degraded wood revealed depth‑dependent reductions in cellulose crystallinity alongside hemicellulose degradation</cite>. 
- Correlation to mechanical risk: severe loss of CrI (≤40–60%) and broadening of h00 peaks generally correlates with weakened microfibrillar order; these can be used alongside moisture to prioritize conservation and estimate remaining mechanical load capacity. <cite id="0b8a7155-4">Peak broadening in wood‑cellulose XRD profiles indicates reduced crystalline order, consistent with mechanical weakening under moisture and treatment</cite>. 
- Cellulose polymorph transitions: partial depolymerization can induce cellulose I↔II reorganizations; an increased contribution from cellulose II reduces d100 and shifts peak positions, so quantify mixed phases (Rietveld/Le Bail + reference standards) rather than relying on single‑intensity thresholds. <cite id="9f793099-7">Cellulose Iβ and II exhibit distinct d‑spacing and intensity patterns vs crystallite size; quantification must reflect polymorph composition</cite>.

Artifact control and best practices
- Moisture: dry and re‑wet to a consistent moisture prior to XRD; or apply moisture correction curves for your wood species based on controlled‑moisture standards; report moisture with each measurement and avoid estimating CrI blindly from “dry” data when samples are inherently waterlogged. <cite id="3adc54ce-5">For Segal CrI<90%, moisture significantly biases XRD‑estimated CrI and L200; controlled moisture or correction is essential</cite>. 
- Added amorphous phases: acid hydrolysis can produce amorphous silica; confirm that any silica peak (≈2θ≈15–25°) is absent or quantified by running a silica reference and mixed‑phase fitting. For very soft samples, support powders with inert spacers to avoid induced preferred orientation. <cite id="3adc54ce-7">High lignin amorphous content is characteristic of waterlogged wood and can dominate the broad scattering baseline</cite>. 
- Polymorph and matrix changes: include cellulose I and II reference powders and lignin in the same scan; use Rietveld/Le Bail fitting to quantify crystalline cellulose fractions vs amorphous lignin; treat cellulose II with its distinct d‑spacing/area to avoid overestimating cellulose I content. <cite id="0b8a7155-1">New WAXS‑based lignocellulose crystallinity methods improve accuracy over conventional models by accounting for mixed phases and scattering</cite><cite id="9f793099-7">Polymorph and crystallite size jointly determine Segal CrI and peak metrics, necessitating polymorph‑aware quantification</cite>. 
- Moisture halo: subtract background attributable to moisture using in‑house baseline spectra of wet wood cellulose at the same geometry/wavelength; or increase count time per point to resolve the amorphous baseline. <cite id="0b8a7155-4">Never‑dried vs treated wood show baseline and peak broadening shifts consistent with moisture and disorder effects</cite>. 
- Cross‑validation and triangulation: pair XRD with FT‑IR (e.g., C–O/H and glycosidic stretching bands) and mechanical tests; use chemometric models to map spatial heterogeneity; in cases of severe decay, use microscopic observations to ensure the sampled region is representative. <cite id="3adc54ce-8">Coupled FT‑IR/XRD and chemometrics revealed depth‑dependent hemicellulose/cellulose degradation in artificially waterlogged wood</cite>. 
- Reporting: include d(hkl) values, 2θ positions, FWHM, I200/I110 ratio, CrI (Segal and WAXS/Guinier cross‑checks), polymorph fractions, moisture, and sample preparation steps; provide uncertainty ranges from replicate scans. <cite id="9f793099-8">Accurate crystallinity numbers for challenging cellulose I require careful geometry, background treatment, and replication</cite>.

Illustrative archaeology case studies
- Shipwreck/waterlogged wood: direct XRD on archaeological wood identified reduced cellulose crystallinity consistent with microbial/chemical depolymerization, aligning with chemical and spectral signatures; this supports a routine protocol of XRD peaks + FT‑IR to diagnose stages of cellulose loss. <cite id="3adc54ce-4">Waterlogged archaeological wood analyzed by XRD showed cellulose crystalline structure changes consistent with decay</cite><cite id="3adc54ce-3">In waterlogged archaeological wood from a shipwreck, both hemicellulose degradation and cellulose crystallinity reduction were detected by FTIR and XRD</cite>. 
- Deterioration mapping in museum/ship contexts: severely deteriorated wood often retains cellulose crystallites and microfibrils, but their relative amount vs amorphous halo indicates degradation; even “slightly deteriorated” wood mirrors modern wood, underscoring the need for controlled baselines and moisture normalization in diagnosis. <cite id="3adc54ce-0">Severely deteriorated archaeological wood can still feature cellulose crystallites and microfibrils comparable to non‑degraded recent wood</cite><cite id="3adc54ce-2">Cellulose crystallinity by XRD (60‑mesh grinding) was used to examine changes across deterioration states in archaeological wood</cite>. 
- Methodological cautions: moisture dependence is strong in many woods; cellulose polymorph (I/II) shifts spacings; added amorphous (lignin, silica) elevates the background and narrows/lowers relative intensities of crystalline peaks; careful moisture control, standards, and mixed‑phase fitting are required. <cite id="3adc54ce-5">Moisture content significantly affects XRD‑estimated cellulose CrI and I200</cite><cite id="9f793099-7">Cellulose polymorph and crystallite size jointly affect the Segal CrI and peak pattern</cite><cite id="0b8a7155-6">Amorphous background subtraction/fitting reduces crystallite‑size bias</cite>.

Putting it together: what to measure and report
- Diagnose cellulose loss qualitatively first: broadening and relative decrease of cellulose h00 peaks (e.g., 100/200), and upward growth of the amorphous halo; confirm by cellulose/II and lignin quantification. <cite id="9f793099-1">Peak width/height evolve with polymerization degree and crystallinity, linking intensity changes to depolymerization</cite>. 
- Quantify crystallinity: compute Segal CrI using I18° shoulder and compare to WAXS/Guinier or least‑squares fitting with amorphous standards; compute crystallite size L by Scherrer; monitor I200/I110 as a normalized metric. <cite id="9f793099-0">Segal CrI is based on 18° 2θ shoulder intensity</cite><cite id="0b8a7155-5">WAXS equations improve accuracy</cite><cite id="0b8a7155-6">Amorphous‑standard least‑squares fitting minimizes size dependence</cite><cite id="9f793099-1">Scherrer width of (100)/(200) peaks yields L</cite>. 
- Correlate to chemistry and decay stage: compare CrI, L, and I200/I110 to FT‑IR indicators of hemicellulose vs cellulose loss, and to macro‑mechanical data to stage deterioration and plan conservation. <cite id="3adc54ce-8">In chemically degraded, waterlogged wood, FT‑IR/XRD showed parallel reductions in cellulose crystallinity and hemicellulose</cite>. 
- Document artifacts and corrections: state moisture, note any silica/lignin peaks, specify polymorph model used, and provide replicate uncertainties; where possible, use perpendicular incidence and consistent geometry for historical comparability. <cite id="3adc54ce-5">Moisture effects must be reported/adjusted for CrI/L</cite><cite id="0b8a7155-8">Perpendicular incidence and amorphous standards cut bias; provide best estimates and error ranges</cite>.

Limitations and remaining uncertainties
Waterlogged wood may contain organometallics (e.g., copper from媒染) and silica formed from groundwater, which can introduce new Bragg planes in the 15–40° range and bias apparent amorphous fractions; include these standards in quantification. Never‑dried wood shows different moisture‑induced disorder relative to oven‑dried, so studies should pre‑specify hydration states and provide moisture corrections. Polymorph changes (I→II) complicate baseline assignment; mixed‑phase Rietveld/Le Bail and reference polymorphs resolve this. Finally, small‑angle XRD is needed for absolute amorphous content across cellulose vs lignin, as the broad 2θ halo integrates both components; WAXS complements but does not fully replace this view. <cite id="3adc54ce-7">Lignin dominance raises amorphous scattering and complicates assignment of broad halos</cite><cite id="9f793099-7">Segal CrI depends on polymorph and size, so I/II transitions and shrinking crystallites must be considered</cite>.

# Executive summary

<cite id="c71da442-0">High‑resolution 3D laser scanning and photogrammetry have enabled rapid, non‑contact documentation and repeatable monitoring of waterlogged archaeological wood, replacing destructive measuring protocols and providing high‑fidelity "virtual archiving" of fragile wood that can otherwise deform or collapse during conservation and display.</cite> <cite id="c71da442-1">These methods address the inherent instability of waterlogged wood, which is prone to deformation and decay if not stabilized, by offering automated 3D workflows that capture surface detail, track changes, and inform stabilization strategies.</cite> <cite id="c71da442-4">They also integrate directly with conservation science, where structured‑light scanning and micro‑CT quantify dimensional stability and internal degradation after treatment to guide curatorial decisions.</cite>

# In situ recording: non‑contact geometry, texture, and virtual conservation

<cite id="c71da442-0">Terrestrial laser scanning has been applied specifically to wet‑preserved archaeological wood to achieve accurate 3D recording that can be repeated over time to detect movement or loss of material during stabilization.</cite> <cite id="c71da442-0">This approach provides a robust digital substitute for fragile objects, allowing analysis and dissemination without repeated physical handling that can accelerate drying-induced collapse.</cite> <cite id="c71da442-2">Repeat scanning experiments demonstrated that TLS captures deformation associated with immersion and stabilization, enabling quantitative change detection in three dimensions.</cite>

<cite id="c71da442-5">Archaeological case work from historic mines shows how waterlogged wooden timbers are now documented as fully textured 3D models that preserve fine tool‑mark microreliefs and joint geometries unavailable in conventional 2D documentation.</cite> <cite id="be6d9c9c-6">In parallel, TLS supports rapid "virtual archiving" and dissemination of wet‑preserved wood, shrinking lead times to virtual access from weeks to hours.</cite>

# Visualization of decay pathways and micro‑structure

<cite id="c71da442-9">At microscopic scales, multisensor integration—structured‑light scanning of external shape combined with micro‑CT—dissects the relationship between macroscopic distortion and internal decay in wet wood, enabling diagnosis and dimensional stability assessment post‑conservation at the scale of cells and pores.</cite> <cite id="c71da442-4">This microscopy‑linked 3D workflow has been used to evaluate stability changes due to conservation chemistry, providing conservation staff with direct visual evidence of drying, shrinkage, and mechanical failure modes to support treatment adjustments.</cite>

<cite id="c71da442-2">Macro‑scale scanning also reveals patterned pathologies—pits, cracks, and worm‑tracks—on the outer surface as detailed surface normals and color maps, improving diagnostic precision under museum conditions when objects must remain inaccessible.</cite> <cite id="0bc02ce9-3">Complementary μ‑MRI and light microscopy can be fused with 3D reconstructions to map moisture gradients and decayed tissue in wet wood, aligning subsurface damage with surface relief for a unified visualization of attack vectors and their progression.</cite>

# Photogrammetry workflows and immersive visualization for maritime archaeology

<cite id="be6d9c9c-1">Photogrammetry has matured into a precise, cost‑effective route to generate fully textured 3D models from still images and can acquire small objects to large sites, making it an accessible complement to laser scanning for documenting wood of all sizes from delicate splinters to ship‑scale assemblies.</cite> <cite id="be6d9c9c-9">Underwater archaeology training and practice now emphasize photogrammetry for submerged wood contexts, enabling close‑range imaging of log boats, piling, and structural remains where light and turbidity are carefully controlled.</cite> <cite id="be6d9c9c-3">Educational tools coupling immersive VR with photogrammetric pipelines allow users to explore scanned maritime wood virtually, providing scalable visualization and public engagement without exposing artifacts to handling or environmental risk.</cite> <cite id="0bc02ce9-8">In broader cultural heritage, 3D assets produced via photogrammetry and scanning support interactive, immersive VR with validated accuracy for heritage reconstruction workflows and public access.</cite>

# Monitoring deformation and taphonomy over time

<cite id="c71da442-1">Automated photogrammetry for 3D monitoring is specifically designed for objects like waterlogged wood that suffer macroscopic deformation and decay unless stabilized, making it well‑suited to time‑series change detection across seasons and treatments.</cite> <cite id="c71da442-0">TLS repeat surveys provide high‑resolution baselines and check‑points in which relative motion of wood components (e.g., beams, joints, frames) becomes visible and quantifiable as vectors and pointwise displacement, informing when re‑stabilization is required.</cite> <cite id="c71da442-2">Immersion and controlled‑drying experiments demonstrate that the combined surface mesh and surface deformation field can be tracked in 3D over weeks to months, linking stabilization protocols to measurable geometric outcomes.</cite> <cite id="9b3e30cc-3">In parallel, non‑destructive X‑ray imaging is used in situ to monitor internal condition and risk of collapse or shrinkage during conservation, complementing optical 3D capture with subsurface hazard detection.</cite> <cite id="c71da442-5">Industrial case pipelines show complete end‑to‑end cycles: excavation snapshot, TLS/photogrammetry acquisition to capture current state, lab re‑scan after stabilization, and VR‑based comparison to validate conservation efficacy and plan future interventions.</cite>

# Integration into conservation science and practice

<cite id="c71da442-4">Structured‑light 3D scanning paired with micro‑CT quantifies dimensional stability before and after conservation, allowing curators to see where shrinkage, cracking, or collapse has occurred at both surfaces and interiors, and to tailor micro‑environmental controls or mechanical bracing accordingly.</cite> <cite id="9b3e30cc-4">Conservation reviews emphasize that waterlogged wood is threatened by collapse and shrinkage, especially after drying; the addition of high‑resolution 3D data and virtual models enables risk‑based display and handling policies, remote expert consultation, and training that minimize exposure to risk.</cite> <cite id="c71da442-9">Standards developed around this intersection show how repeat TLS/photogrammetry can be combined with microscopy and imaging for wet wood, yielding diagnosis and dimensional stability assessment tools that are directly actionable by conservators.</cite> <cite id="c71da442-7">Workflows document wet‑preserved wood as complete digitized objects for research and museum practice, where repeated scans reveal immersion's structural consequences that must be weighed against display accessibility.</cite>

# Practical considerations: accuracy, access, and multi‑sensor fusion

# Summary

Tree shading and canopy cover measurably cool pavement surfaces and reshape their diurnal and seasonal temperature patterns. Field and modeling studies consistently show surface temperature reductions from several to over 30 °C under shaded roadways, with the magnitude governed by tree density/height, seasonal sun angle, material properties, and street geometry. Beyond lowering peak heat, shade shifts the timing and amplitude of pavement heating/cooling, dampens daytime surges, and attenuates nighttime cooling relative to fully exposed impervious surfaces. Evapotranspiration can augment cooling when canopy is dense or persistent, but structural shading of incident shortwave radiation is the dominant mechanism on pavements.

# Magnitude of temperature reduction

- Under tree shade, multiple studies report pavement/surface temperature reductions of roughly 10–32 °C depending on season, species, and site conditions. <cite id="7e59d78a-1">The presence of turf reduced surface temperatures by up to 10 °C, while tree shade led to a 12 °C reduction</cite>. <cite id="7e59d78a-0">Shading reduces surface temperatures by an average of 20 °C, with maximum temperature decreasing by 40 °C</cite>. <cite id="7e59d78a-3">Compared to unshaded condition, tree shade provided the highest cooling benefit of 32.2 °C in summer; differences were observed among pavement materials</cite>. <cite id="989c136c-2">Considering surface temperature under tree shade, N–S and NE–SW oriented roads provided more optimal thermal environments, indicating configuration-dependent benefits</cite>.

- At the urban scale, canopy expansion reduces both air and surface heating. <cite id="989c136c-6">Loss in green cover shifts the surface energy balance through changes in absorption and reflection of solar radiation</cite>. <cite id="989c136c-8">Quantitative mapping of street-tree shade can guide planners on where cooling benefits accrue</cite>. <cite id="989c136c-9">LiDAR-informed canopy morphology reveals spatial variation in shade intensity and its impact on outdoor thermal conditions</cite>. <cite id="989c136c-5">Tree shade can directly lower surface temperature by reducing incident solar storage and convection of heat on land surfaces</cite>.

- Broader urban canopy effects are observed at network or city scales. <cite id="7e59d78a-6">Increasing tree canopy lowers urban air temperature by up to 1.5 °C, with tree canopy ratio contributing 26.7% to mitigating surface heating via shading and evapotranspiration</cite>. At local street level, however, the direct radiative sheltering of pavements produces larger immediate changes than air temperature alone.

# Mechanisms: how shading and canopy alter surface energy fluxes

- Shortwave suppression and longwave coupling: <cite id="989c136c-5">Tree shade reduces the storage and convection of heat by reducing incident solar energy on the surface</cite>. <cite id="989c136c-6">Shade reduces shortwave absorption; transpiration further lowers temperatures, but structural shading is often the primary contributor for impervious surfaces</cite>. This is consistent with observations that impervious surfaces heat rapidly in midday/afternoon and cool slowly at night when unshaded. <cite id="7e59d78a-2">Impervious surfaces warm most in the evening on clear days and during cloudy nights</cite>. Under canopies, daytime peaks are damped and nighttime cooling is moderated relative to exposed pavement.

- Evapotranspiration (ET) and material heterogeneity: <cite id="989c136c-1">Tree shade lowered surface temperatures by up to 12 °C; turf could reduce surfaces by up to 10 °C via additional evaporative cooling</cite>. <cite id="989c136c-3">In summer, tree shade delivered benefits around 32 °C, with differences among pavements by material</cite>. Together, these highlight that ET can amplify cooling where soil patches or porous surfaces exist alongside pavement, while asphalt's high heat capacity and low albedo favor stored heat release under clear skies.

- Geometry and orientation: <cite id="989c136c-2">Street orientation relative to prevailing solar paths influences pavement thermal performance under tree shade; N–S and NE–SW alignments showed more favorable thermal environments</cite>. Shading pattern along the corridor and the vertical morphology of trees further determine how much shortwave is intercepted (e.g., crown height/width relative to roadway). <cite id="989c136c-9">LiDAR-informed morphological analysis quantifies shade intensity and spatial heterogeneity under street canopies</cite>.

This implies that microclimatic cooling under dense canopies coexists with localized mechanical degradation, so shade benefits must be balanced with root management and pavement design near canopy perimeters. <cite id="7e59d78a-0">Shaded pavements still exhibit reduced peaks by double‑digit Celsius relative to unshaded areas, even as materials differ</cite>.

# How canopy cover "reshapes" thermal inertia and variability

- Reduced temperature amplitude: <cite id="7e59d78a-1">Tree shade lowered pavement surfaces by about 10–12 °C relative to non-shaded conditions</cite>; paired with evaporative components from adjacent vegetation, shaded roadways show smaller swings between early morning and afternoon extremes than exposed pavements. <cite id="7e59d78a-2">Exposed impervious surfaces warm most in the evening under clear skies</cite>, which is one reason shaded road segments often display flatter diurnal profiles.

- Shifted timing (phase lag): By blocking the strongest midday insolation, canopy shade effectively imposes a phase lag on the pavement's thermal response, delaying peak heating and accelerating cooling after cloud cover or sunset, provided vegetation persists through evening. This damping is especially apparent on materials with high heat capacity/low albedo, such as asphalt. <cite id="989c136c-2">Orientation that maximizes interception of midday sun shows clearer examples of phase and magnitude damping</cite>.

- Spatial heterogeneity and microclimate "hot–cold" zones: Along a single roadway, shaded stripes under tree canopies contrast with sunlit strips between trees or on the sunny side of structures; measured surface temperatures can vary by 10–30 °C across just a few meters depending on shade fraction and tree size. <cite id="989c136c-9">LiDAR-based mapping quantifies how canopy form dictates shade intensity and thus variability across the pavement</cite>. <cite id="7e59d78a-4">A single tree can reduce street-level surface temperatures by roughly 2 °C via shading and evapotranspiration</cite>. High-value tree species or street-tree arrays can produce multi-degree per-tree-to-per-meter benefits in dense corridors.

- Persistence and diurnal-to-seasonal coupling: <cite id="7e59d78a-6">When tree canopy ratio increases at the urban scale, surface heating is mitigated through shading/ET, contributing up to ~27% of the cooling signal</cite>. At street level, the persistence (evergreen vs. deciduous) dictates whether nighttime damping continues in winter or whether deciduous shade disappears in spring, altering seasonal variability and the extent of "spring re-heating" of pavements.

- Shade fraction and crown projection govern immediate pavement cooling, while ET and albedo shifts influence longer-term energy balance. <cite id="989c136c-1">Tree shade consistently yields ≥10 °C reductions on surfaces</cite>, with higher benefits in summer and under taller/denser crowns. <cite id="989c136c-2">N–S/NE–SW alignments help orient canopies to intercept midday insolation</cite>. <cite id="989c136c-9">LiDAR-informed canopy morphology can target species/planting distances to maximize shade exposure across seasons</cite>.

- Recognize street-scale variability: <cite id="989c136c-9">The intensity of shade and resulting thermal comfort vary with canopy morphology and placement</cite>. Small trees near curb provide modest local cooling; tall canopy trees along medians or walls create wide shaded bands. Complementary vegetation (turf, soil islands) adds evaporative cooling and softens edge effects. <cite id="7e59d78a-1">Turf and tree shade both reduce surface temperatures, with turf providing smaller but consistent benefits</cite>.
