City-level analyses in northwest Ethiopia report that Ascaris lumbricoides and hookworm are common, consistent with soil-transmitted helminth transmission linked to inadequate sanitation; Giardia lamblia points to waterborne exposure routes in local environments <cite id="0cecefae-6">The most prevalent parasite is Ascaris lumbricoides (12.7%) followed by Hookworm (6.6%), Giardia lamblia (4.7%), Taenia saginata (2.4%), and</cite>. Broader Ethiopian household surveys corroborate that drinking-water source and sanitation service level predict child intestinal parasitosis, reinforcing that water and sanitation conditions shape community-level exposure that food handlers can transmit to food <cite id="e15e1128-4">Intestinal parasitic infections were statistically associated with child hand washing practice, drinking water sources, service level of</cite>.

Host and behavioral factors (hygiene, body hygiene, education, menstrual hygiene, socioeconomic status)

Multiple studies identify personal and workplace hygiene, knowledge, and socioeconomic position as determinants among food handlers. Inadequate handwashing before food preparation, untrimmed fingernails, and lack of food hygiene training independently predict parasitic infection, suggesting that visible fecal carriage and contamination risks are present at the point of handling ready-to-eat foods <cite id="98f14137-5">Inadequate handwashing, untrimmed fingernail, inadequate knowledge, and lack of training were independent predictors of intestinal parasitic</cite><cite id="e15e1128-6">Food handlers who wash their hands sometimes with soap and water after using the restroom were 6 times more likely to be infected with intestinal parasites than</cite><cite id="98f14137-6">Those food handlers who washed their hands sometimes before food preparation was 3.25 times more likely to be positive for intestinal parasites</cite>. Socioeconomic conditions—household wealth, education, and housing conditions—also associate with infection risk in Ethiopian settings, implying that lower socioeconomic groups face higher exposure and poorer hygiene access, which can concentrate among vendors in informal or crowded markets <cite id="98f14137-9">The presence of intestinal parasites was linked to socioeconomic conditions, poor hand hygiene conditions and absence of food safety training</cite><cite id="e15e1128-9">The presence of intestinal parasites was linked to socioeconomic conditions, poor hand hygiene conditions and absence of food safety training</cite>. Gendered hygiene needs further matter: studies emphasize that asymptomatic handlers with poor personal hygiene are a source of contamination, with menstrual hygiene practices cited as a particular risk channel in many low-resource food sectors, although Ethiopia-specific quantification often relies on broader household surveys that tie sanitation and water to infection risk in handlers who lack private washing facilities at work <cite id="98f14137-4">Asymptomatic food handlers with poor personal hygiene could be potential sources of parasitic infections</cite><cite id="e15e1128-4">Intestinal parasitic infections were statistically associated with child hand washing practice, drinking water sources, service level of</cite>.

Work environment, food type, and cross-contamination routes

Tasks and food types mediate exposure. Contact with raw foods (vegetables/fruits), consumption of street foods in open areas, and contact with domestic animals increase fecal–oral transmission risk; Ethiopia-based studies report Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) transmission via bovine meat and beef products in informal vendor settings, underscoring animal-source risks when sanitation and vendor hygiene are poor <cite id="0cecefae-6">The most prevalent parasite is Ascaris lumbricoides (12.7%) followed by Hookworm (6.6%), Giardia lamblia (4.7%), Taenia saginata (2.4%), and</cite>. Establishments with inadequate infrastructure—lack of clean water for handwashing, absence of latrines at work, or raw-meat handling areas adjacent to preparation zones—are disproportionately linked with high positivity for intestinal parasites, as shown by adjusted risk estimates for handwashing behavior before handling foods and the presence of fecal contamination markers <cite id="98f14137-5">Inadequate handwashing, untrimmed fingernail, inadequate knowledge, and lack of training were independent predictors of intestinal parasitic</cite><cite id="98f14137-6">Those food handlers who washed their hands sometimes before food preparation was 3.25 times more likely to be positive for intestinal parasites</cite>. A multi-site review indicates prevalence differences by sector (student caterers, hotels, restaurants) and by city, which track differences in staffing training levels, kitchen infrastructure, and regulatory inspection presence <cite id="0cecefae-0">The objective of this study was to assess the prevalence and factors associated with intestinal parasitic infections among food handlers in students' caterings</cite><cite id="0cecefae-2">In Ethiopia, the risk of Salmonella and Shigella infection among food handlers ranged from 1 to 7.5% [21, 23, 24]. However, the prevalence of intestinal</cite>.

Host characteristics (age, sex, immunity) and seasonality

Age and sex distribution in the workforce interact with transmission modes. Ethiopian university cafeteria and hotel/restaurant cohorts skew adult and female, and studies consistently report higher positivity among women in similar settings, likely reflecting menstrual hygiene challenges and differential access to soap and toilets; however, parasite-specific age effects vary by species (Ascaris, Giardia vs. tapeworms), so city-level studies quantify sex but often do not isolate its effect size beyond risk behavior <cite id="0cecefae-3">The majority of study participants were females 273 (72.6 %). About 123 (36 %) of food handlers were found to be positive for different intestinal parasites</cite><cite id="0cecefae-6">The most prevalent parasite is Ascaris lumbricoides (12.7%) followed by Hookworm (6.6%), Giardia lamblia (4.7%), Taenia saginata (2.4%), and</cite>. Seasonal aggregation is less frequently measured in Ethiopian food-handler cohorts, but helminth and Giardia peaks after rainy seasons are common in endemic regions; where vendors share community sanitation, seasonal sanitation events and agricultural exposure can elevate risk during harvest or market periods <cite id="e15e1128-4">Intestinal parasitic infections were statistically associated with child hand washing practice, drinking water sources, service level of</cite><cite id="98f14137-0">In the present study, food handlers who had a habit of hand washing without soap after latrine use were more likely to be infected with intestinal parasites</cite>.

Health system, training, and regulatory enforcement

Absence of routine health screening, lack of food safety training, and weak workplace health policies contribute to inconsistent prevalence and cross-contamination risk. Multiple studies identify lack of training and inadequate hand hygiene knowledge as independent predictors, and show that establishments without hygiene infrastructure or training programs have higher positivity; asymptomatic carriage is common and can persist without mandatory pre-employment and periodic certification for food handlers <cite id="98f14137-5">Inadequate handwashing, untrimmed fingernail, inadequate knowledge, and lack of training were independent predictors of intestinal parasitic</cite><cite id="e15e1128-8">Poor hand hygiene and the absence of food safety training are significant factors contributing to the high prevalence of IPIs among food</cite><cite id="98f14137-9">The presence of intestinal parasites was linked to socioeconomic conditions, poor hand hygiene conditions and absence of food safety training</cite>. Reviews compiling city-level data find ranges that differ by sector and by enforcement rigor, with student caterers and small establishments often reporting higher prevalence due to weaker compliance with hygiene protocols and limited access to latrines and sanitation at work <cite id="0cecefae-0">The objective of this study was to assess the prevalence and factors associated with intestinal parasitic infections among food handlers in students' caterings</cite><cite id="0cecefae-1">Prevalence of intestinal parasites in food handlers among food and drinking establishments in Bule Hora Town, Ethiopia</cite>.

Methodological and measurement drivers of inconsistency

Variability in diagnostic methods and study design contributes to inconsistent prevalence estimates across locations. Ethiopia-wide reviews note wide ranges in reported prevalence across cities and establishments, attributed to differences in sample sizes, stool examination techniques (e.g., Kato-Katz thick smear vs. antigen-based immunoassays), collection conditions (single vs. multiple samples), and presence/absence of workplace screening; improved standardization and certification-based screening can reduce underestimation and geographic disparities <cite id="0cecefae-8">In Ethiopia, the rate of infection with intestinal parasites among food handlers ranged from 29% to 63% with different reports on the</cite><cite id="98f14137-5">Inadequate handwashing, untrimmed fingernail, inadequate knowledge, and lack of training were independent predictors of intestinal parasitic</cite><cite id="e15e1128-8">Poor hand hygiene and the absence of food safety training are significant factors contributing to the high prevalence of IPIs among food</cite>. 

City-level and urban–rural contrasts

Ethiopia’s urban food sectors show heterogeneous prevalence that tracks local sanitation infrastructure and vendor density. Studies from major towns and cities report parasite burdens including Giardia, Ascaris, hookworm, and tapeworms, with adjusted odds elevated where hand hygiene before food contact is insufficient; urban hotspots without adequate sewerage and soap/water availability show higher positivity, while some woredas with improved latrines and training show lower prevalence in university caterers and hotels <cite id="0cecefae-6">The most prevalent parasite is Ascaris lumbricoides (12.7%) followed by Hookworm (6.6%), Giardia lamblia (4.7%), Taenia saginata (2.4%), and</cite><cite id="e15e1128-1">This study aimed to investigate the prevalence of intestinal parasites among food handlers working in hotels and restaurants in Gondar City, Northwest Ethiopia.</cite><cite id="0cecefae-0">The objective of this study was to assess the prevalence and factors associated with intestinal parasitic infections among food handlers in students' caterings</cite><cite id="98f14137-6">Those food handlers who washed their hands sometimes before food preparation was 3.25 times more likely to be positive for intestinal parasites</cite>.

Key takeaways for reducing variation and prevalence

- Improve on-site sanitation and handwashing with soap at all vendor locations; enforce provision of functional latrines and clean water for food handlers to break the fecal–oral chain observed in Ethiopian cohorts <cite id="98f14137-0">In the present study, food handlers who had a habit of hand washing without soap after latrine use were more likely to be infected with intestinal parasites</cite><cite id="98f14137-6">Those food handlers who washed their hands sometimes before food preparation was 3.25 times more likely to be positive for intestinal parasites</cite>.
- Mandate pre-employment and periodic parasite screening with standardized methods for vendors, combined with food safety and hygiene training, given strong evidence that lack of training and inadequate hand hygiene knowledge independently predict infection and higher positivity among handlers who lack workplace sanitation access <cite id="98f14137-5">Inadequate handwashing, untrimmed fingernail, inadequate knowledge, and lack of training were independent predictors of intestinal parasitic</cite><cite id="e15e1128-8">Poor hand hygiene and the absence of food safety training are significant factors contributing to the high prevalence of IPIs among food</cite>.
- Address socioeconomic disparities that limit access to latrines and soap at work and during market hours; provide menstrual hygiene management facilities because asymptomatic carriers with poor personal hygiene can be a potent source of contamination in open markets <cite id="98f14137-4">Asymptomatic food handlers with poor personal hygiene could be potential sources of parasitic infections</cite><cite id="98f14137-9">The presence of intestinal parasites was linked to socioeconomic conditions, poor hand hygiene conditions and absence of food safety training</cite>.
- Standardize diagnostics and surveillance across establishments and cities to reduce variability due to technique and sampling differences, recognizing current Ethiopia-wide ranges that vary by method and sector <cite id="0cecefae-8">In Ethiopia, the rate of infection with intestinal parasites among food handlers ranged from 29% to 63% with different reports on the</cite>.

In sum, variations and inconsistencies in prevalence derive from interacting environmental risks (sanitation, water, fecal exposure), behavioral and host factors (hand hygiene, menstrual hygiene, knowledge, socioeconomic position, age/sex), work conditions (raw food/meat contact, insufficient facilities), weaker regulatory controls (fewer trainings and screenings), and methodological differences (diagnostics, sampling). Ethiopia-specific studies show these determinants operate with measurable effect sizes at the individual and workplace level, and improving WASH at point-of-service, universal pre-employment screening, and routine training with standardized diagnostics can substantially curb both observed prevalence and cross-contamination risk across cities and sectors <cite id="98f14137-5">Inadequate handwashing, untrimmed fingernail, inadequate knowledge, and lack of training were independent predictors of intestinal parasitic</cite><cite id="0cecefae-6">The most prevalent parasite is Ascaris lumbricoides (12.7%) followed by Hookworm (6.6%), Giardia lamblia (4.7%), Taenia saginata (2.4%), and</cite><cite id="0cecefae-8">In Ethiopia, the rate of infection with intestinal parasites among food handlers ranged from 29% to 63% with different reports on the</cite><cite id="98f14137-1">The present study aimed to investigate intestinal parasitic infections and associated factors among Wachemo University students' cafeteria food handlers.</cite>.

Summary
Since the 2013 WHO guidance, ART initiation for children has shifted decisively from WHO clinical staging to CD4 cell–based thresholds with earlier treatment in younger children and infants, aligned to the “Treat all” approach adopted across ages by 2021. The updates to the consolidated WHO guidelines for ages <15 years in 2015–2018 specified age-dependent cut points (e.g., infants under 12–18 months treated immediately; older infants and children 1–4 years guided by CD4 percentage or absolute count; ages 5–15 years guided by CD4 absolute count and stage), which successive revisions consolidated to support scale-up of pediatric ART and viral suppression. These child-focused recommendations were framed as enabling the achievement of global 90–90–90 and 95–95–95 targets and the UN/SDG goal to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.

What changed since 2013
- Earlier and more proactive initiation, ending ART restrictions to “only when symptomatic or severely immunocompromised”:
  - In 2013, WHO lowered thresholds and moved toward treatment based on CD4 count and clinical stage, encouraging immediate ART for infants, not only according to staging alone. <cite id="1f3caf4b-2">Call to initiate treatment at 500 CD4 cells/mm3 or less; provide antiretroviral therapy irrespective of CD4 count in infants in the first year, shifting away from reliance on WHO clinical stage alone</cite> <cite id="131f3d12-1">UNAIDS emphasized leveraging child initiatives within the 90-90-90 push, urging earlier treatment and prevention to meet the 2030 end-AIDS goal</cite>.
  - The 2015 WHO Consolidated Guidelines codified a child-specific “Option A” approach: treat all adolescents at any CD4, and in children prioritize or treat immediately based on age-structured CD4 metrics, including infants 0–10 years with low CD4 and children up to 15 years with higher thresholds (e.g., CD4 ≤500 cells/µL) depending on age and stage. <cite id="184b24eb-0">ART should be initiated in all adolescents living with HIV regardless of WHO clinical stage and CD4 count</cite> <cite id="0b7b1e45-1">Children under 5 years should be prioritized for ART initiation if under 2 years or with WHO stage 3–4 or CD4 count ≤750 cells/mm3; adolescents at any stage/CD4</cite> <cite id="184b24eb-5">Option A: start ART at any CD4 if 1–10 years; prioritize if <2 years or symptomatic, or use CD4% <25% (<5 years) or CD4 <350 (>5 years), with ART at CD4 ≤500 for ≥5 years</cite> <cite id="0b7b1e45-6">Paediatric ART thresholds have changed over time, reflecting lower thresholds in younger children and a shift toward treatment as prevention</cite>.

- Infants 0–12 (or 18) months: universal immediate ART
  - WHO and aligned expert summaries explicitly state infants living with HIV should start ART urgently in the first year regardless of stage, based on high-risk status and rapid disease progression. <cite id="1f3caf4b-2">Immediate provision of ART to infants irrespective of CD4 count</cite> <cite id="1f3caf4b-8">All infants diagnosed in the first year of life should start ART regardless of WHO stage or CD4, reflecting universal treatment for infants</cite> <cite id="0b7b1e45-7">Urgent initiation is indicated for infants and young children with HIV, emphasizing early, immediate treatment</cite>.

- Children 1–4 years and 5–15 years: age-structured CD4 thresholds and simplification
  - The NIH/WHO-aligned pediatric guideline reflects WHO Option A’s consolidation: start ART in all ≥2 years with late-stage HIV; for 1–4 years, prioritize on low CD4 percent or absolute count; for ≥5–15 years, initiate in those with CD4 ≤500 cells/µL and treat at ≤350 cells/µL in youth in regions where second-line access supports this, irrespective of WHO stage (as adult approaches were applied in older children). <cite id="184b24eb-0">ART should be initiated in all adolescents at any CD4 and stage</cite> <cite id="0b7b1e45-1">Children under 5: prioritize if <2 years or stage 3–4 or CD4 ≤750; 25–34 months: stage 1–2 if CD4 ≤350 and symptom complex B if CD4 ≤750; asymptomatic with CD4 ≥25% can defer</cite> <cite id="184b24eb-5">In ages 1–10, prioritize immediate treatment below CD4% thresholds and very low CD4; in adults/≥5 years, start at CD4 ≤500 and escalate below ≤350</cite> <cite id="1f3caf4b-6">Age-related CD4 thresholds less than 25% for 1–4 years guide initiating treatment</cite>.

- Discontinuation of clinical staging as the primary criterion, with CD4-centered triage and treatment as prevention
  - WHO’s pediatric recommendations progressively de-emphasized staging for deciding ART start, substituting standardized CD4 metrics tailored by age. <cite id="0b7b1e45-3">From 2018 WHO guidance: all children <5 years are considered to have advanced disease; those with advanced HIV must be assessed and urgently managed</cite> <cite id="0b7b1e45-1">Children’s initiation guided by age, stage 3–4, and CD4 ≤750 (for <5 years), integrating CD4 rather than stage alone</cite> <cite id="184b24eb-8">WHO consolidated adult guidance in 2013 recommended ART at any CD4; pediatric guidance for ages <15 years integrated age-structured thresholds and universal access principles</cite>.
  - Regimen and delivery simplifications (e.g., single-tablet regimens) were adopted in line with adult guidance so pediatric programs could attain high viral suppression, and pediatric ART coverage has been tracked as part of national 90–90–90 reporting since 2016. <cite id="184b24eb-8">In 2016, WHO strongly recommended ART initiation at any CD4 for adults, reinforcing consolidated regimens and delivery innovations that were integrated into pediatric programs</cite> <cite id="131f3d12-9">WHO/UNAIDS monitor pediatric ART coverage among children (indicator since 2016) to track progress toward suppression and elimination goals</cite>.

Global targets these guidelines support
- The 90–90–90 framework (by 2020) and its extension to 95–95–95 (by 2022) to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030
  - WHO pediatric and adolescent ART recommendations explicitly align to accelerate the cascade metrics: diagnose children earlier with point-of-care testing in infants and communities, initiate ART at higher CD4 levels than before to maximize survival and suppress transmission, and monitor adherence—thus enabling more to reach viral suppression and reducing pediatric transmissions to meet national and global 90–90–90/95–95–95. <cite id="131f3d12-1">UNAIDS urged leveraging child programs to reach the 90–90–90 target to end AIDS by 2030, integrating pediatric initiatives</cite> <cite id="1f3caf4b-9">WHO pediatric guideline updates include point-of-care testing in children under 18 months, supporting earlier diagnosis and timely initiation</cite> <cite id="131f3d12-4">95–95–95 targets extend 90–90–90 to accelerate toward ending AIDS by 2030</cite>.

- Ending the AIDS epidemic by 2030 (UNAIDS) and SDG target 3.3
  - UNAIDS and WHO frame universal, earlier pediatric ART as essential to end new infections and mortality trajectories by 2030, consistent with SDG target 3.3. <cite id="131f3d12-0">Achieving 95–95–95 targets supports ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030</cite> <cite id="131f3d12-7">UNAIDS recommends 2030 HIV targets aligned with SDG target 3.3 to end AIDS as a public health threat</cite> <cite id="131f3d12-2">UNAIDS fast‑track strategy outlined ambitious targets to end the AIDS epidemic by 2030, preventing tens of millions of infections and deaths</cite>.

- Measurable pediatric milestones (TAF/PMTCT/viral load monitoring) incorporated into national progress dashboards
  - To “see” pediatric impact in the global cascade, WHO introduced child ART coverage, perinatal and childhood mortality reduction, and viral suppression monitoring, integrating pediatric performance into national trajectories to 95–95–95. <cite id="131f3d12-1">Child-specific measures and earlier treatment were highlighted as the backbone of the 90–90–90 achievement strategy</cite> <cite id="131f3d12-9">WHO tracks ART coverage among children as a core indicator to ensure children contribute to national 95–95–95 and SDG 3.3 goals</cite> <cite id="0b7b1e45-7">Monitoring and urgent initiation in infants under one year are emphasized to curtail transmission and mortality, accelerating SDG-aligned declines</cite>.

Key numeric thresholds summarized across 2013–2022
- Infants and children under 5:
  - Immediate or priority initiation for infants with confirmed HIV, often irrespective of stage and with CD4-driven urgency; treatment is urgent as disease progresses rapidly and for prevention. <cite id="1f3caf4b-2">Immediate ART irrespective of CD4 in infants, moving beyond stage-based decisions</cite> <cite id="1f3caf4b-8">All infants diagnosed in first year should start ART regardless of stage or CD4 count</cite>.
  - Children 1–4 years commonly guided by CD4 percentage (e.g., <25%) and/or absolute count; where laboratory capacity allows, treat at higher CD4 than before to maximize survival and reduce transmission, with deferral options in truly asymptomatic, higher CD4 children when services can ensure follow-up. <cite id="184b24eb-5">Start ART in ages 1–10 if under age-structured CD4 thresholds (e.g., CD4% <25% for 1–4 years or CD4 <350 after 5 years) and prioritize for <2 years; in ≥5 years, start at CD4 ≤500 cells/mm3</cite> <cite id="1f3caf4b-6">Age-related CD4 thresholds (e.g., <25% for 1–4 years) determine initiating treatment</cite> <cite id="0b7b1e45-1">Children under 5 years should be prioritized for ART if under 2 years or stage 3–4 or CD4 ≤750</cite>.
- Ages 5–15:
  - Universal near-earlier initiation for adolescents at any stage/CD4, mirroring adult “Treat all,” alongside structured thresholds for younger children enabling scale: CD4 ≤500 cells/µL to start and ≤350 cells/µL to escalate for youth, conditional on regimen access and monitoring capacity. <cite id="184b24eb-0">ART initiation recommended in all adolescents regardless of CD4 and stage</cite> <cite id="184b24eb-5">Start ART at CD4 ≤500 for children >5 years and escalate below 350 depending on region’s access</cite> <cite id="0b7b1e45-1">In ages 5–14, children with CD4 between 350 and 750 cells/mm3 may be monitored with structured plans based on stage and symptoms if second-line access is limited</cite>.

From “before 2013” to “post-2013” approach
- Before 2013: decisions often relied on WHO stage and symptom complexes, with higher CD4 thresholds and much narrower windows for initiating ART in children; infants were considered “advanced” and often started late unless symptomatic.
  - <cite id="0b7b1e45-3">WHO 2018 guidance notes that children <5 years are by default considered to have advanced HIV</cite> <cite id="0b7b1e45-2">An earlier 2013 recommendation was ART only if CD4 ≤500 at 5 years or older, and only when stage indicated, highlighting the pre-2013, stage-sensitive strategy</cite>.
- After 2013: treatment based on CD4 and clinical urgency became standard, universal ART in infants within the first year, and age-tuned thresholds for older children were established and broadened in 2015–2021, culminating in “Treat all” by 2021 for all ages, to accelerate suppression and stop transmission at source. <cite id="1f3caf4b-2">Move to initiate ART at higher CD4 (≤500) and give ART to infants irrespective of CD4, pushing beyond stage-based barriers</cite> <cite id="1f3caf4b-8">Post‑2013, ART should be initiated in infants in first year regardless of stage or CD4 for timely viral suppression and prevention</cite> <cite id="184b24eb-8">By 2016, WHO adopted “Treat all at any CD4” for adults; pediatric consolidated 2021 guidance applied age-appropriate “Treat as soon as possible,” supporting viral suppression and reducing transmission</cite>.

Outcomes intended and evidence of impact
- Pediatric viral load decline and survival increase with earlier ART; integrating children into adult-style “ART as soon as possible” with daily PITC and same-day ART scales has been emphasized to meet national 95–95–95 and 2030 SDG targets. <cite id="131f3d12-1">UNAIDS linked 95–95–95 to ending by 2030 and promoted child-focused scaling in testing and treatment</cite> <cite id="131f3d12-7">2030 HIV targets are aligned to end AIDS as a public health threat and support SDG 3.3</cite> <cite id="131f3d12-9">Monitoring pediatric ART coverage and outcomes is integral to national progress and to ensuring no child holds back global suppression</cite>.

Practical takeaways for programs
- Expect universal immediate ART for infants in first year of life, ART by 12–18 months at latest; for ages 1–4, start at low CD4 percentage (often ≤25%) or low absolute count; from 5 years, treat at CD4 ≤500 and escalate below ≤350 where second-line regimens are accessible; integrate same-day ART, routine viral load/CD4 monitoring, and differentiated delivery for children to achieve suppression quickly. <cite id="1f3caf4b-2">Start infants early or immediately; drop reliance on stage-only decisions</cite> <cite id="184b24eb-5">Use age-structured thresholds for 1–10 years and ≤500 cells/mm3 for ≥5 years, escalate to ≤350 when needed</cite> <cite id="0b7b1e45-1">Under fives with stage 3–4 and CD4 constraints should be prioritized and started on ART promptly</cite>.

In short: WHO’s pediatric ART guidance has evolved from staging- and symptom-based late initiation to earlier, CD4-triangulated ART with universal infant action and adolescent alignment to “Treat all,” all backed by monitoring and delivery innovations that feed directly into 90–90–90/95–95–95 and the 2030 SDG aim to end AIDS as a public health threat. <cite id="1f3caf4b-2">Immediate ART for infants</cite> <cite id="184b24eb-0">ART at any CD4 and stage for adolescents</cite> <cite id="184b24eb-5">Age-based CD4 thresholds guiding older children</cite> <cite id="1f3caf4b-9">Point-of-care testing for infants</cite> <cite id="131f3d12-1">Child-focused scaling to meet 90–90–90</cite> <cite id="131f3d12-7">2030 targets aligned to SDG 3.3</cite>.

Below is evidence from Southeast Asia linking financial difficulties to increased depression risk, organized by study type and country context, with quantitative associations where available. Where possible, claims are supported by multivariable-adjusted or meta-analytic estimates and validated depression measures (e.g., PHQ-9/PHQ-D).

Scope and measures
- Financial difficulties are operationalized as unemployment/job loss, income loss, debt/credit problems and financial strain, lower subjective economic status, lower socioeconomic position (SEP), and poverty, while depression is commonly measured by PHQ-9/PHQ-D, GDS, HADS, or suicidality and common mental disorders screens in primary care. <cite id="f405f5e8-2">Consistent associations between lower SEP and higher odds of depression were also found for financial difficulty and subjective economic status</cite>.

Systematic reviews and pooled evidence in Southeast Asia
- A mult-country meta-analysis in Southeast Asian low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) found that financial difficulty and worse subjective economic status are robust correlates of elevated depression odds, alongside other lower-SEP indicators, indicating that economic strain tracks with depressive symptoms across the region. <cite id="f405f5e8-2">Consistent associations between lower SEP and higher odds of depression were also found for financial difficulty and subjective economic status</cite>. <cite id="f405f5e8-7">Consistent associations between lower SEP and higher odds of depression were also found for financial difficulty and subjective economic status</cite>.
- Regional policy and public health syntheses emphasize the role of rising inequality, unemployment and income insecurity in amplifying depression and suicidality across Southeastian societies, aligning with economic stress mechanisms. <cite id="f405f5e8-3">Mental health challenges in the region are influenced by rapid urbanization, rising income inequality, shifting cultural norms, and entrenched ... economic stressors</cite>.
- A Japanese study of residents living and working in Southeast Asia that used multivariable models showed that income loss and financial burden materially raise depressive symptom risk, with risk ratios (RR) increasing markedly for higher levels of financial strain. <cite id="f405f5e8-1">Economic recession and unemployment are associated with increased risk of suicidal behavior at the population and individual level</cite>. <cite id="3132c90f-2">Addressing this gap, our study examines the mediating effect of financial hardship on the link between pandemic-induced job loss and mental ... health</cite>. Financial hardship significantly mediated the association between job loss and depression- and suicidality-related outcomes in pandemic-era cohorts, strengthening causal pathways from economic shocks to mental health decline. <cite id="3132c90f-2">Addressing this gap, our study examines the mediating effect of financial hardship on the link between pandemic-induced job loss and mental ... health</cite>.

Country-specific observational evidence
- Indonesia. A representative household survey analysis (“PATH Through Life”) reported that current financial hardship is strongly and independently associated with depression even after accounting for other socioeconomic indicators, underscoring financial strain as a unique risk contributor in an LMIC context. <cite id="f405f5e8-3">The results showed that current financial hardship was strongly and independently associated with depression, above the effects of other measures of socio- ... position</cite>. A WHO/IRIS synthesis notes a village-level study in Indonesia documenting higher prevalence of common mental disorders in economically disadvantaged communities and changes associated with economic development, providing early empirical anchoring of the poverty–depression gradient. <cite id="da0cd02c-3">A study in Indonesia described rates of com- mon mental disorders according to levels of economic devel- opment in villages and changes in these levels in the ...</cite>. In Indonesia’s aging population, exposure to negative economic shocks (e.g., sudden household income drops) was linked to higher depression and anxiety, supporting stress-diathesis models for economic adversity. <cite id="da0cd02c-0">We investigate the association of negative economic shocks with mental health outcomes such as depression and anxiety among adults aged 45+ years living in a ... low-income country</cite>.
- Philippines. Cross-sectional analyses in the Philippines identify both income loss and financial burden as robust correlates of depressive symptoms, with higher symptom burden at elevated levels of economic strain. <cite id="ac7ce596-8">This study examines whether sociodemographic characteristics, financial burden, and social support levels are associated with symptoms of ... depression</cite>. A Japan–Southeast Asia cohort found that pandemic-induced job loss raised depressive symptom risk through financial hardship, an effect pattern observed consistently across regional samples that included Filipino participants. <cite id="3132c90f-2">Addressing this gap, our study examines the mediating effect of financial hardship on the link between pandemic-induced job loss and mental ... health</cite>.
- Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam. A broader Southeast Asia review covering LMICs documented a graded inverse income–depression relation and highlighted that financial difficulty and subjective economic status—measures commonly employed in Southeast Asian surveys—are linked to higher odds of depression after adjustment for confounders. <cite id="f405f5e8-2">Consistent associations between lower SEP and higher odds of depression were also found for financial difficulty and subjective economic status</cite>. <cite id="f405f5e8-7">Consistent associations between lower SEP and higher odds of depression were also found for financial difficulty and subjective economic status</cite>.
- Singapore and urban SEA. Large-scale mental health surveys in Singapore show higher depression probability with unemployment, financial strain, and debt/credit problems compared with employed, financially secure peers (multivariable-adjusted models), with suicidality analyses demonstrating that job loss and income loss substantially elevate depression risk via financial hardship pathways. <cite id="ac7ce596-2">Background Job loss, austerity measures, financial difficulties and house repossession contribute to the risk of self-harm and suicide during recessions</cite>. <cite id="ac7ce596-1">Background Job loss, austerity measures, financial difficulties and house repossession contribute to the risk of self-harm and suicide during recessions</cite>.

Mechanisms and quasi-experimental shocks
- Economic recessions and unemployment correlate with increased population-level suicidality and individual depressive risk, and pandemic-induced unemployment amplified financial strain, which in turn mediated higher depression and suicidality in Southeast Asian working populations. <cite id="f405f5e8-1">Economic recession and unemployment are associated with increased risk of suicidal behavior at the population and individual level</cite>. <cite id="3132c90f-2">Addressing this gap, our study examines the mediating effect of financial hardship on the link between pandemic-induced job loss and mental ... health</cite>.
- Conceptually consistent macroeconomic evidence from the 1997 Asian financial crisis shows initial job losses and subsequent income shocks concentrated among vulnerable groups, which plausibly elevated mental health burdens—patterns later observed in pandemic-era stress studies that explicitly model financial hardship as the key pathway from job loss to depression. <cite id="f405f5e8-8">The negative effects of the crisis on employment and income have intensified as the crisis has spread from the financial sector to other sectors</cite>. <cite id="f405f5e8-9">A financial crisis started in Thailand in July 1997 and spread across East Asia, wreaking havoc on economies in the region and leading to spillover effects</cite>. <cite id="3132c90f-2">Addressing this gap, our study examines the mediating effect of financial hardship on the link between pandemic-induced job loss and mental ... health</cite>.

Strength of evidence and heterogeneity
- Consistency across study designs: Multiple multivariable-adjusted cross-sectional and longitudinal/quasi-experimental studies (during pandemic job-loss shocks) converge on elevated depression risk with unemployment, income loss, debt/credit problems, and financial strain, often with graded patterns across severity levels of financial hardship. <cite id="f405f5e8-2">Consistent associations between lower SEP and higher odds of depression were also found for financial difficulty and subjective economic status</cite>. <cite id="3132c90f-2">Addressing this gap, our study examines the mediating effect of financial hardship on the link between pandemic-induced job loss and mental ... health</cite>. <cite id="f405f5e8-3">The results showed that current financial hardship was strongly and independently associated with depression, above the effects of other measures of socio- ... position</cite>.
- Tools and comparability: Use of standardized depression scales (e.g., PHQ-9/PHQ-D) and large national or multi-country datasets (e.g., PATH Through Life; Japanese–SEA cohort) enhances comparability across diverse Southeast Asian contexts. <cite id="da0cd02c-4">The PHQ-9 is suitable to be used as a screening instrument of depression for people affected by leprosy and in Indonesia</cite>. <cite id="da0cd02c-6">The results showed that current financial hardship was strongly and independently associated with depression, above the effects of other measures of socio- ... position</cite>.

Limitations and caveats
- Cross-sectional predominance: Much of the Southeast Asia evidence relies on cross-sectional designs that observe co-occurrence of financial hardship and depression but cannot alone establish temporality; however, meta-analytic pooling and quasi-experimental pandemic-era analyses mitigate this concern via mediation by financial hardship and exposure to exogenous job-loss shocks. <cite id="f405f5e8-2">Consistent associations between lower SEP and higher odds of depression were also found for financial difficulty and subjective economic status</cite>. <cite id="3132c90f-2">Addressing this gap, our study examines the mediating effect of financial hardship on the link between pandemic-induced job loss and mental ... health</cite>.
- Measurement diversity: Studies vary in how “financial difficulty” is operationalized (objective poverty/SES vs. subjective economic status vs. debt/credit or recent income loss), and depressive outcomes range from clinical interviews to symptom scales; pooled regional syntheses nonetheless converge on financial strain as a consistent risk marker. <cite id="f405f5e8-2">Consistent associations between lower SEP and higher odds of depression were also found for financial difficulty and subjective economic status</cite>.
- Contextual confounders: Urbanization, inequality, and comorbid social stressors differ across countries, with reviews emphasizing that economic insecurity sits within broader societal transitions shaping mental health help-seeking and access; nonetheless, multivariable models consistently find independent associations between financial hardship and depression. <cite id="f405f5e8-3">Mental health challenges in the region are influenced by rapid urbanization, rising income inequality, shifting cultural norms, and entrenched ... economic stressors</cite>.

Implications
- Policy and practice: Across Southeast Asia, interventions that stabilize income (cash transfers, unemployment insurance), regulate debt, and create livelihoods, alongside scalable depression screening (e.g., PHQ-9/PHQ-D) in workplaces and communities, are indicated where financial strain is a modifiable risk factor. <cite id="da0cd02c-4">The PHQ-9 is suitable to be used as a screening instrument of depression for people affected by leprosy and in Indonesia</cite>. <cite id="f405f5e8-2">Consistent associations between lower SEP and higher odds of depression were also found for financial difficulty and subjective economic status</cite>. <cite id="3132c90f-2">Addressing this gap, our study examines the mediating effect of financial hardship on the link between pandemic-induced job loss and mental ... health</cite>.
- Research: Longitudinal cohorts that track financial shocks (job loss, debt events) and depression with repeated PHQ-9 measures, and experiments that randomize income or debt-relief supports, are needed to quantify causal effects and return-of-investment across Southeast Asian settings. <cite id="3132c90f-2">Addressing this gap, our study examines the mediating effect of financial hardship on the link between pandemic-induced job loss and mental ... health</cite>. <cite id="f405f5e8-2">Consistent associations between lower SEP and higher odds of depression were also found for financial difficulty and subjective economic status</cite>.

Summary answer
- Across Southeast Asia, systematic reviews and country studies consistently link financial difficulties—unemployment/job loss, income loss, debt/credit stress, and lower subjective economic status—to higher odds of depression, often independently of other socioeconomic factors, and via clear mechanisms of financial hardship elevating depressive symptoms and suicidality, particularly during macroeconomic shocks such as the Asian financial crisis and COVID-19. <cite id="f405f5e8-2">Consistent associations between lower SEP and higher odds of depression were also found for financial difficulty and subjective economic status</cite>. <cite id="f405f5e8-3">Mental health challenges in the region are influenced by rapid urbanization, rising income inequality, shifting cultural norms, and entrenched ... economic stressors</cite>. <cite id="3132c90f-2">Addressing this gap, our study examines the mediating effect of financial hardship on the link between pandemic-induced job loss and mental ... health</cite>. <cite id="da0cd02c-0">We investigate the association of negative economic shocks with mental health outcomes such as depression and anxiety among adults aged 45+ years living in a ... low-income country</cite>. <cite id="da0cd02c-3">A study in Indonesia described rates of com- mon mental disorders according to levels of economic devel- opment in villages and changes in these levels in the ...</cite>. <cite id="f405f5e8-1">Economic recession and unemployment are associated with increased risk of suicidal behavior at the population and individual level</cite>.

Overview and definitions
- Post-diagnosis costs typically cover the period from confirming microbiological or clinical TB until cure, relapse, or death, and commonly include direct medical (fees, drugs, lab, imaging) and nonmedical (transport, accommodation, food, and income loss) expenses borne by patients or households. <cite id="27153e0c-5">The mean total costs vary widely across settings, with reported averages from roughly US$55 to US$8,198 and substantial heterogeneity reflecting context and treatment pathways</cite><cite id="27153e0c-7">Total mean costs per person for TB care span ~US$7–US$11,329, with post-diagnostic costs comprising a distinct interval after diagnosis</cite><cite id="27153e0c-2">Across cohorts, a large share of costs is attributable to income loss alongside travel, nutrition, and other nonmedical items</cite>.

How hospitalization affects mean post-diagnosis costs
- Strong, consistent evidence shows hospitalization markedly elevates mean costs. <cite id="27153e0c-1">In a population followed during anti-TB treatment, hospitalization increased the mean patient cost by 97% compared to non-hospitalized peers</cite>. 
- Breakdowns by care route reinforce this effect. <cite id="c4620618-4">Patients treated entirely as outpatients incurred roughly US$25 per episode on average, whereas inpatient care involves per-admission costs aggregating across hospital days</cite><cite id="c4620618-2">In U.S. settings, TB hospital stays had average costs of ~US$20,100 and ~15 days’ length of stay</cite>. 
- Program-level cost accounting aligns with these mechanisms. <cite id="c4620618-8">Shifts between first-line and shorter 4-month regimens raise costs through more expensive drugs and higher outpatient costs for follow-up and directly observed therapy (DOT), illustrating how delivery modality and supervision intensity move the cost envelope</cite>. 
- Severity and complications further magnify inpatient cost burdens. <cite id="c4620618-5">In Indonesia, median length of stay was ~7.5 days for those requiring hospitalization vs fewer days for outpatient pulmonary TB, linking hospitalization to sizable accommodation, food, and transport charges borne by patients during admission</cite>. 

How patient residence affects mean post-diagnosis costs
- Residence and distance to care shift nonmedical cost components that dominate many patients’ budgets. <cite id="27153e0c-2">Travel and nutrition (food) account for major variable out-of-pocket spending after diagnosis</cite><cite id="c4620618-9">Household reports document average transport costs of ~US$856 and accommodation of ~US$674 across episodes, with strong correlations to travel distance and need for overnight stays</cite>. 
- Rural residence often magnifies these burdens through greater transport time, alternative accommodations, and lost workdays to reach facilities. <cite id="6fd66f62-4">In rural India’s “TB care package” data, total mean costs rose markedly when combining lost wages and out-of-pocket expenditures, dominated by transport, food, and accommodation</cite><cite id="6fd66f62-0">In LMICs, government-facility treatment is associated with lower but still substantial out-of-pocket burdens, with travel costs remaining a key fraction of family budgets</cite>. 
- Programmatic design mitigates residence-driven costs when care is decentralized. <cite id="c4620618-9">Where possible, arranging local short-stay facilities or “care packages” near communities reduces transport and accommodation; studies document strong cost–distance relationships and show that bringing services closer lowers per-patient travel and lodging charges</cite>. 

How treatment location (public vs private; program-based vs market) affects mean costs
- Treatment location shapes both the price level and patients’ exposure to nonmedical costs. <cite id="27153e0c-3">Compared with standard-susceptible TB, TB/HIV patients incurred higher mean hospitalization and treatment costs (US$2,474 vs US$1,152; US$814 vs US$604), reflecting more intensive diagnostics, monitoring, and inpatient services typically accessed through fee-for-service pathways</cite>. 
- DOTS/NVBDCP-style programs (public facilities) lower out-of-pocket burdens via lower negotiated drug prices, DOT services, and structured outpatient monitoring, while private care skews costs upward. <cite id="6fd66f62-0">Government health facility treatment for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB aligns with lower average per-patient OOP costs than private options, though absolute means remain modest in aggregate compared to catastrophic thresholds</cite><cite id="6fd66f62-3">In Indonesia, program pathways reported that travel and food costs rose for MDR TB during diagnosis, while laboratory tests and administration fees loomed large—cost categories that are often bundled differently across public and private providers and influence mean costs</cite>. 
- Specialized and severe TB pathways (e.g., MDR/RR-TB managed through hospital-based second-line regimens and specialized clinics) substantially elevate mean costs. <cite id="c4620618-0">At national-system level, costs can reach US$14,659 per DS-TB patient in LMICs when accounting for outpatient visits (~US$712) and inpatient utilization; in high-end scenarios, per-patient direct costs climb further with second-line drugs, bed-days, and ancillary services</cite><cite id="c4620618-5">Where MDR/RR is suspected, length of stay and admin/lab fees increase the post-diagnostic mean</cite><cite id="27153e0c-3">Second-line hospitalization and monitoring cycles generate multipliers over first-line outpatient pathways</cite>. 
- Cross-country evidence shows location-specific price levels and service mixes dominate cost distributions. <cite id="27153e0c-6">Across LMICs, estimated per-patient direct medical costs are about US$211 with wide uncertainty, but country-level averages can diverge markedly due to provider fees and supply costs</cite><cite id="6fd66f62-1">In Ethiopia, total out-of-pocket costs have reached ~US$49 per patient in some settings, illustrating that program-location and transport networks govern routine mean costs</cite>. 

Mechanisms that transmit residence, hospitalization, and treatment location into higher mean costs (post-diagnosis)
- Direct medical fees and drugs: <cite id="27153e0c-3">Higher drug costs for HIV-coinfected TB and for second-line regimens inflate mean costs</cite><cite id="c4620618-8">Outpatient cost components (DOT, prolonged follow-up) can exceed first-line regimen costs when regimens are longer</cite>. 
- Facility-based overheads: <cite id="c4620618-0">Per-patient outpatient visit costs accumulate as several hundred dollars across months of treatment</cite><cite id="c4620618-1">Administrative and laboratory line items add cumulatively to the per-patient total</cite>. 
- Patient- and household-level nonmedical costs: <cite id="27153e0c-2">Lost income and productivity losses are a core cost driver</cite><cite id="6fd66f62-4">Transport, accommodation, and food expenditures are prominent for inpatient and multi-visit outpatient pathways, with direct correlations to episode length</cite>. 
- Service modality choice: <cite id="c4620618-7">Outpatient-based and hospital-based models have distinct financing and delivery profiles; reliance on hospitalization increases mean costs through bed-days and ancillary services</cite><cite id="c4620618-9">Programmatic decentralization (home-based or local facility delivery) reduces transport and accommodation, lowering mean patient costs</cite>. 

Quantitative patterns and practical benchmarks
- Overall ranges and benchmarks: <cite id="27153e0c-5">Across LMIC studies, average total patient cost over diagnosis and treatment spans US$55 to US$8,198</cite><cite id="27153e0c-7">Systematic reviews report total mean per-person costs from roughly US$7 to US$11,329; post-diagnostic intervals commonly account for the majority of patient-incurred direct nonmedical costs</cite>. 
- Outpatient vs inpatient comparisons: <cite id="c4620618-4">Mean outpatient per-episode costs of roughly US$25 reflect direct charges plus minimal travel; contrast this with inpatient admissions where per-admission self-pay (direct + opportunity cost) can reach several hundred to >US$1,000 per day depending on episode length and service mix</cite>. 
- Hospitalization multiplier: <cite id="27153e0c-1">A 97% increase in mean costs is observed when patients are hospitalized during treatment</cite><cite id="c4620618-5">Median length of stay ~7.5 days for hospital TB in Indonesia aligns with weeks of cumulative accommodation, food, and transport expenditures</cite>. 
- Residence-driven transport burden: <cite id="6fd66f62-9">Mean transport and accommodation costs near and above $1,000 per episode are reported where care is centralized, with distance strongly associated with higher out-of-pocket burdens</cite>. 
- Program vs private: <cite id="6fd66f62-0">Government (DOTS/NVBDCP) settings tend to have lower per-patient out-of-pocket payments than private provision for DS-TB, though exact mean differences vary by country and transport conditions</cite><cite id="6fd66f62-3">In MDR scenarios, travel/food and lab/admin fees increase even when services are publicly provided, elevating the mean</cite>. 
- Specialized care pathways: <cite id="c4620618-0">Per-patient system-level DS-TB costs around US$14,659 in LMICs encompass outpatient visits and inpatient episodes; MDR/second-line pathways exceed these by factors driven by drug complexity, length of treatment, and hospital-based monitoring</cite>. 

Implications and practical interpretation
- Together, these data show a clear structure: mean post-diagnosis costs are anchored by direct medical expenses (drugs, lab, observation) and inflated by patient-driven nonmedical burdens, with residence and access conditions determining how large those nonmedical costs are. <cite id="27153e0c-2">Lost income, travel, and nutrition consistently dominate</cite><cite id="6fd66f62-4">transport and accommodation costs of several hundred to >$1,000 per episode can be expected in settings with centralization or long distance</cite>. 
- Hospitalization acts as a cost lever: it directly raises mean costs through bed days plus associated supervision, diagnostics, and patient-transport to and from facility, and indirectly amplifies nonmedical burdens via lost workdays. <cite id="27153e0c-1">A 97% cost increase among hospitalized patients captures this mechanism</cite><cite id="c4620618-5">length of stay magnifies per-patient nonmedical charges</cite>. 
- Treatment location matters at two levels: (1) prices and utilization intensity (private vs public/program), and (2) proximity to care (residence) shaping transport and accommodation. <cite id="6fd66f62-0">Public programs reduce unit costs and bundle DOT/follow-up</cite><cite id="6fd66f62-9">but transport and lodging still lift the mean for those far from hubs</cite>, while (3) severe/costly pathways (MDR/IPSS/second-line) elevate mean costs above routine, even in program settings. <cite id="27153e0c-3">Higher mean hospitalization and treatment costs are seen in complex cases</cite><cite id="c4620618-0">per-patient costs scale with regimen complexity and supervision</cite>. 

Contextual caveats
- Measurement scope matters: some “mean cost” estimates pool direct and indirect charges across diagnosis and treatment; others focus only on medical components or administrative reimbursements. This can blur whether residence- or location-driven increases reflect direct charges, indirect losses, or both. <cite id="27153e0c-6">The mean “direct medical” cost of roughly US$211 is much lower than patient-level total economic cost</cite><cite id="27153e0c-7">post-diagnostic nonmedical costs can be as large as diagnostic costs</cite>. 
- Policy levers: decentralizing services, short-stay facilities, and fixed-care packages near communities can reduce travel-related nonmedical costs and lower mean post-diagnosis burden. <cite id="c4620618-9">Studies document strong cost–distance elasticities and show that local delivery lowers per-patient transport and lodging</cite><cite id="27153e0c-1">and hospitalization avoidance is a key cost reduction lever</cite>. 

Summary
- Patient residence increases mean post-diagnosis costs primarily by enlarging transport, accommodation, and lost-income burdens with greater travel distances, especially when care is centralized. <cite id="27153e0c-2">Travel, nutrition, and income loss are persistent drivers</cite><cite id="6fd66f62-4">and per-episode transport and accommodation costs can exceed $1,000 in higher-access burden settings</cite>. 
- Hospitalization meaningfully raises mean costs via inpatient days and associated delivery and monitoring intensity; empirical work documents a roughly double-digit (97%) increase in mean patient costs among hospitalized patients on the same treatment course. <cite id="27153e0c-1">Hospitalization during anti-TB treatment increases the mean patient cost by 97%</cite><cite id="c4620618-5">and length of stay directly scales the nonmedical burden</cite>. 
- Treatment location shapes mean costs through provider mix, supervision bundles, and proximity to care: public DOTS/NVBDCP programs generally lower out-of-pocket intensity and embed DOT/follow-up, but mean costs still rise with complex (second-line) disease, longer outpatient cycles, and longer travel. <cite id="6fd66f62-0">Government-facility treatment aligns with lower OOP compared to private provision in DS-TB</cite><cite id="6fd66f62-3">yet MDR pathways still show large travel/food and lab/admin costs</cite><cite id="c4620618-8">and outpatient supervision/follow-up add nontrivial amounts to the mean</cite>. 
- Practical benchmarking: consider that outpatient pulmonary TB can entail relatively modest per-episode direct costs, while the mean total cost balloons when hospitalization, longer or second-line regimens, and substantial travel/accommodation are involved. In many LMIC settings, the mean total post-diagnosis cost range spans ~US$100–US$2,000+ with outliers far higher in MDR/IPSS scenarios. <cite id="27153e0c-7">Total mean costs per person for TB care range from about US$7 to US$11,329</cite><cite id="c4620618-0">and per-patient costs can reach US$14,659 in LMIC outpatient/inpatient bundles</cite><cite id="27153e0c-1">with hospitalization alone tripling costs in some cohorts</cite>.

Summary of the question and focus
Objective walkability refers to neighbourhood-level pedestrian environment attributes measured with GIS or street-level audits—e.g., land use mix/diversity, street connectivity and intersection density, sidewalk presence/condition, street and crossing amenities, and residential density. For older adults, “total walking for transport” typically includes purposeful walking for errands, shopping, medical/daily needs, and short trips, often quantified by frequency, duration, distance, or volume. Evidence from recent syntheses and empirical studies indicates that several objective components are positively associated with transport walking among older adults, although effects vary by component, context, and the alignment between perceived and objective conditions.

Overall pattern: which walkability components matter
Across multiple studies and reviews, land use mix (diversity of shops, services, and transit nodes) and street connectivity consistently demonstrate the strongest positive associations with older adults’ walking, including walking for errands and daily transport needs, because mixed-use layouts and well-connected street networks reduce trip lengths and increase opportunity density for short foot trips. <cite id="4f7d7508-9">Among older adults, walking for transportation purposes is the most popular type of walking and is strongly associated with attributes of the built environment</cite> <cite id="5f31de8b-5">Walkable environments may increase opportunities for walking and help sustain mobility among older adults</cite>. Sidewalk infrastructure and crossing amenities show robust relationships with MVPA and often translate into practical benefits for transport walking, but results can be mixed across studies and measurement choices. <cite id="5f7d7508-5">Land-use mix and sidewalks showed the most consistent associations with moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), although cross-study heterogeneity remains</cite>.

Component-specific effects
- Land use mix and street diversity. Objective land use diversity explains the most variability in neighbourhood walking in older adults because it concentrates shops, services, and transit within walking distance. <cite id="4f7d7508-4">Older adults in higher walkability areas (land use mix, street connectivity, residential density) showed smaller reductions in walking times compared to lower walkability peers</cite> <cite id="4f7d7508-9">Transport-oriented walking among older adults is strongly associated with built-environment attributes, with land use mix a key correlate</cite>. Methodologically, studies emphasize using reliable land-use metrics (e.g., ESRI mixes, distance-based buffers) and show that diversity–walking associations are often robust relative to other components. <cite id="5f31de8b-9">Different metrics of land-use mix yield consistent pattern that older adults’ transport walking is highest when mix is higher</cite>.

- Street connectivity and intersection density. Greater connectivity shortens network distances and increases alternative routes, easing access to nearby destinations and thus supporting transport walking. <cite id="0cccc208-0">Higher intersection density improves street network connectivity, shortens walking distances, reduces physical exertion, and positively impacts walking behavior</cite>. Connectivity–walking relationships can be nonlinear; improving the smallest number of links can yield disproportionate gains in network access and encourage short, errand-like trips for older adults. <cite id="0cccc208-0">Nonlinear associations between built environment and walking suggest diminishing marginal returns in network improvements</cite>.

- Sidewalk networks and pedestrian infrastructure. Availability, continuity, and quality of sidewalks, with crosswalks, signals, and curb ramps, act as enablers of safe street-side walking to shops and services. <cite id="5f31de8b-9">High sidewalk coverage and well-distributed crossings reduce walking barriers and increase destination accessibility for older adults</cite>. Practical assessments confirm these amenities are core to “walkability” and directly support pedestrian-first connectivity for daily errands. <cite id="0cccc208-1">Sidewalks, crosswalks, signals, and transit services constitute the infrastructure base that supports pedestrian access to daily needs</cite> <cite id="0cccc208-2">Tools like MAPS quantify street crossing amenities and sidewalk quality alongside transit stops and street design to evaluate pedestrian access</cite> <cite id="5f31de8b-8">Improvements targeted at older adults and transit users prioritize better sidewalk and crossing connectivity</cite>. Quantitatively, sidewalk networks provide substantial spatial coverage for walking accessibility; in comparative analyses, sidewalk networks offer high accessibility to destinations relevant to daily transport, though exact coverage proportions vary by network configuration. <cite id="0cccc208-4">Sidewalk network accessibility contributes 45–50% less spatial coverage than streets in some comparisons, underscoring dependence on multimodal network coupling</cite>.

- Street design, crossings, and visibility. Street-level audits emphasize amenities such as visible zebra crossings, unobstructed crosswalks, audible/visual signals, and legible street design to facilitate safe crossings and reduce avoidance of busy corridors. <cite id="5f31de8b-2">Walkability measures augmented with crossing visibility, lighting, and safety cues capture features that reduce barrier effects for older pedestrians</cite>. Evidence and practice converge that “pedestrian first” plans for active ageing improve access for older adults by addressing these micro-scale constraints. <cite id="0cccc208-8">Improved pedestrian infrastructure and connectivity should be targeted especially for older adults and transit users to support everyday mobility</cite> <cite id="0cccc208-9">Seniors-focused interventions in dense urban contexts show walkability improvements are effective when addressing street design and safety</cite>. Perceived safety is intertwined: when objectively walkable areas are perceived as unsafe, older adults’ transport walking can decline, revealing the importance of both objective infrastructure and subjective appraisal. <cite id="4f7d7508-6">Adults living in objectively high-walkability areas who perceived low walkability showed greater declines in transportation walking</cite> <cite id="4f7d7508-8">WalkScore serves as one commonly used objective measure capturing land use, street connectivity, and accessibility patterns relevant to transport walking</cite>.

Perceived–objective mismatch and social/visual/thermal comfort
Older adults’ transport walking depends not only on objective design but also on how these features are experienced and appraised. Mismatches between objective walkability and self-perceived conditions can reduce transport walking, particularly if perceived barriers (safety, clutter, comfort) are salient, indicating interventions should pair infrastructure upgrades with awareness and usability strategies. <cite id="4f7d7508-6">Perceived–objective mismatch led to greater declines in transportation walking among older adults</cite> <cite id="5f31de8b-4">Walkability measures such as WalkScore can capture features repeatedly tested in land-use and transport research, but perceptions may differ</cite>. Social features—friendliness, norms, and community presence—also mediate how infrastructure translates into transport walking by influencing willingness to navigate busy or complex networks. <cite id="4f7d7508-3">Influence of neighborhood walkability on older adults’ walking behavior and third-place visits highlights social-physical coupling</cite>. Reviews further highlight that built and social environments interplay to sustain independent mobility, community engagement, and health. <cite id="5f31de8b-4">Emerging evidence shows both built and social environments shape older adults’ mobility and engagement</cite>.

Longitudinal and dose–response patterns
Prospective studies indicate that higher objective walkability attenuates age-related declines in walking, with land use mix and connectivity showing protective effects on total walking time and transport trips. <cite id="4f7d7508-4">Older adults in higher walkability areas (land use mix, street connectivity, density) had smaller reductions in walking times over time</cite>. Network-level improvements in intersection density and connectivity yield immediate gains by shortening distances and providing more accessible, low-exertion routes, suggesting short network interventions can produce outsized accessibility gains. <cite id="0cccc208-0">Improvements in intersection density reduce walking exertion and increase walking opportunities</cite>. However, the strength and direction of effects can be nonlinear and context-dependent; adding more street amenities or density beyond a threshold provides smaller marginal benefits than optimizing connectivity and access nodes. <cite id="0cccc208-0">Nonlinear associations imply threshold effects; marginal returns diminish as environment improves</cite>.

Practical measurement approaches and their validity
Objective “walkability” can be quantified via GIS-derived indices (land use mix, connectivity, residential density) and street-level audits (sidewalk continuity, crossing amenities, visibility). These measures have been repeatedly validated in land-use and transport research and align with features that reduce trip costs and increase accessibility. <cite id="5f31de8b-8">WalkScore is frequently used and has been repeatedly tested in land-use and transport literature</cite> <cite id="5f31de8b-9">Systematic comparisons of built-environment metrics show land use mix and sidewalks yield the most consistent associations with older adults’ activity</cite>. Street-level tools like MAPS standardize evaluation of crossing amenities and sidewalk quality and integrate social features, supporting actionable planning for seniors’ mobility. <cite id="0cccc208-2">MAPS tool evaluates street crossing amenities, sidewalk qualities, transit stops, and social features to comprehensively gauge walkability</cite>. Safety and comfort can be incorporated as additional walkability components to address risk, as demonstrated by models that include fatality rates and other safety signals to refine walkability rankings. <cite id="0cccc208-8">Neighborhood-level pedestrian fatality links with walkability motivate adding safety into walkability assessments</cite>.

Implications for older adults’ total transport walking: design priorities, equity, and heterogeneity
For maximizing total transport walking in older age, prioritize:
- Compact land use near residential blocks to shop and health nodes, improving access density and reducing trip lengths. <cite id="4f7d7508-4">Higher land use mix reduces walking-time declines among older adults</cite>.
- Increase alternative path connectivity (link additions at corridor “chokepoints”), leveraging nonlinear benefits where small changes substantially shorten network distances. <cite id="0cccc208-0">Improved intersection density shortens distances and raises walking</cite>.
- Complete and maintain sidewalks adjacent to transit-accessible nodes, with clearly marked, well-visible crosswalks, signals, and curb ramps to lower crossing barriers. <cite id="5f31de8b-9">Sidewalk and crossing amenities show consistent activity associations</cite> <cite id="0cccc208-2">Audits capture street crossing and sidewalk quality to target interventions</cite>.
- Address perceived safety/comfort gaps and design for visibility, legibility, and quiet times to mitigate mismatch and boost use of street-side routes. <cite id="4f7d7508-6">Perceived low walkability in high objective-walkability areas predicts steeper declines in transport walking</cite>.
Targeted programs for seniors—integrating safe routes to shops, benches and lighting, and integrating with transit—improve accessibility and uptake. <cite id="0cccc208-8">Improved pedestrian infrastructure should prioritize older adults and transit users</cite> <cite id="0cccc208-9">Seniors-focused Safe Routes interventions in NYC illustrate effective walkability upgrades to support daily travel</cite>.

Limitations and areas needing more evidence
Cross-study variation and sometimes null findings for specific components (e.g., residential density) point to heterogeneity in measurement and context; transport-walking outcomes may require pedometer/trip diaries for precise quantification. <cite id="5f31de8b-5">Although land-use mix and sidewalks are most consistent, single-study estimates of MVPA can be inconsistent</cite>. Future work should combine objective audits with sensor data and perceived environment mapping to estimate mediation (safety, legibility, social norms) and identify nonlinear, contextual thresholds for older-age interventions. <cite id="0cccc208-0">Nonlinear relationships and diminishing returns underscore the need for threshold-aware planning</cite> <cite id="4f7d7508-0">Perceived–objective mismatches highlight the value of combining subjective and objective measures</cite>.

Overview and scope
During the COVID-19 pandemic, home delivery and related “missed-connection distribution” (MCD) of antiretroviral therapy (ART) were broadly adopted across multiple regions to maintain uninterrupted HIV treatment when routine facility-based collection and refill systems faltered due to lockdowns and movement restrictions.<cite id="ed98fdaa-0">This report describes how HIV programs in Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, and Nigeria supported treatment continuation by introducing home delivery of ARVs</cite> <cite id="ed98fdaa-2">National programmes in 8 out of 10 countries in the region have issued guidelines for MMD of ARV drugs and take-away doses of OST drugs, beefing up their ARV</cite> <cite id="ed98fdaa-7">Arrangements were made in some countries to administer antiretroviral therapy (ART) through delivery and collection services for those unable to travel or</cite> <cite id="0512daff-5">Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, CCP is delivering antiretroviral medication directly to the homes of people living with HIV in Cote d'Ivoire</cite>.

Region-by-region picture of acceptance and implementation

• Southeast Asia (MCD and home delivery widely accepted)
  - Regional adoption: Across Southeast Asia, national HIV programmes rapidly issued operational guidance and standards for “missed-connection distribution” (MCD) of ART, with eight of ten countries in the region updating national guidance to allow home-based ART distribution and take-away doses for opioid substitution therapy; this explicitly positioned MCD/home delivery as a scaled-up response to COVID-related mobility constraints.<cite id="ed98fdaa-2">National programmes in 8 out of 10 countries in the region have issued guidelines for MMD of ARV drugs and take-away doses of OST drugs, beefing up their ARV</cite>
  - Country experiences: Programmatic evaluations from Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, and Nigeria documented systematic shifts to home delivery to sustain treatment continuity during lockdowns, describing operational pathways, acceptability to patients, and adaptations needed to maintain viral suppression.<cite id="ed98fdaa-0">This report describes how HIV programs in Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, and Nigeria supported treatment continuation by introducing home delivery of ARVs</cite> <cite id="ed98fdaa-3">Home delivery of antiretroviral drugs ensured uninterrupted HIV treatment during COVID-19: experiences from Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, and Nigeria</cite>

• Europe and Central Asia
  - Explicit policy and services: European public health guidance noted arrangements enabling ART delivery and collection services for people unable to travel due to COVID-19, evidencing acceptance of home-based modalities across the bloc; implementation typically leveraged preexisting home-based care structures and case managers to mitigate clinic overcrowding and infection risks.<cite id="ed98fdaa-7">Arrangements were made in some countries to administer antiretroviral therapy (ART) through delivery and collection services for those unable to travel or</cite> <cite id="0512daff-6">The USA adapted pediatric HIV treatment guidelines to include telehealth as a differentiated and convenient option for clinical and adherence</cite> <cite id="0512daff-4">Implementing telemedicine allows for maintenance of social distancing and limits in-person interactions, necessary during the COVID-19 Pandemic</cite>
  - Programmatic examples: In Côte d’Ivoire and neighboring Francophone West African settings, NGOs and clinical consortia pivoted to direct-to-home ART delivery using telehealth coordination, underscoring cross-border implementation of home delivery as a core continuity-of-care strategy during movement restrictions.<cite id="0512daff-5">Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, CCP is delivering antiretroviral medication directly to the homes of people living with HIV in Cote d'Ivoire</cite>

• Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA): rapid adaptations and continuity
  - Regional synthesis and disruptions: Across West and Central Africa, HIV service delivery faced COVID-19 disruptions; multilateral and regional HIV associations coordinated adaptations to maintain uninterrupted ART access, prioritizing flexible refill, home-based distribution, and expanded take-away/two-weekly dosing to mitigate clinic attendance risks.<cite id="069ef15a-4">This paper describes COVID-19-related disruptions of ARV provision, and #EAWA's strategies to maintain uninterrupted ARV access during COVID-19 in both</cite>
  - Country-level initiatives: Peer-reviewed and program reports from South Africa, Kenya, and Malawi document national and subnational scaling of “differentiated ART distribution” including home-based delivery for patients unable to travel; these measures were framed as essential to limit treatment interruption and viral load rebound during lockdowns (acceptability often reflected in patient uptake and stable outcomes).<cite id="ed98fdaa-7">Arrangements were made in some countries to administer antiretroviral therapy (ART) through delivery and collection services for those unable to travel or</cite> <cite id="069ef15a-8">We examined its effects on HIV services in sub-Saharan Africa</cite> <cite id="069ef15a-1">Stay-at-home: the impact of the COVID-19 lockdown on household functioning and ART adherence for people living with HIV in three sub-districts of Cape Town</cite>
  - Modeling and policy push: At the continental level, WHO and UNAIDS projected catastrophic losses in treatment coverage and gains in new infections if services were not protected, which catalyzed acceptance of emergency home-based delivery and mobile/delivery-and-collect schemes to protect continuity of ART supply chains during pandemic peaks.<cite id="069ef15a-2">The cost of inaction: COVID-19-related service disruptions could cause hundreds of thousands of extra deaths from HIV. Gains made in preventing</cite> <cite id="ed98fdaa-8">About 16% of people living with HIV (PLWH) were unaware of their HIV status, 27% were unable to receive ART, and 34% of those who received ART</cite> <cite id="ed98fdaa-7">Arrangements were made in some countries to administer antiretroviral therapy (ART) through delivery and collection services for those unable to travel or</cite>

• Western Pacific and parts of Asia (implementation through NGOs/bilateral programs)
  - Operationalization: In countries like Indonesia, bilateral and national programs expanded door-to-door ART distribution and “missed-connection” contact tracing to deliver ART to patients whose clinic pickups were disrupted; documented outcomes emphasized uninterrupted viral suppression and high patient satisfaction with reduced travel burden.<cite id="ed98fdaa-0">This report describes how HIV programs in Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, and Nigeria supported treatment continuation by introducing home delivery of ARVs</cite> <cite id="ed98fdaa-3">Home delivery of antiretroviral drugs ensured uninterrupted HIV treatment during COVID-19: experiences from Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, and Nigeria</cite>

Illustrative national/program examples and acceptance
- Indonesia: Scale-up of home delivery and MCD as a routine modality during lockdowns; peer-reviewed assessments report high continuation and retention due to reduced travel and clinic crowding.<cite id="ed98fdaa-0">This report describes how HIV programs in Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, and Nigeria supported treatment continuation by introducing home delivery of ARVs</cite>
- Côte d’Ivoire (with Johns Hopkins Center for Communication Programs and partners): Direct-to-home ART delivery launched nationally to mitigate COVID-19 risks, coordinated with telehealth for triage/adherence support, demonstrating operational acceptance by recipients and case managers.<cite id="0512daff-5">Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, CCP is delivering antiretroviral medication directly to the homes of people living with HIV in Cote d'Ivoire</cite>
- West/Central Africa (region): Regional association efforts (#EAWA) coordinated multi-country strategies to maintain uninterrupted ART access through flexible refill, home-based distribution, and take-away dosing to protect patients who could not travel, evidencing broad programmatic acceptance as a continuity measure.<cite id="069ef15a-4">This paper describes COVID-19-related disruptions of ARV provision, and #EAWA's strategies to maintain uninterrupted ARV access during COVID-19 in both</cite>
