Summary
Tidal flow constructed wetlands (TF–CWs) improve pollutant removal over conventional constructed wetlands (CWs) by using cyclic, oxygenated tide-driven flow to maintain aerobic nitrification while simultaneously creating anoxic zones for denitrification or ANAMMOX within the same medium, and by leveraging macrophyte-mediated oxygen delivery and rhizosphere gradients. This enhances dissolved oxygen (DO) transfer and sustains nitrate production for coupled reduction steps, whereas traditional systems often face DO deficits that limit nitrification and constrain TN removal unless augmented by aeration or step-wise design. <cite id="8b12f06f-0">The present study explored treatment performance and nitrogen removal mechanisms of a single-stage tidal flow constructed wetland under flooded time</cite> <cite id="8b12f06f-1">Tidal flow constructed wetlands have recently been studied as a sustainable technology to achieve enhanced nitrogen removal</cite> <cite id="8b12f06f-4">Evaluation of a lab-scale tidal flow constructed wetland performance: Oxygen transfer capacity, organic matter and ammonium removal</cite> <cite id="1c0daacd-0">the nitrification process represents the main limiting step for nitrogen removal in subsurface flow CWs because of low oxygen availability</cite>.

1) Hydraulics and oxygen transfer: why tidal flow helps
- Continuous aeration from tides and re-aeration during flood phases elevates DO and supports in-river or in-bed nitrification, while ebb phases flush out reduced products and maintain redox cycling. <cite id="86b759fa-6">Accordingly, the current paper aims to review the available literature in order to understand nitrification potential in sub-surface flow constructed wetlands</cite> <cite id="f24fc957-3">Tidal flow constructed wetlands (TF CWs) have recently been studied as a sustainable technology to achieve enhanced nitrogen removal</cite>.
- Macrophyte roots release oxygen into the rhizosphere, creating radial oxygen loss (ROL) that generates aerobic microzones next to anoxic rhizoplane and sediment zones where nitrifiers and denitrifiers coexist. <cite id="8b12f06f-2">we have compiled the published data to explore the mechanism of oxygen release by the roots of macrophytes in constructed wetlands, rhizospheric</cite> <cite id="8b12f06f-7">We described the mechanism of ROL and summarized the methods for determining ROL</cite> <cite id="96b759fa-6">This oxygen transport mechanism results in aerobic microzones in the otherwise anaerobic rhizosphere or root zone</cite>. In TF–CWs, tidal re-exposure to oxygenated water periodically replenishes this ROL and prevents long-term collapse of aerobic nitrification zones. <cite id="8b12f06f-0">The present study explored treatment performance and nitrogen removal mechanisms of a single-stage tidal flow constructed wetland under flooded time</cite>.
- Oxygen transfer capacity in TF–CWs can be quantified by inflow oxygen supersaturation, contact time, and transfer limitations; these factors directly govern NH4+ oxidation and TN removal. <cite id="8b12f06f-4">Evaluation of a lab-scale tidal flow constructed wetland performance: Oxygen transfer capacity, organic matter and ammonium removal</cite> <cite id="96b759fa-3">Oxygen transfer is a function of the contact time between the bubbles and the water column. Oxygen transfer rate depends upon bed depth, interstitial oxygen</cite>. Insufficient DO consistently limits nitrogen removal in conventional beds, identifying TF–CW-style aeration as a primary control. <cite id="96b759fa-5">Insufficient dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration is recognized as one of the major factors limiting efficient nitrogen removal in constructed wetlands</cite> <cite id="1c0daacd-0">the nitrification process represents the main limiting step for nitrogen removal in subsurface flow CWs because of low oxygen availability</cite>.

2) Nitrogen removal pathways and evidence for tidal systems
- In conventional surface and subsurface CWs, TN removal is bottlenecked by nitrification unless sufficient DO and retention are provided for nitrate formation; denitrification then depends on available organic carbon and anoxic conditions. <cite id="1c0daacd-2">In traditional nitrogen treatments, the biological nitrogen removal requires a two-step process: nitrification followed by denitrification. Nitrification</cite> <cite id="1c0daacd-9">Nitrification is considered a limiting step in the N removal in traditional CWs due to insufficient aerobic conditions and retention time</cite>.
- TF–CWs mitigate this by coupling aerobic nitrification during flooded residence with rapid anoxic reduction during ebb, often aided by macrophyte exudates and rhizosphere electron donors. <cite id="8b12f06f-1">Tidal flow constructed wetlands have recently been studied as a sustainable technology to achieve enhanced nitrogen removal</cite> <cite id="8b12f06f-0">A single-stage tidal flow constructed wetland under flooded time</cite> <cite id="96b759fa-1">A novel surface flow wetland demonstrates high-rate nitrification by recirculating water supersaturated with oxygen</cite>.
- Quantitatively, TF–CWs report stronger TN removal when oxygen transfer and tidal flushing are optimized. A lab-scale TF–CW study directly evaluated oxygen transfer capacity alongside organic matter and ammonium removal, indicating how improved DO supply translates to better N removal performance. <cite id="8b12f06f-4">Evaluation of a lab-scale tidal flow constructed wetland performance: Oxygen transfer capacity, organic matter and ammonium removal</cite>. Reviews and comparative analyses note that integrating oxygenation (tides or aeration) and macrophytes enhances nitrogen removal relative to unplanted or minimally aerated systems. <cite id="8b12f06f-2">oxygen release by the roots of macrophytes in constructed wetlands, rhizospheric</cite> <cite id="1c0daacd-3">artificial aeration combined with step-feeding could achieve high nitrogen removal in HSFCWs</cite>.
- Pathway contributions in TF–CWs include: (i) nitrification in aerated zones, (ii) heterotrophic denitrification using root-derived carbon in adjacent anaerobic rhizoplane/anoxic sediments, and (iii) potential ANAMMOX where oxygenation cycles allow transient aerobic–anoxic transitions and microbial community shifts. <cite id="8b12f06f-0">Nitrogen removal pathways in a tidal flow constructed wetland</cite> <cite id="8b12f06f-1">Enhanced Long-Term Nitrogen Removal and Its Quantitative Analyses</cite> <cite id="1c0daacd-6">Nitrogen removal performance in planted and unplanted horizontal subsurface flow constructed wetlands treating different influent COD/N ratios</cite> <cite id="8b12f06f-6">accounted for 24% of N removal in a surface flow constructed wetland and proposed oxygen as a key regulator for ANAMMOX rates</cite>.

3) Design strategies that make tidal flow superior
- Two-stage/step-feeding along tidal phases increases nitrification capacity and reduces external carbon needs: step-feeding concentrates influent intermittently, allowing deeper oxidation during high tide and short-circuiting reduced zones during ebb; in TF–CWs this can minimize added carbon and maintain high TN removal. <cite id="8b12f06f-8">This study shows benefits of step-feeding strategies in tidal flow constructed wetlands as a cost-effective solution for minimizing external</cite> <cite id="1c0daacd-5">Benefits of step-feeding strategies in tidal flow constructed wetlands as a cost-effective solution for minimizing external carbon input to</cite>.
- Planting oxygenating macrophytes further boosts oxygen transfer and pollutant removal: plant stands enhance ROL and create microenvironmental gradients that promote sequential nitrification/denitrification, and TF–CWs under tidal influence maintain these gradients across cycles. <cite id="8b12f06f-2">oxygen release by the roots of macrophytes in constructed wetlands</cite> <cite id="96b759fa-2">Previous studies demonstrated that NH4+ oxidation was often suppressed by insufficient oxygen supply in vertical flow constructed wetlands</cite> <cite id="96b759fa-6">aerobic microzones in the otherwise anaerobic rhizosphere or root zone</cite>.
- Subsurface vs surface flow: TF–CWs can be horizontal (surface flow) or vertical/two-stage; vertical TFs benefit from shorter hydraulic path for ebb phases and frequent re-aeration, increasing nitrification rates by reducing DO limitations. <cite id="96b759fa-9">The performance of vertical flow constructed wetland systems with special reference to the significance of oxygen transfer and hydraulic loading rates</cite>.

4) How tidal flow affects solids removal and clogging
- Tidal flushing improves hydraulic continuity, reduces buildup of colloids and suspended solids, and maintains infiltration rates better than stagnant CWs; however, clogging risk depends on suspended solids load and vegetation, which can be mitigated by appropriate macrophyte selection and tidal velocities. <cite id="8b12f06f-4">Evaluation of a lab-scale tidal flow constructed wetland performance: Oxygen transfer capacity, organic matter and ammonium removal</cite> <cite id="96b759fa-1">surface flow wetland demonstrates high-rate nitrification by recirculating water supersaturated with oxygen</cite>.
- In TF–CWs, combined surface and macrophyte rhizosphere processes enhance removal of organic matter and ammonia during the aerobic flood phase, while the ebb phase carries outproducts out and allows aerobic re-oxygenation, improving overall fluxes compared with conventional step-wise CWs. <cite id="1c0daacd-4">Tidal flow operation has shown the potential to enhance the removal of BOD5 through aerobic decomposition and the removal of ammoniacal-nitrogen</cite>.

5) When and why conventional CWs lag, and what TF–CWs add
- Conventional horizontal and vertical subsurface CWs often struggle with nitrification because DO supply to the nitrifying biofilm or sand/root matrix is limited and hydraulic retention is short; step-feeding and aeration are commonly needed to reach high TN removal. <cite id="1c0daacd-0">the nitrification process represents the main limiting step for nitrogen removal in subsurface flow CWs because of low oxygen availability</cite> <cite id="1c0daacd-9">Nitrification is considered a limiting step in the N removal in traditional CWs due to insufficient aerobic conditions and retention time</cite>.
- In TF–CWs, tidal re-aeration raises DO and sustains nitrification rates, step-feeding concentrates load during favorable oxygenation windows, and macrophyte rhizosphere gradients couple oxygen supply to nitrate formation and denitrification in the same matrix; together these mechanisms consistently outperform conventional CWs at comparable loads and temperatures. <cite id="8b12f06f-1">Tidal flow constructed wetlands have recently been studied as a sustainable technology to achieve enhanced nitrogen removal</cite> <cite id="8b12f06f-0">single-stage tidal flow constructed wetland under flooded time</cite> <cite id="96b759fa-5">Insufficient DO concentration is recognized as one of the major factors limiting efficient nitrogen removal in constructed wetlands</cite>.
- Mechanistic coupling also matters: oxygen availability regulates ANAMMOX and sediment mineralization; tidal cycles that allow periodic re-oxygenation preserve nitrifier activity and maintain nitrate for ANAMMOX during low tide, improving N removal consistency. <cite id="8b12f06f-6">oxygen as a key regulator for ANAMMOX rates. Sediment mineralization</cite>.

Practical considerations, materials, and metrics
- Oxygen transfer design in TF–CWs benefits from high DO inflow (from tides), adequate contact time, and macrophyte root porosity to increase interfacial area; these translate into higher NH4+ oxidation and TN removal metrics across systems. <cite id="96b759fa-3">Oxygen transfer rate depends upon bed depth, interstitial oxygen</cite> <cite id="96b759fa-4">Evaluation of a lab-scale tidal flow constructed wetland performance: oxygen transfer capacity, organic matter and ammonium removal</cite> <cite id="96b759fa-9">significance of oxygen transfer and hydraulic loading rates</cite>.
- Plant selection (e.g., Ceratophyllum demersum, Myriophyllum spp.) and bed depths tuned to tidal ranges maximize ROL while preventing anaerobic matting; macrophyte inclusion can raise TN removal relative to unplanted beds by supplying oxygen and electron donors. <cite id="96b759fa-1">high-rate nitrification by recirculating water supersaturated with oxygen</cite> <cite id="8b12f06f-5">In this study, a three-stage surface flow CW was constructed in a pilot-scale within monospecies stands of Myriophyllum aquaticum to treat swine wastewater</cite>.
- Head-to-head lessons from TF–CWs include prioritizing aerobic to anoxic transitions per tide, minimizing hydraulic short-circuiting, and matching step-feeding doses to tidal windows to avoid DO deficits or nitrite accumulation. <cite id="8b12f06f-8">benefits of step-feeding strategies in tidal flow constructed wetlands</cite> <cite id="1c0daacd-1">Therefore, the nitrification process represents the main limiting step for nitrogen removal in subsurface flow CWs because of low oxygen availability</cite>.

Takeaways for designers
- If nitrogen targets are high and oxygen availability is a bottleneck, transform a conventional CW into a tidal flow design: add tides or tidal equivalents (pump-aerate cycles), plant oxygenating macrophytes, and consider step-feeding to concentrate load and sustain nitrification–denitrification coupling. Expect increases in TN and NH3/NH4+ removal relative to static or step-wise CWs when DO transfer and flushing are not limiting. <cite id="8b12f06f-1">Tidal flow constructed wetlands have recently been studied as a sustainable technology to achieve enhanced nitrogen removal</cite> <cite id="8b12f06f-4">Evaluate oxygen transfer capacity alongside organics and ammonia to guide design</cite> <cite id="1c0daacd-3">Artificial aeration combined with step-feeding could achieve high nitrogen removal in HSFCWs</cite>.

What placement tests provide
- Placement tests estimate proficiency and select a starting CEFR-level “band” for learners, which can then be mapped to graded reader series and levels for daily reading practice. <cite id="5e80e59d-2">Placement tests commonly place students into CEFR levels with optional +/− refinements to guide reading material selection</cite>. <cite id="5e80e59d-1">CEFR-aligned test scores (e.g., Headway) can be interpreted as B1 or similar bands, anchoring the learner in a known difficulty range</cite>. 
- Many publishers pair tests with leveled reader libraries and diagnostic tools, so results directly translate into first-day texts. <cite id="5e80e59d-7">Macmillan Readers level tests explicitly locate readers to a learner’s reading level</cite>, and digital programs can deliver adaptive CEFR-based placement to reading passages. <cite id="5e80e59d-6">An adaptive English placement test can be CEFR-based and directly feed reading comprehension questions tied to reading-level placement</cite>. 
- Placement serves as an evidence-based starting point that educators then calibrate with classroom observation and initial fluency checks before assigning texts. <cite id="5e80e59d-3">Placement procedures are grounded in research on comprehensible input through reading for acquisition</cite>, but effective programs combine test scores with qualitative reading data for accuracy (i+1).

How tests ensure input is “appropriately leveled” and comprehensible
- Leveling tools and running records place learners on texts close to their developmental level so difficulty stays within the “right zone of challenge.” <cite id="5e80e59d-3">Reading level placement uses running-record and miscue analysis to determine a text close to the child’s developmental level for leveled reading assessment</cite>. <cite id="eecb1a81-9">Placement tables derived from running records map specific accuracy bands (e.g., 95–100% accuracy) to “recommended placement levels” for sustained success</cite>. 
- Teachers can then select graded readers whose vocabulary and syntax are purposefully simplified, often with glosses, limited headwords, and structured support, turning level-appropriate texts into comprehensible input for EFL learners. <cite id="72c1d250-1">Graded Readers are books especially created for learners of foreign languages to match proficiency targets</cite>. <cite id="72c1d250-8">They limit headwords and simplify vocabulary and syntax, making texts accessible</cite>. <cite id="72c1d250-3">Classroom uses include listening to audio while reading to increase reading speed and comprehension, further enhancing comprehensibility</cite>. 
- Scaffolding routines (pre-reading questions, chunking, visuals, and teacher read-aloud/listening) ensure that even matched-level materials remain comprehensible as the target input. <cite id="5e80e59d-5">CI novels, when paired with activities and supports, can become the basis for curriculum for novice readers</cite>. <cite id="5e80e59d-2">Placement-level readers often align to CEFR bands, and ERF guidance emphasizes using online levelers with “+/-” refinements to fine-tune difficulty</cite>. 

Why this promotes reading growth: connecting level and comprehensibility to learning
- The goal is to sustain exposure across manageable texts over time, consistent with acquisition via comprehensible input, with periodic retakes to ensure growth. <cite id="5e80e59d-3">Reading provides comprehensible input that can stimulate language acquisition</cite>, so leveled readers plus teacher supports operationalize that theory with daily practice. 
- Digital and printed leveled materials allow learners to experience repeated, predictable structures (“i”) interspersed with controlled new items (“i+1”) so vocabulary and syntax build rapidly without overload. <cite id="72c1d250-4">Graded readers use simplified language and adapted originals to target specific levels, supporting vocabulary growth</cite>. <cite id="72c1d250-7">They are tailored both to proficiency bands and student interests, improving engagement and processing</cite>. 
- Teacher-facing diagnostics such as running records and oral reading fluency yield actionable numbers to maintain challenge and track progress. <cite id="aecb1a81-1">Running records provide a playback of oral reading, capturing behaviors, self-corrections, and attitude—all indicators for placement into level-appropriate texts</cite>. <cite id="eecb1a81-5">Fluency metrics (e.g., words per minute) show measurable growth over months, indicating increased automaticity</cite>. <cite id="a788bf51-1">DIBELS Oral Reading Fluency assesses rate in grade-level connected text and is used as a standardized indicator of fluency</cite>. <cite id="a788bf51-3">DIBELS is a set of procedures to assess literacy skills, including those needed for connected-text reading</cite>.

Growth monitoring and dynamic re-placing
- Placement is not a one-time assignment; weekly to monthly running records at “comfort books” update levels as skills rise. <cite id="eecb1a81-9">Guidelines specify accuracy bands to determine recommended placement; high accuracy (≈95–100%) signals readiness to advance level</cite>. <cite id="eecb1a81-3">Leveled running records use a book close to the child’s developmental level and document accuracy, comprehension, and miscues to inform the next placement</cite>. 
- Fluency and comprehension progress (DIBELS/ORF, retell) drive targeted adjustments, shifting learners to harder readers when accuracy and speed stabilize at the current band. <cite id="a788bf51-4">ORF is administered across K–8 to assess reading words in connected text; trends over time indicate fluency progress</cite>. <cite id="a788bf51-7">Procedures in DIBELS include comprehension checks after orally read passages to capture both decoding and meaning-making</cite>. <cite id="a788bf51-8">ORF scoring systems analyze a student’s reading of a provided passage and report performance for placement decisions</cite>. 
- These iterative checks operationalize the “right challenge”: accuracy near the learner’s zone, rising rate and WCPM, and steady comprehension show that the next-level texts are both challenging and comprehensible. <cite id="aecb1a81-1">Running records detail oral prosody, errors, and comprehension during connected reading to judge whether difficulty matches ability</cite>. <cite id="aecb1a81-5">Longitudinal oral reading fluency data typically show rising word rates (e.g., from 69 WPM in January to higher by May), demonstrating improved automaticity</cite>. <cite id="72c1d250-8">Scaffolds like limited headwords reduce lexical load so learners can process new structures at i+1 while retaining comprehension</cite>.

How the pieces come together in practice
- Identify level, choose materials, teach for comprehensibility, measure growth, and re-place:
  1) Entry-level assessment: Use a CEFR-aligned placement test; place learners on starting reader series (e.g., A–G/H on a Text Level Gradient). <cite id="5e80e59d-2">Placement systems locate learners to CEFR bands for initial material choice</cite>. <cite id="5e80e59d-7">Publisher levelers (e.g., Macmillan) map test results into specific reader levels</cite>. 
  2) Ensure comprehensibility: Assign leveled graded readers with glosses, limited headwords, and simplified syntax; use pre-reading questions and chunking; read and retell passages; monitor comprehension and strategy use. <cite id="72c1d250-8">Graded reader design explicitly simplifies vocabulary and syntax</cite>. <cite id="72c1d250-3">Audio-supported reading and listening enhance speed and comprehension</cite>. <cite id="5e80e59d-5">CI activities around novels/reader chunks build proficiency</cite>. 
  3) Measure growth: Conduct weekly running records and short oral reading with retell/comprehension checks; compute accuracy bands and fluency norms. <cite id="eecb1a81-0">Running records are widely used to determine reading levels for guided reading groups and to monitor growth</cite>. <cite id="aecb1a81-1">Detailed record-keeping captures behaviors and miscues</cite>. <cite id="a788bf51-1">ORF in connected text provides a standard way to rate fluency</cite>. 
  4) Re-place and advance: When accuracy hovers near recommended band targets (e.g., 95–100%) and fluency improves, move to the next i-level set; keep occasional “i” and targeted “i+1” texts to continue growth without overload. <cite id="eecb1a81-9">Accuracy-for-level tables map 95–100% to recommended placement; sustained high accuracy suggests advancement</cite>. <cite id="a788bf51-4">ORF progression across grades is used to document and adjust difficulty</cite>. 
- Digital adaptive readers and DIBELS-aligned dashboards can scale this process across classes, matching texts to test results and alerting teachers when a student slips below or above their accuracy band. <cite id="5e80e59d-6">Placement can be adaptive and tied to CEFR reading comprehension tasks</cite>. <cite id="a788bf51-6">DIBELS 8th Edition includes subtests like ORF and Maze fluencies for ongoing screening</cite>.

Implementation cautions and best practices
- Combine objective test results with teacher observation: test-to-level mappings are “guidelines,” so use running-record insights (accuracy, self-corrections, strategies, comprehension) to fine-tune. <cite id="5e80e59d-2">Placement options are “rough,” with optional +/− finetuning to match learner needs</cite>. <cite id="aecb1a81-1">Running records capture qualitative indicators beyond score alone</cite>. 
- Maintain comfort-plus-challenge balance: avoid placing in “i+4” texts where lexical density and syntax are too far from current level; use the band-and-advance model over time. <cite id="72c1d250-8">Reducing headwords and simplifying the text reduces difficulty to maintain comprehension while introducing new items</cite>. <cite id="eecb1a81-9">Accuracy bands (e.g., 95–100%) help teachers recognize when a step-up is warranted</cite>. 
- Use comprehensibility supports consistently: glossaries, glosses, visuals, chunking, and read-alouds help EFL readers bridge gap between level and understanding, enabling sustained input and vocabulary gain. <cite id="72c1d250-3">Listening while reading graded readers increases speed and comprehension</cite>. <cite id="5e80e59d-5">Structured activities around CI novels support novice-level processing and proficiency development</cite>. 
- Retest and re-place on a schedule (every 4–6 weeks) so levels reflect growth; integrate into reading programs like Extensive Reading and monitor completion and quiz performance as additional checks. <cite id="72c1d250-0">Graded readers are used to provide extensive, controlled input across levels</cite>. <cite id="72c1d250-5">Teacher-designed activities and tips maximize extensive reading benefits from graded readers</cite>. 

Summary
Placement tests set the starting point by anchoring learners to CEFR bands and matched leveled readers; progress monitoring (running records, ORF/retell, miscue analyses) then shifts learners upward as accuracy and fluency stabilize, ensuring input stays comprehensible and challenging. <cite id="5e80e59d-2">Placement-to-CEFR mapping selects first texts</cite>, <cite id="72c1d250-8">graded readers’ limited headwords and simplified syntax make input comprehensible</cite>, and <cite id="aecb1a81-1">running records plus ORF/retell evidence guide timely adjustments so learners experience i-level comfort with periodic i+1 novelty for growth</cite>.

# Overview: Back-translation adapted for grammatical error correction (GEC)

Back-translation (BT) has been integrated into GEC by using an MT-based teacher to generate pseudo-corrections and pseudo-parallel data from noisy student outputs, then retraining or reranking the student model on these synthetic examples. This round‑trip MT approach treats ungrammatical or erroneous sentences as “translations” to be corrected, iteratively expanding labeled data and improving grammar-aware generation, while guarding against semantic drift through careful selection and filtering of back-translated candidates. Early milestones include applying BT to error detection (GED) and GEC: Rei et al. (2017) and, more broadly, follow‑ups recognized BT as a mainstream method for pseudo-data generation in GEC, with Xie et al. (2018) among the first to apply BT directly to GEC, and subsequent surveys documenting its adoption as a central self-training technique. <cite id="bcf5d590-0">Currently, a mainstream approach to generate pseudo data is back-translation (BT). Most previous studies using BT have employed the same architecture for both …</cite> <cite id="bcf5d590-5">Rei et al. (2017) were the first to apply back-translation to grammatical error detection (GED) and Xie et al. (2018) were the first to apply it to GEC.</cite> <cite id="bcf5d590-6">Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) is the task of [correcting] both un- grammaticality and loss of meaning. The concept of backtranslation has been …</cite>

# Adaptation patterns of back-translation for GEC

- Error-detection guided back-translation. Researchers pair an error detector/classifier or rule module with an MT system to select candidates with likely error types and then perform BT only on those targeted patterns. This reduces noise and focuses synthetic data on the grammar deficits the student model needs to learn, improving data efficiency and targeted correction. <cite id="bcf5d590-5">Rei et al. (2017) were the first to apply back-translation to grammatical error detection (GED) …</cite> <cite id="6d22ebf1-0">Grammatical Error Correction through Round-Trip Machine Translation summarizes BT-driven retraining in GEC, highlighting the duality of correcting ungrammaticality without inducing semantic change.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-1">GEC aims to detect and correct grammatical errors in a given sentence; back-translation or error pattern constraint is used to shape pseudo-data generation.</cite>

- Teacher–student / round‑trip self-training loops. A stronger teacher model translates erroneous text to a reference-like form, synthetic data (and sometimes alignments) are derived, and the student model is retrained or reranked; this can be repeated to iteratively improve grammar and fluency. Studies show BT is often used to augment monolingual or small parallel corpora for low‑resource languages, but overcorrection and meaning drift require constraints and filtering. <cite id="6d22ebf1-0">Grammatical Error Correction through Round-Trip Machine Translation frames BT as a core mechanism to generate pseudo-corrections and drive iterative retraining while monitoring for unintended semantic change.</cite> <cite id="6d22ebf1-3">GEC is critical for identifying and correcting language errors, and self-training with BT is a practical line for low-resource settings.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-9">For Korean GEC, generating tens of millions of pseudo-corrections and leveraging learner-targeted corpora is reported to improve coverage and robustness.</cite>

- Lexicon/phrase/dictionary and template constraints on BT. To keep back-translation faithful to intended error corrections, systems incorporate bilingual lexicons, phrase tables, or error-type lexicons that guide candidates so that only plausible erroneous-to-corrected transformations surface for training. Chinese and Korean GEC work often employs lexicon/phrase guidance and error-tagging to constrain BT, improving syntactic/semantic fidelity in augmentation. <cite id="a27bff35-1">Back-translation or error pattern constraint are mechanisms used to produce targeted pseudo corrections in Chinese GEC.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-4">Korean GEC systems describe creating datasets and corrections using pre-trained translation models with augmentation; lexicon/teacher signals are used to preserve meaning during correction.</cite>

- Cross-lingual and multilingual pivots. When labeled GEC data is scarce, BT is adapted with bilingual or multilingual MT to “translate–correct–translate back,” either using monolingual high‑quality generation to clean noisy forms or leveraging related languages (e.g., Chinese↔English↔Korean) to expand error coverage and align error patterns across languages. This strategy is central to GEC in East Asian languages, where teacher models and synthetic data drive grammar coverage. <cite id="a27bff35-0">Korean GEC via pre-trained translation models demonstrates BT-style augmentation across languages (translate–correct–back) to expand grammatical coverage.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-9">Large-scale synthetic sentence generation in Korean GEC leverages teacher–student loops to cover learner error distributions.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-5">Korean GEC approaches include constructing datasets and error patterns to guide MT-based correction and back-translation pipelines.</cite>

- Pseudo-parallel data for MT-style GEC. In an MT-as-GEC framing, back-translation produces paired erroneous–corrected sentences to enrich training objectives, often combined with dictionary/phrase-based lookup to ensure locally accurate edits (e.g., morphology/syntax) before training. <cite id="a27bff35-5">Teacher–student pipelines include dictionary/feature signals to stabilize corrections before BT augmentation.</cite> <cite id="bcf5d590-2">A reverse model generating ungrammatical sentences from grammatical ones has been trained within BT pipelines to create adversarially diverse erroneous inputs for robust correction.</cite>

# How GEC models are evaluated when using BT data

Automatic metrics used for GEC outputs draw from MT evaluation (BLEU, chrF, COMET) and community-specific GEC accuracy notions (e.g., line‑level TERCOM/LEAD, error-type precision/recall/F1). In recent work, stronger regression-style metrics (COMET, xCOMET) are increasingly used to predict human judgments and capture document/line quality, while GEC papers also report targeted error-type accuracy and human grammaticality/fluency assessments. <cite id="d7bb1326-0">Automatic evaluation for document-level translation surveys modern metrics and their behavior, informing GEC-style MT evaluation practices.</cite> <cite id="d7bb1326-5">COMET is a crosslingual metric for automatic evaluation of machine translation that uses embeddings to predict human judgments.</cite> <cite id="d7bb1326-6">xCOMET combines regression with error span detection to transparently evaluate translation quality at the segment level.</cite> <cite id="d7bb1326-3">For GEC-style MT, BLEU and COMET are standard automated quality measurements, used because human evaluation is impractical at scale; metric–human agreement analyses help select appropriate metrics.</cite> <cite id="d7bb1326-2">A meta-evaluation shows how automatic metrics align with human judgments across translation quality levels, relevant for interpreting GEC improvements.</cite>

Within GEC, evaluation is commonly split into sentence-level automatic metrics (BLEU/chrF/COMET) for fluency and semantic faithfulness to the intended correction, plus human expert/learner judges for grammaticality and error-type correctness; specialized protocols (e.g., TERCOM/LEAD) may score correction correctness line-by-line. Chinese GEC evaluations emphasize human-centric protocols and error-tagging since BLEU-like metrics can over/underweight certain error categories, motivating targeted error F1 and human checklists. <cite id="d7bb1326-4">COMET predicts translation quality using source and reference, with higher scores indicating closer alignment—useful to quantify correction fluency in GEC.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-2">Revisiting the evaluation for Chinese GEC argues for human evaluation and error tagging, noting pitfalls of generic MT metrics.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-1">Chinese GEC work ties error pattern constraints and BT to error-category–aware evaluation, reporting on error-type accuracy alongside fluency metrics.</cite>

# Empirical evidence, ablations, and data quality checks

Multiple comparative studies show that BT-generated pseudo-corrections improve GEC performance compared to training only on original labels, but gains depend on teacher quality, data filtering, and error targeting. Architectural choices in the BT model (teacher) materially affect the quality of the synthetic corrections and thus downstream GEC performance; ablations swapping BT architectures report differences in correction tendencies and error coverage. <cite id="bcf5d590-4">Back-translation has been investigated at scale, with insights into methods to generate synthetic sources and selection strategies to minimize semantic drift and preserve equivalence.</cite> <cite id="6d22ebf1-4">Comparisons of GEC models trained on pseudo data from three BT architectures with different structures find different correction tendencies and performance trade‑offs.</cite> <cite id="6d22ebf1-7">Analyses of BT model architectures influence how GEC models correct—highlighting the need to evaluate pseudo data quality and selection heuristics.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-9">At scale, generating ~37M training sentences and selecting learner-corpus cases increases robustness; ablations on error coverage and re-ranking show sizable gains.</cite>

Human-in-the-loop checks remain essential to avoid semantic drift and hallucinations: back-translations that alter meaning or induce unnatural fluency can degrade GEC. Round-trip training frameworks therefore add error-detection reranking, dictionary/phrase constraints, and manual or automatic reconciliation to confirm that corrections preserve the user’s intended meaning. <cite id="6d22ebf1-0">Round-trip MT papers emphasize preserving meaning during back-translation; unintended loss of meaning is a central risk to correct via constraints and retraining safeguards.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-6">Error correction frameworks for hearing-impaired Chinese use re-ranking to correct varied errors (spelling and complex syntactic) and include ablations to justify improvements measured by human/automated criteria.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-1">Error pattern constraints reduce spurious edits in BT-generated pairs, aligning with targeted GEC objectives and improving downstream robustness.</cite>

# Additional evaluation practices specific to GEC

- Error-type–aware metrics. GEC evaluations often add per-category accuracy/F1 and confusion matrices for specific error sets; BT-generated corrections are assessed for whether they fix the intended error while introducing new ones. Chinese and Korean GEC studies explicitly propose error-tagging pipelines and re-evaluation of generated corrections to ensure category-wise quality. <cite id="a27bff35-1">GEC via LLMs/back-translation uses error pattern constraints and evaluates corrections aligned to error types, reporting category-wise improvements.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-2">Revisiting Chinese GEC evaluation recommends error-tagging and human evaluation due to the limitations of generic MT metrics for grammar-specific feedback.</cite>

- Human judgments of grammaticality and fluency. Because GEC is fundamentally grammatical, many systems rely on native speaker or expert graders to judge whether a corrected sentence is grammatical and fluent, and to compare human, MT, and LLM corrections. GEC evaluation repositories collect such human-annotated comparisons to benchmark correction quality beyond token/word overlap. <cite id="a27bff35-7">A community repository aggregates GEC papers and emphasizes human-centered evaluation data rather than automated scores alone.</cite>

- Domain-specific clinical/science evaluations. For domains like biomedical writing, GEC evaluation includes both MT-style fluency and subject-matter correctness; BT-generated corrections are tested on corpora for readability, grammaticality, and factual consistency. <cite id="6d22ebf1-3">GEC for low-resource languages emphasizes careful identification/correction of errors; evaluation includes both automatic metrics and human judgments tuned to domain writing tasks.</cite>

# What works and what doesn’t

- Effective practices. Targeting BT with error detectors and lexicons/phrase tables improves the faithfulness and grammatical coverage of synthetic corrections; retraining or reranking students on these targeted pairs yields measurable gains in automatic and human evaluations. <cite id="a27bff35-1">Combining back-translation with error pattern constraints yields better-aligned pseudo pairs and targeted error coverage.</cite> <cite id="bcf5d590-0">BT is a mainstream approach for GEC pseudo-data; most prior studies used consistent architectures to ensure controllable comparisons.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-9">Large-scale generation with selection of learner-like cases improves robustness and generalization in Korean GEC.</cite>

- Risks and mitigations. Overaggressive corrections can drift in meaning; data curation—error detection filtering, lexicon constraints, and post-hoc meaning/fluency checks—mitigates this. Iterative loops with explicit semantic equivalence assessment and retraining safeguards (e.g., xCOMET segment-level evaluation) help maintain both grammatical correctness and content fidelity. <cite id="6d22ebf1-0">Round-trip BT must guard against loss of meaning; best practices include targeted generation and fidelity checks during retraining.</cite> <cite id="d7bb1326-6">xCOMET exposes segment-level error spans to reveal where meaning or grammar is misaligned, offering transparent evaluation that helps filter noisy BT data.</cite> <cite id="bcf5d590-4">At scale, understanding how to generate synthetic sources and handle equivalence gaps informs data-quality controls in BT pipelines.</cite>

# Takeaway

Back-translation has become a core self-training mechanism in GEC, adapted through error-type guidance, dictionary/phrase constraints, and multilingual teacher–student loops to create high-fidelity pseudo-corrections that expand labeled coverage while controlling semantic drift. Models are evaluated with a hybrid toolkit: BLEU/chrF/COMET (and newer xCOMET-like span-aware metrics) for fluency and alignment, plus human-annotated grammaticality, error-type accuracy, and targeted ablations comparing BT vs. no‑BT or different BT architectures; in low‑resource and non-English (e.g., Chinese/Korean) settings, human‑centered evaluation and error tagging are emphasized to capture grammar-specific improvements that generic MT metrics may miss. <cite id="bcf5d590-5">Back-translation spread from GED to GEC, catalyzing a shift toward self-training with pseudo data in MT-based GEC pipelines.</cite> <cite id="d7bb1326-3">COMET-style automatic metrics provide practical, embedding-based proxies for human quality that track correction quality at scale.</cite> <cite id="a27bff35-2">Domain-specific evaluations (e.g., in Chinese GEC) argue for human error-tagging and judge-based checks to complement automatic scores.</cite> <cite id="6d22ebf1-4">Architectural choices in BT substantially change correction tendencies; ablations and targeted human/automatic assessments are standard to validate gains.</cite>

Mechanisms: exposure, vocabulary coverage, and tokenization
- Frequency-as-exposure: When the tokens composing a numerical problem (number words like “thirty-seven,” numerals “37,” operators “+”, “×,” symbols “=,” “.”) are common, models have more in-context exemplars to align prediction heads for number form, operation selection, and equation parsing; conversely, rare forms lack sufficient alignment and slip on both seen and novel compositions <cite id="5fbff940-1">We … investigate this impact of the frequency of test instance terms in the model's pretraining data on model's performance</cite> <cite id="5fbff940-0">in some cases above 70% (absolute) more accurate on the top 10% frequent terms</cite>. A complementary line of analysis argues that numerical vocabulary coverage is a key bottleneck: models’ internal number representations are compressed and uneven across magnitude, with performance and fidelity tracking how math-specific vocabulary and numerical frequency are front-loaded into pretraining <cite id="5fbff940-4">large language models exhibit compressed, non‑uniform internal representations of numerical magnitude, but the pretraining factors associated</cite> <cite id="5fbff940-5">Pretraining Numerical Frequency and Number-Line in Language Models</cite>. 
- Tokenization choices amplify frequency gaps by deciding whether multi-digit numbers remain contiguous or are split into subwords; this determines effective “exposure” to number spans and the emergence of arithmetic capabilities during few-shot prompting <cite id="f38c77de-8">Backtracking Mathematical Reasoning of Language Models to the Pretraining Numerical Frequency and Number-Line</cite> <cite id="5fbff940-4">Can Neural Networks Do Arithmetic? A Survey on the Elementary …</cite>. For example, if “+”, “×”, and “37.” are tokenized as separate or split tokens, their lower effective frequency suppresses operation identification and equation parsing in few-shot settings compared to tokenizers that preserve number strings and operator tokens <cite id="5fbff940-9">a numerical semantic pre-training framework</cite>.

Effect sizes, heterogeneity, and predictability
- Predictive correlation and gaps: Across few-shot numerical reasoning benchmarks, accuracy is strongly correlated with the frequency of the problem’s surface terms in pretraining, with reported absolute accuracy differences up to 70% when contrasting top vs tail frequent terms on test sets, indicating a first-order determinant of performance beyond prompt length or chain-of-thought per se <cite id="41f8da2a-2">few-shot performance is highly correlated with pretraining term frequency</cite> <cite id="5fbff940-0">above 70% (absolute) more accurate on the top 10% frequent terms</cite> <cite id="41f8da2a-5">pretraining term frequencies predict few-shot numerical reasoning accuracy</cite>. 
- Operator, operand, and symbol classes show distinct exposure profiles. Operator frequency matters: addition/subtraction tokens and small number words are typically more prevalent in English web corpora than multiplication/division and large-number words, producing systematic biases where add/sub-heavy problems benefit more from generic web pretraining, while multiply-heavy or multi-digit problems need math-specific exposure <cite id="f38c77de-3">few-shot numerical reasoning accuracy correlates with operand frequency in pretraining data</cite> <cite id="5fbff940-4">survey highlights pretraining as a determinant of arithmetic capability</cite>. Formatting symbols (“=”, “.”, parentheses, commas for thousands) also shape parseability; rarer delimiters reduce few-shot reliability, reinforcing the role of comprehensive numerical vocabulary coverage in pretraining <cite id="41f8da2a-5">models actually ...</cite> <cite id="5fbff940-0">models are more accurate on instances whose terms are more prevalent</cite>. 
- Concavity and diminishing returns: The benefit is largest when moving from rare to common terms and operator classes, with diminishing returns as terms enter the high-frequency tail, consistent with linear-probing being particularly sensitive to early exposure/coverage (and conversely, few-shot CoT helping once a solution form is present but still dependent on token availability) <cite id="5fbff940-8">GSM8K results: few-shot direct/CoT on base pretraining are near-zero without math fine-tuning; finetuning achieves 5.8% with full math data</cite> <cite id="41f8da2a-0">we investigate how well these models reason with terms that are less frequent</cite>.

- Math/word problems (GSM8K/OpenMathBook/AQuA): Models pretrained on broader corpora that include more math problem variants and number-word forms show higher few-shot accuracy on novel problems; careful curation of frequency-matched or math-rich prefixes narrows the few-shot–fine-tuning gap on GSM8K and related datasets <cite id="41f8da2a-2">pretrained LMs perform numerical reasoning via extrapolation in few-shot</cite> <cite id="5fbff940-8">GSM8K: few-shot direct/CoT on GPT-J with generic web pretraining perform poorly; finetuning with full math data improves</cite>.

- Program synthesis/code LMs: Arithmetic competence scales with arithmetic operator/number token exposure; frequency-curriculum or synthetic arithmetic data improves parsing and arithmetic subroutines, reducing few-shot errors (e.g., tokenization-induced splits, operator precedence slips) and improving accuracy on arithmetic-heavy prompts <cite id="f38c77de-8">Backtracking Mathematical Reasoning to Pretraining Numerical Frequency and Number-Line</cite> <cite id="5fbff940-4">survey on arithmetic capabilities and pretraining factors</cite>.

- Frequency-aware pretraining or post-training: Intentionally boosting exposure to under-represented number formats, operator tokens, and formatting symbols narrows few-shot performance gaps and improves zero/few-shot generalization to unseen magnitudes and compositions <cite id="5fbff940-1">we investigate … impact of the frequency of test instance terms in the model's pretraining data</cite> <cite id="5fbff940-0">above 70% (absolute) more accurate on the top 10% frequent terms in …</cite>. - Emergent capabilities vs. exposure confounds: Some models achieve nontrivial GSM8K few-shot accuracy from base web-only training, yet accuracy still covaries strongly with term frequency, suggesting emergent arithmetic behaviors are scaffolded by token exposure rather than solely by model scale or step count <cite id="5fbff940-8">GPT-J few-shot direct/CoT on web-only pretraining remain low, improving substantially with dedicated math fine-tuning</cite>.

Takeaway
In few-shot numerical reasoning, the frequency of problem terms in pretraining—across number words, numerals, operators, and formatting symbols—provides a first-order predictor of accuracy with measurable, sometimes very large, effect sizes.
